_childDocuments_.review: Played on Switch with a friend's copy, bought on Steam to support the devs as I played it to the end.Ikenfell is clearly a labor of love and I also wanted to love it so much more than I ended up doing. This is a very conflicted review I'm making, and while ultimately I'm giving the recommendation, there are a lot of problems I have. The following are the biggest things that stuck out to me:+ The soundtrack (and sound design) was the highest of highlights in Ikenfell for me, and up there with the best of 2020. I like or outright love just about everything in the OST. aivi & surasshu and everyone else who contributed to the audio for this game all did an amazing job. I won't bother singing it's praises, just listen to a few battle themes and thank me later. (Special note: Vocal tracks in games aren't always my thing, but It's Showtime! is a groove) + Spritework, character/enemy design, and animation were also great. No complaints there. New enemy designs pop up at a very frequent pace and I can't imagine how much work it was to animate all of those. Props.+ Overall, the game has a lot of charm to it, which I suppose is to say that a lot of the elements work well together and get the dopamine pumping.+ The gameplay concept is great. I love RPGs that reward good reflexes, and adding some SRPG grid combat is a great way to build on that. The game does a great job of easing you into its world and mechanics too.- Unfortunately, I can really only say the concept is great, because it does not get fleshed out in the ways it needed to in order to justify its total playtime. At about 5 hours is when I felt the repetition set in, and it didn't go away (except maybe for part of the final boss, but even that suffers a lot). The spells, enemies, equipment, and dungeons from that point onward, while still lovingly animated and designed, offer little variety as far as gameplay goes. That I might've been able to march through, but enemies, especially bosses, become unforgivably damage-spongey ~7-8 hours in and I had to break out the Instant Victory option to see the game through to the end at all (thank god it was an option), as it was clear I could win (or rather, not lose) a battle, but dealing hundreds of points of damage to multiple boss phases was a total slog, chipping away at them, single digits at a time unless I grinded my way through similarly spongey standard enemies. And for the record, I tried my best to see what each new enemy had to offer before deciding to skip it or not. Enemy attack patterns quickly become samey, and bosses usually fell into the same trap of 2-3 phases, summoning samey minions, sometimes spawning damage-dealing traps that work about the same way every time. I particularly felt that the grid-based combat was not used to its full potential. Just a glance at Ikenfell's SRPG predecessors, Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics, show that there was potential missed. Traps and environmental hazards could've been a lot better.- Over half the main team lacks a satisfying arc until briefly in the (quite heartwarming) epilogue, but then the game is over. Maritte and Pertisia are the only ones out of the team's six who I could say really had any growth at all over the course of the main game. Rook, Petronella, and Gilda started off promising, but fell by the wayside about halfway through the game (ESPECIALLY Gilda - poor thing barely does anything after joining the party, and is left just standing around very conspicuously and very awkwardly in one particular scene where she REALLY should've been rushing to comfort Maritte). Ima is the most underdeveloped of them all, having no meaningful purpose in the story (being easily substituted by anyone else in the team during a certain story event (or really any story event)) and having zero significant development, even getting passed over in the epilogue with, like, one still frame./ Finally, the game is pretty linear. You won't likely be revisiting old areas unless you're trying to hunt for items you missed the first time (or doing one midgame side thing that I personally didn't bother with, or going for a secret boss whom I believe I saved past my last chance to fight). Not the biggest deal but it's noticeable.So ultimately, I got about 6 pretty good beginning hours, and the other 6 ranged from frustratingly uneventful to decent but samey. Was that worth the $16 I paid, and was it worth the time to experience the good bits? I give a heavy-hearted "yes," with the caveat that I'm not sure that I'd be giving Ikenfell's mid/lategame faults a """pass""", or that I'd have finished the game at all, without the Instant Victory option. You or others may fare better than I did.All that said, I look forward to Happy Ray Games' future projects. It's clear that there's passion and talent here, and I hope that the team gained valuable experience (and some decent sales) with this game to make the next one the gem I think Ikenfell was close to being. I want to see another go at it.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of love went into this game and it breaks my heart to make a negative review.However, I can't recommend this game at all. This is a turn-based JRPG about an ordinary girl(non-magical) exploring a magical school to find her sister, who happens to be a witch. The game has diverse characters . . . but failed to make them actually interesting. After 10 hours of playing, I can't describe ANY of the characters for more than half a sentence. The game barely explores ANY of the characters. Instead, most of the cut scenes are conversations about main character's sister . . . a character who I, the player, have yet to meet. The game basically is mostly tell, don't show. There were so many interesting explorations to be done with Gilda and Pertisia . . . but simply didn't. I don't know what purpose Rook and Petronella fills in the game other than being main characters' side kicks or something. Who is Ima again?The combat system is a simple turn-based system with timing press, similar to Mario RPG series. I think the big problem with this system is that the game deliberately attempts to confuse when the player should press the button. When the precise button press is practically required to deal damage, (missing it would deal less than half) I am not entirely sure WHY the game is designed this way. I ultimately found myself using the same moves and same characters that I am comfortable using. Why bother learn how to use other characters or other moves? Not to mention, every move in the combat is drawn-out in order to implement this frustrating combat system and most of the battle feels like a waiting time for the animation to resolve.As I have stated, I can see that the game had a lot of love poured into it. Pixel art animation is pretty darn impressive. After 10hrs, I don't think I am close to finishing the game and the game world is pretty darn big with large areas to explore.I just don't think I will finish the game though.

_childDocuments_.review: I go to some RPGs for tight, precise combat that rewards critical thinking over sheer luck or persistence. I go to some for a sense of adventure in a richly-detailed world full of secrets. Some are for instantly lovable character designs, or a story that seriously changes my outlook. Honestly, sometimes I'm just there for the bops. It's rare that I get all of that at once; in fact it may have been over two decades since a game hit me this good.If you were raised on JRPGs from the SNES era onward and haven't been able to really sink your teeth into an experience for the last few console generations, Ikenfell's got you covered. The fights will test your wits, the twists will warp your brain, the feels WILL bring tears to your eyes...and yes, it lasts longer than four hours this time. Reminds me why I fell in love with this medium in the first place.(Oh and if you're looking for queer representation you just hit the mother lode baby!! At least three canon gay couples, an ace/aro character who stays that way and is never pressured to convert, a non-binary character who uses neopronouns, holy smokes it's incredible)Super validating game in so many more ways than one, please give it a try—it's a steal at twenty bucks, truss me.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic masterpiece in multiple ways.The gameplay takes inspiration from a number of old SNES games, with its own novel spin on the mechanics of turn based tactical RPGs and timed attacks, among others. I encourage everyone who wants to play this game to give the default QTEs a fair try - they are difficult, but that just makes the accomplishment all the sweeter.Unfortunately, there are a few QoL issues with the gameplay that hamper the experience:You cannot view the stats of equipment without keeping one member of your party permanently unequipped.You can view all monster HP for free during your turn, but only through a menu option called "view units," and not while picking your targets.These detract from the game, but if you can get past them the game is still immensely enjoyable.The music is overall fantastic, with one exception. The vocal tracks. They don't match the tone of the game at all, and are mixed above the battle noise during the battles they occur, resulting in extra difficulty that is pretty clearly not intended by the game designers. The rest of the songs portray ambience while still being songs, closer to SNES titles than the ambience of modern AAA games that, when taken out of the game, just sound like noise.The story and characters received just as much TLC as the gameplay.The characters are lovely and more human than the one-dimensional personified individual personality traits that plague games like this.The story touches on a number of dark themes - however the real star is how the characters respond to them. The mature responses and handling of issues such as PTSD, narcissistic family, and self harm are handled with a masterful level of personal experience. As someone who has dealt with some, but not all of these issues seeing these portrayed the way this game did was a refreshing and wonderful experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is the magical RPG game that I have been wanting to play since at least 10 years and now that I was able to finish it, I am left delighted for the experience and sad that it is over.Ikenfell brings with it a promise of magical combat, and that is what you get. There is no mana and there are no melee attacks in case you run out of actions, the only thing that is limiting the player is the timing, because the game brings with it an action command system, reminiscent of Super Mario RPG, Legend of the Seven stars.Ikenfell teaches you very early that timing your spells and blocks of enemy attacks right, has some drastic effects on the battle, more damage from your side or extra effects on attacks, sometimes timing even determines if a spell has any effect at all! This also counts for enemy attacks, foes that would bring poison with certain techniques can be blocked completely without receiving the pesky DOT, as long as the timing is right! And if you are unable to do these timings that is fine too, as you can switch on an option that makes every timing stick perfectly (I completed the entire game without this feature myself, but I can see how it could be important for others). The battlefield also plays an important role, as all skills have a certain attack range, both the players' and the ones of the enemy, with restricted movement, every turn counts! The AI is also what I would describe as "very friendly", as enemies do like to priorize their attacks on your allies that aren't extremely hurt, giving you time to heal up. I really enjoyed that a lot.The game's story follows Maritte, who is looking for her sister at a school of magic, where things have gone south. The plot and mysteries that get revealed bit by bit are interesting and pretty much everything is getting foreshadowed in one way or the other, so nothing is coming out of left field. Though some characters are left a little on sidelines, everyone has their time to shine at some point, magic is even used in cutscenes, showing that it is not just used for battle, in contrast to some other games of the same genre.Every character has a very unique playstile, the energitc Maritte focuses on brute strength, damage and buffing the attack of her allies, while the shy Petronella rather sticks back and throws healing and debuffs at the enemies. The bookworm rook is all about stratgey, he can lay traps steal items an deal strong AOE damage, as long as the positioning is right. There are 6 party members, all with completely unique styles of action commands, magic types and looks too, obviously, and though some of them might be overleveled when you get them in your party, the level disparity disappeared at a certain point where I enjoyed to experiment with my party composition, to take on the dungeons and bosses of the game.Speaking of which, the dungeons are all themed after a magical school, or university in this case. Magical dormitories, weird liminal spaces, and places with books, a lot of them. Though there is a library, an archive and a place called "the stacks" and they all share the same motive of books, all three of them are different in their choice of musical tone (the theme is the same, but they all have cool different variations), enemies and atmosphere. Enemies you encounter in all places share a lot of energy with those of Mother-Series enemies. From goofy birds, to enchanted items and guardians, to creepy and eratic ghosts, the game has them all. Over these foes tower the bosses, that aren't fought in a truly sound pattern, but you can usually tell that a boss is near when you find a kitty lazing around, as these serve as saving points.The bosses themselves vary in their difficulty, most problems I had with early bosses as I was still figuring out the timing of my own and their attacks. Some of them even have cool phase changes that are sometimes to be expected and sometimes are very surprising. Though there is one big thing that bothers me about these bosses, which is that a large portion of them summon annoying helpers at certain HP thresholds that need to be dealt with. Sometimes these can be used strategically, other times you just have to kill them. I did enjoy the battles, as they were very unique overall, but I did have to sigh a little at later bosses as they summoned their predictable 3 goons that had to be taken out.The entire game is painted with a beautiful look, the character sprites on the overworld, their names, battle sprites and talking portraits all stand out and every location has a unique look, making a certain sidequest easy to be done. There are shops to buy supplies and gear but these shops are always where you need them with items that are good for you. No unnecessary backtracking to be found here.An open eye can also find little secrets that hide items or gems of all variety around the overworld, as someone who has found and beaten all secret bosses I would say they aren't hard to find as they are hidden rather fairly, no unfair hidden blocks á la Super Mario RPG.The score of ikenfell has also won me over by storm, some people might recognize the tunes, as the composers were responsible for the chiptune tracks of Steven Universe. Some music tracks in ikenfell even had lyrics, a surprise that, as someone who hasn't watched any trailers, I completely loved. Boss tracks can be a little repetetive if fights are taking too long, but I couldn't stay mad too long after they were defeated.Before finishing off I also have to commend the developers, artists and writers on the casts diversity. With at least three Nonbinary characters, all using different pronouns, it oozed with an air of freedom. The story told me every kind of person was welcome at ikenfell, as long as you were able to cast magic. I personally do not identify as Nonbinary, but I have some friends who do, who will probably love the inclusion of these characters! Ikenfell showed me what a game that is primarily about magic SHOULD be. With fantastic looks, a mysterious story that involved all the characters and a soundtrack that tied everything together I took the game in like sponge thirsty for some water. Give it a try, in case you do miss games like Mother or crave a battle system akin to the one back in Super Mario RPG, or you can stay for the gays, they certainly kept me enraptured too!
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: To put it short Ikenfell is a SRPG-hybrid, timing based combat strategy game, and it really didn't hit the mark for me.I gave this game a really long try, but after about 3 hours all of the magic it started off with faded, and I felt like I've been playing for 10+ hours at this point to try and just get it over with.(+) musicThe boss themes, and environment music is great! Some of the songs that include lyrics are very corny and not enjoyable, but those aren't the majority of tracks. (+) artThe art in this game is quite simplistic, but pleasing to the eyes. It's taking a very traditional SNES era type of lookand uses it well. The color palette can be a bit too bright at times, and doesn't feel very diverse, but overall the art is fun. (-) combatCombat starts out fun, because it is! Fights don't feel extremely long, and timing your skills is enjoyable! First few bosses are fun, and the music really adds to it. Everything changes once you have 3 characters able to be used for combat, and it feels DRAWN. The battles feel EXTREMELY drawn out, especially later into the game. You can have a boss figured out basically, and you still need to sit there for 30 minutes rinse and repeating the same actions over and over.A fast forward feature would be great, but considering the game is timing based combat that is not possible. Also since the game doesn't have mana and only some skills have cooldowns, it makes it that certain defensive skills just get mashed for a whole battle. It makes battles feel EXTREMELY monotonous and lacking in any kind of flavorful strategy rather than just some rinse and repeat use this skill 100 times each battle. For example one character you unlock  has a regen skill that can be used on all 3 members, and since there is no mana or cooldown, you end up using it EVERY time you can. There's no management of using the ability a finite amount of times, or mana management. I think time based combat games work better in a JRPG type of format like Paper Mario or Bug Fables.(-) storyThe story follows Marinette, who finds her way to the School of Ikenfell, because her sister hasn't returned home in months. Soon after arriving she realizes she now has powers, and finds that things at the school aren't normal and nobodyknows where her sister is. It seems fine, until all of the characters start to appear, and they are all stereotypes and have no actual complexity. Ikenfell follows young people, but the lessons here feel so infantile that I'm not sure what you're supposed to take from the dialogue. (~) exploration?The map is quite small, but I personally enjoy a more linear map in RPG games. My main qualm with it is that all secrets,whether it be a hidden door, wall, bookshelf, or anything it feels recycled over and over. (-) customization Leveling your character in Ikenfell is kind of just something that happens, and there are no decisions to be made. No choice of skill, and there is no penalty for ever using different characters because if they aren't in party currentlyyou only lose like 5% of the total battle XP from that combat. You don't equip specific skills you want to use, and there is no mana Items are another problem for me. There's items EVERYWHERE, and at a certain point it doesn't feel interesting to find one."secrets" are everywhere and most of the time it's just an item you can buy, or will get dropped from a boss in 20 minutes.Largest issue with items is there is no hidden weapons or upgrades. You just buy new weapons that give something like 2-4 damage once you get to the point in the game where it's time to get your marginal upgrade. In a long turn based RPG I want to feel like I'm actually progressing something, and that doesn't feel like the case here.FINAL THOUGHTSI think Ikenfell started great, and the overall idea is very fun! The combat feels VERY frustrating and slow though, that it feels like the game time is just tacked on from never ending boss battles, and dialogue that feels unnecessarily long often. I think some people will really enjoy this game, but I found over time it really wasn't for me.OVERALL 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is a grid based, turned based RPG that turned out to be really good. I enjoyed it way more than I thought I would.-The graphics were cute and fitting. Even though the game is pixel-art, it is absolutely beautiful-The combat was interesting. (BUT FIRST I turned off the timer - basically there's a paper mario like timing based combat part of the game. It quite simply got way too tedious, so I turned it off and made everything auto-great.) Each of the 6 playable characters has their own playstyle with their own move-sets. I ended up using Rook (utility damage + steal), Ima (dummy maker + heal), and Gilda (dps) for most of the run. The enemies also all had their own unique moves that sometimes you needed to play around.-The story kept me interested. This was the part that I was most surprised about. I can't believe I was this lured into by the story. Although simple, the writing was good and it really fit the game well.-The boss fights were fun. Now one of the things that was really great about Ikenfell is that if you simply fight every enemy you come across, naturally you will be able to fight bosses without being too weak or too strong. Many of the boss fights I felt that I was just strong enough with healing and tactical dummies to beat them. The bosses also have very unique styles each, and some of them were pretty tough if you were unprepared with heals.Overall, I loved this game, and I highly recommend it!Rating: 9.0/10Recommend Price: Full Price - it's worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cool concept and the art and music are amazing, but unfortunately, the gameplay is repetitive and boring. Each battle is just doing the exact same moves with minimal strategy and very wonky timing for the bonuses (at least at first, but my patience wore out at the bar's basement). I really wanted the story / discovery / and secrets to carry me through a dull battle mechanic, but unfortunately it takes ages to get to the plot and most of the interactions for the first hour or so of the game are just setup, setup, setup. I like the concept and I wish I had better things to say, but this title fell a little flat for me. :(

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend this, as the art and soundtrack are both beautiful, but unfortunately the rest of the game just sort of falls flat pretty quickly.The game play loop starts to get old/overly repetitive only a few hours in, and for story that's cast is so diverse all the characters still somehow end up feeling pretty bland and uninteresting.The combat starts out pretty fun, the boss fights are engaging while never being too punishing, but the random fights on the map start to drag pretty quick.Overall maybe get this if it's on sale, it's not a terrible game but there's a good chance it won't hold your interest for very long. _childDocuments_.review: Gonna chuck this into the pile of "games I wish were better than they are."Like it's cute, it is. And actually the gameplay is great, the other negative reviews really seem down on it, but I think it is A) exceedingly easy and B) pretty fun. But this game was written by someone who seems to have been taught that stories are made entirely out of plot twists (which in the game are framed as fetch quests for the next twist) and it is beyond mentally exhausting how much of the game is ping ponging around Ikenfell trying to clarify what in the hell is even happening. It's frustrating because the game starts strong and it only gets worse and worse, the turning point ironically (or maybe symbolically?) being when they introduce a party member whose sole defining characteristic is that everyone loves zem who then replaces the main character as your party leader for a bit. Welcome to the stage, Miz Mary Zue. Sit amongst the precious darlings who will, with poor justifications and little build up or pacing, go through crowd favorite tropes of heroic BSOD, love triangles, and poorly concealed alteregos. Watch as some nobodies die while hilariously sad music plays so that we know the villain who we have seen maybe twice at this point is actually deeply sympathetic and has a backstory you should cry over guys. The characters are crying so you should cry too. That's how emotions work.I am queer. I root for queer creators and I root for queer games, and I wanted to root for this game. I feel a lot of disappointment when a game wears rainbows on its sleeve and can't rise above the quality of the tropiest fanfiction in terms of storytelling. It is cringe. I played this game and a repeating thought I had as the plot degraded was "you know, maybe games are not capable of high quality storytelling." Then I stopped playing this and went back to Nebula award winning queer himbo simulator , and I realized oh. No.  is just terribly written.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: For those interested in unorthodox RPGs with captivating characters, Ikenfell is a must, a game not far behind the likes of Undertale or the Mother/Earthbound series. Its lavish queer and POC representation is refreshing, and prevents the story from dwelling into some boring medieval fantasy clichés. The gameplay and the frustration-reducing user experience are two other aspects whose quality should be commended. It's hard to be innovative when it comes to a pixelated 16-bit RPG, but this game tries and, if not creative, it is at least fun to play. Ikenfell's timming mechanic goes hand-in-hand with its tactics-like battles, leading to compelling and more dynamic fights. Be it for the story, the gameplay or the carefully crafted oldschool graphics, there's nothing quite like exploring Ikenfell's school ground, a lesson in game development.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr  -- The storytelling and the soundtrack are pretty good.  The gameplay falls off quickly, starting from the mid-game.Early game is balanced well and enjoyable.Chapter boss HP scales exponentially and their damage scales linearly.  Your damage from levels and your damage from gear scale VERY linearly.  Which means your damage will get outpaced starting from the mid-game.  Late game, the bosses start to hit you for 45-80% of your HP while you will hit them for 3-4% of their HP:If you build damage, you deal 4% and take 80-100% of your HP per boss hit.If you build tank, you deal 3% and take 30-45% per boss hit.Either way, the boss fight will take 60-90 minutes and will cycle through the same 3 mechanics.PRO TIP: enable "auto-victory" and click it often.

_childDocuments_.review: As a jrpg, it sucks. As a visual novel, it's good. The game has this awful timing combat, which sounds neat but it's far too hard to use. However, there's an option to turn on auto timing and even instant wins, making combat non-existent. The game becomes mostly an interactive visual novel with those options enabled. That's how I played it. It's up to you whether you play in hard mode or very easy mode. The soundtrack is great too (available for purchase on bandcamp fyi weird that it's not available here too).

_childDocuments_.review: I wish it was longer. It reminds me a bit of Wakfu from when I used to play. This game is a charming RPG with some nice small twists I have yet to see else where in the story. As well as a fun battle system that I wish I had more progress to have fun with. The battles takes place on a 3x12 grid and are turn bass. All attacks are spell with no mana to keep track of. How well you cast  your spell is tied into timing your button presses, like in any Mario RPG. Same with taking damage. The Grid add in far more dept then taking away mana takes a way. I rarely asked my self what spell was most powerful, but instead of what spell is best for this situation. I highly recommend if stander turn bass combat has bored you as it have done for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice mix of turn-based tactics and hit timing. The fact the battles take place on a grid and all actions have a limited range (especially items) makes stuff like reviving allies much more involved than, say, Epic Battle Fantasy. While that can be a double-edged sword (say you've got a party member down while a boss has put traps everywhere), I largely like the system.The story, while not perfect (I wish I got to see more of the characters, if that makes sense, and sometimes the tone of scenes changes a little faster than I'd expect), was enjoyable.The only really irritating part to me was some of the puzzles. Twice I had to look online only to realize I'd missed something that was hiding in plain sight, so to speak. I'm not sure if this means I need to pay more attention or if the clues should be signposted better, but I'm leaning towards the former.If you're into turn-based stuff, I'd recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: -quality pixel art-really good music and sound design-intriguing story-usual turn based combat is spiced up by a QTE-esque system where based on your reaction speed spells deal more or less damage – this keeps the game more engaging and rewarding, but if it’s too much for someone, it can be turned off completely in the settings-Does not respond to keyboard inputs other than the arrow keys-Some tweaking of the UI could go a long way, for example showing HP of combat participants without having to navigate the menu over and over again-Similarly, visual clarity could be tuned up a notch as well, I find it really hard to figure out certain attacks’ timingI expected the usual boring turn-based rpg experience of just roaming menus to pick the same attacks over and over again, but colour me surprised, For more detail on the above points and a look at gameplay, please join me as I elaborate on my thoughts in this video:.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I adore the characters, the art, and the music, and as much as I want to love the game and the wonderful representation it has, I just can't. The combat seemed exciting at first but quickly grew tedious and grindy; fights would take a long time, but I never felt like there was a real challenge and it just felt like a grind. The story often fell flat for me, feeling shallow and uninteresting. My biggest complain though is that it felt like the characters could've been developed way more; in the end they just felt like superficial diversity checkboxes. I tried sticking it out for a while, but in the end I couldn't derive much enjoyment from the game. The representation and diversity in this game is fantastic, but I can't recommend it because of the supbar combat/story.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sad to give this a negative review but as the game went on, it only got worse and worse until I couldn't take the game seriously anymore. The cast is entirely queer, including one person with neopronouns which is nice to see. The story and characters are generally very shallow, and around the midpoint of the game each chapter starts feeling monotonous as the plot takes too many twists and turns to have been planned out beforehand. Combat is generally enjoyable, though in the late game health pools start scaling up and it's hard not to want a defensive build when a couple bad timings could cost 3/4 of a party member's health bar. Assigning equipment is rather unwieldy, as there's too many choices that are hard to compare to each other and become obsolete every other chapter, as well as completely arbitrary weapon upgrades that are just a money sink. There's adequate accessibility options to both autocomplete action commands as well as fights themselves, and also an option to display content warnings which is very much appreciated.The ending solidified my negative review. No specifics, but to its credit, the music is very good, though I think playing songs with lyrics during some boss fights was a mistake. it's undoubtedly the best part of the game, alongside the charming pixel art graphics. if you do play ikenfell, feel free to spin the control stick around in battle to fly into the sky!!
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent music, high-quality animation, a fabulous story, and great battle mechanics. I like that there's an option to turn on content warnings, and that there's a lot of non-binary representation. The timing mechanic in battle has been surprisingly challenging, after playing over half of the story I turned it to automatic (ie no need to press the action button at the exact moment to deal more damage or take less damage). I found it helped me enjoy the story as it got more challenging. Get this game!!!Edit: After about 23 hours in the game it felt like a slog. I discovered an "instant victory" mode which allowed me to skip combat entirely. This let me finish the story even though the combat got kind of hard/boring. Love this accessibility feature.

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is a wonderful game with great characters, story, and music. _childDocuments_.review: Buy it now if you like: Cute stories about magic, simple but engaging Strategy RPG gameplay, good lo-fi music, supporting indie game developers who seem to truly care about your gaming experience.Buy it on sale if you like: RPGs in general-- it's a good one you don't see too often.Gameplay: Like "Paper Mario" or "South Park" RPGs.  You can turn down or turn off the timing here which is great if you suck at it like me!  Settings also have an "auto-win" option for grinding purposes, though I haven't seen much need to grind so far.  Leveling is on the slower side with only 1 or two points gained and  new moves learned every few levels.  Loot is pretty standard so far.Story: Very cute-centric, paced well, and good writing so far.  I'm a habitual dialogue skipper but found myself reading it here because I cared.  Characters are quirky and endearing.  Settings have an option essentially for "trigger warnings" which I turned on out of curiosity.  Warned me so far when a character was engaging in self-hating talk.  It wasn't something that would have bothered me but I appreciate that the devs put that option in for people who just want to have a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: Having played through the game and explored every nook and cranny, the things that pop into my mind is Hogwarts and the Tactics genre. Ikenfell is obviously a game made with love and care, but at the same time it seems rushed in some parts.One of the pillars of the game, is the music. In general it's good and really does something for the game. There are even times, where the music carries a scene, that might otherwise have fallen short.The only music I found slightly off, was the Ikenfell schoolyard, which is a piece you'll hear often in the game. It feels too cozy, considering the urgency of the situation.Another pillar of the game is the combat. The combat is well-made and often a joy to play. Everything is timing based, so every outcome is affected by your reaction skills. I found that fresh and exciting and there was a nice learning curve. The combat is also nicely supported by your character's equipment - I often found myself trying to optimize this part. Further, the cast of characters is both interesting and provides a nice variety in available skills.Sadly, both the combat patterns and equipment variations eventually goes stale. It's too much of the same, over and over. While there are many enemies, at some point they all feel the same. Even the boss battles, that started out great, are eventually just damage sponges with the same gameplay. Equipment feels like it's only upgraded to drain some of your gold.It is not until towards the end of the game, that combat starts getting exciting again.The graphics are well-made and although nothing jaw dropping, it is obvious that the creator has some skills in that department. Pixels aren't easy to work with, so I have great respect for that.The world is made up of a dozen or so areas, that each are graphically, somewhat unique, but it's simply not enough to make up for the gameplay repetition.The game follows a formula of finding an NPC, completing a dungeon of puzzles, fighting a boss only to find a new NPC and repeat the same pattern over and over. It's a well-known pattern, and often works, however Ikenfell seems to be following this too strictly and eventually it grows tiring and predictable.The overarching story initially felt interesting and I often found myself curious as to what would be revealed next. Yet in the end, it turned out... a flat experience.The game took me about 31 hours to complete, which is an impressive length! However with all the repetition, I'd rather it was half the length and half the repetition.A minor issue I had with the game, is the number of errors in the dialogue. Considering it's a text heavy game, there are bound to be a few errors. But this is too much.I also experienced a lot of screen flicker, which impacted combat on several occasions.It's not a bad game per say - it's just too repetitive. I therefore can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is a darling little game. My review might be biased because it's been exactly the sort of escapism I've needed during these uncertain times (lol), but I think it's what everyone could use right now. Charming sprites and environments, a unique combat system (though it isn't always clear how to counter enemy attacks or set off yours), immersive music and characters that you watch grow and overcome personal challenges, who are written so realistically, dealing with those hard-to-talk-about issues that come with the territory of being a young adult. The LGBTQ+ and minority representation is much appreciated, too. I needed this game during my own formative years, but I'm happy it's here now!
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for June 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 6th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.The Humble extra sneak-peek from June 2020 is now a choice, and it’s great to see this game fully. This is a lot of different pieces that come together to make one interesting game.  It’s an RPG where players learn magic and go to a witch school, the combat has timed attacks and blocks, similar to Super Mario RPGs, and there’s a strategy RPG grid of moving characters in battle.  And none of that is a bad thing. The story starts with the main character hunting for her sister, who stayed at school for the summer, but it appears something has gone wrong, and the school is locked down.  The game revolves around fighting enemies to get more powerful and solving rather simple puzzles. There appears to be an interesting challenge here, especially if you’re a hoarder like me. The art is simple, but the designs are interesting and there were quite a few characters I wanted to know more about or see what happens next in the story.  Also, the HP restore system and the save system are activated by petting different cats.  I love that.Pick this up if you want an RPG focused on magical systems and timed actions.  It’s also said to be about 20 hours long so it’s got a good run time, and it looks like it has an interesting tale to tell. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Worth playing, but battle system is kinda flawed.I definitely enjoyed Ikenfell. The story was great, the characters were charming, and the visuals & music felt retro in a good way. Though the game parts, while fun, definitely had a lot of annoying issues that detracted from my enjoyment:* The timing mechanics were wildly inconsistent with some having nice obvious UI while others were unclear and had very limited windows to hit the mark so they ended up feeling unfair and frustrating (ie. Force Punch).* Items were barely worth using. Out of battle, you can constantly recharge at save points that are trivial to reach. In battle, their range is so limited that you have to have the character using the item be directly adjacent to their target.* Status effects were so limited and mild that it's barely worth bothering to stock up on curing items to heal them. * Traps became practically worthless late in the game as enemies started jumping and teleporting so they wouldn't trigger unless you could get an enemy to end their move directly on the trap tile.* Late game enemies and bosses had such ridiculous movement ranges that close range characters were at a huge disadvantage.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: The kind of game that makes you feel empty for a week after you finished it. Awesome RPG, with no male PC and many non-binary characters (yeah !!), which is way too rare nowadays. I was so moved by its characters that I cried ... a lot. Especially the conclusion, after the 12 hours credit scene (due to a very successfull crowdfunding i assume. Have never seen so many names written on a screen. Still in shock). Every main character has her/their/zir personnal music, which makes you love your dream team even more. Some of them are even songs. It's SHOWTIME !!The gameplay is refreshing too. Fights are turn-based but for once aren't slow nor boring. Indeed, every action (PC's and monsters' alike) needs a perfect timing, which is fun but also sometimes pretty complicated. Yet, it's doesn't make Ikenfell a hard game, for there is an option in the game that make those timing easier to play with, which is much appreciated.It took me around 25 hours to finish the game (main story + 3 optional bosses). There is no other secondary quests, the game is focused on what it does best : telling a story. Which also is way to rare nowadays. A no padding RPG, in 2021 !!Thanks for everything, Happy Ray Games, can't wait to play your next game (hope there will be a next game >.<)
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is a game made for and by people who love video games. Ikenfell is a clear love letter to turn based RPGs with a large influence from the Mother series and more specifically Mother 3. While it may pay homage to these games it never lacks in its own identity and charm. The characters have wonderful stories and personalities as well as some of the best and most appropriate representation that I've seen in a game in a long timeAnd not to mention the absolutely outstanding soundtrack and sprite work with the characters and combat animations. A wonderful game for anyone who enjoys the old fashioned turn based RPG charm with modern and inventive gameplay, story, and characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, fairly simple puzzle tactics rpg. The animations are super cute, the characters are lovable and queer and diverse, the story is fairly engaging and has some really nice themes to it. It's a good length (my hours shown are greatly inflated because I left this running throughout the day as I did other things and then came back to it) to do it 100% with all achievements is probably around 20-25 hours. There were some really nice elements in the game, like save points that heal you placed in convenient spots and a teleportation feature to help you zip around campus as needed. PLEASE BE AWARE YOU CAN TURN ON AUTOMATIC TIMING FOR ATTACKS/DEFENSE IN THE OPTIONS!!! I almost returned it before reading that online somewhere and so glad that was available. There's actually a ton of options for customizable gameplay and accessibility, it's awesome!A few complaints (which should in no way dissuade you from purchasing!): some of the puzzles were just exhausting and needlessly tedious (most were fine to fun though). Relatedly, you might find yourself needing to go back through to find gems and some stages because of the puzzle mechanics are an absolute nightmare to try to walk back through to get missed items. There's no reason after completing a section they can't just deactivate all the puzzles and let you just walk through freely. Lastly, I really don't like in games where there's so many items that they essentially become meaningless. The second you get new armor/weapons/accessories, you almost immediately get more and they're all just minimally different. I'd rather have fewer items that make a bigger difference and are either all pretty basic and straightforward upgrades, or are more unique to truly customize each character via equipment. This game tried to do both with just a TON of items and I personally find that frustrating. I would spend all my money to upgrade my gear, only for there to be new, slightly better gear almost immediately. To be fair, there's a lot of items in the game that you can sell for good money, which helps mitigate this, but still, it's not fun to go through this over and over. On top of the items you can buy, you also discover TONS of equipment while fighting and puzzle-solving, so it's just a LOT. These were points of frustration but, in the grand scheme of the game, minor complaints. Overall, this game is extremely well made, enjoyable, and the perfect length for the price point and genre. I would LOVE to see more from this developer and am so happy that I bought this game. Highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: overall i really enjoyed playing this, and can recommend it. the story is a straightforward fantasy adventure, and it pulls it off pretty well. like many children's books, the characters are all quite one note (they're mostly defined by their one anxiety and their one ambition), but not in a bad way. they're all relatable, and their interactions create plenty of heartfelt moments. the variety in character design is the strong core of the game, both in their personalities and in how they play differently in combat.combat is one of the most distinct parts of the game, with a unique blend of Mario RPG style timing attacks and tactics RPG style positioning. the timing windows for attack and defense are tight, and hitting them is extremely impactful (something like 2-3x extra damage/damage reduced), meaning every combat requires a base level of attention often optional in RPGs. i did find the pace of combat a bit slow - everything being on a grid means everyone takes a move action first, and those move actions make combat take a good chunk longer than in something like Paper Mario.of course, adding a grid adds a level of spatial tactics that other games don't have. i'm not sure the design space is very well explored here. on the one hand, there's definitely a depth to the combat that i didn't fully engage in (things like predicting enemy movement patterns to bait them into traps). on the other, i didn't need to in order to clear the game with appropriate difficulty and no grinding. it was much easier to focus on my party's positioning than my enemies, but that didn't add too much thought beyond "keep party close to heal/buff them simultaneously". i think Into The Breach style enemy relocation abilities would have added a lot to the battles, and encourage me to think more than one turn at a time. ultimately, even though non-bosses are entirely optional, i did find encounters to blur together and take longer than i'd like. the worst thing i can say about ikenfell is that there's a feeling of "on paper these are distinct, but in practice they feel the same" that pervades quite a lot of it. there are many unique items but they're a wash of incremental improvements. there are many unique areas, but they mostly play out the same. there are many unique enemies, but not many different things they can do to you. every encounter is unique, but so few stand out. that's doubly unfortunate for the bosses, where so many of them just end up spawning a bunch of minions and not doing much else.  i couldn't play through more than one area at a time without it feeling a bit stale, but that made it a perfect game to play over several 1-2h chunks. and i have to stress that there are many unique songs, and they're all great. ultimately there's a heart to the game, and that's what kept me going. you want to root for the characters and help them face their problems, and i'm glad to have played it to the end. i'm not sure i'll replay it, partially because it ties up so satisfyingly that i don't need to go back, partially because my issues with the pacing would make a second playthrough a slog. i will definitely be thinking about the characters (and listening to the soundtrack!) for a while yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game to 100% completion and while I tried really hard to enjoy it, I just couldn't. The combat gets REALLY frustrating as you progress through late game. It sucked when I faced an enemy I hadn't encountered before and lost a bunch of hp/potential damage because I couldn't figure out the timing right away. I ended up changing the difficulty of the timing in the settings, and while that did make combat a lot easier, battles just became a chore for me after that. And I'm not done here--the boss battles, especially with this mechanic, are PAINFUL. They can't be avoided and are very long. Don't get me started on the final boss battle.The characters are a mixed bag. I really loved Maritte and Pertisia's character development. But on the other hand, I felt like the other characters were barely touched on. Each chapter kept on introducing these new characters I couldn't care for because I didn't really know much about them. The story was the most disappointing for me. It seemed interesting at first, trying to solve a mystery in an eerie, fantastical setting. But with the negatives I faced with the combat and characters, it just seemed to drag on. Entering each chapter felt like an ongoing loop of "no but actually.." to me, introducing huge lore dumps every time. In my opinion, it was like things were made up as the story progressed.The only things that kept me going were the somewhat challenging puzzles and the music. The game may seem charming on the surface, but I don't think I could recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing:StoryIt can be so HARD to make a compelling personal journey. It is equally difficult to pull of a whole new mythos. This game does BOTH and weaves them together thematically to bring both to fruition. If this were a novel alone, it would be worth the purchase price. But it's not: it also has...AestheticsThe pixel art is simplistic, yes, and I give no bonus points for "nostalgia," but the pixel art combined with the emotive faces in dialogue truly pull off the emotional heft of the story and the "cutesy" style really packs a punch during the darker beats of the story. On top of that, the music is absolutely top-class. The chip-tune score is accompanied by vocals for some of the main characters and matches the story beat for beat in a VERY purposeful way. That sense of purpose isn't just borne out in the aesthetics, but also...GameplayHow many times have you started a pixel-art RPG just waiting to realize it's some low-effort nonsense? Looking for that weak point that the creators just didn't have the budget for? This game is relatively small (though I still have 40 hours on it), but it puts in WORK with what it puts into the game. There's a lot I could talk about: equipment economy is spot on, items FEEL good as you get the dozens of new gear pieces; collectibles are well, but intuitively hidden and have real value when you get them; consumables are just right --not cheap enough to spam, but strong enough to make you feel the "hell yeah" when you use them. But I don't want to talk about that. I want to talk about...Party CombatBuilding a full RPG party usually feels something like: Yay! Got the fighter-guy! Whee! Healer-girl! Finally: Wizard-boy! And then... the other ones... This game is amazing in that all six of the party members have a completely different "feel" in combat. None of them are duplicates or upgrades of the others. They are each a delicate balance of novel abilities and strengths that lets you develop your particular "build" when you get into the challenging 3rd-act battles (Maritte, Glinda, Ima 4 lyfe, btw, but PLEASE try them all, because it was hard-fought for ME to decide what MY best team was).Not only are the party members all MECHANICALLY distinct, but their combat mechanics bear out their emotional representation in the story. The quiet girl who always doubts herself has to hang out in combat and support her friends and pop poisons onto the enemy. The strong-willed, level-headed older one is a solid all-rounder that can cover a lot of gaps. Etc. It's an amazing testament to the purposefulness of this game's dev team that the story and mechanics are so well knit together.100% don't bother waiting for a sale: if you like story-driven, tactical RPGs, just buy it now and enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: There are a few issues with the combat. For one you can't see enemy range or attack pattern when viewing their stats during battle so you don't know how far they can reach. Your teammate with the highest speed doesn't even come first among the 3 partymembers all the time. And it can often happen that some enemies have double turns before one of your team even had 1. As for difficulty the only thing that seems to matter is not missing the quicktime events. Especially late game it is the difference between taking 2 damage and 22. _childDocuments_.review: Really fun and unique gameplay, lots of accessibility options/considerations, better LGBTQ+ representation than I've seen in any other video game personally, and a fairly well-written story that didn't feel contrived nor shallow.  Overall, very worth getting the game and playing it.  Will give more specifics below without spoiling anything, but I definitely recommend.Gameplay is turn-based, tactical strategy type fighting with RPG elements, and fights are not random (walking into monsters, obvious boss-incoming situations), plenty of options to save/heal at crucial moments while still allowing for challenge.  Timing for defense/offense can significantly matter, but there are settings to change this if that'd ruin things for you, but default "Manual" setting is fairly flexible while still requiring you to pay attention.  Other accessibility settings allow for more of a "story and item collection" instead of "fighting," but default settings are the details I outlined above.  Also: Once you beat an enemy in a map (i.e. in a building), they are gone until you leave the area (i.e. leaving a building) and return, which is a hugely convenient thing if you're going up and down stairs to find something or trying to figure out puzzles.  You also will not need to grind outside of enemies in the area, don't need to re-fight and re-face enemies over and over again, the enemies in an area will get you the experience you need without needing to get them to respawn.Lots of LGBTQ+ healthy representation, including gender nonbinary, various pronouns, one or two "oops" moments between characters that's handled in a very healthy manner, identity and orientation *not* feeding into some stereotype personality ("gay" does not automatically mean "flamboyantly in your face" for example), a couple of lines showing awareness of how one handles romance/dating without needing heavy focus, etc.Usually I see exactly where a story is going within the first third of a game/movie/show.  I didn't know exactly where this was going.  I had ideas, some were smashed to bits.  Some because of not having all the information, which makes sense for your character, but also some because it went against certain tropes.-----There was a couple of minor nitpicks I have (and I do consider them minor, honestly):Every single person is a different type of gender identity or orientation, which can come off a little token-y... "Okay, so which identity/orientation have I not come across yet?  Yup, new character is one of those, figured."  That said, the fact that their gender/orientation isn't some kind of plot point or major character focus, doesn't define the character's personality, is actually better representation, and the fact that they were considered is better than not existing.I felt like 1-2 character dynamic issues and root causes to issues between characters were kind of ignored or glossed over in the end.  Avoiding saying more to avoid spoilers, but the ending is still pretty satisfying.  I don't expect everything to be perfect, I just would've preferred an additional callout or similar, if that makes sense?  Again, minor nitpick, still loved the story.How the story provided a glimpse into past events felt... overly convenient?  That said, it gets explained, it allows SHOW instead of TELL, feeds further discussion between characters, and doesn't give all answers, just glimpses, so you and the characters aren't getting plot-dumps.---Again, overall, great game, highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: ~10h with victory mode one, without it I would guess it is around 20h 2/10 with Victory mode on, 6/10 without victory mode 1 Yes Yes, I used the following 3: , ,  4 on Astats No No No No No No No No NoWhat a superb game! I really loved this puzzle RPG game. The storytelling starts off a bit cringy but gets better very soon into the game. You play as Maritta who is searching for her sister that didn't come home for the summer from Ikenfall, her magic school. Here you'll enter a world that is very unknown for Maritta, but the characters you meet will also feel on edge because there is something weird going on in the magic world. I love how every party member has their own story and characteristics, which plays a big part in the story. They are not generic party members at all. Another thing I love about this game is the accessibility of the battle system. The game has a turn-based tactics battle system with timing elements. You have the option to turn off the timing elements in the options menu in case you don't like that. You also have the option to turn on "victory mode" that way you get the option to win the battle as soon as it is the turn of one of your characters. I played with this mode on, which makes the game a whole lot easier, but I did it because I wasn't a fan of the battle system. There was nothing wrong with it but I just didn't like it and this way I had the option to play through this fantastic game without being annoyed with the battle system. The game has some great music. Some can be found on Spotify. During one cutscene there was playing an amazing song and I used "Shazam" on my phone to check which song it is and I was so happy to find the song on Spotify. "Yearn To Bloom - Aeldra's theme". Have been playing it while writing this review, I just love it, The game has no missable achievements, after finishing the last boss you can go back to your save just before the last boss. I would even suggest waiting with the final boss and first complete the sidequests. The ending is wonderful but long, and going through it a second time for a minor change at the ending might not be worth it. There are a lot of gems you have to find in the game, those are hidden. There is a great guide here on steam (linked above) which you can use while playing through the game. I did it afterward and only needed an hour to mop them up, which wasn't so bad, and that way you can play carefree through the game. It took me around 10h to complete the game with victory mode on.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent.  Not the best, not the worst.Story was lackluster.  It was unapologetically Harry Potter fanfiction and would have benefited from distancing itself from that a bit more.  Characters were alright, though they felt a bit... soft.  Really did feel like a bunch of kids, which I suppose is appropriate.  Electric girl was the only one I really liked; she was pretty funny.  Actually, come to think of it, that's what was missing - there was hardly any humor.  The game took itself very seriously.Combat was solid, though.  Lots of decisions to make every step of the way.  Each fight is quite time-consuming, so they counterbalance it with big rewards and plentiful interesting boss fights.Core cast is three lesbians and three enbies, which was a bit different, I guess?  A little weird that the character status screen lists pronouns, but that's nitpicking.  Felt a little forced, given the Harry Potter fanfic thing they had going on.  Kind of get the feeling that it's going to color the reviews of the game.  This isn't a story about sexuality and gender identity.Postgame was solid.  Lots of collectibles and three superbosses.  Game didn't overstay its welcome.Worth playing if you like turn based RPGs, but pretty forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: What if the best, most invested, most gay Harry Potter fanfic writers got to make a game?The answer: Ikenfell.Now, that may drive some people away from this game, fanfiction has this sort of reputation of being trash, but that's how most writers start writing, they take a series they already enjoy, put their own unique spin on it, and publish it under some anonymous username for fun. And some people get real good at it. This game's writing, in my opinion, is not trash.It's got that same sort of style to it all though, it's a sometimes whimsical, sometimes serious, very teenage angst filled game about a magic school and a girl who thought she was just some normal person being whisked away into a whole new, wondrous, and dangerous world as she tries to find her sister (who's older but looks way younger for some reason??? Not explained in the game just a thought I had).The gameplay is like if you mixed together Paper Mario and Megaman: Battle Network. It's a turn based, grid movement style RPG where your characters level up, acrue new skills, and most of the difficulty of the game comes from timing your A presses to make sure you deal maximum damage and take minimum damage.But, really, the gameplay wasn't what kept me coming back, as is the case with most of the single player RPGs that I found on a steam sale, the story, the writing, and the characters kept me coming back until I finished the game... then I beat the post game boss(es). And now I guess the only real criticism I have is "dammit I want to play more, why is it over so soon?" When, as you can see, it took me 20 hours to do all that.I think that you should watch a few trailers, maybe the first 1 or 2 episodes of another person's playthrough, then, if the writing looks fun to you, play the game. Even if you're terrible at rhythm or you aren't good at strategy, there are options to make the game easy, and one option even eliminates combat altogether.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played a lot of Undertale, this game has serious Undertale vibes. Definitely grab it.  Maybe the vibe changes later? I'll update if so. I haven't gotten to know them well yet but I'm looking forward to it, OK?The fights take place on a small tactical grid. It's neat! It's not a whole tactics game but a smaller cozier system that's more than Suikoden and less than FF Tactics. _childDocuments_.review: is a game that I really could not bring myself to enjoy. As a big fan of JRPGs and great pixel art, I was excited to see what this game had in store. 9 hours of slowly becoming more and more jaded later, I cannot get behind this game in any light. First of all, the sprite art is alright. Nothing insanely pretty, it’s obviously an RPGMaker game that takes a lot of inspiration from Earthbound and Undertale. I usually love the visuals in these games but in Ikenfell it was only so-so. The character sprites were peculiar to me, opting for 3 different styles, in exploration, in dialogue, and during combat. The most appealing version is during dialogue, where you can actually see the character’s faces, while during exploration they give a strangely large amount of pixel real estate to the character’s hair, only giving 3 tall pixels worth of a face. It makes the characters look very odd during top-down cutscenes and really disconnects me from the characters (because I cannot see their eyes).In addition, I found the combat to be an absolute slog. While I did find the idea somewhat interesting, and the lack of MP gave a lot more freedom to what spells you used, EVERY single fight is dragged on horrendously long. Even the most basic enemies take at least 3 or 4 turns from the player, complete with enemies moving AND attacking AND you having to block it. It turns what could be a 30 second encounter to 4 or 5 minutes, which in the long run becomes agonizingly long. Enemies become insane damage sponges and become entirely dependent on the timing of your attacks (which can be done automatically through settings). Also, the vocal tracks during the boss battles, while a novel idea, did not mesh at all with the gameplay, in fact it really took me out of the game. The story itself felt embarrassingly shallow for how much dialogue there is. I understand in a 10-15 hour game with lots of characters you can’t be expected to get huge development out of each of them, but every character felt so insanely cookie cutter that I couldn’t connect with a single one of them. Each character’s arc just flipped from one end of the other, the mean girl suddenly becomes nice, the shy girl gets brave, it’s just so tiring and I found myself caring less and less about the characters as the game progressed. The actual story of the game is even more unengaging but in the opposite way, plot threads get so quickly muddled and confusing that by the end of the game you’re unsure what is actually happening, somehow the characters talk so much but never about the thing you want to know more about.I respect the hell out of video-game creators, as they’ve made some of my favorite experiences I’ve ever consumed, and I think this is a great team with a lot of potential to make something truly special. But I don’t think this game respects the time of the consumer, it got to the point where I just started using the auto-victory for every boss near the end because it was becoming such a slog. I do think that if you really don’t mind a standard story and you auto-victory through some of the longer, more tedious bosses you could enjoy this game. But as it stands, Ikenfell, to me, is a dangerous combination of a monotonous battle system paired with fiercely rooted archetypal characters and a confusing story that they never bother to truly explain beyond “it’s magic!!”.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful story of us trying to rescue our lost sister at her magic school. Teaming up with her classmates, we immediately learn she pretended we didn’t exist and is also a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥, and our goal shifts to “Rescue her cause she’s my sister, then tear into her myself cause what the ♥♥♥♥ Saf?” Which instantly makes them more realistic siblings than most. That actually sums up the writing as a whole- initially seems rather cliché, but grows into something unique and well written. Characters actually grow and adapt. They respond to criticism, their emotions felt real. I found myself bonding to them rather quickly. The gameplay itself is the type you find in older mario RPGs, where it’s turn based and you do a little timing minigame to determine how well you do. What I appreciate is that near everything has a modular setting. So you can set the timing to automatically hit, but you can time it to do the bonus damage. Or just automatically do it perfectly if you don’t like the style. I had it on semi-auto, if only thanks to a few specific spell timings. There’s even an instant win option, which gives you an auto-victory action during battle. Sounds great for grinding if you need to, though I didn’t. Fight the encounters as you find them and you’ll generally be fine. Also content warning option, which is off by default but appreciated. Nothing that effected me here, but as someone with PTSD I wish more games in general had that.I highly recommend this, it was wonderful. Gameplay was good, story was well written, it’s a bit slow but otherwise quite solid. It's a nice 7 or 8 out of 10. As long as gay people don't upset you it'll be fine. If they do...this might make you combust. However, like all things I love, I am well aware of the flaws. The following is mostly nitpicks,  nothing here was a dealbreaker. But if you want to hear the parts that did bug me, keep reading.~~~~~~~~~- I wish you could just leave the healthbars on instead of having to flick through options to examine the enemies each time. Plus you can’t change settings during a battle, or pause. Which is odd, because it always gives you the option to reset the battle or restart from checkpoint when you die...so if you want to retry you just have to spend a minute dying to get the option. Weird.- Battle can be slow, especially in big battles and when bosses start getting multiple turns per turn, and 5 things act between one of your characters getting to move. looking at you, starhops in Ima’s personal battle.- Everything at the rest cats is optional...except healing. So you can’t save or swap party members without healing. Which doesn’t sound bad, but when you get an attack that’s only useable at half health it can be irritating. Same with cutscenes healing you. there’s no good way to lower your health back either, except hope enemies randomly target the right person.- There was a 6 form boss, with multiple “win in the fight lose in the cutscene” moments, what the actual ♥♥♥♥? - Lashing out in anger IS your fault, actually. Sustained coping mechanisms and your actions while under them are also your fault, especially when refusing to change them. The consequences of your actions are your responsibility. Like seriously, I enjoy reformation and am genuinely glad those people became better. But some of them were genuinely and repeatedly in the wrong, and I’d have appreciated like...an apology that wasn’t met with assurance that it wasn’t their fault. - When you make sure there is exactly 1 of almost everyone under the sun, it can stop feeling like representation and starts feeling like you went down a checklist. It also makes it starkly clear who you left out, especially in the cases you double up. Plently are clear while being subtle. Some are well done while being forward, like our favorite lightning lesbian lancer’s crush playing into who she is and her motivations. But some felt corporate or forced, likely because of the diversity consultant they hired part way through, who reworked some of the story and characters. It shows, because there are a few things just not woven in nearly as well, and sometimes it hurts even the best cases. I end up wondering if this was actually planned, or just the diversity dartboard just hit a good combination through sheer luck when filling out the quota.One of the more egregious examples is a random story crystal in the main hall of chapter 4. It’s the only one that has no before/after cutscene, has nothing to do with the plot, and is never acknowledged in any way by the characters or game. Its main dialogue is Rook explaining to Saf that he is nonbinary, do not call him a guy. He/him enbies are fine, but with him being the only enby not using They/Them or Ze/Zie, combined with the random janky cutscene with no relation to the story, and his gender not brought up outside that cutscene, it just screams last minute change when compared to how smooth most other things are. Not the one that annoyed me, but one of the most obvious.That said these are basically all the issues I had over 33 hours, the game is overall great. But once I found out that most of the faults might not even be the fault of the team it bugged me. Gilda gets a pass though. I know she spends multiple cutscenes talking about how hot your are and muttering about how gay she is, but stream of consciousness and acting without thinking are just how she works, it makes sense. She is delightful.

_childDocuments_.review: Auggghhh I don't think I can finish this one.I am okay with the story and the combat, I wish the combat could be fasten up a bit tho.What I am not okay with was the map/level design.After playing it for 6 hours I could tell that the whole game is going to be like this :- Go to a checkpoint.- Explore some rooms.- Stumble open a locked door.- Find a key.- Fight a boss.Well you could say that MOST games are like that but something felt off about Ikenfell.I am guessing is that the areas look identical with just some reskins done, so it felt repetitive.There is also a lack sense of progression. _childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is a game about a magical school that has a pretty big focus on diversity. We have a variety of skin tones, genders, and sexualities represented, but no one really feels tokenized. It's pretty great. There's a variety of pronoun usage too.The world is interesting. Plot gets a bit dark in places, but is good. There's an option to turn on content warnings and also an option to skip cutscenes just in case it covers something that's a but sensitive for you, though I found it was all handled pretty well and not 'too much' even in some of the darkest bits. If it was using realistic graphics tho, and not cute retro-pixel graphics I'd.. probably have had to skip a few tho.There's other accessibility options besides the content filter. Like, if you'd rather play this game like a visual novel/walking sim hybrid? There's an auto-win option you can toggle. There's also two options to change how combat works. By default combat's a QTA where you have to time things pretty close to do much damage or defend. You can change it so that everything's 'nice' rather than 'oops' if you can't get the timing right, and you can try to get 'great' or for everything to be 'great' by default so it works more like a standard turn based game.The timing is different for every attack which is cool? but also means you need to recognize every attack you make and every attack your enemies make unless you change the settings, which makes it pretty challenging. Grimm's Hollow used a similar system, but the attacks are all shown on a bar so you just have to stop at the same point in the bar, which was. Quite a bit easier than things are in Ikenfell.Due to these systems, all the boss fights feel really unique, and each character also plays differently. One other thing I'd like to highlight is the music? A few characters have vocal tracks, and they're all good! The only thing I can say that's disappointing about them is that I only heard Rook's vocal theme once which is a shame because it's just so good. There's a lot of instrumentals too. The battle music changes based on the chapter you're in which keeps things fresh and doesn't make you get burned out on a particular track.I could say more, but, I'd like to keep things spoiler free, and also allow anyone who plays to get to know the characters and world themselves ^^; Thanks again for gifting me this Rose 💜

_childDocuments_.review: I am quite far into the game, and I have LOVED just about every moment of it. The characters are all unique with actual personality, and the soundtrack is UNBELIEVABLY good. I am enraptured with the story and the setting, and while I don't know if it WILL happen, I'd love to see more from this universe in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: How to describe Ikenfell? Like Steven Universe hit Undertale at a dead run in the middle of a Pride march. Add a sprinkling of Avatar (benders, not blue people) and a soundtrack worthy of standing beside any of its inspirations, and you've got quite the sparkly gem. It's also a lot bigger than I expected it to be, around thirty hours to finish the main storyline and I'm still not done with the sidequests and achievements. If you're just here for the story, you can skip all the battles - yeah, all of them! - but if you're looking for some Actual Gameplay (TM), Ikenfell is about two things: correct positioning and correct timing. Details follow.The fight-monsters, gain-experience, level-up loop is classic RPG fare, but battles play out a little more like a turn-based strategy game (think Final Fantasy Tactics, Fell Seal, Fire Emblem, that kind of thing). The battlefield is about twelve squares long and three squares deep, and each of your characters' spells - and the enemy's moves, come to that - target squares a very specific distance and direction away from the caster. In order to cast your spells properly, you'll need to hit the button at exactly the right time (though if you'd rather stick to strategy you can also turn the timing to automatic). Defending works the same way: reduce damage by hitting the button at the right moment. You'll see a few move patterns repeat later in the game, but rather than feeling stale it feels like you're being rewarded for what you learned before.Summary: Ikenfell isn't just a good story wrapped in a game, it's a good game as well. Worth your money and your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the story is simplistic and the epilogue is cringy, the gameplay and the design are, in my humble opinion, flawless: all of the reaction-based elements are clearly telegraphed to the player, the sound cues are easy to comprehend, the soundtrack ideally complements the activities, the characters are super cute and have their own individual fighting styles, the levels are visually gorgeous and most of the puzzles are well-thought-out for an adventure game. _childDocuments_.review: Cute game, but overall it has a few large flaws that keep it from being really enjoyable to me. The combat being slow with its mix of grid based movement and timed hits to attack, as well as bosses with multiple phases and continually spawning enemies makes just fighting a chore. The writing itself also has a number of moments which are just.. frankly poorly written and feel like they were added just for inclusiveness. Personally, I feel unless Gender politics is a big thing you absolutely adore, you'll find yourself taken out of the game from the multitudes of time the writing wants to hamfistedly shove it into the conversations. If you can ignore both of those parts, and try to see the game around it, I do feel like theres a cute, if a bit sub par and poorly paced story beneath it all. Overall, not really worth it in my opinion, but your mileage may vary.
