_childDocuments_.review: It's a certified A-grade tactical RPG, to be sure, but Ikenfell's true piece-de-resistance is its (in my experience) unprecedented accessibility. Photosensitive? Just pop into the options and switch off the flashes. Trouble with reflexes? There's an option to let you ignore the timed hits mechanic with no penalty. There's even an option to let the player auto-win battles if they're so inclined. Elitists beware; there'll be no ableist gatekeeping here.Oh yeah, and it's stuffed to the gills with PoC and LGBTQI+ characters. Yes, unlike some other magic schools, everyone is welcome at Ikenfell. If that bothers you, perhaps your magical education is best pursued elsewhere. I hear the Scottish Highlands are lovely this time of year...
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed my time with Ikenfell: it has nice battle mechanics, rewarding exploration and a charming story with characters that you will dearly miss once you finish the game; it also has a nice amount of side content that can lengthen an already moderately long adventure, so, overall, it's a very good game worthy of your time.Despite this, the game never achieves true greatness, as most of its aspects have issues which stop the game from reaching the full potential it could have had. They are not that negative, but their impact is still important.The story of the game is a bit simple, but it mostly serves as a a base for the interactions between the characters: this is a fine approach, because if the characters dialogues are well written, it can still result in a deep and meaningful story. This is where the game partially fails: while it never completely fails, the game could have been written better. Some characters are written a lot better than others and some fails in critical moments: for example, the protagonist has a cool moment when the story's stakes suddenly turn for the worse, but it is resolved way too quickly; it's an important turning point for the protagonist, but it fails to feel as impactful as it could have been.There are also some strange scenes that feel either too basic or to different respect the rest of the game, but there also a scene with a sudden conclusion, like it was missing a part, and even one with a continuity error. All of this makes the script feel amateurish in some sections, which, coupled with the fact that the rest is solid, indicates that just more effort could have solved the issues.The gameplay also presents some issues, in part with the basic mechanics and in part with some enemies and moves design. The time based execution of attack and defense is mostly nice, but it can soon start to feel too demanding: the effects between the three levels of execution (oops, nice, great) feel too apart from each other, especially between 'nice' and 'great'; a single attack can be the key to success or a fatal error just by how it is executed. To add to that, stats changes like an increase in attack often fail to be impactful, which make using not-healing item useless.These flaws are more evident in the long boss battles, which can start to exhaust the player and increase the risk of failing attacks, but these battles also point out some design issues. Too many bosses in the later parts of the game starts to summon lesser enemies constantly: not only it's annoying, but it also makes the battles way too long and unforgiving. At the same time, the enemies moves are usually just better than the characters moves: most of the characters move have a limited executable distance and some of them are just not worth using respect others. Overall, it's not too bad and the game is actually a bit too easy, but it all concurs to make the spikes in difficulty way worse.Finally, the game has some very nice accessibility features which are very welcome, like the option to remove the possibility of failing moves or even removing completely the need for timing: it doesn't fixes the problems with it, but it's a nice option for when battling starts getting tiring. There is also an option to enable auto wins, but I wished it was less automatic and its success depended from the player level. Despite all this accessibility options, there a baffling absence of maybe the most important option, controls customization: if playing on keyboard, you are forced to use arrow keys, which, in some layouts (especially in laptops), they are cramped in very little space; I know that it's not always easy to put the option in games, but it's maybe the only strongly objective flaw in the game.In conclusion, Ikenfell it's a game that failed to achieve its best possible form, but that still resulted in a good game: it's a bit of a shame, but if the developers decide to improve it, its issues could be easily ironed out. I hope it happens so, as game like it, especially by being LGBTQ+, deserve more recognition.

_childDocuments_.review: I've gotten into this game and am impressed with the story thus far. It really feels like some of the negative reviews come from right wing dudes. This game is a game that features LGBTQ+ inclusivity as a part of the world they live in. Nobody is suffering because they're queer. It's a delightful change of pace. Characters are instead grappling with their own problems and I'm occasionally surprised at amount of characterization they have snuck into the story-line.The combat is easy to grasp but difficult to master. It's based on a tactical grid system and uses a single button timing mechanic to tweak damage. Sometimes these timings are simple to master. Others can be frustratingly difficult. The overall difficulty is mostly low. Cautious players have easy access to HP replenishing cats that save your game. This isn't a hardcore action RPG- Ikenfell lets you decide how hard you'd like the game to be.Which brings me to accessibility settings. There are options that make combat easier for people with disorders that effect timing or plain don't feel up to the challenge. There is a setting that lowers the amount of flashes in the game to prevent triggering epileptic seizures. There are options to add psychological trigger warnings. I had put them on out of curiosity. While an interesting feature it only adds a warning. There is no option to skip or summarize triggering content. You may however skip combat entirely by using an auto-win setting. I imagine that is mostly for people with severe dexterity issues and not for the chucklenut MAGA ♥♥♥♥♥♥ who are mad because they don't feel represented by this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed the game for the most of the playthrough *but* I can't really recommend the game.The story in general was quite enjoyable yet shallow. For the most part we're getting fetch-quests-like story and real plot point pretty much appears right before it resolves at the end of the game. The character themselves were really shallow too, each being generally one unchanging archetype. I'm not given any reason to like/dislike the characters as the story would want it. Couldn't really fell the immersion.The visuals are pleasant enough. Not top-notch pixel art but well readable and intuitive.The music was alright although some of it felt really repetitive over the course of long fights (which I'll talk more about later). The tracks with vocals I feel like shouldn't be in fight where you have to concentrate on hitting narrow windows of input (Even if I liked Gilda's theme). Some option to disable the vocals or just putting them into cutscenes would be nice.Also the Ima's theme (apart from issues mentioned before) breaking the 4th wall makes immersion even harder to achieve. By the time I got to the credits I got pretty fed up with these.The entire game flow is pretty railroaded with minor secrets sprinkled here and there (). The secrets mostly had some slight visual indicator that there is such but unfortunately there were some that require you either to tap everything or just randomly stumble into it (here I mostly mean  as you can at one point acknowledge that the location exists thanks to one NPC and then be prompted to ask other NPC about it and after long questline you get response that you won't find it anyways which felt like slap in the face). The puzzles are pretty easy but some still require some thought which is nice.The fighting system in this game is great... conceptually. The execution is subpar, feels like wasted potential.I really like in turn-based games to have time the inputs to enchance my attacks and effects (and reduce negative ones as well) like in e.g. Paper Mario but the game just feels unfair at the end stages of the game. Even with great timings some enemies can just bomb you for significant part of your hp. It doesn't feel rewarding to hit those timings - it feels like necessity. There's thankfully accessibility option to force all timings to be "Nice" or "Great" automatically (which I didn't use but I appreciate the option). The other thing that annoyed me is wanting to restart the battle if I fail those early... but there's no such option, you have to lost completely fight to be able to retry it (same with accessing options which I find weird).Generally we're flooded with equipment but later in the game you can't feel these items actually doing anything. At some points you're feeling like enemies are just tankier and tankier and you deal less and less damage. There is shop with items having special effects but they take up the trinket slot and does not give actual stats. Also I felt most of these items were pretty bad.Characters that join our party gather exp and level up. It grants them some stats and sometimes new abilities. Unfortunately I felt that most of them had too situational uses or just doing too little to be viable. We cannot really enchance them in other way than pumping stats. Even after killing every enemy on the way I felt like my party is just a bit weak.We have some quite varied enemies which is nice. Most attacks are quite intuitive to know when to do timed input. Again, in early- and mid-game it is not really noticable but at some point in the game the fights just drag out for long time. The common enemies are sometimes annoyance but not some greater problem. Common strat is to do just one fight at the time, go back to saving point that heals you and continue but if you catch the flow and position wisely your party it's not that bad.Bosses are the real pain. Boss having 200 hp, swarming you with summons (which are for some reason way faster than you and having multiple turns), moving you across entire battlefield while you hit them for 10, 15 with most abilities, maybe sometimes 20-something with good items and setup (I found some ways that could reach even 100 but it was too unreliable to actually play with it) unless you dump resources and precious turns to buff to lessen your struggle... but then you find out you have tons of powerful summons to deal with or boss have 2nd phase when you're out of stuff. Especially at the endgame I commonly spent most of money I've earned through entire run for few expensive consumables that either made it easy-win or (more commonly) didn't made that much of a difference.The game is quite okay for the most of the playthrough but there are clearly some balance issues especially for later stages of the game and lacking meaningful options of character progression.

_childDocuments_.review: These wizards are gay!Let me start off by saying that I loved the representation in this game. _childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent rpg that is both challenging and well-designed. Normally I don't enjoy games with teenage protagonists but this one was so well written that it won me over. These students aren't grizzled veterans, once in a lifetime prodigies or idiot savants that bulldoze through the plot while acting cute. Instead like so many teenagers they are expected to be adults and make life-altering decisions and be forced to grow up before their time.There are a lot of choices on party composition and equipment, and you'll have a lot of fun switching people around as they get new abilities so you'll find the group that suits you best. Every character has their own personality and is really unique on screen.The combat element is nothing short of brilliant. Simple and incredibly intuitive, yet with so many character options with a variety of enemies and enemy effects so it never grows dull or slows down. You are always doing something new.One thing that is very important to me is to have as much fun as possible without grinding or redoing levels. (I like it when a game respects my time) In this game, the difficulty can be customized or you can even have an instant-win button added if you just want to enjoy the story.My reflexes are not great so at first I was worried about the timing element, however after playing a half hour I had a lot of fun with it and hit it nearly every time. (I realized after beating the game you could customize the timing sensitivity or even eliminate it)This game is a well made rpg and well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm rarely the "critics don't know what they're talking about" type but I legit do not understand why the scores for this in the gaming press are so low.This game is a pure delight.Ikenfell is about Maritte, a non-witch who journeys to the witch school Ikenfell to find out why her sister has not come home for the break. And then she gets fire powers. From there, you go on an adventure through the school and finding out what's wrong and trying to solve it with newfound friends. It's Harry Potter meets Paper Mario meets adorable.But before the story, let's talk about combat. Combat takes place on a 3 x 12 grid, your characters on the right, enemies on the left. Based on speed, you take turns moving to spaces on the grid and taking actions. What's neat is that each character gains up to 8 actions and there is no mana; it's all based on positioning and situational stuff. For example, one spell can hit anything three spaces on either side of a character but not the middle. Or that one spell is specifically only ever 3 spaces in front of you. The more limiting the spell, generally, the stronger the attack. Which makes field position SUPER important. Once you choose an attack, you need to figure out the timing to press the button for a better attack. Each attack has different timing as well as defending against enemy attacks. You still do or take damage if you miss, but it's better if you hit the timing. A lot of combat is going to be finding where to sit your character and what is the best spell to use in any given situation. As such, fights in this game are probably longer than most mob fights people playing RPGs may be used to.  On the flip side of that, each area has maybe one or two fights per screen so it's more quality than quantity. You never need to grind in this game, but the option is there if you really want to. Equipment and exp scales pretty well in each area so you never feel underpowered. Fight every enemy once in a dungeon and you'll be fine. Character have equipment that can control your normal stats; Hp, Atk, Def, Speed, Movement. There’s a large amount of equipment that lets you focus characters however you want.The boss fights in this game are pretty great. Most of them try to shake things up, go through phases and really make you use strategy to beat them. Towards the end I will say some of the bosses get a bit...samey and lose some of the uniqueness of the earlier ones. A bit disappointing but not game ruining.The music is really fun. There are also some songs with lyrics; when the singing came in during a fight it surprised the heck out of me. On that note, both of the lyric songs SLAP. So every time one particular character shows up to fight get ready to booty rock.The art is very very nice. The pixelated world and characters are surprisingly expressive for the limited amount of pixels that make them up and the environments are incredibly varied and wonderful looking. I will say that the character portraits that show up when characters talk are super expressive are generally really cute for the characters. I think a couple of them look a  I dunno, but the face just looked like hair on top of a squash. Most are fine.So characters and story. You will either love this or run to your favorite 4chan board to make attack helicopter jokes. All the characters are diverse and there is a LOT of fantastic representation all across the LGBTQ spectrum. Many non-binary characters, people of all attractions, etc. It's quite nice. I would also say the characters GENERALLY have fantastic characterization and personalities. They are complicated people who have very complicated relationships with each other and problems they need to overcome. I quite liked almost all the cast and side characters. It was fun seeing them interact or go through their issues. My only real problem was that some characters get the full lion's share of focus while some others...kinda get forgotten about. I specifically am talking about my favorite character who until she joins your party is developed amazingly, real issues and emotional build-up. And then when she joins your party...they never deal with those issues? She just becomes like...a dumb character who occasionally says something but never talks about her problems ever again. Heck, in a cutscene where everyone comes to some heavy realizations they showed separate cutscenes of everyone finding what they want to fight for...except for her! I was stunned they literally didn't even give her a scene. Just waiting for the others then when everyone gets together she gives a "YEAH! LET'S BEAT EM UP" and goes back to never being important again. Super disappointed. Enough ranting.The story is quite good, nothing astonishingly unique but executed very well. What makes it super solid and more nuanced than a straight "defeat the bad" story is the way it handles "good" and "bad" and how people trying to do good things...aren't necessarily doing them for the right reasons and might not be such good people. I won't go into that more, but suffice to say I was worried it would pull a very common narrative trick to make everything hunky-dory so the characters were very flat morally but it 100% didn't go that route. I was VERY happy about that.So is this game worth it? 110%. I enjoyed my time with this game an enormous amount. It's not going to be the new Paper Mario for anyone but it is the only Ikenfell and I think it succeeds at what it does exceptionally well. It's worth full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: Quite possibly the gayest game I've ever seen.The gameplay is incredibly innovative. I've never seen a game take the chessboard style of tactical RPGs like fire emblem and disgaea and scale them way down for the sake of a pseudo-random encounter based environment like classic RPGs, but it works very well. Each playable character brings their own unique flavour to the game, and paper mario style timing plays a huge part in effectively using or defending against attacks. Truly a unique, tactical, and most importantly fun experience.The soundtrack is great, a nice blend of retro chiptune sounds and realistic instruments, with some vocals thrown into the mix for a few songs.The graphics and visuals are a very cute and retro pixel style, with slightly more realistic sprites used in battle.The characters and storyline are very cute. The message is positive and the setting is interesting. The storyline isn't groundbreaking and definitely seems to drag on towards the end, but still absolutely something worth experiencing. Each of the characters have their own personal hangups and traumas that get worked through throughout the course of the game. It is truly incredibly wholesome content.There is an insane amount of LGBTQIA+ representation, which is definitely nice to see for once. There are lots of accessibility options, including the ability to show content warnings where relevant, a "photosensitivity" mode which reduces flashes/strobing effects, the ability to turn on "auto timing" so you don't have to get the timing right, and even an "auto win" function for if you don't care about the gameplay and just want to experience the setting, story, and dialogue.The one negative point is that the game really does drag on towards the end. The story as a whole feels like it's at a standstill for quite a while as your characters go through dungeon after dungeon to find what it is they need to access the endgame dungeon. The game seems to expect you to grind and/or farm gold towards the end, which doesn't exactly make for compelling gameplay. It is possible to push through the endgame without farming or grinding, but it is definitely a painful experience, especially the last boss. The late game simply feels like a chore until you actually get into the endgame dungeon, and had the pacing been a little better at the end, it would significantly improve my perception of the game.Overall, though, definitely a positive experience and would absolutely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically this game is a joy to play with timed attacks and blocks that are well tuned so the sweet spots feel "right" and predictable. The combat is challenging and engaging, with a decent spectrum of varied enemies and unique bosses.Beyond mechanics though this game really shines with its characters and story. Before the half way mark I was already deeply invested in each of the party members and several of the supporting characters. Their individual struggles, relationships and roles in the bigger story are all slowly built upon throughout the game, and I found myself still humming along with several of their theme songs well after the game was off.There are more feels to be had here than all the games I've played in the last few years combined, and it is definitely worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played! The story is satisfying, the game play is engaging, the characters are interesting, and the music is stellar. It's like if you combined the mechanics of Paper Mario and the feel/puzzles from Undertale. Still, it stands on its own as a game. GameplayTurn-based quicktime combat and defense. I played through it in a little over twenty hours, at about a medium pace (not rushing but also not perfecting it.) The leveling feels nice: it starts to get easier as you level up and then it spikes in difficulty at certain checkpoints. If you want a challenge, I recommend not using items and just over-leveling instead (which is what I might do on a second go around.) The ability sets of the characters makes it difficult to choose how to build your party; they're all super satisfying. This also lends itself to more replayability as you can set up new combinations of party members over multiple runs. StoryI'll keep most of the details to myself. But I promise it's charming. Depending on your experience, you might find it heartfelt, surprising or maybe even a little simple. I don't want to set any expectations on it other than it is enjoyable from whatever perspective you look at it.Cannot recommend it enough. Please treat yourself to this experience, it is so worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly the kind of charming retro RPG I wish we saw more of.* Great retro aesthetic that's handled well* Great soundtrack (which is how I found out about the game, same composers as Steven Universe)* Inclusive story that's fun and written well, strong characterization, and doesn't rely on the "villain evil for no reason" trope so many games use as a crutch. And the game has the kind of authentic charm that I often find lacking in newer high budget games* Combat is fun without getting too repetitive, and while I wasn't a fan of the timing mechanic at first, it really grew on me* Enough hidden secrets to make it fun to explore and hunt around* I'm glad they have the accessibility options. I didn't use them much myself, but I like that they were there, and I knew if I ever got tired of the combat I could still finish the storyI bought this on Steam originally, but wound up playing most of the game on my Switch instead because it's a delight to play in portable mode.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but alas, I just could not get myself to finish this as the combat was tedious and boring.  The art, music, and sounds were fine.  The tactical, grid based combat seemed appealing but unfortunately the execution just didn't hold up to the expectations as the timing aspect for abilities and defenses, while fun at the start, quickly became repetitive and a source of frustration.  I almost gave up there, but figured I'd give a bit more as I wanted to complete it, so I ventured into the settings and toggled the combat setting to effectively eliminate the timing mechanic (automatically get "great" all the time).  Unfortunately, it then felt slightly like cheating (as I figured combat was probably balanced around getting around 50/50 "nice" / "great" timings, so "great" all the time would just be easy mode.  Also, combat still was slow as the animations still played out even though there was no need for them to.  Granted, there is a third option of guaranteed "nice," with the option to get the timing right for a "great," but that still leaves the issue of combat rounds taking quite a long time to resolve--which would be fine if it was complex, but when it basically is the same strategy all the time, the slowness becomes super frustrating.  There is also an option to "auto-win," but then are you even playing, or is it just an inferior visual novel?

_childDocuments_.review: The game's mechanics are alright in theory but in practice are wonky. The timing requirements are unclear for most attacks, lacking the polish and clarity of games like Paper Mario and Mario & Luigi which inspired it. The dungeons also get really frustrating at points which made me want to stop playing (and eventually I did stop)As for the story, the world is pretty boring and generic, and while the initial mystery is intriguing, it drags on for too long for me to care. The characters are all shallow and/or incredibly annoying.You'd have more fun playing the RPGs that inspired it like the Mario & Luigi series or Chrono Trigger rather than Ikenfell.

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is exactly that, a pixel-art game that is brilliantly made... I think, in my opinion, it was just made with love for old Party-based RPG games such as Mario RPG, and Final Fantasy. Now, I might've spoiled the game's score already but who cares; here is why Ikenfell gets a solid 10/10 score later on.Storyline is up first and here you control Maritte, a young, light-hearted lass who, after her sister disappears, heads for the Magic School of Ikenfell to look for her. Safina, Maritte's sister, has joined Ikenfell as a teen and has lived there with her magic pals for over a decade when she suddenly disappeared. Maritte, now in Ikenfell territory, suddenly realizes she can cast Fire spells, a long forgotten sphere of Magic that everyone thought was extinct. She meets a very likeable cast of characters that help her find her sister, like the goofy alchemist Petronella, the bookworm Rook and the sassy rival, Petrisia. All of them young Magic students who've got quite the spells up their... wands! On the other side of this amazingly written story lies the combat mechanics that just use great pixel visuals to convey a sense of Power and spectacular magics. Each character has got a kit of combat skills they can use and there is a specific timing in which you can make that skill stronger; I don't really know how to explain but if you've played Mario RPG in the SNES early on, you'd know precisely what to do, and how to do it. An example of that would be Petronella's Poison Bubble skill, the bubble inflates and right before it comes to contact with your target, press the action button for a "bubble boost", you get the GREAT notification and deal probably triple the bubble's damage... You can use this mechanic when you're defending against enemy attacks as well. The bossfights are plenty and Ikenfell seems to conjure all sorts of creatures against you, from literal kittens, to blobs of flesh that all want to break a piece of Maritte's behind lol. The characters are amazingly written, with, I've noticed, heavy focus on LGBTQ+ stuff... I mean, I don't really mind, but some characters seem to actually force the LGBTQ narrative a bit... But it all fades away once the combat starts. I wish I had done a playthrough of the game, but I enjoyed this  party RPG so much that I lost track of time lol.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: It's a charming little indie RPG with a stellar soundtrack. A small gripe I have is that the LGBTQIA+ representation begins to feel forced very quickly, as it seems like EVERYONE fits into the queer category. Not a huge complaint though, definitely not a big deal. The characters are all so enjoyable to witness. The story so far for me has been interesting, it's rare that games grip me like this anymore! The battle system is pretty nostalgic, as are the graphics. Overall, for me, it's a very solid game, and I love that they got the people who made music for Steven Universe on board. Really fun and brings me back to simpler days.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: An intrigue-laden Indie RPG set in a School of Magic that has even fewer safety-regulations than Hogswarts, somehow. Pixel-graphics, but beautifully animated - and the music is a real treat, with full-on image-songs for many of the bosses. The characters are interesting and nuanced, and the plot is a real work of art - keeps you guessing all the way, trying to figure out just what the heck is going on at Ikenfell.It is not without its flaws, mind. Its approach to elemental attacks takes some getting used to, in the sense that there IS none - right from the start of the game, you'll find yourself fighting fire-elementals by throwing fireballs at them, and that's basically how it keeps on. No need to worry about whether that poisonous blob-monster is susceptible to poison, either - it is, because EVERYTHING is, including things that lack any kind of biological parts to poison. Creates a constant sense of dissonance for anyone who've spent thousands of hours in various RPG's where knowing elemental and status-ailment weaknesses is a core skill.The cast is also kind of... very deliberately diverse. Nothing wrong with being diverse, but it gets a bit grinding when it's this in-your-face about it. A touch of subtlety here and there wouldn't have gone amiss. Though, I couldn't help but have a laugh at how the sole MALE member of your gang of magic-students is also black, making him your classic Twofer Token Minority - the more things change, the more they stay the same, I suppose! Still, in the end, I can't dock too many points for any of that. Maybe games, as a medium, needs to go through a 'very obviously and deliberately diverse' phase in order to reach the point where they no longer need to loudly and repeatedly explain how a minor character has a non-binary gender-identity, but can instead just use the appropriate pronouns and trust the audience not to assume that it's a typo.Either way, it's a thumbs-up overall. I haven't finished it yet, but I very much look forwards to finding out what really lies at the roots of Ikenfell's mysteries...

_childDocuments_.review: I do not like not finishing games......but this just could not maintain my interest due to tedious battle system and threadbare story/plot given in tiny little snippets interspersed through said gameplay.It had some charm and good ideas, but it's barebones in many aspects and just never became fun?I do appreciate the cats though.

_childDocuments_.review: I sincerely wish I could recommend this game but I find it difficult to do so. There are so many things this game does well, especially in terms of representation and many of the relationships between people, but there are so many other things wrong with it.For the first 1/3 of the game it is pretty good, engaging, and while the combat is not for me it has very good accessibility options allowing you to choose how the game works for you. However, after that point the quality starts dropping a lot.The puzzles start to become kind of bad. They become either frustrating with mechanics that don't seem to fit such as stealth sections and sliding-ice puzzles (which works really poorly for a game that isn't tile-based), or they become non-puzzles that just make you walk around and back-and-forth a lot either pushing buttons or blocks. But what really got to me was the writing. It started to become a complete idiot plot. I want to say the majority of conflict comes from either miscommunication or someone not taking 2 seconds to listen to what someone says. Probably one of the most overused and uninteresting of cliche's for creating conflict. There's lots of characters that stand in your way and then go "oh wait you're a good guy my bad". After a while it became difficult to care for many of the characters because of this. Some remain good throughout but not enough sadly. I'd say the ending is very good, but unfortunately the rest of the problems with the story made most of it unsatisfying to me. I do hope these guys make another game and improve on what they have done here, but I struggle to suggest playing this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Battle system was going places but REALLY drops off near the end. Game was really cute with some somewhat interesting personalities -- although I think the game was trying so hard to have a good amount of representation that it overshot the mark and it becomes quite uncomfortable that nearly every pairing is same sex or adjacent. (No hate for the idea, but...wow...that is far from the experience and struggle. It feels fake and forced to me.)Fun little game, but would not recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming RPG with a well thought story and an endearing cast of characters.Ikenfell certainly took me by surprise when I initially opened the game as, tactical turn based combat is not certainly my strong suit, nor is it a combat style that I like too much. Although as the game progressed, both with level scaling and story progression, I found that the game grew on me the more that I played. The story is well written, only getting better as it progresses in terms of the overall narrative. The mystery surrounding the story works constantly to pull the player further and further into the world, as both the player and cast work their way through a breadcrumb trail left by those they are searching for. The cast of characters all mix and compliment each other, both in personality and archetype (more combat-wise). Although I did find that the dialogue was weak and "cookie-cutter" at certain points in the narrative, overall, dialogue between the cast was alright for the duration of the game.Speaking of, my play-through of the game ran about 20 hours for me to complete both the story and all the side content/achievements. This game is not too expansive in the game play, as there are only a few extra bosses and side rooms, although the bosses do quite a bit to both intrigue and add to the combat and challenge of the game. Despite this, there is hardly any replay value in the game, there is some only if you miss the collectible gems and side content although, it is fair to say there is none at all since you can save before the finale and backtrack to complete whatever you miss.In the terms of combat, the game does well to keep the player on their toes both with the timing mechanics for attacks and defenses, and with the variety that the enemies give the player since every character is unique and only a few share similar looking attacks. Bosses, for what i remember, all have unique attacks and unique animations so the timings never get too repetitive through the game. Enemies are also scaled (near) properly to where grinding for levels isn't necessary to get through hurdles that the game sets, though, i would say that these hurdles are more skillful due to the timing mechanics (which is optional in the settings). It is nice that the devs added a "victory" button that is turned off by default. Though redundant to me, i can understand this additions for those that will have difficulty with the game or those that just want to experience the story.As for the soundtrack, the music in this game is especially wonderful. Both for over-world and for the battles. The tracks that ikenfell brings to the table are wonderfully composed and convey the stories emotion exponentially well as more of the game is uncovered. Some of these tracks such as Gilda's theme, are written with lyrics in mind. These tracks are well written and do well to convey character and emotion with the context given by the game at the time.In all, this is a really well crafted game that had tons of love and work poured into it. I certainly loved the narrative and cast through its duration, although as stated, this is a one time experience for most. I could definitely see myself playing this again in 5 or so years, although my gaming backlog is far too grand for another play through.
_childDocuments_.name: Ikenfell

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough. The storytelling is compelling, the music is enthralling, the art is stunning, and the character development is so, so realistic. Conversely to many, I enjoyed the battle mechanics; I loved mixing & matching characters, and optimizing field movement. Moreover, I felt the timing mechanism was intuitive (for me) but even if it's harder to understand timing, the game is forgiving if you save often. And who wouldn't save often, when to do so you must pet a cat (which heals you entirely)?!? Even if grinding out battles doesn't help you with the timing, and you hate the battles, you can just turn on "auto victory" and tap out when the going gets tough. Another reason to promote is for the puzzles. Golden Sun is one of my all-time favorite games and I have been searching for a long time for a game that emulates those out-of-battle puzzle mechanics; Ikenfell comes close, with the hidden rooms/pathways and logic puzzles (though sadly not as focused on interacting with the environment as G.S.).Lastly, if you are an LGBTQIA+ person (or ally) I would highly recommend supporting this game: the characters are well-written, spanning the spectrum, and the banter is charming. We need more games like this!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, great music. Took me about 20 hours to beat. There are several hidden secrets and optional bosses. There's never a point-of-no-return, so you can always go back and find anything that you may have missed.I really enjoyed the combat. It's turn-based on a grid layout, and all attacks and blocks are timed. The timing for each depends on the particular attack, which varies character to character and enemy to enemy. I was personally a huge fan of it, but if it isn't your cup of tea, you can either semi-automate it or fully automate it so you don't have to struggle with the timing. The developers have your back. They also have the option of turning off flashing lights for anyone who is photosensitive.They really decided to go all in with the queer characters. None of the main (playable) characters are cis-het, which is in fact true of some of my own friend groups. They have fun personalities, and my only complaint there is that it would've been nice to explore the characters a bit more because I thought they were all quite compelling characters.There are a couple plot points that felt like they could've used more buildup or foreshadowing. I felt some of the reveals came out of nowhere, and there were a couple shifts that left me confused for a bit before I caught what was going on. In general, though, I liked the plot and thought it was pretty interesting. I'd be interested in seeing another game in this series that went into more of the lore.Overall, this was a really enjoyable game that I would definitely recommend.9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is an RPG that takes place at a magic school. Some might make the comparison to Harry Potter. If you enjoy that kind of setting, you will likely enjoy this game. If you don't enjoy that setting, you might still enjoy this game. With an engaging battle system, interesting and varied character abilities, great music (have you ever heard the music from Steven Universe?), and overall a good story, how could I not recommend this game?Pros:Story - It's fun and unique, with pretty good world building. Good mix of serious, emotional, and funnyGameplay - Tactical combat done well, with timing mechanicsMusic - It's great, and fits the game/styleArt - Good pixel artCons:Battles - Regular battles can get repetitive (bosses rock though!)Difficulty - Can be difficult without using some of the adjustments from the options menu.Dialogue - Felt like some of the dialogue was forced. This didn't take too much away from the overall story though, and was still character development.I really loved this game. You might like it too.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm about to finish 100% and it hurts me a lot to write a negative review on this. Don't get me wrong, this is not a bad RPG, Gwenora side quests are amazing and the simplified stats are really welcome especially for those that are new to the gender, the music is just marvelous and the pixel art is pretty cute. What hurts me the most is that it could have been a masterpiece if it wasn't for the sluggish battle system and a bland and juvenile storytelling.We surely have a lack of QA testing here. The timing hits system is the perfect example of a good idea with a poor execution In theory, it would make the combat  more dynamic and enjoyable, in practice it's just frustrating. In the majority of the cases the game fails to telegraph the player the good timing to hit the button and it doesn't give feedback when we miss it! If it wasn't for the auto mode I'm pretty sure I wouldn't even think to finish the game. Talking about it, the accessibility options feels to me like a big band-aid in a poor game design. It is surely a personal though, and i know some people liked it, but put a victory mode in a game is to assume the battle system isn't fun enough to keep the player interested. This is the part that disappointed me the most. The game has an amazing lore, the gods are wise and mysterious the school is full of secrets and hidden paths, everything is so it's so rich and immersive it could have been the stage for something epic! Unfortunately, it's not the case.I had a really good surprise when I realized everyone in the game is in the LGBTQIA+ spectrum, I found myself amazed and looking forward for an original narrative that naturally presents the characters personality and eventually their sexuality, even because in a place where no one is straight it would be impossible for someone to introduce themselves and then say "i'm so gay" right? Well... not really, the creators were bold enough to create a LGBTQIA+ cast, but it fails badly to trust the player's deduction capacity.  Even late in the story the narrative keeps insisting on the fact that they are not straight, even when it does not contribute to the plot. The problem here is not that i don't want to know about it, the problem is that at this point we all already realized it!  So all the magic the game has built in the first hour of gameplay starts to fade in the repetitive attempt to reaffirm itself as an inclusive work. As a consequence, we have a bunch of stereotyped characters that has little to non importance to the plot. A person is much more than its sexuality, the same goes for a character!Ironically, the most well developed characters are the most secondary ones, Ibn and Bax form a such amazing couple, each time they appear a new nuance is added their relationship. It's a shame a similar dynamic is not present in the main cast.  The rest is a shallow "your princess is in another castle" narrative. With some good moments, but nothing extraordinary.The game could be a masterpiece such as undertale or FFVI but Unfortunately a bad game design and a bold but shallow narrative killed the game's potential in a way i would only recommend this game for die hard fans of the gender.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this last night, and it might have already become one of my favorite games.It's so queer and kind without shying away from difficult interpersonal realities in the sake of pursuing a 'wholesome' vibe. It's fun and funny even as it delves into pain and trauma, and character situations and conflicts are treated compassionately. The playable characters (and most significant named NPCs) are all queer — a big group of nonbinary folks and queer women all dealing with mental health and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥-up states that trauma puts us into.The combat system has a tremendous amount of depth, and it felt perfectly tuned (for me) to always leave room for interesting and reactive combat situations — even in late-game random battles, where my strategy had coalesced around a particular party setup and base strategy, there were rarely situations where any given battle felt trivial or boring. If I had any complaint at all, I'd say that the input timing on some attack animations felt inconsistent across different moves; keeping track of which moves required early or late timing relative to what I interpreted from the animation led to some moments of "Oh, come on!" tension. Aside from that, though, it's easily one of my favorite RPG combat systems.All told, it's just a really beautiful, really gay game that made me happy. It was a joy to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: tl,dr: 9/10 would've paid full price for this game when it came out on Gameboy Color. Magic rules, yo. Pros: # Animations. Let me preface this point by saying I hate pixelated graphics. I have zero love for this "retro" trend happening in the game industry. Making a game that plays comfortably on current-gen hardware does not mean needing to make that game look like it was made two decades ago. (Rant done.)  Ikenfell is exceptional. The animations in the game trailer blew me away. I have never seen so much detailed motion achieved with such simplistic graphics. The animations, of both characters and spells, raise this game well above the pixel mire. The game feels alive.# Magic. (I'm a sucker for magic in games. There aren't enough good games that focus on magic, imo.)  Party members' weapons serve merely to raise their Power stat; they never factor directly into combat. All combat actions are spells. Yes, the early spell mechanics are simplistic enough that one could argue their virtue is merely aesthetic. However, as the game progresses and characters unlock more complex spells, and as the party encounters enemies who deal in status effects as well as direct damage, the mechanics become moot and the action elements of gameplay can only be described as magical in nature, not physical. I very much approve. Ikenfell is a genuine magic game. Oh, and I haven't even mentioned the setting/lore...# Magic resource management. There is no mana in Ikenfell and very few cooldowns. The main factors that govern your party's effectiveness in combat are the turn order (sequencing of spells), field positioning, and spell hit patterns. Oh, and party composition once you have more than 3 people in your traveling party, since every character brings different skill sets to the combat table. All combat in this game (so far as I've seen) takes place on instanced battlefields that measure 3x12 squares. Learning to work within that narrow domain is the key to many victories.# American English is obviously the writer dev's first language, complete with the neglect of the adverb "of" and the recurring failure to use "whom" when appropriate. It is a nice change of pace for me to be able to read a text-based game quite casually rather than straining to interpret poor translations as so often plague Visual Novels.# Characters are handled very well; most of them are given a balanced portion of the player's attention. Most characters are, at best, two-dimensional. Nevertheless, it is easy to become invested in learning more about their personal story arcs as the game progresses.# Music is non-irritating enough that I can tolerate it being on while I am livestreaming. That is very high praise coming from someone who almost always plays games with music turned off.# Though combat is primarily visual, I have found myself relying on some spells' sounds to gauge timing. (Some might consider this a Con, not a Pro.) I appreciate the duality of cues.# There is an Auto timing Option so that you always get Great on your spell timings. I have yet to activate it since spell timing is one of the few ways I as the player can participate in the fight, but it's wonderful knowing that Option exists.# All party members receive equal xp, not just the 3 who participated in combat.# Available vendor gear scales with you as you level. While most gear items can be found during your adventures, not all can, so it's worth keeping tabs on vendor stock. Redundant items can be sold to vendors at about 1/3 value so it's not a huge loss to buy your way into early preparedness.# Ikenfell is a massive oldschool nostalgia trip. Loads of beloved gimmicks and surprise elements are in there; anticipated enemy quirks usually turn out to be true; etc. Many laughs were had.Cons: # Let's get this out of the way: the keybindings suck. I could tolerate them for no more than half an hour, then I dusted 20 months (not a lie) of dust off from my Windows Xbox controller and have been using that exclusively since. Ikenfell is an oldschool, cutsie, casual, turn-based, story-driven game. Why then are the default keybindings on opposite sides of the keyboard so that a player must be sitting upright with both hands ready on the keyboard at all times so as to be efficient with their time during play?!  I wouldn't complain if there were a way to customize the keybindings but there isn't, hence this first and most important Con.# Furthermore, there is no button to go back in dialogue. Every word of dialogue is shown only once. If you accidentally click the button to advance the dialogue too soon, then any words you failed to read will be lost forever. As I have gone further into the game, I have started becoming more anxious during dialogue than during combat. This is just wrong.# The best way to see which party member would best benefit from equipping a gear item is while interacting with a vendor. When highlighting an item in a vendor's Buy/Sell screens, you can see icons over every party member  which indicate whether that item would improve or worsen said party members' stats. Why are these same simultaneous icons not available when the party is traveling and using the Equipment screen?  The Equipment screen is so gawd-awful BAD and slow for comparing and swapping gear.# The Turn Order bar was exceedingly unintuitive to me. I had to rewatch my own gameplay stream and study it in multiple fights just to decipher how it works. The arrow drawn from left to right was what threw me off. I thought the arrow meant turn order would advance from left to right. It doesn't. The arrow means turn order slides, Tetris style,  the right-most position; in other words, turn order actually proceeds from right to left. I feel this should be portrayed less ambiguously to players. Maybe omitting the arrow entirely is the key?# Some sound effects are not well balanced for volume."Meh": # The presentation of some mild LGBT elements has caught me off guard more than once with its overtness, quite abruptly shoving me out of any state of blissful immersion. On the plus side, I guess it's a nice thing that a developer can feel comfortable enough to include such elements in their creative work, right? 	(Edit: I am now over 19 hours into this game. What I had formerly assumed was some sporadic inclusion of LGBT content merely for the purpose of idiosyncratic character development has evolved into an undeniable (albeit minor) theme running throughout the game. Though fairly light-handed and tactful, LGBT content has been presented often enough that I am convinced the game is trying to be a platform for some social issues agenda. This makes me feel like, by giving this game any praise whatsoever, I am also giving praise to this industry practice. I am most certainly NOT offering the latter. Folks, I just came here to play a game about magic. Having been coerced into this ulterior agenda has left a very sour taste in my mouth and has significantly reduced my enjoyment of the game overall. Oldschool games were experimental iterations on having fun, pure and simple. I feel that Ikenfell's corruption of this singular purpose is a betrayal to the purity of the genre whose gigantic shoulders this game is standing upon. Moreover, while I support the LGBT reality of humanity, I am equally and ardently  any instance of the deceiptful practice of co-opting paying customers into being captive audience members to a one-sided "discussion" about an issue that is wholly off-topic from the experience the customers bought into. I don't care if it's for the greater good; this deception just shouldn't be done, imo. I fear that, by abusing the gaming medium to serve as a communicative platform, Ikenfell has doomed itself away from any possibility of becoming a "classic" like the venerable icons on which it was based. That's my 2 cents. And it's a shame because Ikenfell is really good.)

_childDocuments_.review: Content Warning: Some may disagree, might be offended.  You may skip this by scrolling passed this review.The story was great, though I feel like the main point was washed over and swept away in the end.  But at least the journey was good. There were 2 or 3 different plot points that ended up being like "Oh, so we could have just not bothered with any of this and been spared certain grief.", because they are literally like "Hey, we need to go do THIS!  ....NEVERMIND!!"  I picked the game up from the Humble Choice of June 2021 and jumped right in with the whole "Pride Month" stuff.  I saw several people curious about how LGBT impacts the game on the discussion board, and I don't feel the responses really do anyone justice.For anyone wondering about the LGBT tag on this game, I'll just say, I refer to this game as the "Everyone's a something game, so long as it isn't a straight person." game. That is to say, there are no straight characters, everyone's gay in some way or another.  It carries no real impact on the game other than the game makes it clear that they're a "something", and that's it.  Some gender pronouns just throw you off, and every time, say, Ima is referenced, reading it makes me feel like my brain is suddenly trying to fit a square into a circle hole.  Other gender pronouns feel inconsistent.The game could probably benefit from 2 things - A mod that cuts certain LGBT references out the dialogue, and an update to the game that includes a LGBT character dictionary that helps explains the different LGBT stuff and which characters in the game the terms are associated with.  I've seen comments praising the game for the inclusivity and representation of LGBT, but honestly I don't see it, unless you're gay/lesbian.  Then that's basically this game in a nutshell.The game includes an option to turn on "Content Warnings", which prompts messages warning about upcoming content that might bother people.  I think these are way overblown and inconsistent, but I also recognize that someone, somewhere, might have had a traumatic experience with a family member that hordes, or have problems with self esteem or self hate.  Or blood and gore, which I thought was friggin metal as hell.  The option is set to off by default, and you need to go find it in the options to turn it on, which kind of defeats the purpose.  They're also inconsistent.  One character is introduced as extremely anxious and feels worthless, which prompts a warning.  But there's many situations where different characters feel that way, and the game doesn't evenly prompt warnings for each of them.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has it all - I'd backed it on Kickstarter under the impression of "oh a cute magic school pixel art JRPG" and had no idea what I was getting myself into. The art is gorgeous, the music OUT OF THIS WORLD, and the gameplay itself is really interesting! The combat is way more thought out than "press A to attack and win" that other RPGs fall in to, there's a tactics bent to it where positioning is everything. The two most standout things though are the writing and the accessibility options. The story is wonderfully crafted and when it goes dark places, the accessibility options offer content warnings for things that could be potentially upsetting, and make no mistake -this game may look cutesy but it can be incredibly mature and have teeth. (Also if the combat's timing system becomes to much or causes physical strain, once again the accessibility options allow you to turn that off). There wasn't a single cisgender heterosexual character that I could see which I find highly important - it's not "shoehorned" in the way some games will add token representation - all of these characters feel real; they have agency, they have traumas, they have desires and it all shows through their blocky pixel characters via writing that is deserving of awards. These characters feel more authentic in LGBTQ representation than anything I've ever seen in media, and it was really, really encouraging. If you're into RPGs at all, I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ikenfell is an RPG about gay witches solving a big mystery. If that hasn't piqued your interest enough, then the game might be a hard sell for you.The main mechanics of the game are fairly simple to grasp, but can be difficult to get down right against certain enemies, which can lead to a little bit of frustration. Thankfully, these mechanics can be made easier to deal with thanks to the game's numerous accessibility settings.Despite the colourful cast of characters, only three of them can be in your main party at a time, which can be a shame because it is very easy to get a party you like and stick with it throughout the game. However, switching between characters can be done at any save point, and inactive characters still gain experience (although at a slightly lower rate)The story is fantastic and well written, although it can touch on uncomfortable subjects in certain parts. Content Warnings are available in the options menu for those that need them.All in all, this game is a great purchase if you have time to spend on a mid-length RPG and are also a fan of the gays. Wholeheartedly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has potential, but it really falls flat. The combat was described to me as old Paper Mario on a tactical grid, which sold me immediately. But the quantity of enemies on top of the quantity or actions required per attack really just ruins a good thing. On the boss I beat before I quit, it summoned 2-4 enemies 4 times. And most of these enemies required multiple characters to dispatch, slowing the fight the already bloated hp of the boss had done prior.The writing can only be described as juvenile, but safe. Like bubble wrap. Something you would see on preschool television. Any potential conflict between the characters is immediately resolved with hugging and forgiveness. There's a lot of social justice type rhetoric that the creators very obviously cared a lot about, but never really tried to address any of it in terms of the storytelling. On one hand, the classroom of student is a perfect rainbow skin and hair colors, no one generic npc looking like another, but on the other, their gay character is very obviously there for gay representation, creeping on the main character in spite of her being uncomfortable while stating thing like "I'm SO gay." It just seems strange that a game where the devs tried so hard to have the perfect blend of diversity, even going so far to have abnormal pronouns with almost 0 overlap but also use gayness as the butt of a joke?There's a good game in here somewhere, but it definitely needed another round of QA testing for balance and time spent in combat encounters.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, it's usually quite common to find  in video games that interface commands are bound to characters rather than keys, which is both impractical and incomprehensible. In this game, they raised keyboard management to the level of some kind of perverted art.wazd? nope. Change the keyboard layout? Nope, you can't. The keys corresponding to the characters wazd? Nope. Confirm with "space", or "enter"? Nope. Rebind something? Nope. Alt-tab? Depends; If you're lucky. It took me minutes before I found out I could use the directional keys. At least, they warn you that "A" (WTF?) is the key for validation. And B the one for cancellation. It could have been a key next to "A" or something, let's make it more random! Turns out it's not actually B, but… U! At least, on my keyboard, it's next to the A… I'm not sure if it's a relief or not. Oh boy.Next, they talk about some "Y" key. You guessed it, It's not "Y", it's "Enter"…Also, you get a nice mouse pointer, don't hope to use it, it would have made the interface so much better than this mess. Half an hour, it should be enough to review bomb that sorry excuse for a game.Clearly, messing that up to such level must have taken some thoughts and efforts, congrats, hope it was worth it. Thankfully, it doesn't look like the kind of games I would enjoy anyway. Usual humble bundle padding, I suppose (darn censorship).

_childDocuments_.review: I'm extremely grateful to the friend who recommended me to play this game and wish I had taken her advice sooner.Ikenfell has a great story, lovable, gay characters and I fell in love with it. The fighting system is fun, the "timing your attacks and defence" a bit reminiscent of Paper Mario, but with added complexity due to the grid-based fight. Accessibility settings are great - I loved having the possibility to move around and see where the attacks would land, and the trigger warnings helped me. I love the timing-based game, so I didn't take the option to have success (base or better) automatically, but I almost took it for one of the three secret bosses.I highly recommend it. It took me 25 hours to finish it with every achievement and every minute was well-spent according to me. I even cried at the end of the game, which I rarely do, due to themes of healing from trauma which highly affected me.

_childDocuments_.review: On balance a good game, with a lot of stuff you don't see in games - both story and gameplay wise. That being said, it doesn't mean that all of the experiments pay off; in particular, the game has a switch in the options to essentially disable the turn based battles. I'm all for accessibility options, but the game has those as well (which make the timing button inputs either easier or go away entirely); the fact that there's an option to disable a major component of gameplay entirely is suggestive of some problems there. Without spoilers, there's a bit of an issue with Deus Ex Machina in the story as well.Those caveats aside, you've got a rather charming story, and a cast of characters who are non-standard in ways you hardly ever see in a video game. For that reason alone, it's something I'd recommend to anyone interested in stories.Also: if you have AMD graphics and Freesync, make sure VSync is off. If it's on, in full screen FPS seems to drop to a number which is comfortably below playable - no idea why that is.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a great RPG. My only real complaint is that I'd like so much more of it. I wish there were more opportunities to engage in this world and with these characters. Well, that and that one of the character's endings is very bittersweet, at least for me. Vague spoilers from here on out. (Note: Don't take this last bit as a reason not to play the game, it's great, go do it, this 18ish hour indie romp got me more emotionally invested in it's world and characters than nearly anything else this year, and honestly I just want to spend more time with them, I'm just a huge softie who over analyses things.b) This is your chance to stop reading. Ok? Ok...? OOOOK???? ok. One character, though I won't say who, winds up leaving their friends and family without a word after all is said and done, for the sake of their mental health. The only problem is it's not made super clear how this will help them. Their family maybe, but their friends? They do wind up meeting up with one particular character again in the end, said person having sought them out, but It's unclear how long they were separated from their friends, or even if they had any intention to return to them on their own. It's... honestly really depressing, at least for me. Sure it seems to end happy, but it leaves the risk of the character running off again a realistic one. I don't know, maybe I'm just reading too much into things. Hopefully everything turns out alright in the end, again, I'm literally just writing this here because this game is criminally niche and I have no where else to put my thoughts.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR REVIEW: Only buy this game if you are a fan of the Mario & Luigi games' combat system and can tolerate a below average story.-This review contains spoilers.-I'm going to give Ikenfell a positive review, but only because I am not given the option of rating it "mixed".Good sign, I know.Story: 4/10Ikenfell's story is, at best, passable. I would give it a 5/10 normally but frankly it bothers me how there are good ideas nestled into it and none of those good ideas are ever properly expanded upon.First thing's first, the game spends the first major portion of the game unraveling a mystery, all fine and dandy. However, once the mystery was revealed and the intrigue disappeared, I wasn't left with much else. Now a good writer would either cut off the story when the mystery's done so to maintain interest or they would have set up further hooks to keep the audience invested. One might assume the characters would serve this role, but we'll get to that soon enough.So once the mystery Ikenfell sets up is unveiled, all I'm left with are a number of half/quarter-baked characters and a string of plot points messily put together in an attempt to finish the story. It's not that these story beats are bad persay, but nothing ever felt properly earned. There were several seemingly random points where characters would suddenly have an emotional breakdown and arcs would be resolved in such a haphazard manner that I wonder what the hell the writers were thinking when penning it.Characters: 4/10But then we get to the characters. There are a grand total of two characters in this game that I have fond feelings towards and that would be Pertisia and Gilda. Gilda because she doesn't take anything seriously post-growth and mostly just sits around and waits for the plot to throw bosses at you so she can fight them. No secret that I had her on my final team. Pertisia on the other hand is a character that I actually do like in some ways regarding her growth. Her secret is well foreshadowed and I think of all the characters, she has the most plausible growth.However, I would be lying if I didn't say she would still be a low B-Tier character in any other game. No one's arcs naturally resolve themselves, rather the plot occurs and suddenly the player is forced to watch as characters just suddenly feel like developing with very little prompting. The biggest example I can think of is Petronella and Rook, who suddenly get in a spat and reconcile after an equally random fit of anger from Pertisia when someone makes a lukewarm statement regarding some artifact. It felt like the Act 2 breakup trope, except the breakup makes even less sense than in those instances.I could go on and on. Aeldra's sad backstory had no weight because I had no reason to care about Aeldra prior to that point except that she was a generic school authoritarian type for a while, the most I could say is "damn bro that sucks" and that would be the height of my emotional investment. Gilda is entertaining but once she gets told "you're useful, actually", she completely sheds and self-confidence issues and spends the rest of the game as an impatient DnD player waiting for the fights to happen. The final boss of the game was like the final boss of Steven Universe Future, except instead of Steven turning into the big scary monster, it was Aquamarine. Expectations subverted, I guess?Gameplay: 9/10Okay let's get out of the ocean because I'm about to make the case for my positive review. This game's combat system is one of the best RPG combat systems I've played on a purely technical level. Sure, I could appreciate more flair to the game's style (we'll get to that later), but the game has a very clean difficulty curve with a variety of party members to choose from with different roles to play.In the end, I played the game with Maritte (because she's the main character and also her damage buffing is insane), Ima (because Ima's a great all-rounder with good damage and healing) and Gilda (because she's an insane glass cannon ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). Ikenfell is on a very small list of games where I was forced to use my items outside of just reviving dead characters. The latter boss battles require significantly more tactical wit and patience than I was initially expecting, and the combat was good enough that I was able to ignore the subpar story and I could easily recommend the game just for being fun to play. I hope the developers are able to write a better story and are able to refine this type of combat for their next game.As for the puzzles, they're alright. Fairly standard, I'd say. The combat's the real highlight here and if you're okay with turn-based RPGs, this combat system's a real treat. Of course, if you don't like turn-based RPGs and the story as I've described it sounds exactly as pleasant as it was for me, then you should stay away.Music: 8/10In a purely statistical sense, 96% of this game's soundtrack is very good. Aivi & Surasshu are best known for their work on Steven Universe, and while I can't say this game differentiates itself much from that show, I'd say they've got their niche. The music's blend of piano, chiptune, synth and orchestral beats are pure ear candy. Highlights include "Face my Fears", "Rose Thorns" and "Memories in the Mist".But uh, what about that 4%?That, my friend, are the three vocal tracks in this game. They're all bad. I'm sorry to the lovely people who sung them but, they're terrible. They all came straight the hell out of nowhere, were jarring to listen to, and the lyrics made me want to burrow into a hole and die. The worst of this being Ima's theme: "Paint the Future". With crowning lyrics such as "Red like pants of Santas" and "As much as I love pandas, ya’ll the world is more than black and white". The best part about the vocal tracks was that they weren't present in the final boss as I had feared they would be. A shame that three songs would drive down the music score by a whole point, but they stuck out in the worst ways.Visuals: 6/10Before I discuss Ikenfell's visuals, I'd like for you, dear reader, to take a look at three images. Look up the album art for Ikenfell, look at the game's banner on steam, and look up the ingame sprites. Do you notice something off?The visuals of this game are incredibly inconsistent.I like the in-game sprites, but the portraits look terrible. I like the designs shown in the banner, but the designs in-game look horrendous. I don't know what was going on in the design department, but Pertisia's designs from the album to the banner to the game are: "nice looking lady", "mirror baby" and "bell-headed". The portraits do not gel with me at all, the best I could say are Gilda's and Ima's but everyone else has some kind of weirdness. My theory is that the ears are way too high on the face while the eyes are much lower, but that's just me.That being said, much of the rest of the game looks well enough. I like stuff like the Unseen and Agony, and the designs of the enemies are charming enough. The designs chosen for the final game just aren't my thing at all.Overall: 6/10So... is this game good? Sorta? Kinda? My recommendation hinges entirely on the combat. If the combat were any worse than it is now, I would give this a negative recommendation and get on with my day. But still, I can't deny that the combat kept me going. Once I fought Ibn, Bax and Gilda and had to fight tooth and nail to win the 3v3, I was hooked into the game's combat (even if that battle forced me to listen to "Paint the Future"). And in spite of all its failings, I still finished the game with a mildly positive experience.It's got a lot of problems that can't be ignored, but the game is fun enough for me to look past its lesser aspects. I'm never going to play it again, but I'm nonetheless glad I was able to enjoy its combat (and much of its soundtrack) while I could.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to start by getting the trigger warning out of the way. This game showcases a great deal of woke ideology.  I'm perhaps half way through the game, and thus far, the game has made a point of making any mention of attraction between any two characters exclusively homosexual.  There are also several characters who are referred to using recently-invented pronouns or being referred to as plural.  Much like Timespinner, a fairly solid game has had this sort of content plastered on top of it in ways that aren't relevant to the underlying story at all, and it detracts from the plot and atmosphere.  The game does seem to make a point of putting this content front and center, so if you've been bullied/harassed/intimidated/etc by woke leftists or are sensitive/offended by this type of content, you may want to pass this one up.With that said, it seems to be a pretty decent game.  The battles are tactical with spells having a variety of AOE shapes and ranges.  Both attack and defense involve timed A-button presses in a style much like Super Mario RPG.  I think it could have done with auto-healing characters after battle because HP numbers are fairly low, and this leads to a lot of back-tracking to save points for free heals, especially if you miss the timing when attacked which can lead to taking a lot of damage quickly.The characters all specialize in unique a element or school of magic, so each has a very unique spell set, such as casting fire or throwing potions.  Also in a style much like Super Mario RPG, most of the enemies are goofy or at least not too serious.  A lot of blobs and plants and the like, or things like walking pairs of jeans that do flying kicks.  Still, I've decided it's not appropriate for my children because of the focus on homosexuality and frequent use of non-English pronouns.The story itself, apart from that, is mostly light-hearted and funny, with a serious note here and there (abduction, panic attacks, conspiracy, insanity).  The story with its Hogwarts-esque setting is more engaging than the actual gameplay, which is unfortunate, but it's not bad.  The seemingly forced addition of a lot of homosexual characters is unfortunate because it really takes a wrecking ball to the atmosphere.  One moment you'll be hearing about someone's sudden advent of magical power, and then go straight into hearing about how gay she is.  No consideration is made for the majority of players who don't participate in these niche intersectionality groups.  It would be nice if the game had an option or mod available to remove the unnecessary homosexual content and incorrect use of pronouns for those who aren't into that sort of thing.All in all, I think the game deserves a thumbs-up.POST-GAME UPDATE: I just wanted to add a couple things, having completed the game.  It has a very interesting story full of twists and turns and is well worth playing.  When I first saw trailers of the game, I thought the combat looked sluggish and possibly dull, but this is not the case at all.  It isn't fast-paced, but it's full of constant timed button presses that keep you glued to the screen.  I can also confirm that, to its detriment, the game is flooded with gender activism from start to finish.  Almost every character in the game is engaged in a homosexual relationship or expressions thereof.  There is one instance of a moment between a male and female, but it's between a bisexual and one who believes himself to be genderless, so it doesn't count.  Not a single "normal" relationship exists in the game.  Sadly, this is a common logical failing among leftist activists.  It's inclusion by exclusion, an oxymoron if ever there was one, and they fail to realize that this defeats their own mission statement.  it's thrown in your face the whole game.  This leaves me with mixed feelings about the story because the story of Ikenfell and the events that transpire are good, but half of the character development is wasted on shoving this neo-gender activism down the player's throat.  I honestly can't tell you whether the story is worth having to endure everyone talking about how they are "so gay" and "following their big gay hearts" and referring to each other as "them" and "zir" and having boss music that's rapping about Martin Luther which has absolutely nothing to do with the game.
