_childDocuments_.review: The first Little Nightmares is one of my favorite horror games. It had a plethora of beautiful, finely crafted environments and horrifying monsters that made the game an amazing experience. It's atmosphere and theming were heavily influenced by childhood nightmares, and that made it scary in such a fun, nostalgic way. The whole game succeeded at making you feel small and helpless in the presence of much larger, vile creatures. This sequel succeeds in its attempts to explore even more fears in the same way. All the environments are beautifully crafted to tell horrifying stories without use of dialogue, same as the first game. There are 5 chapter, each presenting their own terrifying, unique bosses, with chase sequences that will have you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your pants. Puzzles are easy enough, but made really fun through how well the physics engine allows you to interact with the environment. All in all, it's a 5-6 hour, tightly packed, finely tuned and tailored single-player experience that kept me thoroughly interested the whole time. I see complaints that for 30 bucks, this is way too short, but the game's constant level of quality and polish throughout is enough to justify it, I feel. It's a great sequel that stands on par, maybe even a little higher, than its predecessor.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for an introduction to a horror genre, this game is pretty perfect. It's not really scary, but is tense and has absolutely phenomenal atmosphere and encounters. The overarching lore from nightmares 1 and hidden elements are really well done and for games with no dialogue, really is done super well.However, as a game itself, man the controls are frustrating. There are very good clues for platform sections where you see proper little ramps basically signaling *This is where you jump* but because of how the camera works, right is not actually right, and because the camera moves, sometimes what direction you're holding will change based on how the camera moves. This can lead to very odd and frustrating experiences such as thinking you're holding left to crawl through a hole only to be walking into the bottom of the walkable area and thus moving incredibly slowly. This leads to many deaths in escape sequences because you will sometimes just stop moving.There are also moments of "combat" where you need to use a heavy object to either break walls or enemies... but remember, holding left isn't always properly "left" and so it can be extremely easy to just miss your swing leading to more frustrating and annoying deaths.This can also lead to some frustrations with the platforming as well, many locations where I started looking for alternate paths because I thought I was actually wrong in my choice since it never lined up and I kept missing.... until it didn't?Again... this series and this game as well are phenomenal entries into the horror genre, and the lore behind it is great. I don't remember having this frustration in the first game, so not sure what changed unless I'm just bad, but yeah.... definitely oddly frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, it's a good experience as an ambient atmospheric cutesy horror game. Much like the first Little Nightmares, the art and animation are top tier. The puzzle and action sequences are engaging in a way that never breaks the flow or sense of immersion. I think where the game suffers is the way that the controls and hitboxes were designed and programmed; I don't remember them being this poor in the first game, but I will have to replay that to verify (it's been about a year and a half since I played Little Nightmares). The controls just feel too janky for a game in 2022 with a $40 CDN price tag (yet only has 5-8 hours of gameplay). The game is still really fun to play, but I wanted to warn people about this potential problem. In terms of actual difficulty, casual players will find Little Nightmares II significantly more challenging than it's predecessor; it won't be impossible, but they will become frustrated with some parts. This is partly due to the jank of the controls; things like distance/depth and timing become far more difficult to assess. If you enjoyed the first one, I would suggest trying Little Nightmares II, but would recommend purchasing it when it goes on sale (also there is a free DEMO on the store page which you may want to play first). I paid $20 CDN, and I feel this was well worth what I paid, but I would feel a little bit burned if I had paid the full price of $40 CDN.This is how I would rate various aspects of the game --->Art and animation - 9.5/10Puzzles and action - 8.5/10Suspense and horror - 9/10Pacing - 8/10Story - 7.5/10Gameplay and controls - 6/10Length/content at current price point ($40 CDN) - 5/10Overall grade 76%

_childDocuments_.review: USE A CONTROLLER!!! (no seriously)I'd venture a guess this is a console port. The game initially suggests to "use a controller for the best experience" and out of the box lacks support for full screen 21:9 and 32:9 aspect ratios--workaround being to unpack the .exe, modify a couple hex values, run UE4Unlocker during play to inject .dll and set the FOV (field of view) to somewhere between 75-100... which is all fine but I'd rather have played it on a big TV and gotten the experience set out by the studio.--use a controller extended--Having gone through the first half of the game using a keyboard, I just accepted that the inputs were trash--which is half true. I've never actually played any PC game with a controller nor cared to aside from fighting games. However in this game the experience between using a controller and keyboard is night and day. With a keyboard the gameplay is frustrating at best. Too many times I'd fail over and over due to latent and sometimes non-registered inputs. This turned what were initially amazing and tense moments in the game from "OMG I MADE IT OUT ALIVE!!!" to "OMG finally... that was ♥♥♥ annoying". Honestly I probably still would have grind-it-out with the keyboard if I hadn't gotten to a moment in the game where (no spoilers?) you're getting rushed down and to escape you have to activate via directional input a newly introduced element. After the 15th failed attempt without so much as initiating the push animation I was fed up. "Alright game, you want a controller... YOU GOT IT BABY!". So after a few frustrating attempts to sustain a wireless connection between my PS4 controller and PC (eventually switching to wired) I made another attempt at escaping and progressing the story: BAM first try! From then on the gameplay was a no longer a distraction and I could finally lose myself in this game I'd been sooooo excited for!--the game--It is a beautiful, dark, grotesque and morbidly fascinating experience similar to the original. And like the original I found myself often taking time away from the story to explore and take in all the sights. The puzzles are sufficiently difficult and occasionally left me scratching my head -'what do they want me to do here...?' Having said that... it's missing a lot of what made the original so good.The introduction of AI co-op "Six" from the first (how she got there who knows) often detracts from the fear and feeling of despair throughout the story. The original AI co-op came in the form of small trolls which were introduced as unnaturally moving spies retreating from the corners of sight after tense journeys through quiet and inanimate Jacobs Ladder-esque landscapes. It wasn't until much later in the game did the relationship with them begin.... then subsequently... YOU KNOW WHAT YOU DID SIX!!! That style of slow and suspenseful development in character arc and of the story is missing in this one. It's not the MONSTER the original was but it's a good and fun game for sure. Would buy again!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a harrowing journey in a dark world filled with corruption. The game looks absolutely beautiful, and the different areas offer plenty of variety. Most of the time you will be traversing the world by jumping, climbing and stealthy sneaking when danger is afoot. You will also be solving puzzles and clumsily fighting in some small portion.The game has some trial and error in it’s gameplay, especially in chapter 2. I’m not really a fan of it, some of it can be mitigated by being cautious. But there are places you will die, with no warning. The game however has a very lenient checkpoint system, so it’s not really that big of a deal.One thing you might experience is that your character can be very “sticky”, as you may get stuck on corners and small objects when trying  to hide. But this is something you can adjust for.Had a few minor bugs, mostly in chapter 2, where my character would get launched into the ceiling. Thankfully I didn’t fall far enough to die from falling damage.Had only one more serious bug where my character couldn’t progress through a loading zone. I was able to use some trickery to get the game to place me in the next room, so I was able to bypass it. Overall, the game is fantastic, despite the few cases where you have to progress by trial and error.

_childDocuments_.review: **Mild Spoilers**Overall, a good game. I think it would be better if you had not played the first one. Compared to the first one, there’s less of an emphasis on puzzles, and more from running the ♥♥♥♥ away from things trying to eat you. Which is okay, I’d prefer the former, but the iffy controls often mean you have to do a super cinematic chase scene over and over. A lot of the control and intuition issues from the first are not fixed. More than twice I had to look to make sure I was doing the right thing, just not well enough. Two puzzles in particular were not well made/ the solution not well…advertised? For me, a puzzle game should be complicated, but overall intuitive. Talos principle is a great example. The theme/lesson was less strong than it was in the first, and therefore the acts had a harder time connecting to each other. Storyline is decent, again, not as strong. While the game overall is pretty, prettier than the first one, it’s lost some of that gritty charm now that they had more money. Overall, 7/10. Would recommend, but the first one is strictly better. However, good enough I will buy the third, which I guess is really important.

And the physics engine will freak out with objects flying around the room or your body will fly across thew room if it is hit really hard.Second criticism is that at one point in the game you have to find someone and thematically you just keep going right even though there is literally no way to know that is the right direction and comes across as a bit 'gamey'. Like why am I going right? This person essentially disappeared. A third secret criticism is that your character gets stuck on things too much and doesn't "glide" along surfaces. It can ♥♥♥♥ up momentum or critical moments like the end game sequence where movement is critical and your level space to move is limited.  Other than that its fun. Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The control of this game is absolute hot garbage. I cannot believe the control of this game is still so horrendously bad and clunky after the devs have had so many years of experience making games like this, especially since the control was also terrible in the first Little Nightmares. It's a 3D game presented as a 2D game. The level of frustration caused by the terrible control far outweighs whatever little artistic and aesthetic experience this game has. It's not fun to solve puzzles because you know what to do but you cannot do it because the control is so damn clunky. Playing with a controller, moving the left joystick straight in a direction does not move your in game character straight in that direction, somehow your character is moving either slightly up or down. Climbing and platforming is miserable and sometimes your character simply does not move up so you have to release your left joystick and move it up again then your character now magically holds on to whatever he was supposed to hold on to in the first try. Moving in directions is somewhat okay using a keyboard and mouse but the flashlight control is then garbage. (not that it is good with a controller, just less bad) You have to move it with your arrow keys but then you cannot use grab because the default grab is your LMB, you have to rebind it to some key you are comfortable pressing on the keyboard and you may even have to rebind it back to LMB later.I strongly recommend DO NOT buy this game, you probably would have just as much if not more fun watching a playthrough on Youtube. This is the kind of game that people rarely play twice anyway unless they are achievement and collectible completionists because once you've seen it there is no reason to see it again yet the control makes that first experience miserable. I have played so many genres of games, 2D platformers, 3D games, 1st person games, 3rd person games etc. and I cannot recall in recent years that a game's control is so frustratingly bad that it becomes vitally detrimental to the gaming experience. When I play Cuphead or Shovel Knight, I think to myself that the game is hard and I am bad at it; but when I play this game I just think to myself this game's control is garbage because movement feels like you are playing Fall Guys but someone is grabbing you the whole time.

_childDocuments_.review: Upping their game, the creators of Little Nightmares 2 create new content and characters to improve and expand the Little Nightmares Universe. _childDocuments_.review: This has all the greatness and originality of the first game. It clearly has not been rushed as I worried. I was also concerned that the 'co-op' with an AI companion would be frustrating in this game (as it is notorious for), but LN2 seems to handle that very well. The soundtrack is striking. I'm between a quarter and a half of the way through, and so far this is shaping up to be a masterpiece. If you liked LN1, you'll like this game, but obviously don't expect deep gameplay mechanics and complex puzzles. Little Nightmares 2 is ambitious compared to LN1, but it is still minimalist, using simple puzzles for pacing (like 'Inside') and mostly carried by an incredible presentation.Also, controls and depth perception issues seem to have actually been fixed here, so I'm not sure what some of the big review sites are talking about. (Guys, I think game reviewers might be bad at games.)

_childDocuments_.review: A piece of art. Great visuals, world-building and story-telling.There's this uneasy build up to something really horrible and the feeling is hard to shake off.Nothing is explained in the game. There's no exposition and your imagination will start filling in the gaps.  You'll start asking questions: why am I here? Why did that happen? What's the story behind this place? what's the story behind 6? It's an awesome feeling when your brain asks questions when there aren't necessarily any answers. However, the oppressive atmosphere is often marred by constant deaths and trial and error type situations.For instance, in one situation I was pretty sure I was done using the hammer and left  it behind.  I then immediately got killed with little to no warning because apparently I still needed to drag the hammer with me into the other room.In other instances I was not not sure if I had to hide or run because I just don't know what the enemy was going to do - look for me or run ahead.Quite often I died just because my aiming was just slightly off when I had to jump, slide, crawl or aim for an enemy.There will be times when you're only given a split second decision to avoid getting killed and you'll have to die a few times before you succeed. (the mannequin scene; the final "boss") I died a lot in this game and it kind of ruined the immersion. I also thought the last chapter was a bit weak because it completely went into the supernatural.  I loved the grounded grittiness of the first game.  This game takes a bit more liberties but it's an amazing piece of art nevertheless.Make sure to play at night with the headphones on.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Nightmares was spectacular, and while Little Nightmares 2 holds the same aesthetic, it's a very different game. The puzzles are more timing based (e.g., hitting the right things at the right time; making split-second turns and jumps in a chase; etc.) than clever. As someone who was looking forward to where the story would go with Six's new powers, the late reveal that this is a prequel rather than a sequel was more than a little disappointing. If the game were a standalone, it would be fine, but as a sequel to Little Nightmares, I wish I hadn't played.There were also a lot of glitches, ranging from jumping onto something and being unable to move to key items going missing (e.g., there's a chase scene where you have to move a chair in order to climb and escape, and the chair didn't appear until I restarted the program). It feels like it should still be in beta testing.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, this review says "edited" because I had to change the whole thing. To be honest, about 3 hours in I hit a point where I got so angry at the game I rage quit and wrote a nasty review. I am now here to correct that mistake. While this game has some incredibly frustrating moments, they are still greatly outweighed by the incredible presentation and story.The presentation and visual design present in this game is the best, most creative, and good looking things you are going to get in the gaming industry today. It is unmatched in creativity and mood. The tone is horror but I was never once pissing my pants in fear. It perfectly encapsulates a spooky, dreadful mood, while staying lighthearted enough to play in the dark. There are some very dark themes presented so its not kid friendly, but it isn't outlast levels. This is where the game earns its badge. If this game doesn't win awards for visual design, that would surely be a crime. Now I wish I could say the same about the game-play. The sequences that play out here are incredible on paper. Chased down by a gun wielding maniac through a dense swamp? Incredible idea. I just wish it worked better. As I stated before there were moments in the game so frustratingly bad, I simply had to stop playing. The combat being the most egregious example. There is no way to properly aim a swing, and enemies will be just out of your reach with you having no way of knowing with sparratic movement and weird attack timings. While it may have worked in dark souls, it does not here. There are also multiple stealth sequences that feel forced in and not entirely planned out, with the camera not showing you everything you need to see, and sight-lines being too vague to figure out. Luckily checkpoints are extremely common so if you do get stuck somewhere, you will not re-spawn far from where you died. Still some sequences may have you playing them out many more times than you would like to, so keep this in mind if you are going to purchase this.There is also a minor story that plays out, however it is up to interpretation what it means and why everything happens, but it is still fun to see play out. So in conclusion the game is worth playing for visual design alone, but don't expect a masterpiece when it comes to the game-play. I would recommend buying during a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Nightmares II is a hauntingly atmospheric sequel that expertly expands upon the eerie world established in the original game. Developed by Tarsier Studios, this 2.5D puzzle-platformer invites players back into a surreal and unsettling realm filled with bizarre creatures and twisted environments. With its masterful blend of tension, exploration, and narrative depth, Little Nightmares II captivates from start to finish, delivering a haunting experience that lingers long after you’ve put down the controller.Gameplay and MechanicsAt its core, Little Nightmares II builds upon the gameplay mechanics of its predecessor while introducing new elements that enhance the experience. Players control Mono, a young boy with a paper bag over his head, as he navigates a grim world filled with perilous obstacles and grotesque enemies. Early in the game, players encounter Six, the iconic protagonist from the first installment, who becomes a crucial ally in Mono’s journey.The gameplay focuses on stealth, puzzle-solving, and platforming, encouraging players to navigate through beautifully crafted, yet sinister environments. The controls are smooth and responsive, allowing for precise movements as you maneuver through shadows, hide from enemies, and solve intricate puzzles. The addition of cooperative mechanics with Six adds a layer of depth, as players must work together to progress through various challenges. This dynamic enhances the emotional connection between the characters, making each moment feel significant.The game excels in its ability to build tension. From the moment you step into the unsettling world, the atmosphere is thick with dread. Encounters with nightmarish creatures—such as the haunting Teacher and the terrifying Hunter—keep players on edge, forcing them to think strategically and react quickly. The fear of being discovered creates an exhilarating sense of urgency, making even simple tasks feel fraught with peril.Visuals and AtmosphereVisually, Little Nightmares II is a stunning achievement. The hand-drawn art style combines dark, moody environments with vivid details, creating an unsettling juxtaposition that heightens the horror elements. Each location is meticulously designed, from the grimy halls of a school to the eerie woods surrounding the city, immersing players in a world that feels both familiar and disturbingly otherworldly.The game’s atmosphere is further enhanced by its exceptional sound design. The ambient noises, creaking floorboards, and distant whispers contribute to an ever-present sense of unease. The score, composed by Tobias Lilja, is hauntingly beautiful, perfectly complementing the visuals and heightening emotional moments throughout the journey. Together, the visuals and audio create an immersive experience that draws players deep into the narrative.Narrative and ThemesThe story of Little Nightmares II is layered and open to interpretation, inviting players to piece together the narrative through environmental storytelling and character interactions. The game delves into themes of isolation, fear, and the loss of innocence, exploring the darker aspects of childhood. As Mono and Six navigate the nightmarish world, their journey serves as a metaphor for the struggles of growing up in a frightening and unpredictable environment.The character development in Little Nightmares II is subtle yet impactful. Mono’s relationship with Six evolves throughout the game, reflecting themes of trust and companionship in the face of adversity. Their shared experiences deepen the emotional resonance of the narrative, making players care about their fates.Replayability and CommunityWhile the game can be completed in a few hours, Little Nightmares II encourages exploration and replayability. Hidden collectibles and optional puzzles add depth to the experience, inviting players to revisit areas and uncover all the secrets the game has to offer. The atmospheric design and intricate world encourage players to explore every nook and cranny, making each playthrough feel rewarding.The community surrounding Little Nightmares II is passionate, with players sharing theories, fan art, and interpretations of the game’s symbolism. This engagement adds an extra layer of enjoyment, as players connect over their shared experiences in this haunting world.Final ThoughtsLittle Nightmares II is a masterful continuation of the franchise, successfully building upon the foundations of the original while introducing new mechanics and narrative depth. Its haunting visuals, atmospheric sound design, and engaging gameplay create an unforgettable experience that immerses players in a dark, twisted world.If you’re a fan of atmospheric platformers or simply enjoy a good horror experience, Little Nightmares II is a journey worth embarking on. Prepare to face your fears, solve intricate puzzles, and uncover the mysteries of a world where nightmares come to life. It’s a beautifully crafted game that resonates emotionally, leaving players with lingering thoughts long after the final scene fades to black.

_childDocuments_.review: Just as beautiful and creepy as the first one, but marred by awful, janky controls that weren't a problem with the first one. I was constantly in situations where I knew what I wanted to do, but couldn't do it because the controls were too poor, and I'd get caught on the corner of an obstacle, or get stuck in one animation when I was trying to do something else, or be too CLOSE to an interactable to interact with it.After finishing the game and then going back and getting all the achievements, I see that most of the janky controls are due to the fact that you often have to be in exactly the right place and pressing the controller at exactly the right angle, and if you're not you fail to do what you're trying to do (and usually die), and even if you do know exactly what you're supposed to do it often takes a few tries to get it right. In situations like these, most other games "cheat" you onto the right path if you're ALMOST there to make the controls feel more fluid. This game's credits are insanely long, and I would think that there would be SOMEBODY in there who's job it was to implement that flow.Gonna say this is a positive review overall, because every aspect of the visual and audio design is absolutely fantastic, but with a lot of caveats in the controls department.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Nightmares II is a good sequel to little nightmares and improve on the ideas of not just the first game, but all so very little nightmares, so it's time for the story.A lone boy wakes up in the dark woods as he's tries to survive against a world that's trying to kill him, but soon he's not alone as he saves a captive girl, a girl named six. Now the two must escape and find a safe place but does such a place exist, that is what they must find out.All right the likes; well the atmosphere in this game is still really good, it’s even better as you wander in even bigger place than the Maw, with a feeling of uneasiness throughout the game. The graphics are very good with plenty of scenes in the game that are beautiful, cute, creepy and disturbing and sometimes all of the above.The levels are very, very good even better and pretty varied from a forest, to a city and a school, they are all so fun to explore. The music and sound effects are still good from the music box song and the sound effect of the heavy raspy breathing from the Hunter. I also love the references in the game not just to the previous little nightmare games but other works of horror like that dinner scene in the Hunter's cabin.The enemy designs/looks are very good and freaky; one of the freakiest has to be the teacher. The platformering was okay, it could be a bit frustrating at times. The puzzles were good and fair not that hard to figure out. I do like how they incorporated some of the ideas in very little nightmares into this game at the very end of that game you and a girl team up to escape the enemy known as the butler. In this game Six will help you cross large gaps and will help you push and pull large objects like in the little nightmares DLC the hideaway. The AI for Six was actually good did not run around crazy or run in the line of sight of enemies. The story is pretty good like the first game, the story all so does not have dialogue it's basically show don't tell and it does it pretty well.All right the dislikes;  to start there are some frustrating segments in certain levels like some parts of the school level were hard like dealing with the bullies and their traps, I mean when a bully jumps on us I wish there was a way we could just fight them off us, I mean the bullies are the same size as Mono and Six so we should at least be able to push them off when they tackle us.Other one is the hospital level with its mannequin segment, it was really annoying because the mannequin can move so fast and you have to keep your flashlight on them at all times. Which I wish there was a way to just hold a button down and focus the flashlight on the mannequins, and near the end that last segment with the mannequins was very hard, it just made the game just so frustratingly hard and kind of unfun.  All so there's no hugging in this game, in the first game we could hug the Nomes but in this game no hugs not even with six. I have mixed feelings about the hats in the game on the one hand they are very cute, but on the other hand I wish they had powers like one makes you invisible to certain enemies or opened up a new path.Alright then now that I said all that, Little Nightmares II is a good sequel to little nightmares. It has a pretty good story, still really good atmosphere and very, very good levels. So if you played the first game and liked it, then you will like this one.

The visuals are stunning and every scene is dripping with suspense, mystery and beauty. The sound was also outstanding, I remember throwing a bar of soap at some point and being impressed by the realistic sound it made, its not something many games get right with such precise detail. Overall, a definite 10/10, the story and plot will blow your mind with metaphors, I recommend you play the first game to get a complete exprerience, though. The game is also very scary, creepy and butt-clenching at times, which contrasts perfectly with some slower, more relaxing and atmospheric moments. Congrats Tarsier Studios!

_childDocuments_.name: Little Nightmares II

For example, the controls that are sometimes really frustrating, and since the camera is in 2d, but the game in 3d, you spend your time walking in holes because the perspective is all out of whack thanks to the camera. _childDocuments_.name: Little Nightmares II

_childDocuments_.review: Everything from the first game, that was already a joy to play through, feels like it's been upgraded. The movements are smoother, the environments have become prettier/creepier and even more imposing, the enemies have been upped another notch into absolutely terrifying, and the added mechanics that allow you to fight back and work with a companion are really cool (you get to hold hands, so cute!). I had a horrible moment where my automatonophobia kicked in and nearly stopped me from being able to play, but I soldiered on with some moral support and really had a great time with the rest of it. Ended up deeply invested in the story and wanting to know more than ever what was going on in this world.
_childDocuments_.name: Little Nightmares II

_childDocuments_.review: Little Nightmares II amplifies the crass and demented part of our society by implementing it into a dystopian nightmare. The obstinate characters help puzzle philosophical controversy. The gloom setting highlights the constant generation of infrastructure.  The stubborn characters symbolise the fragility of the human mindset through our generation. The librarian sprawls her neck out in rage when silence is broken. The children react juvenile towards others that stand apart from them. The characters convey segregation and anger easily swayed overtime. The crowded atmosphere surrounding the setting portrayed a possible future into our current lives. The abundance in houses and condos hint a downfall in society due to the sheer fuels put into the construction. The outrageous creatures merely symbolise possible consequences for our actions. Scary and unbelievable  are justifiable ways to describe our fate if we continue to live like this. Little Nightmares II leaves holes mean't to be filled with interpretations and I think that it indicates anti-apocalyptic ideology. This game is a pure nightmare attempting to save our current selves from becoming as the game portrays. One day, we may become the brainless, soulless citizens seen in the city attempting to kill off anything that stands in our path of changing.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Nightmares II is a suspense-adventure game in which you play as Mono, a young boy trapped in a world that has been distorted by a mysterious transmission from a distant signal tower. With Six, the girl in a yellow raincoat, Mono sets out to discover the dark secrets of The Signal Tower and save Six from her terrible fate; but their journey will not be easy as Mono and Six will face an array of new threats from the terrible residents of this world. Will you dare face this collection of new, little nightmares? PLAY A DARK, THRILLING, SUSPENSE ADVENTURE: A host of brand-new residents lie in wait to haunt your steps and disturb your sleep. Outsmart the sadistic teacher, survive the bloodthirsty hunter and flee from many more terrifying characters, as Mono and Six journey through this world together. DISCOVER A FANTASTICAL WORLD CORRUPTED BY THE SIGNAL TOWER: Escape a world that’s rotten from the inside. Your journey will take you from creepy woodlands to sinister schools on your way to the dreadful Signal Tower. Find the source of the evil that spreads through the TV screens of the world. AWAKEN YOUR INNER CHILD TO SAVE SIX FROM THE DARKNESS: Six is fading from this world, and her only hope is to journey with Mono to find what has afflicted her from the Signal Tower. In this world of unknown terrors, you are her only beacon of hope. Can you gather up the courage to fend off your tormenters, and work with Six to make sense of The Signal Tower?

name: Cyber Shadow
detailed_description: The world has been taken over by the evil Dr. Progen and his merciless synthetic army. A desperate plea for help sets Shadow, the sole survivor of his clan, on one last mission to uncover what started the path to perpetual ruin. Your robotic companion, L-Gion, is your only guide through the ruins of Mekacity. How far will Shadow go to protect his clan and the one he loves? Is there more to their bond than meets the eye? Only you can unlock the secrets to your clan's ancient powers. Hurry before you run out of time! The road to redemption awaits in Cyber Shadow, the quintessential Ninja Action game. Features Experience sharply honed ninja platforming action! Dash, slice, and leap your way through the depths of Mekacity as you explore claustrophobic factories, corrupted research labs, fortified coastlines, vast skyscapes, and more! Powered by the lost souls of the ninja clan, Dr. Progen’s army mercilessly hunted down all life forms. As the sole survivor, you must take down more than a dozen apocalyptic bosses, ranging from enormous war machines to your synthetically-enhanced clan rivals. Rescue your clan to unlock permanent Ninjutsu skills and abilities. Attack from afar with shurikens and kunai, or get closer by using your double jump, cross slash, or wall slide techniques. Summon fire, charge slashes, parries and much more to realize your true potential. Experience a gripping story– told both in-game and through animated cinematic story scenes between the action. Shadow returns from oblivion, hurtling through Mekacity on borrowed time for what will surely be his last mission. It’s unclear what transpired before he met his fate, but his clan was betrayed. What has become of the Clan’s master? Who can be trusted when nothing is as it seems? Authentic 8-bit presentation with handcrafted sprites, a detailed pixel aesthetic, and perfect controls. Modern touches like fluid animation, multilayered parallax backgrounds, and evolved game design. Pulse-pounding soundtrack by Enrique Martin.

_childDocuments_.review: We usually get a few Ninja Gaiden-inspired games released each year, but the problem is that many of them just come off as barebones, hardly enough to compare to the classic. So, I went into Cyber Shadow wondering how it would measure up to the rest.The inspiration behind Cyber Shadow is very clear. Not just with Ninja Gaiden, but with NES game design in general, pulling from other classics like Mega Man and even a bit of Castlevania. However, it loses that NES stiffness in the process, offering some more responsive controls and movement. For example, you’re not locked into a direction when jumping – you can freely move around when in the air and even do dash attacks back and forth without touching the ground.The overall combat has a similar feel to it. It is simple, but it is fast, polished, and incredibly satisfying, especially once you’ve got all of the abilities to work with. You start out with just your basic attack, but eventually get ranged attacks, rising attacks, airstrikes, and even parries. That may not sound like a lot, but using all of these effectively can take some getting used to, at which point the combat really shines. This same style of progression can be seen with the movement, such as the unlockable dash attack and wall slide that not only help with combat, but with exploration as well.And on the topic of that exploration, there’s a nice of touch of it to the level design. Hidden walls, secret rooms, and even Mario-style out of level paths, the game has a good amount of hidden stuff to find. The level design in general though has some nice variety to it, taking you from a city overrun by robots to the depths of a reactor and then back to the docks for a fight on top of the water.Each of these comes with their own matching boss fight, fights that are both challenging and unique in their own way. This same kind of variety can be seen with the enemies too. Ranged, melee, divebombing, there’s a good amount there and definitely enough that at least one will bring you pain whenever you see it.I was actually tricked at first, because I was breezing through the first third or so of the game and was like “is this really it?” only for that difficulty to steadily ramp up as the game went on and reach very high levels by the end of it. At that point, I was getting absolutely slapped by certain rooms, some of which don’t even look that difficult on the surface until you’ve actually played them. This all culminates at the final boss, easily the hardest part of the game for me, but a satisfying sendoff once I finally managed to beat it. The game isn’t entirely evil though, there are checkpoints offered throughout and you don’t have to restart the entire game like a lot of the NES classics had you do.The dev placed it at 4-10 hours and I can confirm this as it took me 6 hours to clear. That doesn’t include 100% completion though, which will likely take much longer given that several of those achievements require you to do stuff like “kill this boss without using your sword” or “reach this area without killing any enemies.” The game has a touch of metroidvania to it in that you can go back to previous levels and explore them using your new abilities, which in turn allows you to reach previously unreachable secret areas. Outside of that achievement hunting though, there really isn’t any replayability.The story is mainly told through text-based cutscenes, but also character dialogue and notes scattered about the levels. As the game goes on, it leans more and more on those scattered notes and logs to tell the story, which was a bit disappointing, but again, there’s only so much you can do with an NES aesthetic like this. I personally found it pretty boring and an interruption to the otherwise solid gameplay, but it is there for those interested, just don’t expect anything too spectacular.As with the game design, Cyber Shadow takes on that classic NES-era look, with pixel graphics and all. As someone that has played a lot from that era, I can definitely say that this would be one of the better-looking ones. The sprites are nicely done, the color choices are solid, and the backgrounds are surprisingly detailed given the limitations of the aesthetic.It does this with a bit of a modern touch though, mainly through its parallax backgrounds and much smoother animations than what you would find in an NES game. It also ran perfectly at 1440p and 144 fps, really giving those pixels the modern look. Then there’s the music on top of that. It’s certainly not the best I’ve heard from such games, but it’s definitely not bad and really fits that “cyberpunk ninja”-kinda aesthetic the game goes for.Cyber Shadow offers both keyboard and controller options. There aren’t too many controls to the game, but both options are fully rebindable and I found no issues when testing either of them – although I personally found the controller to be the better fit.So with all of that said, I would recommend Cyber Shadow. It’s an incredibly well-polished NES throwback, with fun combat, responsive controls, and some nice art and music backing it up. The level and enemy variety keeps the experience from going stale during the six or so hours that it lasts and there’s a good amount of content for completionists to do on top of that. If you’re fan of these NES-inspired games, you’re probably gonna have a good time here, just don’t go in expecting it to be a breeze.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game. Its got a fantastic retro look and the music is catchy and pulse-pounding. The gameplay is fun and engaging. It's like those old NES games but with modern sensibilities. The levels are varied with a wide variety of obstacles, enemies, and gameplay. And I would be remiss if I didn't mention the bosses. Loads of challenging, engaging, and memorable bosses! Be warned, though. This game is challenging, but fair. There were plenty of times I quit in frustration, but I always would come back. That's a testament to good game design.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: I had a mostly positive experience, but it took a bit to become positive.Starting off I was getting bored while going through the first 4 or so stages because of the lack of options. I kept going because I knew there was a parry ability later and I wanted to try it out.As I expected, with the parry and then dashing, double jumping and the ability to charge attacks I got much more engaged.Still, all of that comes so late into the game. By the time you get everything the game is already 3/4 done.But what really baffles me is the lack of a NG+ mode... Getting to start over with all the abilities unlocked would give this game quite a bit more of play time.I finished it in 3 hours 54 minutes by playing casually, exploring levels for upgrades and reading all the dialog and lore around. That's a pretty short time.Some later stages can get a little bit annoying due to checkpoints being spread too far. And on the topic of checkpoints: what's up with the different unlocks for each of them?Basically most checkpoints only restore health, but you can pay some currency to make them also replenish the special meter and to give a sub weapon. My confusion comes from why does this currency even exist? All you can do with it is unlock stuff from checkpoints. Wouldn't it have been a better system to just let the player unlock each thing based on the amounts of deaths since they passed said checkpoint? Maybe 1 death let's you unlock the special replenish, and 3 more deaths let's you unlock the sub weapon. I leave it to player discretion if they want to unlock the help or not just in case some want to keep pushing without any help until they beat the section.Oh, and the bosses were a bit too easy. They either have too few attacks so its easy to adapt to them, or they follow a very simple pattern.I still recommend it because it's (eventually) a fun game with tight controls, nice retro graphics and cool music. My only issue with the controls was the dash also being bound to double tapping forward, which conflicts with trying to parry several projectiles in a row, but there is an option to turn off the dashing with double tap forward.I hope to see a NG+ mode added in the future, though! =)
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Cyber Shadow is a very good platformer that does its job quite well by offering a balanced and a fun experience. The fact that it's been developed by a single person makes this game even more noteworthy. It has sweet sprite work and a basic gameplay that turns into a more complex one as you progress. It's mostly linear, but you can revisit the previous areas later on to get some HP and SP upgrades for Shadow. However, it certainly does not qualify as a metroidvania title. The story, when you think about it, is very good. You'll probably won't grasp what's going on on your first playthrough since it can be cryptic at some points, but the more you think about it, the clearer it gets. It basically starts off with an explosion and Shadow, the protagonist, wakes up with cybernetic enhancements and sets out to rescue the rest of his clan from the hands of the mad Dr. Progen. As you progress, you learn more about the characters and I'd easily say that it is very interesting. The only problem regarding the game however, is the controls. I don't know why the developer acted like the controllers haven't been improved since the NES era. I mean, everything is binded to d-pad and two face buttons and it becomes problematic later on. Both sprinting and parrying (both of them are essential abilities that you gain later on) are binded to directional buttons and they both require pressing the left or right directional button twice in a quick succession to execute. Now this input for sprinting can be disabled and can be rebind to another button combination but it doesn't change the fact that this is a very bad input choice for parrying. Another thing I'd like to point out that most people will probably compare this game to The Messenger, another amazing ninja platformer that came out back in 2018, but I'd say don't get your hopes up since The Messenger outdoes Cyber Shadow in almost every way. I'd recommend playing Cyber Shadow nonetheless since it's still a great game in its own way. I believe more content will be added as well considering there is only one difficulty option and achievements are described as "Beat this on normal mode, do this on normal mode etc." I hope I'm not wrong because I'd like to revisit this gem someday!
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so very nearly an amazing game. The presentation is excellent, the gameplay *looks* great when it's going well. But several key things drag it down:  - It eats inputs. For example, if you try to input an air dash while in the recovery animation from an air dash, it will ignore it rather than buffer the second dash. - There is no coyote time (brief period in which you are allowed to jump after walking off a ledge), so jump timing is sometimes irritatingly precise and it's easy to fail to jump. - Invincibility frames after getting hit are incredibly short. Damage boosts are functionally not possible and you will routinely get knocked by enemies into spikes for an instant kill. - The parry window is similarly small, with several minibosses and bosses being designed around use of parries. - The running controls are prone to edge cases. E.g. if you hold the run button and *then* start moving, you walk instead of running. If you're running, jump, and clip the edge of a block, then you *stop* running and can no longer use the dash attack. If, god forbid, you don't turn off the default "double tap to run" control, you can easily start running while trying to parry attacks.As it stands, trying to play this game is an exercise in frustration. There's so much potential here, but it's unrealized.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a bad game. But is does so many questionable things and has mechanics in place that are inconsistent at best. Let's get into a few of the things that, at least to me, downgrade this game substantially. Keep in mind - I'm, at the point of this review, only 4 hours into the game, but I absolutely intend to finish it. It is not a bad game and there a flashes of brilliance sprinkled throughout - it just gets a bit frustrating from time to time.Most of it really comes down to some of the core mechanics as well as the level design.There will be some spoilers as to which abilities you will unlock, so continue at your own risk.You are able to reflect most all projectiles in this game once you unlock this ability. This is neat when it works and a fun mechanic, but sadly it is bound to a flick of your control stick/d-pad towards the projectile. This makes a fun mechanic hard to use and somewhat inconsistent. Obviously when you flick your stick, you move in the given direction. This makes it unnecessarily unintuitive to counter projectiles while moving, while in the air and to a degree on moving platforms. It is absolutely possible, but weird. Especially when at this point of the game there a two face buttons and three shoulder buttons which do nothing. I feel putting the deflect on a button would make it more usable in a lot of circumstances. Sadly, there is also no rebind option available for this move.This feels fantastic - when it works. Once you get the sprint you are able to dash a certain distance forward while slashing. You can even go right through enemies and then chain those dash strikes. This ups the speed of the game and feels super satisfying. It also feels inconsistent. Sometimes you dash through the enemies and when trying to chain your next dash, it just whiffs and you fall down. Sometimes your dash ends within the enemy instead of slashing through it, leaving you taking a hit. It might be I'm just not super used to this move, but I feel I am doing the same thing over and over but getting varying results. And in a platformer, thats a bit of a no-go.This is more of a nitpick than anything else, but always using special meter when performing certain moves instead of actively choosing to use the powered-up version of said move, feels like an arbitrary restriction to the players choice of tools. Also - at times - it leaves you without special meter when you would need it to access a hidden path. Not a big deal, but a weird design decision.Overall the level design is decent, but nothing to write home about. Some decisions just seem off. Remember the dash strike I mentioned above, which ups the speed of the game and can be super fun to use?Well, the first level after you get that ability is the first level to use what are essentially tripwire lasers. This forces the player to either perfect the dash from the get-go (since it allows to dash through the laser) or to take it slow and methodical and therefore disincentivise the use of dash altogether. This could have been a fast, reflex heavy level utilizing and showcasing the dash - but it came to be a stop'n'go. The boss however was fun and utilized the dash quite well.It's a fun game, the soundtrack is stellar and when all things click, it can be a lot of fun.However, I feel like this game needs to be measured against two other games in particular.Shovel Knight (Yacht Club Games latest game) and The Messenger (the most recent retro ninja platformer).Both outperform Cyber Shadow in different ways. Shovel Knight is more varied in asthetics, gameplay and especially level design. The Messenger is more creative, more focused in its mechanics and provides an interesting twist to its formula using the 8/16bit switch. Both games are more mechanically sound and provide more consistent gameplay. Both are tough, but hardly ever do anything I don't expect them to.Cyber Shadow on the other hand feels more sluggish, less inspired and just not as tight gameplay-wise.I'll definitely see it to the end and recommend it to everyone who is willing to see past its flaws. But if you are looking for a great retro platformer and have not played either Shovel Knight or The Messenger - play those first.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: is the video game equivalent of stuffing your face full of jalapeños and biting down. And then doing it again and again. It's definitely one of the spiciest indie platformers I've played yet, a lot more difficult than  or . The beginning is not even that hard at first but once you get your full moveset the game takes off the kid gloves and cranks the difficulty up to 11, all the way to  (NES) levels and maybe even beyond.There are (somewhat infrequent) checkpoints and infinite lives, so the developers went all out with making the game as challenging as possible. There are numerous nail biting sections such as riding a small platform over a chasm of insta-death spikes while fighting off flying enemies and parrying projectiles, where any single mistake will set you three rooms back. Tanking and damage boosting are almost never a thing because the enemies hit hard and there's knockdown and insta-death hazards everywhere.Sadly, the starting moveset is very limited, just attack and jump. But very quickly you unlock shurikens, wall climb (same as in , you slide down walls), upwards slash (with projectiles if you have SP), downwards slash (aka pogo, with a small explosion if you have SP), projectile parry (tap forward when you're about to eat a projectile, then press attack to send it back), and then sprint, teleport slash, double jump and the ability to charge ALL of the above attacks. The teleport slash is the coolest ability by far and the game's main gimmick. Basically when sprinting all regular attacks become teleport slashes, you teleport a short distance while slashing through whatever's in the way. It lets you move very fast, gives a lot of i-frames, and can also be chained, even mid-air. You can double jump high in the air, teleport slash towards an enemy, then teleport slash back through the same enemy to your initial position.The artwork and music are stellar, there are gorgeous anime style cutscenes (key frames only, not fully animated) between the chapters. The game has 11 chapters total which will take you around 10 hours on a blind playthrough, although once mastered the game can be beaten much faster (there's an achievement for beating it in under 3 hours). This is primarily a precision platformer and the boss fights aren't the focus and there aren't too many, although the final boss has 3 phases with no saving or health refills, so you'll have to sweat a bit before you watch the ending. This is not a metroidvania either, it's entirely stage based, although you can replay earlier stages with newly unlocked abilities to access secret rooms with HP/SP upgrades.If I had to nitpick, the shuriken and the parry should have had their own buttons, but the developer chose to embrace a NES like control scheme with only 2 main buttons (jump and attack), so the shuriken is up+attack, while the upwards slash is down+attack (a bit counterintuitive), and the parry is tap forward. Sprinting is double tapping by default, but can thankfully be changed to one of the shoulder/trigger buttons.Here's hoping that hard mode/new game plus update is still coming some day.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: While it's very easy to compare the game to the original Ninja Gaiden for the NES, just saying it's a carbon copy of the game would be a mistake. Don't get me wrong: it takes the action platforming elements of the game such as the quick sword swings and the knockback into death pits from the original game, but it does without feeling horribly frustrating like the original game had at times. It's a clean implementation with smart enemy design, great varied level design, and straightforward yet smart  design decisions to help the player. Boss fights are fun yet not overly taxing, most checkpoints are in locations that make sense, and the game does it all in a great presentation that's not only visually appealing, but sounds fantastic at every corner. It's not surprising that the game is published by Yacht Club Games with the amount of polish the game has, but it also shows the dedication of the dev MekaSkull to how the game feels like a blast from the past without making it feeling like just a tribute to the past.Honestly, the only real downside here is the fact that it's hard to justify the price of the game when it's on the Xbox Game Pass. Now you're probably wondering “uh, then why did you buy it here?” Well, I buy it because I'm a reviewer and it exposes the channel/curator to more people to look at more games. But either way, it's a fantastic game that you'd be remiss not to play, regardless of where you play it.
