_childDocuments_.review: Excellent platformer. The music is amazing, movement and momentum flow very well when you get used to them, level design along with the abilities you get allow for both cautious or fast approaches, Boss fights follow very understandable patterns so you can quickly master them. I enjoyed it so much that I played through it 3 times in a row to get all the achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: This is the sort of game that reminds a person of growing up with the NES, and tugs at all the strings that bind the heart and memory in all the right ways.  On its own, Cyber Shadow is an incredibly fun game that makes the player feel rewarded by overcoming obstacles.  It never feels brutally unfair, only challenging, and getting through tough sections just makes it all the sweeter after a few retries.  Movement and controls are fluid and fun, and the movesets are fairly intuitive while not relying on complicated over-buttoning assignments.The whole aesthetic of the game is beautifully handled, with great spritework and animations and backgrounds that show how evocative the 8 bit limitations can really be.  It definitely will remind a player of Ninja Gaiden III, Journey to Silius, and Shatterfist when it comes to how well done everything really is.  The music is fitting, being completely suitable to the whole dystopian cyberninjapunk setting of it all and feeling like it was all done in 1989.  The whole package comes together nicely, and completes the experience for someone looking for a warm throwback to classic hack and slash platforming.The difficulty is absolutely a thing with this title.  Whether it's a positive or a negative pretty much boils down to if the player enjoys titles like Ninja Gaiden.  If one doesn't like a challenge, and the thrill of learning to avoid the "cheap" hits of scripted enemies, then it won't be a good time.  However, if the player is looking for a game that wants the player to beat it by their own merits and by the development of their skills, then it will be thoroughly enjoyable.  And the game never really feels truly cheap and unfair, but rather that there is a pattern that you haven't learned yet.  It's definitely the mindset of punishing wrong answers rather than rewarding right answers.  There is no easy mode.  The closest thing to easy mode is to grind essence to activate all modes of every checkpoint.  Default difficulty is default difficult, and there are plenty of challenges in the trophies if a player is looking for something harder to achieve.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't for everyone. If you don't like hard games, give this one a pass, because I don't want to see another bad review of this game just because you're bad at it. If you don't mind a game where precise timing is absolutely required to beat it, you might want to give this a try. If you enjoy very difficult games, this is for you. Just don't take it out on the game if you die constantly.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: It’s one of the better NES-style throwback games I’ve played.  Having said that, I'd rate my enjoyment 'just above average', but that's not the games fault and more to do with my preference of genre.  I get a lot more out of something more exploratory like a metroidvania.When taking damage you get knocked back a little bit (not as harshly as in Castlevania 1).You can change your trajectory while jumping.It takes around 6-7 hours to beat.The first half of the game can feel a bit repetitive, making the experience kind of average at times (not the same variety of locations and level gimmicks as something like Donkey Kong Country 2 for instance) but the game does diversify itself a lot more with some vehicular and moving platform stages in the latter half of the game where my enjoyment picked up a tonne.  You gain new abilities over the course of the game which feel good to use.  One gripe here is that you have 2 ways to use your dash, double tapping a direction and a dedicated button.  I have zero love for double-tap to run.  In many games, if you just want to edge on a platform by pressing forward -> releasing -> pressing forward, you end up zipping off to your death when all you wanted to do was adjust your characters position a tiny bit.  Fortunately the problem is minor in this game because the instant you do this and release the button you do not travel very far.  I’d still have preferred if it just gave me the option to choose between the 2 schemes rather than activating both of them (or not bother to include the double-tap).There is more text/dialogue than I would like for a 2D platformer (so I won’t comment on the quality of the writing) but it can be skipped over fairly comfortably.  Unless dialogue is very succinct, it isn’t something I like in my platformers.The music deserves a shout out too.Cyber Shadow is a great retro 2D platformer deserving of its praise.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: I love Cyber Shadow, and it has the potential to be really great! the physics are pitch-perfect, the difficulty is absolutely scalding (in a good way!) and i like how it blended in the story elements- most of the story is conveyed through optional interactions you can skip on repeat playthroughs, or if you just want to skip the story for some reason. While I'm generally getting a bit bored of 8-bit styles in modern games, I can't deny that this game looks and sounds phenomenal! Not only are the graphics and sound design fun and memorable, but it's also designed to be easy to read, even at this game's breakneck pace. Unlocking special moves (powerful abilities that require a resource, SP, in order to be used) allows the game to build up the complexity throughout the campaign, slowly but surely turning you into a Cyber Shadow Master!However, I really believe that the controls could use some more customization options. Cyber Shadow leans heavily on NES-era design, especially in its controls. Essentially, you have the D-Pad, plus three other buttons- sprint, jump, and attack.  Using those special moves I mentioned earlier is done with the context-sensitive attack button. This is annoying enough in the early game- accidentally throwing a shuriken or fireball and wasting SP can be annoying- but there's two moves that really stand out and drag this game down. One is the cross-slash attack: once you receive the ability to sprint, pressing the attack button (the one you're using all the time to just swing your sword, remember) suddenly has the ability to fling you halfway across the screen, and potentially into one of the numerous instant-death traps. Attacking at top speed suddenly goes from second nature to a massive gamble, unless you've already died a dozen times and you know that part of the level like the back of your hand. The other is the parry. You have to tap the D-Pad in the direction of an incoming projectile with the most ridiculously precise timing I think I've ever seen in a game like this. Not only that, but the affected area is still very unclear to me, even after 18 hours. Especially since the parry is controlled with the D-Pad, which means Shadow will be moving while you try to perform it, which makes the distance even harder to judge. While I can understand the cross slash, this just makes no sense to me- i have no idea what developer or beta tester played this game and decided that this was acceptable for a core mechanic. If it had been a separate button, it would instantly be 300% more usable.I understand that this game is trying to emulate the control style of NES games like Ninja Gaiden and Castlevania, but it's too complex for that. And, for the record, I love complexity in games, but only when it can be reliably supported by the control scheme. If you want to emulate an older generation of games for nostalgia's sake, fine. But there's a very good reason Nintendo gave the SNES more buttons compared to its predecessor- to support advanced games like this one! The developer(s) made the right choice in giving players the option to use a dedicated sprint button, and now I'd really like to see that expanded to the reflect and special moves.Let me be clear that I love this game. While I had some problems controlling it, I'd definitely give it a try, because it really is great fun if you like a challenge. The only reason I wrote such a long review was in the hopes that the game could hopefully be improved if this review finds its way to the developer. But, even if that never happens, I don't regret my purchase- these issues don't ruin the game for me. I'm really looking forward to what happens with the developer and with the publisher next.Solid 8 / 10
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Slash-jump-man or: how I learned to stop worrying and love getting hit and knockbacked to land into insta-death spikes that were intentionally placed there with assumption that I'd get hit and knockbacked into that exact spot.Haha.. This is a game with great heart. I wanted to just run ahead like headless chicken and spam buttons but enemies killed me. I would then take a more cool headed approach, think on what I should do, practice and succeed... Then emboldened lose my cool, charge ahead again and die again.This is quality time.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Before you go bashing me for giving it the thumbs down, mind you the question is "Would you recommend this game to other players?", not "Did you like it or not?" That out of the way, good, let's begin:The game starts at what I'd call "Medium-Hard Difficulty", where it is hard but still very manageable... Then a little over the halfway mark you get: Checkpoint starvation, Thousand Spikes Of Death, lots of enemies that takes MASSIVE chunks of your (2, 3 and i think at some point 4 but maybe I'm imagining things), throws a lot of enemies and has a number of speed traps. You'll die way more trying to traverse a SINGLE segment than fighting a boss.The skills are also... A concern. While it's convenient most of them can be used with the attack button, it leaves room for unnecessary SP expenditure or fatal accidents (like soaring into spikes when trying to attack something). This could be fixed with an extra button solely for Skills (with default Neutral being shuriken) and  an option to allow or disallow Skills to be used via attack button.The Equipment availability could be better, since Charge Blaster is recommended at certain points despite being horrible, and some more useful Equipment are misplaced.For these reasons I can't currently recommend the game. If I like it? Yeah I do. Does it frustrate me? Yes it does, but I keep pushing because the places, the story, the musics are engaging enough. Do I want to see this game grow even more? Of course I do. I'd specially love if there were extra scenarios, maybe with a Metroidvania-like progression instead of Chapter driven. One can hope... Oh, it was worth the price, although I paid a little cheaper because of Pre-order
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: A great retro-style platformer on nearly every front. I haven't written any reviews before though from what I understand this game is a bit underappreciated so I figured I'd throw in my support.The game starts out with standard NES Ninja Gaiden style pacing and eventually supercharges your completed moveset in a manner that allows you to speed and chain-dash through levels if you're skilled enough. I would not only say that the game captures the Ninja Gaiden feel but a bit smoother, but Shadow has one of my favorite movesets to control out of any character I've played in a sidescrolling platformer. I've seen some complaints about the controls, such as not being able to crouch, though personally I haven't had much of any complaints with the controls myself. The worst I can say is that parrying being set to double tapping the dpad can be slightly awkward at times, especially if you leave double tap to dash enabled. The most frustrating aspects of the NES Ninja Gaiden games are generally remedied, with Cyber Shadow featuring much more fair enemy placement and very accommodating checkpoints.As someone experienced with platformers I personally found the game to be balanced pretty solidly. I don't think there were any sections that I found to be notably very difficult, though I wouldn't say the game was overly easy, having plenty of sections where I'd have to watch my movement.In terms of presentation, very nice dark spritework combine with a pretty enjoyable story and some of my favorite chiptune music I've heard in a while to construct a very strong atmosphere for an NES style game. Just about every boss fight has unique music which is very cool.I know this game tends to be compared to The Messenger, though that game takes a Metroidvania approach where Cyber Shadow is a traditional sidescroller platformer, generally having you deal with hazards and enemies at a faster pace as a result. If you enjoy retro style sidescrolling platformers I would definitely recommend you check this game out, and even if you're not too experienced with them I feel that Cyber Shadow is accommodating enough to newer players.This developer definitely seems to have a strong grasp on what makes a game fun and I'm very interested in seeing what they may have in store for the future, especially if I get to use a moveset like Shadow's again.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: and give me a follow on twitch if you liked my review, it really helps me out. Cyber Shadow is a pretty decent 2D action/platformer game similar to the classic Ninja Gaiden series, with nothing out of the ordinary that would set it apart from other similar indies. 👍 +The combat and platforming are entertaining enough and ramp up in difficulty as you progress. +The soundtrack is nice.👎-Filled with cheap difficulty spikes most of the half-end where enemies can even kill you from offscreen in platforming sections. -The story was boring as hell. Cyber Shadows story is not particularly bad but it does not feel as epic or interesting as Ninja Gaiden did back in the old days and it doesn't even have these cool pixelated cinematics boss intros or locations and whatnot. But hey you might be thinking, it's not fair to compare NG to CS and you'd probably be right it's not fair to Cyber Shadow a game released in 2021 to compare to a game released 30ish years ago. That would be ridiculous right? Without spoiling the story, you play as a cyborg?! ninja who is given an objective to find and maybe free your clan mates in a futuristic/apocalyptic world that was destroyed and controlled by a mad scientist called Dr. Progen. Things are not as simple as you progress through the game you uncover some things from the past but do not expect anything complicated or even remotely interesting. I found it generic and did not even care one bit about the whole thing. Hell, even the villain of the game has almost no presence whatsoever until the end. A simple, boring story in an apocalyptic world where a hero must kill the bad guy and save the damsel in distress. How cool is that huh? Story rating: 7/10Before you buy this game, just be warned Yacht Club published this game, they did not develop it afaik so make sure you set your expectations properly. Cyber Shadow is a simple 2D action-platformer similar to Ninja Gaiden in a lot of good and bad ways. This is not a metroidvania although backtracking is possible to unlock more health or power bars. It's a linear game where you slash enemies with your sword or abilities you purchase or find as well as dealing with easy to hard platforming sections. The action is far inferior to Ninja Gaiden, which honestly felt more impactful and rewarding. You can't even hit enemies above you unless you use a power nor crouch which are basic things.Only after more than half of the game when you acquire all your abilities and get the upgrade for all of them, things get more fun, especially with double jump and running slash. Unfortunately, that's when things also get a lot more "bullsh#ty" especially in regards to platforming. Enemies will fly through walls, pop up of nowhere, deal insane amounts of damage from off-screen just as you try and deal with the annoying platforming sections. This is not an actual hard difficulty, but a cheap way of delaying the game and forcing you into trial and error moments. Finally, the boss fights are ok at best and most of them are completely boring. I never felt achieved or impressed whenever I defeated one. Gameplay rating: 7.5/10The music was pretty great. I enjoyed most of the level songs and they did help with making the gameplay more enjoyable. The boss fight songs are not as good or memorable which is a travesty. Other than that, there's obviously no voice acting and most of the sound effects were absolutely fine. Nothing truly out of the ordinary or even worth talking about. Audio rating: 7.5/10So the graphics or art style in this case is not the best I've seen from pixelated animations but not the worst either. It's barely acceptable in my books. Some of the locations can look cool but most of them are just boring caves or sewers and whatnot, you know, your generic levels. Bosses and enemies have some variety and coolness to them though that fades quickly and like I mentioned in the story, there are never any cinematic pixelated cool moments like in other similar games. There are a few but they're not that interesting. As for performance and bugs, well you can expect no issues whatsoever. Graphics, performance and tech analysis score: 7.5/10So yeah Cyber Shadow is a decent game, not even close to games like Shovel Knight or The Messenger but still good enough to merit a recommendation from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: "Cyber Shadow" is a fast-paced, challenging action platformer reminiscent of old NES games, especially Natsume's "Shadow of the Ninja" and "Shatterhand". Back around that time, there were a whole bunch of sweet-looking 8-bit action games featuring a distinct futuristic style. Some other examples included "Ninja Gaiden", "Batman: The Video Game", "Vice: Project Doom", and "Kabuki: Quantum Fighter".I've played some awesome 8 bit-style indie games, and "Cyber Shadow" easily matches up to the best of them. It beautifully recaptures the pixel art style of its inspirations, along with the tough, lightning fast, combat-oriented gameplay. As you'd expect from the best of this genre, it doesn't merely copy its inspirations, but markedly improves upon what people liked about them, while avoiding the aspects that were a bit broken. By the end of the game, your character amasses a spectacular array of ninja attacks, wall jumps, dash attacks, etc, far outstripping what you'd expect from an old 8-bit character. However, the game never loses its "pick up and play" feel, since all those moves are accessed with just 3 buttons (Jump, Attack, Dash) plus single D-pad presses. In an age of Metroidvanias, I also love that despite having a couple secret areas, "Cyber Shadow" never gets annoyingly backtrack heavy or loses its emphasis on beating tough, enemy and hazard-oriented levels.If you're a fan of challenging action platformers, I think you'll love "Cyber Shadow" and owe it to yourself to pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the Messenger you can still love this game or hate it; your opinion on that game is irrelevant when it comes to reviewing this game for one simple reason:This game is NOTHING like the Messenger.They were both inspired by retro Ninja Gaiden, that's for sure. But this game is FAR more of a spiritual successor to retro Ninja Gaiden, while Messenger is far more liberal with the inspiration and goes for a metroidvania approach.In its own merits, this game is a true work of art.  Music, sound, graphics, gameplay, are all so crisp I could replay this game and finish it within the same sitting. My only complaints is that this game has a TON of missable achievements, so if you are a completionist, I highly recommend researching the achievements and mapping out your playthroughs before getting started:For example: All the bosses have some kind of hidden-challenge achievement to them, and the bosses cannot be refought without starting a new playthrough. There are more achievements like this, so that is my recommendation to you.I believe MekaSkull could really add a lot of flavor to this game with a boss rush mode. Not only would that be a ton of fun, but it would also allow people to redo the bosses in a fun way to get those achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Cyber Shadow is an initially very enjoyable retro side-scrolling hack and slash platformer that unfortunately grows tiresome as it goes on. There's a purity to its action that is refreshing if you're bored with Souls-like levelling up being put into the mix, as it concentrates on being a test of your reflexes, but it takes this to an infuriating degree.Particularly in the level design, where a lack of saves in the easier beginning stages wasn't so tedious, but by the time it really ramps up the challenge it becomes a slog rather than a fun experience.  This, of course, depends on your tolerance for such things, and no doubt some people will "enjoy" it one way or the other (be they a masochist, or an elitest "git gud" type) Personally it never thrilled me, and whilst the moment to moment action is fine and relatively exciting, as it ramped up in difficulty between the combat and the platforming it began to wear me down at the same time. Upon taking damage you have a very (very!) limited window of invulnerability that is too short to help if you end up being punted into insta-death hazards by impact or enemy attacks.It is especially infuriating when it happens during an intense sequence that involves outrunning some environmental hazard, as they don't tone down the combat encounters when these happen. Unlike most games where they separate these elements and you aren't typically under attack during these challenging set-pieces, here there is no distinction. I think it is this that makes me find it less rewarding than the likes of Hollow Knight / Blasphemous / Ori etc, as they were better judged when it came to being tricky and finely tuned. With those games it got my adrenaline pumping, and despite being tough to finish they were satisfying. This is not and for only this one reason does it fail.The bosses that I have faced were enjoyable and up until a few hours in it was fun, but beyond that point it was too retro for my tastes and it just knuckles down on this design. If you like games being built with health bars for your character that allow you to take several hits, but then contradict this with insta-death objects where you can end up being ping-ponged between enemies into them and then have to restart an entire level, then this is the game for you.If you don't like those things, then it isn't the game for you. I thought I'd like it, and for a while I did, but eventually that wore off when faced with the tedious repetition.  Or the fact that they start putting health refills in places where you are likely to take damage trying to get it, which is an extra slap in the face when you're struggling to get through in the first place. In itty-bitty chunks its tolerable but playing beyond that makes me feel its one to end up siting in the back-log, as something more fun and forgiving takes my attention. By this point the developers have my money, and as it isn't an awful game I don't begrudge them that, but at the same time I honestly doubt I will be compelled to finish this anytime soon. Does that sound like a recommended to you? Because it doesn't to me, and so it's not going to get one.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying Cyber Shadow all over again, originally played it on the Switch. Among NES-likes, it's definitely one of my personal favourites.  From its surprisingly captivating story to its engaging gameplay mechanics and intricate world design, Cyber Shadow sets a high standard for contemporary retro games. It demonstrates a deep understanding that the essence of a modern NES game isn't just about replicating the past but about elevating it to modern standards, and doing what could never be done back in the 90s.The Pixelart is top tier, evokes the best of the NES.  Negative space is used to great effect in the to create the dark atmosphere of Meka-City. The city itself and exploring it is a lot of fun.  The game isn't a Metroidvania but it is a fully interconnected, mostly linear world. You are free to visit almost anywhere you've been any time and some areas come back with new sections later in the game.  Each area has a distinct visual style and several different NES inspired music tracks based around a core melody for that area (multiple songs per area!!).  The music is like a "what could have been" if more NES games had gotten a chance use the VRC6 audio chip like the japanise Castlevania 3 cart.Gameplay is fluid, responsive, and fun.  All the abilities you unlock are hard earned and you must master them to progress.  Shadow's abilities all synergise and build on each other to augment movement/combat (some more than others granted).  They drastically change how you interact with the game as you grow more powerful. Parry feels great, dashing through enemies and flying through an area is so much fun and incredibly responsive.  You have so much control, you can blast across the screen and then correct in air to land on a tiny platform.  It's awesome I am so impressed with how this game feels to play.  My only gripe is that Shadow's move-set starts very simple and it takes a few bosses before it really starts to open up.Enemies are simple but there's a huge variety of them with many unique behaviours, a lot of the challenge comes from platforming during combat against varied groups of different enemies.  Bosses were all great, they feel like the perfect challenge level when they show up.  They don't pull their punches either, they will test your ability to use something you just recently learned alongside the rest of your abilities.  They are all nicely tied into the story as well, and some make multiple appearances.I wholeheartedly recommend Cyber Shadow to anyone who enjoys NES classics like Ninja Gaiden, Shatterhand, Castlevania 3, or modern 8-bit gems like The Messenger, Curse of the Moon, and Shovel Knight. It's a must-play for fans of the genre in my opinion.I actually like Cyber Shadow more than The Messenger 😂
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest gripe with this game is that the controls are so inconsistent. You will find yourself running the same small sections over and over again because nothing will come out correctly.  All of the special moves seem to be only good for getting you self killed. It would be better if they all had their own dedicated buttons instead of input commands that never seem to work when you need them too. Every new skill lures you into thinking its actually going to be useful but tricks you into multiple deaths. This is like playing an NES game that could have been really good except it has all the worst parts of what made an NES hard game. Instead I'm left with the feeling of "Clap! 20 bucks".
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Game took me about 6 and a half hours to beat. Music was great as well as the pix art. Controls were tight and responsive though I wish some moves were mapped to other buttons on my controller. I think it's controls were based on the NES controller as there is only a jump and attack button with combinations with the D-pad to perform different actions. The game could've used more enemy designs along with more levels. Most levels seem a bit "samey". I give this a 7.1/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly pretty weak title compared to most similar games you can imagine. Ninja Gaiden, The Messenger, Shovel Knight, Blue Shadow all do it better. What you see in the trailer is basically the first level being played with upgrades you dont yet have at that point, together with the best song in the game (which admittedly is a banger). The story feels rushed and there is no replay value at all. I finished it in under 5 hours going in blind, and though I have waited for this game for a long time I do not feel that I got my moneys worth. Sad!
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: I remember reading about this game when it was first released, and having been a fan of Shovel knight, one of the greatest platforming anthologies I've experienced, I was super interested to see what Yacht club saw in this game to publish it with MH studios. I was not disappointedGame starts out easy to grasp and as the levels progress and you unlock new techniques, more and more possibilities open up for you and allow for incredibly engaging speed-gaming. Even if it's not your thing, once you get your hands on mobility options it becomes more of a chore to *not* use them, because both the level design and novelty of each ability really tempts you. Boss fights are engaging too, learning their patterns and making as much use of your windows as you can, similarly to the Mega Man Zero series. Again, once you start gathering new powers, boss fights become incredibly fast-paced and tight. I had a blast learning to beat the final boss' first phase in a matter of seconds. Masterful design here, everything seems designed around wanting the player to experiment and explore.The Story itself is pretty standard, nothing too crazy, but still enjoyable. I enjoyed learning about the backstory of Shadow and his clan, discovering what exactly is happening and the ending, despite being quite predictable in my opinion, was still fulfilling and well-done. The Soundtrack was also a joy to listen to. Especially the opening stage theme I have actively listened to outside of the game, but the whole soundtrack absolutely slaps. And, of course, the graphics have their own vibrant charm that makes it incredibly fun to look at and makes you feel really cool when zooming all across the screen.A brilliant package through and through in my opinion. There are  a few little kinks to iron out, some points of the game I literally got confused as to what I was supposed to do but that also might've just been me. Incredibly enjoyable and I would definitely reccomend this to players who enjoy their fast-paced action platformers such as MMX/Z/ZX, Gunvolt, and others.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: I'm someone who enjoys a hard game, but this game feels cheap hard, not fun hard -- and it's not even super hard! It's just the kind of game that isn't compelling enough to make sticking with it worth the irritation.Most of the difficulty comes from instant-kill pits and spikes, and from enemies that attack from odd angles that don't align with your strikes, so deaths often feel like they're due to bad luck or to your character's limitations rather than you own mistakes. Invincibility frames post-damage are very brief, making it very easy to be quickly combo'd into a pit -- which would be perhaps be tolerable if the checkpoints weren't spaced so widely apart that completing a section after several tries feels like you finally finished a tedious, repetitive task you never want to see again rather than completing a satisfying and fair-feeling challenge.And as other commenters have mentioned, the pacing of the ability upgrades feels off, as though they grafted a Metroidvania-style upgrade system -- where you're slowly acquiring new things during the course of a mostly-free-form adventure -- onto a linear action game. The upgrades should have all come much sooner, so that you'd be able to play the majority of the game with your full kit, rather than feeling artificially hamstrung by the glacial pace at which they're doled out. And that's an issue, because the basic gameplay before you've unlocked most of the abilities felt pretty basic to me; jump, slash, repeat.Graphically, it's... OK, but nothing special. The developer may have leaned into the 8-bit aesthetic too hard, if anything, given how flat and limited in terms of color I found the overall look. The music is a standout, though, so full credit to the composer there.Overall, I'd give it a 2/5 or so. If you're someone who's really into old-school action platformers and don't mind occasional terium, you might want to pick it up if it's on sale for under $10, but I wouldn't go above that.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: game revolution's review describes it the best:"It takes Cyber Shadow too long to give the player any abilities that would make the platforming more engaging as the dash and double jump are doled out quite late. But the game doesn’t even make much use of these powers. Instead, it likes to rely on the same types of endurance runs of relatively elementary jumping with an overwhelming onslaught of robots over more satisfying and shorter chunks of skill-based platforming that take advantage of Shadow’s growing move set.Its stunted and underutilized list of abilities doesn’t allow for fun platforming challenges and instead mostly leans on long gauntlets of tediously weaving through scores of fast foes that are hard to hit. Such design seems devised in a way only to suck quarters out of players as if it were stuck in some arcade. Only a small handful of its projectile-light rooms that take advantage of Shadow’s dash and double jump show what could have been as they show a better balance of platforming and combat." it's just a chore and not rewarding at all, boss battles are to easy though so no fun in those too.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: sure is a game that not only goes for the aesthetics of the title that inspired it but also the game feel, and since you’ve already seen this thumb down you know that is not always praise.Lovely retro aesthetic, from pixel-art to music to even the over the top ultra-masculine or silly character design from the 80s.Ninjas are cool, robots are cool, robot ninjas are cool squared, kickass music helps too.It’s very clear what games it’s emulationg and it makes sure you’re getting exactly that.Jump n’ slash, plus some more mechanics unlocked as you progress through the game.Furthermore you’ll get secondary tools usable only in certain parts of the game to further augment your approach to the situation at hand.The moment-to-moment action will often see you traversing a hazard laden stage, platforming while avoiding and defeating enemies.Shadow gets caught in an explosion and wakes up with a fresh metallic body, tasked to find his master he sets off, cutting down all sinthoids that stand in his path.Very generic and just there to get you going, not much happens besides a cutscene here and there to flesh out some aspects of it.The gameplay feels dated, a good nostalgia game should bring back what you remember old games being while using design philosophies from the 30 years that have elapsed since instead of making 1 to 1 copy of it.The biggest offender here is taking control away from the player as your character falls back when hit, now this is fine and dandy if 80% of the game didn’t involve platforming around instakill obstacles, turning almost everything into a stage restart, checkpoints are fairly frequent but restarting a whole section because RNG decided to spawn an enemy underneath you still feel cheap, instakill and RNG never mix well.While there’s nothing wrong with the controls themselves, the level design seems to be made to annoy you, and I don’t mean as in hard, I mean as there’s a ledge that it’s just a few pixels from being jumped on and the enemies around you keep spawning bullets in a random pattern while you’re awkwardly wall-jumping to reach it, defending from bullets makes you drop starting over and countering them has the counter-bullet just a few pixels too low to be used to get rid of these enemies, that kind of stuff.The bullet parry mechanic for some reason is tied to your movement buttons meaning you’ll have to stop wait for the bullets to be one pixel away from you before hitting a button to move towards it that sometimes doesn’t register resulting in you walking up to damage instead of having just a dedicated button for it, again, this wouldn’t be bad if it wasn’t mandatory for some sections.Dash is inconsistent, sometimes you keep going after jumps/attacks, some other times Shadow stops dashing on his own for no apparent reason. The progression curve is weird, you get some four powers almost immediately which feels nice, then a long pause before giving you three more in quick succession, and an even longer pause before giving you seven more all at once and then nothing ever again.Cyber Shadow is an exercise in frustration, bad controls are not good game design because they make the game hard, bad controls are bad controls and from someone that’s either replicating the exact same lack of game design in early games or doesn’t know how to make it feel satisfying.I feel the love poured in this game, but this is about recommending, and 20$ for something that’s has little to no attention in its level design doesn’t seem to cut it.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, great retro vibe. Occasionally frustrating, sometimes highly frustrating on first playthrough (knockback from enemy projectiles and insta-kill spikes, especially), and I found myself frequently angry. But, when I beat it, I started playing it again, and have enjoyed it more since my skill with using the shadow dash improved. Boss battles are great fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Developed by a single man team, Yacht Club publishes yet another amazing retro influenced platformer that not only surpasses expectations but the source material it's based off of.The gameplay here is phenomenal, the movement of the character smooth and responsive, platforming is second nature. Not once did I ever feel like the game was at fault for a death. As you go through about 60% game you'll progressively obtain more moves that you'll need to pass obstacles with. Each new move obtained is satisfying and absolutely crucial to success. Each move plays off of each other incredibly well and can combo into each other, leaving room for strategies and advanced play beyond what the developers probably intended for. On top of the core moves your character gains there is a plethora of power ups that range from a simple sword range increase, to a large spinning field of projectiles to kill anything that comes in your way. The catch with the power ups however is that if you get hit 3 times (or you die), you'll lose it, leaving the most skilled being rewarded with their continued use.The core level structure of the game is segmented into "chapters", one for each unique area. These chapters play linearly, going from one to another. Around 70-80% of the way through though, the game opens back up, letting you revisit previous chapters to obtain secrets that you couldn't initially. Each secret containing health/magic upgrades. The platforming challenges and the fights you'll are varied and no gimmick is dragged out for longer than it has to. Each of the chapters spice the gameplay by throwing new enemies and hazards to combat your increasing power. Challenging yet fun, the levels take time getting used to, rewarding the player with checkpoints when you need them the most.Checkpoints, although generous serve more than to just respawn the player. As you kill more enemies and destroy crates, you'll obtain points, these points help struggling players at checkpoints by allowing them to purchase checkpoint upgrades so that they freely dispense power ups and refill of the player's magic (and in rare occasions full health refill too). Once these upgrades are bought, they are permanent to that checkpoint and don't need to be repurchased, even after death.Hearkening back to the simple games of old, the objective is to beat the big bad guy, and save your people from their evil doings. The story that plays out on the journey towards that objective is presented in a way unlike those old games, however. The game scatters it's major plot through amazing pixel art cutscenes and short bits of text strewn throughout the chapters. The level design too plays into the story as well, portraying gameplay that not only matches it's visual theme but also it's name and it's musical score. The story does what it needs to be with just enough to compel you to keep going and find out what's next.What would complete a retro style game without some stunning pixel art. The visuals excel in the art of retro simplicity, without appearing repetitive and overly flat. The game's palettes and color choices help build the ruined and technological atmosphere of the environments while still remaining easy to read. The backgrounds and geometry make intelligent use of dithering and black pixels to distinguish what can and cannot be platformed on, as well as making colors pop out and contrast each other, leading to a dynamic range of color with the otherwise limited, retro color palette. This game is a great example of how pixel art isn't a crutch for indie games but is an entire art form itself, and when you look at it that way you can gain a whole new level of insight into the intricacies that go into each and every one of these games.Topping the game off is an amazing musical score composed by Enrique Martin and produced by Shovel Knight's Jake Kaufman. The soundtrack is pseudo-retro, joining the recognizable 8 bit sound of classic consoles with higher resolution synths and instruments to create a distinct sound fitting the game's setting. The game isn't afraid to switch the music either, frequently sporting multiple music tracks per chapter, with each track for a level building up off one other, adding more instruments and changing the tempo as you progress through a level, all while making intelligent usage of the motifs it sets up. Overall, a great soundtrack full of action packed music surely to make you stop and listen.I initially thought this would be a shorter game, maybe a 2 sittings, but I've ended up spending way more on this game than I initially thought. It's fast responsive gameplay, fantastic action music, great story setting and art are what define this game. while many may write this off as another indie platformer in the sea of countless others, it's still compelling and a remarkable title to pick up if you're a follower of Yacht Club's games, fan of 2d platformers, or just like ninjas and future technology. While the price tag may seem steep  the content I can say it's well worth it. If you can't stomach the cost, there's always the plethora of sales and opportunities to get the game at a lower values.: Comfortably challenging, responsive gameplay, great pseudo-retro music with plenty standouts, surprisingly cool retro style visuals topped off with a good story. Buy it when you can.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: So it starts out really fun, but after maybe 5 or 6 chapters/levels into the game the difficulty is basically synonymous with annoyance. No part feels fun to play because the level is designed to make player movement and ability options not work well, so it's a "challenge" to get through and if you fail more often than not it's a one-shot death, because suddenly there's spike traps and bottomless holes everywhere.Unlike games like Dark Souls or Sekiro where difficulty is providing a fun challenge that you can feel good to overcome this one creates nuisance after nuisance and calls that "difficulty" (and yes, it's also difficult, hence why the devs probably think they succeeded in that).At some point I felt I was playing Celeste on Steroids, except it also has enemies on top. Every section is suddenly like a puzzle that you have to figure out. use the exact right movement/attack options at the exact right time or fail and restart. That's not what this game is advertised as and I'm quite grumpy about basically wasting 20 bucks for something like that. They even managed to add a Bike section, where I first thought it's gonna be a bit of relief and enjoyment after the stupidly precise platforming puzzles, but no, even that one has the same issues except you gotta mash the attack button at the same time, which I can't do really, since that's just too demanding on my wrists for long periods of time. Also enemies suddenly appear from behind you, so if you're trying to play cautiously but are on the wrong side of the screen you just get instantly hit without anything you can do about it, which is just more bad design that the devs probably call "difficulty" instead of just "booollsh!t"Tl;dr, nice idea, starts out well, gets annoying more and more and ends up feeling more like a chore than a game. Switches basically from an action game to a puzzle platformer and from hard but fair/fun to annoying and frustrating.Cool soundtrack though and graphics are nice as well
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: A sideways thumb.Cyber Shadow is a captivating and challenging modern game that chose to make those old school mechanics work, instead of blindly recreating the artificial difficulty of the infamous console hits. If one decides s/he wants to create a game that plays and works better than those ancient NES relics while giving off a distinct retro platformer vibe, one can actually succeed. CS’s pacing, the enemy patterns, the level layout and the bosses are a beautiful example of that. It plays great.What stops me from wholeheartedly recommending it (despite the 15+ hours of fun it gave me) is the very last(!!!) set of 3 vertical levels right before the final boss fight.  It’s as horrendous as you’d expect.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Ninja Gaiden on the NES and enjoyed it, this will be one of the best games you play for a while.Cyber Shadow is like the classic Ninja Gaiden games modernized. It's mostly a linear experience, is pretty challenging and has very satisfying combat. You unlock new abilities as you finish the first few chapters which are great fun to use and give you a satisfying sense of progression. This is a game that does not feel like it was made by one person. The length of a playthrough is spot on and the level design is top notch. Also the music is amazing, up there with The Messenger's soundtrack.Speaking of, a lot of people want to compare this to The Messenger. Saying "The Messenger did it better" isn't a good review of this game. They both have very different experiences they want to offer the player. TM is more of a metroidvania, has way more laid back pacing, and is overall a pretty easy game imo. If that happens to be your preference, good on you, but any review stating that as the single reason this game should be skipped over should be ignored. It's merely someone trying to push their personal preference onto others instead of giving people their honest thoughts on what is only a vaguely similar game.So easiest way to summarize this review: if the old Ninja Gaiden games (also the NES mega man games too, definitely got mega man vibes from this as well) are your thing, this is a no-brainer.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever felt nostalgic about platformers you played as a kid, only to try them again and realize they were filled with cheap deaths and difficulty spikes ? If so, then Cyber Shadow is the game for you.You're a Robotic Ninja who wakes up only to find that your clan has mysteriously disappeared and the world's been overrun by aggressive robots. Thus starts your quest for answers through a dozen different levels, all of which are flush with secrets and side paths that will only reveal themselves once you've gathered certains movement upgrades. Note that Cyber Shadow is not a metroidvania, since backtracking is only ever needed to obtain optional upgrades (more Health, energy etc...). The game itself progresses fairly linearly, and the challenge comes from how levels and enemy placements are arranged in increasingly treacherous ways.Cyber Shadow's retro aesthetic is fantastic, the soundtrack is perfectly fitting and even the story had me decently involved. You get all of this alongside a game that, while challenging at times, never feels overbearing. There are many checkpoints through all of Cyber Shadow's levels, all of which can be upgraded to give you more health/energy/powerups if you're REALLY struggling. This lack of challenge also helps mitigate your character's movement, which feels inconsistent at times.I really enjoyed Cyber Shadow: it's not the best Retro platformer out there, but it's accessible and very well made.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely incredible, for a specific type of person. It's brief, my playtime totaled 6 hours and that was moving pretty slow, exploring stages, and some time with the game paused doing other things. That's a huge plus in my book, as much as I love an epic in scope game like cyberpunk, red dead, spider man, getting a complete experience in just a day or two will always be my preference.It’s kind of impossible to talk about this and not mention The Messenger, which isn’t necessarily fair due to the scope difference (single person vs small studio), but since they both do pull from the same NES inspiration (Ninja Gaiden) I’ll just say that they are both wonderful games with a differing feel and interpretation of those original mechanics.Things I Loved:So Cyber Shadow I feel is incredibly faithful to what I want out of an NES inspired title. It treads a really good balance between frustration and reward for pulling though a difficult sequence of enemies. Once you are all juiced up with extra powers at the last 3rd of the story you can pull of some very satisfying combos keeping yourself in the air for long periods, slashing enemies and bypassing difficult platforming areas. The story and cut scenes are a really nice touch, they give just enough world building to let your imagination fill in the gaps. The pixel art is pretty great, a bit more on the faithful to NES era side (with bonus colors) than many other retro inspired titles. I find the balance perfect but didn’t love the built in CRT shader the game has, the raw pixels look good but I put CRT Mattias over it after the first level and never looked back, really gave it that CRT feeling of “depth” when used on an OLED display. The music is sublime, I stopped for a second at the title screen multiple times and just listened for a minute before starting it up, also at one of the tracks still pops into my head regularly like it was a track from a Mega Man game.Things I didn’t Love:The ability to parry projectiles was a welcome one but I think I would have preferred it on it’s own button rather than taping forward into the projectile at the right time? I’m not sure, but due to there being a lot on the screen in some cases and several enemies throwing multiples in one volley the parry situation sometimes turned into a bit of finger spaghettis where I either lived or died and felt is was more luck than skill. This didn’t happen that often, which I guess is kind of a side complaint, the parry system isn’t really necessary except for a couple times. The final phase of the final boss was also a gripe for me, again not major I just really don’t like fights that turn into a long waiting period with the boss out of your reach, not terrible but I was hopping for something a little more ninja showdown. Lastly a couple of the hitboxes on wall of floor spikes seemed a little shaky but again nothing major.Knife Fights:The movement on this feels great, I saw some complaints about that in reviews, I just don’t get it man. I’d call this NES+ (I love The Messenger also but sometimes it’s extra smooth character gliding over the background effect just catches my eye the wrong way).Ducking, I never once wanted to duck, the game doesn’t feel designed for it. I don’t think it would be at all useful, in fact I would argue it would get in the way.Instant kill spikes and holes are fine in games as long as it reloads you at reasonably placed checkpoint quickly. I don't get the complaint about these either, this game has a good checkpoint system, allows just enough challenge without making me want to watch the rest on youtube because I've failed the same long sequence 100 times.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Cyber Shadow basically feels like another entry in the Ninja Gaiden series of old. Playing it feels not like playing one of them, but how it feels in my memories of how it was playing Ninja Gaiden 3 as a kid. Great controls, awesome pixel graphics, large boss monsters, and many frustrating sections, but beating each of them also feels exhilarating. I say how it feels like because in many ways it brings a lot of creature comforts the old games didn’t have. Many save spots that alleviate the most frustrating spots (though there are still enough, especially in later levels to not feel too easy).The move set is expanded with various specials you learn along the way, though sadly some of the moves feel badly implemented. There’s just something off about the downward slash that makes it hard to consistently pull off (something which became extremely annoying close to the end with a section where you need to be able to do it to proceed forward, or upward), parry is almost entirely useless and the dash isn’t all that good either. At least double jump is no problem, but the other moves all feel awkward to deploy and just aren’t much fun to use.But given, it’s a large platformer with many and varied levels where you can explore for countless secrets its hard not to enjoy. You can even backtrack between levels to find stuff later if you missed something. And the core gameplay is just extremely enjoyable. There are sections where you go into cyberspace to unlock doors, these were fun too. The boss designs are really neat and once you learn how to beat them, and there’s usually a way to do it, feels very satisfying.Overall, despite its various frustrations, it’s a game I utterly loved to play, a callback to a great game of my youth that makes me remember what was so great about playing it while putting in enough modern touches to not make it as much of a chore and it just looks utterly stylish. There’s are lots of pixel games out there these days, but few manage to look so good, few manage to pin so perfectly old NES visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like a couple of things are weighing down people's impressions of the game:1: The constant comparisons to Ninja Gaiden when this game is absolutely more like Shadow of the Ninja.2: The fact that a lot of things are poorly explained both in-game and out. For instance, how am I supposed to know that I do a dash attack by attacking when I'm already running as opposed to a dedicated command I can do even when walking or standing still? Not helping is that it's hard to intuit what the windows for various commands are.I see a lot of people complaining about how few buttons the game uses, but I think that has its upsides as well as its downsides. For instance, it's incredibly awkward to use three face buttons at once. And you have to do a lot of that in both Shovel Knight and The Messenger, which I see a lot of reviewers comparing this game unfavorably to.Speaking of Shovel Knight and The Messenger, I like how this game takes itself seriously. The plot is really good if you check all the documents and talk to all the NPCs, and it looks like a lot of reviewers are missing a lot. Those other games' humor isn't for everyone, and The Messenger's "quirky" comments when you die get really annoying real fast, especially with all the money you're losing. This game's system of paying for health/spirit refills and items at checkpoints is more forgiving and a lot more creative than just losing money when dying. It helps that you're right back in the game and ready to rock again.The other thing I see people complaining about is the difficulty of speedrunning the game, but that's not necessarily a knock against a game. It's perfectly fine for a game to reward being slow and cautious.The other, obvious, thing is the soundtrack. This game's soundtrack is even better than Shovel Knight or The Messenger's soundtracks as well as Pentadrangle's best work yet. I really look forward to it coming out.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Cyber Shadow is a well rounded experience that takes inspiration from the best of the NES era and is an absolute must buy for fans of this sort of thing. (Though maybe stave off the achievements if you're only a casual player)*Story: This game's story is intriguing, it follows many tropes of cyberpunk fiction but firmly cuts out its own place among familiar works. The protagonist is a ninja who now possesses a mechanical body and must carry out the will of a dragon spirit. Along the way he will encounter what remains of his former clan. The story is primarily conveyed through computer terminals with text inside or cutscenes. Characters in this story are largely static with minimal or no development, but as this is modeled off of NES games, it fits thematically. A few things could be expanded upon or explained a little better, but that could easily be done with a sequel. (8/10)*Graphics: This game's visuals draw tremendous influence from NES games, they are very accurate to the console in question; as opposed to many "Retro" titles nowadays which just use "Pixel Graphics" of varying sizes and no color limitations. Cyber Shadow uses some colors the NES did not have, but it largely stays faithful to the visual limitations of the console. It accomplishes things the console could not do easily, but I think this all works in this game's advantage in that it helps it stand out and be its own game. The game's detailed art direction in particular reminds me of late era NES games such as Batman (1989), Shatterhand (1991), and Vice: Project Doom (1991). Environments and characters in this game are reminiscent of futuristic anime from the late 1980s such as Bubblegum Crisis (1987-1991) and Akira (1988). Finally, the cutscenes take obvious inspiration from the NES Ninja Gaiden Trilogy (1988-1991) but are far more articulate. I consider this game to have top tier pixel art and gorgeous graphics for what it is attempting to be. (10/10)*Gameplay: The gameplay in this package varies wildly between being a smooth, tight, fantastic platformer and being an endless death fest of misery. Despite often being compared to the aforementioned Ninja Gaiden, it also has many aspects in common with Shadow of the Ninja (1990) in terms of gameplay. All of the moves your character learns over the course of the game are satisfying to use and are used regularly. The special weapons are more of a mixed bag though. Some can be situational and not always help you with your current predicament whereas others seem a little too good; all of them are enjoyable to use though. As to be expected with a game of this type, Cyber Shadow has hard difficulty spikes and a myriad of cheap deaths that may kill you multiple times. One minute you are slicing through enemies like butter and the next you dash straight into a wall of instant death spikes. Speaking of death spikes and pitfalls, this game is particularly fond of those, especially near the end. To me the most difficult part of this game is the occasional checkpoint droughts where you must go long sections without reaching any save points. From my experience this game follows the NES tradition of the bosses being a relief from the great difficulty of the stages. All things considered, the gameplay here is pretty good if you're used to the punishing difficulty of the 8-bit era. (9/10)*Sound: The sound is crisp and high quality. Sound effects are satisfying and fitting. Musically, Cyber Shadow excels as well. If I could describe the music in this game, it would fittingly be synthwave made for an 8-bit setting. Sometimes I listen to the soundtrack while working on projects. My only complaint is that not many of the tracks in the game are very memorable on their own. (9/10)*Achievements: To address the elephant in the room, this game's achievements are brutal. Having 100% completed the game with achievements I can safely say that getting all of them is not for the faint of heart. Some you get while just normally progressing through the game which is harmless enough. However, the vast majority are win conditions for boss fights which put you at a massive disadvantage and can take hours if you're inexperienced. The most egregious of Cyber Shadow's achievements are "Fast as Lightning" and "Born Ready", the former is about completing the game in under 3 hours, and the latter being about completing the game without any of the health or sp upgrades you receive over the course of the game. To tackle both of those achievements, I recommend 3-4 playthroughs of the game 1: Your initial playthrough where you get to know everything, 2: Your main achievement playthrough, 3: Your Born Ready playthrough, and 4: Your Fast as Lightning playthrough. If you are a casual enjoyer of games like this I would not recommend getting all the achievements, I only recommend doing so for the completionists out there. The best thing I can say about this game's achievements is that they prepare you for doing the big 2 achievements by making the whole game a cake walk after you finish them. (7/10)In conclusion, Cyber Shadow is a case example of how to make unique and enjoyable retro-styled experiences nowadays. It feels like an NES game released during the late 1980s or early 1990s but incorporates modern conveniences and polish to make it all feel special and fresh. Absolutely buy this if you are a fan of NES or other similar titles from the same era.

_childDocuments_.review: Given its newness and price point (not to mention some of the reviews), I waited a full year before buying Cyber-Shadow, and now my only regret is that it took me so long to try it. What with the sale on now, I wanted to put in a good word for the game and respond to some of the more negative reviews (notwithstanding those written about a previous version). In this game, the design is tight and considered, not unfair: the weakened protagonist's limitations at the outset make it more akin to Mega Man 2 - X than to Ninja Gaiden, and the enemy designs, stage hazards, and bosses all attest to that. The game does demand that you git gud, and that can mean lots of trial and error, but with the steady delivery of cool powerups and even cooler abilities, it's totally worth it. The graphic and audio artistry is something to behold, making you feel like you're witnessing the evolutionary pinnacle of the NES that could never have happened in its time (I recommend letting the title theme loop several times while gazing deeply into the screen to fully understand this effect). Yes, the writing is often very awkward (not that writing is required at all in this kind of game), but there is a strangely authentic, mistranslated-in-the-80s quality even to that. The unfavourable comparisons being made to Shovel Knight (a very fine game) are only by virtue of the shared publisher, and to The Messenger (also a very fine game) only because ninjas. Taken on its own, Cyber-Shadow is a real delight for anyone with the required patience and skill.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall an enjoyable Platformer that’s worth giving a go, just know what you’re signing up for as Cyber Shadow channels it’s NES Ancestors!Controls feel tight and precise, you jump and slash! Not sure what else to say here, character weight and jump distance feels spot on. Levels are primarily linear with hidden paths and secrets to explore and upgrades to find, with a new powerup being added nearly every chapter to keep things fresh. Now lets’ be real here: The game can be difficult, more forgiving that it’s inspirations like Ninja Gaiden, but probably a step up from your average platformer (e.g. Shovel Knight). The enemies are contra-like enemies can home in on you or fire tricky projectiles, damage can deal knockback  and there’s not a lot of invincibility-frames.However Like it’s inspirations, it’s nothing that can’t be overcome with a bit of persistence, patience, and infinite continues. By the endgame everything clicks as your powers are increased and your comboing through enemies and zipping from screen to screen!Pixel perfection! Gorgeous sprite work that really nails the cyber-dark future aesthetic. Special mention to the various Shrines and the game’s title screen cutscene. (I  this art on my wall!)While on a surface level the story is straightforward, there is further depth hidden in various terminals and secrets, with information that leaves a trail of breadcrumbs for further worldbuilding. there’s quite a bit that can be pieced together about events prior to the game.Pentadrangle really nailed this one, a spectacular soundtrack the compliments the stages very well, and oh lawd the boss tracks! My only complaint is that as of this time of writing the soundtrack still hasn’t been released (guys please it’s been 10 months)For the developer’s first outing with the majority of the game developed solo, this is a noteworthy and impressive debut, I look forward to seeing where they go from here.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a real gem for the most part. Engaging level design, an unexpectedly interesting story, dead-on visuals and an obvious appreciation for its source material made this a lot of fun to play. There are some control quirks I disliked - the parry never quite feels precise enough, and the sprinting slash got me killed something like four times in the last boss fight because it came out when I didn't intend to use it (likely a result of the double-tap-to-dash mechanic.)Still, if you're a fan of 2d action platformers, NES games, or even a good fusion of cyberpunk and supernatural storytelling, you should pick this up. It's a steal.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've ever played. Gameplay becomes faster and more technical with each level, controls are tight and responsive, the enemy and level design is rock solid, each area is interesting and mechanically unique, and I love the music and general aesthetics. Dying and restarting is snappy with no downtime, and each area and boss can be blasted through with proper strategy and execution.The thing that consistently shocks me is a vague feeling that reminds me of Mega Man X. When revisiting X1, I'm having less fun until I get the dash upgrade, and once I get my hands on it I think "Now I'm really playing the game." That thought crosses my mind every single time I pick up an upgrade in Cyber Shadow, except I don't feel naked when I don't have it yet. Having the dash at all times wouldn't break X1 and that may be part of why it feels so awkward not having it, but the areas in Cyber Shadow are designed so tightly around the tools you have when you arrive that it manages to avoid making me feel like I'm missing something important.

_childDocuments_.review: A nicely presented game reminiscent of various NES-games like Blue Shadow, Ninja Gaiden and to a degree Mega man. Good music and graphics. Fairly high difficulty with occasionally evil checkpoint placement, though that gives a nice sense of relief when you complete a difficult section. While hard, the game is very fair with telegraphed attacks, taking damage feels like it is due to your own mistakes — that is not to say it didn't piss me off quite a bit at times though. Has a serviceable story that isn't overbearing.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent NES style action platformer but doesn't really hit the same highs that the games in this style that have come before it have. Would easily recommend The Messenger, Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon, or Shovel Knight (obviously) before this. The closest comparison is definitely the Messenger and while that game was weird and long but had a lot of fun stuff in it, Cyber Shadow felt super straight forward with very little nonsense.
_childDocuments_.name: Cyber Shadow

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best new school games with that old school feel.  The challenge is on point and when you master using momentum to slice through a stage, that's when you really see the genius behind this game's design.  I fully completed all achievements because this game is THAT engaging.  The story however is interesting, but convoluted.  You will leave with more questions than answers and not because it is some philosophical mind bender, but because it was all over the place.  Still a great purchase!
