_childDocuments_.review: My husband loves raccoons. I love detective media, including dark, existential and thought-provoking Scandi-noir.We've been eagerly following this game's development for years and loved the demo.As you have gathered from the other reviews, the game resembles the demo in theory only. What starts out as fun and intriguing detective fare abruptly devolves into something much less satisfying.What kills me is that Egg Nut had the fantastic premise, setting and story to make their detective media stand out. There aren't too many popular indie detective games, let alone indie games with such beautiful graphics and a high level of polish.It would have been very easy for this game studio to create a recurring hit with these assets and characters -- but I guess that goes against the "man is keeping me down, stop making meaningless art for public consumption and make half-hearted existential nonsense instead, as praxis" thread running through the game.If you consume media outside of Disney+ and videogames, you will probably find the ending  a lot less original, interesting, and thought-provoking than the people who are defending the last third.Ditto if you're exhausted by "we're all being exploited, this is about the economic downturn with some class critique thrown in" media. (I hope that the people who do disagree politically with the game know what they're getting into...)The script reads like a Creative Writing 101 student's first attempt at writing something existential, then covering up writing flaws by being intentionally mysterious, then claiming "that's the point, it's a metaphor for how we're all alienated under capitalism."The game reaches for basic dystopian plot features and then doesn't workshop them at all. But the really terrible thing is how plot points emerge and recede with no resolution. Which is fine, I guess, for an existential thriller that marketed itself as a fun detective game. But the deliberate lack of resolution and the ambiguity aren't interesting. It's all just rushed, confusing and comes off as bad writing. The demo's premise --  -- is so incisive that it could have carried the game. But it quickly gets lost in a morass of moralizing, competing plot points, and confusing motives.People claiming that others "don't get it" are ignoring how poorly executed it is. We get it. It's just done badly.This is all leaving aside how the gameplay totally changes from non-linear and puzzle-based during the playable demo, to a visual novel with no meaningful choices. This part didn't bother me, but I totally understand why it bothered others.Everything I mentioned would be totally forgivable if the game was, as it billed itself, a noir detective thriller. Or if it handled what it was doing better. Or even if there was any warning in the marketing materials that it was headed this route.I just wanted a raccoon detective game that resembled the playable demo in any way. This game failed to deliver. To add insult to injury, the first two hours (aka the refund limit) are wonderful before an abrupt slide into mediocre absurdist trash. We can't even get a refund, even though this game absolutely did not live up to expectations or resemble the demo at all in terms of story or gameplay.I normally don't leave reviews, but I bought this game to play for my birthday weekend and am so wholeheartedly disappointed by the huge gap between the demo and the game. I hope the studio takes all of this feedback into account when creating their next game.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Light spoilers that I won't get into:I feel many of the negative reviews to come may be reactionary from the epilogue, I was about to go negative myself but this is one of those major art projects that I need to go away and consider to fully appreciate it.So to anyone reading this, expect a movie style blockbuster story with an emphasis on art that I have yet to figure out, the game is good and engaging, but be ready to question everything.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: The game started off really promising with a small time detective finding himself inside something way too big for him.Sadly after about 3/4th of the game, it just totally loses everything. The plot goes totally nowhere, characters just get introduced and dropped off immediately, and nothing that was set up got a proper satisfying conclusion. It's really disappointing since it started out really really well.Sadly the good parts in the beginning aren't even worth it because of where everyone goes in the end... pretty much nowhere.Such a waste, especially since the overall style of the game is really unique and charming.In the end I just felt let down and unsatisfied.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: While this is a very aesthetically pleasing game with an interesting initial premise, the game itself is somewhat short and ends on a bit of a sour note. Personally, I was expecting something a little more open-world, but it's more of an on-rails visual novel (Which isn't necessarily a bad thing). I'd recommend picking it up when it's on sale and you have an evening to kill.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I had an instant crush on this game, some of the design choices and atmosphere are so strong. But as the game goes on the seems begin to show and it becomes clear that it's unfinished (missing assets, rare choppy story elements, long sections with no audio). Eventually, in Act IV the game seems to have bugged and I cannot proceed (stuck laying down, supposed to interact with something but nothing happens).The story is still great so far, I'll try playing again if they patch it cause I want to see how it goes, there are so many awesome scenes, it's just that there's other stuff that makes it unplayable.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Tails Noir is a tale of two halves. The first half of the game is a fantastic detective story with interesting stealth features, while the second half rapidly circles the drain. The developers obviously had deadlines, but I wish the later portions of the game didn’t feel so rushed and thrown together.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the game yet but I have a problem with this game having no chapter selection or a system like that. It's just : Continue / Start a new game. You don't even have multiple saving lots. I'm kind of disappointed but it's not that big to not to recommend it.I hope the developers fix this issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: People complain about how the story changes? It did not bother me since the narrative and tone shift was good. You guys wanted to investigate a cheating husband rather than this? lol I love how it doesn't push the player to figure out a stupid puzzle to move on the story. However, It wasn't perfect. I wouldn't give 5 out of 5. I know this is not an rpg game but I think if our choices caused a bit more difference, it'd have been much better. Dialogs are a bit weak in my opinion and so is the story. It could've been bigger than this story wise. I am guessing the ending most likely satisfied the maker/s artistically, but it did not satisfy me as much. Overall, good and wanna play the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking a lot about this game. While I initially recommended it, after thinking more about it and reading other people's experiences, I think I would advise to skip this one for the time being.First of all, I will repeat what everyone else has said already; the music and pixel art are incredibly beautiful and breathtaking, and I feel like those two things really made a big difference in elevating this game to something special. I greatly enjoyed the character design as well, and the various furry characters were all nicely done. Howard Lotor, a raccoon who is looked down upon by society, was an enjoyable enough MC and a smart perspective to present this altered world.However, in a game like this where gameplay is kept at a minimal, the writing needs to pick up the slack, and it is very hit or miss to be quite honest. I quite liked the dialogue of Howard and I felt like I understood his character and motivations, but many of the others needed more fleshing out. So many different names come and go, and the fates of multiple characters are tossed aside and never explained; in particular, one character is taken out of the story violently and abruptly, yet the game only mentions it once and then never brings it up again. It really feels incomplete and extremely jarring.In general, the story is engaging enough for what it is, but it is important to understand that this is not a detective stealth game like the marketing may seem. The player does not do any detective work besides talking to people as they traverse the entirely linear story; the branching dialogue trees are fun for color text, but ultimately have no effect on the game or its outcome. In addition, the game feels very rushed. The story introduces many different plot threads at a breakneck pace then seems to forget about them just as quickly. There is a massive left-turn of a plot twist near the end that dramatically shifts the tone of the story for the final stretch, with the ending coming even more abruptly.Finally, the worldbuilding was all over the place as well. Even after finishing the game, I still am not very clear on the dynamics of the world this game takes place in; I was not even aware that the city was "walled in" until the middle of the story, which is apparently a major plot point. There was so much I didn't understand that I almost felt like there was supposed to be a supplemental book or manual I was meant to read in order to understand the world. This is simply another fault of the lackluster writing.I tried taking my time to see everything the game had to offer, and while the first two acts of the game felt detailed and I deeply enjoyed them, the final three acts went by quite quickly and left a lot to be desired. Overall, the game is gorgeous and has a lot of great moments early on, but the writing is hit or miss, the world and characters deserve to be fleshed out, and the price is pretty steep for what it is. I am glad to support a small team of indie developers making something different, and despite its flaws I see a lot of potential in a debut game as strong as this one. Check out the free prologue instead of the full game, then come back if you're really curious to see what happens.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: The art direction was wonderful, credit where it's due. I felt like the developers forgot it was a game after the midpoint. After that it's just someone else's philosophical quackery. I wanted to solve a mystery. The only puzzle was in the prologue. There was never any choice or investigating where you had to use your tools; it felt it was restrictive on what you could do. The inventory was pointless. The ending was pointless. I'm not saying you can't make a great story wearing a game like a trench coat; To The Moon did this wonderfully. But there should be something you get from a story. And I didn't get anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Lifechanging game. Went back and forth about buying it, i'm pretty broke right now and saw a lot of reviews saying they liked it but thought the ending was rushed or too out of left field, decided to risk it. So glad I did. The game is immaculate, beautiful, intuitive, rich atmosphere and characters, incredible plot. The suspense kept building and the ending? That "twist" so many people didn't like? My favorite artistic choice I've ever seen in a videogame, maybe ever seen in anything. Its a game that makes you sit down with your humanity. And not for nothing, but for my fellow disabled/chronically ill folks out there? I've never played a game that dealt with that in a way that felt like. Soothing, somehow. Felt very recognized, I guess, in a way im not used to. This is the only review I've ever left on a videogame. If you see this, play it. Devs, thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely a very interesting game. To start, some simple good things about it. The music is amazing. The graphical design, the pixel art and the atmosphere of the game is top-notch. There's some good writing in this game and a lot of conversations sound fairly natural.No spoilers but there is a shift in the story at one point, it feels natural and the story keeps flowing . There's no screeching of tyres as the story is forced where it doesn't want to go.Howard's Vancouver is a dystopia and that infuses the story, yet there is a sliver of hope in some of the characters we meet. It can also raise questions as to how much agency we have in our own lives. A simple decision may lock us in to a path we wouldn't choose and and cannot escape.There's isn't padding in this story and its tale is told concisely. Some people may dislike that and I don't think that this is a game for everyone. What game is though?
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: There's a good story in there somewhere, but the execution wasn't there. There are unresolved plot points due to the story taking a hard turn and going another direction.The visuals and music in the game are great and make up for a lot.Overall, if it's on sale and you're looking for a short visual novel type game; it isn't the worst.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I regret buying this when it launched, back when it was known as Backbone. Around the second half of the game is where it breaks from the noir genre it established from the beginning, which I'm sure many demo players looked forward to (including myself). Honestly, the worst part of this game is that everything else about it is evidently well-polished and sleek; the UI, the aesthetic, and the soundtrack are all on point. It's only the plot, the most vital component to a noir game, that falls flat and doesn't impress. Look elsewhere, because this game only brought me disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know how I feel about this game. Was it good? Yes. Was it the detective story portrayed in the Prologue? No. I don't fault the developers for making the game the way they did, only in marketing it as a detective story. The game is less of a whodunnit and more of a deeper view into life. Kinda. Loose ends are left untied and the ending is unsatisfying, but I did enjoy the game. The ending is left open for further development, and, quite frankly, I'm excited.TL;DR If you're looking for a good detective story mirroring the Prologue-unfortunately, this isn't it. If you're looking for a visual-novel-esque game with a story driven by detective undertones (with beautiful art and music), then try it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this one make me wish Steam had a better review system than a simply binary "do or don't recommend" because I'm really on the fence about this game.It tells the story of down-on-his-luck detective Howard Lotor and his investigation of a missing person in a beautifully rendered 2.5D city inspired by Vancouver. A noir story in its intent, but not execution. It's closer to the modern, bastardized concept of "noir" than the original works of B-roll movies from Hollywood's 1940's heyday. But still, it looks pretty and the soundtrack is very nice.My biggest gripe with this game is the writing. It's a short game. My first run took less than four hours to complete and I don't think I rushed through. Part of that is a lack of content, but also because it doesn't tell a complete story. I won't say it ends on a cliffhanger, it just kind of ends half way through. All in all the way this story is written is really inconsistent. The pacing of the story is not great, you get a really drawn out investigation part where you basically just go and do what another character tells you to do without a lot of choice of where to go and who to talk to. This builds to a big reveal/climax that doesn't seem to go anywhere and you end up spending time in a half-chapter that is completely pointless. You could just cut that entire part out and simply start from the next part on and it would have no impact on the story. Not exactly the hallmark of great writing. Then you're in another half-chapter where you just sit and wait for something to happen, which doesn't happen and then the game ends with a short epilogue told from the perspective of some of the other characters in the story. And again, nothing happens, it's just setup for a sequel.It's also obvious that English is not the native language of the writers. I can't really say the grammar is bad or broken language, it's just that the writing is kind of stale. The language is simple and boring. You don't have the snappy dialogue that exemplifies real noir pieces like the works of Raymond Chandler and the other noir mavens.In the end I landed on a "don't recommend". I don't think the game is bad, it's just bland, inconsistent, lacklustre, and unambitious. For the price though I suppose it's worth picking up if you like pixel art games like this, just don't expect anything special.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: What started as a clever point-and-click detective game with great writing and a really cool pixel-art art style, later became a rather dark monologue about life and our purpose in it. That's where I wish there had been less endless dialogues (that I mostly wanted to skip to proceed with what I considered "the real game") and more "action", even if it were just point and click action. All in all, it's been an intriguing story and compelling to explore so I'd still give it 4 out of 5 stars even if it has been kinda slow after visiting Science City. Do look for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: the story begins to weave very interesting strings that don't tie up in places that they should. much like the gameplay. you do one click and point puzzle mechanic and that's it. you sneak through one major area and that's it. you play as the other two main characters, one partner and one antagonist, for maybe a minute each and that's it. the game is beautiful and the potential is there, but at the end you feel like you've played the equivalent of the small fizzling out which started with a big bang. i think the issue is that the climax of the story was stored in the demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I already played it on a different platform, multiple runs until being sick of it. This is one of the finest pxart videogames of our time. I love the '40s scenario, I love the noir feeling, I love the protagonist being a P.I. as in every good noir and the vision of a living, dystopian world inhabited by anthropomorphic animals. The social division stressed by different "kinds" as a evident metaphor for our class division based on wealth. Genius artwork, deep story and even noir accents in the "love" dynamics between characters. I look forward to playing "Tails", its prelude. This is an absolute must play.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone is beautiful, atmospheric, and pretty terribly written.From the start, the game is a real treat. it is gorgeous and dripping with noir atmosphere, it has an interesting premise and the prologue closes on a very strong hook. That was the demo, and I can definitely see how it got so many people, including myself to want to get this game on release.But then... cracks start to show. Upon replaying the prologue in the full game, my girlfriend and I started to notice that the tone was really off for a noir setting. Way too much modern slang thrown in there, it breaks the spell. Also the general tone is just... very angsty 20 something. Then the real story of the game starts and it has its moments, I will not talk about the big twist, but holy crap you ARE NOT READY FOR IT.However, the more you play, the more every character starts sounding the same. They speak with the same voice, the same tone, they become super aggro on a dime for NO REASON. We played a very mellow play through, our Howard never tried to antagonize anyone, but that did not stop half our conversation to devolve into "the ♥♥♥♥ you think you are" kind of drivel. Seriously, this game needed a script doctor to punch up the dialogue and differentiate the characters AND give a chill pill to everyone, because damn everyone is aggressive in this game.The whole philosophical angle feels... well, I'm in my late 30s so it just feels like something I would have written 20 years ago, so I can see where this is coming from. But it is not half as deep as it thinks it is, and it could have gone much further with more restraint (I mean, the inspiration from Disco Elysium is obvious, but the difference in quality is just as painfully obvious).The whole thing ends in... what is meant as a cliffhanger I assume, and knowing how hard it is to build a game, I don't begrudge the devs for trying to find a good place to cut things to keep space for a sequel. But right now, it feels more like "let's be vague enough that we don't close any doors". I don't want to get too much into details, or even use spoiler tags, but I can understand how so many have felt cheated by the non-ending.I really want to say though: Backbone was fun to play. It is gorgeous, the music is sparse, but what is there is really good, and even if the writing gets a little up its own ass, it has really good moments. I loved the plot, I think it has awesome potential, but I felt like I was fighting the dialogue every step of the way, trying to find the only option that would not make Howard sound like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and even then, so many of the people we talk to end up acting like thugs looking for a fight. Also, SO MANY PARENT ISSUES! This should probably be cut down a bit, I doubt anyone in Renee and Howard's situation would really go that deep into the whole "my mom sucks. - yeah mine too", they have slightly more important ♥♥♥♥ to deal with.As you can see, I don't have a problem with swearing, I mean, I'm French, it's like punctuation for me, but it turns out, there is a way to swear that gives weight to what you say and then, there's a way to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ male it sound like it's trying so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard, it looses all it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ weight and just sounds silly as ♥♥♥♥. I hope this last sentence illustrates my point. Less is more, read Chandler, you can make characters sound hard as a nail without dropping 5 ♥♥♥♥♥ in three sentences, it just makes you character sound like they have no vocabulary, which is not great if they happen to be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ WRITER. (used for effect here)It's really hard to write this, I bought the game as soon as it released, with the DLC, and I even bought it on GOG too to support the devs, and now... I really feel like I wasted my money, or at least, that I should have waited for a discount.I hope the vitriol that has been thrown the devs' way since release will not make it impossible for them to see good faith criticism like what I tried to put together here, because I think the sequel could be amazing, as long as the tone and the writing shortcomings get the attention they deserved.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: The ending gets an unfair rap from the community, it takes a few unexpected turns but was overall very satisfying.Visuals and sound design are absolutely stunning, and the character writing is to die for.While you do lose a fair bit of agency through the course of the game, it fits thematically, and the game plays more as a narrative experience than something driven by personal choice anyways.Highly recommend for the experience alone, wait for a sale if you can but the experience was definitely worth the full price imo
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I'll preface this with the good since I ultimately had to go for a "not recommended" review even though it's a mixed bag.First and foremost, the art direction on this is phenomenal. I love when devs take pixel art to new dimensions by incorporating fancy shaders and realistic water to really pull off a unique contrast. It makes environments pop and it's a style I'm seeing emerge more and more as new indie titles come out, which is great. Props to the artists that worked on this.The writing in the prologue is fantastic and does well to set up an intriguing story with the kind of grungy aesthetic you'd expect from a noir-mystery story. This aesthetic also glows even more when accompanied by the nice soundtrack, and while it doesn't necessarily stand up on its own as an album, it's some pretty great ambience to set the tone. It's also great that this prologue is packaged as the free demo for the game, because it draws you right in to the point where you want to see what happens next.So you buy the full game.Once you get deeper into the story, though, it starts to crumble to pieces as you're holding it in your hands. This really starts to become apparent near the middle-to-end portion of the game, where you've effectively learned the innards of what's happening, and now you're trying to grasp the reason why it's happening. It doesn't exactly help that the story throws you a curveball twist right near the end that you'll never fully understand. Honestly the whole game could have done without it and still would have turned out more or less the same.The epilogue is a little lackluster and doesn't give the story any room to stick the landing, which is really disappointing because this game looks incredibly promising judging by the setup of the prologue and the great visuals.I was on the fence about liking or disliking this game after I noticed some discussion threads on Steam saying the story sucked, because I hadn't finished the game yet at that point and I wanted to give it a fighting chance, but I can definitely see where they're coming from after finishing it.Obviously this is my opinion and I can confidently say the writing might be polarising for a lot of people. Your mileage may vary, but I guess I can comfortably not recommend this game to my friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I start by saying that what you will see in the demo does not reflect the game. I had the impression of a project abandoned in the middle of its evolution. Suddenly the story becomes superficial and cheesy. Honestly I would never recommend him given the negative emotions he left me. Personal rating 5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible game about losing your humanity, told through the lens of people that aren't even human. A lot of people complain about the massive shift in Act 3, but I thought the subversion was an incredible artistic choice. If you're expecting to play a noir game, this probably isn't for you; however, it's an amazing game nonetheless.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Be forewarned, if you're going into this game expecting a gritty Noir experience; know that that's not what this game ends up being.Simply put, the graphics, music, and aesthetic of this game are all a delight, and the story telling holds up well for the beginning chapters.----POSSIBLE SPOILERS----But by the end the story gets complicated to follow, in what starts as a run-of-the-mill noir set up of a PI hired to get proof of a cheating spouse who stumbles into something bigger, that soon spirals into vaguer questions of who holds power and why, and eventually ends with some pretty sci-fi elements with genetic research, discovery of strange things outside "The Wall" and finally a strange symbiotic(?) substance infecting the main character that I still don't rightly understand, but apparently is capable of changing someone's genetic make-up?. It feels like there were bits possibly setting up a follow-up game, but to be frank, I'm not sure.----SPOILERS END----Bottom line: I'd say it could be worth playing for the aesthetic, music, and the first few chapters if you're looking for a quasi-noir/dystopian vibe, but I honestly left this game feeling like I had been duped into buying into a story that wasn't what it presented itself as, and left with a vague ending that was either sequel-bait, or just unsatisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story. I totally get why a lot of people didnt liked how the story just went total bizarre and were unsatisfied with the end. But for me it kept me captivated. Not all games must have a happy end or a conclusion. It is just a story about life. The character made mistakes from which he could never recover. There was no plot armor. Besides that its a beautiful crafted world with a lively pixel artstyle. The soundtrack was great with a lot of Jazz noir some vocalized tracks here and there.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: The detective component of the story sags closer to the middle, giving way to science fiction, and the quest with a choice of dialogues turns into a simple visual novel, which, as it turns out at the end of the game, it was from the very beginning. But all this does not prevent you from enjoying the story of interspecies discrimination and interclass struggle. The wall must be destroyed!
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Starting out, this game is a lot of fun. The first chapter (Prologue) is really great. If they had stuck with that formula then this game would be excellent. Everyone negatively reviewing the game are correct in the disjointed story, the fact that there aren't multiple endings being a negative, and that many of your choices make very little difference except for a few achievements in the game. Speaking of achievements, three of them are buggy and they require you to delete your save in order to go back and get them. The achievements issue really bothers me. I'm not sure why the name change all of the sudden. I bought this game two years ago when it was still called Backbone. Since they changed the name I figured it was okay for me to change my review. Especially after I've had some time to think more on this game. There is a lot to consider when purchasing this game. If you can get it for under $5 I'd say go for it if you like games like this, otherwise, just stick to the prologue. As far as the sequel, I have no interest after my experience with BACKBONE.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: This was a waste. The graphics are at times beautiful but the game quickly becomes drag. It's also quite buggy. I got bugs where the main charactar appeared double on the screen. Going from crouch back to standing up sometimes doesn't work and one time I couldn't get out of the pause menu. And there where more. Pretty weird for such a simple game. But the main flaw is the gameplay. At first the music and atmosphere are good. But it's like at some they just didn't really care about making the game interesting. Cut scenes are barely what you can call a cutscene. Your sometimes staring at a scene where all the characters just sit around a fire and you have to listen to a sentimental song while nothing happens at all. That just completely misses the point. What they also do is wrap up a chapter by going through everything you've found while your character sits on a couch with his partner. There is no music and only some background noises and just piles and piles of text to click through. This game goes to a grinding halt so often that you just want to click through everything to get to the end. It's a shame because the graphics are pretty original and good looking. The story I think could be good but the way they tell it in this game just makes you lose interest. This is a misses opportunity.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I can only recommend this game with huge asterisks attached. From a purely technical standpoint, Backbone is near flawless. There’s some spotty sound design during some cutscenes, but the pixel art, soundtrack, phenomenal world, and its lore make Backbone worth the price of admission in my opinion. Backbone’s environments all feel full of life and have so much detail that it is absolutely insane. Walking down the streets of noir-dystopian city with the mellow soundtrack playing is easily where Backbone shows off its muscles, and if the entire game stuck to the city exploration / pseudo investigation gameplay style then I’d be much more willing to recommend this. Sure, more puzzles and meaningful dialogue choices would’ve also been nice, but the story starts out strong enough to carry the game over those missing features. Unfortunately, things take a turn for the worse after act II, and I can’t say I fully understand what the developers were going for here. Our detective raccoon story gets dropped for something much more rough and it feels unfinished. Someone clearly watched Synecdoche, New York a few too many times and wanted to incorporate similar themes, but the meshing doesn’t really work. I would’ve loved to see a longer third act with a more realized story and especially a more satisfying ending. I don’t think that this game is going to get the MGS2 treatment and become a cult classic down the line sadly, and I’m still not really sure whether the goal was to confuse, anger the player, or both. I would’ve loved to see an actual conclusion to the story that we followed for the majority of the game time, and I definitely would’ve liked to see some more detective aspects to this game that is being marketed as a detective thriller. I hate to come down so hard on this game because like I said, the technical aspects are brilliant, but the story here is simultaneously too complex for it’s own good, and too short to fully explore any of the ideas that it presents. Backbone is something that people are going to play for the graphical merit, its incredible soundtrack, and it's pretty fantastic first 2 acts. It’s just a damn shame that everything else about it will be forgotten.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art and good music.  Ending was a bit anticlimactic and didnt have as good an atmosphere as the rest of the game, but the narrative was very strong and the characters well written, so as long as you can manage an open ended story its definitely worth a play through.  good social commentary too.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and the ending left me in ruins.The art, the sound design, and the writing is incredible. There is a bit of an "ok, redditor" kinda vibe, but I absolutely fell in love with the characters and couldn't get enough of the setting.I had read reviews of the game before playing, so it was spoiled for me that the ending would seem a bit out of place. That was a good thing, because I wasn't expecting it to be generic at all. But damn, I didn't think it would be so sad.We're left with almost no closure. There was no romantic ending, no justice, no formal closing of the cases. This is not a bad thing.The philosophy of the ending was lost on me. I didn't care much for it. The emotional impact, on the other hand? Devastating. There will be no sequel. There will be no follow up. There will be no  time to revel in the success of Howard and Renee's relationship. It's the kind of devastation that made me enjoy La La Land so much (plus Ryan Gosling is in it (literally me)).Overall, I highly recommend this game. It's short, it's fun, and it's impactful. I will definitely play the prequel, but I wish there was more. I wish I only played through the bad ending and missed an opportunity to make everything ok. Just like in real life.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I expected something different from this game. The prologue for this time was not very telling to what this game really was. _childDocuments_.review: This was one of the most unique and memorable experiences I've ever had with a game. I'm a little puzzled by the amount of negative reviews. As far as I can tell, the reasons for that are:1- A lot of people were expecting something closer to an adventure game, where this is a story game along the lines of Night in the Woods or Kentucky Route Zero.2- The story goes places you don't expect and doesn't deliver a conventional payoff for what it sets up at the start.I think this must have been marketed to the wrong crowd. Yeah, this game is way weirder than it lets on at first. Paul Auster's New York Trilogy comes to mind as something that starts with the framework of detective fiction and turns it inside out.The game is visually stunning. It uses sound in some unusual ways sometimes where you get weird ambient sounds in the place of music and expected sound effects. Other times there's a full on original song playing and the game will let you just stop and take it in. The game has a lot of dialogue and it feels remarkably natural. Some of the conversations are thrilling because you don't know if you're on the right track or not. You can get into petty arguments with people trying to push their buttons and then apologize at the end and take it back if you want. It's exactly as awkward as actual interactions with strangers often is.If you like unconventional narratives and atmospheric games, and don't mind that there's not a challenge to most of it, I'd highly recommend checking this out.

_childDocuments_.review: Even after a long delay, the devs delivered only a fraction of what was promised on the Kickstarter campaign.The game feels very short and lacking, even disregarding the expectations the campaign set.Many reviews here will tell you Backbone feels like a rushed, unfinished product.Some refer toOthers talk about the gameplay. And this is where I feel I really have to chime in.I was a backer of Backbone on Kickstarter and developers who don't deliver what was promised to crowdfunders miff me, a lot.I'll go over the devs' promises on :"Collect evidence, interrogate witnesses, connect the dots and follow leads on your own. No hand-holding - move forward through the game by your own rules. Every case has numerous trails, and it’s up to you to decide which one to follow."This simply isn't there. shows Howard using his nose to follow trails. This doesn't happen in-game. The closest there is areAlso, there are not multiple cases, let alone multiple paths within cases. There is only.I wondered if any of the plot did branch and the outcomes could be influenced (didn't feel like playing the game multiple times to check, though). If other reviews here are to be trusted, that doesn't happen, either.Comments on  seem to confirm this."In the animal world, smell is the most powerful sense. Hide in multi-level environments, mask your scent in garbage bins, follow suspects and escape the chase."None of this is present in-game.There are some very short stealth sections, that amount to Howard crouching and hiding behind objects for a few seconds. And that's it. No sense of smell involved.There are no multi-level environments. There are no chasing sequences like the one portrayed on ."The Artifact is a unique ancient technology with unknown origins and purpose. If you learn how to use it, it might change the regular order or destroy it."There is no combat in the game, with or without special abilities. The scene depicted in  is not in the game.One thing to take away from this, though, is that The Artifact was always a planned plot element and not something introduced by the devs later on, for lack of creativity, as some reviewers here have suggested."A rich, living and breathing world waiting to be explored. Backbone takes place in dystopian Vancouver, BC, featuring real locations and breathtaking pixel landscapes.""The planet is sprawling with anthropomorphic animal species. The streets of Vancouver are overgrown with ivy and humongous trees, branches and vines piercing through the concrete, and huge flowers nesting on top of the roofs."I'm not from Canada and have never been, so I can't say if the locations portrayed have anything to do with the real city of Vancouver. From what little I know, from the internet, it doesn't seem to be the case. Also, city maps featured in-game have the name "Vancouver" on them (and, perhaps, they follow the real city's geogrpahy, IDK), but, AFAI can recall, the name isn't mentioned in any other context.What I can say is this: there is no noticeable overgrowth, humongous trees, branches, vines or huge flowers. The closest there is. isn't present in-game and.The  claims the funding for voiceover was achieved. However, the only vocals present in-game are some songs, which have lyrics.The campaign finished in 2018/05/27. The estimated time of release was July 2019. The game keys were delivered on 2021/06/07.It took the devs 2 years past the estimated release to deliver a product very inferior to what was promised. And it's not on Early Access, either, which, to me, seems like they consider it a finished project that won't be added upon, anymore.Even though, on the campaign page, they claimed: "Right now everything is ready for production: the game structure and scope, story and plot outlines, character arcs, world building, level design, and production schedules. All that remains is to get the team working full-time, to release Backbone without wasting any time on other projects.".The changes between the game described on Kickstarter and the final product are so great, it's not even the same genre.There is no investigative, stealth or action gameplay. It isn't even a point-and-click, as there are so little environment interactions and dialogue options are so limited.It plays like a very linear and short (I played through it in a little more than 6 hours) visual novel/walking simulator.If that's your thing and you feel the price is worth it, go for it, but knowing what to expect.I enjoyed the game to some extent.The pixel art is nice, the soundtrack is actually very good and the plot itself is good,.But I simply can't recommend something that feels so  than what we backers payed for.For the very same reason, I wouldn't trust EggNut with a sequel – or any other project, for that matter–, before it is actually released.Saddest thing is: the game, on its own, is OK-ish and I'd probably recommend it (Not for its asking price, but, still.), as a short indie title, if it wasn't for all those promises.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a common expectation for narrative games to provide multiple story lines and a breadth of outcomes. That isn't necessary for a story to be good. This is a story, plain an simple. Your choices change the amount of narrative you are exposed to, but don't detract from it. Sometimes a story is just a story. They don't have to have happy or heroic endings to be good. If you like stories for the sake of stories, with some introspection, you will enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: I really wanted to like this one, but my choices had no effect on the narrative, and the story derails itself with so many points just left unresolved and barely explained by the end, that I feel like I just read a half finished graphic novel. So despite the strong start and solid artistic work on the atmosphere, I can't recommend this one.In-depth:Most frustratingly, your choices make no significant difference in the narrative, and while the story train starts out well, coming out of 'Dark Noir' station strong with great atmosphere and artwork, with some decent framing shots and character introductions included, it tends to erratically change narrative tracks along the way, with little to no explanation or resolution of many introduced elements, from introducing a  story that never comes to any conclusion, to  with no explanation whatsoever, before the story simply seems to carry on without you, and you're dumped into the poor part of town, finally concluding with  and a brief epilogue that only covers a little bit about a couple other characters...No mysteries solved, very few questions answered, and no satisfying conclusions or explanations.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start with the good.The art is amazing, not only is it gorgeous but it's extremely detailed, every part of the city is full of life and they all have their own vibe.And on top of that if pay attention you can catch a ton of little world building details, it's insane reading comments and seeing just how much I missed out on.Unfortunately it's time for the bad, mainly, this game is unfinished.I know the developers have posted an open letter saying the game is like this on purpose and it's open for interpretation, but, I can't being myself to believe it, there's just too much missing.Puzzles and stealth sections are introduced in the prologue and never appear again.The kickstarter showed off combat and the main character walking around with a mutated arm, the game has a scene setting this up but it's never mentioned again.Entire plot threads are introduced and then dropped with no resolution.Characters are introduced like they're supposed to be important only to never show up again.Themes and ideas are brought up but never examined.The protagonist never actually accomplishes anything.The antagonist's plans are never really helped, harmed or even explained by any of the events.Then there's the epilogue.The main antagonist explains her motivating and goal (But not her actual plan) to another character.Neither her motivation nor her goals have anything to do with her previous actions and what she's said before this chapter. This scene is so baffling that I think this was a completely unrelated scene of the antagonist straight up lying to a character, and the development team just stamped the word "Epilogue" on it.I could go on, but the fact is I'm convinced that this game was originally intended to be ACT 1 of the game, but due running out of money they put a bow on it and shoved it onto Steam as a finished product.So I honestly can't recommend it, play the free prologue chapter to check out the art, then imagine a better more complete story for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for Backbone when it first came out, bought the game the day it was released, and I don't regret any of it. The story is completely unexpected. It did not go where I thought it would, and it wasn't the game I thought I was buying. That being said, it was a fun story, and I did get invested enough that I am desperately awaiting news of when I can expect the sequel. The art is beautiful and what the game gets right, it gets right FANTASTICALLY. However, there are bad parts. The demo does admittedly feel more fleshed out and more like a detective game than the rest of the game seems to be. There are parts in the story where you know that it's supposed to have been compelling, but it fell short. A lot of it feels rushed, which I won't hold against the devs. Do I think that these things should be fixed in the sequel? Yes. Do I think that these things make the game not worth it? No, not at all. It's definitely a worthwhile play. It may have been different from what I hoped for, but it was an interesting and fun take on the detective genre. Just don't expect that you'll be solving puzzels--it's more of a visual narrative that you get to be a part of.

_childDocuments_.review: The abundance of negative reviews for a game doesn't usually scare me.Neither do strange and unusual endings scare me.But this time I still should have listened to people.I've never considered myself a very demanding person.And I would have forgiven this game a lot of things: I would have forgiven a vague ending (vague in a bad way). The linearity of the narrative and the lack of even basic variation.(the variation is weaker than in many Visual Novels) I would have forgiven the game for being deceptive about many expectations. Expectations that it itself tried to raise.:What I listed above has rightly alienated many people.But the worst part is that this is not the game's biggest problem.Backbone is weak in the most important part for this genre - the First of all, it's very jagged.None of the themes, even the main ones, are given proper attention. You get the impression that the author just lures us in with an interesting plot and atmosphere, just to then abruptly switch to telling you some of his strange and inappropriate thoughts in the context of the game.Second:Characters who seemingly, as the game progresses, should be fleshed out more and more, become more and more inconsistent and "artificial."And thirdly, as a result we get a "world" which is hidden behind a beautiful and atmospheric picture and music, is actually just a smokescreen (because of this I felt at one point that the 2D background would fall like a cardboard set), hiding some completely , and a collection of some .Unfortunately the narrative designer and scriptwriter just killed this game.And neither the music nor the graphics can fix it.Definitely not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone is a visually rich and thematically unnerving experience, with engaging writing, evocative music, and memorable characters. There are aspects of the gameplay (e.g. occasionally but infrequently used elements like stealth mechanics) and pacing that I wish were further explored and iterated on, but the narrative and tone are the centerpieces, and they are effective ones. Those going into it with expectations of an RPG with multiple endings or large amounts of player choice, or a narrative with clear answers and revelations as rewards for your efforts, may miss out on the experience that is offered here. The game's description is in itself a thesis statement: "There is no choice. We change, but we change nothing. Get to work, detective."This is not a Sherlock Holmes story with logical cause and effect. It is postmodern and Lynchian in the true sense of the term: not just in the sense of a generally "weird" tone, but in the sense that answers, when they exist at all, are not necessarily logical or "satisfying" in a cathartic sense. Life as depicted here is never as black and white or resolved as some styles of popular fiction depict.Likewise, the player's lack of choice in certain scenarios can be seen as thematically consistent and meta, in a sense, as many of the characters (including the player character) feel trapped in their situations. The narrative intentionally drifts from a sense of having choices and seeking logical answers to a sense of choice and answers being beyond the player character's grasp. This may end up going a bit too far, as the ending sections felt less interactive and engaging to me than the earlier chapters. But, while the execution of the idea may not fully be there, I'd argue that the feeling of having fewer and fewer meaningful choices towards the end of the game supports the themes of the narrative (giving in/giving up/accepting) and is intentional, rather than being a mistake or fumble. You change, but you change little to nothing of your world. And you don't control the change you undergo. It's not going to be for everyone, and not all aspects or moments fully landed for me personally. But if you embrace this paradigm--that choice is sometimes an illusion or not offered at all, and that major narrative questions are purposefully not answered, or if they are, they are done so in a subversive or even frustrating way in order to communicate larger themes about self, ego death, and literal death, etc.--you may find that the narrative and experience as a whole offer compelling moments and experiences. In a market where tried and true genres are the conventional bet, I admire this team's guts in putting out a challenging work.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love this game. It was one of the games I was most looking forward to, especially after playing the Prologue, which was one of the best detective adventure games I'd played in a while. The 2.5D pixel art graphics are beyond gorgeous. The music is atmospheric without being irritating, boring, or overwhelming. The gameplay is very intuitive. Some of the writing is even pretty good in the first couple of chapters. So what happened?First and foremost, the issue is that the prologue is misleading. The prologue allowed different pathways through the story and dialogue; it allowed some clever sneaking around; and, most importantly, it had puzzles. In adventure games, it's a must to either have inventory object puzzles (where you can combine or use objects in your inventory cleverly to solve your way through video game logic predicaments), OR to have puzzles where you need to whip out a notepad and solve a code to get you through a lock. I'm a big fan of the latter, and it really looked like Backbone was going to deliver on that front.After the prologue, no further puzzles like that existed. There was one moment where you had to , and another moment where you had to , but besides that, there was no more work required of you as a player. Click through dialogue--doesn't matter which choices--wander around observing things, and eventually, you will run into the ending.And boy, did it feel like you just RUN INTO the ending. What you first think is a small-scale operation turns out to be part of a vast conspiracy that is part of a vaster conspiracy--or is it? Who is good? Who is bad? Who knows. The narrative stacks strange ideas on top of world-building on top of other strange ideas until it collapses under its own weight. Before you know it, the gritty, almost nostalgic noir vibe of the prologue gives way to what is essentially a visual novel about a dystopia you don't really care about.These were great characters in the prologue, and as your choices started to matter less, so did the characters themselves. There were shifts in tone, shifts in gameplay, and at one point, bizarrely, a several-minute cutscene where you listen to a song at a campfire. I picked up so many objects throughout the game that I never thought about or used again. Did I miss opportunities to use them? Maybe. And I haven't even touched on how weird the plot gets. I hate posting "Not Recommended" on a game. I wanted to love this. When I read the mixed reviews, I prepared myself for what was essentially a visual novel and hoped the story would carry it.  But even knowing that, I was still disappointed.The amount of love and care the devs put into this game really shows in the artwork and gameplay, and even in the storyline to some extent. But I hope they will take the feedback fans are giving about this game and, if there's a sequel, turn it into the game we all hoped Backbone would be.

_childDocuments_.review: gorgeous art and immaculate soundtrack, however the story was a bit confusing to follow. Not to a point where it'd make it impossible to enjoy though. This game is one of the reasons I hate the way steam lets you review games, not on a scale of maybe 1 to 10, but whether you recommend it or not. This was definitely a mostly positive experience and I do think it's worth playing. Characters and the world were interesting but I think they weren't fleshed out enough to meet their full potential. This game has a lot to offer, it's really just about what you expect going in. It gives you an illusion of choice, or rather your choices having an impact on the story when in reality they only really have effect on dialogue. It's mostly a visual novel above anything else. The menus were also a bit broken but didn't break the whole game as past reviews seem to suggest - apparently major issues have been patched. Ending was unsatisfying but didn't ruin the game. Wish there was something more. Either way I'm glad to have played this game, ended it with mostly good feelings.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the worst games I've ever played.Don't get me wrong, its not all bad. The Pixel art is great, the game has a moody atmosphere and some very interesting characters. The first half of the game sucks you in to what you think will be a very interesting crime to solve.But all is not as it seems, because everything falls apart after that. Everything that was great about the first half of the game is gone in the second. The choices that you made so deliberately in the beginning no longer matter (and TBH, they never did in the first place). The game is entirely linear, it doesn't matter which dialogue options to pick, nothing changes. The plot somehow got lost along the way and you very quickly go from a detective looking into murder and corruption in the hopes of exposing it all to becoming a science experiment. The ending is a complete and utter letdown and makes you feel as though the hours (only about 3-4 in total) were a complete waste of time.My advice: play the prologue for free as its the best part of the game. The rest is money down the drain.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Review after 3 hours of gameplay: Beautiful graphics with a gripping plot. I like how many interesting dialog options there are; makes the gameplay feel really customized.EDIT:Review after completing game: Oh man, I really wanted to like this game. In Acts 1 through 3, I was hooked. I was loving the detective work and building the story in my head. It was totally gripping. And then, as other reviewers mentioned, total 180 in the story. Suddenly, it wasn't a mystery story. You lose any illusion of control in the narrative, and the story that was building in your mind for hours is suddenly ripped from you. I honestly felt... betrayed? And then the Epilogue shows up before you've had time to process what's happening. There's no satisfaction for your initial investigation. There's no resolution for the character relationships you've built. It's like the whole game was pointless. Honestly, the game was awesome until you hit Science City. After that, the whole game tumbles down a slippery slope. I feel like the creators had a bunch of really fun ideas for the plot, but made the mistake of trying to squeeze all of them in the same story.Really, I didn't want any more twists in the game than I already got in the Prologue. I just wanted to solve a mystery and see the bad guy get her just desserts. I was really having a ton of a fun for the first 4 hours. I don't know. It just feels like this game was trying to shock me... and I just didn't need that. I came for noir raccoon detective and I loved Howard. Then, he's just kind of ripped from you.Final words: So close, and yet so far. Art is beautiful though.

The art is beautiful, the writing is witty, the world-building is exciting and leaves you wanting more, the score is perfect. I didn’t want the story to end just so that I could explore the world more!The game is different from what I thought it would be and I’m happy with what they delivered. I don’t think I’ve played another game quite like this.

_childDocuments_.review: To start off with the positives, the setting, tone, music, and even some of the characters were pretty charming for me. It is nice to see a product like this exist and I'm glad to have played it without any rush to finish it. However, this game feels unfinished in regards toward the ending. I haven't looked that deep into this so I don't know if it was planned for a sequel or not given how confusing and abrupt the ending feels. I'm disappointed on how I didn't feel challenged in any sort of way like with the prologue in the beginning. Everything felt just a little too easy to solve, but I guess if that's your sort of thing, this game isn't that bad if you want to relax and learn about what is going on in this worth. Overall, I wouldn't recommend this product for anyone who sees this in passing as said before, this game feels like it was cut off too early without tying up any loose ends, but what do I know. I don't regret playing this, but I'm not happy with the end product.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really doesn't deserve the mixed reviews it got. A few of the sort of valid cons to the game are..- there isn't much of an ending. but who the hell plays a game for the ending? 80% of the game is awesome, not having a very wrapped up ending didn't matter to me.- for a game that gives you lots of choices, there doesn't seem to be a lot of outcomes. there is only one ending which is the only thing I disliked. However, that is the case with these visual novel kind of visual novel games. Other hit games like firewatch and night in the woods feature a similar lack of changeable narrative.- Lots of walking. Maybe it's cause I played a lot of Poptropica growing up but I've grown to endure a good percentage of my playing time being enjoying the scenery as I run through the map. It's not too bad, especially since the creators have obviously put in lots of love and care into the art. So if you're looking for fast paced and action packed work, maybe this game isn't for you. But if you like to stop and smell the roses? Give it a shot!I fell in love with this game because of its outstanding art, story and intrigue. Going into it, I could have never guessed where the plot was going to lead me. I LOVED the twist! If you like great art, great music, sci-fi, mystery, and crime, CHECK THIS GAME OUTTTT.

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone has very rich storytelling, great characters, stunning art design, and beautiful music. For me, this game is easy to recommend. I expect that my experience of Backbone will linger for some time. However—reading the reviews—I can understand how some people are left unhappy by the twist. _childDocuments_.review: This game was the opposite of what I was expecting. From when I tried out the demo, I had high hopes for the game and waited months to finally play it. Only to finish the game within a few hours. It says I have 11 hours but I completed the game in roughly 7-8 hours then took a nap during the credit screen because I was that furious.For a game worth £19.99 (17.99 on sale), I expect to have a minimum of at least 20 hours worth of game-play to justify the purchase. This did not achieve that. Next, the game was heavily misleading. The prologue offered multiple ways to achieve an outcome and felt non-linear; none of that appeared in the remaining chapters or even felt relevant. There were no puzzles to solve compared to the prologue and it felt like the only thing we were meant to do was to take in the view and go to where we had been directed to go. I felt absolutely no care in the world for the dialogues as they were meaningless anyways, and the ending was one of the most abrupt things ever. The plot-twist was not needed and it felt like the creators of the game wanted to heavily focus on this instead of adding more content and meaningful story to the game that it eventually killed all momentum and the purpose/identities of characters.Honestly so disappointed with how this game turned out. I played the prologue again and felt so excited that I had to leave a positive review, just for the game to do a complete U-turn and drive itself off a cliff. This game does not deserve the price it is asking for.

_childDocuments_.review: Having backed this game on Kickstarter, and after being teased by the Prologue, I was really hoping to be swallowed up by this game. Instead, my feelings about this game after four hours are extremely mixed. The good: Art direction was fantastic, not just in the pixel art, but also the Art Deco UI and text. Visually, this game is stunning. Also (this one's rather superficial) being set in Vancouver was awesome to reminisce personally.The music and sound is hit or miss. There are uncomfortably long songs, and even longer gaps where it's just silence. Silence can be done well in select moments to build atmosphere and tension, but it can also just feel empty (or worse, prompt the player to wonder if it's a bug). The story itself, in the most reductive interpretation, is not necessarily bad. But the storytelling - the way the plot is presented to us - is a mess. There is no semblance of pacing, flying from one plot point to the next at breakneck speeds of which even Call of Duty campaigns would be envious. There isn't enough runtime for this story be presented in a coherent manner. And whereas at least the game tries to pretend you're connecting dots in the first half of the game, the second half loses its marbles and seems to change into a new genre altogether. Gone is the detective work, the puzzles. The intrigue. Without proper time to digest developments in the story, the twists that follow either give whiplash, or subsequently lose all impact. This isn't helped by the inconsistent dialogue either, which for a game that mostly revolves around its conversations is disastrous to player immersion. It seems that every few lines, I encounter awkward sounding sentences, missing words, or dialogue options that seem incongruent with the context or flow of said conversation. Occasionally, it seems to also manifest in the form of joke/meta responses, which might suit Howard's personality, but felt tonally jarring juxtaposed with the atmosphere the game is trying to set. The problem here is that the dialogue can't ever make up its mind, so a number of characters end up suffering from multiple personalities. For all the game's efforts to immerse the player, few things shatter verisimilitude quite like erratic characters. (Speaking of which, the motivations of some of the cast are themselves irrational within their setting, even contradictory at times, and there is no player agency to call them out on it.)Also there's a lot of cursing, to the point where it can sound juvenile.  For me, this game overall feels like hugely missed potential. I went in without having read any reviews, but came out echoing a lot of their feedback. It feels rushed, wildly inconsistent in polish, and became more of a chore toward the end, which for a four hour game is impressive.

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone... Where do I begin?It's... disappointing to see such a hyped game be delivered in this way, especially when its soundtrack and atmosphere is top notch, that's why it's such a shame that the story and gameplay failed. The story starts out strong, lots of questions and mystery, but as the game progresses it seems to just discard it all in favor of a very odd alternate plot point. _childDocuments_.review: Uhh, where's the rest?This might be the most conflicted I've ever felt about a game. I'm giving it a thumbs up but with some colossal caveats. Let me explain...A wet, noirish sci-fi dystopia of anthropomorphic animal people, a mystery of people disappearing, a conspiracy between a crime lord and city officials, all presented in beautiful pixel art with multiple layers and post-processing effects and a really nice soundtrack. Backbone drew me in, kept me guessing, and gave me so many memorable characters in large and small roles. I really wish it had voice acting, but that's something I can usually live without, it allows me to imagine their voices myself.Though the story is quite linear, how my raccoon PI character feels about things and how he approaches dialogue and puzzle solving has a lot of freedom. Do you devastate mourning family members with the truth or be gentle with them? Do you find a way into the night club's private rooms by manipulation, trickery, or friendly persuasion? It matters.The story sure takes some turns, but they were exciting and intriguing and I really wanted to see how ol' Howie was gonna handle the situation he found himself in... when the game just ended, at the darkest moment, what would be the end of act 2 in a 3 act structure. There's a whole climax and conclusion missing from Backbone that's left me with complete narrative blueballs. I checked, there's only one ending to the game and it... ISN'T. Hell, this is a 3 hour game usually sold for £20. Just long enough to make sure players can't get a refund. But I don't want a refund, not really, I want the rest of the story! I want more puzzles, more investigation, more dialogue! I want to know what happened to the characters and how they stopped, or even failed to stop, the big conspiracy.I feel like the kid in Princess Bride demanding to know why grampa read him a book with a downer ending, only in Princess Bride it's a fake-out nightmare and Backbone really does end this way?!?Buy this game on sale, play it, enjoy what there is of it, then suffer as I suffer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the first negative review I've ever felt bad about giving. Mostly due to the fact that I was *really* looking forward to playing this game since I saw it and played the prologue back in 2019. I loved the way this game started out. It had a lot of potential, and it looked amazing. I was hooked right into it at the beginning, found it to be really interesting. Then, as the game goes along you start getting into more details, you get a lot of questions that you want answered. You begin to think that there's going to be some sort of big revelation, that maybe you'll get those answers and have some kind of big mind blowing event, or at least something...Unfortunately, the game, after the third act, just kinda putters down and falls flat... very flat. It's really unfortunate that I can't give games a "mixed" option for reviews, because in all honesty this game is a mixed bag. It's story started out great, but then it completely fell apart toward the end. It took me 3 hours to beat this game and that's only because I took my time looking everywhere I could, trying to get as much out of the game as possible. That's how much I was invested in the game for the first three acts. Then, for the final half-hour of the game, which includes another two acts and a epilogue, there's a big nothing burger. You basically get blue balled, and are left with a lot more questions than answers. It really seems like there's a huge amount of story to be told here, but unfortunately the game doesn't go out of its way to explore it. I really wish there was more, or at the very least a continuation or an update or something. However, by the way the game ended and based on developer response... we're stuck with what we've got. And that's honestly the most disappointing thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the story and felt that it had a strong start. However, it loses all of its momentum in Act 4 and 5. You learn at the end of the game that none of your choices really matter. Motivations for some organizations are never fleshed out. Characters who seem relevant just disappear later. It makes me wonder if this game was supposed to be larger and longer but got cut short due to time and budget.While the mystery, characters, and world building was good, I really did not care for the ending. It is pretty dark even by noir film standards. I also found many sections with zero background music. In a game without voice acting, that was pretty startling. You would think someone would grab some royalty free slow jazz music from the 30s or 40s to include at least. However, the jazz music was often pretty good and set a mood for the game.I hate giving this game a negative No but would struggle to get it a really positive Yes. If Steam had a five star rating system, I would rate this game as a three. Buy it on deep sale, if you like noir films, pixel art, or detective games.

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone is a game with fantastic atmosphere, design, and worldbuilding. Unfortunately those qualities come at the cost of significant substance in the game's moment-to-moment gameplay and story. The game is almost completely linear, which would be fine if its single path was used to deliver a complex and interesting story. For the first two fifths of the runtime, it does. You visit interesting and richly detailed locales with unique characters who help to flesh out the games themes of race, class, and societal decay. From the third act onward, the game takes a jarring turn into dystopian science fiction in a way which is not properly set up beforehand or satisfyingly concluded afterward. Sudden reveals about several characters and their motivations cast the story in far too many shades of grey for any part of the story to truly be concluded. Thematically, this makes sense, as the game explores social issues and how corruption and exploitation is an inherent evil of society (or capitalism, at the very least); but it still left me wanting more. People don't watch detective movies because they want to find out about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the world is, they watch them because they want to see the mystery solved.Ultimately, this game started as a fantastic post-noir detective thriller, but got lost in the third act. I enjoyed many of the twists later in the game, but they're ultimately what prevented it from being a five-star experience from start to finish. If you're really curious about the story, watch a let's-play or buy it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game for months and WOW am I impressed. As you can see with many of the bad reviews for the game, the story and failure to build off of the puzzle and stealth elements from the prologue does hit the game a little harder. However, the writing and story are beautiful, the art direction is unforgettable. and the soundtrack is just perfect.Without getting into any spoilers, the last two acts of this game being IV and V, are weaker than the rest, but still good. It ends on a cliffhanger, and leaving more questions to be answered than there were in the beginning. I hope these are addressed through DLC or a sequel, but the game could have gone without going in this direction.Overall, I do think this was an enjoyable experience, something that does warrant a second or third run to fully complete, however, the ending is what most remember in video games, so there is that. It's a hard to rate game, I am in love with it personally but do see the flaws within it. It is a solid 7.5/10 game, and I hope we see the stor over Howard Lotor and Renne expanded upon, as well as this beautiful world.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited about this game after playing the prologue. I enjoy murder mystery games with puzzles. I'm ok with walking simulators sometimes as well.The full game fell short. My play time says over 8 hours, but I fell asleep twice during dialogue with characters, so my actual playtime is probably around 6 hours. I cannot justify this game being worth $22.49 "on sale" for a game that averages 6 hours of playtime with most of it being dialogue and cut scenes. Cut the price in half and that's more along the lines of what it's actually worth. The dialogue choices were better than I expected, but the story ended abruptly. So much more could have been done with this game. You all spent 5 years with the plethora of kickstarter backers to make a 5-6 hour game then charge over $20 for it?
