_childDocuments_.review: I played the prologue and loved it. Just now getting into the meat of it and It is still as fascinating as the first time I played. The visuals are great and are unexpectedly detailed in a lot of areas. Great game 10/10.Updated After Finishing:I was super hyped for the title and I've been waiting several months for it to come out. I'm not disappointed with the game overall, but I think after the prologue portion the story declines and rapidly. The further into the game you get the more it moves away from a crime novel type of story and the more it moves towards sci-fi and apparently  some undefined  political commentary. The story introduces these sci-fi elements rather abruptly. I honestly was not expecting it and I'll address that more later. Visuals: I found them perfect personally. The meshing between the 3D depth and the 2D landscape was great and I was surprised to see how some of the elements in the game appeared fairly realistic such as the water.  I have no real criticisms on this aspect of the game.Game-play and Controls:There were a few aspects of the game-play that bugged me. For starters, the game auto-saves only. Which means if you have to leave and do something else, if you close the game it will reset the conversation you were having to the beginning of the closest scene. There was also the problem that if you accidentally press a myriad of possible buttons on your keyboard you can pick a dialogue option and you cannot go back, which for a dialogue game seems important. I tried to adjust my volume a couple of times, and for some reason the F8 key-bind also makes you select all the dialogue options rapidly and you can completely lose entire conversations because of that. I actually took advantage of the weird auto-saves and shut down the game and restarted it when I did that so I could run through the missed dialogue. Some of the other issues with the game-play was the fact that the few mechanics introduced in the prologue were not actually used very much in the actual game. There was only one other puzzle and it was not particularly difficult and mostly involved talking and reading. it was mostly minor. The sneaking mechanic only came up a few times, and was really inconsequential. The game became almost totally a graphic novel, which would have been fine overall, but I was really expecting more than dialogue fetching missions if this was meant to be read as a video game. I enjoyed the ability to interact with a lot of the bystanders and make small talk, but it seemed apparent that a majority of these interactions didn't actually affect the story at all. I don't believe your dialogue choices actually affect the story at all and you could probably select any sequence of dialogue you wanted and still progress the story, even in reference to main characters.There were also a couple points where you needed to retrieve objects in order to get through the map, like a key and door system, however, the "keys" were literally right next to the doors. I believe this aspect of game-play is usually incorporated to make players explore the map a little, but when  you literally get interrupted in the progression of exploration simply to have to walk  10 feet and pick up a key, it seems like more of a speed-bump and less of a feature.I don't like how inconsequential is seems with your dialogue choices. I sat on the edge of my seat thinking that there would be points in the story where a bad choice of words might get you killed, but if that option was in there I certainly didn't experience it. The opportunities to fail at any point in the game just really didn't appear.I'm not sure if it's a bug or not but I found that you still got dialogue interactions for things you didn't do in the game. On my second play-through of the prologue, I forgot to check inside the cab of the cider truck outside "The Bite". I noticed I had forgotten only after I received a dialogue option for it in another conversation in that same play-through. Given how I had played that run there is no way Howard had any knowledge of what might have been in the truck, because I didn't interact with it.The rabbit woman I had talked to in the prologue also didn't seem to recognize me when she showed up in the story later, although I had clearly interacted with her and she had explained a large piece of the story early on, which also seemed to break the immersion a little, contributing to that lack of dialogue selection importance I talked about earlier.You also seem to travel through city sections once, and then you don't return, although there were maps in both living arrangements that I expected to be interacted-with like  a pseudo-open world.There appeared to be an allusion to a mechanic that would've let you read hidden messages that were on park benches and stuff if you learned it, by reading some sort of street language? maybe I read too far into that, but I didn't see it again in the game.Story: (I'll not intentionally give out any spoilers but if you're worried about that skip this section of my review)The story starts of very strong with the classic detective drama atmosphere that drew me to the game. The dialogue, although dry at times, was genuinely unique, at least in the prologue, because the options were fairly in-depth and really allowed you to make responses that mirrored what you actually might've thought. This unfortunately doesn't seem to actually matter too much because there aren't really any stonewalls for how you behave, Howard the saint or Howard the devil, you'll progress. You can flirt or jab, but it doesn't seem to matter too much, you cannot romance (I did try), and  very few people will meet you again. The story continues on the detective narrative for a about the first 1/3 to 1/2 of the game, then abruptly and nearly at the speed of light transitions into a sci-fi thriller/horror fest. Some of the plot points don't make very much sense to me either. Why was the search for the girls basically dropped? Why didn't I know there was even a wall around the city until half-way through the game (Doesn't come up in dialogue until around mid-way through)? What is beyond the wall? What caused there to be a wall? What is the purpose of the artifact at all? Why did a particular  main character get killed in the very specific way (Spiked arm)  we saw, and yet we never saw anything else similar happen again, even in intense or stressful situations? What was the point of the bridge section? Why is Clarissa basically omnipotent?  And what was that "Explosive" ending for? It answered almost no questions, and I feel like I've just been left hanging? I'm not opposed to being able to set up a sequel but in order for there to be a sequel, I think I need to know a lot more about what any of it means or what is going on?! Also, y'all did Howard dirty.Story Issue theory?I suspect that the issue for the story comes possible from translation issues, and the need to keep raising the bar on the story, and way too heavy of reliance on symbolism. I believe the developers are from Europe, so a perfect translation was probably going to be hard to achieve, but a few times the dialogues feels a little choppy or repetitive. It wasn't really that big of a problem, though. I suspect that the story got over developed sometime between the prologue and release, although I have no proof. While generally a good rule I hear is "show don't tell" I think the explanations were far too abstract. There was an abstract section involving a parade, showing a lot of symbolism and trying to tell a story, and a significant amount of the story telling floats in the parade were too abstract for me to glean a lot of meaning from. They just looked like angry volcanoes, and I still don't know what they were supposed to mean. I'll give it a 6/10. I'd have plenty more to say, but I think I'm out of room.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: The prologue really made me want to play the game. The aesthetic, the vibe, the ambience, it was all perfect. For the most part, this carried on through the game, and I enjoyed it. but then. it just completely shifted.I've played those kinda psychological games before, that are about life and death and corruption and power and all, and I've enjoyed them. But when a game that doesn't give off that vibe suddenly changes into one of those games, it's pretty anti-climatic. The last chunk of gameplay and story felt very out of place with the rest of the game, and the ending I think was disappointing. Sad, because I really think the game had so much potential, had it not decided to change genres in the middle.Also, it felt unfinished. Some of the dialogue was inconsistent, a few small bugs, just things that should've been worked out in playtesting. They didn't really impact the game too much, just could've been done better.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone/Tails Noir was... somethingIt was fun, the art and style was impeccable and the music fantastic, and between Acts 1 to 3 the story, worldbuilding, writing and characters were perfectEverything after just derails it. Weird sci-fi element gets thrown in and completely derails the story, turning it into something it shouldn't be with very little time to flesh it out.Very disappointing, unsatisfying ending. Don't know what they were doing. Feels like they went for some Disco Elysium with voices speaking to you in the end but it is just totally out of place, wrong and cheap.I don't mind a sad, depressive ending if it is narratively suited - noir is well known for it - but none of the questions in the whole game get answered. You never find out the why for anything in the story, you never really unmask the conspiracy, you never solve the mystery. Its just a total let down, which is made all the more tragic by how good it was from Acts 1 to 3. It lets down all the fantastic art, characters, writing and worldbuilding.Altogether a very unfortunate, frustrating experience because it could be so, so good - it just isn't.I'd love if they just gave it another shot. Rewrote it. I'd love for it to work and be good, it just doesn't. Its painful because I was invested in the story & its characters and they just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it so hard.The game is gorgeous. The art direction is superb and the music wonderful. Its all just such a let-down because of how the story just goes off the rails and ruins a good mystery noir.I just want my cop/mystery fiction with funny animal people and they bungled it >:(
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, I honestly don't get what people complaining about the ending are on about. It's a dialogue-based adventure game full of plot twists, with stylish pixel graphics and a more than decent soundtrack. I had fun till the end, and at no point felt like the devs were trying to wing it to make up for lack of ideas.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely beautiful Noir environmental surrounding visuals. The pixel art and the details are probably one of the best among indie games. And also with very soothing soundtracks and background effects that makes the story all the more thrilling.But after the prologue and second act the story gets kind of weird in name of thrilling and the ending is more weird but not bad, its more of a cliffhanger. Thus i think it will make more sense and the story will be understanding if they decides to release a sequel. But if they just decides to end it here then surely the art wont make up for the story. In conclusion, the game has potential which can be put on good use to make a masterpiece but on the other hand it can also turn out to be a unfinished project with cheap psychology as the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: This game starts off so strong with a compelling murder plot, gorgeous artwork and gritty atmosphere. For the first half of the game, stealth and item use mechanics hold enough interest to carry the plot along. However, the second half of this game feels incredibly rushed, and said mechanics are nowhere to be found. Essentially, the game devolves into a visual novel in the second half, and in my opinion, the overarching story is not fleshed out enough to maintain the compelling gameplay the first half offered. The second half of the game, I felt as though I was going through the motions in hopes that the part I was playing was just a lull in the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: A game rich in storytelling and beautiful pixel sceneries. You play as Howard, a raccoon private eye. As most noir detective stories go, your introduction to the story begins as your client asks you to investigate a missing person. The game took me by surprise when it introduced weird sci-fi to it's noir detective setting. It's what made the story stick out for me- What made me want to explore every nook and cranny it had to offer me. Don't be fooled by the game's looks though: This game is an  disguised as a point and click adventure. It's main focus is on . If you enjoy immersing yourself into a story, and reading, this game might be for you.  The different towns each have stunning pixel art. The areas feel alive with everything that's moving and buzzing. From the slums to the homes of people too rich for their own good, the art sets the mood very well. The visuals are accompanied by end-of-the-world jazzy music. Though, at times, the music seems to fade away for a long period of time, keeping you in long silences. The game offers a few sneaky areas and puzzles, though nothing too complicated. The focus is on it's story, and it sucks you right down the rabbit hole, after you reach a certain plot twist. A minor annoyance in the game is that you cannot  your progress. You need to keep playing until you reach a checkpoint, or lose all progress if you shut the game down too early. Also, I'm quite conflicted about the ending because it's so very very open-ended. Feels like there are so many things left unanswered. It's almost as if the game ended too early. Though I've heard that , perhaps,  and instead sit in these feelings for a while... . The developers shared a little mirror of their souls. I hope this isn't the last we will see of the world of Backbone and that they'll share more in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so very sad to give this game a bad review.The art direction in this game is fantastic, the music, graphics, character design, etc.But the end of the story is too incomplete, like it was made with a sequel in mind and not delivering an entire game. Also back in 2019 when I played the prologue I love it so much because there was a puzzle, some dialogue choices that made you access the building in different ways, but the rest of the chapters feels so lacking. All dialogue options have no impact, there are no more puzzles for the rest of the game,  and the story turnaround at the two last chapters feels so out of place for me.I kinda hope there will be a DLC that at least finish the story, even tho I feel it should have been made into the main game...
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Final recommendation: GO FOR IT! A brilliant narrative experience with fantastic visual flair, emphatic cinematography, and a bone-chilling musical score. Regardless of what you think of Backbone's narrative choices, this game will stay with you.Pros:-Crisply-written dialogue-Masterful soundtrack-Probably best pixel art you'll see all year-Possibly best pixel art of the entire decade-Gripping storyCons:-Story beats might not be agreeable to all
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the noir detective feel that this game offered. Sure there were some typos and maybe one or two glitches here and there but I enjoyed the story line and became invested in the fate of the main character and a few of the side characters as well. I love the variety of conversation choices and how it affected certain scenarios. I definitely recommend this game. The score brings you into the atmosphere of the game and I love the graphics.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What an amazing game. I haven't been this absorbed by a game in a long time. I loved it all the way through. What kept me even more captivated (other than the absolutely beautiful art) is how the story completely turns around at the end of every chapter. It seems like this was a negative feature to some players, as they were expecting a specific game style - from comments I have read, the twists and turns were frustrating for some. To me, that is what made Backbone stand out. The best way to enjoy the game is to just let yourself be immersed by the story. Don't expect a typical film noir detective story - that only lasts for about an hour. The story goes from banal detective tasks to the uncovering of a weird criminal operation, to a mystery around disappearances... to then find yourself in the middle of a high level corruption scandal with grotesque scientific experiments, psychological intrigue and post-apocalyptic wanderings, dotted with haunting abstractions, shocking reversals... I laughed, I cried, I gasped. The rendering of Vancouver is amazing - they really captured the essence of each neighbourhood as they are in real life, but tailored to fit this uncanny valley anthropomorphized animal world. I looked at every detail I could see, read all the texts and dialogues and my playthrough ended up taking about 15 hours. So worth it. I can't wait to play the Backbone preludes coming out next year!
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for games similar to "The Return of Obra Dinn" and came across this recommendation. I really liked the art style and I love crime-themed stories, so I decided to give this a shot despite the mixed reviews.I really enjoyed it. The game was shorter than I expected, and the plot took an unexpected turn and became very philosophical near the end. But it still took me on a great journey and left a lasting mark. I've become so immersed in the Backbone world, and I hope there will be sequels or other games that take place in the same universe. I can see how it was disappointing for fans who've followed the game since the Kickstarter days, but I still think it's worth the play.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Play the free Prologue and pretend it's the full game.Pros:- Great music.- Stunning visuals.- Good prologue, and the two following acts are interesting too.- Simple gameplay that's perfectly fine for this kind of game.Cons:- Sound effects and ambient sounds are missing more often than not.- Weird dialogue writing. It sometimes feels like the characters are having internet conversations when speaking face to face.- After the third act the main plot gets abandoned for a completely unnecessary twist that ruins the entire game. What a massive disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I was super excited for this game after the prologue. It really nails a cool setting and atmosphere with its art and music imo. I just really wish the story was developed better. I'm not a writer and I mainly go off of my own emotions when judging a story, how it invokes emotion into me. It felt like the visuals carried so much weight and meaning in them that the story wasn't building up to correctly. If I were to take any guess as to why I felt this way I would say that the story is developed in such a way that it is a study of Howard as a character and the struggles and achievements he makes as such a smaller cog in a machine, but we never get to learn too much about him. Idk I'm probably rambling but long story short everything about this game artistically great except the story got cut short by writing or game design hell imo.I hope the next game learns from the mistakes of the first installment and uses the success of this game to hopefully fund better time and resources into the story as well for this visual novel.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I have to agree more so with the negative reviews but, I would still recommend this game merely for the world-building and heavy lore displayed here. I love pixel-art games and a good story. I waited a long time for this game and was completely entranced with the prologue. I did expect something different with the final game and with each passing act I was hoping the narrative would catch up with itself but I was left disappointed ...the ending more-so. A large part of me was hoping I had just found the "bad ending" but turns out, it was the only ending. I loved the prologue, I wish so many ideas weren't blended together so the story had a more linear effect and the twists more organic. There's so many questions left unanswered and I feel unsatisfied. Fingers crossed for a part two or at least, a DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game? It's a tough question that I really went back and forth on. The positives are very positive: the art is beautiful and the creators clearly made this with a great deal of passion. They made some risky choices in terms of genre-switching (which many of the negative reviews comment on if you want to read more) which DID make me want to see what they would do next. Moreover, the dialogue choices were extremely well thought out: there was no "good answer" "neutral answer" "bad answer" choices. Instead there was more nuance to it: some characters needed more threatening, others more buttering up, and so the navigation of social situations was really compelling to manage...even if it was relatively illusory (as failing seemed impossible).The negatives, however, are that fundamentally, while I appreciate the risks they took, for me, they didn't work out, and the plot -- while it built intrigue well -- didn't have enough pay off.So I, personally, wouldn't recommend it as a 'this game is amazing and will change your life' game; I WOULD recommend it as a 'you might not like it, but it's worth trying' game. Do with that what you will.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to give this game an up vote though I would prefer some sort of in between rating. Overall I enjoyed "Backbone" for its in game world, beautiful pixel art and often times humorous protagonist. The issues I had playing concerned its story. I believe the first half was stronger than the second as it begins with a detective noir inspired story that reminded me of "Chinatown" one of my all time favorite films. Mid way through, the story takes a genre altering twist that disappointed my expectations for a competent crime thriller. What I got instead kept my interest but at a greatly diminished level. For fans of pixel art and animation, I highly recommend  this game but for people looking for a story in the film noir genre, I think you may be disappointed. Still, I do not regret supporting this game on Kickstarter and was happy to see my name scroll by during the credits.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: It's a visually beautiful game that feels a rushed in it's handling of the main story towards the end of the game. It starts out very detective-like then introduces more sci-fi themes in the later end of the game, that just brings up more questions in a more frustrating way. Despite the ending, the gameplay is nice and the characters all over the game are pleasant to talk to, each one feeling unique. The story is lovely to sit through up into the later halfway part although, but it can be subjective. I can only recommend this if you like more indie styled games, or detective games with a unique narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this makes me wish that the review system in Steam was more in depth.Review are obviously personal and subjective, but i dont know if i would be able to recomend this gameThe music is really goodgraphics are really goodgameplay is simple, but fine but narrative wise? i think it falls offIt starts really really strong, this game has a really cool universe, but the way the story was told and the way it develops i honestly think it just doesnt stick the landing (narrative wise)i still think that if you are curious about it you sould play it
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I kickstarted this game and it had a lot of potential.  Unfortunately, 90% of the potential was poured into the prologue chapter released as a demo a few years ago.  After the prologue, it very quickly sheds any pretense of puzzle solving / deduction and goes straight into a rigidly linear interactive fiction with player input affecting little other than whether a given interaction results in getting a Steam achievement.Unfortunately, while I would have also been happy with a noir VN game, this too quickly unravels as the narrative jumps around and discards plot points it just introduced to focus on new ones, which it then casts off with equal vigor.  While feeling lost with too many loose ends is indeed a staple trope of the noir genre, it makes for a very unsatisfying story when you take a step back and try to make sense of it all as a player.Overall, I don't regret playing it, however I can assure other people that playing the freely available prologue demo is just as fun as playing the "full game" since it's clear that WAS the full game from a development stance.The developers put in a lot of hard work and I'd be interested to see what else they produce, but I hope their next project sees them learn from their mistakes here.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, I wanted to love this game as I loved the prologue but I was disappointed. Don't get me wrong, it's a beautiful game with a beautiful soundtrack, full of details and a great universe is constructed. But it's not what the prologue had made me expect. The prologue had a puzzle and made you use your deduction, the full game had none of this and only relied in dialogue. At first I was ok with the story, for the first three chapters more or less. But, as others have said, the final chapters are substantially shorter than the others, and the story changes abruptly and clumsily.Also, some dialogues are pretty cringe and the protagonist is always whining. If this was written by tumblr I would believe it.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous game with an amazing soundtrack. The story is promising, with compelling characters and an interesting story of political intrigue. The first three acts of the story are great, however I believe it falls off right at the end of Act 3, where it then proceeds through the fourth and fifth acts which have a way different feel than the Acts before. These last three acts are also much shorter than the previous. I was able to get 2 hours each from Acts 1 and 2, however 3, 4, and 5 were collectively about 2 hours.The ending feels abrupt and rushed, if not just a bit disappointing, however it is obvious that the story is cut off the way that it is to leave an opening for a sequel, combined with the fact that this was a Kickstarter game, making me wonder if they maybe ran out of funding for the last leg of development. Regardless, Tails Noir is a good game despite the shortcomings of the ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is beautiful and the beginning of the game was great and intriguing. However, near the end, the game felt rushed and there was so much potential for this game to flush out the world and explore more of the story.  I only got around 6 hours of playtime for a game that costs 25 euros (not worth it in my opinion)
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: This game was complicated...it had BEAUTIFUL graphics, the characters and atmosphere really drew in you in at the beginning, the story from acts 1-3 were intriguing, it's a noir/graphic novel, and I really liked Howard a lot for his personality and sarcasm. The few puzzles were great. Wish there had been more puzzles. Acts 1-3 had a great lead in the story and were smooth. It made you want to learn more and offered up surprises all along the way (as well as interesting characters). Now, the ending...I liked the abstract explanation and contemplation of what was happening ok, but the ending seemed a little jumbled and incoherent?? I don't see how this tied back to acts 1-3 when you were doing something completely different before and the story jumped. It kinda comes out of left field suddenly. It wasn't bad enough to give it a thumbs down though. I just wish it had been a bit more concise and things had been tied off a bit neater/better explanation. If they went back and edited the ending or added more meat (ha!) to the story, I would've easily given it a higher score, but for me this game was about a 8/10. I enjoyed it, ignored the weird ending, and thought the beginning/middle overall was enjoyable. I hope there is a sequel or DLC to continue this because right now the ending was bleak and kinda unimpressive.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I played the initial demo and really enjoyed the pacing and wish that could have continued into the full length. It's not bad awful, but it's somewhat frustrating given the promise of the original demo. Dialogue writing and some bits of the gameplay just seemed unpolished. Also distracted by bites of Disco Elysium. I lost interest after about 4 hours of play and am very glad i got this during a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Howard is a raccoon Private Investigator that gets a job to find out about a cheating husband. Seemed simple, but it got complicated, to say the least.The game is somewhat of a deviant from typical point and click adventure games - for starters, it's not the normal "point and click" - you hardly ever need to use a mouse and most of it is played with left, right and action. Inventory is there, but there's no need to check it except to see the object's icons. This makes the game seem simple, but it gets the depth from the narrative instead - Backbone is a very narrative driven and dependent game, so get ready to read a lot and realise that this is essential to understand the game's experience. Puzzles itself are rare, but those few are actually good, creative and I found them very enjoyable.Graphics are gorgeous, 2.5D pixelart mixed with some 3D objects / scenarios and brilliant placed lighting effects. Music is also something special. This game fits perfectly with Raw Fury's promotion that "Games are Art". It won't please everyone, but Art rarely does, and that doesn't make it less brilliant.Most of Backbone is the player talking to other chars and choosing dialogues - those will allow you to play the story as a polite PI, a caring individual, or if you so wish, an insensitive and verbally violent one. Those choices will affect how you overcome some situations and also some of the game's Steam achievements.This game is a brutal ride. Violence takes many shapes, and Backbone touched a lot of them.Expect several "face slaps" as the story bridges several of our own very real world problems to an animal inhabited alternate reality.Backbone is real, personal real it seems sometimes, and unresolved, but also beautiful, inspired, hopeful and unresolved... like life.Loved it - Eggnut did a tremendous job with their creation.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: Words can't describe how disappointed I am.The demo promised a different game in a lot of ways. It had at least one puzzle, which was fun to solve. It had you sneaking around. It had you observe and manipulate your surroundings. It implied that your choices mattered.Some of the things I liked in the demo are still there. The dialogue is fantastic and flows well. Even the flavor texts are good. The characters and the way they act are convincing. The atmosphere, and the music that surrounds it are consistently good. The prologue and first act are intriguing.I haven't seen any reviews mentioning the computer hacking puzzle, which actually requires a couple of conditions to be met to work. However, you only have to go and interact with things in the same room a couple of times and you can eventually breeze through it easily. It doesn't make you work and deduce enough, which is why it probably doesn't register as a puzzle. What if you had to go take a walk to find the hint-giving parrot? What if you had to check and drag photos and documents on the table or on a board to deduce parts of the password, like in the prologue? What if you had to type out the password instead of choosing from a list of ready-made answers? I doubt any of these changes would've stolen enormous amounts of development time or resources. You'd be using isolated systems that already existed in the game. A couple more of these peppered throughout each chapter, and the ginormous "detective adventure" part of the game's description could've been dealt with.The choices mattering part is tougher to deal with. An extended epilogue where you see the results of your actions throughout the game could've helped. For instance, do you explicitly reveal who told you about the apartment you sneak into in act 2? It is clearly implied that doing so will be bad for the guy who told you about it and his sister who needs medicine to survive. Again, two scenes for each outcome, no animation, just a couple of characters frozen in time and a camera scroll, plus a couple of lines of text. Recycle backgrounds where appropriate. Not the ideal solution, but miles better than the realization that your choices had no effect on the world. Suddenly, you see that everything you did mattered.Another choice: maybe decide whether you're gonna meet up with Anatoly or not after an alien blob attaches itself to you. Being an idiot and trying to contact him kills him. Fast forward to epilogue: you see his house, either Anatoly is looking outside the window thinking dark thoughts about where the hell his friend went, or you see his family in mourning, wondering what the hell happened to the father of the house. Damn that would've been intense. You can still have your depressing ending, and it would've meant something. Whatever you do, and actually do, you end up losing something. Damn that would've ruledThere's a ton of lore and new, weird stuff thrown at you towards the end. But the game doesn't prepare you for them, and it doesn't allow you to spend enough time with the new stuff it introduces you to. In fact, you don't get to spend enough time with anything that is implied to be important. Not with Renee, not with your new friends under the bridge, not with Howard's mother, not with Anatoly, not with the always mentioned but barely seen apes, and not with the harmful "friend" that follows you till the end.I also hate the idea of being forced to sympathize with a serial murdering, drug peddling mob boss who's willing to sacrifice an innocent man in a freak experiment designed to advance her nebulously defined idea of revolution in a city that manages to remain unplagued by electricity shortages or famine despite sitting in the middle of an apocalyptic wasteland. Her excuses and grievances are unconvincing and effin lame. Howard should've stabbed her with his newfound alien tumor powers. Alas, the script decided that Anatoly, a cheeky fellow and great friend, was more deserving of such fate.Here's a couple of nitpicks that aren't nearly as crucial but were still noticeable: no inbetween animation between standing and crouching, no chapter selection once the game ends, and no dialog selection input if Interact is remapped to Z (Because it's set to scroll text up).The very talented team probably had to wrap up earlier than they expected. They probably had all these ideas they wanted to expand upon and found there was not enough time left. I would've been fine with a regular detective story, without the ruined sci-fi world and alien buggery. A cannibal conspiracy in an animal world is already weird and interesting enough. Dealing exclusively with that would've been probably more than enough, and allow the story to pay attention to the stuff that was already there.I feel for the team, and all the effort that went into this, but I can't recommend this game. Ideally, the team would pull a No Man's Sky, ie cut the social media nonsense and focus exclusively on fixing what's already there. But the open letter doesn't give much hope. And it's probably not financially possible at this point anyway. Oh well
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: This'll be a bit scatterbrained of a review, so apologies in advance.Upon playing the game's prologue/demo, I was extremely excited for this game. It seemed to hit all the right notes, the tone, the dialogue, the story, the choices, the puzzles, the stealth, everything....sadly, the only consistency after that, was the visuals and audio. The rest of the game feels like it just kinda loses direction halfway through and completely shifts gears.It also doesn't take long to notice that your dialogue choices kinda... don't really matter. I feel like if you really wanted to, you could just button mash your way through almost everything after the prologue and still leave the game with as much information as you would had you been fully paying attention. The story does very little to fill you in on what's actually going on after it switches it's gears.The text itself isn't horrible, although there's a fair few spelling and grammar mistakes I noticed. Far more than I'd think would normally slip through the cracks.The inventory system honestly feels... like it was also forgotten halfway through it's inception. The items in your inventory often aren't used for anything, can't be examined, or have even already been used for something. So having used items still sitting there just seems kinda pointless. It's hardly even a memento.I still absolutely adore the visual and audio of this game. It's damn near perfect, and I want to see more of it. PLEASE let there be more of this. I just wish the rest of the game was able to match the pace of the prologue/intro.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand where people are coming from, this was a good game. Perhaps this is because I didn't play this game with the same expectations others did, maybe there was some kind of update after those reviews were made, perhaps I'm just someone who finds more enjoyment in things such as poetry, but this game speaks a lot to me. ^^
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: first things first, like everyone has mentioned, the art direction is amazing and so is the music, it's dark, gritty and a few tracks with vocals were sublime.now, on to the bad stuff.i was sold by the free prologue for sure. if only the full game was as good as that. i mean it does include the prologue which i got to play again and basically sped run the thing. and the rest was such a huge letdown to be honest. and i guess it was supposed to make sense with the game title? the story was weak and all over the place. the ending left so much to be desired. the few minutes before the end disrupted the flow of the game. why was i allowed to control different characters? some grammar mistakes here and there also took away the immersion. it's sorta sad to be honest, i really wanted this game to be good. and i only found out about the prologue a couple months ago. imagine the people backing the project since 2018 and waited till now. sorry guys.i seriously hope there will be a dlc or something because the ending is justyea, it's like that.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I was hoping that most reviews were very critical and that I would still find it a fun enough game, unfortunately I was very underwhelmed at the end. Artwork of this game is beautiful and one of the best things about this game. Although even that at some places seemed a bit unfinished for example NPC's appearing out of thin air with no animation that they come through a door or NPC's text balloons not fitting the entire screen so that you miss part of the conversation. I had the same feeling with the music. When there was music it was very atmospheric and added a lot to the game but there were also long scenes with barely any music or sounds to the point that I thought there was something wrong with my headphones. And the story unfortunately indeed went downhill after Act 2. And it's not so much that I didn't like the outcome or where the story was heading, it's more that a lot of ideas were not worked out properly and especially at the end it felt very rushed. It felt like I was waiting the whole time for the plot to be revealed but then the credits start rolling..  I was very underwhelmed. I would not recommend other than maybe the DEMO.

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone is a very interesting game to say the least. I can understand why the reviews are mixed, the direction this story goes into can either lose people or strengthen the love some can have for this game. I fall under the ladder, I really loved this game.The art direction and the cinematic aspect of the game is nothing to overlook, the world building is fantastic and there is always something to look at or explore, even if the story is somewhat self contained. The game-play is very simple but simple is all this game needs to get its message across, and I enjoyed the message. Minor Spoilers below  addressing the mixed reviews: The story takes a huge turn towards the end of Act 3, which from what I have read is where at least half of the players started to dislike the story and the direction it went. For me I was interested in where it could go, and after watching the credits roll what happened doesn't seem like it came from nowhere. It was established early on that the protagonist needed some sort of change in their life, and this was the change they needed to realize something out of pocket, true blissful peace. I see a lot of people angry that some plot threads remain unresolved, for me it seemed like that's what needed to happen, to deliver a message that life doesn't wrap itself up in a neat bow for everyone. It is a good message to internalize and whether or not the game was intending to deliver that or not, that is one of the main themes I picked up from it.I would be interested in this game receiving a sequel, but I also understand if it is a one off story. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Mainly giving this a positive review because I think it's worth playing and many people might avoid it due to its mostly-negative takes. I liked this game a lot, and I disagree with many people's grievances about it.It terms of it being a mostly linear game, I never got the impression from the Prologue that it wasn't going to be. I really enjoy the visual novel genre, that's what I expected this game to be, and that's what it was. Many reviewers were disappointed that it wasn't like Disco Elysium, but I think it's faulty to assume it ever intended to be. Disco Elysium, I'm sure, will go down as a total paradigm shift in the way video games even tell stories. Backbone just had the unfortunate timing of being released as the discourse over DE continues to flood the forums.Others complain about the ending being jarringly sudden and practically no ending at all. I'm honestly only speculating, but I highly doubt this is where the story ends, even if the game itself is over. A better comparison to Backbone than Disco Elysium is a game like Jenny LeClue, which is also a noir-ish story that has a linear plot and a non-ending. As a backer, my sister told me that the game will have two sequels, but when the game dropped the publishers didn't mention anything about it since it took them years to release it. A lot of people aren't aware of just how much time it takes for Kickstarter games to come out. Kentucky Route Zero, a game I really like, took about 7 years to complete, with as many as 3 years in between Acts. It had a development team of three people, one of whom exclusively did music. Games that release in a timely manner almost always have massive teams of criminally overworked employees working 80-hour weeks for months on end.A legitimate criticism of Backbone is its length when considering its price. It takes about 7 hours to complete but it costs as much as a game 2 to 3 times as long.  Wait for it to be on sale, but it's still worth playing. Some of the dialogue trees are a bit clunky, but I'm not a huge stickler for that as long as the game is still engaging. Which Backbone is.This is by far not my favorite game I've played this year, but it's one that deserves more love than it's getting right now, so I'm giving in a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: Backbone Review:Allow me to preface with: I had fun with this game in a broad sense, but this ultimately isn't a fun game or a satisfying story. There may be spoilers.Art: 9/10I'll start with something I'm fairly certain most people will agree on. The art and style of the game is gorgeous, it presents you with a rich and vibrant-looking world that looks and feels lived in. You won't be seeing any sweeping vistas or locations that make you stop to appreciate the view, yet the style works for what the developer was aiming for.Music/Sound Design: 7/10Backbone has a sparse and subtle soundscape, and for once in my life, I would say that works to its detriment. Everything regarding sound in this game is clearly carefully picked to evoke certain emotions and expectations, and there are times where it absolutely nails what it's doing. Such as your first step into The Bite, a night club where a rather gorgeous track is sung, setting the mood wonderfully as you look for an adulterous husband (As private investigators are wont to do in noir detective stories.)Other times, you might not even really register if there's music playing at all, being instrumental, consigned to the background, and often feeling too subtle and non-descript.And admittedly worse is during a late-game cutscene where you're sat around a fire with a rather gorgeous song is played over a relatively static (no animations except idle, no control, etc.) cutscene where nothing really happens. The lack of interesting visuals forced me to skip the cutscene since there was nothing else to it.Gameplay: 4/10Admittedly, this is where the game really suffers. This game has one complex puzzle at the beginning, and one relatively easy puzzle at the midpoint. The former is just obtuse enough that you're going to be spending some time at it unless you have a friend who played it before give you a hint, or you look it up yourself. (I had the former, after spending several minutes trying to figure things out and growing impatient.)This game has absolutely brilliant moments where you're gathering clues and interrogating witnesses and for those shining moments, it feels like you're actually a detective unraveling a conspiracy. But then those moments pass, that feeling fades, and you're left wandering around looking for the next plot point.This game suffers from a lack of interactivity in spite of having a lot you can interact with. You will meet with a fair number of people whom you will spend a lot of time ultimately talking about nothing. It's a nice touch, but it feels like details for the sake of making the world seem larger.Story: 4/10This game has two major problems in regards to its story: Scope and cohesion.This game spends a lot of time building up the world around it, allowing you to interact with a lot of otherwise irrelevant things, and presenting a grand conspiracy involving murder, corruption, and strange science. Yet despite the game's attempts at connecting these concepts, it feels more like you're reading off a laundry list of Bad Things Happening than finding natural connections with the mystery at the core of the game.A major, shocking revelation is your introduction to the conspiracy, and while the protagonist is given an absolutely awesome realistic and visceral reaction to the scene that haunts him through the game, it's explicit, it tells you, 'This is the situation, deal with it', rather than using subtlety and implying this is the case, letting your mind wonder at if what the game is implying is actually the case.This is where the game reveals it has no faith in you by introducing to the character who will guide you through the mystery, who knows some details you don't, sending you to your next point from then on.You follow some tenuous threads that happen to lead to the next plot point, and after infiltrating a home to look for clues, asking around regarding some disappearances, and infiltrating a secure laboratory...Symbolism: 3/10I don't normally bring up symbolism in a game, but I absolutely need to for this one. Bluntly, this game has a lot of attempts at symbolic moments that ultimately don't amount to anything. The aforementioned campfire moment, a long walk at the end, certain activities in the game where you're forced to do some mundane task (making tea) while the protagonist ruminates on events, all of it qucikly feels like time-wasting padding to ensure you won't complete the game under two hours. (This game took me four hours from start to completion.)This game spends a lot of time building up an otherwise contextless world, and at times feels like it needs to explain certain things, like, "Why are there anthropomorphic animals in this setting?" or "What is the racism like in this world?" It feels like the game is trying to convey some deeper meaning behind these concepts, and it ultimately fails to make them meaningful. It fails to give the player a connection to the story.And at the end, the game deigns to give you an epilogue where specific motivations that weren't really hinted at are given, blatantly telling you that power and corruption are a force to be fought against and that there are no easy or truly palatable ways to fight it if you want to make progress.Final Thoughts:This game simultaneously feels too long and too short. For the story it gives you, the padding it makes you slog through, and ultimately the way the plot ultimately resolves, the game could have cut off the fat and kept the game linear and you would have had roughly the same experience. And given more time and content to build up the central mystery and ensure it resolves in a satisfying manner, I could easily see this game lengthened to an eight-hour length where the plot is given more room to present everything in a more organic and cohesive way.Give this game a pass. If you're absolutely set on getting the story, watch a let's play or a twitch stream. If the demo impressed you, I would argue that is developers putting their best foot forward and failing to keep up the momentum.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: If you're wanting a furry game that has a genuine noir theme and story to it, look elsewhere. If you've already played the prologue/demo, you've already played the best part of the game, it only gets worse from there.Long version: WARNING SPOILERS AHEAD:Tails Noir is a game that tries to sell itself as a pixelated furry noir detective game, but it falls short in basically every category, except for the pixelated art, that much, they did well.The plot is pretty standard fare noir, gritty, engaging, mysterious, etc, for the first half. However, once you get outside of Gastown, it veers off into bizarro, modern-day politics, and themes/issues that are completely foreign to the grittiness and darkness that is noir. It almost feels like the first half and second half storylines/plots of the game were written by two completely different people, the first being at least somewhat acquainted with noir and wanted to keep the in-game universe on that track, and the second, someone who is completely unfamiliar with noir, who wanted to graft noir elements onto a grossly hamfisted political message. The only interesting part about the second half was the stuff surrounding "Project Artifact".The second half also has you waste a significant amount of time doing some kind of dumb communist larp with a bunch of people living under a bridge (think the whole CHAZ idiocy, but with furries, and an equally pathetic garden)? This part drags on, and other than a few lines of dialog, is *completely* removed from the plot/storyline altogether, it tries to get you to connect with characters that really aren't all that interesting (including one who apparently smuggles people over the "evil wall" to escape "bigotry" and stuff (things that noir detectives definitely care about), using ill-gotten funds from the main antagonist (basically blood money, which I explain in the next part), and instead you spend this entire time wondering when you will get back to the actual story. Unfortunately, you really don't. The main character dies shortly after, and you're left in a bizarre conversation with the main antagonist who, despite the diabolical things she did earlier in the game (including murdering her own family), the game appears to try and paint as the "good guy" because essentially "the ends justify the means". That part sounds pretty bad already, until you realize that the money she funneled to CHAZ anti-wall/bigotry guy (blood money), to get people over the "evil wall" was obtained by *literally* murdering and butchering people to serve to cannibals (a gruesome discovery you make in the first half of the game), no exaggeration, no lie. The game literally tries to convince you that her murdering and butchering people, and serving them to an elite group of cannibals was totally cool, because the people she murdered were mean people, and by virtue of those horrendous acts, she helped a lesbian rabbit couple escape over the wall. Dude. Seriously. No hyperbole, no exaggeration, that is what the game *actually* tries to convince you of.As for the main character, he goes from being a typical hard shelled, gritty, drunk private eye, something you would expect to see in practically any noir classic, to a spineless doormat who lets pretty much anyone of the opposite sex walk all over him, and who has mommy issues? As in teenage "I hate my parents" angst that just makes you wonder how he became a P.I. in the first place? And in the end, turns into a pile of goo, due to effects from the Artifact.I could go on some more, but you get the idea.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game enough, and compared to a movie in terms of cost/value would recommend it as an entertaining experience... I actually played through it very quickly because I really loved aspects of it compared to many games, but was ultimately left disappointed about what this game was after playing the prologue.  The visuals were nice and I was gripped enough by the story.  HOWEVER, and it's a big however, the prologue presented more physical gameplay (puzzles and sneak action), while the remaining four episodes had minimal to none of it.  After episode 2, the tone shifted in a way that I actually would normally enjoy but there was little to no explanation for what was happening or character building with the new people you met.  I would have enjoyed each episode if they were waaay longer and more involved, with learning about who everyone one and actual consequences for dialogue.  It sort of felt like I was clicking through a book (which, if you take this as a perspective of a graphic novel which I was prepared to, is not a bad thing), but the ending just felt like... they wanted me to purchase a second game to get some answers?  Yeah... if they cut out the last few chapters of any book it's not going to make me want the sequel. I'm sorry.  For a game I mostly enjoyed, I am left with a bad taste in my mouth which may or may not be monkeybutt.

_childDocuments_.review: I found out about Backbone shortly after the release of Night in the Woods in 2017. I had never really played any indie games before but NITW so enamoured me with its visual design, character interaction and soundtrack that I wanted more.The promise of an indie game with a 'post-noir' detective adventure coupled with pixel graphics plus strong attention to visual design and artistic detail - well it had me hooked. Come release day I eagerly purchased it, excited to experience what I had been holding out for so long for. And???Ehh........The artistic details and visual design throughout the whole game are amazing and everything I was led to expect. Gameplay starts out solid if not a little quirky but hey, it's a first time indie studio and a dystopian plot. Soon though you notice the slide. First the decline in puzzles and interactivity, then the sense that your lines of questioning are no longer having any real influence over the story progression.I won't go into any more detail here lest I inadvertently drop spoilers. Suffice to say that I am not alone in these observations and you can navigate over to the Community Discussions if you want to read more in depth.The whole game progressively feels more & more rushed. To the point where the ending comes across as commensurate to walking to the front of the class, hastily still trying to scribble on your paper before you have to hand it in.If Backbone had cost a few dollars on sale or I had played it as part of a game pass subscription I probably would have looked past these shortcomings. However I paid almost $36AUD for barely 5 hours of "gameplay" even with exploring everywhere and aiming for maximum immersion. Replayability? Ha!In contrast, NITW cost me just under $20AUD at release, has provided me over 52 hours of play time and three or possibly four playthroughs exploring the different storylines of each of the main characters.Backbone: It could have been so much more.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails Noir (Backbone) is an indie game by a Belarus studio.The pixel art is gorgeous and the main selling point.The writing is good and music is great.While the overall story starts strong, it does not stick the landing.The game is marketed as a detective or point & click genre game, in reality it is more of a visual novel.The game was very intriguing, promising a hard-boiled noir detective story,but soon devolved from conspiracy to aliens or such stuff.The abrupt ending was weak and did not stick the landing.Also some story elements were rushed, such as the mob boss Clarissa being a misandrist sexist.Nowhere through the story or writing, was it clear to us.Yet in the game, she throws all these feminist/sexist terms at us. Wtf? There is also only a single ending and no way of failure, meaning your choices do not matter.I wish there was more interactivity and agency given to the player.From what I researched, a lot of great ideas and potential has been lost during development.Whole gameplay elements have been removed. Promised to somewhat return in the new Tails game (prequel).I liked a lot of things about Tails Noir, but seeing how I procrastinated 22 out of my 26 hours doing something elseand only played it for like 4 hours, says a lot about this game.I give it a 5.5/10 and got the game for below $5,as there is no neutral rating on Steam, with a heavy heart I will give it a Positive rating (but just barely).
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: I considered writing a fleshed out review for this game but it seems the top negative reviews have already put in words my thoughts and feelings about it. Having been a big fan of the prologue, the only word that comes to mind after finishing the game is, betrayal. Calling an unfinished, obviously rushed, incoherent mess of a story, "subjective art", is ignorant and lazy to me. I'm not sure if the writing was trying too hard to sound "deep and sophisticated" or if they were just writing down whatever came to mind and calling it good enough.By the time I got to the end screen of the game the only emotions I felt were disappointment and pity for all the Kickstart backers whose names were flashing on the screen, and imagining how disappointed the lot of them felt after seeing the support go to this half-baked mess of an experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to ignore my friends when they said that the story ran off the rails mid way through chapter 3 but they were right. It went from PI takes a job and gets way in over their head to "we live in a society" to finally "Suddenly, Aliens" It throws out the noir in favor for a jumbled mess that brings up questions only to never answer on it. The gameplay is simple, you walk around your the area collect clues, interact with the people, hide if necessary. The game itself is short, abour 3-4 hours worth of gameplay with no replayability unless you're going to go all achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails Noir

_childDocuments_.review: It really stretches the definition of a game. The first/demo level has some gameplay elements; two stealth sections and a paper perspective puzzle. The demo definitely gives an unfair impression, I was surprised how the rest of the game was literally just side-scrolling and dialogue. When I was given a gun in the third act, I was hoping that something would happen, but it's only visible (not usable) for a short sequence where you're again just talking to someone.I'm not expecting an incredible breadth of content, but playing the game is pretty much walking from side to side to find the next character to converse with. I'm not sure if there's a fail condition for any of these interactions, so it boils down to just being a VN (although other VNs would probably have more consequences for your actions and more than one ending).  The game isn't an investigation or adventure, it's just going from point A to B.The game has very strong visual direction, probably being the most finished part of the game. The soundscape is deeply lacking however, where I stopped at one point thinking my audio must be bugged with how silent everything is.The story's pacing is off, where the mystery of a cannibal conspiracy is dropped like a hot potato for . I wouldn't mind the change in pace to explore the setting's mysterious wall and what lies beyond it, but the story goes nowhere.  Some people said they liked the story and characters but it feels like it was too compact and there should have been more closure to certain plot points, especially at the ending.It feels like a lot of love went into the game, but so much was again left out for release. It's a game you really want to like for the protagonist and art style, but it just doesn't give much back.I got the game in Humble Choice, so I can't recommend buying it for the 25 EUR is goes for at full price. As far as indie goes, 25 euros would get you much further than this.

_childDocuments_.review: - No spoilers contained withinBackbone's demo prologue sold itself as a 2.5D point & click adventure with both multiple branching game play and dialogue options. Sadly, the actual finished product is much more akin to a visual novel. A very short (3/4hr) and quite muddled one at that.It comes as no surprise that the high point of Backbone is the pixel art aesthetic which is stellar and reminiscent of what "The Last Night" could have been had it ever been released. The game's city environment also feels authentic, detailed and a real sense of world building is achieved with the population and class struggle of the creatures who live inside it. Unfortunately, the story it tries to tell using that foundation could have done with way more time in revision.The multiple choice path selection and puzzle solving of the opening act completely disappear after the prologue, in-turn leading to 4 further (and much shorter) acts of essentially walking along a 2D plane of each scene, initiating dialogue boxes where all the available conversational choices lead to a predetermined outcome, regardless of which options you decide to choose.While the game attempts to keep main character intentions grey and ambiguous like you would expect in any good detective-noir story, this unfortunately has the side effect of making them annoying and unexpectedly 'floppy' in their response behaviour. Not selecting an expected dialogue option makes characters almost completely switch personality at a flick of a switch. Thus, role-playing your main protagonist 'Howard' as anything other than an utter paragon or self centered renegade gives /you the player/ an impression that you are selecting the wrong sequential options and as such missing important dialogue or back story.Of course, as mentioned earlier, you soon realize that none of the dialogue you choose has any real or tangible consequence. The story is very much on rails and will always reach the same conclusion without encountering any dead ends or alternative branching options. Being sympathetic to characters you meet earlier on in the game opens up some (that you can count on one hand) alternative dialogue in later chapters, but other than making you feel good about yourself and unlocking achievements, it achieves little else.The much greater problem than the dialogue options is the story surrounding it. It begins as the expected 'down on his luck detective' cliche - which would have been just fine if it continued that way - (having worked just fine in 'Blacksad' as a recent example). During the prologue, it is grounded in a reality that despite the talking animals, was easy to follow, relate towards and logical.However with Backbone, after the 2 hour mark, it turns into an almost science fiction, 'unknown ancient world' with 'mysterious forces' type affair. The initial murders in The Bite featured in the prologue almost completely dropped in order to dramatically increase the scope towards some greater mystery of what the city and world you live in is and who are the mysterious 'apes' in control.It probably comes as no surprise to you reading this that none of that is sufficiently explained or resolved by the games ending. Despite having 5 chapters, you could even argue that the 'game' essentially finishes after chapter 3. The rest being a long (tedious) drawn out ending, that repeatedly tries to mimic Disco Elysium's opposing inner monologues. While Disco Elysium had game-play reasons for that mechanic being there; enabling you to shape your characters mental disposition in a way that you choose. Backbone has no reason for this, and might as well have just been a cut-scene without yet more pointless dialogue choices.There's also gaping holes in the logic of characters and their motivations, which makes your introduced job as a P.I. who's primary goal it is to understand these, meaningless and frustrating. If Howard has lived in this city his whole life - not a giant one by any stretch, why is he (for the most part) unaware of almost all of the social structure, establishments or people he interacts within it? There's many plot points, such as mysterious symbols found in the park during the start of the game, that are never used or mentioned again. Two interactive city maps that detail a multitude of locations you never actually visit. An inventory system that is never actually used and has no reason to even be included. An incredibly contrived and forced relationship with a character you barely know that has no grounding, history or basis to elicit the responses offered to you. A blink and you miss it character switch at the end that has no reason to exist other than spouting off a few 'hot takes' on feminist political issues which for the entire game isn't mentioned by anyone else. The list really could go on and on..The developer Eggnut are given ample leeway for being a new and relatively small team, yet it is difficult to not compare Backbone to similar games from similar sized studios such as the excellent 'Gemini Rue' a few years back. In the case of that game, they managed to mix a coherent detective story, interesting and varied 2D puzzle based game play with choices that matter and an actual meaningful conclusion to finish. In comparison, if I was describing it as a meal; Backbone is a lot of visually appealing garnish on a meal with no meat that simply wasn't put in the oven long enough to be edible.When '80's era Sierra games from literally a 2 person husband and wife team could tell a complete story from beginning to end /with/ plenty of varied game-play interspersed between the narrative, it makes you wonder if the developers really did any homework on this genre or performed any meaningful play-testing. Both of which would have more than undoubtedly given them the same feedback they're now being bombarded with in negative reviews. When it reaches the stage of a developer having to write an open letter explaining their decisions as damage control, it's fair to say they've messed up either in promotion or in delivery of the product itself.In conclusion, Backbone feels like hugely wasted potential. The sheer amount of character and story threads left unanswered and general lack of closure with the ending hints at a more than likely continuation being planned for this series, yet if no lessons are taken from this debacle and it's just more of the same 'game' demonstrated within Backbone, it's doubtful that many people will be enticed to give them the benefit of the doubt a second time around.**It's also worth mentioning that the credits give a disclaimer of 'No characters are based on real life people, if so it's coincidental" etc. This is clearly //false// as a prominent politically charged twitter user under the same character name and same animal alias is clearly depicted in Act 4 and referenced by name throughout the game. Further-more, Eggnut and BackboneGame twitter accounts are both following this person's twitter account, suggesting that their cameo is either pre-planned or a sign of idolisation on their own part. The same is applied to a lesser extent with an approximated pixel image of FGC E-Sport personality 'SonicFox' appearing on the vending machines throughout the game.If this is allowed is uncertain, but putting false legal disclaimers in your product certainly isn't good practice.
