_childDocuments_.review: I have somewhat mixed feelings about this game. I only played campaigns so far, and that is what I'm interested in. You can play countless games "online with your friends" but the campaign is what makes you return when you're done with the multilayer. And from what I've seen, there is not enough stuff in the campaign mode. The two campaigns are short, and though LP did an ok job with the story, it still feels rushed and patched up together. There is no sense of progression. Neither in the story, nor in difficulty. I'm ok with short campaigns connected by the greater story arch like it was in HoMM3. And I get the point of having one short campaign for each faction. But it's just not enough. HoMM3 campaign scenarios were quite hard and long. SoC campaign scenarios feel short, easy and small in scale. Only one of four scenarios in each campaign feels properly hard and long. Still lacking the story that ties up early-, mid-, and late-game together. Original HoMM3 is a bad choice for inspiration in this regard. Armageddon's Blade or Shadow of Death is a good one. One long "main" campaign with a few smaller supplemental campaigns is a proper way of doing things.I also really miss the optional scenarios from HoMM2 and bonuses for completing them. Like the dwarven or ogre alliance. That is a thing you want to see when "campaign map" appears in front of you. A clear goal, a path, and some options to achieve that goal. Not the linear progression through numerated markers. So much wasted potential.I realize that this is a game on a budget, and there will be tons of new campaign DLCs for $4.99 if the game will win some die hard fans of the HoMM series. But the base game has to offer enough of content. It has to have substance. And we all are aware that SoC is NOT HoMM, and will probably never become one. Unless instead of polishing UI and map generator LP will add a proper story AND lore right in to the campaign. For now it's just a random map generator with a few twists. For the PVP activity I still prefer good old HoMM3. Polished and balanced for players by players, lol.This is a solid indie game with a lifespan of few weeks. Like Humankind, this game wants to be better than game it was inspired by, and a little different for a change. But falls short in substance. It's not the turn based nature, not colorful map, not the "perfect balance" and not the setting that made HoMM a truly great game. SoC just doesn't have the same magic... yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of Conquest is a good and fun game, albeit short and not that deep.In regard to what many would consider this game being similar to HoM&M and Eador, i can honestly say that there are resemblances, but that's a far as it goes. The base building, unit upgrading, tier systems etc. are something verteran and novice players will love and will be made familiar with early on.My main issue with the game is that it's really short, because the campaign only lasts about 10 hours if you stretch it a bit.HoM&M and Eador offer a far longer campaign, and they are more challenging, engaging and quite diverse as well. That being said, i do appreciate what this company has created and hopefully more content (including free stuff) will be added along the way.Personally speaking, i didn't encounter any bugs or anything which is a really good thing. The graphics, musical score, narration etc are all very well done here (although the protagonist kinda acts like being Jeanne D'arc on steroids and that's something i particularly don't enjoy so much).Some smaller gripes like not getting matching gear sets (for buffs & boons), or the option (feature) to sell or break down loot for other valuable minerals or components would be nice to have in the future.I just wished there was more, because it's a good and fun game to play, with a decent amount of quality put into it as well.Like i stated above, hopefully there's a lot more content coming our way as soon as the game leaves E.A. <Fingers crossed>Personal score: 8.5/10 (Highly Recommended)

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved the HoMM Series, then this game is for you!As the game exists on consoles by now, you can even chill and play this game in a couch co-op session with your buddy.The battle system takes a bit to get used to, but it has some real fun tactics and spell combinations, once you get the hang of it.I personally love filling the battle field with Acid Clouds, and then push enemies through them with Repel for some quick kills.If you turn out to hate the combat system, you can still kinda skip it with "Quick Battle", as long as you also hate your own army enough to accept losses. Quick Combat plays horribly bad imho, especially at the beginning of your conquest.If you are not happy with the Quick Combat outcome however, you can actually reverse your decision and play the battle manually, which I think is awesome!The overall gameplay is fun, and you can really feel the effort and love the devs have put into this game.And there is yet more to come in the future. I can't wait!Random Maps do somewhat add to replayability, though a lot of them will look similar over time, as the game seems to constantly try to balance the map layout for all players. Not necessarily a bad thing, though.The Campaign Maps are mostly really time consuming and challenging, so avoid them if you are going for a relaxed session.All of them have various Weilders (Heroes), that will transfer over to the next map, and some of them don't.Unfortunately the game does not tell you which ones will transfer, so check out some of the guides to avoid a frustrating time leveling up weilders, that don't matter at all.I could also not seem to overcome most maps on harder difficulty, without drastically changing my playstyle.That being said: When you do have the time _and_ the mental capacity, definitely try the campaings out. They do a good job explaining the game to you and you get to try some races in a totally different playstyle from your usual conquest map.The real charm here is, of course, the multiplayer mode.As it is turn-based, there is no real downside here for console players, which makes the Cross-Platform aspect better than most other games.Human turns can be played simultaneously (as long as you don't play in hotseat mode). This means a lot less waiting than your avarage HoMM3 session, where you would go grab a bite, take a shower and plan you next vacation between each turn.I totally recommend getting this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of conquest is a love project from a very small team in Sweden.I was lucky enough to get earlier access to the game to provide feedback. The game is heavily influenced by old titles like the Heroes of Might and Magic games, but doesn't just copy the mechanics. They have created their own thing and it works pretty well.For example, Players will have settlements where you can build elements, but it's up to you what you want to build. You have a certain number of slots you can fill (You get more slots when leveling up the settlement) and you don't have enough slots to build absolutely everything. You can also remove buildings and change them for others to modify your strategy. For example, basic resources are generated in the town, instead of an external building you have to capture, allowing you to stop generating basic resources when you don't need them anymore and put focus on defenses, for example.They also have a different approach towards units, as you can't just have all available faction units in your army without leveling up your hero. You have a skill you can acquire that allows you to put more creatures in your roster the higher the level of your skill.Creatures also have a cap, similar to the newer Kings Bounty games, removing the old Heroes of Might & Magic problem of "massive armies" that just destroy everything without any challenge. You can carry a maximum of X creatures in one unit for each creature type. They also allow for having multiple versions of the same creature in your army, as opposed to the new Kings Bounty games, for example. They even allow you to carry base and upgraded versions of your creatures if you desire it so, so you can tailor your army to whatever defensive/offensive approach you want.Magic, on the other hand is quite different from other games in the genre. There are different "manas" and you generate mana of that type based on your Wielder (Hero) and the creatures in your army every turn. Then you will be able to cast spells that have different mana combination costs, each turn. This can get a bit complicated, but it also fixes the problem of older games where you would just cast your most powerful spells always and lower tier spells would get obsolete, or become almost pointless.Progression on the other hand, while similar, it's different too. Your hero will level up and get different skills to improve their combat prowess, exploration capabilities, or kindom ruling efficiency, but every few levels, they can get a special power level up, that boost them in very significant ways, allowing you for further specialization with that hero. You can have one that specializes in combat and kingdom ruling, while another one has beneffits for magic and exploration, for example.If you like turn based games in the Heroes / Kings Bounty stile, you will most likely love this game. Not only the visuals are extremely gorgerous and the music too, but it was done with passion and love and that is something you can easily see immediately as soon as you open the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings on this but I cannot recommend SoC in it's current state. I grew up playing the HOMM games and I was excited to see a new entry in the genre when I first saw SoC at the PC gamer show a few years back. The game brings some fresh ideas to the genre that I really like, but, ultimately, things feel a little bland/boring and there's nothing in that game that really make me addicted like I was with HOMM.The good:For the bad there's really just one significant thing: shallow. Too many systems in the game feel a little basic and suffer from a lack of creativity that would help to improve strategy and tactics. The factions don't feel much different from each other, units feel too similar and lack interesting abilities (both passive and active), there are no unique faction abilities/traits and hero level ups just boil down to additional stats or an extra troop spot in your army. Artifacts are uninspiring; nearly all of them provide just pure stats and those that don't are extra resource generators instead. The concept of the magic system (units generating essence etc) is cool but the spell variety feels weak. Again, most of them are generic stat modifiers and unless you spec into a specific mage build then there really isn't much on offer. Put all of these things together and you end with a game that not only lacks depth but also a hook to keep people interested long term. There are no interesting combinations/builds of specific heroes, with certain skills, units & magic that make for an addictive gameplay loop. Instead it's all numbers and whether yours are higher than your opponents.Overall the game is visually appealing and has some cool features, some of which are a step in the right direction for the genre. But simplicity, blandness and a overall lack of interesting aspects to key game features keep me from wanting to play more past the campaigns and a couple of skirmish games.

_childDocuments_.review: I came for a game like oldschool Homm, and I found so much more than I expected.Being a solid and beautiful contestor in the genre right from early access, Songs of Conquest offers alot of innovative gameplay. Unlike in other games of the genre, you are very flexible with your building paths, having the ability to build any building into different building slots (small, medium and large) which vary from settlement size and level. You can either go classic and go for every dwelling or decide to go hard into a certain troop.Speaking about troops, there is an increase in strength for higher level troops but it is a slighter progression than you might be used to. There are caps on unitstacks, that can be upgraded, but also stop you from building doomstacks from the same unit very early on.Troops also grant your heroe (wielder) essence (order, chaos, destruction, creation and arcana) from which they can produce powerful magic, some troops give just a bit, some give a lot and others do give few but multiple essences. Spells are chosen from a spellbook, you don't have to learn them. There are 4 spells per essence and 20 more that are combinations of 2 of them combined. So you are able to wield powerful magic from the get go. There are multiple well made skirmish maps, 2 small campaigns and a map editor. And a great community to boot.

_childDocuments_.review: Well... I beated Homm3 complete... And though some of this content repairs some of the flaws of Homm3, I would not be so hasty simply telling you this game is better. Its really, really good though. Here is some comparison to Homm3, father of this game.75 Hours on record and I just finished and only the story directly played on overwhelming (hardest setting), so I can compare both as a fresh player and turn based veteran.In Heroes:-You have more fractions-More artefacts-More of and like a lot larger maps and more kinds of buildings-Way more campaign missions-More of moreAnd I will always love it... But you may agree its more or less about town portal and dimension door (and maybe cloak of undead king) and with more comes more of time consumption. Biggest flaw of Heroes III is time consumption.But... In Songs of Conquest -Honestly fights are maybe better and more balanced here-Capturing stuff makes more sense-There is Fog of War and therefore element of surprise-First day first player advantage is not present-Function of towns is more divided into larger numbers of cities and villages-Stacks are limited-There is research-Magic requires skill to use and concept is original and well balanced-Story is short, but I enjoyed every single map a lot. Though it may seem creepy at start, everything will fall into place in the end and you will say just... WoW-Pixelart graphics feels alive-Town portal and dimension door is replaced with beacons of power, non castle points on map serving as fast travel points and magic enhancers. -The only serious flaw is not sufficient diversity of artifacts, units, fractions (should come in DLCs though)-...aaand lack of water, ships, naval battles. I also think units could have alter-upgrade with different abilities and not all the potential of this game was unleashed (yet).Yet still... Everything, even building the town, requires some skill and planning. Though something comes out a little too easy in the end. I cannot wait to test this game in multiplayer as it seems faster paced, more balanced and truly insanely fun in PvP, but I havent tried it yet. _childDocuments_.review: I feel bad about giving this a bad review; and certainly: I do not outright regret the purchase.The artstyle is nice, the gameplay and vision, generally, seem very appealing, but...After having got a good 20hours of fun out of this game (having bought it on sale... (i)), it also grew stale pretty quickly.There just seems to be something about their "remedy" for the perceived "blights" of HOMM[3(?)], in here, that undermine the very stuff that made HOMM (ii) fun to begin with.More generally speaking: I loath this design philosophy (for difficulty scaling/freezing), where the player is hemmed in to very very few options (makes it more predictable for the gamedesigner, what do expect at what phase of the game, in order to "challenge" the player, at any time), were a certain type of game-style may materialize as the one and only "right one"; this seems to be exactly the case, here.Be it the lack of endless troop sizes like in HOMM (not present here; allowed sizes are rather small; and resources and land are very rare, you cannot upgrade everything, being stuck with few options), or the numbers of troops themselves, the game generally opts for restricting freedom rather than playing it wild and loose (with the potential for total escalation... which is fun! (iii)); esp. the latter drives me nuts (3?.... effing 3 troops only at the start?... ffs. that's beyond good and evil...) -- you are basically in a situation, where all upgrade options to your main wielder come down to "more troops", "more troops" and "more troops again", which makes variety basically non existent.And I dislike the magical system, that makes spells available only after a certain number of turns (restricted by troop composition/accessories), which, for instance, has "additional movement" often come too late for certain options in battle.+ why can't I influence/decide, which of my troops with equal initiative should come first in order, which second?The limited options on the battle map, also, does leave much to be desired.The maps are way too small to begin with, both in widths and length -- their lack of variety is boring, also.That, and the options at the start for were to place your troops are pretty bad as well.Like: I have few (often zero) options to begin with, of where to guide my first moves to, in order to take key positions, as it only exposes me to direct attacks from the enemy; meanwhile, troops of mine can be trapped behind other troops, because, after having all 9 troop slots unlocked for my army, that'S also the exact number of slots evailable on the battlemap. Some troops may be fast (>movement points), others may have better initiative (but no ability to have multiple turns in a row thanks to extremely high initiative. That was a huuuuge bummer!), so the fast ones may always be held back by being placed behind the quick (>high initiative) ones, or the latter cannot move forward at all.And I fail to see very interesting abilities in the available troop types.Like: where's the vampires ability to re-emerge after battle?Where is the wielders ability to raise additional skelletons from the battlefield out of fallen allied and enemy troops?Where is the ability of troops to be thrown at enemies as projectile, only to potentially change sides in relatiation?But I am especially missing an ability of troops to effectively trap enemy troops in a position/shutting off entire pathways (there also aren't any giant troops like in HOMM, that would occupy more than a single tile).The ability to punish troops marching through a control-area (even by musketeers during reload? - srsly?!?), just isn't enough; you don't even need "stealth" (ability to ignore control-zones) for that to become problematic, when one round later the feared close range troop may already get in close to the enemy's ranged troops, with just little revenge to fear.Also: the troops die too fast, anyway. Both good and bad!I am not sold on the unit variety, in general.Maybe having some minor factions would help? (see "Endless Legend"?!)And the very punishing way of upgrading them (way too expensive) is offputting for a game. Why do I even have to upgrade them before I have trained them to begin with (before I can even train the higher tier)??? - in many cases it may take a long while, before I have the [very limited] resources ready to upgrade; having to upgrade the rest of the available troop-pool for extra cash (and resources!) seems like a toxic concept.Why not have the number of troops (tier 1 / tier 2) be shared, instead? - it is already well balanced via the different price for recruitment, why double down on that via this weird mechanic? It seems, like you want to make some "inception" of punishing features, which, again, seems anti-player.There are probably more things that would irk me, but for now I lost interest in the game and won't find out.Actually did Alt+F4 a couple of times now, being bored with the game, which prompted this review.I really want to like this game to the point of being able to recommend it, generally.But I can't.And this is not "Early Access" anymore.So the design-vision of this game, for the most part, seems to be implemented already, according to the perception of the developer....i) btw.: it's always a bit doubious, when games go on sale during Early Access. Atleast it got out of EA by now. But still...ii) didn't even play the third one; is that really the "gold standard"?... I did play some later verisons.iii) I get it... that can become very unbalanced. But that is relevant for, and only for competitive multiplayer.And I literally could not care less about that, ESPECIALLY not, for this typ of game.Some game-types are mostly meant to be enjoyed alone. Desperately trying to contain OP-combinations, just for the small minority of players actually concerned with "competitive play", is a really toxic approach to game-balancing, where said game lends itself mostly to a single player experience.Why not have two sets of rules, instead?A true one, and an altered version, for the competitive multiplayer enthusiasts? -- thus players, even when playing with friends, could deside for themselves, if everything needs to be balanced to high heaven, or if fun should not take precedence...

_childDocuments_.review: Song of Conquest’s developers gave no consideration to the internal reality of their fantasy world when designing its characters. They were clearly motivated instead by some sort of cultural activism. There is a diverse roster of real-world racial archetypes for no in-universe reason and no design purpose beyond seemingly self-imposed racial quotas. The physically strongest human units are female in brazen defiance of sense and biology. Every character is designed to be stylish except for the few white men, who are pointedly designed to be ugly. Every white man encountered in the story is a villain, save for one extremely minor exception. Anyone who points out any of these issues on the forum has their thread quietly deleted.Lavapotion compromises their fantasy worldbuilding for the sake of misguided social agendas and censors anyone who criticizes them for it. Valuing activism at the expense of story coherence and player experience has the obvious consequence that the fantasy is not immersive and, by extension, not enjoyable. The gameplay is mostly enjoyable, as covered in other reviews, but this can’t compensate for critical worldbuilding flaws. I don’t recommend spending $30 on Songs of Conquest given its current trajectory. Anyone interested in fantasy strategy games can find titles with richer fantasy and better gameplay for a lower price.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as controls go, plays mostly fine on Deck.  Trading items between wielders is kind of clunky compared to mouse and keyboard.  And minimap is so small on Deck it isn't good for telling you anything but where you are on the map, you can't really judge colors to tell at a glance what is controlled by enemies - having the ability to say push L3 and have a fullscreen map come up would probably remedy this.  Setting both graphic options to medium seems to be the best bet if your goal is 60fps, although the game will frequently stutter when moving the camera for some reason (not a usage issue, and lowering settings does not solve this).  And turn off the handheld performance option, unless you want to save battery.  It seriously reduces frames.I had bought this on GOG during the sale a couple weeks ago, and bought it here during a sale for cloud save between my PC and Deck (can play GOG version on Deck but no cloud save through Heroic launcher) and Steam achievements, since I was enjoying the GOG version so much.This is a good game.  The only real critique I have is that I don't find the music to be anything special, it's just kind of there.I had made it to the 3rd mission of the 2nd campaign before switching to Steam, I find campaign is harder than same difficulty (I'm playing on Fair which is Normal) of skirmish maps, due to scripted events having the potential to screw you your first time through a mission (since you don't know ie. where a scripted enemy will be coming from the first time).  You can set it to autosave at the start of every round, and quicksave is available (10 slots max each for autosave and quickave), so if you have a setback, it isn't hard to reload an earlier save and try again instead of having to totally restart (at least so far, on Fair).Multiplayer is also fun - simultaneous turns (for human players) vs AI is a real time saver.  No coop campaign, just skirmish maps, and a random map generator.I have been playing mostly with quick battle, most of the time I have fewer losses when playing battles myself, but I am trying to catch up to where I left off right now.The game *seems* to be more focused on magic than armies, and magic in this game is not like it was in Heroes of Might and Magic - you cannot cast on the world map, and rather than having a pool of mana that regenerates, you generate essence of different schools of magic while in combat.  You can also cast as many spells as you have essence for in one turn.  I've seen some complaints about this, but at least as far as I can tell right now, part of the strategy is deciding to save spells or cast them when they become available.  You also don't research spells, you just get access to greater power of the pool of spells (which everyone has access to, just need essence) by selecting that class of magic when it pops up for your hero.You have strict limits on max troop stacks (which can be increased with expensive research) and can only carry a few stacks at once to start, but can gain access to having more slots for units by choosing the appropriate skill when levelling up.Overall, very much recommended.  It is like Heroes but different, not as much depth but imo not in a bad way, it makes games go faster.

Changing my review to a negative one.I think Barya campaign is simply terrible.The gameplay of the 3rd and 4th missions in the campaign is focused on the game throwing at you the same enemy wielders again and again. The goal in both missions is to "conquer" all settlements / beacons of power and you slowly progress towards the goal the game keep spamming the enemy wielders you have already defeated every other turn, so you have to make sure there is always someone behind or your main army could retreat in time to get back to protect already conquered bases / beacons of powers. _childDocuments_.review: Wanted this to be the successor to HOMM2 and HOMM3. It's not. Maybe it wasn't setting out to be. _childDocuments_.review: Songs of Conquest knows what kind of game it wants to be and knows its audience. With the obvious influence of the Heroes of Might and Magic series, this game offers the nostalgic feel of 90s games, but with a certain sophisticated and unique mix of mechanics. Unfortunately, despite some interesting features, there are also gameplay limitations (such as unit limits and a strange spell system) that may discourage or fail to convince some fans of similar turn-based strategies in the long run.PROS:✓ Incredible graphics, very atmospheric✓ Four unique factions✓ Local and online multiplayer✓ In-game editor to make your own maps✓ Tactics-based combat like in HoMM✓ Good soundtrack✓ Range of archery units and ability to use battlefield terrain to your advantage during combat✓ Interestingly designed units and brilliant animations of themCONS:- The unit limit in cities and in hero army should not exist- I'm not the biggest fan of the Essence (magic) system in this game- Settlement building feels clunky- No ships and other water elements- Minor bugs but nothing major- Difficulty curve and AI quirks- Doesn't always explain its mechanics well, which can be an issue for some players, especially newcomers

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game after hearing about it online & seeing a YouTube video of the devs playing it with all the ideas they had for it. It was VERY early on in the process. I've attempted to play the game the way they claim it was intended to be played but it's just not something that can be done. DETAILED REVIEW ahead:Let me make some things clear: This is a game that is supposed to be where you move your character (A magical wielder) around the map, gathering resources as you go, getting items, powerups, & even claiming a town in order to use to recruit troops. Along the way you will encounter fights & some people will join you or fight you depending on the story. You'll pretty much select join every time so having a "choice" is an illusion. Also most of the power ups you get from clicking on things are temporary so they are worthless. Only the town economy matters, upgrades matter, & troop size matter.You can have 3 wielders at a time & there are as of now 4 races. (A DLC is coming for a 5th). This is where the game SHOULD shine. You expect a Brood War kind of balance between the races where each one has abilities that the other doesn't have & during the fight you use your unique set of skills & the battlefield terrain (Think the board game Titan if you're old enough) to win the day. However, this never happens. Every race makes use of the same abilities as all magic is powered from "essence" & all races use the same essence. All races essentially have tank units, range units, & support units. Due to this the battles are basically broken down between where you position your units, & when you cast your spells (& remember, you're using the SAME spells). Whereas the Faey race should have "nature" spells & the Risen/Undead race should have "necromancy" one would think.Even playing on the 2nd lowest difficulty & having the biggest army, all my towns maxed out, all my upgrades maxed out - by the 3rd level of each campaign I am SLAUGHTERED by the normal Wielder just walking around. After many trial & errors I've learned that just auto-battling will always yield a superior result. So I sit around building my forces for a few hours, maxing them out before taking on the enemy. You'd think that a FULL POWER you should be able to beat the enemy, but no. They lose 2-5 troops & you lose 30-50 in each & I have 9 troop slots to their 6-8. So I'm not only stronger, have better equipment, but have superior numbers... & auto battle destroys me, & manual battle is way worse. If auto battle kills 50 troops, I'll manage 10. In no way shape or form can I ever come close to what auto battle does. So what is this game? Basically you walk around clicking on things that don't affect the outcome, while slowly building a town(s), until a final confrontation, & then you auto battle many times leveling up (with MINOR customization of your character during this - but you're normally going to pick troop size until you're maxed), & then once you get to the final confrontation you'll auto battle again & die at some point. Maybe it's stage 3, maybe it's 4, maybe it's 1 depending on difficultly, luck, or skill. However, chances are unless you have happened to figure a magical combination out that no one else has - you will never beat this game. There is a multiplayer but what's the point of running around racing to auto battle each other? Shouldn't there be more than just RNG involved in the game? Shouldn't there be strategy of SOME SORT?! And the DLC is only adding more maps & characters & not fixing any of the issues. So what EXACTLY IS IT THAT YOU'RE DOING? A whole lot of clicking. That's what. Now for the positives: The devs do seem to care. They ask your opinions on things. They WANT to know how hard a map is or what price the DLC should be, but here is the thing... despite us telling them, the DLC should have came with the game because it isn't much of anything - I doubt they do that. Despite us telling them to fix the difficulty - they haven't patched it. I've been waiting too long for fixes that never come. As of now this game is going to sit on the shelf & MAYBE in a few years I'll come back to it & see if they made a workable battle system, but that would require reprogramming the entire game & I doubt that. You've been warned if you purchase this.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you enjoy the old Heroes of Might and Magic games? If yes, then you will enjoy this game. Units no longer stack endlessly, giving a reason and benefit to running more than one Wielder. ( Hero )Unit slots are gained by leveling the wielders and increasing the stacks for units is increased by researching which is more of a mid game building once you've established several footholds.Units generate a certain amount of types of essence. Essence powers spells. This adds more strategy to fielding certain units so that you can utilize specific spells. Certain factions will have certain spells more easily available to them based on their units that are available but some rare items/artifacts and structures that you capture in the world can also influence these things, as well as wielder abilities.Battlefields now have more to them. Some elevation tiles increase and decrease the offence and defence modifiers of units.Units have unique abilities available to them. Obviously, some are more powerful than others. I've only played the Human Campaign so far and their abilities were pretty basic. Raising attack/defence of the units around them instead of attacking. Archers have an overwatch ability where they attack any unit that moves within range of their "zone." This zone boosts damage significantly and can be increased with abilities, items and elevation.So far, spells seem to range from useful to maybe too strong. I'm not sure how they scaled the essence costs to damage but they seem to need some tweaking. Chain lightning can hit for 200 several times while another spell that costs 2/3 the essence only hits for 90 and one that costs 1/3 hits for 20.Towns are basically you walk up and claim a settlement. Once that settlement is claimed you claim all buidings that settlement contains and then you can build whatever structures you want in any empty building slots.Building slots can be small, medium, and large. You can increase these slots through upgrading settlements and each settlement you claim has a size and maximum upgrade slot.Defensive structures don't seem to be very strong as far as I've seen. Hopefully they can be upgraded further because the ballistas don't really do much more than tickle the enemy if they have any sizable force.if an enemy has claimed a settlement, you can attack and then you have two options. You can raze 2 buildings a turn or you can convert the settlement to your own. I haven't razed yet so I'm not sure if your wielder has to remain in the city to raze ( which also plunders resources ) but I know if you convert it takes several turns and you do have to leave a wielder.From what i've seen, you have access to an editor where you can make your own maps and layouts and play them out with AI or your friends. I didn't see mods yet.Amount of wielders you can have out are tied to settlement sizes and how many you own. Each wielder appears to have their own set of unique abilities and then access to generic ones like more movement on the overworld or increasing army size.Wielders have equipment slots for weapons and armor you find in the world. These stats all transfer to their units. Stats range from increasing essence generation, increasing offence and defence, increasing maximum troop size ( Called Command ) to reducing ranged / melee damage by a %. The overworld has mines and structures that generate resources used in constructing and recruiting the more powerful and limited units. There is also a structure called the marketplace that allows you to convert gold into resources in case your access to some resources is limited.There are also tons of different events and structures that grant bonuses to stats, generation, wielder boosts and experience and temporary battle boosts. Sometimes these are guarded by packs of AI which vary in strength based on what is being guarded.As far as combat goes, it's all turn based on an Initiative stat and the order is laid out for you. There are several ways to alter this stat via wielder abilities, wielder equipment, buffs and spells.Units have attacks of opportunity. It seems like some can do this more than once on the same unit so walking passed a heavy unit to reach a fragile ranged unit can be extremely punishing.All in all, the game so far is rather enjoyable. I'm looking forward to some of the custom play on maps like the old Heroes of Might and Magic games. It's pretty much what I was expecting based on the trailers and game play I had seen.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of Conquest is a turn-based RPG heavily inspired by the early Heroes of Might and Magic games. But, does it manage to capture that same spark so many of us miss?The Good:+Insanely detailed pixel graphis. You'll be shocked by the amount of moving parts and variety.+Fantastic fantasy soundtrack that manages to match the mood of what's happening on screen.+Four fleshed out factions that are fairly unique mechanically.+Crunchy sound effects make combat a joy.+Fresh take on city-building and combat that make a few new twists to the HoMM-formular.The Bad:-The AI really needs work. The devs are aware and improving it.-With only 4 factions and limited neutral enemies, the game lacks variety. But, the devs are working on it.-A few bugs, namely one that causes slow-down over longer sessions of play.-Despite how well they play, the factions are basically ripped straight from HoMM. The knights allying with forest creatures is the most unique one, so far.Bottom Line:My wife and I initially bonded over the HoMM franchise and have been chasing a decent sequel or spin-off since. I'm happy to report that we've been enjoying hot seat sessions after putting the kids to bed, because Songs of Conquest really manages to capture and build on that nostalgic formular.Does it still feel early access? At times, absolutely. Is it enjoyable? Absolutely, all the time! Highly recommended to fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: In short, don't buy this game if you played any HoMM games before.From small unit caps and wielder having only 3 slots for units needing to level up the hero, uninteresting pixel art, interactable objects that blends into the background objects, nonsense magic mechanics, bugs (I know, early access and all that), to very generic story script.If you never played Heroes of Might & Magic, go buy those instead (1-4) and you will know.Update: Everything mentioned above still stands.The buildings are as generic as it can be (Arleon only). Coming from the HoMM you expect to double click the building and access the menu with all the things right? No. You have to select the castle to get a menu for what you want to do: purchase wielders, draft units or upgrade the castle itself). No purchasing the buildings anywhere. I spent 5 minutes trying to find the menu... You either double click the small icon of the castle at the bottom or click on the empty space near the castle that I thought was just for decoration. That's 3 separate menus for the castle. Now drafting units, they are way more expensive that you expect, struggling to keep a single wielder restocked even with the small unit caps and developers expect you to play multiple wielders due to those caps. You can only have 3 types of units at the start. while fine at early game, it's restricting at mid.As expected you need different buildings to unlock different units and upgrades. Some buildings will unlock two types of units... at least it appears like that, then you realize you have to spend more resources to actually unlock the second unit again. So the "castle" mechanic is just terrible.Now the world creeps, you see the estimated count of units and what the difficulty is fighting the group, which is good. However the difficulty is sometimes misleading, you will face creeps that will annihilate your units even thought it says it's an Easy fight or win without a loss on an Extreme fight.And finally the campaign, that is boring. I just skipped every cut scene and rushed the Arleon levels to level 3, where the difficulty spiked and I died without a fighting chance. You loose any unit you had previously no matter what you had, which I hated in HoMM as well since it doesn't make any sense.You are to defend a small settlement in level 3 against an enemy wielder having a few turns in advance to prepare. I tried twice, managing resources and building the most units I could. Then I saw what the enemy wielder had... three times more units than my two wielders together, decimating everything.I regret that I didn't refund this sooner before it was too late...Maybe they will redo and fix everything at 1.0, but I wouldn't hold my breath...

However, as someone who has played the hell out of HoMM series, this game isn't as fun as those games - and they were made over 10 or so years ago?! Unfortunately this game is lacking in variety.  Your army is capped at 9 units per leader - which is fine, but I just got an item allowing me to have 2 more slots but now I can't use it.  Each faction only hires and recruits from their own race. What happened to the idea that you could recruit anything and get them to fight for your army?? Spells are lacking as well.  No units to summon?  No world crushing power? Each race no matter what you choose basically plays the same way... who cares that there are so many different leaders!  One just gives you 1 more arcana and another gives you slightly better range damage for your troops...it's laughably the same!Also playing against the AI was extremely easy on fair challenge.  I'm not even sure what they are even doing as I didn't even see them until I took over 50% of the world map.  Best to play it on at least "Risky" mode.This game is scared to "unbalance" the heroes and factions and for what?? Is this going to be some sort of tournament game? _childDocuments_.review: Pssst. Hey you. Yes you, the one reading the review (Duh, I mean, who else might I be adressing here?!). Do you know what HoMM is? No? How about Heroes of Might and Magic? Ring any bells? Still no? You are not from Eastern Europe then, I assume? Yea, thought as much, it's the only way someone can be under 20 and not know what HoMM is. Alright, the long and short of it goes like this: Once upon a time there was this wonderful franchise named Heroes of Might & Magic, it was about a turn-based strategy game with, you guessed it, might and magic in it and you had your factions with their unique gimmicks and stuff. It was damned good, HoMM 3 is still considered the best thing since God sent his son to die for our sins by some people and I can't blame 'em, game's something else, it is amazing, you could break it in so many ways that it looped back to being balanced, no joke (except for diplomacy and necropolis, but this isn't about them)! Then everything changed when the french aquired the licence rights to the franchise. They made HoMM 5, which is considered to be the second best in the series and then the series died. Got re-branded to Might & Magic: Heroes and was utter, unadulterated garbage.The many fans of the series sighed in dissapointment and went back to HoMM 3 or 5, based on preference, and that was it. But then, one beautiful day, one frenchman decided to right Ubisoft's wrongs and atone for the sins of his countrymen (which is utterly absurd by the way as sin is not collective but individual in nature, so he was not to blame to begin with, but still, it's the thought that counts) and designed Songs of Conquest, the third best thing since God sent his son to die for our sins and HoMM 3! Thing is, unlike those games, there is a more... let's say tangible balance, you have to earn your way to becoming the most OP piece of might and/or magic on the map through the power of foresight and planning your character skill builds. It might have less factions than HoMM, but what is here is solid, well fleshed-out, looks and sounds nice too! So what are YOU waiting for, go experience a game like there is no other on the market, you won't regret it!PS, if you DO happen to regret your purchase, I am authorized by my powers as an Eastern European to have you sent to a gulag, where is the only place to express false opinions such as yours!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a modern take on the Heroes 3 formula.Some notable changes:You can buy units daily instead of weekly. This makes games MUCH more fast paced.Towns are a physical part of the map. This lets you see the progress your enemy has made. It also lets you attack the town one building at a time instead of all at once.At the time of review there are two full singleplayer campaigns with two more on the roadmap.The map editor is very polished. So much so that the main campaign maps are made with it.The game is constantly being improved and there is obviously a lot of heart and soul put into it.Wholeheartedly recommend it to any turn-based tactics game fan.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played Heroes 3 a bunch when I was younger, I was utterly delighted to discover this new reimagining of the game genre. They added terrain elevation bonuses and attacks of opportunity to combat as a standard mechanic. They also changed casters so that you accumulate magic essence to cast spells based on what units your hero carries around with them, instead of a flat old-school mana pool. You can't stack an infinite number of the same unit in one slot anymore, and you gotta carefully decide on level ups whether to increase the number of unit slots a hero can carry, or pick another passive bonus from a pool.Lots of thoughtful ideas like these add up to create a superb, fresh experience of the Heroes genre. 100% recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun Turn Based Strategy Game.  I have not played Heroes of Might and Magic 3 that a lot of people compare this game to so it stands on its own merits for me.The campaign is a lot of fun and also very challenging (in a good way).  The first couple missions in the current two campaigns get you into the groove of the faction and playing the game.  The 3rd and 4th missions really test your skills and push you.  The skirmish AI is okay, and after playing for 40 hours I have learned how to beat the AI in just about any fair fight that I don't stumble into an army comp that hard counters my current armies comp.  The PvP is a lot of fun and challenging, the only real drawback is the slow pace of playing anything larger than a 1v1, because player turns can easily take 3-5 mins on average and you just stare at your own screen while that happens unless your streaming with friends.  There have been lots of requests for simultaneous turns and the Developers in their own discord are very responsive to the idea.Overall a Very solid Early Access game and definitely worth the price of entry at $30.  If you like strategy games this will scratch the itch and as they add more content will only get better!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a major fan of Heroes of Might and Magic 3, so I was excited to test the sequel. Unfortunately, the gameplay does not have the same rapid, exciting dynamics as the original.The opening section of each game takes place in a perimetered area guarded by powerful creatures. Once you're strong enough to break off, the question is whether the enemy leaders you'll meet are weaker or stronger than you. Because you can only determine the enemy's strength at close range, it's a case of trial and error.Furthermore, scenarios appear to allow control over a single, fixed faction. You are limited to always starting a scenario in the same area, which gets tedious.Finally, there are too many places of interest that give various bonuses, weapons, and goods; their importance is diluted, and they do not have the same impact as the original.The game is significantly more structured than the original; players have numerous options for improving their army, including three fields of research; the factions are diverse and well-balanced; the tactical battles are well-done. At the same time, Song of Conquest keeps its ancestor's key flaws, such as the devastating implications of an early defeat and the fact that, especially at high levels, you are compelled to concentrate all of your army under the leadership of a single leader, which greatly limits variability.Recommended for those who enjoy sluggish, ponderous strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: In what seems like a spiritual successor to the old Heroes of Might and Magic games, it takes a lot of mechanics and improves them for a more robust tactical experience, such as being able to array your troops before combat, with elevation, and obstacles. _childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: Since this review, the game has gotten more optimized and runs better and with no game breaking glitches. I've also come to appreciate the combat more and find it to have more depth than I initially gave it credit for (that said, each fight tends to end in just a couple of turns so there isn't much room for strategic flexibility).Worth the asking price, but a sale is recommended as of this review.Music is great, the visuals are great and most things work well. AI turns are fast to start with but get very slow after a while and my current save is frozen in the middle of an AI turn, which is unfortunate but not enough to not recommend the game. I am sure that will get fixed eventually.Combat is simple and not very engaging, but it's fast and works well enough.The cities allow you to double down on building the same structures so you can mass the same kind of units if you want, unlike in other similar games. That's neat and means you can focus your army.If you like similar games, you will likely find this enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: The game clearly took inspiration of the Heroes of Might and Magic games, which I don't mind at all because I love the original concept & idea of the game genre, they executed it well, the artstyle and sound design and soundtrack is beautiful, good pacing and challenging difficulty spikes, overall a nice piece of work.I am not a fan of increasing the price while it was still in early access though, in general I still think it is somewhat overpriced, since it lacks content and quality of life balance changes. There are 4 playable factions with a limited amount of buildings and troops. These factions are all somewhat original but nothing we've never seen before. Since my early access review they managed to add two new single player campaigns and finished UI, HUD and the overall looks of the game - it looks finished but unfortunately doesn't feel finished sometimes.It honestly still kind of feels like a early access game here and there. I still appreciate what they did with this and I'll improve my original review rating a notch, because they kept working on it and didn't just leave it to die. They are also very transparent with the community and they keep us updated with steam posts and e-mails.  In my opinion this game has the potential to be a 9/10 or even 10/10 game and could possibly be the passing of the torch for the Heroes of Might and Magic franchise, which it desperately needed since the heavy decline in popularity after the fourth/fifth installment. Keep this idea alive. (7.2/10 --> 8.4/10)

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with the positive reviews about the homam feel, and pretty presentation, but it needs lot more time in the oven. Considering it costs 30E, I cannot recommend it at this state. - It lacks depth. All systems are pretty shallow - building, economy, hero leveling- Battles are not bad, but could use some more strategy - wait/defend options, obstacles blocking ranged attacks, more unit skills etc.- Magic system is not great, some spells are very unrewarding and lack impact - homam 3 system was way better imo.- Hard to see stuff on map, you constantly have to press alt to see what is pickable etc.- Artifacts are really boring - looks cool, but only give bonus to stats often. No special effects... - Severe lack of QoLs - cant change keybindings, cant restart the fight if quick fight ends terribly, cant load from fight without having to leave to menu, no comparision of new item vs equiped and many more- Difficulty - campaing have some spike, but skirmish is way too easy imo.- Unit cap - imo bad design or at least not very well balanced.- Stuttering when moving camera on map - even with high fps it doesnt feel smooth.- Needs random map generator really badly.- If you like cosmetic pets like I do - its only avaliable when you pay another 20E for supporter DLC...:/ Cant justify spending 50 on this.Game has very good reviews (although lot seems to be received for free - those are not very objective), but the fact that out of 200k owners only 200 people play it kind of speak for itself. It will take a lot of work to make this game really good, but hopefully devs can do it.

_childDocuments_.review: The obvious point of comparison here is Heroes of Might and Magic series, particularly third entry.Disclaimer: HoMM 3 was one of the first games in my life, and I've played it on and off since release to this day.My first impressions on EA release were a bit mixed. I didn't necessarily appreciate some of the design decisions, such as limiting the stack size per unit type. I also thought that the magic was a bit underwhelming.Also the songs in first campaign were a bit meh. Geez that sounds superficial and shallow...Anyway, I had my reservations, but ultimately liked the game when it came out in EA.But now, after 1.0, getting back to it, I am very pleased. The game consumed my free time for the last week.I am getting close to the point of comfortable familiarity. Some things got improved since EA - most significantly I think the game does much better job now of showcasing potential of its magic system. Songs in later campaigns absolutely slap. The writing and plot is suprisingly decent (for turn based strategy game). Even the stack limits swayed me - they seem to be important element of power progression (there is a research system that allows you to raise the caps on units).All in all it is a worthy spiritual successor to HoMM series - but it is it's own game.And I like this game very much.--PS.:Regarding length: I played a bit when it released in EA, recently I picked it up again and I am nearing the end of third campaign at 22.5h of playtime (measured by steam's "last two week" playtime). I played on "medium" and then dropped to "easy". So I'd say that you should more or less count about 8h per campaign (though YMMV obvs).I'd say that's decent amount of content (there is multiplayer and singleplayers scenarios as well, and map editor, and campaign editor, and mods, and random maps + more content from devs to come).
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful, beautiful spiritual successor for the HOMM series, more specifically the first 3 games with the 3rd being one of my favourite games EVER.The art is gorgeous, it has a very good soundtrack and is very satisfying to play. Sometimes it feels a little too dumbed down, but at the same time this allows for a much simplified gameplay compared to HOMM, good for those who are searching for something a bit more casual. Don't get me wrong - it still has its complexities and depth, but doesn't feel as complex as the HOMM games.And most of all, when I play it I don't feel the need to go back to HOMM, something a lot of this type of games always provoked in me.

_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: It's an okay game. I wouldn't call this a successor to HOMM3/HOMM5, but it is an interesting formula to play around with. Apart from Age of Wonders and this, I don't see any other games combining the 4X genre with turn-based tactical battles.My main issues with the game are as follows:*Variety - Only 4 factions available, 5th coming through DLC. Also, can't mix monsters from other factions with yours which is wasted potential in my opinion. Not all monsters are viable, some are not worth using. This can also apply to HOMM. Little variety in wielder equipment and artefacts, and generally roaming the map is not interesting at all. It seems that the meat and bones of the game lie in the battles.*Missing QOL - Have to essentially click 3 times to move, or click once to designate area to move and press 'Q' twice to move wielders fast. There is no option to enable fast movement. This personally bothers me and turns me off from playing the game. Ideally, clicking once should be enough to move.*AI and difficulty - Developers have some trouble refining AI to suit casual play. Campaigns are hard to get through on easiest difficulty. The AI isn't very smart and cheats, it seems to beeline straight for your wielders and towns from across the map in most instances. This applies to skirmish maps too.The game suffers from the issue of AI struggling to bounce back from losing a battle. The game is basically over after the first battle because the AI doesn't try to retreat and rebuild armies like a human player would. This happens on "easiest" and "medium" difficulties, maybe on harder difficulties the AI can cheat it's way to regain armies quicker.Still, it is worth checking out at a reasonable discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for so long to play this game. I was so lucky to be picked for alpha testing and I had a blast, everything is super polished, the pixel art looks amazing, the gameplay is all I hoped for and even my girlfriend complimented the music which she never does for other games I play.Some random details you might find useful to know about the game:Most importantly THERE IS HOTSEAT.You don't get to build every building in every city, you only get access to so many plots of land in different sizes. So you have to strategize in advance, you can't just mindlessly throw down buildings.Spells points are generated (mostly) during combat by the types of units your hero owns so if you have a lot of chaos units you will be able to cast a lot of chaos spells.There's a full level editor and you can download "songs" (campaigns) that community members made.Armies size capped, you get a maximum stack size which you can increase with research (There are 2 tech trees for each faction)Those are the things I'd wanna know off the top of my head.I hope there's big plans ahead for this game, mostly I'd wish for more factions, more spells, maybe some more "daring" items that do some crazy stuff, and a more complex skirmish system that lets you customize the scenario more deeply.Anyways thanks again to the amazing devs for the key, I highly recommend this game, it's boatloads of fun!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone not familiar with the common comparison of HOMM, the game at first from trailers and whatnot came across as being a 4x game with a lot less depth but in a more 'streamlined' manner, and while the intuitive UI and easy game controls did fulfill the streamlined aspect, the game definitely doesn't sacrifice depth to achieve that, which is so awesome.I was so happy to finish the first mission of the campaign, not sure if the game will hold my attention for long, and then switch to 1v1'ing my friend on the smallest island map and getting an hour into the game feeling like we weren't even halfway done. It does a great job of making you feel the transition from one guy in a hut into a great empire in a satisfying way that doesn't stagnate in weird places.If I were to have any criticism if you could call it that, is I feel like for this game to truly have longevity it will need to put more focus into expanding races, adding new ones, and fully fleshing out the multiplayer, because while I absolutely find myself getting lost in the amazing art and world, the campaign fell short and I wasn't too interested in the 'reward songs'. Game is great as is, add in things such as roster expansions, whole new factions, and multiplayer support, and we have a real long term gem. Good job guys.

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of conquest is fun for a few hours and then you realize its many flaws and the fun peels away fast. SoC begins as a HoMM play style and then changes the goal posts half way through with difficulty spikes that feels unfair and unprovoked. The beginning felt like Heroes of Might and Magic 3 and captured my attention. Beautiful Artwork,  I really love the feel of SoC environments, great soundtrack. Feels nostalgic for the first two missions of the first campaign.The complaints people had in early access are the same complaints I am writing here two years later. I will reiterate the majority of the negative feedback that has not been addressed along with my perspective.  The fourth map of the first campaign is VASTLY more difficult than the previous. The first three levels of the first campaign is where I felt at home with SoC. This was immediately reversed when the AI walloped me without warning and forced me to multiple attempts. Personally, this was such a big turn off for me. The game does not provide hints or tips or gear or anything to help the player understand how to overcome the new challenges. Some players like the challenge, but for me, I'm not going to spend any more time in a game that has become no longer enjoyable. There are physical advantages (vantage points). The tactical appeal distills to a point and click battleground where the winner is determined by the most units. If you are attacked by an enemy with more than you, there is very little you can do to win. The reason for this is because of the lack of damaging spells and the magic system (see below). The campaign maps require a very specific sequence of steps to victory. This does not allow you to build a character, or explore the maps or adventure. If you didn't know the AI would show up on turn 15, you will lose. If you didn't know you had to hole up in a city, you will lose. If you didn't know you had to zerg a city, you will lose. If you didn't know you needed a specific item, you will lose. If you didn't know that the AI knows what you are doing, you will lose. Everything requires insider knowledge. This is simply bad game design. Look at the forums and you will see posts regarding this every day. Upgraded units sometimes have the ability to buff allies if an attack is not preferable. This could almost be a pro except that these buffs should be an implicit ability to the units. SoC seems to emulate special skills by 5th and 6th tier units in HoMM3, except that again, they are buffs that don't feel like they have any weight that could make or break a battle. The magic spells are uninteresting and the spell mechanics don't allow your character to feel special or powerful. I do not understand the reason behind the five magic types because they all feel the same. Not to mention, there are hardly any damage-dealing spells, only buffs/debuffs which are often unnoticeable as to whether the have done any good. I find myself scrolling through each new spell in every fight because they are so unremarkable and unmemorable. This is my biggest gripe. Enemy battles are not HoMM-like, instead of amassing your army and crushing your opponent, you will struggle to feel anything more than an average Joe. At the end of most battles you will find that due to the lack of tactical mechanics, your forces are diminished and thus forced to return to your settlement and restock. This feels compounded by the fact that you are limited to the number of Heroes you can have and gathering units becomes a chore within the game. Its feels like a cheap mechanic to extend the game play. There are too many artifacts in this game which become obsolete within minutes of acquiring them. You don't feel like you earned the gear and the stats they provide is almost unnoticeable. Enemy AI can single shot a full stack of your units despite all the gear you've acquired. But it is almost impossible for you to single shot anything they have due to the problems I have already mentioned. In one battle I lost all 5 stacks of my army because a ranged enemy stood on higher ground and I couldn't reach and I did not have spells with any utility. It was a guaranteed loss and not fun. Simply annoying. You are limited to the number of buildings you can construct until you upgrade your settlement. Then you are locked out of units because you didn't construct the RIGHT buildings. If the AI takes over a settlement, you must take it back and REBUILD everything. A number of these buildings require limited resources and sometimes you cannot rebuild a much needed structure. Heroes are called Wielders in SoC. If an AI is approaching a settlement, I either have to have a hero barricaded in the random settlement they attack or pray to god that the AI will wait for me to send one of the only TWO heroes I am allowed to have. There is so much wasted potential in SoC. It is so close to becoming its HoMM3 doppelganger but it misses out on what made HoMM franchise so great. SoC has the wings of an eagle yet it soars like a chicken. I was very hopeful for this game but it became quickly apparent that the campaign mode and the core mechanics have any redeeming qualities that would make me want to come back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Great turn-based strategy. The inspiration from old games, especially heores, is quite noticeable at times, but I bought the game with that in mind. I like most of the new elements in terms of settlement management. You have to really consider what buildings and units you need at times, and the parcels are often limited in number. The spell casting in combat is also innovated and it took me a while to get used to the way and types of spells, but eventually everything fit :) The campaigns are very engaging, and at times I was pleasantly surprised by a twist in the story. The missions are just long enough, I didn't feel like I was stuck somewhere for a long time. The final ballads at the end of each mission are a great cherry on top, a nice reward and they are awesome! :) Definitely don't listen to them beforehand, they sing what happened in the mission! :) I just have to warn undead lovers that despite the great effort to bring originality and an interesting story to this faction, the bar set by Heroes V with Arantir is still very high. This is not to put down the work of the creators of Songs of Conquest, I just haven't developed such a positive relationship with the heroes of Barony of Loth. However, I am very much looking forward to the next updates and maybe I will change my opinion :)

_childDocuments_.review: As a childhood fan of Heroes of Might and Magic 3, this game is serving to scratch an itch that no other game has quite been able to fill (with the exception of Heroes of Might and Magic 5, but only just). While not a direct clone of the Heroes of Might and Magic 2 and 3, it is a worthy spiritual successor; one that seems to draw aesthetically moreso from 2 than from 3 with its high fantasy storybook-like narrative. Gameplay-wise this manifests most clearly in the town management and combat systems, where new mechanics have been introduced to offset some of the heady rut that HoMM fell into. A part of me laments that the combat, magic, and town management aren't a direct clone, but, across the current spate of Early Access content, I've grown to appreciate the way the game does things. Some quirks of design exist that could use some polish, though, on the whole, it's a very stable Early Access release. The pixel art is gorgeous and I look forward to seeing how the game develops into a full release.TL;DR - For fans of turn-based strategy and tactics, it is certainly worth a go. After 25 hours, I feel as if I've gotten my money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game similar in it's basic framework to heroes of might and magic.The good:     It's combat is very engaging, even without magic or abilities because of zone of control, where units get a free attack whenever an enemy moves away from an adjacent tile of that unit     It's magic system is very fun and better balanced since mana (called essence) comes your units (so you can't have a powerful caster with 1 unit roll over everything). There's also numerous fun combos you can do with magic since there's no limit to the spells you can cast in a turn     Building is modular, so you can specialize to make whichever units you want     Unit stacks have a limit, which encourages you to use multiple armiesThe bad     The game is very prone to snowballing since you lose all equipped items on defeat, gain no xp on defeat, the tendency to lose less units the larger your army is, with no garrisons by default and the garrison building being actual garbage     The UI is lacking and awkward in several areas     several building upgrades for units production buildings make the unit cost high tier secondary resources, making it often better to not upgrade it. For example, the knights->Fists of order upgradeThings for new players to note     The first campaign, while enjoyable, will give you a lackluster impression of the magic system since it's only order magic, which specializes in buffs. The other magic colors are much more fun/unique     You will always be short on resources, so don't build all unit production buildings

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR : beautiful graphics, few subtleties of gameplay, lack of content, and exagerated price tag. Come back when the early access is finished and buy it on saleAs a fan of Heroes of Might and Magic 2 and strategic RPGs in general, I really wanted to like this game. And to some extent I do : it has a beautiful pixel art with an efficient hud and controls, and it successfully implements the core gameplay of the game it drew inspiration from. But I'm not satisfied with it and I'll try to explain why.For instance, wielder magic, leveling and inventory systems are less interesting than in HOMM2, since most of the bonuses each system provides are basic stats that makes you stronger without making any build stand out. Similarly, military units and buildings are actually not that varied and quite conventional in their design, at least for the Stoutheart faction I played.Since the gameplay is not that varied, the clear lack of content becomes a major issue, and simply adding the 2 missing campaigns will not cut it. For now, there are 2 campaigns available, which can be finished in 3 to 4 hours each, and there is a skirmish mode in player vs player or AI, as well as a map editor. I'm sure the community will create relevant content, but I really expect more from the developers.Combined with the AA price tag, this lack of content is what makes me leave a negative review. I do realize that this is an early access game and I truly wish to come back to it one day and change my review, but I simply believe it should cost twice less and offer four times more content. The gameplay part may be more complicated to improve but I'm sure it's possible. It can still become a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I like Songs of Conquest. Songs of Conquest is a Turn Based Tactics RPG offering a retro look and a fresh take on a Heroes of Might and Magic like.Specifically, Songs of Conquest is a more detailed and tactical take on old school Heroes of Might and Magic 3!That’s right: HoMM 3, the one many consider the best of the series.Yes.And more!Songs of Conquest offers all the hex based, hero focused, map exploration, pickup gathering, and turn-based, tactical combat of HoMM, but adds more tactical depth to the combats with different terrain features, plus the very meaningful addition of zones of control: if you try and move past a foe in melee, prepare to be whacked!There is high ground that grants 20% increased damage bonus, creating natural points on the battlefield like hills you will want to take and hold, and now you can put your own troops up on high walls defending your cities, able to take advantage of the position to rain down fire upon the invaders.You also have a similar city building system here, with a default build one building per day, but in Songs of Conquest, the city map is right on the world map, skipping the loading screen when going into the city.Also unlike HoMM, buildings produce troops every day here, so no need to rush back to the city each week, or worry about missing getting a building up in time or losing a boatload of recruitment.So, you end up with more troops on the field sooner; good.However, unlike HoMM, there is a cap to how many units you can put into a troop hex.I really like that, as it creates some kind of reasonable limit in terms of exactly how many knights, or peasants, or skeletons I can stuff into a single hex; 1000s always seemed a bit too much to me…This also means recovery from a big battle is far more possible, as you did not just lose months of recruitment in a one big, painful moment, and this should result in less dropped players after such a pivotal moment in play.Combine that with the free spawn, replenishing guardian troops you get when you build walls, and you have a game where recovery after a big loss is very likely, and pulling out a victory from the jaws of defeat can make it taste all the sweeter.There are many character and gameplay choices to make here; right at the start.There are 4 factions to choose here, right at the start: the human and fey alliance, the necromancers and their undead, swamp lizardmen, and a mercenary and inventor faction.Each faction has 9 heroes, called Wielders, to choose from at the state: they all have different focuses; some prefer magic, others might, others more of a mix; plenty of options here. At lvls 8 and 16, the Wielders get special powers: these are very powerful abilities that help shape that specific hero.When a hero lvls, you pick 1 of 3 upgrades: usually a command upgrade; a hero specific one, and something else.That’s another change from the HoMM formula: heroes in Songs of Conquest here start with a low number of different stacks of troops they can command, either 2 or 3 at lvl 1; very unlike the max you get right from the start in HoMM.This is very good, as it showcases the hero’s growth as a commander more, as they start only able to handle 2 or 3 bands of warriors, and grow to be the great commander.It also provides another meaningful choice for the player to make: do you develop this hero as more of a commander who can lead lots of stacks of units, or do you focus them onto a specific strategy using certain types of units, or magic?Magic in Songs of Conquest is broken down into Order, Chaos, Creation, Destruction and Arcane; with 4 spells each; there are also 20 combination spells that a mix of each of the elements.You can cast as many spells per turn you can afford, this is very good, as you spend some time building up the essences in battle needed to cast.Also, this means you don’t have to camp out in town to refuel your magic points; more exploration and combat, less city camping.A random Map Generator has been added as well, a feature that was sadly lacking from the early HoMM games; they are present here to help keep the gameplay fresh.Set maps are also a prominent feature, in case that is your preference.Songs of Conquest also comes packed with a map editor, in case you are the type who likes to make your own maps. Both Local Co-op hotseat multiplayer, and online Co-op and PvP are present, in case that is something that interests you.Controller Support is present, at least it was on the map, but I was unable to move my units or cast spells using the gamepad; this is also an issue I have seen reported on the Steam Deck as well, so I would urge caution currently getting this if you are committed to using a controller / deck.Thankfully, mouse and keyboard is present, and felt great.While I do like Songs of Conquest, I did come across some areas while playing where I feel it could be even better.Please let me know if anyone thinks any of this is out-of-line, or off-base.For example, by double clicking during the movement; it would be a welcome feature.The keybinds on the gamepad say it is pause, but that does not work.I’m aware this is being worked on, but as I was assessing the current launch version of the game, I have to mention it.Currently, there are issues with the controller and the Steam Deck, with it flat out not working in battle for myself when I tested it with a controller.The devs are aware, and are working on it, but I have to mention it.I know there is that yellow circle under the Wielder, but all that does is tell you if you have movement left or not, not any apparent indication of how much is left.Maybe there could be a radial yellow circle bar under the hero that decreases as you move, with the yellow dimming as the movement left fades.This would make it far more visually apparent how much movement each hero has left, without having to click around to see what they have got left every turn.It seems that you or the AI will just instantly win upon finding the super special thing: there is no countdown timer, no notification prompt that it has been found, no need to take the super special MacGuffin to a special place to use it, empower it, or destroy it to win, nop!You, or more likely the AI, just instantly win. :(Currently, this victory condition is not very exciting…Thankfully, you can just not use it when setting up the map, which is what I would recommend currently.Note: This is a launch look at Songs of Conquest so any bugs or other oddness is not representative of the final product, as updates should be coming to continue to improve the game.Anyway, my hopefully helpful suggestions aside, I really like Songs of Conquest.Songs of Conquest is a fun Turn Based Tactics RPG Retro take on HoMM 3, but packs even more depth in to the combats, and is easily well worth a wishlist and a watch.Watch?
