_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty new but already having a pretty hard time wanting to load the game up. - It all feels lifeless, like absolute disconnected from my toons. When my troops die I only feel bad that I don't care at all... - The game plays like a checklist without the checklist, almost like everything you do anyone else who played would be doing.- The graphics suck. I get it's a style, but it's somewhere between on old RPG's and old Arcade games. VICTORY at the end of a fight makes it feel cheesy to me. To me there is no feeling to the world, it's all bland and basic as if to make it quickly. - The game is very quick, so quick it feels like it's about giving you everything up front to the point where I already don't want to "explore" because well, I'm simply following a very very predictable trail of bread crumbs. - I don't feel like I'm building up a kingdom, it's not mine... it's the Devs. No heart, no nothing... You pick seemingly nothing, rather you color in the bubble with a number inside to let you know what color to use. ---------------I get that people like games like this, I'm not here to poop on that. Buying the game I really hoped it would have depth but this game appears to have none... it feels very much like a MEME game, popular because it's something slightly different, made to be consumed faster than a glass of sugar filled grape juice. I say all this because people who might want to put down money might only see the positive comments, and that's fine... but maybe that person looking at the game from the outside might feel some of what I'm talking about and want to avoid it but fanbois only hype hype hype... and then run to consume the next game in 2 weeks. What I was looking for was a game that I could play over years, load up even after I forgot about it and just play over a week leaving it loaded up all that time... This to me feels like you play knowing it's ok, kinda fun maybe... up until you remember it's all by the numbers... you just repeat, repeat and repeat. It's boring imo. I'll still try it, maybe I'm wrong and I'll change my answer here, but this game feels like the art style, short cut after short cut to just pump out a game, but it seemed kinda cool and so it sells millions before everyone forgets about it.

_childDocuments_.review: While playing campaign the levels are forced to end before you have a chance to explore the map.There is a time limit and enemy hero forces you to fight him, and you end up finishing the level with half of it unexplored.They came up with a game dynamic that works against the presentation of the content they have created, I have no idea what they were thinking but this is quite ridiculous.Post 1.0 Update: They have broken the game balance. You start the levels completely underpowered and random armies just decimate you, leaving you unable to complete the campaign. Just read the reddit threads on difficulty imbalance - Devs don't care about the enjoyability of the game at all. What's even funnier - you have much higher chance of winning a battle on auto-resolve (and have much fewer casualties) compared to manual play, which again brings me to the point above: They have introduced a game mechanic (auto resolve being less punishing on armies) that forces you to SKIP game content (manual battles, animations and spells). What were they thinking, was this game a weekend project for them? Did they have no play testers? _childDocuments_.review: I have been having the honor to stream through the first main campaign with my community and have lots of thoughts! There won't be any spoilers since I really want people to try it themselves. As an older kid who enjoyed watching my parents play HOMM from their deskside, Songs of Conquest feels like an amazing foray into the genre and an absolutely wonderful spiritual successor. The units are all beautifully designed and animated, the campaign itself that I've been through so far has been very fun and full of interesting lore, and I've really enjoyed all the characters and scenery the game presents. There are, in the later levels, a large difficulty spike that forces you to really be as efficient as possible; mission 3 our of 4 made me restart it entirely due to not really knowing where my town goals were, and while it was a little frustrating, I really enjoyed it actually. Going through the mission entirely blind and then using what I've learned to be more efficient and go through the level more effectively adds a lot of repeatability and really helped me appreciate my own ability to adapt and overcome challenges that I felt were previously insurmountable. As for skirmishes, I don't have anyone in particular to play multiplayer with currently, haha, so I suppose I won't focus on that as much as I haven't gotten to play it. Game mechanics wise everything feels very sound, although I do find that some of the units being incomplete for some factions and other factions being able to have a stack of 100 vs a max stack of 50 for a base unit is a little... not great? I believe some balancing could be put into place, but it's generally pretty fair. Along with that, this IS a week one review, and I'm sure we'll get additions and stuff later on!Lastly, while it does not effect my opinions on the gameplay itself, the dev team have been extremely kind and friendly with not only me, an extremely small content creator, but with their entire community and love to get feedback. I just wanted to note that Lavapotion have been absolutely stellar and I'm excited to see the support they give to the game in the future; we just don't have enough developers that are this devoted and lovely nowadays and wanted to give them a shoutout. Ahh, also, the music in this game? Absolutely stellar. The sound effects all help to feel like you're playing in a fantastic ballad of an epic tale. Along with that, you get little songs for every chapter you complete in the main story, and they are all fantastic!!TLDR: If you enjoyed HOMM or just like turn-based strategy, I think SoC could be a really fun game for you and highly recommend it!!

_childDocuments_.review: A modern classic that draws inspiration from but tries to improve upon older titles, it succeeds enough to set itself apart from the past and is an interesting game on its own merits. A great game for fans of  who want something fresh, and a game that is approachable to beginners.The world is filled with conflict, and discontent. The Rana are enslaved, the Baryans crippled by debt, and the Barons are at each other’s throats. Yet times are changing, the Faey are restless, the Unseen Society is stirring, the Rider comes, but all these conflicts are transient, yes, things are changing, because only Aurelia is Eternal. The story is explored through four roughly concurrent campaigns, each telling the story from a different perspective and giving the player added context and a deeper understanding of the conflicts at hand. Distrust, old wounds, arrogance and fear serve to make matters worse, but each faction has their own hopes for the future, and fight to make things better, their way.I like that. The characters are heroes in their own stories, there is no true villain because they all do terrible things, but they all have justifications for doing what they do and their own visions of a new world. Whether or not their arguments are reasonable is another discussion but the fact that it can be debated at all is more than you say for certain games.So, you meet a colourful cast of characters, such as the honourable, and courageous Silkspool of Barya; the slave turned freedom fighter Rasc of Rana; the murderous tyrant Cecila Stoutheart of Arleon; and the illuminati. There are several more to be acquainted with, like my favourite Bighli, the protagonist in the Barya campaign, and my runner-up, Brother Hillar. However, what I especially appreciate is that dialogue changes depending on what commander initiates it, of course this is all flavour, but it is a nice touch that things change ever so slightly.However, I notice one issue as early as the first campaign, which is that endings do not really conclude much at all and leave a lot of things unresolved never to be brought up again. This problem is most apparent in the Arleon campaign, they introduce a problem and Cecila has to solve it, but midway they switch tracks and decide the campaign should be about something else instead and so they functionally leave both plot threads with unsatisfying conclusions. It feels very abrupt.Yes, every campaign has a suitably epic finale, but there is no epilogue at all, it feels like they are hinting at a sequel or an expansion, which does not sit right with me. I love the campaigns, and the stories, but would have preferred that they release two or three longer campaigns with an epilogue on full release and have the rest as DLC. has some of the prettiest pixel art I have ever seen, it is absolutely beautiful, home to wonderful aesthetically pleasing regions, units with a surprising amount of character, and it is simply very nice to look at.Even if you set the beauty aside you will still find a game that is easy to read, completely free from units that are hard to differentiate and one that has a variety of creatures that are rare to see in fantasy games. Rana is definitely the standout for unorthodox units having a selection of creepy-crawlers, amphibians and a few more. Yet even the archetypical knight faction, Arleon, has its fair share of diversity, as they also include the Faey.The OST is nearly as good, songs like the main theme are magical, and almost make me tra-la-la while the tracks for Loth are a bit more imposing and ominous, but they all make me think of fairytales, sometimes the happier, epic ones and other times the desolate, vengeful ones. There is a song for each conceivable mood that a strategy-RPG can invoke in you. My personal favourite is probably , , , or , but the entire OST is great, so I had a hard time picking out the ones I liked best.They also made songs of conquests, imagine that music about your victories, amazing. These songs are not only nice rewards for completing a new campaign mission, but they are also great on their own, giving you an in-universe bard’s tale, providing each faction with their own flair, and showing the people’s perception on what is going on. My favourite is probably Barya’s song, , or , both are great, the latter gives me shivers, while the former is simply captivating., like the rest of the genre, splits its gameplay in two. You have the adventure map where you need to think strategically, capturing resources, modifying your compositions and generally working on the big picture; and then you have the combat, where you make use of your equipment, and compositions to tactically outmanoeuvre your opponent.One of my favourite aspects of the genre is the adventure screen and  does not disappoint. You have numerous artifacts to find, strange and varied resources to capture and sometimes dozens of settlements to conquer.However, this is where we run into a problem, and that is that is map knowledge. The official campaigns are mostly free from this issue, but it is a risk you will face if you play skirmish maps or community content. In  you require large cities; you require celestial ore and the other rare resources. If you do not have that, you cannot upgrade your units, increase their stack sizes or even access your most powerful units. So if you are a beginner of average skill and forced to meander about for turns on end you will most likely be facing an enemy too powerful to beat, and that can be annoying.As stated, this is not much of an issue in the official campaigns, anymore, because the developers are aware of it and are typically good at signposting, so the missions feel fun, with the right amount of variety in terms of objectives. The major issue is campaign length, there are only four missions per faction one of which is a tutorial so while the finales are grand and epic in scope, especially the fourth one, you will not explore the factions as much as I would have liked, that is left for skirmish mode.Perhaps the most important thing in 's combat is your unit compositions. Each creature generates essence and that can be used to cast a range of powerful and effective spells.This also means that even weak units can have a part to play and that you are less likely to sack a creature than in . You want to keep at least one soldier alive, if possible, they might be completely useless in an actual fight, but they generate just as much magic as if the stack was completely filled.You might be inclined to focus on a few spells, using a monolithic army but being able to cast fireballs every few turns. Maybe you prefer a diverse army with more flexible magic solutions, maybe you simply prefer having a strong army of Baryan gunpowder. Whatever you like there are pros and cons but one of my personal favourite tactics is a mass of Musketeers and Canons and buffing them to shoot twice each attack. Of course, they do need to reload, but why would I worry when my enemies will be dead before they reach me? Here be no dragons, only craters and corpses.Yet combat is not perfect, it plays great and is fun, but siege in particular has some annoying issues. The vertically messes with your positioning and sometimes you are unable to place someone in an opening because you can only highlight the hex in front, but the AI has no such weaknesses and that can be annoying if they have a particularly challenging Wielder.

_childDocuments_.review: TL, DR: It's worth full price. It's an excellent successor to the HoMM franchise that innovates enough to make its own mark while retaining enough of the old designs to scratch that itch for ye olde HoMM. Buy it. BUY IT NOW.First the campaigns: A besieged kingdom loses its patriarch: in his place rises a hard-nosed daughter intent on proving her worth. With dark rumours of cultists, power-hungry neighbours, and restless Fey at the periphery the only question is how far she'll go to bring stability amidst a crumbling Empire.Amidst the fires in the desert, an orphan slave is freed and returns to his home, now with a thirst for vengeance against those who have oppressed his people for so long. It doesn't matter if the world is burning as well: his people  be free from the tyranny of man.There are four factions: Arleon (the remnants of the broken Empire) are the archetypal human kingdom but with some fun twists thrown in. Crossbows and longmen, swords and shields - backed by oathsworn Fey that bring the fury of the forests into the mix. Barya are merchant-states to whom contracts are law and anyone can be anything. Great for discovering new technology. Also great for enabling slavery. Win some, lose some. They rely heavily on firearms, barriers and giant brutes - including an awe-inspiring cannon that will bring the end to any battle it sees use in.Rana are the slave-race of amphibians, dwelling in the marsh amidst giant insects, spiders, carnivorous birds and an ominous threat you'll have to discover for yourself. The Barony of Loth is a kingdom in extreme decline. Their armies are gone, their cities are ruins and no hope left. Well, almost. You see: they're not just going to lay down and stay dead. The Barony of Loth will rise again, even if its rotting citizens must slaughter the living to see its power rise once more. Cultists and skeletons abound in this cute twist on the typical Undead faction. Needs a tad more necromancy in-game, though.Finally, a quick summary of the tweaks the game has made that have put it, at least in my estimation, as an excellent successor to the HoMM franchise. - Settlements have specifically sized building slots that ensure a single settlement isn't  enough to build everything, but it's enough to conquer the neighbours. This makes the game vastly less centralised than HoMM is. This is a huge positive in practice because it means many more settlements changing hands throughout the game, as each map tends to have at least 6-8. - Stack caps. Gone are the days of 300+ crossbowmen that snipe you from across the screen. Now each stack has a certain number of units it can fit (increased via research): if you want more crossbowmen, you're going to need to have multiple stacks of them. This enables a fair bit more variety in army make-up and also ensures that there is a hypothetical limit to how big a single army can be, encouraging multiples. - Range is not infinite, units have zone of control, and there are height differences in the map that actually matter. This is pretty common among HoMM spiritual successors but is still worthy of note. - What magic you have is based both on your hero and on your army. Each unit you buy generates essence associated with them. A swordsman might generate Order, for example. That then fuels Order spells. This is honestly a surprisingly fun premise that lets you build armies and heroes to compliment each other - like setting up a fireball mage with a bunch of destruction-essence units so they can start raining destruction with impunity. Though it also means as your units die you tend to have less and less magic to turn the tide. Gotta be careful. Nothing is truly expendable.  - Special resources, like stand-ins for mercury and crystals, are so bloody scarce that when you get the option to have a hero generate them it is unironically a compelling choice. I didn't quite like it at first but the more I thought about it the more it forced me to make difficult decisions: do I want 20% more damage, or do I want the ability to upgrade this unit or buy this research? All that said, there are some bits that are...  great, but this is also an early access game that looks like a finished game worthy of its full price. Mostly my issues boil down to the following: - A lot of factions have units that do the same thing - this unit debuffs offense/defense/initiative in an area around them, this unit can skip their turn to provide a mild buff to all your units, etc. It has the unfortunate element of making the factions feel a bit too same-y, like they're just reskinning some units. I don't think that's the case, ofc, but I'd like to see more asymmetry where the factions are a bit more distinct in the buffs/debuffs they give and what they do.  - The Wisdom skill still exists. XP sharing I get, but "get more XP" just seems like a feat tax that we've moved past design-wise. Either it's an auto-buy or it's a trap; there is no in-between. It doesn't lead anywhere and, honestly, it doesn't make the game more fun. IMO: toss it and embrace exploring other possible skills. Not everything has to be HoMM-derived. - Small creature spawns seem a tad low. It's more manageable once you get more settlements but starting off it tends to be a bit rough. Either that or I'm bad at the game. Pls fix. >:( - The amount of Risen you get after a battle (as the Barony of Loth) is negligible, which is a bit frustrating because they take up a slot and there doesn't seem to be a way to improve the rate. That said this is early access so I'm hoping this will be addressed over time. - The campaign songs - the ones the game is named for - are  lackluster. Their pacing is weak, the rhyming rarely fits neatly. It's not even remotely a big deal, ofc, since you can just skip it. It's just a bit awkward given that it is a titular feature. Maybe they warrant remaking in the future, depending on how successful the game is. Y'know, just in case you get No Man's Sky money. ;3cAll in all it's an excellent successor to the spirit of HoMM3. It innovates enough to make it unique but maintains a lot of the elements that made the game fun to begin with. Plus I dig the pixel art. It gives the game a very unique style. I think if they continue to evolve, making the factions more distinct from one another, it will be worth way more than their current asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: I post this about 2 weeks prior to the 1.0 release.It's an absolute blast. Imagine taking some of the best elements from the table-top styled turn based games with world maps and battle gameplay, then painting it with some stellar modernized pixel graphics. It's responsive, a lot of fun, with the ability for your heroes to both gain levels (with you picking their specialization) and equipment. It's quite rewarding to level up your heroes and the battles feel and look great.A thing I really appreciate is the limitaitons on how many units you can have in a battle. This created issues in some other games I've played in the past, like a completely broken late-game. That can be fun in its own right but I'm personally grateful that it's not a thing here.The base building available came as a surprise to me when I started playing. It feels really well-designed and thought out, allowing for various outposts to grow into towns and cities. The limitations also endorse experimenting with different types of builds, which is a lot of fun thanks to the robust unit design and battle mechanics.The music is also really good. It shows that the developers and visionaries for this title really cared about how these types of games are played and what draws you in. And they show it without stifling innovation or sacrificing enjoyability. This is the best take on the genre I've seen. Possibly ever, even when compared to some of the older titles. At the very least it shares a top spot among some absolute legends.

_childDocuments_.review: As entirely anyone would think this is HOMM, (Heroes of Might and Magic). You aren't completely wrong. Is it entirely copying everything about HOMM? No is the short answer to that. This is already shaping up becoming into one of my favourite games out there. Let's do a summary of what this game has to offer. - Towns are built outside, so you'll get a nice overview on the map, how the city grows from a humble village into a prosperous metropolis. - You can mish and mash buildings pretty much in any form or way, making decisons so much extensive. I wouldn't recommend building small buildings on medium or large, but you get my point. What you have available, you can pretty much do whatever you fancy. - There is a Research/tech tree involved here. Further bolstering your troops, economy and magic in various ways, some are really unique if fully researched, as every single tech can be researched three times. - Unit caps, and unit commands. You start with 3 commands, which is how many different troops you can have, adding more command with each level, you can expand your army. Unit caps make units don't exceed crazy numbers which you could aquire back in HOMM. There are limits, but you can always combine the same units creating many flexible combinations. Some work better with others. Units create Essence. Essence is your form of magic, allowing you to cast not just one spell at the time, but as much you desire, as long you have enough essence, Combat is fun and strategic, and they keep on updating the game constantly, promising more factions for the future. Even so, 4 factions already included so far. Note, I may not remember all the names. Arleon/Empire consists of Humans and Fae creatures. Rena/Lizardmen Consistst of Lizards and FrogsThe undead faction which I can't remember at this moment, consists of Undead and humans. And finally the Orcs combining with human faction. Each are very different, I'd say that's all you have available from Early access is more then enough. Cute sprite animations, I ain't fuzzed about the decision, it looks bloody amazing. It's worth the price, give them support if your interested into the fantasy genre. Or wait until full release. It's going to be my new staple of playing games similar to HOMM for the future. Does it mean I will just abandon the HOMM roots I have? No, but this is damn close. However is it completely without some faults I'd like to address. No of course not. For instance, I feel artefacts providing command could've maybe been replaced or maybe just the limit of the command could be decreased, skill wise that is. So that an artefact providing command would be more liable, as in the choice of matter in late-game, I always choose a different artefact, because command only provides what the skill already does. Specially if you put all those level up points into the same category so you can have the biggest army right from the get-go. Leaving it with a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Elitism and nostalgia aside-- apart from the basics of the gameplay loop, this is nothing close to HoMM, despite all the stuff they said in the trailers. I feel lied to. I get this is alpha-- but if these are the foundations of the final product, and from I've seen in their Discord they don't plan any significant tweaks to bring it to closer to its roots-- then I feel outright stupid for buying this and the supporter pack alongside it.Sense of wonder: nonexistent. 'Formulaic' is the best word to describe it. Mystic vibe: personally gone, just 'yet another high fantasy game'. I've seen more original worldbuilding on deviantart.Music: only a couple of tracks stand out. Rest is absolutely nowhere near the ambient music Paul Romero composed. (Ironic as the game's story quite literally revolves around living through ballads sang by bards).Story: only thing I can remember at this point is it being about some discount Meve from the Witcher series. Second chapter, or 'song'? So forgettable that even with being only 40 hours in, it's already out my mind. Maybe you want it just for a good bit of skirmish? Well sucks to be you. As of now all that's on the table is extremely limited options (handful of maps), laughable variety and a joke of replay value-- essentially stuck with the dog water campaign, as it has the most meat on its bones.Lastly, all the low-key out-of-nowhere pandering in the campaign, and throughout the game overall? Nice one. Truly needed in a HoMM-like... Took me back to the ye olde days of debates on 2016 YouTube.Don't bother. Save your hard-earned money for a rainy day or keep an eye out for when this evolves into something worth your time.It amazes me how a handful of guys in 1999 could have came out with a complete game such as HoMM3. Without all this modern fancy techniques, software and pipelines, with everything from logistics to communications being tens of times more bothersome than now-- yet they still managed to create an all-time masterpiece. Yet in 2022-- whole 23 years later-- something so lacklustre gets a pass because 'it's in alpha'.90% positive reviews-- I must be living in some alternative reality by the looks of it. Genuinely disappointed with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: I'd recommend WHEN ITS FINISHED.  At the moment it's definitely still going through all the Early Access issues.  If you're cool with that, then you should support it, especially if you're a fan of Heroes 3 and want these kinds of games to keep being made.Keep in mind when comparing this game to HOMM 3 that Heroes 3 has had a long time to evolve and develop.  Very few if anyone ever played HOMM 3 in "Early Access," so trying to compare this game in its current state is a generally unfair comparison when you stack up all of Heroes' little changes, expacks, and evolution along the way - especially if you count any fan patches or similar content.The Essence (aka: Magic) system feels both more and less exploitable than HOMM 3's magic.  It's hard to even gauge where this is going to pan out since the game is still making major tweaks to things like essence generation or spell damage - not to mention just the interactivity of effects.  The ways these can interact with particular troop mechanics can also be baffling at times.  Sseth's "I'm not sure where mechanics end and exploits begin" is a good line, because it's hard to tell right now since things are being developed and changed routinely.Still, the game is generally beautiful both musically and artistically.  The two campaigns released thus far feel good, and probably take about 10 hours each to play through.  Again, comparing them to Homm 3 campaigns isn't really too fair of a comparison as the sheer breadth of Homm 3's campaigns would take you easily over 200 hours if you counted all the expansions.Ultimately if you think Heroes 3 is a good game, you should support this - if for no other reason than it's better than giving your money to Ubisoft who either forgot (or simply never knew) how to handle the Heroes franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write a lot of reviews, when I do i really love the game or dislike it. In this case, I am not a fan of the game. As a player of HotM3, AoW4 & Endless Legend & Space 2, this game doesn't live up to its expectations.- The online multiplayer is clunky, if you make an enemy out of someone, you immediately can't play simultaneously anymore and have to click them "friendly" to play simultaneously again, like why? I want to play, not have extra wait time. Really dumb mechanic. Take a look at Endless Legend and how they have done it.- All races are basically the same. Upgrade your towns to it's fullest and reap your rewards, only the leveling of your hero can tweak it a bit, but each game feels the same because of this.- Don't ever go for any battle beyond fair with auto-battler. You basically lose 80% of the time and will have a crap game.- More different winning conditions would be fun. Like maybe someone is going for the beacons while another is going for another objective. Or like in AoE maybe someone is building a wonder. These are things that can be easily made better I think. - The (paid) DLC they are currently coming up feels very lacking. I would only pay for a DLC for this game if it has at least 1 new race and a big new mechanic to change the monotone gameplay.-The price point is really high. I bought it on sale, but I think 33 euro's is a very steep price for a game that doesn't bring that much new to the genre.Some plusses:- The art style is really lovely and captures the mood really well. While Im a fan of this, the playstyle of each race feels very much the same, building and build wise, disregarding the unique styles of each race- Every turn you get some units. This is a very welcome change to other games like this where you either have to wait a few turns and stay idle. You can always crank up a weaker hero with some new units.- All in all its a chill game, if you want to play this solo, definitely do. I'm used to playing these kind of games with friends for sessions of 2-3 hours, thats why the review maybe is a little bit harsh.2 Bonus ideas for the devs but if you could crack the auto battle to be a little more strategic like maybe have a pre-setup for each battle you can set or maybe "defensive" or "aggresive" mode. The other idea is to have "daily mode", where each player in an online game can take only 1 (or 2) turns a day. This could be really cool for people with more busy lives that still want to play these kind of games. I can really imagine people having whatsapp groups over this and having these weeklong games.All in all, I see potential, but it's not there yet!

_childDocuments_.review: A reimagining of Heroes of Might & Magic 2~3 , and a pretty good one at that. While being true to the formula of these games, there are tons of improvements, quality of life features and gameplay tweaks that are well designed, and some still being smoothed out.The game has 4 factions, which in my view is a bit on the low side, and one of the areas where the game seemingly falls short of its examples. Factions share between them the pool of spells, each gaining access to 3 different schools of magic.  That being said, the units each faction offers are well thought out and there is a lot of (hidden/implicit) synergy to be found between them and the spells you get. Another cool endgame feature is the addition of research to improve kingdom and unit features, among which one key element where Songs of Conquest differs: unit stack sizes are limited.  This counteracts the limited choices each faction has, since all of them remain viable. Low tier units get higher stack limits, while top tier units can easily be limited to 3-5 units. This is but one example of a gameplay tweak that makes Songs of Conquest familiar, yet unique.Looking forward to seeing this game get finished and expanded upon.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe it took this long to have a new game in the genre of HoMM3. Visually speaking, what an update! The game is visually gorgeous, the pixel look within a 3D space is a great way to give it a fresh modern look while still calling back to its retro origins. Every sprite is carefully crafted and animated and it is so nice to see them move.The world map movement and interactions feels every bit the same as HoMM3 and I would not want it any other way.The most notable change is that your town and every building in it is physically present on the map. I think this is a great add-on because because it makes the action of making your town and expanding it much more tangible and satisfying.Speaking of it,I love how they handled the town building. You are offered with a limited amount of spots for your buildings but you are allowed  to decide the locations, types and quantity of buildings you want to have in your town. It is a nice additional strategy layer that lets you specialise your towns for your needs. You could potentially have a town that only produces resources or one that is made to focus on creating as much units as possible. It really does feel like an improvement to HoMM3.I would say the combat is the part of the game that changed the most.The tactical aspect stays true to its origins, while adding features that only deepen the experience. (The elevations that gives you defensive or ranged bonuses are a welcomed improvement). Units have a variety of special abilities that gives them a specific play style. For instance, I am still on my first game with the Barya faction and I love how the spearman has extended reach and can attack through other units. It is something that I don't think was present in HoMM3 and it makes for fun tactics. That said, I really hate that the musketeers need to reload. The spell slinging is probably one of the more unique aspect from the game. You don't have just one type of mana, you now have 4. From what I have seen, they are mostly affected by the hero you chose and the type of units he carries with it. During combat, you start with no mana and you accumulate it depending of which actions you make with your troops, mixing the different type of mana to cast various spells. Compared to HoMM3, it changes the relation you have with your mana. Where you once saved it for strategically important fights, you are now encouraged to use it as soon as you have it. It makes casting spells something you do on a much more regular basis, which is nice. But the sad thing is that you lose what was once an important resource to manage, making the choice of using spells a much more trivial one.Like I said, I have been playing for almost 5 hours and I am having a blast!There are things I am not 100% on board with, but in this case the good definitely outweighs the bad.At this time, I already have the feeling that this is a game I will be coming back to on a regular basis. For an Early Access, this is extremely solid. There are tweaks and balancing to be made but I am confident the devs will be responsive to the community and tackle these issues as they come up.With the success it already has, I can only hope there will be new factions, maps and scenarios overtime because this game surely deserves it.For any HoMM enjoyer, this game is a must buy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal. If you are looking for an amazing Turn-Based Strategy game with a lot of unique mechanics, this is a game for you. Now if you are looking for a game exactly like Heroes of Might and Magic 3 or 5, why? These games are still perfectly playable today. Songs of Conquest does a lot of things different than HoMM and in my honest opinion this is what the genre needed. First of all you don't have any Mana, you need Essences to cast spells. How do you get them? There are Artifacts, Buildings on the Map, Research nodes, all these are options to gain Essence. But your main source of Essence are your Units. Each Unit has a specific amount of Essence they give you on each of their turns. There are 5 different kinds of Essence, with each having 4 different Spells that need an increasing amount of Essence and a lot of Spells that need 2 kinds of Essence to cast.So not only do you need to get a good variety of Units to fight your enemy, you need to make sure you get the right kinds of Essence to cast spells. And let me tell you, you REALLY want to get the right Essence. This might change later but right now during Early Access Magic is completely busted. Don't believe me? Have fun fighting against an enemy hero with a bunch of rats. The game tells you this fight should be "Easy" but then your enemy casts Fireball, Armageddon, Magic Burst, before you can even move your first unit and your Army just got completely destroyed.Right now there are 4 factions with more to come with 8 upgradable units each with a big variety. The units for each faction aren't just reskinned, every faction feels like a different playstyle. But let me tell you one thing, Rats are literal GODS in this game. When your enemy attacks you and he has 500 upgraded Rats, just reload. Trust me.For anyone interested in Campaigns, there are currently 2 campaigns with 4missions each. There will be more, possibly 1 campaign for each factions. It took me 23hours to finish the first two campaigns which were not only extremely fun but the last mission of each Campaign is a beast. The game has no difficulty setting so you better get good cause otherwise you gonna have a really hard time completely the campaigns. (They already nerfed some missions so I guess there were a lot of people having trouble.)The game also comes with Mod-Support and a World Editor right from the beginning. So for everyone interested in Skirmishes against friends or AI, so you gonna have enough Maps.But what is the current state of the game? Well, its buggy. Unit Numbers might be wrong here and there, interactible buildings on the map might be invisible, but the worst thing atleast for me is the camera. When ending your turn and you are fighting against multiple AIs the game laggs so much that the camera is not able to properly show you what your enemy was doing when he did something in your area of view. This resulted in quite some frustrating situations cause I knew the enemy did something in my area but I had no idea what he did and where. So I really hope this gets fixed.But overall, this is an amazing game. Its way better than I expected and honestly, right now its my game of the year. If you are interested in a new Turn-Based Strategy game or are looking for a game to get into the genre, please try this out. You might want to wait for a few patches but this is 100% a must-play for everyone even slightly interested in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty fun game.  It's somewhat similar to Heroes of Might and Magic II and III.It has some (mostly small) differences which I'll get into later.Combat is almost exactly like HOMM.  That is, it's tactical, but more casual/simple as far as tactics can get.You move units around on a hex gird, and if they are next to each other they can attack.  If they attack, the enemy may retaliate (unless they are destroyed by the attack).  Some units are ranged, and they can't shoot if an enemy is next to them.Most units have some kind of special ability, ranging from pretty subtle to pretty important.  Some units can move next to enemy units without triggering attacks, making them more mobile.  Knight-like units can charge enemies and hurt more based on how far they've traveled.  Guard-looking units tend to give buffs to nearby troops.   Units with a shield can block ranged attacks.  Some units have the anti-ability of needing to reload every other turn!  Some of these abilities are lifted directly from HOMM.One difference from HOMM is that there are map tiles which have elevation, and being on higher ground makes your archers shoot farther and hurt more, and makes your melee guys have an advantage too.Another difference from HOMM is your hero's MP (magic points) comes from your troops.  So each troop type gives a certain magic type, and after the troop takes its turn, you get MP, which you can cast spells with.  It's an interesting system but the net result isn't that different from HOMM; you can cast various spells inside combat.  It does mean you can never cast spells on the world map though!There are four factions in the game.  They're ok, they either lack a bit of personality or they are copies from other games/ideas.One of the factions contains knights and faeries.  Half their troops are knights, half are faeries.  So there's a bit of a split personality going on there.  In HOMM, the faeries were one faction and knights another seperate one, and here they are smashed together for some reason.The second faction is a total mess.  I has some goblin looking things, humans with muskets and cannons, some hyenas, and feels totally random and pieced together.   It's fun to play as but thematically it's not cohesive.The third faction is undead.  It's similar to what you'd find in any game, including various HOMM games.  Skeletons, zombies, necromancers, and stuff like that.The fourth faction is sort of a swamp-themed faction.  There was also a swamp-themed faction in HOMM but this one is more original and is probably the most original faction in this game.  You have some frog-looking spearmen, some fat frog guards that protect the other frogs, and some frogs which ride giant birds and giant spiders.  Also some spiritual turtles and dragons because why not.  Pretty neat.In-between fights, you move around on a map.   On the map you claim mines which make money or resources.  You also pick up resources, initiate fights, take over towns, and find equipment.  Overall it's a carbon copy of HOMM.  But, they got it right, and it feels fun.The game has pretty good pixel art.  In a world filled with a lot of pixel-art games, this doesn't particularly stand out, but it looks really nice and definitely makes the game more fun to play.  I think the animations don't have as much personality as in, say, HOMM2 though.The music is pretty much well-received by everyone.  I think it's pretty good and fits the setting really well.This game doesn't do much that's new but it still is pretty fun.  If you like this kinda thing, may as well get it.On the downside, there are only four factions and mostly they are kinda not that interesting.  On the upside, everything is pretty solid, bug-free, and a pretty streamlined and fun experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The balance for the game is made by people who either never bothered to play their own campaign or feel like having to fine-tune all your skills and actions to the point where one wrong choice leads to a mission replay is a good idea.After several nerfs the Arleon campaign victory achievement is held by about 3% of players. Nuff saidUpdate: Rana campaign is a joke, at most mission 3 may give you a bit of trouble, but it is so far the most comfortable and easy experience despite the units themselves being the least interesting, you just send in wave after wave of units because they are just that good when upgraded. Mission 4 also is the only one where you are allowed to actually build dragons but every enemy hero has a combination of units and artifacts to cast Justice, nullifying any and all fun you might have had with them.Update 2: Barony of Loth campaign is also an absolute joke after mission 3, at which point it becomes near unbearable. It looks like instead of following up on ideas that worked for other similar titles developers tried to make something completely new, which is commendable, but they failed to understand what makes the crazy Heroes 3 videos of zero losses fights with one peasant possible.Last update: The Barya campaign is the best one so far. If every campaign was as well done as this one and the army was as beloved as Barya I would give this game a resounding 10/10 ngl. So far it is the army with the most unique abilities, the best magic and overall the best one to play. Last mission is a drag because you have to deal with the constantly respawning undead armies but after 5 tries I finally beat it. The amount of people that beat the campaigns on any difficulties stays way under 5% for all of them, so unfortunately Lavapotion didn't do well on their balancing department. Unless you know what you are doing or are a HoMM veteran or something of the sort, the game does not like you. So if the devs intended for this game to only be only for HoMM veterans, suppose they succeeded. Overall nice try admittedly, the magic system is fun despite being broken, there are some units that I absolutely adore and the art style(except hero portraits, they look very different from the cutscenes) is stunning. I would still play any more campaigns and see the continuation of the story but unless you are in for the long run I don't see new players buying this.

_childDocuments_.review: Gonna say no for now.It's OK, but far from loving it. Visually beautiful and great sound too, but the gameplay loop is boring. Exploration is also too basic - premade maps are nice for preplanned strategies, but no procgen maps means no thinking on your feet. Not to mention, diversity of units is basically just all the faction units as NPCs hanging about. It really needs much more to this.I've tried a few different factions now and they all feel pretty much the same barring a few different abilities here and there, but what sets them apart is essence and spells, which is also what makes the game both really interesting (initially) and then boring.Once you figure out that, for example, Rana is capable of dictating the entire flow of a fight due to having creation as their main spell stat, and initiative + essence farming is the gold standard for strategies, you realize the games strategic layers are quite thin. Loth are second strongest, but a pretty distant one, largely because they don't have the ability to control movement as well as Rana.Doomstacking can definitely punch through a lot of spell spam, but it requires such an enormous econ investment vs basic leveling of a hero alongside certain units with wide stacks that the cost benefit is just way out of whack.It's not that spells are "broken", but rather that there are some obscenely good spells that you pretty much should always use with the faction you play, and completely worthless spells that are situationally okay but for the most part a waste of essence. You pretty much funnel into those spells because everything else just isn't worth the cost, and building gigantic doomstacks of rats or cheap units is a no-go long term because they've arbitrarily set limits on qty. of units. I don't know why they did this.I dunno, there needs to be more to this. Once the initial "cool" factor wears off with the spell system and you do a little theory crafting, the game turns into a pretty repetitive grinder and fights can be trivialised with the right spells and positioning - to the point of negating almost any other strategy.Needs work. Aesthetically brilliant, and I dig the game, but right now it thoroughly earns its EA status.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic adaptation in the HOMM-style turn based strategy games. Everything feels familiar whilst adding new things to mix up and balance the formula.If you enjoy turn-based strategy or looking for the next step in getting your HOMM fix, this is a very good contender. The game does taking some relearning to do even if you are a HOMM veteran as the magic system, unit stacking and hero levelling is all quite different.Four factions with more on the way. They all look and play completely different whilst still being balanced. No faction feels straight up better than the others in terms of balance.Beautiful pixel art, either you love it or you hate it. It compliments the game world very well alongside a great soundtrack, somewhat peaceful sounding.Four campaigns, one for each faction, again to be expanded on to continue each factions story. Usually I don't care too much about the stories in HOMM games as they tend to get lost a bit in their stories. Discovering how each faction and character crosses paths and learning their fates was really enjoyable.Be mindful the campaigns are on the more difficult side as you get to the end mission of each campaign and may require a few attempts. Your hero/wielder carries over between missions making it important to level them up throughout each mission.Over-all this game looks to have a very promising future created by developers that clearly care for this style of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Literally just Heroes of Might & Magic, but with pixel graphics. They should probably consider removing "kingdom management" from the description, since all you really do is move your avatar around the map and claim resource buildings - there's no real "management."There are plenty of older, better Might & Magic games on Steam, or similar games like King's Bounty, and all of them have better graphics and sound at lower prices.All in all, there's nothing that really makes this game stand out from the rest of the pack - although there is a map editor and a multiplayer mode, so it *might* be fun playing with a friend. If you REALLY need Pixel Graphics, I highly recommend Eador Genesis - it has much deeper strategy, *actual* kingdom management and better writing. And it's only like six bucks here on steam - and that's when it's NOT on sale. Edit: Whelp, Steam didn't let me refund the game, so I went and sunk another 14 hours into it, and yup, my opinion hasn't changed. The highlight of this game really is just the map editor - though I never did try out the HoMM 5 map editor so I can't really make a direct comparison. If you design a custom map with dozens of claimable towns in it, THEN you can think about calling this game a kingdom management game.The essence / magic system definitely has something of a learning curve to it - basically at the start of each unit's turn they grant essence to your wielder with the type of essence depending on the type of unit, then you cast spells using said essence. As for the spells... they could use some work. A lot of them have very little impact or feel super gimmicky, although there are some cool ones like the Swap spell (swap positions of any two units, friend or foe alike, within a certain range of each other, which is great for getting past body blockers or pulling ranged units out of position) and Dimension Door (teleport a selected unit a small distance)DOUBLE EDIT: After extensive testing, I have discovered several things, and none of them can really be described as "good" - although some of them are so un-balanced that it's actually amusinig. A lot of other negative reviews have complained about this, and it's true. They AI has no real understanding of the core concepts of the game and will just blindly throw units at you, while casting bog-standard damage / buff / debuff magic and none of the really cool ones like shoving enemies for free attacks of opportunity or using Dimension Door to pop a melee unit right next to your ranged units. The "smartest" thing I've seen them do is use the Swap spell to swap one of my front-liners with one of my back liners, but honestly I do that myself so my ranged units can move into deadly range without getting the -50% ranged damage penalty for moving and attacking in the same turn. Here's the thing: in this game you build buildings to produce units. An individual building will produce a fixed number of units per turn, which are then stockpiled and become available for purchase using gold.For example, Laboratories produce 2 Toxicologists per turn, so if you only have a single Laboratory, it'll take 10 turns before you can get a full stack of 20 Toxicologists. The AI can build however many units they want as long as they have the gold to do it, and I'm 90% sure they also get boosted gold income compared to the player. Plague Rats are NOT glass canons - they're just glass. They get hard countered by massed Troubadours standing perfectly still and doing nothing but strumming their lutes for a stacking +10 defense per Troubadour. Also because Loth upgrades are divided into "Human" and "Undead" categories, and Rats don't count as either of those, they have absolutely atrocious scaling. Exchange buildings are one of the only buildings that don't require any strategic resources to construct, and once you have 5 of them the buy / sell exchange ratio improves from something like 3:30 to 9:10. So yeah, its WAY more cost effective to focus gold production and just buy the resources you need. Not that you have much of a choice, since the only strategic resource buildings you can actually build are for Lumber and Stone - the rest you need to pick up from the map. - At least when it comes to combat. There are some skills available on level up that give gold per turn or +1 strategic resource per turn, and some skills that focus on scouting for pickups, but not every Wielder has access to those.Because of the way essence and supporters work in this game, it is ALWAYS better to have more army slots. Essence gained and buffs granted are dependent on the number of army stacks, regardless of how many units are actually in that stack. A single Troubadour will provide just as much Essence production and will buff just as hard as a single stack of 50 troubadours - whats more, 5 stacks of 1 Troubadour each will provide FIVE TIMES THE BONUSES as a single stack of 50 troubadours.If you focus on skills that provide passive buffs, you're going to get out-buffed by Command armies with large numbers supporter units, and if you focus on skills that boost your magic, you won't have enough units to provide the essence to actually power that magic. See where I'm going with this?Anywho, TL:DR, this game could definitely use some work. Admittedly the charm of the pixel graphics is starting to win me over, and I'm sinking way more time into it than I thought I would by breaking down the mechanics and min-maxing how fast I can beat the AI on that one skirmish map that everyone plays, but I know that kind of repetition certainly isn't for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played heroes 3 and 5 as a child this game scratched that itch. I also like that the game encourages having multiple wielders with good armies instead of one hero having it all, limits on troops was excellent idea.I'm hoping for good single player map adventures as I'm not into multiplayer.Base building is also something that suprised me and it is very well thought out. In this game in order to win you have to sacrifice a lot in order to get ahead, you have to tailor your playstyle to your starting hero, resources that are available in the starting area and the map layout. You also have to be careful about how you spend your movement, remember it is all about calculated sacrifice, as a player you have to choose if you sacrifice moves to get resources or get towns, to get artifacts or get vision on key areas on which enemy is most likely approach (lookout towers very important). It is basicly a chess game and in chess you have to sacrifice to get ahead.This game will require you to feel pain in order to win and it is very fun because it teaches you that victory comes at a cost. Of course there will be defeats, a lot of them and it will suck but that is necessary in order to learn this game.Highly recommended and I'm looking forward to further development of the game.P.S. _childDocuments_.review: So, my feelings on this game are mixed.On the plus side - I enjoy the central premise, the graphics and the music.The game if almost completely bug free from launch. Other developers (Ubisoft) could learn something here.I appreciate the difference in the look and feel of the different factions.I approve of the map generator and the potential for many maps to emerge from the community.I think the strongest original feature of the game is the town development section. I love the fact that you can not get everything in every city, and that choices matter.The tactical combat is fine - it's not original in any sense of the word if you're used to HOMM, but it works.On the negative side, there are two main concerns.1) The lack of dimensions in faction setup. You have your main faction - and your hero, but the hero matters little in terms of how the game plays past turn 10. Compare that with AOW, where the combination between race, class and specialisations changed the dynamics of the game completely, all the way into the end game.2) I don't like that you can choose the hero you wan't and I find that you level them up in much the same way.3) I think research if not fully implemented, but more of an afterthought. Once you build the research buildings, you can research all the stuff for cash.Overall, I'll recommend the game, but I do hope to see more mechanics fleshed out as the game matures in Early Access. Otherwise replayability will suffer.(A caveat: I don't play single player or campaign - strictly multiplayer - So I have no idea if the campaign is any fun).

_childDocuments_.review: Is Songs of Conquest the best game ever made and you should definetly buy it?I dunnoBut even in early Access it delivers what it promises on the store page, which is more than most EA games do (and just games in general sadly enough).Could it be better?Sure, I guess.More stuff, more Factions, more Spells, more Units, more SP content.But it still is in EA, the Devs are fairly communicative here on Steam and much more so in their own forums/discord (weird how common that one got btw I guess it's cheaper and easier to manage than a dedicated 2005 forum these days) and are open to suggestions.So far we got 4 factions, vastly different units BUT with the same roles overall, interesting magic system via essences whcih differs from HoMaM IIIUNIT CAPS so it isn't about murder stack v murder stack (although even wit the caps a full teched 9 stack of T3 units wrecks stuff).And just overall a great experience.Check out Seeth's video for a more indepth review, I can't be arsed.Good stuff +1

_childDocuments_.review: i will say, this game is super fun and has tons of promise, and i'm super into this style of game. i played through the entire human campaign in about 20 hours and it was really fun.however, beyond that campaign, i think there r serious balance and difficulty problems that make this game really hard unless you're apparently following v specific strategies for specific levels. e.g., the frog/rana level 3 has been incredibly difficult - enemies spawn constantly, with way more troops than you, and you can never catch a breath. i then shifted over to try to play a skirmish map with 3 AI players, and not only do they spawn constantly and attack relentlessly with a serious resource advantage, they apparently rarely ever fight each other and only focus on you. basically, game as it currently stands is v promising, but pretty frustrating for me, so i think i will wait until the balance issues are resolved. can't really recommend in its current form, but looking forward to the updates

_childDocuments_.review: Its hard to avoid comparison with HOMM3 when you talk about turn based stratgy . But SoC is able to offer alternative unusual mechanics. This gives the chance to attract both HOMM3 fans and fans of the genre in general. My personal top unusual mechanics :1. The approach to magic is magnificent and fresh. Every unit in its turn give some essence and you spend it on spells. It can be every turn -cheap spell, or you can accumulate essences and use powerfull spell2.  Unique urban development. You upgrade you city and get places for small , meduim and large buildings. It can be a lot identical buildings, or a bunch of different buildings. You can build too much tier 1 units buildings and play too fast, for example.3. This leads to interesting squad planning mechanics. You don't necessarily have to play through all the unit tiers. You have a limited number of units in a pack (this is improved in a special building). So instead of trying to develop into several tier-S units, it is sometimes better to take hordes of low-level units. There is no need to necessarily develop into elite units, and this works here

So if you expect a good experience in multiplayer I doubt this will be a good choice in long term.Pros are mechanics of gameplay, different take on Heroes of Might and Magic, with limited troops count and lords skill tree, but even then there is max command skill best of all the rest of skills.Graphics are bad, but before buying this game I knew how it will look, so I don't count it as a Con or Pro.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so, it's not a horrible game by any means. But I don't think it's worth it yet.The campaign is pretty flat early on, with a ton of identical battles, nonexistent army comp options, execrable writing, a pretty rough UI, and a lot of hitting end turn. The skill system is very poorly laid out; for some reason "increase my army size" is a skill, competing with a bunch of other non-skills that barely affect battles compared to the massive increases that unit cap gives, so the first 10 levels are all just "increase army size" with absolutely no choices necessary aside from the Power choice at level 8.I love this style of game so I stuck with it for a while, but I was pretty bored by the end of the second mission. There's really only so many ways you can fight the same battle with the same 3-ish usable units.So all in all, I'm not too bothered that the 3rd mission was the same for 20-30 turns until you get a massive attack on your home city with 1 turn warning from a spawned-in army. I was actually kinda happy to finally see another welder. But I thought about retaking the city, and realized I just didn't care enough to try.The game definitely has potential, and I'll come check it out again in the future. I wouldn't recommend it for the campaign though, that's for sure, or interesting skill tree choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Good things:This game looks nice, the mix of 3D and pixel art really makes it stand out. Faction design is quite interesting, the game doesn't look like it is set in a generic fantasy world with zero thoughts behind it. The music is simple, but it fits perfectly as a background for this game. Bad things: Too reliant on random and rock-paper-scissor type mechanics, also quite unplayable in coop (especially with 3 people or more) because of the ingame limitation that only allows 1 player to participate in combat (others just need to wait even if they battle a completely different enemy on the other edge of the map). Units are very limited and boring, upgrades are just "+10 of this stat and +5 of that stat". Magic seems either useless or overpowered, if your character is not fully equipped with magic items your spells will rarely deal more than 5% HP to the enemy you are targeting. As you can see, the game seems and looks good, but absolutely fails in every aspect of gameplay. At least it's price tag is reasonable.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the very positive reviews this game has recieved, most of the negative reviews I've read don't seem to be doing this game any justice. As a matter of fact, they almost prevented me from purchasing this gem. The 66% discount luckily negated this preconceived bias. After spending 50+ hours in conquest, and if I had a time machine, I'd wholeheartedly go back in time and pay full asking price, no questions asked. Paying them the remainder they are owed isn't in my nature and I'm not made of money either, but if the developers ever decide to release an expansion, I can see myself buying it without hesitating twice. Trying to make up for what feels like stealing in a sense, probably compelled me to try and counter the negative reviews that influenced me. I hope by doing so, the negative reviews won't play as much a part in deciding if this game is worth a try for you.It should be noted that after scrolling through the negative reviews again, some of them are just plain comparisons with HoMM, which in this case is a non-constructive way of reviewing. Don't get me wrong, you can easily compare the two, in their respective genre. But comparing a new game with a classic game by a different company and then burning Songs of Conquest because it's not the succesor you wanted, isn't fair. Most of the other negative reviews seem to be written with only 10+ hours or less, which always sells any game short, but in this case those reviews definitly rub me the wrong way. Let me explain;You see this game seems simple enough at first glance, and on lower difficulty settings this might be the case. Walking around collecting things, encountering enemies, conquering bases, winning the game. But did you play optimally?The thing is, and let's be honest, I only really started thinking about my moves after I went up a couple of difficulty levels. It's not as simple as it looks. Yes, options are limited (also one of the biggest grievances the negative reviewers come up with), but almost all of the time you can't pick all of them. And so, limited options means making more decisions. This is true for the base building and your army setup, and most of all; your movement. To go back to some of the negative reviews, someone said; "I feel more like a cleaner than a knight." and again, this feels true for lower difficulty settings. You should know from the start that clicking everything shiny indiscriminatly isn't a great tactic anyway. But the difficulty in this regard ramps up quickly. So after losing a couple of games almost instantly to a bulldozering AI, I started looking at it from a different angle. And that's where the game actually started clicking for me. You can't do everything, and doing something affects your entire game. This also means that the AI can actually decide the best routes to take based on everything that's visible to it. After my 50+ hours, I'm still regularly making small misstakes here and there. Now that for me constitutes good game design, easy to learn, takes a while to master, and the AI can kick your ass if you're not paying attention.I'd like to commend the team behind this creation, as it definitly scratches an itch for me. It also feels like a passion project, a labour of love, love for the genre or an era? I can't help but be positively affected by a product like that. Apart from the game's mechanics, the pleasing pixel art, and the soundtrack, the fact that it has old-school hotseat play is a huge bonus for me personally. (Yes I'm positively biassed here) Not many games of anything within this vast  genre of turn based tactics, and especially in this day and age, add any local multiplayer options. Currently playing coop hotseat with my spouse, can't wait to challenge her to a 1v1 some time soon. [UPDATE: She won. Although it was a close one. Could've seen it coming, didn't adapt to her army. Next time, Next time!]As for me, the days of gaming on a potato have long gone, but my predisposition towards any game that runs on almost any modern machine out there still remains. If you can't, for whatever reason, get a new machine right now and you have to make due with what you have, you probably can play Songs of Conquest.After looking at the Songs of Conquest website I also discovered how easy the developers made it to mod this game a little. I quickly made two new Wielders for fun, based on the sprites provided, within less than an hour. Drawing the sprites yourself would be a little project. An honourable mention to the map editor on that front aswell, easily accessible from the main menu! If you like to come up with characters or campaigns of your own, they got that covered.I'm very curious what the developers have in store for the game in the future,Eventhough I'm nowhere near done with the game as is,Thanks everyone at Lavapotion!

_childDocuments_.review: What to say? Its one of the greatest game I ever played and its worthy succesor of Heroes of Might and Magic III! _childDocuments_.review: its an easy recommendation for someone who likes HOMM series.and its inevitable to compare the two while reviewing this gameI feel like MIGHT heroes in this game are not as strong as the MAGIC heroes in this game. its impossible to preserve your tropps even with defense or attack boost from the MIGHT hero. and since you can only bring limited army per stack, so there is no such thing as having 1000 of the weak units that can oneshot a dragon stack, for example. and unlike HOMM, you can only have 1 hero at the start of turn 1 - so you can't play the usual strats of main hero gets the experience, while a sacrificial hero just go activate all the locations on the map.. you need to level up your town to at least level 3 for that. they really went creative with the units here, there are units that can burrow underground, can charge like a bull, can attack safely from two hexes, can build a wall to name a few.However, imo the ranged poison troops i feel are so OP,In addition, you can't mix unit from other factions, since any town you captured will be automatically converted to your factions building and units.and unlike HOMM, there's no "your unit has high morale allowing them to move again" There is no more OP spells like HOMM's Blind and Expert Town Portal. More over, unlike HOMM, you can cast multiple spells per turn, which will end up into crazy combos.what kind of crazy combos you ask?just look at the achievement list for some ideas.

_childDocuments_.review: A spiritual successor to Heroes of Might and Magic 3 but with unique features such as troop stack caps. unit upgrades through research, stack expansion, a whole new spell system and mana generation and building system. All heroes can cast all spells by default, as long as you generate enough mana.After playing through Story Mode with all races I'm itching for more, and more is promised from the studio with a set plan.The pixel art is crisp, fantastic. Spell effects are also great!Although I'd love to recommend this, it comes with a few (but very minor) flaws. Interactable objects on the map doesn't show which bonuses they give until you interact with it. In other words you can't inspect them, and thus have to memorize what they give. This got pretty frustrating at the start, but as I played and started memorizing I get better at prioritizing what could be left behind.You also can't interrupt a hero's movement mid-walk, so you have to commit to each step.The story started out great, very front-loaded - but fell off a bit towards the end, and some dialogue felt tired.All in all a fantastic game, and with some polish and expanded race alternatives (maybe even some spells) this could be a new classic worth of pulling HoMaM 3 off the throne!

_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've been waiting for this game for a few years. I've just finished the first campaign and in general it has a few key issues. But let's start with...The Good:- Art style is nice. Not the best, but nice. Pixel art is not my thing but models and animations are acceptable. The problem though, due to being pixel art, nothing is too clear (compared to Heroes games, especially Heroes 3). On the adventure map, a lot of buildings are non-descriptive or non-characteristic. But still, they look nice.- Flow of the game in general is quite good. When you get used to the mechanics, like recruiting units instantly from your other towns with Rally Point or casting unlimited amount of spells per turn is bit different but kinda welcome. The unlimited casting thing has a down side but I'll get to that in a minute.The Meh:- Factions are... not very special. Main faction in the first campaign is literally Castle/Haven with a twist. Necros are as expected, skellies and rats. Mercenary faction is pretty bland from what I've seen so far. I think there is also a Fortress faction but I haven't seen much from them yet. They are mostly in the second campaign I think.- Units are not specifically special either. The game has a unit based mana mechanic, which is different. Each unit has a mana type and they generate that when their turn comes up in combat. Then your hero can cast spells with those mana types (think like MtG mana but creatures generate the mana instead of lands). From what I understand, there are Might and Magic hero types (and we obviously had the Might hero as our main hero in the first campaign) and once again, Might focused heroes suck a bit. More to that later.The Succ:- The absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ imbalance, especially in the campaign. Even after the latest patch to balance it out, enemy heroes in the last mission of the Castle faction has almost infinite amount of units. I had to restart the mission twice, took parts of the map inch by inch, lost some parts and tried to retake to lost towns again and again... It took literally 10 hours to finish the last mission. I might've got cancer while trying to finish that last mission. PS: If you can manage to sneak in your hero to the top leftmost town and kill the guy in front of the town, it's over. But enemy's wandering heroes are literal gods with constantly fully stacked armies, sooo good luck.- The spellcasting. I mentioned this a couple of times but as different and refreshing as it is, unlimited spell casting becomes absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with Magic focused heroes. You can get hit with 2 Armaggedon, 2-3 chain lightning and a few other fireball-like spells at the same time and lose every single unit while winning. While Magic heroes can do this, Might heroes can... boost troop defences a bit, give a little bit of initiative or grant an extra turn to a unit (which is probably the saving grace of Might heroes). - Autosave/Battle Save system: After playing Heroes 3 HD+ for years, I really got used to the battle save that let's me replay a battle or take me to the exact moment before I engage the enemy. This game however, doesn't even have a decent Autosave feature. To be fair, it DOES autosave but it usually take you a few turns before, which you need to replay again. I can't even remember how many times I had to replay a ♥♥♥♥ ton of turns just because I forgot to make a quick save. I even had to play a few major battles just because of a simple mistake I made later and forgot to make a manual save. Btw, yes, the game allows you to customize the number of autosaves and autosave frequency in the Options menu but it still doesn't fix anything.In short... This game has a lot of potential to be a very good one. It may not be a classic like Heroes 3 but it won't be forgotten quickly by the fans of the genre, that's for sure. BUT, I still can't recommend the game in this EA state. It still has a lot of balancing issues and some of the features should be reworked. I'll wait for the full release and if the issues get fixed, I'll probably recommend it then.Edit: After numerous updates to the game, the addition of map generator and all the other features, I can now wholeheartedly recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: A marvellous experience that I was lucky to discover - I have not been a fan of pixel graphics before, but decided to give it a go, and, oh boy, I absolutely loved it. I realized that pixel graphics are not outdated, but are its own style, and was never put off, instead being immersed in the gameplay.The game is crafted with such quality and love, the factions are distinct and having their own style, but also balanced and interesting, the world is built with such quality, I sometimes have been just moving the camera around and feeling as if I am present there. I have been playing for hours on end, doing the campaign (I recommend the difficult setting) and trying some standalone maps, but leaving them until I am done with all the chapters of the campaign first.Over the past couple of months, I saw that new official maps have been added, with the game also having a map editor and community already coming up with some great maps of its own. The game has huge amounts of fun to discover, and you can absolutely get lost in time when you notice yourself sitting and trying to finish a map in the early morning hours on a weekend. A masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, but id wait to actually buy it for a year or more, or till dev reaches a more finished product. The biggest issue at the moment is definitely performance, turns take a fairly long time, even early on, you maybe have the ability to move 10 or so spaces, and fight, maybe build a building, before you end turn then have to wait sometimes 2-4 mins or longer for enemies to calculate/finish theirs. It starts to rack up quick and I found myself thinking about just playing something else.Again, its not bad, but it makes the game tedious to play.
