_childDocuments_.review: I finished the campaigns and I enjoyed it. I almost gave it up during the first campaign, it was un-exciting. For example the militia have to reload after they fire one time. Dude who wants that. But it gets better once you get to the frog hero. The undead campaign is also cool. The soundtrack is neat. Still, not as good as heroes 3 for a few reasons. For example the high tier troups, other than dragons, are very dull. The archangel was the best for the humans, but in this game you have to be ok with knights and cannons. The biggest let down is the Magic system. In heroes 3 you had super cool spells, including dispel which seems to be absent here. And teleport is limited to two squares. It takes all the fund out of it. It took me 10 hours to figure out how it works. Still it's very weak and you need to achieve a very high level before your spells count. I played for 40hours, and I lost interest after I finished the campaigns. Still it's a very good game and it can keep you captivated. I wished the campaigns would pay different and give me a choice of the end. For example I'm invested in the undead hero, but after I leveled it up, the story kind of ends and I'm forced to finish the story with a different race (the mercenaries which are ok and it would have made for a better story for the undead to "win").I was able to finished most of the campaigns on Worthy setting  (with some Saving and Loading). However, for the last campaign, it gets impossible since you can't beat the turtle hero that's blocking the pass at the beginning of the map. So I had to dumb the settings down, which was still hard.Overall I recommend it and hopefully there will be some new addons with cool campaigns.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Not really sure why some are saying that enemies come out of nowhere and wreck them.  Usually if an enemy tries to gank me, they regret it.  The key is playing aggressively and exploring as hard as you can.  You get a good amount of wielders to do this with.I wasn't a HoMM3 kid, in fact, I never really played it other than a few times when my wife tried to get me into it.  When I saw this game I noticed the similarity, and overall I found it easier to take to.  If you wanted to get into HoMM3, but maybe found it a little overwhelming, try slowly sinking into this.  Play the campaigns, have fun looking around the maps.  I really enjoy the graphics, they feel lush for pixel art and make the maps really come alive.I also really like the automatic battle option, as I am not as skilled in manual battles yet.  It makes "big-picture" gameplay more accessible, as I have only to worry about composing my squads and overall map dominance.  You can even accept the results of the automatic battle or try your hand at a manual outcome.Froggo campaign alone is very fun, and in general the game is very enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: This was sitting on my wishlist for a while and I finally pulled the trigger. I have never played HOMM so I am new to the genre. I'm on the last mission of the first campaign and have to say it is really fun. I have the general flow of the game down, although there are still new things i'm encountering.The exploration of the maps is fun, planning out perfect pathing with all your wielders to be efficient. The battles are tactical and have very interesting mechanics with how getting mana and spell casting is done. There is an optional auto-resolve button for the battles, and if you don't like the results you can do it manually instead. I've had some close calls and able to turn an auto-resolve loss into a win, really fun pulling that off.I can definitely see myself enjoying the game for many hours with just the campaign and custom maps, however, I am interested in trying pvp and co-op eventually. I think that brings the most longevity to any game. I know the main focus is the campaign in the road map, but I hope there will be some multiplayer updates as well to keep the game alive.Highly recommend for tactics/strategy fans.

_childDocuments_.review: A very well-made game. It is heavily inspired by HoMM 3, yet it manages to distinguish itself by introducing a couple of unique mechanics, which drastically change gameplay.- City building system, coupled with stack limits allows for a lot of build diversity.- Magic system is unique, interesting and powerful, if used correctly.- Visual design is of a very high quality.- Campaigns present the story pretty well - the musical cutscenes are a nice addition.Still, there are a couple of areas in which the game could use a bit more development.- Some minor QoL features are missing. Moving troops from the town defenders to your Hero is a bit of a chore, you can't replay auto-resolve, you can't repeatedly shift-cast spells e.t.c.- The game lacks simultaneous turns. They might get added later, but so far the multiplayer is pretty slow, especially if you are playing something other than a duel.- Unit abilities and faction mechanics are too similar. The majority of research upgrades are pretty much the same across the factions, units have a lot of same-y abilities. A bit more diversity would be nice.- While the campaigns are pretty good, they only cover 2 out of 4 playable in-game factions, and are pretty short on missions - each campaign only has 4 of them.All in all, the game is pretty enjoyable to play right now and has a lot of potential in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: PRO: Decent Heroes of Might and Magic clone, heavy on nostalgia. Innovative magic system for spell casting.CON: Incredibly short. Still technically early access at the time of this review, but according to devs the meat of the game, the campaign itself, is done. I finished every mission from start to closing credits within 10 hours of playtime. Felt like I was gaining a level every 2 minutes, progress is really fast. Even getting it on sale, it wasn't worth the price.My advice would be to wait for it to officially release and don't pay more than $15 for it. The game will barely last you a weekend before you see and do everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and Beautiful. I just spent most of the night playing the last chapter of the first Campaign. After playing it a while I'm happy the Quick Battle option doesn't waste units like I imagined it would and I also like so much that you can overwrite the result with a Manual Battle if you really don't like the result. The pixel art is just so precious and done with love.I like the UI and the story and that I can take my time reading flavor text of the events and things I find in the world. I'm curious about how would that change when Turn Time Limits are implemented  that's going to affect the Single Player experience or if it's just for the Multiplayer which I'm also excited for. The only thing that throws me off is the cinematic for when you finish an episode in the Campaign with an uncanny-valley 3d bard. I love the song, don't get me wrong, but it looks so different from the rest of the game I'm hoping it's a placeholder. _childDocuments_.review: HoMM never did much for me back then. By the time I was finally able to get my hands on the family's computer, the only thing I wanted was my cousin's copy of Diablo II. That and to raise a burning fever on that old Pentium brick by clicking the hell out of it as another clueless, pixelated barbarian.Those were the early 2000s. Flash-forward a couple decades and here I am, still putting my mouse on chokehold, a  habit that forced me into reloading Songs of Conquest after more than a few misclicked hexagons.It might be the flimsy plastic of modern wireless mouses; a little too thin to rest one's finger while scanning through the best spot to cast a disastrous fireball. Or perhaps the culmination of all those hours spent as a kid hacking 'n' slashing the undead, unconsciously building up this unstoppable force that clenches - unruly - kept untamed into my thirties. This Y2K's dungeon crawler rendition of a common index finger just begging for the devs to add a rewind button - though it also helped rush through the pointless bursts of dialogue during all 4 campaigns.SoC lacks in its narrative, but so what? I'm not running strategy games looking for a bedtime story, I'm playing it for the immersion: To be consumed by my own 10min-long dissertations of "what should be my next move..?" then fumbling around immediately after. One could call it torture - I call it fun (and slightly torturous).Should you play Songs of Conquest? If you've read this whole thing, then it might entertain you. Just like this post the game is somewhat unbalanced. Unconcerned about its long ramblings. Every so often pushing towards an unnecessary obsession over small, little details.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a fun, but difficult, turn based strategy. The fun comes from the fact that, with good enough skill, anything can work. Want to run 800 rats? Have a firing line of Muskets? Have a swarm of frog people? As long as you build a wielder around that, it's viable. Even though it's in Early Access, it's still quite polished. The game is decently balanced, with the four factions having strengths and weaknesses of their own. There are very strong strategies and builds, but with enough planning and know-how you can counter them.I like this game. It fills a niche that really no other game fills, and fills it well. The game runs very well on my old PC. I'd say this game is worth full price, especially if you've got friends to play with.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: I can totally recommend this game to all Heroes of Might an Magic fans, the atmosphere and the feel of the game is very similar and at the same time it has enough differences that it does not feel like a clone. The game could benefit from having more than only four factions and a handful of neutral creatures. Right now after playing the campaigns the enemies feel somewhat repetitive. I really hope the game will get some DLCs that expand it a little bit more.Differences from HoMM:* Stack size limit. The weakest creatures may group up to 200 units in one stack, the strongest only up to 3 - 5. I guess it makes balancing easier, and it was not a problem for me when I played.* Magic system. Instead of spell points you have 5 varieties of 'essence' that you gain from your troops, hero skills, artifacts and map objects (spires). Instead of learning spells from mage tower, you have all the spells known, and amount of essence of each type determines which spells are available right now. Magic can make a really big difference, feels satisfying and quite different from HoMM.* More complicated factions. Instead of following just one theme, each faction in this game is a mixture of 2 parts. For example humans are in alliance with fey creatures, undead go along with their living masters and so on. Still there's only 7 types of troops for each faction, but you can really specialize.* City building right on the map. There's no city screen like in HoMM, each time you upgrade a settlement, a number of 'build sites' of various sizes become available around it. You can build whatever fits in this site, so instead of having all 7 types of creature dwellings, you can specialize a city in producing only one or two, or focus on the economy.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: First game I've played like HoMM. My friends tell me this is a lot like HoMM 3?I am thoroughly enjoying this game! It's super easy to get into but strategically has so much depth. Every time I think "Oh I understand the strategy now!"... no... no I don't. There is so much to consider in a given game: proximity to enemies, nearby resource producers, alternative win conditions available, what strengths your faction has and how it all interacts...Chill game to play co-op with friends as well.2 big downsides so far:-in multiplayer: only 1 battle can be fought at a time across all players. Since battles can be the most time consuming part of the game, as the game goes on in multiplayer, the time you wait on others battling grows and grows.-AI at difficulty Challenging and above are very strong an aggressive early game. In small maps I feel like I have absolutely no chance which is very frustrating. Sometimes I want to sit down and play a quick 1v1 in one sitting but I find the gap between AI difficult annoying (the difficulty below Challenging is a joke)Overall I highly recommend this game for the price. I already have gotten plenty of enjoyment out of it at 43 hours and don't plan on stopping anytime soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Credit where credit is due.With release 1.0 I can wholeheartedly change my review and recommend this game as of late May 2024.TL;DR: it is now worth its price.Previously SoC was wonky, unstable, bugged, messy and directionless, but now, most of the issues were fixed or patched enough, to actually enjoy the game.There are still issues like playing against 7 AI where performance sags a bit, but so far, from what I tested, most annoying visual glitches, poor AI, broken starting positions, odd seeds for random maps and probably a couple more things, are working properly.Game still does start to bleed resources after a while, but it's not like previously, where after 30 turns, it would take almost minute to end turn, or worse, get into decission loop causing computer players to fail to end turn and corrupt save, or freeze.I now do believe, dev team have proper road map, goals, and enough resources/manpower, to push this tittle into perfection.Rare, but welcomed, redemption arc.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game in the spirit of the old Heroes of Might & Magic titles, but with many more balances twists on the formula.Long gone are the days of powerstacking and one Hero being the whole power budget of the player.Campaigns are fairly hard, but the new Simple difficulty mode should make it easier for newcomers to the genre.4 base factions are iron balanced, with many powerful builds, but no obvious one trick that rules them all.I heatedly recommend Songs of Conquest to anyone who may enjoy some non-tolkienesque fantasy story where everyone is both the good and the bad guy at once, and for anyone who may want to play a new HoM&M style title.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put. I LOVE IT! Just one more turn...There are a few hiccups here and there. Some minor performance issues on larger maps, and I found the 4th mission in the Arleon/Human campaign to be a tad bit unbalanced or OP in the AI's favour. It's not impossible to beat but unless you know exactly how to beat the chapter in advance or have been lucky from the start and done the right approach it gets bogged down and you have to reload a lot or even restart. The devs have announced that they will nerf the campaign AI however so it will probably be fixed in an upcoming update.Apart from those minor issues I haven't really found anything to complain about. - The AI in Skirmish play seems balanced and fair. It pose a challange but seems to play by the same rules as the player and doesen't cheat. - The game ooze of amazing atmoshphere with its beautifull and sometimes very calm sountrack, and stunning artsyle and visuals. - The factions feel very reminiscent of something you would find in the older heroes of Might & Magic games, especially HOM 2. But manage to distinguish themselves with their own original feel and look. From what I have played of the story/campaign its quite good and I got invested in the universe and lore. Some will miss the traditional town screens from other titles in the genre but I found it refreshing, and once you get used to how towns work its great fun and not overwhelming to manage your towns. Remember, this is not Heroes of Might & Magic. It's a love letter to the genre and a revivial of the old school feel. Which is something the game achieves excellently! But this is for all intents and purpose Songs of Conquest, a new and original title. Not Heroes of Might & Magic 2,5 or 3,5.There is so much detail and passion put into this gem. The gameplay is fun and addictive. The atmosphere is spot on. This game feels like coming home or seeing an old friend. But at the same time its something new you havent quite seen before. And I think this is the closest we will ever come to relive that feeling of discovering Heroes of Might & Magic for the very first time again. This is also an excellent entry for new players interested in the genre who can't come to terms with how dated a lot of other games in the genre has become over time, or find them hard to run on modern hardware. The game is in early access so its missing two of its campaigns and there aren't too many skirmish maps to choose from. But the game comes with a map editor so the community can make their own maps and even campaigns. Considering the game just launched things can only go one way from here. UP!

_childDocuments_.review: Well let's say it's still developing and I'll try it out from time to time to see if it's gotten any better. Though I don't see the hype around it. It certainly has good visuals, and my first thought of "oh it seems too cluttery" was not at all an issue (other than one specific issue below). The animations are crisp and unique, mechanics are well fleshed out and it's totally in a playable state. I also haven't encountered any bugs.My issues with the game:- Even the "easy" AI is too hard (you're bound to make mistakes the first time you're playing) and it's not forgiving at all.- The sprites will sometimes steal your mouse clicks when a big building has something behind it and your general will just go off on their merry way, with a second right click (which would normally cancel such movement) making it faster. There's no option of changing sprite clicks to tile clicks (i.e. clicking on a tile will send you to that tile not to the sprite's core tile which is god knows where).- Combat evaluations are really bad. Sometimes it will say easy on a combat and you'll get your ass handed to you (well, you still definitely win but with half of your army gone, that's hardly a victory). I guess my understanding of easy is different than the game developers'.- One last minor gripe is that the loading times take too long even though the game is installed on an SSD. My guess is that it loads the entire map every time you enter and leave a combat, which shouldn't happen when you have enough RAM. The AI also takes too long to do stuff. Total War's turns take a shorter amount of time with 100+ AI nations in the mix.

For an indie game this is as good as HOMM3

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: 4/10. Feels like the game is actively trying to make me not want to play. I don't want to fight the game for enjoyment, so I'm refunding. Biggest issues ruining the game for me are ranged unit range limits and a wonky magic system. Needing to spend *entire* turns only moving to get ranged units into firing range feels absolutely horrible. And the magic system is weird - you get essence mainly from your troops and it's used as mana, basically. It's a very awkward system that's unnecessarily complicated. It makes me want to just use autobattle, which means (to me) that the game has failed. I should *want* to fight most fights.It's a shame because I can tell they were trying to be creative, but the game just feels weird and boring simultaneously. Weird/boring units, weird/boring design decisions, weird/boring graphic style, weird/boring combat, etc. Boring heroes with boring upgrades.Editing to say I looked at other negative reviews and the word "boring" keeps showing up over and over. Obviously I'm not the only one who feels this way.
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: As a veteran of HoMM I love this game very much. I would already recommend the game to play.Pros:- Really good art style. Still need some tuning for better visibility and readability. - Music and sound the top- Cut scenes - one of the best design in years, no details to don't spoil- Settlements mechanic is really fun also, though lack of a single management screen, too many clicks- Exploration of maps is really fun as wellI am not going to say cons as it's early access, but rather potential improvements:- Magic system - This is my biggest complaint at the moment, it's really dull as of now, not fun to focus on it and no feel of progression at all. Essences system is cool, but it would be much better if you can learn spells from exploration, research, items and skills. So overall magic system has great potential but needs a lot of work. Hope to see it much more developed.- Consistency - too much of random enemies and wielders appearances out of nowhere. It kills strategic element for some maps. They should come out of settlements otherwise it's just game against random events.- Battle system - ground levels (high/low ground bonuses) is good addition to classic, but wait/skip should also be there, without it the whole tactic is to hold/attack and apply spell. No full or even multi-round planning. The same as feature to flee the battle. - Research system - would be more fun to have some sort of a tree rather than everything available at the beginning. Also limit either time for researches or how many you can do in a turn.- Settlements - like it very much. Though It has a lot of potential to be even better, more upgrades, specializations, and more control for defense. Overall settlement development is very quick and it would be great if we have more space and buildings for development along the exploration. Now it takes just few turns to fully develop a settlement. Few more minor changes would be nice to have:- more contrast for settlements on the map, to clearly see and differentiate from regular buildings- more wielders or at least some mechanics to deliver army. Building chains of logistic is a very satisfying.- ability to replay battle manually after quick battle results- compare artefacts with already equipped when hover mouse

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure: this was gifted to me by the developer, but I have enjoyed it so much and I had already planned on supporting the project, so I have gifted a copy of this to a friend who also enjoys these kinds of games.As a long time fan of the heroes of might and magic franchise, this has been on my radar for some time. _childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of Conquest is a pretty decent light version of Heroes of Might and magic with pixel graphics, with one glaring difference that completely ruins combat (and thus, the entire game) as it currently stands in early access.The magic system is entirely broken.  If you go into combat with an AI wizard that is at all leveled up they will, for the most part, delete your army before you get a chance to do anything.  Rapid firing spells one after the other, all on one turn, that do massive damage.  I'm sure it's possible to make a similar character as a player, but that brings the combat down to "who has the fastest unit" which again, is not a fun game and basically invalidates military characters and units.The music has a very good ambient feel but nothing really strikes me as being special, which is fine.  The unit depth is similarly good but not great.  There just aren't that many units to play with except for the undead faction which has way more for some reason.  I assume this is an early access issue.  The graphics, while pixel art is not my personal favorite, are very well done, and they mix in some great effects that make the game look better than the screenshots might suggest.  It's just so unfortunate that the magic system basically makes everything else irrelevant.  If they can fix it the game will be a solid if not spectacular HOMM like.  If they can't then it is simply unplayable.  For now, I don't recommend purchasing it.  If it gets fixed, then certainly I will update my review.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR polished turd is, unfortunately, still more or less a turd. I'm not hating, but a LOT of reviews for this game are positive only due to HoMM nostalgia. Game has potential, but it's not as ready as some would make you think.As a longtimed Heroes series fan and someone who was really looking forward to this game I'll be first to say: the spirit of HoMM3 is strong in this one. Even though I'm not a fan of pixelart (HoMM3 sprites still look better than those in this game), I have to admit the level of polish is quite good. Music is especially well made. Base gameplay is solid and you can feel a heart put into creation process.Should you be rushing to buy this one then? No.Despite being a small game with pixelart graphics, it struggles with keeping consistent fps even on high end hardware.Campaigns are short and really not that creative in terms of a plot. Sure, it's a turnbase strategy, but even latest Heroes incarnations could put a good story.Balance is all over the place, game heavily promotes magic casting, basically forcing you to cast at every possible turn and invest in magic oriented skills. If you won't do so, you'll be blasted to pieces by an AI wielder shooting offensive spells faster than AR-15. Example: in the first campaign you encounter a setup with AI not only starting with more cities (that's expected) but also with a sh*tton of magic resource generators meaning fighting their wielders is a suicide until you patiently try to remove all those external generators first. Or you can simply run 2-3 armies at once into enemy wielder to secure a victory and leave yourself open to attacks from other enemy armies. Fun times. Did I mention that AI has apparently unlimited resources, almost instatly brinding back defeated wielders and coughing up army after army?Speaking of armies - some units have clear advantages over their counterparts, which you'll discover only a few hours into the gameplay.Battlefields size is an illusion, you'll get 1 turn to setup your units before an actual engagement and that's if you're lucky. This one might not be a downside for everyone but for me - in tactical turnbased game, it's a huge no-no. If we want things to get fast, we have combat speed and autoresolve for that.That brings us to buildings. While the whole system works quite nice, some buildings have requirements stating that other, usually rather useless building (e.g. lumbermill) is erected first. The thing is, once you build the building you want, you can simply destroy the required building freeing the space and getting resources back. What's the point here, delaying me 1-2 turns longer?I'll wait for it to exit EA, then we'll see about changing this review. Good news is - most of problems are a matter of tweaks and adding content, not rebulding the core of gameplay so there's a solid chance the game will come up good.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been mulling over the merits of this game for a bit in my head and couldn't quite place my thoughts in order until I read some reviews to get others' opinions.The part of other peoples' comments that clicked most with me was the magic system.  While playing, I didn't really understand the magic system.  That's because it is purposely obtuse for no good reason.  It seems to me they changed it simply because they realized the rest of the game (except the city building aspect) was a lesser beat for beat remake of any Heroes of Might and Magic-like game to have existed.  They felt the need to "spice things up".  So they changed and castrated the "magic" part of Might & Magic.  This essence nonsense not only isn't fun, it's limp-wristed and a numbers game.  Further, it doesn't make any sense.  Why do Wielders get their powers from the troops under their command?  I suppose any half-way decent writer could come up with a mystical excuse, but it's still stupid.  Even more so from a gameplay perspective, because it implies that the Wielder isn't a real character, but an amalgamation of their troops.  In fact, that is a further problem I have with the game, the Wielders don't feel interesting or powerful.  They don't - feel - like they're in command.  The army just exists to smash into another army, and the Wielder is just their mascot.Another thing that others have touched on was something I didn't even notice.  The lack of overworld magic.  That's huge for a game like this.  A large part of the strategy in these types of games was the magic you used in the overworld, to buff your army, or hinder your enemies.  Now this is just... gone?  And that's an improvement?So much for the "magic" part.  Now let us speak briefly about the "might".  It's... here.  It's not really interesting either.  You have stacks of units that do things and toss them at other stacks of units that do things.  None of the units seem very interesting.  Some are downright bad (Militia) and some do quite well (any undead unit).  Many have said the battle maps are too small.  I tend to agree.  The maps are a bit smallish and the engagements are very quick.  The terrain isn't interesting, you generally have flat ground and you have high ground.  Not much else.  I will say one thing I very much do not like about the "might" system is the stack caps.  This, again, is a balancing "fix" to the formula.  All units now have a cap on their stack size, which is very off putting to me.  The whole allure to this type of genre is that it abstracted battles but still gave you the illusion that you were in command of a mighty force.  In Heroes games you could have thousands upon thousands of troops under your generals.  Each unit could represent many thousands of soldiers.  Each bit of a damage to that unit was dozens, if not hundreds, of people dying each blow.  Now?  Eh... 50ish units per stack.  Can be increased some more via research.  What?  Even Disciples games did a better job at creating an illusionary battlefield with it's four units than this.  Because somehow, Disciples battles, while quick and streamlined like this game, were more compelling than the battles here.The game overall itself is serviceable.  The graphics, for the style they were going for (pixel art) is fairly attractive... except for the horrific slo-mo close-up shots of the final hit in a battle.  These can be turned off, thankfully.  The music is fine, but nothing outstanding.  The overall pace of the game is steady and a good homage to Heroes games.  The city building is actually something I do like, though I do wish it was somewhat less restrictive.  The fact your city exists on the map instead of a separate "city screen" is a nice change.  The game is a safe, by the numbers tribute to the Heroes games.  If that's what you're looking for, you'll enjoy it... for a time.I'll admit, I never played Heroes of Might and Magic 3 - the supposed gold standard of this genre.  I have played 4, 5, 6, the Disciples games, and a lot of "clones" in my time and I enjoy the format.  Though I think the problem is that it has grown very stagnant and a lot of people are trying to basically reinvent the wheel instead of inventing the automobile.  I feel this game is good, but plays it safe and tries to "balance" the game; which always means to dumb it down and strip things out.I feel I gave this game too much leeway in trying to see the good and ignore the bad.  As such, I have crept past the two hour refund window and have to eat the rather somewhat steep price for what's on offer.  I'd caution anyone else to wait and see how the EA develops, but even then I think the fundamentals here are just too safe for a hallmark game; but just another Heroes of Might and Magic wannabe that is a flash in the pan and may even be forgotten within a year.As I said before, if you're desperate for a Heroes-like game, you'll find a decent one here.  It takes many of the right ques from that storied genre and does them quite well (magic, notwithstanding).  But ultimately, the question I ask myself and you should do as well, "Is there any reason to play this over those old games you probably already own?"  My answer would be flatly, no.  And despite all the work gone into this game and the nice little pixel art on display, that is the most damning verdict of all.  If you're looking for a Heroes-like game that has poor modern day graphics but fantastic gameplay and an actual creative approach to moving the genre forward, I suggest you skip this game and take a look at the Conquest of Elysium series.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time turn-based strategy player, I truly enjoy Songs of Conquest and it has become my favorite game that keeps me occupied with figuring out different tactics and replaying skirmishes just to go on more adventures with my favorite wielders (Wielders are equivalent to heroes in Heroes of Might & Magic genre.).The game (both campaign and skirmishes) may present itself that it is all about having more units and without tactics. This is because, in easier difficulty, a player could choose to wait several turns just to get more troops and upgrades before progressing through difficult fights.Tactical gameplay shines when playing on higher difficulties and in competitive multiplayer. Without tackling difficult neutrals early on with minimal loss, the enemy would be way ahead of you. For this reason, you are motivated to play efficiently. Besides the famous meta like combining the right essences for spell damage, you could have fun through the use of buffs and afflictions such as shooting multiple times with your ranged units, making your frontliner almost invincible with melee resistance, or keep repelling a deadly stack away from your mages.These tactics might not be obvious to you, unless you see an enemy AI uses it, or you get to try the "Challenge Maps”, by which you have to progress through difficult fights using a given wielder and limited amount of troops and resources.Factions, units, and wielders have unique appearances and identities. For example: Each wielder has his or her own appearance and animation in the world map, instead of using the same generic rider with different portraits. Units are drawn beautifully and they fit in very well together.The trade-off is that there are lesser factions and unit types, which is a letdown for some fans of Heroes of Might & Magic. The good news is that the developers have listened to the players and it is very likely that there would be more factions in the future, given that the game sells well after 1.0.Besides numerous conquest maps, challenge maps, user-made / modded maps, random map generator (RMG) is also available and there are multiple templates to choose from. RMG is arguably the heart and soul of the turn-based-strategy’s replayability and I’d say that Songs of Conquest has a very good one compared to many other modern games. Most of my 1,000 hours of game time are from replaying RMGs. I keep creating a new game each day, feeling like going in a new adventure. It’s been a lot of fun for me.There are things that could be further improved, such as template variety. All templates tend to share a similar characteristic: having multiple entrances, equal distance between each faction’s base, and an absence of high-powered artifact zone. This could make a new generation a little bland.However, this already started to change because the developers have listened to the players and made improvements on some templates. Furthermore, not only that players could create maps using the map maker, they can also create their own variant of RMG. How cool is that?Throughout Early Access, the AI has improved so much. It is like night and day. Since the hardest difficulties are not yet at the level of competitive players, they do have resource and unit multipliers. This might change in the future, as the AI continues to be improved by some very passionate developers. Meanwhile, the ‘Worthy’ or the AI with no advantages could give turn-based veterans a lot of trouble if they are still new to the game.You can do both hot-seat and online multiplayer. When playing online, one of the most requested feature is simultaneous turn, where both players could play during the same turn without waiting for the other. The game did not have this feature at first, but the developers have listened to the community and added this feature.As of now, you can play simultaneously in the same turn, but only one player can use the combat map (no sim-battle), so if your multiplayer buddy is in battle, you cannot get into battle until he or she finishes. Sim-battle is expected to come in a few months after release, due to the fact that the developers have to re-write many lines of codes to make this work.Meanwhile, if you feel bored of waiting, the game does provide another feature where a player is randomly selected to play as the engaged neutral arm. You can, of course, turn this feature off.Songs of Conquest is a polished gem with some rough edges. Since it is crafted with much love and dedication, I have no doubt it would be further refined in future patches and DLCs, given that the game sells well after 1.0.

_childDocuments_.review: About a year ago I thought I would take a stab at developing a HoMM 3 clone because as far as I knew the genre hadn't had a serious new entry for years (decades?). After a couple days of investigation I realized just how large in scope such a game dev endeavour would be, and I shelved the idea - the amazing thing is that the folks at Lavapotion ACTUALLY DID IT and added a whole lot of style to boot!If you ever wanted another "good" Heroes of Might and Magic, this is as close as you're probably ever going to get - and these are big shoes to fill. Songs of Conquest makes the HoMM enjoyer feel right at home, but it comes with its own brand of art, lore, and music that adds layers of freshness to a tried and tested genre. While lots of mechanics will feel familiar to any HoMM fans (building, upgrading creatures, hex-grid-based combat, artifacts, overworld movement, and powerups), Lavapotion have also brought in some changes to address some of the more dated game design principles found in OG HoMM3. For example, gone are spell points that heroes (wielders) would need to gather through level ups and powerups - instead we now have Essences, which are incremented each time a unit has a turn in combat; these essences start at 0 each combat and are reset once combat ends, so you no longer need to worry about using all your spell points in 1 battle - let loose! And neutral armies that are greatly outnumbered simply flee and give you XP rather than making you choose between fighting for XP or leaving to find a more interesting battle.The town building also feels really well balanced, as at the beginning you don't get enough spaces to build every single structure. There's a strategy to choosing what to build and when, when to knock down a structure you no longer need and add a new one. The visual aesthetic of towns are also fantastic as you can see them grow in the overworld rather than having a separate town screen in HoMM (both are great, but this definitely works here too!).The only downside I can think of (and this is a stretch) is that ranged units feel a bit overpowered especially in the end-game, but maybe I haven't tried enough of the factions / played around with the difficulty settings enough. But this is a really minor point - if you haven't noticed I'm struggling to come up with a negative take to balance the praise :DVisually and acoustically, the game is bliss. It creates a super relaxing atmosphere that you can get lost in, and I found myself captivated by even the "simple" pixel art style of the wielders, each of whom gets their own custom in-game art (again more than you ever got in HoMM, aside from character portraits).Overall, this game just works! Did I mention it also had 0 bugs in my 17 hours of playing? And it even has a map editor that's way more intuitive and user-friendly than any HoMM game ever had.My score: 10/10 This game scratches EXACTLY the itch I know a lot of turn-based strategy lovers have been dying to scratch for a while now. If you like HoMM, get this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Songs of Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so great! It reminds me of the glorious days of Age of Wonders and Heroes of Might and Magic. It especially draws parallels to Age of Wonders 2, but that might be due to me being partisan towards Age of Wonders 2 since I've played it so much during my whole life. Songs of Conquest has a great campaign with a captivating story line that teaches you how to play while you're playing (why can't every game do it like this). You get attached to your heroes and units. The battles are kept interesting because units differ vastly from each other with each unit having advantages and disadvantages, their own upgrades and unique abilities that can change how you play. You get to build and upgrade towns and buildings, helping you to increase and strengthen your army. There are even quality of life buildings that adress issues appearing on larger maps, but I don't want to spoil that.I played on the second difficulty level - there are three - and the AI felt worthwile, sensible and strong enough to keep me invested in fighting them.There are some things I would like to see implemented:- In battles, I often look for the log of enemy spells. Whenever they cast something, I want to see the effect on my units or what the spell is supposed to do. That's not always possible. I wish I could hover the enemy's spell name in the log.- I would like to have more building complexity that interacts with each other, like in Age of Wonders: Shadowmagic where you could build a Spire and a Portal in the very late game to teleport your units around, or maybe some buildings that let you build cross over units, like merged units between factions when you have buildings of both factions. Something like that. Otherwise I can see myself play one or two games of one faction and never touch that faction again.- I would like to have a different spell book per faction.- I would like to research spells. For that there would need to be more spells in total.It's a great game and I played 2 days straight, which doesn't happen too often lately anymore. Give it a try and see if it scratches that itch for you too!

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following the development of this game for quite a while on twitter due to the wonderful pixel art. In my almost 5 hrs playing I have only almost finished the 3rd mission on the 1st (human) campaign so there is plenty of content for an early access title.I have not played a Heroes of Might and Magic game in.....20 years? So I don't really remember much about them. Regardless I think Songs of Conquest stands on its own.I'll not give a rating as I am not actually that far in and it is an early access title so I expect things are subject to change. I am very much enjoying it so far though!The pixel art is excellent and you can tell extra care went in to making the animations. (I especially like how the final blow at the end of a fight the death animation is in slow mo. A very cool cinematic effect that adds to the whole experience.)I actually got dunked on by the first (mini?) boss. I thought it was supposed to be a scripted loss or something but I just was not understanding everything yet. In Songs of Conquest, you control 1 or more "Wielders" (Heroes/commanders) and move around a map collecting items and visiting locations that give various buffs/debuffs/resources. You collect/recruit troops which you use in order to defeat enemies and defend your settlements.In the first couple missions the fact that you have to "end the turn" in the over-world map doesn't make a lot of sense. Like there is little or no reason to not just get all your production running then sit in your settlement and spam recruiting troops (there is a daily production based on what buildings you have) and new turn to power out an army. (It also seemed a bit silly just moving and ending the turn just to move again.)In mission 3 you see why that is very much not a good idea. You need to be on top of making every turn count.You see, normally you wandering around the map will discover enemies and are free to engage them. They don't chase you and even if you run into them you can withdraw before the fight starts.Mission 3 enemy Wielders roam the land. This opens up a whole other aspect of the game. Defence.You can garrison troops (and wielders) inside of settlements in order to have an advantage if an enemy wielder attacks and if you have built a tower (and upgraded it) you get a Ballista to help with defence.If you lose, your Wielder will die (sometimes meaning the mission will fail) and you will lose the settlement. (Which means you lose the resources it was producing as well).As I said before I am enjoying the game but here are some comments based on how things are right now.The tutorial(s) could be implemented in a bit more player friendly way. Tooltips that pop up are great but it would be nice to be walked through things a bit more as new things come up. The systems seem a bit intimidating and not entirely intuitive. (How does combat actually work? What does the number of troops mean? How is damage calculated?) It's probably in the info and tutorials but its a lot to read through. (I have muddled through so far though so it is not that bad.)If troops/enemies are close to each other it is VERY easy to miss-click and instead of attacking who you are engaged with, move, take two attacks of opportunity for disengaging and then die.And finally at the end of the 1st or 2nd mission you encounter another character and there is dialogue that ends in combat. This seems like a good place for a choice to be (As the character doesn't seem to want to fight you at all). I do not know if the devs are planning on making points in the game where you get to make choices in how you deal with other characters in the story but it seems like a natural thing that just isn't there right now. (At least so far.)All in all Songs of Conquest is an engaging and beautiful game and excellent for an early access title.

_childDocuments_.review: The artstyle and the music are really good and the spellcasting system is interesting for a bit, but I unfortunately can't recommend this game simply due to its lack of tactical and strategic choices you can make.The game is very clearly inspired by the Heroes of Might and Magic series and it wears this comparison on its sleeve. The thing is it doesn't do enough to innovate on a 30 year old formula and while it is a solid reimagining of HoMM, it is quickly apparent that gameplay systems from the 90s don't stack up well when compared to modern innovators of the genre like Age of Wonders and Endless Legends.The unit roster is extremely limited and you don't have a lot of ways to customise your units or spells, outside of upgrading them once. This means that even after a few games, you'll notice that you're constantly doing the same thing without something exciting to look forward to in the late game.Both the strategy and tactical maps are limited in what they allow you to do and how complex they can be. No strategic spells, no roaming barbarians, no destructable environments and very little variety in approach. Again very reminiscent of HoMM, but in 2024 I want more interesting ways to express myself in my 4X games.Maybe Age of Wonders 4 has spoiled me, but when playing this game I felt like my nostalgia glasses fell off and that I am no longer entertained by game systems that were all the rage 30 years ago.

interest with heroes 6 and what came after, in the games that is not the genre.and here comes songs of conquest, this game does everything just right, on the face of it it looks like the great heroes of old, and plays allot like it too, at least in the ways it should. but what really took me is the things this game innovates on and makes it its own experience,its manly expresses though the none linearity of it all, a few examples of this are the castles and the magic system and how you set up your army. there is no castle screen, your cities are part of the world map, and you build your _childDocuments_.review: I'm really at awe with this early access - I think they game does justice to the game that inspired the developers - remember that this isn't a remake of HoMM, it is inspired by it. With that said here are my feedback from playing last night and giving it some thought over some sleep. Remember, this is my thoughts on the game, and you can agree to disagree if you want!----------------------------------There are currently 4 factions;The Arelon, a knightly faction that employs Fay creatures as well as classic "castle" style units.The Rana, a froglike lizardmen race that are fighting to break free of slavery - they get dragons!The Barony of Loth, Cultists and scholars excavate old battle sites for arcane artifacts and call the Oathbound legions to serve once more. Loth will rise to its former glory, even if it means bringing back the dead.The Barya, slavers and merchants they specialize in tinkering and use gunpowder weapons and machinery to defeat their foes. * More factions - not really a bad thing, as we are in Early Access, but I expect more factions to come in as well as either a) more units or b) more upgrade paths (see below) - but most of all I just want more factions :DMagic works by using essence. Essence is generated by your Wielder (skills etc.) and units every turn they are activated. Some units have skills to make more essence and some spells allow you to gain more too. You use essence (advanced mana) to cast spells which comes in 5 forms; Order, Chaos, Arcane, Destruction and Creation. As you gain essence, you can see the spells populate the left side bar, but that is not all spells you can cast, you can always click the scroll to see them all. You can cast as many spells a turn as you want as long as you have essence to do so. This means, if you want access to specific spells, you get specific units and skills that give you that type of essence.Spell levels are upgraded through the skills of the wielder itself and you have access to all the spells on all wielders. * The system is great, but I miss spell research. Right now you just have all the spells available to you at once. It can get overwhelming and it lacks that randomness in getting the bigger spells.You have 8 different units, each with an upgrade for each (except Rana Tremors) that are built within the cities. Each unit has different stats and grant different essences to the user.Unit stacks are limited to a certain amount of units pr. stack, but you can bring several of the same unit with you - stack limits can be improved with research. This is a bit similar to Kings Bountys unit system.There are no "wait" or "defend" action for every unit, BUT it does become available to some - in one form or another. * I think the lack of "wait" and "defend" actions work just fine, as it keeps the pace up in the fights. The limit makes good sense, as you can't just stack up a bunch of units on a single wielder and call it a day. It forces you to make several armies and to think about what you do - I like that.Cities are integrated into the map - there are no specific city building screen, instead you build them on the map itself. This makes the cities feel much more alive and a part of the game. * In cities it can sometimes be hard to know exactly which buildings are need to upgrade buildings later on, this could be made better. The city UI needs to be optimized as setting defenders and moving units around / upgrading is a lot of clicks right now.The campaign options right now are two - one for the Arleon faction and one for the Rana faction. Each campaign consists of 4 missions. The Arleon campaign serves as the main tutorial to learn the game, but from what I hear the 3rd and 4th map are very hard and can be discouraging.  * Currently I'm playing through the Rana campaign, and I feel really attached to my wielder - the story is compelling and I feel engaged in it. Right now the Rana campaign is really good, but I've not made it far enough into the campaign to talk too much about balance.  * The music is absolutely incredible, albeit sometimes it does cut out and stop playing. More music please!People can create custom maps for the game - as it comes with a map editor built into it. People are already creating custom maps for campaigns. There are set maps for skirmishes that can be played in hotseat or online multiplayer. * * Skirmish/AI battles makes the game laggy at times - turns can take a while since there are no simultaneous turns or anything to do while waiting for the AI or other players to take their turns.-----------------------* Right clicking everything (except for casting spells!) is annoying - To me right click is secondary and left click is primary - so making that change in my brain is hard. Maybe make it an option you can switch the buttons around (or just let us change the controls)* You can not continue on set path - You can't hit "space" to continue the movement of your wielder, you have to click the spot you want to go to every turn.* There is no "you have movement left" warning when you hit end turn - there is an advanced mode, but it doesn't do the trick, only limits the mistakes you can make of ending the turn for a wielder, instead of the entire turn.---------------------------I’ve played many of these strategy games, from Heroes I-VII to Kings Bounty I-IV as well as Disciples I-IIIThe latter, especially the second iteration, had a great system for units that I hope you guys will implement down the line.Right now we have 8 units with one upgrade – which I feel is enough units to fill the armies needed.Instead of adding more units to the game, I would advocate for more upgrades, but not just linear upgrades, but split upgrades.Split upgrading (my term) means that you pick a path for a unit to upgrade it, and by picking said path you lock the other path.An example could be the Rana Hunters, they can now be upgrade to the Storm Guards after which two paths could be available.One path would lead to the Storm Guards getting a ranged attack while the other path would make them much more tanky melee units.Both paths would have unique artwork to show the upgrade. The upgrade should be global for the scenario, so you can’t pick another path in another settlement.This would add a lot of diversity to the game as well as expand the types of units in the game without having to add completely new ones.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only what... three hours into playing this game and it FEELS like HOMM3 but modern day; punchy graphics, upgraded systems and several overhauls to game mechanics that make the game feel GOOD to play. I have played just about every HOMM game that has come out and none of them have captured the charm and essence that HOMM3 brought to the table, this game does that in spades.The good...The cities: I LOVE the city design, it's completely unique and really adds to the game because while it limits you in some ways (total number of buildings) it stands apart from the rest because you have that modularity to make what you need and choose what kind of production the town does, such as resources early game and units lategame. Maybe you need to have more of a garison present defending the border town that gets constantly attacked, you can. I like this a lot.The magic system: In a lot of the HOMM genre you see magic done on a mana pool based play, where magic is strong but it can leave you weak if you use it. Here you're not only encouraged to cast spells often, but it doesn't help NOT to cast spells because you get mana each turn of combat that is reset at the start of the next combat so saving it isn't necessary. I really like this, it gives the player a good sense of commanding the battlefield with magic.The Bad...The POIs are nice, I like their strengths and weaknesses that come with them, but I find great distaste in the way the game doesn't want to tell you what they do until you activate them. Discovery is fine, I like that and you shouldn't know what they do until you've activated them once... but once you know what they do, the game shouldn't go back to hide that information. It seems like needless tedium that wastes the players time. Does this structure give me a permanent buff or is it a temporary one? Does it give me a buff/debuff that I don't want for this hero... I can't tell... Visual clarity is something really needed.Heroes leaving party: They take everything they have on them with them when they do so. Did you load up your army and items on one person to maximize the strength? Great. Their leave of your party takes everything with them without any warning or ability to take what you need/want for your current ongoing map. I don't like this. Give me a prompt that it will happen or the ability to trade/take things from them. I can understand if it's something like an ambush or rockfall that cuts the two off suddenly, but if the characters obviously have the opportunity to shuffle around gear, give me the chance to do so.Overall I give the game a solid 9 out of 10. The above critiques really detract from the gameplay in ways that as a player I really find distasteful. That said, as a person who loves this type of gameplay; its an absolute MUST purchase. Especially if you're the kind of person who's looking for a solid spiritual successor to HOMM3

_childDocuments_.review: Song of Conquest (SoC) is a turn-based RPG in the style of the Heroes of Might and Magic. This is an early access indie game made by 4 people that has a multiplayer component that lets you play custom maps with friends or with bots and another that is a single player mode with 2 campaigns with 2 more coming out later. The campaign tells the story of 2 different characters that have to gather armies in order to conquer empires.I’m going to admit that I have never played any game similar to Heroes of Might and Magic before, so my review is going to be from the perspective of a newcomer to the genre.It’s a game that surprised me. For years I had heard “Heroes of Might and Magic is great and you should play it or games that are like it” but I never bothered with any of them until SoC, and I have to say… this game made me a fan. I think the thing that intrigued me the most is how deep the magic system for each wielder is… right I have to explain that to you.Wielders are the generals of the map, each one has different spells and equipment, you can have multiple wielders in the same campaign, you just need to find them or recruit them.  The combat takes place in a grid of 13x9 hexagons, SoC offers you the option of auto-resolving most encounters but most of the time you are better off fighting each battle by yourself. During combat each unit has 1 movement action and 1 attack action that they can use per turn, there is also a magic system where your wielder cast spells and gives you all kinds of advantages against your enemies. Most of the objectives have to be completed via combat, you really need to become proficient with the magic system of the game.The game auto selects some spells but in order to defeat the harder enemies and to avoid being stomped in multiplayer, you have to dig into the “spell book” menu and find spells that really fit your playstyle and what your army is good at.During your adventures in SoC exploring is the key to success, because you gain exp to improve your wielders capabilities and equipment that improves your army stats. Depending on what wielder you are using, each level is going to offer you different interesting options, something that I really like is that there is not a truly bad option with spells and perks. You just need to know how to adapt it into your strategy.There are a few “city builder” mechanics in the game, which is just building stuff in your bases in order to get more combat units, other wielders or generate resources passively. But nothing really worth talking about, it’s very simple but fun.If you are a fan of turn-based RPGs or Heroes of Might and Magic inspired games. This is an easy sell, even with this game being in early access this is easily one of my favorite games of 2022. For $20 this game is more than worth it.Rating: 8/10Great game.

_childDocuments_.review: is a turn-based strategy and tactics game inspired by older titles like . It’s a nice blend of city management and tactical battles, without giving too much attention to either of them. is all about using large strategic choices to influence small tactical battles. You will manage a handful of cities and need to strike a balance between growing your economy and your military. It’s pretty straightforward, with only 10-15 buildings per faction. Some buildings produce soldiers while others produce resources. Many of them have synergies, such as a castle requiring a peasant hut in order to upgrade the units it produces, but that’s as complex as it gets.Then you have the tactical side, where you use the units you’ve trained in a turn-based battle. This is where your army composition matters and you start mixing together magic spells, unit abilities, terrain advantages, and a handful of other variables. It can be a little overwhelming at first, but even early on, I found it enjoyable. Your wielders (basically a general for your army) have various skills to unlock that allow them to specialize in certain combat styles. This allows the same faction to have wildly different playstyles depending on the army composition and the wielder in charge. Sometimes you can make major mistakes that cause you to lose the fight, but you can also pull off great comebacks thanks to the sheer volume of tactical decisions available. also features two distinct modes: campaign and skirmish. In campaign mode, you play as a specific faction for a handful of levels, while skirmish mode has you playing a standalone match with support for both singleplayer and multiplayer. The developers are mostly focusing on the singleplayer aspects during early access, so I’ll start with the campaigns.Currently, there are only two campaigns with four levels each, but they are much longer than I expected. You can easily spend an hour or two on a single mission, especially the later ones. The campaigns have their own stories and seem to serve as introductions to the factions. Each mission introduces something new about the faction, and it seems to be leading you towards skirmish mode as the main focus, at least when it comes to replayability.Skirmish mode has the same core gameplay, the main difference being the lack of plot and optional multiplayer. At present, multiplayer is a bit of an afterthought, although the devs are now adding simultaneous turns to try and improve this aspect. In singleplayer, it’s fun to be able to play as any faction without the restrictions the campaigns tend to place on you. Ultimately, I prefer the story mode, but thanks to modding tools,  has the potential to build a strong community that helps extend the game’s content.Even though only the campaign mode features a central storyline, the developers clearly put a lot of thought into it. It isn’t the most well-written story and it wears its influences on its sleeve, but I still enjoyed it. The world-building is top-notch with plenty of lore and backstory breathing life into what would otherwise be a by-the-numbers fantasy world. The factions are all interestingly designed and their gameplay is thematically consistent with their individual lore. Ultimately, the story elements are a net positive, even though in a vacuum, they’re underwhelming.I was pleasantly surprised by how excellent the audio and visuals were. Many strategy titles tend to slack on these because the gameplay is the major focus, but  manages to excel at both.Graphically, it’s gorgeous. The art style uses modernized pixel graphics to give off a retro feel while meeting the high visual standards of today. When coupled with the silky smooth animations, you have a recipe for success. The world map obviously looks great, but the visuals really shine once you get into a battle. This is where you get to see the animations in action and they add a lot of weight to a combat system that already feels brutal, especially when the last unit dies and you get to watch a slow-motion closeup of it.Thankfully, the sound design is no slouch either. The soundtrack fits the game perfectly, both as background music while you concentrate on strategy, and when you hear the bard songs after completing a campaign mission. The bard songs can be goofy, but because they are played straight without a hint of irony, the silliness becomes endearing, kind of like a Rennaissance fair. isn’t a great game yet, but it’s built on such a solid framework that I would be surprised if it doesn’t significantly improve in the next year or so. Even now, it would be good if it was a full release, the only negative being the lack of content. I expect two new campaigns to be added on at some point, hopefully along with some new factions. If this happens, it could wind up being one of my favorite strategy titles ever. As it stands, it’s a terrific game that simply needs more time in the oven.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited about this game, which is why this was a hard one to downvote. Unfortunately, this game suffers from a range of bad and DELIBERATE design decisions which sadly make it just a mediocre nice try and a forgettable experience.Some of the major bad design decisions include:1) unit stack caps! seriously, what the hell? who ever thought that this was ever even a remotely good idea?2) no wait and defend in battles, you basically just throw the two armies at each other with close to no strategy3) the spell variety is severely lacking, and the spells, overall, have negligible impact4) the artefact system is shallow and it allows for very limited builds; this also means that the best-in-slot items are very clear-cut and that strategically creating an impactful build around the situational needs of the moment is not really an optionI might add more items to this list as I keep playing, however, so far, the above are enough for me to say that this title has completely failed to meet the expectations that it built up by labelling itself the spiritual successor of HOMM3, which could not be further away from the truth. _childDocuments_.review: This game could very well pass for a spiritual successor to the Heroes of Might and Magic franchise.  The gameplay is fluid and definitely what you would expect for the genre.  The only downside to that is the low number of empires to pick from.  Did a single campaign map and then went into a skirmish map with the random map generator.No real surprise that the random map generator, on its first run even, created a map that had at least one inaccessible area to it.  Fortunately the map was generated in the Map Editor so it was quickly fixed by simply moving the offending tower out of the way.Combat is fairly solid, and the commanding hero doesn't even need to have the Tactics skill to set up the army prior to battle.  Most of the skills from Heroes 3 are present, but embellished to great effect.  The combat spells can be cast is rapid succession, limited only by the amount of essences you possess throughout the battle.  Yes, I did manage to cast three separate spells in the same turn with no trouble.Not sure what the reasoning behind it is, but when dwelling upgrades are built the base unit's production halts entirely for that city, though any accumulation up to that point in time is kept while a new counter starts counting up for the upgraded version of the dwelling.  Upgrading the base unit to the upgraded one in the army works like you'd expect, but it must be done manually for the settlement.  This is told to you by the tutorial popup so it isn't some sort of hidden feature / annoyance to get surprised by, and it still costs you the relevant upgrade costs.Three campaigns to pick from, with the fourth faction of mercenaries not having one.  The fourth campaign choice is instead reserved for custom, community content.  What I have seen with the one level I played, the developers are definitely putting in a decent story to everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of Conquest hearkens back to the style of classic strategy RPGs like Heroes of Might and Magic. Visually the game looks great, the character sprites are detailed and expressive with colorful maps to traverse. However, sometimes wandering around the map to collect resources is a bit tedious when there isn't much else going on around you. Gameplay is easy enough for a beginner, there are helpful tutorials that can be toggled on and off, but it also has enough depth for those seeking to immerse themselves in the more strategic elements such as building up your town's defense and productivity. The UI is simple enough to navigate and doesn't make you feel bogged down by menus. Building your settlements is fun and watching the buildings evolve as you upgrade them to produce more soldiers and resources is satisfying. The battle system incorporates the usage of terrain and elevations to give advantages or disadvantages depending on your positions. It's simple enough to pick up the battles, but mindlessly attacking won't bring you to victory so it's important to think about how to use your troops to their capacity. Despite being melee troops, the footmen seemed awfully weak and felt like sending paper soldiers off to battle. The Rangers on the other hand, were extremely useful. You can also upgrade the different troop types as you advance your settlement. The music is...present. It's not bad by any means and sometimes there are cutscenes with bards singing songs but it didn't feel very memorable. Overall the game seems very well made thus far and is a very enjoyable experience if you like old-school strategy RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very rare for a game that's a "spiritual successor" to a childhood favorite to live up to that expectation. Often those sorts only seek to copy a formula instead of building upon it, repeating design mistakes the original may have had, and ultimately ending up inferior to the original.Songs of Conquest not that. Goodness gracious is it anything but that.This game is a brilliant continuation of the Heroes formula, to a point that I almost want to consider it separately from those games, injecting new ideas into a tried and true formula while discarding outdated mechanics. The pixel-art is gorgeous, the music is incredible, and the basic skirmishes have perfectly captured that same hot-seat co-op fun I grew up with in Heroes 3.I want to highlight some things about the the combat and magic system here, because I'm seeing in many reviews that people are calling it shallow, or lacking impact, being generally down on many of the systems. This is ABSOLUTELY not true, but I understand many of the complaints. People are trying to approach this as if they're just playing another version of Heroes of Might and Magic. That is a mistake, Songs of Conquest has a different flow than what's came before, and you will not experience it at its best if you don't adapt to it.First off, the magic system. Songs of Conquest does away with spell points in favor of a Magic the Gathering sort of mana system. There are 5 different schools of magic, each tailored around a specific theme of magic. Order magic primarily revolves around buffs, Arcane gives some fun board manipulation spells, things like that. Each unit in the game is connected to at least one of these schools of magic, giving at least one orb (Basically a spell point) of that school every time they take a turn. The more orbs you have of a school, the more powerful magic you can cast of that school. In addition to that, there's many skills heroes can learn, as well as artifacts to find, that generate additional orbs and boost the power of spells in many different ways.And at first, this does feel a little lackluster, combat spells barely tickling opponents and buffs being barely noticeable. Add to that that spell generation feels far too slow, and you'll be left barely remembering to use spells!But then you start working *with* those mechanics. While the spells feel lackluster at first, they grow EXTREMELY powerful once you start gaining hero skills related to them. Movement spells like dimension door increase in range, eventually hitting a point where you can instantly dive a backline with slow, hard hitting melee units and delete ranged units before they ever get the chance to fire. A 'pacify' debuff doesn't feel all that great when it only lowers an enemies damage by 25%, but after taking some Order skills on your hero that jumps to a whopping 75%, invalidating powerful units entirely! I have had more fun with this games "swap unit" spell than I think I've ever had in a Heroes 3 games, being able to invalidate an enemy players strategies by swapping their frontline of foot soldiers with their backline of archers, then walking up and instantly deleting that stack is something I'll never get tired of.Adding to that power spike is how you build your armies. Each stack of a unit generates spell orbs, meaning that if you build your armies in a way that they are all producing orbs of a single school of magic, you'll quickly find yourself with more magic than you know what to do with. This is especially fun in Songs of Conquest, as unlike Heroes of Might and Magic you can cast multiple spells on the same turn! Some units act as magic 'batteries' specifically for this purpose, the Baryan's Piper unit is pathetic in combat, but generates two Order orbs and has an ability that gives every ally extra turn priority if it hangs back from battle and plays its music. Split that stack in two, and that immediately gives 4 Order orbs and ensures every other unit in the army is going to move before your enemy gets a chance too. Which, if you followed up on that with more Order producing troops, means that you can pacify any ranged units the enemy might have while charging forward with an insanely buffed front line! It's an extremely addictive system that marries the 'might' and 'magic' systems of its predecessors in a way that compliments them both!This game builds on its predecessor in other ways. Between adding unit stack caps and allowing no sort of 'Town Portal' map traversal ability for your wielders, the game encourages players to have multiple powerful heroes at once to attack or defend on multiple fronts. The unit stacks make spells more effective, as those armies can no longer grow to a size that debuffs become invalidated. And the elevation differences in battle, while being such a simple idea on paper, completely changes up how encounters function as both sides try to compete for the high ground. Again, the swap spell, it's hilarious to walk up to a powerful unit on the high-ground, trade places with it, and use that advantage against them.There's so much more I could take about. Bases allowing you to build multiple of the same production structure allows hilarious strategies like building ONLY plague rats and drowning opponents in a sea of rodents. Or how being able to delete and refund structures allows you to rapidly shift from a thriving economy to all-out troop production. But I think I've made my point with this review. Yes, this is a spiritual successor to Heroes of Might and Magic, and yes it is enjoyable in many of the same ways that those older games are. But it is also an evolution of that formula, and trying to play it in exactly the same way is a disservice to the mechanics the game possesses. Just try to keep that in mind while playing, because once pushed to their limits these tools are an absolute delight to play with!(Just one last thing. Campaign missions (While disappointingly short, I do hope they get expanded in length) end with a tavern minstrel singing a literal Song of Conquest about your exploits in the mission you just played. That's awesome. More of that in every video game please)

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of conquest is a spiritual successor to homm but offers refreshing new takes and mechanics to the decades old Genre. Let's start out with the good stuff+ City building. From what I've seen so far there are 4 different city sizes from small Hamlet to bustling city. Depending on what size you have they give different amounts of base income as well as offers a different amount of construction slots. The construction slots is what makes the new city building mechanic great as it allows you to either have a city that focuses on economy, unit growth or defence or a bit of everything. There is a also a building which allows you to train troops from any city you own which means no more mules. All of this together let's you really plan out your empire in a different way than in previous titles. Only negative thing is that I think the defensive buildings are a bit weak and could use a buff.+ Unit caps/wielder caps. The cap to max amount of units in each stacks means you have to think more carefully what type of units you use and also promotes the use of multiple wielders as opposed to just putting all your units into a single "doom stack" which your entire playthrough relies on. + Magic system. The magic system resolves around essence which is generated per round and depends on what kind of strategic map bonuses you have and what kind of units you bring to the fight. Different spells require a different combination of essence there seems to be a bit of a learning curve on how to best use your essence, on which spells and when. So far I've found some pretty powerful combinations like making a squishy DPS unit that just attacked an enemy in from an overextended position untargetable until the next turn, blocking off the only approach to your ranged units with a spell. From what I've experienced the damage spells might need some buffs as a few of them are a bit underwhelming+ Research. I know other titles also offer research options and some titles don't. I think it's a neat way to spend resources in lategame and offer a small albeit not insignificant strategic depth.And for the main pain points I've encountered so far.- Optimization. The game suffers from a few optimization issues such as fps drops and problems loading assets when a large part of the map is explored and especially while zoomed out or during the ai turns.- balance issues and qol. there are still a few things that need to be balanced better or improved most of which I have touched upon above. There are also qol stuff that needs to be expanded like settings, no edge panning sensitivity, no key bindings Overall I think the game has good core on which to expand upon
