_childDocuments_.review: “The spiritual successor to Heroes of Might and Magic 3”Well… maybe ? Let’s get into it. (Keep in mind that this game is still in early access and anything mentioned here can still change in the future)First the good stuff:- The graphics (and music) are absolutely beautiful. It might not suit everyone but I love this pixel art.- The gameplay is fun and engaging. Combat is fast and thanks to the fact that your monster stacks are limited in size it doesn’t really allow you to overcome your enemy by sheer numbers. So you have to at least think about your tactics. - There are currently 4 factions. Each has a personality and multiple valid playstyles. You can spend multiple hours just trying to figure out multiple strategies for just a single faction.- There are some interesting new ideas, for example research. Which (even though a little bit pricey) allows you to specialize in your faction even more. - There is a very nice map editor included which allows you to create custom maps or even story missions. There is also a hub accessible from the game to download maps (and later mods) from the community. This might spell a really long life for the game.- The developers engage with the community regularly and you can reach them pretty easily on the community discord. - The overworld gameplay is pretty shallow, even compared to Homm. You just collect resources and artifacts,  fight monsters and level up your Wielder (Hero). There are special buildings which provide extra monsters, experience or temporary or permanent stat boosts (There is also one which involves combat) but that's it. No underworld, no ships, no “looking for holy grail”, no overland spells or artifacts which would affect the way you travel. - There is no spell unlocking you just get all of them (more on the magic system later)- The hero skills get boring pretty fast. Every hero level you get to choose from 3 skills. 1st is a new skill, 2nd is an upgrade for your existing skill and 3rd is a command skill. Ignoring the fact that the command skill is more powerful than any other skill you are offered. ( Because it allows you to carry more army and by proxy generate more essence (this games’ version of mana, more on this later)) The skills are overall pretty bland. They usually involve some kind of stat increase, be it offense, defense, mana regeneration or spell damage, in some rare cases resource generation, But i would expect something more imaginative from a modern game. Every 8th level your hero also gets a new “big power” (or upgrade for it) which also usually involves something like +1 damage or +1 range or +2 HP to your troops. Which amounts to nothing.- Same goes for the artifacts. They are just simple stat increases you just get best in slot for your type of gameplay and you are done. No inherent gameplay comes from them. You can also enable an option for the game to just choose the best in slot automatically so you will just mostly ignore them.- The cities. The developers didn’t want to use city screens because “it’s just a fancy way to present menus and submenus to the player”. So they came up with building sites. Which are even worse. Your city is in the overworld split into main building (where you buy new monsters and manage your defenses) and building sites. These come in 3 sizes small, medium and large in which you can build different kinds of buildings. This causes 2 things. First the cities can get too big in the overworld causing issues for map makers because they have to account for this space otherwise you can get your hero stuck (Happens even in official maps). Second you still have to click through multiple submenus to do stuff but this time you have to look for it all over the place. Now the bad stuff:There is only one thing I would call bad about the game and that’s the magic system. (If you are not looking for a Homm successor and just want to play fun strategy game you can skip this part)The magic system is original. There are multiple types of essences (mana) generated by your troops (usually weaker monsters generate more and more powerful essence and stronger monsters weaker less useful esense) This essence allows you to cast spells in combat. Depending on the essence type (there are 5 types) you can cast damaging spells, supporting spells or utility spells affecting the battlefield. There are even more useful spells using combined essence types. Also the different factions usually only have reliable access to 3 types of essences from their troops. They have to get the rest from hero skills, research or artifacts.- I said that the magic system is original… but just for the sake of being original and it causes more issues than it solves (it solves none compared to the standard mana systems in games like Homm). The spells are too weak and too powerful at the same time. Some of the spell effects, mostly the damaging ones, are by default too weak to be considered useful or even fun to use unless your hero specializes in spell damage. On other hand if your hero specializes in spell damage (and the correct essence types) you can obliterate half of the enemy army at the start of your turn. Because the spells have no cooldown or even limit except your essence (which is reset and generated a new every combat anyway, so you don’t really use any resource).- There is no fun experience of discovering new spells. Because you just have them all in your spellbook and can just read up on them.- The essences are generated only in combat so don’t expect magic in overworld (probably ever).Summary (TL;DR):Overall this game is a fun strategy game with beautiful art design. For now I would give this game 7 / 10. (Early access version of the game)If you are looking for Homm 3 succesor I would probably recommend reducing the score by 1 point. If not or if you disagree with my rant about the magic you can increase the score by 1 point.Let’s hope at least Fanstratics will be more faithful to their roots.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Updating this for the Steam Awards, it's an excellent game :DThis is an excellent spiritual successor to the Heroes of Might & Magic series. Check out my video to learn more about it:TL;DR - This game is enjoyable enough for a full release, not just Early Access. There are only 4 factions and a limited number of official maps. , the factions are nicely varied and there is a really good map editor with mod.io integration so you can download community maps easily.You can grow your cities and armies however you like. Do you want to spam a single unit? You can do that. Would you rather have every unit available for your faction? Also possible! Cities do have different maximum sizes (limiting how many buildings you can make) and armies have a limit for how many units you can have in a stack. This prevents deathballs and putting all units into a single army and works just fine.There is some limited research, which lets you buff your units, heroes (wielders), economy, and unit limit for a single stack.Magic is interesting. Your heroes can natively generate a bit of essence (like mana but in 5 different flavors) but most of essence is given to you by your own units. Every time a unit takes its turn, you get a bit more essence. The longer a battle lasts, the more powerful spells you can cast. You can gain more magic faster by spreading your army wide.  by doing so you take greater risk, because every time a stack is destroyed, an enemy army gains a stacking buff. It's a nice balance of risk&reward.The AI is a bit lacking. It does better on maps with a lot of cities but makes some questionable choices on the battlefield. Currently, there's only an easy and medium AI available, though both are quite easy. However, you can also play this game in hot seat or online.Pro tip - . This will let you set up teams and play team games.In general, a great game with a few minor issues, I had a ton of fun already, and I can't wait to find out what's coming in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game has massive potential. Wonderful art, cool ideas, and the ability to tap into the greatest aspects of HOMM3. However, it is (very) far from polished and the developers need to focus on fixing the many bugs that are present. I think I've seen enough so far to revisit this title in a few months and see how things have improved.One note, though. I was a big fan of Stellaris. The problem Stellaris had (and still has, if I understand it correctly) was that the developers had no interest in fixing the underlying code of the game to make it playable late-game. Instead of fixing the core game, it's developers started cranking out purchasable DLC. I quit playing (and chose not to purchase any DLC packs) when I realized the developers were never going to address the glaring structural problems inherent in the game's code. I mention this because I hope SoC's developers realize that the title will succeed or fail on whether they make it playable. Before new factions or maps or other game mechanics (window dressing) are introduced, they need to fix the underlying playability. No crashes. No major bugs. No frustrating slow-down post round 50. If they fix these issues, I'd happily play this game (and buy DLC) for years to come. If they don't, then I'll move on to something else and readdress this comment.

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of conquest is a very mediocre game through and through. I have never played HoMM so you can be assured that there aren't any biased comparisons with that series in this review.Nice artstyle - very neat, pretty and quite refreshing. Good soundtrack - the tracks are very comfy and fit well to a fantasy setting. the songs which play at the end of each campaign mission are charming and aesthetic. Campaign missions are just mindnumbingly boring. there are 4 campaigns (one for each faction) each consisting of 4 missions. I've played 2 campaigns so far and there aren't any unique objectives or set pieces in the missions. every mission I've played so far is just some thinly veiled reason making you go from some point A to point B while fighting some enemies. it is so ponderous and feels like a chore honestly. All factions play the same. the factions aren't asymmetrical as they seem. you don't need to adopt new strategies or tactics for each faction. the unit abilities are different but the basic unit functionality remains same. the magic spells being mostly shared among factions doesn't help either, each faction would have been better off with their own separate set of magic spells. the magic system is quite weird, sometimes your healthy army can get nuked by the enemy wielder just before you wipe out their last standing unit. There's no easy way to put this but the writing is abysmal. the characters feel extremely disconnected from reality and feel like they are cardboard cutouts with no depth, no charisma or any thought put into them. I can point out several instances or scenarios which play out in the campaign that aren't convincing at the least. the factions themselves don't have any buildup or much lore behind them to make them interesting, the game makes the fantasy setting completely generic and as bland as possible. the settlement management, exploration are all quite basic and uninteresting. there just isn't much to it. overall, I don't recommend this game to anyone looking for a good single-player strategy game, its gameplay is serviceable at best and the campaign narrative is ridiculously bad. I will update the review after I force myself to finish the remaining 2 campaigns in-case I find some of my criticisms to be wrong,--------I have  changed my mind (so this portion is entirely an optional read) but I have more thoughts on the issues of the game and some other things which I wanted to substantiate: the mission ending songs and the art in them are better than I gave credit for. they were really rewarding and motivated me to finish some really frustrating missions (looking at you barony of Loth and Barya 4th missions). all factions feel same-y due to lack of unique mechanics in the overworld as well as in battles, before any SoC veteran starts picking up their pitchfork and torches, please hear me out: 2.1. In the overworld, each faction could have had unique stances or attack modes. for example: Rana, who are the faction of reptiles dwelling in swamps could have something like an ambush mode in swamp territory which would enable vanguard deployment for some of their low tier units, similarly you can imagine unique mechanics for each faction like baryans getting contracts for wiping out random mobs, etc etc but sadly none of the factions have any such thematic mechanics like this. all factions play the same in the overworld.2.2. unit abilities also fail to be thematic and impactful, let me give you an example: the Rana have chelun eldars which are basically tortoise sorcerers and Loth have necromancers, they both have the SAME special ability which is charge essence. they could have some interesting or fun additional abilities like turtling into their shell for the chelun unit to mitigate anticipated damage, thus making them formidable battle tank-mages and reanimate dead friendly human units for necromancer or hell, let the necromancer stack come back as an undead necromancer stack with half the stats. 2.3. similarly, arleon knights - no charge ability or something which could damage and push enemies back a tile, the rana frog infantry - have no long reaching tongue lash ability or even something fun like climb walls during siege (because they are frogs lol), Loth undead units could maybe reanimate based on a certain chance during the battle, and so on, but instead several abilities are lazy like stat increases or essence charging. the point is there is a lack of unique and fundamentally distinct units (they only look distinct in appearance and stats). 2.4. besides these, the gameplay still isn't engaging to me, especially when enemy wielders gets these toxic army comps and magic builds which stomp and neutralize you before the start of your turn, forcing you to build an entire army around especially countering them, this isn't really good when the game limits the number of wielders.2.5. minor complaint but most of the turns are spent in taxi-ing armies and waiting for units to be made. it might be just me but I started to feel that the unit variety was lacking nearing the end. I was pleasantly surprised that the undead faction's story was not the usual "undead == token bad guys in the setting" but overall the writing still isn't good and the campaign missions don't get any better. I do believe I understand the issue why the writing is underwhelming:3.1. each faction has total 4 missions and the writers are forced to introduce, flesh out ALL the wielders of that faction within these measly 4 missions which is a difficult task. no wonder the writing feels rushed/contrived/unnatural. also just when we think the story might be picking up, it ends, that's how abrupt the campaign. the game universe does have potential but it just falls flat, it's such a shame. final words: I still do not recommend the game for its campaign BUT you should give it a try if you plan to only play it only in skirmish coop or multiplayer because then your perspective as a multiplayer/skirmish enjoyer will be different from mine, a purely campaign only person.

_childDocuments_.review: A magical distillation of HOMM2/3/4 -- streamlined to make competitive & cooperative play feasible, fun, and quick. As an enormous fan of HOMM3, and an outspoken apologist for HOMM4, it was disappointing to see the series disintegrate, so I'm so happy to see someone fill that hole in my heart so elegantly.SoC takes all of the classic base-building, exploration, RPG-elements, and tactical combat from HOMM and shapes it into a far more balanced and board game-esque mold. Gone are the limitless troop pools and legions of heroes. Hard caps and choices based on limitations are everywhere. But this feels far more freeing rather than restrictive as the game is pleasantly designed around a more predictable growth progression that takes you to the gates of your opponent right as exploration starts to wear out its welcome. The map design and expansion logic of the skirmishes often gave me the feeling of some kind of turn-based Starcraft with how its resources and build-sites are dispersed and managed, and I think that's a very good thing. HOMM often fell into repetitive patterns of snowballing and clashing until one person gave out. Here, intelligent choices in army composition, battle tactics, and base management are way more important. I know some people have been turned off by SoC's magic system, but for me it's a perfect summary of what this game does right -- make every decision the player makes interesting and impactful. Never have I seen a system like this one, where your army composition has a tertiary effect of defining which spells will be available to you and how often you can cast them. And the opportunity to demolish and reshape my bases allowed me to experiment with these compositions in a synergistic way with the kinds of spell damage I wanted to inflict. I have gripes too -- the game feels bereft of content, especially considering its price tag. Part of what made HOMM3 so incredible was the sheer depth of the world and how much you were sure to encounter. Within a single skirmish I felt like I'd encountered most of what was available -- and even though the custom map system is amazing it's still limited by the base variety the game feeds into it. TLDR; it's HOMM perfected for multiplayer, it's beautiful to look at, and I wish there was way more of it. It's still in EA so I hope more gets added -- not only another faction or two but just more random beasties and dungeons that could help flesh out this wonderful world.

_childDocuments_.review: After some 50-ish hours with this game in its early access, a couple hundred hours in various Civ games and probably a couple thousand cumulative hours in HoMM 1-5, I'm by no means an expert, but certainly an avid enjoyer of the genre in general and this particular niche within it.Songs of Conquest is not without annoyances, but, let's be honest, none of these games are. The main difference here is that you probably already love HoMM if you're considering this game, despite its flaws, while SoC has yet to prove itself to you. Well, let me tell you, it's much more than a bland imitation banking on HoMM's pitiful current state and its beggars-can't-be-choosers-fans; rather, it is a daring reimagining of the genre with its unique takes on mechanics, balancing, and priorities. First things first: the game looks absolutely stunning, and plays smoothly and intuitively. The factions – while limited – have a nice selection of units and are defined and explored in depth in their respective campaigns. The soundtrack is gorgeous, too, and the inability to pause the game before taking 'just one more turn' is as present as ever. Now for the rest. With a set of decently written and well designed campaigns – personally, I'd argue that they are more entertaining than HoMMIII's –, a nice selection of skirmish maps, and a lively (albeit modest) community playing and designing their own maps, the promised future updates and continued work on the game are more of a bonus. Ultimately, it feels as if the team has decided to depart from the HoMM formula a little, because if they tried to copy it, they'd never come out on top. Instead, they've created an alternative.As it is, Songs of Conquest is a wonderful breath of fresh air for anyone who loves Heroes but feels like in just a little bit of a rut, or, contrary, never liked Heroes but always wanted to. Give it a go and support a small game studio working on learning from our collective gaming past to write a love letter to the genre in the present.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the first campaign and a skirmish map to see the top-tier units. I understand it's work in progress, and I like the core of the game, so I'd recommend this one.: * It does capture the HoMM feeling well, kudos to the team for that* There's good unit variety for each faction* Graphics, music are very good. * Magic system looks like an interesting evolution of what I've seen in HoMM games: * This is a con for me, but maybe a pro for others. There are not enough fantastical units I can relate to. The earlier HoMM iterations (aka the good ones) had relatable creatures from folklore: dragons, medusas, titans, imps, orcs, etc. This one takes a more original approach with lots of made-up monsters. I'd be happy with made-up monsters if I get loads of background lore and context, to familiarise myself, which is what we automatically have with folklore, which is well known. Here, suddenly you see armies of creatures A,B and C that you know nothing about and they just look like fantasy creatures.* Story felt a bit meh, maybe the are fantastic to somebody who hasn't played many other games in the genre, but it's typical subpar HoMM fare. Good HoMM 3 examples not seen here so far, were the stories of Crag Hack, Gelu, Sandro etc. * 8-player map with AI is still quite slow. I suspect this will get improved later on* Magic felt a bit underpowered and spells were not directly in my control. I tried a destruction magic hero, hoping I'd be blasting creatures away, but I kept getting several irrelevant spells, e.g. 1/5 available spells at any given time were destruction magic, and that was not because of essence imbalance. * I'm not sure what to think about town buildings being available on the map as slots, as interaction is minimal, they complicate moving around them and they add a layer of micromanagement (go physically to marketplace to trade)This is it so far, I'll keep updating as time goes by! _childDocuments_.review: Way, way better than any sh** ubisoft is planning on doing with HOMM series.Review:Gameplay: 10/10 Art: 10/10Sountrack(comparing to the greatest soundtrack in games-Homm3): 7/10Multiplayer: 9/10 Written review:This game is amazing, simple as that. It builds on HOMM3/4(where it draws inspiration from) and creates something new innovative solving a lot of HOMM3 problems, and adding a lot of variety to the mix.Problems it solved:Lots of heroes - Heroes of might and magic, as the own name says was known for it's many heroes, but this mechanic got abused as any player would have 10 heroes with one town creating these gigantic "supply lines" and kind of breaking the game a bit. In songs of conquest the heroes are aligned with the number of towns and how evolved you're, so you can't just start spawning thousands of heroes. And these heroes have a relative high cost so it's not the best strategy Shallow battlefield combat - HOMM3 is great for a lot of things, but one of it's flaws is the battlefield combat, it's mostly a wait to play mess and stronger vs weaker situation mechanics are not that deep. Songs of conquest adds elevation *Insert Anakin it's over meme here* where better positioned units do more damage and take less. And you can play around the field for better results, locking up tiles so they can't reach your archers. Spell throwing gods - In HOMM3 we had these wizards that were basically gods once they've reached a certain level. But in SOC you only throw spells as long as you generate the mana(essences) in battle. So another problem solved.Some of these problems were also what made HOMM3 kind of fun sometimes, but I see them in a step in the right direction, I don't acknowledge anything UBI is doing with the franchise at the moment which is kind of sad. The bad:Multiplayer needs some working - Some crazy disconnects and I would surely enjoy simultaneous battles instead of one player occupying the battlefield, but I don't know if that's a viable solutionBut this right here is the true HOMM IV successor, it builds upon the great things that HOMM III and HOMMIV brought. Keeping the great styling asthetic that we fans loved so much and adding a lot to the mix.Keep it up guys!

_childDocuments_.review: Having spent a significant amount of time exploring Songs of Conquest, I’m excited to share my thoughts on this captivating turn-based strategy game. From its vibrant art style to its engaging gameplay mechanics, this game has certainly made an impression on me.One of the standout features of Songs of Conquest is its stunning art direction. The hand-painted landscapes and character designs create a visually enchanting experience. Each region feels distinct, from lush forests to arid deserts, and the attention to detail is commendable. The animations are smooth and add life to the battles and exploration, making the entire experience immersive.At its core, Songs of Conquest combines classic turn-based strategy with resource management and tactical combat. Players are tasked with building their kingdom, recruiting units, and engaging in battles with rival factions. The gameplay feels familiar to fans of the genre, yet it introduces fresh mechanics that keep things interesting. The game allows players to create diverse armies by recruiting different units, each with unique abilities and strengths. The unit variety encourages strategic planning, as you must consider your army composition when facing different enemies. The depth of army customization adds layers of strategy that enhance the overall experience. The world is rich with resources, secrets, and lore waiting to be discovered. Exploring the map is rewarding, as players can find treasure, hidden artifacts, and various events that can turn the tide of battle. The sense of discovery is gratifying and encourages players to venture beyond their initial territories. The turn-based battles are well-designed, requiring players to think critically about their moves. Positioning, unit abilities, and terrain all play crucial roles in determining the outcome of each encounter. The battles are intense and rewarding, with a satisfying sense of progression as you level up your units and unlock new skills.Magic is a pivotal element in Songs of Conquest, adding an extra layer of strategy to both combat and exploration. Each faction has access to unique spells and magical abilities that can influence the battlefield in significant ways. Players can harness various magical abilities, ranging from powerful offensive spells to defensive shields and support effects. The ability to strategically deploy magic can turn the tide of battle, allowing for creative combinations with your army. The magic system encourages players to experiment with different spell combinations, adding depth to tactical decision-making. Utilizing magic requires careful resource management, as spells consume mana. Players must balance their use of magic with other tactics, making every decision feel impactful. This resource management aspect adds an intriguing layer to the gameplay, requiring players to think ahead and plan their moves accordingly.The music in Songs of Conquest is more than just a background element—it is a key component that shapes the atmosphere and immerses players deeply into the game’s world. The soundtrack is beautifully composed, featuring memorable melodies and orchestral arrangements that evoke a sense of epic adventure and mystery. Each track seems perfectly tailored to the environment and situation, whether it's the calm exploration of a forest or the intense buildup before a crucial battle.The music doesn’t just accompany the game; it enhances it, making the emotional highs higher and the quiet moments more poignant. It becomes a significant part of the storytelling, pulling you in and making you feel like you're part of a living, breathing world. This level of integration with the gameplay means that the soundtrack is truly unforgettable and, for many players, it will resonate long after the game is over. It’s not an exaggeration to say that the music is half of the game’s atmosphere, elevating every scene and encounter.The game features four distinct factions, each with its own unique lore, playstyle, and perspective on the unfolding events. What makes the storytelling particularly compelling is how the four campaigns are interwoven to narrate the same overarching conflict from different viewpoints. This multi-perspective approach allows players to understand the motivations, struggles, and ambitions of each faction, adding depth to the narrative. Each faction's campaign presents a different flavor of strategy and storytelling, whether it’s the noble struggles of the Arleon knights, the arcane ambitions of the Barony of Loth, the primal ferocity of the Rana, or the industrial ingenuity of the Barya. This approach ensures that the game never feels repetitive, as each faction offers a fresh set of challenges and a new angle on the same events. The choice to tell the same story from four different perspectives gives players a fuller picture of the world’s politics and conflicts. It’s fascinating to see how each faction perceives the events and their own role in the grander scheme. This adds layers to the narrative, as players uncover new details and reconsider the motives of characters and factions they may have previously judged.One of the game’s strengths is its challenge. The AI is smart and adaptive, providing a worthy opponent that forces players to rethink their strategies. The game also offers multiple difficulty settings, making it accessible for both newcomers and seasoned veterans of the genre.The variety of factions, combined with dynamic map events, the magic system, and customizable army compositions, ensures that no two playthroughs will feel the same. The different campaigns and the ways they interconnect create a narrative that invites players to replay the game to understand the full story.Songs of Conquest is a delightful blend of strategy, exploration, and storytelling. The stunning visuals, engaging gameplay mechanics, rich lore, intricate magic system, and unforgettable soundtrack create a compelling experience that is hard to put down. The four interconnected campaigns masterfully tell the story from multiple perspectives, giving players a deeper understanding of the world and its conflicts.Whether you’re a longtime fan of turn-based strategy games or a newcomer looking for an engaging experience, Songs of Conquest is well worth your time. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a game that balances depth and accessibility, with plenty of opportunities for strategic planning, tactical combat, magical mastery, and an epic musical journey.

It was not uncommon for me to report something to the team, then seeing a patch that addressed it just days later. I would especially like to bring attention to #ai-adventure and #ai-battle channels which are being tended to by dedicated AI coders 24/7. No feedback there goes unread, and it really shows, comparing an AI from couple months ago and now, the difference is insane. Most if not all reviews about pushover AI are outdated by now.And the future of this game looks very bright! We can expect an extensive post-launch support promised to solve most of my few gripes with current gameplay. There are even rumors about a 5th (with lore and early builds hinting at a 6th!) faction in the works. I can't wait to see what Lavapotion has in store for us.

_childDocuments_.review: Songs of Conquest is a game that you'll probably buy because you are a massive fan of Heroes of Might & Magic. If you are one of those, I can tell you that you can buy it and be satisfied, it is quite faithful while introducing many new things that don't ruin anything. Trust my word as someone who has played all Heroes media over the course of 20 years.If you aren't a fan of Heroes, then this review is for you.Playing through Songs of Conquest is a great experience, something you'd curl up to during a fresh may day and immerse yourself in while hearing the birds chirping outside. It is quite relaxing and stimulating. I'll try to explain the pros and cons of the game as best as I can during the course of this review.The game is divided into three parts. The management, the adventuring, and the combat.The management and adventuring are neatly combined together so I'll talk about them first. There is no one singular map in the game, rather many different maps with different goals and playstyles. On each map, your goal is to go around the map collecting resources and treasure to amass power for yourself, whether it is empowering your wielder with artifacts or getting access to stronger armies by buying them with the resources you have gathered. This part of the game is very good, with a nice ambient soundtrack, and some amazing visuals. (Which we will get into later) It has a nice sense of progression, as better loot is typically guarded by harder enemies, which you have to face in combat.When in combat, you are put into an entirely different game, seemingly, as you then have to use the troops you have to fight enemy creatures in a chess-like environment, with a field that has a hexagonal field. There are many different aspects to combat, such as elevation giving bonuses to your units in combat, terrain you cannot move your units to and through, as well as magic that your wielder can cast to turn the tides of battle. It is always quite tense and exciting as you would optimally not want to lose any units, and in late-game battles, it can become insane.Your wielder is the person which will be leading your armies and moving around the adventure map. It gives a very nice RPG element as you can give them new skills, and upgrade existing ones, of which there are many - all the while giving them differing equipment and artifacts. There are also trade-offs when leveling up with your hero in the skills that you choose, so it is always going to feel more personalized the more you play and the hero you have sees so much progress.On a technical side however, the game suffers. There are currently a substantial amount of bugs, thankfully none of which seem to be too gamebreaking. This is fine in my eyes however as the game is still in early access. The graphics are great, however, giving a sort of Stardew Valley kind of vibe.There are also some balancing issues where there are some blatantly overpowered and underpowered things in the game. In the campaign, there is also one very insane difficulty spike which struck me as odd.Overall, though, the game is great, and I'd easily recommend it, especially as the devs are relatively nice to the community and transparent, with many updates being churned through. I'd give it a higher rating maybe in the future, but for now, until the bugs and balancing issues are fixed, as well as the relative lack of content, I am giving it a

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time HoMaM player who have played 1 through 5 (I hated 4, and 6 + but despite my dislike for 4 I played it anyway. Don't make me start on anything after 5) I'd basically say that overall, SoC is very playable and likable. It does try to bring back the nostalgia of HoMaMs 1 - 3 albeit with major differences and in some cases general deficiencies. I would recommend the game to diehard retro 4X gamers and those who enjoyed HoMaM1 and 2. I personally don't care about the pixel graphics at all. It brings back the nostalgia of 640x480 gaming, and the game certainly loads a whole bloody lot faster than current era 4X games, some of which makes you wait for more or less half the time you spend playing.That being said, there are TONS of stuff that require improvement for this to become a long lasting hit. At its current state, although good, SoC misses the mark by a very LONG margin and I hope that the devs seriously look into the shortcomings.Good points:- Quick loading.- Includes a map editor, which is very important for people who enjoyed HoMaM5.- Music is great.- Most of the tooltips are really helpful.- The moment you get used to the game, it's pretty much not fussy to play.- Good enough graphics (albeit with weaknesses) for a nostalgic 4X game.Now, on to the problems, and bear with me. LAVAPOTION! PLEASE READ THIS!- Campaign is DULL AS HECK! I play HoMaM and SoC for their MP, but with the campaign like THIS, the game    will have a big issue getting players to like playing the campaign. Characters also lack flavour as well. This    being said, players NEED to know that SoC is totally new and the lore isn't deep like in Might and Magic.- UI is horrid in many ways and NOT INTUITIVE. The tutorials are pretty OK but the UI is still a very bad   experience. Interaction between wielders (Heroes in HoMaM) and settlements and other cities are just not   quick and simple.     = For one, moving troops around isn't intuitive at all and require too many clicks to do.    = City building and interaction is also an issue. Again it's not intuitive and there's not "city screen" where        everything can be done easily. The current city popup is very messy and frankly quite frustrating to use.       The controls are thrown everywhere in the popup and nothing is grouped into proper areas.    = For stuff like moving troops between entities (wielders and settlements alike), instead of going for a        single-click to move, or a combination of a key and click to split, the game instead pops up a tiny        context popup that makes you select either to move all, split evenly or otherwise select how many       troops you want to move. This makes for a very bad UX as players will end up clicking too many times       when moving troops.    = Placement of icons for settlements need to be clearer, more pronounced, and on a more proper location.       Right now the weilders and settlements are on different places on the screen (weilder on the left side       and the settlements are on the bottom left corner just to the right of the mini map, which are practically       invisible to the player). Again, the placement is seriously unintuitive and I only noticed the settlement       icons like five hours into the game or sol.- The pixel graphics brings some issues as well, and this issue was also apparent in HoMaMs 1 and 2. Items   can end up being hidden behind other objects, especially big objects like city buildings. This not just make   them very difficult to pick out especially since we're using bitmaps, it's also very difficult to mouse-over or   click on them as their Z-stack is behind the bigger obstructing object. There's a need to do something   about this.- There's actually not that much difference between the factions at the moment, but I personally consider   this to be a small issue as I believe that there'll be more distinctions and further factions that Lavapool will   make.- The multiplayer maps are very limited now, and TBH reminds me more of HoMaM1 and 2 instead of   HoMaM 3 and 5, and I consider 3 and 5 to be a lot more fun. The settlements are just too limited in many   of the maps, and the procedurely-generated random maps can sometimes make the home cities smaller   so you may end up starting with a Large Settlement instead of a City.- Some capturable buildings and visit sites don't say what they do in the tooltip.- The AI is not very good, which is a fact that Lavapotion admits, but to let the AI cheat by giving them more    resources even at "Fair" difficulty is just horrible. This actually makes the game less fun and personally I   found it very frustrating to have to suddenly deal with an impossibly souped up enemy wielder with tons of   upgraded forces when I KNOW very well that there was no way I was able to do the same. LAVAPOTION!   LEAVE STUFF LIKE RESOURCE BONUSES TO AI PLAYERS AT VERY VERY HIGH SETTINGS INSTEAD!- Tactical Combat-wise, I'd say that I'd want an EXTRA button for the current unit's skill on a FIXED    LOCATION on the screen as that's more intuitive. Currently the buttons on the whole game are so small    that I often needed to squint to look for them, and in tac-com, having that small button placed on the unit   itself makes it tiresome for the player as the location would change when the unit moves.- Tac-Com: There's currently no "Wait" ability except in certain units which makes combat slightly less    tactical than newer HoMaM games like 5.- Currently, there's a really bad screen tearing problem whenever I scroll the map around. This needs    SERIOUS ATTENTION as screen tearing is seriously bad with unoptimized Unity games.Conclusion:I have more to say, especially in regards to where else Lavapotion can improve the game, but this review is long enough as it is. I've yet to try the multiplayer function, but when I do, I'd be adding more comments and constructive criticism.I've already decided to keep the game within an hour playing the game, even when I noticed all the issues it has. I personally feel very positive about the game and am hoping that Lavapotion would change the game to make it a lot more playable and enjoyable.At its current stage, I can still recommend the game to players who prefer retro and nostalgic 4X games like HoMaMs 1 and 2, but to young futts who just think that fun = graphics : stay away from this title.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game right as it went public for Early Access and after playing a bit decided to wait until the full release. It was promising but really incomplete at the time. As of full release it improves upon some shortcomings of HOMM3, adds new ideas but ultimately it doesn't quite get to the point of quantity and quality to really satisfy the urge for a fresh new HOMM3-like experience.I didn't wish for it to be a clone of the HOMM3, of course, and Songs of Conquest has plenty of new mechanics to differentiate itself. It's just that those new mechanics are hit and miss, with a slightly more emphasis on the , unfortunately. The  essence is gained on the battlefield through different troops which provide different kind of essence. Basically the bigger and more diverse army you have the stronger and more efficient you magic becomes which kind of defeats the purpose of magic? While you can gain wielder abilities that improve the essence gain I don't feel like investing in those abilities when I still need an army, I'd rather invest in offensive abilities because if I have a really strong army then I probably don't really need ice bolts and chain lightnings that much. In the  I found myself not using much of magic cause I had plenty of powerful long range troops. And while the enemy AI was more apt and willing to use magic against me, it didn't help it against the strong army at all, dealing maximum of 1-3 troops worth of damage against a stack of 30-40 troops. And in the  most of the magic available to you is defensive magic, which is neat but not really engaging as you'll probably just use Shield and not much else.The random map generation is where the meat is in a HOMM3 experience. I respect the developers for putting a lot of time and effort in the campaign still. And the map generation is OK, I guess? The maps are very linear, often there is only 1 valid path to the town, combined with the lack of underground and seafaring (and classic freeroam magic like dimension door or fly) makes it a rather straightforward experience. There are portals, which I've seen in other people's gameplays, but I've yet to encounter one in my games, it seems to be a rare occurrence:/Also I feel the artifacts (artifact generation?) are lacking, while in HOMM3 you could really make some powerful build with the artifacts, make combos or just find cool artifacts that elevate some aspect of your character (necromancy/magic/skills etc), here the artifacts seem not only one dimensional but just really sparse. In all the games I've played there wasn't really a lot of interesting artifacts (or just a lot at all). 90% of the time I managed to get maybe helmet/armor/weapon set for my main character and find maybe 3-5 useless like +4-6 weapons and that's it. Artifacts feel underwhelming too.I really don't know how to assess the AI in this game. The AI seems to have just 1 main player, that has the majority of the troops while all the other AI wielders are left with 1-2 half-stacks at best, which on medium-lower difficulties creates an unfair advantage for me, cause if I know that I've destroyed the main player of the AI team I can just send my secondary or tertiary wielder to just clear out the rest of the team with minimum troops. The AI wielders also behave really weird because they are weak, in my experience, only the main enemy wielder is exploring the map, while for some reason all the other wielders just chill in of the towns. I've encountered the following situation twice: I come to an enemy town and there are like 2-3 wielders just standing there with almost no troops.On the higher difficulties AI seems to have unreasonable advantages in troop counts. On day 10 I was completely destroyed by an AI with hundreds of different troops while my day one dwelling was able to generate about 50 or something troops in total, and the others even less (while also having two towns by that point).P.S.  It's really annoying when the AI turn takes twice or thrice as long as yours, especially when they are in Terra Incognita yet it feels like the game is processing their turn in real time as if you're watching their moves. That kills the enjoyment quite a bit.I am OK with the town system. It strips away the uniqueness of every town, since now they are converted into your fraction and the only difference in them is their size, but it creates interesting opportunities since you can build any building as much as the quantity of that building size permits. I love that you can build Rally Points to get the troops from different towns in one place. It's just essential since traversing the map can become quite tedious.Playing it in 2022 for a few hours and returning to it again 2 years later and hearing the soundtrack I immediately got a Déjà vu/nostalgia like feeling I get when I get into HOMM3, even after those few hours years ago the soundtrack was still deep in my head. It's really amazing. Though I wish the soundtrack was more varied. I don't have a problem with the style at all. I love it, but I don't like how points of interest are too unnoticeable, they tend to blend in too much with the rest of the map. While I can play with highest graphics possible I tend to put terrain on low, so at least it creates a nice contrast between the terrain and what's on it (still, I tend to miss some things quite often).

_childDocuments_.review: I am one of those players who grew up playing and loving the HOMM series, but over time I got to know King's Bounty  and I liked its mechanics more... However, I think we won't see any new parts soon , only endless remasters/remakes. I thought this genre was done for, but then Songs of Conquest bursts into version 1.0 with both feet, and most importantly, the game turned out to be good.I'm not claiming to be a grand-master in tactical turn-based games, so it was enough for me to complete all the campaigns to pour out my opinion.First of all, I was captivated by the game's appearance. Pixel art is hyped and continues to be hyped, and still, games are developed that cause a "wow" effect. The game has its own original style. This is probably the first thing I noticed.Secondly, it is, of course, the painfully familiar gameplay , but with its own features. To me, the most challenging and unusual aspect is magic. You can actually sit with a notebook and a notepad to calculate all sorts of powerful combinations since the magic you cast depends on the type of troops you use. You also need to manage and rebuild cities correctly to avoid getting stuck. If I was sweating in the campaign from time to time to buy just the right amount of units and defend my castle, it's scary to imagine what happens in multiplayer. Each faction offers a unique experience and different playstyles. At first, I was upset that units have their own capacity in a squad, but over time I appreciated that this contributes to gameplay diversity instead of just overwhelming the enemy with numbers.Although the campaign didn't hook me at first, it gradually builds up and leads the player to the finale, where all the threads come together . In the last mission, at least for me, I felt like a strategist, as I constantly had to react to various threats and calculate my moves. The campaign also features richly and interestingly designed maps, all of which are seasoned with dialogues or lore elements that will surely appeal to meticulous players.It was challenging, it was interesting, and it was dopamine. Most importantly, the success of this game gives confidence that the genre is not going anywhere and there will be more similar games in the future .

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10It has been a long time now. Finally Songs of Conquest is fully released and all of the campaigns are here for us to enjoy. Is this the fresh new take on Heroes of Might and Magic 3? Is this gods gift to man? Nah, not really, but it is a neat game that does many things right.Songs of Conquest is a turn-based strategy game in which you control a hero on a map, claiming loot and capturing towns and buildings to streghten your stats and economy. When you get into a battle, the game changes into a grid-style board in which you take turns controlling units and trying to outstrategize your opponent. Just like the Heroes of Might and Magic-series. The game is presented in beautiful pixel-art with great lighting. The soundtrack is also very fitting for the game. I have a little nitpick in that I sometimes would like some more detail in the character-designs, as they now look a little too compressed in the facial area, a consequence of the art-form.What is different from Heroes of Might and Magic, then? Well, mainly two things. First, it is how towns work. It is a little tricky to explain, but basically you have a twon center and build-sites where you choose what buildings to place, based on how big the site is. This means that you cannot make a town bigger and bigger until you have all the things, you need multiple towns to be able to get all that is offered to your faction (of which there are about five in the game). This is an interesting choice, as it forces you to make some hard choices in priority and no game ever feels the same for your faction. The second change is in combat, with something called "essence". It is basically a form of mana that translates to that every school of magic has its own mana-pool. Essence is gained in various ways, both in and outside combat, and using spells is very important when it comes to winning fights (arguably just like in Heroes of Might and Magic).The campaigns and writing is very good in Songs of Conquest. The game is pretty and the strategy challenges you. But not all is perfect here.Having each scenario end with a little bardic song is cute but quickly becomes gimmicky and tbh I did not "like" any of the 20 second songs that much. It is fun in concept but meh in execution. I also do not enjoy the UI for how your army is composed at all. I would very much like to clock on a unit to get more info and just have a little window where I can expore more about each unit-type. I miss this from Heroes of Might and Magic 3 and 5, specifically.All in all, this is a neat little game that has its own identity, for better or worse, and I had fun with it. I hope the developers keep making fun games and that they are proud of what they have done for the genre. I sure am.

_childDocuments_.review: A lukewarm recommendation. There's plenty to like about Songs of Conquest, particularly its art style and audio design. Exploring the map is surprisingly fun given what you're doing is pretty basic. But there's lots of things I'm not so keen on. The big issue for me are the battles - they're just not that interesting or engaging, and I find myself auto-resolving them 99% of the time. I don't like that the Wielders, essentially how you're represented in the game, don't take part in the battle aside from casting spells and providing passive buffs as a result of the gear that they wear (doesn't make a lot of sense either). However, it's one of the few strategy games I've enjoyed playing on the Steam Deck so it gets a bonus point for that. Overall it's a decent game but I'm still left searching for something to scratch the Warlords/Heroes itch.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: The multiplayer in this game is only enjoyable if you take a group of drunk friends and randomly move your pieces until 1 person cries and leaves the game. Do not buy this game without a friends group to play multiplayer with, it isnt worth it. I want to preface this review by saying I received this game as a gift from a friend, so I personally didnt end up paying for it, he did. Additionally, I only write steam reviews on games that I have a very strong opinion about. That is the case here. I am not a campaign player myself. I played the first mission and got bored on the second mission of the arleon campaign. The campaigns are just special custom maps made by the devs and if you played through it once, you will experience the same scenario again. That makes them unappealing to me, since all i have to do is find the correct sequence of moves and then it is solved. [Skirmish and Multiplayer Skirmish]The skirmish portion of the game is much more fleshed out. There is a custom map maker built in and thus there are countless of custom maps. The devs recently added randomly generated maps as well, which allows for us to play 1v1 many times in a row without any meta gaming happening on the map. Good. The main issues with skirmish come from the way multiplayer is implemented. You have 2 choices, Play either 1 turn after another or you play with simultaneous turns. The first option means you sit there for 2 hours in a 20 turn game and the sim turns means that after doing all the Neutral Battles, you crash the game the second your opponent spam clicks on your Hero and you can start over again. Additionally whenever a player enters a neutral battle the game locks up and you cant move your hero until the fight is over. It is UNBEARABLE unless you are in a voice chat with the players or do something on the side. [AI Fights]There are neutral Fights on the map, guarding treasures or production buildings. Winning the fights early gives you a massive boost to your economy and is the difference between winning and losing. The best players are capable of taking fights very early with very little units and taking little losses. How does that work? The neutral fights cannot use magic. You can. There are MANY ways to cheese them abusing this fact. The community complains that the AI is not smart enough, but Ive been trying to do a better job than the AI by playing the fights from the AI point of view and if the opponent is smart with how they use their magic, then there is NOTHING you can do. Also, since we want to take fights early and with very few units, they will take LONG since we cannot burst enemy units 1 by one. This is again an issue with the current implementation of simultaneous turns, the opponent waits for 5-10 minutes each time unable to interact with the game. [Community] There is no Ranked matchmaking, so if you want to find games against other players, you have to either join random lobbies or you go to the official discord and beg for someone to play you. There are no competitive minded players on that server. I am a tryhard myself, every game is a mismatch and unfun. [Balance] The game is insanely snowbally in nature. If you get a fight 1 turn earlier then that will make more of a difference than some missing stats on the units you use. This puts a high emphasis on early AI-Fighting units+Heroes and factions that get them nerfed or simply dont have them are automatically unplayably bad, unless the opponent is just as bad at the game as your faction. This also means that if you want to play a strategy that doesnt have a way of doing early AI fights, then that strategy is just bad. It limits the game ALOT. Fights against humans end within 2 turns, there is so much movement magic in the game that you can cross the entire battlefield on the first turn and decide the outcome of the fight. [Learning Curve] This game takes a while to learn. But it isnt satisfying having learnt it. Everything in this game is just a matter of optimization and once you know how to do things the most optimal way, there is NOT A SINGLE THOUGHT required anymore. It only seems like a deep and intriguing game to people that dont have the time to actually spend 10-20 hours actually practicing and optimizing their pathing, creeping and building management.Conclusion: This game can become good eventually, but in its current state it can only be enjoyed if you can actively overlook how shallow the mechanics of the game are. Additionally, there is no competitive community left on the official discord, so the devs have to figure out the most broken Cheeses and Abuses of AI and maps and Factions on their own, which I havent seen work in the past.

_childDocuments_.review: This is almost certainly going to be a good game. A lot of the decisions the devs have made are great upgrades from the HOMM 3 formula and so far I have not encountered anything that made me go "hmm, this is a bad decision". However the game also needs a lot more development. I would like to see more factions, some variety in spells across factions, but most importantly the game needs significant AI improvements. My first skirmish, with no knowledge of the game and with the AI on the highest difficulty it can be (normal), was a steam roll. I think most people will not have friends to play in multiplayer, so better AI is a must have for the longevity of the game. As a short term fix, rather than AI skill improvements, I would consider adding higher difficulties where the AI just cheats (by getting more resources, lower costs, etc). A better AI on an even playing field is obviously the ultimate goal, but cheating AIs have worked for many AAA games.

If you manage to setup economy and unit recruiting properly and balance out expansion/recruiting, then you will win easily. The most fun part about this game is finding this kind of balance.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of comments are saying this game is a successor to "Heroes of Might and Magic" (which we  desperately need because it is an amazing turn based strategy game that has been exploited and forgotten).In my opinion, this statement is true but unfortunately the missing pieces leave a major impact. For me, the issue is that when I play HMM 5, for example, I am so excited to upgrade beyond the starting peasants/archers/swordsmen onto the much more impressive griffins/knights/angels. And in/up-against other factions, the units that excite me are the bone/shadow dragons and the succubus and the unicorns etc etc etc. It gets so exciting in HMM 5 to use your army of 1000 tier 1 units (peasants) against an army of 20 tier 5 units (vampire lords) or whatever.Meanwhile in this game, I am only done the human capaign so far so maybe my opinion isn't worth much, but the fact that my end game army is the same as my starting-game army (a handful of archers and swordsmen) feels pretty dissatisfying when in my mind I am comparing the game to HMM 5.My request to fix this is that the devs should consider the units they have currently implemented into the game as their "lower tier" units, and then literally double the amount of units in the game, to make a second half on units that are the "higher tier" half. Available in much lesser quantities. "50 swordsmen and 3 Angels" sounds way more fun than "50 swordsmen and another 50 swordsmen" to me.I think the game would also benefit from resizing the units in combat. Making the weaker/basic units smaller in size would help portray the difference in strength between something like humans versus wraiths.Obviously I give the game a thumbs up though, because it is a hella good game. And their Roadmap seems to be providing tools for modders, so maybe my requests will be answered in modders' additions to the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Update: I'm disappointed in the newest campaign. It lacks both depth and breadth. It's short like the others with only four scenarios, but the first two of those scenarios are also tiny and set up like you're first playing the game. It's unnecessary. This is the third campaign. I expect introduction scenarios in the first campaign, not all the way to the third one like I haven't been playing the game. It's especially noticeable because it takes until the fourth map to get any real depth, and then ends abruptly. I really don't like the approach you've taken. You use the campaigns more to introduce the faction then to give a satisfying experience. Campaigns are what I enjoy most out of this genre and you've really neglected them.Really awesome game. If you're a fan of HoMM this hits the sweet spot. It's really cool to see your town built in real time, and having a natural limit on the amount of buildings in a town is a great way to diversify town building. The campaigns have been really fun to play, and each faction feels different. I really hope to see more campaigns as that is what I always enjoyed the most from HoMM.There's one major critique I have for the game. Magic is overpowered, much like the original HoMM, just in a different way. It's not just really easy to quickly cap your essence, but it also has a huge impact each time it's used. The wielder with the higher initiative has a huge advantage in battle because of this and initiative checks can often outright decide who wins a battle. I really don't like the approach you've done for magic here. HoMM at its core is about troop strategy and town management. Magic should be supplementing that, not overwhelming it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, like many other's said, a tactical-strategical 4X-like, commonly reffered to as HoMM successor, feels indeed like a spiritual successor of Heroes of Might and Magic 3 in terms of general feel and gameplay loop, but that is where the similarities end.The developers managed to spin a tale about a captivating world, where all events are intertwined, and each mission has at least couple of a certain *deja vu* moments, where we can connect the dots, and see the bigger picture after "hearing" each Song of ConquestThe game itself consists of 4 factions as of now, each with their own well-crafted short "song" or campaign, where our heroes (or wielders, how they are called in this game - because they "wield" their troops, and their essence), which are of varying difficulties (the infamous Loth 4 mission comes to mind) but all are perfectly doeable, all offer some replay value, and have 3 levels of difficulty to choose fromFactions are all very assymetric, but still somewhat balanced, each one offers different tricks to playMy only minor gripe would be that building "Might" heroes is counterproductive - magic will always be stronger than troop bonuses in the current balance. I would alleviate it by making might skills more gimmicky than straight up bonuses

_childDocuments_.review: Song of Conquest is a exceptional turn based strategy game that emulates games such in vein of the Heroes of Might and Magic era (Before the game became ♥♥♥♥ do to ubisoft.) adding some cool twists  ideas on the use of how using spells and abilities works, the usefulness of units so on and so forth. this game is phenomenal there is still a good deal of things to be done for balancing. there's a lot of combos and ways to run armies and wielders and more will be discussed / improved upon as the Early access continues but for now for 30$ this game gives you more than enough bang for your buck. the story is well written, you have interesting characters and challenging levels for the campaign setting and for multiplayer this can go up to 8 players total. leading to some fun interesting and intense games. if you love turn based strategy games and enjoyed Heroes of Might and Magic this game is definitely worth looking into and possibly picking up.

name: Digimon Survive
detailed_description: Digimon Survive presents a hybrid visual novel and tactical RPG set in a mysterious world filled with dangerous monsters and deadly battles that will test your ability to survive. After getting lost on a school trip, Takuma Momozuka finds himself transported to a world inhabited by ferocious foes and new allies. Join Takuma and his friends as they fight their way back home. Craft your story in this thrilling visual novel with turn-based combat. - A Rich Visual Novel Experience Unfold a dark tale about friendship and survival that is jam-packed with exciting drama, a unique cast of characters, and potentially grim choices. - A Mysterious World Explore otherworldly areas filled with hidden secrets and Digimon to recruit. - The Power is Yours Your choices affect gameplay: you bond with other NPCs, your Digimon's evolution, and the outcome of your adventure. - Thrilling and Strategic Gameplay Persuade your opponents to join your team and evolve them to fight alongside you in thrilling turn-based battles.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a clear no from the Digimon side as well as the gameplay side for me.- the story -I love Digimon - even though to this point I have not heard the word Digimon drop. If you had copyright issues with the term surely the title wouldn't be Digimon survive? So why still call them beast in new game plus?I'm not too much bothered by how slow it is (Freakign dragged out though, feels like I am voting on decisions, and then they just keep on going on the same topic for another 1-2 hours until finally, we get a move on).I also get that this whole subject is supposed to be about survival. But it feels so draining/boring / torturous to have the characters argue about everything every step of the way and 5 chapters in still not trust their partners. I am playing a game because I want to have fun with the Digimon universe. That includes them bonding with the team / the partners. Yes, the world can be scary and dangerous. But don't rub it under my nose every 20 seconds. I'm not that dumb that I need constant reminders to take the situation seriously.If you wanted a dark souls / corpse party sort of universe perhaps a new monster taming / strategy IP would serve better.- the gameplay -The deaths I've seen so far feel absolutely pointless to the point of drama/shock factor though. You can have the highest relationship with a character, invest every free action in them, talk to them at every opportunity, explore every location on the screen, not lose a unit in combat and still have them die? With the audacity of the characters guilt tripping you into "we have seen the signs, yet did nothing." What did you want me to do more? Throw my controller to the screen because mashing the A button on them would not let me talk or make them see reason? What is it linked to then though I wonder? Karma? Cuz then by all means Karma is a trash system taking away gameplay purpose if you can only choose one Karma / Path to make them live.Just have the right karma type and you are immortal to the threat of deathtraps! You did not resolve this by being smart about finding a way out, trusting the right people or making a plan beforehand. Nope, all you had to do was be red more often than green or yellow!And the idea of having a New Game + path that's possibly the only save-all? Sorry to disappoint, but I do not have the patience to go through 30 hours of false advertisement (my choices matter, but actually only the total number of karma points matter) and then still hold the motivation to do it all again on a 2nd playthrough.- the combat -Having an option for free battles is good. You could recruit 105 Monsters in the Dex, at least you won't lose the units to unavoidable death. Just a shame they can't use the talk command and therefore feel like a worse choice than the main Digimon. The fights themselves feel needlessly slow and sluggish because moving 2 or 3 fields per role type is just nothing. Mob KI sometimes keeps running from you to defend dragging it out even more. I haven't felt much of an effect for elements either. You side attack and back attack and gang up on them and punch them to death. No point splitting up anyway with so little movement.Grind evolution items by flipping on auto battle (exploration doesn't give enough plates for a full team of free digimon to evolve) and I was overleveled enough to beat the final boss without giving a care about even wearing equipment or using healing items.

_childDocuments_.review: A bunch of people are talking who stopped after half an hour so take it from someone who rushed to get through all 12 chapters. As a longtime fan, this is the game I've always wanted out of this franchise. It's a bold new take on the series that's surprisingly dark but still has you trying desperately to befriend everyone because the characters are so charming. Even the characters who made me hate them were so human and that made me want to see them overcome their struggles. The more mature parts of this game threw me for a complete loop in the best way possible. And I ended up really enjoying the combat system despite being skeptical of it at first. I wouldn't say that combat is incredibly hard, but you do have to use your brain and there were a handful of battles where I got a bit stuck. Not to mention the fantastic art! Having dynamic lighting for the characters really made a huge difference in the game's atmosphere.Although it's a departure from what fans of the series may know, parts of the game pay homage to the original Digimon Adventure anime in ways that make you feel rewarded. I wouldn't say this game is perfect because towards the end of the game certain parts became a bit more predictable and I felt that it had partially lost that initial spice that came with realizing this wasn't your average monster collecting game. But as a whole I think the fun I had with this game more than makes up for any parts where it felt a bit slow. And yes this is a visual novel so people who don't like reading may not have nearly as much fun with this game. But it's a game that I believe is worth playing to the end, and personally I can't wait to replay it some more to find every collectible and unlock every secret.

_childDocuments_.review: Its different so I wont knock for not being the same so I'm judging it for what it is not what other games in the series are. If I had to boil it down.The game is like a dating sim/strategy game with a digimon backdrop.  The story is good but downside is you have to replay for the TRUE ENDING which honestly I didn't really feel like replaying it to completion as it definitely did feel extremely repetitive as the "Gameplay" of the game is pretty much just basic strategy that is uninteresting. I understand the locking a true good ending behind difficult gameplay or to experience the story in a worst case scenario can be good but I didnt like that you basically have to reset entirely even through the handholding tutorial sections at the begining of the game. I think they should have done a NG+ with built in skiping options of the earliest sections as they are just a slog to get back to the jumping off point for the dark/good path.  I'm not super into the do all these dialog options to see different things happen as its super repetitive. Yes I'm aware there is an auto battle option however lets be real they really should have just had the option to replay the story and choices if you wanted or to Jump to major decisions and track which things you've experienced yet or not otherwise its a bit boring. That may all seem negative but is pretty standard for the genera which I'm not super a fan of. The story is good and the concept is interesting enough to keep you entertained. The gameplay  and repetition is really the downside.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever played an srpg or read a visual novel, you know within the first 5 hours that digimon survive is a mediocre slog at bestPros -Nice spritesChompHandful of older mons getting the spotlightCons -1. Game is far too easy. Outside of the last 3ish bosses per route you can have auto battle on and win every battle with ease, even on hard mode. Combat boils down to move to the side or behind enemy and then use whichever of your 2 moves (wow! 2 whole options!) hits harder. Digivolution is supposed to be used sparingly as it drains your sp, but if you use even one SP item to increase your max you will NEVER run out, and that isn't even factoring in passives from other digimon that'll randomly regen your sp with no input. Balance is all over the place and most free digimon you can recruit are better than your party members until your party members get to mega, and there's 0% chance you can fail a recruitment since you can just savescum and constantly reload a map with no consequence. Don't forget that there's no limit to how many stat items you can feed a digimon so you can make agumon an invincible god within a few chapters. And guess what? stat items can also be savescummed and rerolled so you can get him max attack or defense with 0 thought2. Game and story are slow and repetitiveMany, MANY moments in the story have dialogue repeated ad-nauseum, if you got to the sewers you know exactly what I mean. Characters will all have the exact same problems at the exact same time and you'll have to respond to each of them the exact same way and they'll all respond the exact same way with no variance. Lots of the actual game is just flipping through menus to go from point a to point b to point c to get 3-4 lines of dialogue that don't add anything to the story and then moving on. If you don't have acceleration charge good luck finishing any battle in under 30 minutes. Most Digimon move only 2-3 squares in maps that are 200x200, and it's extra ♥♥♥♥♥♥ because bosses will just sit and spam defend until you're within 10 blocks so you can't even count on them to speed things up. Think turning off animations and canceling animations will speed things up? Enjoy your digimon running in circles and buffing themselves repeatedly, never even attempting to attack.Difficulty and slowness aside, there's dozens of points in the story where you'll do 5-10 battles on a row in the exact same map with the exact same enemies in the exact same spots. In the sewers you go through like 4 seadramon fights with that one healing robot in the center, in the library you fight 10 waves of god's notdigimon on the exact same layout library with way too many walls, the 400 fights with bdsmwolfmon in chapter 2 it gets really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fast, ESPECIALLY because the ai will always act in the same way every time as well. It also doesn't really feel particularly good having digimon limited to 1 move and a basic attack if you actually want to have stat increasing gear on them.3. Routes diverge way too late and your choices don't actually matterNo route choice until chapter 8/12, none of your character's affinities affect their deaths with the sole exception of ryo in ng+. Deaths are always forced per route and what ultimate decides your route is a red/yellow/green option at the very end of chapter 8. What's even the point of having moral/wrathful/harmony choices if all it does is affect Agumon's evolution? it doesn't affect ANYTHING else and you can put 100% of your points into harmony but still choose wrathful because ecks dee. Also in ng+ even though you get to save lopmon and shuuji, the entire cast will still immediately think all digimon are evil because of lopmon despite nothing actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ happening to warrant this fear in ng+4. Worst translation for a digimon game periodCharacters constantly flipping genders and blatantly wrong translations are the least of the problems here. Biggest issue is that if you gave me a script and took out the names I wouldn't be able to distinguish any characters except dracmon, lopmon, and ng+ ryo. every character (in english) is written to talk exactly the same way with no variance and again, it just gets ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ oldStart bat!5. "Free time"No reason for this to exist. It functions exactly the same way as normal story segments but with a timer and sometimes the normal story segments have a hidden timer anyway6. The musicNone of the music is particularly BAD, but when they choose to use the same 3-4 songs for 99% of the game they'll make you want to blow your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brains out by the end of itOverall for gameplay? Just go play kamidori alchemy meister, castle meister, any disgaea game, or any fftactics gameOverall for story? Literally anything else

_childDocuments_.review: A quick disclaimer, I haven't beat the game yet but I feel I've played enough to form a valid opinion.It's a shame the name, Digimon Survive, created the wrong expectations and at the same time acted as a crutch. This game tries to capitalize on nostalgia and it didn't totally suck but also didn't quite hit the mark. At first, I thought that it had a great visual novel aspect and mediocre to bad gameplay and with that in mind I would have given it a recommendation, BUT like I mentioned before, its name’s sake gets in the way of the great visual novel aspect. Having watched Digimon Universe: App Monsters recently I honestly feel that Digimon Survive would have been better off as Digimon Universe: Survive or Survive: A Digimon Universe Game. This would have enabled the game to have even more free reign over the characters' monster companions whom are a bit underutilized throughout the story. Due to the slow-moving story and un-astounding gameplay, it makes it hard to recommend to anyone except for those who are Digimon fans and are familiar to basic Japanese folk lore. If you’re a visual novel fan you’ll be frustrated by the combat gameplay and if you’re here for the rpg gameplay with Digimon you may be frustrated by the slow story. And all of this doesn’t factor in the full priced tag on a game that doesn’t bother including an English dub, ouch.

At initial glance, I was a little put off by the visual novel aspect, but I found myself falling in love with it. The relationships built between the characters on each of the routes really drew me in and gave me a unique love for each character. The battle system is fun, though not super complex. I found it challenging enough to keep me engaged, but not overly difficult. There is end game content in the form of 'Mugen Recollection' battles that proved quite challenging. I love the way the story explores the relationship between human and Digimon. Playing through this game feels more like watching a Digimon anime than playing a Digimon video game. The story is like what Digimon would be like if written for adults. I loved the dark and gritty themes.
