_childDocuments_.review: I had little experience with visual novels before Digimon Survive, but so far I'm impressed. Characters are likeable and clearly based on those from the Digimon anime without coming of as clones or cheap knock-offs.The tactical battles with your Digimon start after roughly two hours. The time before that is used to establish the characters and the world. I didn't mind this, but it's probably to slow for some people. After those two hours you can battle as much as you like to level your Digimon or talk the wild ones into joining your team.There are at least 30 Digimon to find and all of them have multiple evolution lines (some of which are obtained by making choices within the story). As someone who has not watched Digimon in twenty years I thought it had a nice variety and some cool monster designs. If you're really into Digimon you might miss some of your favorites since there are apparantly more than 300 of them.In conclusion: give it a try and you might be surprised by how much you like it. I know I was.P.S. Labramon is a good doggo :-D
_childDocuments_.name: Digimon Survive

_childDocuments_.review: Consider this as a weak "not recommend", because I want to write a review but there isn't an option for "neutral". The game isn't great, but isn't bad either. It kept me playing to credit roll after all, and it was overall enjoyable. However, it is not a game that I would tell my friends "hey you should check it out".If you want to play this game, make sure you know what you are getting into: "hybrid visual novel and tactical RPG", in the official words. More specifically, I think this game has some problem on balancing the two: the first few chapters are story-heavy but less gameplay, while the "tactical RPG" part kicks in in later chapters but story becomes weaker. So if you expect engaging battles when starting the game, you will be disappointed. But if you expect visual novel first, it can keep you interested and catch you with fun battle system later on, making it an enjoyable experience.I bought the game at full price because ultimately I don't care, but I think many other reviews have a good suggestion: get it on sale. The game has good elements (e.g. visually pleasing), but overall it feels like a game worth half of its price tag only.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay. I can only recommend this if you're already a diehard fan of the series, and even then, you'll probably still get bored with the gameplay. The storyline doesn't feel fully thought-out, and most characters are one-note. This game also has the P5 issue where your bond with teammates is its own progression separate from the actual story, and you'll see development there that has no overall bearing on the plot, where characters seemingly "forget" what they've just done.The VN "gameplay" consists of searching every map for items, and picking the right dialogue choice when speaking with other characters to see a number go up, then reloading if you picked the wrong choice. There are a few different distinct routes that you arbitrarily pick based on which "flavor" of response option you pick for story dialogues, and doing the other paths involves a ton of repeat gameplay. The story splits off about halfway in, so you're going to see almost the exact same stuff for half of every playthrough. You're expected to play the game at least twice to get the "true" ending, so you have a lot of repetition on your plate, which brings me to combat.Combat (which feels like it would have been the focal point of the game) feels tacked-on and not very well thought out. There aren't enough interesting mechanics for combat to feel varied, so you're just going to repeatedly pick the guys with the highest levels, evolutions, and type advantages. There's a positioning system, but it doesn't make a big enough difference beyond encouraging you to step into a certain spot before attacking. A lot of the repetition in combat boils down to the fact that there isn't really any gameplay progression to make the RPG elements feel meaningful. Numbers go up, but your brain activity doesn't.I really wanted to like the game, and there's a lot of soul put into certain parts of it, but as a whole, don't bother unless it goes on a steep sale or you're a huge Digi-head already. I don't regret the time I put into Survive, but it could have been a good game instead of a playable game if the dev team had more time.

_childDocuments_.review: Alrighty, time to redo my review with some more hours under my belt. Might be a longer one, but I'll try to maintain a format that's easier on the eyes. With that said, this review will be entirely spoiler free as I think it's best to go into this game blind and be surprised by its writing and storytelling first-hand.  Most negative reviews here seem to be of people that weren't really sure what it was they were buying and getting into. Though the visual novel format is much more interactive and involved, taking a spin on the genre similar to games like Tokyo Dark (which I also quite liked). As such, it relies heavily on its story and atmosphere to carry you through the game. That said story is clearly written by a team passionate about Digimon and exploring new facets of the world that haven't quite been fully considered yet. The writing is captivating and convincing at every step of the way, with a constant feeling of uneasiness to break through the surface of what is otherwise a diverse cast of individually interesting characters with their own charmingly exaggerated personalities. With that said, the story displays a very clear resolve on the side of its development team in their efforts to continue to double down and dedicate their attention to Digimon's more mature general audience when compared with its monster collecting counterpart which shall not be named. The game plays out like an anime, which is a commendation rather than a criticism; it feels natural, it feels immersive, and it feels far too special to be credited as anything less than a masterpiece. Be warned that the story will not be void of  (vague spoilers as to a theme present in the story) and other more dramatic elements; though I suspect this may be a draw for many. The battle system is pretty fun, reminiscent of other tactical RPGs including Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem Three Houses, etc. Though understand that the fights will take a backseat to the story, as this is where that same aforementioned theme comes in regarding the story playing out like what you would expect form a serialized anime or written story. Battles are present when they fit in the story, and the team behind the game did not attempt to force battles down our throats more than necessary in this clearly story-based game. With that said, I think that the impact that choices you make during the game's story has on your actual combat and evolution is a fascinating mechanic in the game, as well as their more intricate elements including specific Digimon stats and equipment options. With this said, most fights aren't particularly difficult in my experience, with exceptions (or at least up until a point where there is a bit of a difficulty spike). Regardless, I don't actually have too much more to comment on in regards to the battle system in the same as while it holds its own as an engaging and enjoyable experience, it's definitely not what makes the game special. As mentioned at the start of this review, this is going to be spoiler-free and also make a consistent effort to avoiding giving any information that isn't absolutely necessary as to allow anyone to have a surprising and special first experience with this game. Though seeing as the story is what gives this game staying power and sets it apart from others, it's definitely important to mention or comment on here. The game jumps out with a bang as a precursor to the events of its main story by showcasing two very young children facing a life or death encounter, the results of which I will leave for the game story itself to reveal. At its core, Digimon Survive follows a group of student who were going on a class trip to explore an old school and learn about the culture and shrines of the town it is located in. Leading up to and during this trip, constant reports of natural disasters were present in the surrounding area, as a cause for concern throughout the class. Continuing onwards and fast forwarding briefly through the story, our main cast finds themselves in an unsettling and unnatural version of their world; a rough imitation where everything feels slightly out of place, but is familiar enough to set some panic to rest. As the group tries to get their bearings and learn about the situation they've been thrust into, the horrifying events around them quickly make it apparent that their class trip has become a lot more dangerous, and a lot more horrifying. For the sake of full transparency, I genuinely have zero complaints about this game or its content. When I say that I find it to be a masterpiece, there's no understatement to be made there. Though I did want to briefly mention what others seem to find issue in with the game.The first, of course, is that buyers hadn't expected the game to take as much of a story-focused approach and had wanted more combat out of the game. While I think that the interest in that sort of game is perfectly valid, it has never been advertised as a game so heavily reliant on its combat and quick looks at any of the game's descriptions or even their trailers (aside from the initial reveal) should also make this apparent. I find it disingenuous for others to be reviewing this game poorly due to poor diligence being paid on the reviewer's behalf to determine what it was that they were buying; no disrespect to those posting the reviews themselves.Otherwise, it seems like some people are having trouble with the game on the Steam Deck. While I don't own the device, it's worth mentioning here at least until the issues are patched out. Given the love and effort clearly put into this game, I suspect we can expect to see it resolved in due time. Hardly an issue for the majority of players though, of course.I can say with confidence that if you're at all interested in this game, it is absolutely worth a try. Whether you are an existing fan of the Digimon franchise, are curious about diving in, or are completely unfamiliar with it, this game is a stellar option for diving in and continuing to explore the world. There is something to be said about a game that very clearly knows what it needs to be, what it wants to be, and what it is. For some this may inspire complaints as to the story focus of the game, its lack of a more expansive array of Digimon, or the story-based evolution mechanics. Though for me, this brings about nothing but praise and surprise in the amount of love that's been poured into this  game by its development team and writers over the course of these long 4 years waiting.After all, it really says something when a game is special enough to really break me out of my shell to have me sit down and throw my thoughts out to the endless sea of reviews in an effort to hopefully be a deciding factor for at least one other person getting to be able to have the pleasure of experiencing this story themselves. I would consider that a win.The game was worth the wait, the game is worth your money, and the game is a worthy addition to the Digimon franchise. I have over 900 games on this account, and this is one of my favorites. I unconditionally recommend this to anyone ready for a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot has been said in other reviews about the characters and visual novel elements in Digimon Survive, but I'm going to focus specifically on the tactical gameplay in this review. Since this was the main appeal to me as a game and what I spent the majority of my gameplay time doing I'm going to talk about what I liked and didn't like in some detail here.Digimon Survive has a Final Fantasy Tactics-esque grid based combat system with teams of up to six Digimon that take turns moving attacking and moving around an arena. Digimon all get assigned a general affinity type (Vaccine>Virus>Data>Vaccine) that acts as a weapon triangle, and have unique passive abilities, skills and elemental affinities which shape their matchups against each other and allow different Digimon to shine in different scenarios. You can equip each Digimon with up to two items which either grant them useful buffs like extra heath or speed or gives them access to powerful skills that can dramatically increase the utility of a character. Additionally, the ability to evolve your digimon and "talk" to them in battle allows you to time specific powerups at key moments which can turn the tide of battle but aren't unlimited so require some planning to use effectively.You don't really need to pay a whole lot of attention to these mechanics if you just play through the game normally, because on Normal difficulty most of the standard enemy encounters you run into don't put up much of a fight. Hard mode seems to be tweaked to inflate enemy stats to the point that you can't mindlessly charge into a group of enemies and expect to win. Most people don't seem to know how to even change the game difficulty, however- it's not in the settings menu for some reason, instead you have to pick it from an optional menu that you can only pop up right before a fight begins. Even on Hard mode though, while you do need to have some decently built teams to win, the story mode really doesn't have any missions with particularly complicated strategies or particularly challenging enemies outside of boss fights. It's not like a Lunatic mode in a Fire Emblem game where you have to exploit every game mechanic to the fullest just to survive, but the game does have its moments where you do have to stop and think. It helps that training new Digimon recruits is very easy to do thanks to a forgiving XP curve with low level Digimon recruits.However, once you beat the game you get access to a NG+ exclusive dungeon gauntlet with some of the most complex and challenging battles in the entire game. Enemies will start getting combinations of extremely powerful skills that force you to not only change up your strategy constantly but approach battles as a puzzle that needs to be solved rather than a group of meatshields you can just steamroll through. You will need to start making use of mechanics like buffing/debuffing, status effects and elemental resistances to make your party members effectively respond to specific threats. Coordinating also matters because intelligently splitting up enemies and dealing with them one at a time can make seemingly impossibly tanky or overwhelmingly powerful foes suddenly become a lot more manageable. There's some real depth to just how far you can push your team and with all the gear and potential recruits you unlock in a normal playthrough you have a lot of meaningful strategic decisions to make.One of the most interesting fights in this postgame dungeon has you up against two bosses on opposite corners of a very wide open map with minions that charge you in the center. Both bosses have a skill that gradually inflates their stats every time a minion dies to the point that if you beat all the minions first the bosses become nearly impossible to hit or damage. To beat the level you need to split your party in half and figure out a way to simultaneously bypass the minion swarms, beeline directly towards both bosses at the same time, and take out the bosses before the minions that are chasing you the entire time manage to grind you down. It's a complicated tactical dance that is very easy to screw up and felt way more intense than any of the standard missions that I had to deal with in the main story.You can of course simplify all of these missions dramatically by turning the difficulty way down, but you're cheating yourself out of some great fights if you do so. However, if you're just trying to grind levels and items it's fine to just beat all the missions on Very Easy mode because the rewards/XP are all the same.One complaint I have about the combat in the game is that there is no way to buy specific items. In the story this isn't an issue but this is a huge problem in the Mugen dungeons because you will never get rewarded items for winning battles that cure status conditions or restore significant amounts of health. Confusion/freeze/paralysis is a huge problem in some of these missions and if there's a healing skill that fixes them I don't have access to it. Maybe the story mode should be less stingy about giving me these items instead of dumping me with a bunch of useless Bandages that don't do anything but take up space in my inventory.The biggest issue I have with the combat though is with enemies that will just randomly decide to constantly run away from the party while spamming guard and never trying to fight back. Not all enemies do this, it seems to be some sort of AI trigger that certain defensive Digimon are set to use and there's no way to influence an enemy to be more aggressive. This is frustrating enough in the story missions but when it happens with postgame enemies that have skills that reduce damage, attack and guard on the same turn or regenerate health (sometimes combinations of all three!) it's absolutely infuriating and can massively lengthen what would otherwise be a short and sweet encounter. The majority of missions thankfully don't have this issue (or just have maps that are too small for it to be a problem) but when it does happen it can be a demoralizing time sink.Overall, other than these relatively minor issues I still felt like the combat was very satisfying the vast majority of the time and offered a surprising amount of tactical complexity and depth. Anyone who dismisses the game as being too easy or too simplistic is really missing out. If you like the idea of tinkering around with a team of powerful monsters until you can coordinate against seemingly overwhelming odds will definitely get a lot of enjoyment out of Digimon Survive, though you definitely need to invest some time into the game and play on the harder difficulties to experience this at its fullest.

_childDocuments_.review: I can understand why some people do not like Digimon Survive. It is very different from a vast majority of media produced from the IP, in tone especially. However, that is exactly why I love it. I love the being able to coax out constantly different dialogue and finding small details in the environment. Second only to the overall plot themes, of course. This is how I want digimon plots to be explored going forward. Ideas of them being folklore creatures have been teased in the past, but hardly ever so substantiated in this way. In fact, you can argue a lot of what is going on in this game is what happened in the first digimon anime, but just given a proper tonal shift...As much as I praise it, though, remember I said I understand why people do not like it. It is a slow, dark VN for much of its run time, broken up with RTS battles and some RPG stat elements. This suits me just fine, but it is not the lighthearted creature collector with 3D turn based battles people have come to expect. (And rightfully so, considering Cyberslueth and prior.) If you like Digimon and do not mind the elements I have mentioned, genuinely give it a chance. However, do not be afraid to set a timer. It is not for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: 106.7h (100% achievement, finished the game 4 times) 50.1h Yes (1+1 achievement). Yes (29 achievements). No.Have you watched ?  is a visual novel with an adventure theme similar to that anime, albeit with a darker theme. It tells the story of several children that got transported to another world where they have to... survive. It also has a turn-based tactic element for combat with adjustable difficulty.- 4+1 endings- Adjustable difficulty for combat- It still takes a while to reach the story branching to get other endings even with the fast-forward option- Some parts of the story might feel inconsistent, redundant, or offIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 uses a blend of 2D and 3D in its visuals. Character portraits are depicted in 2D with some pre-set animations while backgrounds are made in 3D. I couldn't tell whether the Digimons are 2D or 3D though; they appear to be in a similar style to the 2D character portraits, but the shading tells me otherwise. That being said, both of them blend well with the environment.The game seems to be lacking presentation in its action scenes. Both the visual novel and tactics gameplay don't present them well - character portraits that are used for the visual novel scenes look stiff, while models used in the tactics gameplay hardly have any animations. There might be some cutscene portraits for end-game and evolution scenes, but I wish there would be more for other scenes in the early game.The story in  can be a hit or miss for some people. It gets a light horror vibe at the beginning, and it can get dark later on. Characters are in constant danger, and people are getting desperate. If you are new to the Digimon franchise, Digimons can evolve into a stronger form, and evolution feels more appreciated in this title since it can really turn the tide of the battle.Characters tend to be one-dimensional. In addition to the main story, you'll have to increase relationships with other people. However, I found them to be too fixated on one concept without going into details. While I don't mind such things, it makes the relationship part to be useless and empty. I wished that they would focus more on the main story instead.Your choices don't matter. Despite providing a lot of options to choose from throughout the game, the events will eventually converge to what the script intended. Sometimes, the story flow breaks either due to repetition or oddities, with other characters bombarding you with facts to switch your decision.The endings are decided not because of your actions, but because of your choices. The game will basically ask you to choose which ending you want to get in the middle of the game, with karma affecting the options that show up. Moreover, two out of four endings are too similar with slight differences that are based on the script. Luckily, the other endings have different stories to compensate for it, allowing you to choose which one is canon to you.The story becomes inconsistent because of the branching. A character forgets what they were talking about a few chapters ago, dialogues being served for a certain route that isn't adjusted for another route, and people switching sides in a heartbeat are things that I found odd in the story. The story was good, but these aspects clearly need to be addressed - I played two routes with these in mind and couldn't focus on the story because of it.The gameplay was divided into three parts. The first part is the visual novel section where you read the main story and make some decisions from time to time. These decisions will improve your karma, which will be the deciding factor on which ending you can choose and wild digimons' recruitment chance.The second part is the exploration section, where you need to use your in-game phone to look for objects and talk to people. The game will allow you to move between areas to scan for objects and talk to other people to increase their affinity from time to time, with a marker of which area to go to progress the story. However, it can be tiring to reexplore some areas in the first few chapters. You need to progress the game several times and items can shift around each time you do that, with some characters having optional events that can help in increasing their affinity. It can be annoying to reexplore everything just for these small changes, although luckily, it only happens at the beginning.The third part is the tactics section. You can choose which Digimons to be deployed to the fight, which can consist of other people Digimons and wild Digimons. Recruiting wild Digimons can be harder as you progress since the success rate depends on your karma; the highest Digimon stage, Mega, can have a 5-20% chance depending on your karma gain. Luckily, it's fast to level up early game, making it easier to build your party early on and stick to that instead. The issue comes if you are a completionist that wants to recruit everything - it can take hours to recruit Megas with a ~10% chance.I finished the game at 50.1h in my first playthrough, which mostly happened because I took my time and tried to recruit all Digimons that I could find. I ended up replaying the game three more times to see the rest of the endings and recruiting other wild Digimons that I didn't have. That being said, it still takes hours to reach the story branching even by speeding up all dialogues.As for the difficulty, you can adjust the difficulty for combat. I played in the easiest mode, and I could say that it was easy - I didn't even feel the danger that some of the battles pose because of this. You still need to think of some strategy later on though, and level up some Digimons whenever necessary. is a unique take on a Digimon game, presenting you with a darker story and higher stakes. Personally, I liked the dark take that the game took, but the game also has a lighter story in one of the routes if you prefer that. However, I wished that they focused on the visual novel section more instead of the tactics gameplay, and either ditched or improved the relationship system. I was more engrossed in the main story and want more, but the other sections hinders me from enjoying it further.Although some parts of the story don't sit well with me, I still enjoyed reading it. It caught my interest many times, and the intense moments always deliver. I could recommend it to people who like visual novels and don't mind the cons, but as much as I hate to say it, the current price can be to be too steep for a visual novel of this quality, so I would recommend buying it once it gets on a cheaper price. Also, don't buy it because of the turn-based tactics - you'll be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's a Visual Novel first and foremost, tactical RPG second.  If you don't like reading a lot?  You're going to wanna pass on this one.  The choices you make change a lot of things, and you need to be a bit of a completionist to get the most out of this game.  It's the story and characters that carry this game, not the combat system.  And I'm already planning my next playthrough to see how different choices change things.EDIT:  Adding a section of spoilers at the very end, for anyone who wants to complain that your choices don't matter.  They do.  They really really do.Longer version:GAMEPLAY - It's a VN, that has as much combat as you want technically speaking.  There's almost always a Free Battle available to do if you want to grind out XP or other Digimon.  But you'll spend a whole lotta time talking to people to get to the fights that matter.  I thought I'd mind it more, but honestly I actually like this.  The cast have clear nods to other series, but they do feel like their own characters.  The various Digimon are also really good characters as well.  It strikes a good balance between it's serious tones and lighter ones, to not leave you too far one way or another.  And the story gets told in and out of combat as well.STORY - As a long time Digimon fan, Digimon Adventure Tri really struck a nerve for me.  The kids were older, more mature, and capable of not only seeing what Digimon can do, but actually understanding that if a giant dinosaur fights in the streets, someone is going to get caught up in it and could get hurt or even killed.  This game really took that idea and ran with it, and I love it because of that.  Some people won't, and to them I suggest other Digimon games.  Cyber Slueth is more light hearted adventure.  This is not a kid's game.  The darker tones here hit a lot all over the spectrum.  Shock, anxiety, depression, anger, guilt, the list goes on.  And how it tackles these topics, and how you respond to them in the game matter quite a lot.COMBAT - Combat shows the signs of good design and bad design.  The worst of it is that some levels just aren't all that interesting.  Height and positioning matters, and it feels a lot like I'm playing Final Fantasy Tactics (in a good way).  The type power triangle is at play (Vaccine>Virus>Data>Vaccine) but it's never been a make or break thing for me.  Being attack from the front or sides makes a huge difference.  And auto-guarding if no action was taken feels like a streamline.The biggest issue with combat is that it feels like it was made to be accessible, and it's somewhat shallow because of it.  And while it makes perfect sense in the world to do so, encountering Free Digimon versions of your partners removes the uniqueness of it all.  You can very easily acquire doubles, and evolve them differently.  Most even have their own Evolution Tree, different or easier to access than the partner versions.  It leaves a weird taste in your mouth because of it.This is also not a catch em all type game.  Smaller roster than most people expected, and you will likely miss out on some Digimon cause of this or that reason.  But it has a bunch of fan favourites, some to bloat the roster, and just focuses a lot more on the Partner Digimon and their relationship with their human.SYSTEMS - The real treat here is the Evolution system, and I like it a lot.  It feels faithful to how Digimon do grow and evolve.  It's not level based like most games.  Partner Digimon grow and evolve based on their bonds.  They evolve to higher levels, and then revert when they run out of energy.  And as the story goes along, they unlock new evolutions.  If you make difference choices, the evolutions will change.  (Much like Tai forcing Greymon to evolve, turned him into SkullGreymon.  While their more natual bond grew and instead unlocked MetalGreymon.)  Free Digimon you befriend Persona style (by talking to them in combat, yes.) can gain levels as you use them, but require special items to Evolve.  Free digimon (no partner) don't devolve though.  Their changes are fixed, and you can choose directly what you want them to evolve into.The differences between the various evolution states is interesting though.  Their skillsets change, and while the stats will all grow, who they change into will change which stats gain more power.  Defenders get more defense, while Attackers get more Attack, etc etc.  Different stages can change their type as well.  A Defender can turn into an All-rounder or Attacker.  This means the Digimon will play differently based on how you evolve them.  Doubly so for Partner Digimon who evolve in combat each time.  You may want or need skills from the Rookie or Champion stages, and once per turn you can freely swap between them.  The Champion level might have a type advantage, but the Ultimate might have more move speed.  There's also a SP cost for evolution so you don't want to just evolve and forget.  Though the cost is low, and I haven't had any real issues unless I spam out high SP cost attacks on a Digimon with lower amounts.  Devolving lets them regen, and items are picked up all the time if you look for them.To get all the items, attacks, specific evolutions, you also need to explore EVERYTHING.  It's a fight of tedium in some cases, as things will unlock in an area you just cleared out right after talking to someone.  This is how I got most of my items, and got into most of my battles.  For some this is just going to be tedious amounts of busywork, and you'd be right.  But there's also varoius rewards hidden behind the tedium.  The game does reward you for doing it all.  And there's a ton of character development and world lore packed in here that I found myself wanting to know more about.  The choices I've made also determined how the relationships I've been fostering ended up turning out.  Talking to the right people at the right time will get you items or affaction rating.ART - Not much to say here.  I just really like it.  The sprites are laid out in 3D space and you can tell if people are together or spread, even in the same area.  And there's enough variance to tell emotional changes easily, and sometimes subtly.  It's really nice.CONS - As for real problems?  I couldn't get my controller to work at all.  And using the mouse is not very good either.  The hit detection on the boxes really suck.  I hunted down the keyboard controls and started using them.  It was annoyingly hard to find the info, should have been the default until controller input was found.  But to give credit where credit is due, you can play this game easily with one hand on keyboard.  Left me with the ability to eat foods and such without stopping.Summary:  It's a darker and more mature game.  The story is it's focus, and it doesn't hide this.  Combat is a little shallow, but it's fun.  I think a couple replays will have value if you stuck to one way through the game's story.  Taking other paths or getting items you missed on the way will add more value.  If you hate VNs or want a lighter story, you might wanna go elsewhere.  But this is a good take on Digimon, and I'm honestly loving this game.EDIT:  As I said up top.  Adding a section here that is SPOILERS for people who aren't sure what choices actually change.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay time for an honest review.+ Story is amazing, never expected a digimon title game to actually hook me into the story (I'm looking at you Cyber Sleuth).+ Art and visual are by far the best part of this game, the 3d background that shifts around with the 2d characters are executed seamlessly.+ Combat difficulty can be lowered if you're mostly interested in the story, meaning you don't have to dedicate your game time to only farming.- The amount of playable digimons are really, really limited. A lot if not most recruitable digimons end up evolving to a similar evolution line to one another.- Translations, sometimes you'll find a few mistakes and it wouldnt ruin the experience, but one that I've found involved a certain event where a character obtains their ultimate evolution line, but then again, digimon titles are known for their mistranslation and bad QC.- Combat is fine at best, it feels bland and takes a while to clear. Auto battle exists to help solve the latter issue. - It's 70% VN, you'll be spending most of your time conversing with characters, exploring areas, and do a lot (and I have to emphasize this) of reading. This may not be everyone's cup of tea, so do be warned what you're getting into.Overall its a very enjoyable standalone digimon title game if you're looking for a darker story with your favorite digimon character that fleshes them out more than just mascots. Also make sure to give Lopmon headpats, poor guy needs it.

_childDocuments_.review: I long for the days when they are going to do proper sequel or remaster of original Digimon World, when i saw trailer for Digimon Survive, i was actually pretty hyped about initial premise a tactics based digimon game. Now what most ppl might already know or don't know is that this game is roughly ~70-65% visual novel and rest is tactics battle, so going in you have to be okay with VN elements, if you aren't that might take lot away from your game experience unless you find the combat very redeeming. - Game actually offers lot bang for the buck, being roughly ~25h long with the moral path (There are multiple endings, true ending being only accessable with 2nd playthrough in NG+) - The 2D Assets are actually pretty neat and look good. Game doesn't suffer from any optimization issues, loads up fast and FPS is solid, however not many options to adjust graphics outside of VSYNC and resolution- Some of the cast can be rather annoying at times and keep going on mindless tantrums out of the sudden in very whimsical manner... - OST is too small, too few tracks, which makes lot of BG music play on the background 80% of the game in multiple locations- For a Visual novel game its not a masterpiece story or anything, rather predictable one if you have seen a single digimon series in the past. - For non-VN fans i wish there would've been more battle stuff and more VN content locked away for optional stuff than mainstory line dialogue, which at times felt like beating a dead horse by repeating same fears and problems the same characters mentioned trillion times already. Ultimately Digimon survive is a decent game, however it could've been lot better if it had more budget to work on different elements and other aspects that could improve QoL like sound design. I Believe a sequel game done in similar manner could perform well if it did overhaul thing or two.

_childDocuments_.review: A neat concept so I decided to check it out since I enjoy tactical games and the classic Digimon World series (even with all their flaws). I can talk at length about how much I enjoy Front Mission, Disgaea, Tactics Ogre Let Us Cling Together, Fire Emblem 6-9, and the more modern Troubleshooter: Abandoned Children. Digimon World openly leans heavily on Utawarerumono influences. However, Utawarerumono and subsequently Digimon Survive both rely heavily on their visual novel segments compared to these other games which has a much more detailed combat mechanics and character building focus. If the VN segments were compelling to me, I could enjoy it, but the story is very strongly targeted towards young people. I don't enjoy this, the characters are annoying and uninteresting to me. If you're a high school boy and interested in Digimon, visual novels, and tactical games, I recommend this. If not, play something else, I think. A thumbs up seems too generous but a thumbs down seems too harsh, because I believe the target demographic that would love this game, but the game falls short elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Took 84 hours to 100% this game (completing all 4 story routes and collecting all 117 Digimon)I would recommend this to two types of people:- People who love Digimon, because this game really captures the spirit of Digimon.- People who love visual novels, even if you’re unfamiliar with Digimon. The story is essentially "the beginning" of Digimon (the opening sequence takes place in 1970 for reference) and throughout the game they aren’t even called Digimon since they aren’t defined as a species yet, except in one of the four endingsThe most important thing to note about the plot is the lack of evolved partner Digimon during the written story. There are many instances where you might think, "this could have easily been prevented if they evolved here." Both the humans and Digimon have no idea how evolution works. Evolution just sort of happens randomly, even if the gameplay suggests otherwise. There are no Digivices or in-universe documentation on how to evolve at a moment's notice.I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone expecting a serious SRPG. The important fights can feel fun, but are way more about eye candy than actual gameplayDigimon Survive is a visual novel with dark horror elements mixed in, the writing is genuinely 10/10 for me. It’s hard to praise the half-baked SRPG gameplay elements. If there were a "baby's first Final Fantasy Tactics" this would be the baby's first version of baby's first Final Fantasy Tactics. I played the entire game on Hard mode and only had a single game over. I didn’t need to grind either; I just retried and won. Monster recruiting is a pain, in my opinion extremely unfun, and not very well thought out—you’re better off using a guide. Also, evolve each partner Digimon once to each of their new forms to ensure they’re added to your field guide. Garurumon and Kyubimon are examples you can easily missVisually, the game is beautiful. I love the character art during the story, and even though the gameplay is pretty bland, the battle sprites are nice. They aren’t super animated, but they’re fun to look at and represent each Digimon wellThe soundtrack is super killer, I’ll be listening to it for years. My favorite track is the evolution theme, which shares a common motif with a few other tracksYou need to play the game at least four times to 100% it. It took me 84 hours from selecting "New Game" to finishing the fourth ending. This is one of those games you 100% once and never touch again

_childDocuments_.review: I am really disappointed. I've been a Digimon fan all my life but this really feels like a low quality game right from the start. The decent voice acting stands out in a bad way when paired with 2D images and low quality animations, it really feels like they planned for it to be better, but ran low on time and resources. The characters all come across as almost bland replicas from the Digimon Adventure series and Digimon Tamers Series, there is very little nostalgia for fans of the franchise. Admittedly, I just began skipping through the dialogue at points, so there's a possibility that I just missed it, but with that being said, I'm pretty certain that they don't even use the word Digimon, throughout the entire story. Even though, they make direct references to the 8 kids and their partner Digimon from the Adventure series.Absolutely not an A-list game though, this is a 29.99 game at absolute best so far.**After "completion"Yeah.... it really doesn't get any better, and anyone praising the "dark" themes, seems to be acting like we didn't already cover the majority of these concepts back in the 3rd season of the anime. This was nothing new and I would say is even pretty close to just being a bad copy of the Digimon Tamers Anime.I honestly don't know what "twist" they're asking people not to spoil, but at no point during the entire novel, (and no, I won't call it a visual novel, because that would imply that there's more than flash game level graphics) was I even remotely surprised.I haven't even touched on the technical flaws behind this game either, from the bad translations, to the mechanics required for recruiting Digimon to your team, the bad PC port, the flash level animation, the use of VERY repetitive single sound bytes, the lack of any need for complicated JRPG mechanics because a toddler could stroll his way through the fights. LMAO as a matter of fact! There is actually an Auto Battle feature!  You can literally have the game complete the battles for you, even specifying whether it should focus on Attack, Defensive, Evolution, whatever your fight style, just click and walk away, then come back and make some more nonsensical dialogue options.If you wanna read Digimon, go grab the manga, it'll cost you less and you're honestly getting the same experience. Unless you speak Japanese, then you might actually find some enjoyment here, as the voice actors do sound like they're trying their best.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of visual novels and strategy RPGs, this game doesn't do a particularly good job of either. I enjoyed the ending I got , but it was an absolute slog to get there. The game angles for a little bit of a horror vibe, but I don't think it quite goes far enough. The "strategy" aspect is really quite flimsy, with every digimon only having a basic physical attack move and ONE-yes ONE- other move that could be anything from a heal to a buff to a more powerful attack. You can expand this with equipment, but that's also very limited, with there only being two equipment slots per digimon; if you give a digimon a new move, you sacrifice giving it further stat boosting equipment.I can't speak on this authoritatively, but the translation also felt dodgy, with a few chapters in particular having characters accidentally misgendering each other all over the place. I can't help but wonder what else was lost along the way, you know?MAYBE pick this one up on sale and if you're already a digimon fan. It was a treat as a fan of Tamers from way back to see Renamon tearing things up, but it wasn't worth the well over half the run time of the game where I kept playing out of sheer stubbornness.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really hard to define this game at least in relation to Digimon Cyber Sleuth, which was the only digimon game I've played recently and thoroughly enjoyed (the original, Hacker's Memory not so much). This one feels much more like a visual novel as there is far more focus on story and characters, with tactical gameplay sections in between long stretches of narrative. I found the story far more enjoyable this time around as the writing and inclusion of many digimon as their own characters made it much easier to get invested. Fans of the original Digimon anime will likely love the story as well. The only objective flaw I found was the translation, while far better than Cyber Sleuth's, had some confusion with digimon references that made some of the middle parts of the story a bit immersion breaking. It will also feel slow paced; you won't get the full story until the second playthrough at the earliest. The story branching was actually bold and not what I was expecting. My first playthrough went to some dark places, and I imagine it could have gotten a lot worse had I ignored the affinity of each character.While I preferred the battle system of Cyber Sleuth, I really liked the story and characters of this title. Here's hoping one day they'll get the best of both worlds in a digimon game one day.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been fantastic so far! The story has been dark and compelling and I found myself loving each of the characters (besides one who, in all fairness, seems to be going through some ♥♥♥♥ at home). If you’re a fan of the digimon anime and the story Digimon Adventure and Digimon Tamers delivered, you won’t be disappointed. I would even recommend this game if you have a passing interest in digimon, as the themes and story highlight what digimon is all about. There were a lot of scenes that, while I expected some scenarios to turn out the way they did, still left me with butterflies in my stomach waiting for it to happen. I grew to care about the characters and really want to see them, and their relationships with each other, well, survive.The children and their partners are great together. A problem I’ve had with digimon games previously is that you don’t really care about the digimon you have in your party. You just collect a bunch of monsters and switch them out for whatever is stronger or cooler looking. There’s no emotional attachment. In cyber sleuth, your first digimon is also just a slot in your army that sooner or later gets replaced. But In Survive, there’s a huge emphasis on the relationships between the tamer and digimon. I find myself really appreciating the moments where the protagonist or one of the other kids are confused and uncertain and their partner is there to comfort and support them. I know there are a lot of people upset with the amount of dialogue, but it’s a visual novel first and foremost. Its a text adventure with an emphasis on story and exploration first and combat second. That being said, for the combat playing second fiddle, it actually uses a really solid system that focuses on positioning and planning ahead. It’s a lot of fun and reminiscent of Devil Survivors, Fire Emblem, and Shin Megami Tensei. I do find myself wishing there was more of it throughout the adventure.  Though free battle is unlocked eventually, which allows you to battle whenever you want as many times as you want, letting you scratch that trpg itch. Although, there have been moments where a story sequence is interrupted by combat and I really just wanna get back into the drama that was just taking place. Which, if anything, shows how good the story is. Hopefully, future Digimon games will expand on this combat system further as I’ve really enjoyed it.  I was worried that the long wait raised my expectations too high, but the game has delivered an experience that I’m wholeheartedly enjoying.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, after what i saw in this game i am legit surprised it is rated 12+. _childDocuments_.review: I haven't played much of the steam version, but I did complete a playthrough of the switch version, so the review will be based more on that. Minor spoilers ahead but I will try to keep it to a minimum.Gameplay: First of all,  if you really enjoyed games like Cyber Sleuth then this might not be for you. What you are getting is a Visual Novel with some strategy type combat. A little bit of thought may be required during these fights but most of the time you can just turn your brain off, go full on child mode and look at all the cool evolutions or something. Now for the hot take: this is actually good for the game. As I mentioned the game is a visual novel and should be approached as such. That is its main appeal and having the combat be good could work against it, as people would just skip everything to play it.  During the story you will be presented with certain options, either tilting you towards an alignment or giving you a chance to improve your relation with some of the characters. The choices wont really matter until you reach the mid-late game, where depending on that you can follow a different path, changing the story significantly. Therefore the game will be the same for about 60-70% of the story for a few paths, except for the true ending one, and different for the last bit. Once you finish the game once you unlock the new game+ option, making the game even more of a breeze while unlocking a certain optional combat area which may challenge you a bit. But you are also able to skip through most parts of the story, so while you may expect your first playthrough to take about 30 hours subsequent ones may be half that.Story: This has to be my favorite story in a Digimon game, no matter how low of a bar that is to set. At moments it feels like a darker retelling of the original adventure and long-time series fans will definitely spot many nostalgic tidbits and references. The premise is simple: you get isekaid to another world and try to return home, learning more about that world in the process. Where the story shines is how it takes the characters in consideration regarding to this fact. They are all children and the world is hostile. This alone makes certain exaggerated character moments work pretty well and helps quite a bit with the development of those characters. Some of them are, of course, better written than the others but I did like most of them. The story is darker than most Digimon games, with some rather shocking moments that feel well paced out. Kind of. The story itself is not that dark, its just that there are some heavy moments and themes, while the setting is grimmer than usual. Some chapters felt like they were dragging on more than needed, but that may have been because of me grinding for no reason at all. Despite that It still remains a Digimon game, with the kids and their partners complementing each other and the growth of one reflects on the other. And this is what the game does best: the Digimon feel more fleshed out and not just a yes-man to their respective tamers.Visuals/Sound: I love the art direction they went for with this game. The environments look great and each area feels at least a bit unique, while the characters models look great. honestly just looking at the screenshots on this page should give you a good idea of what to expect visually and whether you like it or not. The voice acting is great and I really like the music too, both of which seem to be a great fit for the story told.Final Verdict: The game is a great experience for long time Digimon fans, as long as they don't hate visual novels. It is not for everyone, but it is an amazing option for its target audience. If you like Digimon and VNs then give it a try. If you do not like either or both of these then maybe skip this one.Objective rating: 7/10Subjective rating: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: No crashes or errors here.Cool game. Never played a VN before, but I guess it's kind of like watching a long anime movie. _childDocuments_.review: Digimon Survive is a game I had been looking forward to for the better part of 3 years now, having to wait time and time again due to a troubled development cycle. As someone who enjoys visual novels, loves Digimon, and absolutely adores turn based strategy RPGs, I was really hoping for an absolute slam dunk of a title. The reality is that, while this game is worth picking up if it looks interesting to you, it's nothing truly innovative or special in any significant way.- Surprisingly good writing (and given how this game is primarily a visual novel, I'm grateful this is the case)- A good length for the game (about 20-30 hours for a first playthrough) with a decent amount of replay value to see the other runs- Good variety of Digimon- Great art style- A disappointingly high number of typos, misgenderings, and grammatical mistakes- 3:1 ratio of visual novel to strategy RPG- the combat is very simple (not necessarily bad, but I personally was hoping for something more complex and engaging)- Recruiting free Digimon (Digimon without a specific character attached to them) is a hassle. It's almost identical to Persona 5's recruitment of the different personas, but the answers feel random, there's only a handful of questions, and even if you do pass the threshold to ask them to join you, they have an abysmally low percentage chance to join for seemingly no reason. This would be a bigger grievance if your roster wasn't mostly tamer Digimon anyway- Exceedingly long tutorial- There's really only 1 choice that has any significant impact on the game- Replaying the game to view other endings can be really, really tedious, even with auto battle and skipping seen dialog- Minor mechanics spoiler - Minor story spoiler - Major story spoiler All in all, I enjoyed the game enough to 100%, even if I was fairly checked out after getting through the game once. I'd say the promotional material is honest about what the game is, and your feelings of deciding if this game is worth playing or not can accurately be decided based on it.

_childDocuments_.review: A well-appreciated gift for old-time Digimon fans.Important note: This game is a Visual Novel first and a Tactical RPG second, you'll spend more hours engaging with the story than doing actual combat, the combat part is good enough for me, but what I do really enjoy is the story and I think it is what truly matters for a VN/TRPG game like this.My experience:I enjoyed this game, it has a good enough combat system for me, a great story, a very beautiful music, and it provides a sense of nostalgia for longtime Digimon Adventure fans like me, so it is an overall positive experience for me.Overall:- Combat 8/10- Story 9/10- Nostalgia 10/10- Miyuki's Song 100/10Conclusion: 9/10 would recommend this game, especially for longtime Digimon fans who are familiar with the Digimon Adventure series (or any other Digimon series) 👍

_childDocuments_.review: The story is excellent (if slow to pick up - YMMV though) and the characters are all portrayed realistically. The tone this entry has is exactly the kind of tone I've been wanting from a Digimon game since the Tamers TV show a couple of decades ago. That alone makes this game worth purchasing, if only when it's on sale.That said, it's clear that most of the budget/focus went to developing the story and world-building. If you've ever finished the Devil Survivor games (especially Overclocked) then Survive's gameplay will feel like a joke in comparison (though I admit this comparison is a bit harsh - Overclocked is a masterpiece in general, not just in the scope of SRPGs) except maybe in the final couple of chapters. Simply put, there isn't much depth to the mechanics of this game and that makes it simply okay to play instead of great or even good.The game also has a glaring problem in how it integrates the gameplay and story together. Over the course of the game, you are given the option to participate in free battles to get more Digimon, but their involvement within the actual story is outright nonexistent. That's fine but it's totally jarring to be able to assign other units to battle when Takuma (the player character) is alone with his buddy Agumon, and we're told no other help is available. Granted, this sort of encounter is kept to a minimum so it's not like it ruined the rest of the game for me. Still, I feel as though this could have been handled differently.Definitely get this game if it's on sale if you're a Digimon fan.

_childDocuments_.review: I consider it an 8.3/10. It has great aspects of story telling and I really loved the mature/dark tone that they presented. I know that it is a visual novel with some gameplay mechanics but from what little experience I have with the genre (only really played a fate stay night VN) this 30-40 hrs of story telling feel weak. Besides this degradation of quality for the time played I think it has what it needs to build and amazing sequel

_childDocuments_.review: One of the major aspects of this game is its story and most gameplay elements are tied to it, albeit in a hit or miss way at times. A majority of the runtime of this game is attributed to you reading story dialouge and making choices. Without any spoilers and with the context that I've fully played through one route of the game I actually found the overarching plot to be fairly engaging in the choices I made (flavor dialogue allowed for deeper characterization at times) and fairly interesting as a lot of mystery and tension loomed throughout the story until a certain point before the story locks you into a route based on the choices you have made. After the story branches into its separate routes the one I played seemed to get a lot of answers for the major mysteries of the plot that was set-up; however, the plot's narrative seemed too quick and focused on two characters while leaving everyone seemingly in the background. I'm not sure if this is true in the other routes as well but at least the ending was ok, it tied up the story well without any major plot issues but most of the main characters felt so rushed in their individual arcs the ending felt pretty anticlimatic to said arcs. Now although I actually think the main story to the game is great the individual plot you play through every chapter (part) can feel as though it drags on in some places; however I feel this doesn't detract from the pacing of the story until near the end of the game. This next part of the section contains spoilers!  Overall the story is a pretty great mystery. It has some interesting and profound themes dealing with more intimate human experiences and trauma.  This game is a visual novel and a pretty fun Turn-based strategy game on top of that. I've seen some people say this game is similar to Fire-Emblem or X-com but honestly it's kind of it's own thing within the genre. Many of the gameplay elements this game has is similar to the  games in terms of actual combat; however this game as a TBS emphasizes the positions of your Digimon and how you plan for their attack or defense against enemies given they only have one action in a single turn phase. I played this game on the hardest difficulty the first time and the only two problems I had for actual combat were that animations for moving take too long and that generally the late-game maps were far too large allowing for enemies to stall out even normal battles for far too many turn phases and minutes spent. Now with that being said about the actual combat; the preparation and numbers for combat in this game is by far one of the worst balancing issues for any RPG I have seen since Elden Ring or FE3H Maddening Difficulty. There are no shops in this game, meaning that your items are replenished through limited exploration and a majority of the time normal battles that start to give diminishing gains while still taking an egregious amount of time to complete late game. There is an affinity system in this game where raising affinity with a particular character allows their partner digimon to digivolve; however the free time given in this game doesn't allow for affinity to be raised for their partners to evolve on par with Agumon so most of the mid-story to endgame they will likely be benched or punching above their weight in fights. A lot of the time your units on story maps are force deployed meaning that if you don't keep everyone an even level there are some fights where 1/3 of your deployed party will get rolled pretty fast, which isn't bad considering there are only a few maps you can fail from a unit dying in a battle other than Agumon. This is fairly balanced out by being able to recruit Digimon in this game. The only issue with party preparation is that Stat boosters and evolution items are few and far between so experimenting with different builds or a different party composition that the one you've started with recruited Digimon or beefed up partner Digimon is very punishing if it doesn't quite turn out the way you wanted to, especially when it comes to evolution items. Because some parts of gameplay are tied with the story there is some ludonarrative dissonance from several instances where your gang of survivors is under time pressure but in gameplay you can explore leisurely and wander around to gather items and even sometimes do free battles with Humans or Digimon absent from the group at that moment in time. The gameplay at it's core is pretty fun as a TBS and can even be relaxing at times but due to the tediousness of balance numbers and the restrictions placed on party composition the gameplay can get repetitive especially towards the late-game and on repeat playthroughs. (Though there's potential for lots of challenge runs)  There isn't much to say about this game graphically due to it mainly being a visual novel. The sprites look clean and the animations are pretty smooth. There aren't any anime cutscenes or hardly any animations/special cutscenes for really big moments a la Danganronpa, so some big moments can feel a bit drained of energy when there are only certain sprites for characters to emote instead of a big cutscene. The backgrounds are nice and the areas are pretty cool run-down locations of common settings like amusement parks or cities which creates a gravitas atmosphere. Though (probably due to budget) set-pieces are used incredibly often and it can be a bit jarring. The gameplay presentation works and is completely functional; but, the sprites for each Digimon are all Chibi which is fine but the scale and power of a digimon relative to size is somewhat odd since they all are the same size on the battlefield. The sprites themselves are a bit inconsistent with some Digimon like Floramon looking wonderful but others like Mermaimon looking somewhat stiff. The hud in battle is functional if not looking a bit boring and the phone UI is very pleasing aesthetically to look at. The soundtrack is generally great.The presentation for this game works overall and is functional but has some major aspects missing for bigger story and gameplay moments which makes said moments not as satisfying as they need to be. I personally loved this game and see myself playing more! Objectively I think it's great with it's main sticking points being its intriguing story and characters along with TBS gameplay that isn't incredibely deep but is still fun to play. Its only drawbacks are mainly balance issues in gameplay and some narrative structure issues that may pull players out of the story. I generally would recommend this game to anyone who loves Digimon or visual novels, you'll have a great time! I recommend that you play something like X-Com or Fire Emblem instead for deeper gameplay if that's what you seek.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about the game and when it comes down to it; this game surpasses any Pokemon game that has been released thus far. The music is amazing, 10 out of 10. The music is composed so well that you don't ever get tired of hearing it or a different rendition of it.I really hope they win some sort of award for it.The story is great, I won't spoil anything, so I'll just leave it at that. But, boy...was that prologue a little too long though. And one of the endings I got was a little meh, I haven't gotten the other endings yet. But hopefully they'll be a little better than the one I got.A lot of the characters are hard to like in the beginning, but by the end, you become pretty attached to them, even the ones you thought were annoying and would never like.I love, that your choices affect people and outcomes, I've been waiting for a Digimon game like this for a long time.Overall the game is great and worth buying, a solid 8 out of 10.But that isn't to say that it doesn't have down sides, which is why it isn't a full 10 for me.The biggest issue for me was the English dialogue/translations.Please, Bandai, hire competent English writers and English/Japanese translators. HECK, I will volunteer to check your games for any grammar mistakes and send you the corrections. No payment needed. Seeing a Digimon being referenced as a "He" one minute, and the next "She". Or reading sentences that made little to no sense, took away from the experience for me.That was probably the worst thing about this game.A few other things that bothered me:I wish they had full voice acting in the game. It was little jarring when the characters be fully voiced one minute and in the next scene, I would just see their mouth moving and see the text. Expecting to hear them talking, only to realize it was a part that was not voice acted.The illustrations and facial expressions definitely could have had more variety throughout the game. One minute someone would have a good illustration of the them freaking out, showing the insanity/horror/etc that they were faced with. But then in another epic scene, another character would look like they weren't phased by anything that was happening to them or around them. When they should have been.In the end though. I don't regret toughing out the overtly long prologue, and some of the most terrible translation errors I've ever seen in a game. The music was worth it and so where the characters. All of which I've come love, despite illustration flaws.And I highly suggest you don't let the flaws of the game deter you from what is a pretty good game.And please go back and tweak your game Bandai, this game is a diamond that needs to shine.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a visual novel ashamed to be associated with Digimon.This is NO modern Digimon game. If you are looking for something comparable to Cyber Sleuth, this is not it. Nor is this the next step forward it has been advertised as. Its playtime mainly consists of distracting you with generic anime characters who wear their personality in their hairstyles. Digimon are not the focus and "Survive" could only be referring to the tolerance modern Digimon fans are allotting this game.Survive consists of the usual point and click gimmicks that exist in most shovelware vn's. The main one being elements of paranormal mysteries to stretch "gameplay". It's as if you were actually investigating something that the game will just explain to you once you've exhausted all dialogue. If you actually choose to read the entirety of dialogue presented at the start (excluding the tutorial) it will be beyond an hour before you yourself are actually battling with Digimon. If you are looking for an immersive Digimon GAME, this is not it. This is a vn broken up with anime quality cutscenes that consist of static poorly animated Digimon you're intended to recognize.Now there are two things I cannot comment on confidently: The complexity of combat and the quality of the entire story. I didn't stick around long enough for either. In battle the Digimon sprites are hideous. They are animated to bob around but it's stiff and distracting so it only takes away from the experience. I imagine their low quality and limited animation is only to implement new Digimon later, as sprites are A LOT easier to make. There is a tactics/xcom battle system, but there are many better examples that take full advantage of the genre. This is just a generic version of that. BUT instead of fireball, you launch "Pepper Breath" making it a Digimon tactics game. I understand this game went through delays, but poor production is not an excuse. Right down to the UI it is obvious that polish was not a concern. I know this is a cheap critique, but yes it is a phone quality game. A bulk of the intro is the main character looking through and accessing his phone. The cast of characters are vapid and will no doubt go through various Jeri level horrors that somehow make the game and themselves more "interesting". Unfortunately there is no subtlety or nuance so the whole thing feels like a re-skinned Danganronpa with Digimon. Horror is always around the corner so there's no genuine shock or intensity, just going through the motions of what's intended to be an unsettling RPG. There are sim and morality elements. So if the ensemble cast and pre-scripted Digimon are interesting to you, that would be something to enjoy, I guess?If you just have to see Digimon on screen I really recommend exploring prior titles. By supporting this product you are only guaranteeing that these low effort "games" will continue to be made. If you have any familiarity with VN's you would know that they have become the bread and butter of independent game developers. Many that could put aspects of this game to shame. But then again it's month 1 edition. Maybe by month 2 it will be a brand new game that consists of more than exhausting NPC dialogue and clicking random points on a panoramic JPEG.The only reason I wrote this review is because I'm noticing a lot of the positive reviewers are approaching the consumer as the problem. This game is cheap. It is written on the wall. Do not feel ashamed for not enjoying VN's. It is not even great for a VN, it is adequate AT BEST. The cutscenes consist of anime production value. Then return to static character PNGs and poorly animated Digimon sprites. It leaves the whole experience disorienting. Clicking through JPEGs and anime cutscenes does not a good game make.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. I like that it's a visual novel but the pacing is just way too slow. I'm 26 hours into my first playthrough and I still haven't reached an ending yet. I've learnt that you need to play new game+ after your first playthrough to get the true ending...I just don't think I have the patience to get through the rest of this first playthrough and then do a second one after that. I really dislike it when stories in visual novels drag on for too long and this one does. I just find myself not caring what happens anymore. I keep trying to push through it but I also just want the story to end already so I can say I finished it. Some of the characters are just down right unlikable. So much so I found myself feeling glad when something bad happened to them. The combat part isn't fun for me, I just use auto battle. I wouldn't pay full price for this game. if you want to try it get it on sale. As for the positives. The art is really beautiful and I like the music too. I found the first few hours of the game really interesting and it was my favourite part about it. I like how the story is similar to the first anime. I loved that anime as a kid and it's what got me into Digimon in the first place.I don't know if I will end up finishing it...at the moment I feel like sinking so many hours into it just isn't worth it. There are times when the story feels like it's not progressing and just keeps going around in circles. It also feels like your choices don't matter. I just don't know what the point is anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts with a young lad and gal running through a fog filled forest with something in the shadows chasing after them. Just when they think the children are about to be caught a couple of mysterious creatures suddenly jump to their rescue. This is where you will go over the basics of the game, how to move, using the camera, attacking your enemy etcetera. After a short battle, where you take control of the mysterious creatures against a powerful enemy the girl is pulled in to the shadows as she helps the young boy who is pulled in to a nearby portal, after this tutorial the game will start. After the tutorial, is the Prologue where you find yourself at school where some of the members will be heading out on a camping trip to visit some ruins. It’s a typical morning, when over the news they hear about landslides caused by an earthquake nearby to the ruins they plan on visiting. The usual cautions have been urged by the local fire and police departments however, the school trip is still to go ahead. You will interact with a host of different characters such as Takuma, Aoi, Minoru, Saki, Ryo, Shuuji, Professor and more. At times you will have to make decisions which may not be liked by one character or more. They’ll be times when you will not only be able to interact with characters but with your surroundings. Anything of potential interest is indicated by a magnifying glass, although those characters which have a Red Exclamation Mark indicates that they have some important story information. Sometimes there will be things which are hidden but using your smartphone’s camera will help bring them in to view. These could be items, clues or they could reveal some creature hiding out in the shadows or undergrowth. How you respond with other characters will have an effect on your Affinity with them. Your affinity with the characters will have an influence on the combat field through the Battle Backup, this will give you some sort of backup such as replenish some of their health. You will gain different results depending on if you decide to treat everyone similarly or whether you just build your affinity with one person. As you progress through the story each of the main characters will gain a friend, a Digimon monster who will fight besides them. Although, it will take time for some of them to trust each other but once they do then your new friend will evolve in to a new monster. The Digimon they can evolve in to multiple different types of monsters, all of which can be used in battle when require as long as you have the necessary resources (Skill Points). This will increase your Digimon’s abilities and will also change their skills which is great if your current monsters' abilities and skills aren’t cutting the mustard.  The combat field is divided in to square tiles over varying terrains with each tile also consisting of different heights which can come in handy for getting an advantage over your enemy attackers. Another way to get an advantage over your enemy is to attack from behind or their flank, this can inflict greater damage than a frontal attack.  At the start of each combat, you will be able to choose which of the current crop of Digimon's will you send to the combat field. Depending on the situation you’ll be able to send a number of your monsters to the battle field. You can place the monsters on the yellow tiles which are found somewhere on the combat map. Each of the Digimon’s have their own class types some are all-rounders, others more for attack or defense. Each character and enemy will take it in turns moving and carrying out an action such as Move, Attack, Item, Evolution and Talk. Selecting to move will allow you to move around the field, it is determined by highlighting of the tiles in blue. Attacking will allow you to attack an enemy within its range, this will determine on the Digimon and their attack and abilities (will use Skill points for abilities). Selecting an attack will highlight the tiles in orange to detail the attack area for said attack or ability. Item will allow you to use an item from your inventory, Evolution lets you evolve a Digimon if you have enough Skill Points.  The option Talk lets you talk to others in your group or the enemy. When you talk to an enemy, they will ask you three questions, depending on the answers you give them will determine if they’ll trust you and in doing so, they will offer you two choices, to either take an item or to join your group. However, they won’t always join you and may run from the battlefield instead, which looking on the brightside of things is one less monster to fight. Talking to one of your friends will give them encouragement giving them Rally Effects which will last for a few rounds of battle although use it wisely as a character can only use this feature once per battle. Defeating all enemies will result in a Win, this will increase your Digimon’s stats in the following, Max Health Points, Max Skill Points, Physical Attack and Defence, Skill Point Attack and Defence and Speed. You may also gain some other Rewards which will be stored in your inventory. While you will find battles as you progress through the story, you will unlock Free Battle which you can find on the World Map after unlocking Exploration. Free Battles let you gain items and be able to recruit new monsters to your group. Exploration will unlock new areas around your current location such as at the school. School corridors, gym, cafeteria will become unlocked allowing you to visit each of these areas and checking for clues or to chat with anyone in an area. As you visit these areas new ones will become available each time furthering the story. There is quite a lot of chat in the game so be prepared for that, you don’t do any walking from one place to another like in your typical RGP games. The graphics are great and so far, I’ve enjoyed the story and I’ve only had a couple small problems in my time playing the game. The first of my problems was when using my Xbox One Wireless Gamepad, you use the LB/RB buttons to move from one target to another when scanning an area for clues and chatting to others. However, I was unable to move to the next target off screen to the left no matter what I did using my gamepad. In the end I decided to play using keyboard and mouse and with no troubles. The second problem I had was the game would freeze for a good ten seconds or so, however, there has been some updates since this happened and I haven’t had it freeze on me for a while so fingers crossed this has been sorted. Steam Settings - Display, Antialiasing, V-Sync, Shadow Quality, Field Depth, Bloom, Aspect Ratio/Resolution, Keyboard and Gamepad. Sound - Background Music, Sound Effects and Voice Volume Sliders. Dialog - Dialog Skipping, Post-Decision Dialog Skipping, Text Speed, Window Transparency. Positives  + Good story + Nice graphics + Has achievements + Has cards Negatives  - Controller scanning issue to next screen over - Froze on me a few times Recruit new friends to help you against dangerous monsters as you try to survive in a mysterious new world while trying to finding a way home in the visual novel, tactical turn-based combat game, Digimon Survive. 8/10
