_childDocuments_.review: Fun puzzle-platformer that takes inspiration from games like Another World, Flashback and Prince of Persia - for those uninitiated, that means the controls in this game are intentionally clunky for nostalgic reasons (I already see the complaints in the reviews, even though it's supposed to be that way). However, I have to say that this game does not feel exactly like a cinematic platformer in terms of cutscenes and how the momentum was executed - the running jump is fixed and much easier to do than in any of those classics (for better or worse, depending on your preference). That said, not a bad game, just not what I expected. I think the humor is done very well, there are many creative and unexpected ways to die, if you into that.This is one of those games where you will die a lot, which is actually something that cinematic platformer genre is known for (the beginner traps). You will often find yourself in a situation where the solution is not obvious right away, so you kinda have to test the waters, see which path does not lead to your demise. Perhaps the best aspect of this game is just the creativity and mechanical side to the puzzles, you have to think outside of the box to solve them. There are many cool elements to the game that will test your patience, such as not running on the ice or not jumping from the high elevation. Even though the game does not look as good as some of those 90s classics, the pixel art is still pretty good, clearly, a lot of effort was put into this experience. + in my opinion, hilarious+ lots of creative puzzles+ a TON of cool ways to die+ achievements  - they were okay for the most part. The only thing I noticed that you can occasionally screw yourself over like in the area with radiation, it saved when I did not have enough time to get through - although I managed to fix it by exiting completely instead of restarting. As someone that holds 'cinematic platformers' very close to my heart, this game looks familiar with the delays on the actions, but still feels very different from the classics due to how the momentum was executed. However, looking at it from the perspective of a regular puzzle platformer, the game has a good sense of humor and many creative puzzles. Again, it's a little clunky, that is intentional.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? If you consider Another World (aka Out of this World) a masterpiece, then yes. It is a puzzle-platformer. Simplified, your task is to get past a multitude of obstacles to reach the next screen. Living in a dystopian state, you have to win a TV reality show to get your freedom. This show is designed in a way that noone does survive it, of course.Gameplay consists of running, jumping, pulling up ledges... game veterans will get a little Flashback here. You push stuff, pull levers... and listen to other characters. Not all other characters are enemies, many of them (including a crow) have to say something. Enemies (guards, policemen, soldiers) should be avoided (be sneaky or fast) or killed (using the environement, your character does not use firearms). Nearly all enemies kill you, also the environement kills you in many different ways. Falling down from too high hurts you, or instantly kills you if it was from high enough. Your job is just to stay alive (and reach the exit). If you reach the exit, you are presented with a new situation, the game does not feel repetitive. It is not too long, too.The jumps usually require precise timing and look like they were taken out directly from "Prince of Persia". I'd rate the difficulty with average, there are some sections that most players probably will have to retry a few times to get past. The game uses pixel art, looks a bit like "Songbringer". Gamepad works fine.Dark humored, pixelated puzzle platformer in the vein of Flashback or Another World.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hoping for a dark themed game, which in the more we advanced, the more it gets darker and darker. Kinda like George Orwell "1984", with a fully controlled society and no escape. Instead i get a would-be-likeable character, who is ALWAYS joking arround with bad jokes, seriously the jokes never made me smile and the game does it so much that it become super cringe. The main character is so dumb and joyfull for nothing that he becomes unlikeable. People don't die, they have special suits, so dying is a option, even for side characters. The scenario is given in a really bad way; a third person talking over a picture in a wall that is placed very conviniently where you just pass by. No exploration, no reflexion of your own.Just with theses elements, the game has lost his principal value; the oppressive atmosphere (which "1984" have).Now, lets focus on gameplay; Plateforms are actually great in this game. Well though and require some reflexion, it's not perfect but it does the job. Pretty cool.But the controls are very rough. The jump button especially. It feels terrible. it almost requires you to stop, to jump either forward or up. And for a plateformer game, it is a huge no-no. You can't have a bad jump button that nullifies your gameplay and action-rythm on plateforms. Especially when some jumps are timed and requires millimeters precisions, literally.It's a shame; I had high hopes for this game and It could have been a great game.  , there is far better games out there who deserves your 15 dollars money. There's even better games with only 10 dollars. This one does not deserve it.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay itself is fine, great visuals, some cool mechanics, although the platforming feels very unsmooth it is still fun to play. My big problem is the overall theme. In short, it is super poorly done. The description says it is inspired by 1984, but it plays like someone read a oneliner about 1984 and decided to make a game about it with a TV-Show twist. Basic themes of 1984 are lost, all thats left is "surveillance state". Wow, big deal... Even the humour got twisted like hell; it is so incredibly unfitting and lands rarely.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been craving for a game like this since the times I've played Flashback and Out of this World. Not only Ministry of Broadcast is an excellent platformer with smooth controls, great pixel art and animations, it is also utterly hilarious. I've literally laughed my way through the whole hallucination level, it was incredibly delicious. My only wish is that the puzzles (and the game overall) could have been a bit more difficult. I've certainly had some amount of fail/retries, but overall no parts of the game were near as difficult as some of the sequences in Out of this World or Heart of Darkness. All in all, this is a very refreshing and well-produced game. Even the collectibles are great (protagonist is looking for suitable shoes throughout the whole adventure).

_childDocuments_.review: Unless you love clunky controls that feel like doing brain surgery using a hydraulic press, or an extreme masochist don't waste your time. _childDocuments_.review: "Ministry of Broadcast" was recommended to me as a title that I would enjoy based on the plot and mechanics. At a high level, it does seem to offer a novel idea and has a neat Orwellian vibe about a dystopic world fitting somewhere between the authoritarian Warsaw Pact and "The Hunger Games". While clever and a bit silly at moments, this 'high art' concept fails on implementation and goes on far longer than the joke actually permits.The main complaint here is not the story, but the unforgiving and torturous mechanics of the . As a platformer, it is almost unendurable and the character will die consecutively on the many platforming elements, even if the player knows exactly what they are trying to accomplish and how to do it. "MoB" has the same design problem as "Mirror's Edge" or the many terrible NES platformers from the 80's where successful gameplay requires continuous failures due to platforming elements that could never have been predicted before they appear. The neverending traps, hazards, and pitfalls are slow death to the player's enthusiasm which quickly ebbs away to nothing by the end of the first day - and there are four more days to go in this title.The story starts out interesting but it lingers on-and-on without significant development as the title drifts through it's own inertia with the continuing chapters becoming boring like a joke that has become stale after repetition. There might be some recovery possible in later days if there was a new plot device or a platforming mechanic or other catharsis, but it's all the same like the devs ran out of budget for writing and just kept copy-pasting assets to stretch out the length. The late game doesn't become more intellectually challenging, but instead throws more stupid split-second platforms at the protagonist and there is no health or fatigue system - every miss whether small or large is instant total death and back to the last checkpoint.Let me add an important note about the content as well. "Ministry of Broadcast" is an attempt to make a work of dark humor, with it's exaggerated totalitarianism and comic purges of dissidents. The ginger-haired protagonist of the story will often have to resort to the barbarous methods of his captors to advance in the games, and the writers try to extract plenty of satire from their mildy morbid contestant. However, that message only works for as long as the humor lasts, which for "MoB" only stretches through the first hour. By the time that the shoeless cipher reaches the mid-to-late game, the joke has begun to wear thin and now the act of building a bridge from human remains or cremating the living to clear a room has an impossibly macabre quality. It's possible that another audience might receive the game differently than I did, but after you stop grinning at the story then you begin a new and emotionally exhausting journey through casual manslaughter - and I think the devs still believe that you're smiling along with them.Finally, the game ending rewards the player with a conclusion that is both predictable and wholly unsatisfactory. The two canon endings are both miserable rewards for the player that gave so much of their patience and willpower to arrive here with both feeling like losing scenarios. There are some secret (better) endings as well, but they were a bit too secret for a player that wasn't looking and I feel like they would pass by more casual players who weren't that invested by the end, which would be most players. Of the secret endings, there is one that is barely tolerable but requires work that the average player wasn't aware of throughout the title. When I played "Silent Hill" years ago, I got the worst ending without realizing there was a choice and never picked up another title from that franchise for years - "MoB" felt like the same feeling again."Ministry of Broadcast" is overlong, underdeveloped, and both bloated through repetition while also emotionally-draining. The character is only mildly controllable, the objectives are asinine, and the story is only entertaining at a high-level but fails the more that it unfolds. I can only give the developers credit for the attempt at crafting a unique world and some of the early storytelling, but it is anti-fun as a playable game and not unique enough to stand out from other (better) attempts at world-building.

_childDocuments_.review: I received press code for this back at release to stream it but just managed to finish it several months later.This game is very strange but in a way I generally like. It's part puzzle game, part Prince of Persia style platformer, part darkly comedic social commentary and just part WTF. There isn't much like this out there and while I do appreciate it for that, there are some caveats with this that are important to know before deciding on it.Pros:-Really cool pixel art style.-Minimalist but well done soundtrack and sound design.-Snappy, witty writing with a story that messes with you right up until the end.-Lots of varying challenges.-Some interesting comments on various elements of society and politics if you read between the lines.Cons:-Story will be impenetrable to some. I like to think I'm reasonably smart and I still don't entirely get it.-Controls are slow and mushy, much like the original Prince of Persia. You will get frustrated a lot with some of the platforming puzzles.-Checkpolnts that are sometimes frequent and sometimes really spread out in maddening places.-A lot of puzzles that just require trial and error to figure out.-Some levels feel a bit like they wear out their welcome early.I really enjoyed this overall and if you're a patient player, I think you will too. This is a pretty unique experience and one I believe worth experiencing if you like more abstract stories in games.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like hard platforming games that require turns on a dime and near perfect precision? Do you also like when those games have ♥♥♥♥♥♥, slippery, inconsistent controls? Because I sure don't!Do you like when games are inconsistent in what they communicate to the player? Do you like when they combine these inconsistencies with those same inconsistent controls? Because I sure don't!Do you like when a good story is ruined by confusing story telling, difficult to understand happenings, and an overall inconsistent tone and delivery? Because I sure don't!Would not recommend for the above reasons. If they had managed to make the controls tighter, the story in any way coherent, and the overall experience at least somewhat consistent, then I would have, but they didn't, so I won't as well.ADDED THOUGHTS BELOW:If the developers see this, I want them to take away the following:I get that this was made with older narrative platforming games in mind. Old platforming games with bad controls had bad controls because they were old games. They didn't know yet how to make those games feel good because they were made a long time ago. There's a reason most games have good, tight, responsive controls. Difficulty isn't the problem with the MoB game - but shoddy controls are. (Think - the puzzles were great! But the terrible controls used to complete them weren't.)In addition, this game has tons of good ideas. The developers were inspired by something. I want them to develop more. Maybe not a sequel, maybe something else. But they can and will do better, I am sure of it - it's just that this isn't the best game to show that. I want them to get better and make better games.

_childDocuments_.review: The Ministry of Broadcast mixes an Orwellian dystopia with dark humor, and they work surprisingly well together.  The writing in-game is absolutely top-notch; the sarcasm and defeatism work well in bringing the player through the story, and I often found myself poking around areas I wasn't supposed to just to get a bit more of the dialogue.  If you're after a narrative, Ministry of Broadcast is the absolute epitome of fantastic writing; you'll cherish it if you take your time.The puzzles were very exciting as well, and a solid break from the narrative that is woven. Only one puzzle stumped me at the end; they're all very much doable as you explore the room that you're stuck in, and after a bit of trial and error you definitely get that coveted 'Aha!' moment as you send another survivor tumbling to their doom.  If the game consisted entirely of a narrative and these often enjoyable puzzles, it would be an absolute classic.As with many things, however, there is a caveat, a dead horse in the backroom that you'll inevitably come against as you progress.The platforming controls leave a lot to be desired, and there are segments that you'll have to perform the platforming flawlessly in order to continue.  Flawlessly to the point that if your character takes a singular errant step at any point in the sequence, you're best left to simply restart the entire segment.  You'll likely break a controller during two specific segments, and the first comes around the four-hour mark; when you see reviewers with ~ 4 hours played, they got stuck there and shelved the title.Not that I could blame them; the character controls much like the classic title , which was acceptable when it originally released back in 1991; now imagine attempting to frantically platform using that movement scheme.  Even when you aren't pressed on time, you will end up leaping errantly to your death when you're simply trying to grab the ledge right above you.If the writing wasn't so damn good, I probably would have quit when the others did.Aside from the controls, the only other issue I have with the title that there isn't more for me to devour; the ending wrapped things up nicely, but what I'd do for more of the narrative and dialogue is likely shameful to my family.If you're looking for witty and brilliant writing while solving some puzzles, Ministry of Broadcast is right up your alley.  If you're looking for a platformer, your princess is in another castle.  Hopefully, Ministry of Broadcast Studios can take another pass at the control scheme and make things a bit more user-friendly in the near future, and the game would be flawless.All in all, I strongly recommend this title, and future titles would be well received from this studio.--------------------------------------I received this title for free from the developer as part of my ongoing work in-game journalism as a freelance writer.  While my works can be found on a couple of websites, the heft can be found at .  This did not affect my scores, as I'm far more interested in developing a trusting reader base than making nerdy developers happy.

It makes sense within its own logic and feels more like a fever dream, that keeps you pushing forward to the conclusion, no matter the cost.The levels are diverse and pose new different mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: "Ministry of Broadcast" is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro pixel platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.This crap and badly made platformer is a thematic ripoff of "Papers Please", but the gameplay is a slow, plodding "narrative platformer", which just means all the fun aspects of precision platforming has been removed and replaced with plodding, unskippable, badly written dialogue.  Once more we see developers fail at understanding the basic principle of delivering narrative through the game itself, and pretending their game is a crap E-book instead of doing their jobs properly.  Nobody wants to read all that garbage. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.The controls and game handling are notably very clunky and unsmooth here.  It's janky and unsatisfying to play... and any experienced gamer will tell you, the handling, responsiveness and general gameplay feel of the control scheme must be well polished for this kind of game to succeed.  Unfortunately, this is something the developer seems to have phoned in, with little to no apparent gameplay testing.  They dropped the ball on this one.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.Some of the defects in the game can be attributed to the choice of using the GameMaker Studio construction kit/toolset.  This is a very poor quality toolset favoured by amateur developers as it's cheap and requires little in the way of development skill, but unfortunately has very limited capabilities.  Just as you can't make a silk purse out of a sows ear, you can't make a great video game if you use a terrible engine.  GameMaker Studio is most commonly used to make retro pixel shovelware and cash grabs.A strong argument can be made that construction kits like GameMaker Studio should never be used to make games for profit, as the "developer", Ministry of Broadcast Studios has done here.  These construction kits are intended to teach people some of the basic principles of game development, and to make small demos to pass around with friends.  They're not intended to replace to actual work of real, professional game developers.  So it's inappropriate when amateurs try to use these for profit, without any actual, real game development effort taking place.  This doesn't result in products that have any real meaningful value for gamers.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.You're forced to sign a highly questionable yet legally unenforceable End User License Agreement... for such a relatively low effort, low quality game this comes across more as a delusion of grandeur than anything else.  This agreement includes questionable requirements that may attempt to revoke consumer law protections that gamers expect to have, which is also highly problematic.  Developers must learn they are here to serve gamers, not control them.  I had my cat walk over the keyboard while the EULA was displaying, which fixed that problem for me."Ministry of Broadcast" has the preposterous price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  It's really insulting when developers who can't even work out how to do computer graphics properly and dump pixelcrap onto Steam think they can charge this kind of money for their garbage.This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: When I have strong feelings about a game, they're typically positive. Usually, I'm either neutral on games or I quite like them. There used to be only one game that I could say I genuinely and thoroughly disliked ("Gods Will Be Watching," for those curious). Now that I've completed this game, it has officially been added to that list.I'm sure the team that worked on this game worked really hard on it, it won a lot of small awards and people clearly enjoy it for the most part. I acknowledge that this is a personal opinion and that I'm not in the majority, but I walked away from beating this game having felt like my time and money were both wasted.I want to start off with a few things I liked: the visuals are quite stylized and certainly not bad for the 16-bit constraints. The dialogue is often amusing but not overambitious in its writing. The rewind / restart from checkpoint function (something I had to use too often in this game, but more on that later) is smooth and usually quite quick. Many puzzles (though not all) have helpful hints from the signage on the walls, which helped me along more than once. Now, onto my issues with the game. Firstly, the movement mechanics make the puzzle platforming part of this game (which is most of the game) a miserable grind. When you get to a ledge, depending on if you walk off, run off, walk off while jumping, or run off while jumping, you will have slightly different trajectories outwards as you fall down. This sounds neat on its surface, but there are many parts of the game where only one of these four options will result in you landing where you need to, so you have to try all of them until one works, and then memorize which one you need to do and make sure you do it every time you get kicked back to a checkpoint. You have to do it *perfectly* in a lot of cases as well. Firstly, the animations for walking / running do not actually end when you stop pressing a key to go in a direction, making timing off by *just* enough to mess up a lot of maneuvers, but it's always off by different amounts of time depending on where in the walk / run animation you were when the key was released. This is especially troublesome when you factor in that this game requires pixel-perfect timing on many jumps, so you're hosed if youre even a fraction of a second too early or too late. In addition to this, the ice mechanic adds nothing to the game except for a slightly amusing cutscene near the end, but is an otherwise infuriating rather than challenging or interesting addition. Even without ice, the fact that your character skids when coming to a stop after sprinting is also problematic when you have to alternate a lot between sprinting and not sprinting in certain long stretches of jumping puzzles, making small platforms and icy areas particularly frustrating. I had to restart so many areas SO many times, just because my jump timing was off, or I did the wrong kind of jump, or the puzzle wasn't clearly conveyed (again, some are very well conveyed, but some SUPER aren't, which is a shame) so I often had to throw the poor protagonist's corpse at things over and over again until something finally worked. And don't even get me started on the timed sections -- most of these probably took me at least a dozen tries, with a few even taking a half hour by themselves. The last one took me the longest at about 40 minutes from the start of the cliff-climb, and it took almost 20 minutes just for me to get through the final stretch with all the goats, as I was often off of the timer by just a fraction of a second and would need to start over from 20 seconds prior AGAIN. The level of precision needed makes it so aggravating that by the time you get done with a puzzle, you've been on autopilot for the last several attempts spitting out exact keypresses like a robot, and you don't even feel proud by the time you beat it, just exhausted and annoyed. Especially when the game gives no indication that your progress is saved, meaning the paranoia is intense after completing a particularly hard puzzle as you pray to any god that will listen to keep you alive until the game stealth-auto-saves your progress. I really wanted to give this game a chance and get through it to see if at least the story and world-building panned out, even if the gameplay itself was disappointing, but I honestly wish I hadn't. For how cool of a concept the Ministry and and show are, you're given almost nothing to work with as far as lore, and even the small amount you do get is so vague that it quickly lost my interest and never gave me enough to gain it back. I'm all for cryptic and hidden storylines, but the best of those are good at feeding you enough interesting tidbits to keep you wanting to learn more, and this game did not. By the time I got to the end, I was completely un-invested in the story or its characters and just wanted salvation from my suffering, which shouldn't be how you want your players to feel after playing your game. The last timed sprint was the worst nightmare of the bunch, and the ending was nowhere near worth the effort it took to get to it; it was about as rewarding as a wet fart directly in my mouth.In short, I really wanted to like this game, but it never gave me any reason to, it only gave me reasons to put it on a list of games I regret playing and really disliked, which was a list I didn't think would ever get another game added to it. I got this in a bundle with Beholder, which was easily one of the best game series I played this year, so to learn that this game is almost as bad as Gods Will Be Watching was a huge disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: Wow.  There are very few games that I will play and finish, but this one had me hooked.Ignore the play time, it didn't take me that long, I just left it running for a few days.Ministry of Broadcast can be described as a platform puzzle adventure game. Graphically it's simplistic, with pixel art, and very few options. Full screen or not. If you choose to have it not full screen, the window is tiny. Other than that, the graphics are serviceable, and in most cases, quite good. Would I like to see a higher res game? Yeah, sure, but these work and work well.Sound wise, the game is quite good. The audio really enhances the atmosphere of the game, and if you turn it off, you can really notice the difference. The game feels bland and boring without the audio. Which brings me to the one issue - you cannot separate the music from the rest of the audio. It's all or nothing. And pausing the game means the music plays louder than it does in game, because the background "noise" has stopped. It often meant pausing, turning the audio off, doing something else, then coming back to the game, turning the sound back up and resuming the game. Minor issue, but an issue none the less.Game play is where the game shines. You control a new contestant(?) on a game show, and you're tasked with completing the levels at the start of each day.  You run, jump, push, climb and fall your way through each level. There are puzzles and obstacles in your way, these include guards, dogs and NPCs. One thing to know, you're going to die. A lot. The game does rely quite a bit on trial and error. However, the game doesn't get frustrating. If you die, you usually only have to redo a few seconds to a minute of game play. And you generally realise very quickly what you did wrong. Then it's just a matter of adjusting what you did or trying something different and you get by.Rarely have I played a game to completion in recent memory. I often get bored, run out of time, or find it gets beyond my skill level to continue. This game was not like that. The difficultly gets harder, sure, but never to the point of "%#!^ it, I'm out".My one final gripe, are the controls. They're basically perfect. Use the analogue stick or digital D pad to move, A to jump and X to "use" and the triggers to run. Any work and they work well. Except to reset you press the 'Play' button and to pause you press 'Back'. I reset so many times trying to pause it was not funny.Overall, aside from a few minor issues, this game is a hell of a lot of fun, and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little title that any fan of Abe's Oddysee will like.Game includes regular difficulty that is "old school precise" and easy mode for those more interested in the Truman Show'esque story.Clearly a lot of love was put in, as the game reeks of tiny details and cute jokes.The nine hours I spent on it gave more impressions than some other games I put four times the time into.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. If I had to combine two games, I'd say this feels like if Portal, Hotline Miami, Papers Please, and Lisa had a baby.It has really fun puzzles that for me always felt fresh (good mix of novelty, thoughtful solutions, or speed running) amidst a great atmosphere of a Soviet-y 1984-esque state. It balanced a story that never tells ALL but tells ENOUGH to make you really care about the main character, while being peppered with a lot of fun and dark humor.The annoying-est part is just the fact that the character control itself takes getting used to, and at some points it felt like some luck needed to be involved for grabbing a ledge at a particular time. But you spawn back immediately, check points were often enough it never bugged me, and the multitude of deaths felt less annoying and more part of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: If Prince of Persia was set in a modern dystopia ala 1984 (A reference the game leans on HEAVILY) The controls can take a bit to get used to but it's so much fun to play. The easy mode changes very little from the normal mode but if it's what you need then it's an option for you. I can't recommend this game enough for people who enjoy a challenge in their platformers. The biggest hurdle is learning the controls especially if you're coming from a modern baseline of game knowledge. It's not the same as a Mario game, don't expect it to be. I see real speedrun potential in this game, look out for it in a marathon someday.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: Full review: Ministry of Broadcast will inevitably be of niche taste with players, particularly those who find heavy politics in narratives icky. With (generally) cooperative controls, a heavy variety of activities to struggle with, and puzzles for all those puzzled out there, this piece of art is little less than an articulate, passionate movement. Without question, something that should be captured at least once, for those looking for pain with a point. It knows you'll make the right choice.+ Horrifically beautiful narrative that builds with time+ (Normally) intuitive control scheme and mechanics+ Great variety in activities and puzzles+ Looks astoundingly good- Fast-paced platforming can be a pain- Certain puzzles' difficulty could be toned down to prevent pace breaks
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: Ministry of Sound takes the art style and gameplay of classic puzzle platformers such as Flashback and Another World and creates a dark and humorous experience unique from any other.  There is a deep story that begins to unravel as you go deeper into the narrative.  It truly is something to dive into on your own, as merely describing it feels like a bit of a spoiler.  <3+Some of the best sound design I have heard in gaming, either AAA or indie.  Every dog bark, gun fire, etc. was perfectly placed.  The music hit every right tone through finding humor, dread, and solitaire.  Just perfect.+Wonderfully realized puzzles kept my brain thinking without ever stumping me entirely.+Pixel art and animation felt appropriate to the game's world.  Even something simple like shooting imaginary bullets with a  hand gun was creatively realized through the minimal pixels.  Every death felt gruesome in this manner, as well. </3-It must be said, but the gameplay, even if it felt quite intentional, felt very sluggish and delayed.  Again, much like the games it was influenced by, seems necessary.  But when timing is important, it became the primary cause of failed jumps and climbs more times then I cared for.VERDICT: Must be checked out, immediately.  There is some joy to be found in this lovely puzzle platformer by all.  9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: A work of art! Stunning pixel graphics, an outstanding (and very complimentary soundtrack), along with a highly intriguing dystopian, Orwellian-esque setting. The story line is very intriguing and I foresee a massive twist coming up. Obviously the developers were also inspired by Prince of Persia (in terms of gameplay), but unsuprisingly there are major gameplay advancements when comparing to the former (seeing that we are in 2020). The gameplay does feel very versatile, and it isn't strictly a puzzle game as there is action and some 'finger shooting' on behalf of the protagonist (you'll see what I mean when you play it). Well worth the price - a definitely recommended little gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: Received for Streaming Purposes. Absolutely loved this game. Despite my own personal frustration with a couple of "timed" areas, the game is really good fun for anyone who liked the dystopian atmosphere of "Papers Please" and the puzzle platforming of games like "Another World/Flashback". If you haven't played these games, what you have is a story-driven platform game where you must cautiously jump, climb, sidestep or even just RUN through a perilous reality competition. The controls are tight, despite my terrible joypad - and completing each section was fun. The pixel art is beautiful and really sets a nice atmosphere, with some great attention to detail. The music completes the package, with some disturbing melodies as well as jaunty tunes when needed... and for added sprinkles - the writing is very tongue in cheek, with some sly comedy in throughout.Completion was satisfying, something I cannot say with all games. Difficulty is just right, with me dying a lot, but enjoying each gory death and able to restart quickly. Several times I thought the section would be impossible, only to try again a few times, and reach the next checkpoint.  Then when reaching the end - this does allow you to rewind and revisit areas for that extra insentive to find hidden objects (as well as alternate endings!). Definitely recommended, to anyone that values the grimy hopelessness with a side of fun and a decent challenge. :P
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: MoB was a very interesting game I played the gameplay was great but in some areas i felt that the animations or the actions Orange made were a bit slow for the challenges they gave - more specifically in areas where there was a "timer" or where whatever you on was falling. Its kinda hard to keep up with these challenges when it takes 2 or 3 whole seconds just to get up. You could make these a bit faster or maybe you could give orange i-frames aswell during these small actions. Or you could make some of these sections with a lower timer and add more thought to the section rather than reflexes like most of the game is based around. The puzzles were REALLY well made and thought out which is the biggest chunk of the game. Its usually trying to find a way around something which can be difficult or maybe easy. Even when you mess up the game is very fair with check points and if you permanently get stuck you can always reset the puzzle which is usually where your checkpoint started. I don't recall anytime you could get stuck like that but if you did rewind is always there. The difficulty always progresses at a good pace and the game doesn't throw you with a huge difficulty spike. The game rewards patience and looking at your surroundings as well as out of the box thinking. However while this is great for the type of game it is I felt like the puzzles and challenges never did give more than one option to do get over a puzzle or obstacle. Aside from a very small portion i feel that the game could use more than one way to solve an issue Orange has to face. Like you can still have it puzzle oriented but also reward different ways to do a puzzle. I say this because I feel like after you beat the game there isn't much reason to go back to it other than the boots because once you know how to get through the puzzle the challenge is gone. In other games with puzzles like these like say zelda. Zeldas main focus isnt just dungeons and puzzles meaning theres way more reasons to go back to it even though the puzzles are the same. In this game the puzzles make up majority of the gameplay. Now making the challenges challenging while also adding different ways to do them is hard in of itself. So i don't drag the game for not doing this. Im just offering ways I think it could be improved. Either way the gameplay itself is really well made and polished for their first time making a game. Now the story is a bit confusing with not much details or explanation given. But i really think that actually adds more to the atmosphere of this dystopian. Which the atmosphere is really on point. It nails it making you feel immersed. The music is hit or miss or usually quiet but for the same reason it adds a crucial part to the atmosphere so its actually a good thing for the most part. All in all for 15 bucks i'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzles or even trying out something new. It brings a lot to offer and it really well made. You'll have fun with this game if you puzzles or dystopian stories.
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: While fairly short, its a lot of fun.I love games that are a bit mysterious with its story and leave some things to the players imagination. Specially when some things, that are minor and not entirely relevant to the story, remain in darkness.  Only thing i wish the game had, was the option to skip dialogues after you heard them and respawned.Made a few passages in the game rather annoying than fun. Definintely recommending this game if you love puzzle platformers with tight controls
_childDocuments_.name: Ministry of Broadcast

_childDocuments_.review: Indie pixelart? Check. Good ol' platforming? Check. Engaging storyline? Check. Immersive music, self-aware jokes, nationality of the authors? Check. Check. Czech. Only problem I've had was unintentional falling to my death after pressing the Up key while holding the Left or Right key. Space key also makes you jump, so I don't see a reason why the Up key should be used for jumping as well - especially frustrating when it's not possible to turn it off. Second thing missing was the inability to set the difficulty - when you get stuck, you're stuck. The crow could give hints after several unsuccessful attempts (that would cost something). Otherwise great fun, 8/10 would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Ministry of Broadcast is a narrative-driven single player cinematic platformer mixing Orwell’s 1984 with modern reality TV. A country divided by The Wall; to cross it and reach your family, you must compete on - and win - a reality TV show broadcast by the Regime.

name: The Forgotten City
detailed_description: WISHLIST DEAR VILLAGERS' NEW GAME Awards & Nominations About the Game Travel 2,000 years into the past and relive the final days of a cursed Roman city, where if one person sins, everyone dies. Combat is an option, but violence will only get you so far. Only by questioning an intertwined community of colourful characters, cleverly exploiting the time loop, and making difficult moral choices can you hope to solve this epic mystery. Here, your decisions matter. The fate of the city is in your hands. Explore an open-world ancient Roman city with historically authentic art, architecture, costumes and customs Investigate a gripping, non-linear mystery with multiple endings Become entwined in the lives of richly detailed, deeply interactive characters Grapple with moral dilemmas which have life-and-death consequences Play as whoever you want, by choosing your character’s gender, origin and backstory Solve problems with reason, charm, bribery, intimidation, violence, or by cleverly exploiting the time-loop

short_description: The Forgotten City is a narrative-driven time loop adventure in ancient Rome. Discover the ruins of an ancient underground city, travel 2000 years into the past, and unravel the mystery of who destroyed it by cleverly exploiting the power to wind back time. The fate of the city is in your hands.

_childDocuments_.review: Revealing what makes The Forgotten City so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ marvelous risks compromising the experience for new players. Don't even watch the trailers. Just get out your wallet and do it. If you -must- consider broad points about why it's getting overwhelmingly positive reviews, I present the following extremely low spoiler arguments:- The threshold between narrative and gameplay is blended really well; playing the game well feels like interacting with the story.- The writing is actually really high quality; believable characters, negligible plot holes, and genuine philosophical conundrums.- The mysteries are compelling to investigate; you're not following a series of quest markers to get this done, you actually feel clever for figuring things out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I have made it to 1 ending out of 4, so it's from that perspective.It is one of the time loops game like outer wilds, where you learn something new about the world and the characters every time you restart a loop and use the information you have to figure out the mystery. All the threads that I chased or was chasing felt pretty intuitive. And I always had something to chase, which is very important in these types of games because if you feel stuck with nothing to do you get frustrated.A very good detective and puzzle game, one of the best probably that you can get.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I was interested in this game because of the comparisons to Outer Wilds. I think that's a pretty unfortunate comparison for this game, because I think it just doesn't come close to living up to that experience. While I think the voice acting is nice, there really isn't much depth to the various characters, and many of the subquests are very trivially resolvable. The game is quite short, and there's just not much depth to either the exploration or the puzzles. Adding to that last bit, the game uses a hints system for the puzzles that defaults to on. It didn't occur to me to check for that until after some surprisingly direct prompts, so I turned it off at that point... but then found that everything remaining was direct enough that it didn't really matter anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game was just pure fun! History, drama, mystery, horror, you name it, it was in there. The world is pretty, the music is nice, and there's an eerie feeling all through it. And all the spookiness was balanced by some actual human warmth in the characters. I did get 2 out of 4 endings in about 5 hours and left very satisfied. This game goes so far out in the end you have no idea what you'll get, so just go in blind and with no expectations. Will definitely play more to get the other 2 endings.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: You will enjoy this game. That's a Desius Guarantee, but just in case: You can do a driveby shooting on a roman, which by itself is totally worth the pricetag. Luckily, a lot of love and care went into the development of this game, which is just, breathtakingly awesome as a "Whodunnit" puzzle adventure with plenty of loveable and hateable characters, and some philosophy that may or may not shake your belief system. If none of that sounds fun to you, then that's unfortunate for you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: As many others have said, this game was originally a skyrim mod. If you've played the mod, you probably already bought the game, but for those few who think "why buy the game when i have the mod for free?", let me tell you: this game blows the original mod out of the water. While the plot is still basically the same, the setting and gameplay change necessitate a lot of other changes that are all for the better. Even if you played the mod, the ending will still blow you away.For those that haven't played the mod, this game is an excellent time loop mystery. You can take your time figuring things out across multiple loops, but if you're clever enough to figure things out quickly, you will be rewarded by a mechanic that saves you a good amount of time by taking care of the more immediate problems you'll face on each loop. The "canon" ending is definitely worth the trouble of getting everything just right.I also recommend this game if you're a fan of Roman (and older) mythology and history. Can't spoil the surprises, but the whole thing is very well written. Please buy it and support these devs!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It was alright 6.5/10.Definitely feels like a skyrim mod. With all the stiff that entails.I thought timeloop mechanic was pretty shallow, feeling more like a non standard game over then something that really impacts the story. It's like the game says "oops, you clicked the wrong dialogue option and now you need to reset the game. Now you know what to say next time!". The only thing that the time loop really impacted was that you get to keep your inventory and skip some dialogue. Otherwise uncovering the mistery was fun enough with some nice twists.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It's nice and all, but personally I can't say that it's actually worth investing time in. To start with the game is all story, which is not at all a downside, the problem is that the story is not all that interesting. I thought it was funny that in the main menu the game had a disclaimer telling content creators to exercise caution and spoiler alerts so as to not spoil the plot to their viewers, but the spoilers only matter if you know the mythology that the game plays on in advance.From a technical point of view, the dialog system falls short (lacks branches) and the save system lacks actual save points. After the first time that I happened to waste around 20 minutes I learned to never take my fingers off the quicksave/quickload keys.Bottom line, it's alright, if it's on sale maybe get it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really glad I finally got around to playing this game. I can best describe it as a story-driven puzzle game, where you have to talk to various characters to solve mysteries and collect items in order to progress. There are 4 endings, and I had a fun time figuring out how to get to each one. I really hope this development team gets to create more games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This initially stared off as a Skyrim mod. If you knew that, you probably played the mod. I'm glad to say that this standalone game provides a lot of new and interesting things for those who have played that. The story is similar, but the setting and the additional content adds a lot. Overall it's an extremely well-written adventure game dealing with some moral and philosophical questions.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a particularly long game and it's certainly not a difficult one and the story itself isn't even something entirely unexpected, but there is clear dedication and appreciation to the main goal of trying to tell that story in a wonderful and unique way.  Time-travel and groundhogs-day loop games are uncommon enough, but this one goes out of its way to really help you experiment, make mistakes and want to see all the subtle differences each time you run through.  And beyond that, quality of life decisions such as letting you skip actions you've done multiple times before by having other NPCs do it for you so that you don't need to frantically run around fixing the same problems is an incredibly smart and natural inclusion.  Easy recommend, though given it is only a 6-8 hour game if you stretch it, I would recommend waiting for the price to get closer to 10$ to reflect that.  As with these games, once you beat it and see all the endings and paths, there is not much in the replay value department and 20$ is a bit of a high asking price for the comparative hours you get from it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It was a pretty interesting and lore filled game ! The scenery was really lovely ! I really enjoyed exploring, running around and talking to everyone!I liked the Greek/Roman setting with hints of civilizations ! I wish there were more games with this setting !Also I really enjoyed ending #4 !If I would make any suggestions I would have loved for there to have been a clock to keep track of the time of day. Maybe a bigger map with more fun puzzles too!I will be looking forward to more games made by them ! 9/10 !
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game.Ir's clearly quality over quantity in terms of content: There is quite a bit to explore, but the map is really small, there is only a limited set of people to interact with, and if you read rather than listen to the dialogue, you can get through everything in about 5 hours (provided you read fast). This limited set means everything could be connected meaningfully, and doing things can influence multiple people at once.And the canon ending is very rewarding. :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A really good narrative based game. Forgotten city throws you in an interesting world where everyone is walking on eggshells. It's up to you to conduct investigation on what the city is, how to escape and who would be responsible for their ominous fate by using the time-loop mechanics in the world.PROS:   - Good likable characters.   - Some puzzle aspects are fun to figure out.   - Great application of time-loop mechanics. This is probably my favorite part.   - Good story. There's a mystery involved and is interesting once uncovered.CONS:   - I wish it was longer.   - Some bugs here and there. Especially the delay of texture pop up after a loading screen.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very good. I mean most people would rather love to be exiled in this place than live in reality. But the game is still bugged and at occasions I keep falling in between worlds and NPCs talking to me between walls and several floors above. Please fix these issues.But I finished this game on me own in a single day and did two ending scenarios, for anybody playing this game new just try to deduce the outcomes and reactions on your own and this game is most savoured by a thought out verbal war with the supposed "gawd" in this game. The cannon ending of this game was trying to be quite inspiring and its the best. Because a true hero saves all and without any expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Bravo.Well realised characters. Engaging story. Story design to make you feel like you solved it all on your own, even though you were gently guided to the solutions. A few twists and turns. Allows you to try almost all solutions to the story through the clever time loop. Not too long. Not too short. It is very hard to find fault with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I have really enjoyed my time with the game. so much in fact, that I felt compelled to make a review of it. I liked the game mechanics, the core idea of the game and even the way the endings are presented and lived through.  I can't go into details lest i give spoilers, since part of my enjoyment was revealing the layers of the history embedded in the game. but it was a great journey through human history.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game on sale for 10 bucks.  And I definitely got my money's worth.This game is a first person exploration game, primarily.  You investigate the mysterious town, and you relive the same day over again until you beat the game.  There is some action/fighting/platforming aspects to the game, but it is definitely not the focus of the game.The true focus of the game is the question of morality itself.  This game is story rich and driven by your own actions when dealing with the complex and well-written characters of the game.  The heart of this game is a conversation about the concept of moral choices, and it forces you to examine your own decision making process when making moral choices.It reminds me a lot of Knights of the Old Republic 2, particularly the character of Kreia when she scolds you for giving credits to the begger, only for him to be targeted by other beggars and killed.  It is that level of complexity that the game forces you to consider your own notions of morality, and I really liked that a lot.Without getting into specifics or spoilers, you could see each character that you come across as an aspect of your own self, like pieces of the whole, and when they do an action, you can question yourself if you really see them as so different than yourself if you were in a similar situation.There are villains in this game.  But at no point did I feel like they were evil for evil's sake.  Rather, they had compelling reasons for their motivations to act the way they do, and it is possible to see yourself in them.I highly recommend this game.  It was very thoughtfully executed.  I also really liked the facial expressions and character designs of the characters, and they were all endearing in their design, their personalities, and the skillful writing of their script.I do want to say that I think 25 bucks is too much for the game.  I'm very picky personally these days.  And I want twice as much value for every dollar I spend.  Perhaps selfish, but money is tight these days.  So do what I did, and wait for when it goes on sale for 10 dollars.  The game has limited replay value, because once you've gone through the story and received the canon ending, there is little reason to return to it.  You could in theory watch a longplay of the game on Youtube, but I thought the experience of playing the game myself was worth it, for 10 dollars.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is an incredibly charming game. I didn't expect to beat it in one two days, but here I am. While the game is obviously made by a smaller team, it does a lot of things better than other time loop games I've played. It doesn't waste my time, and leaves several ways to approach the same problem. I would also recommend Jacob Gellers video "After a City is Buried" that talks about the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: An utterly amazing game: one of the best I've ever played. Brilliant story, fun gameplay, likeable and interesting characters, really interesting ideas and a fantastic mystery all build upon a great premise and unique ideas. For a game made by such a small group of people, it is very good quality and the voice acting and music is superb. I definitely reccomend this game. It was brilliant.

_childDocuments_.review: It felt like playing a *good* Fallout game, but with a less action/shooter mechanics. Overall I enjoyed it and I look forward to this studio's next offering. _childDocuments_.review: I played this game totally blind knowing nothing about it other than it had good reviews and a time loop mechanic, which I enjoy in games.I only got one ending so far and plan to get the rest, but I thoroughly enjoyed going through this game, figuring it all out on my own, learning about the characters, solving little mysteries that lead to bigger ones, etc...I highly recommend not looking up guides or walkthroughs as that will spoil a lot of the enjoyment I think, but to each their own.Reading other reviews, people have complained about the AI? I feel like that's a weird complaint since the game is almost completely scripted. It's like complaining about the AI in a point-and-click adventure game. The only issue I encountered is that on maxed out settings the performance chugged just a little at times on a high-end system when new sections loaded. Only lasted a second or two when it happened every 20 minutes or so, so I didn't notice it for the most part. I encountered no bugs.I reached my first ending in just under 4 hours, which was 6 loops in the game. I wonder if anyone can beat that blind :D

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game. It very much feels like a standalone version of a Skyrim mod made by only a couple people, but that's because it is. I've never played the mod myself though, and I went into this completely blind [which I'd highly recommend!]This game is all about solving mysteries, talking to interesting characters, and choosing your words wisely. I went in expecting not much more than that but there's also a bit of combat and enemy evasion which kept me on my toes.I did run into a couple bugs, but one was easily fixed by  and another required me to look up a guide and backtrack to a old dialogue option missed in the beginning, but in the end this game was a very enjoyable experience which never dragged and always had something new to explore. It took me a little less than 8 hours to finish but every moment kept my interest and the multiple endings were fun to discover.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Groundhog Day: Philosophical Ancient Rome Edition. A first-person mystery adventure game that's short, small in scope, and low budget... but engaging!The writing is surprisingly clever (aside from a part of the canonical ending that actually made me groan out loud with how clichéd it was) and philosophical, the setting is interesting and atmospheric, the characterization is  (characters are well fleshed-out with their own unique back stories, personalities, and drives, which together with well-written dialogue means that characters that are meant to be likable really  likable and characters that are meant to be unlikable  unlikable - which makes it even more shocking when something is revealed that completely changes your perception of them), and the acting is punching well above its weight for a small indie game.Go in as blind as you can. Even if some plot twists might make you roll your eyes, you don't want them spoiled.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Intelligent, well-written, well-designed mystery that rewards paying attention and thinking outside the box. Many leads are resolved simply by doing what makes sense, often with several different plausible routes to take, which makes the world and its characters feel all the more real and fair, while referencing the specific actions you took or the order in which you took them makes it feel alive and reactive. Conversational boss fights are passed not with skill checks or dice rolls, but by learning about the world, understanding who you're talking to, and supporting your argument. Even when there is an obvious right choice, having to think about your responses and engaging with the game on its level is still very satisfying.There are a few rough edges (clunky movement, inescapable level geometry); the characters and dialogue are overall rather shallow; and it might feel short for the price, depending on how long it takes you to explore and solve the various mysteries; but these are minor flaws compared to the overall experience. A well-crafted labor of love, more than worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, I don't like to rip on games like this, games that were made by a small team and clearly had a lot of heart put into them. I just really did not enjoy this game. I sat through to the end because it was intriguing in a way that a high school production of Peter Pan is intriguing: promising at first, then Peter Pan hits the window at full speed, and then you're glued to your seat for the rest of it so you can watch the set fall down. Here are the positives:-The way the city is structured,  is very, very cool. -The dialogue is snappy, and the player character has a great personality. -Very well researched and depicted when it came to history and language -- excellent use of Latin, especially in the graffiti.-Time loop mechanics are fun to play in. There are ways to bypass certain events so that you don't have to waste time doing them repeatedly, which is very convenient. Now for the negatives: -No map and lack of quest markers made the city nigh impossible to navigate. I get that there are secret parts of the city (and they were the coolest parts) but there are ways to hide those things on a map. This is a basic accessibility feature that makes the game less frustrating for  and it baffles me that it wasn't included. -Certain puzzles, usually the ones that affected the very fabric of the game, were easy to figure out, while the minor puzzles were nigh impossible and blocked certain areas. I had several major mysteries figured out far before I could put them to any use, because I couldn't figure out how to get past minor obstacles. The game's "guidance mechanic" wasn't any help, either -- it said stuff like "it's all up to you". -Despite the game being based around a time loop mechanic, time didn't seem to matter at all. Major events are triggered by the player walking up to certain characters. It made me care considerably less about what was happening around me, because I knew that if I didn't want a certain event to trigger, I could simply avoid that area. -Too many characters, too little time. I didn't care about any of them (except possibly Equitia). The character models are a little bit uncanny valley, and all the characters take several seconds to start talking to you once you engage them in conversation. Since so much of the story comes through dialogue, this is just annoying.-Story seems to be missing any sort of structure. I could only define act 1 due to an event that was clearly supposed to be the end of it. I couldn't define the second and third acts. Act 1, though, took far too long and was far too confusing.My biggest complaint is the lack of structure in the time loop. Without a defined limit, you feel no urgency. This also means the  feels no urgency. Certain areas stretch out for far, far too long, even if you're trying to nip along smartly. I think that there's technically a defined end point to a loop, but it takes so long that it doesn't matter. Technically, the following are spoilers, but I will keep it vague: Overall, I just really didn't enjoy this game. I went in expecting to love it, having heard all the excellent reviews, but it failed to live up to expectations in almost every way. At least include a minimap next time. 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: This is a pretty good story telling game with a story that I subjective find intriguing. It is, however, a bit pricey as it only takes me 7hrs to 100% the game.  This game is, in my opinion, a story telling game. There aren't really hard puzzles or detective works that need to be done. All you have to do is just do the leg work, talking to people and exploring your surroundings. The side quests mostly ties back into the main plot so things you do are almost always relevant. The world is small so exploration actually gives you meaningful clues to solve the case. Even if you missed something, you can easily run back and forth in a very short amount of time. There are also a bit of action sprinkled on the puzzle solving to prevent you from getting too bored. The story has a few twists that, although somewhat cliche, interesting in presentation.The only thing I'd complain is probably the fact that exploration is not rewarding enough. There are a lot of money around that you can grab but if you know what youre doing you dont have to spent any money on anything and can still get the best end easily.That being said, I'd also agree with people who did not recommend the game. The characters do not react in the most natural way and the gameplay can be something more engaging, like making the game a platformer, instead of just a story telling game with some actions. I personally didn't mind these issues because the plot alone is enough to drawn me in and kept me playing.

At present, they are optional aside from a few key story areas, so not really optional if wanting to finish the main storyline. But I acknowledge that this is more of a taste/preference thing.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve never heard of The Forgotten City until it came out and everyone was talking about it. But apparently, originally this title has been a mod for Skyrim. As a mod, this sure would be amazing. As a standalone title, though? Yeah, it’s pretty good.This is a first person perspective action adventure game with a time loop as a main story gimmick. And it starts in a very promising way – you find yourself in an ancient underground city, surrounded by extremely lifelike golden statues that seem to follow your movement. Then you travel to the past and learn about this city’s Golden Rule, where if one of the citizen were to sin, the entire city will be punished. What is considered a sin? Who is going to endanger the entire city and you in it? And can you escape the time loop and return to your own time? It’s a very neat setup and a lot of the gameplay is fun as well, as you follow different leads and try to use your ability to start the day again to your advantage.But the game never really goes beyond the basics that this setup allows. Yes, resolving side quests and main quest issues via several loops is a cool idea and you get interesting interactions with characters as you learn more about them. Yet, apart from one additional gameplay mechanic, that was a pleasant surprise to me, you don’t get many genuinely fun moments or ideas explored. Lots of situations you must resolve involve just one or two steps, most of which can be done in a single loop. And after it’s resolved, there’s absolutely nothing you may do with the characters involved in it, their stories are just “done”. Most of the city isn’t that fun to explore and more exciting locations are, more or less, a one-off trip, unless you somehow trigger the loop reset while in there.Which is really the big disappointment with this game. There’s a lot of promise and a lot of multiple solutions for things, but none of them are inventive or necessary or even fun. Movement in the game is dull as locations are covered in invisible walls in the most unexpected places, Paradise Killer this is not. Finding some NPCs during the day is a chore, since some of them don’t have a set schedule and semi-randomly wander around and even those who do walk along predictable paths cover so much ground, that you still have to spend a lot of time before you can finally find them to ask some simple thing you couldn’t before. And boy oh boy how many bizarre bugs can happen in this game. None of them broke my playthrough, but a lot of them are shocking.If I sound overtly negative about The Forgotten City, it’s not because I consider it to be bad. Quite the contrary – it’s a very decent take on this type of adventure game and I liked playing it. But it is vastly underwhelming. The plot doesn’t get any more interesting after a few early revelations (there are twists coming, mind you, they’re just not interesting). The gameplay doesn’t get more exciting. It’s no Shadow of Memories, The Sexy Brutale or Outer Wilds – I don’t love these games (in fact I didn’t even finish Outer Wilds), but they were far more exciting than The Forgotten City. But hey, it’s certainly pretty good anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game relatively blind and suffice to say I thought it was a breath of fresh air, and astonishingly well done from such a small studio. _childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is a phenomenal experience from beginning to end despite being named like a hidden object game.Forgotten City is the first of 3(?) time loop games to come out in 2021 and I honestly think it’s the best. This game falls on the side of Outer Wilds’ philosophy of time loops. Exploration and conversation are what reward you with further knowledge of how to advance your way to escaping an unending time loop. All this is served in the frame of very well-written and performed characters who serve to make you love, loathe or suspect them. Furthermore, this is all framed in a historical setting of ancient Rome where the creators of the game spent extra time to ensure this is well represented. I enjoyed this game immensely despite its short run time for a first playthrough.The only downsides of this game really are due to its origin as a Skyrim mod. What little combat there is is awful, there’s pop-in on higher FOV and texture issues periodically as well as the characters having stiff animations that are reminiscent of animatronics. All that being said, the performances outshine the stiff delivery and the combat is a very very small portion of the game.Really, to say too much more would be saying too much. This game is very short and deserves as blind of a playthrough as possible. There are some great surprises throughout the game for those who have an interest in ancient civilizations and their mythologies. This game is an outright must-play and is among the very best games to be released in 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: While I'm not sure it rises to the level of Outer Wilds and Return of the Obra Dinn, The Forgotten City earns its reputation as a compelling and well-made discovery-based puzzle game.Like the others, The Forgotten City has a mystery that unravels as you make further discoveries.  Where Outer Wilds' discovery is based on exploration, and Return of the Obra Dinn's is based on observation, The Forgotten City's is largely based on conversation.You'll participate in many (well-voiced) conversations with a handful of characters while you work out what's going on, and what you can do about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I stumbled across this from a YouTube video ages ago. The concept seemed really interesting so I bought it and finally got around to playing it a couple months later. _childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is an exciting adventure that is best discovered on your own, so I ask you proceed with caution as I will discuss some aspects of the game in this reviewThis time looping adventure isn’t particularly inventive as other games but its constantly progressing story and excitement make it unique. It was originally built as a Skyrim mod and gameplay wise, is nearly identical to that game, just with less combat and more focus on characters and story. What it excels in is its cast of characters that aid you on your adventure. While interactions with them aren’t particularly deep and are honestly rather surface level, they are charming characters who fit their roles well. Even the villains and the more mischievous characters are fun to interact with, particularly the side missions with Desius. The story has plenty of intrigue, a mysterious city where no one can leave, a missing daughter, a Golden Rule where a “sin” committed by one person leads to the death and destruction of everyone. The unraveling story provides genuine twists and turns that progressively get more interesting the farther the story goes. The game also has multiple endings. They have less to do with decisions you make and more to do with when you decide to jump off the ride. I accidentally reached ending 2 much earlier into the game, but didn’t get the true ending until I played the game a few more hours. Ending 4 felt like the true ending to the game. It has a really heartfelt ending that was definitely corny but really cool nonetheless and deals with some interesting philosophical dilemmas. These themes deal mostly in discussion regarding morality. While they never reach Philosophy 102 level, they are welcoming nonetheless. When taken as a whole, the intrigue, great ensemble cast, and world make this game easy to recommend to fans of laid back story games. Another plus is that the game can easily be beaten in a weekend meaning the time commitment is low. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game though the ending was a bit cliched for me and I finished everything in under 10 hours. _childDocuments_.review: I finished The Forgotten City a few days ago and I'm still finding my head spinning with how wonderful this game was. This is genuinely an incredible game. The writing was incredible and this may be one of the best written story games I have ever played. I had high expectations going in but this game surpassed them all by miles. It is full of plot twists and interesting developments, and the ending had me ugly sobbing (in a good way). I'm reluctant to say more for fear of spoiling anything, but this is a story that will stick with me for a long time.One thing to note - this game does have a few jumpscares. There is an option to skip most of these, but I'm unsure how it would work as it seems like you would miss a big part of the story if you skipped this part. I am a gigantic baby when it comes to scary bits in games and I coped (mostly) so I would suggest not skipping this part if you can.
