_childDocuments_.review: As one of the many who have experienced the Skyrim mod this game is based on, I was excited when this game was released 4 days ago. I knew the developers were working on a standalone game with quite a few changes, but I actually did not know what to expect overall even after watching a YouTuber stream the playthrough for a bit. I was intrigued and now that I have beat the game around 1:45 this morning, I am highly impressed with what Modern Storyteller did with the story line as well as with the graphics and technical aspects of the game.I only experienced one crash but I think it was due to a few other factors outside of the game. Otherwise, I did not experience any bugs or further crashing. This is one of the most important aspects to me.I did not expect the story line to take place during the Roman Empire era let alone expect there to be real world historical references, and a few subtle references(more like jabs to me lol) to this year/2020. I found all of this to be well written and highly intriguing. I personally took my time to get to know everyone within the city(in order to get the results I wanted) and each character was unique and interesting. I rarely skipped lines and when I did, it was only because I needed to do something very quickly. Other than that, I enjoyed listening to what they all had to say, especially Galerius(I never used the dialogue option that rushes the conversation). Furthermore, I actually wanted to debate(not just selecting dialogue options I wanted, but also voicing my stances out loud, regardless of the fact that this is a game) with some of the characters in the story LOL.The character models actually looked real good to me, pretty realistic. So much so I ended up kinda developed a sort of crush on Horatius LOL. :P I was surprised by certain revelations closer to the end(given the path I chose) and thought it was cool. I could go into more detail but that will go into my actual beliefs(Monotheism) and how I would interpret polytheism, for example, which Steam would rather us avoid since it is under the Religion banner. Let's just say I was impressed personally.I expected this game to be longer than the mod but shorter than the games I usually play and I was not disappointed. Not to mention I can replay the game and do things differently if I wanted to.  Personally, I think this game was worth the price I paid(got the bundle).Btw, Steam did not record my playtime for some reason, I have been playing this game for at least 10 hours total. :)Overall, I love this game and I am looking forward to see what Modern Storyteller as well as Dear Villagers will come up with next. :D
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: When I first started looking at reviews for this game to see if I really wanted to invest in it, I was left unsure whether or not it would be worth doing so due to the lack of detail contained within said reviews.  Seeing that the reviews were showing as 'Overwhelmingly Positive" I decided to persist.After purchasing it and loading it up, I wasn't quite how to take it when one of the first screens I saw in the game requested that I withhold reviewing the game until a certain point in the story.  If anything, it made me all the more worried that I might have made a bad decision in blindly purchasing this game without digging into the reviews.Well let me tell you, I am very glad that despite all my early concerns I managed to press on through to the finish of the game.This game was wonderful and kept me guessing as to what was going on until the very end, something that it seems is becoming more and more rare in games these days.  I will not be going into much further detail both out of respect for the developer's request that I mentioned above and out of respect for the experiences of anybody reading this review.  The story is wonderful and engaging, and I highly recommend that anybody who is on the fence over this game due to the ambiguity of reviews or feels concern over the developers' request to not spoil the story give this game a chance.I am certainly glad that I did.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr:Mystery game with very little in regard to "hard game mechanics" (text adventure adjacent), but boy, oh boy the characters and the story!If you like games like Call of Cthulhu, this one is a no-brainer!Slightly longer:The game is mostly about listening to dialogues and making decisions based on them, so it is VERY good that all the characters, you talk to, are very destinct (if sometimes a little sterotypical) and have interesting things to say!The theme is fairly heavily based on philosophical discussions about right and wrong, but don't seem to be to academic or too preachy. Mostly it is a joy to hear what some of the folks have to say and to get angry about some of the points of vies :)About the game mechanics... they work. It's not the main focus of the game, but (without any spoilers) they include clever ways for avoiding annoying back-tracings, that otherwise plague similar games.Also, I LOVED the epilogue of the 4th ending!Things, you might NOT like: -walking around and talking is mostly all you do. There is a stealth section and an optional "action section". But if someone were to call the game an "stealth action RPG" they either never played the game or doesn't know what these words mean.-You might get stuck. It's an adventure game. Sometimes there is a riddle and if you can't solve it, the game won't progress. GIYF, but this can be annoying.-There are themes like self-harm, abuse and even... health-care... if you will. Also, if you don't like politics in your game then... well, there is literally an election in this one, so... decide for yourself.

The fact that this is a finished game explains the time taken since it was announced a number of years ago. I highly recommend this game to everyone, especially those who enjoyed the original mod.10/10 Great game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily in my running for GotY. I waited for a sale, but it's completely worth it at full price if the concept intrigues you.This is a smartly-designed, smartly-written adventure game that lets the player feel smart too. Can't ask for too much more than that. The setting is intriguing, the concept is fascinating, and each character feels fleshed out without needing to dump their whole life story on you. (Some will if you ask) The plot has some really good twists; it all makes pretty logical sense despite the supernatural elements (give or take some "shortcuts" in the writing to keep you from replaying quests and having the same conversations in later loops); and it raises interesting arguments about morality and punishment. It's cool for a game to respect its audience enough to discuss that frankly, engage the player on the subject, and, in contrast to real life philosophical arguments, all in a setting where Godwin's Law doesn't apply...It also lets you be stupid, I accidentally stole a loaf of bread Elder-Scrolls-style, invoking godly wrath on the population. My bad, folks. Thankfully, most items can only be examined, so you won't be doing that too much. And it is clearly labeled when you'd be stealing; just practice good "trigger discipline" when you're poking around. (Might be one of the few instances where a Windows-style "Are you sure?" pop-up would be appropriate. "Are you sure you want to steal something in the town where everyone dies if you steal something?")Mechanically and graphically, it kinda feels like an Oblivion mod, complete with these staring-contest conversations with the city's inhabitants and a few uncanny animations. There's also some pretty casual archery-based combat, and one quest does turn things into an action-horror game for maybe a few minutes too long, now that I think about it. (Made sense narratively, at least). Most challenges are puzzles and exploration-based, and even that action segment can be bypassed by exploring other options (apparently).Most quests have multiple solutions. You can try to acquire items legitimately or attempt to steal them and survive to start the next loop. A lot of times, bribery is an option, but so is exploration. Even "boss fights" can be talked down, not with a "speech stat" but with sound, philosophical discourse, closer to later Deus Ex games than Fallout. The game itself has multiple endings, but there is a "true" one that it guides you to pretty obviously. I *do* wish the game was a bit more consistent about what items are "stolen" and which are harmlessly taken. I kinda sorta broke into a guy's house, which was fine, but was just allowed to help myself to his house key to keep exploring it? Most things laying around in someones house would be "stolen" if you do more than examine them. And I have a bit of criticism regarding one of the last big reveals:  It's really nothing ruinous, just mildly disappointing. I was still completely enthralled by the story after a brief eye roll.Oh, and the game has a very smart system to keep from getting repetitive, putting this himbo at the start of each loop that won't ask questions and will go do quests you already completed for you, because he's just a swell guy. Galerius is the real MVP.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow. I came in with no expectations, and was completely blown away by the end. This game might very well be my game of the year. It warms my heart that this game was made by a core team of only a few people who had a clear artistic vision and a story they wanted to tell. Consequently, the writing, the exploration, the storytelling, and the voice acting were all superb. I thought I knew a lot about the Classical world, but this game taught me even more I didn't know, while captivating me with its riveting timeloop mystery from start to finish. I also respect the game for respecting my time. Although it took me only 6 hours to complete this game, it was an extremely dense and high-quality 6 hours, in which I enjoyed every moment I spent with it. It left not a single loose plot thread behind, and made sure to give the player as much closure as possible. Everything was just really really well written. This game might even approach The Outer Wilds for the title of most well-done time loop mystery game of all time - an extremely impressive feat for such a small game by a small team.  TLDR: just pick this game up and go in blind. Approach this game as you would approach the Outer Wilds. Explore every nook and cranny, and actively connect the dots as you go. You'll be handsomely rewarded for it.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those few games i will hold dear in my heart for the rest of my life. Just like with subnautica, i wish i could forget just to rediscover it over and over. Its a interesting game, with a story worth listening to, with 4 endings, one that feels like you are cheating the system, one that feels like a bare minimum solution, one i havent found, and the canon ending. The canon ending, without spoilers, is beautiful. Its a mindblowing situation, that at the same time wonderfully resolves and gives you all the answers to all the questions you might have. And i know this might sound insane, but the ending of the ending, the part where you are done with the city itself and see the aftermath, gave me a reminder of something i havent thought about for many years and with that kinda changed my perspective on life. I cried for a solid 20 minutes at how beautiful the message was, how wonderfully alive the characters felt, how rewarding it was to take the long and hard ending, how philosophical the overarching topic was, and how well the story pacing was.This is a MASTERPIECE, maybe not by its graphics and gameplay flow, but its story definelty makes it one. Play this game, you wont regret it!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get it out of the way immediately: The Forgotten City is no Outer Wilds. As in: it's not a particularly challenging game and the time loop aspect is not used that much mechanically. The logic consequence is that TFC is more of a narrative and dialogue-driven game than a true investigation or puzzle game. It's also pretty short.But as a narrative and dialogue-driven game, it is bloody fantastic. Though it has a couple of questionable lines and doesn't always allow you to say the things you want to say (you don't really learn anything until you reach a flag that says you do, even if you figured that out yourself beforehand), TFC is fantastically written and voice acted, with compelling characters, interesting and well explored themes and a great underlying mystery that gets unfolded at a steady, absorbing pace. It's really immersive, and the atmosphere is exceptional. You really get awed at any major discovery or twist, and it's a testament to how well this is put together as an experience. Plus, it also looks good for the size of the team that worked on it, even though the characters's vaguely crossed-eyed stare bothered me a little every now and then.Overall, you could be slightly disappointed if you are hoping for a more involved mystery and deduction game, but if you take it for what it is, The Forgotten City is absolutely recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical that this game would be able to reach the same heights the original mod did for me, especially since I could remember most of the plot twists. I am happy to say however, that I was wrong.While players of the original will recognise characters and plot threads, and be able to predict some of the twists before they happen, there is still lots of new stuff here that I loved.it's an improvement on the mod in almost every single way; the game delves a lot deeper into it's themes of morality and properly fleshes out a lot of the underdeveloped plotlines of the original. There's also some new twists and genius writing, but none of it feels unnecessarily tacked on so the game doesn't overstay its welcome (something I wish more games would take note of).The only negatives would be that the game can be a little janky (very Bethesda-esque) but it really doesn't impact the experience when the writing is this good. I also didn't find the canon ending quite as satisfying as it was in the original, however I think the improved writing and voice-acting throughout the rest of the game makes up for that.To say much more about The Forgotten City would risk spoiling the experience, just play it, it's a truly brilliant experience and a definitive game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: Its like a playable episode of Star Trek Enterprise.A neat little timeloop game, about philosophy, justice, entitlement and the impossibilitry of being moral.While the mystery is very intriguing and well written, the philosophy ts a bit blunt and on the nose. It asks the bit questions, says there´s no way to answer them, but still finds one and ties it with a neat pink bow on Top.In classic Kirk fashion, you even beat a higher entity, by talking it into a logical conundrum.Mechanically its a mix of the dialogue structure from RPGs like Gothic, or Elder Scrolls, with a bit of clockwork Metroidvania sprinkled all over it. _childDocuments_.review: Youre trapped in an ancient underground city and any crime, even stealing a loaf of bread, triggers a death curse. And the only escape is a portal back in time, resetting the whole day. Youre mostly walking around talking to people trying to figure out whats going on. The catch is you keep items and knowledge from previous loops so at some point youre basically insta solving quests by walking up to someone and saying "yes i know heres the thing you need" and the game factors that in with different dialogue. _childDocuments_.review: I don't usually rave about games, but the fact that four people made this blows my mind. _childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is a neat little adventure game. Very reminiscent of old school point-and-click adventure games: you spend most of the game exploring the map, talking to NPCs, solving problems for NPCs, and unraveling the overarching mystery. There is some combat, however most of the game's challenge comes from figuring out what words you should say to various NPCs in order to get the outcomes you want. The game revolves around a mechanic first used by The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (and originally ripped off from the movie Groundhog Day) -- you're stuck in a time loop; the same day repeats over and over -- however you retain any knowledge or items you picked up on previous days when the world resets. Therefore if you ever piss off an NPC so much that they won't talk to you anymore, or if an NPC dies, and you needed to talk to that NPC, there's no need to reload a save: just start the day over afresh and all your mistakes are wiped clean. It's a short game; I got the best ending in one seven-hour sitting without using guides. Speaking of which, you absolutely should not use guides or spoil this game for yourself in any way. It's a rare, creative gem. Highly recommended if you can get it for $15 or less.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it. The character writing here is good, the overarching narrative and mystery is compelling, and it doesn’t overstay its welcome. I wish they had done more with the time loop - there’s very little of the “oh at this point in the loop X person will do Y thing, so I need to do Z” kind of thing that Outer Wilds did, but that’s more of a missed opportunity than a fault of the game. I also don't think the combat stuff really fit here - I would have much preferred it to have been purely focused on the adventure aspect. Looking forward to seeing what comes out of Modern Storyteller in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to thank the developers of this game for thinking about the plot at least as deeply as I did. Early on, when I learned about the main story conceit, and how and why the time loop resets, I thought, "wait — that seems like it wouldn't work! What if..." — well, I won't spoil it, but you get the point. Imagine my satisfaction later on when some of those questions I was asking out loud were things that  could ask other characters in the game — like, practically verbatim.Now, this isn't the first game that has allowed me to express in-game skepticism about the plot or setting. But typically it's done to "lampshade" a weak point in the story. It's a well-known tactic: if the story acknowledges the weakness, and tries to explain it, the player will be more forgiving, even if the explanation isn't that good. Not here.   skepticism, and somehow its plot gets stronger the more you examine it.This is a short game, so you may be hesitant about the price, but it absolutely delivers. If all games executed their concepts as well as this one, they'd be bargains at twice the cost.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this well done narrative driven mystery-focused game. It took only a couple hours for me to reach one of the endings at a moderate pace, but the story is so intriguing that I am going for more endings which I rarely do for most games.Because I recommend playing the game blind, I will use spoiler tags when giving certain tips with vague story impact that I wish I knew and could also help for people who feel stuck or confused.  Overcoming the latter can be satisfying for some people, but I also know that its irrelevant for people who want to stop playing as a result.  Here is what you need to know:+Very nice look and feel to an ancient part Rome, with great audio & voice acting.+Dialog options are excellent, and at times amusing, though...-I don't expect mocap, but character mouth movements & lack of mouth fidelity are somewhat distracting because they could be better.?This is not a first person shooter, so any combat you could do is quite basic, which is understandable because the game is far more about exploration and mystery.+Different objectives you can get and do are quite varied, some objectives can be done multiple ways, if I got stumped on most of them there was always another objective to make progress on, and way points are optional. When using waypoints though...-There are certain objectives for talking to certain people or going to certain locations that do not display any waypoint what so ever, even if you have met the person, or a location is known to you or most people.  This resulted in some unnecessary frustration for me.-Auto saves are ok but only appear to be invoked after completing some objectives or going to a new area that requires a bit of loading time, but in my opinion it should be done more frequently before talking to some new or important people.  Otherwise...?There are two ways that you can redo a conversation that's not going your way: Cause the time loop to restart, or reload a save before that conversation happened. Other objectives can be done during the current time before time loop restarts?Being aware of when you save is important because your death does not restart the time loop, and simply asks you to reload a prior game save.??+

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend The Forgotten City to fans of great writing, stories, puzzles, and philosophy.  An exceptionally well-written story with a dash of action/adventure that unfolds beautifully over the course of a dozen or so hours, though its density and richness make it feel longer.  It's best to play spoiler-free, and I'll do my best to ruin nothing in my review.It's surprising how much the creators were able to do with a simple gameplay loop that is essentially walking around and talking to people.  They manage to constantly present enough new fun things for the player to see and do that it never becomes a chore.  This also goes for the many quality-of-life elements that eliminate what would otherwise quickly become tedious.The twenty or so characters feel unique and well-rounded, each with their own perspectives and attitudes.  Through dialogues with them it becomes clear how deeply the designers thought about the moral and philosophical ideas presented in the game.  There is a delightful clarity that comes from not just being presented with a thought, but having first been given the opportunity to experience the events that gave it life.  It is sometimes heavy and other times uplifting, but always feels honest.The shape of the story and its execution are superb.  It's rare that a project is able to deliver any twists or revelations as striking as the many delivered by this game.  The game's ending is also immensely satisfying, with the designers understanding and delivering exactly what players want from a resolution.  There are even a few memorably laugh-out-loud funny bits of dialogue.There are many games that are not as well thought-out or thought provoking, are less polished, demand more of your time and deliver less than The Forgotten City.  Fans of great writing will enjoy every hour they spend playing this game, and will not regret the money they spend on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I begin to explain this? I have so, so many things to say.           First off, the soundtrack is phenomenal. The soundtrack "Let Us Live, Since We Must Die" adds a beautiful choir in the background while completing your quests and exploring the game. It truly makes you feel out of this world, and the beautiful scenery just complements the music.          Secondly, as mentioned, the scenery and graphics are beautiful as it's made with Unreal Engine. I can tell you one thing- the golden statues are REALISTIC. Almost indistinguishable from reality. The details on the gold are beautifully captured and it's visible that the developers put effort into this. Though a small suggestion for the scenery in this game is to tone down the light that's showing from the opening of the mountain/hill/whatever it's called.          Lastly, the voice lines! The voice lines are well acted, and definitely brings an adventure in your game. While voice lines and NPCs don't seem as glamorous in other games, the developers of The Forgotten City knows how to make them well and interesting enough for you to stick around. All of the NPCs that you will come across have different personalities and things to say so that nothing will be bland or non-interesting to you.           And to finish off this review, I want to say one last thing. The creators of The Forgotten City wanted to take a new and original concept and I can say that they almost perfectly executed this concept into the form of a realistic video game. Holy moly. This game overall makes me feel like I'm in a different world, and hell, it is amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: What I like about it is the exploration aspect that opens up new areas without too much gimmicky puzzle solving.  The animations are a combination of realistic and cartoony.  The time loop is not as annoying as it could be, but can be stressful knowing that you have to run back to the portal while being shot at at the end of every day or when a "crime" happens.  I prefer adventure/atmospheric/exploration/walking sims that  let me take my time, and the run away aspect makes me want to rush.  So far I haven't found a clock that tells me when the end of the day will happen other than getting dark.  The other thing I'm not fond of is that, especially in the beginning you are bogged down in tedious dialogue that really slows things down.  I don't mind reading interesting period texts in such games, but these characters come across more like boring Skyrim NPCs.   They seem very wooden and one dimensional, and basically used as examples to promote various social justice issues, which is a very big problem with propaganda that doesn't understand the art of subtlety.  So far it isn't terrible so I'm giving it a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: „The Forgotten City“ is an interesting game. You play as a stranger that, after getting seemingly lost stumbles into an… well… forgotten city that is inhabited by people that lived in Rome around the time of Emperor Nero. The city is well ordered, has the social hierarchy, morals and believes of that epoch but it also has a dominating feature, that determines all live there. The so called “Golden Rule”. Allas this is not the one they thought you in philosophy or church (“Do as on to others as you would want them to do onto you…” – if you did not pay attention …) but a more sinister version: “The many should suffer for the sins of the one…”. Which means that if one person in the city commits a sin, all others will be punished for that sin. And the punishment is severe. Problem is, apart from some very obvious sins like murder and theft (yes, not “picking up whatever the player likes when no NPC is watching” in this game, at least not without consequences), it is not always clear what will constitute a sin. And somebody is going to sin anyway, always. So, the search for a way out as well as for answers begins…All in all, it is a great game with some nice jokes/references. But it is absolutely story driven. Although you play form an ego perspective and there are a few weapons, there is nearly no “action” and fighting. There are some moments but they are limited. The people of this forgotten city are interesting and have their different characters. But you must like games where you have to watch and listen a lot. Also, due to the nature of the game mechanics, you must be also interested in games, where there is a certain amount of repetition. What people I believe should be aware of is, that this game is not set entirely in ancient times. I somehow missed that. You, as a character in the game, come from the present day (this is not a spoiler in any way since it is clear from the moment you start a session) and this gives the frame for your approach and the conversations. The framing of the story also has an influence on the reasons for the existents of the forgotten city and its rule. While I found it interesting in the end, people that really want to play a game set strictly in the ancient world of old Rome or antiquity might be disappointed. All others how a not bothered by this but are interested in the epoch in general most likely will have a blast. So, if its sounds like a game for you: Go on that river boat ride, leave Karen behind, jump into the world under the small temple and find out what misguided moral superiority mixed with love can bring…And never forget: “The Many shall suffer for the sins of the few…”  and they might get a golden teint.

_childDocuments_.review: I told my DM I was tired of the old beat everything down until you win shtick, and how awesome it would be to play a full Pathfinder/DnD campaign using wits, diplomacy, intimidation, retreat, etc and no violence. Then I picked up this game and really enjoyed the challenge, the interactions with convincing characters, the puzzles involved in doing just that! I also love theological and mythological history so it was great becoming immersed in a world where you can experience these things for yourself across multiple "ages" and beliefs in time. It also renewed my jaded feelings about the value of philosophy, even poetry, and was a though-provoking exercise in the truth of morality. GO FOR THE GOOD ENDING! The validation and gratitude for your compassion and determination is well worth it! It gives a wonderful sense of accomplishment. From the things I learned along the way that are applicable in real life, this was probably the most valuable game I've played since it gives more than fantasy escapism.Years ago, I played the Skyrim mod that originally inspired the devs to make this game and it was mind-blowing. Furthermore, at 4K, lock on 60 FPS and high settings (not ultra), even though the game runs more or less fine (still there are rare dips), it managed to utilize 99% of GPU. This is mind-blowing. _childDocuments_.review: This is a phenomenal game.  The setting, characters, world-building, and the balance of mystery/discovery, are in a league of their own.  I (a tired dad that usually can't keep his eyes open after 10PM) found myself playing until 1AM during a play session that started around 9PM, with no idea that so much time had elapsed.The closest comparison I could make to another game would be Outer Wilds.  I love that game as well, but The Forgotten City presents a world that is actually lived in, rather than simply static ruins.  A cast of 20+ characters, all well and fully voiced, with tons of interesting things to say, that react to the actions and choices that you make... this is a rarity in a smaller indie game like this, and it would be impressive even if it weren't done so well.  I found myself genuinely liking and disliking characters, in a way that didn't feel hypothetical or performative. The story felt intellectually challenging, in ways that are particularly relevant today.  Its themes of ethics, religion, history, and human nature feel timeless, despite the ancient setting.Even though the game has many hours of fascinating and engaging content, I definitely finished my time with it wanting more.  I want to live in this city, with all of its terrors and its flaws, it started to feel like home in a way that few games have before.  For now I'll have to settle for waiting for whatever comes next from the talented folks at Modern Storyteller. Or maybe I should start collecting old Greek coins?

_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is a mystery adventure involving ancient Rome and time travel. The game has you 2,000 years in the past in a hidden city in a chasm in the mountains of Italy, somewhere off the river Tiber. You're trapped! The people living here that aren't all gold explain that this city is ruled by an unknown god and that they follow 'The Golden Rule' which states 'The many shall suffer for the sins of the one'. The golden statues are those that failed this rule, but what exactly is considered a sin? Nobody is sure, but the denizens of the city are convinced that if one does sin, the entire population will be turned to gold.How did you get here? Who is the 'unknown god' that rules this place? Is 'The Golden Rule' even real? Wait... did that statue just whisper at me?! Was it always looking right at me?!If you are at all intrigued, go in blind and stop reading my review, only real complaint I have is it only took me about 8 hours to get all 4 endings, but if you need more:

Amazing story, beautiful art and environments, the voice acting was superb, dialogue was outstanding, and a classical historian and philosopher's dream. Makes me want to reread Epictetus and Seneca. It was the ending that really got me though. I failed to send Galerius on his errands, and thus did not save everyone, which bothered me as I did not realise how attached I had become to each of the characters...until the end. I greeted them like long lost friends. I cannot recommend this game highly enough. If you like puzzle-adventure games, with a bit of a twist, just play it. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a while to finally purchase this game. Although people kept praising it, it always looked a bit off. But I can definitely agree with most people: This is a great game! If I had to compare it to others, I would say it is in some regards similar to the outer wilds but in ancient times and more philosophical in nature.Great fun!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A fun premise involving time buggery. A puzzle game that involves learning about all the events that take place within the Forgotten City, and figuring out how to best order your involvement.I personally had more fun with the original Skyrim Mod, from memory I just enjoyed the aesthetic more. But most likely it is because that was my first experience with the story, and once you know the plot it becomes less impactful.That being said, it is still an enjoyable experience which puts problem solving and a love of history first and foremost.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, it's not a long experience, but it wasn't a full AAA price so that wasn't a huge deal for me.A fun world to explore with a good number of mysteries and problems to solve through repeated loops, and it has a clever in universe way to remove the tedium of solving the same problems again and again each loop.slight spoiler But yeah, a good fun game in the "Break the loop" genre
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The story is well composed, I enjoyed my playthrough unraveling each secrets the game has to offer. As many suggest it's better to play this game without knowing anything beforehand. My suggestion is that the game will have slow buildup early on, and it will make feel a bit lost and stuck. Just play through it, follow any lead with clear pathway, once you reach some points in the story, it will become a good ride.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This is a campy game, and that's not a bad thing in itself. The one-note characters are full of petty drama (bullies, rheumatism, cartoonish greed, and so on), and the plot zips around tropes, cliches, and high school ethics. It's fun. (It's also frequently unintentionally funny too, which I enjoyed as well.)The problem was that the game never develops well. Each of the 20+ suspects has exactly 1 issue with 1 solution, and then that character is done for the rest of the game. (Some characters don't even have an issue, like Sentia.) Money is used for exactly 2 things and then it's done. The timeloop mechanism isn't really used for anything in the game either outside the first hour either -- you'll be reloading a save file about as often as you bother timelooping, and you won't find substantial branching paths that requires resets to explore. I was disappointed there wasn't more interlocking characters/time stuff.  It was an underutilized mechanic. (In part because there's no in-game clock. You're never like "what happens to X character at noon?" or "how can I solve two problems that happen at the same time?" or "what order should I solve problems in?" Instead everyone just stands there.)The game also starts you off with a whodunnit, which was fun -- but then veers away from that hard. It felt like the game had an Act II that was cut -- which would have made the timeloop more necessary, developed some of the ethical themes they wanted a bit better, as well as given some variety and more twists -- like an involvement of the present in some way. The thing I enjoyed most was the beautiful buildings and the layout of the city, which never got old. The interiors of buildings were incredible to walk around in. The voice acting was also better than I expected, even though some of the modern diction made me laugh. (In the beginning of the game, the Centurion solemnly describes Time Paradoxes as if he had grown up watching Terminator -- the other characters are similar, sprinkled Latin not-withstanding.) The attention to historical detail was great -- it was so random to be able to look at Roman artifacts in this game -- it's clearly a weird merger of interests that made the game distinctive.If you play this game, you'll have to manage expectations: it's a game made by three people, and at first there was enough polish to hide this -- but in the end it shows. I enjoyed some of those limitations -- it was funny they would play clap audio without clap animations -- and didn't enjoy others. (Characters that never develop.) It's also much campier for a game that was praised so seriously -- not in a bad way -- the canon ending was sweet -- it was just unexpected.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I find this to be a nice gem of a game. I went into this without any pre-watched gameplay or spoilers of any kind and I certainly recommend this method for others too. The game is dialog/narrative driven with a well thought out story, along with multiple endings. I picked it up at about $25 and it was well worth it. Modern Storyteller has a new fan!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Short, sweet, and a wonderful puzzle experience. This game excels at drawing the player into a unique and interesting world while also challenging not only their problem solving, but also their ideology and their take on the nature of man. With only a ~$20 USD price tag you should definitely give this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply a masterpiece. I can't think of even 1 bad thing about it. It's got a great storyline, so many twists and choices and very interesting characters with great voice acting. Multiple endings too. I went for the best one in my first run and I am glad I did. It's so satisfying. The music is just so so good. Easily one of the best ever. The little combat that is in it is simple but well done.It's also very short so it's easy to replay and check out the other endings.Final score : 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A well-written investigative mini-RPG with a fail-forward time loop mechanic. The graphics, controls, and animation are simple for the era, but enough as to not be a malus. What really sells it are the dialogue trees that account for all sorts of actions, various states of success or failure, and quests with multiple solutions. The characters are nicely rounded and nearly all of them have an extra layer or two beneath.I do wish the logical/philosophical aspect was a little broader - as it is, succeeding in conversation challenges is usually pretty simple, often just involving "exhaust your conversation options but don't pick the one that is obviously picking a fight."All in all, the game is short, for the price, but it's an experience I'm glad I had.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The fact that this game was made by a core team of 3 absolutely blows my mind. The Forgotten City has an extremely intriguing narrative that unfolds in a very satisfying way as you learn more and more about the city that was forgotten. The actual gameplay itself is somewhat basic, being largely conversational based with some light combat mechanics, but the focus of this game is by far it's curious characters and the predicament the town has found itself in anyway.This game is 100% worth trying out if you enjoy logic-based puzzle games and/or games with quite deep narratives, and definitely lives up to it's price point.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: If you like going around investigating weird ♥♥♥♥ in a well contained but diverse world, this game is ideal. There's a little action involved, but most of it is voluntary. It's a cozy kind of creepy (unless you do a specific quest that the game will warn you about, which is creepy af) and in spite of being a time loop game, you don't have to go around repeating ♥♥♥♥ you've done before - the game offers you great shortcuts for things you've already figured out.Tons of little details of roman/greek mythology spread around the place, and also being the core foundations of the game, is also highly enjoyable.You can probably go do a full completionist run of this in less than 8 hours - I don't feel like I've missed much, and I took it very casually and have made some extra restarts to check things out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of history of ancient civilizations, debates of morality/ethics/religions and sometimes their parallels and contradictions and all set in a very intriguing and thoughtful adventure mystery title that sprung off a Skyrim mod...I cant not recommend this game enough. Sure, it started slow and rather boring. But, as the game got going there are some very good social commentary here from a lot of different angles with some great characters. Not to mention, we got a Legionaire constantly quoting Stoic philosopher Seneca. Whats not to like? In our crazy modern lives coming off 2021, We need more Stoics.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, this is not a game that hands everything to the player on a plate. It's not a game where you can build up your character and fight through any scenario. In short, it's not the sort of game that I normally play......but I loved it!Here's why I bucked my own trend...The rest of the reviews may praise the graphics, sound, dialogue... I do, too. They may criticise some aspects. Like any game, it's not without fault, but the few that I found were minimal compared to the pros.Cons:1. I have a medical problem with memory. I'd have liked a map. In some games, this weakness of mine is critical. In this game it was a minor problem, but I'd still have liked one.  To most players this will not be an issue.2. Whilst I like quests that have no "See it, do it!" markers, on a couple of occasions, that philosophy gets a bit extreme: you're going to really have to dig in to your source of patience, at times.3. "Googly Eyes!" In general, I loved the NPCs (non player characters), but at times their eyes are a bit 'spooky'. My advice is to get over their gaze and listen... don't look into their eyes! Their voice acting is great!4. Err, that's it.Pros:1. Graphics are great on my PC. I do have a system that allowed me to set everything to 'Epic', though.2. Voice acting is great. Trust me, that's very important.3. Quests are good. Again, they don't always have defined markers, but that's spelled out for us in the download page. Explore! That's my tip.4. Historical info is there to be discovered, for those (like me) who like that sort of thing. It seems to be very well researched.5. Re-play value. I messed it up a bit, first time around. I knew I had and went back and tried again. The result was worth the effort (all I'll say in a review). There is definite replay value in this.6. I don't know if the overall mechanic of the game is unique, or not. I played a version of this on Skyrim. It is certainly unique there. It's definitely unusual, charming and compelling.*7. The story and history is where this excels. Epic!So, for me at least, the few gripes were far outweighed by the tonnage of plus points......I'd still like the 'googly eyes' sorted out.* For those, like me, who played a version of this as a mod on Skyrim, don't worry! The plot is similar, but not the same. It's well worth doing and you won't get it right, if you only base your ideas on that mod!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: really fun and clever game. Good replayability, lots of fun hidden things to find and stories to learn. I love the little historical touches (like the graffiti that mimics modern graffiti and might seem like a joke but it is actually similar to real ancient graffiti that has actually been discovered). Though the replayability helps, I am still left with the feeling that I would like this game to be a little longer/broader. I wish there was a DLC
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The concept and setting are great but the execution was kind of lacking. Characters and writing are fine but nothing incredible. I never felt like I was solving anything, you basically just run around exhausting dialogue trees and following objective markers. The time loop mechanic is also poorly used. There is some pretty bad pop-in, and annoying loading screens between certain areas but the game is pretty overall. I did run into a few bugs with NPCs floating, getting stuck in conversations, etc, but for the most part its technically sound.Could've been great but it needed more time in the oven.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best story-driven game I have played in a very, very long time. I just finished the main ending and was so blown away, I had to leave a short review.For playing this, I can only recommend you turn off the option to show quest progress. That way the whole experience will feel less like a game and give you the freedom to think and connect leads for yourself, which is something games rarely do today.So on a last note, what did I enjoy about this game so much. For one, the writing is superb. Every single action any character makes is something I would expect them to do, based on their personality. Not only are they non-contradictory, quite a few are also really smart. Even if these characters have some piece of opinion or worldview that on first glance seems irrational or cruel, they are always able to explain themselves and make a sound argument for their position.By the way, did I mention you can have debates with smart characters where you are able to change their mind and they might just be able to change yours? On interesting topics of philosophy???For me personally, this game is one of the best experiences I had in gaming in quite a while. Thank you, @TheModernStoryteller :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This is what I'd call a social time loop, trapped in a mostly Roman city under an intriguing Golden Rule: if any commits a sin, all will turn to gold. Who could enact such a rule? How would they know a sin was committed, and what exactly counts as one?It has some great plot twists and an extremely satisfying ending. I really enjoyed playing it with objective markers turned off!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: If you're interested in or are studying narrative design, get this game.I don't care how you feel about Roman history.  I don't care how you feel about first-person exploration games.  I don't care how you feel about walking sims.If you're interested in or are studying narrative design, get.  this.  game.That said, if you're looking for an RPG in the vein of Skyrim (which, interestingly enough, this game is a standalone version of a Skyrim mod, which I also highly recommend) or New Vegas, where you can roleplay and fight to you heart's content...this isn't really that.  You can pick gender, color, and origin stories for your character (which can affect how the game turns out), but that's it.  There's some combat, but its locked to just a couple of sections (which is for the best, because it isn't good).  There's no leveling up or picking new traits/perks.  And the game is much shorter.  I got the canonical ending in four hours.  But what a four hours it was!I wish I could go into details about the story and characters, but the details would spoil the experience for you.  And yes, I hate it when people say 'I can't say anything, just buy and play lol" but that really does fit here.  So much foreshadowing and easily-missed details that flow together to create a grand story that really sets a new bar for game-based storytelling.Once more, with feeling: If you're interested in or are studying narrative design,
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. A friend casually recommended this to me, and I am glad I jumped on it immediately. This is one of the best story-driven games I've played. There is so much polish, right down to the portraits on the credits. The voice acting is so good. The story and main time loop mechanic were done really, really well. There were a couple parts that were actually genuinely creepy, where I had goosebumps the entire time (this doesn't generally happen to me, not even in actual horror games where it should). I played through it in around 11 hours, and loved every second of it. During the hours I wasn't playing, the game was never far from my thoughts, and I think it may stick with me a while, yet. I didn't complete all of the quests, but still managed to get the canon ending on my first try. I am interested in going back to finish the quests and see if I can get the other endings. Oh, and speaking of game endings, I thought the way the ending was done in this was so good; I love that it - and how it - gives proper closure, and doesn't just gloss over everything in a 10-second wrap up. I really am hopeful that Modern Storyteller will come up with another game in the not-too-distant future, though it may be hard to rival this one... I hope they come close.There are some games that, when I complete them, leave me with no desire to play other games for some time, as the story and experience just weighs heavily on me. I have a hard time jumping from a game that leaves me in a melancholic state, into anything else right after. NieR (the original game on PS3), my current #1 favourite game of all time, is one that did that very well. This is another. The feeling is one that I for some reason enjoy to sit in. I'm so glad to have played this game, and I enjoyed several lines that really made me ponder life, outside of the game.This is as close to a perfect game as it could get, with only one minor problem for me: the inability to turn off the dialogue text. This game is entirely voice-acted, so there's no reason to have text on screen. It detracts from immersion, as well as the fact that I always end up reading it ahead of the voices, and that's irritating. I can't seem to stop my eyes from drifting down and reading - it takes real effort - and I hate it. But it's a relatively minor issue, and one that wouldn't stop me from buying, playing, loving, and recommending the game to anyone.I played through this with Proton, so many thanks to Valve and all the developers over the years who worked on that... Would have never got to play it, otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City
