After learning how to do that ending (no guides, just picked up on it from talking to one of the characters) I couldn't resist and I expected every part that happened next, which is certainly not a bad thing as i was laughing about it for about 5 minutes straight
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is a fantastic mystery story that is best experienced knowing as little as possible. Go buy it now.The opening is a bit rough but stick with it for like 30 minutes and you'll soon be hooked. The first dialogue you have is weird and might give you the false impression that the writing is bad. There are story reasons it is the way it is, the writing is actually stellar throughout, just talk to more people and it will become apparent. Seriously, the writing, from nuanced characters to a beautifully unfolding plot, is all excellent.The main reason to play this game is to solve/discover the many mysteries that it contains. While there are the obvious big mysteries you'll ask yourself within 10 minutes of starting (why am I in an ancient roman city? Whats up with the gold statutes?) there are also many smaller mysteries to solve along the way like finding a missing person or figuring out why a guy is angry. That is really the hook that gets you, wanting to know every detail. As a big fan of mystery media in general it is unfortunately often the case that fun questions often don't have good answers, creators only worrying about the intrigue and not the integrity of the reveal. I believe that almost every single mystery or question this game presents is immensely satisfying to uncover, leading to some wonderful moments.I also firmly believe that despite being almost exclusively about seeing mysteries unfold, this story could only be done in a video game. Sometimes I encounter story driven games only to ask myself why this was a game not a movie or TV show. Not here. This story could not be told any other way, a real shining example of the power of an interactive medium.But before I suck this particular ward against the evil eye too hard, it is of course not perfect. Most of the gameplay is just talking to people and clicking every available dialogue option, and while you talk the camera is locked onto a not very impressive face (its a team of 3 people that made this, its a miracle it looks as good as it does, but still...). While there are some "action" sections, the gameplay in those is pretty weak. So most of what you actually do is... well, its ok. It is functionally just there to facilitate the story and it does that, and no more. But all this really only matters for the very, very few people who hate mysteries. If you truly cannot get behind a good story told well, and NEED some more typical video game gameplay, then, and ONLY then, might this game not be for you.Aside from that small (possibly theoretical) group of people, you will like or love this game. And if you really are not sold yet and need just a tiny push, know that at the end of the game
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: What an excellent game!  At 15 hours it was far shorter than I expected to spend on it, but I feel every penny was well-spent on what I did play. There is very little I can say without spoiling, so I'll make it point form.- The 'major' ending was an excellent surprise to me, because in order to actually achieve the solution, I had to completely change the strategy I went in with.- The additional endings were each unique and satisfying.- It would have been incredibly easy for this to start feeling tediously repetitive, but the systems put in place to speed up repeated sections keeps it well-paced and satisfactory.- I expected to spend longer because I expected to get stuck on puzzles.  I did at a couple of points, and looked up a couple hints to continue, but honestly most of it was designed in a way that made the solutions instinctual without feeling like hand-holding.  Wonderful design!- Upon achieving the final, 'major' ending, I haven't had such fun with an ending since Dragon Age: Origins.  I wish I could talk about it but suffice it to say it had that feeling of having traveled a great way in order to get to that one final, triumphant, fulfilling walk through the ending - and again, comparing how much time I had to spend in DA:O to get to THAT ending, that's saying something about this game's ability to get you invested in achieving the best possible result in a much shorter amount of time.I haven't really 'finished' yet. I'm going to dive back in and try and get more acheivements and such - but I already feel that this game deserves all the (if you'll excuse the time-appropriate word!) kudos it has been given.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of really good ideas in this game.I don't want to get into spoilers, so I'll keep this review short. The writing is clever and interesting. The world map is interconnected, easy to traverse, and fun to exist in. The game isn't long, so it's punchy without overstaying it's welcome. The only points I would take off are for annoying loading points and for strangely stiff character bodies during conversations, but I think that's remnants of this game originating from a mod. Even with those minor annoyances, this game is well worth the cost of entry.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Strong writing. Clever puzzles. Some elements a bit easy and snowballs pretty heavily once you have some stuff figured out, but there's some catharsis in that. It's not flawless for me- mechanically it's a bit clunky so the action segments left me cold, and I found some issue with it around the time you're replaying the game for different endings (left vague to prevent spoilers) but still a strong recommend overall.

_childDocuments_.review: It's everything I wanted in a game. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely my game of the year. I didn't expect much, but it's truly amazing, in-depth, and absolutely beautiful, with fantastic voice acting and compelling, complex characters. There are a few bugs (I fell through a rock into the abyss once,) but nothing incredibly game-breaking (especially if you spam quicksaves like I do lol.) Also, trying to keep this as spoiler-free as possible, (only spoiler-tagging for those who are very picky about knowing nothing going in, it's very light!)  To reiterate that in an incredibly spoilery fashion that I do NOT recommend those who haven't played read (but I had to get out, and man, I hope the wonderful writing team reads this because it means so, so, so much to me,)  There's not a single character I thought was written poorly. Almost nothing I would change. This might literally be my favorite game ever, no exaggeration. "Winning" the first time  I already thought the game was amazing, but getting my second ending cemented this game as an absolute eternal favorite in my mind. Just... wow.The one thing I'd change is that I'd like a map or minimap, since I'm kinda directionally challenged and found myself getting lost on the beautiful map constantly, lol. I spent like 10+ minutes trying to figure out how to get up to the Bluffs and ended up Googling it. But generally? Just... wow. Thank you to the team behind this for putting this masterpiece out into the world. Seriously.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the Skyrim mod several years ago, and absolutely loved it.  I was cautiously optimistic about this game - was concerned there would be nothing new, that it would essentially be the same story in a new location. I'm very happy to say that's not at all what this game is. Although some of the story lines and characters are similar, they are not exact duplicates, and they definitely stand on their own.There may be a few inconsistencies in dialogue due to the inherent looping nature of the game, but the stories are excellent and the characters are well developed. The writing is very well-done, there is an ever-present feeling of dread (recognizing at any time you can say or do something that leads to the...end... of the many) and generates a strong drive to continue on. I'm also really glad that mechanics exist (and are very well built into the story itself) to prevent the looping from feeling like a reoccurring grind.

So, when I wanted to use only the flashlight, I would unintentionally also use the gun, which made me shoot accidentally twice pfft well, it happens anyway. Perfection does not exist, as in the main character says to Pluto heheI'm very excited about what this game publisher will bring next!!!

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful entry in the time-loop mystery genre. I would ask you to read no further and instead just jump right into it, knowing as little as possible about what is going on in this game. That said, I will not spoil any core story threads, of course.I am a huge fan of Outer Wilds which is why this game was recommended to me. Time loops are wildly fascinating to me as a concept and The Forgotten City delivers a very well designed implementation. That said, this game's time loop is quite different from the one in Outer Wilds and both games have very different strengths and weaknesses in my opinion. So do beware if you were recommended this game as being very "Outer Wilds-esqe", there are some key differences.The main one, in my opinion, is the way progress is made. In Outer Wilds, knowledge is everything. You can get to all of the game's endings in the first loop if you know what you are doing. This is not entirely the case in The Forgotten City. Here, that concept exists as well, and you'll be able to finish the game in far less loops if you know where to go and what to do. But it is a little more linear in that you need to find certain key items to proceed in some areas and quest-lines which you carry through loops.I will now list some pros and cons that specifically stood out to me while playing The Forgotten City. I will try to keep it as spoiler-free as possible, but still, as a last warning, if this game just sounds intriguing to you, especially if you think you'll enjoy the Roman/Greek setting, read no further and just start playing.The story is very well thought through and the twists and turns you encounter are very interesting and at times quite shocking. I find this to be the most important aspect of a story-driven game like this by far and I was very pleasantly surprised by the quality of the writing in this game.While playing the game, I felt a strong sense of agency. It felt like many things I did had some real consequences and changed the city in meaningful ways - until the start of the next loop, of course.The characters are incredibly well fleshed out and every inhabitant has their own, very distinct, personality. They each have their own values and goals and really feel alive in that sense. You will grow to like certain characters and dislike others, not necessarily because the game is designed around forcing these sentiments on you but just because you might work well with certain character types and not so well with others.The game has a strong philosophical undertone and deals with very heavy subjects like good and evil, different types of moralities and different ways to exert power over others. But it never forces a certain view on the player, instead remaining open minded and asking questions rather than providing answers. I find it fascinating how well this is implemented here.If you enjoy lore about ancient civilizations, this game will hit a lot of the right buttons for you. It is heavily grounded in Roman and Greek mythology but does extend to other civilizations as well. If you know a lot about ancient mythology, you may see certain connections way earlier than someone who does not which I personally find to be very rewarding.The (English) voice acting is great. It conveys emotion and tone very well. This is quite impressive to me considering the small size of the development team.However, exactly that small size of the development team brings me to the biggest con in The Forgotten City - the graphics.To be fair, the graphics of the world itself - the textures, the landscape and the buildings - do look good. Nothing groundbreaking yet quite immersive. But most of the game is not spent running through the streets and caves or marveling at the architecture, it is spent in direct dialogue with the inhabitants of the city.And the facial animations look... rough, to say the least. They seem very robotic and uncanny and while the voice acting itself is great, the NPCs' mouths don't reflect what is being said at all. They do show a certain degree of emotion through facial expressions, but they are often too subtle to notice or too extreme to look pleasant.I would not be surprised if this turns some people away from the game. That said, it did not bother me a lot while playing. Sure, having amazing graphics can improve immersion by a ton but at the end of the day, this game is about its story and the secrets you find within the city, not about photo-realism. So let me end this point by asking you to try the game anyways. Graphics are a big part of a game's first impression but this game is definitely worth pushing through that barrier.The controls are sometimes a bit difficult, especially when it comes to interacting with certain objects or jumping between platforms. This might be a personal issue but there are times where I died unnecessarily because I was unable to correctly interact with zip lines, specifically. That can be rather frustrating but luckily, it did not happen all too often.To reiterate: The first impression of the game might be a little rough due to the facial animations. But once you get to the core of the game - the story of The Forgotten City and its inhabitants - you will quickly forget about that and find yourself enthralled with the many layers of intrigue and moral dilemmas that the game throws at you. And once you beat it, each ending (except one which should become very obvious very quickly) will feel fulfilling in its own way, even if there is one "canon" ending.Tl/Dr: If you enjoy mystery, philosophy, mythology, ancient civilizations, time loops and/or great stories, look no further and give this game a chance - you won't be disappointed.

The first hour is a bit much, like all these characters talk to you, random quests pop up and the map looks more confusing than it really is. _childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game. A little on the short side and could really use a map, but a very engaging story and a great mystery to solve. One of the few games I've played that claims to be about morality and doesn't boil it down to Jesus or Genocide, the character in this game feel more complex and well realized which makes everything feel much more immersive. I look forward to seeing what the team come up with next.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It always feels weird when you have to swim against the stream.I really have no idea why this game is being lauded as such an example of an excellent narrative. The story and writing are certainly solid, but nothing to write home about. The characters work well, but they're in no way special or memorable. What actually impressed me the most was the action and platforming sequences.I really struggled with whether or not to downvote this game, mostly because it was developed by such a small team and I want to applaud their efforts and hope they'll go far, even if their game didn't really click with me.Also, I feel better about my Thumbs Down knowing that it will be drowned out by the myriad reviews from people who seem to love this game.

No trailers no screenshots no nothing.The first few minutes of the game made me think that he played some joke on me because in the beginning the game felt bit weird. However now, after completing the game several times I can say that it was really amazing, So I guess thanks for the recommendation friend you earned my trust!I can really only recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished playing with 60% of the achievements in 10 hours, with no hints / spoilers.  I finished with two of the four endings, including the canon ending.This was a very pretty and satisfying game.  I was under the impression it was a "puzzle" game but it is more of a detective/investigation game - almost entirely conversation driven.  The path is relatively straightforward, and  doesn't require much skill or finesse to find your way through.  Fun, entertaining, light-weight (in terms of effort).  That said, there is also a fairly heavy ethical question being explored regarding the nature of right and wrong.  Definitely heavy subject matter if you are just looking for mindless entertainment.My biggest complaint: you can never put anything down (as far as I could ever tell), which means your inventory can fill up with duplicates and flotsam.  Not that it matters, really, since your inventory also manages itself and you never have to actually dig through all of it to find the note you want.  Based on 10 hour length, visual appeal, interesting topic, and relatively low challenge - 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: So good! Its a detective style story where youre running around in a strange world trying to put together pieces that never fit like you want... until suddenly they all do and then you get to satisfyingly reap the rewards of your work. Very beautiful game, and well designed to help keep you on track and not frustrated. Also good level design to avoid tedious backtracking. Great game, give it a go if you love a good story and world to explore!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Going into this I didn't expect it would involve explaining the concept of memes to an ancient Roman lady, I was pleasantly surprised. You can comfortably see most of what the game has to offer in less than 10 hours, but it will be a very worthwhile experience. I'd recommend going into it completely blind if the concept of doing detective work in an ancient Roman setting involving time loops remotely interests you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a well written, excellent game and well worth playing. It's funny but I'm the type of player where if a game hasn't grabbed me within the first 30 or so minutes, I'm usually done with it. It needs to be(or to feel, at least) compelling from the very beginning. With "The Forgotten City," it took some time to gain any sort of traction; obviously, the only way you can advance the narrative & plot is to keep talking to people. All of them. It takes some time for a given plot line to reveal itself but once it does you're off and running. This game was beautifully put together from start to finish in all aspects. It almost puts me in mind of "The Talos Principle," in a way, although the games are quite different. In this game, it's like the puzzles are the people themselves and you use them to unlock the clues you need. But there's a lot of world exploration and lore to be discovered as well. Definitely one of the three or four best games I've played this year. At least an 8.5 out of 10!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: In an age where games can push 40+ hours in length before you can get the "full" experience, and yet is packed full of frustratingly inconsequential filler, it's incredibly refreshing to have a game which takes a nice round 10 hours to beat, but feels so incredibly rich, and dense in the content that it gives. I never played the Skyrim mod this was based on, but I had heard good things about it over the years. I'm glad I finally took the plunge.The story is brilliantly thought out and the city feels very reactive to everything you do. The developers clearly did their homework regarding the mythologies and cultures on display, and they didn't skimp on the voice acting and animation to bring it all to life. As far as indie passion projects go, this is well up there as one of my favourite experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent mystery adventure game with a cast of memorable characters and plenty of twists and turns. In a way almost reminiscent of The Swapper or The Talos Principle, it builds its world around some key questions about morality and culture, and explores them through every part of its world. It also features genuinely engaging dialogue, where you need to make meaningful choices geared towards the perspective of the person you're talking to. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: so i have done everything there is to do in the game. my review really doesnt change. i personally wasnt a fan of the story, but all in all, still an excellent mystery game. i spent a lot of time with the game paused while i did other things. so if you rush through it like i did, i got about 5 hours of actual game play time, and i knew (or could accurately speculate) the entire story after ending 2 about 3 hours in. at that point it became a race to the finish and was no longer a mystery unraveling before me.ORIGINAL REVIEW:Alright so lets start out with the bad. The writers for this had absolutely no clue how to write characters. Each character is basically one overly exaggerated emotion and no real personality what so ever. Along with this the story feels very forceful, you try and choose to turn left and the game says nope your going right. Its pretty rough stuff, but onto the good.I went into this expecting something closer to skyrim... and boy was i dissapointed. This game is nothing like skyrim, heck you cant even freely kill people without breaking the world. However, when i started playing forgotten city, i accidentally found something amazing. This game is by far the best mystery game i have ever played. In fact i have been gaming for over 20 years, and 15 of which i have been searching for good mystery games; and in that time, i have never found a mystery game that satisified me to this extent. Forgotten city is by far a 10/10 mystery game. Character writting is rough in fact its like a 6/10, but the story and mystery aspect of it is so good, that i cant help but it give it a fantastic recommendation.

Took me around 9 hours to get two of the four endings, so it's not a long time but is a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: What a huge let-down.  I was cautiously optimistic about this one, and was hoping that I could really immerse myself in _A_ story.   But wait! -- within the first minute of the game I have to choose one of four classes, each of which has a unique advantage.  Which one should I choose?  I have absolutely ZERO information at this point, so how can I possibly make an informed decision?After choosing one at random, and wandering around, I encounter my first NPC, and I am given the choice of telling him either the truth, or a lie.  Again, with ZERO information (is he a good guy?  a bad guy?), how can I possibly make an informed decision?  Am I expected to just guess randomly, and make tons of quick-saves, and go back and re-load if I make the wrong choice? If there are numerous decisions of this type, the number of possible branching options will quickly become unwieldy, and I don't have enough extra brain cells to try to remember which of multiple saves consist of "OK, I said FOO to this guy, and BAR to that woman", but it turns out I should have said BOO to that woman, so try to remember which save file corresponds to BEFORE I talked to that woman,  ....The final straw in the coffin lid was -- after a very cursory search -- apparently the game has FOUR endings!!!!  WTF???  When I read a story, I want AN ending, not FOUR different possibilities -- ESPECIALLY if my choices are going to determine which ending I'm going to get, AND I'm given ZERO information with which to make an informed decision, so it's basically 100% guesswork.Couldn't the devs even decide how the story is supposed to end?  Reminds me of those annoying movies, where you sit through two hours, finally see THE end (most movies only have ONE), and the end makes no sense whatsoever, and I look up reviews and find the director -- and this happens WAY too often -- says something like "Oh, yeah, well, you see I didn't really want to have an ending that actually makes sense, because I wanted each viewer to have their own interpretation of what happened, and make up their own mind what happened at the end".I want the creator of the media to have a well-thought-out ending, not have me try to figure out what they may have been intending -- that's just lazy storytelling, and it's why I am PAYING  them.  I DESERVE to be lazy, and NOT determine how the story is going to end (based on my decisions which are essentially purely random decisions; with no information I may as well be sitting next to my computer with a pair of dice, and just rolling them whenever I'm presented with a dialog choice [izzat supposed to be FUN??])) -- that's why I'm PAYING for a story that somebody has actually thought out, including how it ends ...If, on the other hand, I had been given a bunch of information, and I had to sit back and think it over, and enough factoids could be teased out of conversations that I have already had, books that I may have read, observations that I may have made, etc... and THEN I was expected to make an important choice, THAT would be fair, as long as I am given enough clues to work with, but that is emphatically NOT the case with what I have seen of The Forgotten City.Rant over - if you like this sort of thing, the game looks gorgeous, runs incredibly smoothly on my middle-of-the-road PC, then go for it, but not for me ....

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game. The dialogue and the choices you make actually feel as though they have weight. The story and the mystery revolving around the small city the game takes place in keep you locked in, and personally I lost track of time playing because I was so invested in it and didn't want to segment my experience. Not to mention the atmosphere has was so well done, it persuades you to stay there, no matter how many times you loop, and the music is beautiful, captures the Ancient Greek and Roman feeling so well. In terms of gameplay, I guess you could call it a walking sim, but more like a rogue lite,time looping,walking sim. Most of the game you're speaking to the npcs, trying to figure out why you're in the city, and how you can escape, while picking up a few side quests from them that'll help in that as well. Most of the quests revolve around speaking with more of the really well acted and fleshed out npcs, and looking for a key item that'll solve the side quest; certainly not super long, branching, rpg quests, but this isn't an rpg. Combat is basically nonexistent, except for one side quest where it's mandatory. There's a few physical "puzzles" in this game that mostly consist of making yourself some platforms, but the story and dialogue are the only "puzzles" you'll really need to think about, connecting the dots to better understand the story. The looping is pretty simple, the only times you'll really need to loop are if you actually did something bad and the game forces you to loop, or if you have to speak with someone about something, and you're unable to interact with them in your current loop (death, angering them, and the like). There's also a time limit for a day, but the time for each loop is really long, the only time I ran out of time was when I decided to knock out all the longer side quests, and even then I got them all done, plus an extra 1 or 2 of the shorter ones before I ran out of time. I went in completely blind and on my first ending only needed 3 loops.I tried my hardest not to spoil anything, since the story is everything for this game, but it is worth it. I only needed 6 1/2 hours to see all the endings (due to me just loading up a save for the last 3 after my initial playthrough) but I can say with certainty that it was an amazing experience. I don't even like these kinds of game but I took the dive and was blown away.So yeah, just buy this game, and I hope the experience sticks with you as I feel it will with me

_childDocuments_.review: I might be a bit biased since ancient Rome is my favorite part of history, but being able to walk through the city, meet the citizens, discuss real philosophical topics of the time, and enjoy the meshing of Roman, Greek, and Egyptian culture in a profound, intelligent story full of interesting characters—for me personally, there isn't much better concept in gaming. I find it especially difficult to compare  to anything else because it is so rare to find a game that offers a compelling adventure storyline, meaningful RPG elements, and occasional, fun action sequences that never last too long for you to get bored of them. The first game in years that I've bothered to 100%, including all the achievements. If I had to pinpoint some negatives, however negligible, the loading screens take a bit too long for a game made in 2021. Also, the price tag seems a bit steep, considering you can finish the game within anywhere between 1 and 8 hours (depending on endings; 1 hour if you rush the worst ending, 8 hours for all endings), and getting achievements that I've missed during my first playthrough took me about 12 hours in total playtime. Then again, I got the game through Humble Bundle for basically pennies, so who am I to complain? Overall, a solid 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a true time loop, but more of a progressive time loop. Luckily, the time loop mechanic itself shouldn't be considered the main selling point. If it weren't for some light gameplay mechanics, I'd consider this a walking sim and it definitely seems to scratch a similar itch. The game is short and I really enjoyed the journey so I give it a thumbs up and look forward to whether this team creates more stories in this vein.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a sucker for time loop puzzles where you have a set amount of time to figure stuff out before looping, but the fact this game is set in an ancient Roman society is what makes this game stand out for me. The attention to detail and historical accuracy is amazing, mixed with an extensive understanding of Roman/Greek/Egyptian mythology and how it played into their everyday lives, elevates the quality of the gameplay to the point where I FEEL like I'm exploring a real Roman city. I am yet to play a game that captures anything close to this experience.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: This is a...really good video game.Time loops are ripe for video game potential and it's kind of surprising it's taken this long for there to be so many of them. Dying in a video game and coming back to try again with knowledge of what's about to happen is in nearly every video game, and is actually pretty similar to a time loop, only game narratives rarely take that aspect into account. Deathloop, Returnal, Loop Hero (actually I don't know if this is a time loop?) and even an expansion to the first time loop game I can think of, The Outer Wilds, came out this year, so maybe something's in the air, like when Armageddon and Deep Impact came out the same year.The Forgotten City's version of the time loop has you mostly talking with people and solving their problems mostly through dialogue and exploration. Since so much of what you'll be doing is talking to people, it's important that this aspect is good, and it is. The voice acting performances are great and the facial expressions are impressive for a small indie team. If there's an issue here, it's with the strange way the screen centers on the people you talk to and they continuously stare straight into your eyes. Since the game is first person, I honestly have no idea how this problem is solved, and seemingly neither does anyone else. And you get used to it, so it's not a big deal.I don't want to talk too much more about the game for fear of spoiling something, but the act of figuring out what's going to happen, what problems are there every day, and what can be done to solve it is rewarding. This is one of the best games of 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a must-play for anyone who loves ancient history and immersive storytelling. Despite starting as a Skyrim mod, it stands on its own as a polished and engaging game.The attention to detail in the world building is impressive, though some secondary areas could use a bit more life. While there are characters moving around, some areas can feel empty. Nevertheless, this is a minor issue that doesn't detract from the overall experience.The writing is one of the game's strong suits, delving into issues of morality, power, and human nature. If you are the type of player who doesn't like to spend time reading or talking to other characters most of the time, maybe skip this one. The dialogue choices ultimately affect how the story unfolds.Gameplay-wise, the focus is primarily on exploration, with some occasional "fights". I also found the game to be bug-free, with no crashes or technical issues. This game can be finished in 10 hours, maybe more if you want to explore all endings and/or get all achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: If you remotely love history--especially that of the Roman Empire and past that--I have to give this an immediate thumbs up. I think most people know this was originally an Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim mod created for that setting in mind, but as a standalone game, it's set in our world. With that comes some interesting implications as you explore the story. It is best to go into it blind. The gameplay is not difficult and it's better off for it. The main enjoyment comes from the puzzle solving of the plot and getting to know the characters and solving the mystery behind The Golden Rule. My first time playing it had me sitting there in voice call for a friend for 4 hours straight, only leaving at around 5:30 AM. It's a great time and a memorable experience. I hope the devs continue making more games.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing Outer Wilds, I really didn't think any game would capture that sense of exploration and discovery. I'm so pleased I was wrong!If you've played Outer Wilds: this is basically the same game transplanted to the Roman Empire; there's less content in terms of locations to discover, but there is a lot of fully voice-acted dialogue that you need in order to figure out what's going on. The theme is classical mythology rather than sci-fi, can't say more without spoilers.If you've not played Outer Wilds: this is a hard sell but basically don't read anything about the game before playing it. If you like classical mythology, classical philosophy or Roman history you'll probably get a bit more out of it, but the main focus is on discovering what the various characters are up to, and those are human stories that are relevant in any era. There's a small amount of combat but it's not complicated or difficult, and it's not the main focus of the game.Very good game, keen to see what these devs will come out with next.

_childDocuments_.review: That was exactly what I wanted. _childDocuments_.review: This game was exceptional. I went in with 0 expectations and boy was I shocked. As a historian, I really really liked this game (despite the shoddy Latin pronounciation from the VAs, can't blame them though). I loved how I could walk into a random villa and I could just hover over a mosaic or pot and the game would tell me all about what they depict. Not to say this game is a walking/museum simulator... far from it. This game challenged me in a way I haven't felt since Disco Elysium. I wanted to figure out the mystery presented to me to solve. About an hour in I felt like I did as a child when I was reading a choose your own adventure book where my fingers were shoved between so many pages at once, except it was my brain shoved between threads and lines of inquiry.If you want to play this, stop reading other reviews and just delve into it blind. _childDocuments_.review: If your bar for quality has dropped so low to the point where this is some of the best writing in gaming, please seek help or play more narrative video games.For a game made for "Adults who like figuring things out for themselves" the mission path is extremely straight forward, and there isn't much thought required to get through the game. Just go with the blatantly obvious solutions or just cheese your way through it because the game breaks at the slightest hiccup. And aside from a single moment, nothing really feels clever. For a game with a timeloop mechanic, they do nothing to give you interesting puzzles or narrative beats to get around by using the timeloop. Most solutions basically play out with you choosing dialogue until you say the wrong thing. Then on the next loop you go back and say something different. And it's not like you really have much input either as the options are pretty rigid and several times the game would not let me say the one thing I very easily could have said to sway the conversation in my favor. It's so surface level and rigid that I can't fathom why anyone would think the dialogue or choices are interesting. I mean I literally got the "True" ending on my first run through and I didn't even feel like I did anything special to deserve it.Speaking of the ending, the big reveals in the last act are unbearably corny and play out like something you'd probably see in a random Gmod level or a porn game. And despite coming out, what, almost a decade after the mod? It still looks a plays like a skyrim mod, though I'd argue the original mod's visuals almost fit better and Skyrim's facial animations are about on par with this 2021 release. I seriously can't believe this game was made in Unreal 4. It looks like it was made Unity, by people who don't understand lighting and post processing.I just don't understand what anyone sees in this game. The illusion of choice is paper thin, the ending is eye-roll worthy, and it's just kinda corny as a whole. The 4th wall breaking jokes are facebook level humor and having a "Karen" joke literally 2 minutes into the game does not set a great tone.

_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is sort of a whodunnit, set in an ancient roman settlement. Tunics and pottery galore. But there’s also fantastical elements, like science fiction and time travel mixed in. The twists is that no one’s been murdered, per se. Instead, someone triggers a cataclysm , ending society. And if it ever comes to that, you get to loop through time to start the day anew.The setup is great. I just wish the game was a little more complex. It plays out sort of like a side-quest from a role playing game. Characters and scripting feel very rigid. Uncovering the plot boils down to chasing quest markers. Meanwhile, the time-bending aspects turn out to be more of a narrative hook than a gameplay one. Let’s face it -- a time travel mechanism that lets you restart the level with some progress saved in between is not that interesting.It’s fine though. But I’m constantly reminded of games like Paradise Killer, The Return of the Obra Dinn, and The Painscreek Killings -- games with a design ethos that permits them to leave the player to their own devices.There’s a lot more agency there. A lot more resting on your shoulders. If you can’t figure out how the web of intrigue connects, you’re out of luck. No quest log or map markers to make the process more digestible. Just deduction and observation. I miss that in The Forgotten City, along with a narrative that’s a little more interestingly weaved than just exposition spouted from a series of characters. But it is what it is I guess. It’s a careful recommendation from me.

There are a few bugs here and there, but all in all, this game is a hidden treasure.

_childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic entry into the strangely more and more frequent genre of "time-traveling mystery games". Not that I'm complaining, The Forgotten City is addictively intriguing and designed so that solving mysteries in any order you'd like is always a smooth and fun process. You're goals are always clear and there's multiple endings that match the player's investment in solving the mystery. I do think the mystery elements fall off a bit as the game often hands you the answers for free with little warning.However, what takes the mystery's place is a large cast of organic, varied characters and surprisingly snappy and often blunt dialogue. The game also raises several interesting philosophical discussions without cramming any one answer down your throat. It makes you think about your view on morality and how you view others' actions with a level of elegance I've seen from very few games. If the concept of the game alone has you interested then please try this one out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game that I enjoyed and left me wanting more, however that is the biggest issue as well, the content is good but there is not a huge amount of it. In my 4 hours I finished the game with the "Canon" ending saving everyone possible. I think for many people a 4-9 or so game might be a big ask for almost 30CAD. I will be looking forward to what they put out next though, the story and mechanics are great, there is just not enough of them, especially the latter. Keep that in mind if you're someone who buys games for longevity. Also it's a little on the easy side. Some of the whispers are nice especially early when you're unsure if it's on your side or not , but overall the puzzles and combat could be a little tougher :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original Skyrim mod (or Skyrim in general) but I thoroughly enjoyed this game! I love anything that's story rich so I decided to give this a try. The world was amazing and I loved exploring the city. The voice acting was also top notch, it really brought the characters to life. I think the way the time loop was utilized was clever and was used to it's full potential, as opposed to just being used as a "do-over". I do wish we could've personalized our character more and created more relationships with the other characters; it felt when it came to who was "with" and "against" you was pretty set in stone. The game is also a bit on the short side, but for such as small team it was super well done. If you like story rich games with a basis on exploration and a bit combat (use of a bow and arrow), you should check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through two endings at this point and I have to say that this game was a gem.  I don't know why Steam's suggestions never landed me on this game because this was right up my alley.  As someone who spent a chunk of their life as an archaeologist, the attention to historical detail was tickling.  I wouldn't mind getting stuck in the atmosphere of this game for eternity.Beautiful game, interesting characters, well thought out details/dialogue/story, and lots of little surprises along the way.  The golden statues are the most unique "enemies" I have ever encountered.  Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing, absolutely amazing. It has a great and intriguing story, with 4 different endings. I have the first 2 so far. I remember when this was just a Skyrim mod, and this is even better now. It really benefits from being its own thing and using real history instead of Skyrim lore, it feels amazing to play even though I'm already familiar with most of the twists. There is some clipping through walls here and there, but for such a small team it's quite impressive. 10/10 experience overall, recommended for anyone who enjoys solving mysteries, history, or is just wants a break from the low quality stories in AAA RPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: "This is a mystery adventure with multiple endings. It rewards thoughtful conversation and exploration, not brute force. The fate of the city is in your hands." This message from the beginning of the game sums it up pretty well.While the facial animations are pretty barebones, this is easily overlooked thanks to great voice acting, a fantastic atmosphere provided by the soundtrack and graphics, and a solid A++ story. With memorable characters, surprising and interesting twists and turns, and rewarding payoffs for both individual character arcs and the overall story, the plot of this game had me hooked from beginning to end. The game is only 8-10 hours long, but it's as solid an 8 hour game as I've ever played. Well done, devs!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: is a creative masterpiece of storytelling and RPG. Very few games, be they indies or triple A, come even close to its level. This is a refined story-rich experience in which your choices truly do matter. It doesn't hurt that its premise is a philosophical conundrum the keenest of philosophers have struggled to adequately address for ages. If any of the keywords above sounds like something you're interested in, this is a must-play for you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. I binged the heck out of it, on a mission to get all of the endings. I really enjoyed the world, getting to know all of the characters, and unraveling the mystery! Listen to the other reviews! Go in blind! Don't look anything up! It's worth it! I hope there will be more like this!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is an impressive accomplishment for only 3 devs. Remarkable, really. Tight storytelling, good dialogue, great voice acting, well-rounded characters you care about, suspenseful plot. Should appeal to anyone who likes adventure games, puzzle games, roguelike/timeloop games. Think of the roguelike Hades crossed with Groundhog's Day.  Interesting historical quotes and philosophical musings serve as garnish. It does have some flaws - it starts really impressively, and peaks during an intense action sequence around the 2/3 mark, but I found it sagged a bit in the home stretch, and there were a few bugs that while not game-breaking, did damage the immersion. In one case, two characters got stuck in a door and kept repeating the same dialogue loop. In another, a message flashed that "_______ will be unavailable until _____ has finished his errands", but he never finished them so I had to reload and closely follow him during his errands to make sure nothing went amiss.That said definitely worth playing if you're tired of the gaming wasteland populated by cynical cashgrabs, copycats and tryhards, and crave something crafted with care and detail and...brains.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: My friends know me as a gamer, and recently one of my friends asked me "What is the best game you've played in the last year?" Without hesitation, I said it was The Forgotten CityIf we're being honest, I think many of us have played time loop games, and many of us have played games with mystery and intrigue. However, not since I was a child have I gotten so wrapped up in a game's story. I found myself sitting at work trying to work out different bits and pieces of information and forming theories on what was happening. Until beating it, I quite often found myself eager to get home so I could play more and see how the story played out. A fair warning, I get creeped out easily, and there are some things in this game that sent chills down my spine. There are definitely some creepy sections. Also, I got the best ending on my first playthrough, and didn't see much point in replaying.Last tip is DO NOT LOOK UP SPOILERS. Go into this game blind and you won't be disappointed :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Skyrim modding, I of course was one of many to play through and enjoy the Forgotten City for the original Skyrim. The original mod managed to stand out and remain memorable amidst a sea of other mods due to its focus on an interesting time-loop mystery. A little more than half a decade after its first release, Forgotten City has been re-released with a revised storyline and in its own engine, and I think this remake still shows its quality.Sent back in time, the protagonist is tasked with saving an ancient Roman city from committing a sin that would devastate its people. I found the story pretty interesting with some nice twists around and the characters to be alright. The voice acting is very passable; I personally have a low bar for that sort of thing, so none of the voices nor the music felt grating or irritating to me. Overall, the immersion was solid.The gameplay is a little lacking, however. Most of the time, you're doing puzzles to achieve a goal, like how to enter a locked manor, or fetch quests, like finding an item for an npc. There's a light amount of combat that's a bit iffy - it's all ranged combat with a bow, and sometimes it feels like arrows that should connect with enemies don't do so. Still, you're given what feels like a surplus on arrows and health so it's a non-issue. The gameplay definitely takes a backseat to the story.Overall, The Forgotten City is a fun mystery game to get through.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Fairly short game, i finished in 7 hours with all endings.The map is small but it feels dense, walking doesn't feel like a chore and generally things make sense for natural progression. In fact, I don't think I used the active quest line, there was generally a good progression that you should be able to track which is great. This time traveling detective type game was fun. There was a lot of different ways to approach things.theres a decent chunk of back tracking and some situations are annoying when you have when you missed something, but the game kept me very entertained.Question system could use a little more depth, but the conversation flows were interesting and made a lot of sense with each character.I think the game could have been a little more detailed (more searching for clues rather than running around), introduced more combat situations/ enemies, but otherwise I am happy to have played this.5 is average8/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I'd describe this as a great soup with a few grains of sand mixed in. I loved the character writing, this game has some fascinating conversations, I especially enjoyed one that you have near the end of the game, about a person trying to defend their beliefs in a crisis of faith. The topics covered put a large smile on my face, I felt like most of the conversations let me express myself as a modern day history nerd sent back in time, to confront the people she had only read about. I was let down by the ending though, it featured a trope that I'm not the greatest fan of (though it was excecuted in as good a way as it could've been in my opinion), and it felt a bit too cheesy for my tastes. The gameplay that isn't talking or staring at the immaculately crafted world, was a bit weak as well. Though it overall didn't detract much from the massive smile on my face this games conversations and attention to detail put on me.

It has some fairly intense action as well, which I was not expecting, but it was well done. I encountered some very minor bugs while playing, but nothing game-breaking.Most of the puzzles involve talking to various people, figuring out what they want and how to get them to trust you. Thankfully the dialogue is very fully explored and I rarely found myself unsatisfied with the dialogue options provided.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as this game did have points of enjoyment, I cannot recommend it at its current price or stage in development. Other reviews draw comparisons of this game to other much better games, skyrim, fallout, outer wilds, and to be honest I see no comparison at all to Skyrim or any RPG other than how the game looks as an unreal port of Skyrim walking mechanics. The gameplay is a very intense visual novel, It seems like the developer wanted to write a story instead of making a game but then had to find a way to translate it into a game. Every 'puzzle' that could be possible is either ridiculously easy or literally explained by the game. 'Choices matter' comes down to dialogue mattering for when you talk to a character, that's it, there is no RPG element. There is no development of your own character, and all the unlockable items/ equipment are extremely simple. Comparing it to a game with a somewhat similar plot, Outer Wilds is like this game but an actual video game complete with environments and care putting into blending gameplay with narrative. This game feels like all the work was handled by the writing team, there is very very few actual moments of gameplay.Spoilers on the Narrative structure of the game:

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time playing this game! I enjoyed it a lot, and that enjoyment stems from a plethora of factors - of which the largest were the world's architecture, the characters, and the multiple endings. The architecture of the The Forgotten City is aesthetically pleasing, the characters were interesting to get to know, and I found the multiple endings to be an excellent feature to the game. The multiple endings add to the experience instead of detract, unlike other games that put up the appearance of being multi-choice but actually force you into a specific scenario no matter what you pick, and it is probably the biggest contributor as to why I had such a great time; knowing that my actions had consequences and could lead to different endings was exciting.Overall The Forgotten City is a terrific, engrossing game that I highly recommend. Furthermore, if you're out to learn a bit about the history and culture of Rome, then this game is likely for you.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since I was this immersed in a game's story, and even days after finishing it I miss it a lot and wish I could reexperience the whole thing with a blank slate. _childDocuments_.review: A fun little Groundhog Day mystery, set 2.000 years in the past.I liked trying to piece the mystery together, even going so far as to take notes on all the residents. Enough to recommend the game, but only just.The game is horrendously optimized, to the point of almost making me quit.For a heavily narrative-driven game, the action and horror elements felt very misplaced. Especially considering it's a game of trial and error in a time loop, where the MAIN appeal of the game is talking with "suspects", being able to die in the game and having to reload felt very silly and tiresome. Having a conversation and accidentally making them mad at you? Fine, I'll do something else and try again on the next loop. Having a conversation and accidentally making them kill you? "You died - reload latest savegame". Completely immersion-breaking. Now I - me in real life - know not to say that, but my character died and does not. Why they couldn't work in to the story, that dying triggers a time loop, is odd to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten City is a great mystery adventure with a small touch of action. The star of the game are all 20 characters and your mission to unravel their secrets, issues, complots and mortally. The amazing writing, voice-acting and many dialog options makes this task extremely enjoyable (even so there is a little bit of the uncanny valley in some of there eyes).Exploring the background of the hidden city, the Golden Rule and trying to find a way out it, is as fun as well and takes you on a philosophical journey of the meaning behind sins and human nature.The structure, pacing and freedom is amazing in the game, which always gave me something to do, but never overwhelm me. Every step felt natural following the previous step, without the game forcing me down a path. There just a few issues with the game. The combat felt completely unnecessary and was not fitting to the overall gameplay. There isn’t much of it, but it was never challenging or having a bigger purpose. Having puzzles instead would be much more fitting for the game. The game is full of invisible walls, which makes the game sometimes confusing. Some places appear to be important, because of the lack of invincible wall. I wish the game would feature more cleaver level design. The graphics and style look great overall, but many assets feel like, they were bought in an asset shop of the Unreal Engine. Overall an amazing game. A must-play!

_childDocuments_.review: I can not recommend this game enough.The premise is that you get caught in a "Groundhog Day" style time loop, replaying the same day over and over again, gaining more knowledge and items as you go. The people of this ancient city you find yourself in live under one law: "Many shall suffer for the sins of the one". Basically, if one person breaks a law, everyone dies. You are tasked with finding out which of the 20 or so residents is going to break the law, and to try to prevent them, causing a time paradox that will fling you back to the present day.You can try your hardest, but you will have to live through a time loop at least a couple of times. Every single character has their own personality, and you will come to either love or hate every single one of them by the end.This game does a brilliant job of making you feel smart, as though you're a real detective. There are 4 different endings that can be achieved, but you'll have to work out how to get them on your own.There is only the one main quest that you can follow all the way to the end within a couple of hours, but I highly suggest following all possible side quests and threads you can find.The only issues I really ran in to was that one quest was sort of bugged and never got checked off of my side quest list, but by the end it resolved itself. The game can also chug a bit from time to time.If you're even slightly interested in this concept, do yourself a favour and stop reading anything about it. Play it yourself, and avoid spoilers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This was one of the best narrative games I've played in years. Definitely amongst the top handful I've ever played, and narrative games are my main genre.The first 20 min or so was the most awkward part of the game, but it played superbly well. I'll be looking forward to this studio's future releases.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully designed game with wonderfully designed quests. This game is, as a time loop game, pretty good, and it's great at doing what it does in terms of storytelling. The story beats unfold pretty well, and although I kind of spoiled myself halfway in, the game still does a good job of guiding you through the story while also giving the player a huge amount of freedom.While The Forgotten City is great in most regards, I do have some problems with it, mostly the ones carried over from its origins as a Skyrim mod (although this game is made in Unreal Engine, I believe). The facial animations, dialogue trees and even the combat are very similar to that of Bethesda games, and while I'm fine with the first two, I really don't think the combat is that good, although it takes only a very small and optional part of the game. I do get the feeling that the design of the city and the graphics are also very Bethesda-like, although that's more of a good thing than anything, while the lighting does look a bit dated. The entire Ancient Roman aesthetic and the deeper levels with even older ruins are a nice touch, too.I really like how much thought the developers put into making the game as friendly to players as possible. You're given an overwhelming amount of choice but there are choices that are recommended by the developers' decisions. There's also some pretty solid writing and voice acting in here, with characters' relationships going very deep - there are about 20-30 characters in total, and since they all live in a small town, they all know each other and as such their quests are very much interconnected. Every single quest flows into another one, with useful items you can get from one quest being able to help you out in another. The focus on dialogue and also, towards the end, philosophical debate, is also a nice touch - instead of using skill checks to be able to convince people, you have to use instead your wit to figure out a line of debate that can win people over, or you can go do another quest that might give you some more leverage. The fact that it's a time loop allows you to try things over and over again, and the nifty addition of Galerius as a sort-of messenger makes it way easier for you to go back to the beginning of the loop and just not do a lot of the tedious work needed to save everyone. There are also pretty helpful notes from the developers, telling you to do things like getting creative to solve a problem, or warning you that you might not like a quest ahead if you don't, for example, like horror elements. The ending (the canon one, at least) is also extremely satisfying - most media I consume like to leave endings up to the interpretation of the audience, and that's fine, but I honestly like a more drawn-out ending that allows you to actually see your effects. The amount of time and effort you've put into helping people, too, determines your choice of ending, and having such a satisfying ending feels very much rewarding.While the game's runtime might seem a bit short, it's a great game to just sit down with for an evening and binge, and I think the quality really justifies the price more than the runtime does.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, this game was great! A very tight, fun story with great gameplay mechanics and multiple interesting hooks. It didn't take super long to get through, but going through the various endings was excellent and fulfilling. I especially loved the 4th ending. In this game you're a modern person put in an ancient world, and this pays off with the highlights of this game: philosophical discussions about the nature of morality and punishment, connections built with each individual, and the knowledge you gain along the way that can be practically applied. The further you get, the more you feel like a true farseer, messing around with different timelines for clues, and plotting how these pieces fit together. It's insanely satisfying, and the world reacts as you manipulate the fates of the city. The game is quite beautiful, especially the architecture. The characters look alright, but their writing and personalities are really what set them apart. You come to appreciate some, hate others, and some you may never even meet in the city. Your choices and dialogue very much effect the way people interact with you throughout, and by the end they can even give fewer details depending on their relationship with you and the results of your choices.With 4 endings (I got three out of 4 in my last play sessions) you'll have different ways to finish the game, but the 4th ending is the real highlight, and doesn't require that much more work.Overall an excellent title that kept me paying attention the entire time, and replaying the ending to find every last detail.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Best played going in blind. Come for intertwining storylines and characters, and the intricate ways that they all interact.There are some action segments, but that's not really the main point of the game. It's more about people management and making choices. My #1 advice: Don't be afraid to try the wrong thing. Experiment.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so as a massive history nerd whose favourite videogame genre is choice based narrative games (especially ones with time travel puzzles) this game feels like it was literally made for me. I loved it so much! The story was amazing! it had great depth, it was thought provoking, it had mystery and interesting plot twists, that characters were all well fleshed out with their own unique backstories and character arcs. What a journey! And the history, I loved how researched it was - I even learnt a few new things. It all worked together to make the world feel so real even with the supernatural/time loop. The writing made me laugh out loud quite a few times, especially the more meta lines like talking about living through a pandemic and how memes have ruined the name Karen xDIt's amazing what the Dev team have been able to come up with and I thoroughly enjoyed myself. 20/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game, a bit short for the price, but that's fine, the overall experience is super memorable. Gameplay wise, the game is a masterpiece, can't believe it was made by such a small studio as their debut. But their inexperience rears its head in the writing, while the plot and the characters are super well-written, the ending kinda hits all the cliches of a game like this (can't go any deeper than that for fear of spoilers, I would 100% recommend this game to everyone though), its still well written for what its doing but there's also that feeling of experience something amateurish. That's not a bad thing imo, they can always improve from this. They have already announced that they are working on a second game, can't wait to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really sucked me in with its world-building and engaging dialogue.  It's a fairly small world that has been masterfully crafted and populated with interesting characters and a really good mystery.  It also delves into some philosophy and the psychological implications of living in a world under a 'golden rule'.  The Forgotten City has some basic gameplay to help provide some variety (ie. climbing, exploring and arrow combat), however this game is placing most of it's focus on the story and having conversations with the characters.  It's a good thing that the voice acting is amazing and the characters look good.  But the actual writing is what hooks your interest.  It really made me want to choose all the dialogue options and I got excited when a new dialogue option is open up.  Learning more about the world and its characters, as well as unravelling the mystery keeps you going. Some games make me want to skip the dialogue, but I listened to the vast majority of the dialogue, which is a testament to how everything comes together.  The good news is that the game won't frustrate you with its puzzles and you're constantly rewarded with new reveals at a steady rate.  Perhaps it could have given the player more opportunities to figure it out for themselves or play around with potential solutions, but this could have easily made it more frustrating than fun.  I doubt you're ever going to be stuck in this game, but that just means you get to experience this amazing story without any roadblocks.  I experienced two bugs that fortunately didn't stop my progress, which I would say is really good considering how many possibilities there are with what happens. Overall, I got the final ending in just over 9 hours which is the perfect length for a game like this.  If you enjoy interesting narratives then definitely get this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

Overall I found it very pleasant and spent about 10 hours playing. Would definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. The first thing I saw was the unique concept. The game brings up a lot of philosophical questions that question morals and make you think. They made the plot have multiple endings, and none of them contradict each other which is surprising. The game also includes a good amount of mythology, and while I'm not an expert on ancient mythology, from what I saw everything that wasn't deliberately changed for the plot was correct. I also really enjoy time travel mechanics like the game uses.The second thing I loved was the art style. The game is beautiful and contains several different types of architecture that matches their IRL counterparts. The character design is beautiful, which is especially important because the majority of the gameplay is interactions with characters. The characters could be animated slightly better, but it's not awful currently. The third thing I enjoyed was the gameplay. The game itself isn't that long when getting all of the endings, but the achievements require a little more dedication to find. There are unique elements, such as not being able to utilize some elements until you find things hidden around or acquire them from other characters, and I appreciate how the game has something so that when you wind back time, you don't have to redo anything that is necessary for the plot again and again. My only complaint is that there were one or two parts that weren't clear to me how to advance.The final thing I liked is probably the most significant aspect of this game. The story is amazing. There are several stories, all of them are elaborate and connected. Some of them are essential to the plot, others you have to dig around a little. Either way, they are immersive and make the game feel more real.Overall,  is a good game. Its story and style combine nicely to immerse you into the game and make you question what you know as right and wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City was a fun game that I recommend. TFC is a puzzle adventure game where the player is stuck in a time loop and has to figure out the mystery of how to break the loop.  The game basically takes place in an ancient roman town where the main game play is figuring out how to manipulate people so they'll cause some action that will cause some other person to react the way you're hoping. There's environmental puzzle solving along with Machiavellian puppet mastery.  Sometimes I'd say the wrong thing and p.ss people off and kill any chance of progressing further, so I'd just commit a sin real quick, which triggers Armageddon and then restart the loop. The narrative revolves around basic religious philosophy where all the towns people will be killed if any body commits a sin. There is a ton of dialogue that I was tempted to skip through from time to time. This really is a more narrative driven game than I usually play, but the narrative and exploration went really well together in this case. I liked how they showed that the different ancient religions have all been basically the same gods just renamed by each new group of people that comes into the land. It was cleverly conveyed. The Forgotten City was a lot of fun and a compelling play. The game took 7.5 hours to finish and I mostly played it in one sitting. I got three of the four endings, including the real ending. The 'cannon' ending was bit wacky. Personally, I liked the ending where some jerk gets burned alive causing the time loop to be broken.

The amount of detail, time, and effort the creators put in was amazing. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: This was a magnificent experience. _childDocuments_.review: Note: My playtime does not reflect my actual playtime. I bought the game after I already finished it.An intriguing little game with a cool concept. It has a great atmosphere and great voice acting. It's not particularly challenging, but you do have to think a bit. The videos and screenshots might give the impression that this is an action game, but that is pretty far from the truth. The game is 90% talking and solving various issues, and a tiny bit of action. _childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The forgotten city is a time loop puzzle. A formula that is slowly starting to become more ubiquitous as people figure out better ways to utilize the medium. From the outset the game has an attractive premise to it where mystery abounds in every corner and avenue.It's a shame that the game doesn't trust you to solve it. (OH DAMN)This game is getting a hard recommendation from me. This is a medium that is completely carried by two things. It's writing and it's avenue of discovery. Outerwilds, I still hold, has the best container for their story, as well as the best avenue of exploring it. But the forgotten city has an edge that none of the others have, great presentation. By siphoning some player agency, the forgotten city has a much better tailored experience to present to the player.However the game is TERRIFIED that you will get stuck. A quest journal is fine, it helps with making sure that a player has referenced material (even if it is a little on the nose.) But you are rarely invited to figure out solutions yourself. It really boils down to one issue.The "quests" are broken down into way too many steps-Talk to person A receive quest to talk to person B (quest marker)-Talk to person B and receive quest to investigate site A (quest marker)-Site A has a linear tunnel to go through-Learn something new, go back outside to continue to the next quest.Quest markers and step by step layouts betray the power this bottle'd time loop experience have to offer. There is not that much territory to explore and not that many people to talk to. ~15-20 people total, and running the entire distance of walkable space is about 10-15 minutes. You do NOT need to hand hold in this environment and it severely detracts of the natural experience of feeling really clever when you do figure something out.But about that presentation. This. Game. Has. Got. "IT". This natural desire to complete it just to experience the full story it's trying to tell. I am spell bounded to say the least on how to win. A proposition that continually gets more complicated the more I discover.Summary: I am enjoying the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game. I just fear it's not going to be very long. It's too damn hand holdy in trying to get you to the end of the game, but the story and writing is so good I honestly have no idea how it's going to end even at my estimate, 70% done. Few games can overcome their flaws with their writing. Especially flaws so close with their core designs, (quest markers really?!) . In my personal opinion those games always deserve to be celebrated.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't long, but it's wonderful. The story is intriguing, well-paced, and the world feels believable and lived-in. The game world isn't large, but it's generally memorable and easy to navigate after a little exploration.  It's also a visually pleasing game despite being made by just a few people. The basic gist is that you're stuck in a time loop and you need to cause a paradox to break out of it. But you're in a city where The Golden Rule is in effect. If someone commits a crime, everyone is turned into gold statues and you'll need to run to a portal and start the day over again.The game has four endings, the easiest of which can be accomplished solely by you killing the right person. The game runs decently as well. I typically had over 60 fps on a 5700 XT at 1440p. Didn't have much in the way of bugs and crashes either, which is almost funny considering this is based off a Skyrim mod.  You can get the good ending in about 5-6 hours (My internet went out when I played the game for a 4-6 hour stretch the other day, so ignore my playtime) and there are plenty of reasons to speedrun. Some achievements are tied to doing things in the fewest number of loops. The game is mostly spent walking around and talking to people, but the dialogue is splendid, as is most of the voice acting. There's some action and a bit of horror elements, but the most you'll do is shoot a bow (or gun, but you really don't need to bother with that.) FYI, when the lady at the beginning asks you about yourself, say you're a fugitive. That lets you run faster. That's the best perk there is.

They also kept the gameplay suitably close to the Skyrim original, that means there is quicksaving, retro-style fast movement (thank ♥♥♥♥), Skyrim-style stealing and sneaking, and a conversation interface which is uncannily similar to Oblivion's.
