_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City started as a mod for Skyrim, an seed of an idea that lived inside the world of one of gaming's most popular franchises. Four years of hard work later, the fragment of an already excellent story is now a full standalone experience and it is one of the best narrative adventure games you can play today, akin to games in its narrow subgenre like Outer Wilds, Return of the Obra Dinn, and Paradise Killer.To avoid as many spoilers as possible, I will keep this vague. You play as a stranger who discovers a hidden underground city set back in the Roman era. The twenty-or-so townspeople live in fear of a Golden Rule, which deems that if any one person commits a single sin, the entire town dies. It is up to the player to thwart these sins as well as figure out the roots of the mysteries of the lost city, as well as the way you can escape. The story takes some wild swings, but is always right on the mark and delivered an engaging and intricate clockwork of stories, lore, mythology, philosophy, and moralism wrapped inside a tight package. There is no filler here. Almost everything you do contributes to the overall mystery, or at least allows one of the many faces to open up to you about the various secrets around every corner. The majority of the gameplay is based on dialogue; talking to the townspeople about their past, their morals, and their needs allows the player to find clues and leads to further the plot. The voice acting and writing through all of this is superb, with several notable standouts. This is a group of people you will want to help break from their prison, and there are many ways to do so. While you can brute force your way through some conversations, trial and error in discourse as well as in your actions allows you to see the machinations of the setting, and finding which levers to pull is the game's greatest draw. The game also does an excellent job of resisting repetition, giving you a character who will carry out tasks that you have already solved so you can focus on new objectives. There is a minor amount of combat, almost all relegated to a specific section of the game, but I found it mostly pretty fun, if not a little clunky and outdated. Those adjectives can also describe the animation style of the NPCs, as they have a certain Skyrim feel in following their daily routine as well as in conversation that takes some getting used to.That said, the world is designed to mastery. I first tried playing this game a few months before actually diving in and I got lost in the cave system, but the Forgotten City is really poetically crafted to always lead you to somewhere new, poke the player to look at something from a different angle, or even to return to a location with fresh eyes. You can very easily get around from place to place, and a zipline upgrade early on helps alleviate some of the burden of movement. There is more to the city that it seems on the outside, and diving into all the locations was a blast as I slowly peeled back every layer and locked door. Not only is the game complex, but the game's performance was nearly flawless, and the music was simultaneously grand and ominous in setting the tone.The Forgotten City has multiple endings, but they all can be achieved without restarting the game. The "canon ending" is a wonderful conclusion to the journey, no matter which way you tackle it. I was really impressed with the way Modern Storyteller was able to have a perspective on morality and philosophy without being heavy-handed and snobby about the affair. You can have some really funny and goofy moments with it, and you'll have some serious twists and turns, but as long as you aren't expecting an action-packed blockbuster, The Forgotten City is one of 2021's best experiences and makes for an excellent new entry into the "Metroidbrainia" subgenre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A free-roam exploration/puzzle game.  Most puzzles aren't the normal prop puzzles (find something somewhere, use it somewhere else) or puzzle puzzles (move switches in the right order), instead you have to talk to numerous people about everything until one of them tells you something useful.  Gradually you learn what sort of things are useful and that reduces the list of thing you need to try.It lacks signposts early on, so you flounder around for the first two hours without much progress.  You do achieve a few objectives, and the game does mark them as achieved, but it's not obvious what good they do you until later.  The game has one dialog option which can lead to voluntary combat and carefully labels it, so you can avoid it if you don't like combat.  You can win without it.  I like being given that notice.It's an Unreal 4 game.  Map is medium-sized and theres some scope for getting lost in caves, but after a while you realise the cave network is small.  3D models of places and people are excellent and as realistic as you could want in this type of game.  Atmospheric lighting and convincing water flow make this game a tour-de-force of realism.  If anyone complains that it's hard to make a computer game look both good and realistic, I'll point them at this game.At this stage, a week after release, there are still glitches in the mission scripts and other small buts, but the developers have already put out two updates, and are paying a lot of attention to the Steam Discussions, posting replies and responding with fixes of things discussed on the fora.There are some annoyances and inconsistencies in the world-building and plotting, but they're not annoying while you play, only if you sit back and think about it.  And without them the game wouldn't be any fun.I'm not sure how the game got either the mass of 9/10 scores from professionals or the worst of its negative Steam review.  If you enjoy exploration / chat/ character games, buy it.  If you enjoy Myst-like games, or need to learn about Roman culture, perhaps wait until it's discounted and buy it then.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This was a very well executed mystery in a very well thought out setting. For whatever reason, there seems to be a renaissance of 10-15 hour narrative mystery games involving time travel right now (Outer Wilds, Obra Dinn, Heaven's Vault) so I was obviously comparing it to those in my head during my playthrough, and here is what was good and bad (The only reason the Bad is longer than the Good is because they're smaller nitpicks and I can't really talk about all of the good things in detail, I still think it's a good game):Good:Bad: Again, it was overall a good game with a very imaginative story and ending. I would rank it as better than Obra Dinn (which I thought was kind of cliche and annoying) but not as good as Outer Wilds or Heaven's Vault because of the lack of another gameplay mechanic to break up all the dialog trees and puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A nice little adventure that both feels gargantuan and unconquerable within the first few hours, yet also feels short once you finish it. It took me about 7 hours to get the true ending, so you need to pace yourself accordingly and try not to speedrun it or something. That being said, the dialogue is nice to listen to, and the game is logical with rarely any inconsistencies.Do I think it's worth the pricetag? For the work the developers have put in, I'd say yes, as their small team has clearly put in a lot of love and care to making this world work as well as it does. If the price puts too high a burden on you, or dangerously raises your expectations for how good you expect the game to be, maybe wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: As good as they say. I've been looking for a game like Curse of Obra Dinn and it definitely scratched that itch. Solving a mystery with very uniquely fleshed out characters keeps me engaged and caring about the people of this city. As a fan of ancient history, this game also tries to teach ancient culture and beliefs if you'd care to learn and is surprisingly accurate in doing so. The time loop aspect is just the icing on the cake and brings this storytelling to the next level. It feels like Deathloop without the combat but rather focusing on the story and mystery.This game was an absolute joy and I do hope they continue to make similar games.It keeps the gameplay fresh by introducing a few puzzle elements and even a tiny horror element, but nothing that overstays its welcome. It also has a point and click mystery game feel as it makes you want to just click and look at everything in case it may be a clue. If not, it at least comes with some history tidbits to learn.The only negative comment I'd make about the game are the character models. They just look a little odd? Cheap? Like they were generated from some character creator. They tried to have the characters look somewhat realistic but crosses into the uncanny valley a little bit. I think I would've enjoyed it more if the characters were more cartoonish instead of going for a realistic look that ends up looking a little akward. The character models were the only thing preventing me from being fully immersed, but overall it's not a big deal. Also, the character choice at the start really doesn't matter. It's clear they had an interesting idea at the start, perhaps a leftover from the Skyrim mod (I've never played it), but it ultimately doesn't really do much nor adds any replay value, so I feel like they could've taken that out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun story-driven RPG with a few puzzle-like mechanics. The game is not visually spectacular, but  fans of Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, etc will find it familiar and have no problem with the graphics.The theme of the game, looking at classical history, is very fun - although if you are already well-read on the topic some of the story may be apparent before it is revealed.The game is mostly dialogue driven (although there are some dungeon-esque and action elements) and the time loop elements are very well handled. The game cleverly avoids you having to do repetitive tasks unlike in other time loop games.Would recommend (although probably wait for it to go on sale)
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent "figure out the secret of this world" narrative experience. The mystery is fun to wrap your head around and the various story thread intertwine nicely together. Everything comes to a head for a satisfying "true ending" moment. Do not buy if you are a gameplay first gamer, as there is little to no substantive gameplay on offer here. The game mechanics simply exist to enhance the delivery of the narrative. Also, a full playthrough unlocking all endings could take as few as 5 hours depending on how quickly you figure things out, though it seems around 10 hours is more common. I personally think the game would be worth the full $25 price despite the short length, but know that before you buy.Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys an interesting narrative, uncovering secrets, and unraveling mysteries. It was a great ride!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The lost city is a narrative-driven walking simulator with a few short combat segments. The bulk of the story is learned by talking to people you'll meet along the way. It is very reminiscent of Outer Wilds in all the good ways.The game holds your hand a lot more than Outer Wilds, but a lot less than Firewatch. It took me about 11 hours to get to the epic/canon ending without looking up any guides. Due to the short nature of the campaign, the characters are mostly one-dimensional which is probably the weakest part of the game. Still it's a solid 9.5/10 for me.Mild spoiler: I thoroughly enjoyed how the plot tied together The Forgotten City runs great on the Steam deck.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: Buy it on sale.Long version: Never played the mod, so went into it with a blank slate. It's visually beautiful. Voice acting is top notch. The concept is pretty interesting, especially if you're a history buff and/or like time looping. For $25, it's kinda short (~10 hrs). Zero replay value. And hate to say it, but I thought the canon ending was pretty cheesy. I am a little worried about the people who said it made them cry. Are y'all okay...?
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fantastic game! It's visually appealing, although the people do look a little wonky. You can definitely explore and talk to all of the characters and finish under ten hours. This place is really cool, and you can tell a lot of research went into creating this. While some parts of the plot were predictable, the game still had several plot twists that took me by surprise! I've read reviews that mentioned the script seemed a little heavy-handed at times, but I don't think it bothered me too much, and I feel like it did suit the story. the voice actors were really good at making you like the characters, and aside from the main plot line, there is so much going on that you uncover. It's a very fun and engaging game! I have only played it one time through, and accidentally stumbled onto The Canon Ending; I'm not sure about the others because there was one I really wanted to avoid during this run through, but your choices definitely matter for the ending, and The Canon Ending did not disappoint. I will definitely play this again!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Fun mystery, time-loop adventure story with a historical twist. Decent writing, story and characters. I enjoyed the inclusion of Ancient art, pottery, statues, poetry, philosophy, architecture and culture. Unfortunately, the experience is tarnished with the inclusion of modern politically-correct historical revisionism. Ancient Egyptians were not sub-Saharan Africans, Ancient Greeks did not look like modern Greeks and Ancient Rome was not tolerant of sexual deviancy. Were it not for those forced revisionist elements, it would have been a flawless historical mystery adventure. Here's hoping the team can be more fact-based and objective with their next project.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: If you see this review before checking out the trailer for this game, I hopefully can recommend it and let you experience it blind before too much is revealed.  That is if you like more narrative focused games, I would relate this to Outer Wilds, or Myst.  Games where the story and narrative are front and center, but with you the player driving the narrative.  This game has a good setting, story, and characters, but my favorite part of narrative video games like this one has to be not knowing the full story, or setting, or plot.  Just as my character I am along for the ride, and with each new revelation I myself experiencing this world in a new light.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this game to fans of mystery, fantasy or historically-inspired genres. The time-loop mechanic never became tiresome and I enjoyed the game from start to finish (about 10 hours to finish my first playthrough). However, because there are 4 endings, I will definitely be returning to the Forgotten City. Definitely worth purchasing, even at full price, to support such a promising developer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This review will have no spoilers... because it'll be short. I mostly just want to give it a thumbs up.This game is worth all the praise it's gotten. It is what interactive storytelling should be, IMO. It's well written, fun to explore, and paced fairly well. The puzzles/logical choices are all very reasonable, there's no blind "oh, I need to rub item X on thing Y". To be fair, the puzzles are not very challenging... but that's the point. The point is that the game is designed for you to enjoy the rich story and setting. In my relatively short playtime I've completed the game, but it really felt packed with things to discover. Every time I thought I had it figured out, something new would open up.You should avoid spoilers and just buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the original Skyrim mod, this game not only brings what made that mod special to a new setting, but improves upon it as well in so many ways. I loved exploring the story and getting to know the characters. I also appreciate the mechanical elements that made the game more accessible for me as visually impaired player (the option to be guided to your current objective, and voice acted journals for example.) I can't wait to see what's next from the development team.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly can't recommend this game enough, but if I say too much about it I'll end up spoiling it. Suffice to say, The Forgotten City is a well-written, poignant and intelligent story and one of the best games I've played in years. It's clear that the developers have put their hearts and souls into it, and the results show.Without giving too much away, if you enjoy games like Pathologic or The Outer Wilds you will enjoy The Forgotten City. Go play it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: "The Forgotten City" is not just a game; it's a thought-provoking exploration of ethics, morality, and human nature. It raises questions about the consequences of our actions and the complexities of decision-making. The characters you encounter in the game are wonderfully written, each with their own motivations and moral dilemmas, making it a philosophical journey as much as an adventure.In terms of drawbacks, some players may find the game's slower pacing and dialogue-heavy nature less appealing if they prefer action-packed experiences. Additionally, a few technical hiccups and minor bugs can occasionally detract from the immersion, but they do not significantly impact the overall experience.In conclusion, "The Forgotten City" is a masterfully crafted narrative-driven game that excels in storytelling, character development, and its clever use of the time-loop mechanic. It's a game that will linger in your thoughts long after you've completed it, making it a must-play for fans of narrative-driven adventures and those who appreciate thought-provoking storytelling in video games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: • My personal experienceI absolutely love the way the story is written and delivered. The fact that it was a Mod from Elder Scrolls V, it really does deliver a similar take to the same story they pulled off years ago. The aestheticism of this game convinces me I'm actually in this long forgotten place, a city buried deep within a chasm. Best part about this this game is the learning of the Roman Era and other distinctive parts that come into play surrounding greek mythology. It sets the stage for this game as it originally focused on the Ancient Dwarves of Elder Scrolls and that took a huge fascinating step.I can't get enough of this game, I find it educational in its own way and entertaining adrift of the aspects that is left for us to pick up later on. What makes myself more eager to play it again, and again are the multiple endings they've placed and rediscovery of ancient history.• Sound/Music DesignWhile spending the first three hours of the game, I took some time to adjust my settings regarding sound and other various pieces and I took notice of the background ambience. It's breathtaking, and it relates to the locations I find myself in as I dive deeper into the chasm. Underground caves express a dark deviating tone while being outside the fresh air outside the light blooming sun, there is life and nature and it's so vast and luxurious in its own way. I have a deep love for OSTs. Soundtracks bring spark and life to a video game, especially when you're presenting a story filled with adventure, mystery and conspiracy. This game's soundtrack is definitely an eye-opener and truly defines what kind of game this was meant to be. • PlayabilityUser playability is a must and being able to freely change what kind of controls I want to use for my game really shows how much effort the devs have put into their settings.• GraphicsAs much as I have a very specific preference for detail in graphics, The Forgotten City's graphic design makes it more realistic and at the same time plausible based on how other users find it dignifying. I can certainly say it is undoubtedly awe-inspiring and I would still mesmerise over it.• ConclusionIt's only been a hot minute, and I've already found myself attuned to this enjoyable adventure packed, star gazing theme joyed conspiracy story and it puts me on the edge of my seat when I engage in dialogue, filled to the brim of excitement and stress inducing contentment.Hope to see what the developers have got planned in their next game as I have had a fantastic journey with this one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: this game has been an incredible adventure. the idea of ancient ruins coming to life & time travel has always intrigued me. the story line coming together is classic & done very well. It reminds me of why outer wilds performed so well. different concepts, similar flow with the time loop situation where you’re slowly pulling the pieces together. the developers did a very good job at showing us how to feel about the characters. The voice acting, clothing and mannerisms really suited them all. i really admired some & really disliked others. i loved the ancient world from the get go.  it’s stunning aesthetically and there’s a good amount to explore that kept me interested. it does get creepy & eerie in a couple locations and there’s a whole different place too so there’s a good amount of variety in the distinct environments. it’s been a pleasure to step back in time here into this ancient soft magical world.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful story, incredibly satisfying ending(s), fantastic characters and voice acting. Go in blind for sure.I highly recommend picking the "soldier" background, because running around ancient Rome with a glock is cool as heck.And if the apparent "clunky-ness" of movement and combat in the trailer is giving you second thoughts (as it did for me), it's not a huge part of the game and isn't an issue at all - don't let that stop you from enjoying this seriously incredible experience!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This being my first steam review, so I ask myself where do I begin.The Forgotten city, being my first ever steam review should lend credence to just what a perfect piece of artwork this game turned out to be. Starting out as just a simple add on for Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim, I was a bit weary as to how good this game would be.I have nothing but praise for this game an excellent and interesting premise that as a bit of a History buff pulled me in right from the get go. It has been a long time since I've been captivated by a game the way this one has, what makes it all the more unbelievable is it was made by a studio that works out of my home town/cit of Melbourne, Australia.I'd like to go on into further aspects of the game mechanics and story, however I feel that to do so would ruin the experience. Just go in almost blind as I did and solve the mysteries for yourself, trust me you wont regret it.10/10Best game had the joy of playing in quite some time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I am speechless, not a RPG, not really an adventure game; So sad it is finished after only 20 hours of play, and 2 more hours to get the missed achievements. As it is said in-game: breaching the golden rule does not mean the end of the game; if you really want to explore the game you actually NEED to breach or let other(s) breach the golden rule. A really nice concept, hidden gem in the world of gaming; I wonder when I will have the privilege to stumble on the next one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down one of the best adventure games! I’ve gotten 2 of the endings so far and I’m already itching to unlock the rest. The narrative is incredible, the graphics are pretty and there’s always something new to find with each path you choose. I discovered new areas that I hadn’t ever noticed when I replayed, and I’m positive that will happen again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: First: Is this game worth it? I'd say with a fair debate- yes. Pros:There are multiple endingsThings change according to how you doYou don't have to commit to a pattern in your "Groundhog Day" cycles so you have the freedom to change things up!You can get people their come-uppins without violence... Or with! Just... Know you gotta run. There's small nooks and crannies of secrets and tidbitsThe voice acting is quite nice along with the animationsBEAUTIFUL SceneryOnce you complete a quest/achievement, you don't have to do it again infinitelyCons: Minor minor things. Invisible walls that protect you from falling into the deep abyssIf a mistake was made, you gotta nut up and set up your project again (BUT! ... that doesn't take long at all)Okay, maybe my review is rushed because I'm comming down from a high of completing ONE ending and I'm not usually one to replay just to see other endings for myself but... I'm about to. I might be biased. I enjoyed this game. It was pleasant, straight forward, fun, immersive and you have the luxury of rushing through a bit of dialogue if you've been "through the dance before".I played nearly 6 or 7 hours and was cresting the hour past midnight when I realized the time in REAL life and felt that I was SO close to finishing the game, only to find that there is SO much more, and that I could do more and there were more secrets, so I WASN'T near the end at all! Finished one ending in 8 hours of my running around, fuming at the mean people and realizing the story plot (Because when I game RPGS, I have no brain on, just watch movie) Try it. _childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Its a single player adventure. The game, and the story is pretty interesting, content feels like a cheap copy of assassin creed, but still is very fun to play. Reminds me the old single player games, like Little Big Adventure, Monkey Island, Full Throttle, etc... It feels like a classic, and is fun to play. I can say is fun to play and interesting to discover, something that has an old point of view, and with not much they handled to do a very funny game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I was sceptical about the Forgotten City! It's based on a Skyrim mod, looks similar and I'm not a big fan of Bethesda's style in RPG creation. Further it was focused on doing things that bRPGs aren't particularly known for - investigation and puzzle solving. Could this work?You bet your last sestertius it can!The Forgotten City excels above all at atmosphere. You feel on the ground in this strange place, and that makes the story hit hard with every step you take. It's an easy place to fall into, with characters you can identify with and want to help. Solving the mysteries of the city takes you into some strange, unsettling locations - and I was on the edge of my seat the whole time!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: Dear Devs, I gave you some money. You gave me much, much more. I've had the pleasure to enjoy good writing in games before but this was out-of-this-world. I cannot even fathom what Herculean task it must have been to make all the pieces fit. Thanks for taking me on this magical adventure.My fav part for anyone who has played it:

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun, rewarding game with a great story. I hit a glitch in the quest "the gilded" which took me some time to work around, but still thoroughly enjoyed. _childDocuments_.review: I was surprised at how much I liked (no longer do) this game. It is well made. Nevertheless, the ending is the dumbest and worst I have yet seen in a video game. It does nothing to uphold the game I previously played and ruins the whole thing.Why did the ending go down as such? It is not novel. I have seen this trope play out before. I enjoyed the game about the Roman city, but ‘No’ we must forget all of that. Boo. Thumbs Down.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very pleasant experience. I played the Skyrim mod before but the standalone game is something much more immersive.If you've played the mod, you will recognize many mechanics from Skyrim.The characters are all very interesting, with their own stories and voices. The visuals are also very great and you really feel like exploring a Roman town.The action sequences are lacking pace but since they are not the main aspect of the game, they are still enjoyable.This game is definitly worth its price.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The most satisfying, story-driven game I have played since Disco Elysium. Everything from the character dialogue to the incredible use of history and archaeology hits perfectly, and it all comes together in a beautiful mix of science fiction and ancient mythology. Each character's personality shined so vividly, and I found myself highly immersed with their stories. I felt fear, joy, sadness, hatred, and heartbreak.If you are a history buff with any interest in ancient Rome, Egypt, etc., or a Sci-Fi fan with an affinity for 'Isekai's, this game deserves your attention.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the original mod a few years ago and still remember most of it, yet this game still managed to draw me in and get me hooked up on the story/characters/conflicts. I was worried I wouldn't appreciate the Roman/real world setting as much as the fantasy setting from the original mod, but not only have they managed to retain the atmosphere of the original work, I'd say it's heavily improved upon. If you like story-based games with exploration and dialogue choices, you can't go wrong with this. I'd recommend not researching too much about the game/setting as it can spoil your first time experience somewhat if you already know most of what to expect.pros:+ beautiful graphics, considering the minimum/recommended specs+ amazing story and characters with decent writing+ exploration doesn't feel like a chore and there's a lot to uncover in most nooks and crannies + satisfying gameplay loop+ fair regional pricing (something that's getting rarer and rarer for those of us outside of the US)cons:- a few minor bugs on my end (quest markers disappearing at random)- can be short, depending on your playstyle/how fast you uncover stuff (only listed as a con because this game is genuinely good and I wish there was more of it to enjoy)
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game is heavily driven by story, barely any action. For the most part, you will be reading and learning about the story of the game. Roughly, about 80% of the game will be you reading. The other 20% is putting the pieces together and taking action. If you don't like reading, you will not enjoy the game. If you do, you will lose track of time, enjoying the masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A magnificent example of how to make a time-loop adventure game that both punishes and rewards exploration.Authentic Roman, Greek, and other histories blended into the story, which adds gravitas. and a modicum of edutainment. Pure excitement and player agency, once you understand the world you are trapped in.  The ultimate puzzle/mystery game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The short and skinny (I had to re-write most of this review):The city is very fun to explore, great characters, great pacing, great themes, and an excellent plot with some crazy clever twists and moments. The narrative is the entire point of this game and it does it well.I recommend avoiding quest markers (you can do this by "focusing" one of the main quests which doesn't give you any explicit hints to follow) to get more immersed and familiar with the city by heart. If you're a history buff, the references in this game will be extra sweet.I got it as a gift (thanks Angel!), but the price is a bit steep in my opinion. I wouldn't want it to be longer or anything, but anything that's not narrative-related (graphics, music, gameplay, etc) is uninteresting and/or janky. It all depends on how much you value a good story. And I do geniunely recommend playing this for yourself blind, it does improve the experience.TLDR: Laser-focus on narrative, if you like good stories you'll like this. Bit pricey but absolutely worth it if you can afford it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: First, I'll say that I usually wait to buy games until they're on sale, but when I read another review expressing how glad they were to have purchased at full price, I went ahead and gave it a shot. Boy, I am so, so glad I did.First: There's something in this game for everyone. Most quests have the ability to be solved multiple ways with equally favorable endings, so whether you prefer to fight your way through, sneak around, or use your wits, there's a place for that. While you're exploring, you can pick up any number of artifacts around the city to learn more about them from a historical perspective. Dialogue options also revealed interesting historical and lore-driven information that delighted the history buff in me. The gameplay is smooth, and the world is absolutely stunning. You get to begin exploring on foot, then unlock options for faster travel as you progress. The time loop mechanic gets creative use as a plot point, or as a nice reset if you're not sure where to go next. I cycled through multiple times to see all the different endings and dialogue options, which is huge for me (tbh, I usually google tricky quests to get the exact right dialogue because I'm too invested in getting a certain ending :X)The only thing I'd like to see is an in-game map (I found a beautiful one by Francesca Baerald that was a great help!).Overall: 10/10. I would recommend this to literally any of my friends, regardless of where they fall on the gamer spectrum. Fantastic game by a small company. Devs are responsive to issues and push out updates as needed. Buy this game; you'll love it!

_childDocuments_.review: It doesn't bother me at all that I paid $20 and the 13 hours I've put into this will likely be all I put into it.  This was a good purchase.  It's an interesting mashup of game play style: problem-solving that achieves dialogue "richness" without feeling dialogue "heavy".  NPCs with personalities that are engaging without being cumbersome to uncover.Additional thoughts: I really couldn't care less about Steam Achievements, but I did genuinely want to achieve various outcomes with this game just for the sake of the outcomes. I enjoyed the various characters to be encountered and genuinely cared about their fates.   I wanted to see how the world would react to choices I made.  I felt satisfied with each of the 4 outcomes, and enjoyed that there was still some variation to how "complete" those individual outcomes could be depending on your choices.  I typically avoid First Person style games, because I get motion sickness from a lot of them (despite growing up playing FPS games), but it wasn't really a problem with this.What you see in the screenshots is what you get.  It's a story-driven, problem solving interact-able.    It's not an RPG.  It's not an Action game.

_childDocuments_.review: A really great game, you notice the skyrim heritage in both good and bad things, its got the detailed and interesting to explore world, but also some of the jankier things like NPCs rotating to face you before talking.I would say if you like exploring lore and mysteries in RPG's you will love this game and should try it, I 100%d the game because I wanted to see everything of this world I could.I played with the hints turned off (They are on by default) and  the game isn't too difficult but does require a bit of thinking sometimes, I recommend playing through in a couple of session closer together so you can remember everything, even tho the game does make sure you wouldn't be entirely lost.TLDR: Great game, not very long, stop reading reviews and play it blind if you at all enjoy figuring out lore/mysteries in games such as fallout/skyrim/divinity because youll almost certainly love it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: It is rare to find a game that gives you the agency to find leads on your own, in the order that you want to tackle them, and how your choices actually matter (for the most part, and doesn't give you the illusion of it). If you're not paying attention when you're speaking with a character and choose the wrong dialogue option, you can piss them off and they won't speak to you (for the rest of the time loop anyways). Or worse, it can lead to the dreaded Golden Rule being broken.Resolving leads gives you clues on other leads. It is really satisfying to resolve a lead or you manage to find a creative way to find a clue or to access a locked area. The game doesn't hold your hand and trusts you to figure it out (and if you need a little help, you can turn on hints). Dialogue is really engaging; Roman history (mainly), themes on morality, natural law (and others), and the characters are a colourful bunch. While it is mostly serious, there are humorous moments here and there that have made me laugh here and there.Based on how much of the mystery you've solved, it rewards you with an appropriate ending. Should you want to take the easy way out, you can, but you will probably feel bad about it. However, by uncovering the mystery, you will be rewarded with a mostly rewarding canon ending. Highly, highly recommend it. 9.5/10The cons*The combat is very clunky (however it's only a very minor part of the game).*The hair... especially on the older lady is... not great. *Canon ending - while I do think that the final confrontation is really engaging, I do feel like it's a little too easy to solve it. But the rest of the ending is emotionally satisfying and resolves almost all of the murder mystery questions (with the exception of a few very minor questions).

_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This is an example of a game that is perfect in length and scope. The developers have done a great job of creating a compelling world all set within the confines of a small Roman city.  The time loop mechanic feels necessary as opposed to a novelty, which many games of type fall for. The setting and art direction go a great job in showing what life would be like 2000 years ago and has a very eye catching antiquarian feel. The game's highlight is the meticulous writing and script which breathes life into these ancient characters. The layers of mystery I uncovered from the first person you meet to the final revelations were engaging and thoroughly enjoyable. The writing of particularly difficult and thought provoking questions such as "What constitutes a sin?" and the variety of answers given by the diverse range of npcs, really did make me have to stop and ponder for a moment.Overall, The Forgotten City took me 6 and 1/2 hours to achieve all four endings. Surprisingly this is actually a strength of the game as each of those hours was filled with meaningful content and never left me bored. It is a testament to the game that can be completed in an afternoon and yet I still wanted to come back for more.This is one of the best narrative puzzle games of 2021, and I would highly recommend it to those who wish to see a time loop mechanic done right or want a very well written mystery.I look forward to what the developers pursue in next endeavour.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a blast! It has a lot of smaller flaws, but I was just so roped in by the premise that I never really cared about said flaws. The flaws are noticeable, so you'll have to suspend your disbelief purposefully. it's stuff like like, "hold up, how did x not know y after learning the name of z?", "did no one else see these easily noticeable patterns in this topic everyone would've talked about at some point?" or "Okay, I just told x y, so now he should now angrily want to do z, but he's not doing anything and seems to pretend the conversation never happened. What gives?". That being said, I personally had no trouble suspending my disbelief in spite of these flaws. There's some action elements that are rather clunky, the game is a drain on computer resources, and even then, I can still recommend it.Because it's fun!The premise that I don't want to spoil is just so good that you can't help but be thrilled to play a role in it. The surroundings and scenery are just so beautiful that you really feel like this place exists, in spite some flaws with the AI. The dialogue is, in my opinion, pretty dang good. It basically never happens that you get stuck with a quest or a puzzle, making you feel like you're making constant strides in discovering how to complete the game, which is also just fun. In a way, the game just grips your attention from the first moment to the last in this fun ride, and when it's over, you just feel satisfied, really. I did, anyway. It was 4 AM by the time I was done. >.>So yeah, I can strongly recommend this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Great game full of memorable characters, exploiting the time loop is a fun mechanic that is seldom seen in games and it works really well here with QOL features to automatically repeat your actions at the start of each loop, so you're not constantly having to do the same things over and over. It's fun and feels a bit cheeky using knowledge learned on previous loops to sway your interactions with characters the way you want them to go. Definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: So, I want to take something out of the way. The loop mechanic is pointless. If you're someone who likes video games for being punished when failing a challenge, you're going to argue that the loop is integrated with the story or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ you want to make up. The thing is, it is perfectly possible to make a game like this, with certain modifications and adaptations, without having a loop mechanic to hinder the player. Because it is only that: a hindrance. There is something I find very disturbing in most video games which is a need to prevent you from walking freely around its world – even in most indie games, which are those in which you’d expect to see less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Again, the loop is just a mechanic. It is expendable in regard to the game world or its design. With that out of the way, I want to talk about world building and design, which is what matters. In this regard the game excels, and I risk guessing that this is why the game (deservedly) received so much praise. It is hard to explain, but there is an organicity in how the city and its inhabitants are designed that strongly compels you learn more and more about the world – specially, of course, if you like exploration. I felt compelled to explore every nook and cranny and to exhaust every line of dialogue because the world and the way information is delivered was very well designed.  But another problem that hinders exploration are the branching conversations. This is another element that comes from triple A games because it gives people the illusion that choices matter. Well, they do not. Branching conversations are just an annoyance that prevents you from fully exploring the world. What is intriguing to me is why an indie studio would want to include such an element because you'd think these are the kind of remaining pointless elements you see in high budget games that are included only because (supposedly) they allow the game to be marketed as something most people want.Nonetheless, despite the negative aspects (which are few), I still highly recommend this game if you like exploration and thoughtful design.

It is SO worth your time, and you will thank me.

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten City is a fun little game with an incredibly unique premise, that makes good use of the increasingly a-la-mode time loop mechanic. Sadly, its over-ambitious nature coupled with its faithfulness to its predecessor bring it down a notch. Highly recommended for those with a fondness for history, mystery, or both, but not so much for those looking for intrigue or action. Perhaps fittingly, it was only once I had beaten Forgotten City that I learned it originally came from a Skyrim mod. Indeed, throughout my playthrough of the game, I was constantly bombarded with a strong sensation of deja-vu, which I couldn’t place. NPC animations so jank that they look like statues, even before turning to gold? Poor dialogue writing and even poorer voice acting? Stealth archer being the most viable combat strategy? I’m amazed I never drew the comparison. I say that my discovery of this fact is fitting, as perhaps the most memorable moment of this game is built on a similar premise. Forgotten city has the player trapped in a time loop in a seemingly inescapable underground roman city, where one slip up means a rather gaudy death for everyone in the entire city: The golden rule of the bible is taken quite literally here, everyone shall turn to gold if this is not followed. . Frustratingly, as interesting as this premise is, along with the questions it raises, it is thrust to the wayside for the main focus of the Forgotten City: The golden rule itself and the morality behind it. The Forgotten City attempts to tackle deep questions of philosophy and morality in a game that only lasts about 5 hours, maximum, and it does so very awkwardly and unconvincingly, sometimes even going against the arguments the game makes itself. . The whole of Forgotten City can feel this way sometimes. Time loops, although an excellent mechanic and well deserving of its newfound popularity, require a real focus on an airtight plot, as players reviewing the same story over and over tens of times will rapidly notice any plot holes that would go unnoticed in a more linear story structure. And let me tell you, the Forgotten City’s plot is like a slice of Emmental. This often breaks immersion, or worse, can accidentally trick the player into focusing in on details that were supposed to be overlooked. Although this review has been primarily focused on tearing the game apart, I loved my time with this game, and still very much recommend it. The story, although awkward, was gripping and the plot twists were fun, unique, and well planned. The NPCs, although one-sided, are still loveable, and the effort put into their complex, interwoven interactions between each other is commendable. The way the game incorporated your ability to loop through time into the story is incredibly unique, and the fact that . Although it was at times very much over-ambitious and dragged down by its reliance on its roots, the fact that a game of this comparable quality and scope was made by three people is impressive in its own right. And hey, it has less bugs than the average actual Bethesda title on release, so there’s that too. Hopefully, someday in the future, a lead dev will pick up the unique idea, and, just like the original mod, rebuild the concept of the forgotten city into something even more polished and interesting than now. But until then, I still recommend you give The Forgotten City a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I'm sad that it's over. I wish I could spend more time in the beautiful world of The Forgotten City. But those are just details. The game is full of wonder and meaning and heart. It will make you think, it will excite and exhilarate you, and it will widen your eyes. The Forgotten City gives and gives and gives, but when it's over, you still haven't had enough. This game is a gem.Verdict: SUPERB

_childDocuments_.review: The original mod was an interesting curiosity with potential, but this is next level. There's a few ways in which I would like the game to be more responsive but generally it does a stellar job with player choice, the story is fascinating, well layered, there's plenty of reasons to experiment, and, more importantly, when crap like the TLOU2 can win awards by making you hold foward until the next cutscenes, a lawyer who quit and thew his savings at retreading his Skyrim mod with 3 other guys can give us an amazing example of a story that can ONLY be told through an interactive medium. I want to see what Nick Pearce does next.

_childDocuments_.review: Really excellent game. Stories that work within a time-loop don't always get the balance of repetition and novelty right, and I think Modern Storyteller did a bang up job of it here. Whether you made a mistake, or need to move forward of your own accord, each loop brings new elements and handily removes the need for repeating steps in quests ad nauseum. The story is engaging and the characters are all well written. It's a nicely rounded cast and I enjoyed spending time with them solving the puzzle of the loop. There are a couple of diversions from time loop problem solving that gently up the game play ante and I thought them well done. A welcome change in pace and tension. I'll add, the game/puzzle is structured in such a way that failure is not punishing (quick-save exists, too), and experimenting is fun. It's not particularly challenging in its solutions, but it is clever at how it arrives there, and the writing team use the dialogue to say a bit more about the world as they see it than I was expecting. It's by no means a 'message' game, but the messages it does contain add some soul to the proceedings that I appreciated. A strong recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: After hurting my thumb recently my friend gifted me this game as it wasn't as action packed so shouldn't require much in the way of dexterity. Going in I didn't really know what to expect, didn't really ever hear about this game and for some reason always getting it confused with the Sinking City (a Cthulhu adventure). This game had absolutely nothing to do with anything with Cthulhu and really did suprise me.For anyone thinking about playing the game, I'll refrain from spoiling anything in this review since I feel more people should really give it a go. The game is dialogue based which means most of the time you'll be spending talking to people to discover more about what's going on. Not to say that's all of the gameplay mechanics you'll be facing but without spoiling anything I cannot elaborate.The game's story is where it really does shine, thrust into an ancient Roman city it's up to you to decide the fate of it's inhabitants. The game sort of straddles a rogue-lite element with some time travel being involved however has some mechanics that makes this element nonabrasive. The game really comes into it's own with the attention to detail and interesting dialogue, from the start I found myself engaging with philosophical thoughts that really encompassed some tough topics, this only evolves as you progress through the game's story culminating in some brilliant dialogue and action.Really would recommend this game, anyone who is looking for a less action based game would be right at home here, fantastic work especially as the development team consisted of three people!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A short narrative game, with a compelling plot containing plenty of twists and exciting developments. For those who have played the Elder Scrolls mod that shares its name with this full game, there are enough changes to the story to make this worth playing as well, though obviously some of the big twists may already be known to you - still, there are new endings and a backstory that mean the ultimate mystery that needs to be solved will remain unknown to you - don't go looking for spoilers.Lovely aesthetics, nice ambient soundtrack and I really liked the quality of the voice acting. Solid title.

_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: A time-travel walking simulator which is  well done. I've played literally hundreds of walking simulators, and this game is in my top 10.For reasons I won't spoil, your character is transported back to an ancient Roman city shortly before its complete destruction.  Your job is to prevent its destruction, learning lots about the inhabitants along the way. The story has lots of good twists, and a great ending.Don't get confused by the aesthetics - this game is  like Skyrim. While there is a small amount of (rather poorly designed) combat, that is not the main focus of this game. In fact I think combat can be avoided completely, if you want.The game has about 8 hours of content.  There's more than one ending, but with a little save-scumming it's possible to see them all in one playthrough, meaning the game doesn't have much replayability.Because the game is so story-centric, it's hard to explain anything more without spoilers. Suffice it to say, if you're a fan of story-based game, this one is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I preface this review by saying I'm definitely in the minority here. I really, really wanted to like this game. Also, my downvote is in NO way a reflection on the time and effort clearly put into this game. The devs did a commendable job for which they deserve to be compensated, so I am glad that others enjoy it.It's just... for whatever reason, there's something about the experience that feels INTENSELY boring. Every time I looked at it sitting there in my Steam library, the thought of going back in felt like a chore.When I think about other games I dislike where I am in the minority, I notice a common theme: resetting. It's not like this is a new concept - repetition is in many ways the very core of gaming - and some of the games I have enjoyed and played the  most (Banners of Ruin, Invisible Inc, too many puzzle games to count) as well as many movies or TV shows I like (Groundhog Day, Edge of Tomorrow, Russian Doll, ST:TNG's "Cause and Effect") prominently feature resetting as a core element.But there's a certain genre of games as of late that try to blend immersion and resetting mechanics, two concepts I find utterly antithetical to one another. Every time a reset occurs, it feels like a distraction that has been imposed artificially, where the hand of the game designer is a bit too explicit and directive, where overt design yanks you straight out of suspension of disbelief, plops you down at the beginning and excitedly giggles "again! again!" This sudden disruption of narrative momentum completely undercuts the rest of the gaming experience.Maybe it's just that I felt like this whole trope was played out well before The Stanley Parable dropped. The wry, self-aware humor calling out its own tedium is a large part of why I enjoyed that game, but also why I didn't spend long in it.Or maybe it's just that the whole Sisyphus aesthetic hits a little too close to home. You might notice that most of the repetitive narrative entertainment I mentioned also prominently features dark humor, often as an explicit statement that the whole time loop thing is not fun.TL;DR - I couldn't get into this game for the same reason I hated The Outer Wilds. Take that for what it's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: ++ Excellent story with great twists+ Beautiful environment+ Gameplay is fun and engaging+ Mostly great voice acting+ Great ending- Repetitive combat (game would have been better with less of it, honestly. It gets very boring after 5 mins because there's only 1 weapon and only 1 enemy type).- "Canon" epilogue is far too long. I'd rather not know the boring modern details of every single character after the fact.-- Uber-wokeness in games like this is honestly exhausting. Every conceivable box is checked in this game; nevermind that its supposedly ancient Rome.    - You choose your character's "Body Type", not your gender.   - The bad guys are, of course, the old white guys + the two capitalists.   - Egyptians are portrayed as Black- which actual Egyptians find extremely offensive (modern left is trying to erase them from their own history- see Netflix's Cleopatra controversy).   - Not so subtle anti-Christian message. Christianity is referred to repeatedly as a "cult", "intolerant", responsible for burning Rome to the ground, and ultimately shown as having the "wrong" beliefs.   o To be clear, I'm perfectly fine with having a diverse cast in the game. It's just the same tired tropes and completely ahistorical left-wing box-checking exercises that I object to. This is supposed to be ancient Rome, not a Berkeley gender-studies class.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forgotten City

_childDocuments_.review: The Forgotten City is a mystery adventure game of exploration and deduction. Travel 2,000 years into the past and relive the final days of a cursed Roman city, where if one person sins, everyone dies.  Combat is an option, but violence will only get you so far. Only by questioning an intertwined community of colourful characters, cleverly exploiting the time loop, and making difficult moral choices can you hope to solve this epic mystery. Here, your decisions matter. The fate of the city is in your hands.

name: LIBERATED
detailed_description: Buzz More from our friends About the Game Open a playable comic book. Hear the rustling of pages. Maybe you’ll even smell the ink. Immerse yourself in a dark, rain-soaked city. Finally, LEAP into the ACTION ! Unravel a cyberpunk story paying homage to modern and cult pop-culture inspired by Black Mirror , Mr. Robot , The Matrix , and even Fight Club . Enter the bleak streets of a dystopian near-future. Here, human rights crumble as governments and megacorps join forces to make you their pawn. THEY want to trace your every move. THEY want to shape the way you think. Will you obey? Or will you FIGHT ? Jump, sneak, solve puzzles, and keep your 9mm ready. Liberated is a white-knuckle action-adventure game presented within a graphic novel. The comic book story intertwines with a pure side-scrolling shooter. Kill them first, ask questions later. Get ready for a visual tour de force. Witness gorgeously hand-drawn panels reminiscent of Frank Miller’s and Will Eisner’s graphic novels. Liberated combines the legendary comic book styles with the aesthetic influences of ‘40s and ‘50s noir cinema. Let the interplay of light and shadow leave you breathless. Bring upon the revolution.

_childDocuments_.review: Liberated is a game that is a lot better on the outside, than on the inside.Aesthetically, I love the comic book the game is going for. The dark sketchy lines look great, and watching cutscenes on a physically rendered book is really cool. You can even move the camera around and see the light bouncing off the paper.The atmosphere and pacing of cutscenes is relatively compelling, and I thought scenes were presented in interesting ways.Unfortunately, gameplay took a backseat here, which is a shame since this is a video game after all.There are long stretches where you will just be walking to the right without anything happening, and then suddenly, out of your field of view, an enemy will pop up and engage you in combat.The game promotes stealth play, however it is truly frustrating to pursue.In any game where I get the option, I always take the stealthy route, however in this game I found it far less frustrating to just gun my way through everyone.Not only do enemies catch you off guard easily, forcing you to inch your way slowly to the right if you don't want to blow your cover, but sometimes they can be obscured by foreground.The most frustrating bit of all though is actually trying to take them out, the way the game intends you to.There are spots you can hide in. (Which aren't obvious until you run right by them and see the prompt. And sometimes you'd expect to be able to hide somewhere and can't).You're meant to hide, and wait for the patrol to come backwards past you, and you click a button to take them out.However, if you want to trail them without waiting for them to come back, it is a miserable experience. Getting too close will make them turn around because they hear you.So instead, you can sneak, which is silent, but sooo slow. No matter how many times I tried to find the right balance between moving forward quickly, and then sneaking closer, I could almost never take them out successfully. They would most of the times just turn around and take me out.In the end, shooting everyone proved more time efficient.Honestly, the shooting doesn't feel too bad either. It's very simple, but relatively satisfying to pop a headshot, or take down a drone.Although I didn't find that there was much variety to spice it up.I am also normally someone who doesn't outright hate quick time events. They have their place, as long as they are used sporadically.Well this game is by far the worst offender I have ever experienced.You will be prompted to press the correct button during cutscenes throughout the entire game. Not only multiple times per cutscene, but multiple times PER ACTION.As in, you are driving a car in a cutscene, and for one drift, you need to press 3 buttons half a second after each other. I have absolutely no idea why they thought that was a good idea, but literally not a single time in my time with the game did I have to press any QTE once. It was always three times, aside from one cutscene where I only did it twice.Overall, I can't recommend the game.While the art style is awesome, and the world can be intriguing, sometimes voice acting can be a bit off, and cutscenes can drag on a bit. But the worst offender, is that the gameplay is quite a slog to get through. It pains me to say it, but it's how I felt. It's worth noting that I didn't get through the entire game, but I just didn't feel motivated enough to push past the 2 hour mark.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes there're games that are hard to rate properly. One of my favourite examples is Fallout 4 that is technically a shooter (and it sucks as a shooter).Why did I mention it? The thing is,  is more of a 2D shooter than anything else as well and I'll explain this point further on. is a noir graphic novel set in a cyberpunk/dystopian near-future world where human rights are violated by the government. A group of people called "Liberated" is trying to shed light on the crimes of this government. This story is being told via comic book issues/chapters.The main "cool feature" of this game are comic book pages and action that is happening there. And it's really well implemented - great work with Unity here. Hands down this feature is amazing, looks beautiful and stylish. Now let's talk about gameplay. We read amazingly drawn comics and from time to time we're getting some action, be it a mediocre shooting, nice puzzle or crappy QTE. Sounds good, right?The problem is, from 3-3,5 hours playthrough (for 4 main chapters and 2 DLC ones) ~70-75% of playtime you'll be doing a "mediocre shooting" part. It wasn't a problem for me as I mostly liked it, but it's not something that you would expect from this game when you're looking at it for the first time.Another weird thing is a filler story that could be described in a few sentences. I can't say that it's unfinished, but it's so minimal that it looks strange even from a comics perspective.All in all,  was a positive experience for me but I believe that it could've been so much better if it was more story oriented.
_childDocuments_.name: LIBERATED

_childDocuments_.review: A digital interactive comic book set in a noir cyberpunk world of complete government control, eerily reminiscent and very close to the course our own blue ball of yarn is spinning into at the moment.What excites about Liberated is the way it's presented. Through a slick, black and white comic book, complete with textured panels, sounds of flipped pages and reflections. You even have the ability to tilt the view around the panels a bit. It's a complete experience of reading a comic book. I can almost smell the paper. The art is wonderful (brings to mind Frank Miller's Sin City, even a hint of Torpedo and some other noir comics) and the way the panels are framed really glues your eyes to a single panel, letting you linger on it as long as you want.The story, spread over four comic issues, follows a group of rebels fighting against government control and some of the points it serves strike close to what is happening now. It subtly nudges you to think about things most of us already know, but choose to ignore. People being a part of a giant online community, invasive surveillance, fading of paper money and the move towards a cashless world for easier tracing, infallible police and a lot of other tiny things we don't really think about. Orwell would have a field day here. It does have some flaws and holes, but it's an ok noir cyberpunk tale.Sounds are good, but the soundtrack is a bit monotone and forgettable. Voice acting is well done, even with the cringe worthy moments, managing some unexpected voices you wouldn't really attribute to a person's physique.Unfortunately, the gameplay part that happens through interactive panels isn't something that will send ripples of excitement down your spine.Most of the game is played, or read, by flipping the pages and following the story. At certain points you get control of characters in a side scrolling shooter of a run and gun type. The game does feature two difficulty options, but it's easy no matter what you pick. The gunplay itself is kind of wonky. Shooting is ok, but the way the characters draw guns seems a bit slow and just slightly off. There is a stealth mechanic, but your character moves very slow when using it and the enemies have a tendency to spot you off screen, or off panel. The entire mechanic is completely not needed for gameplay, apart from a few instances where the game forces you to use it. Just shoot everyone in the face.There are exactly 7 puzzles in the game and 1 extra in a DLC. They are not overly complicated and shouldn't prove a problem, but I don't really know why they're there. They really don't bring much to the run and gun gameplay except breaking what little flow it has. Quick time events the game features bring even less. I'm not opposed to them, I like me some Telltale QTE's, but here they're really not needed, just like the puzzles. It feels they're both there just to shovel in some gameplay moments, so the game doesn't turn into a visual novel with okish run and gun scenes.Two free DLC's released are a nice touch and flesh out the world a bit more. The first one is really a visual novel, the second one has a couple of action scenes and both happen after the main story.I've noticed a couple of bugs and glitches. Enemies strangely becoming immune to damage while shooting you back, weird getting off the ladder animations that get you stuck in place for a few seconds like the game is loading something and some scenery glitches where your character gets stuck. And the game is also not easy on the hardware, spinning up the GPU fans much more than you'd expect (played on an i7, 32GB RAM, RTX2070 and an SSD).It's a very cool concept, a digital playable comic book, but the final product here doesn't mesh the mediocre run and gun gameplay parts and unneeded QTE's and puzzles with following the narrative Telltale style story presentation. Kudos to the Atomic Wolf, L.INC for trying something different and I hope they work on developing the concept further, but I can't really recommend this just on the merits of great art and presentation. And the price is a bit much considering how short the game is and what it offers.Take a peek inside the  if you like to walk off the beaten path and only sometimes return to the main roads. You might find something worth exploring. And if you do, thank you for the visit.: 6 story achievements, 2 ending achievements, kill x enemies, some missables. Comic issues can be replayed when you finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? It certainly is a NEW game concept, and I'd say I had my fun with it.It is a short b/w comic book with animated panels, with speech and sound effects. Quite nice, but the real novelty is that many of the panels require interaction. Sometimes simple (timed) decisions like YES/NO, sometimes QTEs, puzzles like from a hidden object game, sometimes long action sequences where you run, jump, sneak, hide and shoot through a 2D environement like in a run'n'gun game or a simple car chase. In short, you read an animated, fully voiced comic strip with different minigames popping up at various points. Really cool. That's what I call an interactive comic strip. When you fail an action sequence you just restart it.Taking place in a near future dystopian world, with survaillance cams and police drones everywhere, where citizens are supposed to be part of the online community (and allow the government to observe them that way), you play a small time hacker with a prominent father but without social media presence, with cash instead of an online account and with highly sensitive data on your computer. You just manage to encrypt it in time, before the police raids your apartment. You still get caught, and then you have to make a decision...Voice-overs and ultrawidescreen support. Game is saved automatically. Switch to story mode to have easier action sequences.Interactive comic book. Read, take decisions, play through little action sequences.
_childDocuments_.name: LIBERATED

_childDocuments_.review: Here we go.If this game was a graphic novel, I'd be ok with it. But, it isn't.The story of a confrontation between an evil police government and free rebel citizens called Liberated. Orwell, 1984, you know. Someone here trying to convince us, what not everything so simple as a first sight. But in fact, the problem is - everything here is simple and predictable. Gray moral doesn't work in the game. We already know who's truly bad even from 1st chapter. I am sure, developers wanted gray morale here, because they show us the story in different angles and both sides.  That's all about the plot.As a game, Liberated is empty. All we need - run from the left to the right and shoot. If an enemy shooting you, and you shoot him back, your bullets with 75% probability will fly  through the target. But enemy's not. The game has puzzles. Seven. This is not seven types, this is seven times.DLC1 has only story elements without gameplay, or maybe it is visual novel genre, then I'm sorry. Cardboard characters you don't sympathize with. Even their 3d-models looks bad.I  expected The Sin City, but have got 1984 Orwell's  retold in short.Glory for heroes!

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, sure, throw a 4-button QTE that lasts a 1/10th of a second at the very end of the first level.Yeah, sure, kill the main character just because I inevitably lost that one QTE, forcing the rest of the game to go on without him.Yeah, sure, put a checkpoint the second after I fail so that in order to get the best ending, I have to replay the last 30 minutes of your slow-ass walking sim just to save the guy's ass.Guys, it's okay to have a short game, you know? You don't have to wring 30 extra minutes of playtime from me by forcing me to replay levels I've already done just for a single game-changing QTE at the end. It really doesn't improve my impression of the game when you pull that crap.
