_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue 3: how to squander two decades of goodwill in one colossal disappointment.I really loved Shenmue 1. There's no doubt it's a product of its time, but the game hooked me immediately. The story got straight to the point: dead father, murder mystery, vengeance, go. Along the way, main character and gacha enthusiast Ryo Hazuki befriended a lot of people and was constantly reminded that the path of revenge is not a road on which he can backpedal. The theme was tight, the fighting was fun, and the final battles were thoroughly enjoyable.Shenmue 2 had a lot more of the same, but it did feel like the rudder was adrift. While there was more fighting, there were also more QTEs and a lot more wandering around, doing nothing. For a concept that started off as a Virtua Fighter RPG, Shenmue already felt like it was getting caught up in all of its sidequests by the sequel.Shenmue 3, long awaited after almost 20 years since Shenmue 2, is astonishingly bad for one single reason: it is boring. S3 is full of extraneous junk to keep you occupied, but the game never feels like it's getting off the ground. Making it to Bailu Village at the end of S2 was this momentous occasion. S3 starts off with Ryo faffing around in Bailu for nearly 20 hours before he moves on to Niaowu to spend another 20 hours faffing around there. The game wants you to be engaged with all of the things to do, but all of this is entirely optional mini-game garbage that only serves to waste your time. The main game is agonizingly torturous in its pace because, if it didn't throw plot roadblocks at you, you could clear the whole game in well under ten hours.At this point, Ryo Hazuki is supposed to be an unstoppable force of nature, kickboxing his way through everything and everyone. However, he repeatedly gets his butt handed to him because the plot wants to slow you down so you can take the time to appreciate the pretty skyboxes. He also has to jump through hoops for the world's rudest senior citizens, who are fond of subjecting him to fetch quests in another effort to drag out the story. There's not enough game in the game, and it shows because the game is more padded than a hockey goalie. By the time you make it to the second main area of the game, you have to wonder if you're even getting close to your objective, and since it's never quite clear what you're working toward anyway, the whole endeavor feels like a complete waste of time.Even more bewildering than the story is the fighting. The first two games had a complex but tight system of arcade-style controls. You could mash buttons and get by, but advanced players were able to chain aggressive combos to put the hurt on enemies. Shenmue 3 does away with all of that in favor of actual button mashing. The game just kind of shrugs and tells you to hope for the best while hitting buttons. You can train Ryo to build up his attack and defense, but bizarrely, Ryo never gains any experience in his stats when engaged in an actual fight. That means the game expects you to waste more time training Ryo so you can survive the scripted fights, and you will spend literal hours training Ryo to improve his stats. All of this happens so that you can get to an end boss battle that concludes with the game admitting it is a filler episode that did nothing to advance the plot, which is just criminal.It was after I had picked my sixty-ninth plant in Niaowu that I realized I was losing my mind because this simply was not fun. In fact, the game had not been fun for a very long time, possibly ever., and I could not bring myself to finish it. There are plenty of callbacks to familiar characters and places, but it feels like gratuitous wink-and-nod fanservice for the series veterans who wanted something more after waiting nearly two decades for this game. Other games do what S3 does far, far better. The only QTE you need to do for this game is quickly forget about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I backed Shenmue III on Kickstarter at the physical copy tier. While it's nice that they finally ended up providing a Steam key to backers (which is a joke in-and-of-itself considering you had to fill out a survey a year ago to opt-in), it's too-little too-late. Any goodwill that was present at the end of the Kickstarter campaign was completely destroyed by either ineptitude or disdain for the people who helped fund the project enough to have it bought up by Deep Silver and have its exclusivity rights sold to Epic.From slipping timelines, no communication, switcheroos on deliverables (they still haven't delivered all the physical rewards...), and other half-truths or outright lies, this company has done it all. Being shipped a storefront installer without any data on the disc I received is a pretty good parallel for this project and this game. Promises of something; delivery of nothing. _childDocuments_.review: The original Shenmue games polarised the audience on their release. Whilst technically ambitious, they were slow, boring and mundane. That was also part of the charm. The appeal of a realistic world set in 1980's Japan and China, before the heights of modern technology, allowed the games to set themselves apart from more contemporary peers. A world created in celebration of a time that had already passed.The original games are eccentric, but contain beautiful moments that even to this day show the potential for gaming to champion it's existence as an art form to be respected.They also teach patience. Resilience. The importance of friendship. The importance of doing what is right. Some players will consider the original Shenmue games as some of the best ever made.Shenmue 3 however, is a problematic sequel. With a limited budget and scope, it was nigh-on impossible for YsNet to create a game that would reach the heights of the previous two entries; pleasing Shenmue fans and attracting new players.They have achieved it - mostly, but the game is not without its flaws. Those flaws are for you to decide. The reviews are mixed - both sides are correct. Shenmue 3 is as polarising as the games that came before. It is so incredibly meta, brave and takes risks that should be commended. It also includes some very bizarre decisions in its presentation for you to discover. Shenmue 3 for me, is a lesson in accountability. It puts player choice at the forefront of its design whilst creating a balance between positive and negative outcomes from the decisions you will make - a yin/yang if you will.You will read lots of reviews from players that were frustrated by the stamina system, the difficulty of the combat system (Ryo has been NERFED!) and the money “gates”. All of these frustrations stem from player choices but this only becomes apparent once you’ve spent a large amount of time with the game. If you try to rush through the story and ignore the world around you, you will become frustrated. Mechanics wise, Shenmue 3 improves almost all aspects of the previous games. Navigating the world is easier now that the tank controls are gone. Investigations in 1st person are smoother.The Virtua Fighter battle system has gone, potentially due to licensing reasons and has been replaced by a new engine that is passable. In multi-person battles, Ryo can now target specific enemies. There is an element of button mashing but move variety is required in order to progress as enemies will block repeated actions. You can learn the move commands but there is a slight input delay. This can be offset by assigning 5 moves to a hotkey but the removal of throw moves and the strategy that comes with the previous VF engine does harm the experience. You can still evade, block and look for openings but the new engine just doesn’t feel as good. A stamina system is now present. Activities and the passage of time will deplete stamina. Endurance training can improve it and purchasing food can refill this when it’s low. A low stamina status will only allow Ryo to walk, which slows down the experience. Earning money in Shenmue 3 is far easier and more fulfilling than previous titles. Ryo can complete jobs to earn money, be it chopping wood, fishing, collecting herbs or driving the forklift. He can also gamble or compete in a martial arts tournament to earn tokens, which can be redeemed for prizes and then sold for money. You can also do exchanges at pawn shops, such as capsule toys, game prizes and specific items from stores for move scrolls or money. The game also includes an adorable hunt for special ducks in shops, which can be exchanged for move scrolls. There are plenty of options to consider but it’s up to you to focus on what you find fun and what Ryo needs at that time.Some players will end up in a cycle of doing jobs to earn money, to spend on food for stamina, to deplete by running around everywhere. They will also use gambling. If it isn’t working for you, take a step back, review your options and make some changes. Everyday is a fresh start! Story wise, Shenmue 3 is a continuation of the saga. Fans of the series will know that this game was never meant to be the end and the lack of progression considering the wait is frustrating. However, Shenmue’s story progresses by location and YsNET were limited by what they could achieve in the locations presented in this story. The story elements, whilst hit and miss, also include some of my favourite moments in the series. What we do get is a deeper relationship with Shenhua and answers to some burning questions from Shenmue 1. There are also deep references to Shenmue 2 and I thought the implementation of this was a highlight. Shenmue 3 tries to implement the best of both of those worlds. Shenmue 3 is a hard game to recommend to newcomers but if you have patience and want a game that takes its time, this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue III is flawed and awkward, and unfortunately not the game it could have been were it made back in 2003 or whenever it was supposed to release. Sometimes a stiff facial animation, weird looking muppet man, or a mismatched piece of dialogue mid-conversation will very much remind you of that. And losing the Virtua Fighter engine combat probably hurts more than anything. However if you;A) Enjoyed Shenmue I and IIB) Realize this is not a AAA Sega/ Sony funded gameC) Know what PS2 graphics actually look likeyou will probably enjoy the game for what it is. The environments are actually incredible to look at and explore, Ryo's down-time dialogue with Shenhua is fun to listen to, the music is still top notch, and if you're into it, there's plenty of fanservice and call-backs to the Dreamcast titles. And continuing the trend of easing up on the players patience, there's plenty more skip-to options if you do not feel like traveling to an area/ feel like waiting a couple of in-game hours for a person to show up/ store to open. Story-wise, this game is certainly lighter than the first two titles and it definitely feels more like a game inbetween games. If Shenmue IV ever sees the light of day, this probably won't feel as strange. But without spoiling anything, the tail end of this game is mostly a set-up for Shenmue IV, or however Yu Suzuki plans on continuing the story. Also I originally played this game on a PS4 Pro, running it at 45FPS or so. On PC, it runs great and feels great at 60+FPS. Overall, if you really do like Shenmue, give it a shot. If you liked the idea of it or just liked it in passing, this game probably won't do much for you. 6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, Shenmue 3, how I have longed for the light of your presence to shine upon thee...Heads up to those who peruse this review: I'm a HUGE shenmue fan. I backed this game on kickstarter and have played the game twice on Sony PlayStation 4.Let's forget all of the nonsense associated with Deep Silver and the Epic Game Store exclusivity. How is THE GAME?A mixed bag.Let's start with the graphical presentation. Shenmue 1&2 were AAA games back in the day; the most expensive games every produced up until that time. Shenmue 3 is a AA game; as such you cannot go into this expecting the latest cutting edge graphics.With that said I was very impressed with the quality of the environment. Bailu Village is beautifully rendered with an impressive level of detail. The faces are another matter entirely though.Some faces are acceptable, others look like rubbery Halloween masks.Moving on to the gameplay...Shenmue 3 features a stamina system. Some reviewers have complained about this because for a large percentage of the game it is frustrating to see your health deplete before your eyes. It's incredibly frustrating. I actually think the inclusion is a welcome feature, but it is not balanced properly. As you work on your stamina training this becomes less of a problem in the game. In my new game plus I could run around all (game) day on a single charge. The new fighting system favours gamers who are not big fans of fighting games (like me) In Shenmue 1&2 you could purchase skill books and you would instantly "master" them. Although not really. I found it hard to remember and pull off the more powerful moves.Shenmue 3 does things quite differently. Once you buy a skill book you must practice that move oever and over again until you have truly mastered it. Once you have, you can add it to a "pull list"In a fight, simply pull the trigger and watch Ryo execute a perfect move! I love it, others don't. I guess it depends on your love and skill level of traditional 3D fighters.Rummaging through drawers has never been easier. The chunkiness of Shenmue 1&2 is gone, the lock is perfected. My only quibble is the red highlight around the selected objects, it's a bit “gamey" for my tastes.It's a little weird that cut scenes keep blacking out between transitions and the music abruptly cuts off when entering new areas of the game.QTE's are ridiculously hard. The game simply does not give you enough time to respond. When you fail, you simply have to try again, unlike Shenmue 1&2 there is no branching paths.The story (no spoilers) is a bit of a disappointment. Much of the information you "learn" is actually things players have already learnt in Shenmue 1&2. The new stuff is very welcome, but after waiting for so many years for this game I selfishly wish we could have gotten a little more.The Shenmue saga comprises 17 chapters.Shenmue 1 covers chapter 1.Shenmue 2 covered chapters,*3,4, and the beginning of chapter 5#. Shenmue 3 covers chapters 5,6, and 7. *Chapter 2 was cut from Shenmue 2 which featured the Ryo's adventures on the ship travelling to Hong Kong)#Shenmue 2 was supposed to end on the top of the Yellowhead Building. Yu decided to ship the game with the beginning of Chapter 5 (Guilin) because at the time he didn't know if he would ever get to finish the story and didn't want the work to go to waste.Because of this, the opening of Shenmue 3 is a little weird. It's not a big problem though since this game features a recap movie which is available at the main menu.I've been extremely nit-picky with this review. It's because I'm a Shenmue uber-fan. That said I am really happy with this game. If I wasn't I wouldn't have gotten the platinum trophy on PSN or played it twice, or bought it again on Steam, or created an achievement guide... lolYes, I love this game, warts and all. I believe if you are a Shenmue fan who has been waiting for the Steam release you will be extremely happy with this release. If you are coming to the game fresh having never played Shenmue before, or if you are a casual fan of the series you probably won't enjoy the game.Shenmue 3 was made for the fans. Other than the recap movie, no effort has been made to broaden its appeal or to engage with a wider demographic or pander to more mainstream open-world sensibilities.I hope my review has been helpful and as non-biased as possible. If you decide to buy the game, please check out my Achievement guide also available on Steam :)8/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's widely regarded that Shenmue was ahead of its time when it was released in 2000. Yet in 2020, a future where open world games are plentiful, I think it still holds true.Shenmue 3 is a game that follows the formula of its predecessors so closely that it feels like something out of a time capsule from the early 2000s. Too many open world games have gone in the direction of creating big empty violent playgrounds with just enough filler content to pad out their playtimes and give customers their $60 worth. Shenmue 3 contrasts this with an open world that's small, detailed, grounded in realism, steeped in mundanity, and all with a homely feel. It succeeds in creating that world, but fails to use it to its full potential.There's no hiding that Shenmue 3 is a bad game, and I'd have a hard time recommending it while looking a person in the eye. It's even a pretty bad Shenmue game. The hybrid health/stamina system is not a welcome addition, the combat is a step backwards, and the story fails to clear the low bar the previous games set out for it. The dialogue still sounds like it was both poorly translated and poorly written, new story elements join old ones that still don't make sense, and side content still lacks depth and quantity.This game can be easily criticized, but there's undeniable passion and effort here, giving its flaws a campy feel that you can still find enjoyment in if you're open to it. I do, however, believe Shenmue 3 does enough right that I'm not only enjoying it just because I can laugh at it.The game is segmented into days, in the morning you'll open your notebook and be given a main goal for the day that'll slightly advance the story if you choose to do it. Even if you finish the day's key item, you'll often get free time to spend on optional mini-games and side quests, or you can just skip to the next day. There's a time limit for completing the game, but it's generous enough that no one should reach it naturally. The game won't even tell you it exists unless you're getting dangerously close. A different game would've told you near the start, giving every moment a sense of urgency, but that's not what Shenmue 3 is.Shenmue 3 is very slow, and very repetitive. It'll happen multiple times that the big thing you do for a day is something mundane, something like catching chickens. Yet even without the threat of impending doom, Shenmue 3 still does a good job of making you think of time as a resource, and getting you to care about how you spend it. You'll feel a certain way knowing you could've spent the day in the noble pursuit of martial arts, but instead you were out save scumming the gambling mini-games. You'll go home to your platonic roommate, she'll ask you how it is you make your money, and you'll lie.It's easy to fool oneself into thinking this game's world is deeper than it actually is. Problems within the world are solved intuitively by engaging with the world. The result is an environment that feels less video-gamey than bigger budget alternatives, even if there's less to do here.This isn't a game that relies on maps and quest markers. If you need to know something you ask someone, anyone, literally anyone. Shenmue 3 has lots of NPCs, and most of them have voiced responses for nearly every step of your main quest, sometimes multiple responses, and not in a cheap "go over there" kind of way either. NPCs will frequently respond in ways that are unique and explicitly referencing of the thing you asked about, sometimes they'll even throw in a line or two of flavor text. Having NPCs be this useful makes them memorable.All of the NPCs have names, and they look and sound unique enough that I never noticed any obvious clones. Many of them have unique daily routines, and you'll see them often enough at different parts of their routines to begin to piece together stories for them. It's really pleasing to play an open world game filled with NPCs wandering around, and being able to pick a face out of the crowd and think to yourself "hey I know that guy!". There are limits however, and in terms of actual interactions you can have with NPCs, most are limited to only the main-quest-related dialogue options.Of all the characters, the star in this world is Shenhua, a character only just introduced at the very end of Shenmue 2, whose grand role in the story is so far a mystery. Each day is book-ended by interactions with Shenhua, and she'll be the only character you can talk to in what this game's idea of branching dialogue trees is. These interactions quickly became the highlights of my days, and the later half of the game suffers as she fades into the background. She'll still accompany you, but nightly conversations will be replaced with early bedtimes, and the peering in of windows as one sleeps.Ultimately, this game has two sides to it which appealed to me, the one being that it's "so bad it's good". It's from this side that I was amused upon hearing, after almost two decades, that Shenmue 3 wouldn't be a grand farewell for the series. Yu Suzuki has a vision, and he will not compromise. That's not to say that commercial and critical failure hasn't at all tempered his expectations. The originally planned 16 chapters of the Shenmue epic has been refined down to a modest 11, still enough to get us to a possible Shenmue 5. I was amused by the ending we got in Shenmue 3 and I'm eagerly awaiting a possible sequel.The other side of Shenmue 3 lies in the feeling that somewhere within the Shenmue formula there's a great game. Even if none of the Shenmues fully realize it, if they're the only ones out there trying, then they're the closest we have.

_childDocuments_.review: >> Hey Shenhua.<< What is it Ryo?>> This game is disappointing.<< It's disappointing?>> Yeah.Steam compared this game to Final Fantasy XV, I really liked the trailer, and friends said they loved Shenmue I and II, so of course I bought it. I'll start with a warning: don't buy this game if you don't have a controller. When I started it up, it said that playing with a controller was recommended - and you really should. The mouse doesn't do anything, in the menu at least, and there is no way to find out what keys are linked to what commands (settings only change language and sound). After accidentally selecting "credits" (with arrows and enter) and being unable to exit (the backspace key started the credit roll and none of the other keys made it stop), I gave in and borrowed a controller.  I'm sure there are online guides that tell you what the standard keys/buttons are, but I shouldn't have to use Google in order to start my game. With a bit of practise and a controller, the controls are okay though, and the fights are fun. They basically recommend you button-smash, but after a few training sessions it's possible to level up specific moves.The next thing that struck me were the flat dialogues. The dialogues are the best thing about FFXV so the low quality of the ones in Shenmue III was surprising. There's a sample at the top. Five minutes into the game I could predict 80% of the dialogue because it's so repetitive. It could be a fun drinking game if you play in a group or watch a stream. In general, the game feels like the developers just took the game they made back in 2001 and added new plotlines. The graphics are higher resolution, but that only makes it more obvious how basic they are. Clouds are sheets floating in the sky for example. I'm going to continue playing because I'm curious what happens next, but I'm not sure I would have bought it if I had known all the above.Edit to add after a bit more playtime: turns out the game is not only repetitive in its dialogues, it's also repetitive in everything else. On top of that it promotes gambling (not the only method of getting money, but the most efficient one). Don't know if I can finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game. THOROUGHLY. I do genuinely hope that Shenmue 4 will be a reality but I still have to post this as a negative review due to a few key factors. Firstly, this was a chance for Yu Suzuki to modernize the Shenmue slice of life formula and build newer systems into the game engine. Instead they chose to go for a retro style game with modern graphics.The upside to that is lovers of the old games get a sense of nostalgia as it feels like playing Shenmue 2 remade for the new age but with clunky old systems and the jank that we all know and love. The downside is that there overall ethos of development has left the franchise is a state of stagnation, stuck in 1998. Secondly, the timed exclusive deals with Epic game store crippled the reception of the game just like other titles that choose to go the Epic games routeThirdly, the old formula meant that there was a lot of busy work and tedium baked into the story beats. Locking out progress in areas due to not having X amount of money or X item without prior warning plus requiring a long grind to obtain said money or item means that the game had areas in which it grinded to a hault and forced you to do things you didn't really want to do to continue. Such soft locks are present in many games as ways to pad out play time and I hate it.Shenmue 4 please. Make Shenmue great again.

_childDocuments_.review: Like many I had written this game off after some bad reviews that made it seem like an absolute disaster. Still, after having played the first 2 games again, I was interested enough to finally give it a chance regardless. Imo it really is not a bad game at all, but the transition to modern day gaming surely left a lot to be desired.+ Laid back exploration: Like the classics this game still lets you take your time and enjoy the atmosphere and mundanity of its locations. If you feel like experiencing the day-to-day life for a few weeks with a mixture of discovery, fighting, money earning mini games and gambling, you can feel at home. Taking your time I don't think the infamous wealth roadblocks are a problem at all and quite similar to Shenmue II.+ Controls: by foot or in a forklift this game controls much smoother than its predecessors.+ Mini games/jobs: From lucky hit and arcade games to fork lifting and chopping wood, they are more pleasant than their counterparts, though I definitely would have loved a bigger and more lifely harbor area.+ Awkward charme; Stilted dialogue, weird (non) reactions, a certain B Movie charme, if you valued that in the original games, there's still plenty of that to be found. + fighting: Despite other people's opinion, I actually prefer fighting in this game. In SM I and II it really felt like pressing YXX again and again was the most efficient way to win fights, while here it's a bit more about timing and using a previously trained and saved one button press combo. I'm generally not into fighting games though, so I can't judge if I'd enjoy it otherwise.~ Art direction: The environments can be very beautiful for sure, but some of the characters just look goofy and don't feel like they belong into the game. The earlier games showed a bit of that too, but apparently cartoony 'larger than life' unreal engine models just feel wrong, while the old dreamcast tech could still get away with it. ~ Locations: The game starts right where SM II ended and lets you experience the first third of the game in a small rural chinese village, followed by another bigger location afterwards. Sadly both of those lack the charms of Dobuita and Hong Kong, but still make for an interesting enough setting on their own, even though they feel artificially crafted to include game mechanics like gambling and fighting. - No (new) memorable characters: Shenhua is the person you spend most time with and imo she is not the best choice to pair with Ryo, as she can be almost as stoic and bland as the man himself. It's great that you eventually get to meet someone else from the past games to liven things up with, but sadly other people that get newly introduced either don't leave much of an impression or just don't get enough of a presence in game.- Lack of life-like simulation: NPCs with routines, destinations and overall purpose to their actions were a huge deal in the first games. he locations felt really lived in, like places that would still exist on their own once Ryo left for another adventure. This game uses the tech to make locations more beautiful, but at the same time they feel very artificial in comparison. NPCs don't feel like they have much of an agenda as most of them will just stand at a location throughout the whole day. Nobody to watch in the mornings on their way to open up a shop, nobody to play darts against, no other people actually working at the harbor, etc. Nobody reacts to rain at all and there seems to be tons of freshly prepared food on every restaurant's table, despite the fact that there's absolutely no one around to enjoy it. It feels like they either deliberately tried to hit some sort of uncanny valley design or just lacked the budget to follow through with ambitious ideas.- Meta stuff everywhere: A few references to the original games could be pretty charming, but this game just gets crazy with it: Shenmue characters/self referential material on t-shirts and in capsule toy machines, a whole building dedicated to the game series itself and worst of all Kickstarter backer rewards with their faces/names to be seen in various locations later in the game. This is just very immersion breaking, especially in a series most famous for its attempts of immersing the player in its setting.- Timed side quests: For some reason you could miss out on side quests if you don't trigger them in the exact time frame in regards to the main story. So if you want to see them all, you almost need a guide.- Achievemnts: If you're planning to 100% the game, you might want to rethink. They really force you to delve into some of the more tedious aspects of the game, the worst contender being 1000 fish to catch, which will take many hours and layers of your thumb's skin.All that being said, I'd still recommend it if you enjoyed the first two and feel like continuing Ryo's journey. It's not as charming or memorable, but it can be a good time and it certainly didn't ruin the series for me.

I get nostalgia, but for everyone else, I don’t think they’ll be able to see the charm as this game feels rough. _childDocuments_.review: I will honestly say, this is genuinely the worst video game I've ever played. And when I say play, I mean actually playing the game at least a decent amount of time. I'm sure there are some low quality asset flips that I've played for 5 mins that are worse. But in terms of video games I've either played to completion or have at least put in enough time to have a decent understanding of them, this game is the worst. And yes, I have played both Shenmue 1 and 2. Not only is Shenmue 3 absolutely terrible in practically every way, but it does a massive disservice to the franchise. Completely abandoning so many of the things that made the original games novel and interesting. Such as the Virtua Fighter inspired combat system. Or the more open nature to puzzle solving and progression. Shenmue 3, despite being a niche game for old time fans, decided to massively dumb itself down, in what I can only imagine, was some ill fated attempt at cultivating a new audience. So what we end up with, is a combat system that would make Skyrim look impressive. As well as puzzles and progression systems, so transparently designed to pad the game and waste your time, you'd have to be a stupid baby to not realize it. And I mean that, A stupid person would still see how insulting this game is. You'd literally have to be stupid and a baby to not see how absurd this game is with wasting your time and padding out nonsensical plot points. I could go into further detail of the amateurish usage of a stamina system, the RPG aspects and gambling, but the only people who would defend this game, are the most dedicated Shenmue apologist. You might still think, "But what about the story?" And my answer to that is simple, Yeah, what about the story? The game barely has one. 90% of the game is either retreading things from the past games, or waffling about doing nothing. The entire story of Shenmue that has any real substance, happens in the last 20 mins or so of this bloated game. I'll sum up right here. Lan Di, gets Phoenix Mirror. You fight Lan Di, You lose. The game ends with Ryo swearing to get him next time. Also Ren showed up. 0/10

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't exactly wait 18 years for this game like the people that played Shenmue 2 on the Dreamcast back in the day, but even I feel betrayed.This "game" is frustrating beyond comprehension. Let me list the reasons why I despise this game:- There's an absurd amount of grinding. Even when you're not doing side-quests or achievements, the game creates this fake longevity by forcing you to grind in almost every single activity in order for the story to progress.- The pacing of the story is so slow and boring. Some people used to say that the Shenmue games were boring, but screw that, THIS IS BORING. Which is even more unnerving considering the fact that there's barely any story at all! This is barely a completed game, considering it has been in development for ATLEAST 4 YEARS! And don't give me the budget constraints nonsense, there's no excuse for the quality of this thing.- Despite spending 2 games fighting assassins, goons and all sorts of martial arts experts, somehow Ryo is a wuss in this game, and needs to train endlessly because some anemic bastard stepped on his pinky toe too hard. What a joke.- Despite being a game released in 2019, it still feels like it was made in 1999: bad voice acting, terrible subtitles in the japanese option, outdated controls (really? you couldn't look at the way other video games were made nowadays? you had to go with the "nostalgic route" and keep all the things that are wrong with the game?), cutscenes that fade out and fade in mid-conversation for no apparent reason, etc, etc.- The fighting mechanics are completely ruined. Whatever fun players had from the flexible and satisfying Free Battle mode of the previous games is gone, and replaced by a stiff ass boring new fighting mode in which you can't tell if you're actually hitting the opponent or not. Also training new moves is guess what? More grinding! Got a new move? Train it by repeating the same thing 1 million times. Fun!- The stamina mechanic will make you want to kill someone. Who the heck thought this was a good idea?! Ryo can't run more than 10 steps without having a heart attack what the heck is this nonsense?!- Interesting characters from the previous games such as Ren and Shenhua are reduced to useless side bimbos. Ren serves almost no purpose in the story, and talking to Shenhua in this game is like talking to an AI sexbot. We had more meaningful and interesting conversations with Shenhua in the last 10 minutes of Shenmue 2 than the entire duration of this stinkfest.- Enjoyed having missable content from the previous games and having to start a new playthrough because the game is infested with timed events? Congratulations! The game now has triple the amount! Really annoying specially for someone like me who has achievement OCD. Enjoy replaying this dumpster fire.- I hope you enjoy the ending as well. 18 years for this cop out of an ending. I can't be mad at Shenmue 2's cliffhanger but this? What a giant disappointment.No wonder this game is trash, Yu Suzuki says he doesn't enjoy playing video games.I hope Lan Di comes out of the screen and kicks him in the balls.

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation is yes, but only if you like life simulators. Sure Shenmue 3 (as with all of Shenmue) has action elements BUT for the most part the focus of Shenmue is the detective work, asking where sailors or the next temple is, and living ie eating/ sleeping and a little bit of entertainment. If this isn't your thing you won't like this game.Pros: But IF that is your jam, I HIGHLY recommend FIRST Shenmue 1 & 2 (takes ~40 hours to complete the two) than this, Shenmue 3 (~40 hours on it's own). Though it has been 20 years between release (plus controversy due to this being made by different dev houses... different devs but the same director and likely lots of the same staff I'd assume. Though this game is a PERFECT transition from Shenmue 2, all the people, jokes, most of the game mechanics (some, like the fighting system, were Sega's property thus could not be carried over but the new one is very similar some don't even notice the change) it's all there as if the games 20 years ago was yesterday, Cons: Realize that Shenmue is a massive 5 (or more) part series so take this lightly but seriously, Shenmue 3 is kind of like the filler episodes where you get to know one of the main characters but ultimately do nothing at all to advance the main storyline. I don't know about you but I like filler though, it's got one leg to stand on and that's entertainment- thus IMO you'll get the BEST entertainment out of filler.Overall S3 adds some welcome techniques to the Shenmue series that shows the difference between a 2020 game and a 2000 game. It's still not everything to everyone, it still expects you to know Shenmue 1 and 2 (there is a recap video, but I still highly recommend you play 1 and 2 first, both are available in an updated package on steam), and to some, it is still made in an old school (tank controls, dialog that tends to skew to the corny/ anime side) frame of mind. For this, I can't give this game a perfect score but still a highly recommended 7/ 10. If you don't like 'coffee talk' filler than it might more of a back burner 5.5 to 6/ 10 but surely TRY Shenmue 1 and 2 to see if you like it than at the very least put this gem on the backlog cuz it's a LOT of fun at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Before starting my review, I'd like to point out that we really need a mixed review option on Steam. I hope Gaben will hear our prayers one day. Anyway, as most of you know, Shenmue III is the highest funded Kickstarter game and it is definitely one of the longest awaited one. How long was it... 20 years? I'm not a loyal Shenmue fan, I didn't wait 20 years for it, in fact, first time I've played Shenmue was a few months ago but I was aware of its significance and contributions to the video game culture of course. I also didn't contributed anything to its Kickstarter campaign but putting myself in one of the loyal fans' place, I'd be extremely disappointed by this game. Especially after waiting nearly 20 years for it. Although I have no doubt that Yu Suzuki and YS Net did their best to bring a solid title to the fans, they've made a grave mistake by striking a deal with Deep Silver. 1 year Epic Store exclusivity was straight up disrespectful towards the people who contributed to Kickstarter campaign. Hopefully, they will learn from their mistakes with Shenmue IV. Anyway, let's take a look at the redeeming qualities first... This might be considered as a negative attribute by many people but Shenmue III is like a PS2 game rather than a modern one. The way characters talk, voice acting, mechanics, they all are very similar to older Shenmue titles. I loved it and I'm pretty sure fans will love it as well. Landmarks, overall world design, and the soundtrack are beautiful. Interacting with the world is much easier compared to older games. You will also have a smoother experience navigating around the environment. The most beautiful thing about Shenmue III however, is the dialogue between Ryo & Shenhua. I highly suggest you to talk with Shenhua whenever you get the chance since you'll witness the bond between them growing. Compared to these redeeming qualities, there are many bad things about Shenmue III. First of all, voice acting scales from very good to worst, same applies to character designs as well. There are much more minigames compared to older titles and levelling up your fighting moves is much more straightforward but the whole story revolves around them and they get repetitive very fast. Both parts of the story are the reflection of one another, and the only significant event happens right at the end of the game, but it will leave your frustrated whether you're a fan or not. I don't want to spoil anything, you'll have to see that for yourself. In spite of highly interactive world, it feels shallow due to the fact that Ryo responds almost everything with: "Hmm... This is...". He says nothing of importance, thus it feels like most of the interactive objects are just there to create the illusion of being interactive. Combat on the other hand is a mess. Grabbing is gone, it feels like you're not even hitting your opponent and on the top of that, it is simplified. Instead of using the face buttons, you just choose the move you want to execute and hit RT. You can still use the face buttons but it's not as efficient as hitting RT. Also, don't even think about playing it with keyboard and mouse because the layout is terrible! I don't know if you're allowed to change the layout or not, but it definitely cannot compare to gamepad. QTE is also way too precise. It wants you to react almost immediately. I'd highly recommend dropping the difficulty during the chicken catching section, trust me on that one if you value your mental health. If you're planning to obtain every single achievement and "enjoy" everything that this game has to offer, you'll need a lot of time and patience since it has one of the most tedious achievements out there such as catching 1000 fish and collecting every single herb. They make the game extremely grindy and it's such a lazy way to extend the gameplay time if you ask me. To sum up, Shenmue III is worth your time if you're interested in the story but anything other than that is worthless. _childDocuments_.review: It's a shame that the most popular videos for these games (the third in particular) only serve to give it a bad reputation, and through a lot of misunderstood hyperbole. Yes, it's much slower paced than the last two - - though I find it fitting coming off of the ending of the second - - and yes, it's needlessly grindy in the beginning (there's a mod called "Kiwami" everyone should get for that), but I don't see why anyone who loved the first two wouldn't enjoy this one. Very relaxing game that improves on and at the very least maintains what made its predecessors so lovable, despite the initial tedium. You'll be making a lot of jokes over the fact Ryo was once able to beat 70 guys in a few minutes, but has to practice horse-stance. Still, the music is almost as good as the first two, the setting is gorgeous and arguably the best in the series, the mini-games are better than ever, the characters are lovable, and the combat is more challenging than the original. I just hope there's a fourth, because it ends on a weak note.

_childDocuments_.review: It only took them, what, two decades to make Shenmue III, the intentionally slow middle act in the multi-part poorly-written, poorly-translated epic kung fu quest. It's such a weird game. It's admirable how close it sticks to the original games' design, and while I appreciate that, it also hurts the game quite a bit.I'm happy the game plays just like Shenmue I + II -- I think that was the right route to take. Where I think this fails is simply down to pacing. Shenmue I and II, despite feeling like archaic products of their time today, were *epic* in design. The settings, the scope, were massive and detailed; the story's peaks and valleys were, while not, you know, technically good, at least diverse and unfathomably ambitious.It has one major change from previous entries: Combat has been completely redesigned. Most folks are hating on it, but I actually loved the changes. No longer am I just using the same two or three moves over and over to win every fight. Enemies getting familiar with your tactics means you have to learn -- really memorize -- new moves and plan your fights dynamically. Those skills being weak without training means you have to go to the dojos and train. It's not perfect, but it's a step in the right direction.Shenmue III still plays and 'feels' the same, but it doesn't share the prequels' ambitions. Reviews that bring up the lack of progression aren't kidding. Despite the game being just as long (or longer) than Shenmue II, there are only three regions to explore, and the quality is all over the place.Bailu Village, the opening chapter, is my favorite, and it felt like the perfect continuation of Shenmue II's ending. The quests, the look, the pacing, are all exactly what I wanted from a sequel. (This makes sense, as apparently Shenmue II's ending was meant to be the opening of Shenmue III.)Niaowu, the second chapter, is beautiful to explore and full of *so much detail* it's awe-inspiring. The environmental detail surpasses any of the previous games, and it's still a comfort to end every day talking to Shenhua -- but: The quests take a dramatic dip in quality here. Everything is transparently a fetch quest, and you just spend every day jogging to the same 5 or so locations throughout the city, which highlights how poorly designed the city is at the coarsest scale (i.e., just large corridors connecting to one another).And the castle. The closing chapter is incomplete. It's a single linear corridor that slams a bunch of story twists at you which otherwise feel disconnected from the Bailu village and Biaowu story progression (or lackthereof). It has the most awkward, bewildering fetch quest squished into the start of it.It's great seeing Shenhua and Ren again in HD. It's great hearing Ryo's wooden voice-acting hammering out the hammiest lines again. It's great to explore a relic of 2000-era game design, even if it doesn't quite live up to the past. Still, I can easily recommend this to fans and still hope we see a Shenmue 4 some day soon. :)

_childDocuments_.review: The first was a gradual awakening to the layer of dirt beneath the surface of a teen karate prodigy's pleasant hometown.  The second was a stevedore-funded tunneling through a high-rise hive of criminous humanity.  This third game is almost a vacation for Ryo Hazuki, being a laid-back, low-pressure romp in the Spring sunshine, and it's one of the most soothing -- and aesthetically pleasing -- games of my year.Despite having a fraction of  or 's budget,  is every bit as Shenmue as the previous pair.  There is a change in feel, however, that comes from the game's central, pivot-of-action spot in the projected quintology (long stories are always slower in the middle, it seems) as well as from the new rural setting.  Here is the dimsum noontime of the series, a contemplative mezzanine where Ryo must  the meaning of Master Xiu Ying's Leaf of Patience (it's in your inventory at the start) -- a slow getting-to-know the gorgeously green Chinese countryside as it exists in the Shenmue universe:  the very place, you'll remember, where the stone mirrors originated.  This one is short on big plot reveals, but incredibly rich in atmosphere and environmental detail.  The story is less serious this time around, too, maybe even a bit  in parts, but it is a true continuation, not a retcon -- and good on Yu Suzuki for not speeding up his narrative pacing and , which some "fans" insisted on (as if it was something they wanted to put behind them forever).First comes Bailu, one of my favorite locations in the entire series:  a sprawling mountain town where it's always so refreshing to leave Shenhua's cottage by sunrise, looking out on the golden prospect while thinking about what you're going do with the day.  Should you . . . upgrade your fighting stats with a wooden kung fu dummy?  (I  loved doing this!  What could your lizard brain enjoy more, I ask you, than grinding for strength with satisfying QTEs?)  Hunt the verdant lands for medicinal herbs to sell for heaps of yuan?  (The hours I spent scouring every flowery meadow and pleasant valley for these things!  Collection obsession at its finest!)  Gamble at turtle racing and Lucky Hit in the venture areas?  Chop firewood?  (This was another favorite; if you hit the log dead-center, you get  chunks to exchange for cash, and every streak of center-hit three causes the music to rev up and  you up.)  And since this is a Japanese game, you  you can fish every body of water deeper than a puddle!  There are so, so many fun ways to make money -- meaning you're not stuck doing something like carrying box after endless box while De Lin and Congo throw ♥♥♥♥♥-fits on you.Niaowu, the riverside city where the second half of the game takes place, has a few strengths of its own.  You get all the money-making, time-spending options you had in Bailu, while having the chance to take in some  detailed architecture; the variety of shops and especially the richness of the many Buddhist temples will blow you away.  It did disappoint me, somewhat, that Ryo couldn't talk to every single person on the street like he could in ; the game restricts you to questioning only shopkeepers and a few notables in Niaowu.It was a fine game for sure (I hope I've made that clear!) but it wasn't  roses.  I would have liked:-- More dialog options!  Though being a monomaniac is in keeping with Shenmue tradition, I would have preferred our protagonist to  question every person he talked to about things already obvious to him.-- Better fighting mechanics!  I came to grips with 's controversial system pretty early on . . . but there were no throws this time, and no regular counters, either!  I didn't feel as if I were engaged with opponents as intimately, as , as in the other two games.-- Better story DLC, and more side quests in general!  Good to see slab-faced Zhang again, but did they really have to recycle those same few thugs from earlier in the game so much for the DLC?  Did they  have to make us set up chawan signs randomly around the city for  to get this slice of nothing?  I felt like I was playing grab-a$$ with every drinking vessel in town.-- A more robust finale!  The castle architecture and new character designs in the endgame were excellent, and I know that the game was  to end on a cliffhanger, but there should have been a more dramatic, drawn-out confrontation.  C'mon!  After the Seventy Man Battle, the seventeen-storey dungeon hack, and the epic journey to Bailu seen in the previous games, the wam-bam-goodbye of  didn't quite cut it for me.However, I  come back around to this point:  I enjoyed playing  more than any other game this year save its predecessors, with which it ties; they're all certifiably Shenmue, and each expresses that quality just a little differently.  I was always thinking about the game when I wasn't playing it, and, with the strong exception of the DLC, I never got bored in the fifty hours I spent with it.  I honestly didn't think it would be as good as it was, but the aura that hit me as soon as I stepped into Bailu was so warm and rich that I immediately expected Ys Net to hit every single note I craved -- thus the stumbles listed above stood out to me more than they otherwise might have.If you really like Shenmue -- beauty marks, fuzzy warts, and everything else -- and  just the technological innovation the originals represented back when they released, you will adore this game.  Please, Sega or somebody, help Yu finish this landmark series; if he could do  with Kickstarter bucks and a from-scratch engine, just imagine what he could accomplish with big time backing!(Not a criticism, but it is absolutely  how every white guy in this game has a face like one of the plastic cowboys from Primus' "Winona's Big Brown Beaver" video.  Now, I know what I said earlier about the boxes, but I kind of wish I could have worked with Riff Tamblyn hauling a few -- just so I could have laughed my a$$ off at his big, lumpy face turning red with rage as I went butter mitts on yet another one!)

_childDocuments_.review: The original Shenmue is probably my favorite game ever. I also enjoyed the sequel when it (finally) came out for the Xbox. I had pretty low expectations for Shenmue III due to its numerous subpar reviews, but not playing it was simply not an option. Now that I've put 12 hours into the game, I can safely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the first two iterations.Yes, the combat is not as enjoyable as Shenmue I or II, however, it's fairly easy to figure out so that you can enjoy knocking out "thugs" without too much frustration. However, where this game shines is in its beautiful setting, slow, relaxed pace, and (of course) its tried and true adventure game mechanics. Personally, I think the graphics are great, and I don't mind hunting for herbs, spending money trying to score capsule toy sets (which is actually pretty important in this game), and leveling up my kung fu. I guess these aspects make it slightly "grindier" than the original, but I think it's still really fun, especially when taking a slow pace. TLDR; Loved Shemue 1 and 2, and number 3 definitely does the series justice!

_childDocuments_.review: Updates 11/28/20: So I finally completed this game. I must say at the end I feel a little disappointed, not because of the limited progress of the story, which I already knew before I made the purchase. I am talking about how the town is designed to feel real. It was a huge achievement of the previous installments, especially Shenmue 2. The two old games were significantly limited by hardware 20 years ago and therefore resulting in low-poly boxy environment with very low resolution textures, and the map was separated into multiple chunks. But despite those limitations, the development team created a living town/city that feels believable. Now all those limitations no longer exist today, but what appear to be large, beautifully-textured towns in this game actually feel like soulless, empty movie sets. You can see all those things that don't make sense at all. It wasn't that bad in Bailu Village it wasn't that bad, although you may question why there are three restaurants serving a population of 30, with identical layouts across the three locations. If you are a Shenmue fan, you know that in previous games you NEVER see cookie-cutter layout in stores and this is what Shenmue distinguish itself from other games. (Godfather and Mafia 3 are the opposite examples.) By the way, how did Shenhua's house suddenly getting a new, separate bedroom for Ryo to sleep? Remember he and Shenhua slept on separate beds in the same bedroom the night before they went to find Shenhua's father missing. The game may take 20 years to release but within the game it were only several hours separating Shenmue 2 and 3. Oh by the way, Shenhua's clothing mysteriously changed between 2 and 3 for no reason. And her father's name was En Chouju as written on the letter to her at the end of 2. But in 3, his names is now suddenly changed to En Unshin. Did they actually do their homework when picking up this project?Then you move to Niaowu and the environment design becomes a full-blown issue. You may remember in Shenmue 2, how much Wanchai looked different from Kowloon, and within Wanchai and Kowloon how each building and street corner look different from each other and has its own identity. Tall buildings have elevators, clothing stores have fitting rooms. You find facilities like parks in the towns, and you there are various non-retail locations like a town should. But here in Niaowu, excluding a warehouse for you to play forklift missions, buildings are ALL of identical architecture elements: roof, walls, pillars, and windows. Its supposed to be an old town with hundreds years of history, but looks brand new and more like a modern town plan by a single land developer in a single project. Looking deeper, you will find there is no apartments or houses for residential purpose, not even separate building entries for residents. The hotel you stay has no bathrooms. Everything on the first floor facing the streets is for retail. It doesn't feels like a town at all, but more of a Chinese theme park or outdoor shopping mall. Once you get into those stores, things are getting more ridiculous. Using the appliance store as an example, in Shenmue 2 you saw all those things popular in the 80s and their design matched the real stuff at that time in Asia: stereos, two-in-one washer/dryers, portable TVs, wall fans, PCs, and fridges. I had many of them at home 30 yrs ago. Everything just looked real.  In Shenmue 3, not only you see much less items, but they also apparently are stock assets probably purchased from those online asset markets. As result, you see stereos from the 90s, and AMERICAN-style blenders and fridges from the 50s, in a Chinese town supposed to be in the 80s. I still remember reading the game magazine articles telling me how much effort they put researching Yokosuka and Hongkong when they made Shenmue 1 and 2. This time, they apparently made ZERO effort how a Chinese town in the 80s would look like. I understand this is no longer a AAA production and the resource is limited. That's exactly why they should've directed the limited resources to get the things right, not blindly making maps big or just creating more capsule toys. Then you get to see those restaurants, where for some reasons, they put their food on empty tables for whole day. And they cook on old, American stoves.Losing the feel of believable environment is taking so much away from this game. You can compare clothing stores, restaurants, barber shops, herb stores, martial arts specialists, drug stores, every type of retailers to those in previous games. You will find every store in the current game are like pointlessly piling up stock assets that are out of their place, completely lacking souls and touches. English books stored in a Chinese gang hideout? Check. Only English-labeled drugs in drugstore? Check. The size of this game is as large as any AAA games today but such lack of background variety is stunning, especially when comparing to Shenmue 2 which was restricted by both the GD-rom and Dreamcast memory sizes. Higher polygon counts can't hide the less organic environments. Higher resolution textures don't save the poor design. To me, Yokosuka in Shenmue 1 and Hongkong in 2 are places I enjoy to walk aimlessly even after completed the game. You can feel they were trying hard to replicate a town you live in. Niaowu in Shenmue 3? I have no intention going back at all. It may have 130 retail stores but it is as fake as it can be.Then you have those NPCs, which are way scarce than in Shenmue 2 despite the 20 years advance of technology. For most of the time, the streets in Niaowu are either empty or having less than 5 people. And the NPC pop-in in previous games is still here. You have to walk to within 100 feet from Bushindo to see the guys practicing martial arts showing up in front of it, for example. And you probably have noticed that unlike the previous games, NPCs here no longer use umbrella when raining. In fact, they behave like nothing happens, walking in calm pace or sitting on outdoor tables watching their dumpings soaked under heavy rain. In fact, they just sit there doing nothing for the whole day, instead of walking in to a restaurant, sitting down, eating food like in Shenmue 2. In Rokakudo, you see the Miko holding a broom cleaning the same spot without moving morning to night. The stiff, rigid NPC behaviors take another big chunk from this game. Oh, and the conversations are also very mechanical, including those with Shenhua. At home, your conversation with her always follow the same pattern. It certainly doesn't have the polish like something that has been brewed for 20 years. Overall it is still a Shenmue game but if I give Shenmue 1 a 7/10 and 2 10/10, this one I would only give it a 5 or 5.5. Lots of easter eggs and the Bailu/Niaowu setting obviously references Yokosuka/Hongkong, including that you have free place to sleep in the first and must pay for hotel room in the second. It plays like Shenmue but but it is a shame that they lost so much thoughts and attention to details in stage designs that made the previous settings charming and believable. To much is done for each surface but too less for how things look together in whole. If one day Shenmue 4 is coming I am still going to buy, but I hope they will find the magic back. It shouldn't be just how it plays, but also where it is played at. ---------------------------------------------------------If you know what you are going to get and feel comfortable about it, this can be a nice game for you. In many aspects this game doesn't quite meet today's standard.  It is a game that you can slow down your pace to enjoy, with solid graphic and smooth music. It is a shame that it doesn't conclude the story in a meaningful way and I don't really expect another game would eventually be made for that purpose. But it is still a nice experience, an old-time entertainment with old-fashioned story without today's SJW censorship/contamination.

_childDocuments_.review: **My personal experience of the game as a fan who has been waiting so long is overall positive. I followed the game quite closely so I am aware of the difficulties that presented themselves during the development and some of the compromises that had to be made as a result, and find the end product a more than acceptable labour of love by Yu Suzuki and YsNet.Shenmue III may click with you, or it may not, but it's worth finding out all the same. A recap movie is included to fill you in on the story details from the first two games should you decide to jump straight in, but if you're unfamiliar with the series Shenmue I & II are also available on Steam and are also recommended as epoch-defining games from SEGA's short-lived Dreamcast. A blast from the past, a triumph of determination for the fans and the developers, and ultimately a unique experience you wouldn't get from any other series or any other developer. Shenmue III is all these things and more. That "more" might be positive or negative depending on who you ask, but Shenmue has always been divisive, and Shenmue III more than usual because of having to overcome the hurdles of an 18 year gap between entries, inherent cynicism of the age we live in; and the obvious fact it is attempting to be a sequel to two of the most expensive games ever made on a sixth of the budget and manpower.Shenmue III succeeds on that last point, and is a closer approximation of the original titles than most would reasonably expect. The budget is however creaking with strain, which is apparent on almost every level. While Shenmue III recreates a number of essential systems that formed the backbone of the original games, alongside various additions and improvements, the relative level of polish the first two games had isn't present and it's clear corners had to be cut to achieve a finished product.It could also be said that Shenmue III fumbles the ball on core elements you would expect to be a priority, but I redirect you to the "relative polish" comment above. The game has to spin a lot of plates just to even feel like a proper sequel, and given the challenging conditions it was developed under, some leeway has to be given for an acceptable level of falling short of quite high expectations given the opulent development environment the first two games came from. Shenmue III succeeds majorly on the small things that makes the series unique, and most notably the vibes and atmosphere that make the Shenmue games genuinely world class at worldbuilding without making it feel particularly signposted and gamey. The game is best played at its own pace, which is with few exceptions relaxed. Whether you're ingratiating yourself with the locals in Bailu during the first half of the game, or playing tourist in Niaowu in the second. This is not a game for adrenaline junkies. This is for the patient, observant, and curious.On that basis I will readily say the Shenmue series is not for everyone, and perhaps Shenmue III less so because it has to compete on a different standard today, but it's worth finding out if you're the type of person Shenmue will appeal to. Sometimes these games just click with people who have the right personalities and tastes, and it's worth taking the plunge to see if that's you.

_childDocuments_.review: Very early into the game but so far, it's definitely shenmue. For those that always wondered what a higher res shenmue would look and feel like, this is it. The same wonky dialog, bad lip reading and social awkwardness is all there. I heard the first few hours are slow and they are but what's cool is the ability to wake up and do whatever you want. For me, i started a routine to train and then spar, then work or gamble to earn money then continue on the main quest. Combat is lacking but not the worst.. what i  wish it had was a side quest style to it like most modern games. Only difference being, ryo is in a real world and his quests would be helping the local village like helping capture fish, or repair a boat or put out a fire or any other task that would help build a relationship with the townfolk. As much as this game wants to be a real-life simulation, it's still on rails as far as the story goes so it wouldnt hurt to put in more side content/mini games etc. It's actually not a bad game whatsoever. I feel guilty for getting this as cheap as i did. Never thought i'd play it. I was a fan of the first two and best them on the og dreamcast. When i revisited those games a few years back in prep for this release, i could still see the charm but the games aged like milk. This is a worthy continuation of the story, even if it doesnt progress much. Not bad for the budget but if they make #4 (doubtful) it would benefit from some more modern, quality of life improvements. Adding things like stamina (hate it in every game) is a chore, not an immersive game mechanic. Get rid of it or at least have it autogenerate instead of having constantly manage it.

_childDocuments_.review: With Shenmue II being an excellent game with an incredible atmosphere, great characters, and , it would be an understatement to say that Shenmue III had a lot to live up to. However, with Shenmue II costing Sega tens of millions of dollars and not selling great, it seemed like Shenmue III would never see the light of day. However, thanks to an incredibly successful Kickstarter and some backing from Sony, Shenmue III was eventually released over fifteen years later. Despite the time between Shenmue II and Shenmue III's release, Shenmue III feels right at home with the other titles, for better or worse. From the detailed environments to the high level of interactivity, Shenmue III feels like it takes everything from the previous games and finds a way to make it feel new. However, despite doing a lot right, there are plenty of things that Shenmue III does wrong. The biggest is that it plays like a Shenmue game; the tedious tasks, drawn-out sequences, and annoying aspects of the previous games are very present here. Moreover, in some ways, Shenmue III is even more tedious than the previous games. While this isn't necessarily a bad thing, it is what Shenmue is known for, I would've liked to see at least some progression in the design philosophy, considering how much time has passed since the last game. Outside of the gameplay, though, the story leaves a lot to be desired. In fact, despite Shenmue III being a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for the story to be wrapped up, the  despite little being done to move the plot forward. When it comes to the visuals of Shenmue III, things are somewhat mixed. At times, Shenmue's world can look stunning due to the vibrant colors, solid particle effects, and great character models for the main characters. Yet, at the same time, the game can have a very Unreal Engine 4 aesthetic, if that makes sense. As for the performance, being a game running on UE4, there are stuttering issues. While it isn't the worst I've seen, it is very noticeable when traveling to a different area of the map. Along with this, despite having an uncapped framerate, it is clear that Shenmue 3 was designed to be played at 30 or 60 FPS; I could not get solid frame times when playing above 60 FPS on my rig.Overall, while Shenmue III has many issues and can feel very outdated, it's a decent entry in the series. Even though it is my least favorite Shenmue game, there is still a lot to like about it. Due to this, if you enjoyed the previous games, I would suggest giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually really wanted to like this game and realized probably about 20 hours in that I hated it, but felt I needed to see it through to the end. I'll be listing my thoughts on this review of what I hated about the game.1) I did not play Shenmue 1 or 2. I've always had an interest in Shenmue because I love Yakuza and wanted to find another game series similar that I could fall in love with and thought the newest would be the best because the graphics and clunky nature of 1 and 2 really turned me off.  This whole storyline read as a filler to me. The voice acting was terrible and I just didn't feel a connection to these characters. There is a severe lack of emotion, both in the main story and their pathetic excuse for sidequests.2) With Shenmue 3 taking as long as it did to get released, why the heck are we just ending the game with a "The story continues" the story continues, when? 20 years? If you can get funding? Why not show the dedicated character base (Which seemed heavy when I did research) a proper send off for these characters? 3) This game is essentially a grind fest with limited energy levels and a difficult way to keep up with income. All you do in this game is grind and because so many achievements are missable you cannot really get into this storyline at all because you do one or two steps and then if you don't run to this character on vendor avenue to help them out before you do step three they change their mind or something. Why is everything so missable? It was consistently frustrating and ridiculous.4) The DLC had no purpose. It should have been part of the game. I do not care for a DLC on a fighting race, for games that were already free in the game, and I definitely don't need a DLC with more pathetic side quests.Ultimately, I would not recommend this game to anyone. I guess I can say I've experienced it but if they ever come out with Shenmue 4, I will not be playing it. _childDocuments_.review: I've played this through 3 times, twice on PS4 and once on Epic.Ok so let's get the elephant in the room out of the way. Epic exclusivity. While I personally don't care what launcher a game is on I can see why backers may have been upset, however it does not impact the games quality in any way, shape or form, nor shoudl it define a review. A game is a good or bad game despite the launcher. It should also be stated publically, as has been done so by Cedric Biscay of Shibuya that Deep Silver sold the exclusivity rights, not YSNET and YSNET didn't see any funding from the deal. The game...Quick recommendation for anyone new to the series, as this is a straight lead on from Shenmue III I'd recommend playing Shenmue I, II and III back to back and you can see Shenmue III fits right in with the way it is presented. Almost like it was caught in a time bubble. We also have to remember this did not have the budget that the first two games did. It was a Kickstarter, with Deep Silver coming on board later. So there are clear concessions made here. Some animations are a bit stiff, the English dub can be a little out of sync at times (though the Japanese is great) and graphically it isn't AAA but it still looks beautiful, translating the art of the DC presentation to Unreal well. It plays exactly like a Shenmue game should, taking your time to immerse yourself into the world, building routines, training, playing mini-games and progressing the story. This could be mitigated by the fact they had to change the ending last minute and also spent the vast majority of the development time building the games systems (70% was the figure quoted in a recent interview)There are some valid critisisms though. The story doesn't quite move on as much as I'd have liked but it does set up more games. The fighting system doesn't have throws and has been overhauled with minimal tutorial. I'd recommend checking out some youtube videos on the new system. Once you get to grips with it the system is perfectly serviceable. The training, for some might be a little grind orientated (and you need to train in this game) but I enjoyed it. Overall the game is Shenmue through and through, yes it isn't as polished as the first 2 games and doesn't hit the heights of Shenmue II but it is a good continuation. Shenmue 4 will build on this games strengths I feel. 7/10 if you're giving a more unbiased opinion for me 8/10 (I'm biased and really loved Bailu village)Enjoy it, savour it, this is the game that we were all told would never exist. It does, we made it happen, let's continue the journey!

_childDocuments_.review: The Shenmue series is not for everyone, and I think everyone who enjoys it perceives it a little differently. I never played Shenmue 1 or 2 until the collection came out about 2 years ago. I'm a bit of a SEGA nerd, and both the history of the series and the hype around the 3rd game intrigued me. I don't think that they hold up that well. That being said, they are very influential games and are packed with enough charm that, overall, I did enjoy what I played. I don't mess with the Epic Store, so I like many decided to wait an extra year until the game came out on Steam.Was the wait worth it?Yes... mostly.If you expect completely modernized gameplay with top tier presentation, maybe lower your expectations. The game mechanically feels a little smoother, but nearly the same to the original games. The dialogue is still very stilted, with most performances being either completely overacted or incredibly underacted. It feels like an HD remaster/remake of a Dreamcast game.Here's the thing: I love that. Not everyone does.I really enjoyed Shenmue because of the quirky presentation. It's got a mildly interesting narrative that, at the same time, shouldn't really be taken seriously (and doesn't really take itself seriously for that matter). And while the pacing can be all over the place because of what some of the tasks you have to do require, it's really cool to be able to go from fighting to fishing within the span of an hour. It's a really interesting experience.What a lot of people would call flaws in design, end up enhancing the charm for me personally. I don't really have too many issues with the game in that regard. I didn't like the HP system at first, and I could still do without it. But I adapted to it and don't really take issue with it being here anymore. The biggest problem for me would probably be the ending. It feels... abrupt and maybe even a bit anticlimactic. I think the people who have followed the series for years and were disappointed by the ending, have the right to be disappointed. The series was originally envisioned for 5 or 6 games and the ending definitely gives me "halfway through the story" plot beat vibes. I personally doubt we are getting another game in the series though. I don't think the Shenmue 1+2 re-releases did very well, and given the controversy around Shenmue 3's release, combined with the fact it didn't do well critically or financially (excluding Kickstarter obviously)... the future of this series is VERY up in the air in my opinion.So TL;DR: In terms of presentation and mechanics, it feels exactly like a Dreamcast game with some updated visuals. The narrative could be disappointing to longtime fans. But if it's the charm you are after, it's still here. I definitely had a fun time overall.Shenmue 2 is still my favorite though.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite it not being as great as the first 2 games, Shenmue III is still a game that holds its own. A lot of people say that this game has "PS2 graphics" well damn, that must mean that every anime game in the world has Sega CD graphics! It's a kickstarted game, so you can't expect it to have RDR2 or Detroit Become Human graphics. The world is amazing and you can interact with all of the NPCs with all of them having loads of different dialogue options. The combat while not being as great as the first 2, is okay and you'll get used to it. There is a lot of activities to do throughout the game like play arcade games, go fishing, get a wide range of capsule toys, train your martial arts and get stronger, and collect herbs to sell them for money to buy food, scrolls, clothes, or other things. My only complaints are the stamina system which has your health go down rather quickly, you can train and get more health, but it's rather annoying still, I hope if we get a fourth game, they remove it (you can download a mod easily that removes this problem though, but it still shouldn't of been in the final game). The last problem is that the game sorta copied and pasted a story with a gang in the second half of the game. Overall Shenmue III is a decent game, it has flaws, but it is worth checking out if you are the least bit interested It's not like Yakuza at all, so don't go in expecting that. People compare it to Yakuza, while Yakuza wouldn't have existed without Shenmue, they are basically the exact opposite in terms of gameplay and story. Shenmue is more of a detective game with a combat system.
