_childDocuments_.review: Its Complicated.If you haven't played a Shenmue game before, I cannot recommend this one to you.If you have, you may find something to love, but only if you are willing to work for it.I did like this game, but not without reservation.Having started the Shenmue series a couple short years ago, instead of back in the prime of the Dreamcast, I found myself loving the series for its commitment to the small stories and mundane tasks that ground its larger themes in a way I have rarely seen a game do. In this series you will have to work jobs in order to make money, which are not made to be exciting so much as demonstrative of a commitment to your goals. Shenmue asks for you to be as disciplined and committed as its main character Ryo, a studied student of martial arts and a paragon of virtue.Shenmue 3, in many ways, is the biggest test of this commitment. It is the first game to introduce level meters for your various martial arts skills. Where once you could master a button combination to pull off a new move, it is now with repeated training and effort that you need to 'master' these skills. It is in this area I probably found myself losing the most patience.I love the idea of needing to train and improve Ryo, even with the awkward juxtaposition with his past accomplishments where the character had already in many ways proven himself an accomplished martial artist. It still feels nice to see you slowly work your way up the ranks against your opponents. However... this is also where this particular game pads things out. No way to get around it, Shenmue 3 becomes a grind.Instead of being implemented in a complimentary way to the story line, the frequent need to grind your martial arts training becomes an unnecessary and substantive barrier to all the games story progress. It felt that every major revelation in the game was accomplished only after you spend large amounts of time grinding. It eventually undermined the tone and the feeling of accomplishment these tasks were supposed to make you feel as Ryo, and just started to feel like an arbitrary way to extend the games length.With all of this you need a motivation to make it through, and with Shenmue the story and characters are the typical carrot on a stick. The promise of the resolution of the various plots from the previous games was enough to keep me sticking it through. Was it worth it? For me, barely. Do not get me wrong, I loved the characters, and we did see some progress in the story. However it was not quite as revealing and substantive as you might of hoped or expected. Without revealing too much: Many of the series threads have started to come together, but I feel much of the potential for big moves were squandered.All said, it is Shenmue. The weird characters, the slice of life gameplay, all the small moments of zen that people love about this series are here. For the Shenmue fan .... you probably will want to play it even as it is. For everyone else, try the original games first and see if the juice is worth the squeeze.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first Shenmue game, and I've got to say that it was enjoyable, but not worth $49.99.I liked this game because...I really love the level of detail that went into this game. Every single NPC felt really unique, like they had their own story to tell and secrets to share. Its very easy to get lost in this world.All of the side quests and minigames bring a lot of variety to this game. Whether you want to spend your day away in the arcade, fight your ways through the ranks of the local dojo, or relax with some fishing, there's plenty to do here.Now onto why this game isn't worth $50...The first thing to know about this game is the absolute grind. Grind your kungfu level up, grind more money, grind kungfu, grind money... It can be relaxing and "zen" for some people, but I understand others might not be so inclined to it so if you are looking for a nice action game to blast through, this is not the game for you.The combat is lacking. There's really nothing to it. Press a sequence of buttons (or RT) and hope you attack lands. In the end, all that matters is if you leveled up your kungfu high enough.The voice acting is all over the place. Some characters sound so lifeless, you would think they were acted by zombies. Other characters are acted out really damn well though. And then on the other side of the spectrum, some characters are acted to bizarrely they completely ruin the immersion of the game.The graphics are outdated and there are noticeable framerate drops and random glitches in the cutscenes. It really does not stand up to anything else made in 2020.Overall, I would recommend this for die-hard Shenmue fans or someone looking for a decent life-sim / action game and can look past the quirks. Otherwise, I would move on. $50 can afford a really well-polished triple A game these days, and this game just doesn't really stand up to that quality.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful game, and one which we never thought we would see. It absolutely feels like Shenmue, completely immersing you in its environment, and the experience that Yu Suzuki and team were able to achieve on such a tight budget has far exceeded my own expectations.The locations are  – so much so that you'll find yourself stopping just to stare at them. It's rare to see colours in games matching what we see in the nature around Bailu/Hakkason, and the beautiful architecture and lighting at every time of day in Niaowu/Chobo is a sight to behold. The choreography of the martial arts scenes and the main character models themselves are seriously impressive, taking Shenmue right into the modern era. The extent of the areas also goes beyond what I imagined – they're large in size, and every nook can be explored and examined just as in the original games.With 20 years having passed since the originals, it's such a joy to spend time with the characters again and see the next chapter in the story. We get to know Shenhua and her history, see Ryo reach his next level in martial arts, and can even call friends from the original games from the hotel in Niaowu. There are a lot of funny, quirky moments, as well as some deeper ones, and many fun new characters. I would have loved to see the plot taken further, and the sub-stories developed more, but this was a game made on a shoestring. The fact that it exists at all is something of a wonder.There are faults for sure – the combat system isn't as extensive as in the first games, and the food mechanic can be annoying (though casually browsing shops for gyoza, yaki-tori and steamed buns does bring a certain amount of happy nostalgia for anyone who has been to these kinds of street markets/yatai in real life!). The English dub is no doubt as hilariously (deliberately?) bad as the first games too, but it can easily be switched into soothing Japanese. As a whole the game tows a halfway line between the decades-old Dreamcast gameplay and modern-day expectations, and for me it strikes a good balance.I think the game serves as a fantastic basis for Shenmue IV, should the developers be able to get the go-ahead. The foundation and engine are all there now, and if the story and depth can be taken to the level that Shenmue II reached after Shenmue I, we're going to be in for a real treat. I'm hopeful that the re-release of the first two games combined with the anime will provide the developers the audience to go all-out next time around, bringing out a release to appeal to a modern crowd, with the fan service not being so necessary in future instalments.I'm perhaps something of a closet Shenmue mega-fan – it in no small part led to me learning Japanese, living in Japan for several years and even visiting all of the games' locations along the way, from Yokosuka to Dobuita, Wan Chai, Kowloon and Guilin too. Anybody who has spent time around Yangshuo will see how fantastically the southern Chinese countryside has been portrayed here in Shenmue III, and I just can't wait to see what Suzuki-san will do next.For anyone unfamiliar with the series, I & II are out now as HD remasters, so there is no longer any excuse. Look at them through the lens of the year 2000 releases that they are, and it's easy to see how extraordinary they were for their time. I get that it's niche and obviously not for everyone, but in my opinion their open worlds and story still hold up today. For me there has been nothing like them since that comes close to their level of immersion, but Shenmue III goes quite some way to capturing that same feeling. As fans we should really support and encourage the teams to see the conclusion of this epic adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue 3 is a long awaited sequel to a Dreamcast classic. The original games pioneered the open world genre and were ahead of anything else at the time. Many game creators today speak of the influence Shenmue had on their careers. If you were a fan of the original games then I think you will need to temper your expectations. This game is not a big budget sequel but an indie title made on a limited budget so a lot of compromises had to be made. To me personally, the Shenmue games were some of the most influential games of all time but I'm going to say up front that this game or series is not for everyone.The game is very slow-paced compared to the last one. The overall story doesn't progress much and the story cut-scenes are very scarce compared to previous entries. You can still find and work jobs to earn money. You can improve your martial arts through sparring or training. There are mini-games that you can play to win prizes. You can now pick and collect herbs. Collecting full sets of herbs or capsules can be traded in the pawn shops. Gambling to make money faster is again possible. Some of the new gameplay mechanics like fishing really fit that Shenmue feel. Menial, repetitive tasks that you have to do daily to earn money. Or practicing your martial arts to level up to beat a strong opponent. Being able to change your clothes to customise how you look is also a welcome change. You will still have to play detective by opening numerous drawers and cupboards and searching rooms. Arcade machines are still present although don't expect to be playing any Sega classics as they've been replaced with original works. One new mechanic that really should not have been introduced was the energy drain mechanic. Your health will deplete gradually and even quicker if you run so you will have to purchase food to replenish it. Basically a survival game mechanic that really just breaks the flow here and had no place being in the game. I suspect it may have been included to artificially extreme the length of the game. Fortunately there is a mod available to disable it. Other issues I have are the technical issues the game has. There are stutters and pop-in sprinkled regularly throughout the game which hampers enjoyment. Framerate also jumps around a lot but will rarely drop below 60 fps if you have a decent rig. Characters can appear and disappear even when they are next to you. With all the grinding and repetitive tasks that you'll be performing the thing that I find missing from this game is the payoff. In the previous entries there would be lots of repetition too as it's a Shenmue staple but there would always be plenty of payoff from scripted story sequences to QTEs but here it is just lacking. I'm guessing the budget attributed to the lack of cut-scenes and set pieces here which is unfortunate. There are side missions thrown in throughout the game which gives you something extra to do and forces a bit more exploration which is nice. Visually I think with the budget that they had that they've done a good job. Character models are hit and miss. Some look good whilst others look just strange. Facial animation could use improvement too. Environments are a different story. Some areas do actually look beautiful. Amazing colours and scenery that you sometimes will stop just to look at. I did my first playthrough on hard and the QTEs were extremely fast and difficult to react to. So I can't imagine what they will be like on the hardest setting. The music also feels neutered here. Nothing had that epic feel anymore. A lot of tracks are just remixed from older tracks which makes me wonder why they couldn't just use some of the older orchestrated tracks. It's not bad by any means but it did disappoint. The combat has also taken a step back in this game. Firstly throw moves have been removed completely. Secondly it has been simplified as well. Once you get used to it then it's still enjoyable and as in previous entries one of the highlights of the game but it's a shame that they went backwards here. Overall I still enjoyed the game despite my many grievances with it. To live up to the expectations set by the other games with the limitations set upon the team, with the limited budget would be impossible. I really hope that we get to see the Shenmue series finished someday as it's always deserved more fanfare than it ever received.

_childDocuments_.review: If there's any game that's an argument to break Steam's "Recommended" binary for something with a middle-ground, it'd be this game.The graphics are inconsistent- and yet, ultimately convey the Shenmue look with all its warts. Environments legitimately have a lot of charm and good color palettes. Interactive NPCs all have names and there's less of a focus on the "generic NPC" like Shenmue and especially Shenmue II. However, you can't talk to everyone like you could in the originals. That, and the stamina system turns the game into a slog at times.The locations are larger than I had assumed they'd be (but not large at all by modern open world standards), but one modernization I would've liked would be the ability to backtrack to Bailu after getting to Niaowu. The game has a looser plot with less tying Ryo down so it would've worked fine.The fighting system is confusing at first and is more like a command-queue system. There are some improvements over the original fighting system (like targeting) but almost no one is going to find it an improvement over the original games. It almost feels like they were going for a simpler, beat-'em-up style of gameplay, and if that's what they were going for, they should've made it more visceral and immediate. As it is, it feels sloppy at first and the ragdoll sometimes results in unintentionally hilarious posing. Snake Power is basically "I hate this fighting system" juice. Throws are absent, too.All-in-all it's a slow, sleepy title and not a whole lot happens until everything happens. I think this was always the intent, but the execution and budget rush hurt it more. The final events in the game happen so quick and unexpectedly that it completely ruins the narrative weight of the actually-quite-large developments that happened. It feels like it's all brushed under the rug by the time it's said and done. It's over in minutes.Even with all this, I still really liked this game. If you can still play the old Shenmues to this day and enjoy them, there's still a lot here to enjoy. Just keep your expectations tempered.One last criticism that comes to mind has to do with the way backers and Shenmue-fanservice were integrated into the game. It's immersion-breaking and disrespects all the work done on the game. It turns it into a "product". You shouldn't be able to buy capsule toys of people Ryo knows (or of himself!) and see super-deformed Chai hanging around in the arcades. That and that dang building right there in Niaowu! They should've integrated this content out-of-universe somehow (for example, maybe provide the Shenmue-themed capsule toys as gifts for progress, that can only be viewed in the game's menu, and Ryo is never seen physically handling it or retrieving it). There's also a fight near the end of the game where it's a bunch of very-not-Asian looking people and you just have that realization "I bet this was a backer tier".

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game through on PS4, and I have tried to pick it up again, but the only thing that kept me playing on PS4 was the hope the story would progress, but that didn't happen. So now I'm going to rip this game a new one because it's terrible. Let me start with the good. The game when I was playing it through, hoping for story advancement, wasn't bad, and definitely had that nostalgia factor to it because I am a fan of the original two games. It held my attention, and the environments were beautiful and worthy of praise. Now let's get to everything else. The models for the characters fall in uncanny valley territory - it's like watching a badly-drawn cartoon be turned into a 3D model that makes you kinda wince when you realise the strange look isn't intentional, and even more when you realise these are supposed to be the "improved" models - the original ones were even worse and were changed after immense backlash. The dialogue in this game, which unfortunately comprises most of what you do in the game is next-level awful, seemingly fitting with Yu Suzuki's strategy of rounding up bums from the bus station, getting them as drunk as possible and then corralling them into a recording studio. So often you find yourself talking to an NPC and they respond to a question nobody asked or even thought about. Then you have the voice over from the original Ryo actor who phones his performance in so hard it sounds like he was flipping through pages on his phone while recording his lines. And his dialogue is among some of the best in the game. Then there's the plot - a first-rate idiot plot, in which Ryo is led around like a dog on a leash and made to do idiotic fetch quests until the plot runs out of steam, and then it's "oh, I need expensive wine" or "oh, I need this expensive move book", and off you go like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grinding for hours, expecting some move forward with the plot, and nope -- more trolling from egomaniac Suzuki. I remember I kept playing, hoping, praying, for more content. Hoping there'd be some resolution to what was going on, and sometimes it'd happen, only for it then to throw up another mystery. In Guilin, the only mystery that gets resolved is, Ryo's dad was here and wrote a note for his mother - why? No idea. What does this have to do with the plot? Nothing. Eventually it conjures up a reason for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ off to another city, and away you go, and you're back at 0 again. The grind resumes, and then eventually after hours and hours, and zero advancement in the plot, you're told that, oh, wouldn't you know it, but that building across the water? He was there all along! Oh, and also, Ren's here to stop the plot from falling apart.There's also a segment where when you get to this building, that apparently is decrepit and derelict, you meet Chai. Yes, the man has such amazing martial arts that he can survive being jettisoned into the middle of an ocean, and swim to another continent, all just to be once again, given a thrashing and then thrown away.He was a tiresome character even when he had a position in the plot, but when he came back from the dead and appeared in Shenmue 3, I felt like throwing my controller at the TV - the absolute epitome of lazy writing. They throw in a joke as though look, it's hilarious we have Chai here, and at that point all I could think of is all the hours I've wasted trying to get this story to progress, and then here's Yu Suzuki metaphorically just laughing in my face at even the suggestion that the plot would progress.Then the story finally sputters across the finish line, with us meeting a new "boss" so incompetent she sets her own base on fire because.. reasons?  These are the most incompetent criminals ever - any two-bit chump could easily overtake their organisations by just buying a gun and shooting these fools, but apparently the mystery of their martial arts is what keeps them going.Also, these people are supposed to be high-level drug smugglers and big-time crime bosses, but they're always for some reason just sort of hanging around waiting for a young man to turn up and try and defeat them. Doesn't Lan Di ever at least try coke and hookers? Isn't he interested in the obvious perks of a criminal life, or does he mainly just sit around in a fancy room with henchmen waiting for nothing?Then there's the second-worst, which are the gameplay mechanics. We're all of course familiar with having to eat black garlic after walking 3 meters down the street so we don't pass out, but having this idiotic mechanic in a game is surely some kind of crime against gaming and reflects Yu Suzuki's decades-old thinking about game mechanics.Then there's the fight system which is the gaming equivalent of being drunk and trying to button mash for combos but not realising you've got Gran Turismo in the game console. I mean, there's an excruciating lag in the input, and when it all comes down to it, you're forced to level up arbitrary skills so your attacks actually do damage, but when it's all said and done and you max it out, you end up just using the same two or three moves because they're short enough to connect without getting hit. The fighting is just arbitrary. The models all look like they're just shuffling around a board game, and there's no real AI to speak of, they just hit harder, so if you learn to mash the same attack over and over again for 20 minutes, you can win the fights, or go off and spend hours with the dumb training mini-games which also level up your fighting abilities.And then of course, all of this culminates with the absolute worst thing about this game. It does not resolve any of the mysteries around the story, it adds MORE mysteries which are unexplained, and leaves the game on a cliffhanger which is pretty much exactly the same as the previous, the only difference being the last one is a cave, and this one's a wall.Now, my final bit will be reserved for bile for Yu Suzuki. I loved the first two games, and Yu Suzuki seemingly doesn't realise how much of a financial disaster they were for SEGA. The game sold well in terms of numbers, but relative to its cost, it sold extraordinarily poorly. When Yu Suzuki got this second chance, he should have seen this as Shenmue's swan song and appropriately acted to try and wrap up the story so that fans could at least have some closure on the series.Instead, Yu Suzuki decided that he'd stick with his insane vision of having 14 chapters or whatever it was, and absolutely refused to even move the story forward even a scintilla. This egomaniac still seems to have it in his head that he's going to be making Shenmue 4 and onwards, and given this game's obviously dreadful sales figures, that's not going to be happening soon. And it's a shame because the game would have had some nostalgic charm for me if it hadn't just been a big shaggy dog story where Ryo learns two moves and then gets ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up by Lan Di.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue III ReviewDialogues: 1/5 – The dialogue feels unnatural and often lacks emotional impact, making conversations less engaging.Graphics: 3.5/5 – The game showcases well-crafted environments and nostalgic art design, though it falls short of modern graphical standards.Sound: 3.5/5 – While the music adds a nostalgic touch, the voice acting and sound design are inconsistent, sometimes detracting from the experience.Fighting Moves: 5/5 – The combat system is a standout feature, with a variety of moves that are responsive and enjoyable to master.Characters: 4/5 – The characters are unique and interesting, bringing life and personality to the story.Story: 4/5 – The narrative continues Ryo Hazuki's journey with intrigue and loyalty to the series' past, keeping fans invested.Ease of Understanding: 4/5 – The game is generally straightforward, allowing players to grasp the main objectives and mechanics without much difficulty.Ease of Use: 3/5 – Some aspects of gameplay could be more user-friendly, with certain mechanics feeling dated or cumbersome.Animation: 3.5/5 – The animations are solid in most areas but can feel stiff at times, which may break immersion.Overall Rating: 6.5/10 – Shenmue III is a heartfelt continuation that appeals to long-time fans with its nostalgic elements and engaging combat, but it lacks the polish and modern feel to captivate new players.Recommendation for New Players:To fully appreciate the story of Shenmue III, it's essential to play Shenmue I and Shenmue II first. These games provide vital context and deepen the narrative experience. Additionally, for smoother and more comfortable gameplay, using an Xbox controller is highly recommended, as it offers optimal ease of control and responsiveness.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue 3 (and possibly the series as a whole, especially considering the ending of this one) relies waaaay too heavily on padding - go here, talk to person x; oh, x said they don't know about subject y, but said person q on the other side of town knows. Go find person q, but person q isn't here today, come back tomorrow. Exploration is severely dampened by artificial restrictions (and the fact that there's really nothing to find). What's this path that branches off? I haven't been down there yet - Ryo stops dead in his tracks, woodenly mutters "There's nothing that way." What? I see some buildings, what do you mean there's nothing down that way?Speaking of, well, speaking, the dialogue in this game is one of the worst I have ever seen in a game. I know the first two games were bad, but they've got nothing on this. Dialogue is disjointed, with characters seemingly responding to different lines than what the other character is saying.The visuals don't bother me much, and I was charmed when it started raining and the dirt paths took on a muddy look. But every other surface is oblivious to the rain, including NPCs. Their behavior is completely unaltered, so even in a downpour you'll see them doing the same things they'd be doing on a sunny day - including having a meal in a restaurant's outdoor seating area. Maybe the restaurant they're at markets this as bottomless soup? Another caveat to the visuals - the character models are hideous.

_childDocuments_.review: An acquired taste in every sense of the term. Give it a chance.I am a Shenmue fan and Kickstarter backer--already spent dozens of hours with the PS4 version. Honestly, I love this game and will defend it until the day I die. HOWEVER, even I have to admit that this is a niche series that's difficult to recommend. It's not your average action/adventure game. It's much more unique.Will you like this game? It depends on the following criteria:1. You appreciate Chinese/Japanese culture2. You enjoy anime, martial arts, etc.3. You enjoy bad voice acting (this seems to be deliberate in Shenmue 3. Japanese audio is an option if this isn't your cup of tea).4. You enjoy quiet, immersive role-playing games with emphasis on exploration and story.5. You are AT LEAST familiar with Shenmue 1 and 2. Playing them isn't required per se, but you're otherwise going to be lost in terms of story. Luckily, the first two were recently re-released on modern platforms and PC.WITH THAT BEING SAID, here is my personal opinion broken up into categories:Pros:- new additions to the Shenmue sandbox are minor, but GREATLY improve the experience: a radar/map in the corner, a more robust journal/quest list, improved controls, less restrictive exploration, more mini games, a stamina/hunger system, skill trees and leveling up, etc.- beautiful graphics and art style. despite being a Kickstarter game, it's gorgeous to look at.- Music composed by Ryuji Iuchi is fantastic.- Funny and lively characters with their own unique backstories.- varied environments with plenty of quests and mini games to entertain you.- The game FEELS like Shenmue. The modern additions make it simultaneously retro and modern in the best possible ways. As a fan, this was the most satisfying aspect.Neutral:- the new combat system. It's less complex than the previous two games, but S3 incorporates new practice modes, Dojos, and a skill leveling system. I really enjoyed this new system, but I can see why other fans were disappointed.Cons:- the art style can sometimes clash (characters being exaggerated with environments looking realistic).- The last quarter or so of the game kinda dragged for me. Too many grindy quests with little payoff. The previous two games were guilty of this too in some respects, but it seemed more glaring in this installment.- the plot is lacking. The story progression from Shenmue 2 is disappointing. It moves VERY slowly despite having some pretty awesome moments (Lan Di, anyone?).Bottom Line:  Give it a chance. It's not for everyone, but it was DEFINITELY for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of Shenmue. I played Shenmue 1 when I was a kid and then played it again as an adult along with Shenmue 2. I love both games despite their flaws. I think the part that hurt the most was the fact the game does have parts that are interesting and it somehow certainly had enough to drag me along, but it's not until I was nearly done, that I felt kind of sad because this game could have been something more. Yu Suzuki certainly can be credited with creating an amazing game series, but his commitment to his vision really hurt fans like me by not giving us any closure. In fact, this game really feels like a prologue to another game that may never come to be. Probably worthwhile for fans to check out. It will draw you in enough to keep you going, but you too will feel this deep sense of disappointment by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue 3 is a game that we hardcore fans have been anticipating for years with no avail. 2015 however saw a change in this with the announcement of Shenmue 3 being in development. 4 ½ years later was when we saw the release of the game on PS4 and Epic Games Store and today (November 19th 2020) we see the release of the game on Steam and GOG. Shenmue 3 takes place immediately after Shenmue 2 with it continuing on from the cliffhanger. Again we are in Ryo’s quest in China to take revenge for his father from the hands of Lan Di. This new chapter goes into more detail with Shenhua, the girl you met in the forest originally in Shenmue 2, with Ryo able to get into more of her backstory when you are resting at her house. More new characters are introduced that help Ryo on his journey who feel like they belong in this game world.   One of the new features introduced in this 3rd chapter of the series is the stamina meter that you have to keep an eye on so food items are actually useful. One aspect that was changed that I miss is how you purchase items. 1 & 2 has you picking up what you want to purchase whereas 3 just has a menu to choose from. Fighting system has also been changed with it being more simplified by having the option to either input the command for a combo or executing the combo with one button. You still have to grind out moves just like the previous games so get ready to train the same move over and over again. New moves are also obtained by collecting scrolls just like 1 & 2.    Graphics looks exactly how they are supposed to be for what they are. Has the same art style as it’s predecessors except the Unreal Engine 4 gives it a more next gen polish. The level of detail in all the houses, stores, temples, etc is incredible and has the same exact feel as 1 & 2.  OST sounds exactly how a Shenmue game should be with one of the original composers actually returning for the game. They even got the original voice actor for Ryo in both the English and Japanese versions which is a nice touch. Attention to detail with sound design to the world is also here with birds chirping when you are in the forest and the sound of city life happening around you in the more urban area. NPCs are also very interactive with Ryo being able to talk to practically anybody to find out about clues, pawn shops, part times jobs, etc. I played through Shenmue 3 twice since it was originally released and can say it definitely meets expectations for hardcore fans. It was supposed to be a game for the fans first and it shows for better or worse. Newcomers might want to start with Shenmue 1 & 2 as a litmus test before jumping into 3 because if said players don’t like how those original games play then they will also feel the same way about 3. Hoping for a Shenmue 4 in the future and with the future anime series coming out will maybe bring more interest in the series to make 4 a reality.

_childDocuments_.review: FIRST AND FOREMOST If you are going into this expecting it to be like Yakuza because of the vast amount of influence that Shenmue had on Yakuza STOP RIGHT THERE! while yes it did have a huge influence they are both entirely different games, play entirely differently, and are overall entirely different experiences, Yakuza is more Fast paced, where as Shenmue's gameplay is more about slowing down and taking your time, and exploring around, also unlike most open world games where the details are focused on the macro scale, Shenmue's details are focused on the micro scale, thus exploration comes more in the form of searching cabinets, table settings, bookshelves, etc... sure the trailers make the series look like high action, and while the games do have their action sequences, they are not (as I stated before) about fast paced action comparing Shenmue to Yakuza in this regard is like going into Mega Man, and expecting it to be like Mighty No. 9, or Banjo Kazooie and expecting it to be like Yuka Laylee, or Sweet Home and expecting it to be like Resident Evil, again the previously mentioned titles had massive influence over the formentioned titles BUT those examples are also completely different, with different styles of gameplay and are completely different experiences. Now with that out of the way I want to say that while this game is the low point of the series having played it on ps4, thanks to Deep silver (yes it was them and not Y's net, nor Shabuya productions doing that ...you can look up the interview with Cedric Biscay where he himself specifically said that he had no opinon on the exclusivity deal and stated that Deep $ilver did that to make up the money that they felt they would be loosing on this title, and I do have my gripes about it such as how the energy bar works) I did still get some enjoyment out of, just be aware that these games are not about high action, they are more about slowing things down and getting lost into it's universe, I believe that maybe why alot of people jump into this series and end up not liking it, as they end up playing it in the wrong way. if you can muster up the patience, and let your mind wander into the ingame world of Shenmue you will find that the series is actually quite enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: This review can be summed up in one short sentence: "It's true to the original."That's all you need to know.If you have any love for the first two Shenmue games you can stop reading right here and buy  because all the criticism this series has gotten are just things you will take for granted. The stiff and awkward dialogue, the slow pace, the silly plot, the non-negotiable 9PM curfew, people who tell you to "come back tomorrow" for no apparent reason, the fact that Ryo has the emotional spectrum of a cucumber... All this you will gleefully accept as part of the charm that makes Shenmue such a phenomenal and memorable series.So we're back on Ryo's quest for revenge after nearly two decades of waiting. Starting a new game is like visiting an old friend: simply everything about this game calls you back to those turn-of-the-millennium days of the original games. The music, the sound effects, the animation, the various gameplay modes, the architecture, everything has that unique Shenmue ambiance around it. It can't be stressed enough:  is a work of love that was made for the fans.In terms of gameplay vs. action: this one is somewhere between the first and second game. There'll be quite some street fights with thugs, but it doesn't have a rollercoaster of violence like the end of the Kowloon episode in .The graphics are good. It's not ahead of the competition like the original games were, but it offers an interesting and very much alive world full of detail. One weird thing though: half the characters are modelled for realism whereas the other half have ridiculously exaggerated features, as if the graphic design was done by two different teams working in isolation.Some notes on the story. What follows should not be a surprise, but here's a spoiler marker just to be sure: Ultimately, it's difficult for me to give a rating for this game. Hell, I'd give it 10/10 just because I'm thrilled that we got the this game against all hope after all these years. Compared to the other Shenmue games, I'd give it 8/10 because it simply doesn't break new grounds the way they did, yet ticks all the boxes of what made Shenmue so memorable in the first place.I had a wonderful time with this game and I hope that one day we will continue the journey in  (hopefully before the year 2040).

_childDocuments_.review: While the credits rolled, after more than 100 hours after I first launched it, full of fears and expectations, I was simply thinking one thing : "Yeah, Shenmue is definitely not a franchise for everyone."The first Shenmue was, to put it simply, a revolution, a title ahead of its time. It was also a game that some players found utterly boring, and I believe it's understandable. To me, even if I was drew by the promise of a revolution at first, I quickly became attached to the atmosphere and the story delivered. Also, Shenmue is the title which made me want to learn english (which isn't my native language), it is a special game to me. I was waiting since 2002 for the third opus to come out. Needless to say, when III was announced in 2015, I nearly cried tears of joy, even if the first trailer wasn't anything special. Then began another wait for the game to be available. I waited one extra year for it to became released on Steam. During this final year, I heard so many negative thoughts about this game, I was spoiled the ending... When I launched the game, I was expecting it to be garbage...But no. The game is really good. At one condition : don't expect a revolution or something akin to the release of the first Shenmue. The third one follows closefully the footsteps of the two first episodes, in all their aspects, both bad and good. To put it simply, Shenmue III is a game where patience is the key, you can speedrun the game if you want to (and know exactly what to do), howewer, Yu Suzuki and Ysnet wants you to fully live your life in the world of Shenmue. Life isn't always about forcing your way trough everything, but it is more like enjoying some simple things, like fishing (I'll come back later on this point, promise). The game (and the series in general) has always been about emulating life, with the fun elements, but also the boring aspects, while also proposing an interesting story. Not the best, surely, but interesting nonetheless.Story in III don't really progress, there is some new elements learned throughout the game, new characters appear with returning one, but don't expect a conclusion. When I was spoiled, I was thinking "what is Yu Suzuki doing ?", but now that I have completed the game, I understood that it was to soon to see what all Shenmue players want to see, but I was also thinking that Suzuki-san could have reduced the scope of the saga and end it with III...However, if the scope wasn't as large, I wouldn't have had the world I desired for 18 years, vibrants of details and activities. I have a potato laptop, yet was able to play at the lowest settings, with some lags and long initials loadings, but nothing really bad happening, QTE and fights weren't affected by the low capacity of my laptop. The game is surpringly stable on PC. I really want now to buy a better computer to play it again at full capacity, even if it's an AA game this time, Bailu and Niaowu are some really appealing places I want to know to their full glory.The game plays like I and II. Yeah... You will have from time to time the feeling to play not Ryo, but a tank. One other inconvenient is a new element added to the gameplay : the feeling of hunger. At the beginning, it's a plague, really. You've got no stamina and wants to buy others things than black garlic, but can't. But once you've increased your stamina with the one inch punch and the horsemen stance, it's better balanced. For the rest, expect the wide range of activities usually offered in the series, all with interesting mechanics, like fishing once again. However, a mini-game stuck in my mind, simply because of the sheer insanity of the QTEs : the chicken catching. The only advice I can give is to be patient, lower the difficulty if necessary, and observing the chickens.The soundtrack is a bit disappointing though. The tracks are really good but there are simply too much tracks from II in some areas, especially in Niaowu. But the tracks themselves are really great !Now, for achievements hunters... there are a lot of rare achievements to get but they can get quite ridiculous and that's when I bring back the fishing game on the table : 1000 fishes ?! Seriously ? What were they tinking ? The fishing game is really cool and a good way of earning money in the game, but you have no idea of how long it is to catch 1000 fishes. I got it the day before departing to the final zone of the game, and I began to fish almost at the end of Bailu. That's how long it is... Once again, patience is the key when looking for achievements but despite that, they are well tought since they are a guide to showing the depths of the game.The game earned a full fledged recommandation for me, but it comes with a warning : this isn't a game for everyone. If you want something similar, but more action-packed, look for the Yakuza games. If you are interested, I give two pieces of advices to you :-Go play the shenmue I and II compilation to see if you like the atmosphere and gameplay. Sure there is a recap movie at the menu of III, but it doesn't replace the experience.-Tell yourself that III plays exactly the same way (despite some improvements), and that there is no end in sight.That's all. Yet again... The story goes on...

There are some beautiful graphics at times, mini games are distracting but entertaining, and of course, capsule collecting is fun/frustrating. _childDocuments_.review: - A year after it's release on the consoles, Shenmue III makes it way to the PC platform. The long awaited sequel to Shenmue II is finally here. I got in on Shenmue late. Despite owning a Dreamcast, I never had the opportunity to enjoy Shenmue on it's original platform, so you can imagine how pleased I was when I learned of the HD rereleases for Shenmue I & II on Steam. After playing through both of them several times, I finally understood why Shenmue was spoken of so highly. It's among my all time favorite titles now. Shenmue III is no exception. It has the same unique charm and flair of the originals, despite being roughly eighteen years apart from the last installment. As others have put it, it really does feel like a Dreamcast game made in the modern era. To some this may be off putting, but to others including myself, it's well welcomed. Shenmue III really is a dream come true for fans of the series. It's not just a win for the Shenmue series, it's a win for the industry as a whole that a series long thought abandoned can still make an incredible come back. Shenmue III is not perfect, mind you, especially for new comers to the series, but there is a lot to enjoy here. If you have not already played through Shenmue I & II, I strongly encourage you to play those first and come back to this when you're ready. They're not required to enjoy the game, but it greatly enhances the experience for you.Shenmue III gets a big thumbs up from me. I can't wait to see the story continue in Shenmue IV.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a little late to the party on the PC version, I did finish the console version though along with the DLC. I also wasn't affected by the EGS 12 months exclusivity deal (I backed a physical PS4 copy) and I bought it on EGS at release and I bought it on here too.I am a huge Shenmue fan and have been since the original release on Dreamcast, which I still own along with both 1 & 2.It is easy to recommend this game to a die hard like myself that was just looking for more Shenmue, however it is not without fault.The good...Everything you expect from Shenmue is here, good looking locations, great soundtrack and tons of things to do.The training system is really good and feels like more than just an after thought like in the first, you will find fighting gets easier the more you train. There is loads of moves to learn and collect and there is plenty of opportunity to use them unlike the first two games (I loved em but there wasn't too many fights in em) so there is a reason to collect them and see what works best for you.There are plenty of mini games like fishing and arcade games to keep you busy, just like there has been in the originals.All characters and npc's have that Shenmue quirky look to them, all the interaction we know an love is still here and the game is stunning to look at.Pretty much a love letter to the 90's and Shenmue from the modern era.The bad...The story is just flat out pointless.The plot moved about an inch in a game I waited 18 years for, and it all feels very rinse and repeat. The first two broke upthe grind with story but this one can not because the story wasn't there to do so...The story DLC feels like it was stripped to be sold back to us, mostly because it plays like it was.The dialogue is honestly worse than the first game, broken replies that make no sense and the pronunciation is really annoying (Chi is Che...)The combat is just a mess, input lag on all moves and combos. The block system is broken and no counters, throws or parrying of any kind.For anyone with an ultrawide monitor, there is no support for ultrawide of any kind. You will need a mod to do so and you will also only be able to run at borderless windowed mode when the mod is used.If like me you are a big Shenmue fan, get the third one. There is enough good to out weigh the bad but get the DLC story pack because that was definitely meant to be part of the main story...And for newcomers, there is a story recap for those that haven't played the first two games.But If I was new to the series I would wait on a sale if you are unsure.For a game that was always big on story to sell it, this one just doesn't progress enough to recommend newcomers at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue 3 feels like an old Dreamcast game painted over with modern graphics, and what I mean by this is that instead of building on or learning from Shenmue's old mechanics and fixing the problems that plagued those two games, Shenmue 3 decides instead to embrace those problems while adding new ones that make Shenmue 3 feel like an incredibly outdated game. It's almost incredible how issues from the original Shenmue can still be found 20 years later in Shenmue 3, so much so that Shenmue 2 will sometimes feel less outdated than Shenmue 3, which is my biggest issue with this game.I still love Shenmue 1 & 2, and I consider them two of the best gaming experiences I've ever had. Shenmue 3 should've built on top of those games, but instead, it remains trapped in 1999 along with its creator (Yu Suzuki) with no plan to change anytime soon, which makes me very anxious about the future of this ip. (Also wtf did they do to the faces of Ryo and Shenhua?! Why is Ryo's face so much rouder now?? and Shenhua looks like a completely different character, like ffs I miss the old designs.)

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the first two games recently, and having enjoyed both, I wasn't sure what to expect coming into the third. I'd heard it was faithful to a fault (this coming from AAA consumers and journalists and being untrustworthy), and I'd also heard that it was modernized somewhat (something I feared). It's on the faithful end, having QOL enhancements carry over from Shenmue 2, but ditching the tank-controls is its modern concession aside from performance.I'll touch on the combat, which is what I've mainly seen criticized, and then the story briefly.The combat is frequently targeted as the Shenmue 3's largest shortcoming, and that isn't the case. I'd have a hard time saying if I prefer the new combat over the more Virtua Fighter inspired combat from 1 and 2, but it's a different kind of complexity. Whiff punishing is more rewarding since a bad dodge results in you getting smacked as opposed to a neutral-reset in the previous games, and your spot-guard isn't free anymore and depletes a gauge over time. I'd say ditching the directional inputs for sole button-combos is a smart move since target-switching during crowd fights has been implemented. As far as the removal of throws, it makes sense that Ryo would start to figure out that Jiu Jitsu isn't cutting it, and he needs to figure out Bajiquan if he wants to keep pace with these martial arts masters (lore reasons), and I also found them interchangeable with other moves. They look flashy and do good damage, but a hit's a hit. The game has also streamlined how training and move-acquisition feed into each other. In the first 2, a move got better as you kept using it and it was on you to find more powerful attacks. In Shenmue 3, any move you upgrade increases your overall attack power, and many of the minigames and various items you collect can be exchanged for new moves in a less costly and more time efficient manner than the previous games (no need for excessive money grinding; you can get everything just by playing through the content). Since these systems all interlock now, it's easier for everyone to build a strong Ryo. I think I preferred the original 2 letting me tailor my Ryo's move-set specifically instead of spoon-feeding me, but it does fit his character-arc better to have him grow in all areas instead of what I was particularly interested in.The story is another point of contention. I could be wrong here, but, if I had to guess, Shenmue 3 might cover chapters 6 and 7 of Suzuki's 11 chapter script. Could just be chapter 6, but I felt like it covered a lot of ground. If anything, it seems rushed. The generosity in terms of character interactions and letting bits breathe is missing here. The lower budget is definitely something I noticed in terms of the story's pacing. Guilin seemed a little quick but more or less on track, and then the back end of Niaowu hurtles toward the end credits. I honestly feel like Suzuki should've told less story more thoroughly here, but he was also trying to appease people that don't really remember his game from 1999 that well (and that probably didn't care for it in the first place).I like Shenmue 3 a lot. I'm glad to see it. There are some people that supposedly like the first two, but don't like the third. That sounds to me like they never liked the first two, and just grabbed them because they were blockbuster releases at the time.So here's my recommendation. If you actually like Shenmue 1 and 2 (as in, you like them RIGHT NOW when you turn them on), grab Shenmue 3. Everyone else, stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad to criticize it harshly, but it's spectacularly boring.First, lemme start with what I liked. The atmosphere is very immersive and beautiful. Maybe it's because I'm a big fan of the "Ancient Asian village" aesthetic, but the time I spent bored from the gameplay was spent looking at the absolutely gorgeous background. Second, the story seems pretty interesting. I've never played any Shenmue games, so I had to see the recap movie. From what I saw of it, the story looks incredibly interesting.And that's exactly the reason I hate to say this, but... this story in this game is agonizingly slow. After 3 hours, I've completed like 2 mini-missions, mostly because of a slew of mechanics that slow down the game. A core mechanic to getting anything done is asking around in a village of around 20 people hoping that one random person might have a clue relevant to your search. And then, when you do find the clue, what follows is one of two things: another round of talking to everyone in the village or a jog across the map to find the next person with a clue in what feels like a wild goose chase by just the 5th time around. Slowing things down even more is a stamina system, where you gotta eat to keep up your stamina and health, which are the same thing for some reason. Just ran across town to fight someone? Well, you're gonna have to eat before you fight them or else you die in one hit. Don't have food? Just do a boring minigame for 2 minutes and you'll earn enough to buy enough to refill your energy.Which brings me to another complaint: the slew of boring minigames. I'll admit that I was excited to try the first few. But then they became a core part of the actual gameplay. Want to make money? Boring minigame where you press a button when the slider's in the right range. Want to get stronger so you don't get your ass beat in half a minute? Play a series of minigames with such thrilling mechanics as pressing a button once a second to make sure your arms dont fall below 4 feet above the ground like flappy bird. Hell, they even BLOCK you from progressing very early on in the game unless you dedicate a good amount of time into it.Then there's my last gripe, which might be more personal. The fighting system is either bland and boring as hell, or there's a lot that the tutorial didn't explain. At this point, it could be either or both. The only thing the tutorial tells you to do is press buttons. Literally nothing but that. If you look a bit deeper into the instruction manual, you can find instructions on how to block and do special attacks, but very little is explained about them and they work far fewer times than they don't. So, with little actual instruction and a hell of a lot more confusion, all you can do is follow their advice and buttonmash while you hope that you played the flappy bird minigame long enough to have enough endurance to survive the fight. The fighting system plays more like a stat-based RPG that emphasizes grinding instead of any fluidity, reflexes, or awareness.All in all, 3/10. Maybe get it if you want to admire the scenery or if you're a long-time fan of the series or if you're far more patient than I am, but, if you're new like me, don't expect much in terms of excitement.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put over 10 hours into this and I don't want to play it anymore. It's simply awful, they ditched tall he best parts of Shenmue I & II (the exploration, discovery, story, variety in gameplay), then kept the terrible controls, and even made some parts worse (terrible dialog, terrible acting, terrible cut scenes, terrible cartoon-ish characters), and topped it all off with horribly monotonous gameplay (buying and eating food, leveling up your fighting skills and health, earning money, collecting herbs, gambling to earn money and exchanging for prizes and selling those items to earn money). I totally spent $17 so I could spend hours practicing the horse stance.Is there anything good about Shenmue 3? The graphics are decent but not great by today's standards, feels like it was made for the Xbox 360 or PS3. The controls are a marginal improvement over the original. There are a few entertaining moments, but they are few and far in-between. There's not too many nostalgic elements which is a positive for me, there's way too much of that nonsense coming from Hollywood and the gaming industry these days.I didn't have high expectations for Shenmue 3, I knew it was crowdfunded and didn't have a huge budget. But even then, I'm left sorely disappointed. It's clear that lots of effort went into this game and there was huge potential despite the relatively small budget, but the effort was focused on all the wrong areas of the game. Shenmue is very much about the plot, dialog, cinematics, and cutscenes; this is very much where most of the time should have been invested in. But instead they put in far too much time and energy into developing annoying gambling games, food, leveling up, collecting herbs, and other uninteresting monotonous gameplay elements. And then they force you to focus large amounts of time on these portions of the game, whereas you could mostly ignore these portions in Shenmue I & II. There's also very little continuity between this and the first two games; it's almost as if the first two games never happened. For example, you start this game as a complete amateur in martial arts which feels so wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: 2/10This game came out in 2019. It is a sequel to a game that came out in 2001. Although this game has been in pre-production for a long time, it required a very successful Kickstarter for it to see release. If you backed this game I feel quite sorry for you. What you received in the end was probably not worth your money, your hope or your time.Taking my score into account, I obviously think that this game is awful. It takes concepts that were cool from a bad game in 1999 and does not expand upon them at all. To be fair, this game absolutely feels like a Shenmue-game, but that is because nothing has changed. What was cool in 1999 is no longer cool and what was bad in 1999 is perceived as absolutely atrocious today. This game is 19 hours long when it could have been three, and even so it would have been bad. Why is that? Let us get into it:Shemue 3 continues right where Shenmue 2 ended. You play as Ryo Hazuki who is trying to find and get revenge on the man who killed his father. Note that in order to even understand what is going on you NEED to have spent the 30-40 hours it takes to complete Shenmue 1 and 2 (which are bad games that you should not play so there's that). The game is still a third-person social simulator, beat'em up, exploration, detective, open world game with tons of hidden interactions, minigames and stuff to explore. Your tasks often consists of "talk to this guy, find out where the thugs are hiding, buy a thing, wait for this thing to happen". Most often your task is to figure out where a certain NPC is and to go to them for a little chat. They will then point you in the direction of the next NPC and sometimes give you an additional task to do before you can progress (play a minigame, buy a thing that requires you to grind for money etc. etc.)What is good about this game? The lighting. That is it, really. What is meh about this game? The minigames, the controls, the music.What is bad about this game? Everything else, but let us talk about the most prominent things:The pacing. The game runs on an in-game clock in which a day is about an hour long. Some things can only be done during certain hours of the day, which often means that in order to progress to the next task, you need to wait a day. Luckily, the devs have introduced fast-forwarding mechanics and sometimes fast-travel to the next objective, which really helps (but accentuates the poor design of the story and the way in which you progress it). The story moves at a snail's pace, with conversations draging for ages, loading screens being required to do the most basic of things (move a chair, open a door, pick up an item). There is never a sense of urgency or pull in what I am tasked with. It is always a matter of talking to people until I figure out where I am supposed to go next, talk to the NPC in question and either being pointed to a new place or being faced with a task that ALWAYS just feels like a time-waster in order for you to not rush through the game. In my review of Shenmue 1 and 2 I complained about there being sections of the game in which your progress is locked behind an in-game paywall and/or a grind. There are absolutely sections like this in Shenmue 3 as well. There are TWO times where a paywall is used and thus, you need to grind through one of the many boring ways to earn money in order to progress. Will you chop wood 25 times, each time taking you about three minutes? Will you save-scum and gamble, hoping to strike a jackpot enough times so that you can win some money that way? Will you drive a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ forklift again over and over? The fact that the first paywall is 2000 yuan and the second is 5000 makes it feel as if the game is testing your patience. That is not a good way to present a game at all.The writing. It has not changed since 1999 and even then it was dreadful. No character feels like they have ever spoken or expressed a thought before in their lives and close to everything falls flat. Nothing is emotional, funny, intense, heartbreaking, heartwarming or any other thing that writing in a story-heavy game is supposed to convene. It is just stiff and unnatural.The voice acting. The Japanese voices are okay, they are just hindered by the poor writing. The English voices, however. Whoooooo boy, it feels intentional, how bad these actors are. Just like in 1999 it feels as if the devs asked Siri to record audio for the game. Watching compilations online is fun, as you do not need to do anything else than listen to weird/bad voice acting, but when you actually need to play through this absolute trashpile of a game it really stops being funny quickly.The combat. It strike me as odd how the developers not only seem to have ignored other games with a beat-em-up combat-system with slight focus on martial arts (take Sleeping Dogs, Sifu or Yakuza, for example), they also managed to make the combat WORSE than how it was in Shenmue 1 and 2. There is input-delay and the characters rarely show any sign or consequence of being hit. Sometimes they block, sometimes they do not. Regardless, they react in the same way, as if a fly touched their face. Other times, you knock them down and they magically go flying. This sounds cool, but is not, as you need to wait for them to get back up in order to start hitting them again. You can get through most fights with just mashing the "punch"-buttons, and the secret kung fu-techniques are COMPLETELY optional to use. They are not fun to use, so why bother?The character-designs. Apart from the gorgeus lighting-effects, the animations and the characters (as well as most items and environments) really do not look good. Feels 2007-2009, maybe? Hard to describe, but very ugly.This ties in to something that one could call a nitpick, but I still want to adress that I feel as if this game is depicting most Chinese people in a way that I can only simplify as racist. Just as in Shenmue 2, most commoners are either stupid, sly and/or greedy, evil or something in between. The exception is, of course, hot women. It feels quite unfresh in 2019, but is not too uncommon in Japanese games. But still, the way that Chinese people are portrayed does not sit well with me. However, as a white man, I leave accusations and harsh critique in that matter to those who are targeted and who may or may not take offense.Overall I feel very dissapointed after having played through Shenmue 3. The game would have been bad if it came out in 2002 and feels unacceptably bad in 2023. It feels as if the developers learned close to nothing in the 18 years it took to get this game released. Furthermore, the game is also not the final one in the series. The story is clearly written for a Shenmue 4 to continue this absolute atrocity of a series. I said that Shenmue 1 is a piece of history, as it introduces very interesting and cool concepts that are sadly packed into a terrible game. Shenmue 3, however, has no excuses, no identity and no respect of mine. The game does not even feel like it is made with love, who could express love by designing a game this way? I shake my head in dissapointment at Shenmue 3 and hope to never see a game like this again.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, most of the negative reviews are less than 2 hours into the game. Anyone can have an opinion of a game, I get that. At one hour I had barely learned how to sell herb decoctions, and had about 3% of the basic functions done. If I stopped at that point I could understand how it would be boring. That really doesn't make a good review though.The people this was aimed for was for people who remembered how great this series was in the 00's. Even a lot of the professional reviews are like "This game doesn't have good graphics and the translation sucks." Yeah, that's what it was like back then. It is almost exactly like the original so they did a great job recreating what the game was like. As an 18 year old today playing this game, it'd probably suck, but as a 40 year old getting to finally see a continued version of a game I loved, it's awesome. They could have made it like a completely new game but this is perfectly fitting.Price-wise I can understand if people don't like it. At the sale it had during the opening though, $30 bucks or less is quite fine, especially for people new to the game. I personally wouldn't buy it if i didn't play the first two games. It isn't a AAA game, as people phrase it. That isn't the point. Hugely anticipated game, but just because a lot of people wanted to see it happen doesn't mean it had sparkles coming out of every orifice. It'd be like a Qbert 5 coming out. 8 bit graphics would be perfect for it; doesn't mean it needs to look like GTA V.So far, I feel the game has been done perfectly. I love collecting lil toys, the combat is just like back then, and the dialogue is the same as in the original. Once I've got to the end, I may change it, but so far I feel like this is an authentic and nostalgic version of the original. Again, if you are new to the franchise, you'll probably hate it. If you remember how awesome it was back in the Dreamcast days, you'll find it worthwhile.

_childDocuments_.review: Would you like to try lucky hit?Oh man, how long has it been? So many years.Jumping into this game all the nostalgia rushes back in.This game is way more LA Noir than it is Yakuza. There isn't really a comparison between Shenmue and Yakuza, both are good and very different. The level of detail in Shenmue is incredible, no other game like it that I can think of.Because of how detailed and complex it is, this game is going to be a turn off for most people looking for a Yakuza-like quick action fix. Int his game there is training, and you aren't just a badass like Kiryu right out of the gate. The fights are also not quite as dynamic as Yakuza, but slower and more controlled.The visuals will not be appealing for many modern players, but they are very much in line with the original, which I feel is a good thing in this game, as it's a continuation of a story and the fact that it looks like SI/II feels authentic and not overdone.The design is beautiful. Everything is highly detailed, a trademark of Shenmue.So. Many. Minigames. And yes, they are just as infuriating as they were in SII.The controls are pretty much the same as they were in the original - weird but you get used to them. Definitely recommend controller, and nice in Big Picture mode.The dialogue is just as awkward and unintentionally hilarious as the past games, actually found myself laughing randomly because of the dialogue and how little our protagonist seems to give a ♥♥♥♥.> "You stand before a great Chen Tai Chi master."> "Ummm, yeah, I'm good, thanks."For better or worse, SIII feels just like SII, take that how you will.The game does keep moving forward in time without you, which can annoy people who like to explore absolutely everything, when they are forced into the next scene not having finished looking around the previous one.It's a very slow burn game that requires patience to appreciate, and the amazing soundtrack helps. One of the chillest games in my library.Personally, I can't wait to lose way too much time in this immersive sim.Basically, if you enjoyed SI/II you will fall in love with this game. If you hadn't played them, give this a chance and you may learn to love it. For $17 this is a steal.The truth is, I secretly bought this game to maintain my lucky hit addiction.

_childDocuments_.review: I am FOREVER grateful to Yu Suzuki for bringing this saga back, it always saddened me to see the Shenmue saga just fade away when it definitely did deserve to continue on.This game plays in the spirit of Shenmue I & II, but with updated graphics, so Shenmue III was meant for the fans. With that being said those who have not played Shenmue I & II may not understand Shenmue III, or like it's journey... but the journey will continue on either way.Bear in mind the Shenmue saga is not a fast paced action game, instead it's a slow game that is all about the journey.The Shenmue saga is about a young man named Ryo Hazuki from Japan, who is on a mission to avenge his father Iawo Hazuki's death by the hands of a Chinese man named Lan Di. If Ryo is to ever stand a chance at defeating Lan Di he must practice and conquer the martial arts, which will take time, patience, and dedication, so this will be no quick task for Ryo.With all of this being said Shenmue III is not the end, it's more than likely far from it... I am sure we will be seeing more of Ryo and follow along with him on his journey to finally conquer the martial arts and go toe to toe against Lan Di one day.Lastly, I will end the review with this;Please do not let any of the negative reviews deter you, if you have played Shenmue I&III give this game a chance you won't regret it. The majority of the reviews that are negative stems from "review bombing" because a lot of people are angry that Shenmue III was backed on Kickstarter, only to end up being an Epic Store exclusive for a year. Yes I admit the whole Epic Store fiasco wasn't a good move by the publisher, but I strongly believe in forgiveness. I also believe that reviews are not meant for personal vendettas, it's meant for reviewing the game itself.I firmly believe a true fan of the Shenmue saga would wish to see it continue on, they would not let something like this cloud their vision and cause them to forsake the whole series.It's good advice to never judge a book by the cover, it's what is written among the pages that truly matter. ~ Laozi I nominated Shenmue III for the "Game of the Year" Award 2020! Hopefully it wins, it deserves it!~ Shenhua Ling

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: This is a review from someone who has actually played and beaten the game (four times on PS4) and not just blind outrage to fuel a ridiculous PC storefront fanboy war.As a happy $1,300 backer who does not require outrage warriors to feign concern or anger to speak on my behalf, I am very satisfied with the Shenmue 3 we ended up getting. Like many others, I played the original games on the Sega Dreamcast in 2000, and jumping into this title in 2020 it is impressive to see a relatively new studio come back 20 years later with a follow-up that perfectly retains the spirit of the original games albeit with some minor modernised touch-ups. So many games have either been rebooted, re-imagined, remade or fallen victim to emulating tired AAA gaming design choices that they end up losing their identity and homogenise themselves into a boring cluster of same-old-same-old with prettier graphics. For YS Net to remain steadfast in their approach and create a retro-style sequel more concerned with retaining the essence of the originals (clunkiness and 90's cheesefest awesomeness included), rather than blindly chasing modern trends in a desperate attempt to appeal to mainstream crowds, makes for a bold and refreshing change as we drown in a sea of identical experiences that are now all too afraid to take risks. YS Net deserve credit for building a sequel which not only delights with fan favourite mini-games and Easter eggs, but features a brand new combat system, two intricately designed locations right down to the mundane, and two fully voiced dubs for over 200 characters to create an aggressively uncompromising Shenmue experience. I wish so many other games had the same degree of boldness to retain what made them unique in the first place, rather than changing their identities to adhere to a boring checklist.

_childDocuments_.review: Shenmue III is probably one of the worst console ports I've ever seen.  It's a third person arcade brawler/cutscene simulator (I'm not kidding, endless, long, unskippable cutscenes... like once you get past the first bunch of them and can play the game at last, you run 10 metres and hit another cutscene).   I think even the cutscenes have cutscenes.Anyway, they tell you that you have to use a console peasant childrens toy gamepad to play the game, and the keyboard controls are terrible, and locked.   That's below standard for PC.  The developers never actually saw a mouse before, so they didn't consider that in the control scheme.  You have to use your keyboard to move the camera around.  Yeah, I know, it's a joke. What isn't a joke is the sheer scumbaggery from Deep Silver.  They teased this game on Steam then pulled the rug out from under gamers and took CCP money to withhold the game from Steam, which turned out disastrous for them, just like it did with Metro.  So they came back to Steam and ate their crispy dead crow and got only a fraction of the sales they would have gotten if they put gamers first.  So they got what they deserved. Unethical, morally bankrupt developers aside, the console port here is garbage.  Whatever hope this game may have had for success was eroded by the terrible console port.   Once more, consoles ruin gaming for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally got around to this one, and I have mixed feelings, but overall I enjoyed the adventure.The graphics are gorgeous, I enjoyed exploring the world here,  It looks like they took a lot of time designing these locations, and it shows.  There are pumpkin patches, rocky cliffs, birds flying above, cities nestled on the riverbank.  There is also a nice score to go along with the game.  The opening intro theme in the quarry is pretty epic and I've listened to it in the truck a few times.The gameplay is more or less classic Shenmue with the exception of the combat.  Its inferior to the previous entries, but it gets the job done.  You can acquire skill books through completing side quests or by collecting/buying items and trading them in pawn shops for the skill books.  I must have collected a couple dozen of these and never used most of them.  You can level up your combat thru sparring at a temple or by practicing against wooden dummies via tedious mini-games.    There are two large locations to explore in the game with plenty of activities, mini-games, shops, fights, and gambling (including lucky hit!) much like the last two games.  There seem to be fewer quick time events in this one, but they're there.  A major gripe shared by others on here is that your stamina meter constantly decreases which means youll need to purchase food or rest to replenish it.  Its a very tedious game mechanic.On the positive side, the gameplay really does capture that "Shenmue" feel from the earlier titles such from the jilted bad dialogue to asking random people on the street for directions to the local fortune teller.  It definitely hit you right in the nostalgia feels.The story however is basically filler, with very little progressing in the overall plot.  Ryo continues to search for Lan Di, his father's killer, and Shenhua's father who has been kidnapped.  There isn't much to add to that honestly.  Personally I feel If there is a Shenmue 4 it'd be nice to see the story wrapped up instead of a new episode every decade or so.Score:  4/5  (One point given for nostalgia to be honest).  Perhaps 3/5 for new players.

Pros:Good classic gamplay / simple controlsbeautiful locationsbasic jobsgood mini games / arcadessimple side quests and straight forward quests with the odd one that you might need to look up onlinedojo`s you can fight at / trainingitems you can pick up to make medicine and so much more... Cons:The only real cons i can see so far after getting into the big city is the health dropping as you run now, and a bit of a missed opportunity on expanding on the Shenmue world by adding more to do even something like running your own dojo, or being able to buy more objects that operate in the game a bit more than what they have since the first Shenmue. Also being able to talk move around a bit more freely without the old blocks as that does make the game feel a bit dated in a time where we now have the tech to open those areas up more without taking up too much data.Overall:I`m one of the few that wanted this game for years and was over the moon when i heard it was being developed, but sad when it was only released on Pc and Playstation but now i finally have a system to run it, Its definitely worth it especially for the low price you cant go wrong. It feels & plays like the original with some nice small new updates, with only a small few cons.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I begin I should probably mention that I backed this game on Kickstarter and have completed the Epic Games release of it.  If you're expecting a modern day masterpiece then Shenmue 3 probably isn't for you.  Other than a visual upgrade not a lot has changed since the previous installment in the series all the way back in 2001, which is a double edged sword really.  On one hand you can seamlessly pick up where you left off in Shenmue 2 but, on other hand this game isn't going to be all that appealing to new comers to the series as it plays like a early 2000's game (not that there is anything wrong with that) but, then again was Shenmue 3 really made for anyone other than fans of the series.The good; At last fans of the series get to continue where they left off back in 2001 and it's a almost seamless continuation in the series with a few graphical updates.The bad; The battle system isn't as rich and fluid as the first two games and the other than introduce certain characters to the series fans have been waiting a long time to see the story doesn't really progress that much, this is only bad in the respect of not knowing when or if we'll get a Shenmue 4.The ugly; It's what long time fans wanted but, it doesn't do itself any favours to attract a new audience, unless the fans are going to pay for Shenmue 4 in another Kickstarter or something like that then this just might be it for the Shenmue series.It's the weakest game in the series but, if you liked the first 2 games and want more then this is the game for you.Score 7/10
