_childDocuments_.review: Never heard of this series before I was bored and found this game on Steam and decided to try it out. It seems to check a lot of boxes for me. I enjoy games with a group. Being able to gear up said group. Big damage numbers. Farm and repeat. I was not disappointed. The game has an amazing soundtrack and is very similar to Final Fantasy games. The same music composer for those games is also responsible for the OST in this game. It takes several hours to actually get to the main loop of this game and that will be a huge turn off to many. The campaign is pretty much a giant tutorial. You're very limited as to what you can upgrade/aquire. The real farm doesn't start until you're at least at extreme difficulty and up. Most of the battles are fun because the combat is so well done on this game. It's very similar to Monster Hunter, except on here you can actually move and it doesn't feel like your character is stuck in pancake syrup. Most of the battles in this game seem pretty balanced and fair, but there are a few that just seem broken, not fun, and Elden Ring levels of aggravation. Like I truly wonder if these missions just didn't get noticed by how ridiculous they are because they make me hate this game at times. They're very few, only two like that so far. Vyrn is a complete idiot I wish I could get a duct tape sigil to shut him up permanently. Speaking of sigils, having a sigil to increase your damage capacity is the most outlandish, stupid idea ever. It's the core foundation in a game like this to upgrade your gear to get bigger numbers, then you have an artificial ceiling that you have to periodically raise even though you've already done that by upgrading your gear. So Vyrn and damage cap sigils need to be taken out in the next patch.+Fun+Fun end game loop if you make it that far and don't give up+Smooth, fast combat-Vyrn sucks-Damage cap sigils suck-Some fights raise my blood pressure too much Side note this game on steam deck is almost unplayable. It's just not strong enough, especially when you get in heavy fights with a lot of adds the game slows down way too much to be able to keep up with the colossal amount of crap on the screen. My rig has a 4090 and going from 4k 120fps locked constantly to steam deck performance about made me have a seizure.

This game has exceeded my expectations as this was my first JRPG I have ever played through to the end, I won't say the story is anything outstanding but the atmosphere within towns/cities was amazing, the world felt super lively, most random NPCs have been voiced and is doing their own thing; like 2 npcs playing at a puddle chatting away being playful, or a group of kids play fighting outside the church etc, these things especially stood out the first time you get into these towns.The combat is fantastic, fast action hack and slash, there is a great deal of difficulty towards the end game where we have to fight multiple bosses consecutively in one session, mechanics are super fast paced, hits hard and any silly mistakes can cause us to fail the fight. There are many characters to choose from which varies significantly in playstyle, each character have their own set of skills (only 4 can be picked) as well as combat gameplay with their unique weapon. I have personally been playing siegfried who uses a two handed great sword, a slow heavy hitting playstyle where each attack needs to be timed for it to be efficient (not too difficult to pull off) and I am enjoying this character the most at the moment. There are other characters such as Charlotta, a mobile fast hitting melee character or Io who is a mage that charges up powerful spells. Outside of characters there are sigils to build whatever our needs are, such as being as tanky as possible, or being a glass cannon full dps(really not recommended and is not needed at all), the progression of character mastery(just upgrades for a character), weapon upgrades, the best sigil builds etc will take up majority of your time in end game which I personally enjoy. (I have played it off steam previously)However, there is a major flaw to this game, after we have finished the main story, this game is primarily a multiplayer/co-op game, which requires a good matchmaking system, and it is not great. There is no cross play between console and PC, no cross region matchmaking, depending on time of day you may struggle to find a match with other players. It seems majority of players play on the Japanese server, where most players change the download region on steam to jump over to JP server and when it is later than 3AM over at JP server the matchmaking dies fast. It is suggested that people install the global matchmaking mod so we can queue into any region without being region locked, though occasionally it can still be a struggle to find a match. It would be way easier to have some friends to play with.I would give this game a overall 9/10, highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Early review for people that are interested in an early buy:My RIGRyzen 7 5800XRTX 3080 10GB VRAM16GB RAM (running multiple apps in bg)Ultra settings 2k resGame is running fairly well, I see a lot of people complaining about game not even launching, IMO skill issue.There are frame drops in some areas like in the forest it dropped to 90 or in town it dropped 80 from 120.I feel hardly pressed to complain about it, because it's still smooth, unlike some other releases from last year that would be hiccuping hard even with DLSS turned on and whatnot (like for example Remnant 2).This could still be improved but is not a major problem since the game is still playing smoothly.IMPORTANT: Does not feature Ultrawide Support and max refresh rate is 120HzDone with performance talk.I'll combine my demo experience from PS5 with what I played here.The combat is very satisfying it's kinda of a meld of Platinum Games' and recent aRPG style Final Fantasy games.Like Platinum games it has very fast paced and fluid combat with cancellable at any time attacks with big dodges (features the limit to the 3rd dodge being slower like in Darksiders for example, you can continue combo after dodging like in PlatGames' tho!).The animations and character presentation is top notch also not unlike something you would find in a Platinum Games' title.All characters feel very distinct and have their own quirks and gimmicks, some of them might feel familiar if you played Granblue Versus, like for example Gran/Djeeta feature a chargeable heavy while Narmaya also features a stance.These gimmicks are at core of each characters gameplay and it is key to utilize them to maximize each characters' potential.Where the game is similar to Final Fantasy is it features a similar skill wheel, when you hold R1/RB your X/Y/A/B buttons change functionality to allow for "Skills" which are self explanatory, starting from a basic fireball, heal or a big sword swing to something like a parry or a team wide buff.Speaking of teams, game heavily leans on teamwork and has a lot of very interesting features that will be key to playing in coop.Enemies have a Stun Gauge that when fills up you can activate a Link Attack simultaneously with another character (or in COOP with a player) and will fill a Link gauge that when full will buff the entire party.This gauge is filled through other different means, one of them is Skybound Arts.This is essentially a Super meter not unlike in a fighting game, once you're at 100% you can activate a Skybound Art which will deal significant damage HOWEVERThe more interesting part is that using Skybound Arts will fill other characters/PLAYERS Skybound Arts gauges that can be further combo'd and if all 4 characters use their Skybound Art they will activate Chain Burst.This Chain Burst will not only damage but also stun the enemy for inexplicably long time and is key for getting higher ranks on your quests.Mastering all these mechanics is the meat of this game and provides the depth and satisfaction to an otherwise already very competent aRPG.Story? No comment, I have only 40 minutes so far but it seems at the very least interesting and the characters are very vibrant and likeable.Even if the story turns out to not be great, the mechanics and presentation is already great enough to be at least a satisfying game,

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Worth full price if you love Action based JRPG games with character interactions. Absolutely a must-buy if you were also waiting for this game since 2016 or later. A flawed masterpiece. Lived up to my personal high expectations so I highly recommend this game.As someone who has waited for this game since 2016 when it was first announced, this game is an absolutely flawed  that lived up to my 8 years of high expectations. If you are on the same boat as me or if you're a big JRPG fan like me who loves character interactions and flashy combat with substance, this is an absolute must-buy. You dont even need to have played any of the Granblue games as the game comes equipped with a glossary that you can open mid-conversation to read to know the lore if you want to. It even comes with 'Fate Episodes' that tells you the detailed backstory of each of the characters as well as a journal that gives you a synopsis of each character too. So dont worry about being out of the loop!Some notable day 1 flaws (which hopefully will be patched down the line) are stuff like not being able to rebind controller buttons, no option to swap button prompts to the PlayStation prompts despite the game being able to support DS4/5 controllers out of the box without Steam input and the audio being strangely low volumed for whatever reason. Cmon guys, its 2024. Some of your fellow Japanese competing companies have already implemented either auto-detection or an option to swap to PlayStation prompts. Get with the program already, sheesh. Not everyone plays with an Xbox controller.Story:We're tossed into non-stop action back to back with some gaps in between. So far the game has been very well paced in terms of story, and its quite an action packed narrative.Combat:Absolutely smooth and damn near perfect. Its responsive and snappy, its got all the flashy fireworks and teamwork/team interactions you can expect from an anime styled Action JRPG game. Its almost on the same level as Bayonetta series. Almost. Common things that this game shares with Bayonetta series are being able to smoothly dodge cancel any attacks while still being able to continue your combo/charged attack the same way the Bayonetta series allows you to. Every single character has their own unique playstyle and while some may share the same archetype like caster or combo attacker or the combo into charged attacker, all the characters vary different enough from each other that you will find yourself enthralled in the combat system. Performance: Its perfect for me, though depending on your rig, your mileage may vary as this is the huge bottleneck as to why most reviews day 1 are negative leading to a mixed score. Besides that, the game ran absolutely smoothly with no stutters or crashes and with a constant stable 120 FPS (you can toggle between 30, 60 or 120 only). Such a feat is worth mentioning as most modern games so far have released with hilarious amounts of performance issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, I have now finished everything in the base game content-wise, and even though when I initially made a review for this game after 9 hours I severely believed I didn't even need to, it turned out I was right and the gameplay loop for this game is indeed way too good. I went into Relink thinking it'd maybe be a decent multiplayer experience at best, but what I ended up finding was an incredibly fun game with so many great intricate systems. The best way to explain the gameplay is to say, "what if your turn based rpg was an ACTION RPG", AND IT ENDED UP WORKING REALLY WELL?Gameplay is fluid throughout multiplayer and single player, the bots that control your party members do the best they can, for the most part, with the characters they're given to control, and the same can be said about randoms or even your friends.I say 'for the most part' because there are a very few amount of characters, like Ghandagoza and Vaseraga (the two massive beefcakes) that the AI doesn't make the best use of, in the sense they don't execute Ghandy's perfect timing hits or Vas's charge attacks.As of the time I'm editing this review, there are 19 playable characters with 2 coming in the extremely near future, all with extremely varied playstyles. You're given access to unlocking them pretty easily as you follow the main questline, the only time you'd really have to "grind" for one is to unlock whichever final character you choose.My initial impression was a low level of disappointment in how some character's had shared mechanics, but after delving into every single one I now realize I couldn't be more incorrect.On top of each character having a fully unique design, they're each given a passive that HEAVILY impacts their gameplay, and definitely require you to use the customizable skills that come with each character to use them to their full potential. So much of the customization in skills comes in the form of how you want to output damage, how you'd like to support your team, or how you'd like to support yourself, giving you a decently varied playstyle just for a single character. I'm fully min-maxing my 7th character right now and I cannot express the amount of joy each one gave me.Also in case it needs to be mentioned because we live in a world where the gaming landscape is controlled by the idea of "viability", yes, every character is viable. Some will do more damage, some will have more utility, and others will do a bit TOO much damage, it seriously barely matters. The ONLY TIME IT MATTERS is when you get to bosses with damage checks, but this is more like the game is gating you off from content until you're actually SERIOUSLY ready for it.Every character is designed to have a specific role and be able to play for the team in the form of buffs or debuffing the enemy if you don't feel comfortable in being the main damage dealer, and you'll more than likely be doing your part as long as you play the game and try not to die! Healing, debuffing, and buffing is also NOT REQUIRED IN ANY PART OF THE GAME, I have played the entirety of this game solely super-armoring through every piece of content with Vaseraga as I let my starving, piss-stained AI companions grapple onto me like my children as I do all the damage. ALSO, YOU DO NOT NEED TO PLAY THIS GAME HYPER MECHANICALLY IN ENDGAME CONTENT, ANYONE WHO TELLS YOU TO DO THIS IS A GARBAGE DELVING RACCOON ON A KEYBOARD, but you can definitely play mechanically if you'd like. :)The game also allows for even deeper customization in the form of Sigils. Sigils are stat amplifiers that can support everything from your damage, crit chance, percentage based damage based on certain qualifications, lower cooldown times, decreasing cooldowns every time you do damage, and the list goes on. Every time a game has stat amplifiers like this it seriously makes me so happy, and I constantly spend hours theory-building and testing to get the perfect build for how I can get the highest damage while also catering to my playstyle.The mechanics of this game, separate from characters, are mostly in the form of guard breaks, blocks, dodges, and your Super Burst Gauge. Dodge rolling and blocking can both be perfectly timed and give you an amazing buff if you do so in the form of making you invulnerable to damage for a few seconds (which can by the way be buffed with the aforementioned sigils!!), letting you get off some more of that sweet sweet dps as long as you can stick to the enemy. The Super Burst Gauge is this game's form of giving each character a cinematic chargeable ultimate, that is actually able to be combo'd with any of your teammates. The purpose of this mechanic is seemingly to put it together for a massive elemental combination burst after combining each one, but a tip for players going into the endgame, you can actually use your SBA to stall out damage windows for you and your team, and more than likely get more damage than you would have otherwise.As for the story itself, I can't say I care for it! It has moments where it has a lot of fun with itself, but for the most part it takes itself very seriously, and what it takes very seriously is SERIOUSLY campy. This is for the most part an intensely cookie-cutter anime turn based rpg storyline. But I seriously don't care! I appreciate the amount of effort put into the game and it's story as a whole, but I also really appreciate the amount of effort put into allowing me to skip every cutscene I'm not in the mood to sit through! There are some seriously flashy and cinematic parts to the main story that do make it pretty entertaining when you're actually PLAYING THE GAME though, so i'ts definitely not an entire snooze.Problems though! Only 2 that I can FORCE, but they do exist. I understand the need for a damage cap, and even though the game itself actually gives you a certain amount of ways to INCREASE the damage cap, when it comes down to it there's an actual concrete damage cap eventually. I wish I could say it would be somewhat difficult to get to, but if you play this game to the degree of maxing out multiple characters, it does ultimately come to chance, but for the most part you will be hitting the damage cap on a few characters you put effort into building. Granted though, a damage cap for this style of game is pretty important, and does balance out multiple characters that otherwise could very feasibly beat endgame content in seconds, which is already possible.Probably the only other actual issue I have with the game right now is that there aren't enough bosses for the EXTREMELY LATE endgame content in this game! Farming in the EXTREMELY LATE endgame has you fighting around 9 of the same bosses multiple times, and that doesn't even include the final boss that for the most part is grinded out separately for other reasons I don't want to spoil! These boss fights get pretty repetitive, especially if you're doing what I'm doing by building multiple characters to appreciate more of the content put into this game.There is more content post-release that does appease one of my more fair complaints, but the only form of said content that's been actually shown is in the form of a new endgame boss coming out a month after the game's release date. There are some nice bonuses with the arrival of two new characters and some sort of paid dlc in the next couple months, but past that I have to just hope the developers see how much people love this game and desperately wish it gets even more extended content.If you're a fan of games like Monster Hunter (but hate how long hunts can take), or crave something akin to Genshin's party system in a fully fledged multiplayer system, maybe interested in the fantasy anime RPG elements, or even love the chaos but synergistic gameplay of DMC or Bayonetta, seriously type into your little Youtube search bar and look into the game, because I definitely can assure that this game would be worth your time and money, ESPECIALLY at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Monster Hunter World, Final Fantasy XVI, Xenoblade Chronicles (all of them), and the original gacha game, this game feels like it was made for me, though I'll try to be as objective as possible. As of the time of this review, I've played everything in the base game, including the final challenge. I'll also not acknowledge the Assist Mode, as I never used it and it cannot be used in the end-game anyways.Granblue Fantasy: Relink is an attempt to take the world of Granblue Fantasy and put it into an action setting, which I believe it succeeds at marvelously. Characters are represented beautifully and faithfully from their gacha counterpart, right down to a lot of NPCs looking very similar yet also immediately recognizable from the gacha. Many mechanics from the original gacha game are here in ways that make sense, such as every character having four skill slots that have cooldowns after uses, weapons having level caps that need treasure drops from quests to uncap further, and a wishlist that players can add treasures to so they can easily find which quests they can farm them from. But there's NO ACTUAL gacha here, this is not a pay-to-win game you can whale at, this is a full-fledged game.And I want to emphasize that you DO NOT need to know Granblue Fantasy to enjoy this game, the whole point of this game was to introduce the IP to more people. I have friends that know very little about it, only what they've heard from me over the years, and they enjoy Granblue Fantasy: Relink just as much as I do. Every character has Fate Episodes you can go through, which most are just still-images with text on a screen voiced by that character. The first 2-3 Fate episodes per character are their backstories, so you can learn what you need to know in-game. In fact doing Fate Episodes grants stat increases for that character, so you're encouraged to do just that. Some Fate Episodes do have quests attached to them, these also have important unlocks you will want.Aside from the visuals, the first thing that will stick out is the story, and this aspect of the game can be polarizing. The story is only okay, and yet I think that's okay. As a fan of the original gacha game, it just feels like another side story event. It's not bad and not great, just with a much higher budget and visuals. But the core of this game is the multiplayer aspect, which doesn't fully unlock until the story is completed, which can hold people back. As with the original gacha game, nearly all cutscenes can be skipped, which are accompanied by a short blurb detailing what happens in the scene you're about to skip, so players wanting to jump into multiplayer ASAP can do that and still have a basic idea of what's going on. The story can take somewhere from 5-20 hours depending on just how much of the cutscenes you actually watch and how through you are in scouring the story quests for collectibles.The game is a mixture of character action like you'd expect from Platinum+ (who actually assisted in the initial development), raid mechanics like you'd see in Final Fantasy XIV, and 4-player co-op like from Monster Hunter. This doesn't sound like it should work, but it does spectacularly. There's over a dozen characters, starting at six with others unlocked over time, with each having a very different playstyle from one another and granting every player to find their own way to play and express themselves. Each character has their own unique traits and combo system, and unique skills they can pick from. While they can only bring up to four into battle, they each have a handful of unique skills to pick from. You're encouraged to try them all out and find what works for you, or more importantly what works for the quest you're tackling. While some characters are a little more complicated and difficult to pick up than others, the ease of controlling and attacking with them makes jumping into Granblue Fantasy: Relink an immediately responsive experience. There's also a training area where you can practice using a character without worry or failing a quest; you're highly encouraged to utilize this. As you unlock more skills and sigils, you'll need to figure out what works well together.The meat of the game is the post-story multiplayer. While playing the story, you'll gradually unlock Easy and Normal level quests, and they can be played in multiplayer, but they're so easy it's not worth the time. After completing the story, you'll unlock Hard level quests, and the Monster Hunter-style progression will begin. Clearing select quests will unlock more and harder quests, granting access to more bosses, materials, and more to strengthen your characters for the next challenge to come. While there is a variety of quests such as surviving an onslaught of weaker enemies, the ones you'll spend the most time doing are boss battles. They start out with simple mechanics like finding a way to deal with a goblin with a massive shield or avoiding a giant rock monster as it tries to roll you over, but slowly get more in-depth and eventually introduce breaking boss parts to either gain rewards or stun/disable them. As you advance to Very Hard, Extreme, and higher, the boss battles get harder, add new mechanics, and do everything in their power to put you down. The final level of challenges get especially brutal, making it all the more satisfying when you finally overcome them.The music is incredible! In the early years of the original gacha game it was composed by Nobuo Uematsu, legendary composer for Final Fantasy, and those compositions are rearranged as well as new compositions by the current composer Tsutomu Narita. I'm not really good at explaining how and why music is good, but as with the original gacha game there's quite a variety of thematic styles. Seriously, just go online and listen to some of the boss themes for this game. I recommend Managarmr's theme.Granblue Fantasy: Relink is incredibly fun and gorgeous, with a vibrant and colorful art style that can make you feel like the world is alive and gameplay that's very satisfying to play, though it takes a while to get to the really fun part. Depending on your skill level and ability to learn MMO-style raid mechanics, you may find the game challenging right away, or take a long time to reach that challenge, but I assure you the challenge is here and waiting for you to find it. And with post content on the way like Lucilius's Dark Rapture, I promise the challenge will only intensify.

_childDocuments_.review: In the sea of mediocre dogwater games that have been releasing back to back for the last couple years I finally found a game that leaves me with my jaw dropped from the start. Holy moly.The art direction, the graphics and visual style, the atmosphere and world design, the visual & combat FX... phenomenal.I feel like I'm really in a fantasy picture book. This feels like when you watch anime and the characters are playing a video game and you're like wow I wish video games were really like that. This one is really like that.Not only that, the story chapters are so immersive from the cutscenes, to the boss fights and world exploration, to the scripted panning of the camera and event sequences. I don't know how to explain the feeling I have playing through the story but the best I can describe it is that it feels like I'm playing a game in 4D. If you've played so much as the prologue then you know what I'm talking about. I'm so tired of playing these story games where you just walk through a soulless generic world doing random tasks that a plumber could do, let alone a hero, and there has really not been one moment where I'm not fully hooked playing this game. I'm not finished with the campaign yet but I'm looking forward to finishing it this weekend and start gearing up my characters to tackle boss fights together with friends and fellow GBF enjoyers online.P.S.: Yes, I am aware some people are experiencing bugs at the moment. If this concerns you then wait for the first patch / hotfix cause this game is worth it.P.S.S.: Tbh there is literally no reason to buy the special edition as it gives you no type of unique special edition cosmetics or profile showcases. I'd argue that the special edition actually hurts your overall experience since it gives you a bunch of money, skill points, and upgrade materials that you'd have way more fun coming by naturally. If you want to buy it for the color packs then just buy the base game + color pack 1-3 which will be the same price as the special edition which funny enough comes with color packs 2-3 but not color pack 1.

_childDocuments_.review: Granblue Fantasy: Relink is a visually stunning masterpiece that captivates players like myself with its gorgeous graphics and an engaging albeit short main storyline that leaves you craving for more. While the journey through the narrative may conclude too soon for some, the game compensates with an abundance of end-game content that promises countless hours of fun. The gameplay is thoroughly enjoyable, blending classic elements with innovative mechanics to keep players hooked. A beautiful and immersive experience, Granblue Fantasy: Relink is a testament to how games can be both visually appealing and deeply satisfying in content. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm immersed in a captivating world that scores an 8 in my book, with the potential to hit a solid 10 for anime and manga enthusiasts who invest in the storyline. While the system is well-structured, there's some grind involved for those aiming for extreme levels of mastery. But, if you're ready to invest the time, the payoff is worth it.The cinematic experience is an absolute standout, earning a perfect 10 in my rating. The game's cut-scenes and cinematic sequences are breathtaking, seamlessly blending with the narrative to create an immersive and visually stunning adventure. Every moment feels like a carefully crafted masterpiece, enhancing the overall enjoyment and making the storytelling truly memorable. Granblue Fantasy Relink is a game where the story's potential for anime and manga enthusiasts, diverse gameplay options, and the challenge of late-game progression combine to create a thoroughly enjoyable and rewarding experience.Story  -----------------> 8 ( if you like anime and manga and invest in the story it will be a solid 10 )Game-play  -----------------> 10 ( You have so many ways to play the game is unbelievable )Progression  -----------------> 8 ( if you are planning to go to  extreme and dive in late game you will have some grind )Cinematisc ---------------------> 10

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to be enjoy this game, and for parts of it I really did: there are some really fun and cool set pieces, the characters are sufficiently fleshed out, and if you want it there's plenty of lore to read up on (especially if, like me, you didn't play the mobile game that this is a sequel (sort of) to).So why don't I recommend the game? Because the story is irritatingly inconsistent and becomes immensely frustrating. I understand that's not a blocker to some, in which case enjoy the cool set pieces and the combat. For anyone who wants to know what I mean? Well, if you care enough to read on, let me explain:Firstly, 'irritatingly inconsistent': the game just isn't consistent within itself, which means - in my view - that the plot suffers significantly. Your team's power level is one major example of that - your team are heroes that have defeated an empire and the equivalent of deities, and yet the group have trouble against goblins; an hour later, they are wrecking something akin to a demon, then another hour later they're struggling against some soldiers. This happens constantly, and I've never played a game where the apparent power level of the main characters seems so all over the place (and yes, I have played several of the Trails series!). The worst offender is Another inconsistency relates to the motives of the main antagonists: Final example I'll share (though there are so many!), towards the end,  Why was the boss still alive? Why could it suddenly defeat the entity that had just beaten it? Because the game is inconsistent.What about 'immensely frustrating'? Well, front and centre are the four occasions where the game forces you to lose a fight. This is, to my memory, always after you have just utterly wrecked some horrendously powerful demon-like creature, which means any high you have after achieving victory are immediately dashed (and tie in to inconsistent power levels as per above). Also, the forced losses are always just as you're about to , which makes the whole of the story feel frustratingly repetitive - nothing you do, at all, matters until you get to the last Chapter and the game decides you're allowed to finally win.Also, to a lesser extent, are the 'pulled right out of one's arse' plot contrivances. The game does have a lot going for it, but for me, I just couldn't enjoy the experience as a whole. I played to the end of Chapter 9, hoping it would get better, but it actually got worse. I haven't played the end game experience, partly because the motive that's meant to push me to continue is one I just absolutely can't bring myself to care about.

_childDocuments_.review: The game runs exceptionally well on my PC, no framerate drop even on the busiest battle scene, staying locked at 120fps on Ultra graphic settings. The PC version is also superior in terms of the Multiplayer/Co-Op compared to the PS4/PS5 version because we have a Lobby/Room Select while the PS4/PS5 only have Matchmaking System a la Call of Duty.That said, I have 4 complains with the game right now:Other than that, I have no other complains, because the game is exactly like how I imagined it back when it was still called Project Re:Link in 2016! The combat is fluid and responsive, the characters are lively and expressive, and the Japanese voice acting is superb and on point. Definitely worth the price I paid for, and I hope that Cygames will address the issues I listed above and all the other complaints that other players are experiencing.

There is a also really great design choice why this game does not respect your time: you can only sells or trade with limited amount while you have a bunch of sigils or stone you want to trade (oh and hope your mouse button or controller button really good as you will need it to speedup the process of transmutation for sigil or stone). How about old sigils ? Well once you get to sigils V, you can put sigils I below that to trash (+ your resource to upgrade them too).2. Oh it has lot of character, looks like it will fun....... NO !!! Due to reason number 1, you will need a freaking lot of time to build your character. And you know which is good ? You get terminus weapon for character you never use. Yeah.... Let's put your effort down to drain (or keep farming terminus weapon and hoping it drops for your character).3. Oh look, there are a lot of sigils with different effect, it will have variety of build right ? NO. This game only ask you 1 thing and it is DPS. Heck even for the best weapon, it ask you to have below 45k HP to get the buff. Thus screw those health sigil, screw those aegis sigil, etc. But but but... I still can have other build right ? Lucius patch (new patch) even make this more clear. New sigil = moar DPS, his mechanic = moar DPS as if you lack DPS bye bye your HP (thus making tanky build is a void). In addition, they basically put a bad mechanic in this game: DAMAGE CAP. Thus in endgame, you will need a bunch of this sigils to unlock your character power (I mean DPS).4. Lot of lazy design to make the game harder. What I mean for this, in proud difficulity, you will fight a group of boss. But there is a caveat, the boss which is not the main boss will do only 1 or 2 move. That skeleton boss which you fight has some move ? Now it becomes not main boss and what does it do ? Spam AOE.Unless you are into this kind of thing, I fully not recommend this game.

name: Noita
detailed_description: Noita is a magical action roguelite set in a world where every pixel is physically simulated. Fight, explore, melt, burn, freeze and evaporate your way through the procedurally generated world using spells you've created yourself. Explore a variety of environments ranging from coal mines to freezing wastelands while delving deeper in search for unknown mysteries. Pixel-based physics: Every pixel in the world is simulated. Burn, explode or melt anything. Swim in the blood of your foes! Enter a simulated world that is more interactive than anything you've seen before. Your own magic: Combine spells to create your own magic as you delve deeper into the caverns. Use magic to crush your enemies and manipulate the world around you. Procedurally generated world: Explore a unique world every time you play. Discover new environments as you adventure deeper. Action roguelite: Death is permanent and always a looming threat. When you die, don’t despair, use what you’ve learned to get further on your next adventure. Noita is being developed by Nolla Games, a company set up by 3 indie developers, all of whom have worked on their own projects in the past. The three gents in question are: Petri Purho Petri is best known as the creator of Crayon Physics Deluxe. In his youth he also made a lot tiny freeware games. He has also made a bunch of board games, but he hasn't told about it to anyone. So please keep it a secret. Olli Harjola Olli is known for the award-winning, mind-bending sci-fi puzzler The Swapper. Besides indie games, he also dabbles in music, live visuals and making programming languages. Arvi Teikari Arvi is also known as Hempuli. Over the years he has released a lot of tiny experimental games, so many in fact that he is unaware of all of them. One of the games he remembers making is Baba Is You.

Procedurally generated world: Explore a unique world every time you play. Discover new environments as you adventure deeper. Action roguelite: Death is permanent and always a looming threat. When you die, don’t despair, use what you’ve learned to get further on your next adventure. Noita is being developed by Nolla Games, a company set up by 3 indie developers, all of whom have worked on their own projects in the past. The three gents in question are: Petri Purho Petri is best known as the creator of Crayon Physics Deluxe. In his youth he also made a lot tiny freeware games. He has also made a bunch of board games, but he hasn't told about it to anyone. So please keep it a secret. Olli Harjola Olli is known for the award-winning, mind-bending sci-fi puzzler The Swapper. Besides indie games, he also dabbles in music, live visuals and making programming languages. Arvi Teikari Arvi is also known as Hempuli. Over the years he has released a lot of tiny experimental games, so many in fact that he is unaware of all of them. One of the games he remembers making is Baba Is You.
short_description: Noita is a magical action roguelite set in a world where every pixel is physically simulated. Fight, explore, melt, burn, freeze and evaporate your way through the procedurally generated world using spells you've created yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a super unique action roguelite where every single pixel in the game is physically simulated. So if you played powder toy or any of those types of games back in the day this is like those but its a roguelite with crazy and fun random spells and combos.The main draw of this game is as you can tell, every single pixel is physically simulated. So when there is an explosion or fire if it touches wood it will start to burn it and it can catch you on fire but if you can find water to douse your self off. you can get rid of it. If there is gunpowder it will cause a huge explosion if blown up, and even the enemies have blood in them so if you kill them you can douse yourself in their blood to get an effect.All this means that the world and environment you are in is just as interesting, if not more interesting, as the enemies.Beyond the world being simulated pixel by pixel, the spell and wand system in this game is the other half of this incredible experience.Each wand will have various stats along with several spell slots and most of the wands you pick up in the world already have several spells in them.So every time you pick up a wand in the environment they are all going to feel completely different from one another because there are so many random variables that make each wand unique. Firstly you have all the stats that I talked about but then you have the spells and what order the spells are in. So you keep getting crazy random wands that all do super quirky and unique things and that is a ton of fun.And if that was the only thing wands had that would be fine but instead there is actually a crazy amount of depth these wands bring with them because you can fully customize them.you can take off all the spells from them and mix and match them together and almost create your own sequence or program of how your wand will fire.So you could do alternating spells in a wand that will make it fire two different spells or you can use modifiers to maybe make the spread of your wand crazy high but give it a lot of damage.There is a ridiculous amount of depth in this part of the game and I would be lying if I said I understood it completely because it seems like you could do some 500 IQ plays with combining and mixing and matching spells to create super powerful wands.But what I like about this game is that even though it has this crazy in-depth wand customizing system it’s not that overwhelming because you could just never customize your wands and instead only use the pre-built wands you find randomly throughout the cave and you would still have just as much fun and could still find some crazy powerful combos.Obviously if you get really good at the game and can learn the system then you will definitely do better and that's awesome because it is rewarding the player for learning the mechanics instead of punishing a newer player with extremely overwhelming mechanics.So overall if you are a fan of roguelikes and roguelites or just want a kind of fun sandboxy pixel world to explore I would highly recommend this game because there is absolutely nothing like it to compare it too so if you want this type of gameplay Noita is really the only game I can think of you can play.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of game run around parading the label "roguelike." They aren't. I won't get autistic about the definition, but those are all roguelites -- games that either heavily take RNG into consideration or feature a procedural generation mechanic or two. However, you'd be forgiven for making such a mistake of distinction for Noita. In all but visuals, Noita plays and is designed as close to the spirit of a real roguelike than any other game trumpeting the term. It's very random, it's relentless, it's a ton of fun, and there are tons of unintended consequences.Ignore my hours, I've played this for dozens on another account. I could continue to do so but wanted to support the devs. FAIR WARNING: to determine whether you'd like this game, go play Brogue. It's free. If you don't like Brogue, or rather the rules of Brogue, you won't like this. The game can be utterly merciless at times and you will restart frequently; the only progression is your knowledge of the mechanics, just like any actual roguelike. The physics are amazing and lead to total chaos much of the time, and here and there the RNG can get downright unfair (being hit with a nuke the instant an enemy sees you, for instance). But if you are a connoisseur of real roguelikes and understand the grit, gain, and punishment of playing them, you'll love Noita.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun roguelike. The tinkering with wands and spells makes it very fun and can get incredibly crazy pretty quickly. It's a shame there are so many cool secrets and riddles that are so difficult to discover in normal play, but otherwise a pretty neat game. Pretty staunchly RNG based in my experience, more so than Binding of Isaac, etc. but I still would recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn I wish there were more games just like Noita - physics-based, pixel roguelikes that is. I mean, I know there are similar games but they don't scratch this very specific itch like Noita does. I remember I used to play this old Java game back in the day - it was called just like "Sandbox" where you just sprinkled random materials like sand, dirt, water, gas, acid, lava, fire, etc. and they would collect at the bottom of the screen or float and interact with each other. I downloaded that on my computer in the days before smartphones at a time where I was going to be without internet for an indefinite amount of time and it managed to entertain me. The physics part of Noita feels a lot like that.

_childDocuments_.review: At its current state. I would avoid Noita. I've had my ups and down with this game, but this ends with a down and out unless they change a couple of mechanics.There are no instructions or introductions to any of the Wand mechanics. I would highly discourage people playing this game blind.  You have 4 wand slots starting with some basic wands that will shoot basic bolts and a few bombs.  You find a few wands in the map as well as able to purchase ones in between maps. What they don't tell you is that you can mix and match the effects on each wand, taking some effects one wand and placing them into another. So, if you're unaware of this, you'll be going through an already brutal map with subpar wands doing very little damage.That's fine and good after you figure out how to make and craft good wands.  But the reason why I'm quitting is that the game can stop your 45 minute - hour run completely based on RNG outside your control. So, in between maps there is a safe room that is under the main level.  The way to get into this is going into a portal on the bottom of the level.  But you could use and acid ability and melt the material to get you a path in.  If you do this, you "anger the gods" and spawns an invincible Lich that will demolish you in the safe room and will chase after you if you're able to avoid it somehow. The problem is, if an enemy does this, the game will blame you and will spawn the Lich.  Enemies will attack other enemies.  So if one has an acid attack, and starts attacking another enemy, they will be able to melt through and trigger the Lich.  This can happen offscreen without you knowing what's happening.  So you'll be going through the level and all of a sudden "You have angered the gods."  The more commonly way this occurs is that there are big worms that spawn at random and will burrow quickly around the level.  They will trigger the Lich pretty much guaranteed.  There's no way figuring out if there is a worm burrowing around unless you see it. Getting the right wand effects, getting good perks, and getting health drops is already tough enough with this game.  Getting your 45min -1hr run ruined by an RNG worm burrowing through the safe house and angering the gods is the cheesiest and worst way to end a run.Update: Continued to play it after a few updates and they partially fixed the worm burrowing angering the gods.  It still occurs but not as frequently.  I want to like the game, but I still do not recommend it.  The gamer relies completely on which wands you get in the first few levels.  There are times where you don't get a single wand on the first stage which puts you at a major disadvantage enemy wise as well as limiting you to what you can explore.  If you look at posting of crazy wand combos, don't think you'll get those at all.  They require specific rare wands, rare spells,  as well as RNG based perk availability to work with the wand. You're left with pretty much crafting single fire heavy spells (missiles, bombs), or rapid fire SMG-type spells.  I'm getting sick of spending an hour exploring almost the entire first and second floor, only to be rewarded with 1-2 life gains, cruddy wands that only attack, and sub optimal perks. Going to stop playing until they give a significant update to the availability of spells, wands, and perks. Or being able to explore without being reliant on getting specific spells, wands, and perks.

_childDocuments_.review: (Edit 4: I'm nearing 160 hours. I've discovered parallel worlds which you can enter by tearing through the solid stone on either side of the map, then using some combination of ambrosia potion to stop the radioactive damage of the barrier stone, black holes to dig, a wand that's powerful enough, teleportation spells to reach the other side before it trickles quickly through hundreds of health. I had a single 16 hour run through three entire maps. I became some sort of demigod that finally only succumbed to a potion that turned me into a 5 health sheep. Secrets... So many secrets to discover. So many wands to make. How did I end up handling health after so much time? I had a boomerang wand full of "heal friendly" spells. Before I found the boomerang spell to make that function properly, I actually threw the wand on the ground in front of an enemy and allowed them to fire wrecklessly at me until my health was full, because that's what they do with any wand they find. The possibilities of wand creation are just... Unimaginable. There's a teleport spell that shoots out and blinks you to the location, but there's also a "return" spell that pulls you back to a location after a short moment, yet you can combine the return spell with another spell with a trigger, so you can "return" to a location in the distance, not unlike the teleport spell. So much logic, and so many possibilities. There's a spell to fire from the nearest enemy, so you can play it safe and find explosion immunity, then use a static projectile explosion that you cast from the nearest enemy. They simply explode violently. I made a wand today that has an "always cast" trait that uses a spell that gives all your shots an aura of damage, so I coupled that with little bouncy spells that increase the shot speed of the wand, then another modifier before those that drastically increases shot speed with no respect to your aim. Instantly, I'm surrounded by an entire screen of projectiles which all have auras that deal damage continuously. Everything dies mostly before I see it, yet I know, all it will take is some little slip up and my run is over regardless of that strength. The possibilities... Are endless.)(Edit 3: Star date 41016, 41 hours in. This latest 1.0 launch has proven to have something unexpected. A level of diversity and possibility I hadn't considered within a game. I've felt the strangest urge to explore it deeper, after having so many unique little details strike me with this new patch. I cause a fire only to see it covered in water suddenly. How? Oh, it seems the simple heat from the fire caused the snow above it in the snow biome to actually melt and put it out. I get a perk that caused me to freeze everything around me, so I walk on water and imprison an enemy under it where he drowns. Later, I almost cage myself in a fountain of frozen blood. Over and over, over and over, new random and ridiculous occurrences happen so naturally. Enemies trapped under a metal floor, then I see them surrounding me, all because a monster that shoots acid happened to end up in that room. Something... Something about this game has taken hold of me. I can see something within it, and I must go deeper. End log.)(Edit for 1.0 launch: Tons of new stuff and changes that makes the game feel a lot less consistent, but technically a lot more awesome because of that. The game already has the physics/variety for tons of crazy emergent gameplay, but that just multiplied with simple changes like no longer starting with the same wand/flask every time.) The physics are amazing. Reminds me of Powder Toy except there's an actual game attached to it.At first, I was amazed by the physics, then I started doubting it had the depth I'd want from a roguelike, enough that I was wishing it was a rogue-lite, because I felt like it was missing some progression to keep me interested.Turns out, the game has a few surprises.1. Finding random wands was cool. Finding random wands with random powers was cool. Realizing the shops after each level allowed me to completely edit all the spells on every wand made me want to keep playing. I even found/bought a few "spells" during my first few games and had no idea how to use them, but it turns out they can all be put into your wands in any crazy combination. It reminded me of everything I loved about weapon personalization in the original Mass Effect, and how cool it was to put together your own weapons in an earlier patch of 7 Days to Die, except this game is far more extreme.2. There are a lot of perks. Perks that change everything up. I mean, I said you can edit your wands in every shop. Turns out there's even a perk to allow you to edit them anywhere. There's a perk that makes you immune to explosions. There's a perk that gives you giant spider legs that completely change movement. There's a perk that makes you immune to electric while electrifying everything you touch, so you kill yourself from an explosion because you step in water that's near an explosive barrel. 3. Combining everything I've said, Level 8 is a b**ch, and I know there's some sort of insanely OP combination I can find that would allow me to crush everything like a crazy run in Binding of Isaac. Hell, here's one just from what I've found so far. Perks: Explosion immunity, unlimited spells, combined with a wand I found once with a nuke shot. 1000 range explosion. I'd just shoot that over and over until I destroy my way down to whatever ending exists in the game.

And sprinkle in a lot of difficult gameplay mechanics on top.This makes noita very adversarial, especially when you, the lowly gamer, see the many alpha gamer's videos on their reaching of the final mega secret area of the game.Beating the main run part of the game is definitely not an impossible feat, even for novice players, due to the ability to occasionally just get absolutely busted wands, but it's still a very challenging game, especially when everything seems so complex.The duology of Noita is, Noita is simple, do not get hit, do not light yourself on fire, do not die, get to the end to win(??)Noita is terrifyingly complex. _childDocuments_.review: I put off this review for quite some time. This game is great, but it's a game that made it 99% of the way to godhood and then fell off completely.Is it worth buying? For most people, probably. Those people that don't delve far into the game, play through to the most straight forward end and then never touch it again.For everybody else, development seems to have ended for this game. There are bugs that make the expanded content unplayable (literally sitting at 2 FPS in a PW (don't look up acronyms if you don't want spoilers), the game demands that you experiment yet the game engine is bugged out and breaks your flasks if you have them carefully sat on the ground, deletes your spells/wands/items. Any physics object that gets ejected out of player view has a chance to be deleted from the world.There's an entire alchemy system in the game but the buggy game engine won't allow you to store items on the ground, it deletes them/smashes flasks seemingly at random as you exit and enter the area, thus you are prohibited from experimenting. You also get 4 inventory slots, so, without cheating with inventory mods the game makes it mandatory for you to store items on the ground.Some spells crash/lag the game, some objects never appear due to bugs. Some quest related world objects get destroyed immediately due to worldgen. I could go on and on, it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mess.I have a capable computer, I'm in The Work in a PW and the game crawling at 2FPS is the final straw.It's sad how such an amazing game that just needs a bit more polishing is left in this state. Nolla Games, you guys were so close.

_childDocuments_.review: Risk of Rain, Terraria, Binding of Isaac. These games all have some core elements that I have really enjoyed, and Noita has a lot of the greatness from those games. I'd recommend before giving up on the game, go look for a tips for beginners video or something. DunkorSlam is a great content creator for the game and a lot of his videos helped me get over the initial learning curve so I could enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Game puts you into spots you both cannot foresee nor prevent that will just randomly happen and kill you.  This functionally takes agency from the player in a way that both confuses and frustrates.  It is confusing because the game does not give you information beyond cryptic messages about what's happening, and it's frustrating for me because if you play games to achieve mastery of mechanics, you cannot have random elements in the game that the player cannot interact with.That said, if the intention is to create a game that while you play it you just sorta randomly die, it's not a bad game. _childDocuments_.review: It's a roguelite, plain and simple. The particles are fancy and the combat can be suddenly brutal but end of the day it is a roguelite through and through.You will die and you will try again.The point where Noita stands out though is the wand/spell system and flasks. The former is where you have a set amount of wands that roll different stats like number of spell slots and/or cast speed. Between that and what spells you find along the way (or more commonly rip off of other wands) replayability is high. And then there are the flasks. Flasks let you abuse the particle physics Noita is proud of much to the detriment of your enemies. It's a tool for subtle puzzles or not-so-subtle panics and works very well with Noita's emphasis on.....uh, creative solutions.If you're a fan of roguelites you'll find Noita a pleasant break of form while still being familiar enough to jump right in. If you're more of a tinkerer who likes to break a game's systems you'll also enjoy the game, provided you can get far enough. And if you're like me and enjoy both you'll resign yourself to playing into the wee hours of the morning without realizing it. As is tradition.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a wonderful game for it's low price, to put it simply. The way the developer(s) have implemented thousands of ways to tackle any given situation without making the game too complex is wonderful. The world you play in has been jam-packed with secrets in every nook and cranny, allowing for endless replayability. Another thing to take note of is how the game is a roguelite, each run starting from the start until you die or complete it. Knowledge about the game, what spell/wand combos are the best and how to deal with many problems is the only thing that carries over between runs, allowing each one to usually be better than the last. Also, the vast modding community allows you to change the game in any way you like. Overall, Noita is certainly a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's how it's been going:I die. I die a lot. I find good things, I die. I run a floor again and again and again, dying every time. I begin learning the mechanics and the basic layout - the [REDACTED] over there, the [REDACTED] that sometimes spawns over here, the [REDACTED] that is so tempting and which I fell to twice and never again, and I die once more.I die. I die a lot.I go into the mountain. There's a gloopy, misshapen, tumorous blob hovering in the corner, caustic acid dripping from its guts and burning the dirt. Below it, giant rats scurry, sharp claws clicking against the pebble-filled dirt. A dull roar can be heard from the darkness, and after a hundred deaths and a hundred more lives, I have come to understand that roar as the sound of a demon with skin of fire - pure fire, no flesh - whose sole purpose in life is to shoot me dead.And despite my sure knowledge that jumping down will be the end of me once again, that my hundred deaths will become my hundred and one deaths, that I may die from acid, I may die from fire, I may die from freezing mist or an outpouring of water and slippery tentacles from an eldritch dimension I dare not dream of, that I may die from my very own spells, turned against their maker like so many rabid dogs, I leap down into the unknown. And, as always, I die.I die. I die a lot.And yet every time I die, every time I make it a little farther than I did before, equipped with spells and abilities and spiderlike limbs that itch where they join to my skin, I find myself happy, loving the thrill of exploring the deep unknown, uncovering the remains of the [REDACTED] and finding the inklings of knowledge budding in the back of my brain, not unlike those poison-filled blossoms that curled around my wrists and ankles as horrid monsters with a hundred segmented legs encroached upon me.I die. I die a lot. And, admittedly, after fifty deaths and fifty-one lives, I will often find myself rage-quitting. But within a few hours, I find myself loading up the game again, standing before the tunnel that leads down into the mountains where I know I will meet my fate and, potentially, riches beyond my dreams, and against the knowledge of my sure death and potential failure, I enter the unknown once more.I die a lot, yes, but that's not always a bad thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow this is the most frustrating, difficult game I've played in quite some time, dying all the time, starting fresh 5 or more times in one sit down, yet is one of the most fun and addicting games I've ever played. Every playthough you learn something new: how this spell works with that spell, how this potion can get me through this otherwise tough section, how this enemy reacts and fights, etc. Even though on a surface level, it seems as if you are repeating yourself going through the same areas, every game will be different, with different challenges you have to adapt to. You are never not kept on your toes.If you are just starting out on this game, allow yourself the time to soak in everything. You will not beat this game quick, even if you have seen gameplay before you play it, you need experience and alot of it. You have to be a wizard, a warrior, an alchemist and a strategist simultaneously to achieve good runs, and that takes time and experience.My personal favorite thing about this game is the fact that the descending progressing levels of increasing difficulty with the final boss at the end COULD be all that there is to this game and it still be a good game. But there is an entire WORLD surrounding it in all cardinal directions, filled with secrets, quite frankly to the brim. So if you get good at the game and beat the boss, try exploring a bit more, and see what challenges and strange places you may get yourself into. And most importantly, have fun. Don't become attached to a run, understand that the more you play, the more you learn, and with each death, you become a better player. But still pray to our lord and saviour RNGesus, because sometimes in this game, a single pixel could set off a cacophony of unfortunate events, one of those events being your ultimate demise.

_childDocuments_.review: So, please note that this review is after playing 2 hours with the very first release of the game.I feel like anyone who watches the gameplay trailer will immediately know if they want to buy it or not.  Either you'll see the physics and go "Whoa, that looks like fun!" and you'll want to get it to play around.  If you've put hours into playing with the "Falling sand" web tools, than you'll probably like this game.  If that doesn't look interesting to you, then it's probably not the game for you.  Nuts and bolts though, how does it play?  2d exploration with a very malleable, very organic world.  Move/fly with WASD and mouse aim.  Combat is fun and works.  Enemies are interesting and varied.  Death is easy and just around the corner.  It is very easy to set yourself on fire and get coated in poison where you're losing life over time and the only way to heal is to find some water to rinse off in. That's not a bad thing, if you like challenging games.  This is a game about being methodical, taking your time to and paying attention to your surroundings.  It can be frustrating to have a kick-ass arsenal of powerful items, and lose it in an instant because you blew up a wall right in your face and died in a fire.  So far every death feels like a mistake I've made, not the game being unfair.  Still, you are the glass cannon that rains down fire on your enemies, and blows up easily. Magic system takes same great notes from magicka in that each wand has slots that you can drop spells into it.  You have to find, or buy the spells, but you can mix-and-match to come up with new effects.  This is also a game that you will only beat by learning the mechanics and the systems.  There are no "unlockables" that make you more powerful, and the game easier, over time.At this point, there is nothing that I've seen in the game beyond fight enemies, get to the level exit, buy some upgrades, and find the occasional scroll with cryptic text.  That's OK.  I'm happy with the dungeon crawler-physics sandbox.  It feels like an old-school title, not like a retro title.  It makes me feel like I've just fired up my old 386 computer with sound blaster pro card to stay up all night playing games.  Just me, the pixels, and a world to explore.

_childDocuments_.review: Things you are expected to see upon immediately playing:- Wands are initially un-creative, and simple- Monsters are simple, and un-creative- The world is very linear- High damage, but low health- Limited wand creativityHowever, the more you explore:- New Spells and Wands can be discovered- Monsters variety grows the further you explore, especially off your intended route.- The world is infinite in all directions. The limit is your computer resources.- There are ways to reduce damage, evade, negate, and block damage, then there are ways to increase your health.- If you play long enough you'll find a perk that will let you modify your wands, anywhere.Additionally, there are secrets, and the developers have made these secrets very cryptic. Their are symbols, tablets, and books littered throughout the world. There are strange interactions with mixing chemicals, or eating specific things... It's like layers of interwoven secrets. I bet many of the people that have down rated Noita, probably never found the Pyramid past the giant skull. This is a game designed to reward explorers.Although a lot of the reviews say that your are bound to RNG luck, and you'll only survive if your lucky. That is only true if you let RNG control your luck. There are some guaranteed combinations, and all that's required of you is to use the knowledge you build through playing. There are even a mod someone has made, that let you experiment and learn wand combinations to help you learn these seemly secret interactions.The most common thing that kills me in this game, is my own greed.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is getting a lot of good post-launch updates, however the devs keep adding stuff without balancing the rest of the game. With the every update we get more perks and not more possible perk rolls per level, this makes it almost impossible to get a properly function build together at the time of the review.  It's still one hell of a funny game, though.---------------------------------------------------------It's Good. Very funny in the beginning due to physics shenanigans and the experimenting. After a bit of time it becomes very frustrating to die from enemies with perfect aim that stunlock you or chain reactions that are set off off-screen. The game is a case of roguelike that is simply too random. Sometimes you can pass an hour without finding any usable staves or spells, sometimes you find strong stuff right at the beginning. Needs a lot of refinement but the concept is definitely there. You can really easily get OP once you got the hang of it, I wish it had unlockables or something similar, once you reached the perfect ending and tested most spells the game ends. Not saying that the time you'll get out of it will very probably be your money's worth, you can buy it at full price without regrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing the early access thus far and this is surely a very unique take on a side scrolling platform shooter. Very cool voxel 2d physics based idea and pulled off very well. I want to gain something from each run and make myself gradually more and more powerful for subsequent runs. Without that there is little replay value for me personally. But I would hope that is in the works. Will check back later.Update: The pixel dynamics of this game are completely unique and well worth the entry price. The difficulty makes it frustrating. _childDocuments_.review: Really a wonderfully fun rougelike game. The wand crafting system is simple enough to pick up right away, but deep enough to keep you wanting to make the most overpowered wand you possible can. Gameplay can be harsh to the point of unfair and unforgiving, but most of the unfairness can be dealt with as long as you don't rush. _childDocuments_.review: Before I start this review, I want to mention that, yes, I'm aware Noita is a roguelike and I am aware of how roguelikes work.I REALLY love the game. It's clearly absolutely brilliantly designed. Being able to experiment with the vast number of spells available in the base game, plus the ones from mods, gives this game almost infinite replayability. Something about blowing up a pile of explosive barrels and completely ruining the environment just never gets old. HOWEVER...I think it would be a LOT more fun with some sort of progression system between runs, mainly with the wands/spells. Some sort of overhaul update, alternate gamemode, or mod that essentially removes the wand and spell pickups, possibly even the health pickups as well, could make this really fun. You start with nothing but a pea shooter. You pickup gold and try to progress as far as you can. After your run, you're left with a shop that sells wand upgrades and new spells, and some sort of progression tree to better and better spells also means more gold required for each spell of a higher tier. This lets you customize what you go in with for each run, and makes the ascension to godhood much slower, but much more meaningful when you finally get to the wand of infinite black holes that just eats through anything and everything in its path. The progression could also be made with health upgrades, something that costs exponentially more the higher your health gets.I would be very excited to see this alternate gamemode, or perhaps a new game entirely, made with the Falling Everything engine. That being said, this game is still extremely fun, and I don't regret any of the time I've spent playing aside from the hundred or so times I have killed myself due to environmental hazards.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Worth full price, _IF_ you don't mind high difficulty.  I'm not joking, I'm 100+ hours in, and have yet to join the ranks of the 11% of players who have won the "victory" achievement.  I only got past the fourth level once! (That's the halfway point.) Overall Difficulty:  I put in 100 hours, and have yet to get past the fourth level, and have yet to meet much less kill as single boss. (There are 7 levels in the main dungeon, two secret dungeons that are 50% longer than the main dungeon, multiple optional/secret boss fights, and more planned secret areas).  RNG Difficulty:  Over half the time, you can easily beat the third dungeon level with the base wand, and two guaranteed items.  I rarely make it that far because I get greedy.  The other half of the time, very unfair elements exist: enemies that hit you off screen, insta kills, "shopkeepers" getting angry due to offscreen monsters wrecking the shop...  The devs are trying to reduce unfair difficulty, but have been unsuccessful thus far.  Luckily, they introduced modding (beta), so mods exist to eliminate the worst parts of the game.Trivia Difficulty: There are hundreds of ways to die. I feel great satisfaction when I die to something new - that means I've made progress, and am one tiny step closer to victory.Skill Difficulty: Nearly every attack can be dodged, if you keep calm and aren't distracted by other enemies.  Your character is a tad slow, but so are most projectiles, so it evens out.  There exist starting area items that can one shot even the "shopkeeper", but they require skill and setup to use.Crafting Difficulty:  The wand crafting system is very intuitive and clear.  You can predict exactly what a wand will do just by looking at it.  That said, which spells you find is up to RNG.  Even if you get unlucky with wands/spells, with experience you can find combinations that are good enough to get you through the next level.Greed Difficulty: The #1 killer.  The urge to find one more wand, a key spell, another clump of gold, the potion needed to cheese the next area... it will drive you to fight minibosses with starting items, while at low health... and then you will die.  Of course, if you aren't greedy, you won't find sufficiently powerful items to beat the game...Environmental Difficulty:  Although the environment rarely kills me, about half of the damage I take is due to the environment.  The enemies are merely the ones who get in the last shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Rewriting this after doing the 33 Orbs of Knowledge Ending as well as the Sun/Dark Sun EndingNoita is a roguelike with the main gimmick of it being based around the custom "falling everything" engine, in which each pixel is simulated (kind of like those web browser sand games you'd play in computer lab). This results in chemical reactions such as water turning into steam, then condensing on the ceiling to drip down again. Gunpowder igniting when fire hits it is also a great example. These interactions are just a fraction of what the game has to offer however, the battle/crafting system of customizing wands with spells you find is incredibly intricate and takes a lot of trial and error to learn (Hell I don't even have a full grasp on it still due to all the nuances it provides!). Wand crafting is a key factor in getting a good run, as well as understanding how spells work being vital towards a lot of late game content.The art direction, monster design, general atmosphere, and music are also incredibly well done for this game, nothing feels out of place. The weather on the surface also cycling through different events adds a nice touch to making the world feel lively as well. Music in this game is also adaptive/seamless, meaning that it'll switch tracks depending upon the events or enemies near you.I don't want to spoil it for new players but I will say this game is much more expansive than you think as well, any wall you see in the game can be broken and there's most likely something waiting for you on the other side. Besides the main path you journey downwards through you'll run into smaller connected biomes and whole other areas with monsters way to strong to fight at the current moment, as well as runic puzzles scattered throughout the world. The design and organization of the full scope of this game's map is insane and thoughtfully crafted.Despite all the positives it should be noted that death/dying by your own mistakes many times is a gameplay feature in this game. Noita IS a very hard game that has quite a bit of a learning curve, primarily due to how unique of a game this is! There really isn't another roguelike or game structured like this. But besides that once the game clicks for you IT CLICKS.Overall, especially after doing some of the late game quests (I haven't completed all the unlocks/finding enemies, perks, etc) this is a very special game and easily skyrocketed up to the greats for me. What this game provides is a nearly endless combination system for combat, exploration is theoretically infinite, and so much more.9/10 would die in the first area via fire again.

_childDocuments_.review: Years after release and the name of the game is still "getting stuck on random pixels on the screen that refuse to go away when you blast it with explosives". The game is fun when you are in mid air, casting spells and hitting things from offscreen or being immune to damage. In literally any other situation you are just asking to get clipped into some random pixel and die because you are now stuck for several seconds until the game figures out you are stuck (yes, being stuck is so ingrained into the game that there is a system that noclip the player after several seconds).If you move at high speed (fall from high elevation/acceleratum) you'll randomly clip into parts of the wall and get yourself stuck. You can sometimes squeeze yourself through into tight areas and be unable to get out even though the terrain has not changed. There are spells that spawn objects with collision box (summon cart) and you can instantly get yourself stuck the moment you cast them (they explode btw). Use the teleport spell against a ceiling and you'll randomly get stuck in it (sure you can escape by shooting elsewhere, but why does this even need to happen in the first place?)The worst part is that even undamaged walls can sometimes just cause you to clip into it. The clearest example is the dense rock wall that surrounds the chasm east of the mines, but realistically any wall can do this. If you fly against these you'll randomly get stuck, and to make it worse you'll be stuck in a flying state which means you can't even regenerate your flight gauge to get out.I sincerely cannot recommend any platformer where getting clipping/softlocking is a literal feature at this point.Edit: I enjoyed the game during the beta but a lot of things seem to have been changed for the worse since. The game is barely playable without proper digging spell and now there are so many random crap spells diluting the drops that you'll have a tough time getting one. Let's be very honest: nobody cares about 20 variations of fireball/bombs that don't even dig through steel, which can appear on the literal first level. To make it worse there are some really nasty enemies now like the swapper enemy and the ghost that spawns with random wands. I really don't understand how these add anything to the game other than to add "lolsorandom XD" deaths and piss off the player.It used to feel like a reasonable roguelike game, now it's just a glorified tech demo with some bare minimum attached.

_childDocuments_.review: Steep difficulty and unforgiving explosive death will greet you at every turn, but this little game has a lot going for it. Firing a found wand is more likely to destroy you instantly, this is also true for using spell components. If you have a low tolerance for unfair death I would be wary as a several hour run can be cut short by an unforeseen disaster (such as enemies teleporting into safe zones, explosives erupting unexpectedly or lava/acid/toxic sludge pouring onto you from above). On the plus side, even after 200+ hours I am still a novice with many areas still to explore, endings to find and bosses to face. The randomly generated terrain continues to surprise and there are a shocking number of secrets.
