_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much more than what you would expect. This is the type of roguelite where you dont keep items/gold/xp when you die, but knowledge. And this knowledge is very important.Along your journey you will die many times, many many times. You will get shot, burned, blown up, polymorphed into a worm, get stuck in walls, killed by your own wand or die in any of the hundreds of other unexpected, insane and hilariously frustrating ways.In these runs you learn about the layers of the dungeon and how to survive in them. You learn about the enemies, causing them to become easier to avoid and or kill in the next run. Enemies that were major threats become trivial, even with a basic wand. You learn about the wands and all the mechanics attached to them, which have to be exploited to get far in this game. You learn about the physics of the game and the various magical fluids that initially seem a hindrance but then become a tool in your arsenal. You learn about all the mysteries and hidden secrets that, if you knew them from the start, would change your entire approach. Some even allow you to bypass entire sections all together.And then once you have 'completed' the game, perhaps because of that one lucky run, you realise you have only explored a fraction of the world and are really not as powerful as you thought.Noita has such a distinct vibe. I have not felt this in many games recently, it made me think of how it felt playing games when I was younger. The feeling I got when I explored this world at times where so horrifying in a good way. The game doesn't tell you what to do or where to go. It's just there waiting for you and uncaring if you dare to enter or not.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. The world is incredibly interactive, from burning down wooden structures to bombing the whole world away, which is extremely satisfying. This game is quite difficult, and it takes a long time to adapt to that, but once you know the basics, the fun can begin.I have managed to beat the game once, and I want to share some tips that made the game way more fun and accessible for me:-  This is, of course, easier said than done. Deaths are part of the game, and at times it can be out of one’s control to change anything about it. In the runs, you gather valuable information to assist you in the next run, like how to dodge certain enemies, how to use the world’s tools correctly, and what spells or wand properties you really like or dislike. Use that to your advantage. I personally like to play more slowly and defensively in order to avoid getting surprised by hordes of enemies or other unexpected dangers.-  I personally don’t really like watching guides or rankings for specific spells, but instead, I discover things myself, which can be quite rewarding. I use the knowledge from past rounds to build wands I really like. For example, I prefer rapid-fire wands to mow down my enemies, and therefore I often look for wands with fast mana regeneration and short cooldowns instead of high mana capacity. In combination with my wand, I try to find cheap spells with infinite ammunition and supportive spells to decrease cooldowns even more or shoot multiple projectiles at once.-  Even basic spells like the green bouncy ball (I don’t memorize names) can be quite good when combined with the right wands and spells. You just need to know how to get the most out of the spells and wands, which you achieve through your collected knowledge. Don’t be afraid to try something new, even if it may turn out to be worse than your other plans. Maybe you find a new playstyle you enjoy. This way, you open up your palette of spells and wands to use and decrease your dependency on RNG giving you exactly the spells you’re looking for.These are my personal tips I would give to newcomers. Remember, my tips are not rules you must follow; they are just guides to make the game more accessible to some people. Follow your own playstyle and do what feels right to you. I hope they help you unpack the amazing game that Noita is :D
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: My favourite roguelike. This game does not hold your hand. The only tutorial you get is what the controls are. Everything else is a secret for you to figure out, either by playing or searching online, on google or some wiki page. Be prepared for that.This often results in you losing your hours long run, (you can save and quit anytime you like to continue whenever) just because you decided to fire that random wand you found that had spells you've never seen before. Polymorphine potion makes it so you can get one hit KO'd even in a god run (there are ways to prevent this)Very frustrating. But the wand building mechanics and the secrets in the game make it all worth it.In Noita, the question is "Do you want to win the game, or do you want to build an epic wand that will eventually end up killing you?"And most people, including me end up choosing the latter; it's just more fun.The game advertises that every pixel is simulated, but doesn't advertise its wand building mechanics (or the abundance of secrets, some of them still an unsolved mystery!) as much as it should. Underrated gem.I'd tried the game for an hour when it first released in early access, didn't like it much because I was focused on clearing levels rather than the wands. Recently I started seeing clips on YouTube of crazy wands in Noita, and I bought the game for a cheap price. 120 hours in (no mods, finally finished the main route), I can say that the price was well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Noita combines many different mechanics together into a uniquely organic and addictively challenging experience. Rogue-like random generation, a beautifully rich physics interaction system, wands and spells with virtually limitless combinations, super difficult enemies, and did I mention secrets? This game has secrets. This game practically ~IS~ a secret. Noita has the mark and feel of a game that was lovingly hand-crafted with a clear vision, and I am very glad to have discovered it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exceedingly hard for me to review properly, but I'm going to take a stab at it.Firstly, I recommended this game because I love this game.  It has the right amount of challenge, can be played at whatever pace you feel like, and when you get that itch to go exploring, well this game's got that covered, too.  I personally have taken on the challenge of becoming consistent at the game, having held the early access world record for most consecutive wins with 11 (and, I did it by doing only 11 orb runs).  But know before getting into it that there are some clear downsides to Noita, especially with the 1.0 release, that I would like to speak to first.  These changes made it very difficult for a casual player to get into the world of Noita, unfortunately.  However, if you are seeking out a challenge, Noita is definitely for you.My main point of contention is that 1.0 added forced randomized starting loadouts (previously they were opt-in by way of doing the daily instead of a normal game) that sometimes give you different spells and a different flask to work with.  These cause needless suffering for new players for 3 reasons:1) You can get a primary wand with a single spitter bolt on it.  This single spitter bolt wand will have low range, poor accuracy, and poor speed, and can leave players vulnerable to enemy attacks.  Even veterans can become overwhelmed if they suddenly find themselves surrounded by enemies, but new players are especially susceptible because they won't know what the correct enemy prioritization is, resulting in heavy damage or death.  There are other bad primary wands as well, but the spitter bolt is the worst, and my hope is that spitter bolt - and anything with short range, really - gets removed from the initial primary wand pool.  Great alternatives are spark bolt, bouncing burst, summon arrow, or magic arrow.2) You can get a secondary wand with no explosives on it.  While a rain cloud has its use (see the next point), the ability to get out of potential soft locked situations with an explosion is invaluable for new players, and not having an explosive spell to do so hurts new player progression.3) You can get a random flask.  This is the most inexplicable decision to me, because water is EXCEEDINGLY valuable at all levels of play: it can be used to put out fires, neutralize toxic sludge, make the player not take fire damage while stained with water, and kill one of the more challenging first zone enemies, the stendari.  My recommendation is to ditch whatever flask it gives you when you start - even if beneficial - and replace it immediately with water.  Water can be found to the left of start under the tree (you may have to dig, and you may not have the tools necessary to do it, but sometimes it's free), to the right if you're willing to climb the mountain with an appropriate explosive in the wall (ie: anything but a bomb) and find the lake, or if you start with the rain cloud wand.Honestly, it is my opinion that Nolla should revert this change and make it opt-in for the daily only, or even enable it as an option for full runs.  Why I find this important enough to bring up first is because there's literally a whole WORLD of things to explore and learn about this game to have to also deal with the frustrations of a randomized, and sometimes underwhelming starting loadout.  Players are going to have their hands FULL tackling every challenge this game throws at it, and as you get deeper into the game those challenges grow bigger and more difficult.  And THAT is what I LOVE about this game.This game pulls no punches.  You WILL get shot by the shotgunner.  Repeatedly.  You WILL die to enemies with a freeze wand, or a nuke wand, or machine gun concentrated light wand.  You WILL kill yourself experimenting with wand building.  You WILL find enemies you have absolutely no idea what they do, even after the 50th or 100th time you kill them, because, darn it, that enemy is going to die before you find out what kind of terror it will inflict on you!  You WILL be running about panicked or scared because you know you can't deal with that one particular enemy, and now you're running headlong into a bunch of other enemies and... well, game over.There's a REASON win streaks in this game are hard to come by, and that's because the game is HARD.  It makes you stop and think about what you're about to do.  Is going down this hallway without checking above and below a safe bet?  Is there a propane tank lurking in the snow you're about to dig in that you can't see?  Is that underwater chest going to have a thunderstone?  Did I just hear Ukko or is that the wind?  Often, second-guessing yourself and staying as safe as possible is the key to victory in Noita.If you're a speedrunning type, Noita has got you covered.  Runs of this game can be as short as 2 minutes, and involve absolute chaos, tight dodges, teleporting blindly into new territory, and trying to find that one boss-killing wand to finish the game as quickly as possible.If you're an exploration type, ignore the usual seven zones and explore the world around you!  Find out what's at the bottom of the pit to the right of the lava lake, what's outside to the left of the tree, or to the right of the mountain.  Journey into the sky, or fight your way beneath the temple of the art to see what my lurk there.  Traverse impossibly thick walls on either side of the map and see what might be on the other side.  Fight optional bosses with unique mechanics and rewards.  Discover strange quest items and try to figure out what to do with them.  Learn the secrets of alchemy and be blessed with endless health and wealth.If you're a completionist type, you'll be interested in what's at the top of the tree - pillars of meta-progress that grow as you unlock more endings, more spells, and more challenges.  I myself plan on doing a NG+28 33-orb run at some point.  I expect that run to take *weeks*, and to think that one drop of polymorphine can end that run is a scary but exciting prospect that will keep me on my toes the entire time!If you're a mad scientist type, wand building is where it's at.  There are so many spells with so many spell combinations in the game that you will be hard pressed to get a win with the same wand twice.  Sure, there are repeating themes: homing mist wand, trigger chainsaw wands, speedy bouncing burst wands... but in the end, you get to craft your own tools of destruction from what you find in the game, and that's one of the most rewarding things about this game.So overall, my recommendation for new players is to expect the game to be challenging and hard.  If you're going into this blind you are going to die, quite possibly hundreds of times, before you get a win.  If this is not your style, this game may not be for you.  But if you're willing to learn everything the game has to offer, you will be rewarded with a rich world of mystery worth exploring, satisfying wands of mass destruction, fulfilling victories against challenging bosses, and the thrill of winning the game on your terms.That is, in between bouts of stepping in polymorphine and getting one-shot.Best of luck, noidat!
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: You're looking at my hours played, and at the Overwhelmingly Positive rating, and you're wondering why I'm not recommending it. Well, I'm wondering too. This was one of the very few games I actually felt hyped about, and I bought it as soon as it was released. I've had fun with it, and it's a competently made game with a fun central gimmick. So what gives?At its core, it's pretty simple: While Noita is fun, it's also really miserly when it comes to doling out that fun. And that's something that just really rubs me the wrong way.One of the frustrating things Noita does is something more Rogue-like games do. The game's mechanics are conditional under a tax you have to pay, and that tax is you being forced not to use the mechanics. In Noita it comes in the form of a time tax and an inventory tax. See, when you start a new game, Noita isn't fun. Your starting items are garbage, so you have to find good items before you can start having fun. But the first level is purpose-made to be absolute trash to navigate with a fresh character, and the items you can find there are often poor. There are other forms of time tax, such as the character being really slow, but most of it is that first level. The other tax is the inventory tax. See, the point of Noita is that you make your own magic wands from wands you find in the levels. These are random and often not very good. In standard play you can only edit items in the saferoom at the end of the level, which means you always have to sacrifice one of your four and slots to carry found wands to the end of the level.Yes, yes, I know, complaining about RNG in a Roguelike. The problem is, a good run in this game depends on luck to an extreme degree. For instance, there's no real healing in Noita (with a scant few exceptions), and you  take damage. In fact, the reason you now start with a flask of water is because catching on fire before you could get one was a run-ending first level problem. So your capacity to look for new stuff depends on your health, which you can increase with an item found in the levels. If you have bad luck and don't find many, that's most likely a junk run for you. Can't find good wands or spells in the levels or at the saferoom? Junk run. Bad perk selection? Junk run. Bad luck in one level makes you much more susceptible to bad luck in the following level, because it directly limits your capacity for exploration. And it doesn't end there, oh no. There's a wizard enemy who can teleport your butt to random places on the map. Better hope it's not too harsh. The worms that traverse the level can straight up destroy the saferoom, for which the game blames , spawning a strong enemy in every saferoom that you have to fight. It's even in the enemy placement, because damage comes easy in Noita. Clear an obstacle and see a lightning wizard? Good luck with your new run. In the correct quantities these mechanics are all fine. The way Noita piles them up makes the game feel extremely arbitrary.Noita's core mechanic is that it simulates every pixel, being probably the first real game to actually have a good reason to have pixel art. It's pretty cool, not gonna lie. The fact that you can empty a flask and dip it in liquid in the level to fill it up with is pretty unique. But it... doesn't really do a lot with this. Despite the environment being fully destructible you'll only rarely use it to tackle problems, and then half the time only by accident. There's very little interaction between the environment and the player aside from digging passages to get somewhere. When you get down to it Noita is basically just a sidescrolling shooter where you sort of get to decide what bullets you shoot. Even the kick your wizard can do to move loose objects is horrible. There's a massive delay, it's inaccurate, and sometimes barely moves an object. Oh, and enemies that are too close to an object when you kick it are likely to get no damage. This all comes back to the game just plain not wanting to give you the tools to have fun. The explosives in the levels are a good resource to blast passages if you have no digging tools, or just blow up enemies with. So why is my only way to move them around the worst kick in video game history ?You still here? OK, look, Noita isn't a bad game. It's more what you'd call a diamond in the rough. But boy, it's rough. You're going to have fun with it, no doubt about it, but you're also going to get pants-on-head frustrated by it. Because it's a fantastic idea marred by execution that's both really arbitrary and really afraid to give the player too many tools.Oh, and I almost forgot: One of the new features added is a perfect example of my complaints. Your wizard can drink liquid present on the map. If it's a potion or similar, you gain its effects. If it's inert, it simply disappears. Previously, you could keep doing it, and it was somewhat of a tool to lower the fluid level somewhere. The developers thought this was too powerful a tool, apparently. Your wizard now has a limited amount of stuff he can eat/drink. I wasn't aware of this thing breaking the game in any way, but OK. It doesn't end there, however. No no no, you  take damage if you overeat/drink  overeating/drinking reduces your already slow movement speed. This isn't fun. This is a garbage mechanic with no purpose other than to limit the player. The only other game I know that has a similar mechanic is Kingdom Come. That is a game with an autistic dedication to realism. This is a game where you play a spellcasting wizard with a jetpack. If I want to chug a trench of whiskey because the game hasn't deigned to give me proper digging tools yet, can you just let me do it? This feels too much like playing D&D with a DM who feels threatened by your character's capabilities.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and addictive game. I've seen comparisons drawn to Spelunky and Terraria, but to me this is nothing but a good thing. _childDocuments_.review: Brutally difficult, but incredibly addictive. Expect to die a lot while playing this game but don't take it personally, everyone does. After a 10 hours of practice you will be able to consistently make it to the second level with some decent loot. After another 10 hours, you will be able to make it to the third somewhat regularly. After another 20 or so, you might be able to make it to the endgame levels on a semi-consistent basis. But it doesn't matter how strong you think you are, or how powerful your wand is. One day you definitely will be polymorphed into a sheep and killed in one shot or electrocuted for opening a submerged chest with a booby trap in it. The wand building is fantastic, the world physics and particle nature of the environment are intuitive and repeatable and provides lots of potential for environmental kills (or deaths), and these two factors provide endless replayability. Watch some youtube videos on wand building and try to remember the important stuff such as triggers and multicasts, as well as things like chainsaw which are almost a little game breaking. As soon as you get to level 2 you can build a wands so in level 1 very important to know what wands to pick up and what to leave behind. Cast delay and Recharge speed are critical but it's not going to help you if your Mana charge speed or mana pool are too small. Lots of people talk about how important it is to have a non-shuffle wand, but in the early game after level 2, a fast want with low recharge speed and cast delay with a single projectile spell will be a lot more helpful. For example if I have no other option, I will almost always switch my projectile from my main wand to my "bomb" wand at level 1, this gives me a much much higher fire rate. Also, learn how to polymorph, teleport or dig (but watch out for steve) out of the Holy mountain, this means that you can go back and build wands mid level. Not too important at the end of the game when you can dig your way back in but helpful at the start. A teleport bolt is the best and safest solution, but in a pinch you can use polymorphine to sneak through the doorway, but watch out for mobs so you don't get 1hit killed. Once you have a bit of knowledge you will find that you're much more able to survive and the game gets much much more fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: I am conflicted and ultimately will leave a positive review, but this game does have some roughness.Is Noita a fun game with fascinating aspects? Yes, absolutely. Is it too hard and obtuse for it's own good? Also a resounding yes. Based on achievements, there is a very good chance, almost 90% that you will not beat this game. It's difficult in a way that Spelunky is - there are hidden hazards that will outright kill you in the blink of an eye, so the acquisition of knowledge is your greatest barrier to success. Knowing what is and is not truly dangerous is incredibly important, and it only comes via a torrent of dead runs on every level.There's a whole hidden game withing this game - the main path only requires you defeat the end boss after a few levels, but there are a slew of additional bosses, dozens of additional biomes, and secrets so secret they are absolutely unobtainable without a wiki. Even then, you have to have gotten good enough to be MUCH BETTER than just being able to beat the game to access them.Wandcrafting is fascinating and definitely the strong point of this game, along with the particle-based physics engine. Wandcrafting starts slow, as the early levels don't push your abilities as much as the later levels, where you can craft doomsday weapons that obliterate everything. It's quite fun to tinker endlessly with spells to see if you can eke out some advantage or push your craft.All in all, great game that could have been better by being just a little less murderous in slightly unfun ways, and a little less secret about it's secrets. I have spent a lot of time in the game and been rewarded for my effort, but that wasn't without some frustration at many lost runs.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: This game has soooooo much content! The game is meant to be played with curiosity. you are NOT MEANT TO JUST TRY AND GET TO THE BOTTOM, BE CURIOUS AND EXPLORE!. Take the game casual and slow. The game at face value is about 10% of its content, the rest is everywhere else but directly down. I have no idea why so many people are bi***ing about the difficulty. If you lower it, the game will become too boring. The challenge of making it just that little bit further is great!. Please do not base your purchase on the fact of difficulty or lack of content because the people who write those reviews have no idea the things you can do or find in this game, You can go up or left or right if you want, BE CURIOUS! you can go wherever you want!. The idea of a game is to challenge you but yet reward you for your curiosity. For the love of god be curious! and you don't have to go down! There are mysteries that are yet to be uncovered, and places unseen to most players. Tutkia!

_childDocuments_.review: tldr; This game is pretty and should be a hardcore take on Powder Game-style physics simulation, but its mechanics are too shallow to keep one's interest, with a headache-inducing difficulty curve, and so much variability that it fails to keep players interested past the first few dives into the fray. It feels very much like the game wants the player to experiment and learn mechanics, but also constricts how the player can use mechanics to their benefit.Noita is a roguelike with a great focus on both spell augmentation and alchemy through the combination of different pixel materials, as you delve deeper into the bowls of the planet for vague reasons.Great effort to trying to teach the mechanics of this game with as little dialogue as possible, with most lore being hidden away in obscure challenges and descriptions for items and spells alike being brief, to put it mildly.The graphics are very good overall, though I would note the darkening effect on projectile hits can darken a piece of level geometry so much that it's virtually invisible, making weaker weapons feel like they are slowly whittling away at a destructible surface when in reality it isn't.I do not recommend this game overall however, and the biggest issue I have with it is how unilaterally it fails to achieve its goals. As both a wand game and an alchemy game, it just does not work well enough so that a player can use either system to progress down through the dungeon as more difficult monsters appear. Hence, the difficulty in this game is just dumb, with scaling in the enemies being very brutal, but the player scaling is much less concrete.To cover why the two primary systems fail, let's start with wands. You get spells pre-equipped on each wand, you can hold up to four wands, and many more spells in reserve. However, the augmentation of spells onto your wands can only be done if you're in a safe zone, areas of no return which you can swap around your spells on your wands.Big issue is that you can't do this for a majority of the game, making wand management a headache if you want to upgrade your wands base stats but want to keep the spells on it. There is a perk for this which literally allows you to just change your spells on a whim, which is silly, because it makes the game so much less difficult that it makes the perk overpowered, but also begs the question of why this isn't a base feature.Alchemy requires bottles, and bottles are in such short supply. You toss a bottle, it's gone forever. And that is the only real way of collecting liquids to then perform alchemy, of which there are shockingly few interesting interactions to prepare offensive of defensive brews to players knowledged in how mixes react. Most of the time it's all about adding water to a hazardous material so that you don't instantly die, which is shallow and begs for a system of advanced concoctions to take on enemies in an alternative to wands, either through buffs or debuffs.A buzzkill for the flow of the game is how a large proportion of your progression is tied directly to the map generation. As a roguelike, it has randomly generated level layouts, determined by seed. Unfortunately, wand and potions are scattered randomly, with their spells and contents randomized. This leads to dumb runs with overpowered spells and some strong potions effects, to many limited use wands and another bottle of material that you cannot use in the slightest. That's assuming you get anything, many runs are just dead on how little consistency in progression there is with multiple bottles but no wands.I've tried with this game, twice now I've played for quite a while before the flame going out. This game is one of many which only makes some sense with a proper wikia/gamepedia article to back up its mechanics, but the one there is just doesn't cut it.If you're a masochist, there are better games out there that reward your patience and dedication than this one. Shame too, it had potential, and has improved quite a bit since I last went in. But it just doesn't have enough traction for new players to latch onto, to get then invested and further into the game every time. Learning game mechanics in heavily nuanced games is what keeps roguelikes great in my books, but this one has so many game mechanics with such little depth.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of rougelikes, although I struggle to find one to fully grasp my attention for hours at end. I have had this game since 2019 and from what i played of it then I enjoyed but there wasnt much direction and I didnt have the patience for a game like that then. Since picking it back up I have loved it, learning about different spells and wand builds; I want to keep going back to it. Exploration has been fun too, from finding bosses and getting obliterated to finding treasure or tripping absolute sack on some mushrooms; this game keeps me coming back. Once you are able to put together a good perk build, it can change the feel of the game completely. For example, there is a telekinetic kick perk that allows you to grab and throw inanimate object and hurl them at fast speeds at your opponents. That, with every pixel being simulated makes for an exciting experience. With procedural generation, every run feels different and I cant get enough of it. All in all I'd give it a 9.5/10, this has to be my favorite rougelike so far; but holy **** it is hard.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a clear lack of polish to many elements: There is not even a main menu, and the game reboots to give you a new seed / dungeon to explore. The records after each run don't save, you can't enter a seed. However, I haven't been able to put this game down beyond that. The combat feels strategical and like everything is purely in your own control. The spell customization is expansive and is easy to pick up, but difficult to master (It'll take me a few dozen more hours to figure out modifiers and multicasts). The generated dungeons are expansive and interesting, and destructible to the point where every corner is interesting despite being "yet another mineshaft".Keep in mind though, this game is difficult. The first stage is kind of easy, the second stage already requires a lot more to pass, and the third one I have barely reached. The fourth I reached once but instantly got obliterated by a skeleton wizard with a yet-inpenetrable shield.Good luck.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of factors that go into making a good game, but there’s one that I don’t hear about very often, perhaps because it doesn’t have a good name. It’s the chaos that arises from getting an insane build in Binding of Isaac going, or the chaos that erupts from grabbing a poorly-placed idol in Spelunky. It’s chaos that doesn’t always favor the player but wreaks absolute havoc on the game world, much to the delight of spectators. This chaotic special sauce can improve the fun factor of just about any game, and titles like Noita that build their action around it come out as some of the most fun of all.Noita might still be too Early Access for a story, but wizards don’t need much of an excuse to ruin ♥♥♥♥. You start your journey at the mouth of a cave, adorned with some very helpful runes that inform you of the controls. Descending into a network of disused mines, you find all manner of zombies, goblins, and gooier things in your way. The first of your two wands will make short work of foes, while the second will make short work of the environment in spectacular fashion. These tools are only the tip of the magical, exploding iceberg, though, as you find grander wands that scatter fireballs, launch black holes, summon acid clouds, ignite everything on the screen, and more. If you can manage to defeat your foes and not vaporize yourself in the process, you might just find what lies at the bottom of these caverns.Admittedly, there’s not a lot of direction to Noita at the moment besides going down. Each level is a large, sprawling complex of tunnels, shafts, and chambers that eventually lead to a portal at the very bottom. The portal always leads to a temple where you recover your health and spell charges (if any), buy new wands or spells, and get a perk to make your little murderwizard even more murdery. Once in a level, you’ve really just got to survive, and enemies are only half of the threat to your survival. Every pixel of the environment is modeled and is ready to collapse, drain, burn, or flow at the slightest provocation. You can imagine what happens when you drop a lantern into a pool of oil, or blast out the supports for a tank of acid, but watching the chaos unfold is a whole new level of fun, and surviving it is a whole new level of challenge.This is the core of the Noita experience, taking ridiculous weapons into ridiculous levels and watching ridiculous things happen. You can absolutely play it safe and cautious, mitigate risks, and focus on reaching the end of the game, and at some point you’re going to want to do that. But honestly the real appeal is finding a wand that fires six nuclear warheads in 0.1 seconds and finding out what happens to the entire level when you push the button. There are wands that shoot lasers, wands that shoot eggs that hatch into flesh-eating monsters, wands that are actually chainsaws, and wands that do all the of the above with each shot. You’ll find wands that do crazy things but they’re really just containers for spells, which you can pull out and affix to other more appropriate wands to make whatever implement of chaos you desire, like burning sawblades that explode into acid clouds.The catch is that you have to find the odds and ends to do that, and it won’t always happen. I’ve had runs in Noita go absolutely bonkers with wands that could instantly vaporize half the screen, but those are the minority compared to how many runs I’ve played straight with wands that shoot arrows or bouncy balls. Make no mistake, this is a solid roguelike platformer with excellent movement, controls, and combat, but the real magic is left for the RNG to give to you, and it won’t always deliver. And maybe it shouldn’t, considering how potent the biggest, flashiest spells can be, but I can’t deny how many runs I’ve been on where I was left wishing for more bombs or more chainsaws or just that wand I found last time that I killed myself with all too soon.There’s still plenty of ground for the developers to cover in terms of fleshing out the game world and balancing the tools available, so if you’re more in the market for a full game experience there’s no harm in waiting. But you can’t look at the gifs on the store page and tell me that doesn’t look fun, because I can assure you it is. Some of my new favorite game experiences have come from my worst Noita runs, like hucking 4x dynamite all through the ice caves or shattering an entire shelf of potions and rolling in the magical runoff as it enchanted me with everything at once. The potential for hilarious chaos here is at a record high, and as long as the rest of the game coalesces around it eventually, Noita is sure to be a classic.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing design for a game.  Most games that have this sort of "hardcore" type mode where a death means you start over, rely on giving you upgrades you can purchase each time you die, so that next time you can progress further.  This game however, relies on the player learning more about the world they're in.  I really like the take on discovery in this game, where you're constantly learning more about how the world works, and how you can use what is around to your advantage,  Learning how the spells interact with each other, testing the wands you create yourself, finding what perks can help with the spells you have, figuring out what liquids you want to take with you in your flasks for future use, and so much more.  There are probably plenty of people that would get frustrated with the game at the start, because it can seem very difficult, but for those who like a challenge, there is so much to discover in this game.As quoted from the game itself"The sacrifice of oneself to the pursuit of knowledgeIs the highest tribute to the gods."To me, it's the type of game where I'm always wanting to learn more, and there just seems to always be even more to discover within the game.If I had to say something negative about the game it would be that there is a few too many unpredictable deaths within the game, and they definitely could be toned down a bit.  Even after knowing what I'm going to come across, sometimes there is just nothing that can be done to avoid all the attacks without making the game tedious/boring.  Not everyone wants to tunnel/dig everywhere, but it is by far the safest method of navigation.  It simply allows the player to skip a lot of enemies they may have had to face, but I think it would have been better if the player could more reliably deal with the enemies directly.

_childDocuments_.review: If there's one thing that's clear about the overwhelmingly popular reviews for this - it's that people still love randomised zero progress roguelikes. Noita is a roguelike pixel simulation where you play a wizard who collects randomised wands that shoot randomised spells. The whole world is made of pixels with their own properties, depending on what it's made from (wood, metal, gunpowder etc). There's a ton of different liquids that all interact with each other (water, beer, oil, slime...). It's a very clever experience that's quite short-lived and too random to keep my interest for more than a few hours. It's made by a small Finnish team though which is awesome.+ Animation and artwork is beautiful+ Cave diving is interesting - feels a bit like Starbound+ Pixel simulation of materials and liquids is very impressive+ Ability to use the environment to your advantage+ Interaction between liquids works well; water acts a bit like a fire shield and you can wash off blood, poison and oil- There's no progress between runs which is the main thing that puts me off. Each run might last 10 minutes, then you need to re-learn everything for the next run where you pick up different things- No explanation of mechanics, although you pick it up within an hour- I don't like the randomness. The maps, enemies, spells and wands are all different every time, which kind of keeps it interesting, but also introduces a few flaws. For example, on one run I hadn't found any other wands, and couldn't afford any upgrades. The perk I got added an 'always cast' ability to my only wand. The spell it added was random, of course, but I couldn't tell what it was because you can't hover over tooltips. Whatever it did, it stopped my only wand from actually shooting anything, which meant I was defenceless for level 2.

_childDocuments_.review: is a very interesting, but frustrating roguelike that I beat recently for the first time after over 130 hours of playtime (Well, first without mods, I beat it in  once before, and some of that time may have been with the window minimized, but I digress).There's a lot of things to like here, but there's also a lot to dislike. What counts as a positive may depend on what you like in your games, and how much you like of it. There's also a lot of "____, but ..." when it comes to talking about the positives of the game. Ultimately though, I'd say their is more good than bad here, which Is why I recommend this game. I have re-written this next part of the review twice now (about mid-way through the first paragraph each time), as I thought about how best to approach talking about this game. One of the difficulties with reviewing  is that there's a lot of things I could talk about, to the point where it'd probably go past Steam's character limit if I tried to mention everything. On top of that, some people may find it more fun to dive in without a whole lot of knowledge on the game. So for this review, I'm not going to get too much into detail, and will generally try to avoid spoiling anything (even if its not particularly secret).Noita takes a very hands-off approach when it comes to learning what to do. You learn the basic controls, and from there on out, the game lets you do everything on your own. On the one hand, this lets you feel like you're doing everything yourself, whether it be discovering a good use of your spells, a trick to make things easier, or a mechanic you didn't know was in the game, you can feel like you earned every step of progress. However, the downsides to this is that there is a LOT to this game and it will take you forever to learn everything yourself. On top of that, Noita can be a very difficult game, and not knowing what you're doing can quickly end a run, sending you all the way back to the beginning. This can be very frustrating, and you will likely become incredibly familiar with the first biome/area (And the other main areas, too, later on) by the time you start having semi-decent runs. And even if you do decide to look up things (which I recommend, especially after you've done a few dozen failed runs of the game), the game is still heavily RNG-based, and incredibly challenging. Whether or not the RNG gives you decent wands/spells/etc. can make or break a run very easily, especially when you're just starting out. You might not even be aware of the true power of some of the things the game gives you until you've looked it up or played/experimented for a long enough time. The heavy reliance on RNG adds to the replayability and variety in the game, but the difficulty it comes with works against other aspects of the game. For example, the player is normally encouraged to experiment with the spells and other mechanics in the game to learn how everything works and be able to have better runs, but because of how dangerous experimenting can be and the fact that you start all over from the beginning if you fail, you may find yourself not testing out something that looks like it'd be a lot of fun solely because you don't want to have to go through the first area for the millionth time. It should also be noted that the RNG can sometimes make the game incredibly easy (at least, by comparison), making experimenting unnecessary.There are also a lot of secrets in , but without help, you'll likely find it difficult to uncover most of them, especially since many of them have extremely vague hints (or in most cases, none at all!) to what you're supposed to do and where the secrets are. Secret finding is made difficult as well due to the previously-mentioned difficulty and restarting from the beginning, so you aren't likely to take as many risks as you need to to unlock everything. In addition, even some of the mechanics themselves aren't explained very well in-game, so if you only use what the game tells you, you probably wont even know what some of the things do (unless you dedicate a seemingly-excessive amount of your life to playing this game).Overall, the game is enjoyable, and there's a lot of crazy things you can do and find, but I feel the game tends to withhold a little too much from the players (although this was made slightly better with an update that added more hints). You likely aren't going to get the most you can out of this game without looking stuff up, even if you only intend on just beating the game. Another option that many players do is using mods at the beginning that are designed to help you learn the mechanics and get them down before attempting serious runs (such as , which basically changed the game to an area where you can experiment with wands and spells to your hearts content, or , which removes one of the obstacles in the game that prevents you from experimenting with wands).I recommend going in blind first, trying out the game, and then after you find yourself not making much progress, allowing yourself to look up stuff so you can understand what's going on, how to play the game, and how to find secrets (and what to do for some of those secrets, as you'll likely never find out otherwise).

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a game of surprising depth. It's dev team, Nolla Games, undersell the game as a simple showcase for the game engine they have developed; a pixel-based physics game in which every pixel is 'physically simulated'. My own initial interest in the game was as something that I'd anticipated to be a kind of 'pixel playground', with a side interest in magic spells.I was very wrong.Playing Noita is a joyous punishment. With each comical death, you learn hard lessons. You are told no rules, but given tools and the facilities to learn how to use them. On first presentation, the game which looks like a funky Terraria clone reveals itself to be more of a roguelite with a little dungeoneering thrown in for good measure. It's only once you've died around a hundred times before you're awakened to some of the scale of how wrong you were intitially. The procedurally generated levels are new with every rebirth, but you come to learn the patterns of the landscape; you come to identify the mechanics of the (increasingly obnoxious) mobs and the quirks of specific spells in combination with each other. All of a sudden, you're beginning to see that this simple physics based roguelite game is actually a comprehensively punishing 'game' based on precision, intricate knowledge of the game mechanics and unflinching desire for more... More gold; More spells; More wands... More Power.After 282 hours I have beaten the game twice. I have died upwards of 500 times. I refuse to play the game any longer. It showed me a side of myself which scared me. I had become a man obsessed with discovering the secrets hidden within; secrets which Nolla Games have painstakingly laced into the very fabric of this 'magical action roguelite'.I can only give this game the highest of praises. It showed me the flaws within myself. I was left humbled and defeated by it.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: This got recommended to me by the Discovery Queue, and I thought it was an interesting concept, but didn't bite at first. I then saw some streamers play it and thought it was actually super interesting, I should've got it when Steam first showed it to me! I then got gifted it by a friend, and now I immensely regret having seen anything about this in the first place. After a lot of anticipation and excitement over my warped perception of how the game would play after watching immensely skilled players, I now realize Noita is extremely mistaken in how it presents itself. I happily jumped into it expecting an extremely creative, expressive game where you could easily annihilate both you and your foes with a wide variety of spells. What I ended up getting was a grueling, agonizingly slow and restricted experience where you just get nuked immediately before you even get the chance to cobble together something somewhat funny."Every pixel is physically simulated." The appeal to messing around in pixel sand games as a kid caught my eye. Unfortunately it rarely seems to make use of it in any particularly interesting manner. Seeing acid melt through everything and looking at the holes it leaves looks cool. When a bunch of liquid flasks get smashed at once, the way they pool together looks interesting, assuming the visual appeal isn't ruined by witnessing Invisibilium and Berserkium go to waste. But unless I'm missing some extremely radical, extremely important underlying mechanic that specifically  every pixel to act the way it does, it's just purely a lag generator and I don't see the need for it.Oh wait, there is one: Alchemy! Did you know, that depending on your seed, mixing a random first liquid with a random second liquid on top of a random solid makes Lively Concoction, a liquid that massively heals you on contact with it, and is one of the extremely few ways you can heal outside of making to a Holy Mountain? Did you also know that if you combine a  randomly generated combination of two liquids and a solid, you get Alchemist's Precursor, a liquid that which upon having meat thrown into, turns EVERYTHING into gold?  Well I sure as ♥♥♥♥ didn't either until I looked up a YouTube video about it! There is NOTHING in-game telling you these exist at ALL! There's lore tablets hidden in secret nooks and crannies around the world that extremely vaguely  they MIGHT maybe possibly exist, but I'm not gonna instantly figure out I should pour deer urine into blood after reading something saying that people don't like dying! What the ♥♥♥♥? Despite having an overlying theme of alchemy and mixtures and the secret powers of science, it hardly bothers at all actually integrating it into gameplay. Aside from extremely mundane and common interactions like many liquids turning lava into rock, or water purifying toxic sludge, there's very little of substance at all when it comes to understandable aspects of Noita's chemistry. Unless you're really, truly expected to just randomly pour ♥♥♥♥ together and hope that something might happen, there's nothing at all to do with the many wacky liquids and powders other than the utmost basic and obvious, like pouring water on yourself while on fire, or drinking Berserkium to deal more damage.  In terms of exploration, there is none. Or rather, the exploration you  to do is locked behind ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, while you're forced to trudge through massive, awkward to traverse tunnels in the mountain in order to scrounge up wands, golds and max health increases that you  skip out on easily. During the select few times I've managed to make it up and over the mountain as opposed to entering it, I was blown away. Massive rolling hills, gigantic fossils, many more entrances to other underground locations, a gargantuan tundra, there is SO much more than what the game appears to be. But the means of finding them are extremely limited, essentially down to chance, and if you get killed at any point while exploring the overworld, it's right back down to the bottom with your rinky dink starting set babey!!! Finally walked right for 20 minutes long enough to find a secret entrance to somewhere? Whoops, you got instantly blown open by the enemies hiding in there! Too bad!This is a problem that's omnipresent in Noita I've found. If you're at the wrong place at the wrong time and you don't have the reaction speed of The Flash, you just get instantly eviscerated. Foe that you didn't see picked up a wand with Magic Missile? Bye bye. Found a secret spot in the first area, looted it, and the game decided it wants to spawn an endgame foe in front of the exit from there? Have fun. What about when it spawns a Kummitus, equipped with a powerful wand you crafted in a previous playthrough right at the beginning of the game and shreds you before you can even process what's going on? Well that's just on you. Maybe you just shouldn't get hit. Maybe you shouldn't dive into an acid vat you couldn't see while under a  from a Sokaisunmestari. Maybe you should play more carefully. You should've known that singular pixel was actually lava. Back to the Mines, with your measly little Spark Bolt and Bombs and Water Flask, you stupid nooblet. Why would I want to bother exploring this weird new area, or trying out this new potentially lethal spell when if I mess up, I'd just be sent straight back to the start with nothing again?Good luck figuring out how to make a decent wand in this hellish environment. I sure didn't. Wand crafting seems extremely interesting, and there's likely a lot of depth to it, but most spells just aren't that interesting or useful, and I found myself always resorting to just slapping basic projectiles on a wand with a low cast delay and recharge time and using that. Many spells are overwhelmingly dangerous to the user, have limited charges, only serve extremely niche purposes, or are just outright garbage. Some are even all of the above. Why the hell would I want to spawn a giant vat of lava underneath myself? What's the point of Toxic Mist? Summon Rock? Poison Arc? A lot seem potentially useful on paper, but in practice I just ignored everything and resorted to just Magic Arrow, Summon Disc Projectile, or if I could find it, Lightning Bolt. Given your small inventory space of only 4 wands, and the inability to change what's on them without being in a Holy Mountain or having the spell Edit Wands Everywhere, I just ended up tossing out wands only dedicated to casting a single niche spell like Rain Cloud or Circle of Stillness because I just didn't end up using them that often. You absolutely can happen upon insane spell and perk combos, like using Homing Shots, Explosion on Drunk Enemies, Mist of Spirits and a trigger spell to create a rocket launcher, or slapping together a bunch of Chainsaws to create a machine gun, but between the overall absurdly hard to utilize spell list, quality wands only consistently appearing in the lowest depths of the mountain, and handful of hardly noticeable or outright harmful perks, obtaining a strong build seems mostly up to chance. One time I happened upon a wand with Triple Scatter and three Lightning Bolts while I had Electricity and Explosion Immunity and I've never had a run come even close to that level of strength ever since. Runs were mostly just me taking 10 minutes scrounging pick-ups in the Mines, getting unlucky, then just getting shredded in Coal Pits or Snowy Depths due to lack of quality spells. Noita feels like a massive waste of potential. Much like pouring water into toxic sludge, the heart of creativity and exploration is melted by the mind-numbingly slow pace and extreme difficulty until it's just all one big unbearable mess. At its current state in early access, I wouldn't say it's worth getting.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaotic experimentation, lovely physics and oh so much to explore. _childDocuments_.review: Noita is a game that caught my eye with its stunning pixel physics, especially the way fire can spread and consume everything in its path. I was curious to see how this mechanic would affect the gameplay and the exploration of the procedurally generated world. I was not disappointed.Noita is a roguelike game where you play as a wizard who can wield various wands and spells to fight enemies and manipulate the environment. The game is challenging and unforgiving, but also rewarding and addictive. Every run is different and full of surprises, as you never know what you will find in the next biome or what kind of wand or spell you will stumble upon.The game encourages experimentation and creativity, as you can customize your wands and spells with different modifiers and combinations. You can also interact with the world in many ways, such as digging through the terrain, setting things on fire, creating floods, or even summoning black holes. The game’s physics engine is impressive and realistic, as every pixel has its own properties and behaviors. You can see how liquids mix, how materials burn, how explosions affect the surroundings, and how enemies react to different elements.The game is not easy, though. You will die a lot, and sometimes in very frustrating ways. You might accidentally kill yourself with your own spells, or trigger a chain reaction of destruction that you can’t escape from. You might also encounter enemies that are too powerful or too fast for you to handle, or traps that are hard to spot or avoid. The game does not explain much to you, either. You have to figure out everything by yourself, from the effects of the spells to the secrets of the world. The game does not have a tutorial or a difficulty setting, so you have to learn by trial and error.But that’s also part of the charm of Noita. The game is full of mystery and discovery, and every run is a new adventure. You never know what you will find or what will happen next. You might discover a hidden temple, a friendly NPC, a rare spell, or a powerful artifact. You might also encounter a boss, a curse, a trap, or a deadly enemy. The game keeps you on your toes and makes you adapt to the situation. You have to use your wits and your magic to survive and progress.Noita is a game that I bought for the fire pixel physics, but ended up loving for the whole package. It’s a game that is challenging, rewarding, and fun. It’s a game that makes you feel like a real wizard, with all the power and the danger that comes with it. It’s a game that I highly recommend to anyone who likes roguelikes, magic, and physics. Noita is a game that is worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a surprisingly complex and fun side-scrolling rogue like game. You can have fun playing slow and strategic or fast and frantic. The whole world seems designed to punish you for carelessness, but WHO CARES when a stray spell tips a lantern onto a pile of gunpowder stacked against an acid barrel? WHO CARES when you reluctantly develop a vomiting disorder and realize you can use it to put out the fire that is about to kill you? There's abundant fun to be had and the game is pretty and oppressive at the same time, an art style all it's own, which has me coming back for more failed play-throughs every day.

_childDocuments_.review: LIKE WOAH. the amount of crazy things that can happen in a run are just woah.okay so 1st off the physics based gameplay is just super on point. kick a lantern n watch the fire spread. throw a rock on an enemy, destroy the terrain n watch it fall on monsters. its all pretty satisfyingwood catches fire, water evaporates , oil makes you slippery and flammable, etc etc etc... and theres a lot of magical elements as well. alchemic reactions is the name of the game if you wanna stay alive.so whats the gameplay like.... well it feels kinda like terraria except with only just wands. sort of..(im just talking about the combat) Thats by no means a bad thing. 4 wands can be equipped and scroll through with different stats and spell slots. example you can start  a 3 spell slot wand with ok recharge n cast time with idk firebolts and another wand that shoots bombs. you can later find a wand like 7 spell slots but with a spells you dont like or are useful. getting to an alter you can put your firebolts into your other wand and add modifiers like speed up projectile make 2 or more shots come out or just any other spell like the summon bomb on your 2nd wand but it will be random and not recommended since bombs have limits. you can mix and match and make some ridiculous overpowered wands. this is the reason for the replayability also because things can go south real quick.secrets... you like secrets in games. this game is in early access and yet there are so many secrets to find. not to mention different areas to explore. each run is a new random world to explore and its huge. my 1st few runs where about the same until i learned of the different areas you can reach and started finding new paths and learning the combat and the mechanics greatly helps to make these paths available to you. wood wall blocking your path? burn it. concrete door in your way? blow it up. dirt rock and just about everything can be dug out if you have the right wand. ive even used acid to burn through certain areas. my favorite rouge-lite game is "dead cells" yet this game feels on par with it. thats gotta count for something.two vastly different rouge-lites. dead cells is more fast paste action, its got speed running elements, lots of enemies can be tossed at you and if skilled enough you can deal with them all pretty ez, while noita is slower it has for more moments where i'm scheming up battle plans with the terrain. trying to get this thing to hit that or make this fall just right. also a lot of experimenting... a looooot of it. running into multiple enemies is harder to deal with and probably best avoidable if you wanna live. of course if you are overpowered and get cocky you'll probably just wanna kill everything then die because you missed a shot it bounced back and sawed my face off... damm you "blade summon" spellso overall its a unique type of game which i'm all for. i can't wait to see what else they will add. excuse me while i go play some more

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better rouge-likes out there.4/5tl;dr: Every pixel is mutable and reactive, every spell and potion effect reactive and additive.GFX: Pixels!MSC: Decently atmospheric.SFX: Reactive, tactile and distinct, all things a game with this much going on needs.STRY: I'm sure there's something? But where? The hieroglyphics?GMPLY: Treacherous exploration. Every shadow is death. A simple guide to improve survivability: Is it on fire or toxic? It could become so at any time, use caution. Is it glowing/does it take damage? It'll probably explode and/or spew fire/toxic, use caution.Is it moving? It probably wants to kill you, shoot it before it does the same to you.Lightsabers all day...

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and nostalgic, kinda hard!This game will age like fine wine with its similarities to platforming gems, combined with rougelike level generation and the combat of a Terraria-style game (to put it simply). Beautiful music, sound design and of course, immaculate use of pixel art for a uniquely timeless graphical style. The wands and perks allow for lots of different options when formulating a build, while having just enough constraints and drawbacks to keep things interesting. _childDocuments_.review: They say there's no progression in this game, that it's a true roguelike. That is false. There IS a form of overall progession... your knowledge. Okay, bare with me. I know what I just said sounds really stupid, but just hear me out. Noita is a game where there is a LOT to learn. I have 40 hours and I still feel like I've barely scratched the surface. Every run I learn something new, find some new spell, learn of some new interaction. The game is very challenging but somehow 90% of the deaths are my own fault. Every time I die to something I did I take note of it, and remember it for my next run. Just the other day I got a wand that let me summon 5 giant explosive barrels at once, and a perk that made most "consumable" spells have a limitless amount of charges. I went around the entire stage throwing hundreds of them into a pit, shooting them with a fireball, and watching the "fireworks" as the game slowed to compensate for the massive mess I just made. Needless to say, I ended that run by blowing myself up, as I dropped barrels into a pool of water which I accidentally touched with lightning, detonating them.There is so much to see and do in this game and I feel like there are limitless possibilities for spell combos. Despite "breaking the game" and becoming god multiple times I still haven't beaten it lmao. The more I learn the more I want to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely wonderful game that I will probably never finish. The mechanics of the game are as follows: It's an on world creation seed based randomization (Meaning you create a world, get a seed, and the seed will be the same every time) with absolutely liquid mechanics. The wand crafting alone is worth getting this game for, even if you never actually play the game. The randomization is to the pixel and they're not joking when they say every pixel is simulated. Everything interacts and moves like you think it should, including with your wands or enemies;potiens and liquids and everything having it's own density and combining together in somewhat believable ways. It's certainly a feeling when you crush some weird blob with a mine cart and find out you get double gold for it, then get killed instantly because you lost focus for a microsecond.Above all: This game is hard to play. Solidly in the: "Oh god I looked away for three seconds why is everything on fire" range of hard. If that's what you want, this game is perfect. If you don't wanna be slapped repeatedly with your own charred corpse, maybe not.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of game, go in knowing you will die and enjoy each death as mechanisms are working behind the scenes that are sometimes announced, but more often than not add elements to future runs keeping the game fresh. _childDocuments_.review: MY NEW FAVORITE :) I've been recommending this game to all my friends. PROS- amazing magic system! The variability of wands and spells means you'll be making new and interesting combinations for countless replays -perks are super cool! You can combine things like explosive immunity with a super reckless wand that blows up everything to become unstoppable-Enemies and locations are unique and cool. Their attack patterns will surprise you and the threat from each enemy is rarely just about dodging-stains are a unique mechanic. You get wet, covered in slime, alcohol, blood, etc. and each has different effects. -And of course.. The sand pixels. Omg I have never had more fun dropping a sea of acid on a dungeon and watching how everything burns away. and its all the more exciting when your reckless antics can kill you - permanently. Cons-sometimes the particle physics can make you lag. Usually this only happens if you make a ridiculous wand that spews a million flaming particles-you will die completely randomly. A lot of enemies can just one shot you, which feels pretty bad. Maybe I just suck, but get one-hit-killed always feels unfair. -friendly fire will also kill you a lot. Again, I'm not the best player, but the number of times I've just tried to test out a wand and accidentally chunked my health away is ridiculous.-worms can sometimes destroy the safe zone, and then the game punishes you for destroying the safe zone. Pretty unfair. Overall: 9/10 highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most complex games I've ever played. It has so many mechanics that you can use, abuse and kill yourself with. Actually, it is so easy to kill yourself in this game that you don't even need to try. You are your biggest enemy, your greed is your biggest enemy. Also, everything has physics. _childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could give this game a neutral review instead of positive or negative, and I will be giving it the latter as my experiences with it lean more to the negative side overall.BUT, I must mention that said experiences are very subjective and someone with diferent tastes might enjoy it far more than I do.While its amusing at first, it gets boring and repetitive really fast; And while the spell/wand customization is fun in theory... you are mostly going to for the same sort of stuff every time unless you wanna die real fast, as the more quirky and fun spells are really just gimmicks or ways to get yourself killed super fast.Still, fun to play for an hour or two every few months, when you got nothing better to do.Again, I really wish I could give it a neutral review instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Real review: Neutral. Noita is fun for the first 30 hours, but then quickly becomes a grind and joy-draining. The game gives you a lot to explore, so you tend to ignore all of its issues while it lasts (20-30 hours). After that, all its flaws stick out and poke you like thorns. You'll bleed frustration, because the game doesn't let you play it. NOT FUN => Getting stuck on a pixel. - Why can I easily move into a space but cant exit it just the same?- This game should not be >= 1.0 with such a glaring issueNOT FUN => Missing the fine print of your wandNOT FUN => Coming across a new spell without a warning it will harm youREALLY NOT FUN => A once harmless spell now causes damage to you because of a spell modifier- It's very easy to lose hours of progress because you missed the always cast explosive on a new wand, or you find a new spell that fails to mention it will cause damage to yourself (which is confusing, because some explosive spells dont harm to the character), or a spell that was once safe is now harmful because of a modifier. NOT FUN => Needing mods to enjoy the mechanics of the game- The game is already really hard. Modifying wands anywhere and infinite spells dont make the game easier, but it does make the game funner. Those should be built in from the start. There's too many wand options and combinations to NOT have these be active all the time. NOT FUN => Getting killed from an enemy off screen on their first shot. DEV MIGHT BE AN A HOLE => Having no check points with all these issues- Self explanatory

_childDocuments_.review: A game that is absolutely brimming with great ideas! Highly recommended just for the innovation it brings to gaming.However the developers should really consider some changes to ease the player in more and give them more saftey to experiment with the various systems. Even Spelunky didn't start the player in the dark! And this game does that + has fire and acid everywhere! I love it! _childDocuments_.review: Noita is a procedurally-generated 'rogue lite' platformer that you had better make sure revolves around weapon customization and optimization, depending upon exactly how frequently you like to die. It's also got a complex game engine based around particle physics that makes each and every pixel behave according to its kind and occasionally makes my framerate slow to a crawl. This can create a lot of what the kids call 'emergent gameplay' or it can ruin your day real fast. If you're not a fan of either of these things, you probably shouldn't spend money on this, but if you are, then it'll be the most fun you've had with a roguelike in years.This game is a real cool dude, and I know that based on science, and I'll tell you how. It's because of the fact that even when it's wrecking me, which is a thing it does a lot, it still makes me feel like a spell-slinging badass. I feel like Corvus, I feel like Tim the Enchanter, which I didn't really know was something I wanted. I feel like any practitioner of totem-based magical destruction you might care to mention. I maybe even feel like Drake from Stonekeep sometimes, and I definitely didn't want that. It also strikes me as the sort of platformer early DOS devs would have made if they had been able to do so. The particle physics always fill me with warm memories of exploding the screen to death in Scorched Earth.Like any roguelike, it'll sometimes screw you over in ways you can't possibly control, but if you're willing to learn the lessons it has to teach and develop an approach to wand customization and perk selection that fits your play style, of which it can accommodate several, you'll most likely find it a rewarding experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Noita

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a hidden gem of a game. What's unique about Noita is the physics engine and wand mechanics; what's good about the game is a bunch of things.I really appreciate the fact that there is basically no meta-progression, with each run you start from scratch. Many recent games are supposedly rouge-likes but the meta progression really rob them of what makes rouge-likes great (in my experience).Also the game has some cool secrets and I would recommend new players resist looking up spoilers for those as much as possible. Although, it is useful to look up information of some of the base mechanics.Anyway, great game, two thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot more depth than meets the eye, I decided to play it just on its merit of having "falling sand" particle physics and found so much more to enjoy. _childDocuments_.review: have you ever piddle away hours on end messing with the falling sand / powder toy?this is that but an actual game. a rogue-lite where you basically can blow up everything, all pixels are physically simulated. you collect wands and customize them with a bajillion different spells, modifiers, etc. and create immensely crazy effects from combining stuff. the wand system is seriously the most amazing thing i've seen in a game like this probably ever, and they keep adding more and more stuff to play with. the game doesn't hold your hand at all and it is punishingly hard at first but you just have to die over and over and over again until you realize what's going on, and understand also the massive perk system which can also effect your spells and the environment. the enemies are tough and crazy and spooky, also there are giant hellworms that randomly show up and eat through the map, and like, floating octopuses that try to fondle you. the combat is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ intense and unpredictable and often you will be like dodging attacks and environmental threats with 1 health remaining. there's also a ton of secrets that can help you. i sunk at least 100 hours into it, it's just so fun and the randomness, the excellent psychedelic soundtrack, the frequent updates, and amazing modding community make it infinitely replayable. the art is also beautiful. you will die, frequently. but you will learn and eventually become a god. i just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ much.

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a wonderfully complex roguelike game that's full of secrets and discovery. The goal (initially) is to explore different environments under a mountain, making your way downward through progressively more difficult levels. While you're exploring you'll gather randomized wands, potions, and other items that you can use to improve your chances. If you've played many modern roguelikes and roguelites this should all be pretty familiar to you, and you'll see a lot of genre staples here like game-changing perks being doled out at set intervals in 'safe' areas that also function as shops.There's a few major differences that set Noita apart from other games in the genre. The engine that this game runs on was featured pretty heavily in Noita's marketing, and for good reason. Noita's 'gimmick' is that every pixel is a simulated material that can interact with other pixels independently. If you've ever played with those falling sand, powder game type webtoys, picture that but as a frame for an excellent roguelike. You can dig through the ground, set stuff on fire, electrify metal, evaporate liquids, everything you would expect. While it's very cool, it isn't enough to make a good game.Luckily, Noita has a lot more going for it than just a neat engine. I mentioned earlier that you'll find wands while you're exploring the caves in Noita. Wands, and the spells inside of them, are the primary way you interact with Noita's world. Each wand you pick up will have different stats, and a different number of slots to hold spells or modifiers. You can think of these spells as bullets, and the slots in the wand as space in a magazine (yes I'm American, why do you ask?). Your wand will fire the spell in the leftmost slot first, then fire the spell to the right, and so on. You can put spell modifiers in these slots (flaming shots, extra damage, more speed, etc.) that will be applied to the spell that comes after them. At certain points in the game, you'll be given the opportunity to rearrange the order of these spells, switch them between wands, and essentially craft a unique sequence of spells. This is a meaty mechanic, and you can create some truly insane combinations doing this. Noita is an extremely difficult game that ramps up very quickly, and creating powerful spells is mandatory to completing it. You're in an arms race with the game, and you're both encouraged and expected to do everything you can to bend the mechanics to your will.It will probably take you a few runs (and some wiki diving) to get comfortable with this mechanic. But once you do, you'll be creating wands that would make Gandalf piss his pants in terror. With wands like that, you'll have no problem beating the main game. At this point you may realize that you can pretty much dig through anything and go anywhere with your collection of super wands, and you may try going outside of the game area. And when you do, you'll find that you've just discovered the rest of the game.Noita is huge, and the main levels are just one very small part of a much larger map. There's danger and secrets in every direction, just waiting for you to discover them. Spend some time exploring on your own, but once you feel like you've seen everything consider heading over to the wiki to read up on some of the more obscure secrets and quests. It's borderline impossible to discover everything on your own, so if you want to see it all then this is required. Noita is a great game that you can sink countless hours into, and it's absolutely worth your time. Dive in, and don't forget your water flask!                                                                                                                                                                   -----------------------EDIT: I swear I know how paragraphs work, steam formatting is just awful. Fix your ♥♥♥♥, Gaben. TLDR: Buy Noita or I will break your kneecaps

_childDocuments_.review: What else can I say about a game where the overall player reviews are overwhelmingly positive? Well, for starters, this game is unforgiving in a way that you'll only understand by playing it.It's Roguelike, so by it's nature, it will kill you... A LOT! It has the nostalgia of an old school game (If you know, you know), but with superb physics built in, and everything  (YES EVERYTHING), even down to the last little pixel is destructible in one way or the other. The game doesn't hold your hand... You start, and you figure it out as you play. The controls are simple, and the objectives are easy to figure out... If you're one of those die hard gamers that thinks they're better than everyone else... please do be my guest.. I like to see people be humbled by entertainment...The "unlockables" in this game are MANY, and the combinations of wands and spells are insane. This game will challenge you, run, after run, after run, and it doesn't get stale. IF you're easily frustrated, perhaps it's not the game for you... Or perhaps it is, and it's an opportunity to quell that rage and frustration you harbour, because it will break you... at some point... unless you're weakling and run from a good fight. The only thing I can leave you with, is this... Buy it, try it, OWN it... It really is a must have for any serious game collector, and is definitely one of my top favourite games to play casually in between more demanding games, it's one where if you have only 5 minutes to spare, this game can do that... or, you know... consume your entire afternoon with run after run.I highly recommend this excellent game!

_childDocuments_.review: This game lets you eat things you cannot eat in any other game. You can eat dead enemies, blood, vomit, grass, psychedelic mushrooms, and so much more.
