There's tons things to eat that give the player a debuff or no effect at all, and there are very few things to eat that benefit you. There's not much of a reason for the player to eat stuff (unless you have perks), but the game still allows you to eat anything and that alone makes it worth playing.Really though, this game is phenomenal. Banging soundtrack, beautiful art, active modding community, and tons of secrets to discover (it'll take you many tries before you beat the game once, and once you've beaten the game you've explored maybe 10% of the game world). This game can be obtuse and hard to figure out, but do yourself a favor and try to stay off the wiki to avoid spoiling yourself, at least until you've finished your first run. _childDocuments_.review: Noita is a rare gem of a game. It may seem like a simple 2 dimensional platform action and exploration game at first, but it has incredible depth and complexity to experience. While many games over-tutorialize, or handhold new players, this game forces players to build their own understanding of the lore and mechanics which drive the world. While exploring and fighting a wide variety of unique enemies, the player is also encouraged to build an understanding of wand-crafting and alchemical mixing of potions and elements to reveal secret areas and defeat bosses which are both fantastic in scale and rich in lore. While the game itself is quite challenging, and there are a lot of extremely dangerous obstacles to overcome, it is a rewarding and interesting experience.Procedurally generated worlds with dynamic alchemical rules.Dangerous environmental and enemy monster effects. Complex and rewarding "wand programming" mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been absolutely phenomenal in its art style, mechanics, and general design.The expanded world looks promising, I assume  areas will be worked on and more fleshed out later in development so on to the actual part that we can truly experience right now.The dungeon is a strange and unforgiving territory. I love the difficulty and the intensity of the game as is but it is quite overwhelming starting at just the second area. There are very rarely any breaks to yourself, safe areas or just open terrain to help avoid each projectile. It seems as though each enemy knows exactly where you are and when you kill anything of its type sometimes they will swarm. The projectiles can be hard enough for many players not to mention the relatively small amount of levitation that's available but even when you inevitably get the hang of the projectile dodging the game feels punishing to kill the enemies. The mechanics of allowing creatures to "bleed" is unique in itself but so many enemies seem to carry harmful or debilitating blood that makes it worth avoiding the ground at all costs when killing swarms which also make it near impossible to pick up gold nuggets to continue to survive in this descent. It's a shame to experience so many creatures and not be able to pick up mental knowledge on them or even realize their existence sometimes when later on it's just a race to get to the holy mountain. One last thing before I move on to my own personal experience that makes me want to keep coming back as it fills me with endless entertainment are just two mechanics that feel a bit off. Crouching is really only there to make you go down in water and sometimes barely duck behind some rock to avoid shotgun or sniper fire if you even have the liberty of staying still in your own area. And kicking is somewhat more useful in being able to kick around various explosive barrels and crates and even the lamp oils if you're careful enough to use instead of bombs to access areas. Kicking can sometimes be strange as it follows your cursor but does not necessarily follow up on where you're supposedly aiming since it can be screwed up by even the tiniest bump in the earth.My own personal experience has been filled with laughter and amazement. Using the worm egg to dig through the tree and down into the tunnels which, by the way, the worm sometimes doesn't 'dig' as in destroying the terrain and instead just seems to swim through it? I'm unsure if that's a bug. To using a chaotic polymorph flask to put out a fire as I was surrounded by enemies and turning into a giant worm with a health bar which I assumed to be the final boss?? I lived as I was able to control it and tear through my foes and terrain alike. When testing a black hole orb inside the holy mountain I chewed through the wall and "Angered the Gods" which spawned some holy demon that was protected by some sort of shield to punish me. It's all just a true new experience each time, a full on rogue like of which I fall in love with.Oh and one thing I'd like to suggest is:When polymorphed you should still be able to see your health bar becomes there are multiple times I have died polymorphed, or more specifically chaotically polymorphed and finding out I've been damaging myself the entire time.Sorry for the long ramble of a review it's my first real lengthy review and I tried convey my passion for this game within it. Thank you for reading if you came all the way through!Edit: Moved self comment into reviewAnd just played a couple more games and already have experienced stupidly wild things XD I became a yeti, a wolf, and an enemy became a giant fire worm that spilled lava out its eye. Also teleportitis apparently still teleports you when you're in the holy mountain. And not only can it teleport you forward in the level but it can teleport you BACK to the place you just were before that holy mountain.

_childDocuments_.review: Noita's simulation of the interactions that all the different materials, enemies, and objects in the world have with each other allows for interesting emergent situations you'll have to deal with. The game mechanics are clear-cut enough; you can collect things that sparkle, kick other loose things that dont, stain yourself with liquids to gain new properties & status effects, throw consumables, & eat or drink many things you're standing over.      Everything else in the game aside from your main goal of progressing deeper underground is actually fairly obtuse. It's intentional, for what it's worth. Players who enjoy serious secret hunting have much to discover. The world is considerable larger than the immediately apparent main path.     Noita is unforgiving. You'll need to experiment with the Wand customization mechanic to understand it's quirks, & trying new things usually leads to death. It's fine though, the game restarts quickly & you can try again, just a bit more knowledgeable. Sometimes it feels like things beyond your influence happen & get you killed; it's seriously helpful to have a mindset where you can examine the events leading up to your death & how it might be avoided in the future. Even then, you could still get "Noita'd," but treating surprise bad luck as just another thing to play around can lessen the salt.     Weak cpus beware.

_childDocuments_.review: Been looking forward to this one for a while. These are my first impressions, from a guy who has loved Nolla Games' output since Crayon Physics Deluxe and loves roguelites in general.First, bear in mind that this game is mega-Early Access at the time of writing this. There are numerous elements that need polish, such as Fullscreen (Windowed) pretty much just being standard Fullscreen, and so on. The game is plenty playable, or at least it was on my rig, and runs very well especially considering its main gimmick.Speaking of, yes, the gimmick is awesome. My concern with this game was that Nolla Games would just lean back on the gimmick and then just make a generic roguelite off it, but no, they really exploited this to the max and I am so happy.  On top of that, enemies drop twice the loot if you kill them with the physics system instead of just relying on your normal weapons, which is great.Speaking of though, THE WANDS! These are also really awesome. Equipment is in two categories, Wands and Items, and you can carry 4 of each. Items are just that and don't do more than what they say on the tin, but between each zone, Wands can be customised and the customisation system is very deep. Just on my first playthrough, I quickly assembled a wand that fires a magic arrow, that bounces once and upon hitting a target or a second wall, it leaves behind an imminently-exploding mine that blasts in a vertical cross shape, and a constantly-burning wand that can indeed set fire to stuff at close range passively, but can also shoot a rolling fireball (that's honestly more like a grenade launcher) that resurrects everything it kills.The customisation system is difficult to describe, but I'll try: Each Wand has a set of specific stats unique to that Wand, like how many spells it can hold, how quickly it can fire, its mana cap, and so on. However, the actual spells it fires aren't set in stone, and you can shuffle them around between the zones, buy new spells for your collection, ecetera. You can strip wands for their spells then discard them, or pick up empty wands with no spells because said wand might have really good stats, so next floor you can make your B.F.G. The spells themselves, and their order, determine the behaviour of the Wand. For example, you might have your basic starter wand that's setup is 2 Spark Bolt, so it fires two small bolts in succession and then reloads, but if you apply a "Y-shape" behind those Spark Bolts, it'll shoot those two bolts at the same time in a cone pattern instead.There's also the items themselves, which are mostly Potions, essentially some liquid that you can toss out at a moment's notice when you need to. You can even drop Potions and shoot them to create a barrel-like leak effect, spray a small amount of it at foes, or just toss the whole thing, and Potion effects vary from teleporting anything in the liquid to a random location in the zone, or turning anything into a sheep, or literally just being lava, and the liquid , so you'd better make sure you don't need to traverse where you throw a potion, or you might just be doing it as a sheep.Some other things to note that might affect your purchase decision:

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Steams text formatting is borked. Hope you like bold text. Sorry!It is very hard for me to describe Noita effectively.So, i'll just say "it's good" if you're super lazy.But, if you've got time, here's a quick read. There is a TD:LR at the bottom if you don't want to read my wall of text, so feel free to take a peak if you're just passing by.Despite the fact that it is in Early Access, I really feel like there is a massive world here, and the player character, be it a representation of us, or it's own being,(I used to call them "The Alchemist", but further research has revealed that they are infact the "Noita" which is Finnish for "Witch")  is just one of many cogs in the machine, albeit a seemingly very important cog.From what I can tell of the very, very minimal storyline (there is no speech from characters, or at least none i've encountered)  I myself have never reached it past "level three". (The spoiler is really minor, and a bit speculative.) EDIT: I beat the game, but there is still so much more to discover.Of worthy note of what I've discovered about this game, is that it seems there is only one "map" (in the game sense). The portals at the bottom of each level bring you to a new location in that map, separated from the previous by a mostly invulnerable barrier of ancient, worn stone bricks. What's even more impressive is that every little interaction is saved.  I remember seeing a video in my YouTube recommendations saying "exploring the overworld of Noita" or something of the like. Haven't watched it yet, don't like major spoilers. (which is why i'm keeping this rather, but not entirely vauge.) EDIT: The video is "Exploring Noita's massive surface for its many secrets" from FuryForged. Cool guy, great videos.Noita is a dungeon crawler rougelike set in a strange and mysterious 2D world. It's got great music, and naturally evolving combat based on it's arguably revolutionary pixel-based physics system. (I love squares! :D ) You are The Noita, a Witch who must use the treasures and traps in the caves below them to make themselves more powerful as to not be killed off by it's inhabitants. Your primary method of survival are various pre-generated wands that appear throughout the dungeon on display. Some have traps, so watch out. Some of them have infinite use (I call em' Cantrips!) and some have limited usages before they need a recharge, and that can only be done between stages. (Spell slots! ... Is this D&D...? Somethings tells me it's not.)Lastly, Noita has a very interesting "fog of war" like effect. You can only see in the area that you've been in, and even then they have to be lit for you to properly see them. I get the impression that the... inhabitants, of the cave system have a very similar vision system. It doesn't appear to be cone or radius based. I get the impression that they have a view of the world very similar to your own. Of worthy note is that regenerating health mid stage is extremely difficult. If you get your hands on a wand or potion that can heal you, treasure that thing, because it will save your life. Not it "may" save your life, it WILL save your life.Finally, I have some suggestions for the developers.Noita is a very well made game. Despite the fact that it's in early access, it already has a massive amount of content. On a less serious note, I haven't been this confused and engaged since about the story since

_childDocuments_.review: Game is great, but has balancing issues currently. I also miss some sort of progression as Rogue Legacy has it. My gamer reflexes are very poor, and because of it I rarely get very far until I die. And while I do learn some tricks as I play, I still very much feel like it's becoming a chore starting over again and again without the first part getting somehow easier to overcome. It would be awesome if you could built your character, wand and spell roster somehow over time. Perhaps be allowed to bring one or two things over with you every time you restart, to slowly built a cool noita.Cons at the moment (aka "things that get in the way of pure enjoyment"):- Frustrating as hell when the game pulls instadeaths on you out of the blue. You can be playing for 30 minutes and die due to something you have no control over.- Quite severe balancing issues- Relies A LOT on luck when it comes to what you get- Killing levitation when getting shot at is annoying as hell. Quite often you'll be floating down into a new place and get shot by an out-of-view enemy, then instantly get dropped to the ground where 4 enemies are further shooting at you, making it impossible to get away. Instadeath!- Wand and spell system is extremely confusing and hard to understand. Whenever I think I get it, it does the opposite of what I expect- Very little opportunity for experimenting with wands and spells. Got it wrong? Too bad, when you die you won't see this wand again- Gold disappears too quickly- Player feels overly fragile. You'll end up tiptoeing all the time once you learn that instadeath is everywhere. And it's very often due to game design flaws as described in my other points.- Very little opportunity to regain any bit of health during a level- Fire and acid is a bit too chaotic at the moment. Maybe just tone down how long fire burns and how much acid is spewed from monsters and containers.- The big beholders are too bulletspongy for my taste, especially since they continually spew out smaller beholders. Unless you have a good weapon, it's bye-bye (at least for me).- No difficulty options. This is a single player game so why not have one? We don't all have super reflexes. I'm slow with these things, and I would like to enjoy this game more.- Monster hideouts. I hate them! Drop down somewhere and suddenly there'll be 20 monsters shooting at you instantly. DEAD! Nothing you can do. Goodbye cool wand and progress.- Many monsters give little to no chance to react to them before they fire a perfect shot right at your face. This is especially true for the snipers and flying gunners. They will instafire on you when you are in their sight. And you can't shoot at them without them being in sight most of the time. So you will loose health no matter what.So why do I still recommend this game? Because the potential is insane! And it IS fun to play, 2 out of 10 rounds... So there's glimpses of brilliance throughout. The physics mechanics are really fun to play around with and the monsters are cool. It's just a matter of dialing in the gameplay and balancing issues and adding some sense of follow-over when dying to give a sense of progression.Pros:- Pixel physics are a major upside to this game! It makes for some nice dynamic gameplay.- Weapons are fun!- Potions are fun!- Stat boost selections between worlds are fun, but a more permanent character progression system would be cool in addition to it.- Enemies are nice a varied. Well-designed too.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly one-of-a-kind, software simulation marvel that's as physically expansive as it is technically adept and yet...It just wasn't for me.I was waiting for that moment for the game to "click", and I just never found it. And it's something I've battled with for a while now...I think the biggest turn away for me was the difficulty. I'm no stranger to difficult games, but this one is on a different spectrum. It's less Sekiro and more Dwarf Fortress, in the fact that the world can just decide you're going to die whenever it wants. The big difference being: in games like Dwarf Fortress, the reward is often a unique story to tell, and maybe some tidbits of useful knowledge to guide your next run. While I see  of that narrative reward loop in Noita, it just doesn't feel nearly as gratifying. The difficulty, combined with the length of the runs and the randomness in general, makes learning the game a slog past the first two levels. Sure, I've just figured out an amazingly powerful wand setup, but unfortunately my robe grazed an electrified surface, now I'll never see it again.  I'll be able to build something similar, but it'll take me 10 hours of runs to find the a similar setup. Or more commonly: I've finally gotten to that next level deeper, only to get one-shot by the first enemy I see. So what did I learn here?...You see what I mean? It's a punishing cycle with little to no reward. And like... I guess that's part of the point? I know there's tons of cool and crazy secrets, but what are they worth if I can never find the right wand combinations to properly explore them?Still recommending, at the end of the day. It is as advertised, and I think the modding scene can address most, if not all, issues I'm complaining about.

_childDocuments_.review: For a very long time, I only gave the ranking of the “best” video game to Bloodborne. Then, Factorio came along, and that game also deserved to have that title. A few years later, Noita appears in early access and I buy it to support the studio for doing something new and for that sweet 15% off. It was fun, but it felt repetitive for someone like me who wasn’t willing to use the Wiki or look up guides, so I never played it again after my initial 15 hours.Recently, Noita’s final update came out, and I can easily say that this game deserves a spot at the top with Bloodborne and Factorio. The almost infinite amount of content, the incredible customization, the hundreds of secrets and the incredible gameplay that is just the perfect amount of satisfying and infuriating makes this game a must-buy. Noita is an amazing game, but it is also a love letter to the gaming world. This game set a new standard. It pushed the limits, creating something that nobody thought could exist (yet). Sure, this isn’t the cool video game we thought we made up in our mind when we were 12, but this is almost it!You like Terraria? Get itYou like Roguelikes/Roguelites? Get itYou like feeling like God? Get itYou’re particularly masochistic? Get itYou’re the edgy friend that keeps calling yourself an “agent of chaos”? Get itYou’re an achievement hunter? Get itI’d only tell you to skip it if you enjoy a well-crafted story and don’t care about gameplay.Fair warning, I’m really good at roguelikes/roguelites and I haven’t won a game after 30 hours of playtime.Good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: a brilliantly programmed and original game, made inaccessible by how opaque it is and how brutally unwelcoming it is to new players. I'm not recommending this game, and the reason I don't recommend it does not have one thing to do with the game from a purely technical point of view. it's incredibly well made, the gameplay is incredible, the sandbox side of spellcraft is immensely rewarding, and in a lot of ways it plays like a roguelike. the good kind.no, the reason I don't recommend is because so much of the game relies entirely on looking up guides, trial and error, and immense time sinks that often lead to lost progress on the part of the player. hidden mechanics you'll never figure out by yourself. overwhelming difficult spikes or completely random off-screen causes of instant death (on a game with permadeath and no one-shot protection of any sort, no less!). to "truly" beat the game you must embark on a journey that can take upwards of 10 hours to complete - at any point, you risk dying to something you could not predict. I played most of my time of Noita in Offscreen mode, I actually have somewhere between 80 and 100 hours in the game... and I only beat it once. Just once. There's nothing wrong about making difficult games. Dark Souls is absolutely incredible. Dead Cells also. Hyper Light Drifter is certainly no cakewalk. however the truly frustrating thing about Noita (in my experience) is that mechanics entirely possible in the game are deliberately kept out of a player's reach for the sake of difficulty. regeneration? does not happen. digging? you better luck out on the spells you find. you can't even edit wands outside of specific areas (Holy Mountains), which means often leaving very good wands behind because you can either pick a wand with excellent stats but a suicidal random set of spells and modifiers on it (and you lose a functional wand in the process, and now must pass most of the level with one of your wands being a dud at best, and something that kills you instantly if in a high-stress situation you cast "Explosion" or "Giga black Hole" just by scrolling over the wand and clicking by accident while hastily trying to douse your burning robes and not die.The game is moddable. to hell and back. and that's part of what got me to conclude that I don't like it. even modding so many of these personal gripes away, the game remains obnoxiously, frustratingly complicated. alchemy is a striking example. you could make the case that "it has a learning curve" but... nope, it doesn't. alchemy, one of the most unique and honestly fascinating mechanics in the game, is randomized each run, so there's never much you can carry over from one run to the next. this leads to the other issue. the RNG is so overwhelming that it often feels like you only go anywhere because today the game feels like letting you get anywhere. getting something like Explosion Immunity on the first level is a night-and-day difference to most runs where a single misused bomb will delete you (or most of your hp, anyway).I simply do not recommend it. it's not a game everyone can or will enjoy. i certainly quit. I've been picking it up one and off for the better part of two years, sometimes diving into it, only to be swiftly remembered that I'd have more fun playing a game that isn't actively designed to be frustrating, or that doesn't demand me to memorize 20 specific guides on youtube just to understand what the frick the anvil at the hiisi base does, or the signifficance of hand statues in the ice biome, or the part where it's really, really, really, really not a good idea to even try and defeat the boss found past the lava lake. if you enjoy something akin to terraria (2D exploration, combat, some mining-ish vibes, terrain manipulation, crazy combat and powerscaling, high difficulty in some areas) but would prefer a far more volatile and challenging game, this might just be for you. But it's certainly not for me. And I don't want to keep trying to make it so. no amount of modding on my part can fix the core gameplay issues I have with this game. it is, still, a hell of a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: 80+ hours in, and I have just scratched the surface. This is one of the best games I have ever played. Nominating this for a Steam award for sure!Noita is is a gorgeous rouge-like chaos-worshiping neo-retro adventure shrouded in profound mystery that can only be revealed through exploration, tinkering, and dying over and over again. There are hundreds of spells you can choose from and combine to create the goddess-tier "wand" that maybe, just maybe, will finally win you the game. This will take a long time, however, as you burn, bleed, melt, drown, and get punched right in the nose harder than a pack of dinosaurs stampeding over your face.Literally anything and everything around you can be destroyed in a variety of ways, especially you. As you progress deeper into Noita's seemingly endless ice caverns, psychedelic mushroom jungles, and metal fortresses, you will be introduced to new mechanics, monsters, perks, spells, and environments to master. This game takes patience, but don't worry, it rewards people generously with plenty of interesting, unique content to unearth. The posabilities of building your character and turning them into an overpowered demon of pure destruction, like my wife, are truly endless. If you pay attention and be patient, you will unlock the secrets waiting for you far below and high above. There is far more to this game than meets the eye, and death is only the beginning.Some of the enviroments and ideas present in this game are so unique, and I personally have never seen them done before in the hundreds of games I have played over the years. The developers give such a high attention to detail with this game; it truly is impressive, and I am more than stoked to see it come out of beta and fresh into the world. Although casual players not looking for a challenge may dislike this game, gamers seeking a mind-bending adventure that doesn't hold their hand are in for a real treat.

_childDocuments_.review: I officially play this game more than any other in my inventory, though I feel the hours played are not accurate perhaps due to playing offline. Of the roguelike genre, this one satisfies every checkbox that i look for. The synergies available vary immensely, and offer much creativity. The perks can be very satisfying and the world-building is excellent. Considering the vast content and amount of procedural generation per world, I'm surprised how sparsely I run into "bugs." Magic building games are my favorite to play and Noita absolutely contends for top place in magic system, chaos, and creativity. The mod community is rampant in their efforts to continue building up the game and in general, the Noita community is a blast, pun intended. I hope you all find as much enjoyment from this game as I do, and of course, get Noita'd.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since I've fallen in love with an early access game, but Noita is an absolute gem and is chock full of content for the asking price.As is standard roguelike fare, it's not an easy game by any stretch. Some runs you'll feel like a god, raining down magical death on your foes only to be smacked face-first into a pool of lava. Other's you'll be inching your way through the world bit by bit with some more underwhelming spells. Either way though, I've always had fun in my attempts to beat the game.Noita is all about wands and potions, you find new wands and items throughout the world and use them to advance. Between areas in the main cave you can move spells from wand to wand and craft some really fun death sticks. There's a shop, some health and a spell refresh for limited use spells and a selection of perks too. The further you get, the more deadly both you and the enemies will become.There are tons of secrets to be uncovered by the inquisitive player that upon finding will offer a slight advantage in future runs should you revisit them. There are several places to explore, tons of enemies and even a secret ending that I've yet to find. There are secrets that will destroy the uninitiated, enemies that will make you hate them from the first encounter and more than a few clever tricks that can help or hinder you.Some light advice I would give before you begin:-Check the controls: This seems simple enough, but you'd be surprised how many people just throw and waste their potions because they didn't know you could spray them!-Throttle your levitation: This will ensure you achieve maximum flight time and you may even reach new places or avoid certain death.-Enemies with guns tend to not be able to shoot straight up: Get the drop on them by floating overhead and raining down death where possible.-Exercise caution at all times: You never know when a worm might appear out of nowhere and turn you into a snack. To that effect, keep your sound on.-Kick!: This is easily missed by most players, but kicking is a very useful mechanic. When you kick an object it will fly toward your cursor, this makes it incredibly useful for taking out enemies, removing obstacles or even making a path in some cases.-Take note of liquids and how they work: Several liquids may interact with each other, pouring water on lava makes rock, pouring water on fire makes steam, etc. Some of these interactions are incredibly useful. Some enemies are also especially weak to specific liquids.-Take the time to learn about wands: Knowing what each stat does is a good way to judge if a wand is good or rubbish. Shuffle can be good or bad with certain spells, capacity might not matter for some wands, recharge speed helps many spells, etc.Overall Noita has been a delight to play since launch. The devs are constantly pumping out new content, including new spells, enemies, secrets and even mod support. The latter even comes with an official mod as of my last session that gives you more varied starts to your runs.I can honestly say I'm plenty happy with the current state of the game and I couldn't be more excited to see where the devs will take it.

_childDocuments_.review: This response is largely personal, since I know there are a large number of people who enjoy this game. There are very, very few people who I believe could get past the suffering and the unenjoyable portions of this game to really make it a fun experience. Hours of careful progress through caves, stepping around each and every obstacle so delicately, get ruined in a single instance of a snagged pixel or an enemy from off screen setting off explosives. Even heavily modding the game can't redeem this game's negative qualities. It's so absolutely random that nothing matters, no progress (temporary or permanent) is ever made. I have tried to replicate the same techniques that I have seen online, but I just don't have the time in the day any more to spend on games that are such an incredible time sink for no feelings of gratification or reward.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't honestly recommend this game to anyone.It has a lot of positives, but they are overshadowed by negatives.--Have you ever thought of yourself - hey I wish I played a sandbox game with permadeath that has a vast map that's largely filled with nothing and gives you no fast travel options (outside of spamming teleport wands which just doesn't cut it as it still consumes considerable time).--Have you ever thought of yourself - hey I wish I played a roguelite game with only 1 boss and fairly static areas, but that also lets you explore additional areas and fight additional bosses... BUT only once you break the game and become able to oneshot virtually everything?--Have you ever thought of yourself - hey I wish the game didn't give me any useful information in any shape or form and only lets me learn through panfully dying over and over again, within roguelite runs, and only after the extremely tedious and repetitive early game? (or by metagaming)--Have you ever thought of yourself - hey I wish I had multiple 16 hour runs in a permadeath game?--Or alternatively have you ever thought of yourself - hey I wish I played a game with permadeath... but while opting out of the permadeath feature by means of exiting the game and backing up my saves manually every now and then? (or by writing a shell script to semi-automate the process)If you ever thought you wished for any of these things they hey maybe this game is for you.Otherwise - yeah the game's design quite often makes zero sense and enjoying it requires a certain level of acquired masochism.The wand building system can let you do a lot of fun things but to me it feels more like programming (with imported spaghetti code libraries) than like actual gaming, as you'll likely need to read through many pages of the extremely cryptic documentation on the wiki or watch video guides in order to get anything done within a reasonable timeframe.The whole "every pixel is simulated" slogun is just marketing crap. Yes, there is in fact pixel-level physics simulation but obviously not "every" pixel is simulated. It looks cool though, but it also runs like crap when you start truly approaching the "every pixel is simulated" situation and you start seeing the chunk loads despite your framerate dropping to single digits or the game crashing (as you'd expect).On the positive end, besides the more obvious ones, the game does have modding support (but if you want achievements you'll have to play vanilla cuz why not) and has improved slightly after EA. The biggest change from EA is that there's now little basins on the holy mountain exits; so you don't get oneshot by a horde of enemies camping the exit to the snow level. I'm not sure what else has changed, as I quit playing the EA as I got rapidly tired of getting one-shot over and over again in the snow level (currently there's much more variety in the where and how you get oneshot, so I was able to have some fun with it)Edit: Fixed some typographical errors and added clarifications here and there.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly neat and engaging roguelike/lite game if you have a thing for exploration and experimentation. Noita is one of those games that are quite simple on the surface, but houses a vast repository of secrets just waiting to be found quite literally, beneath the surface. The game has a lot charm, and it's so easy to get hooked on it. There a few different portions of gameplay that work together and form the incredibly fun experience that is, Noita.For starters, you're a wizard. Sweet, right? You've got a cool magic wand and a dope purple cloak. Unfortunately, you happen to be in the middle of *seemingly* nowhere, at the mouth of a mountain's tunnel. Where is anyone, or anything? Who can you show off your stunning duds and fancy destructive magic sparks to? Maybe if you venture into the cave before you, you'll find out. There's a few large stone tablets that go further into the mountain's maw. Cryptic messages from a time unknown, glowing bright as you walk past... messages from unknown beings that explain to you the very simple controls of the game. You venture further in, slipping down a steep decline. The cave opens up in a vast, winding maze around you. It's dark. It smells funny. It is now you realize you're not exactly alone down here. You've found the "anyone and anythings" you were looking for. Unfortunately, they seem to want you dead.... and this is where the fun begins. A primary portion of your objective in Noita is exploration. A sizable portion, as there's a whole lot of darkness to delve through. Danger in the form of the environment and all those that inhabit it. Secrets and strange places; relics and magic. Fortunately, you're quite good at handling magic. You know, being a wizard and all. Your main goal is to dive downwards into the mountain until you can go no further. What's down there, lying in wait at the very bottom? If you can survive long enough, you'll find out. While this is the main objective, Noita's world is actually quite large. There's a number of destinations with their own hazards, rewards, and sense of mystery. You look around, find an obstacle, look elsewhere, find a way to overcome it, and the cycle repeats. You slowly piece together the puzzle of Noita's world, always finding something cool while you're doing it. One cool thing happens to be the very earth you stand upon.There's a numerous amount of materials that form the game's environment. Dirt and gravel. Ancient brickwork, dense volcanic rock. Ice and slush. Piles of sand and... gunpowder? Pits of lava, vats of sludge. Deep lakes of water, or some various liquid from a potion that spilled somewhere. You interact with your environment in a number of ways in this game, and the way it reacts to various disturbances is incredibly cool - each pixel has a simulated property to it. Objects have weight. Liquids flow and spill; they mix with each other and create different concoctions of potential benefit or hazard. Your enemies bleed various substances that also can have effects on you. All these liquids can be bottled for use later, frozen, burnt... they can even give off gases and vapor, and these gasses react to various things as well. There's just all this neat stuff going on at once that keeps you on your toes that you can use to your advantage or fall victim to. So, in a scramble to hold on to your life and find some answers, you press forward. As you trek through the caverns, you'll notice that someone left some wands around. Just floating enticingly on some cool pedestals.  As far as you're concerned, they're yours for the taking - granted that some creature doesn't get to it first and decides to use you as target practice. This is the beginning of your descent into madness and unlimited power... potentially. The next portion of Noita's formula is that of wands and spellcasting, and man oh man. You're in for a wild ride.Upon starting each run, you'll be granted two wands. A simple wand that fires one of many basic projectiles, and another wand that can create explosions - useful for blowing through the ground, obstacles, and enemies alike. Each wand has spell slots, and these are occupied by a basic spell that is good enough to get you to a certain point... and then you might notice you'll need some more firepower. Like mentioned previously, there's a number of randomized wands all around the caverns. Each with their own unique set of spells and characteristics that can be either amazing or... not so much. The madness advances when you realize that you can actually tinker with these spells slots - customizing combinations of magic and magic modifiers. And goodness gracious, there's so much to work with. Anything from making your wand become a torch that sets things on fire, to casting projectiles that leave trails of fire. Maybe that trail could be poison, acid, or light... what if the projectile itself *was* light? What if that light had an electric charge that stunned everything it touched? Or accidentally killed you if you held it while swimming in liquid? Liquid you can make out of thin air? You can make it rain. Rain what, exactly? It could be whiskey, toxic sludge, maybe even blood. Maybe you'd like to cast a sphere around you that freezes the liquids you've just made a pool of. Or perhaps you can drill through your frozen brew and the earth with your chainsaw-drill-lazer wand. A black hole that eats the ground is a much cooler, though. Why drill into the dark when you can light up the map and know where to go? Got yourself in a tough spot and need a shield for a quick breather? There's a spell for that. Do you want to fill your entire screen with tentacles that pound everything they touch into a pulp? Do you like explosions? Like, a lot of explosions? In various shapes and sizes?There are so many possibilities. If you're creative, you can make something truly spectacular. Possibly ungodly, but spectacular nonetheless. And if that wasn't enough, there's a plethora of mods to find in the Workshop that adds even more insanity to the already chaotic mess. Maybe you want mods to have less chaos, even. Quality of life? Custom character sprites? New spells? Flat out cheat? Sure, why not? Again, there's an incredibly huge amount of possibilities. It should also be mentioned that Noita isn't exactly an easy game. You're going to die, quite a bit. That's what makes it fun. You have to be smart about how you react to the environment and use your tools to handle the situations you find yourself in, and craft tools to bend the situations in your favor. Some runs will go better than others, but that's how things go with games in this genre. Try again and discover something new.To echo my statement at the beginning of this review - if you're into exploration, tinkering with things, and leaving a part of your fate up to the RNG gods... Noita is absolutely worth checking out. Fantastic game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! It is all about the gameplay loop, and it is wonderful!The options are immesurable and so is the fun. Really deep and solid system.The main thing is that it is a wondrous world with so many secrets. I thought I "broke" the game (infinite floating) and reached places that I was actually meant to reach! It totally blew my mind!Move far over these so called AAA games with their limited level (and game) design and mechanics.Cons:-Too unforgiving-Sometimes unfair (RNG)-No second try (in base game) and VERY limited healing-No quality of life... at all!If you are easily frustrated with dying and it being unfair here is a nice and balanced mod list you should try to make it more fun. None of them (IMO) are game-breaking and only enhances the experience:-Configurable Attract Gold - Attracts golden nuggets when very close, good for pickups from hazards.-Quad Life Gold - Changes gold nugget despawn time to 15-20 seconds, instead of the default 3(!). So that you can actually clear the room and reap your rewards after.-X3 Inventory - Gives you 3 times the inventory for spells. Quite handy when you like many options.-Vampirism+ - Gives the vampirism perk double heal. The default perk is crap and not worth it.-Health containers - This mod might be borderland "unbalancing", but I think it is a nice addition. Sometimes enemies drop health containers that fills up some health.

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is one of the hardest and most punishing games I have ever played. If you do not play tactically, you will be punished for it. Knowledge is the one thing you can take with you between runs and every death will hammer that point into you. This game does not hold your hand and most of the people leaving negative reviews expected it to do so. Noita will play dirty and expect you to use everything you have available to scrape by with a win.The updates are consistently good and change progression in a good way. A new way of healing was just added and I was afraid it would devalue progression but it is hard to obtain and use, so it doesn't overshadow other methods of healing in the game. Health is limited, so the ways you get health are very important. The new liquids are also very interesting. If updates continue at this quality, I expect this game to have a bright future ahead.This game is not for everyone. If you want a laidback experience with low-risk gameplay, this may not be the roguelike for you. Noita is for people who want to test themselves in an incredibly unforgiving world and find community through solving puzzles and finding secrets the world has never seen before. The "true" ending of the game has yet to even be found yet and you may even have a part in finding it.Do you have what it takes to obtain true knowledge?

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game where you will probably spend too much of your time playing. It is a nearly perfect game that is updated frequently enough and of course as it says, every pixel is simulated. It plays like Spelunky had magic and a physics engine. It is very fun and full of secrets. I have all of three problems with this game.1. Once you have beaten the final boss and go to explore the massive world you will soon find that secrets are a bit hard to discover. They are everywhere but the ingame hints are very vague and best. Luckily if you really want to do them you can always look online for solutions2. The game can be slow if your computer is not powerful enough. I have an eighth gen i5 intel CPU and it sometimes has trouble processing everything post final boss as I destroy the simulated world.3. Enemy health scales sometimes to ridiculous heights. They are easy enough to beat if you know what you are doing with wand creation but the game gives no tutorials to make wands. I suggest that you research wand building through youtube or on the Noita wiki if you want to play this game.Other than that I love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun game with a very high replay value. Lots of hidden gimmicks and secrets, lots of combos and lots of fun!Even at its full price it's worth it.Also runs smoothly on Arch Linux without flaws!

_childDocuments_.review: Every Noita run, you will learn and gain something new. It makes a stoic scientist out of you, whilst occasionally sending you into fits of hysterical laughter, disbelief, or rage from witnessing how you died. But then you make a mental note of how you died so that you don't die in the same way next time, and fire up another run. The online Noita community inspires you enter the cave again and again, hoping you'll survive until you can find more interesting spells and wands, or stumble across wand components that synergise in fascinating ways. You learn and tinker with different spell combinations like some alchemist scavenging and salvaging pieces of wands and spells hidden throughout each stage, as you slowly become consumed by the manic thirst for knowledge of the Noita witch itself. This is not a game to binge. Noita is a hobby that is nurtured with time. I found a single typical Noita sitting to last 30 to 90 minutes - I stopped when I found myself rushing through runs and dying. Sometimes I stop playing for a week, but then I come across a Youtube video of some ridiculous Noita stuff so I return for a while. Again, this is not a game to binge, but one to enjoy over a long period of time. Hopefully, one you'll keep on revisiting to have these nice moments too.

_childDocuments_.review: I like roguelites, but something i dislike about this game is how every enemy always has sniper like aim. It feels genuinely unfun that you have to always have peak movement to dodge. For example, I was fully invisible, shot an enemy, and in the .5 seconds it took for my projectile to travel he turned around and took a chunk of my life before it died. Standing still, even with the element of surprise, gets you killed. The spells are interesting, the whole "pixel" system is neat too. There are a great number of secrets and variety of enemies. This could be a great game, but the vanilla version feels like it has some arbitrariness to it. Unlike other roguelites, where I feel like I'm always progress and getting better all the time (both as a player who understands mechanics, and as a character who might unlock more items) in this one I feel like luck is more important than anything else. Once you grasp the mechanics there's not much else to do but hope you get some good wand combinations and enemy spawns that aren't too terrible.  If you aren't constantly playing as carefully as possible, you will die. Despite what I have described as arbitrary difficulty, I recommend people try the game and interact with its mechanics, but don't expect to beat the game anytime soon.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam offered a Neutral review. Noita is interesting, but it has a problem a lot of other roguelikes do not seem to have - stinginess with resources.Noita was recommended to me because I enjoy Roguelikes immensely. I've played and beaten a myriad of them, and never even came close to completing others (such as ADoM) but still enjoy the run. In a good roguelike, from beginning to end, you always have a chance. "The RNG giveth, the RNG taketh away", but there is often a consistency to your resources - Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup is fair with giving you a variety of loot even though it is unforgiving with your fights, FTL is beatable with every starting ship due to a fair run of shops and gear, and the Binding of Isaac gives you at least two items a level. In any of these, even if the run ends badly, you never feel unfairly screwed by the RNG, as resources were available and usable. Making it to the final challenge, even if you fail the final challenge, usually makes me feel satisfied in a roguelike. In Noita, it just made me dread the next run.Noita, by contrast to those listed above, is much more inconsistent. The wand crafting system is astounding, understanding it lets you get further than ever - but the problem is, you need decent wands and some usable spells to get anywhere. This is where Noita falls flat on its face. First, you need to find wands - you can hold up to four at a time. You probably want a wand for killing things, a wand for digging, and a wand that carries some useful utility. So you have one remaining slot for testing new wands and taking along spells, assuming you find any - sometimes, after clearing the entire first level, I found a singular wand that could be reached with my starting bomb wand. Oh well - maybe we'll find one later? Well, as you go down, many of the wands you find are strictly unusable - they either have a fairly good chance of killing you when cast or end up doing next to nothing because the spells are chained in a nonsensical manner. "That is alright," you, a clever wand crafter, claims. "I will simply fix the wand!" Well, about that...You can only edit wands in the Holy Mountain between levels (barring a perk you can get), and therefore only remove spells from wands for later use in the Holy Mountain. The Holy Mountain offers a small selection of either wands or spells - but with the wide variety of spells, it is unlikely that any of them will be helpful for putting together a good wand for your continuing progression. But maybe you'll find a spell that could make your damage wand a death machine. Do you have the money for it? You see, gold disappears after a little while (barring picking up a perk). The curve for buying items from level to level gets a little high, but enemy health increases multiplicatively, so beyond about the third area, if you cannot buy that nice Lightning Bolt you found, and you don't find any usable resources to avoid having to fight the enemies (wands, or even potions, or perhaps the invisibility perk) you won't be able to kill them in a reasonable timeframe and you will likely miss out on the gold drops, putting you further in the dark - not that half the crap in the Holy Mountains are good anyway.But more importantly, lets say you found two spells that would be useful when combined on two different wands outside the Mountain - as I mentioned above, you probably have one wand slot remaining for carrying and testing wands. So are you going to get rid of that utility wand or your digging wand? Barring circumstances of good fortune, you might not be able to get it back - the Mountains are a one-way trip without spells that can dig through the hard rock of the Mountain or side of the world. But if you have those, you probably are not lacking in resources anymore. The tedious early-game is only punctuated by the lack of usable resources that most seeds have. The curve of enemy health gets absurd in the fourth area - if by the Holy Mountain of the third area you do not have a good wand or fortunate perks, you should simply give up. Your impoverished wizard should simply open the menu, and select "New Game". But if you have resources, then the game and physics engine open up greatly and you can have great fun chasing secrets, exploring the levels, and playing around with the alchemy. The game is very enjoyable during those moments - and then, when you inevitably die, you have tedium rather than fun for the next hour or two. Some people advocate for using mods to fix these sorts of problems - several friends have said "Yeah, beat the game for the achievements and then just mod it to fix it." Various highly subscribed mods offer the perks to edit the wands everywhere or to not have the gold disappear from the start or more ways to get your spells, and the sandbox is very interesting when you have the resources to play with it. However, I do not feel that excuses the inconsistency of the base game at all and the tedium that inconsistency brings. Many roguelikes respect my time and do good work to put tedium by the wayside by offering a variety of resources from early on - I would never mind having Yet Another Stupid Death if the game wasn't a miserly thing.As it is, I don't want to dissuade anyone from the absolute blast of a physics engine and the amazing wand crafting. Just be aware - Noita does not respect your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Went to the left instead of the mines because I knew there was interesting stuff over there.Climbed the side of the mountain to get a mysterious egg.Used all of my bombs and blew holes in the bottom to drain the water and climb up to snag another mysterious item.Get attacked by a worm that's burrowing through the level and destroying terrain.Escape the worm and get attacked by a cloud of eyes throwing acid that destroys the world.Somehow kill all of the eyes and survive.Go back and follow the worm tunnels.Enter the Abandoned Mine with all sorts of nasty creatures including more acid monsters.Get knocked down to 2 HP.Find the corpse of the worm, uncertain how it died.Kill a dozen enemies to keep surviving, being as cautious as possible.Go to pick up a Flask of Water next to a friendly little frog. _childDocuments_.review: Noita, as it currently stands, is one of the most unforgiving masterpieces I've experienced; now, I've experienced many games I would consider to be masterpieces, but nothing as brutally unforgiving as Noita.Noita has you play as a witch, but doesn't actually give you a task; Although there are goals with which you can achieve, you're never told what these goals are, nor are you handed any objectives, instead you have to think about what you want to do and then find a way to achieve it.When you first appear in the world, you're standing in front of a cave entrance with some boulders in and around, these display carvings that serve as instructions on how to control your character, Mina; and with that, that's all the instruction you will ever get (kind of), you will receive instructions throughout but unlike those in the beginning, they're often designed to be cryptic, they exist for you to figure out.As you head further into this cave, you'll begin to come across some bad guys, and although what you see appear feral, or overly hostile, or even grotesque, that's nothing compared to what's to come. A lot of enemies in the beginning can be dispatched with ease, but don't ever become overconfident, because they may be able to see you when you can't see them, and they have the reaction time of a computer.Noita contains a fog of war, effectively covering up everything you can't see unless you've been to an area before, and so if a bad guy is in this fog of war, it can catch you off-guard without warning; in order to stand a good chance of surviving down below, one must move slowly, consider the possibilities, and take caution; make sure you're well equipped as well.Moving onto your means of atta... Defence, you have wands, and each want will have varying stats that can make them better or worse, along with a number of slots; you see, each wand can effectively be "programmed" with spells, placing spells into these slots can yield different outcomes depending on which order the spells are cast; you can also apply modifiers to your spells to produce entirely different outcomes. Learning to program your wands will give you a leap toward winning, but don't forget to practise caution as even your own spells may hurt you depending on what they are.Overall Noita is a game about trial and error; when I began playing, I had already seen a few streams of it, but never truly understood what was happening; I've seen other who have watched countless videos and streams on Noita who have gone on to "win" within their first few attempts; and I've heard of some who have gone in blind, attempting to discover everything on their own, even without help from the Wiki, but no matter how you choose to play, just remember that death is a major part of this game.You are going to die, and respawn, and have to start over right from the beginning, and each time it happens, you'll know what not to do the next time you're down in the depths. Keep on trying, and keep on advancing.

_childDocuments_.review: Middle-earth: Shadow of War is an action role-playing video game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. It is the sequel to 2014's Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor, and was released worldwide for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One on October 10, 2017. While it is possible to use any old Orc to get your required tasks done, both the Middle-earth: Shadow of War Epic and Legendary Orcs are equipped with traits that make them considerably tougher fighters. You are restricted in recruiting Orcs up to your current level and no higher, so if your current squad isn't doing the business, then adding in some higher-tier Orcs to replace them is an excellent way to give your armies the extra boost needed to assault or defend those fortresses. There are several ways to get Middle-earth: Shadow of War Epic and Legendary Orcs, with some of them proving more reliable than others, so we've put together the various methods of recruiting these powerful soldiers below. This one is a no-brainer. As you adventure through Mordor, you're going to run into a ton of Orc Captains, and some of them will be Epic or Legendary. What rarity Orcs spawn at is out of your hands, but it's worth tracking down these warriors and claiming them as your own. Most of the time higher tier Orcs will have some immunities and strengths that your run of the mill captains don't. When hunting an Epic or Legendary Orc, it's worth tracking down a Worm to find out more information on your target so you can be prepared. For example, if you're a player that prefers to fight from range, it's definitely a good thing to know if an Orc is immune to arrows. This is the cheapest way to get Orcs, and it's not too hard, but you also can't predict when an Epic or Legendary Orc will spawn. You can hack and slash through the regular captains in an area and wait until more rise to take their place, but there's no guarantee one will be the Orc you're looking for.All in all it's a bad game.

_childDocuments_.review: Noita is a very refreshing and unique take on roguelites and in my opinion, one of the best.The physics and wand crafting system alone makes this game nearly infinitely replayable.The sheer amount of spells and combinations you can make is ridiculous.The world is massive and filled with crazy secrets and bosses to discover.It has workshop support, is very well optimized, AND it's cheap!What more could you want?

_childDocuments_.review: My view on Noita will not be supported by most, but i think it's important for people to know.Noita is not a "game" game. It's a tech demo.Is it technically very impressive? Yes, it most definitely is! It's an absolute amazing piece of tech that's neatly folded into a rogue like type of experience, but don't be fooled. I'm not calling it a game on purpose.This is the reason i'm not reccomending it. 20 bucks for a tech-demo is just too much.Why is it no roguelike-game?And i could go on... but i won't.I don't want to bash the developers or anything, as i said, it's a mighty impressive tech-demo. I'm really looking forward to what they'll do with this tech, when they can use this engine and actually focus on the "game" part of the experience and focus on a fun experience.If they can add "Hades" type of progression to a game like this, with some minor explanations as to how things work, this would be f'in amazing.Give me the tools i need to beat it, and i will beat it no matter how hard it is, but shroud the tools in mystery and give a "bang head against wall" type of progression and it loses all it's fun. At least, for me.- inb4 GIT GUD kiddo's join in.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a peak (a peek and a pinnacle, really) of true insanity. Just when you think you've delved into the deepest depths and explored the most ridiculous recesses of it's madness, you find out that there's even more lurking beneath. It is hard, it will absolutely break your balls. But it's also beautiful in it's intricacy, giving you freedom to experiment, combine, and synergize different pieces together to make the most catastrophic monster of a spell your brain can imagine. And you're gonna have to do so if you want to see what's waiting behind the walls which hold the parallel dimensions of the universe together. No, by the way, that's not an exaggeration. name: Beyond Blue
detailed_description: Beyond Blue is a single-player narrative adventure that takes you deep into our planet’s beating blue heart. Set in the near future, Beyond Blue explores the mysteries of our ocean through the eyes of Mirai, a deep-sea explorer and scientist. Become a part of a newly-formed research team using groundbreaking technologies to see, hear, and interact with the ocean in a more meaningful way than has ever been attempted. Features: Throughout eight different dives you'll explore the untouched world of our ocean and use technology at the edge of our understanding - tracking sea creatures, unraveling mysteries, and interacting with the ocean like never before Experience an evocative narrative with full voice cast - Anna Akana (YouTube), Mira Furlan (Lost, Babylon 5), Hakeem Kae-Kazim (Black Sails, Hotel Rwanda), and Ally Maki (Toy Story 4) Listen to a captivating and entertaining soundtrack featuring an original score and music from Miles Davis, The Flaming Lips, The Edisons, and more Unlock sixteen unique mini-documentaries called Ocean Insights that feature original footage and interviews with science’s leading ocean experts Take beautiful pictures to share using the brand new Photo Mode , featuring dozens of filters, lens settings, and more Embracing the same inclusive development process that was used to create Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna), E-Line’s BAFTA award-winning game about Alaska Native culture, the company partnered with BBC Studios (developers of the acclaimed Blue Planet II), OceanX Media, world-class game makers, and some of science’s leading ocean experts to craft an experience that reflects the awesome wonder and unbounded mystery that infuses our planet’s beating blue heart.

_childDocuments_.review: There was a lot of effort put into the realism and authenticity of this game. The experience reminds me of the old Endless Ocean series for the Wii. The game is fun, enjoyable, relaxing, and enriching to experience. The music is also incredible and I will no doubt be spending some time in the sub to just listen to it. The voice acting is incredible as well.However, I do have a few issues with the game. Nothing major or deal breaking, this game is exactly what it is advertised as: an educational and enjoyable experience. And yet, I felt that there was too little content. While the content that is present shines, the lack of more dive locations and story was hard to miss. I feel like there could have been so much more the game could have had.Thus, I would like to ask the developers to please consider a sequel to this game at some point in the future. It made me realize just how much I missed learning about the ocean through video game format, and I would love to experience it more.
