_childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue is a game that was awaited by many people, who have a deep love for oceans. However, your expectations are at the core of how you will perceive this project in its release form. Chances are high, you will feel like you've bought an aquarium screensaver from the 2000-s.If you wanted something for pure relaxation - get it. The graphics are pleasing and the models of animals and surroundings are well-done. There are no brain-wrecking quests, so it will serve you as an interactive aquarium to take your mind off.If you wanted something more - oh well, oh well... The storyline starts just fine, but feels rushed by the end. Most of the subplots have been abruptly cut, so when I saw the epilogue cutscene after just 2 hours, I was surprised. The story of the sperm whales, miners, and pretty much everything else contributes nothing at all to the story. Besides, the dialogues (that feel frankly artificial) and half of the voice-acting don't help either.Scanning (and identification in particular) is another part of this game, which had a huge potential that's been lost somewhere. Identification is one of the things moving the sperm whales storyline, but considering that all the animal models and textures are the same, you won't feel any difference between finding whale A12 and whale A7, for example. Therefore, there's not much interest in scanning every single creature unless you want to have 30/30 achievements.Exploration is definitely not the strongest part of this game either. The locations themselves are quite small and barely have any landmarks worth finding. Most species don't interact with the environment at all.I will get back to Beyond Blue as I love oceans; and spending another relaxing hour in this blue world sounds like a good idea to me. But I can't say I would recommend it to anyone, who has gameplay and story-driven project at the top of their gaming priorities.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A must play for casual gaming, on the surface Beyond Blue is an underwater exploration game. But, the story, the collections of fish, videos, and music and the immersion in the Science of the underwater research teams make the experience much more. The music is refreshing and full of energy as well. The gameplay is entirely peaceful. No death, no survival, and no collecting of resources to progress is really required. Certain story objectives appear in each dive, and accomplishing those triggers the end of each dive. While doing those objectives, you swim around scanning all the fish for your collections. But, after completing all the dives, you will be able to free dive in every location at will to find all the fish you still need. So, it is really very relaxing. I don't think the choice questions changed very much in the way of the story. I noticed that you could replay each conversation in the captains chair of the sub, and make different choices, potentially changing the story I suppose. But, I didn't try that out. In a way, this reminded me of the relaxing experience of collecting seashells as a child. But, it is enjoyable for gamers of all ages.If you enjoy underwater exploration and casual games, then this is a great choice. Total play time depends on how much time you spend playing all the music tracks and videos, looking at the fish and their behaviors in your collection, and swimming around in the water. I spent about 12 hours in the game with all that. But, the achievements took about 10 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Endless Ocean franchise, it literally took 5 seconds of footage for me to be convinced into buying this game.What I liked:- The beautiful graphics - The realistic animation of wildlife - Free diving mode that is unlocked after completing the story- Controls were easy to learn - The mini documentaries- Endless Ocean like fish catalog where you can unlock new species upon scanning them- Deep sea diving locations were especially interesting What could have been improved upon:- I personally did not care too much about the story. I simply wanted to swim around among the wildlife studying it in awe.- You can only zoom in specific story related animals (mostly whales)- Lack of different species, especially notable with bottom crawlers (shellfish, sea cucumbers, etc.) and plant life- No gulper eels (my personal favorite fish and one of the most bizarre looking animals on the planet )- While most of the animals were excellently animated some like the tubeworms and the starfish were just plain 3d models. I can't help but to compare this to Abzû where even the smallest of sea life was skittering on the seafloor.That all being said Endless Ocean 2 Blue World still holds the crown as the greatest ocean exploration game ever made.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue can definitely be beautiful, watching all the different kinds of sealife go by in the underwater enviroments. However, that only gets you so far in terms of actually having fun with the game. In Beyond Blue, I more often than not feel forced into doing boring busywork. Scanning the sealife, taking samples, picking up or placing beacons, etc... All while having to slooowly swim from A to B to C. The scanning sealife bits can be cool in certain cases, but this too just gets overdone at a certain point. Not to mention the rather infuriating controls of the 'zoom scan drone'.As for the story, there's no real overarching thing here but still, it's mostly as interesting and even emotional as the visuals are. But it's also quite short and, at least for me, the entirety still isn't captivating or interesting enough to compensate for its gameplay.I like and respect the idea of the game, and the sealife looks . But overall it's much more of a visual experience rather than a game. There were many parts where I lost the want to play because most of the objectives just felt like one big chore to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: As a marine biologist myself, I can only recommend this game. While it seeks to educate and even includes several optional small insights from Blue Planet II, it also offers a relaxing and beautiful underwater experience. It's truly a joy to just swim around and explore wonderful oceanic regions, such as an atoll, the open ocean, and even the deep sea. Marine biologists were involved as advisors and it clearly shows, such as the current oceanic issues the game brings up, which adds to the realism this game offers.If you want a great diving experience while learning about the ocean along the way, then this game is for you. However, if you seek another Endless Ocean, or even an artistic game like ABZÛ, you should pass on this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I always liked animals quite a lot, whether it's in real life or in-game. Whilst there are a lot of  farming games about animals, I would say it's rare to come across a game that revolves around those that reside in the ocean. All the games I played before, that implemented fish, were only the ones where I could fish for different kinds of marine creatures, although it is nowhere the same experience as swimming through their natural habitat with them. Lucky for me, Beyond Blue fulfilled my wish through and through and I could finally experience the beautifulness of the ocean with all its residents without actually having to go underwater in real life.Mirai is a female deep-sea explorer and scientist who became part of a recently founded research team with new but useful technology. Thanks to its help, they can see, hear, and even interact with the marine creatures in the ocean they are exploring. Whilst Mirai is the only one going underwater, she loves observing her whales, although a few problems are coming up along with the worrisome fact that a few species are close to extinction.Beyond Blue doesn't contain a breathtaking story, yet it still connects just well with the tasks and happenings in-game. And so, Mirai hosts live streams, where she shows her viewers the natural habitat of her beloved whales, or just has to look for lost items such as trackers. I kind of liked the personal touch of Beyond Blue as the story isn't only about the expedition of the cast but her own story gets explained as well as some family drama that takes place between the exploration of the beautiful ocean which spiced it up. However, I wouldn't say that the plot is the most appealing part of this game.Admittedly, I judged a book by its cover in this case and straight out expected a typical survival game underwater where the character might have to get some fresh air once in a while or at least avoid getting eaten by dangerous species underwater. However, this wasn't the case at all with Beyond Blue, as this game is solely about exploring the ocean. That means the player can just take their time and visit every corner of the ocean without having to worry about dying at all, as it's not possible in this game. Although there are still dangerous animals appearing throughout the game during Mirai's exploration, they are all peaceful and won't hurt her.As aforementioned, the exploration of the ocean is the main theme of this game. There is a short tutorial at the beginning that explains its player everything they need for spotting the suspicious noises as well as scanning the marine creatures thanks to the advanced technology. As the player is diving through the ocean, they can scan all sorts of creatures they come across. Completionists will have a lot of fun, as they can look for all animals to add them to their digital collection and can read more about them in a science log.There are eight different dives available that work like chapters. The game changes back and forth between the underwater and submarine sections, although the latter only gets visited after completing a dive. In the submarine, the player can either take care of calls or listen to voicemails that are required to continue the story. Additionally, when visiting the submarine, I noticed that various objects, such as books or pictures, differ each time.  Even though there isn't a lot I could do with them besides examining them, there is a radio available all the time where I could choose what I wanted to listen to between a few set tracks.Beyond Blue is quite linear, although the player can freely roam around in the ocean for each dive. Something I appreciated was that I could always see on the map where I am supposed to go next so I couldn't get lost. I felt like this feature was necessary for such a kind of game as the player can still freely swim around before taking care of the story elements, yet, completing specific tasks is required before being able to move on to the next one. Although the fetch tasks were not special in this game, I still found it awesome to check out all different marine creatures, especially since I was already familiar with a lot of fish thanks to my experience with prior games that included fishing.After scanning the animals, the player unlocks them in the science log. While being in the submarine, the player can look at their 3D models and even select between different animations, although more are getting unlocked when scanning creatures. Although each species is scannable multiple times, the animal itself can only be scanned so if the player, for instance, encounters the same whale once again they won't be able to examine them again. In addition to that, there is also information available for each species and even documentary videos the player can watch during their stay.Whilst I found it was an interesting feature, I only took a look at a few fish in the beginning but stopped quite soon as I only wanted to start the next dive instead. It might come in handy when the player wants to check one or another animal they're interested in but other than that I didn't want to check every single of them. I was slightly disappointed, as well, that big creatures such as the whales or sharks only had a quite small 3D model and thus, I couldn't admire them in their full form.Now, let's dive into the most appealing part of this game: The graphics. I found that the environment and animals all looked stunning, and I was impressed as it looked a lot better than I expected. It was kind of heartwarming to see the same species swimming together as a swarm, just like I pictured it in real life. The game switches between day and night time, so the dive sessions look different from each other and presented a great ocean that I couldn't help but admire during the tasks I had to take care of and I might have wandered off sometimes because I got distracted by some creatures.One thing that wasn't very pleasant in this game was the character model. During the dives, the main character is covered in her diver's suit, so I couldn't see her anyway. However, once I finished a dive and was in the submarine, I immediately found that she looked quite off, and her face looked emotionless. Luckily, these moments didn't happen often, yet, it sadly had an impact on my immersion.First of all, I loved the soundtracks! They sound relaxing and just fitting to the emotional ocean theme, although I have to admit that during diving, I enjoyed various sounds the bigger creatures, such as dolphins and whales, are making, as well. I never looked into these kinds of sounds before, yet it sounded utterly adorable when I could listen to the fish, well squeaking which made the ocean quite lively at the same time.Beyond Blue is a beautiful exploration game that is somewhat similar to a walking simulator except that it takes place underwater. Whilst the game is very short and can be completed within a couple of hours, I had a lot of joy diving through the ocean and meeting all sorts of creatures on my way of completing different kinds of tasks. However, it should be kept in mind that the story is rather simple, yet revolves around important topics that are still relevant in real life, as well. That being said, Beyond Blue truly is a game that will be enjoyable for any ocean lover and became a quite memorable game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: As a marine scientist who has been cruelly kept away from the ocean by the pandemic, Beyond Blue was an absolutely wonderful experience. A few things require a bit of suspension of belief but by-and-large, this is the closest I've felt to the ocean I love since 2019. The models and animation are extremely well done, and anybody who has spent time in Indo-Pacific reefs will feel at home here. As other reviews point out, the 'story' is questionable (to put it politely). It's great that they've attempted to discuss serious themes like marine pollution, mining, and HABs, but the execution has much to be desired and quickly gets annoying. Fortunately, it is relatively easy to ignore this and once you unlock the free-dive mode after a few hours, you don't have to listen to it any more. If you're looking for an engaging story or gameplay, look for something else. But if you're looking for the closest you can get to swimming in a reef without actually getting underwater, this is it. I loved it!
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended with caveats.1) If you are looking at this wondering if it's like Subnautica - it's not.2) If you are looking at this wondering if the game is like ABZÛ - it's not.If you are looking for something that is high-action, high energy, high drama, high danger- you are in the wrong place.It is a beautiful underwater grindy walking-sim. Except you are swimming.It's a very chill game that can be very frustrating at times.There is a story- it's somewhat shallow- there was room to go into the different parts of the story more deeply.And if you hate pro-environmental activism or messaging- walk away now. This is very much a game for environmentalists h who enjoy educational material mixed with a somewhat relatable fictional story.Help save the whales. Help save the sea turtles. If you are cool with that- maybe you'll appreciate the story.The music is good, with some really awesome tracks you can choose to play while on your submarine. The art is beautiful, but has some issues with clipping and occasional blobby/melty rendering in really busy areas.The controls- well, they kinda suck. Both kb/m and controller feel clunky or awkward. And the camera controls are awful in certain situations (using the manta drone to scan creatures in particular). And the character's walking animations on the sub are stiff and jerky. The diving/swimming animations are much smoother, but there are times where you bump into invisible walls or get hung up on terrain that it feels like you should be able to glide over smoothly.The game runs fine, but is not optimized as well as it could be, IMHO, There are numerous instances of flashing lights and quick lighting changes that could cause issues for people with Epilepsy or other light-induced neurological conditions.For people with vision problems and color-blindness- there are quite a few areas where a lack of contrast may make details hard to distinguish, may cause headaches, or may be really hard to see due to the color palettes used.  The map in particular- targets on the full map are pale orange circles on a light blue-turquoise background. There is no option to change map colors to make it easier to see, even for people with perfect vision. This was an issue for me, and I can usually see low-contrast colors fairly well. Poor design choice for the full map.You will need both hands to play this game- whether kb/m or controller. Both feel awkward and clunky. I do not have an Adaptive Controller set-up to test it on, so I can't say how the game will be using one, but I suspect the controls will still feel very awkward unless you have a very (expensive) specialized set up,There really are no puzzles to solve, just targets to find and scan or collect, which can be tedious.There are some distressing subjects being dealt with involving dementia, death, inter-personal relationships, and industrial waste and destruction of the planet. Emotional triggers that might be painful for some people, that may not be mitigated by the hopeful moments and successes in the game..********************************************************************************All that said- yes, it is beautiful, and has a lot of good educational material. It is pretty chill and slow-paced. I am enjoying it, but not as much as I had hoped to- mainly because of the controls and the totally wonky camera during certain activities. I will finish the game up, and will recommend it for people looking for something slow and grindy, but chill- walking sim enjoyers, basically. I would say get it at a significant discount. Though I appreciate the educational value, and the message of the story, the sloppy controls and wonky camera make it impossible to recommend at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue is more an educational tool than a game.Inspired by BBC's Blue Planet 2 documentary,the game is simple down-to-Earth walking simulator in realistic to marine life ocean.There are so few decent atmospheric underwater games:while ABZU is pure art, SUBNAUTICA is "horror" survival.Beyond Blue takes the realism niche.It can be completed in 2-5 hours (ignore my 18hrs, I fell asleep) and the price even at discount seems a bit much (especially as none of it goes towards marine life preservation...)Decent product.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I've read some reviews on other platforms where people have stupidly believed this game is similar to Subnautica...and as such they think this game is boring. Two completely different games.It's an exploration science game really, made obvious by it's trailer and synopsis. In that regards, here is what I liked about it:1) The graphics are very smooth, the creatures on offer all look very good and the environments are nice and crisp. No performance issues either.2) Swimming in the sea is very calming, I'm the kind of gamer that has spent hours playing No Man's Sky for simple reason - it's very relaxing to just mindlessly swim/fly somewhere with pretty background music.3) As a science game, you get the chance to learn things about underwater creatures and unlockable documentaries allow you to get invested in the ocean.However its not perfect and for me, as an exploration game i would want more.1) Small selection of creatures. 47 animals on one map may be fine for some, but considering the ocean is one of the most densely populated areas in the world I would have expected more. 2) I would have liked for them to have more diving maps around the world, but at £15 its not much of a criticism, more of a suggestion as potential DLC.3) The story isn't necessary. Too be honest, a game like this doesn't need a story. People playing this will have an understanding on what the game is, theyre not expecting heavy narrative decision making. They just wanna find fish. Taking the story out completely may have opened up more map options, and maybe customising suits or your sub. Overall I liked it. After 5.5 hours I'm done. It's a pretty, fun little game that just lacks meat. I would be interested in potential DLC content because I would definitely dive back in. As it stands, there isn't much incentive to free dive continuously once you've discovered all the species. I would recommend it for anyone who loves the ocean.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I won this game in a giveaway, but I was not required to review it or promote it in any way.I feel like this game is for a niche audience, and I happened to be part of it. It's more of an experience than a traditional game and has an emphasis on being educational. It can also be 100%'d in under 4 hours (and I play at a relaxed pace), so  keep that in mind.It's absolutely beautiful and calming and does manage to teach a fair amount. I love to take a break from my more "standard" games and chill out in games like this, with bonus points if it's teaching about a subject I love. Its main two draws are its relaxing atmosphere, allowing you to swim freely with all sorts of beautiful sea creatures, and its educational side, which includes short videos from marine specialists, as well as allowing the player to learn more about a creature simply by encountering and scanning it, letting you play a bit of a biologist yourself. This is honestly a wonderful example of how a game could be a teaching tool; it's certainly more engaging than a textbook, and students would likely be learning without even noticing!It does also have a story to it, and frankly the human side fell flat on me. But the whales' story? That fully drew me in. I won't spoil it, but you're following a specific pod throughout the game, and it gets more emotional than you might anticipate.So basically, pick this game up if you want a calm break from your other games, or you're the type of person who loves animal documentaries (like me!) and would love a safe way to feel like you're part of one. Just be aware that it's quite short and the only replay value you'll have is swimming in set areas (it's not a big, open world) and looking at/photographing sea creatures.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - This is not a regular game, it's an educational game.  It's decent on its own merits, at least on sale.  There are spoilers ahead.So here's the deal: there isn't much "game" in this game.  You follow a series of objectives until you reach the end, none of the objectives are all that difficult.  Once the game is done you can re-visit old dive locations.  If you're crazy for completing Steam achievements you can 100% this game in four hours or less.  If you're looking for serious gameplay you should pick up another deep-sea game such as Subnautica, Abzu, or Aquaria.Likewise, there isn't much "story" in this game's story.  The protagonist was raised a diver, loves sperm whales, and works with OceanX to follow a pod while collecting and tagging things on a worldwide livestream.  The protagonist also has a sister having trouble in school and a grandmother dying from dementia.  The resolution to both tangled storylines is in an epilogue cutscene.  It didn't feel satisfying, but that may have been part of the point: it's about life as a marine biologist, with emphasis on "life."That's really what this game is: it educates you on marine biology and the lifestyle it involves.  You unlock short videos of real-life marine biology researchers explaining things you see in the game, and scanning all of the wildlife unlocks information about these creatures that is (presumably) completely factual.  For those looking into some manner of aquatic career this would be a handy introduction, especially if you can overlook the quirky stuff (no oxygen tanks, being able to dive 4000m below sea level, having an infrared light that does nothing, etc.).In terms of being gorgeous: the game is absolutely stunning.  Beautiful dive locations and background music pair together to make a serene environment you could almost get lost in, at least if it wasn't for the predefined area of each biome.  Even with that limitation it's obvious the devs put a lot of care into fleshing out this region of the sea.I personally enjoyed this experience, brief as it was, and after realizing that one of the four voiced characters was Mira Furlan it hit me differently.  Life goes on, and people we admire are gone.  But even I do have a mild regret of paying full price for this experience.  If it goes on sale it's more worth it.  Ultimately, though, it is worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately I can not recomend this game. Such a letdown to be honest.- No exploration (there are no landmarks to see)If you want quality level design, like sunken ships and such, play Maneater.- Frustratingly tiny maps, dives are very limited- Lazy level fidelity. Almost no floral variation. Kelp? Nope, Corals? Nope, Only Rocks and some grass. Mobile game roots are showing.- Minimal selection of animals, no interaction possible. - There is no active eco system, just fish props in a void- Annoyingly whiny eco-warrior plot (Humans = bad, Greenpeace is good etc.)
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed going through the game. I like the fact you can explore on your own, there is also a story and plenty of extra material so you can learn more about the ocean. The graphics are pretty awesome, the music and sound set the right tone to the entire atmosphere. Hell, there is even a mode where you can take a picture and edit it. However, one thing that I cannot get over and it irritated me throughout the gameplay was the voice acting... It is the most annoying thing I have heard in a long time. And trust me it is terrible. It is like listening to teenage valley California girls talking about the most irrelevant stuff ever (although they talk about quite important issues in the actual game). After 2 hours I wanted to shoot myself in the head to not hear these voices ever again, luckily for me, the story line was about to end. I give the developers props for trying to make the story telling entertaining.Overall, it is a  worth your time and money. It consists of 30 achievements, some of which can be very time consuming, and counts towards game collector badge. Trading cards for this game do not exist.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue is a chill and relaxing diving game with some story.Gameplay is very basic but the game delivers a very satisfying experience and some interesting story. You dive into the ocean and explore the area. There are few areas to explore. Each one has story objectives which usually require you to scan the sea life around and some objects. Once you're done with that you can go back to your sub/ship where you can listen to music and watch video logs. It's also the place where you talk to other characters using a phone.There are two stories going on. One is related to the ocean life and its safety, pollution of the ocean. A lot of stuff is explained through real videos which you unlock by doing activities underwater. Those are real life videos presented as documentary. It's a pretty educational game.Another part of the story is personal family story which is fine but nothing special.The game is very relaxing, no hard gameplay sections or time limits or anything. Also after completing the story you can dive into each area and just explore. It's a good time to go for missing achievements then.Controls can be a bit annoying sometimes but nothing too bad since there's no rush. Collectibles also are marked on the map but it's very subtle so look closely.Graphically the game looks very good. Underwater areas are pretty small but look amazing. Just sit back, relax and enjoy. Sea life also looks great and highly detailed for an indie game.There's a photo mode which allows you to take some awesome screenshots.Sound design is good too. Voice acting is alright and being underwater feels immersive.It's a good game for those who likes relaxing games and cherish nature. It delivers a message and provides entertainment while being educating.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: The "story" isn't exactly a story. I was really hoping this would fill the void of Endless Ocean and Endless Ocean 2:Blue World, however I was a bit underwhelmed. I think there is potential here, with more story and different missions, but the final product was a bit lackluster. It still is beautiful (the underwater parts, at least) but I wish there were more areas, species, and interactions you could have with the animals you encounter. I find these kind of educational underwater games can be enthralling, but this fell a little bit short. If anything, I hope I helped a great cause, there did seem to be a lot of care put into this game, I just wish they went a bit further. I look forward to updates, but for now, it feels like an incomplete experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game! I personally don't care for the family drama portion of the story, but the game play itself is amazing! You can swim up to sharks, Orcas, GIANT SQUID, Angler Fish, etc., without the fear of harm coming to your character. There is no bad guy you have to fight. The game is literally a scan and explore game. You don't have to gather resources/supplies and build tools, structures, etc. If you watch all of the videos, you do get an achievement for it FYI. You can play this sober, drunk, or high and still have a good time. Also, if you don't like the music she plays in her sub, you can turn the sub music down to zero because otherwise you have to mute it every time you enter the sub. All in all, it's a pretty great game. My only complaint is that you can't go back and visit the other parts of the objectives, as it only goes with what you choose and you can't visit the other option once you've made your decision. Devs, if you're reading this, please make this a thing!*Addon* Devs, the game reset some of my progress, which is super frustrating! Also, I should have everything scanned, yet it now says that I don't. Please fix this, as it's impossible to find fish when they don't show up on any of the maps! Also, if we have like one more fish in a group to scan, please mark that fish (especially if they swim in groups like the baby turtles, as I can't tell which ones I've scanned the tag and which ones I have not)!
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: The developers could learn a lot from playing the Endless Ocean series on Wii. I know they were trying to go for educational game here, but they forgot the "game" part. There is absolutely no reward for playing this game, except for the visuals, which I admit are pretty well done. The story and gameplay though... Yeesh. A few things that would make this better: 1. An element of danger... Every species, and there aren't very many of them, completely ignore the player. Even the sharks in the game bump into you like brainless robots. I think the Endless Ocean series did this best by pulling you out of the ocean and back to land when you got too close to dangerous animals. If I remember correctly, it gave you fair warning, then bam! dive over.  The sharks don't have to eat you, but maybe make it difficult to scan them or make them hard to get around. 2. Make scanning rewarding... I've completed the entire story (in less than 4 hours) and I still don't see any reason to scan a species more than once. I know that you can unlock Blue Planet clips, but I've already seen the Blue Planet series and if you're playing this game you probably have too. Maybe if you complete all the scans of a certain species you unlock something that changes the game? Like a new suit, faster swim mechanics, new equipment that changes how you're able to explore, etc. 3. Kill the sub... This game is about diving with sea animals. Why am I spending time on the sub listening to the developers horrible taste in music? Let me learn more about the species that I'm diving with WHILE I'm diving. Don't make me go back to the sub to do that. And if you want me to spend time on the sub, entice me with things to do on the sub, don't just use it as a means to progress the absolutely horrible story line. 4. Kill the scan view... I played this entire game with the scan view turned on because.... You guessed it! This game is about scanning sea life. Unfortunately, the scan view has this weird dithered pattern around the edges that gives you tunnel vision and obstructs your view causing you to miss out on what is happening in your peripheral vision. I found myself popping off scan view temporarily just so I could see what was going on around me, then quickly popping it back on. Developers, just incorporate scanning into the non-scanning view. 5. What's with the different colored flashlight... I found out in the last 15 minutes of the game that you can change the color of your flashlight. Regular, black light, red light, something else, and turned off. You press 'Y' on the controller to change your light. Don't know why you would though, because it basically does nothing. How about, if you change the flashlight color, you are able to pick up animals/objects that you wouldn't normally see? Like, make them near-invisible until I use the red light. That would cause me to explore the small maps using the red light to make sure I uncovered everything (and if I uncover everything, give me something for it>see point 2 above). 6. You don't need a map.... I didn't use the map once. There is no reason to use it because the game force-feeds you way points the whole time. Just point yourself towards the whale icon and swim. In Endless Ocean animals that were know to stay around a certain area were shown on the map in that area (RDR2 does this with wildlife). First, make scanning rewarding (see point 2 again), then make me use the map to find the animals I need to scan. 7. Don't waste money on music licensing... This game, no joke, gives you an ipad-like device that just controls the music in your sub. You are not going to like being on the sub in the first place, you are really not going to like being on the sub if you're forced to listen to crap music. I used the ipad every time I was on the sub...to turn off the autoplaying music. Who is coming on to the sub and turning it back on when I am diving anyway?I appreciate what the developers tried to do here. Taking care of our oceans is a worthwhile cause, but you can educate the people about that issue while letting us play an engaging game.For anyone else still reading. Go find a way to play Endless Ocean for the Wii. You won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Experiencing the completion of the main storyline in the game is truly wonderful. Upon finishing the narrative, you unlock the captivating Free-Dive mode, the game offers a delightful Photo Mode, providing an excellent platform for creating stunning screenshots.In Free-Dive mode, players can select from a diverse range of eight unique dives, each set in expansive maps teeming with a rich variety of ocean life. It's a remarkable experience that brings you as close as possible to the sensation of actually swimming in the ocean. The attention to detail and the vastness of the underwater environments make Free-Dive mode a truly immersive and enjoyable extension of the gaming experience. Whether you're a fan of underwater exploration or simply appreciate the beauty of marine life, this mode offers a fulfilling and visually stunning way to engage with the game. It's an aspect that adds significant depth and replay value to the overall gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve always had a fascination with the ocean. I had no idea there were games that actually had you diving and doing research until I found Endless Ocean on the Wii as a kid. I absolutely loved that game and have been looking for similar games since then. Beyond Blue is exactly what I was looking for! It's been many years since I’ve had the joy of playing Endless Ocean but from what I’ve played so far, Beyond Blue blows that game out of the water! The modern gameplay and graphics are beautiful! It's also great to not have to deal with forced motion controls, haha! I’m super excited (and a tad terrified) to start diving into the deeper and darker parts of the ocean to experience more of what this game has to offer.Scanning marine life for more info is wonderful, fun, and relaxing. HOWEVER, I suffer from some bad motion sickness and the zoom in for scanning is a bit much for me while moving around. I would love to get a setting that drops the zoom in while scanning. I can only play this for about 30mins at a time before I have to step away. Besides that, I love this game and if you love Endless Ocean or Subnautica and want a more relaxed underwater experience, this game is for you!

_childDocuments_.review: + Absolutely gorgeous atmosphere+ Catching narrative + A lot of cognitive information and videos about the ocean and its creatures+ The game is not afraid to talk about ocean pollution and its species’ extinction+ A set of educational and informational videos + Professional voice acting + A perfect game to chill in after a bad day- A bit awkward model of the protagonist- The story of the protagonist and her family doesn’t unfold that much- The game itself is not long and can be completed in 3 hours maximumIt’s always great to see the games where the player can clearly see the help of professionals during the development. It will be safe to say that Beyond Blue is a perfect example of what I am talking about - the developers teamed up with scientists, marine biologists, and with a crew of a few pretty popular BBC documentaries to create this game. The main goal of this game was to draw public attention to the problem of the ocean’s pollution and the extinction of its creatures. So Beyond Blue it’s not only a short entertainment and an atmospheric game, but it’s also a pretty good way to learn something new about the ocean and its problems. I can’t guarantee that players will know everything about the ocean after this experience, but what I know for sure that this game can surely stir up the interest of the players to get to know the ocean. The game comes with a short story about Mirai, a professional marine biologist who dedicated her life exploring the ocean, learning about its creatures, and researching the behavior of dolphins, whales, and other ocean species. Mirai has a small team and they came up with a pretty interesting idea of streaming every dive into the internet so people could watch it live. It sounds a bit weird and not realistic, but it’s the game, after all. Beyond Blue also tells us a touching story about Mirai’s family through the short phone calls that she can make from her pod between the dives. These calls help us to understand the difficult relationships between Mirai and her sister and this adds some extra charm to the game. The gameplay is presented as a third-person diving simulator, where the player has a chance to experience eight different dives in different locations. To begin with the mission during the dive, Mirai goes to the buoy that shows her the location of needed creatures and once the player touches it, the map shows them from one to three marks on the map of the current goal. When Mirai reaches one of them, she has to scan them to gather the needed information about this creature and this allows her and her team to continue their research. It’s interesting that after finding the specific creature, Mirai can launch the drone to have a closer look at this creature. I have to say that the level of the details they put on the design of these creatures is simply outstanding. The player can explore the whole creature from every possible view for future research.Every single dive has a different vibe and atmosphere in it. One of them is set during the early morning, the other one happens in the afternoon and there is also diving in the evening, where the player can also see a beautiful sunset from the underwater perspective.To progress with the story, the player has to reach different waypoints on the map, to gather all the needed samples and information and then move on to the next dive. After that, the player can freely explore the ocean, scanning all those fishes, whales, dolphins, and even sharks. Speaking of sharks, I really enjoyed that the developers busted that myth regarding sharks being dangerous, killing people at the first sight and being extremely dangerous - Mirai swims side to side to small and bigger sharks freely and this is a beautiful experience.Mirai streams her dives online for the big auditory with the help of her team and they always continue to comment on everything that’s going on and why they are exactly doing all these dives. So the player always knows their main goal and all those dives make sense. There is a small submarine, where Mirai can rest and prepare herself for the next dive session. This place is actually a so-called hub of the game, where the player can check some of the personal stuff, listen to the music that Mirai prefers to listen to, and call her team to talk about the results of her previous dive and the job that still has to be done. Mirai can also call her sister and this is where the game adds a little bit of drama, showing us their pretty specific relationship and the family problems they have there. However, this story has not unfolded that much and I am still not sure why they added this storyline, sometimes it felt like they did only to fill the space. The saddest part of the game is that it’s pretty short in terms of a story, the game can be completed in one session, a little bit more than three hours. After that, the game can be used as a meditation tool, where the player can dive in for a few hours just to chill, enjoy the environment, and scan everything on the map.When the player finishes each dive, they unlock educational short videos about the ocean and its nowadays problems. So the player can learn a bit more about all the species they’ve met during the game and how we would treat the ocean and the whole planet in general, to save their lives. The game has decent graphics and mild pleasant colors of the water during the dives are really eye-catching. Beyond Blue worked a lot on the design of the ocean and its creatures, so they did not pay too much attention to the human models. As a result, Mirai’s face, which you can see only on the submarine between the dives, looks a bit plastic, without any expressions.  The whole game is filled with different sounds recorded by the real professionals to never lose the feeling that the player really explores the ocean. You can always hear dolphins squeaking, whales moaning, and a lot of different atmospheric sounds during this short adventure. Beyond Blue also has a pleasant background music during the diving and a collection of lyrics tracks that Mirai loves to listen to between her work assignments. Mirai’s team members have been dubbed by professional actors and it’s a pleasure to listen to their conversations.Beyond Blue has a brilliant atmosphere and chilling gameplay with an educational purpose and it’s definitely a great move from the developers. Games like this one let the player pay attention to all the problems that the ocean and our beloved planet have and I truly believe that it’s very important to talk about such things. It’s a shame that the game itself doesn’t last long with its story, but other than that, this game is gorgeous.

_childDocuments_.review: While Beyond Blue has its positive aspects, such as its educational elements, beautiful environment, and relaxing gameplay, its negative points should be considered, particularly if you are looking for a more compelling story, visually stunning experience, or a game with longevity and replayability.- The story is uninteresting and rather underdeveloped. The narrative lacks depth and does not add much in the way of emotional impact. The dialogue is also almost constantly running while you swim around, which can be a bit fatiguing to the ears (or was for me when I just wanted to chill). - Beyond Blue has a rather repetitive gameplay loop with the main mechanics consisting of swimming and scanning, which all becomes monotonous over time as you find no real variety in your findings or rewards. This all leads to a declining lack of engagement and excitement.- The game offers a rather short duration and has limited replay value as what you obtain throughout the game is additional content like short documentary-like videos, descriptions/details/and factoids, etc. -- none of which is exciting to go through and reunlock as the gameplay offers little content.Aside from this, Beyond Blue immerses players in the depths of the ocean to explore and learn about marine life. While it caters to specific aquatic enthusiasts, it didn't quite appeal to my personal taste. The game's focus on education and exploration is commendable, and the simple controls make it easy to navigate and interact with marine creatures in a beautiful environment. The audio design is impressive, with realistic sound effects and excellent voice acting. Although Beyond Blue provides a serene and informative experience, its short duration and limited appeal may not resonate with a broader audience. I can't recommend it as it was just too short of an experience and not one that has struck me as particularly memorable.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s short. I completed the game 100% in 7 hours, which involves scanning every creature in the game, but in that short time you get to see  of beautiful underwater life  take part in a beautiful story as well. Much like Firewatch, Beyond Blue doesn’t exactly end perfectly. Things are a bit murky, as is the water in which you plunge.  Beyond Blue, while set in a not-so-distant future, tries to keep things as real as it can. And they do a great job.In fact, Beyond Blue may be the best game I’ve ever played where the in-game story ties to a  message, and it’s one of immense importance. It’s not something like a life lesson like “believe in yourself” or “the power of friendship”, although fine messages in their own right, but it’s about the tangible and concrete benefits of a healthy and thriving ocean. Most of the dialogue surrounding the marine biology, and the heart-to-heart conversations between the characters feels real. Some of the interactions between the sister and the protagonist feel a bit awkward. But overall, the interactions sound good.The game doesn’t  amazing. It’s just very simple swimming with a “sprint” key and a left and right click, but for an underwater game it controls fine. This is why I categorize this as a bit more of a “walking simulator” than the current tags would lead you to believe. For maybe the most direct comparison that people will understand, this game is even more of a walking simulator than ABZU, which had some light platforming kind of aspects with momentum and rings to hit as you swam. Beyond Blue doesn’t concern itself with that. It’s more about beautiful sights and visual/audible wonder as you are told the story. Playing it is a good experience, though. And you can return to the areas in a level select after the game is over, because you will surely miss some of the cuter and more interesting animals during your initial playthrough. You can also look at the animals in a model viewer and see what some of their “behaviors” look like. It’s a nice add-on!Another thing you can “play” is a series of original videos made concerning the oceans, marine biology, marine conservation, and other related topics. They’re beautifully made and really cool to see in a video game! I’ve never really experienced anything like that. The soundtrack features half original score and half curated music. It’s soothing! I’m a  fan of original scores so I  wish it didn’t have any licensed music, but the music they added in, specifically with how it plays while you’re in the hub adds a sense of realism to the game world.There is only one group for whom I would I not recommend Beyond Blue, and that is people with intense fear of the deep sea, as some levels in the game would really trigger your fears or phobias because you can hardly even see any geography and are almost entirely surrounded by empty water in almost all directions.Otherwise, Beyond Blue is a strong recommendation from me toward practically anybody, as I think anyone could use a relaxing game like this with a beautiful and important story to tell! It’s not the most engaging and exciting thing there, in fact almost none of it is “exciting”, but it was still pleasant and nice. I’m very happy I played.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I adore this game and absolutely love it and will tell you why, but first you need to know a few things.  This is more of walking simulator (or should I say, swimming simulator) where you swim around and scan various aquatic life.  That's it.  There is an underlying plot to this game, but it is not the focal point.  I would say it is worth about $10, although I got it on a deal for $4.  It is extremely repetitive, and the voice acting of the main character is atrocious.  Now for the good.  This game is exactly what I wanted.  I wanted something relaxing, with realistic graphics, where you get to swim around with various marine animals, and not have to worry about a big objective or getting eaten.  If that's what you want, then buy this game!  The graphics and movement are amazing,  there's a wide variety of marine animals to see, and you can swim anywhere you want within certain boundaries.  The different times of day to swim at are so cool too!  Also, you can save anytime, anywhere which is awesome.  I've only played this game for two and a half hours and felt like I had to write this review so people will buy this game!   I'll update it once I finish with how long it took me to play, and how the ending was.Oh, and whoever tagged this "horror" was crazy.  I've played kids games that are scarier than this!  And if you like this game, check out Abzu!  Abzu has to played with an Xbox controller in order to enjoy, but is still worth your time!Edit:  I just finished the game and it took me 4.6 hours, and that was seriously taking my time.  It was definitely worth it, and a lot of fun!  The ending was pretty anticlimactic and left a lot of questions unanswered, but I would say it is still worth getting!  And if you love nature documentaries like I do this is just like being immersed in one!

_childDocuments_.review: The writing is the weakest point. _childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue is a gentle, relaxful game of ocean diving and scanning sea life. In your high-tech wetsuit you don't need to worry about water pressure or air supply, nor do any predators take any interest in you. Missions usually involve seeking out various kinds of whales, noting any unusual animals that happen by, or finding locator beacons that need their batteries replaced. You (usually) know exactly where your objectives are and (usually) have a map to help you find them.There's no unlocking, gathering, or building. Instead, the missions serve to further the plot: you play Mirai, who wants to follow a family of sperm whales (with a new baby!) and collect data on them. In your underwater habitat between missions you get phonecalls from André and Irina, whose technology you're testing and whose research you're furthering; and from your sister Ren, who is caring for your grandmother who has dementia.The plot touches clumsily on the evils of underwater noise pollution and on the importance of family; I say 'clumsily' because these threads don't really get handled in a satisfying way. There's some tension between André and Irina, for example, that I never really understood nor saw resolved. And the gameplay is kind of clumsy as well, with fish that just, well, swim around; you're told when you've recorded various behaviors, but you never actually get to see the behaviors taking place (aside from a few in cutscenes).All in all I'd say that the plot itself isn't memorable (aside from its educational aspect) and the gameplay is oversimplified (would be good for a kid or for somebody who just wants to swim with sharks without getting wet, but it lacks depth). So for those reasons I can't really recommend the game.The one reason I *would* recommend the game, though, is that one of the characters is voiced by the late Mira Furlan, perhaps best known for her roles in 'Lost' and in 'Babylon 5'. All of the voice acting in this game is superb (given what they have to work with), but it's bittersweet to hear her in one of her last roles.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  is done and dusted. This is fairly unique inasmuch as it’s on one hand an ocean exploration game and on the other, an actual documentary. Both sides focused on understanding ocean life better and on environmental conservation.Before I dive into the fun stuff, I want to talk about the game’s issues, which can be significant. The game will sometimes refuse to open, point blank period. The game will also likely hard crash, and there’s not one set of circumstances causing it. It can happen at any time. Once that happens, the game won’t recognize your save files if you hit continue when opening the game back up. It’ll just sit in loading screen limbo. The workaround is to direct load saves. However, that did not work for me until after I uninstalled and reinstalled. The devs have shown no interest in fixing these widely reported issues.When you consider the importance of the game’s message and the fact that it’s tied to a conservationist and scientific exploration and research organization, the relative lack of post launch support is unacceptable.With that said, this game is special. It’s basically a fictional parallel to what OceanX does in real life, on the game side. On the documentary side, it does a great job of informing the player as to the organization’s goals and accomplishments. Which serves to offer the player a personal attachment to their mission. The story does feature a bit of personal relationship stuff to flesh out the characters. I’d say it was a complete joy to experience, but there is a moment of deep sadness in the game, so I’ll instead say it’s about 96% pure joy, 4% apprehension and sadness.The gameplay itself was very relaxing. You mostly swim in a special rebreather suit around the ocean tagging various ocean life, from jellyfish and clams to dolphins and whales, and plenty in between. You will have other objectives such as investigating an illegal mining operation and trying to save aquatic animals from algae based illnesses. Through all of this, you are tracking the lives of and interacting with a family of Sperm Whales, which is your primary directive in the game.You will retire to a special submersible which the main character stays in during the game, after each day of diving. Inside, there are some story building knickknacks; your dive suit; a computer that logs all the wildlife you’ve tagged, tracking their habits and such. You can also watch the Insight videos as they unlock (which is the documentary part of the game). Finally, it is here where the protagonist will have the most interaction with her two mission leads, as well as having the chance to call her sister, which is the largest part of the personal relationship aspect of the game. Oh, and you have some tunes you can flip through as well.The in game graphics can be quite stunning, and some of the places shown in the documentary (Insight) video clips are awe inspiring. You could easily invest many hours just swimming around and taking everything in. The voice acting is good. Not great, but good, and approachable for sure. You can easily connect with the four story characters. The music was really cool and there is a decent selection of songs which I would characterize as mostly alternative pop. Just an all around fun soundtrack.I played on the Steam Deck with the highest settings and everything enabled. Outside of the issues I noted previously, it performed immaculately. And those issues are 100% experienced across platforms and regardless of personal rig specs.This game has been bundled five times, so while I think the cost vs value combined with the mission and message is definitely there at full price, you certainly couldn’t be blamed if you wanted to wait for a deep discount or for it to be bundled again. Even with the issues I discussed, I do think this game falls into the category of must play and I highly recommend giving it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue is a good but not great game. Lacking biodiversity, it is very short and lacks much-needed gameplay features which the Endless Ocean franchise had in abundance. Small things like being able to surface while diving and look around, zoom into small patches of coral to find tiny fish, occasionally walk ashore to find terrestrial or avian animals, explore ruins, and befriend and swim with dolphins were left behind in Endless Ocean and not brought into this game.Considering Beyond Blue was released in 2020, it shamefully falls short of the precedent set by Endless Ocean and Endless Ocean: Blue World which came out in 2007 and 2009 respectively. There is not much of an excuse for this because of the profound technological improvements made since this game and the fact that this game was made for the PC and modern consoles, which could easily have run a much bigger and in-depth game. Beyond Blue is an atmospheric game, with great ambiance and excellent graphics. Not a fan of the pop music, but I am likely in the minority here and the music will likely be enjoyed by most. Some of the captions did not match up with the voice lines, and at least one of the captions repeated. There was a particularly obnoxious glitch that would appear whenever I focused on an animal. As I focused on an animal, regardless of biome, a manta ray would randomly appear out of nowhere swim towards the fish within view of the camera, and then disappear as soon as it finished zooming. It really killed the immersion. Game is comfortably worth $10.00 USD, not $20.00.If you played this and loved the concept but felt the game itself was lacking, I insist that you purchase Endless Ocean and Endless Ocean: Blue World for the Wii or run it on an emulator in high definition (it looks a million times better in HD, and I hear there is an incomplete high-definition texture pack online for Endless Ocean 2 which you can patch onto the ISO which may improve the game a bit, but I have never tried it). You will be very pleased.The soundtrack for Endless Ocean is beautiful and features Celtic musicians such as Hayley Westenra and Celtic Woman. Though you will notice technical inferiorities such as less polygons on models and a lack of voice acting, it is hard to deny the game is far more dynamic and provides a superior gaming experience. There are also many more species and environments to discover, and you get to hunt for treasure in both games. If you do decide to take my word for it, you will not regret it. Final verdict is 6/10. Good but not great. If you liked the concept of a scuba diving simulator, please play Endless Ocean for a more refined experience.

_childDocuments_.review: You're taking on the role of Mirai, a diver/scientist studying ocean life (mainly pods of sperm whales) and her research team composed of two others.  During the expedition you'll spend 8 days (dives) where you'll study a wide variety of oceanic life, and see some of the effects humanity has on the ocean.While going through this, you'll also learn about Mirai's family, and home of the hardships she and her sister have dealt with.  The graphics are great.  models and textures look impressive, the game scales up to 4k and looks fantastic from what I understand (I don't have a 4k monitor so it's not something I can confirm.)The music.  During the dives the only music you'll have is ambient tones from the wild life around you (Primarily whales) which doesn't sound like much, but does provide a feel you're expecting from a diving game, in between dives you'll have a pretty wide selection of music which is a nice personal touch too (though you won't spend too much time listening to them.)If you're the type to like story driven games in an oceanic setting, yes.  That sounds like a very niche genre and it probably is.  But, I do think a lot of people can find something to like about this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to look at fish and learn a thing or two about them don't bother. There are about 20 different fish in this game and they all swim away from you if you get remotely near. If you want to hear the personal drama of uninteresting burned out lesbionic characters while swimming miles back and forth in order to listen to various whale songs this is the game for you.This is just the most unbearable kind of trash. It's a mobile phone game with a minimum of content where all interactive elements are just repetitive fetch quest tier time wasters to pad out the game in order to stuff more of their bad character dialog in. All you can think about while playing this is some developer team meeting with BPD freaks bleating "yes, we're making a game about diving but what about MY interests?". It's obvious they never wanted to make a game about the ocean but instead some kind of self insert story where they can vicariously become interesting people with, like, complicated but totally enviable lives.I love diving games and would have been willing to overlook any number of flaws if they just gave me a pretty environment with lots of fish to look at. _childDocuments_.review: Beyond Blue is a short (about 4 hours), relaxing, nice-looking underwater exploration game with unfortunately too many issues to recommend it.You play the diver of a small ocean research team, exploring underwater areas at various depths. Your missions include tracking and scanning whales, surveying rare ecosystems, and streaming the experience to interested (fictional) viewers. During these missions you also get indications that something isn't quite right with the whales, and you'll investigate further. Unfortunately the story hardly goes anywhere - it starts slow, eventually begins to get interesting, and ends soon after. The main story arcs get concluded in a narrated epilogue, which makes me think that the game was originally planned to have more content. There is some closure, but it feels rather rushed.The game is set in the here and now, inspired by documentaries about ocean life. It tries to depict realistic situations like a nursing whale baby, a whale mating "dance", or predators feeding on a swarm of small schooling fish. Unfortunately, each of these events only happens once in a scripted scene with no interactivity. And while the scenes don't look bad, you can easily find real footage (e.g. of the baitball or the nursing whale) or CGI (e.g. of the "sperm whale vs giant squid" fight) that looks much more impressive. There is also a disappointing lack of detail in these scenes - for example, in the nursing scene, the two whales don't really touch, but you don't see milk being ejected into the ocean either. There are also no small fish being attracted by the milk. It feels as if the developers took a list of the most-viewed Youtube clips of life underwater, and then tried to remake some of them with much less detail for their game.Outside of these rare events, all animals just swim around and don't interact with another (or their environment) at all. While exploring, you never see animals hunt, feed, play, or do anything else apart from slowly swimming around. Due to the lack of interactivity, the scarcity of depicted animal behaviors, and the lack of detail in the aforementioned scripted scenes, the game unfortunately largely fails to capture the magic of true underwater life. I think it might still impress players who have never seen a documentary, but even for that part of the audience, watching one of those would probably provide a better experience than playing this game.The lack of detail continues in other aspects of the game. For example, your diving suit has a helmet (which explains why you can talk to your colleagues), but you don't have any visible air supply - no oxygen tank, no AirBuddy, nothing. You also use the same flimsy diving suit in depths from 10m to 4000m, which is completely ridiculous. The game tries to explain that away in the voice-overs with a vague reference to "new technology", but this is really just a lazy cop-out, considering that the game obviously tries to depict a mostly realistic experience overall.Occasionally the game tries to educate its players, which I appreciated, but the information remains disjointed. I believe that there are many, many more interesting details that could have been included. It didn't help that the menu area where most of the trivia information appears - the scan log - kept bugging out and didn't show me anything half of the time.You spend most of your time exploring the fairly large maps and scanning animals. On each dive you get a couple of objectives, but there is no quest log, your mission progress only gets shown briefly after accomplishing a step. Most of the missions are completely linear - e.g. you may have to scan 4 dolphins, and only after that is done, your colleague will give you a waypoint to the next objective.Scanning an animal is as simple as looking at it and pressing mouse buttons. But frequently you have to also scan a specific spot on its body, which involves rotating the camera around the animal with very clunky controls that I found annoyingly unpredictable.Occasionally the game wants you to find things like an animal tag that has come off, or take probes from 3 locations, but all these tasks work in the exact same way: you swim to the location indicated by a mission icon, you press "F" to interact with the target once you reached it, and that's that. While the game tries to make these tasks feel differently by giving them different context in the voice-overs, they do feel repetitive and uninspired after a while. There's a lot of wasted opportunity in the mission design.Optionally, you can ignore mission tasks and just try to scan all animals on a given map. You'll get achievements for accomplishing this, but it has no effect on the story.The graphics are beautiful and mostly realistic, though I would have liked a bit more anatomical detail. But generally the graphics and animations are the game's strongest suit. That said, I have seen other underwater games that looked better. Granted, those depicted fictional worlds, so the artists could take more liberties. But then again, there _are_ amazingly beautiful underwater places in the real world, and the locations in Beyond Blue feel a bit bland compared to those, though they certainly don't look ugly.Sound and music are pretty good. Some of the songs that play in the submarine may sound a little odd, but I appreciated the diversity, and I liked listening to languages I never heard before. The voice-overs are decent as well.Beyond Blue provides the standard graphics settings that you would expect (AA, bloom, ambient occlusion, etc.), and 7 separate volume sliders to fine-tune your audio experience. There are sensitivity sliders and inversion options for both axes of mouse movement, but keyboard controls are unfortunately fixed to WASD, plus Ctrl and Space for vertical movement. Since the key for the map ("M") is impossible to reach when your fingers rest at WASD, you constantly have to break immersion and look down on your keyboard, which is really bad for a game that tries to deliver immersion above all else. The idiosyncratic UI design doesn't help, often you have to press keys like F, R, or V where I would have expected mouse clicks or at least the Esc key to work.You can save the game at any time, which is nice.My experience with the game was severely affected by bugs. I was never able to view the video clips on the "insights" tab, clicking on them just consistently crashed the game. The scan log (a page with images and trivia about all the animals you scanned) only showed me "closed lock" icons half of the time. Trying to change the graphics options to "low" froze the game. Clicking "Continue" in the main menu froze the game (though loading a save thankfully worked).It hurts to give a thumbs-down to a very well-meant game that I really wanted to like, but I can't recommend a game just for good intentions. I believe that it's extremely important to make more people care about life in our oceans. They are a massively important part of our planet's ecology, yet we treat them as an unlimited global garbage dump. As such, every game that tries to depict realistic underwater life is welcome.But Beyond Blue simply fails to deliver the level of detail that would be needed for that, and it doesn't have enough interactivity (or an engaging enough story) to make up for that. Hence, I would recommend watching actual documentaries (or good, detail-rich CGI) instead of playing this game. Though if you're just looking for a relaxing experience of diving, swimming around, and watching various animals as they don't do much else than also just swim around, then you can get a few hours of enjoyment out of it. Otherwise, it's (sadly) mostly a wasted opportunity.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't awful - but in it's current state I feel it really misses the mark on what it tries to achieve.As a game, it's bland - you go through the environments, which are areas bound by invisible walls where you can only really interact with the environment and animals by scanning them. I started the game excited to explore underwater, but most things don't really react to your presence. You don't connect with them and I felt detached from the world and it's inhabitants. You can swim over volcanoes and it not have any effect on your character, even swim into them from above and nothing. The submarine you visit between chapters doesn't feel fleshed out, there's books and objects but for the most part it's look don't touch. See this person has books but you can't experience them. The voice acting isn't good and the personal stories between the characters fell flat for me, I didn't connect and often conversations come to "I don't want to talk about it" and the choices it gives you are totally meaningless, even the ones where it asks you what you want to do. As an education game it's okay, the micro-documentaries are pretty and quite interesting... they slightly flesh out things that happen in the game and the one cool moment I experienced with the bait ball. The 3d models of the fish you can investigate with on the submarine are cool for a moment, but they're a bit weak as educational devices. I'd love them to highlight parts of the animals and tell me their names, maybe the function of the fish - videos of the fish in the wild. Looking up the scientific info tells you what depth those fish live, it tells you the scientific name of the animals... but it doesn't give you more information than that, I'd love something to connect with the wildlife more! I'd love some documentary footage, facts, lifespan, general information about them! I'd love to be taught, but I found as I was streaming it people in chat were educating me more on those fish.As a narrative experience the game falls flat, the 'livestream' way the game pushes parts of the stories forwards is scripted for the most part and you don't ever feel like you're playing a role as your character, interacting with a livestream or interacting with the other characters you're introduced to. It's all incidental, it lacks interactivity and the game's just middling. Also, the game has some serious audio issues where if you turn up the in-game volume too loud audio peaks and distorts - some videos are MUCH louder than others and the game insists on playing music to you when you're in the submarine by default. I want the ambient music but I don't want to be hit by licensed tracks but you don't have a choice and it doesn't remember when you turn the music off. The audio isn't levelled well in conversations either, the quality and volume is inconsistent and when you have a phone conversation between three characters and one is noticeably louder than the others, it's just a strange detail that could be easily resolved if the audio was properly compressed.It's not a fun education experience like Bee Simulator, it doesn't land emotionally as a piece of environmental activism, it's not a compelling experience like Journey or Abzu and although the micro-documentaries are good quality, they could be separated from the game and still be just fine and I didn't feel they really improved the game or my personal connection with the game - also they felt a little disconnected from the character I was playing in a narrative sense.I don't usually score games, but this is like a 3.5 out of 10 for me. It feels like with polish and the want to deliver a game, it could be improved - but I don't really see it being more than something kind of middling and disappointing without a complete re-haul of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest its not a long game, even if you're going slow the story line is maximum 6 hours long (and that is only if you're trying full completion of the all the achievements at the same time as the story line). But what you don't get in story you get is the actual game play. The graphic rendering of all the sea live is simply stunning. You get the opportunity to get close to sealife, even the sealife you wont ever be able to get close to in real live (  ).And another point in favor of this game is that the animals are non threatening in this game, so you can watch the sharks and the whales all you like in this game, which is way more accurate than nearly every other simulation game I have ever played where sharks are in the game. In a survival game it makes sense that the wildlife is super aggressive like every animal is starving to death and you are the only eatable thing within miles. But a game like this with more natural behavior is a breath of fresh air to me, and has more educational value to be honest.Which is a good point to explain that this game has actual a lot of educational value, I'm not the only biologist to review this game (and I have even seen some marine biologist in the comments) but beyond some far fetched reasoning  in the storyline, (and some points of this story line is as far as I know currently researched, like the auditory  disturbance mining a vent would have on different species and other problems with deep sea mining.) it is quite accurate in the description of the animals shown and also in their behavior.

_childDocuments_.review: What I thought was most interesting about Beyond Blue was how they managed to make a game all about the ocean so incredibly dry. This is a narrative driven walking (swimming?) sim where you go on a number of dives, swim around, "scan" a few things and follow an oceanographer and a pod of sperm whales through a short narrative.  You can also learn a bit about the ocean and some other underwater critters on the way.   Don't say gaming never learns you nothin. I think this is badly overpriced, but one of the characters is voiced by Mira Furlan from Babylon 5, so that's something. I'm going to give this a "maybe" because it's well polished and has professional production values, a surprisingly rich soundtrack, decent voice acting, all of which make up for the rather dry and somewhat uneventful plot (this is not close to Abzu in terms of unfurling narratives, anyway).Worth buying on steep sale if you're a fan of walking sims and/or BBC documentaries about the ocean.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: is a mostly calm, at your own pace, ocean exploration game that focuses on education and the importance of ocean conservation. The gameplay here is mostly of the "find it and scan it" genre, with a few other tasks thrown in as well. There is a story involving the characters and the animals you're studying. I don't want to spoil anything, but I will say it might get close to home for some folks.The animation is smooth and the animals look and behave wonderfully. The visuals of the ocean are well captured in this style as things often just appear from out the blue or deep in the darkness. You might get startled once or twice, but nothing is here to hurt you though. You can swim right up to any animal you come across without worry. You can also inspect them in a database back on your sub, which acts as a home base of sorts. While you're there, feel free to listen to a nice selection of music and watch the mini documentaries featuring real life ocean explorers and conservationists.Once you've finished with the main story missions you can return to any location and swim freely, taking in the atmosphere and snapping as many photos as you'd like. I've 100% the game now and can see myself booting this up from time to time just to soak in those calm ocean vibes.If you're a fan of walking, or in this case swimming, simulators, then this will probably be perfect for you. Regardless, this game lets you explore a part of our world that most of us will never get to experience in person, and that's pretty neat if you ask me. I do recommend picking this up, but totally understand if you'd like to wait for it to go on sale first.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond Blue

_childDocuments_.review: As it stands, this is kinda the only game doing this on the market. It's a peaceful ocean exploration game with beautiful visuals and as someone who's loved ocean life for about as long as I can remember, getting to swim alongside so many massive, majestic creatures (even if they are digital) is a little bit of a treat. And as someone with a bit of thalassophobia, it was also somewhat thrilling! If this game had anything approaching violence I might've not made my review quite as gushing, let me tell you.
