_childDocuments_.review: Things I liked:*Graphics - It's a very pretty game! Great environments and models. The 2D character portraits are well drawn, too.*Music - The soundtrack is fantastic! The previous game also had a top notch soundtrack, so I'm not surprised that quality continues*Gameplay - It's not terribly complex, but it's fun. Reminds me a lot of Starfox, but smoother and faster. I've played through 5 missions so far, getting all the optional objectives for the first 4. There's a good variety of mission types so far and I like that it's not all just run in and blast everything. There's moments of intensity broken up by moments of rest. It's these later that give you a chance to look around and admire the vastness of space, before you once again shove missiles into bad guys.*Ship appearance customization - There's a lot of different skins and colors to choose from. I think just about everyone will find a combo that they like.Things I'm neutral on:*Story - It's decent. Not great. A few things stood out to me as not really making much sense. When you replay a mission to try to get the optional objectives, you can skip past the dialog and story, so if it's not your thing, you don't have to sit through it. There aren't any real cut scenes, but there's voiced dialog screens, like in an old RPG, which brings us to...*Voice Acting - They all sound good and seem to be fairly talented, but I think the script doesn't do them any favors. As I said before, it's not bad, but it's not really great. There's too many things that (at least so far), aren't really explained or fleshed out. Granted, I'm at the beginning of the game, but if this changes, I'll come back and update this.Things I'm not a real fan of:*Opening card packs - There's a temporary-ish card system in the game that allows you to keep an active upgrade card at all times. At the end of each mission, you get a (random?) selection of new cards and you can keep the one you're using or swap it for one of the new ones. You can only have 1 at a time and the others are turned into cash to buy stat upgrades for your ship. The system itself is fine. I like it well enough and it gives you way to shift a small bonus around based on your play style or the mission objectives. I would prefer you get to keep a small number of cards to swap in and out without melting them all down, but not enough that it bothers me. The reason I mention the card packs in this section of the review is that when you get new cards, you have to hit a button to "open" the pack to see what they are. While I like opening packs of cards IRL, in the game, I don't like the extra step. It's a really minor thing, but it totally disrupts the flow of the post mission screens, IMO. You're watching all this stuff happen automatically, and then you think you're about to see your cards, but no, you have to hit the button after staring at the screen for 30 seconds waiting like a clown. Maybe this is just a me problem (probably), but I'd prefer the game just show me the cards.*Some enemy patterns - I've had a wave or two of enemies seem to spawn behind me and move into the screen from behind the camera. Usually this ends up in one or more of them slamming into my ship. There doesn't seem to be a way to defend against this other than knowing when it's gonna happen and positioning yourself accordingly. Definitely not a fan of this.And that's about it! If you're looking for a modern, fast paced, arcade style space fighter combat game, this is definitely more than worth the price. I really liked Redout and I'm glad to see the developers are continuing to make great and fun games!

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, game isn't bad. I had mixed feelings on first few chapters because game was really focused on on-rail gameplay parts but the further you go in campaign, the more freeflght sections there are. And in my opinion they're well-made. Especially those from last 3 or 2 chapters.However I miss post-endgame content. After you're done with campaign... there's nothing interesting to do. All you can do is replay previous missions and blast every enemy with maxed out ship. No campaign+, no campaign reset, no custom missions / training fights against bigger ships. That's a shame.But still, I won't give it a negative review. And unfortunately that's only because of its low price. Again, shame. I hoped for PC game, not for a mobile port where story (which happens too quick in my opinion) tries to be "realistic", but on the other hand you need to collect big, floating coins and blueprints in the space. I mean, c'mon. I finished this game in 7 hours with a bit of grinding and have anything more to do in it. I wish there was at least a simple multiplayer with bots or something, to give it at least a little bit of replayability.Because replayability of missions is not really good. After starting one mission over and over again to complete secondary objectives I have to listen to parts of long conversations over and over. And yes, I'm aware of "skip all" button, but some missions still plays dialogues even after skipping the entry. Solution to this could be making more interesting "loading screens" at the beginning of missions (which are literally just some sentences thrown on a black screen - 0 effort), which could contain some simple, pre-prepared cutscenes.You had so much time to do all of that! Where it all went???

_childDocuments_.review: I’m not sure where to begin with Redout: Space Assault.  I supposed we could talk about how the game is deceptively using the “Redout” name to lure in potential customers who were fans of the 2016 anti-grav racing game or maybe we can talk about how this is a poorly conceived mobile game ported to the PC with little effort.  No matter how you approach it, Redout: Space Assault is just not a very good game despite having some superficial charms.Screenshots and trailers are quite deceiving for this one, as I jumped into the cockpit expecting some awesome space combat action along the lines of Star Wars: Squadrons, but instead I found myself locked into an on-rails arcade experience I would expect to find in an arcade or maybe in VR.  While a few missions actually do open up and allow you limited freedom of flight you’ll find yourself trapped in a very small bubble of exploration before getting reattached to those rails.This is a tough review because I would love this game if I was playing it in a sit-down cabinet or 10-foot screen at Dave & Busters or even on my Oculus Rift, but as far as a standard PC space shooter Redout: Space Assault just comes off as an obvious port of a mobile game with limited vision.  The broken HDR issues at launch kept me from even playing the game for several weeks until it was patched, and even in its current state the graphics are still washed out and unattractive with a simplistic design better suited to VR.  Despite the poor graphics fidelity the level design and space vistas are quite spectacular and thrilling to fly through.  The game lacks the flow you’d expect from a fast-paced arcade game due to its awkward difficulty and boss choke points that force you to grind previous levels for credits before advancing, and you have no idea how much you need to upgrade to overcome certain obstacles, so even that becomes try-die-repeat.Read full review at

_childDocuments_.review: Let's address the elephant in the room: this is a mobile game port. If you are looking for a star citizen/elite dangerous/eve online experience look elsewhere. This is a pick up and play game, but it doesn't mean it's bad.Now that that's out of the way:It starts a bit slow but then progresses nicely, around 6 or 7 missions in you start to get a good number of enemies on screen, your classic enemy formation that flies in front of you and starts shooting. A nice mechanic is the take on bigger ships, alternating between chasing and "locking" onto them and moving so as to shoot them from all angles, with the possibility of targeting sub systems such as shield generators, turrets etc. I just spam the fire buttons, but if you want to be more precise the option is there.With asteroids and all sort of debris flying around in space never feels "empty", and you can boost/slow down as required to make it through the narrow passages. Or the opposite, as some missions require you to fly through "gates" that keep your turbo up in order to be quick and escape There's a reward and an upgrade system, albeit a basic one, and a "card" system which lets you choose between three temporary upgrades for the ship. Nothing ground breaking, but I like the possibility of customisation.Will get back to the review when I have more time in the game. As it is, I recommend it, bearing in mind its intended audience.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - This game is painfully mediocre and not worth your time.What makes it so bad? Well there's a saying that the whole is worth more than the sum of it's parts and unfortunately Redout: Space Assault is made from a litany of cheap and half-assed parts that fail to come together. The OST is dull and generic with some occasional electronic music thrown in to indicate "HIGH STAKES TENSION" occurring while otherwise being un-noteworthy space opera esque filler. The voice actors all sound bored out of their minds and have no passion for the dialogue that they're sprouting, which is unsurprising as it is utterly banal. The combat is all over the place as it attempts to mix on-rail space shooting some free flying sections, with the former lacking the nuance and excitement of other games such as Star Fox as enemies pop-in, scatter the screen in visual effects then jog-off without making any impact. While the latter are just dull as you mosey around the same generic space areas with the same props scattered around them looking for objectives which aren't well sign posted. There is an upgrade system but it basically just exists to incentivise the side missions as the rewards are infinitesimally minor and don't have much of an impact on gameplay (seriously you need to buy +missiles around 10 times to get one extra missile per salvo). Your ship has shields and a hull, the former regenerates while the latter doesn't, which would be fine but a lot of enemy attacks just straight up ignore your shield and most missions give you hull regeneration pickups anyway. Death has no punishment aside from taking away any currency you've obtained during the mission, but this currency only exists for the upgrades that don't do much. There's a barrel roll mechanic, but it doesn't work against most enemy attacks as it only exists to avoid missiles, which the enemy uses in abundance and which cause the game to beep aggressively at you like an irate microwave. Last but not least the mission designs sucks as there is a wildly oscillating difficulty curve, repeated bosses (Act 1 and Act 2 have the exact same boss, but now there's a time limit yay) and random fail states (some missions just end out of nowhere while others drag on and on).I guess to summarise this is a Eurojank version of Star Fox as it "shares" many of the same ideas and controls. Unfortunately it's aggressively boring and has none of the charm or dynamic routes through the campaign. Even as an avid bargain bin enthusiast who avoids AAA games, I can't recommend this one. It's just so incredibly DULL and has 0 charm to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, it's a simple game. Even SIMPLISTIC I would say. But if you like old fashioned shooters, buy it on a sale. It's a fun, relaxing game for when you want to turn your brain off.Really, criticizing this game for several reasons makes no sense: it is exactly what it aims to be, and it succeeds. Enjoyable, not too challenging, with a nice gradual introduction to mechanics and learning curve, and can be taken in short sessions if you wish so.Ok, the 3D mechanics on rails can be a bit confusing at times compared to classic 2D shooters, but again... it's not a flaw of the game: it's inherent to the style of this game. What IS a flaw is the lackluster controls: at times you can hit stuff even if it's on rails, and this is not acceptable.Good fun, not AAA and not much depth, but I'm enjoying it.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout: Space Assault, the prequel of the original Redout that came out in 2016. Though, unlike being the AG Racer, this one is a Space Sim/Arcade on rail shooter. The game itself is pretty simple with only having 4 stats for you to upgrade, which is Hull, Shields, Weapons, and Missiles. Although the stats are very simple, combat is even more simple as you only need be behind something to be shooting at it and launching missiles just locks onto the nearest target to the player. Though, through it's simple gameplay, it's pretty fun in my opinion and inherits some of the breakneck speed from the original game in some missions involving either pursuing or retreating. And the music is really good, just like the previous Redout in which I adore with the soundtrack taking a special place in my head as an extremely good soundtrack.My biggest gripes with the game though is through it's balance of difficulty between enemies and the voice acting. Most levels in the game are manageable until you get to the cargo smuggler missions in which you never receive any instruction on how to fight it even though it is a special enemy and can't be fought through simple combat mechanics. Second gripe with these smugglers as that the devs cranked the damage through the roof with the smugglers as regular enemies took a bit to get through the shields, meanwhile the slightest touch from a cargo smuggler instantly downs your shields and evaporates half your health. Now the voice acting in this game has some of the most corny and generic voice acting I have ever experienced, especially with the protagonist, whose character isn't very well defined as he initially seems to be a by-the-books protagonist but becomes a loose canon when the plot demands it. In the game, every character stuck to a theme, like the scientist whose research you have to retrieve from smugglers having a generic German accent, much like every, single other generic scientist character from media. I felt like the devs should've just stuck with no voice acting like they have with the original Redout.TL;DR: Gameplay is simplistic but enjoyable and music is very good. Though, voice acting is remarkably generic and difficulty between enemies is inconsistent. Overall, I'd say the price is agreeable for the game. I really wish there was a neutral option for reviews

_childDocuments_.review: Redout: Space Assault is a mobile app that's been dumped on Steam as if it was a real PC game (it's not)... it's a cash grab from greedy mobile devs.  You might be fooled as some token effort went into porting this to consoles and PC, you can even change the resolution and controls, and the graphics are polished... but that's just to cover up the low poly assets, a limitation caused by the iPhones this mobile app was designed for.Trying to play this is a decidedly unpleasant experience... it's a basic rail shooter (you know that old, dead game format that vanished when PCs became capable of full 3D, user controlled movement?).  It's a rail shooter because mobile phones aren't capable of true 3D, fully user controlled, high fidelity gaming.  Fine for mobile gamers, but this is PC.  What's a mobile app doing here?  Not belonging, that's what.  To play this mobile app, just put your finger on your iphone screen to point at the bright flashy enemies and your ship will autoshoot them for you.  Incredibly shallow stuff. From a technical perspective, as a mobile app, this doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.  To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold on PC as if it were a PC game.  This is unacceptable and somewhat insulting to PC gamers.  It's a good demonstration of the poor attitude the developer has towards PC gamers, and this attitude has resulted in yet another defect in this mobile app.Because this is a mobile app, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the iPhones that the mobile app was designed for.  These are unfortunate handicaps and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was an afterthought for the iPhone developers who are to blame for this.  The mobile app is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for mobile phones forces upon a game.  Once more, mobile devs have made gaming worse for everyone.  I didn't spend thousands on building a gaming rig just so I could pretend it's an iPhone.These technical defects push this mobile app below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Redout: Space Assault has the ridiculous, laughable price of $10 USD (TEN BUCKS FOR A MOBILE APP!!!!), for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the mobile app, coupled with the unrealistic price, and the questionable ethical nature of the developer and/or their associates (as outlined above), this is impossible to recommend.The game peaked at 35 players, immediately at launch, and that player count evaporated immediately overnight (suspicious), leaving just 1-2 players loading this up every week or so and quickly uninstalling it when they see how bad it is.This mobile app features a number of suspicious, likely fake positive reviews. The reviews all appear at almost exactly the same time, within 24 hours after the mobile app launched on Steam, all have a direct Steam purchase of the mobile app, and all have very similar wording and writing style.  This is highly unusual given the very low quality of the game and poor player counts.  After those reviews, there's just a tiny number of reviews that dibbled in, in line with the markedly low player counts for the game.If these reviews weren't present, the game would have a markedly different review score.  The "Positive" review score on this mobile app should be taken with a large grain of salt.  This might be done to deceive and scam gamers into paying for a bad product.

_childDocuments_.review: Gratuitous missiles and energy weapons explosions, but good enough for a mobile game.The story, while plot points were predictable to me, felt like a nice addition to give the game some identity behind the core mechanics.The core gameplay consists of spamming weapons and strafing around a bullet storm on rails for most missions. Free roam areas provide some leisure when not in combat, but otherwise are difficult to pilot without a dedicated control scheme. Sparse race events provide a neat challenge reminiscent of perfecting a racing line in the original Redout, but hardly comparable.The progression system keeps things invested for the player, but may be balanced to induce a little grinding. (Ran into a roadblock for a mission that practically requires level 3 weapons early on, but apart from it, no real roadblacks)Challenge objectives provide needed incentive for experienced players to play the game well, though I see no limit for respawns during levels. However, hidden timers on objectives can be irritating.Overall, I enjoyed the game. Though, I'd recommend waiting for a sale as it's not something to exceed in expectations.If you liked Redout, don't expect the same flavor from this rail-shooter, but if you'd like to experience some of the lore behind the space colonization. This might feed that craving.(Really wish they had done a full fledged console release, the idea of space dog fighting with Redout's inherent sense of speed does sound awesome. Just the execution with this game feels about average, and more attributed for being aimed at mobile devices.)

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a trailer for the game and thought it looked like playing Starfox 64.  Yep, that is mostly what the game is like.This is not a freedom-of-movement space sim, nor is it always on rails.  Just like in Starfox 64, much of the time you are on rails and your control is strafing without changing the general direction you are heading, but sometimes you are free to fly around in any direction.  It can be frustrating when it switches between these modes in the middle of mission without any warning.As far as I can tell you can just die over and over and over in missions without any real consequence, other than in some missions when a bonus objective (which is not required) is to not respawn.  This does somewhat make the game seem a little easy.  About halfway through the game as of writing this, I have only had to replay a mission once.  It was a mission where you had to destroy a cruiser quickly or it got away.I have encountered a bug once where suddenly The view is so zoomed out that my ship was only a few pixels big and nothing seemed to progress.  That mission did require a restart, but then I encountered no troubles.So, a few minor problems I have with the game.  But if you like the Starfox series and expect to get similar gameplay, you will probably like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stunning art & animation. Some of the best I've seen in an indie game outside of cuphead.Unfortunately there are a number of missteps in its game design.- Battles don't feel varied enough, especially in the first area. You slowly wipe out hoards of the same few enemy types.- Each character starts out with the same incredibly dull set of moves. Unlocking enough for the game to feel like an actual beat em up is tedious.- The feeling of beating things up isn't as snappy and satisfying as many other beat-em-ups.- Temporary equipment you find during a run is underwhelming, to put it mildly. - The tutorialization is ridiculously overdone. I'm almost surprised there's not a tutorial on what a tutorial is.- There's a ton of mandatory dialog that tries to be clever, but really bogs the action down in the context of a multiplayer action game.I guess categorize this as one of those "I really wanted to like it but..." reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: Sorely lacking in content and variety, which is even more disappointing seeing how much this game was delayed. If I had known the game has zero new progression elements after completing it the first time, I would of refunded it. Four hours of gameplay to defeat the final boss with zero post game elements besides grinding for more random lore drops is absolutely atrocious especially with how little content is present the first time around.Immediately on starting the game up, the main menu looks basic; and players are thrown into the experience with little opening exposition. Not much is done to establish the context of the world besides simple, hurried dialogue with shallow characters. And even that mostly only serves to provide weak canonical excuses for why certain game mechanics exist. Why is Hat Kid in this game, and available to play from the start as a part of the core roster. They contrast heavily against the rest of the character cast, yet are unlocked from the start with absolutely zero explanation given. Almost as if the developers just desperately wanted a character cameo in the game, while having zero respect for the actual canonical integrity of the game itself. This combined with how rushed the opening of the game feels, makes it just look amateurish.The actual combat is decently satisfying and engaging. But there's virtually zero enemy variety, and no room variety. Each of the four zones only has a room worth of unique enemies, which you will encounter in full almost every room. Meanwhile each room is simply a rectangular arena with absolutely no unique hazards or geographic elements, only discernible from other rooms by the different background art. Literally; playing one room of each zone exposes you to nearly all the content that zone has to offer. The room rewards are relatively stock rogue-lite currencies and perks; nothing especially unique or exciting. There's little choice making or resource management or anything to diversify the experience besides the occasional admittedly interesting lore comic and very repetitious challenge rooms.When players defeat each boss they unlock the ability to buy a significant health and damage upgrade at camp, which players can only get to by being defeated themselves or ending the run. This combined with the upgradeable health potions results in a very obvious and artificial attempt to forcibly limit how much the player can progress in each run by forcing them to return to camp for purchasing major statistic upgrades after each boss. Even worse; these upgrades also destroy the skill unlock aspect of the progression system as players must choose between buying blatantly advantageous statistical upgrades unlocked from bosses, or buying new skills to simply make combat more interesting. Players actually are forced to choose between fun and progress essentially. The statistic upgrades cost so much that while buying them players will need to take more than a couple runs to beat the final boss; if they want to grind enough currency to also buy any new skills before finishing the game. So players are punished for beating the game too easily.The game presents a decent challenge but even with the blatantly artificial gating of statistical upgrades crucial to survival, I still managed to complete it within four hours while only needing half of said upgrades. Just to discover that there's no higher difficulty tiers or modifiers or anything, no new enemies or any boss variants either. After defeating the final boss the game straight up just tells you that there's no more content, but you can keep grinding if you'd like. Why bother, everything is going to be exactly the same past this point there's zero variety to the rooms, enemies or bosses and little variety to the perks or challenge rooms.Yet there's also various frustrating elements to what is there. The game extremely encourages combination attacks and avoiding damage, but it's possible for enemies to spawn or get knocked off screen so players lose their combo meter because the last enemy is temporarily out of bounds and thus inaccessible. The combo meter also continues ticking down during the death animation of an enemy, so in the time it takes for an enemy to die and the game to trigger the reward sequence the combo meter can go down a tier and lower your reward??? Some enemies also have questionable hitboxes that allow their attacks to hit the player even while standing behind said enemy. And that later game enemy that randomly will spam the same area effect attack potentially six times in a row while being nearly impervious is just obnoxious. The game also has problems with visual clutter, which can hide incoming attacks, both due to how clustered together enemies can get and because of how large the damage indicators are.Incredibly disappointing and downright disturbing to see a rogue-lite game delayed for so long yet released for twenty dollars with what amounts to only four hours of content. And even that four hours of content is filled with constant repetition as each room is just a nice looking box populated with the exact same enemies over and over. There's little point to having multiple characters in a game that is so easily completed and so un-replayable. Statistic unlocks are bound to each character, by the way, so you have to re-experience the artificial progression gating with each one. While grinding for lore you'll probably only read once and skills that don't really matter much after you've defeated the final boss.Despite the awful introduction, along with the artificial progression gating and terrible unlock economy, as well as the extreme lack of general variety and badly paced story; the engaging combat plus interesting character backstories had me on track to recommend the game. I completed it in four hours convinced the post game would introduce new difficulty tiers, modifiers, enemies and boss mechanics to explain the initial deprivation of such during the first playthrough. That is not the case according to the popup message the game gave me. This game was delayed multiple times and yet the only part of it that doesn't feel rushed is the character variety. Honestly it seems like this game was originally designed to be linear, but then after multiple delays the developers played Hades and decided to cobble together what they had made into a ramshackle rogue-lite instead. So at this pace I would be more than willing to recommend this game once it is actually fleshed out and appropriate for a full monetized release as a rogue-lite; ten years from now.If you're interested in finding some games that I do positively recommend they can be found on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, especially since it has Hat Kid. The art style is eye catching, the game runs smooth, the combat feels impactful. Sadly the game just felt very repetitive to me. When you enter a new zone you see most of the enemies you're gonna be fighting in that zone within the first screen and it just repeats several times until you get to the boss. _childDocuments_.review: Tunche is one of those games that is kinda fun at times but fails on so many levels that it can’t be recommended. Let me start with the fun parts, the game looks and sounds great. Figuring out the bosses for the first time is a lot of fun and learning your characters moves and how to combo effectively is enjoyable. The moment to moment gameplay is good and fast and you feel in control most of the time, you can cancel most moves to dodge for example. The enemy design is pretty good and varied, some of them can really cause problems if you don’t prioritize them correctly.Things I don’t like about this game: First of all the tags for this game are wrong, it is neither an Action Roguelike nor is it a Hack and Slash game. Instead this game really is a brawler or a beat em up. Why is this game not a roguelike in my opinion? The game only has 20 different powerups called cores. You can start with 6 and at the end of a run you will usually have at least 17 so every run is basically the same. Also the cores don’t really matter, once you are done with meta progression you don’t need a single one to win, some just speed up the combat rooms. The game really goes hard with the meta progression. Not only do you have to unlock basic moves such as your combo-finishers and special moves with every character separately but also general stats. You start with 100 health after you upgrade you can have 500 health and an extra 60% damage. Once you upgrade your characters the game is an absolute joke.The worst thing about this game is the story unlocks, to 100% the game you have to watch the story of every character. However if you do get to watch the story or not is random, also the story can only unlock in order and only in the correct act. So if you don’t get the unlock in act 1 your best action is to start over and replay act 1 again. If you miss for example the story in act 4 you have to replay acts 1-3 to have a chance to see the story in act 4. The game is already repetitive with the characters having similar movesets the story requirement adds an obnoxious grind for no good reason. This could be easily fixed by guaranteeing the story after beating the boss twice.The game also has a lot of bugs, enemies repeatedly spawn off-screen and the only way to kill them is with projectiles. Sometimes you lose your ultimate charge without doing your ultimate move. Some ultimate moves can get stuck such as hat kids scooter and qaros tornado also sometimes the game softlocks. To be fair it isn’t the biggest deal as the game saves after most rooms still annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't regret buying and playing this game, but its hard to recommend because of a lot of haphazard design decisions. A lot of the reviews talk about how repetitive this game is, and they're completely accurate. And it is not just because its a beat 'em up so obviously you're going to be fighting the same enemies a lot. Playing Final Fight 10 times in a row is less repetitive than beating this game once. Every area in the game outwears its welcome halfway though them. You'll be fighting the same hordes of enemies multiple rooms in a row before something gets shaken up. And I do mean hordes. The achievement for defeating 1000 enemies is more than twice as common as the achievement for beating the second boss.As for the rogue-lite elements, I really wish they weren't there. Progression is terrible and there are only a handful of useful items, 2 of which are completely busted. Every run will play out the same since most items don't have much of an impact.Game's pretty though

_childDocuments_.review: Hello, this is Lich and this is my first review on a game. (And sorry if my english is not great. It's not my main language, lol.)So, I've been waiting for the launch of this time for quite some time. I think it was since last year.Probably most of you have heard of this game due to it's guest character, Hat Kid from the aclaimed A Hat in Time.It was the same for me, but then i searched deeper into it and found it's page on kickstarter. (which unfortunately, i got too late for being able to pledge anything.)I got some interest on it and started watching it.Now that i got my hands on this game, let's get to the review:Pros:A game themed with the folklore and environment of the amazonian rainforest. Few games use this theme for games, but i think this one might be the best i found so far. That's a plusMy passion for roguelikes, and my liking for Castle Crashers also got my interest in this game. So that's also a plus.The art style of this game is gorgeous! It feels like i'm playing a real cartoon, and i find most of the characters really cute! (I want to hug Nayra like a plushie!) and it's hand drawn? Now that's a plus too!The story is quite interesting. I played the game enough to be able to beat it and i liked it! Another plus!The Cons:This game might be gorgeous at many ways, but it does have some flaws. I'm going to list them, but try not to be scared by them.Even though this game have a good gameplay, and hitting stuff is quite satisfying, it starts to get a little repetitive at some point. But i won't complain too much about it, since most beat em ups are repetitive at some point, and i'm quite used to repetitive stuff. Thankfully, it's roguelike elements help a lot supressing this game weakness, but then, it takes me to another weakness..The game is challenging for those not used to play this kind of game, but for serious players like me, i found the unlockables of the game a little... scarse.Don't get me wrong! The game have some number of content and it's not like you would be able to get 100% of it in one day. It might take a while for being able to level up all your characters and unlock all colectibles and other stuff might help on your future runs. But for serious players, they might find that something is missing?And lastly: The game is suffering a little with some bugs and glitches, but the devs are being very active and comucative with the community, and they are working very hard on fixing these bugs. So don't be scared!Conclusion:I find this game worth it if you like roguelikes and beat em ups, and the art is super beautiful! It's sure to give you some fun for some time (especially with friends) And it's chalenging yet fair. It's content take some time for a casual player to unlock it, but a skilled player might get bored after some time and find them somewhat scarse.I'm pretty sure that this game will have big future updates with new content and the game will have much more content than it have right now. What i'm trying to say is: The game doesn't have too much content, but i will have more later on, and that hopefully will fix the three flaws i mentioned. The repetitiveness, the scarse content and lastly: the bugs and glitches.Besides, the game just got fresh out of the oven it will only get better.  =D

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Cool aesthetic designHas a Hat Kid in it somehow (Literally the reason i got the game tbh)More combo-focused-slasher-y than the usual beat'em up gamesHas coopCons:Super grindy for what it isGets boring and repetitive after literally an hour of gameplayCharacters are not different enough, And they still manage to have an apparent diff in power level that serious that it is a problemRoguelite elements have little impact on gameplay varietySpecific wall of text describing my experience in the game:I have been enjoying slasher games for a long time, appreciating DmC-style Combo mad videos in different games and searching for something new to try doing sick combos in. So i tried this Tunche game, expecting it to be similar to Aztez i guess (ty Epic for the actual gem given for free), the 2d beat-em-up roguelite with a simple but actually not so simple combat, with hidden abusable mechanics of course. Also "Roguelite", so there must be some RPG Character building involved. At first it went ok, the combat was fluid, easy to understand and a bit satisfying. The kit felt kinda basic, but i have expected that, "this is a roguelite afterall"- i thought, "there must be some progression and different items that might alter the gameplay".  There is a big problem. Characters start with around the same moveset with slight differences in range and speed, and have their "unique" skill trees. 90% of the unlockable moves are shared between all the roster with slight differences in range and speed again. Also the experience isnt shared between characters, so you have to unlock the same thing on every character (5 times in total) if you want to actually compare their full potential gameplay. Aritfacts you find are permanently upgradeable and their level stays between characters, but it takes a long time to max even one of them, and you might not find it in the run. The combat is done well overall, but you really lack tools to reach variety in combos, and you are not rewarded enough for it, the damage is the same, if not worse, than just using a grounded move spam. There is a DmC-like style meter in the game, i guess, and it activates some dps artifacts if you have them, but there is no guarantee you get it. The final thought: Try the game, it is easy enough for a casual gamer i think, and use cheats to skip the grind and have some more fun. Also new content might be up. I'll give it a 6/10, 3 out of them are for Hat Kid, and that's enough to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: it kills me to not recommend this, i like beatemups like castle crashers, i like the art style, but there's just so much of the game that just kills it for me. i played with 2 friends and we were optimistic, but eventually it just got miserable. i think the real crux of the game is that the roguelike elements do not mesh well with the beatemup gameplay at all, making the game just feel very grindy, which you do not want out of a beatemup. i refunded the game, so bare with me as i only played an hour and 17 minutes before making the decision refund. it was a hard decision too, cause i do want to like the gameso let me guide you through my experience. you choose a character, you fight enemies that feel like they either have more hp than they should or you aren't doing as much damage as you could. you go screen to screen facing more of them as you go. you get a little variety in the enemies, fine for early game, but few enough that seeing them gets old quick. eventually they throw so many of the same enemies at you that the screen is just flooded with the enemies and you can't see what's going on. not so bad, but since you havent done much yet, you're stuck with mashing the x button to do your basic combo, with a slam-the-enemy-into-the-air button to spice things up. its not much. eventually so much stuff is going to clutter the screen that you'll take a hit from something you never could have seen or avoided and realize "hey that one attack took out 20% of my hp wtf" but whatever, you keep making your way through the game. sometimes you'll get an orb that serves as a minor upgrade, but its not much. for example, one is a better air dodge that makes you go further.  sometimes rooms won't have enemies, but rather NPCs. maybe you'll unlock a cutscene, or use a shop or something. or maybe you'll find the llama and have to spend your in-game currency to do a special challenge, but the challenge is something dumb like push enemies into a grinder to damage them, which doesnt sound bad, but the hitbox on the grinder is so much smaller than you'd expect. it looks like you can push the enemy anywhere in the middle, but no, the hitbox is finicky and it just wasnt worth the effort, especially since you have to waste coins to even attempt it. i didnt bother with that a second time tbh, i know my limits. even with friends helping, it was too much of a pain. so after all that, you finally get to the boss. its a rather simple boss, avoid telegraphed attacks and attack any chance you get, but what makes it such a pain is its shields. see, it has quite a lot of shields. once you break the shields, the boss is knocked down for about 3-5 seconds or so before recovering with all of its shields. now then, the boss has quite a lot of health, about 2500 hp, iirc. with i think 1800 shields. i dont remember if these are exact numbers, but it was roughly in that area i believe. now, here's the problem, you do virtually nothing to the boss. each character has different damage numbers, but its not a high number either way. as hatkid, i was doing about 7-12 damage per attack i think, and my friends weren't doing much better. we spend a couple minutes on the boss then die, as the boss still has 3/4 of its hp leftback to camp, we notice a lot of the NPCs we encountered are now resting there, but we can't really buy anything yet, so its back to the grind. we do the same thing all over again but this time we die just before the boss. we get back to camp, we buy some stuff, now we have a couple more attacks. whoopee. back to the grind of seeing the same enemies in the same forest to get to the same boss. it's here that we really feel the trial and error. so we get back to the boss and do a little more damage to him before we die, so instead of 3/4. he had 2/3 of his hp left... progress i guess. it got pretty unbearable though since one of us died early on in the fight, and then i died a bit later, so i was just watching my last friend just solo this boss for like 2 minutes straight, doing virtually nothing to him, since i think damage numbers might scale in co op. back to the grind again.we buy more stuff, and get back into it, but by now we're drained. we almost make it to the boss, we die, i alt-f4 and refund the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunche is not the game you would expect from looking at the screenshots. It's actually more of an arena fighter where you choose your next rewards before getting a new wave of enemies. It's also not a roguelike at all, despite what the description says. Now with that cleared up, how is the game ?The presentation is definitely one of its strong suits. The game looks great, the animations are nice and fluid and the menus are clear. I found the combat, which is at the heart of the gameplay, pretty fun too.You pick one of the five characters and embark on your journey to get as far as possible, gathering ressources to bring back to your camp and buy upgrades, skills and trinkets. There are 4 worlds, with about 10 fights in each one before reaching the boss. Said boss, once defeated, unlocks a life and slight damage upgrade for your next runs.Seems short ? It is. But that's not the main issue. You will most likely need 4 or 5 runs to reach the final boss for the first time, and you will have to go through the first few worlds everytime, which gets boring very quickly. The more you level up and grow stronger, the more boring it becomes. And that's for one character ! If you want more from the game than the 3 hours this will take, or simply experiment with other characters, you will have to go through that same process again, because ressources are not shared. I think this is just a flawed progression system, and adding shortcuts to later worlds would only make an already short game even shorter.There's still fun to be had, and I enjoyed it for what it is. I loved the art style, juggle combos are satisfying to land, the bosses are interesting... The characters' stories weren't really to my liking, but others could enjoy them. It's a shame the whole thing is dragged down by a system that almost puts you off from going for another run. I could even see players giving up on the game after finishing a run and realizing they have to go through the tedious beginning all over again. Wouldn't blame them.It's not easy to recommend Tunche, but the game has a lot of charm. If you can put up with the annoying progression system, the rest of the game is high quality and filled with good ideas. Because of this, I'll give it a positive , and hope the studio comes up with another project with that same quality everywhere. Good attempt !

_childDocuments_.review: I remember back in the day when Castle Crashers came out and it re-introduced me to my love of the beat ‘em up.  I’ve lost plenty of quarters even further back, supplying as many lives as I could run through to beat an arcade’s campaign in one after-dinner romp at whichever restaurant my family was at.  This genre has a lot of good memories, so when I see a new title, I immediately get excited.  Come on Tunche, don’t fail me now.Deep in the heart of the Amazon lies a troubling foe, as monsters of all kinds have ravaged the innards of the bustling forest and have terrorized its inhabitants.  Warriors from all flocks have tried to seek the source of terror, but none have made it deep enough to face it.  Many have been captured or have gone missing, leaving five tribesmen and women (and one Hat-wearing kid) to dive into the source of the terror and eradicate the evil within and restore order to the forest that they call home.While Tunche off the bat isn’t trying to reinvent the wheel with beat ‘em ups or roguelikes, it tries to blend the two well enough to run a fun and efficient package.  Character controls are simple: buttons for melee and ranged with a launcher for additional combos to start.  Ranged attacks use a separate Mana bar that is refilled primarily with melee hits, allowing for synergistic combat.  Each character takes a specific style into the jungle, with Pancho being a heavy hitter, Rumi utilizing mana-based attacks, and Hat Girl smug dancing.The Amazon is cut into four different areas, with multiple “stages” to do battle in before facing the area’s big boss and trudging forward.  If your HP hits zero, it’s all the way back to the beginning, with no checkpoints available.  But every run allows your character to get stronger with the various collectables found in each level.  XP upgrades your character and unlocks new combos, Essence upgrades Cores found in the jungle, and Gold allows you to grab run-specific items as well as grabbing cores before each run.When you’re venturing through the Amazon, you may notice the same thing I did at first, that man: this game is .  Tunche boasts hand-drawn graphics and it pops with a colorful vibrancy that remains soft and enjoyable to look at in motion.  Tunche runs super smooth and I never ran into any hiccups while playing, which is crucial in a beat 'em up and every moment matters.  The bosses all look super cool and provide a neat range of attacks that are again, super cool to look at.  It was a real treat seeing these for the first time.  Especially Boss #3.  So dope.But in terms of how much I enjoyed the game, well, our mileage may vary.  The inclusion of roguelike elements is always a neat mechanic for added longevity, but the game has to be worth the grind in multiple aspects for it to stick.  And going through a few characters and beating the game with one, I can say that for how much is unlockable with what I’ve been given to play, I don’t have much incentive to complete this game fully.Tunche has a weird problem of being too easy yet artificially too hard.  Characters have simple button mechanics that make it an easy pick-up-and-play, especially with up to four players that can have a go at each run.  But all characters are woefully underpowered to start your journey: not that a big deal since Tunche provides a  of unlockables to find (samples of lore for each enemy and boss, storyboard-like past plots for each character, a whole camp of people trapped in the Amazon, etc.), as well as bolstering your character to bigger and better stats with each run.  The problem is that these unlockables are at complete random, more notably the plot for all characters.  Since Tunche’s stages are picked by the provided icon above the selected area, showing what players will unlock when they complete the room, these rooms are cycled randomly with a chance that no big collectables will unlock.  The first three runs I had with Pancho gave me none of his story bits, which I found out later each one is unlocked in a certain stage: if you don’t get the proc on stage 3 or 4, you’ll have to play the whole game over again in hopes you get it.  Kinda sucks if you’re curious about the character and just roll your imaginary dice badly.Tunche also expects a loss after each new stage, with each boss defeat giving a substantial upgrade to your character once you’re back at camp.  If you’re like me and clutched Bosses 2 and 3 in one run, I was able to upgrade my character to a point where the rest of my runs were exponentially easy.  There’s a super move for each character, but I couldn’t tell you Pancho’s because I was so powerful with normal attacks it was never needed.  After beating the final boss, I was left with a ton of things to unlock for most characters and I was still missing parts 3 and 4 to Pancho’s story after my 6th run.  Tunche then throws it’s hardest problem directly in the face of New Game+ players: there isn’t one.If you’ve beaten the story, you can go back into the Amazon and run the gauntlet again, blindly rolling for the things you need, but there’s no challenging incentive to return other than a curiosity of the game world and a juvenile need to punch down at your smaller foes.  With the combat scarcely hiding numerous infinite combos to whittle down any foe with ease, and the numerous power-ups that raise your character’s efficiency above the trees: the combat becomes stale very quickly, especially if the return to the Amazon to check boxes doesn’t get checked after several runs.Even bringing friends along for the ride doesn’t help as much as it should.  We were only able to find one story bit for our three characters in the 4-5 runs we had, and the amount of enemies on the screen borders on the ridiculous.  You can get lost really easily on screen where we got defeated several times but couldn’t tell you as to what did us in.  If all our characters were more upgraded, we probably could have worked out better, but for bringing in friends for a plug-in-play, getting blasted with a deluge of enemies did not give the best impression.So it puts me in a weird situation: I want to recommend Tunche for the beautifully drawn art and its smooth and simplistic combat.  But I can’t recommend Tunche for it’s artificial inflation of a game that just does not feel finished.  Putting so much to unlock behind the luck of the draw loses its luster when most of the game is seen within an hour or two.  Having extra modes, harder difficulties, anything to give a different angle to what was shown would’ve done wonders to have me keep playing and buy-in on everything to see in the jungle.  But with the one trail available to be retread ad nauseum, it’s not worth buying in.

_childDocuments_.review: *TLDR;*Game is fun, you need to do A LOT to unlock the cool stuff, L3 for potions is weird.- What I enjoyed:Aesthetically the game looks really cool and game plays pretty wellMore runs leads to more upgrades which lets you get closer and closer to being the "peak" of your character and you can feel yourself getting better as you equip yourself with more upgrades in the hopes that "this will be the run" and it's honestly really cool.When you fight a boss, the health bar tells when they shift phases so it gives you a good idea on what to expect for a boss/see how close you were to beating it.I enjoyed playing this game a ton, that doesn't mean I liked all of the game. - Nitpicks/Annoyances/Potential Bias?:You get OVERWHELMED with enemies the second you add another player, I assume it is supposed to scale with the amount of people playing but even at 2 people people it felt like a lot of enemies were thrown in and since you don't have a screen clearing move or a super move at the beginning of the game, you need to just hold out and take everything on.(Okay updating this statement here, in one of my runs I got the leech ability meaning I gain health every-time I defeat an enemy, so I get the overwhelming enemies part can be a bad or a good thing depending on your circumstance. Just wanted to be fair in my statements, anyway back to the complaints and such.)There's a lot of the game you have to play before getting to the good stuff, like unlocking the supers I referred to or additional combos, I got to the first boss about 4 times before being able to upgrade a decent amount of my moves on the skill tree, if you have the patience for that or can at least distract yourself by playing with friends then you're prolly fine (I'm prolly just trash)The essence needed to unlock skills are quite a lot, so I assume you need to make some real progress in order to get some of those abilities, as in not be struck on the first zone, I'll admit the reason why it's taken me a while is prolly cuz I'm trash.Whenever you clear a room, you don't always know what reward you're getting? Albeit gold, essence, mana and so on. which kinda sucks since I'm not always able to go "cool, this room gives me essence"Speaking of which I don't think it reminds you what each symbol means? Cuz I've had multiple times where I forgot if this symbol was a core or gold or what have you, so a reminder screen of the tutorial screens you encounter for the first time would help.You can't config your buttons which I would prefer because I double checked, R1 or RB does the same as L1 or LB, which are your super moves. Both of them don't NEED to be your super buttons, so why is L3 the button for your potions?Adding onto that is the fact the game doesn't visually show you instructions with your controller inputted, I'm using a ps4 controller which plays well and has no issue.Even though you can see your controls for multiple controllers in settings the game has still used the xbox layout to get its "point across", which is kinda annoying visually, but since imma PRO GAMER, I myself had no real issue.The current build I'm playing has some graphical issues, although I don't have it recorded, sometimes menus will stay on screen in the middle of game-play after picking up a core, but go away upon picking up another itemThe control scheme glitches into the other control screens if you hit pause while on that screen and go back to the controls option, then goes away when you're back at that control scheme.(this I DO have recorded at the 5ish minute mark: - Overall:Even though I spent a good minute complaining about some technical/personal issues, i still found the game to be an overall fun experience and worth the time to play it.Maybe down the line it will implement some quality of life updates and/or additional content to better the experience.But this by no means is a bad game, it's just lacking in some departments.*TLDR;*Game is fun, you need to do A LOT to unlock the cool stuff, L3 for potions is weird.

_childDocuments_.review: There used to be a big review with criticism here. I develop my own games myself, and delve into game design. There are a few controversial points in this game, but overall everything is fine. I was wrong about some things, so I'm changing my review.Thanks to the game developer for the answer! It helped me to understand the game a little better. It's funny, but when I played the game in the morning, I didn't encounter the problems that I noticed in my review. And it's not that they were fixed, but that I was terribly tired and sleepy when I played the game. In fact, I just needed to get some sleep! x)At the moment, I really do not recommend playing if you are tired and want to sleep.I still have difficulties playing the Nayra character. Rather, the character's problem is that he is overly situational. For example, the third finish attack X,X,X, Y often leads to damage and it is extremely difficult to do it correctly. There is another problem with this attack: Sometimes it does not pass through enemies when you hit them. In addition, this attack practically does not give any increase to the rank, but according to logic it should.I thought a little and came to the conclusion that the problem I'm experiencing is not related to the character and how he moves, but with the intelligence of the enemies. They behave extremely uncharacteristically for the bit m up genre.Many enemies make a jerk attack. The game warns about their attacks, and in theory it should be fair, but it becomes a problem when you beat the crowd, and one enemy can just pass through you and you will get damage. In such situations, you cannot react because it is difficult to interrupt the attack animation. In addition, enemies can attack you diagonally while you are making strikes.After going a little further, I noticed that the bosses are very long and boring. In the genre focused on the combat system, it feels very strange that you have to dodge the boss's attacks for a whole minute, and only at certain moments beat him. The game genre implies that you have to beat the enemy and stuff combos, but the game does not allow you to do this fully when it comes to bosses. Boss fights are the weakest and most boring part of the game. They are not spectacular and long. When there is a boss fight, I want it to end as soon as possible.So I came to the conclusion that it's not about the skills of the characters, but about the intelligence of the enemies and the bosses. Due to the atypical behavior of enemies, fights are difficult to read. In many other representatives of the genre, the intelligence of enemies is made differently. In general, Tunche reminds me a lot of modern Battletoads in terms of game mechanics. It wasn't the most successful game in the genre.Tunche is a good game, but for an amateur. I don't like it because of the large number of controversial decisions, but I won't make a refund, because it's clear that the developers tried. The game has good animation, good music and location design, soundtrack. An unusual setting.Despite the fact that I don't really like the game design and the intelligence of the enemies, I will continue to play the game. There is a progression here, I want to see what will happen if you pump up the characters and complete the game completely. Maybe my opinion will change. I don't want to offend the developers of the game, because I know what it's like to invest time in something, and then get a negative review. No need to get upset, bitter experience is also useful, and everyone will not like the game. I'm sure this game will be great for many, and that's enough.

_childDocuments_.review: and often has that "Just one more round" aspect. I found myself losing track of time on multiple occasions.The character designs are adorable and Really well done. Each character feels somewhat unique and brings something different while also being similar enough to be able to pick up a new character without too much difficulty. It does take a lot of skill to beat the bosses but just remember that while it is challenging, it is possible. Like in most other roguelikes sometimes it feels like slamming your face into a brick wall again and again, but eventually, the wall crumbles and your head stops hurting. One of my favourite parts however is the integration of Hat kid. At first it doesn't really make sense as to why she is here other than for a popular cameo character for people to jump off of, but her story parts are very well done and in my opinion her lines, or rather emotive faces, fit her personality well. _childDocuments_.review: I was pretty darn excited for this, but the game simply lacks content. Even worse, the combat lacks any sort of variety. The combo system works on a DMC/Bayonetta "stale moves" type of deal, which is perfectly fine until you realize that you don't really have any other moves. You have a 1-2-3 melee on the ground and air (which count seperatly), a piss poor ranged magic missile, a launcher, a meteor, a charged ult move, a variant for your dodge, and a finisher for each step of your 1-2-3 that all feel pretty piss poor. This is the same across all characters with very minor changes. That's nowhere near enough to keep the combat fresh past the first few hours. Admittedly I found myself enjoying stringing together combos, finding new ways to keep air time, etc. but it gets old very quickly, and seeing my combo meter stale out after 3 melee hits so I'm forced to do one of the awkward finishers doesn't help. Neither does the lack of enemy variety or patterns, which mostly amount to 3 or 4 different types of attacks, with most of the enemies tanking a good chunk of damage from you, turning many fights into priority attrition battles where I fail to notice I've been hit half the time.I'd be fine with the limited content if the combat was simply more diverse and built up, but it feels like they did the bear minimum and called it a day, focusing more on the (admittedly fantastic) visuals and reminding you that Hat Kid is just here in this Amazonian jungle for some reason, completely breaking the style and sticking out like a sore thumb. There's just not enough video game here to justify a 20 USD purchase, I'm afraid, unless you want to have a one or two off co-op sesh with the gang.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I have only played this game in 2 player couch co-op.Art style looks good, but hinders gameplay. Being 2.5D but with characters in 2D makes it hard to see what attacks will or will not hit enemies. There are also no grouping abilities. The combat is very rigid, stopping you dead in your tracks whenever you attack, making it hard to correct for attacks that you miss. Enemies flash white when you hit them, they also flash white when they are you to hit you, so it is hard to know when an enemy is about to attack. It is also sometimes completely impossible to know if an enemy is about to attack, as enemies are consistenty obscured by either you or other enemies. All of this is a problem because the game relies on combo score. Over half of the Rogue lite upgrades you find throughout the levels rely on reaching an A rank score to activate. Something which is interrupted with any hit from an enemy. This makes most runs feel completely identical, since most of the variation you get will never activate at all. And when they do; they do not change your playstyle. The art style also makes it difficult to see where a boss' hit box is. It often feels paper thin, despite the boss seeming so large that hitting it should not be an issue.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunche is a roguelite beat 'em up. Unfortunately there is not enough content or depth to justify the rogue-LITE structute of this game. In beat 'em ups depth can come from enemies or from player character's combos. This games has does both poorly.There are 4 zones/regions and the enemy variety is bad. The first 3 regions just spam you with their own version of the fodder enemy that comes in 3 different colors and sizes (small, medium and big), but they all have the exact same attack pattern and only differ in hp and damage numbers. As a rule there are two special enemies with like 30 fodders per wave, but they die really quicly and fail to change the gameplay in a meniangful way. The last region doesn't have the fodder enemy and the enemies that it has are interesting to fight. As for the combo variety. Due to being a roguelite characters start out with basically nothing (which is probably expected): a basic 3 hit combo on the ground and in the air, ranged attack which uses mana and ability to lauch enemies in the air. Unfotunately after you unlock everything, there is still barely any variety. At their peak characters end up with the following:, ground pound, ability to cancel basic 3 hit combo into a heavy attack, ability to bring enemies to the ground from the air, 2 supers, and 3 specials unique to each characters that work on cooldowns.This game has 5 characters, but you won't use all 5. That's because designers made the brilliant move to have each character have their own progression. So you will have to unlock 2 supers and 3 specials for every charcter. But's that's not all. There are number buffing preks in the skill tree that are not unique to characters. Instead 2 of them unlock after defeating a region boss. These perks are +100 HP/MP (the base amount is 100, so the first upgrade doubles your health/mana) and +15% damage. But they only unlock for the character that you used to beat that boss. These are the most expensive and significant upgrades in the game and you will have to grind for them on each character separetly. This essentially lock you into the character that you started upgrading and if you want to change characters all your progress is gone.Since this game is a ROGUE-lite. In the actual run you will be offered a random upgrade. Good thing - none of these apgrades are number bonuses. Bad thing - almost all of them are completely wothless. A third of the upgrades require you to achive an A rank combo to activate. Unfortunately in the first 2 zones enemies die to quickly to do it and bosses have long invulnerability phases which drop your combo. And a rogue-lite tradition, there is one upgrade that will win you the whole game - this upgrade will contiously heal you untill you are reach one quarter of you maximum health. If you have enough HP upgrades, the Final boss will literally be unable to kill you as he cannot deal damage fast enough.   Speaking of the boosses, they are ok, passable. They can all be beaten without taken damage. So I would like to desribe them as fair, however their hitboxes are something else. In general this game has a problem with lingering and oversized enemy hitboxes, but bosses kick it up to 11. The game will generously show with a red outline where the enemy projectile will land. But the outlined area is a lie. Because all of the projectiles explode, and the explosion is 30% bigger than the outlined area. And that's not all. If you see a projectile explode on the ground and the explosion is already gone and the only thing that's left is dust, don't think you're safe. The hitboxes lingers for almost a full second. So you can be hit by air. If you know all that, these bosses are kinda fun. But new players are definetly screwed.Final thoughts, this game has like 2 good things going for it - visulas and sound and everything else is either mid or bad. _childDocuments_.review: Our review of Tunche will contain NO SPOILERS. We will give a brief synopsis of the plot and we’ll talk about how the plot is handled with different characters in the story.Tunche is a very fun roguelike game. If you’re not familiar with the roguelike genre, its origins comes from the classic video game Rogue. It’s a kind of genre where you play through procedurally-generated levels (randomized levels) and the character has permanent death, meaning you have to beat the entire game in one life.Tunche is a modern roguelikes and is, of course, much more forgiving than classic roguelikes. The levels are randomized as with any other roguelike, but the developers were careful to put limitations so that it’s the gameplay doesn’t end up repetitive or extremely difficult.For instance, when you play through a level with a character you can speak to story-relevant characters and get plot exposition. If you die, you’ll need to go through the level again, but you don’t necessarily need to go through all the plot exposition again.When you die and have to replay a world, the characters will give different lines of dialogue. Most of the new dialogue is usually much faster. I died to a boss at the end of one of the levels in Tunche who originally had dialogue where they introduced who they were. When I returned to the level to fight that boss again, they said something to the effect of, “Maybe you’ll actually put up a fight this time!” instead of repeating old dialogue.When you begin the game, you’ll be able to play as one of five protagonists. Their move sets are all unique, but you don’t need to be worried because you can viably beat the game with any of the characters. The combat is action-based, and you can either strike enemies physically, you can toss them into the air with a launching physical attack and then combo them, or you can use projectiles to shoot enemies from a distance.Your use of projectiles is limited, and you’ll need to restore a gauge by attacking the enemies physically to use more projectiles. You cannot switch characters on the fly and you will need to complete a run with the character you chose. If you want to change characters, you will need to die, and then you can choose which character you’d like to use at your camp. Local co-op gameplay with multiple characters is an option, but in our review we played the game by ourselves and thankfully the game wasn’t too difficult.Because the protagonists have similar move sets, you should be more interested in choosing the protagonist whose story you’re most interested in because their backstories are significantly different. The basic premise is that each character wants to find Tunche to grant them a wish.Rumi is a shaman and from the second she was born she was destined to be the leader of her people according to her family’s goddesses. She wants to get knowledge from Tunche to be a good leader for her people.Qaru is a hunter who was cursed when he hunted a sacred beast in a forbidden part of the jungle. His arms have been replaced with bird wings. He wants to find Tunche to get rid of his curse.Nayra is a warrior, who inherited her mother’s spear and wants to find Tunche to prove how strong she is.Pancho is the humble protector in his village. Unfortunately, his village has been affected by natural disasters such as landslides and rains, and he seeks Tunche to protect his home.And everybody’s favorite – the Hat Kid from A Hat in Time video game! You can play as her with no problem, even if you never played A Hat in Time because the plot of that game and Tunche are unrelated (she’s just a cameo). Tunche has four main worlds, each taking about 45-60 minutes (the latter worlds are on the longer side). In each of these worlds you’ll progress through a number of randomly generated rooms, but you can somewhat choose the types of rooms you go to. Each time you complete a room, you’ll get randomly generated rooms to go to next represented with icons, and you choose which one you like.For instance, the first main world will have mostly frog and forest-style enemies, which will not be present for most of the latter game. The developers were friendly and have put easier kinds of enemies to defeat in the earlier parts of the game, to help ease you into the game.You’ll have to progress through a certain number of rooms in the world to progress to the boss, which then leads to the next world. I’d estimate that it takes maybe 15-20 rooms to get through the each world. At the end of the world you’ll find a unique boss, and each of the four worlds in the game will have their own bosses. These bosses are not unique to the protagonist that you choose.It’s a bit tricky because you’ll need to learn the bosses’ patterns and defeat them while minimizing damage because you’re likely worn down from doing many stages in the world. All of the bosses are certainly learnable and you can dodge and avoid all of their moves.If you get past the boss, you’ll progress to the next world of the game. The gameplay then repeats itself until you beat the game. If you die at any time, you’ll need to restart from the beginning all over again. It’s not bad though because you will carry over your experience points, which you can use to permanently level skills on your characters. Some skills will allow you to use new moves, and other skills allow you to be able to hold more potions at once, to name a few.As well, defeating bosses will unlock new skills that are powerful, such as increasing the amount of health your character has. The only downside is that you’ll need to die to access the skills shop after defeating the boss.You can also find Spiritual Cores as you progress through the levels and you can also purchase them, as well as upgrade them at the camp. These Spiritual Cores grant bonuses for your character. There’s a combo system in the game, where if you use different varieties of moves you will get a grade from D up to A. One Spiritual Core would shoot thunder from the sky while we maintained an A rank combo, for instance.When you die you go to a camp. You need to unlock the story NPCs, but usually you find most of them within the first world. You talk to these story NPCs to purchase skills for instance. Another NPC will allow you to view all collectibles you’ve found in the game. These can include enemy information if you defeat enough of each type of enemy.You’ll eventually need to beat the entire game in one-shot without deaths to see the ending of the game, which means beating the four worlds of the game and its bosses without deaths. With the shopkeeper present in each world and getting some powerups after dying it’s not too hard, but you’ll need to learn the enemies’ and bosses’ patterns.I explained earlier that the rooms in each world are random, and you’ll need to find these comics in rooms with a book icon. I was able to get comics in world 1 and 2 very easily, but I wasn’t able to get them on 3 and 4 (I only did the latter worlds 3 times), so they can be a little tricky to get. I do wish it was easier to get these comics, they were very fun to read through. I wouldn’t want to grind through the whole game again to view them if I missed them though, I’m surprised these kinds of rooms didn’t appear more frequently for me.Overall, it’s a very fun and addicting roguelike game, even if you’re playing it solo. You’ll definitely struggle when you first play through the game, but as you die and learn from your mistakes you’ll get through it more easily the next time. The protagonists, enemies, and world designs are full of colorful 2D artwork. Sure the graphics aren’t impressive from a technical standpoint, but the art direction really oozes with charm. If you’re a fan of roguelikes or even just want to try this as your first roguelike I encourage you to give this game a shot, it’s a very original and unique new IP.

name: Hell Pie
detailed_description: Hell Pie is an obscene 3D platformer that takes bad taste to the next level! The game sees you grab the horns of Nate, the ‘Demon of Bad Taste’ . He is given the honorable task of gathering the disgusting ingredients for Satan’s infamous birthday pie. To do so, Nate must venture out into the overworld and do whatever it takes to ensure those ingredients are secured in time, or there’ll be hell to pay! Luckily Nate isn’t alone on this quest, his ‘pet’ angel Nugget is there to offer support. Nugget offers his holy insight when needed, but more importantly is chained to Nate, so can be used like a grappling hook or swung around as a weapon. Nate can also equip horns he finds across the world to give him new hellish abilities. Together Nate and Nugget will explore insane environments, meet tons of repugnant characters and witness some truly shocking sights. Hell Pie is a seriously twisted take on the classic mascot platformer, come along for the ride if you think you can stomach it! Become a demon: You're Nate, demon of bad taste, the 8th deadly sin. While not taken very seriously in hell, he is feared on earth (by some...a few...2-3 people at least). Heavenly support: Nugget the angel does not only look cute, he's also useful. Throw him like a grappling hook, use him as a weapon and let him be your guide. Freedom: Use the extensive moveset to overcome obstacles the way you want. Filth: It might look cute, but there are violent characters, illicit drugs and sodomy. Stuff: Collect things! Lots of things! Hell and above: Explore 4 big worlds and survive challenging platforming levels. Fashion: Buy outfits. You're the demon of bad taste and should look the part. Random bullet point: Did you know? Necrophiliac ducks exist.
