_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice story-centred game, with very nice imagery and questionable accessibility.The text is a bit too thin and violent for my impaired sight, with no options to change palette nor size. The interface can be zoomed in (a bit), at the expense of seeing what's around you.Messages and responses are timed as well, once it's gone it's gone, which is even more of a problem when you're a slow reader and/or in one of the many time-pressured areas. No option to change that either.Controls are few. It can be played with a mouse (click, drag) or probably a controller. There are (limited and fixed) keyboard options for sonar/examine, switch to movement mode, and progress to highlighted node.  The problem is that to go somewhere unexplored,one needs to: ping for new nodes, select the node, press the forward button or switch to movement mode - align dial - press forward, and each is defined by the animation speed. Ok, but not great when you're time pressured and you have a motor impairment
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Expectations were high, the waters were deep,Promised adventure, but I fell asleep.The reviews sang praise of the grand ocean floor,But playing along, it was nothing but bore.The currents, they whispered of danger ahead,Yet all that I found was a yawn instead.No creatures to chase, no thrill to be found,Just irksome tedium, no treasures around.And here I now float, adrift in my dreams,Where the game is as thrilling as it first seemed.But alas, awake, it was nothing to keep—Expectations were high, but I fell asleep.ZZZzzz... 😴
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: this game is approved Does Not Trigger My Thalassophobia. great message abt ethics. simple interface, and what it "lacks" in visuals it certainly makes up in audio immersion + great imagery in text. the ui design is just so pleasant . Would love to see more of this specific ocean xenobio niche that doesnt rely on direct visuals too much
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun little indie title. Think if subnautica was a text adventure. Gameplay is a bit shallow, I wish there were more puzzles, I wish there were more things to go back to, more branching paths that were previously inaccessible. There's an inventory system and many collectables but not very much to do with them, out of the dozens of in-game objects only a handful offer any way to interact with the world. For what it is, it's great, but it feels like the foundation of a game screaming for more. As much as I wish there was more I would still recommend playing through it.I played through the game once and 100%ed the save slot with a final time of 6h49m, which includes reading every bit of flavour text, reading through all the "lore entries", some idling, and visiting every single place there is to go.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game about exploration. It's essentially a text game but the limited amount of interaction you have really gives it something more. The subtle stresses that they put on you are great ways to make you feel the tension as you read. The mechanical elements exist to complement the writing and not the other way around witch i very much appreciate.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I have tried for about an hour. In that time, I almost fell asleep once and fumbled with the controls no less than a dozen times. Playing with a controller, switching submenus regularly screwed up my brain when it came to pressing the next button. There is no time limit (as far as I am aware of) or punishment for pressing the wrong button, but it still annoyed me. I regularly play games with a controller, from Dark Souls to even some 3rd person shooters (blasphemous, I know), but rarely do I get confused with the controls as much as in that one hour of In Other Waters.Gameplay aside, it's a narrative game that in that first hour has failed to provide a hook for its existence. Without any visual stimuli, the story needs to pick up the slack and it sure did not in that hour, as pages upon pages of fungi descriptions do not make it for me, sorry. Did I mention that I almost fell asleep? Anyway, the music during the intro was beautiful and I was prepared to suspend disbelief and sink into an underwarter world of mystery, but it took only a few minutes to realize that that music was probably the best part of the game (for me). I will probably not continue with this, not with hundreds of other games from my backlog vying for attention.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters floats somewhere between an art project, a work of speculative fiction, and an experiment in minimalist UI design.  I'm not sure I'd quite call it a game.  It's better understood as a slightly interactive novel.  In Other Waters has already decided what story it wants to tell, and your input really only controls the order of a few branches of that story.This all sounds more negative than I intend - the music is beautiful in a haunting-synths way, the story is well-told, and the interface is as much a part of the story as it is a means to interact with it.  If you're looking for a peaceful, contemplative experience, as opposed to a twitch-fest or constant battle of wits against NPCs, you've found it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Short: This is one of the best indie games I've played in probably years. Great sound design, story mechanics, and generally awesome all around.Long: This game is fantastic, and I highly recommend it. The sound design is unique and intriguing, and the soundtrack is equally beautiful. These, combined with the simplistic design, create an incredibly unique experience that I have gotten nowhere else. The gameplay is surprisingly rich, not to mention smooth and very well thought-out, and the story is amazingly interesting and will leave you wanting more every time you pause the game. As long as you don't mind a couple spelling errors (which is a given when a game has this much text, since even triple-A titles screw up their grammar), In Other Waters is a must-have for indie lovers looking for a fun, relaxed experience.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game upended how I think of computer/video games... I think of intense visuals, action, noise... This game has little to none of that. I have visual "memories" of the game, but they are just my imagination. I constructed an elaborate world in my mind based on text prompts and a basic control screen... If you're not keen on biology and imagination this might not be the game for you, or perhaps just a very different experience from mine. Anyway, I greatly enjoyed this and would love to follow Ellery on other planets.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, I have not completed this game - and normally I would not review a narrative game until I had - but it is so compelling that I want to recommend it now.Firstly, this is not a fast action game. If you go in expecting something like that, you will be disappointed. It takes its time, unveiling its secrets one by one, upping the ante each time. You have ample time to get used to a mechanism in the game before the next one is introduced, and it makes it eminently playable, and a puzzle that you always feel has a solution.The game focuses on discovering the underwater ecosystem of the planet you find yourself on, following in the footsteps of another researcher. You collect specimens, research them, and use their abilities to your advantage to help you get around. The twist is that you are the AI of the suit that the main character wears, so you see everything as the AI would see it - as radar images, icons and text.Travel is achieved by selecting pathfinding waypoints, some of which can lead to dead ends, but all of which help you explore the world that is presented to you. There can be a sense of being "on rails", but there is so often something to discover or interact with, that the game always feels interactive - though I have had a couple of rare occasions so far where I have had to get from one of the fast travel points to a distant objective, and it can feel a little long, but it's a very minor gripe.Presentation all round is excellent, and the sense of satisfaction as you gradually complete your database is palpable. I would say that you should go in prepared for quality minimalism, and if you enjoy that, you won't be disappointed with In Other Waters. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: "In Other Waters" is a love letter to our world just as much as it's an exploration of the possibility of life on other ones. The story is achingly beautiful and equal parts tragic and hopeful. The mechanics are challenging enough to be engaging, but easy enough to be fun, and the graphics, while simple, are very well done. The game is a gorgeous example of environmental storytelling, and you only have your gathered clues and the musings of Dr. Vas to guide you to your conclusions about what happened on this mysterious planet. The speculative fiction is almost uncomfortably on-point with problems we face today with capitalism and climate change, and the alien marine biology is thoroughly-researched and meticulously detailed. Amazing game, no notes ❣️
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Music, UI, Excellent. Loved the minimal art style and colour palettes throughout.Everything else: Passable...Perhaps a limitation of the minimalist direction of the UI, but the gameplay is barebones and never really improves. At every stage of the game you will be endlessly repeating the exact cycle of scan, click, move; scan, click, move; scan, click, move...  The early areas have some basic puzzles to them but after that, you're just dropped into empty expanses to move through until you hit each story point.Story was decent, it picked up at the halfway point and I finished the game in one sitting from that, but there's zero payoff to it. Several of the main plot points don't get fully explained, and the game builds up to one of the most underwhelming finales I've played: It just feels like nothing happens. I was just left staring at the credits thinking "Was that it?". Wait for a sale and don't expect too much of it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica... kinda... except you don't need to witness the terrifying deep ocean.The gameplay revolves around the exploration and documentation of a largely water planet. This is achieved through the ui of your underwater vessel, showing a map of what's around you, oxygen, among a few other elements. This ui and gameplay designs are the best & most unique aspects to the game, which pair nicely with the biological exploration the game focuses on. Other factors such as the story and ost both complement the setting and vibe of the game, making for a pretty well-rounded experience. Though it should be noted the slow-paced gameplay isn't for everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Such an atmospheric and novel-like experience, I'm now 50% into the game progress and thoroughly enjoy it. Unlike most SF games (e.g. No Man's Sky?) that explore the biology of alien worlds using stunning graphics, In Other Waters relies on narration, sound & music, and imagination, completed with a scholarly taxonomy literature and discovery behind-the-scenes. I feel like my dream of being an exobiologist comes true.My 8yo daughter also enjoys playing the game with me. She's more focused on the story (asks me to explain every details in the EV notes), and nicknames Minae as "Mini".
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: beautifully seamless UI coupled with some very nice music and descriptive writing really transport you into an alien world. in a lot of ways this reminds me of reading a good book. i am hooked by the premise but what's magic is how my brain is filling in all the details around me. games will spend $100m so you can see each individual pore in the character's face but nothing really tops your imagination. this game also made feel like i was playing a very stripped down pilot simulator. once you get the hang of the gameplay loop it becomes very satisfying in that workmanlike checking-every-box kinda way.says i played 31 hours but in game time was closer to 5, for the record. i had this running in the background quite a bit just fwiw
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's beautiful and atmospheric, with a gorgeous soundtrack. The UI does a great job of representing the underwater world, though the movement mechanic can be kind of frustrating. I initially really liked it for the meditative quality of the gameplay, but the story also ended up drawing me in so much more than I expected. Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: an incredible story, experienced through the eyes of an AI, and therefore told mostly through text and environmental clues provided by scanners, equipment, and your interactions with the only human on the planet. slow, meditative, very chill and relaxing to play. beautiful and elegant as a game and a story. my only complaint is that it's hard to know which way is forward and which way is to side quests while exploring, but it's only so frustrating because the game is chill and enjoyable enough that it makes you want to play it to completion.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a relaxing dive into the newly discovered marine ecosystem of an exo-planet, played entirely through a beautifully designed UI and very good sound design. Despite not having a true-to-life visual render for most of the things encountered, the game does a fantastic job of sparking the player's imagination through text, atmosphere and a clever visual design. Highly recommended for any marine biology enthusiasts. That being said the ecosystems presented, while fairly detailed, are  reminiscent of life found in our own oceans. To the point I felt the organisms described did not feel alien enough for me to buy into this world being an alien planet. As a marine biologist myself, I put down the controller feeling like I had seen it all before, as no life-form is truly unique and it all has a very strong sense of familiarity. Narrative wise, the game was a major let-down for me. The mystery uncovered throughout the playthrough is somewhat interesting, but similar tales have already been told and paired with the already familiar ecosystem, mediocre monologues and one-sided exploration of environmental ethics, I was left with a sense of indifference towards both the characters and life-forms of Gliese 667Cc, as well as the larger universe presented. If interested, get it on sale. Worth a playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A short, unique, and enriching experience- more or less Subnautica without gameplay.It delivers the story and experience almost entirely through written elements, letting your imagination take the lead. This concept is written into the story in a unique and convincing way. I've never played anything like it.Ending is underwhelming, failing to answer some of the mysteries it spends so much time setting up.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The concept seems interesting, but the execution didn't work for me unfortunately.The gameplay just feels like rather a clunky way of turning pages. And if you took what you read in the game and actually put it in pages it would amount to a lot of exposition on fictional fauna...At least for the first two hours... Which is all I could bearThe interface looks like you are piloting a submarine, but the truth is that you are just clicking predefined waypoints. Exploration in games is always gated to an extent - and really an illusion, but to me this is too much. At least if you could just click on these waypoints directly.. But no, you need to scan them first, then click of them.Sometimes you need to drag and drop stuff you acquire to open up new paths... Othertimes you need to pick up stuff with an interface element (you slide a slider, then you click two buttons then you click another button - then you have picked a thing up)... but just feels like extra clicks with no real thought behind them.The survival/exploration elements are so light that they just feel like busywork rather than something to play around.It could have worked better as a visual novel... If there were actual visuals. You just get a heightmap and colored dots representing the cool stuff. Apparently to figure out what something looks like you first need to figure out if whole life cycle and take samples of every single aspect of its biology... I get its meant to be the reward for completing stuff, but its still funny that you have to sit through all these elaborate descriptions and still have little idea of what they are portraying till you get the drawing and then realize you had it all wrongIt might be a bit harsh to judge what probably amounts to 20% of the game like this. But to me that should be the hook of the game, rather than something to endure.If you enjoy reading and finding out about fictional fauna, you might enjoy it. I just figured out I need more to keep coming back to a game. To me the solution would be to either make it an actual exploration/survival game or just trim all the fat and make it a choose your own adventure/visual novel type of thing. Having the interface of the former with the gameplay depth of the latter is a match made in hell
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a gem. The whole concept of discovering the alien ecosystem really got my imagination going. Discovering this little world was a pleasure the whole way and everything about the design helped that along. Great UI (I played on my touchscreen the whole way), great sound design, lovely writing and artwork. Everything fits together, nothing feels superfluous. Anybody who likes story-oriented games will really enjoy this melancholy and hopeful take on life beyond Earth and humanity's relationship with it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a unique and incredibly charming game.To call it a walking simulator would not be quite accurate, though most of what you do is essentially just 'walk' around... swim really.You play an AI built into a divesuit being used by a xenobiologist on a foreign planet, your job is to guide her around in search secrets and to catalog the planets wealth of diverse alien life.The primary gameplay loop comprises the task of vectoring pathways for exploration, gathering samples, managing suit energy/oxygen, very occasionally using the additional tools and puzzle mechanics.Samples gathered can be used as fuel sources for either energy or oxygen, this varies based on the sample, and can also be used to interact with environment in several ways.The tools obtained along the way are themselves powered by your oxygen and energy.All told the gameplay isn't quite simple enough to call a walking simulator but is never quite complex enough to call it a resource management sort of fair. exploration really is the best word for it.Through elegant simplicity the game portrays the feeling of being a marine biologist.Stylistically the game is utterly superb.I am subjectively a huge fan of the games aesthetic but on an objective level every detail is masterful.What I mean is that every piece of menu and map, world and organism; have insanely well crafted and minute animations. The game lacks specific visual graphics, instead offering maps and menus, you are an AI after all.What we do see is incredibly polished, the sound accenting every tiny motion and detail, the result is a completely believable world.This game is perhaps my new favorite example of mastering simplicity. Few games have so completely immersed me in alien worlds as this one does with only a handful of topographical screens to look at.The writing is a huge component here, while there were some small typos, I want to say there were three in total, I noticed because they were in stark contrast to how professionally done all the entries were.There is a fantastic consistency of character here, and masterfully done entries for all the organisms. I wanted to catalog everything so I could see the illustrations I would get as a reward.Finally there is narrative to cover,I enjoyed the overall tone but I did have some slight problems.it is a bit political and preachy, it gave enough for me to say it wasn't wholly unoriginal, but I will say I liked it more at the start than at the end.I appreciated the characters and their relationship to one another, the big reveal had ramifications that slightly flatten the wonder of discovery throughout, but it wasn't so predictable so I could almost forgive it...I'm struggling not to get into spoilers...So would I recommend this game?I guess.. I really liked it but I'm not certain who this game is for...I sure love roleplaying a xenobiologist but like... who else is that gonna please...just look at all the screenshots on the store page, if that is enough for you than you will definitely enjoy it, otherwise probably go elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems simple and even repetitive on the surface, but the strength of the world building and the narrative drive of discovering the mystery of what has happened on this strange planet absolutely captures your attention almost before you notice it happening. I found myself going back to previous mission areas just to try and learn more about my discoveries, and was absolutely delighted when the game pushed back on that decision. It made my choices seem like they mattered, even in a fairly linear exploration experience. This is the game I needed to play right now.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Very relaxing but also mysterious experience overall. It's an exploration by essence but also visual-novel-like. I was genuinely interested in how the story would pan out. The ending might be, in my opinion, not super compelling. The UI design and interactions were fun but I wish the scan toggle and untoggle button was unified to space bar only. That way I could focus more on exploring rather than feeling "hitting left control button is kinda tedious."
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loving the game so far. a stylish, intelligent & meditative experience. It's quite refreshing.Minimalist presentation is clean & slick.  Sound design is off the charts.  Writing is smart with enough leads to keep you wanting to explore just a bit more.Overall it's an extremely polished package with a serene vibe that couldn't have come along at a better time.Kudos to team JOTA.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game. Its slow paced, but I was so entranced by the story. Admittedly it isnt much of a game, being just some yellow dots on a HUD, but the story told through text was amazing. To me this game served as a contrast to the tone and pace i'm used to, and gave me time to think. Music is great too.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'm refunding this game. You'll see my low playtime, and think this is a review to just gloss over, but hear me out.I think this is definitely something to try, I don't doubt there's a fantastic story being told here, and the game design is wonderful. It's nice and sleek, efficient. The sound design provides a whimsical dose of serotonin, hearing complex beeps and boops as you punch buttons and turn dials.However, I'm not seeing myself recommending this to anyone, nor am I going to try to finish it.The game gets stale, fast. I usually don't mind repetitive tasks, but this one just takes the cake.Prepare for an hour of traversing Gliese 667Cc by repeating the same 2 clicks, and hearing the same beeps and boops over and over and over.It doesn't help that In Other Waters doesn't offer much to look at, most of your discoveries are going to be symbolized by little dots on your screen, a constant yellow and blue, melding into each other. Exploration feels stale and stagnant as Waystation A fails to pry itself apart from the appearance of Waystation B.Worst of all, In Other Waters fails to get me feeling w e t. I look at my cyan-glazed screen and I feel no closer to the Ocean than Ellery is, sinking ever so deeper into the ocean.The lack of imagery, and engagement failed to immerse me in her story, in your story.What I'm trying to say here is, In Other Waters seems like an artistic journey, rather than a game. You're sort of just there for the ride, and you aren't going to be doing much.I played and completed Citizen Sleeper, if you found this game through that, just as I had, then I'd really recommend you rethink what you're looking for in a game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is rad!  First of all, I love the unique framing.  Seeing everything through the lens of a navigation system gives the game a strong identity.  I enjoyed the slow rhythm of exploration, reading  and movement.  It can be a bit tedious but overall it creates a cool vibe.It's really cool that you're not directly seeing everything, you just have your sonar screen {which looks incredible and still manages to show you beautiful environments} and a whole ocean of text to read from the main character's observations.  This game is mostly reading, but the game around that adds a lot to the experience.  The minimalist style and constant  brief prose descriptions of the environment go very well togetherThe ecosystems you explore are fascinating, I especially enjoyed how symbiotic relationships are so fundamental to each one.    I loved learning about all the different species and I love the scientific writing.   The main character makes observations, speculations and discoveries ... it gives a lot more flavor to these text entries. You're not just reading encyclopedia entries,  you're going along with the journey of cataloguing stuff for the first time. I have some minor complaints about underutilized potential (especially with some gameplay systems) and I don't like the direction the story chooses to go in. That's not enough to hurt my recomendation for this great experience
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica meets a text adventure. This game brings you to a unexplored oceanic world and leave you, not as the intrepid explorer, but as a digital assistant. You must guide others through the world that you experience fundamentally differently.Low in threat and rich in narrative, this game feels like a exobiology lesson coupled with a visual novel. There is plenty to explore and collect, but ultimately, you ride the current of the narrative, learning about the characters and world, until it gracefully ends.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Sublime underwater sci-fi experience! Fuelled by a great story, great UI presentation, and your own imagination! On a desolated planet a female scientist asks your help to control her diving suit, in order to investigate what happened to her colleagues who did studies on this planet decades ago. A friend xenobiologist of hers arrived long after after they vanished to find out what happened to her mother, this friend also disappeared. She left bits of research behind, but she didn't leave clear logs behind. What was the reason for this? Together with Ellery, our companion, we slowly but surely find out what happened to this underwater planet! Normally I don't look up too much about games I'm going to play, so I expected some visual presentation of any sort. This game plays entirely inside an UI. A compass-like control panel when you're navigating the diving suit, and a menu representing the base. It remotely feels like a very old DOS game, that makes an appeal to your imagination. This game does that superbly well! When the UI changes colour to match the environment, it hits like a hammer! Thanks to the great writing of this game! Is it all fantastic? No not entirely. To move around you have to click four times. You can speed this up by using the keyboard, but I don't see the point for this. Also taking samples is rather mundanely done. It feels a bit like artificial gameplay, to slow down the progression. There is a lot of extra lore to be explored. Every waypoint is described by Ellery, her observations. At times she conveys her thoughts. There is one part packed with lore, but you are losing oxygen. When you run out of oxygen you are 'retrieved' to the nearest droppoint. Since I was very interested in all the lore I have had a few resets. Later it appeared that I took the least favourable route. I find it odd that there is this conflict of much lore and having to hurry. There is a catalog function of all the samples you gather. For some reason this didn't work for me. Every sample gave an error. I must have done something wrong, no idea what... Such a game would be perfect with voice acting! It already has very atmospheric music, with good sound effects and voices such a game would be so immersive! I hope the devs will make more games like this, there is plenty material for a sequel! This game could use achievements. Many people just enjoy them! 85/100I  loved the ending, but it left me with some questions...
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up in a town with an oceanographic museum that we frequently visited, I was instantly drawn to the strange sensations of the aquatic alien wildlife and the astonishingly atmospheric soundscape. I felt like the little kid I was decades ago, exploring aquariums, display boards and monitors emitting the sound of waves and low fidelity documentary.I never really understood “cozy games” so far and while this does not have that specific tag, I still feel like this is my kind of cozy game. Never too hand-holdy, never too hard, always nudging you in the right direction while still giving you a great sense of exploration and a lovely chill vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: 'In Other Waters' is a good, albeit slow, text-heavy experience. There is quite a lot of exploration, but very little 'game' per say, as the same 4 buttons are used the whole game with little in the way of variation. This is made up, however, in the depth and complexity of it's world-building.The writing is about average, but the world building is where this game earns its price-tag. Exploring and learning about this strange, almost Permian world is a joy to behold. When I say text heavy, this is a book first and a game second though an enjoyable one at that. Not to mention the amazing thematic soundtrack, it is rather immersive and really strengthens an already strong sense of presence to the world.The story starts really strong with the emergent sense of wonder, but slows down and can get a bit tedious right around the midpoint of the second arc. By the final arc, however, things pick up sufficiently to carry you to the story's conclusion. The game can probably be completed in 4 or 5 hours if you maintain a good pace; this might constitute about one or two gaming sessions. It took me a total of 7h 45 minutes to finish the game to 100% tax completion.If you enjoy a bit of a slower, text heavy gaming experience with an immersive world 'In Other Waters' will certainly be a treat.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly immersive and atmospheric game, given what it is. Kind of annoying controls at times, but the creatures are interesting, and getting to roleplay as an off world biologist study aquatic life is certainly fun for those of us who'd imagined that humanity would be further along the tech tree than we are in real life.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game cause it looked unusual, and it's really fun. There's almost nothing to see so far (~1.5 hrs into the game at time of writing), it's mostly top-down topographical maps and circles representing plants, animals, and fungi. Despite how it sounds, this game is entrancing. There's a sense of wonder about every new step, and each discovery is as interesting as the one before it. Highly recommend this game if you like slow-paced, thoughtful games.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, thought-provoking, enrapturing... It's so easy to sit down and just play this game. Without any spoilers, let me put this as easily as possible. You learn with this game in a way that will become very evident from the first 5 minutes, all the way until the near-end of the game. You're MEANT to not know what you're doing, not know where you are, but as much as you are a guide for Ellery Vas, she is a guide for you. And what a world does she discover alongside you; Gliese 667Cc is teeming with incredibly interesting lifeforms, not so outside the scope of terrestrial marine life that it's completely impossible to relate to and understand, but alien enough that each sample you retrieve is worth the knowledge you gain. The science put into this game is really amazing as well; I was blown away each and every time I gained a new entry in the taxonomy files.I only wish the game were longer, and that more could be said for Minae. There's a very hopeful and determined note that this game is ended on, but with how the game sweeps you up into its story, you want to see even a glimpse into that future. Regardless, it was really amazing. Insane atmosphere, really academic, and emotional despite the game-play style. Loved every aspect besides wishing the ending were more substantial.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Impressive format that felt really fresh. The writing was excellent, and I could see the rich ocean world unfold before my eyes. The story was beyond captivating, and really made me appreciate the life we find on our planet and really drove home the terror of the thought that we are actively destroying one of the universe's most beautiful creation. The only question that I have is why it took me so long to discover this game. Thank god for LudoNarraCon or I would've completely missed out on this masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a remarkable little gem, although It is a pretty niche title for sure and a lot of people might not quite gel with it (I can totally understand that), but personally I found everything about it just perfect, the story is truly captivating and will leave you thinking long after the end credits have rolled. The gorgeous UI, sound and topography design is also so satisfying to navigate.The soundtrack is up there in my top 10 game OST's as well, pure ambient bliss that captures the feeling of the vast unknown depths with a splash of the melancholy and wonder thrown in for good measure.Well worth checking out if you dig story driven indie games that do things a little differently.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very special beautiful game.It is a joy to explore this games alien ecosystem through the tactile interface of a diving suits controlling Ai, sensor readings and your partner/ocuupants' descriptions of the local flora and fauna paint a fascinating mental image of a truly alien ocean as you slowly unravel a mystery tied intimately with this environment. This is a truly phenomenal and wondrous sci-fi story and this game will likely end up being my GOTY.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Completed game at 96%, Linux, 6.7 hours.First, I would like to say that In Other Waters is not your usual game. There's no combat, no flashy cinematics, multiple characters or anything like that. Instead, I would define In Other Waters more as a journey, a journey through the sea directing the steps of a biologist around the sea of an exoplanet while she maps and collects samples and searches for a lost friend.In In Other Waters you take the role of an AI on board of a diving suit and choose where to go, what to collect, what to keep and how to use everything. If you don't mind, I will not spoil the story ;)The game is very atmospheric, and although the graphics are very simple (just lines of similar height, showing the limits of objects and of the terrain), the music and the sounds accompany you throughout the game very well.The two only minor points I have 'against' the game are that sometimes you barely have time to read all the descriptions of every nook and cranny and different species of aliens that you encounter. And that the cycle of scan-select destination-move can be a bit tiresome after a while.So, my summary is: if you want an atmospheric game, go for it. 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: feels more like a UI study than an actual game. It's a mildly interactive sci-fi story in the form of an interface of a AI-controlled suit that a scientist explores an alien ocean in. You can do reasonably many different things in this game, but the method if delivery was just too detached for me to empathize: instead of seeing an alien ocean filled with unique lifeforms, I saw dots on a screen with flowery descriptions—and, unfortunately, nothing more.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those texts that convey the preposterous wonder of life in all its forms.  is imbued with such thoughtful speculation and imaginative detail, and is a demonstration in how to streamline the design of a game to support its narrative. As long as that hard sci-fi mystery sounds up your street, this is a get.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Loved this game! It had a dynamic atmosphere that worked so well with the colors, UI, and sound design. At some points I was on the edge of my seat waiting for something to ambush me! In my opinion, this game was designed well to do a lot with a little. The interface is clear and simple, and even realistic when you consider you're playing as an AI in a suit who receives data, not imagery. The way that would change colors combined with the sounds made for such diverse areas, which were essentially just topo lines on the screen. The descriptive entries and monologue made my head explode with imagining what this place looked, felt, and sounded like. This has truly diversified my concept of what a "video game" really means!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so cool! It can be frustrating, navigating the map by moving from point to point, but on the other hand, it lets the player take their time in exploring. The alien creatures encountered are very unique and creative, thoughtfully made, and inextricably linked with the rest of their ecosystem. I recommend this game to anyone who likes chill, scientifically-minded games.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Exploring the unknown,  places the player from the perspective of an AI helping to guide xenobiologist Ellery Vas after she was called to planet Gliese 677Cc by her colleague, Minae Nomura. What she discovers is for the player to find out. The game is minimalistic yet beautiful, stowed away in a world that rests entirely in the imagination of the player, aside from some of Ellery's research sketches, a topographic map that you explore, and also simplistic representations of the life within the oceans of this planet. Moving around within restricted vector points on the map, you will uncover the story in bits and pieces, every bit driving you to try to find out some more. What drew me to the game at first was the set of screenshots seen in the store page. Not too much time spent in the game later, I realized that's pretty much all of the visuals I will be seeing. Fine, no problem. The game's pull on my curiosity by involving my imagination did the trick. I read through all of the observations surrounding each vector point, I try to explore as much as I could, I tried to see every corner that the game was willing to present to me. Several hours later, I realized that I had been very slow in progressing the story, but instead making every effort to identify every organism I came across and to gather whatever samples needed to examine in detail later in the lab--which is an automated procedure, of course. Only Ellery's scientific research logs and her brief diary entries serve as larger sections of reading--even then they are optional. The rest of the game is trickle fed through small observations and Ellery's brief interjections as she documents the newly discovered organisms or she voices her thoughts mixed with her memories.And you will find yourself doing much of the same, scanning the waters, reading observations, moving from one vector point to the next, etc. Some of these will have organisms, remains, etc. for you to sample. The sampling mechanic is very simple and easy to use. After that, you will find that some of the samples will help you by giving you more power, more oxygen, or they may assist in altering the organisms around you so that you can then further your explorations. There will be a few areas that you might come to that are basically locked off until later in the game when you have an additional tool equipped, but for the most part, there will be very few limitations.Should you decide to dive into the game, the game gives no hints on what you should or should not be doing. You have a set of tools available, and so you will be able to use them however you wish. A few spoken hints from Ellery gets you going, but really, you are left to explore the game for yourself, including the way that the mechanics work. I think this works well for a game like this, it truly is as if you are an awakened AI system whose memory banks have been wiped but are able to carry out the functions. In turn, you discover more about your own identity as well as the story unfolds.An engaging atmosphere to accompany the minimalistic game is difficult to accomplish, especially when the game primarily features lines of text here and there for the player to read. But  accomplished it, by combining a beautiful ambient soundtrack with location-specific tracks, excellent sound effects that hint at nearby curiosities and/or immediate dangers, a fleshed out world through the well-written revelations, the simple use of color/topographical map, and that continuous pull on the player's imaginative curiosity.It took me right around 11 hours to complete this game to its very last detail, explore all of the nooks and crannies, and to see the story to its end.  I imagine that now knowing everything and if I wanted to just to run through the story from beginning to end in a new game, it would probably take somewhere around 4-5 hours, that would mean me rushing from place to place, doing everything I can to progress the story but doing as little as possible to explore unnecessary paths or to collect the optional samples to complete the research entries. I have seen people posting screenshots for 100% in as little as 8 hours, so you should have a relative idea of how long you will be expecting to spend with this game.In my final exploratory dives to complete the sample collections, I may have wished to have an on-screen pointer that could guide me a little bit more. But is it necessary? Absolutely not. The game's not all that big, and the world being divided into the vector points really is not too difficult or too long to discover in its entirety. There were also occasional grammar errors that I can expect from a game with so much writing. Of course, the occasional glitch encountered put me off a little, but nothing game breaking.The game allows you to Save + Quit anywhere within the game, to continue at a later point. You can also complete the story first and then return to the game after to complete whatever optional research items you have not completed. I would have gone through the main story a bit quicker had I known the latter. So, now you know as well.You only need a mouse or a controller. They both work perfectly fine. I played with the mouse to start and switched to controller about midway through. You can toggle the button prompts for the different actions on-screen with your controller any time, and they are not intrusive to the visuals. I kept them on for the most part.There is very little that the screenshots do not already tell you. It's minimalistic and text based, with very little visuals.Amazingly put together and absolutely crucial to the overall experience.So this game will inevitably reach fewer people than it deserves, because of its heavy reliance on text. I know plenty of people who do not want to read, even in games. But in all seriousness, if you do not want to read through the game, do not play it. (It seems that if you cannot handle ellipses in monologue, they may also bother you. To me, the use was mostly reasonably done to convey Ellery's excitement, disbelief, or being deep in thought. A few unnecessary ones were not going to bother me much.)Base price is set at $14.99 US, which is reasonable. That accompanying PDF DLC is a bit pricey though, and I think a lot of people are going to skip paying an extra $9.99 for it.The gameplay mechanics became a lot more smooth-flowing for me after a couple of hours, so I was mostly fumbling for an hour here. While I say that it's okay to watch the beginning of the game because it is not very revealing, part of the charm of this game is to discover everything on your own, including how to work through the controls while being fed the story in small chunks. The video is here if you wish to curse at me for clicking the wrong thing again and again for inefficient use of time, but I won't hear you, so that's okay. is an absolutely recommended game from me, and it's one of my favorite indie games of 2020. I enjoyed every fumbling and stumbling minute I had with the game. I thank you for still reading this review at this point, and I hope you take the time to enjoy this wonderful gem of a game as well.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: What starts off on a high note with its otherworldly soundtrack, interesting narrative and feeling like you're exploring an alien ocean drags itself to a hault by the third hour. The clunky traversal system means you spend most of the game waiting to get to your destination. And the overwhelming amount of text thrown at you can get super tiresome. It sort of has some survival mechanics but they are easy to manage and ignore. Where they just shouldn't have existed. I don't like criticizing games that are different like this but this really should have been a book. Or even a visual novel but there is just so little visual storytelling going on. To the point where I skipped large amounts of world building because it was large text info dumps. Which don't really do anything for the marrative and arguably hurts the world building.Exploring alien oceans is one of the things I enjoy most in gaming but In Other Waters it was mostly exploring the world in my mind and listening to the music. That makes it hard to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting concept. I first played a game around 5.5 hours and got about halfway through the plot, got bored. Ended up starting a new save a few months later, and finished the entire plot in less than 6 hours. Super short game, in my opinion. I personally didn't love collecting all the samples and was more interested in following the story, but it was short. Good story, but really short game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The most fascinating thing about In Other Waters is its premise: you will play as an AI controlling the systems of a suit worn by a researcher, exploring a huge underwater ecosystem. The role of the researcher, in addition to purely narrative, is to be your eyes and ears, providing you with information (via text descriptions or dialogue) about your surroundings and the next steps to take, even going so far as to ask for your opinion in certain situations. I find this idea very interesting, but I must admit that the gameplay loop became very tiring too soon, crippled by a sense of repetitiveness that made me stop playing after discovering that the point where I had arrived was not the ending, but only a climax roughly halfway through the game. Although the writing is top-notch and the setting is extremely well-characterized and interesting to delve into, from a gameplay standpoint you are limited to repeatedly clicking on the screen to select the next location to reach 90% of the time, with the remainder devoted to very simple environmental puzzles and researching samples retrieved from the ecosystem. I want to emphasize that by this I do not mean that all point-and-click adventures come across as dull and repetitive, but that In Other Waters feels much more like a short novel filled with xenobiology than a point-and-click video game.So why do I recommend In Other Waters, despite dropping it?Because overall the game is definitely not bad and I realize that it could be greatly appreciated by a niche of gamers willing to try something a little different, even just to read about a very inspiring world capable of stirring the imagination.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: finished the game, 100% species examined takes you to a planet far from Earth, where you meet a xenobiologist who is trying to find a lifeform and reconcile with her friend. Deep dive into a planet full of water to find specimens and study them.- Simplistic UI- Relaxing gameplay- Unable to open lab to check previously collected specimens when you are exploring- Dialogues are auto advanced, forcing you to read the dialogues when you have no time to do soIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 provides a simplistic design. It plays out from a top-down view, where you can see everything through a radar-like interface. Although the simplistic UI looks neat after you get used to it, it is confusing for first-timers to operate. There is no information on what each button does and you need to do a trial end error to figure out what they do.Despite the story being one of the main focuses of the game, the design seems to encourage you to skip it. It takes too much effort to advance the dialogue manually when you have nothing better to do with no hotkey support, while it can be problematic to read when you need to do a lot of actions in a short time since it automatically advances after some time has passed. The best that you can do is to read everything through the message log, which I always did most of the time, not only because of how the dialogue advances, but also because the story tends to be hard to grasp unless if you read the whole paragraph at once.If you are interested in reading alien lives, the game has a lot to offer. You'll study different specimens, tracking your discovery in your journal. This journal takes form in a full report of the specimens' behavior, images, and theories of the xenobiologist. However, since they all are non-fiction, I don't find any benefit in reading them, especially since they have a lot of texts.As I said before, the game takes form in a radar-like interface where you can scan the area and order the protagonist, Ellery Vas, to move around. However, the game barely has tutorials to understand how it works, and figuring out how to walk took more time than it should be. Moreover, the interface seems to encourage you to do everything with your mouse, despite it will be easier to play with a keyboard. Fortunately, keyboard shortcuts for some actions like scanning an area and moving forward are available, which help to cut time in exploration.As a xenobiologist, you can research the specimens on this watery planet. This can be done by taking samples of the specimens in certain spots and bring them back to the lab to do more experiments. You'll bound to get extras from the sample gathering, and these can be used either as a fuel or as a tool to manipulate your environment. Some specimens can be used to clear obstacles in a short area while others can help you to provide an O2 area in poisonous areas.Although the specimens will be more focused on environment manipulation at the start, you'll explore more dangerous areas as you progress. Your engine and O2 supplies will deteriorate faster than they should be, and you must use extra specimens as fuel to keep going. This also makes the end-game areas to be a chaotic mess, forcing you to rush the areas before you run out of fuels. Standing still is discouraged, whether it's to read the story dialogues or the small texts that are always available on every node in your path.I finished the game in ~6h after collecting all specimens. Some specimens are only available in optional areas, forcing you to re-explore previous areas and remember the areas that you haven't explored to find them. This also means that it's best to explore an area in one sitting, especially since you need to visualize the rough map of the area to prevent yourself from getting lost. The difficulty is easy as long as you focus on exploration and not spending your time reading the texts too much in the dangerous areas.The game doesn't mark the next objective at some point near the end of the game. The UI is also not intuitive when it notifies a diveable area. I got stuck in the game twice because of these problems. You also can't check the previously collected specimens when you are exploring an area, and the limited amount of specimens that you can carry at once might prevent you from progressing too much to prevent the use of non-duplicate specimens in the process.Being a relaxing game that is focused on exploration, it feels boring at first - you only need to scan the area and move around on repeat. It started to get better once the path branches out, letting you explore more areas and find rare specimens at the end of the road. Despite the story being hard to read in dangerous areas, it does a good job in killing the boredom, forcing you to finish the task quickly. However, people who had a hard time visualizing a map on their heads might have difficulty with the game, especially since some areas tend to look similar. At the end of the day, it's still a nice relaxing game, one that will be enjoyed for those who like to explore.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it in the tiny teams festival, really interesting experience. Even with minimal art and mechanics (creatures and plants are dot's on a topographic map, you control the diving suit by scanning and walking between waypoints) it does a great job of evoking a sense of mystery and exploration. The writing is very good, and reminded me strongly of the book Children of Ruin. Slowly coming to understand truly alien life.Would recommend to anyone who doesn't mind a text heavy game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet little game. Super simple, just point and click. The music was super relaxing and matched the "vibe" of the game super well. I enjoyed the UI and the overall look of the game. For being such a short game (main story is only 3-4hrs), the amount of content in it is really cool and detailed. There's a bunch of different species you can discover, theories behind them, and even sketches. You can tell a lot of time and creativity was put into this game. And if you're interested in it, you can spend many more hours past the main story just discovering everything.I think the only thing I wished this game had: achievements lol I'm a sucker for achievements but obviously it's not necessary.Because it's so short, I would definitely recommend buying this game when it's on sale. But if you like story-driven, point-and-click game/text-based games, or you're super into marine biology, I think you'll enjoy it!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is a particularly exemplary game if you are willing to accept its occasionally obtuse gameplay. More than the awesome atmosphere and noteworthy soundtrack, what makes In Other Waters a great game is the fact that it contains some of the best writing I've ever had the pleasure to witness anywhere, not just in video games. The balance between deeply astute observations of the life on the planet and the incredibly poignant dialogue displayed as the story unfolds is breathtaking. It challenges what a game is and should be in the most beautiful of ways. Though it isn't my favorite game and something I most likely won't return to, it is an amazing experience I would highly recommend to anyone whom loves art video games.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is relaxing. Unique.  And quite captivating.   Such rich, colorful, text-based imagery keeps me deeply engaged as I explore this alien oceanscape, discover and catalog new lifeforms, and unravel the mystery of my pilot's missing colleague.  How do the developers/writers know to scratch a marine biology itch I didn't even know I had?
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Overall good. An unfair description would be "minimalist walking simulator Subnautica". 3 out of 5 as a game. 4 out of 5 as a concept.I did not enjoy the first 30 minutes of the game at all (scan, move, scan, repeat) but eventually I got into the mood of it, taking one "dive" each day, spacing out the story. It felt like some aspects (the prelude to the ending and the collection mechanic) had undergone some revision during development, but the narrative was well thought out.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very short experience, but it's a real pleasure. Gorgeous UI and world, and I thought the story was very compelling too. You'll probably guess the broad strokes, but I thought all the details were interesting and creative, and there's a lot of lore to bring the world to life.Two things: I was not totally sure how much impact my decisions made (except one, which I *think* certainly would have made a big difference in the ending). The other thing is, I really wish there was more art (even static art like the sketches) to depict characters or things that you're seeing.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful game, and beautifully written. Very classic science fiction in a way: an alien world, a mystery, strange creatures. The graphics style is quite abstract but works well.My only complaint is that the node-based map movement feels quite constraining and makes me feel a bit railroaded at times.(Note: I backed this game on Kickstarter.)
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting story told by means of a linear gameplay and a very calm, slow pace. Your willingness to read the text and picture the situation out of it will play a big role in how much you'll enjoy the game, since most of the time all you can see are lines and dots. Resource management is simplistic, and exploration is streamlined, but rewards you with additional info about the world, which I found interesting. All in all a good game, would recommend if you are looking for something soothing.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly one of the most well thought out games that i have played in a really long time. The amount of detail and work put into the story as well as the biology behind how each organism works is astounding. On top of all that the graphics of the game are very satisfying to look at, everything is really smooth. moving around is a little tedious but the content of the game has outplayed anything i've seen in a while. 10/10 game
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't really delved too far into the game yet, so this is more of a review about the mechanics and gameplay. While the interface is different than what I'm used to, very barebones and simplistic, it's easy to navigate and use, and pretty easy to get fluid with. The game doesn't have much in the way of vibrance, but it makes up for it with it's cool topographical maps, scanning system, and the soundtrack is very calm and relaxing. Overall, I'd say it's definitely worth the time, and it's easy to lose track of time while playing.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: If the idea of being an ai companion to a xenobiologist as you explore a complex alien ecosystem sounds interesting to you then you will love this game. While there are more additions themetically which i won't spoil, the games focus is always on the ideals of science, and how that can clash with less noble interests. The great writing manages to keep this interesting for the duration of the playtime, with a lot to say about it's themes.Also this is one of the prettiest games, both muscially and visually that i have played in a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: So I got this game because it looked very different and it is.  It has an immersive good mysterious storyline and the controls will take some getting used to but that's also part of the story and learning them isn't hard.  Its also all about exploring and that ties in with learning the UI nicely which gives it some very innovative gameplay.  So I'd recommend this for anyone who likes exploring, solving easy (imo) puzzles, and a good story.  For me this under-rated game was well worth the cost and time.Bear in mind it is slow paced and some people might find the UI too restrictive/structured?
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest, were it not for a friend's recommendation I wouldn't have looked twice at this game. The info on the steam page left me feeling 'eh', and based on the graphics I could see i thought I'd either be really bored, or it'd make my brain hurt. Fortunately, I was wrong.I absolutely loved this game. While it is fairly minimal in gameplay, there is enough to keep you engaged. The story is absolutely amazing, though. I don't want to say much for fear of spoilers, but we'll just say I played this until 3am because I couldn't put it down until my eyes refused to open anymore. There's also the taxonomy of all of the species you can find - holy hell that DETAIL! I'll admit I didn't read all of them, but I did look at all of the sketches. Absolutely astounding. I also really appreciated that post-game, it gave you a chance to go back and find what you were missing. I was at 98%, and apparently I just forgot to scan something I already had in my base :,) But it allowed me to 100% it! And as someone who doesn't 100% games unless it's 1) easy or 2) I love the game, I hope that says something :)I did have a few problems with the game - it gets kind of boring going straight on the paths where there is nothing to scan, it bugged out a few times and told me I couldn't go deeper/less deep when I could and I'd have to leave the point and come back, and sometimes I didn't notice the game dialogue going because I was so focused on the radar, and seeing as the text auto-advances, I definitely missed some. There is a way to access to log at least, but at the time, it was kind of annoying. Overall small annoyances compared to the amazing positives.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's not that it's bad, it's that it's only about 3 hours of game. But look at my play time. Nearly 20 hours. That's because I actually fell asleep multiple times, or simply got distracted by Reddit for an hour and a half by accident cuz I was so bored. The problem is, it's just a regular visual novel. All the game mechanics are essentially just complicated ways to see the next sentence worth of story drip out--which is far too often a reiteration of something that was already said. As far as visual novels go, it's just okay. The concept is pretty cool, it's basically The Abyss + Subnautica. But it's not that great apart from concept. There's only one character and she spends most of her time repeating herself. There's numerous points where the writing is just plain awkward, like you'll go into a facility and she'll say "Oh, this was an industrial facility. People worked here." And then literally in the next room you enter after that she'll say "This isn't a lab....this is an industrial facility. Like...?!?! We know!The 'gameplay' is constantly getting in the way of actually absorbing the visual novel, too. For at least 50% of the game the environment will be killing you gradually, either from oxygen or power diminishing, or both. But the game feeds you the story by giving you information to everything you click on as you go. So basically you end up skipping reading all the details, because you don't wanna sit around reading while you're literally suffocating! It's maddening a text based game was designed in this way, and it makes me think they either just designed it poorly, or it's a deliberate attempt to prolong the game by making it more stupid. I don't know. I really respect the developers for making this, and I hope they keep making similar things. But this one was just a bit too little butter spread over too much bread for me. A good game if you're looking for something to play before bed, I suppose.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: As a training biologist myself, with a soft spot for marine biology, I picked up this game thinking it'd simply be a collecting game, entertaining enough! But it was so much more than that- I hadn't expected to encounter a beautiful story that sucked me in, really made me think about humans in function of a whole, an ecosystem. The xeno-organisms were tangible enough to visualize, their anatomy made sense as it used elements from real life organisms we find in our waters today, but it amazed me that the developer found ways to combine said elements into something wholly new. Every dive, I looked forward to discovering new creatures, seeing where they'd belong in Ellery's taxonomy, and analyzing samples I'd picked up while exploring. PROS:- amazing visuals. simple and clean.- the soundtrack was mesmerizing. - story rich, definitely recommended if you'd like to be fully immersed in something new.- the science is accurate, and I was honestly so happy the game didn't shy away from using biological lingo. do not worry though! it's not incredibly complex, so if you don't think you have enough of a scientific basis to go off of this won't be a huge struggle. + if you manage to unlock the sketches, I find that all the gathered information joins together beautifully as a whole. - as a fan of taxonomy, aka the situating of organisms within a hierarchy based off of molecular similarities/morphological similarities, identifying these creatures, describing them, giving them names, etc. this game really captivated me! I'll definitely remember how fond I was of the little details for years to come.CONS:- the way one navigates through the world is through repeated scanning, lining your vessel up to the next destination, and traveling there. while it can be good to traverse the world in a slow pace so you can take it all in, if you're trailing through an area for the second or third and onward time, it gets tedious to have to keep doing so in small bursts. - the game isn't very forgiving to people with a poor sense of navigation (aka me) ! in order to complete the game fully, one needs to collect all the sample data from specific locations, which are only shown on a map back at the base. this map becomes inaccessible once you are actually out and about, hunting for these samples. this combined with how tedious the traveling method is, uh. it gets frustrating fast. - I had a bug that sadly wiped out most of the samples I had stored in my base. No, I am still not over it, even if I can go out and collect them again. -_-Overall, if you don't mind somewhat repetitive gameplay, and a game with a beautiful plotline and world to explore, I'd highly recommend trying it out. This game favored telling a story over providing convenience to its player, and I wouldn't say it isn't worth it because of it. On the contrary, I feel like this game has a lot to offer if you have the patience for it. It's wonderful, easy to get into, and I know I'll cherish it even after I've 100%'d it. Try it out!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Chill exploration game with a lot of reading and collection objectives.Play an AI dragging a marine biologist through an alien water planet. Its by no means a fast game nor a particularly exciting one, but good nonetheless if you like calm methodical explorative games. I only played for half an hour or so but probably won't go back to it as its a little too slow for my tastes. Seems to be a great game, just not my thing.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game bizarrely has no settings menu. Want to mute the music or just turn down the master volume? Want to remap the 4 buttons? Want to change the speed/size of the text in a game that's all about reading text? These seem so obvious to include that their exclusion must have been a deliberate decision. It doesn't matter whether the motive was laziness or the developers' "vision". It's inexcusable.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A bittersweet love letter to nature. It'll take a bit to get used to the interface, but don't let that deter you from a beautiful story. There were parts like Subnautica that took my breath away- no graphics, just description and atmosphere. As a scientist, I can say their speculative science writing for is top-notch.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I really enjoyed this game. The smooth and simple graphic style is a nice change from the ever more realistic games that are made now, and the music does a good job of conveying the creepy but intriguing feeling of being on another world. The game conveys most of the information to the player by text, however, so those who don't as much enjoy having to read everything or may not have the fastest reading speed(dialogue is timed) may not enjoy this as much. I do like reading though, and enjoyed that. The only other thing to mention I would say is that this game is not super long. I completed a 100% run in less than 9 hours, and I'm generally pretty slow at finishing games, so take that as you will. Overall, I would say that if you enjoy reading about all of the story rather than watching it unfold yourself, and are into sci-fi, then this is a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: every once in a while i come across a game that redefines what a game can be. In Other Waters is one such game. i put off playing it for a long time; honestly i was pretty deterred by the way the gameplay looked. i was worried i'd be bored, or that it would be too simple. but this game has so much depth, heart, and scale that completely took me by surprise. i should've known better, after having played Citizen Sleeper, but i admit i was still unsure. this game totally exceeded all the expectations i had for it.for a game that is comprised entirely of looking at a HUD, there is so much rich storytelling, so much emotion. in fact, what is the most poignant about the gameplay experience is what is *not* seen. the deceptively simplistic design leaves room for the player's imagination, builds suspense, and allows the player to interact with its world in a totally unique way. it is also addicting, and easy to lose oneself in. heightened by amos roddy's magnificent score, In Other Waters has catapulted itself into my list of favorite games. i can't recommend it enough. if you have doubts: DON'T!

_childDocuments_.review: There are bits of this game that are beautiful, and I enjoyed the xenobiology, and I might even return to it at some point if I need a breather, but there are a few elements where this falls flat that outweigh the good. 1) The gameplay is clunky - This feels 'on purpose' rather than by accident, collecting samples requires a few clicks, and I can understand this from a perspective of *really* feeling like you're piloting your suit, in the same way that some mech games have you flick a few switches to turn on. This is neat at first, but becomes tiresome when you're retreading known areas to find a sample to learn more about some cool plant and it's just annoying. 2) There are times when the game requires you to move quickly through environments - given that the visuals are incredibly simple and the mechanics of the gameplay itself are not particularly fun (see #1), if you have the skip the reading parts, it becomes very difficult to see why you're playing at all. I struggle to see how these sections made it past testing, unless the testers were already familiar with the environments. 3) The 'exploration' element is hampered by the rail-like way to move around. I can see a potential post-hoc explanation for this, you don't know what part of the terrain is passable until you explore it etc, but there are times where it's really hard to see why you can't just go in a certain direction to take a shortcut, or getting somewhere feels unnecessarily painful (again, especially when you need to retread your steps).This was a borderline 'no' from me - the music is good and there are points I was really into reading about fungus stalks, but the annoyances of the gameplay get to a point where it feels like you're doing chores to get morsels of rewards.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Lots of really cool speculative xenobiology and an interesting mystery to slowly piece together. I love the amount of thought that was put into this game -- its characters, its story, its world, and especially its creatures. Some of my favorite moments were times where I just got to explore and learn more about this amazing alien world and its life forms. It was a very calming experience. I loved hearing Ellery's thoughts -- she possesses a curiosity and awe that really made these discoveries enjoyable. The game also has its fair share of haunting and evocative moments too and I enjoyed those as well. The writing and story in this game were really wonderful, and I'd say those are this game's main selling point besides the interesting xenobiology stuff. The soundtrack was really good and it was fantastic at establishing the game's atmosphere. It did a great job at capturing the emotions of each scene. The soundtrack is mostly pretty subdued and calm though, so I recommend wearing headphones to get the full experience out of it (that's what I did). The UI is pretty simple, but it has a very clean, polished look and is easy to use after figuring out how it works (it was a touch confusing at first). You don't get to see a lot graphically speaking -- most of what's in the game, besides what you find in Ellery's taxonomy sketches, is represented in the form of symbols. This isn't a bad thing per se, as it was an interesting and pretty cool experience to try to build the world (and before getting sketches, the creatures) myself in my own imagination, but I do wonder what this game would be like if it had the lush graphics of say, Subnautica. The whole experience rather reminded me of reading a book but mixed in with the exploration and puzzle-solving mechanics of a game. I enjoyed this aspect of the game but it may not be for everyone. I have only two real complaints with this game: 1) Backtracking can get rather tedious with the travel system that this game utilizes2) The text will move forward on its own if you wait for too long Thankfully, these are relatively minor annoyances overall and they don't detract much from what makes this game really good. I highly recommend this game if you're into leisurely-paced/atmospheric and insightful science fiction (or if you're a hardcore biology nerd, or both :) ). It's a wonderful hidden gem. It's kind of weird and different from most other games I've played, but I liked it quite it a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game that represents a modern version of the text-based RPG genre.The game is about an AI that controls the diving gear of a marine biologist. Being a machine means that the player's perception of the world is very restricted - but this is something that actually enhances the gameplay experience. The visuals are limited to dots and geometric shapes that appear on top of an elevation map, as well as colors that provide ambience to the location currently visited. _childDocuments_.review: In other waters was a unique experience that you don't come across that often. You have a lot to experience and discover in so little time, that you may want to rediscover some of them next time you open up the game. This Sci-Fi /UI game has a lot to offer if you don't mind reading the games like reading a book and have some patience. The game's details in words and the information you get out of lab, makes you wonder about a planet with a whole underwater life in it. Most of the time you are wandering around these waters and your scientist keeps taking notes of the thing you come across.   When you first enter the world of In other waters, you may be kind of disappointed, but if you keep going; read all those data about species you encounter back in the terminal , unlock those spectacular sketches of those living creatures, the game makes you want to wander in this vast world with good graphics.
