_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a beautiful, wondrous, unique experience. The writing (which is copious) is extremely detailed and believable, which helps solidly build the world you're exploring even though you can't see it directly. The mystery plot on top of that creates an extra element of intrigue and suspense that adds to the existing atmosphere and kept me hooked.The interface design and the soundscape do a fantastic job as a substitute for a direct graphical representation of your surroundings. Nothing is just a radar blip - each item of interest has its own characteristics, which I could associate with them when reading the taxonomy entries. I also like how the interface changes to show when you are in different areas. Combining that and the sounds with the terrain graphics, every region is distinguishable and interesting. Exploring is very rewarding, especially because it gives you more background on the environment.Some reviews mention the power and air management as a negative. Maybe if you're expecting a purely casual experience, it can be a bit jarring. But I thought it was a great feature of the game that added a bit more "gameplay" and also added to the immersion. I never had major issues with the system, because you can almost always find enough samples to keep your levels up, even though I read every single flavor text as I went along. The interface does a good job of keeping you aware of the systems without being distracting. A couple times I turned back when my levels were low, but it turned out there was an exit just ahead anyway.One thing I thought was a little underdeveloped is the depth system. You'll be at the same depth most of the time, and then towards the end you go to some more extreme depths, but there wasn't very much in between. Most of the depth changes are traversing caves and shafts. It seemed like there was a lot more opportunity there, but it's understandable that the game did need to be finished at some point. Another thing that some other reviews pointed out is it would be nice to be able to see your current position on the overall map, although I usually had a pretty good idea of my position and heading. Lastly, as a completionist, I was hoping to find out whether I found every map node, point of interest, etc (other than the solitary missable: ).I think the length of the game is very good. It took me 10 hours to get 100% according to my save file. If you beeline the story and don't stop to smell the flowers, that could be a lot lower. I was always eager to dive back in and see what came next. Of course, there's still a lot more we could see on Gliese 667 Cc.I've never seen or played a game quite like In Other Waters and I thoroughly enjoyed the experience. It does take some patience if you want to get the most out of it, but it's worth doing.

_childDocuments_.review: I think In Other Waters is the perfect example of when someone has a really cool idea for a game, genuinely seems to sink a LOT of time into making it, the world around it, the aesthetics...Only for that game to run head first into the giant brick wall of "This is an interesting gameplay mechanic, but it's incredibly tedious." And maybe that's part of the point, but it does make it hard to recommend. The "Gameplay" isn't there in the sense most might like, but I found myself immersed in it nonetheless. While the narrative is interesting, I think it gets a bit 'loose' towards the end, unsatisfying maybe? Finishes too quickly? And I personally believe that's just a product of how the game plays. I think the people/person who made this game realised that this kind of gameplay can only go on for so long before you get tired of it, and so wraps it up when they do. That's not to say the story is incomplete, it isn't, but I just wish I got another hour out of it, for things to simmer a little more in the mystery.So with that out of the way, lets get to rambling!Genuinely, I think what the developer(s) had going on here is a FANTASTIC base for a game. There's something so unique about having the player see and interact with the world in a limited way, while having their view INTO the world you inhabit seen through different eyes. You're an AI in a suit. You don't... see things the same way the person wearing the suit. You see lines, dots, triangles, topography maps, lifesupport meters, all the utilitarian stuff. You are someone's body, their eyes, in your own way. Just like they are yours, in their own way.I love Ellery's view into the world. It's great. The best part of this game is going out of your way to scan things, collect samples, and try to understand the world the best you can while using Ellery's research notes and sketches into a really well thought out and interesting alien world. ACtual thought went into the roles of how creatures all take part in their own ecosystems, even if just in a narrative sense, and I think some games that want to emulate alien ecosystems could do with taking a page from this game's book and putting a lot more thought into how their fauna and flora interact.It's... a chill game. There isn't much to it other than clicking, dragging, clicking, dragging, and the very rare resource management and puzzle solving. It is, mostly, a narrative experience, with nice art, an interesting gmimick, and *really* cozy music. I want another game like this, in a similar style. Oh, to be the AI, unsure of why it exists, but just... simply is, seeing the world through a different lens that a person does.Pick it up if you feel like doing a LOT of reading. And you're okay with... a lot of clicking and dragging and clicking and dragging and waiting and clicking being the vehicle for a fairly short, if not decent story with some good vibes. Sometimes, I'll switch my view to the bottom deck, sonar, wait for Ellery to walk into the observation room and sit there, watching spores and alien life flitter past on the sonar. My eyes, the sonar, is different to her eyes... but yet, I share this quiet, ponderous moment with her. Staring aimless into an alien sea, through different lenses. I think that's why I like this game so much, I find I get this kind of nerd ♥♥♥♥ out of games a lot nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a slow burner, I played it gradually over the course of half a year, though my total play time is just 15 hours, my one save/playthrough only has 12 hours on it, so some of that is due to having it on standby. Anyway, I got 100% of the biology notes on the different critters and because of that got the secret epilogue. So that's where I'm coming from with this review.This game is solid and well written, but tricky to get into, the text based style with the three clicks to move in any direction was frustrating at first as it felt slow, but in hindsight, you play as an AI in a divesuit using third party software for a task you're not meant for, so it makes sense it takes three actions to move. Even with that said, it was a little annoying until I got used to it, I got past that by focusing on the notes Ellery takes to describe each node. She's a real godsend as a character. Ellery is introduced to us at the start of the game so no real spoilers here, she's the lady you’re helping navigate the waters of planet Gliese 677Cc, is here because her former coworker and ex lady love Minae (They’re are many benefits to being a xeno-marine biologist) sent for her and then when she arrived on the completely isolated planet was nowhere to be found and the dive suit she’s in has an AI not designed for so she can't navigate independently and has to rely on an unfamiliar AI that take three clicks to move in any direction, (her priority is still worrying over Minae tho, whipped lol). She’s a very sympathetic character and you can really feel her wonder at all the life around you, her notes on the creatures you help her documents really bring the world to life, which is necessary as because you’re just a confused baby computer AI you can only see the vivid world she’s exploring vicariously through the notes she takes. Good thing she’s competent at her job. The gradual growth of your bond with her as her sole confidant in this vast world is really well articulated too.In other waters is that golden indie find the entire indie game industry aims to be for people, I accidentally found it and I can tell it was probably a real labour of love for the developers and while there were moments were it dragged and the belated realisation that you can't access part of the bloom until you continue a story beat of the plot was very annoying because I tried to get to this one node for ages before realising, those moments were totally outnumbered by the many moments of wonder and curiousity and just interesting things there are to find and experience on Gliese alongside Ellery. If you're looking for a solid exploration game and you're not the impatient type, then I totally rec testing the waters with this game. I had a really fun time with it and the ending moved my heart.

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a short but oh-so-sweet adventure game with an interesting narrative, fantastic soundtrack, and a short playtime. I usually dislike shorter games, especially ones that claim to have a powerful story behind them. If it's only 6 hours long, then how can it deliver on this promise? This game delivered. I went for 100% completion, which took about 8 and a half hours, and I loved every second of it. The story is fascinating and doled out in small chunks, giving you time to wind down in between each truth bomb. The graphics are minimal but beautiful, with soothing colors and interesting representations of alien seafloor topography, and the soundtrack has that certain je ne sais quoi that enhances the experience artfully. Gameplay is fundamentally repetitive, but different areas bring new environmental effects and obstacles, so it never truly feels boring. But the writing, oh the writing! For a game where you cannot see anything your companion is describing, visualizing what she says is effortless. From rock formations to alien life to the very ocean around you, the writing used strikes every chord needed, and then some. Every little node on this game's gigantic map prompts some commentary, and all of it is flawless.10/10 game, worth buying even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Something about this game stuck out to me when I was browsing the Steam store.Usually I play games only if they have achievements, but this one was different enough. A game about underwater exploration as a scientist. Okay...we'll try this out.Turns out this game was more mentally and emotionally investing than appears on the surface.In Other Waters plays like a visual novel, point and click, maze-like game with tons of lore on the ecosystem and a backstory that you will have to discover on your own, as that's the crux and the reason for the gameplay itself. I found that by the end of the game I wished it had been just a bit longer, but the length was reasonable for a game like this.You get to catalogue different creatures and bacteria, take notes on their roles in the local ecosystem, and how their relationships with other fungus and inhabitants of Gliese667Cc function.If you are looking for something with a meaningful story, a decent amount of lore, and not a too-taxing amount of backtracking and exploration (think of a plot map,) then you should generally enjoy this game. More than any of the other previously mentioned features, the story of Ellery Vas and her discoveries on this planet is the biggest takeaway, and it will leave you with a strong impression.Please enjoy the story.

The music in this game was incredible as well, and the atmosphere throughout was fantastic. I really enjoyed the dialogue with the protagonist, and simple interactions you have with them simple as they may be. It takes a lot of patience, and the right mood to finish, but I don't regret any part of it for a moment.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is a criminally underrated game. From its immersive soundtrack to its intriguing story, I was invested from beginning to end, and even invested enough to go completionist--which is not typically my playstyle. While the story could be considered predictable, any plot points I called ahead of time didn't hit any less hard when they arrived just because I saw them coming. It's not predictable, the plot is just well-supported and foreshadowed. Elleya is wonderful company and I'll be thinking about her story for a long time. I've recommended this by word of mouth to pretty much everybody I know and I'll continue to do so while I listen to the soundtrack until the end of time.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An insanely well-written game where the worldbuilding, plot, gameplay, and UI all come together to define a single coherent experience. It's like the TIS-100 of diving underwater. If you liked Tacoma but thought it was too short and leaves more to be desired, this game somehow achieves more with less. There's no vague, loose ends in the plot or worldbuilding. Everything that needs to be there is there to back it up. This game does what 99% of games on steam tagged "story-rich" can't.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Reminiscent of text-based games, In Other Waters follows the journey of a marine biologist as she explores a completely foreign ocean planet teeming with life, while looking for her friend. There is a story of intrigue present but the main focus is definitely the novel underwater landscape laid out for you to wander.If you've seen the footage, don't expect groundbreaking graphics, with the controls and display being on the rather analogue end. It's basically stark lines and blips that requires a fair bit of imaginative heavy lifting but it adds to the overall feel of the game and plays a deliberate part to the story as well.So, reserve an afternoon to document unique lifeforms and get lost in the depths. Just don't forget to watch your oxygen levels.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game. A lot of the gripes I've seen with it are about the choices made regarding the control scheme and visuals, and while I agree they aren't streamlined for ease of use, I do think that was on purpose and is supposed to add something to the game. In the very beginning, you're told that you're an AI that has been uploaded into a dive suit that it isn't compatible with. I felt like learning the controls as I went, non-intuitive and needlessly complex as they were, was a smart way of reflecting that. Of course I need to push four buttons to move - I'm incompatible with this hardware. Of course the game looks like a radar map - I'm an AI, that's how I perceive it. I appreciate that the devs did something new and interesting with this game.I do think the game has its flaws, though. It pretty much ends at the climax, which is hard to pull off and did leave me feeling a little underwhelmed. The story builds up a handful of big questions you're asking as you go through it, and they're left pretty unresolved at the end. This isn't poor writing, it feels intentional - there's only so much you can find out from what you have, it makes sense that you wouldn't be able to extrapolate every answer to everything - but there were certain big things that I think would have benefited from getting a little more content in the game. The ending feels a little abrupt.If you're interested in playing it, I recommend it. I got it on sale, and am satisfied that I did. Full price may feel like a little much if you don't love this type of experience. The game can likely be completed in 2 - 3 hours if you only do the main story and nothing else, and would probably take closer to 7 - 9 if you took the time to collect everything.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting experience with an intriguing world, an engaging mystery, gorgeous interfaces and intense curiosity on a background of "humans are a plague on this beautiful universe". However held back by an ending line that feels like it invalidates the philosophy of the entire game. Still worth playing though, I just was angry when I finished it. Also if you do play it, the first hour or two may feel a bit long / lacking direction, but don't worry, it changes soon after when the game turns into a thriller.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I've played it only because it was in the humble monthly package. I've liked it in the end and 100% it, but I would not recommend it to anybody with patience lower than a Buddhist monk. I will change to recommended if:* the GUI will be reworked to not being infuriating for about the first hour of the game, * suit inventory will be bigger or allow a stack of samples,* the map will be available not only in the lab, and height marks would be the same in the map and in the game,* and sound options would be added.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: i have no idea when or how i ended up getting it, and i only decided to download and play it because i wasn't interested in anything else at the time. what i found however was one of the most peaceful and intriguing games i've ever experienced.playing as an AI your visuals are limited- deliberately so- as you're woken up by a person and together you explore a strange alien planet. they learn why they were called there, and you learn where you came from in such a way that draws you in despite how limited the world is for you as a machine.while it's not for everybody, those that enjoy heavily narrative experiences and exploring an unknown world will definitely enjoy this unique experience.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the game and I felt compelled to leave a review, but I'm not sure where to even start.This game is a journey, an adventure, a legitimate piece of art, not a product you play for a while then throw away, like the vast majority of games ever made. I know this sounds vague, but I don't want to get bogged down into the mechanistic details of it. It's not perfect, to be clear. It's a bit linear, and it's rather short, but don't let it detract you, because it's still far superior to most plot-driven games out there.This game shines in its excellent depictions of unique oceanic ecosystems. I think most biology lovers could agree that these fictional ecosystems were meticulously constructed and made to feel believable. Even if their exact scientific details aren't always accurate to the last iota, they echo the complexity and awe-inspiring interconnectedness that so characterizes real ecosystems here on Earth. Playing this game evoked in me the same deep curiosity that reading about biology or watching footage of the intricate creatures that surround us does. The same feeling you get when you watch a great David Attenborough film, to put it simply.And now to the plot. I don't think it's perfect, but it does tie this game together. Otherwise, well, you could simply watch National Geographic or read about microbiology to a greater effect, simply because these are real. The plot drives you to explore more of the game's environment in order to piece together the human story that transpired on Gliese 677Cc. I don't want to go into it, even in general details, to avoid spoiling anything, because, as I said, the mystery drives you forward. I will say that what you uncover is a poignant story that touches on some of the issues that we deal and dealt with as a species for the last couple of centuries - the antithesis between human development and growth and our environment. Yes, I know, this is isn't the first and definitely not the last time this topic is explored in art, but the developer's take on it is still valuable and unique. And maybe more importantly, the story set within that context is interesting and touching.In Other Waters isn't a game I will forget. It's one of these games that will come to mind years into the future when a friend asks me about the best games I ever played. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, although it is not a game I myself enjoy. I would recommend it to those who like a reading heavy journey through an underwater alien world, a lot of exploration and a good bit of interaction although not thrilling gameplay. I have to mention the amazing sound and visual design too, although I feel like it really speaks for itself.So yes this game is very pretty and unique, but you have to enjoy reading general information about the various things you explore. You have to really enjoy reading to enjoy this game. I do not mind reading (okay I do) but to me this feels more like an interactive book than it feels like you are truly exploring something.I believe this game is for someone, but with the "gameplay" it has to offer that someone isn't me. I like a good story, even if I have to read. But the reason for why I play games is to experience a story coming together with nice visuals and sounds/music and great gameplay. This game shines on 3 of those things, but lacks "proper" gameplay elements.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely worth the full price of $15; even more so when it's on sale.Pros:- beautiful story- simplistic controls- beautiful music- graphics are immersive even though they aren't super high qualityCons:- literally just that there isn't any kind of "how to" in the beginning for movement. It tells you to move to a spot but fails to reveal that you have to click/select the spot you want to move to, press the movement key to set a course, then press the movement key again to actually start moving.Possible improvements (targeted to the developers):- playing would be quite a bit easier and more immersive (in my opinion) if you could see were you were in the world map (or at least within the region) while actually exploring; it's way to easy to get lost while searching for samples and/or points of interest- it would be really cool to see(hear) some voice acting for the main character. Being able to hear the intonation in her dialogue would make the story much more immersive- maybe as a DLC or as a sequel, I'd love to pursue the story of repairing the planet and/or studying more new species on said planet
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'm undecided about In Other Waters. In some ways, it's a nice concept - you play an AI navigating a topological map with a human. It's got a curious concept and a hopeful philosophy which I liked. In other ways, that's all it is - you move around the map, you occasionally chat to the human and you sort of solve puzzles. It's hugely repetitive, a little dull and the graphics are really simplistic - it's essentially a glorified text adventure, because you only get descriptions from the human and occasional sketches. It took me just over five hours to complete and although there's other bits and pieces to explore, I was ready to stop.Really, it made me want to transpose the world into subnautica's, because that would be amazing - but as it is, it was interesting but a 3/5 to get in the steam sale.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: There is a dramatic tonal shift halfway through the game, which shifts the genre towards horror and introduces disturbing elements such as [spoilers]death, suicide, body horror, and genocide.[/spoilers] I would not recommend this game, because I feel that those elements were badly mishandled. *** SPOILER/CONTENT WARNING ***Halfway through the game, we learn that Minae Nomura has committed suicide by diving to an unsafe depth, but been preserved in a comatose state by a parasitic plant. Ellery Vas insists that Nomura is alive, and that her consciousness has merged with the plant. The player is presented with no reason to believe that this is true, but the narrative frames them as morally suspect for doubting it.Near the end of the game, we learn that Gliese 677Cc was inhabited by a sapient species known as the Architects, who were almost all killed by the Baikal corporation. We learn nothing about their culture or society. Though they are portrayed as extremely powerful, the narrative does not suggest that they attempted to resist the Baikal corporation in any way. I found this portrayal dehumanizing, and, in combination with the narrative's insistence that the Architects were "in tune with nature", reminiscent of the racist "noble savage" stereotype.At the end of the game, Ellery Vas descends to the abyssal plain. Previously, throughout the game, returning to base required a map of the area you were in, which could only be acquired by visiting specific sites. At the end of the visit to the abyssal plain, despite not having visited such a site, Ellery is inexplicably able to return to base. Because I did not predict this, I viewed descending to the abyssal plain as effectively suicidal, and the fact that the game forced me to do so to progress was distressing.*** END WARNINGS ***
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: If you like deep, intriguing story-lines or are a big fan of biology, then this game is definitely for you. I cannot recommend this game enough. I have played through it two times at this point and the story hits you just as hard on a replay. Both times I finished In Other Waters I was left stunned and that feeling has stuck with me. It might sound boring to some people, but I promise that it is a delight all the way through.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Not quite, but it is a good story told in a different way. You play an advanced diving suit that has suddenly become sentient, and explore the ocean of an alien planet together with the scientist just wearing the suit. You need to figure out how to use your suit and ensure the survival of the scientist, who is completely fascinated by the alien world and the extraterrestrial lifeforms even though she is stuck in a malfunctioning diving suit.Lots of writing, not so much visual treats. The game gave me the same vibes as I once had when playing "The Portal" from Activision (1986), in case anyone remembers that. It can be played with a gamepad.An engrossing and fascinating story of exploration, well-written but a bit depressing, and with a slightly tedious interface.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I am very much a casual gamer, and this was perfect for me. I'm really interested in science, particularly unusual underwater creatures, and I love AIs and robots and aliens, so just the theme of this game already felt almost like it was custom-made for my interests. That, combined with the low-stakes nature of gameplay, made this such a fun and rewarding experience. The story was engaging and thorough without being dense, and I loved that I could choose between strictly progressing the narrative vs taking some time to explore the wildlife. I stretched out the gameplay for as long as I could - I never wanted it to end!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is such a strange game. It would be really easy to dismiss it, it's slow on the verge of tedious and once you've finished the game you've read thousands of ways to describe stoney pillars.However, notice that I wrote "once you've finished the game". As slow as it is, it sucks you in with it's incredibly beautiful stylized look and the increasingly growing need to learn why you're trapped underwater on this foreign planet and what happened to it. Hell, I even 100% it although there's no trophies/achievements and the only reward are some pretty dry descriptions of the sealife on the planet. Not because I felt forced to but because I actually wanted to keep exploring.In Other Waters isn't a game for everybody, but if you want a game you can just recline and play through without stress, maybe in increments, and like if you the exploring part of adventuring then it can certainly scratch your itch.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Did you ever think it would be cool to be a diving suit?  Me neither.  In Other Waters, the wishes of absolutely nobody have been granted, as you get to be a diving suit.  But wait, there's more.  Exploring the minimalist (yet somehow still un-user friendly) interface, you get to go on a plodding console ported interactive novel/point and click adventure where you cart a scientist around an alien ocean.I appreciate there's a badly written visual novel story here if you're willing to work really hard to dig it out of the convoluted and unsatisfying interface.   But I can't think of any gamer I'd tell to stop playing CS:GO so they can wrestle with this bundlemess. Also there's the comedy price of $15 USD for this bundle spacer.  The same money would get you a AAA game on sale, one where the developers knew how to do 3D graphics, so this is going to be a no from me.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is a simple game. I thought the color scheme would wreck my eyes, but it didn't.Pros:★ Leisurely (you can't die)★ Interesting and emotional writing★ Well thought-out alien ecology★ Good sound design★ Good music★ Very few bugs, and those are easy to ignoreCons:☆ No options, even to adjust volume(!) or remap keys☆ No achievements, even low-stress, no-competition ones for story progress☆ The mother of all railroads: there's no free-swim mode, even after finishing the story; you are literally limited to a designated set of waypoints and can never deviate from them, and you can't even take the map with you when you dive☆ No resolution of the plot, except to some nebulous, off-screen entities, leaving more loose ends than my middle school D&D campaign☆ Wildlife sketches are so washed out and the labels are so small I had to use the highest magnification of my glasses and put my nose almost on the screen to read themIn conclusion, someone who loved  (totally understandable) filled a notebook with cool ideas for a game, added some boilerplate corporate hubris, dangled some plot threads into some cyan-dyed water then published the whole thing with a Unity interface and never came back to do anything with what they started.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the minimalistic style and simple mechanics fool you - In Other Waters is one of the best exploration games out there, and it's incredible what it accomplishes with such a clean and elegant UI, all thanks to the amazing story it conveys. To analyze the game, actually, we should start precisely there: the visuals. If it were a full-on 3D first-person exploration game, In Other Waters would have a completely different experience. In fact, it'd probably be a horror game (this assertion will make sense once you play it, trust me) or at least a Subnautica-like experience where, if it's not an in-your-face horror all the time, it borders that territory frequently. We'd be so in our heads with fear and defense that it'd probably also have some sort of combat mechanic to deal with all the strange creatures we find along the way. In short, it would definitely not stand out in the vast sea - pun intended - of exploration games we have nowadays. But In Other Waters is nothing of that - and that's its strength. There's no combat because you're not in the role of a human that must "tame" all wildlife they find just because it's our "duty" as "superior beings". And let's be real, if we had to combat anything in this game, it'd be ourselves, not the creatures in this alien planet that are minding their own business. The real horror isn't the alien aquatic fauna and flora, but the prospect of what human greed and selfishness can do to an seemingly untouched ecosystem. The game doesn't shy away from this message - what can happen with Gliese 677Cc is precisely what already happened with Earth in the game's universe and what currently happens IRL. This is one of the few games I deem as almost "necessary", specially for younger generations who grow up with increasingly ecophobia and general fear of the future. There's still hope out there, somewhere - we just have to collectively fight for it. And to find that hope in-game, you'll play as an AI guiding a scientist - a xenobiologist, to be more precise - who travels to this unvisited alien planet after receiving a strange message from a former research partner. From this point on, In Other Waters develops into such an incredible narrative that I won't comment any further as to not spoil it - just bear in mind that the writing is phenomenal and captivating, with the exploration really tying together all the mysteries you uncover. I saw some people comparing it with Outer Wilds, and in that regard, this comparison kinda makes sense. You don't have to be a biology aficionado to enjoy this game, but if you're one, you'll obviously have an extra layer of enjoyment than the regular folk. The creatures' descriptions are really well-made and make everything seem realistic. As not a biology aficionado, however, In Other Waters is easily in my top shelf no matter what. Buy it, you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game so badly, and for the most part I do. I really liked the world it was building, the premise is pretty neat, and the gameplay is a good mix of puzzle solving and exploration in a nice, relaxing setting. So why am I not going to recommend the game?Two reasons. Firstly, the movement method is just so clunky, especially when you factor in having to frequently toggle between different HUD menus/ modes.Secondly, the dialog with our NPC companion... It's all done in this.... really annoying,and,i guess, supposed to be awe-filled kind of... style?  As in, it's written exactly like that for every interaction, to the point if found myself just completely ignoring it and missing out on world building.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is an absolute gem of a game that I cannot recommend hard enough to the sort of person who will enjoy it. A deeply contemplative and meditative experience, you play the role of a mysterious AI helping xenobiologist Ellery Vas as she unearths the mysteries of the alien ocean in which her colleague vanished. Everything is done through the interface that controls the functions of the dive suit, and you perceive the world through topographical maps and sonar, while occasionally communicating with Ellery via yes-no answers. Even via this simplified interface, there's a deep and evocative sense of wonder that this game manages to generate through the dialogue, observational notes, and taxa descriptions. Over the course of about a 10-hour play time, I felt absolutely compelled to progress the shockingly deep story and unearth and classify 100% of the alien taxa you encounter.I did have some minor quibbles. It's not always obvious when dialogue is about to show up, and I wish it was more obvious when Ellery was talking to you. It would be nice if the chat-log didn't vanish whenever you exited the game as well. The timer on the dialogue also felt pointless, as sometimes I'd barely catch a chat before it vanished, and it didn't serve any mechanical or flavor purpose in the game.Minor gripes aside, this game is an absolute gem, and if any of the things I've described above appeal to you, you owe it to yourself to pick it up. I'll doubt we'll see anything else like it for quite some time.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I 100% recommend this game.First and foremost I will say, as others have said, it's not a game for everyone. It is very textbook with lots of reading.The entire world of the game is a mystery to you as the player, and you only see a map with which you guide the main character about the ocean of an alien planet. Regardless, the descriptions in the dialogue paint the picture of the world for you and as you study it you get small peeks into the looks of the creatures via sketches drawn by the main character. These certainly help to fill in any gaps in your mental picture of the world and it's a beautiful way to play.Don't be fooled by the minimalistic appearance and simple gameplay. The story is haunting, beautiful, fascinating and well written. I found myself completely drawn into the mystery of it, wanting more, and was sad when it ended. The soundtrack (and simple atmospheric sounds at times) really do a wonderful job of setting the mood and helping you feel what the main character was feeling. The interfacing is gorgeous with a lovely color palette that I found very pleasing to the eyes. The colors change throughout, also aiding the atmosphere and overall feeling to the game.All in all this game is a beautiful and unique experience and I really have nothing at all bad to say about it other than I wish it was longer.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful exercise in worldbuilding, speculative biology, and collecting all the things, all contained in one minimalist romp.While it's a shame we can't see the creatures beyond text descriptions and scientific illustrations, this game has been a significant fixation of mine, to the extent that I've created nearly over 100 lifeforms of my own to flesh out this panthalassic world even further. The kind of experience you can get done in one session, and then come back to when you want to research things a little more.Oh, did I mention that there's a TTRPG module based on IOW coming out soon? In case you ever wanted more of this wonderful setting.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is as many things as it isn't; it is alien, unique, pointed, and interesting. Instead of dramatic mechanics to sell a pressing or bombastic story to the player, everything about the game is reflective, almost melancholic, and more about discovery than action. What brought me to it was the interface and sound - the presentation is spot on, matching the beats and tone of the story excellently.It's not without fault - in some areas the design clashes with what you feel you need to do and what the game wants you to do, but the descriptive prose and mystery that brings Gliese 667Cc to life is more than worth the bumps and taking the time to experience it.I'm a sucker for games that push the interactive medium in interesting ways in order to tell their story, and In Other Waters succeeds fabulously. If you're at all interested in a unconventional game or like exploring alien biology, give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This was a very, VERY, differnt game and one that i reccomend.i have a few nitpicks, like the Xenobiologist instantly knowing and making correct suppositions about everything, and the story going a bit for the usual evil megacorporation stuff, but i really liked everything else.If you want a novel that feels completely different form anything you've ever played this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Stunning visuals and a great, atmospheric soundtrack. The writing is fantastic too - I enjoyed the characters and the narrative, and the biological entries are very convincingly written (to a layperson). Your interaction with the game via the very slow and purposeful scanning and movement mechanics probably won't work for everyone, and they can get frustrating at times if you get lost or stuck. It's also strange to have such interesting text for each movement node, and then frequently put you in a position of being under time constraints so that you can't actually stop to read any of it. That aside, it's well worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: One thing this game excels at is the sense of scientific exploration and discovery. Very much starting off like a mysterious science fiction yarn where a computer boots up and you play as an AI are conversing with Ellery, a xenobiologist. You're in an alien planet's ocean helping her out in discovering the local wildlife and exploring the area. The blue-and-yellow aesthetic and UI are pleasant and so are the little animations, making for a relaxing experience. The gameplay loop of discovering a new plant, going back to base, scanning, and then unlocking its properties and behaviours, eventually unlocking a picture of the fauna, is satisfying. The music is incredibly memorable, and the main driver to keep me going. However, the lack of any direction gets to be obtuse. The loop of blowing up obstructions which reload each time you return to go back to base gets to be repetitive. Ellery stops talking to you after an hour, so narrative incentive to continue goes away. I got stuck trying to get to the east side with a roadblock and with several trips to flank around it, while going back and forth between the base because you have to manage your fuel, I got frustrated. You can't look at the map at any time, you have to be back in the base to view it, so I ended up taking a screenshot and alt-tabbing to it while playing, or playing in windowed mode to check up on where I was going. There are no indicators to show where you've already been so I ended up in vain going around in circles. I won't fully give up because of the sunk cost fallacy, and maybe once I get past this area, the rest of the game is relaxing again and instil the joy of discovery. Highly recommended for anyone into text adventures, relaxing atmosphere, science, and hard science fiction but be wary that the lack of direction can become frustrating so look for a guide before diving in.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Words cannot describe the experience of this game. And it truly is an experience. What started as a fun little exploration and discovery game unfolded into a story of exquisite writing and deep emotional investment. It's only 8-10 hours. But it is nonstop investment from start to finish. Its tight. Its clean. It's wonderful. Not to mention the message is very strong and unfolds organically.Not to mention the music. Every track is ear candy. It's a sort of mix of surreal synth muffled to give it an underwater feel. It truly feels like the soundtrack of an alien ocean and it is perfect for setting the tone of each area.It's not without flaws though. Avoiding spoilers, the agile creatures near the start and the really tall creatures are both a pain to scan down. And there are a few cases where you have to move to a very specific spot to trigger the story. But they're relatively small nitpicks since the game as a whole has no time limit or enemies to evade.Lasty, can I just say that the ecological papers presented in this game are not dry. Somehow. The writing in this game is amazing as a whole. The characters. The story. A lot of people can write those things very well. But a fictional research paper? I've NEVER seen anyone write one of those and it be interesting. But, somehow, it was managed here.The game as a whole is not for everyone. There's no action. There's a lot of reading. But if you wanna chill with a good story or just want to feel things this is the game to get.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Alright this one's a gem.It's extremely simple, but it's a neat concept being the companion AI to a character in the game in regards to the story.It has a very Metroid prime feel where you go around scanning things and learning lore. There are things in the environment that can kill you, but overall it's quite chill.Definitely recommend if you like that style of exploration.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely not a game for everyone, but it's great for its niche audience! Playing as a suit AI without real eyesight was interesting as a way to experience a world only through the UI, and the story of the world and the xenobiologist you are helping to track down her colleague got me surprisingly hooked
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Quite possibly the greatest storyline I have ever played. And I own 160 games and counting. I have scavenged Steam front to back hunting down the highest of quality, inspiring storylines I can possibly find, and this easily makes it in the top five. The story never lacks in substance the entire way through, and my only regret is not finding this game earlier.Please get this game. I wish I could pay more for it, and will be following these developers for as long as they make games.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say I can strongly recommend this game for a few simple points.The story is VERY much a tell-and-not-show affair from the time i've put into it.  Namely in that my inputs as the player occupying the role of a dive-suit AI feel pointless.  The protagonist can come to a conclusion about the environment around her in a very silly way, by just forming her observations to fit the narrative she wants based on first observations.  She can say 'Do you think plantyMcOceanblob behaves this way because of MysteriousOceanForces?' and you can say either yes or no, and of course I say no because her assumption has no where near the amount of evidence needed to conclude that.  But then she just replies with 'Hmm... I wonder' instead 'Yes I think so too what a marvelous discovery for science!  I hope this gets us closer to my missing GF!' And thats the hook, her GF is here as a lone biologist cataloging the planet and she's missing.  Somewhere. Mysteriously.  And nothing about that developed much in the 2.5 hrs I put into the game before putting it downThis could be interesting if the story developed more but it didn't seem to beyond just being mysterious and over-assumptive conclusions about the ocean planet's marine biologies.  If the flawed thinking was intentional, I love it when stories intentionally are written with characters who come to assumptions due to flawed ways of thinking and how it affects their role in the story.  But I have no reason to assume this is the case in this game because my protagonist companion is essentially the narrator of both her internal monologue and the story overall.  I cant imagine I'll have a very interesting twist at the end should we find her thinking is flawed because well, in 2.5 hours our protagonist has not narrated more than a simple story with merely unanswered questions as the hook.  I've played games like this before and dropped them as I did this one because I've found they almost never pay off in the end.  None of the other reviews I read suggested I'd encounter some mind bending twist partway through, or that this is a slow burner of a title, so I decided to not spend more time hoping for a payoff I was pretty sure wasn't coming.Games that succeed well at this build more than just unanswered questions along the way, but storyline aside they also need to have gameplay that builds along with their story.  So the lack of the above coupled with the very shallow gameplay left me feeling kind of let down.  The topographic UI is actually really compelling in design but I didnt get to meaningfully interact with it because its essentially just an on-rails waypoint system.  There's no free exploration so I can't get a sense of feeling my way through the world because I know nothing is Over There Waiting To Be DIscovered because anything that is To Be Discovered will be on the rails.  On a gameplay level, its the difference between being in museum walking along individually manicured but ultimately narratively and meta-mechanically shallow exhibits vs. being in a new environment feeling out the systems and setting organically by learning, akin to a child discovering a toolbox and finding all the things they can do with the things inside and the ways they can shape their experiences through them.  Most creatures in your environment are just lore or gate/key puzzles and also dont have meaningful interactivity.  Its also just not fun to move around on these rails or through these gates.  Its just not fun to build a marine biology (i.e. lore) compendium for its own sake without a compelling story or gameplay reason to do so.  It's not fun to build my waypoint map if the story doesn't drive me to feel good about finding the next unanswered (or forcibly answered) question.  The gameplay just isn't compelling or even passably entertaining, its mundane if not really just a facade for the uncompelling story.In fact its more like a dressed up visual novel.  And that kinda sucks.  The fantastic presentation is all window dressing for a flavor of game I really don't care for and don't even think is that well written despite my tastes.  And sadly, Visual Novel isn't even in the list of tags for the game so I don't think I would have been able to determine this without a LOT more nitty-gritty research.  I don't feel bamboozled, just disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like, the only serious review I've ever made, it was just so damn good that I had to write this when I completed the game.Simple UI design, unique style of storytelling, a great atmospheric soundtrack. A must for people in marine biology who like games, highly recommended for everyone else. Amazing themes of scientific exploration, corporate/human arrogance, environmental damage, dealing with conflicting emotions over a lost lover, and just some chill ocean exploration.Might be a bit slow, but I liked that since I could savour it for longer. Also liked the background story about the sapphics, made me think of my girlfriend.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a game that captures your imagination like no other. There is a level of beauty in its simplicity that lets you fall in love with the world it creates. The music and sound design is immersive and the interface is satisfying while still being easy to understand. I have never written a review for a game previously but there is something special about the world of Gliese 677Cc. The storytelling truly makes an impact on your view of humanity and its entangled greed, lust for power, corruption, but more importantly, the hope to preserve and make things right. If you are not the type to mind reading, this game is truly a masterpiece and I'd recommend giving it a chance! :D
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully written and genuinely inspired game about exploring an alien ocean. A genuinely unique enough experience that it's hard to compare to much else!It's closer to a visual novel / interactive fiction than a more pure "exploration" game, which isn't a bad thing, but do be aware of it. Nonetheless it really, really does have the "feeling" of exploration to it.One important caveat. In Other Waters has a  of beautifully imagined alien environments... but they are almost entirely delivered through text. While the text is filled with very good imagery, in the end you need good mental imaging to fully enjoy this game and appreciate its environments. If you are too aphantasic, this game might not be for you.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10 Decent.In this game you control an AI of a diving suit. The diving suit is controlled by Dr. Ellery Vas, a marine biologist on an alien planet. You work with Dr. Vas in controlling the suit, swimming around the planet via waypoint markers, cataloguing all the alien species. As you catalogue them, you have to set out and collect samples so that Dr. Vas can do her more in-depth examinations and research.Gameplay is a basic UI where you click on commands to navigate etc. It is basically like a map that you scan and click on points of interests. There are obstacles to overcome with the use of puzzles, and you have to keep an eye on both your power levels and the Dr’s oxygen levels.You can only respond to the doctor in terms of yes/no prompts, so this is a curious journey in an alien world between them and you that progresses as you explore. Dr. Vas has a reason for being on the planet, they wish to seek out another Biologist, a Dr. Minae, so you have an investigative story to follow as well as the cataloguing of aliens etc.It is a fairly chill game, and one I enjoyed, but I think towards the end it got perhaps a little too heavy handed with its message, and it also failed to innovate further from what was a fairly engaging first half. The first half has you navigating obstacles with the use of items, but the second half is really just a run against time due to your oxygen and power levels being reduced quicker. That’s kinda lame.Still, a commendable effort and a decent game to look into if you want to chill and read a fairly heavy exploration game. Don’t come here if you’re into graphics though.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It was a bit tricky at first, there was one part where I was stuck because I didn't see the spot I needed to go to, it was the only time the symbol blended into the scenery, however it was called "Hidden shelf" so I can't complain that much. Besides that one issue it is very addictive, even though this is just clicking buttons simulator, once you get into the flow it's hard to stop yourself for going on 'just one more run'.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant game.You play as an "AI" that manages the protagonist's suit. You dictate where the protagonist goes, identify points of interest in the environment, help the main character collect samples, and manage the computer systems. You essentially manage the protagonist, except that you are not her. As the story progresses, she fills you in with sparse details about what is going on as she recalls them. And since this is her first time down here too, it works out narrative wise.What I love about that is just how the premise fits the player's agency. Every bit of detail and gameplay is just enough to build the world mentally. When I imagine a 3d version of this game, it loses a lot of the narrative structure. The way the game/interface was designed allows the player to experience the story through the character's thoughts as a story, not through cognitive dissonance by trying to be the character but then you do your own thing. This game does not allow that to happen by letting you be the suit and having the character speak to you instead. When you control a character in another game, you are in charge of managing their perspective and movement. You are tasked with being the character, which is an unrealistic burden in terms of your relation as the player to the story being told. Since you do not specifically control the character, only their direction and when to progress, you are free to imagine that she has her own awareness. The game supports this well by giving her  of dialogue. Even when you click on new waypoints, the description is just her observations vocalized!It shouldn't need to be mentioned, but it's not an action game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Feeling sorry for the game receiving so many negative reviews. There are much worse pieces in this shop that have 90+% positive ratings, and it just does not make sense that score of In Other Waters is so low.It is compact, in all senses: story, gameplay, and visuals. Still, it is also interesting, pleasant to interact with, has a dramatic enough story to keep you motivated to unravel it (although with a somewhat weak finale, as most dramatic stories go), and offers much fun in exploring of detailed fictional ecosystem (only other game with such motive I can recall is Waking Mars). Moreover, it does not mutilate existing scientific knowledge as Subnautica and No Man's Sky do, but treats it and ones who produce it with proper respect.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly not sure if I should recommend this or not, but let's just say if you have a few free hours, a little patience, and can get it at a discount it's definitely worth it. The gameplay isn't great at all to be honest. But it's not about that, it's about the exploration, the world building, and the story, which I think are very good.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game - I played it for a while, then left it to sit and recently finished it. You explore the alien oceanic ecosystem, represented mostly by writing and abstract shapes. But, once you collect enough data, you are rewarded with a sketch and detailed description of the various creatures that you so far had to just imagine. All this is happening while you are uncovering a corporate secret related to this world.This storyline is not especially innovative, but the storytelling perspective is fresh and I also enjoyed the design choice to leave most of the visualisation to your imagination. Also, the music score is great.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I am a bit torn between recommending this game or not. Don't get me wrong, I like this game a lot. Tldr: the game's atmosphere, story line, concept, and soundtrack are very good, but the mechanics and game play loop can be better. The sound design is immaculate, the soundtrack is doing a lot of heavy lifting for a game with very simple mechanics. I can listen to it for hours. UI wise, I think the game's minimalist design is great because the game focuses on discovery, data collection, and record keeping aspects. As a big fan of ecology and xenobiology, this is a perfect game that scratched my nerdy itch. The aesthetic of the game is very unique, the topology navigation map is very creative and fitting to the tone of the game. From a biologist perspective, however, I feel like there's a lack of diversity, monotonous, even. But I understand the complexity of creatures are limited by the scope of the game, and not everyone wants to read 100+ species entries. I still wish there're more things I could do with my discoveries, like breeding and extracting materials (like crafting). Most of the texts seems to be fluff materials, even though the data entries of the species suggested that they can be utilised in many other ways. Therefore I feel like it is a waste of potential by making  "fetch quest/data collection" as the core game play loop.This game is short, relaxing, and atmospheric. For a game that marketed itself as a scientific discovery/exploration game I feel like they can do more about it, but maybe that's just me rambling about pretentious features that no one cares about. For a casual game, it is very well made. I wish more games can lean into the wonder and joy of discovery.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a game, its a linear click through story book. Applied for a refund and was rejected. Because I was stuck with it I played through all of this and citizen sleeper and was deeply disappointed. _childDocuments_.review: Wow, I will say I have no been through a lot of the game yet, but the idea of it has me really interested from the get go. _childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I was a super early fan of Subnautica so this game intrigued me based on that. This isn't that game at all but it's kind of similar in that it gives the player that sense of wonder of "what lies beyond" If you played Subnautica and liked it, I would say this game is kind of like a text adventure version of it. Very different games and story of course, but they both take place on an alien planet that's all ocean and your job is to explore and discover its mysteries.If you never played Subnautica, that's okay! You can still enjoy this game very much. However to enjoy this game and get the most out of it I would say you have to like to read a lot. You explore by sending your character's vessel to these little triangular nodes. There are a few hundred throughout the whole game I'd say. At each one there is a very small descriptive paragraph about what the main character sees. I suppose you don't have to read them but it's the best descriptors your going to get and if you have a good imagination it pairs very well with the surrounding abstract look of your environment. To add to that, you will discover samples of flora and fauna which you can analyze back at your lab. Some of these push the story forward and some may trigger small optional side quests that lead to unlocking more reading material and details about the world's surrounding life and ecosystem.To fully appreciate this world the devs created, I highly recommend reading everything. If you don't like to read stuff in video games, the game is still enjoyable but you may find the game play a little boring after a while. This isn't an action packed sci-fi adventure and I found myself enjoying the game the most in 1-2 hour sessions. I completed the game in about 10 hours or so.Remember when I mentioned traveling via the nodes and reading small paragraphs each step of the way? It's this that leads to my only complaint with this game. It's only a small part and it was more of a minor inconvenience than a complaint. There is one part of the game where the area you're traversing is kind of poisonous and your O2 levels drop much faster if you linger. Well I like to read things slowly so navigating through this area forced me to move along quickly. I wasn't able to take my time reading the descriptions for fear of dying for not moving along quick enough. It was a small part and it's really the only thing negative I can say about the whole experience.I enjoyed exploring and uncovering the events that took place on this planet. Everything is very well polished, the sound is fantastic, and the shift in color of your HUD as you enter certain areas was a nice touch. I recommend playing with a nice set of head phones for full immersion.TL:DR: An oceanic text adventure with charming abstract graphics, sound, and environments.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Continuously disappointing.The first thing the game does is pop up a small window, asking you to for graphic and input/keyboard settings. How could I possibly know what keys I'd want to rebind, having not played the game yet? Is this menu really NOT available once I'm already playing, when I can actually see how the settings affect gameplay? And even if you do want to change any settings, the window to do so is hilariously short - perhaps 5-6 lines tall, requiring a ton of scrolling. Already a poor impression, and the game hasn't even started yet.Once you start a new game, you're forced to wait through unskippable credits. Put these at the END of the game! I don't yet care who worked on this thing, because I haven't yet experienced it. Finally, the game begins, and I find out... it's a glorified text adventure. Okay, that's fine... I've played and enjoyed plenty of those... but this one automatically advances the "spoken" text with a little timer. You can manually advance to the next line early, but you cannot stop the automatic advancement. Ready or not, if you didn't read everything, too bad! (Mercifully, there is another menu you can go into to see a log of the conversation.)This also wouldn't be a huge problem, except that there are usually a total of TWO text fields that you are expected to read - the dialogue, and the... I'll call it the "logbook," which contains written observations of the alien world - for both locations and organisms. So if you're reading and digesting that, and the "spoken" dialogue times out, then whoops! I guess you gotta go look at the log to see what you missed!This is compounded by the fact that some of the items in the logbook are of creatures that zip in and out of the frame, so you need to click on them before they leave, or risk missing some information that might be important. So really, there are THREE things you're expected to read and comprehend simultaneously - creatures, dialogue, and locations - from most to least urgent. Have you ever been forced to wrestle a book?And the text IS important... the locations and creatures in the game are nothing more than circles, triangles, and squares. The entire interface is extremely abstract, consisting of not more than 4 colors. This also makes it a bit hard to figure out what you're even supposed to do, and how to do it - though, that's the point, and I'm okay with that. You're a weird machine on an alien planet. Things are gonna be kind of weird. I've played and enjoyed Myst and other games like it. I like to call these figure-out-what-to-do games, "Oops! No manual!" ...games. That's a lie, I just came up with that right now.Anyway, the developers don't seem to truly understand how to make a "Oops, no manual!" game. For example, to take a sample of the environment, You have to CLICK on a panel to open up the sample collection menu, then CLICK AND DRAG some sort of control, to line it up with a glowing dot... then CLICK on some other part of the interface, which moves half of a... thing... then CLICK on another part of the interface, moving the other half of the... thing... and finally, CLICK another button to actually collect the sample.So, why 5 clicks for an action that could simply be 1 click? Well, because it's a little puzzle to figure out how to do it, right? Here's the problem: Once you've figured it out, you still have to do it, every single time. There are no CHOICES involved. And because the game has no combat, there are absolutely no gameplay consequences for doing it slowly or incorrectly, like risking being attacked by a creature. And there's no reward of any kind for being faster or better at performing this action. It's not even a quick-time-event. It's worse. It's a waste-your-time-event.Not having combat is a perfectly fine choice for a game. But then you can't ALSO have these little time-wasting tasks. This is what i'm talking about when I say the developers don't understand how to make a game like this. Well, it's one example. Here's another:The interface itself is buggy. For absolutely no discernible reason, sometimes I simply CANNOT spin the... I don't know what to call it... the vector-chooser. This is how you direct your diver on where to go. It's important. And 10% of the time, it just doesn't work. When making a "Oops, no manual!" game, you better be absolutely sure there are no bugs like this, because the player won't be able to tell the difference between the interface not working because it's not SUPPOSED to work that way, and the interface not working because of a BUG.Oh, and that vector-chooser is just another example of the game adding unnecessary waste-your-time steps to your gameplay experience. Why can't I just click on the location I want to move to? Why do I have to move this stupid vector-chooser on top of the location first? Also, why do I have to manually scan my surroundings at every new location? Not doing so means that it's impossible to advance, so, you HAVE TO do it. And it's not like it takes a ton of in-game power, either. So there is no discernible gameplay consequence for doing it constantly. (Maybe it drives away some creatures later in the game. I don't know.) So it's just another waste-your-time event."If the choice is always the same, cut it out of the game!" -Me. I said that. Just now.Anyway, I made it to the first milestone, a base, and I just couldn't bring myself to care about my next objective. The dialogue is constantly telling you about how cool the alien world is, but all I see are a bunch of circles and squares. All it really served to do was remind me how Subnautica is 10,000x better. You actually get to SEE the alien world. And while there are bugs, at least there are no waste-your-time-events. Seriously, go play that game instead of this one. It's fantastic. And don't look up any spoilers. Don't even watch the trailer, just buy it. I wish I could play it again for the first time. That's why I'm here, actually. I just wanted a game that scratched the same itch for exploration that I got from Subnautica and Zelda: The Wind Waker. But this isn't it.Oh, one last thing, which I know is incredibly nitpicky, but it's not why I didn't like this game:"Animals," "plants," "fungi," and even "bacteria," are EARTH phenomena. They do not and can not exist anywhere else in the entire universe, unless they've been brought FROM Earth. If life is found on other planets, it will NOT be appropriate to use taxonomic classifications from Earth, like this game does.Referring to aliens as "creatures" or "fauna" is fine, but "animals" refers specifically to the kingdom "Animalia." All life on Earth has been found to have stemmed from one single abiogenesis event, and therefore shares at least some fraction of DNA or RNA, which is incredible. If we ever discover extraterrestrial life, a whole new taxonomy would have to be developed, with branches stemming from its own, independent abiogenesis event. (Or MAYBE the same one, but further back! That hypothesis is called "panspermia.") Alien life might not even use DNA or RNA. Perhaps it'll use some other molecule.You might say, "Wait, bacteria might exist elsewhere in the universe!" Well, there could certainly be bacteria-LIKE organisms... microscopic, fast to reproduce, able to survive and thrive in extreme environments.... but those won't be "BACTERIA." They'll be something else. "Bacteria" has a very specific meaning. So, yeah, even Subnautica gets this detail wrong.Like I said, this is pretty nitpicky. But then again, this whole game is ABOUT life on another planet, so I'd have hoped that they got this detail right.Anyway, that's all from me. Join me in my next review when I'll surely be be b*tching about how movies rarely make sense from the villain's perspective, or how trophic dynamics is rarely, if ever, considered. (You want giant monsters? Then you better also have an enormous, lush ecosystem to support them!) Bye!

_childDocuments_.review: Hello Im Skill Incarnate and Welcome to My Games Review Series.My reviews cover indie games that i have bought, had gifted to me and have been provided by developers for review.In This Episode I cover one of the hottest new indie games on steam, In Other Waters.This title is a mix of exploration, puzzle solving and storytelling which uses a minamalist visuals with a fantastic soundtrackin order to bring to life an Alien world filled with beautiful sights and hidden danger.The player takes the role of an Artificial Intelligence in an advanced underwater diving suit. You must attempt to guide the current owner of the suit, a Xenobiologist who has been stranded on an underwater alien world. You will need to work together with your new friend, guiding her through a beautiful and sometimes hostile environment, studying the the flora and fauna, gathering data, and unlocking the secrets of the planet in an attempt to locate a strandedloved one.In other waters is a perfect example of how Video Games can be an artform and is recommended for all indie game enthusiastsDisclaimer: I was not paid by the Developer for this video. _childDocuments_.review: Chill, melancholy SF. It balances the wonder of discovery against the loneliness of ... well ... being the only person on an alien planet, while keeping the impending total ecological death of Planet Earth as a poignant background note. This is as much a piece of Interactive Fiction as it is a video game - there are graphics, and challenges to overcome, but if you're not ready to do the heavy lifting in your head it's not going to work for you. I loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this as of 100% beating the game for the first time, this is incredible. Not only is the story narrative nothing like any other game I have ever played, but the way the game portrays these creatures and how they act without you being able too see them is a new experience. The sample collection barely feels like grinding, and I loved how the entire story can be completed in a few hours without feeling rushed. 9.9/10, my only complaint is the game not telling how to get the last creatures for the taxonomy without just searching, but even that was fairly fluid.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games with environmental storytelling, then you'll love this one. I would advise you take your time progressing through the game, read the various descriptions to get a feel for the world, and don't rush for the end right away. This game is also an experience, with a world that is expertly crafted to simulate a nautical ecosystem, and In Other Waters does a remarkable job of building a detailed environment with very little in the way of fancy graphics.I supported this game during the Kickstarter campaign and am glad to say I was not disappointed!10/10
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Text adventure with some graphics and gameplay elements like resource management and navigation. Sadly, the navigation is frustrating because the overview and detail maps do not match up; and neither map has any way of recording where you have been. If you can put up with that, the game does have some novel elements, and a decent if somewhat predictable story. As you can tell, this is a rather lukewarm thumbs up  review. I like to support solo developers. This game does suffer from a common solo developer problem; game elements like the map layout are way too obvious to the developer, but not to the novice player. It gains from a common solo developer trait. There is nothing else out there quite like it, it has its own unique feel.  For that reason, . I did think it worth the sale price I paid for it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: If you have ever fantasized about being the person in the chair, guiding an extraterrestrial explorer through an unknown world, this is the game for you. It is simplistic, but engaging in that there is always something new to find and read about. On the topic of reading, you have to enjoy reading to enjoy this game, as almost all aspects of narrative and progress are based around text boxes. It would be cool to have some voice acting, but for what this game is, it is super fun and relaxing.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't for everyone, and its something I'd reccomend playing in half an hour sessions at a time. Its very slow paced, methodical, and repetitive, which can drag a bit, but when played in small doses, its easily one of the most calming and wonderful games I've played in a while. You basically are an AI controlling a mech suit from the perspective a computer program would have. You're manipulating instruments and compasses and dials to move around rather than walking or floating freely. It uses these restrictions to it's benefit to give you a one of a kind immersive experience. The most fun I have playing this game is completing the alien 'pokedex', as the game is very good at creating a truly wonderous and mysterious alien world to explore with each new piece of information found about a creature bringing more questions than answers and leaving you curious to see what else you can dig up about them. Absolutely watch gameplay of it first, because this is not going to appeal to everyone and might really turn off some folks, so if you watch some footage and instantly think you'll like it you should absolutely get it. Its a great game to wind down after a tough day for like 30 mins.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Roughly on the border of liking and disliking the game. On the one hand, I am glad that I finished it and I enjoyed the story. On the other, the gameplay was rather plain and somewhat tiring. The story kept me interested just enough to follow through and find the answer to the mysteries that come up during the game. My main gripe is that I would liken the game to a walking simulator. It was a decent 'book' with a somewhat interesting story but interacting with the pages wasn't particularly enjoyable. The landscape and interface was quite interesting and I liked the stylistic choices. I would simply say that the gameplay loop was not enough to carry me to loving the game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cool experience and in a way it's like the walking sim of older adventure games, in that there is never any real danger and it's more about being immersed in the setting. My issue is that the writing isn't as good as I would like it to be. I'm about 75% of the way through the taxonomy, and though the entries have been enjoyable to read, the characters don't feel real. The diver that is your only companion is more of an excuse to have someone explain what is going on, but has no personality beyond that. I can only think of one time something they said made me feel anything.Would suggest everyone give this game a try. Game devs can learn a lot about minimalism from this.
