Exceptionally designed all-aroundOh and with a fantastic soundtrack.It's a sort of graphical text adventure where you explore an underwater ecosystem on another planet. It's very good. I needed this.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique game! It has an odd, indie charm that I enjoyed, though the controls could have used some help. Though I wonder if making the controls easier would've taken away from the atmosphere in a way. Beyond the controls, my biggest complaint is the super tiny inventory, that was annoying.Overall though, I recommend this game for anyone who's looking for something unique.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting, fun, exploratory game worth your time. Explore, document species, and learn the depressing & chilling history of the planet & a corrupt corporation. It's a great game. I honestly did not think this game was too slow, I thought the pacing & speed was perfect. This game is very obviously one of those "labor of love" types; you can really tell the developer cared deeply about his project. I definitely recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: So, I finished In Other Waters and it is absolutely beautiful. It’s very minimalistic, so sensory starvation appears somewhere in the first hour of the game, but then you greedily read all the reports and descriptions that the game generously provides you with and you begin to really “hallucinate” the world around you.The game is almost 80% pure Subnautica and 20% Roadwarden. You swim through a vast open world, explore the nooks and crannies, scan animals and all sorts of strange plants, and stumble upon a cunning and twisted plot that will turn everything on its head by the end of the game. There is even a base where you constantly regroup and plan forays.Steam says that I played for 10 hours but I really think there was a lot of AFK and a couple of times I re-visited some locations to find the sample I needed. So realistically the game will last about 5-8 hours.In general, a very interesting indie game, very solid in the sci-fi department, well voiced, nicely written and leaves a good aftertaste. The downsides are a very minimalistic game loop and an almost complete absence of a fail state, which puts the game closer to a walking simulator (swimming sim?). It’s forgivable to miss it, but if you want to read something underwater, then this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is, in many ways, exactly what I want out of independent development. It's smart, it's well-written, and it makes the most of the limited budget. I'm not interested in summing up what the game is -- there's a summary section for that. But I'll break down what I love and what few things could use some patching.You won't find much about IOW that's flashy, but the minimal UI is gorgeous. Small, subtle changes to the lighting do some really heavy lifting in terms of setting the mood. The idea of operating a suit as the player-character isn't new, but the interface is excellent at reinforcing the idea that you are inherently mechanical.The writing is terse, but conveys a wealth of subtext and feeling. It's pretty amazing how much a sense of place you can achieve through the minimal mapping and high-grade writing.On the critical side, there are a couple places that I found cause to complain. The first of these is that there are still a number of UI-related bugs. None of them were game-breaking, but it wasn't uncommon for a scanned object on the map to revert to appearing unscanned, or for the Taxonomy UI to lock up. None of these forced a restart or caused any loss of data, but they were annoying. Hopefully they get patched soon.The second issue I found was that I wanted to enjoy the writing, but felt pressured to skim and move quickly during certain sections. I'm not sure what should be done about that, but it did mean that the more threatening areas didn't leave as vivid an impression as the others, simply because I wasn't able to sit around and absorb the descriptions.Overall, highly recommended, and one I'm probably going to annoy all my friends talking about.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I knew what I was getting into before purchasing the game - something that mainly has you interacting with a limited UI to move around and tell a story. I figured if the story was compelling enough, I would enjoy it.Well... the story was compelling and I still didn't enjoy it. I actually would have given it a thumbs up if it were a visual novel and told the same story but after a while I just couldn't be asked to go collect any more samples and click click click my way through the ocean. Quite frankly, the game portion is far too boring. Additionally, the map will drive you absolutely bonkers. Somehow humankind has mastered the ability to travel to distant planets but not to pull up a basic map to see where the heck you are supposed to go OR where you have already been.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game achieves having a silent protagonist knowing nothing of the world and a driven character having feelings and opinions by differentiating the human from the suit. You are the AI; steering, measuring, acting on behalf of your human. The communication between the two is yes/no at best and a bit underutilized. Having only a abstract view of the surroundings makes it more interesting to find all bits of information about flora/fauna to finally get a sketch of the things you encounter.The difficulty is very low. There are resources that get restricted at times, but gathered samples can be used to replenish them. The other obstacles require some upgrades you find during the exploration - at worst you need to look around more for the right samples. It's a good game to play a bit at a time. Most of the UI requires some "extra" clicks to start an action, which I find charming, it feels a bit more like you are controling something other than rushing trough to the next node on the map.The selling point is the atmosphere of a unknown planet with lots of things to discover, the UI changing color with the current mood of the place - if you dislike "walking simulators" this game won't be for you.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if you could call this a 'walking simulator' but that's one of the closer descriptions I can think of.  is a fairly linear story-telling experience, and a fascinating one at that. The tale is told almost entirely through in-game UI, to the point that a new icon appearing, or the screen darkening, caused an emotional reaction in me. Aside from that, there's character logs, a few yes/no answers, and a lot of exomarine xenobiology. It kind of reminds me of Subnautica, including the resource management aspect, but it's very much its own game. is a game that is going to be huge for some players and a non-starter for others, and that's okay. If you're looking at this description and think it sounds boring as hell, then you've probably accurately assessed how much you're going to like this. If interactive stories and sci-fi mysteries are your bag, you may enjoy this.If it has flaws, it's the gameplay - in particular, some traversals are awkward or close enough that they can be difficult for players, and sometimes the direction isn't as clear as it could be. It's fun to poke around and explore - that's a huge part of the gameplay - but sometimes you may want an objective marker. If you can get past that, I wish you the best.Related games:  (vibes)
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The story of this game, is great. The controls (PC) leave something to be desired, as movement is quite clunky. There's a discrepancy for wanting to move through an area due to a hazard quickly, and wanting to read things. The map I would have to say is it's worst feature. I would still recommend giving this game a try, especially if you love biology.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A serene, powerful experience. A truly beautiful game, breathtaking and full of passion. Brilliant, utterly believable writing, from the characters and setting to the plot and the story development. An elegantly simple interface that is perfectly designed to give the feel of being in the main character's situation without getting in the way of gameplay. Music well suited to the environment and the speed of play. Enough urgency in certain mechanics to give a sense of threat when needed without making things feel impossible. Full of mystery and discovery, tells a profound and sad but hopeful story, does a great job of letting the player think and interpret.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely loved this game. The story was fascinating, the music helped you get engrossed in this new world, and the pacing (while slow a times) felt realistic as you learn more and more about this complex ecosystem around you. I am someone who works with and around ecosystems professionally, and I feel like this game encapsulated the wonder I feel about the little details and grand systems in the world around me! Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Not for everybody.Slow paced, repetitive and no graphics to mention.But the few assets it uses, music, ambient sound, atmosphere, and overall design of the game are well done.Feels a lot like a cross of walking simulator and a old test adventure, in a good way.6-10 hours of game play depending how thoroughly you read the descriptions and explore the map.Thumbs  up.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: At its core it felt like a minimalist Subnautica which is not a bad thing. It has a lot of neat ideas that just unfortunately fall flat. The exploration was too linear with few extra locations to scan. The UI and mechanics are interesting at first but shallow. More involvement in certain suit and base features would be welcome along with more opportunities to use them and more features to play with. That also goes for interactions with the flora and fauna. Every single movement has something to read but you're often put in positions where you're rushed due to an area draining oxygen or power so you can't relax and take your time to read. A simple pause while there's text would alleviate this. The story just suddenly stopped and while I was fine with the end, there was a lot more that could have been shared before it did.Love lore so collecting stuff to get sketches and see what the representative dots actually look like with information dumps is great.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Dear god, this game. This game is beautiful. It's nothing short of amazing. It's awesome in the sense that I am in awe at the sheer depth of it.It's worth it for the atmosphere alone. The calming music and pleasant visuals, work so well to immerse you in this deep, wonderful ocean. It's a great mix. Don't even get me started on your first deep dive, that segment is so well done. And your final dive into the deepest part of this three sunned planet is emotional to say the least.Most of my time was spent reading. It's a game mostly about reading and that perfectly suits the narrative. I can't overstate how engrossing the environment descriptions are. Add on Vas' observations of the flora and fauna of Gliese 667Cc and you get a scenic image of an ever changing world of fantastic creatures and places. The taxonomy may be a little simplistic, but I don't think it should be much more complicated. In concert with the exploration it provides enough challenge to feel massively rewarding yet quite feasible. The entries on the animals behavior and theories on how they could operate outside of the window of the game snowball into the pulsing heart of this fictional setting. The drawings of the living things you and Vas find are so... right, in a way. I'm not a 100% on this but, I believe that these seemingly small and minute yes or nos you give while playing do have an almost profound effect on your relationship with your meat friend. The ending line in the trailer about whether or not Vas can trust you was never encountered in my play through which means there's at least one more ending and very possibly more. You'll just have to find out for yourself.It's hard to explain but everything in this game meshes extremely well and the developers knew what they were doing. It's one the most comfy games I've ever played, maybe even my favorite story game too. I'm glad to have been able to experience this, this amazing piece of science fiction that seems so grounded despite it's watery setting.Edit: I feel like I should add that I completed the game 100% in two play sessions, the first one being a little under 8.5 hours and the second being just over 4.5 hour, just to show how overwhelmingly engrossed I was/am.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a 'meh' rating.It's fine but falls short of being good.Its' theme is about exploring the alien world but it either keeps you stuck on rails or makes you rediscover areas because you went there before the game was ready.The game play is adequate at best and tedious at worst, especially when going back through areas you've already been.The writing is almost good but lacks any impact because nothing happens meaning it's only good when it's an aquatic alien safari.5/10, some great ideas unfortunately diluted with unfulfilled potential
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It was very comfy. I love reading walls of texts, details and fleshed-out worlds, and the visual minimalist take is interesting and fits well enough in the story.It's maybe a bit niche, and won't appeal to everyone. I had some gripes, most of which other reviews mention, but it was still nice.Mostly posting to say that "bundle filler" is a pretty rash and chauvinistic way of saying "It's not my kind of game." There is a lot of quality in this, and different games can be interesting in different ways.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable short sci fi trip.It doesn't go too deep in its story but it still finds a way to create a compelling environment where you want to find out more about the place.It is about the journey really and letting your imagination work so you see the world and not just the little yellow dots.the descriptive writing is really done well although many a times some of the writing wont be read since there is a conflict within the game that other reviewers have pointed out as well.Need to move vs need to read.I enjoyed my time with it and can recommend to others who don't require non stop action and can enjoy a slow burn story.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I almost wish I could provide a more ringing endorsement for this game. The storytelling is beautiful and there's a serenity to exploring an alien ocean that is hard to rival. The limited interface and bare-bones graphics allow your imagination to run free, visualising all these exotic, strange creatures and their habitat.The problems however, lie in the game's controls, structure and most painfully, in the story it tells.The controls are the smallest problem, at least for me. They're clunky and unlike pretty much anything else I've ever used, but I got used to them over my time completing the taxonomy. An issue that remained to the end however, was that movement was painfully slow, unless you make use of your limited supply of oxygen (more on that later). Even when you do activate your speed boost, you're still restricted to travelling strictly between nodes, often frustrating you as there is a clear path between one point and another, but because there are no nodes connecting them, you are forced to take an enormous detour, completely negating the whole point of being underwater and able to maneuver in three dimensions.That oxygen system is also a limiting factor in other ways. Every node you click on, brings with it exposition about what your companion is seeing (as an AI, you don't have eyes as much as sensors), likewise, she'll occasionally speak up with her thoughts about the situation, as you explore. This is all fine and good when you aren't under any pressure and can take the time to read these notifications, but in many areas, your oxygen reserves are being actively drained, either by some corrosive bacteria; brine pools; or just being so deep that there's nothing producing oxygen down there. This puts a time limit that still ticks down, often quite rapidly, while you're trying to read what's going on. Finally, the story... It's painfully trite. Spoiler alert for anyone interested in playing, but I regret to say that the narrative is nothing we haven't seen before and hits the exact same notes that have by now become boring! Humanity's ruined our own world and is strip-mining lifeless exoplanets for resources. A corporation finds this brilliant new world and immediately tries to exploit the life it discovers. In so doing, the corporation drives a vital species to extinction and causes an ecological disaster. Oh no, how terrible, humans are bad, our corporations are bad, we're killing our world and are a blight on all life. Boo hoo. How many times do we need to hear this same environmentalist doomsaying and flagellation, before we've heard it enough? Frankly, the whole affair leaves a bitter taste in my mouth, that mars the entire experience.In short, while I at least mostly enjoyed my time with In Other Waters, I won't be playing the game a second time, as besides the interface and worldbuilding, it does and says nothing that a hundred movies and games have not browbeaten the viewer/player with before.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An artsy game. A decent premise that goes a bit heavy handed on the "Humanity is the real monster" trope but its fairly interesting to get you to keep playing. Gameplay is odd but sometimes baffles with certain lack of QOL stuff like a Dive map which would be helpful with getting a better ballpark on some of the samples you need. I also spent a lot of time clicking through wonderful descriptions of stuff because I simply didnt have the time to read it as my Oxygen was depleting so fast. The descriptions are nice when you have the leisure to take them in though.I'd recommend this well enough. Got about 5 and half hours of entertainment from it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A great game where you explore life in an alien ocean and uncover mysteries left by a previous visitor! I loved this game and have no regrets buying it.I will say it probably isn't for everyone. Half the game is exploring, looking for different lifeforms and then reading the conclusions that the biologist draws based on specimens. If you aren't really interested in the discoveries/readings and only really care about the main storyline you may not get as much enjoyment out of it. However, if you like feeling like an explorer/scientist it's a lot of fun!I ended up liking the main story more than I expected as well. Without giving too much away I would say that it does a great job at keeping the mystery interesting and compelling throughout the whole game. In general, the game is a lot of reading with little reliance on visuals (beyond the interface you see in the previews). I enjoyed the visuals and mechanics of the game, but if you are expecting detailed depictions of the sea-life and ocean beyond a collection of sketches you would be disappointed. I didn't mind this at all and was fine with letting my imagination fill in a lot of the blanks, but be aware of this if you think differently.Overall, I highly recommend this game if you don't mind any the points above! (Not sure if this is relevant to anyone, but the recorded play time for me is wrong. It took me around 9 hours to finish everything.)
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be played slow. Take your time, read, explore.In Other Waters is a take on text-based adventures of old mixed with some time based tasks, some heavy worldbuilding into ecosystems, graphical minimalism. It reeks of atmosphere and subtle details of an alien ocean. You get to experience it in your minds eye, helped by music and visuals. Take your time, read, explore. The game has really solid worldbuilding that is both consistent and realistic. It's the weirdest book I have read by its form. If I was a biology teacher this game would be my "additional reading".Of the control methods I tried I found controller to be more interesting, albeit it heavily ignores the platform conventions (no clear "negative" button), the game somehow feels much more real with the controller.I did find some glithces (picked up some microbes just by exploring and story didn't consider that option), but overall the experience is pretty smooth sailing. If you are an aggressive explorer, there will be a moment in which you want to go off the tracks exploring a newfound toy but you'll find that path closed until you advance the story "in the right way".I would highly suggest it if you ever see it at 7€ but it's not expensive experience considering the polish factor.EDITS: finished the game so added remarks about worldbuilding, the railroading and also upped the suggested price a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The game is unfortunately very confused about what it wants to be with multiple systems fighting against each other.One excruciatingly grating part was managing your O2 supply. Traversing certain areas of the world sees your O2 supply actively being drained, even while standing still and reading text or scanning your environment.This means that these parts are usually raced through with ignoring all exposition that's being provided. All the while you are actively hating on the UI design for being such a clunky mess when trying to * locate the next travel node (ping with Button B)* wait for the travel node's scan to complete (hold R stick pointing at node)* exiting the scan mode (press Y), line up the next travel node (hold L stick pointing at node)* and continue your journey by pressing A. All while ignoring any text that's appearingThis is even hurt more when trying to place some of the specimens that would provide you a bit of breathing room. To add insult to injury, the O2 system is mostly inconsequential: * You can't die. Even in areas where you can't request a drone pickup you will always be saved. You are merely reset to your starting point for the current expedition * Saving & reloading seems to restore O2 & power levels to fullAt which point I beg the question - why even bother?The areas where managing power levels was required I found less grating since these didn't tick down in realtime but with actions taken, which was a more fitting mechanism for the presentation the game is going for.---The presentation also seemed to be at odds with what the game wanted to achieve - immerse me in an alien world full of aquatic life. The text snippets while exploring were rather fragmented and painted a rather incomplete picture of the world around me - which I couldn't see. The sketches in the lab you unlocked _after_ researching everything about a lifeform, were able to fill a few gaps but by then you already moved on.---The story felt a bit hand-wavy, far removed from hard scifi. The points where the protagonist got on their soap box to preach against the injustices done by the evil bad company felt rather on your nose and could have transported more subtly, fleshing out the world and putting the actions in context instead of just having the protagonist ramble.---Give this a pass unless you are really into aquatic life and don't mind confusing presentations.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Some of my coworkers would call this "chill, lo-fi". And it is, although a little bit of that slow pace is enforced by the awkwardness of the UI. And it's not a perfect match for my personality - there's some really good writing here but I'm often wanting to move along faster than the text appears on screen, and so I don't fully read it before making my next move. Particularly bad during the second major section, which has a time limit and so pressures you not to read the text.There's a human-interest story overlaid over the biology and puzzle-solving; because there's a _game_ here I find it a lot more interesting than most "walking simulators". The puzzles are light - so far, everything is obvious; there were a couple of places in the first and second sections where you become aware of things you can't get past yet, but in the third section I've found a tool that should get me past them when I double back.Speaking of doubling back: to do all the biology tasks requires a fair amount of backtracking, but I don't think you need to do that to get the story, and it's not a long game even if you're trying for completion.Review at 70% task complete, who-knows-how-much story complete. Just now with a couple of big reveals, some of the theming has gotten heavy-handed; we'll see how it plays out.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A soothing, articulate, atmospheric journey through an alien sea. Rather like finding yourself AI on the computer of Subnautica's diver but in the best possible way! It is amazing that games like this are being made, that break the mold and present brilliant new, creative ideas on how to make video games.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: unbelievably good. basically an interactive sound novel played through and as the interface of a diving exosuit. gorgeous minimalist art design allows martin's careful character writing and xenobiological science fiction to bloom in the player's mind. plan dives, take dives, take it easy"It's... beautiful in here."
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so glad I played this game! In general, it's basically a text adventure with a unique UI. That might not be for everyone, but I really enjoyed it. You'll have to learn how to use the UI, but it's very satisfying, especially when supported by *fantastic* sound design and music. I've never played such a biology-focused game, and I certainly can't say all the long taxonomy reports interested me, but I was always excited to find a new sample and go scan it later. Exploring is fun, if a little meditative, and even if you hit a dead end you're usually rewarded with a unique sample. I had some tense moments running low on power/oxygen, but it was never harsh enough that I died. The story was very interesting and paid off the mysteries it set up in a way I found satisfying and creepy. It really asks you to use your imagination since it's all text, but that's better in some ways. I got chills a few times! I got the credits after 5 hours, and I'm on the fence for whether I want to try and get all the samples/scans. Some things I read said the "final" ending is not totally satisfying, so I'm not sure. Either way, I'm really happy with what I've gotten out of the game already.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games that I've played, despite the (relatively) limited content. All of the lifeforms in game were incredibly fascinating, and exploring this underwater realm was very satisfying and, with the exception of some of the regions, relaxing. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game, especially to fans of speculative biology.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful little narrative. It's text based but with a key part in exploration. The graphics are minimal but it's very much like being an AI that seeing things only through a map and text.I think there are things they could have pushed a little further in terms of the relationship with Ellery and the AI, as well as building tension and suspense throughout the story. The more intriguing things got me most invested about 2+ hours into the game (or at least at the pace I was exploring). There are some segments where it can feel a little slow but when you get more used to the controls and UI, things start to pick up and get interesting.I think there is a lot of intrigue to keep you exploring and going. Though it can get admittedly a little grueling going from place to place or trying to navigate to get small samples. It's good to play it in small portions, I think the potential for this sort of narrative of a text-based UI exploration game style could be explored more. It certainly made me feel excited to discover new things in this way!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: 2-D bird's eye view world explorer with very simplistic graphics. still manages to feel like a very immersive feeling of the environments with music and color. if you like being a nature cataloger then this is definitely for you. its fun to see how the different species and biomes interact. each of the 4 biomes has its own major obstacle to deal with, from coral to strong currents to poisonous algae blooms it definitely keeps you on your toes. the alien life still feels strange but still feels interesting and cool and less scary. the "story" starts with a severe amount of mystery and confusion in this new world environment, and the game will have you theorizing a good portion of the game. the second half of the game gets very creepy and dark despite there being no enemies. you should also note there is some heavy handed political message in the second half of the story bit about global warming and how humanity is poisoning earth. personally i thought it was TOO strong, making humanity seem like we are a virus that destroys everything we touch. i understand the message and its important but in this game, it clashes with the softer, more neutral aspects of the nature exploration of the game, and also demonizes the human too much while making nature seem incorruptible, while in reality humans right now are just dealing with our society growing too fast industrial wise and are coming to terms with that fact. most governments have agreed climate change is a serious threat but societally and economically haven't been able to deal with that yet. nature as well, for all its grandeur and pretty aspects, is also brutal. everything is in competition for everything else to survive and we aren't shown that side of nature is this game. i know im ranting on about the political nature of this game but it is really, really verbose about it. its a great game with an amazing exploration aspect, and has a great woven story. really although i complained about the politics of it i do enjoy the messages and how it tells the story. plus for a 2-d game with simplistic and linear exploration it has good visuals that can both scare and interest and blow you away, sometimes at the same time.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely adored this game. The thought and effort put into the writing and sketches, and all the lore of the planet and its creatures, motivated me to fully complete the game which is more than most other games can do. You can really tell the game was made w/ passion and thought, and though the minimalism of it had me sceptical initially, I became fully immersed in the story super fast. If you don't like exploration, item collection or reading, maybe it's not for you, but I happen to love all that so it was perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: this game is unique in that you don't get much instructions, you got to experiment with everything to learn. i started out unsure and a little frustrated, but once i cracked it I was delighted! it was so worth it. The story line is like no other! i love all the little clues and hints of the past and they do amazing world building {galaxy building} with few words
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I saw the trailer and I was eager to play the game, and now that I've finished it, I'll probably never forget it.The things I thought most interesting were the UI, music, story, and the taxonomy. The UI is simple and captivating, the music really gives off vibes of what you're experiencing, the story is very interesting, and the fact the game has taxonomy is awesome to me. 10/10 game, it was better than I expected.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I love the idea behind In Other Waters. I love the aesthetics and execution. It’s a beautifully realized game that figuratively and literally dips its toes in uncharted water. It’s mainly about exploration and science, charting taxonomy and topology along the oceanic floors on a foreign planet. It’s very abstract compared to a lot of other games. Meaning that you’re not actually controlling the character. Not thematically anyway. Instead, you’re controlling her diving suit as an A.I. with full access to all the relevant functions. That’s why you’re not seeing the game from a classical perspective, and why nothing is rendered past a colorful user interface. It’s limited to a sort of overhead view, populated with blips and blops, icons and menus. It plays out exactly like the screenshots describe, which isn’t often the case. Still, it’s not a game for everyone. Unless you’re following along with the story, there’s very little to dive into mechanically or otherwise. You’re pretty much clicking markers throughout and seeing if there’s anything of narrative interest there. Despite this, it’s still a beautiful and claustrophobic game, where the color palette swaps to darker tones as you descend deeper, and where you can feel the main character’s state of mind at every turn. I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone. But you are missing out on something unique and interesting if you opt out.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing it, but acquiring samples when they are far from the waystations can be frustrating as it is easy to get lost, because you can only check a pretty basic map back at your main base which only includes large landmarks and only shows the general area where you can get the sample. You have no map when out in the water and can only remember what locations look like to navigate.Moving throughout the world is done by entering scanning mode, scanning a place within ~15 merters where you can go, moving there and scanning for another place where you can move (you can move only to places you have previously scanned, but you only have to scan a position onece). Each of these positions have a short, written description, which is where you will get 80% of the information about the environment you are in, the rest comes from Elery's comments and research about various creatures and places you discover.I think the story is interesting, but it left some unanswered questions.I belive this game is worth your time if you can look past some tiring mechanics and are interested in discovering a bit about life on Gliese 677Cc with some twists and turns.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some amazing moments for aspiring xenobiologists, but it also contains some incredibly stupid humans.It goes from a cooperatative adventure on an alien planet to being forced to go along with several insane leaps of logic from a clearly defective science human.Spoilers and overly exaggerated summary is below:Your science human went for a booty call on an alien planet to chase down a woman who left her to freeze to death on an alien planet, AND ruined her carrier in the process.The woman your science human was trying to find injected herself with alien dna so she could dive into the abyss, only to basically kill herself, and then she exploded into plants in the medbay.The super space corp discovered this planet basically a generation ago, establishing several long term bases, even in the deep trenches of the planet. They then ruin everything forever. Not only ruining the ecosystem on a planetary scale, but causing the extinction of a possibly sapient race that was not only a quantum super computer, but also a magical gene editor. And then they abandon the planet and forget where the left it or something?Overall its a 9/10 game that's brought down to a 6 because of the humans being just that dumb.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this game!  Author had great pacing throughout... learning the controls, navigating the maps and descriptions (almost D&D-like in the way a description paints the picture for you), encountering and overcoming constraints, building the taxonomy of things, obtaining and using new "skills",   Once navigating, etc. became more formulaic the plot pace increased and expanded orders of magnitude.  Relaxing fun. If you don't enjoy reading or purposely having to stub your toe a few times to learn a mechanic you may not enjoy it.  If you are a botanist at heart or think you'd enjoy a more cerebral and text-based Avatar-ish story than this may be just the right game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful 2d Subnautica, with a really nice UI.The UI plays you as you are: The controller of a suit, the manager of it's functions. You move it, boost it, sample with it, and everything else a player would normally do - yet unlike Subnautica, you . The only thing you can see is a map, and important object markers made of lines, curves, and dots. (I mean, also the fact there isn't any crafting.) Yet, somehow, I wasn't bored with this. The game never gets too repetitive, ending things just before I get bored. You move around via chains of premapped triangles, and sample species to use as fuel or oxygen. I really enjoyed the fact that the game never made you do supply runs between each important story checkpoint, most were traversable without bringing more than the raw essentials (1 fuel item, 1 signal orb, and 1 oxygen item). I only made 3 resource runs, lasting less than three minutes each, in the entirety of the game. As your pilot talks to you during story events, the music is dynamic, having notes play as you press the 'next' button to dialogue - this makes the scene far more immersive than a music loop fading in and out of sections. Speaking of music, the atmosphere it creates is perfect - suspense or wonder or just a curious calm, it manages to fit the scene every time. The game even changes the colors of your UI at times, to really put out that vibe of the area you're in.Although it's a strange comparison, this reminds me of Katana Zero: Beautiful music and visuals (even with only curves and dots), and a short playtime perfect for the well-written story they portray. I finished the game in 3.7 hours (222 min), and I would ABSOLUTELY recommend buying it, In Other Waters is something you won't find anywhere else.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game a lot, but I really wish I had known going in something that the gamess marketing and the vast majority of the reviews fail to convey: This game has some pretty graphic horror. It is "nonviolent" in the sense that there are no combat mechanics, and it isn't "survival horror" in the sense that it doesn't use the gameplay conventions of the survival horror genre. But what you're getting here is something really more akin to Annihilation than to Subnautica. Obviously, this isn't inherently a bad thing. The game is well-written, and the gameplay is just deep enough for the length of game that it is. My main complaint is that the game often institutes the harshest time constraints in areas where the writing is the best and the most plot details are being revealed, discouraging exploration and spending time on actually absorbing the text, and putting the mechanics at odds with the story. While the pressure is fairly mild and easy to survive in a mechanical sense, its presence still detracts from a game that is so text-based and narrative driven. I feel like some people are also going to be dissatisfied with the amount of content for the price tag. It took me 10 hours to 100% everything without a guide, and two of those hours were spent trying to force my way into a couple areas that I didn't realize I wasn't actually supposed to be able to access yet. I'm personally okay with this, as I'm generally willing to pay a little more for the sake of giving indie creators a living wage. If you're really looking to maximize your hours of gameplay per dollar spent, know that the full sticker price might leave you wanting in that area.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly an ecologist's game as well as a sobering and thoughtful work of art and social commentary in its own right. I can vouch that great effort has been put into the construction of this alien ocean and the life forms within. On multiple occasions I found my uni training leading me down the same lines of questioning as the protagonist. This is the best speculative biology I have seen in some time. It's possible I'm finding it easier to understand some of the science in here as I can imagine a handful of places where the info comes in hard and fast and one might miss something. It's never anything mission-critical though. Make use of the logs on the Esc screen.All this dovetails beautifully with the writing. Considering the protagonist is a dot that spits out lines of text, the connection established is very fulfilling. Strongly encourage players to sit back and absorb the picture Ellery paints for you. The plot itself is a crisply-presented variation on a well-worn sci-fi trope. I suspect the time/attention constraints of the genre cut off some of the plot and character development, but it is complete as is. Some very relevant ethical questions are presented for the player's consideration, which is as much as I should say without spoilers.The environment here is a character in itself. You interact with it, it provides just the right about of time and forward planning tension, and insofar as it is a puzzle it doesn't feel out of character for the ecology of the place. In fact I think the strongest point of distinction I can offer this game is the perspective it takes on the environment. Ellery is, despite having very good reason not to be, unfailingly generous in her interpretation of the intentions and capabilities of the environment and the creatures you encounter. Nature is beyond our morals, and it is infinitely creative. This is an attitude that many real ecologists can struggle to internalise. Very few portrayals of ecology anywhere depict someone truly coming to grips with this truth.There are three gripes I have, which seem frustratingly basic in hindsight. 1) there's a lot of clicking involved in getting from A to B. A problem that could easily have been solved with a few more keyboard shortcuts. If you get this game, check the 3 shortcuts on the Esc screen as soon as you understand the controls, you will save yourself a lot of clicking. 2) You can't get to the map screen while you're outside of base. The terrain is well-crafted enough that waypoints are not necessary, but use of compass directions is. 3) The logs clear every time you start a new session. It'll be hard to remind yourself of the flavour if you resume after a long gap.Music is absolutely on point, the sketches are pretty and biologically accurate, and the postscript in the DLC booklet puts a nice wrap up on the story. If you're into that sort of thing, get the full package and I promise you will not be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It really takes guts to make something like this, especially these days.In the age of the ever-shrinking attention span, this game grabs you with all the immediacy of a biology textbook--one of those scary old-school ones with huge walls of text and hardly any pictures.Yeah, what Heaven's Vault was to archaeology this one is to marine biology.  That means that it, too, is definitely not for everybody, probably even more so.Once again you play a scholar in a depressing future who's spent a career scouring distant worlds--this time for alien life instead of ancient words--and coming up empty.  You finally hit the jackpot when you track down your former colleague who ran off to an unexplored ocean planet.  Of course, since both of you work for what's basically the Weyland-Yutani Corporation, there's more to it.  Nothing can ever be simple, huh?  In practice that translates to spending most of your time crawling around the ocean floor at the pace of a sea slug, conducting a painstaking survey of the local marine life.   You drift from node to node, musing upon interesting features of the undersea terrain and gathering up samples of various critters that you haul back to the lab for analysis.  When I say "you," by the way, technically you're not a person but rather an AI in someone else's dive suit; but since you're the one doing everything it's kind of beside the point.  Anyway, the reward for of all your hard work is a text-filled compendium of the anatomy and behavior of the creatures you discover.  Some of the bits and pieces you find can also be put to use in more practical ways; and meanwhile you're unraveling the mystery surrounding your sketchy employer and the fate of your colleague.  Whew.A game this weird could only be made as a labor of love, and the author's delight in this unusual material really does shine through.  It must have taken quite a lot of effort to create such a deep and detailed picture of an imaginary alien ecosystem.  An impressive amount of thought clearly went into dreaming up all the various life forms and considering how they would work together in each of the regions, which range from shallow subsurface plains of shimmering flowers to poisonous algae blooms to inky abyssal depths teeming with phosphorescent wonders.  At least, it all looked pretty convincing to me; and that was the key to establishing this game's distinctive style of immersion.So at this point it probably sounds like it's going to be a wide open player-driven exploration game, huh?  Maybe even an X-Com sort of thing where you have multiple layers of mechanics--exploration, retrieval, research, engineering, etc.--all running in parallel and influencing one another to move you forward?Not even close.While you do have some latitude to poke around each area and look for stuff at your leisure, the overall structure is highly linear.  It starts off subtle but as you go along the main story gets more and more insistent about taking the wheel from you, until by the end you're pretty much forced to pull over and let them drive.  At one point I tried to take a little detour to go open up a door I'd run across earlier and the game actually yelled at me about it.  Geez, fine, be that way. In general you're better off ignoring your video game instincts and just going where you're told.  Backtracking is incredibly tedious on account of how slowly you move and the lack of detailed visual indication on the map to show where you've already visited, and following directions at least helps keep it to a minimum.  Your home base winds up being another red herring. It's divided into more than half a dozen separate modules which at first look like they'll play an important role in your mission, but you never even use half of them. The sample analysis is a one-button, no-brainer procedure, and so the whole place is reduced to a library and a transport hub for jumping between waypoints. Pretty underwhelming.When it comes down to it, without any real freedom or decision-making involved you're not "exploring" the regions here any more than you explore the dungeons of a JRPG. You basically run them in order to reach a fixed goal. Like levels, each one has its own theme: the magic forest, the poison marsh, the electric cave, etc. Taken individually they're pretty neat to see, at least on the first pass, but this structure felt awfully strange in a game that initially seemed to be aiming to simulate a scientific investigation. Even the story turned out to be much more personal than discovery-focused.So where does that leave us?I think the main thing is to go into this one with your eyes open; otherwise the premise could leave you wanting a totally different sort of game.  As long as the basic idea appeals to you, you'll be happier without the distraction of expecting it to be something it's not.  Then you can just sit back, listen to the chill music and let your imagination run wild as you sink beneath the waves in search of space jellyfish.Really, it's fine.  Keep your killstreaks and lootboxes.  I'll just be over here reading about globules of alien mucus.You can find more indie game reviews at  or visit my   Thanks, and enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting setting; clearly a lot of work has gone into creating it. Great sound design and music. The game is very good at prompting your imagination to fill things in. CAPSULE comes to mind as another game with similar setting, atmosphere, and presentation (although that game is much smaller and much less chill). If you liked one you'll likely enjoy the other.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Charming, minimalist, just enough challenge to make it not a walking simulator.The story is well told via a series of journal entries and observations, and while it's a bit dark it's also hopeful.If you like the idea of a game about exploration with some very minor resource management and reaction-time challenges (click on a startled organism to examine it before it leaves scanner range, and the like), this is probably for you.   If I had a complaint it would be that the controls are a bit obtuse and movement is a bit slow.  This is not a game for the impatient.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: If the idea of zooming around an alien ocean discovering life sounds appealing to you, then stop reading reviews, buy this game, and start playing. This game is impeccable in design (visual, audio, and gameplay). The user interface is brilliant. The amount of work that went into species descriptions and drawings is incredible.My first playthrough took a bit over 6 hours, during which I was able to catalogue every species. I played it over multiple hour-ish sessions, which was good for leaving space to think about what happened.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fundamentally a minimalistic, guided narrative wherein you uncover the mystery of what happened on the planet you find yourself on - serving as the "AI" guiding the stranded scientist as he explores the planet with your assistance.  The story itself is quite compelling (if slow to get to the interesting part), but numerous typos in the dialog, a clumsy UI that had multiple glitches for me, and being forced to navigate waypoint-to-predefined-waypoint all ended up making this feel like more of a slog through a point-and-click nonadventure than a compelling game.  I wish it progressed faster / was a bit less clunky, because the underlying premise is great, the music is nice, and I dig the aesthetic - but after ~5 hours to get through the "main" story...I was over it and had no desire to continue point-and-clicking my way through waypoints to finish mapping out the planet.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Meh... It's kind of sweet and a decent, albeit unoriginal story. It's point and click with only text to read. It's all about alien biology, which is not really interesting, since it's all made up. If this taught you about real, Earth ecosystems it might be better.Kudos for making a non-violent game though!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a fun SciFi plot. In Other Waters is a great game to play when you feel like other games sound like too much. Listen to pleasant music and enjoy the low stakes of this very fun game. Only complaint is that it was so short. That said, any longer and some of the taxonomy and tasks would have gotten stale. Would recommend for something to play in between things.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Certain elements of the story remind me of Subnautica, which isn't a bad thing. There's more of a focus on the science, discovery, and character aspects, overall feeling a bit more mature in its themes, and the tongue-in-cheek satirical humor is missing. The game itself plays more like interactive fiction with a stylized graphical interface, which may appeal to you or it may not. I certainly enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A really nice narrative game. It pulls right back to the barest core gameplay, and builds a really nice world and story around it. The music is beautiful, and the graphics, while minimal, are nice. My only complaint would be that it would have been nice to include the illustrations within the game scan, rather than a separate enclyclopaedia back at base.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It's essentially a purely narrative game, a bit like as if someone took the atmosphere from Subnautica but conveyed it purely through text (all you see it an abstract 2D scanner map, never more) and descriptions, while also eschewing the danger that game could have.This sounds boring. And don't get me wrong the game is certainly not for everyone. But its atmosphere is also impressive, and it conveys it well. If you thought the raw feeling of Subnautica was far more important than the building, the escaping or the upgrading, give this a spin!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Try it for one hour. If, by the end of that hour, you're still annoyed with the interface, just stop playing. For me, the neither the core gameplay loop nor the story was intriguing enough to justify my pushing on through the game's intentionally clunky UI.The problem is it all felt like *work*. And it's not very interesting work either - you just collect samples while your companion Dr. Vas does all the talking, all the theorizing, and all the mentally challenging parts of being a space botanist. I honestly feel like this "game" would work better as a novel, with pictures and biographies of alien life laid out alongside Vas' thoughts about her expedition. The player seems to be unnecessary to the narrative, and it takes so long to learn anything new that it hardly feels worth the effort. Sometimes it's even dangerous - for example in the Bloom area of the map, pausing to read all the flavor text depletes your oxygen. What was the thinking behind that design?
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I can easily recommend this game to people who enjoy point and click style games, or even books. To everyone else, you're going to want to skip this one.The story is pretty good, and the setting details are creative and exceptional. The majority of interesting moments in the game are simply reading the descriptions of some plant, creature, or environmental feature. Oddly, I found the relatively simple graphics very compelling when coupled with the vibrant descriptions in the game.Mechanically, this game is very boring and will never really expand in an interesting way. There is some light puzzle solving, simple oxygen and fuel management, and a slightly frustrating inventory system that comes standard in games these days.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games!!! What first attracted me to the game was the minimal and simple style and color combos. The overall experience was satisfying and relaxing (although, SPOILER ALERT, there are some intense moments), and the soundtrack is pleasantly immersive.SPOILERS: there are some backtracking moments that feel tedious, but it's important to fully understand the story (and for you to know you explored and places). Also, after my 3rd run, I felt somewhat melancholic, because there's enough space to add more lifeforms, and we only explored a tiny part of the planet, so I wish there was more to explore.Regardless, In Other Waters is a must play, you won't regret it!!!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: ugh, this hurts. this game is special, there is clearly love put into it the worldbuilding is great, as is the user interface. if that's all you're after, go ahead and buy it. i however did not enjoy it and will be returning it. there's many small issues that make basic things, mainly movement annoying. the way you have to switch between scanning and movement mode in order to move, and the way that you cant move to unscanned when in movement mode. this somehow turns moving too unkown nodes aka;exploring, a seemingly key facet of this game into a three click movement, that's three clicks per node. trails are often 10+ nodes, taking a few seconds for the character to move between.for some reason... the main character.... talks like this a lot. it seems small but waiting for those tiny bastard dots always annoys me. i'm sad that i'm not the kind of person this game is made for, its good, great even. but i don't enjoy it. i want to explore this world more, i want to see all the cool critters, but i know this game will enevitably sit gathering dust in my library forever
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not recommending this game, because there is no neutral option and as a warning because this game may not be for everyone.The Good:-Lovely visuals-Nice sound design-interesting story-Different colour pallets for different areasThe bad:-Repetitive game-play-Too short music loop in the base-Text heavy-Fake sense of explorationConclusion: This is a good Indie Game, but it is more akin to a walking simulator. If you expect an exploration driven or puzzle game, then this isn't it. The game makes you believe that it is about exploration, but it is very linear with very few minor branches. There is the main quest and along the way you can pick up samples that will increase your knowledge of the fauna for no other reason than to read about it. In this game you're more of an observer than someone who can act on it and it feels like you never really have the control of your actions. Worst offender was when I unlocked the torch and wanted to first go pick up a previously unobtainable sample before continuing with the main quest, but it would keep me from even getting close to that area forcing me to proceed in only one direction: Very immersion breaking.Finally, everything is described through text and that isn't a bad thing per se, but when you couple that with oxygen loss in certain areas, you feel rushed to read the text, rather than taking it in and getting immersed in the game. It would have been wiser to be able to pause when reading.All in all, if you like the demo and the visuals you can get the game, but don't expect it to grow anywhere beyond that.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A very immersive game that manages to evoque a beautiful alien world with simple 2 color shapes. The gameplay is not that deep (no pun intended) but it serves the story well. The descriptions of the environment are very well written and the story is engaging and fun.Overall a good little game, for the passionates of exploration and discovery.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautifully crafted game with a unique atmosphere. It has a very strong sense of style, which is most obvious in the game's UI and sound design. The original soundtrack by Amos Roddy is amazing, - much better than the sounds from the kickstarter. I love how with the combination of great sounds and minimalistic ui they let the player imagine how this underwater ecosystem might look like,  which felt both mysterious and dangerous, even though you can only see some bright dots on a minimap. The only thing that annoyed me, is that sometimes the main character will tell you too much about what's going on, not letting you to find out for yourself. However, that helps move the story forward and it has a very nice pace, so I recommend it to anyone who likes games with good stories.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: My save file says 88% complete at time of writing and I don't think I'm super close to the end but this game is amazing! The fungus ocean is so interesting, the creatures are unique, and the music is beautifully mesmerizing! Might just be lingering paranoia from other underwater alien world games but I keep half expecting to find something huge and terrifying, but as far as I can see the game is true to the tags and calm!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Unique and absolutly captivating exploration based game with a charmingly abstract style and presentation.If you are even mildely interesting from the screenshots and trailers I truly recommend giving it a try!I just started my play trough at the time of this review, and will update it once I either finnish or abandon the game^^But as the first 1,5 Hours really managed to be a great start, I am quite sure the overal "YES PLAY THIS" tone will stay.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this review, I am only 5hrs into the game and don't really have a clue how the story is going to play out. Nevertheless I felt inclined to write a review, since I have already fallen in love with this game.First things first: I bought it on sale, not really knowing what I was gonna . Now after having played it, i can say it is more of an "experience" than a game. An interactive story that unfolds thanks to your actions as a player. What i really like is the atmosphere that is brought to life by outstanding sound design."In Other Waters" manages to induce a very immersive experience, similar to how H.P. Lovecraft did in their stories. All that  whilst maintaining "minimalist" graphics to say the least. And maybe that is not , but  of that very fact - by not showing the player what things look like (i.e. landscapes, different alien lifeforms) it gets your imagination .Following that, I felt very motivated to gather samples and complete studies on these extra-terrestrial lifeforms, after all the  player is rewarded a faint sketch of a study subject once every part of analysis has been completed. Additionally, new little mechanics to traverse the  are being introduced so there  is a  of variety to the gameplay.Now this is not a game to rush through as fast as possible, quite the opposite - for me at least. If you've had a long day and you just wanna relax a little, take in the scene, the story, heck maybe even close your eyes for a few minutes and just enjoy the sounds and BGM, go spin this bad boy up and you won't be disappointed. In that sense, I'd like to compare it to Stardew Valley, which had a similar kind of chill to it.But to  on your excitement, this game may not be for everybody - if you're not interested in slow storytelling, working towards- and reading about how the authors imagined life on another planet might look like and rather find your satisfaction in rich gameplay, you may not want to So far, my playthrough went  and I'd like to thank the team behind "In Other Waters" for this beautifully  experience.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I went into In Other Waters expecting a game about discovering and cataloging alien sea life, and it is that, mostly, but on top of that I ended up surprised by just how emotionally affecting the plot could be. The atmosphere is perfect, the gameplay relaxing, and the UI beautiful (although it did take me a bit to get used to on a controller.)Bonus points for the lesbians, I love those.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this. It was impressive how they could use really limited (although aesthetically pleasing) visuals together with quite simple game mechanics, combined with great atmospheric sound and well-written flavour text for an extremely evocative result. The sense of being a scientist exploring an alien landscape was really effective. I was totally drawn in to it, and I can't think of anything similar.The only thing I would consider changing about it would be that the map in your base will instruct you to take samples from a location, but the minimap when you go out in the wild doesn't have the same markers. For a lot of the game it doesn't matter at all, because you still have lots of exploration to do and you don't really need to head for a specific spot - but as you get closer to the end, and you want to finish your data collection, you really need to go to those specific areas, and it can be a little frustrating to find them. The landmarks you can use to guide you are extremely sparse and vaguely defined, so you end up aimlessly wandering around in roughly the right area, hoping you will just stumble upon the right location.I guess the feeling of being lost might even have been intentional, but it just broke the immersion a little for me, and I didn't think there was any narrative justification for your minimap to offer so little help when trying to navigate. Still, definitely not enough to put me off the game, and I enjoyed it right to the end.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game was not what I expected, but do note that I stopped playing after 1 hour. I wanted it to have the kind of feeling you get when being immersed in water. The isolation and wondering what lurks in the dark. Further, the graphical style did not appeal to me. I did not get a clear enough picture of how things look just by reading about them in text.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Thought it was a lower-quality graphics version of Subnautica.  While it is slimmed down from them, I think there is a real case for In Other Waters having a better story.  It doesn't have the fancy graphics or voices, but make great use of the minimalistic HUD, colors and music.  Kinda short, beating the story and most of the objectives in 10 hours, but memorable.  Definitely worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like it. The story and such was intriguing. The controls are 'ok'. But I didn't come close to finishing this short game. Why? ... the map. Or lack thereof.So, we have the technology to travel to other planets, explore their oceans, and painstakingly catalog the life we find there. We also have a handy, digital map of the area we're exploring. But the map ... for reasons unknown ... can ONLY be accessed while you're docked at a base. Apparently we don't have the technology to show you the digital map, while you're out in the ocean.Horrible, horrible design flaw. I'm sorry I bought this one, even on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A silent, small discovery journey, minimal and intimate. It is though, apart from searching and finding the story points on the map, a very linear story with no "real" choices. The taxonomy is beautifully and detailed, but I feel the detailed biological informations do not really intertwine with the main storyline, i wished there were riddles of some kind, where you have to really study the biology drawings/text to come to conclusions.... but this is not necessary at all, You can also not look at 80% of the artwork/content and still pass through the story.  I would have loved the textbox a bit bigger to be able to read easier and give more space to the story line - the visuals are not that important here, honestly (apart from the taxonomy sketches and the gerneral minimal feel, which is awesome! I wonder if i will fill out all the taxonomy entries anyway - they are beautifully written and the drawings are great. Just for curiosity - and thats cool!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An odd text-based adventure game set in an alien ocean where you study the native species. There are no graphics, just lines and dots on your HUD as you read a description of each room and the critters you find. If you do enough research on alien organisms you can unlock some rough sketches giving you some idea of what the aliens look like. If you progress, you can eventually to figure out the secrets of what happened to the last expedition to this planet.Not for everybody, but if any of that sounds interesting you might like it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This is not just a game, it is a masterpiece and a work of art, both in terms of design as well as storytelling. Truly impressive how so much satisfaction and emotion can  be conveyed with such minimalist graphics. I cannot believe how this one crazy guy from London basically created the game mostly by himself (apart from the music which is not any less brilliant in its own right). This is true gaming innovation, and shows how games can be the most complex sort of art.
