_childDocuments_.review: Like others I was immediately drawn to the premise of this game (and the premise is brilliant), but for a game that sells itself on adventure, exploring and discovering alien life in an alien sea, it does a lot less to market the fact that it is essentially a text-based adventure.  "Discover alien life that you will never see".  "Explore an alien sea by staring at a topographical map with some pink overlay lines".  "Go on an adventure by selecting the next pre-determined vector point triangle".This is an indie game with a small team, I understand that there are limitations that come with that, but there are also little steps that can be done to emphasise the feeling of being an AI guiding a lone explorer.  Here are three things that I think really detract from the game and the concept:1. Lack of voice acting.  There is one character (potentially two).  Voice acting would have been a very simple addition to the game that would have captured the feel of a person monologuing towards an AI or leaving logs behind, rather than a click-through text adventure.  Instead of feeling like a technological observer to the conversation I'm instead diverting my "AI resources" to staring at text as it generates.  I'm sure the dev/s could have found a single person to read out their script in front a microphone to reinforce their "you're an AI" selling point.2. Exploring through a 2D topographical map makes no real sense for this AI; how was this topographical map generated when you're the first explorers (who are documenting) to go there?  If you're generating the map with your AI features, why is it only in 2D?  Why is the point of reference above the explorer? Are your sensors really so useless that all life you catalogue can only be pinged as a dot instead of even a basic outline, even though it can map entire reefs and advanced topographical information?  Instead of the play area being a very technically-accurate topographical map, it would make much more sense and be a lot more immersive if, instead of a pre-developed map (that you can see outside of your scan ranges), you were developing the map/topography as you travelled.  Not in the form of a pre-established topography map, but in the jaggy outlines of a half-discovered rock wall that then gets converted to a topography map (for example).  If that's too complicated, just give us jaggy lines instead of an accurate topography map to better reflect the feeling of scanning the area as we explore.3. Perhaps my biggest pet peeve: "Oh my god everything is so beautiful!"  The explorer constantly drills into us how beautiful everything is.  "Oh my god, alien life, I can't believe my eyes!" "Wow, it's so beautiful!"  "Everything is so colourful!"  "Look at how elegant and beautiful everything else with how it gently and seductively sways in the soft currents of the ocean with air bubbles dancing magnificently like little ballerinas amongst the most colourful and vibrant corals you will ever bear witness to in a thousand lifetimes!"  Like, we get Clarissa, you can see and we can't.  You don't have to rub it in every five steps.  Everything is beautiful and here I am watching a dot follow a pre-determined path in a recurring sequence around an enclosed area of topographical lines.  Breathtaking. :/Concept art of the creatures/areas would have gone a long way. For example, the explorer could have "taken a snapshot" of the discovery that gets uploaded to the database/catalogue you're creating, so we have a basic visual point of reference for what's being described (the animals, the plants, the reefs and the rock walls etc. etc.).  I believe there's artwork that can be downloaded, but without it being in real-time as you explore or integrated into the game that really just falls under "a book in the same universe with pictures of some things".Overall, and I believe other reviews have touched on this, this is a game for people who like *text* adventures.  Don't go in expecting to see a single thing you've "discovered" or "experienced", you're just a dot moving around a topographical map with other dots moving around and text describing the various dots and movement of dots.  There are also info dials on things like oxygen etc. and you can collect samples (described through text of course) and do stuff with them, but I didn't really get far enough to unpack all of that stuff because text-based adventures aren't my thing.  From what I've read there's depth to be found in those mechanics, but for me the experience felt very linear, pre-determined, almost solely focused on reading text and all about how beautiful everything I couldn't see was.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really neat game. It looks amazing, and despite the minimalism, it manages to convey a lot. The sound design is also top notch.It immediately reminded me of Mu Cartographer and Capsule, although this one is far more narratively driven.The game is very mysterious, and and first hour or two are great as a result. Unfortunately, the story is rather slow to unfold, and many points fail to develop properly and ends up rather unsatisfying.It's also a very impressive feat, creatively. There is a whole ecossystem of a maybe 10 to 20 organisms described and drawn out. As much as I love this, however, their existence is 90% flavour text, and it's presented through rather dry log entries.I stress it again, it's very impressive, but it's such a failure of communication, in my opinion. Most people (myself included) wouldn't read a dry description of insects or fungi or what have you - so why would we want to do so about an imaginary ecossystem? Life is often stranger than fiction, too.So this seems like kind of a wasted effort. Commendable, but ultimately feels like it was a rather "selfish" creation; it doesn't do much for the player other than maybe show off the writer's imagination (and research).Finally, the gameplay was also very underwhelming, especially in respect to the ecossystem.Early on, there were elements of Waking Mars - where you were collecting samples which you could deploy in the world to interact with other creatures (to inhibit growth and clear a path; to catalyze growth to block a current). Unfortunately, these were completely ditched and never developed later. This would have helped, I think, in making the flavour text feel more relevant and interesting. Perhaps it could contain hints about where and how to use different elements, etc., to solve real problems.I tend to find pure flavour text tedious and irrelevant; it's a very different matter when the text is tied to my *actions* as a player.There is also some resource management but, once again, very very minimal and almost irrelevant. You can use samples to replenish oxygen or power, which you need more of one or the other depending on the area. But you almost always get whatever samples you need in the current area you're exploring, so you don't need to map or catalogue anything.Worse, the game encourages you to collect and bring back new samples to the base, but these occupy precious inventory space - and the movement is rather tedious, so going back to the base is a hassle.So yeah.I still enjoyed the game quite a bit. The story's payoff was a bit disappointing, but it still kept me interested throughout, so it was cool. Visual design is really excellent, and so is the audio. Writing seems very competent, but also far too wasteful and ultimately dull. Game design is also very basic, although it hints at more (which makes it feels more unsatisfying than if it hadn't been there in the first place!).Also, I used to love these kinds of quirky games, and somehow touch with them over the years. This game reminds me where my attention to should go again!

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a very charming game. It is an extremely calming, relaxing, zen sort-of game.  However, I do unfortunately feel as though it is lacking. The concept is incredible - however at it's core, this game is simply a point and click game. A story that progresses every time you click. That's fine, I like point-and-click games as much as the next guy. However, I feel like this idea has so much more potential than this. The game is sort of "narrated" by the xenobiologist that you follow, which is fair enough considering we can't see anything. But the writing lets it down. Everything is pointed out to you in a very straightforward way. Perhaps the best way to get the story across to everyone, but not the best for the game I feel. Nothing is left to your imagination, while also not being overly descriptive. Overall, it's a very cool concept and the game itself isn't terrible. I do feel like the core idea here has so much more potential though. It's a great story that doesn't convert well into being a game. Or at least, hasn't been converted too well into a game. Of course this is my opinion - I would prefer things to have a bit more intrigue, a bit more description, etc.At the end of the day, it is a good product. The UI is lovely and the sound design is great all around. Just not my cup of tea. Also, I see a lot of reviews comparing this game to Disco Elysium. Either I've missed something huge here or these reviews are crazy. Disco Elysium is a completely different game altogether, despite having some similar mechanics here and there. Just wanted to clear that up with all these other reviews.TL;DR - A nice little story that didn't translate too well into a game. Well designed. Simply not for me unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty good game.It took a little bit to get used to the gameplay. Coming off of other videogames with a million mechanics and stats and things you need to watch out for this game brought me back somewhat to flash games with the benefit of a weird amount of immersion aided by the gorgerous UI and amazing sound design.The story might not be everyone's cup of tea. Our protagonist is a self described depressed biologist out on a wild goose chase looking for someone with the only lead being their call, minor amount of drama ensues. Personally I did enjoy the story and found it interesting to see what happens next.The environment is abstract on your UI map including the numerous alien species you will scan and study along your journey. During my playthrough initially I thought that I had to scan everything in an area before moving on but as you progress the story you'll acquire a few upgrades that are completely necessary for achieving that goal so ideally don't waste 3 hours in the first are like me. The descriptions of the aliens are gorgerous and the writters really nailed the writing there its extremely realistic in a way it didn't even need to be.This game, atleast to me with my sound system felt weirdly immersive especially a few hours in once we got down to the lower dephts. As someone with thalasophobia I expected that to be triggered but it never was. Sound design is stellar.Slight criticism I have is of the lack of a menu to mute the music, I don't dislike the ost its just repeating alot when you are exploring a certain area and I would rather keep just the ambience instead. There was also some strange issue with one of the biological samples in the first area where the laboratory didn't seem to scan it despite having two pieces and clicking them one after another. Fixed itself seemengly because later in the game I backtracked to get 100% and took another simple which worked this time.I am not sure if this was intended that I had to close the game and open it back after getting 100% for the final sequence of conversations and cutscene->credits to trigger.Overall would reccomend for people that like to read and have a little bit of patience as well as those that enjoy staring at UI.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful.It's sold mostly on it's narrative and worldbuilding but that's not to say that it's a pure visual novel/ walking sim, or that what game play there is isn't fun. interacting with Gliese 677Cc's ecosystem as you study it makes the planet feel real and immersive.  is an example of an early exploration mechanic that makes the game's scif-fi ideas feel tangible.On the topic of those sci-fi ideas though, this game's worldbuilding is dense, fascinating, and brilliantly presented. This is hard sci-fi, every entry you log will be filled with biological speculation and chemical readings. But even if you don't care about all that, the ecosystem here is filled with unique and interesting wildlife:  None of this overshadows the story however, which is well written, affecting, and gets you thinking about all the things that good sci-fi does. The history you uncover of Gliese 677Cc is steeped in colonialism and humanity's arrogance, but its future is an open question.I found this game to be completely captivating from start to the 100% finish.(plus it gets points for having casual lesbian rep)

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing, peaceful, and surprisingly immersive for a game with no voice acting.  Gets round the limitations of being a one-man-developed game by making you an AI of sorts, nurse-maiding a marine biologist around a mysterious ocean.  Actually, it's far more elegant than that.  Being an AI explains and enables the symbiotic relationship you have with the scientist.  Neither of you can function in the world without the other, a nice link into the ecosystems you quickly discover.It's a real labour of love, with a lot of work and care put into it.  Very recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick:4/5  I wholeheartedly recommend this game.  It is one of my favorite game-play experiences that I have ever had.  I am extremely biased in my opinion of this game due to my personal interests.More:     In Other Waters is a unique game.  I have never played anything like it.  As far as I can tell, it is an atmospheric game.  All of the enjoyment of playing this game comes from the player's immersion in the story and the music.  It is like reading a book.  The more interested you are in the topic of that book, and the more you enjoy the author's writing style, the more you will enjoy reading that book.  I am very interested in marine biology, astronomy, astrobiology, and science fiction.  Therefore, this game's topic interested me very much.  This is one of the reasons for my bias in this review.  Minimalist gaming experiences have also become an interest of mine recently.  Therefore I easily became engaged with the designers methods of conveying an experience without an abundance of visual stimuli.     There is no tutorial as far as I can tell.  The game hits the ground running and expects the player to figure things out as they go along.  I thought that the interface would be more intuitive than it was, but it worked out just fine once I got the hang of it.  It took me a few minutes to understand the basics and I was off... exploring an alien ocean.  The narrative pulled me in immediately.  It is delivered at a comfortable pace and it holds back just enough information to keep the player invested in what is going on around them, without spoiling the surprises.  I was surprised at how emotionally invested I was in the little dots which represented characters.     I do have a few issues with the game.  The minimalism is taken too far in some areas.  The lack of an active map isn't that big of a deal.  Yet, when you have already traversed an area, and you want a better reference point by which to orient yourself, you do not get one with this game.  This led me to waste a few hours searching for something that I still don't know if I was able to find.  That search points to another issue that I have with the game.  I am unsure if I encountered a bug during my play-through.  My belief is the reason that I am unsure is connected to the sometimes extreme amount of minimalism.  During my search for a sample I repeatedly returned empty-handed.  I was unable to find out why this was happening, or even if I was supposed to be searching for it at that time.  There was no distinguishing feature, at least one that I could see, that could tell me if I was searching in the wrong spot, or if the search itself wasn't supposed to occur at that time.  This failed search and the game forcing me to pursue another objective irritated me extremely.  It was the one time during my play-through that I was pulled out of the experience and not enjoying myself.     Other than a few minor gripes, the game is great.  I love this game and I can't wait for more developers to begin making games like this.  Every discovery and piece of information that you find is more rewarding, because there is less flash and flair bombarding you every second.  The descriptions and artwork of the alien life forms are a prize well worth the effort when you uncover them.  This game is an imaginative exploration of a possible world.  I hope that you experience it, and that you get as much out of it as I have.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: It was very interesting in the beginning, but in the end the mechanics are clunky and frustrating--understanding where you've been already, reading the map, and pursuing completion of the 'compendium' , we'll call it, through map specific sidequests is quite painful for a number of them. It feels unbalanced and not thought all the way through per collecting resources and managing your inventory. Then there is the writing, its heavy handed too often. This is a game about not taking global warming seriously as a society and the massive consequences that entails. Which are real and it deserves all attention possible. But In Other Waters makes the serious error of suggesting humanity will destroy the earth ala 'its now the moon'--when its the earth that will destroy humanity and move on, as it has many many times for epochs of death and new eras of life on this planet. Life is actually very hardy once it digs in, as science understands today. The game talks a big game but reveals itself to be lacking in a serious understanding of ecology or the biological history of the planet. The plot also has issues, the character we follow comes to one or two very key conclusions that do not make sense in the abstract or in the details found by you in your exploration. There is also too much evidence of ideas that didn't get implemented,. fleshed out, or acted upon but the foundation for them are there.  That adds some dissatisfaction that's hard to ignore, and it might have been unintentional. But in a video game, everything is a chekov's gun and something big that is just there to look at is something to be disappointed in. And this game had a Chevok's Gun and had some very interesting narrative possibilities that it didn't follow and ended up being underwhelming.  It was a set of very interesting ideas that made for an uneven experience in the end but it was ambitious and that deserves a lot. If my critiques seem uncompelling, give it a shot.I didnt realize this team went on to make Citizen Sleeper, I think this was a stepping stone to that and clearly they are very talented. Getting this to support them would be worth it. But the game is frustrating, in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved and was completely consumed by my playthrough, any small complaints I have - no sound volume adjustment, no map makes manuvering unnecessarily difficult - are eclipsed by just the sense of wonder in investigating and charting a new world.The way the game tells its story and world building is so engaging while being so minimal, and is a lesson in how strong writing can reduce the need for any visuals.I was originally hesitant in getting this, as I'm directionally dyslectic, and the promo pictures looked to me like a fully map-based game, but I found the exploring more intuative than just directions, and the struggle of figuring out how to get somewhere worth it to unlock all the data entries.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I have two major gripes with this gameGame-play: Imagine aim-labs but their is no recoil and only one of the targets move.Controls are obtuse for no particular reason. Instead of having me press the scan button, scan the dot, press the stop scanning button, and then move to the dot, why can't I just move to the dot? Secondly, theirs this whole mechanic of taking samples and using them to affect the environment, but after the second chapter, it's completely forgotten. why have it in the game then? lastly, the game is far to linear while under the guise of being open. You aren't exploring, the game tells you what your allowed to find. Example, after you find the blow torch, you are not allowed to use it until you progress the story far enough. Which really Blows :)Story: If you cry when you remember that lumberjacks exist. This game is for you.The story has the depth of a lobotomized child. To sum it up quick, think "humans were the virus all along." you could replace any character with "Lenard the talking crab" and it would honestly make it better. The story is bare bones. you have evil corpo that is evil because..... profit? and you have good aliens that are good because they speak for the trees. but you? you are on the good team because you are the rare breed of persons that is able to understand that nuking a planet isn't profitable. Side note, if you collect all the samples and then do the final mission, the character decides to stay on the planet forever away from all humans, then immediately informs you the antenna is repaired and that you should contact everyone for rescue.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game's biggest assets are its innovative mechanics/interface and its chill atmosphere. Unfortunately for it, the innovativeness of the former sometimes feels clunky, awkward and uncomfortable. That, and that I keep finding myself indifferent to the story, means that I only play for short periods of time. It's an interesting game, but not on my list of personal favourites.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it, it's a chill game with good ambient music and a nice minimalistic design. Writing is decent and the different biomes are entertaining to wander around. Of course it isn't perfect, some game mechanics force you to keep moving so you don't have time to read the logs, and some people may find the missions a bit samey. However, I think it's a good one, specially if you're into these kind of chill interesting games.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: |  | A relaxing and intriguing experience. If you are a fan of detailed world building (or even the clinical documents detailing SCP entries) reading through the notes of Dr Ellery Vas as she studies and analyses alien fauna and flora is absolutely delightful.I will say I'd recommend using a mouse, as I wasn't totally satisfied with the level of controller support. Which is a shame, because I found the methodical game play of pushing forward in an unknown environment, step-by-step, scanning and sampling everything that you reasonably can to be the perfect match for the game's story and lore.However, my biggest gripe is that objectives that are marked on the 'over world' map in the Waystations, are not flagged on any type of compass when you're exploring, which lead to me getting turned around and frustrated. To be fair, I was attempting to 100% clear areas, instead of pursuing the plot, so that might be a feature that appears later on.All-in-all, lovely, imaginative, sapphic, experimental, but not for me. Well worth giving a try <3
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal atmosphere achieved through convincing sound design and extremely pleasing user interface more than makes up for the lack of traditional game graphics. Engaging story keeps you coming back to the game's many surprisingly grounded alien ecosystems. Lots of alien taxonomy to comb through for those interested.Traversal can feel slow and unnecessarily grindy at times but keyboard shortcuts alleviate this issue somewhat. Dialogue is frequently a bit on the nose, undercutting natural player curiosity about the world and desire to experiment with mechanics. Overall, highly recommended for biology or speculative biology nuts and those who looking for a unique experience gameplay-wise
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a tranquil and explorative point and click for the curious mind with a penchant for discovery of the unknown. The story eases you into the world and you will find interesting lifeforms at the bottom of this alien ocean. The soundtrack is one of total immersion if you listen with over ear headphones, one that morphs into play at the right times. The UI is simple enough to use without the need for much text as it is quite intuitive. Without revealing too much, you will learn more about why you're there and the events that transpired. It's a short game that you can dive into and have a chill unwind with.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: While I am recommending the game, I would definitely say it is not a game for everyone. The UI is quite good though, and you'll spend the whole time playing basically looking at this beautiful graphical interface rather than actually being "in other waters" if that makes sense. I would say it is most comparable to a walking simulator, with a sprinkle of Metroidvania without spoiling too much.The sound design and writing, as well as careful use of color really adds to the immersion of the world you're exploring even if you don't get to see the world with your two eyes. The story is engaging enough and there are enough changes as you explore to keep exploration engaging and interesting. It is a lot of reading, especially if you feel like finding out more about the marine life living on this foreign planet.If all of this sounds alright to you then I recommend giving it a shot! It was short enough, completed in 3 sessions or so for me and the story was interesting from beginning to end, ramping up in complexity as you progress. I applaud the dev for trying something very different.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Wow... What. A. Game! As an exploration-driven adventure,  is designed to intrigue; to tell a tragic yet hopeful story; and to make you marvel at a gorgeous alien oceanic planet that's "shown" to you through incredibly-descriptive text and top-down visuals consisting "merely" of simple shapes, colours and animations. You won't be exploring this lively alien planet alone though. After all, in this game, you play as a seemingly-conscious AI in a diving suit that had malfunctioned. Your job here is to guide your "operator"-slash-companion, a xenobiologist called Ellery, who's here in response to an urgent request by her friend, Minae, to the places she wants to go as she tracks down her friend and eventually find out what Minae had intended for her to find... which includes a wonderfully-diverse yet immensely-interconnected ecosystem of alien lifeforms and a tragic mystery involving the exoplanet mining corporation they both work for.Part 1:Part 2:Now, I'll have to admit - the game can be a tad bit "slow" mainly because of the way you travel from one point to another in this game... personally, I'd prefer if scanning my surroundings is done automatically whenever I moved... but trust me when I say that if you persevere, you'll be well-rewarded with a beautifully well-written and paced story that, in combination with superb graphics and sound, will completely immerse you, making you feel everything that Ellery is feeling and experiencing everything that Ellery is going through. You know those games that no other game will ever come close to? Well, In Other Waters is definitely one of those games.I also enjoy exploring the different sections of the ocean planet, discovering and cataloging new species as I go. It's not very different from "collecting" new Pokemon but since this game is more science-y, you aren't collecting specimens just for collection's sake... you are also examining parts of a creature, and monitoring their behaviours and habits. Best of all, you can use natural "signals" to get the local flora and fauna to do what you want, whether it is to shrink certain flora, like how a mimosa plant would when touched, just to reveal a new path or to make the local plants expand to slow down the currents so you could cross a channel. The process is very methodical and the sampling process is very non-invasive as well... in case that's of concern to you :)Plus, being of a scientific background (biology, in fact), I've got to give the devs and the writing team props for making sure to use the style of writing that a real biologist would use. Every plant or animal you discover is described in brilliant detail, and once you've collected all the samples needed, you can even see Ellery's sketch of it. There's a bit of resource management too with different environments affecting the drain on your energy and your oxygen levels differently. Thankfully, resources are pretty abundant in this game - it's obvious that the game isn't designed to be hardcore - and you could easily restock up on oxygen/energy-giving materials as you travel. That said, it's always wise to bring along some spares.I've also got to give huge props to the graphics team for having the ingenuity to use simple shapes, colours, and animations to bring a whole alien world to life, and to the sound team as well for creating soundtracks that perfectly suit the events that are unfolding or lend gravity to the realization that's dawning upon me as I read the texts. These "little" things really make a huge difference when it comes to immersing a player in the virtual game world he/she is experiencing - and boy! Was I completely reeled in!+ Fantastic storytelling, mostly done through texts. Expect lots of reading! + A gorgeous life-filled alien oceanic planet to explore. Makes you feel like a true xenobiologist! + The more scientific aspects of the game are all very well-done. There aren't too many scientific jargons (that I've noticed) that'd push laymen away from the game.+ Offers an ingenious way to not only visualize the alien planet and everything in it, but also to show how lively it is (in most sectors).+ Some resource and inventory management since you have a fairly limited inventory to store samples and that those samples can be used by your suit to restore some amount of energy and oxygen.+ The main storyline is fairly short but sweet! Less than 5 hours if you only focus on the story.  + Worth its asking price. I know that $2 for an hour of entertainment may come across as being expensive for some, but that's not including the several more hours you'll need to collect all the samples you'll need to fill up your catalogue, and the experience is very much worth it! - Suggestion: I think it might be a bit less tedious if scanning is done automatically whenever you've made a move from one point to another. - Suggestion: Maybe there's a way to make it so that the player can queue up multiple discovered points before moving the suit?  - Bug: When I click on a sample in my inventory just to view its details, my energy/oxygen level will go up as if I've "used" the sample. The sample remains in my inventory and is definitely not "used up".To put it simply, In Other Waters isn't just a game - it offers a breathtaking experience; a chance for you to explore and document an alien planet as a xenobiologist would, and to join Ellery in her journey to track down her friend Minae and hunt down the truth behind the weird phenomena she's seeing on said planet. It's a game I would recommend to others without hesitation, especially to those who enjoy a really good story and love experiencing a game that's so unique and innovative.Hands-down one of the best indie games in 2020... and it's only April!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I'd describe In Other Waters as the love child of Subnautica and Sunless Sea. It feels so good to just glide along the ocean floor, exploring and sampling and drooling at the candy colour palettes (the colours are so freaking nice! I actually can’t describe them in words!!). There’s a story but the real joy is in just moving around and doing quiet xenobiology among the floating silt and the gentle waving of the alien deep sea species. It's a quietly beautiful game that deserves more recognition.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely game! I was really on the fence about buying it but decided to make the jump. I really thought this would only hold my attention for an hour or two, but I was really captivated by the story and very focused on making sure Dr. Ellery stayed alive. I remember in the beginning of the story how Ellery told me she relied solely on me, but came to realize that as much as she needed me, I needed her. Her descriptions of the environment, and the sketches she provided turned the simple mini map ui into an unforgettable lush underwater jungle in my head. I am left wanting for more, but i can only appreciate a game that knows how to end properly. Definitely not a game for everyone but definitely a game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game with a fascinating story. However I wouldn't recommend for people with short attention spans, The movement function is rather repetitive and slow. Secondly, this game doesn't seem to have any achievements, not a big deal but kinda demeaning after hours of grinding. Third, text doesn't give you much time to read it, only a second or two per text box, there is no log keeping track of it either. Forth, without a log it can be difficult to keep track of what objective you are following. But all in all the game shows passion, has a good message, a great story, AND MY GOD I feel bad for the writers fingers! There are hundreds of movement spaces in this game, and each has its own text box describing it! I rate it at around 6-7 out of 10, no corporate malice here, Just a small indie gem vibing in the ocean. good suspense too, anyway Imma go make a sandwich. relog after 100% it for the final cutscene btw

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy games that are highly artistic and story-driven like Journey or Monument Valley, you'll get a lot of mileage out of this. The game also reminds me quite a lot of Horizon Zero Dawn, if you know the story and lore of that game. The only thing I can think of that would drive you off is the lack of... well, gameplay. In Other Waters, you only do three things:1. Read text2. Collect samples of indigenous flora3. Move across several pre-set pathsThe game is VERY story-driven and VERY linear. I was a *little* disappointed by how few choices you have (the AI you play only has the option of responding "yes" or "no" in response to what the scientist tells you). But I don't mind, because the story is awesome: full of intrigue and accompanied by brilliant music. I'm hoping they make a sequel, because they set up a sequel perfectly (leaving the ending open to interpretation but not baiting a new title). The only other thing that might put you off is there are heavy... humanist sentiments here. From the game's perspective, mankind is portrayed as an arrogant, meddlesome species that wants to profit off whatever it finds. Also, according to the game, there is no God. Planets and species evolve or were genetically engineered. Many of you will be fine with that but I find the need to point it out. If those things don't bother you... buy the damn thing and play it. It's amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely, hands down, already one of my favorite games of all time. The writing is wonderful, nuanced, sensual, and has already made me tear up. The art style, with its clean lines and colors is simple and yet beautiful. The world is alien, interesting, and I already want to know more. I cannot recommend this enough.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really relaxing game with nice sea music. Most of the gameplay is exploring.The thing i dislike the most about the game is the controls and the pretty small field of view but it's probably the point.If that kind of game interests you and that the graphical style is your thing go ahead and try it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Like many of the other 'negative' reviewers, I wanted to like this game. It's different, its UI is lovely to look at, and it tells a story of exploration and new life. I think I'm near the end, but I don't think I'll finish it. The story seems feels too familiar to be compelling, and the moment-to-moment play simply isn't 'fun.'But my main frustration is actually with the UI itself. It looks great, and while it is very spare (not even offering you, e.g., the illustrations you've already jotted in your log to remind you of which of the many similar creatures you're encountering) and would appear to be very good for one thing: navigating. It's essentially a very simple topographic map, after all. But it's actually of little use--it doesn't allow you to mark spots of interest to return to, to even know what general direction a point of interest the game's already noted for you is in, it doesn't even offer legible topographic information.There are many things to credit this game with, and I'm disappointed to be putting it down. But ultimately a game that offers us a unique visual design, leaning so heavily on a mapping aesthetic, falls down for providing so few cartographic tools.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters gave me the feeling of truly being on an alien world and being in awe of the creatures Ellery Vas and I were discovering and documenting. The story is very well-paced and of high writing quality as I have come to expect of Jump over the Age after Citizen Sleeper. It's good to see that despite this game being older, the writers were already amazing at their job! Its themes are depressingly real in this day and age, about ecological preservation, the destruction of our planet by climate change and corprorate greed, but it's a story that's important.There's only really a couple of flaws I have experienced with this game, mostly the backtracking feeling a little tedious sometimes when you're doing the sample collection missions. The point-to-point navigation system is interesting, but considering that once you have "seen" them, there's no way of checking to make sure you haven't gone there yet. I did also find that some of the story points didn't really conclude properly? Like the whole thing with Minae and how she ended up where she was and what exactly happened to her.But I do think that the game left me in wonder and amazement. I love that the species documentation missions didn't feel like tedious grind work, I was out exploring and learning so much. It does help that I am a huge nerd when it comes to world building and speculative biology. But also, the more you learn about the ecosystems and the main story, the more you notice they complement each other, and understanding one side helps you understand more about the other.All in all yeah, this game is good and it has a very unique atmospheric vibe to it that I love
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The first two areas are extremely boring in my opinion, and during them you are still getting used to the clunky controls and interface. I had to force myself to keep playing in order to get past them. Once you arrive at the third and fourth areas, things get very interesting, very fast. After that, you're hooked onto the story, and can intuitively and quickly use the controls. Rest of the game ramps up the fun exponentially. Game is about ~5 hours, if you do all the story missions in a row. There are a few sections very similar to parts of Outer Wilds if you've played it. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me of the Geology Game, but since everything is hypothetical and concluded to be correct by the reasoner's own opinion and backed by popular opinion, it must be.... fiction. So they charge you for it.The interface only works when it is convenient. Spinning the direction guidance system in first instance doesn't work at all even when aligned with a way point already clicked on, but later there is auto button on below it. I presume this is so the dialog can not be outpaced. Having gained some patience with it, there are artificial limiting factors, some things you can do and some you can't do for no obvious reason. Loading samples that may be a future solution for instance. Rather than write alternative time lines to the story they just don't allow some items to be loaded to take and test. This is suppose to be a non imperial scientific game about hands on experimenting.After a while even though you need to collect things or "cut" into large structures the game is stopped and won't let you. This is game is single track downhill.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very unique and atmospheric game. If you are interested in the story, everything flows together at a good pace and really brings you into its world. Great use of UI, color, sound, and music brings the minimalistic world alive. I definitely enjoyed it and would recommend it to anyone who wants to get lost in new, mysterious world.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice story driven indie title that does a lot to be different. I'm sure this won't be for everyone, but its going to be hard to find another game like this.As can be seen in the screenshots for this game, there's not much going on visually and might come across as a bit confusing to look at. But the unique art design really does lend itself well to the concept of playing as a navigational AI. It might not make sense at first, but once you get into the swing of things you'll quickly see that all the pieces fit to create an immersive experience. And that experience consists of helping your human explore and research the flora and fauna on this alien planet. To complement all this is some good writing that really that does encourage the relaxed play style.If you're looking for a story driven indie game that plays like no other, this one is a good pick. Very much worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Do you know what speculative evolution is? Do you enjoy small, well direct game worlds? Does the prospect of a quiet mystery and exploration of an alien world interest you? This might be a good way to spend some time, then.The writing is good as well as the pacing. Explores it's story and game ideas fully without overstaying it's welcome. I can see some people having a hard time getting past the fairly simple visuals, but I love maps so I adapted fairly quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I've seen a couple negative reviews about the clunky movement. If you hit esc in game it displays all the hotkeys. Pressing W will move you to the next point, pressing space goes into scan mode, pressing control goes back into move mode.As of this review I've played for about 8 hours and I think i'm nearing the end (my taxa completion is 75% and it feels like i'm somewhere near the end of the story). My compy specs are: i5-4460 3.2ghz, 16gb RAM, GeForce GTX 980, Win 10. I've experienced no crashes and a couple small bugs with the inventory eating my items and the thruster not working occasionally. The inventory eating was a pain because I lost a "rare" sample and had to go all the way back to base and swim out to it so it would respawn however, the dev has already acknowledged the bug and is activley trying to fix it. The thruster not working hasn't really bugged me as you can just turn the thruster off and on again and it conserves the oxygen that wasnt used.Overall, wonderful game, beautiful and brilliant. The game surprised me at many points. At first I thought it was going to be a sort of interactive novel but, it makes clear that you're in control from the start. You must navigate Ellery around a very large section of ocean all while observing your environment, collecting samples, maintaining power/oxy to the suit and solving some light puzzles. The game UI may be a 2D top down and most things are represented by yellow dots but, that running narrative just lights up your imagination. Despite only reading about most of these places and creatures I feel like I really experienced it through the detailed narration. In fact when I finished research on my first creature and unlocked the drawing I was pleasantly surprised that it was near how I imagined it. It appears a great deal of love and attention were put into this game from the mechanics and narration alone however, after awhile I started doubting that Ellery is really a xenobiologist (especially from the future) with some of the random comments she makes. (although I suspect the comments in question were added to clarify things)I'm struggling to find more to say without spoiling the game. If you like exploration games and are looking for a nice chill expierience, this is a great one to pick up. It does have it's intense moments (like exploring The Bloom, ugh) but, for the most part it's slow paced with tons of descriptive narritive to read or not if you wanna skip it. The game is very generous to the observant and attentive tho, and often you can make tough spots a lot easier () with some creative thinking based on the observation Ellery is taking.Conclusion: Fantastic game, can't really think of anything I didn't like about it. 10/10 and I hope the dev makes more games like this or even a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The focus of this game is exploration and discovery. The pacing is slow, but enjoyable. .The story is interesting but I think that the main focus is discovering more about the various life forms on the planet and enjoying the environment around you.By finding samples and encountering specimens of those life forms you get to learn more about them and, once you've collected all relevant samples, you get to see sketches. Unfortunately, due to the slow movement, getting every type of sample becomes a little bit of a chore. This is only made worse by the absence of a map once you're outside the base, leading you to getting lost more than once.The thing that makes this acceptable is that every inch of the world is hand-crafted and interesting, leading to the sense of wonder that I suppose the creator is trying to instil in the player.Then there's the UI. Oh god, it's beautiful. Minimalist but expressive. It really gives you the feeling of exploring the world around you. Even though the creatures around you are just yellow dots, with the way they're animated, they feel alive. Overall I'd give this game an 8 out of 10. It's short but interesting. Unfortunately it doesn't really have any replay value, but it sure is an experience I would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, that's it? A very simple, ultimately not-very-interesting game masquerading as nuanced and complex. The graphics are minimal, the environments mostly described in text accompanied by a handful of sketches. This works well with the atmosphere. The interface is fiddly and cumbersome, which contributes to the overall story at first, then becomes tedious as you progress. The entirety of gameplay is in scanning nodes for journal entries, then proceeding to the next node. This is essentially page-flipping to get to the next few lines of story.The story is the big weak spot. The first half is typical, but engaging, golden-age science fiction wonder-of-exploration fare. This is well done, as you slowly fill in the nooks of an alien ecosystem. About the halfway point, your narrator flips on you and becomes incredibly one-note, and this is where the story turns uninteresting. After all that exploration, it turns out this is just more Final Fantasy 7/Captain Planet, Luddite, Malthusian, anti-human, anti-technology, Gaia cult greenie extremist fare. Blah blah blah, Shinra's pillaging the environment again. As usual, here comes humanity and corporations despoiling all the pristine, harmonious nature. The lady piloting an exosuit to explore a planet in a star-system far from Sol whines constantly about how humans ruin everything with their technology and exploitation of resources. You've heard it all before, we should all move back to caves and eat the bugs, etc. etc.The story spins its wheels in this boring, predictable way, then just ends. There are a couple of intriguing threads left hanging, but these are never resolved. Roll credits. The only 2 interesting things going on are simply never mentioned again. Don't forget to fill up your log of alien flora and fauna! You don't even get an acknowledgement for 100%, but do it anyway. Yawn.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I was close to liking this game, but ultimately it wasn’t for me. I think it is a good game, for the right kind of player. It looks stylish (though the graphics are monotonous) and has atmospheric sound design. The story just about maintained my motivation to keep playing, though playing essentially meant a lot of boring mouse clicking to slowly get around to reveal the story. I can’t say I enjoyed the process. I felt I had no agency in how the story developed or was revealed. I was pleased to discover I didn’t need to identify all life forms to progress through the story, so I ignored all those prompts on the map and never bothered to look at any of the taxonomy, which also meant a large part of the game was redundant for me. I’m just not into collecting, cataloguing, or reading lots of details for its own sake. I was very curious when playing In Other Waters, but only about the big picture story, not about the minutiae of the life forms. I’m not a details person. Those who are might really enjoy building and reading the taxonomy, and therefore derive much more value from the game than I could.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A very beautiful game. I'm leaving a review before finishing it because I don't want to burn through it quickly, but so far I'm really amazed at how well the narrative is paced. It's interesting because the game is very 'on-rails' - that is, most of what I've done so far has been following the script of the game without deciding what to do for myself - but with a really high level of involvement from me as a player. I'm not tasked with problem-solving, but I still have to operate the game's 'exoplanet extractor' instrument as instructed by the NPC scientist piloting it - I think the player character is actually meant to be an AI built into the scientific instruments, which means that the only way we can interface with the planet being explored is through the scanners and tech systems in the explorer's suit. That might sound boring, but the UI is the best part of this game - just the right amount of fiddly; it's unintuitive but easy to get into the flow once you've figured it out. I'm playing with a gamepad and it feels like the game was made with this in mind; it's a wonderfully tactile experience which suits the scientific narrative perfectly. Hugely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Simple, sufficient graphics. It was a fresh experience for me, gilded by the well-matched music.As it starts out it was lovely. A sci-fi exploration with an eye for the minute notes, leaving caches of lore for the curious mind to unveil. I didn't even mind that it was largely on a rail. The music made the monotonous three-click combo of movement into a ritual of meditation. Unfortunately, the story is also where this plummets. The tonal shift towards the middle is of a preachy variety. Suddenly the contrast must be applied and lo it is a glum one. The aspects of exploration are cut down and our protagonist turns into a political misanthrope. Humanity bad. Woe is the privilege of living. Erase the evil machine and embrace the noble savage. Play it for the music, the novelty of xeno-biology or to praise the cult of gaia. In the end I can't recommend the full playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: My initial impression is to be annoyed at how the user interface deliberately requires a bunch of unnecessarily inputs to operate. I can't simply right-click somewhere to move. I have to scan, click a point to select it, click back to movement mode, and then click a button to move there. And I can't move a long way at once, but only to a nearby node. Then I have to repeat the process starting with a new scan. Taking a sample isn't a simple button press. Instead, I have to switch to sampling mode, drag the selector over the sample, click the left side, click the right side, and then finally click the button to take it. If there are multiple samples, I have to repeat the steps for each sample.This artificial slowing down and dragging out of the gameplay makes me not want to go back into the map to gather more samples. Maybe the game would be too short if they streamlined the UI, but I'd much rather have that than forced tedium. Don't waste my time!I understand that they're trying to present me with a slightly complex, alien UI that I have to figure out through trial and error. The UI puzzle was interesting for the first few minutes, but after that it started to get annoying. It would be nice if, after figuring out how to move and take samples for example, it unlocked shortcuts to let me do them with one click or button press.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Turn-based subnautica. You are exploring an alien ocean but instead of it being free form you instead move from node to node along pre-determined paths. There are often several branches and to unlock "secret areas" you need to use the environment or progress in the story to unlock new equipment to deal with strong currents or blocked passages.It is interesting how the "side quests" are all about exploring the local flora and fauna to discover more about them. Despite it being pretty low-tech graphics, if you completely explore a species it does come with a new taxonomical sketch that lets you better envision what the biologist pilot is describing. Interesting story and really scratches that "exploration and discovery" itch without needing combat mechanics. Instead you're mostly stressed by your shrinking power and oxygen having to decide if you cut and run back to base or push just a liiiiitle bit further...
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a beautifully designed game, down to the finest detail, and through its vast and amazing story. If you're looking for a nice relaxing game to play in your down-time, as if you were reading a book, except this book sat you right in the middle of the beautiful atmosphere with its stunning music and sound design, by Amos Roddy! In Other Waters is great for a relaxed, immersive session to draw you into the alien world it presents. The story is the biggest selling point for this game, as well as the documentation if you're interested in analysing amazing new things about an alien world. If you prefer to have more varieties of gameplay, or aren't that into collecting or games for the bigger story, then In Other Waters might not be the best fit. But In Other Waters did what it set out to do, and I loved it! The atmosphere, the story, the world and the design, all of it was mixed together perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a unique experience. I've never played another game like it. If you enjoy a good SciFi novel, odds are you'll love this game. It has unusual but intuitive controls that I enjoyed mastering over the course of the story. To an extent the game encourages exploration, and reading what material it had to offer made me nostalgic for the fantasy novels I read as a child. The closest thing I can liken it to is a SciFi version of 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea, if that book were written today as a visual novel with robust gaming elements. If any of this intrigues you, give it a try.Extended review, spoilers ahead:I picked up this game a while back because of what I'd heard - that it was a peaceful experience about alien marine biology. Feeling nostalgic for games like Endless Ocean for the Wii, I assumed it would be similar and bought it. In Other Waters is not Endless Ocean, or really anything like any other game. It's not a visual novel, exactly, but nor is it purely a game so much as a story, and it isn't entirely a walking simulator either, though it freely picks through all those for its framework. The graphics are clean but utilitarian. You start out as an AI in a diving suit on the alien planet Gliese 677Cc, and must help a marine biologist named Ellery Vas navigate the alien waters and uncover its mysteries.If you're not a fan of reading, I would suggest turning back. While the graphics are minimalistic, the writing is far from it. I've spent the past 9 hours reading paragraph after paragraph of descriptions of everything from alien life to random rocks. Ellery is going to write her heart out and the meat and potatoes of this game is listening to her talk and occasionally giving her yes or no answers, when you aren't using the unusual but genius controls to guide her around. My one complaint with this game is that, with the controls being so non-standard, it could have used a bit more nudging towards how to use everything. Then again, there was something innately satisfying about figuring out the console and becoming a master of it by the end of the journey, so maybe that was intentional. [spoilers] My only other complaint is that we don't get to see Ellery's notes on the Artificers, or even what they looked like beyond their exoskeleton's description as 'radiolarian'. I do suggest looking those up, by the way. Radiolarians are gorgeous. [/spoilers]It's been a long time since anything has engaged my imagination in the same way this game does. When I was younger I consumed novels left and right and my imagination filled in the blanks in the most incredible ways. These days it's harder and harder to find that same level of creativity, but In Other Waters strikes this gorgeous balance [spoilers] using the sketches in Ellery's notes as a reward for finding all the collectibles associated with each creature. This method ensures that you have an idea what they look like, but still gives you leeway to imagine what Ellery is seeing [/spoilers] .This game is a masterpiece. It's the breakout game of its type, really, and I could think of no better pioneer. I enjoyed it from start to finish and I hope you do as well.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: amazing game. it's a classic minimal-mechanics indie game, and those mechanics really shine in their simplicity. the entire game revolves around slowly adjusting yourself to the world through the very restrained UI, which works beautifully with its narrative. the sci-fi is loving and detail oriented, and every aspect of the game reinforces its primary theme of learning to love the world around you through a filter of mechanical alienation. there is some annoyingly monotonous backtracking at times, especially if you want to learn more about the planet beyond the main narrative, but the reward is nearly always worth it. if you like how it looks, you will probably love how it plays!

_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: What a little gem of a game! It's definitely not a game for everyone but those who are fine with stopping to smell the roses and take their time will really have great time with it! It's about the journey not the destination. If you love sci-fi and a little mystery this is for you!The sense of atmosphere this game manages to create it astounding! Amos Roddy's evolving soundtrack and diagetic sound scapes. The phenomenonal world building and descriptions of unique species! ....And of course the simple but beautiful UI with it's map contours and changing colour palette that reflect the different environments you find yourself in. It gets your imagination flowing in the best possible way!The game mechanics were smooth and intuitive, and worked well on my steam deck (the only issue being text being a little small but it wasn't that much of a hindrance personally). I only have a few nitpicks, mostly with the way the game got caught in a few areas with trying to create tension by having your oxygen or power getting eaten up faster but with that putting pressure on the player to speed through, and thus miss descriptions of that area and worldbuilding unless they heavily prepared for it which seemed like a little bit of a shame. There definitely still is more time than you think but the pressure did push me to rush things and not take them in properly.Overall I really enjoyed this game, it was a deeply human and breathtaking piece of work!

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is FTL the walking simulator. I mean this in the kindest way possible. The main gameplay loop sees you traversing a graph overlay on a topological map reading tweet-length descriptions of geologic features. What's fascinating is that even subject to the severity of these constraints this game manages to ooze theme, tell a compelling story, and offer just enough collectibles to make exploring engaging without overstaying its welcome.This is a good game, memorable in the right ways for the right reasons. It might not be replayable, but it is enjoyable, and worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The art and narrative made me interested in this game, but i just couldn't stand actually plaing it. This game is just kinda tedious, and honestly more suited to mobile than pc. Presentation is good, and narrative is also alright, but there is little game here. Since you can only navigate between preset points in the ocean, it feels less like exploring and more like being on rails. This also makes just moving around very annoying and needlessly tedious. To move, you first need to press a button to scan for places to go, then click on the next point you want to go to, plot a course, and finally actually engage the drive and go there. This process is repeated for every single small stretch of ocean you want to move, and gets super annoying very quickly, eroding my patience in under an hour. I got this game for a fraction of the listed price on steam, but still wouldn't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a fun and worthwhile passion project.  Although the action seen on screen is rather minimalistic, it's quite easy to sink one's teeth into this and let imagination take over.  With very few tools to work with, this game somehow gives a true sense of exploration and academic discovery through the masterfully crafted interactive environment.  I enjoyed every second of this, despite a few moments of repetition and treading old ground.  Overall, In Other Waters--while always working within set parameters--is a perfect example of limitation leading to creativity and focus.

_childDocuments_.review: Compelling story and a real air of mystery. Although the graphics are pretty minimalist, each creature is uniquely represented and has a personality that's conveyed well considering the limitations of the style! Different areas having different colour pallets is also a very nice touch that immerses you in the moment. As a biologist myself, it was incredible to play a game that has a focus on discovering and recording new life, and seeing my suspicions about the nature of the life on this strange planet prove true!The main draw for me was the movement, it was pretty clunky and despite getting the hang of the keyboard shortcuts, it was a bit of an annoyance. The painstaking nature of this was somewhat lessened by the wonderful flavour text at every node you can navigate to – if movement wasn't so slow to begin with, I would have slowed down myself and stopped to smell the roses (the roses being the lovely prose)! I wish it was longer, completing it in around 9-10 hours, but not a bad price for it!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A unique experience, unlike any other game I've played. _childDocuments_.review: A lovely and entrancing voyage of discovery, ultimately both bittersweet and hopeful. It strongly reminds me of the astounding "Heaven's Vault", combining exploration and classification with a strongly directed art style. However, "In Other Waters" plays out more as a kinetic novel, following Dr. Vas's observations, spiced up by your own character's reactions... and a couple of key choices. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters has such an innovative system of delivering game and story content, that I fell in love with it instantly just based on that.  As you can see from the promotional screenshots, the main part of the game is played by navigating around a sparsely detailed topographical map using a well-designed interface meant to simulate the controls of a powered dive-suit.  Then, the fictitious wearer of the suit reports what she is looking at in a series of concise descriptions to give the player an idea of what is going on and what all the little yellow dots actually represent.In my opinion, the elegance of that system alone is worth an enthusiastic up-vote, especially considering that the writing of the descriptions in question is absolutely on point.  So, basically, the core loop is well designed and well-presented.  So far, so good.  What else?The theme of the game is one of science and exploration.  You're on a fictional alien planet, jetting around under the surface of the ocean, making observations about alien life-forms, and in some cases collecting samples to take back to the research station at which you are based.  All of this, to reiterate, is communicated either through well-crafted text assets, or through the stylized abstraction of the "suit" controls themselves (the UI of the game).  Personally, I love this sort of idea, so again, I give extremely high marks for the roleplay conceit underlying In Other Waters' core loop.  Wonderful.Then there's the story itself, the narrative being related about the fictitious marine biologist with whom the player is partnered during play.  I can't comment on it much at all, because I'm only a few hours into the game right now.  It's shaping up well?  Certainly, I can say it's presented skillfully by a storyteller who knows what they are trying to do.  No complaints from me.BUT...  well, I think I'm done playing this game.  I do this sometimes.  Crack open a nice juicy title like this, love every minute of it, but then put the product itself aside in favor of just kind of day-dreaming about how cool the idea was, and musing about how it would be awesome to one day make something like that myself.  Lame as I feel about that, I am still very pleased with my purchase of In Other Waters, and would whole-heartedly recommend it to anyone reading this.  Don't miss out on this one, friends.10/10 nigh perfect

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is a great game! At first, I assumed I would feel lost in such a large map, and at times this was true, but the paths are simple. Despite the fact that it's not very difficult to get to where you're going, the feeling of scale and many side-paths make traversing the map feel quite rewarding and discovering unique sample sites feel like an accomplishment. On top of this, the designs for organisms are really neat and their adaptations are believable, if a little complex. One of the most engaging and purposeful biology games I've ever played!

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxed, low-key; the story isn't always there (there's a lot of exploration wherein the human wearing the suit you inhabit isn't saying much of anything), but some of the exposition hits hard. The soundtrack is repetitive, but relaxing, and the transient sound effects are well-produced.I could conceive of the exploration getting frustrating for someone aiming for completionism -- not having access to the full map except when at base makes for confusion trying to figure out how the short-range and long-distance maps intersect.If you want a high-stakes, high-tension game this isn't your jam (there are some areas with time pressure -- which is mostly a good mechanic, but annoying insofar as it disincentivizes reading the text, which displays slower than I can read), and the only time I nearly killed my wearer came from a controls issue in such a time-sensitive scenario; but if you're looking for something that's fairly low-stress but that tells a story that sticks around after you've stepped away, I do recommend this. It's not Braid -- new mechanics are introduced fairly slowly -- and I'd welcome a more interactive conversation system than just "yes" and "no"; but it's a good game nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is an incredibly unique and well designed game that uses everything from it's stellar ambient soundtrack to the UI itself to fully immerse the player in a unique way that no other game can. Jump Over The Age wastes none of this immersion by creating a truly incredible story with twists and turns that you simply must experience for yourself. It can take a second to adapt to the pacing of the game but once you do, you can easily lose hours as the story unravels. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a more casual game that prioritizes storytelling above all else.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not difficult to recommend In other Waters. It offers an interesting narration-driven experience in a Sci-Fi setting with a strong emphasis on exploration. The atmospheric world-building and meticulously crafted xenobiology truly left a lasting impression on me. However, it's important to note that this game might not appeal to everyone. It presents a minimalistic gameplay approach, primarily through a beautifully rendered 2D HUD view that encourages thorough exploration and narration.If you're the type who rushes through objectives without taking the time to catalog the intricacies of alien biology, you might find that the experience resembles a visual novel devoid of traditional visuals. The game also has aspects of a resource management simulation but strategic thinking is pared down to a minimum, as you only scavenge materials along your journey to power and oxygenate your suit. The game's progression lacks the complexity of a traditional Metroidvania, omitting platforming, combat, and puzzles. There’s only some light backtracking expected and advancement is streamlined to ensures no crucial upgrades are missed.In conclusion, In other Waters offers a unique and immersive experience that rewards players who savor deep exploration and narrative engagement. However, it's not designed for those seeking conventional gameplay elements like combat, puzzles, or a branching storyline. If you're prepared to embrace its distinctive minimalist approach and appreciate the beauty of its storytelling and its distinct atmosphere, then diving into the depths of In other Waters could be a captivating journey.

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters : By Triple F"In Other Waters", developed by Jump Over the Age, is not your typical underwater adventure. It's a captivating blend of exploration, science fiction, and resource management that casts you as the AI of an exosuit exploring the depths of an alien ocean teeming with unknown life.The game takes place on Gliese 677Cc, a planet harboring a vast and mysterious ocean. You experience this world not through the eyes of a diver, but through the minimalist interface of the exosuit's AI. This unique perspective creates a sense of wonder and isolation, as you rely on data and readings to paint a mental picture of the vibrant ecosystem below.The story unfolds organically, pieced together through snippets of dialogue between the exosuit pilot, Ellery, and various research logs. These fragments hint at a past expedition gone wrong, a hidden connection between the alien lifeforms, and a looming threat to the entire ecosystem. The narrative is subtle and requires active engagement, rewarding players who piece together the clues scattered throughout the game.The game's soundtrack, composed by Amos Roddy, is as captivating as the visuals. Haunting melodies and ambient soundscapes evoke a sense of awe and mystery, perfectly complementing the vastness of the alien ocean. The use of silence is equally impactful, amplifying the feeling of isolation and amplifying the subtle sounds of the underwater creatures.Gameplay revolves primarily around managing the exosuit's resources and guiding Ellery through the depths. You scan the environment for new lifeforms, analyze collected samples, and monitor crucial parameters like oxygen and battery life. Every decision carries weight, as resources are limited and venturing too deep without proper preparation can lead to dire consequences."In Other Waters" isn't about conquering challenges or slaying enemies. It's about exploration, discovery, and unraveling the secrets of this alien ecosystem. The game rewards curiosity and careful observation, encouraging players to analyze data, experiment with different approaches, and learn from their mistakes.While not overly complex, "In Other Waters" is a slow-paced experience that demands patience and attention to detail. Players seeking an action-packed adventure might find the gameplay repetitive. However, for those who enjoy a more contemplative and thought-provoking experience, the game offers a unique and rewarding journey.To sum up, "In Other Waters" is a breath of fresh air in the gaming landscape. Its unique perspective, captivating narrative style, and emphasis on exploration and resource management offer a deeply immersive experience. While the slow pace and minimalist gameplay may not appeal to everyone, the game rewards patient players with a thought-provoking story and a sense of wonder at the mysteries of the unknown.
