_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: The start of my journey resembles a movie intro, soft sounds guide me, already in the first seconds the strengths of the soundtrack and the sound design are revealed. But suddenly... a system crash... The in-game interface reports an error... we are gently rebooted and find ourselves underwater with Dr. Ellery Vas. We are in a fully automatic diving suit a few meters below the water level on the planet “Gliese 667” which seems to be completely covered by the sea. Ellery asks us to continue on our way and to take over the navigation. Slowly I realize ... I am not with my colleague in the diving suit ... I am the diving suit ... or to put it more precisely I am the AI system which controls and operates the suit. My operator, Dr. Ellery Vas, is an astronaut and xenobiologist in search of her long-lost colleague and partner Minae Nomura, who may have made a groundbreaking discovery. A dark secret that wants to be unfolded.Immediately noticeable is the unique user interface which has been designed with great attention to detail and color harmonies. A feast for the eyes of any graphic designer like me. We quickly learn the reduced handling of the suit and explore the rich underwater landscape, which we can only capture ourselves based on the minimalistic data input. Little by little we unlock simple tools that help us open up new areas.With the new areas, there also come some survival elements and mild resource management. (but mostly you get all resources where they are to be used.) In addition, it is important to examine and document every found creature and object in our home base to fill our encyclopedia of living organisms on "Gliese 667" piece by piece. Here you can also unlock sketches of the life forms which have only been described in text form so far, but you have to finish the research on them first.What is crucial is to read the numerous but passionately and carefully written dialogues, descriptions of the environment, research reports and journal entries. Every line is full of detail and emotion. This is where the atmosphere, the sense of this world, and the true immersion is created - in the narrative and not in the visual input of the game. If you don't like to read or if you just navigate quickly through the areas, a crucial part of the story is missed. We can respond to the occasional questions from our partner Ellery with yes/no answers from time to time, but I doubt if it has any effect on the gameplay.A good sense of direction is required, because an overview map is only accessible in the home base, which serves as a starting point for our research trips. So it can happen that you get lost in the labyrinth of paths from time to time and overlook a nice dialogue or a research object.During all our journeys I began to like Ellery very much. In the dialogs and journal entries, you learn a lot about her relationship with the missing Minae, the fate of our Earth, the ambitious company "Baikal" for which she is working, and about herself. But most of all about her love for this vivid world filled with life. The story of Ellery, Minae and this strange world is revealed piece by piece and unfolds in a touching way. Is it a visual novel, a walking simulator (swimming simulator) or even a visually beautifully packaged short story? It's a bit of everything, but above all a well-told story full of deep thoughts and an ambitious thirst for the unknown. This game is for patient reading enthusiasts who are willing to take the time to explore and experience a story. It receives the Seal of Recommendation from me.RATING:Story – ⭐ ⭐ ⭐ ⭐ ⭐Graphics – ⭐ ⭐ ⭐Sound – ⭐ ⭐ ⭐ ⭐ ⭐Gameplay – ⭐ ⭐ ⭐Fun Meter – ⭐ ⭐VERDICT:+ a deep and detailed built storyline+ refreshing visual user interface+ exciting description and sketches of the alien underwater life+ comprehensible character motivation+ no achievement pop-ups (disturbing the immersion)- missing mini map feature- repetitive navigation and sample collecting tasks- unfortunately no spoken audio dialogue (would have been amazing)- little variety in level design- lost potential in more home base features (some are constantly offline)
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: An OK game that offers a good proposition for a gameplay basis, but does a bad job at refining the experience. Most of the taxonomy research can be summed as "click the white dots, until orange, search the samples candidate for question marks, and then follow the paths til you get in a dead end and get the sample from there", rince and repeat for all species.The story itself holds well together but is also very cliché and will probably not leave a deep mark.One major point to appreciate is the work put in the world-building, map art, and the sketches rewarded for completing a taxonomy entry.Overpriced for a 5-6 hours of play, I recommend to get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game, with a good story at it's centre that really promotes the feeling of exploration, as well as the notion of being alone in a vast alien world. The UI, which of course is your main interaction with the game, is quite intuitive albeit a little repetitive at times. Though the keyboard shortcuts help tackle some of this. The delivery of the story and your surroundings via the text descriptions given by the main character are fundamental in selling this to you. I advise you read everything you can as you go through this game, to feel as immersed as possible. The art style is beautiful with colour scheme being a huge highlight. The soundtrack is best described as a delicate synth that climbs to layered complexity at key moments, which was very effective in giving me a sense of calm and inquisitiveness throughout. If you want to feel like a lone explorer of an unknown world, and also enjoy unique methods of storytelling and don't mind reading a bunch then this is probably worth a go for you :)
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically a "walking sim" with some very distinct, stylish visuals and excellent worldbuilding. If you get turned off by reading a lot of text or a more minimalist aesthetic then this game is probably not for you. But if you're looking for a chill game with a gently unfolding narrative (with some nice twists and turns), then I can't recommend this one enough :)
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: cool alien creatures and chill, but engaging, game play. looking forward to the story and completing every taxonomy as much as possible. Not to hard for a person who does not play a ton of games, as i feel like i can take my time with learning the mechanics. all in all, i am loving it! if you are the type of person to scan every creature in subnautica and read their entries in depth, this is probably a game you will enjoy. edit- i loved it, but this is not a game for everyone. I felt rushed in some areas (although i liked the strategy of bringing the right items and managing power and oxygen), and some areas were difficult to navigate, as you can only access the map from the main hub, but i loved filling in the taxas and reading through their information, and i felt the story was engaging and a touch tragic and bittersweet.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant, stylized experience that amounts to mostly a linear adventure, despite branching movement.  It has simple controls that can occasionally be annoying if you don't keep yourself in the mindset that you're underwater and can't move :: snicker :: fluidly.  The story is there as a backbone and is adequate but is also fairly simple, though the ending felt like it came too soon.  Trying to be a completionist I clocked the game at around 5 hours.  The drive for 100% is either to get the taxonomy entries (which are gorgeously drawn) or for your own sense of accomplishment as the game features no achievements.  The music is wonderful and pleasant.This is billed as a relaxing game.  The music is nice, the colors muted until some of the later parts, and the only sense of urgency is that you CAN run out of power or oxygen, in which case you just get a fade-to-black sequence that puts you back at the main base.Enjoyable and pleasant.  Worth playing through, though its linear nature means you likely won't be replaying it any time soon.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is kind of like a classic text adventure game with a minimal UI. The story is linear and compelling. The excellent writing and effective use of colors captures the imagination and transports you to this alien world. This game does a lot with very little (visually speaking). So while fauna and flora are represented with simple dots, those dots have a lot of personality. The world feels very alive. You can also discover beautiful sketches of the various plants and animal life. Overall I had a great time with this game. I really enjoyed the story and the setting. It doesn't overstay it's welcome at just under 6 hours of game time. (It'll take a little longer to discover all the collectibles but that's totally optional )
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters puts its creative and sad story before its original, if a bit clunky, gameplay. It was really nice to experience a narrative focussing on environmental themes instead of psychological issues. Furthermore, it looks and sounds absolutely stellar. The overarching narrative can be a bit predicable at times though, and simply moving forward or picking up an item can take up to four clicks, which is a bit much. If you can put up with that and a lot of reading, you'll be rewarded with one of the more unique experiences you can have in this medium.In Other Waters is one of those games of which I wish there were more: it knows the story it wants to tell and the feelings it wants to evoke so well that it refuses to be restrained by gameplay tropes, player expectations and basic quality of life features. It is a niche title with a niche audience that is even smaller within the current gaming landscape. If you are not willing to play by the game's rules, by a game's idea of what it should be, and still hang on to the notion that the player should be king, then you might be frustrated. If you, however, are willing to immerse yourself in a setting that uses limitation as one of its central design-tools then you'll be rewarded with a beautiful, story, vibrant alien landscapes emerging from your fantasy, and an ending that will leave you thinking.By now you probably already know that you're playing an AI in a xenobiologist's suit and have to help him exploring an alien planet teeming with extremely detailed and thankfully skillfully described lifeforms. Over the course of the game, you'll spend most of your time reading various descriptions of fish, coral, algae and more, while navigating your suit from dot to dot, from time to time using items in your limited inventory to progress further. The game has a bit of gameplay, but, as expected, it is neither very hard, nor does it take center stage most of the time. There are some more taxing expeditions mostly in the middle of the game, but even then you'll be provided with ample resources and hints to very probably see them through in the first attempt - and you can't really die anyway.Similar to other exploration games, In Other Waters replaces the barely existant gameplay with a strong focus and story and creative narrative design, and thankfully mostly succeeds in that. It was refreshing to see a story mostly focussing on a landscape, an exterior object, instead of the player character's psychology. Don't get me wrong, you'll learn quite a bit about your biologists and yes, he comes with the expected baggage, and I don't want to erase the need for "actually this is a metaphor for depression" titles but it was a nice change of pace, that's all I'm saying. The overarching plot is good as well, maybe a bit predictable, but otherwise beautifully melancholic to downright heartbreaking with a very important message for all of us.The feeling of melancholy and liminal dreaminess is further pronounced by the minimal graphics in beautiful and stylish pastel colors, the absolutely amazing ambient soundtrack and the pleasant UI design. Some people have complained that the text went by too quickly, and this might be a problem for some, but it wasn't for me. But as a heads up, if you are an extremely slow reader, this game might pose some problems.The only thing that really irked me was the deliberate clunkyness of the interface and general gameplay mechanics. Everything just takes so many clicks. You can only move from dot to dot, but to actually move, you have to click to scan the surroundings (to make the next waypoint visible), click the waypoint, click again to chart a course and click again to actually move. This is a ton of clicking for a simple movement action you'll do hundrets of times. Picking up objects is even worse. Even activating your booster takes about three clicks, if I remember correctly. It is all done for immersion - it is a complicated piece of tech you're wielding here, but it becomes really grating after a few hours. It is still not a dealbreaker though - just something I wish the developer had thought through a bit longer. you are fascinated by environmental storytelling. If you are into hard Science-Fiction. If you are looking for a unique experience. If you don't mind reading a lot of text.  you are a slow reader. If you have no patience for clunky mechanics. If you mind reading at all. If you prefer gameplay over story. If you are looking for an open world exploration game. The Other Wilds, Genesis Noir, VA-11 HALL-A. If you find yourself in the "buy this game"-category, then absolutely, even without a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: This game surpassed my expectations. I was expecting a fairly dull and unimaginative text based story game, but the developers put exceptional effort into making the 2D landscape feel alive and active with shockingly little graphical complexity. Reading about the environment and history of this watery world captured my imagination as a biologist and an alien life enthusiast. The story was also excellent, and it kept me glued to my seat until I got through it all. The post-game pdf that includes amazing images of the life on the planet and continuation of the story tied my experience together in an unforgettable way. Anyone interested in alien life or the oceans should pick this up!
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters is quite frankly one of the best games I've played this year. It utilises minimalist graphics and gameplay features to deliver a beautiful story and paint a picture of an alien world. You play as an AI controlling a suit, you guide a biologist through the waters of this planet and uncover not only the rich marine life of an oceanic planet, but also the history of the planet, and why you're there.It's beautiful, it's well-made, the limitations are leaned into fantastically in a way that immerses you more in the game's world and settles you into the role you play in the story.I loved this. Nearly eight hours of gameplay, and I'd play it all again just to have a new appreciation of earlier parts knowing what I do now. You could definitely take more or less time to play the game, and it can easily be played on a laptop whilst you're on holiday and bored. It's excellent.As well, the attention to detail in the taxonomy, the way everything is well-described and put together in a way that just looks like an actual biologist's notes? It's fantastic. Part of the reason I kept coming back to this was just to read these entries, and discover more creatures. The sketches you unlock are especially interesting, giving you an actual visual of what these creatures are after only seeing them described. You put the work in, and you get to finally see what these things you've been helping study are. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: From the perspective of a marine scientist, and someone who as studied the environmental, biological, physical, and chemical conditions of the oceans, this is a wonderful, rich game to enjoy. The detailed, and accurate (at least, for xenobiology) field notes, the taxonomic classifications and analyses, the way Ellery muses about how these new organisms might interact with each other and be affected by their environment all felt quite real and familiar, almost as if I was back in my biology courses, being introduced to new and fantastical creatures. I haven't finished the game yet, I want to savor it and take my time, but from what I have played, I've very much enjoyed it. Though, a menu that lists all of the controls would be helpful, as I tend to forget what controls do what if I put the game down for a while. The graphics are crisp, and extremely well done, with excellent font choice and overall UI design. I'm not a composer or musical in any regard, but the sound design and theme are top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: In Other Waters doesn't deliver on its premise of casting you as an AI. It's got a beautiful aesthetic, but it's more of a visual novel than anything else. In my playtime, there were no decisions to be made, no puzzles to solve, and no agency. Instead of feeling like I was exploring an unknown planet through the eyes of my human companion, I was just clicking on a lot of predefined waypoints and reading text. I think I'd enjoy it much more if it was advertised as a visual novel instead of an exploration game with a unique and unfortunately unfulfilled hook.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of speculative biology and games with unfolding mysteries, In Other Waters is the game for you. A compelling package with a beautiful soundtrack, simple yet appealing visuals (the turquoise and yellow diagram/map style really works), and chill gameplay that is keyboard and controller-friendly. The writing and unlockable illustrations make you really feel like you are exploring an alien world. The only flaws I noticed are that the UI can be a little unresponsive sometimes and that a startup dialog box prevents the game from being launched with only a controller, but these are minor issues. Overall, solid 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Calm exploration with text descriptions and simple iconography, intuitive UX design, and beautiful music makes this a joy to play. The story is engaging, as is discovering new life, and studying it by finding specimens and samples. Short game, less than 10 hours to complete 100%, but worth it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant, beautiful game. This is one for those who love detail, written description and using their imagination - not for gamers who want fast action and constantly changing images. In Other Waters is like a sci-fi novel that slowly reveals itself to you as you walk the ocean floor.  The aesthetics are stylish and soothing, the fact that your view is constrained to a radius of only a few metres forces you to be in the moment, taking in your surroundings and being constantly aware. There is a lot of text but the world building it achieves is astounding. The score is ideal too;  constantly supportive, never overcompensating and at times genuinely moving. I absolutely loved this game and highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: From the outside, this game is hard to understand. Looking at screenshots doesn't help much and even when just starting playing it the confusion can remain. However, it won't be long before any such feelings will fade away...In Other Waters is a videogame that closely resembles a book. Books are very simple, as they are just a bunch of words string together (some say a monkey with a typewriter could write any book, given an infinite amount of time), so, much like videogames, they require a lot of work from the reader: if videogames require action from the player, books require imagination; the book just guides the reader mind to create the world it's describing.In Other Waters is very simple mechanically and doesn't require much action from the player, but like a book, it requires imagination: it's an exploration game that shows very little of the world to the player, by using simple contour lines for the terrain and dots for the living beings you'll encounter. So, the main job of the game is to immerse the player to enhance their imagination and this is a job that it does very well: the intricacies of the controls make every action feel more impactful and the simple, yet beautiful, color palette changes based on the environment, with the accompanying music following suit. After playing for a bit, the controls will feel like second nature and the deeper the world is explored, the deeper will be the emotions felt.Despite this, the game also does a good job at not feeling too obtuse. While the game can be played with just a mouse, there are some keyboard shortcuts that can make the game easier to control and, overall, the game is also designed to be lenient in deaths and with some actions. Also, the game rewards the player with sketches of the living beings you studied to completion, catering to players that could want some more substance.Finally, the game's story ties everything together, with many questions for the protagonist to answer and parallels for the player to find with the real world, with its themes of environmentalism that, despite not being the first time they have been presented by a media, are still foreign to a frighteningly major part of human beings.In Other Waters is a unique and imaginative game that any person with a fervid imagination and/or a love for nature deserves to play.
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played the game for like a minute or two, and I'm ready to give a negative review.My reasoning is similar to my negative review of ; this may not bother you at all, but for others it's a huge annoyance, or even an actual problem.The issue is that the text auto-forwards after several seconds.Standard fare for some games, one might think, but almost every game I've played, certainly ones without voice-overs, have had an option to  Not this game. In fact there's no options menu in game at all.I read at an average rate at my current age. (Slower than I used to, when I was middle/high-school age.)I also get distracted easier these days. I often play games while watching shows on my second monitor.I was giving this game my full attention, with no other media playing, when I started this game. I got distracted with a "something in my eye" sensation and missed a bit of text in the first couple minutes of the game. But even before that I was annoyed by the auto-forward and looking for a way to stop it. Most of the time I read it all before half the time is up, other times I need to read something a couple times, if I get distracted, or if I'm feeling a bit tired which increases reading time, it gets close to or does run out.There is a text log in the pause menu, so if you miss something you have to press Start to open the pause menu, then press down, then A, to read the log...Oh... and from what the dev said in the forums (and other forum posts & negative reviews); if you save & exit the game, the whole log  so you can't read what happened if you take a break and want to refresh your memory.You movement navigation thingy is controlled with left stick. When you press the map ping button is switches away from the navigation guide, then you must use right stick to have a cone overlap a point of interest to scan it. There's no reason I should need to move my right thumb from the buttons to the right stick and use that, no reason for it to not also be left stick as you can't have both up at the same time AFAIK. It's something that slows down gameplay, and takes away from the experience IMO.I recommend reading this other negative review for more detailed info:
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

_childDocuments_.review: Play as an Artificial Intelligence guiding a stranded xenobiologist through a beautiful and mysterious alien ocean. A non-violent sci-fi story, enter a world of wonder, fear and vulnerability, unraveling the history and ecology of an impossible planet. What will you discover together?
_childDocuments_.name: In Other Waters

name: THE LONGING
detailed_description: Buzz "Players can expect one of the most unusual video games of the year with The Longing from Studio Seufz" - heise.de, Germany "A very original and atmospheric gaming experience and a fascinating experiment." 82/100 - PC Gamer, Sweden "[...] we wish to accompany the Shade throughout his life, and he will accompany us even in our absences." 90/100 - , Spain "The Longing shows beautiful art and unhurried gameplay." 4.2/5 - , Brazil "The only flaw I can find in this little pearl is that we will hardly replay it, but it was created as a unique experience and so it will be for all those who buy it. You will not regret." 95/100 - pcguru.hu "The Longing is a fascinating adventure as long as you remember that it is not intended to be played in one, or even ten, sessions. " 80/100 - , Finland About the Game Unusual mix of an adventure and an idle-game. Play as a lonely Shade, the last servant of a king who once ruled an underground kingdom. The king's powers have faded and he falls asleep for 400 days to regain his might. It is your duty to stay in the earthen palace until he awakens. As soon as you start, the game inevitably counts down the 400 days - even when you stop playing and exit the game. It is now up to you to decide what to do with your solitary existence beneath the soil. Don't stress yourself, you have plenty of time. Choose your playing style Start the game and simply come back after 400 days to see how it ends. You actually don't have to play the game at all. But the Shade will be even more lonely without you. Or explore the caves and collect items for your comfortable underground living room. Just send the Shade to take a stroll - the walking speed is slow, but luckily there is no need to hurry. Read tons of classic literature from Nietzsche to Moby Dick right in the game - or at least have the shade read them. After all, time goes by faster if you learn to keep your mind occupied. (The little Shade in the game finds ONLY English books for now.) Ignore the king's commands and advance to the outer regions the cave. It will be a long and dangerous journey into darkness... Features Slow exploration of a vast, hand-drawn cave. Atmospheric Dungeon Synth soundtrack. Various endings. Lots of well hidden secrets. Time-based puzzles. A lonely but cute protagonist. NOTE: The game time keeps counting down even if you quit the game or shut down your computer.

short_description: An unusual mix of adventure and idle game. In utter loneliness deep below the surface, it's your task to wait for the awakening of your king... for 400 days.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant and totally unforgettable. I think about this game all the time. It's dark and tender and moving. I was under a veil of calm and menace whenever I had it open. At first I tried keeping it on in the background, but I'd soon drop everything and focus on the window, taking in every step and turn. The choices I made in this game still haunt me.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most unique and deeply-touching experiences I've had with video gaming. Please, give it a go. It isn't really 400 days, there's ways to speed it up greatly. I went for all the achievements, and there's still secrets I hadn't figured out yet that aren't on achievements, and I really recommend to go for it. But please, be patient. This game will demand a lot of patience, and if you don't think you can tough it out, it might not be the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: If you aren't getting enough self isolation from the stay at home orders , you might want to try this game. This game uses real time to make you wait 400 days alone in a cave. The puzzles are thought provoking and you have ways to make the 400 days literally fly by faster. My only suggestion is that you need to play this game with headphones. It feels tedious since you're alone but the puzzles are aural as well as visual.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I love idle games alot, especially when i'm always busy irl with work and other stressors. It's nice to have a game that's not time sensitive daily. Depending on how you play, it won't actually take a whole year! I like taking care of the shade and making him happy in his little home, it looks so cozy I just wanna jump right in!
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is an incredible game. I bought this right as covid hit the US, played it for a week and then didnt touch it again until the 400 days were up. finishing the game, especially if you invest time into the game itself so you can become more attached to it, is one of those endings that hits different. having took so long to complete, you reflect on how the world had changed around you during those 400 days, how much you as a  person have changed. I cannot recommend this enough
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The perfect game to play in quarantine: beautiful, charming, eerie, and easy to get lost in! (Literally: find a map!)Edit: April 6th, 2020 (day whatever of the COVID pandemic and social distancing/quarantine)I was drawn to this game for the dark art style and the unique premise: as a lonely humanoid, you must wait 400 days to awaken your king. To pass the time, you can wander the beautiful labyrinth of the kingdom, start a mushroom garden, read some books, draw a few pictures, look for other signs of life, or try to find a way to escape.The soundtrack is absolutely incredible and adds real depth to each part of the kingdom. Kudos to the composers!I can see how some people might not see the appeal or find it to be slow-paced, but trust me: everything you do in this game makes the waiting worth it. I strongly recommend this game, especially to people who may have nothing to do in quarantine.We all long for our lives to go back to normal. We don't know when the longing will end, but we are not alone.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I actually haven't finished this yet and have been meaning to come back to it.  If you are stuck at home right now in some kind of lockdown this is the game for you.  This game and a few others (Noita, Outer Wilds) give me a sense of mystery that has been all but lost in modern games.  Mystery is the most magical feeling you can get from a game and when these few games make me feel it I suddenly remember how good games were when I was younger.   The music, the art, the long painful waits before a discovery, the cryptic lore, all cast a spell on me and I can tell you that it is rare that I get this enthusiastic about a game.I really cannot praise this game enough, whoever thought of this concept really nailed the execution.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this game 10 months ago and I still can't stop thinking about it. It doesn't look like much in the screenshots, but I don't think any game in recent memory has affected me on a personal level as much as The Longing. Even on a purely objective level I have to admire the use of gameplay mechanics to explore the well-worn themes of loneliness and isolation in such a fresh and poetic way.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: After years of playing the prologue (waiting to buy the game), I can finally start playing with my shade friend!While my play time is absolute rookie numbers in the grand scheme of things, this game has been one of the most profound and meditative experiences I've had as of late. I ran out of meds and this has affected me by a lot when it comes to my mental state and anxiety management. Not saying that this game is essentially a replacement for those, but I can't doubt that having the humble little shade do tasks at their own pace alongside me is comforting. Its a lovely reminder to not rush things and that a lot can be done in such relatively little time, including being mindful of things.This is the only game that makes me say "I can wait to finish it"
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don't know how to feel about this one. One thing this got me to do, better than 90% of games in my library, is care about the protagonist. I genuinely wanted the best for the shade. I wanted him to be happy, I wanted him to see the sun, I wanted him to see the world. It felt good getting stuff to make his room better, finding books for him to read, Was it worth that wait? Maybe. I can't say for certain.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: No I'm not a troll. And no I'm not a hater. But I can't understand how so many people are giving this game a positive review. Maybe I'm just an old man who believes his games should be actually worth the money they're asking for but this is ridiculous.Now look, I'm not gonna go too in depth here. If you want a more in depth look and with actual gameplay then check out my video review I did on my youtube channel (link below)But the basics are this.Pros:-Great Artwork-Great Soundword-Great Original IdeaCons:-The game is super slow-The game charges you too much-The game is an idle game. But not an interesting one. It has an interesting story, but the gameplay mechanics are executed poorly.-The game offers you almost nothing for your 15 dollars. You won't get anything interesting until 400 days after you buy this.And I mean...that's legit. The artwork is good. The Sound is good. And the idea is good. But all the executions to form these ideas into a game are terrible. Everything about this game, from the basic mechanics to the plot, is a giant waste of time. No one is gonna remember this game or come back to this game 400 days from now. You know why? Because in the next 400 days we're getting at the very least 25 AMAZING games. Here are some examples:-FF7 Remake-Resident Evil 3 remake-Cyberpunk 2077-Evil Genius 2-Baldurs Gate 3-The Last of Us 2-Watchdogs Legion-Doom EternalAnd I could keep going. No one is gonna be thinking about this game 400 days from now and yet this game requires you to pay attention to it for the next 400 days to enjoy or experience what you paid for. No thanks. Not gonna happen. Not with all those games coming out this year. Spend your money on something more wisely or save it up for something more worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game and overall experience is: GREAT. Although this is very slow pace and casual game I loved it! Usually i play hack and slash fast games but this one was quite the opposite. If You are into killing/destroying and fast games this is not game for You. This game gives You no pressure of timing, You can play it with the slowest pace You can imagine. Game is artistic, intriguing, soundtrack is awesome, and immersion into the world is fascinating. I find story of the game original and exquisite. Also when observed from my pair of shoes it was worth the money.GG for the developers. ;-)
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I pirated this game yesterday... Didn't have to wait 400 days to buy it... I just had to support the developers and this really special game.It's definitely not for everyone! The game is super slow paced. Enjoy your 400 days! No, it definitely won't take that long but hey, don't expect action or something. Exploration, isolation, depression... fantastic atmosphere, beautiful ambient soundtrack. Waiting is exciting. Weird, isn't it?The shade is a really cool character actually. For some reason, you can relate with him. You enjoy being quarantined? Probably not. Well, that's what he feels too. Really, a special concept this is. Does it worth the price? Well, I'll figure it out, but worth or not, the developers made a game with soul, that already worth it. To make it possible for them to create other gems, support them! Whatever the end is, I never will regret supporting them! Beautiful stuff!Follow the hints, your diary, explore, wait, close the game, relax return to it and see if something changed. You don't need to look for guides I think. So far, it explains things for your. Since I started the game with that version... Let's call it a "demo", I already have about 6-8 hours in it.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Let me sum up this review in one line: The Longing does not respect your time.Is it beautiful? Yes.Does it say something? Yes.Is it worth your time? No. So, it's trying to make you FEEL like the character by dragging out the experience. Unfortunately, it's not fun or rewarding.Now, I do like that some things are time dependent. That's clever, and fun, because it gives you something to look forward to. It's clever to have the timer tick down while you're not playing. However, the designer didn't maximize this feature.There's a neat bookmark function where you can "remember" a limited number of paths to a destination. That makes sense, but it's very limited, and it doesn't show where these places are in relation to the map, There's also a nice function to walk to a random place in real (slow) time.This is where The Longing fails. It takes forever to get anywhere. You can use the bookmark function to set your character in motion, log off, and when you come back, you'll be there. Unfortunately, active exploration is purposely slow, and meant to torture you.I love games, but I have real life things that I must attend to. I'm not nine years old, or ninety years old, with nothing to do.The Longing would have been amazing if I could have unlimited bookmarks, via a map, and randomly explore, offline, until I found something new. This would make every log on a fun experience, but no.The Longing just wants you to suffer. I got the message, and I'm passing that on to you for free.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: There is no game in existence where it should take MINUTES to walk through an EMPTY room that fits on a single screen. That's where I'm drawing the line.I know, I know, it's supposed to be an idle game.I like the premise (quite a bit actually) but I just couldn't do it. I'm sure for those that are extremely patient, there's some good stuff here.You can't just cut the walk speed of an average exploration game down to 15% to extend the 'content' and call it an idle game.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game. This is a weird and interesting experience. But honnestly I can't recommend this game to people. Everything is painfully slow. I understand it's the point of the game, but it means that you don't want to experiment with it. Sadly, this game needs you to experiment to complete it (or go to the wiki and completly spoil yourself which ruin all the fun).Try it if you have extreme patience to test.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to start off by saying this game was definitely not made for someone like me, so take this review with a grain of salt. You start off talking to the king, he asks to be awoken in 400 days, my first thought was 'this is going to take irl 400 days, that's awesome!'. First off, it will not take 400 irl days, this can be shortened in many ways which kind of makes the 'it will take 400 days to beat this' comment false. This is not really a negative aspect of the game, we hate waiting, so anyway to speed things up should inherently make us happy, but doesn't really work with this game as it kind of makes you not want to explore and just sit on the couch to speed things up. The next part is my biggest complaint, the exploring part, before going on this was all intentional game design, and like i stated earlier this is not a game made for people like me. Exploring is just extremely boring and often underwhelming, you move at an extremely slow pace and many times have i been left with the same question. 'that was it?'. Often the destination is not exciting, not to say there aren't some really cool places, it's just that you'll see the same stuff over and over. Another part i hated about exploring was getting lost, MINOR SPOILER AHEAD, there is a room where you find a map, i thought this was really going to help as someone who forgets things quite easily and often gets lost, but no. This map you get to look at for a bit, but as soon as you walk away from it, it disappears. You also had to wait to 'decipher it' so i thought maybe the shade would have drawn it and you would be able to pull it up to check whereabouts you were. This made the map useless to someone like me. Again, this is not a game made for someone like me, this game has some fantastic ideas, and some really cool places or things, but for me the time investment just isn't worth it, nor was the money. I also am only on day 107, i will come back on day 400 to see the ending, but will not actively play or explore anymore. Hopefully the ending is somewhat good.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: OK this is an early review, having only spent 24 of the 400 game days so far in 9 hours playing time.This is a brilliant game, so different from everything else I have and even tho it is an idle game it is strangely ENGAGING. I have already developed an emotional attachment to the pathetic Shade. Yes, you need patience, or at least be able to set things in motion and wait and wait and wait and wait....The ability in the game to do nothing or to just pass time at your room with minimal objects is 'fun' or at least cathartic, but there are many 'quests', puzzles and secret paths at hand and I'm doing my best to complete them.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game certainly is an experience.How would you spend 400 days in an underground cave, all alone aside from your sleeping creator?Will you explore? Will you go mad? Will you long for your wait to end and whatever fate is in store is revealed to you? Will you try to escape, or make the best of the situation and make yourself more comfortable?This game may not be for everyone but I's still suggest you give it a try, especially if you like idle games.You have 400 real time days to help Shade explore the cave and in that time some things will change opening new areas to explore, so you'll need some patience to get a payoff. There are several endings as well, even if the game is really just intended to be played once and it's ultimately up to you how Shade's story concludes and what you learn from it.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I was not expecting to love this eerie idle clicker as much as I do. You essentially  but do not  keep a little character company by playing the game. During the 400 days you'll be guiding the shade on meaningless tasks as the two of you explore caves and castles, decorate one humble abode, possibly venture beyond time and space, play music, and ultimately await the awakening. Not my type of game but you fall in love with the mopey little guy. If the animation of the screenshots interests you and you like relaxing/creepy this is worth trying.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: A very immersive experience. It does take a while to do anything, but that's kind of the point. Also, don't worry too much about the 400 real-life day timer, as you can take actions to both speed it up or beat the game prior to the timer counting down to zero. Also also, you can just open the game once, wait for the intro cutscene to finish, close it, and then come back 400 days later and beat it that way, if you really need to.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing requires a lot of patience. Every, second, counts. Four Hundred Days of this. You will be alone. No one else but you and who knows what else could be in the caves with you. The more you do the more the cave changes as time passes, things can grow and vanish, moments and chances will come and go as well. Don't let it get you depressed, don't spoil yourself with guides, do not cheat neither, you will be punished. This is a journey to see how long you can last with dwelling alone in this unique, but sad life as a Shade. Try gathering coal for the fireplace, and reading, there is much more to literally, pass the time. It's not all that restrained to doing so.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game that has a lot of potential, from the empty feeling to the excitement of finding new items and location to the realization that thing happen in real time; like waiting for a door to open in 2 hours of grinding time (real hours not game hours) or watching a puddle get bigger over a month. This is a game that will test both your patience and sanity and I am in for the long hurl of streaming it once per day to get further and further in the game one day at a time
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: How to describe this game without going into too much detail? It is an experience. A journey. The destination doesn't matter. This isn't a game you "play" so much as a game you hang out with. You are given a simple task, wait 400 days and then wake up the king. Time passes in real time but keeps going while the game is closed and the more stuff you find to shove in your room the quicker time passes while in there. You can find paper to draw on, books to read (with stuff like the full text of Moby ♥♥♥♥, The Illiad, and The Count of Monte Cristo), and various other decorations like rugs and crystals to make your home more "home-y."Explore the caves, come back to places multiple times, look around and try to find secrets. You can look up a lot of stuff about the game online but part of the journey is trying and discovering stuff for yourself. There are multiple endings but you only get one and then the game is over. So make what ending you get a personal experience. Give the shade a name, spend time with the little fella, take him on grand adventures to the edge of the kingdom. Or don't, you can just leave him in his room, he'll happily stay in his chair, and you can boot up the game 400 days later to see an ending.There are multiple places you can get hints for some of the puzzles within the game. Sometimes it's after the shade has finished a book, he'll leave a note on the last page that is a hint to something else in the game. If you really want you can manually flip all the way to the last page or you can just set him to auto read and come back in a few hours. There is a face that you can trade items to that will give you hints as well. The few hints I'll leave here are:1) Try everything multiple times, some stuff will only work after 3 uses type thing.2) There is a door that appears in random places when midnight passes, see if you can find how to track it.3) 400 - 365 = 35. Don't forget to be there when the clock ticks over to say Happy Birthday to the little guy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the definition of a walking/waiting simulator. You spend real-life hours and even days waiting for ingame events, but it doesn't take too long in reality (it took me about 4 days to access all the time-gated sections) because you speed up the passing of time by making your home more comfortable.The game is really about the story it tells you about Lorn and you learn to care for him and about him, it's really fun and sometimes sad to read his insights about his situation. Walking is extremely slow so you pay close attention to the details around you and you really start to appreciate how pretty the game is in terms of visuals and music. Over time, though, you start going AFK as you send Lorn on longer walks because you've seen it often enough.This game is fun if you're looking for a casual experience hunting achievements, but most importantly if you're patient enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Arguably the most fun screensaver I've ever had.All jokes aside, this game is good if you're in a slump and don't have the brain capacity to engage in more fast paced games that requires you to pay attention.It's very zen, the shade becomes your pandemic isolation companion that you check in on every now and then just like we did with our "tamagochis" back in the day.One of my favorite things about the game is the silly little grin the shade gets when the cave is nice and he's about to sit down and read Moby Dck for the umpteenth time, my man just wants to read.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is an odd game, but that's what drew me to it initially. Most of the time it's a game where you play for 10-20 minutes and get something started that'll take a while to finish. The game continues while it's closed so you can start reading a book, start digging a hole, or start a long walk to the other side of the caves that the game takes place in. I bought this in the middle of Jan 2021 and have just passed the 400 days mark as of today 6/22/21. I played about 15.5 hrs but in theory you could play only a few minutes and still "complete" the game.  It's an interesting game to hop in and try to find something new to make some sort of progress although I'd say it's less progress and more just to see what else is down in the caves. I recommend this one but only if a game without any real goal beyond waiting and exploring over a long period of time sounds appealing to you. I had a good time with it and feel that there is a lot down in those caves I never uncovered.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best experiences I've ever had with a game. _childDocuments_.review: I would steer clear of The Longing if you're looking for a game to play.That being said, if you're interested in a story, an experience that lasts then I recommend The Longing 100%.This is a character study and exploration game, though all exploration is intentionally slow and methodical. The shade has 400 days until they have to do the one thing they're born for; they aren't in a rush to get anywhere, so they walk everywhere. They don't try particularly hard at most things, and most of the time in game is spent waiting for things to happen. In order to enjoy the game, you must understand the shade's mindset. Waiting for 2 hours for a door to open isn't an issue, and when it does open it's okay if there's not much behind it. The shade is interested in exploring his environment. If there aren't many surprises or big revelations then that's to be expected. The point is just to pass the time - although as a player, there is incentive to help the shade on this venture.As you add things to the shade's home, you will find ways to speed up the wait faster and faster. The game could be completed by opening it once, waiting 400 days, and opening it again. You could also explore with the shade, hear their thoughts, and gain not only a deeper understanding of them as a person but also be able to complete the game in a much shorter time frame.Ultimately, I would very much recommend The Longing. It's probably my favorite game of 2020 and I don't see that changing in the future. I urge you to buy it if you're even slightly interested in the concept, and have the patience to wait for it to play out.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of game that scratches a very particular itch. When it is quiet, and dark, and you have nowhere to be but with your own thoughts, this is a really good choice.The brooding, lonely atmosphere really clicks for me. The music, the slow, intentional choice, and the expansive feeling the world that is really so extremely small. It all worked for me.I took breaks, playing an hour here or there over about 12 months. I intentionally saved this game for when I was really in the mood. Sad, angry, lonely, any of those darker feelings. Because there is so much time where you do so little, you have to leave your phone in another room. Have to force yourself to live in the tedium.In any other game, I think that would be a list of problems. But here it all comes together into something that's really lovely in a cathartic kind of way.I don't think there are many typical considerations that work the same way here. Gameplay is intentionally limited. This is essentially a point-and-click adventure style game. The visuals and audio are great for the mood, but you probably don't even need a graphics card. It all comes down to whether or not the environment and emotion of the game connect with you. But I also think if you put in some effort to meet the game on its own terms, it's really amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Because we live in an age where everything is fast paced and no one has time to be bored, I'm surprised that this game has received so much positivity. (But obviously not enough to make this a negative review.) It focuses on the exploration of an underground kingdom that has next to no life. Your reward is that you get to experience a Grimm-fairy-tale-ish world, but at the speed of a snail. It's enjoyable if you have immense patience and need something idle to do while thinking deep thoughts or chatting with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing stands out as one of the most captivating gaming experiences I've ever encountered. The 400 real-time days timer creates an unparalleled sense of immersion. With its minimalist visuals and atmospheric soundtrack, you are drawn into its underground world. I understand that this game is not for everyone; however, to me, it has been a surreal introspective adventure that nurtured patience and encouraged self-reflection. I highly recommend it.P.S. If you want to experience all the possible endings, make sure to keep a backup of your save folder found in "%USERPROFILE% \AppData\LocalLow\Studio Seufz\The Longing" (for Windows) right before you experience the ending. As soon as you do, replace your current save with the backed-up files to resume from where you left off."

The only way to access the game is to wait well over 2 hours of in game time for a door to open just so you can actually see the game isn't even worth your time.There's no game here. _childDocuments_.review: This game is more of an experience rather than a traditional video game, but that does not mean that it's not worth trying.You are controlling a lil guy called Shade that has been given a task of waking up his king after 400 days.That's it, that's the task. Because the time goes on when the game or even the pc is off, you can finish the game in a few minutes of gameplay by starting it, leaving it for 400 days, and coming back to wake up the king and watch an ending cutscene, but the game is so much more than that.In most games, you are rewarded for your skill, knowledge, reaction time, strategy, and stuff like that, but this is one of the few games that i can think of that reward you for... Patience.I still has puzzles to solve hidden behind cryptic clues, and a pretty big place to explore, but everything in this game requires patience. And not just any regular amount of patience where an enemy is a bullet sponge and you need to keep attacking for some minutes to kill it. No, i'm talking about waiting a month for dripping water to fill a hole so you could reach a ledge you could not otherwise. Yes, you can do most of the long waits with the game off, but even walking, mining, and other stuff that requires interaction takes a really long time - and that's the point, at least one of them.This game will teach you, or remind you, that although you have you may have a lot of time, and it may seem to pass slowly, it passes faster when you are occupied, and also, that even if you are just waiting, the world is still moving, and you can miss important things if you don't pay attention and let the time pass by. It may teach you about loneliness, The Longing, the happiness of small things, existential dread, the joy of discovery and more - but only if you give it time, attention, and most of all, patience.Of course, this game is not for everyone, and because devs know it, there are a variety of things that let you pass time faster and other quality of life things to make it more bearable for those impatient, but the game is still slow.The puzzles are very cryptic sometimes, and if you are the completion type, there are a few great guides, some that are very spoiler free, that may help in both exploration and execution of things. I would recommend however, using guides and other external resources as little as possible, because it does diminish the experience. I regret it a little that i could not hold myself back and looked up some stuff that i would have enjoyed a lot more if i found it myself...There are a lot more things that i would like to say, but they would inevitably be riddled with spoilers, so i won't.It is a hard game to recommend because how unique it is, and it is definitely not for everyone, or more like, it depends a lot on your current mood, expectations, and even at what point in life you feel like you are.It reminds me of some books that were boring or hard to understand as a child, but got more interesting or held different meaning when i read them later in life. I would have hardly bothered playing this game for more than 15min or so, if i played it 10 years ago.You wont know if you like it or not until you try, and you may not even like it on the first try, but you will most likely remember it, and think about it for a long time if you do.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great experience, and as a fan of the medium, absolutely recommends to other as unique take on idle and adventure games. However, I cannot recommend the game to anyone that expects/wants more of a "game" instead. I'll try my best to explain why I loved this game, and also completely respects friends of mine refunding after playing 15 minutes of it. :THE LONGING: feels more like an experience than an actual game. The satisfaction in playing is enjoying all the details, interactions and immersion the developer created. The tying of thematic with mechanics is just perfect, and makes me wonder why it took so long for a game like this to be made; making an idle game where waiting feels so natural to the context. I mean, why make the main character run if you have to wait 400 days? There's no rush to climb stairs, open doors, waiting weeks to a stalagmite to fall. Jesus, one of the first interactions of the game is , and I don't know if that is brilliant or just stupid, but I loved it.The waiting feels therapeutical, and really gave me a break from the constant action/frenetic games I've been playing lately, like a breath of fresh air in game design.However, as magical those first moments of discovery will be throughout your first hours playing (assuming you just didn't refund the game after the first 5 minutes of climbing one set of stairs (which I find the most perfect way to introduce what the game is all about)), the game, if not ironically, very slowly start to stale.Don't get me wrong, there will still be a lot of surprises and cool discoveries during the ~40-50 hours of playthrough, but the start becoming more and more sparse as the game progresses. Sure you have a ton of books to find and read, but after you realize it's just impratical to use the game to actually read any of the books and it's just another activity to keep your character occupied that loses a bit of meaning after a few hours. The same goes for finding crystals or painting. It just seems the massive world that was first introduced  to be explored and filled with adventures to explore while waiting quickly shrinks and you find yourself without much to do except rushing to get an ending. I really wished the game had more content and activities to discover and do, after I got to about 300 there was nothing else to do except keep my little shade reading, or . This is one of my biggest complaints of the game, and I would considered it a masterpiece if not for this.The game also has a few bugs, mostly visual artifacts every now and then or just rarely freezing for a moment. But nothing that ruins the experience, and understandable given the game was made, as far I'm concerned, by one person.Well, this was, and most likely will forever be, the longest review I make for a game here, but I wanted to externalize my thoughts on this little gem. TL;DR:You should buy this if you love games as a medium and like try different experiences. Bonus points if you want a slow paced/idle game to chill every now and then. Don't buy if you just want immediate payoffs or the thought of having the main character walking like a turtle for 40 hours is nightmare for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I get the general idea of the game as a sort of low-time-pressure idle experience that you can come back to and explore when you want to chill. However, the pace is excruciatingly slow - not the development-of-events pace, but just the walking pace itself. The way the walking mechanic works requires hands-on guidance until you've explored enough to know what connects to what, and that's complicated given the labyrinth of connecting doors and tunnels. So while there is a "go to this place I've seen before" option to let your character navigate on its own, my experience 80 minutes in is of an extremely dull process of plodding across screens, occasionally enlivened by finding something I can use as a crayon. I like the concept of wandering around finding things to amuse myself - books you can actually read, coloring aids, a musical instrument, things to start fires with - but the amount of time I have to spend double-clicking a screen edge and watching my character slooowwwwwllly cross over is just tedious and frustrating. Doubly so given that it's essentially a big maze, one of my least favorite ways to add play time to a game without adding anything interesting, useful, or moving. I'm really regretting the money I spent on this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I stand before two familiar protrusions from the ground. I’ve made it a habit to come here every two days. The scenery which they dwell in complement the warmness I feel from visiting these towering obelisks. The plain in which these stones sit on has a sunset, so bright and restful. The light dances off the top of the hill creating a stirring display of luminescent rays on the columns. My gaze shifts into these halated halls.The shade is sluggish, slow -- painfully slow. But in this, we are meant to and can easily equate to the timescale of life, as just as all things, change is slow and gradual. When playing as the lone shade, our lives are comparatively colorful. Yet, the shade represents the dichotomies of the human experience: duty vs desire, belonging vs solitude, creator vs creation.  The shade battles with these values, just as humans oft do, yet the most profound element we both share is the motivation of seeking humanity where humanity is absent, taking action in the face of despair. The King who created the shade tells it hide itself away from the outside of world, instead impressing upon the shade to favor the empty society it rules alone. This is the first longing of which that can only then be adopted into the barren order he had created, grand and isolated, but neither natural nor human. The mountain Father created the world, and then created the world for a sole creation. Yet how can this world be the King created be wrong in any sense? The natural order is vast and barren, yet stable. Father created the world, and then created the world for a sole creation. The creator is powerful, yet weak; his waning power parallels all the misfortunes in the world, moreover stands as  evidence that contradicts the existence of an omniscient god. But a weak god can still be loving, his pre-slumber message implored the shade to be safe, providing our young conduit its sole instance and beneficiaries of parental love. However stable, the realm is insipid. Is this the human experience in which on must always align? I argue the dichotomies of man are merely a shift in perspective. Pleasures which are forced on us can become constraining, yet the mundanities of our lives can become great presents of joy and peace.The Longing so far is a beautiful dive into the trials of life and look forward to the continued experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Singular, beautiful and probably one of my all-time favourites now.The Longing put the adventure back in 'adventure game' for me, not just because it's so mysterious and strange, but because it harks back to a time when you'd spend months with one single adventure game, trying to work out what to do to progress. In The Longing, however, you don't get 'stuck' so much as you just have to... wait, for things to happen, whether it's for some moss to grow or indeed to wake the king after 400 days.Although it's described as an 'idle game' mixed with an adventure game, I think that term undermines just how engaged you have to be to uncover its many secrets, and that's not to say you have to be watching the game constantly either--the game quite happily ticks along when you exit.It's not for the impatient or for those wanting something to do all the time. It's slow, meditative and rewards the observant. There are some tough, introspective decisions to make here and while the length of the game makes these heavier and more final (you get one persistent save), The Longing has plenty of clues if you're paying attention.It must be said too, that the game's muted but detailed and evocative visuals are complemented by an incredibly atmospheric (and unique) dungeon synth soundtrack. It all works together so well and I'll be listening to it for a long time to come.I'm sad it's all over now, as is often the case when you finish something so absorbing, but the longing had to end.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so... upset.I'm so frustrated that this game didn't land for me.And it's not even because it's a bad game. It's simply because I never really got to experience it.I was really looking forward to a game about being alone, being isolated. I have a lot of personal experience feeling alone. Probably more so than most. At one point in my life, I moved to another state, struggled to find work, and finally landed a stable job where I worked by myself all day, and didn't make that much money, but I was so scared of looking for another job after nearly becoming homeless multiple times trying to find work that I stuck to it anyway. I had no life outside of working alone and going home to be by myself, and this lasted for many years... a game about solitude had the potential to really strike a cord with someone like me.But... well... The temptation to play always came to me when I felt most alone.I liked the idea of being immersed in this kind of world to fully appreciate its tone.I wanted to play when I was away from home, on my own, with my laptop...without internet. -_-Yep, this whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ buildup was just to tell you that the game doesn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ work without an internet connection.It doesn't seem to be DRM related, the game will open initially, but then it says "oh there is no connection, how disappointing" and then close. Even my lonely game about being lonely isn't there for me when I'm lonely.How ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ironic.Maybe it's not fair to judge the game based solely on this, but it did, in fact, ruin the entire experience for me. You can see my achievements and the only one I have is beating the game, because I never got a chance to do anything else with the little bit of time I did get to spend with it when I did have internet. I hope I can try again one day, and maybe I'll "get it" then, but after having this game on my mind many times throughout the year wanting to play it and never being able to, I'm only left feeling extremely disappointed, and I just had to complain somewhere, so here we are.Who knows, maybe a sequel will take into account lonely, disconnected people like me.Fingers crossed! -_-

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is unlike any other game I know. It’s tedious, slow, it has you backtrack a lot, it’s isolating and lonesome. There is VERY little to do in terms of game mechanics, (just walking really) and it can actually be completed even if you don’t play at all.. But despite all that, it’s one of my all time favorite games. Now, understandably, it’s not a game for everyone. But if you’re like me, and you like stories that reward you for caring about the little things, you will love this game. THE GAMEPLAY:The Longing’s primary mechanic is waiting. Waiting for doors to open, things to grow, rooms to change, ect. And this waiting can take hours, some times even weeks real time. As mentioned, the only thing you really do in terms of playing—aside interacting with a few objects—is walk. And you walk very slowly. The Shade is in no rush. It isn’t a game you’re going to sit down and play start to finish, but more of a friend you’re going to check in with once in awhile. See how things are going. And if you do check in often, there is so much to uncover!Creating art, finding secret rooms, new books to read, and so on. THE VISUALS:It’s a unique art style and one I’m very fond of. It has classic children’s book vibes, like Where The Wild Things Are.THE SOUNDTRACK:I like the music a lot. Dungeontroll does a great job, and if you like dungeon synth in general I think you’ll like it too.THE STORY: The Longing will teach you about patience that you never even knew you had. The mundaneness, the sense of longing (pun intended) the loneliness.. It’s all very real and The Longing handles it in a unique way that honestly felt very cathartic to me. I felt so connected to the Shade (the main character). Their plights, and their happiness meant so much to me because I could relate to how they felt, and I genuinely wanted to see them get better. The story will change depending on your own playthrough, and how much time you want to invest. CONCLUSION:This game is a great reminder to slow down. To enjoy the little victories, and to not rush to get to the end. It’s a game about mental health in a way. The struggles of feeling alone, and unwanted. It’s a game about waiting.. For what is up to you to decide, but I believe, the best things in life take time..

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely little point'n'click'n'wait adventure.The sense of scale and discovery - both in spatial as well as temporal terms - is fresh and at points awe-inspiring.The protagonist managed to build more character, depth and emotional attachment for me than many other recent story heavy titles.Unfortunately the game offers little to show for content-wise after you managed to push over the initial set of boundaries it gives you. There's a few lose ends and strings that strongly hint at cut content, which is a shame.A few of the puzzles are heavy on the moon logic side and there is a bit of item/pixel hunting so be warned. Best team up with a friend when playing this game or be prepared to consult a guide.Regardless, I enjoyed the time I had with The Longing, it managed to captivate me and come back to complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a relaxing little idle game, with a bit of surrealist humor (and a small amount of horror) that you'd expect from people influenced by eastern European cartoons. There are several endings, two of which are a little hard to parse the meaning of, and only one that I would call "happy," though even that one is a little tragic. There's an interesting little story in here, though it's not likely to blow your mind with its emotional depth. You'll probably get at least a little attached to the shade, the character you control, since they narrate their thoughts so much, and they're surprisingly polite to what little life there is underground.It's also worth mentioning that you don't have to literally wait 400 real life days. Doing so only nets one of the 5 or so endings, and even then, if you decorate your home, it'll speed up the game's clock while you're resting in it. It seems to make the clock move a half second faster for every decoration you add, and reading a book also speeds it up. Near the end of my playthrough, I had decorated my home to the point that more than 20 seconds were passing in-game per second in real life, meaning that hours were passing in mere minutes.I'm glad that I finally played until I got a happy ending for the shade. I'm not sure if I'll ever come back to it to get the other endings, but I did enjoy the game and got pretty much everything I wanted out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is a game where you walk slowly towards a goal, then are able to walk slightly faster towards another goal, and then can walk slightly faster still. The goals rarely open up new activities (- some do! There are about 3 of them and they are the highlight of the game), achieving those goals doesn't really feel satisfying, and they aren't great rewards in themselves more than being a pebble in your collection of pebbles.You know, I just don't think this is really a great game. I should be the perfect audience for this, I'm all aboard for idle and tiny achievements and the aesthetic, but I don't think there's enough reward to justify the build up. My suggestions for tweaks would be things like: Rewards being incremental, so the next hurdle would make doing one activity thrice as productive, with more agency in those activities. Maybe the option to significantly change the home, more than just a faucet and some doodles. Maybe the shade or the environment could become more shade-y or less shade-y-looking as he chooses between his two overarching themes. Maybe there could be about 20 more opportunities to make that choice between his two options. I was surprised the art didn't seem to be playing any role in this. I don't love that there's no "best ending", but I think there might be people who appreciate that for the theme of the game, so that might be personal preference.I think there's enough here for a game that takes several days, but this is really TOO slow, because it gives so little back. Positive feedback:Amazing map! Never seen it done like that, the puzzle was A+. I laughed.Those few items that open new activities were executed well, and at the right point of the game for balance, but there should be more of them, that deliver you more agency, or else the game should literally be shorter.A couple of things added to the home are things that Shade "likes", which comes with a certain reward that makes sense for having things you like in your home. That is a really cute way to reward the player and also help them feel connected to Shade. There could be twice as many of these.Anyone remember Kittens from back in the day? That is an idle game unlike others, that keeps surprising you with how small you really were on the scale before now. There's still a whole new plane of existence with new things to do after you reach a level you think must be the end, every time. The Longing really feels like it COULD have been that, with illustrations and semi-automated gameplay, but instead you just have a dozen pebbles that become slightly faster to earn with each pebble. I would look forward to a larger sequel with better time-cost/reward balance, but I can't recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals of the game are beautiful. As I am personally not into synth, the soundtrack begins to annoy me after a while, but even then there are places such as Shade's room once it is decorated, .The initial awe of exploring and trying to figure out what is actually going on is indeed a lot of fun, just as figuring the answers to some of the puzzles (how to get into the treasury or the secret library, and my personal favourite: the mushroom planting). However, once you figure them all out, there indeed is nothing more to do than waiting if you have your eyes set on certain resolutions. (Still you will check on your shade every so often, because you can't just leave the poor guy alone there.)While I sense a lot of emptiness in the game (which yes, is part of the longing, but come on, one or three more little puzzles?) and the lack of replay value for any other purpose than a different ending (which you can find on YouTube anyway), the game allows for obtaining all achievements in one go if your timing is good.As a piece of artwork it had a good potential to provoke thoughts on multiple psychological subjects. As it is executed, it falls out of the category of classic games, as the story is slow, unchanging and clearly stated at the very beginning, there is no score to keep, and no prize to win.I am still mulling it over with the stork.
