_childDocuments_.review: It is quite rare that games fascinate me the way this one did. I am far past my 400 days (which in the end were less because of some tricks you can use to increase the rate in which time passes), and still thinking about the lonely shadow in its caves of stone. Let me explain why this game affects me so much.First, and that may be the main point anyone makes, this game is so different to anything out there that I even cannot determine the genre. Point-and-click? That would be to far, because there is no real story and no puzzles at all. Walking simulator? Well... kind of. Closest to home hits idle game, but to say you pick it up every day to do your "duty" would be wrong as well. It's you who decide how often and in which way you play this game. Will you walk around and seek the unseen caves, the new things to discover, the beauty of the crystal caves and the glowing mushrooms? Or will you just sit in your armchair and wait for time to pass? It's okay, do how you feel like.As you may have guessed already there is nothing else to fulfill than waiting 400 days IN REAL TIME to wake up your king. He is a giant, sitting there on his throne, all reddish stone. And you are a shadow, a small human-like figure entirely made out of pitch-black shadow. Only these yellow eyes stand out and stare into the dark. You are a shadow, and you are depressed. And lonely. But you can find relief in the small things. Picking up the coal for example, your "siblings". The soundtrack is just great. Without, I would say "There is potential, but something is missing", but the soundtrack is so epic and moving and fits the void of the caves so well that I can't do but praise it. Please listen to it while you randomly wander the paths. And there is a lot of spare time, because you walk agonizing slow. That's part of the concept, of course. The slowness, the time, the ticking clock, they blend together into a feeling of eternity and dimension.Before I talk to much, here is my conclusion: Play this game. It truly is something else even though I do not like how often this is used to describe something unique. But if you love games for this stir it gives your heart, the moments you just plunge into the alien ocean (metaphorically, there are only puddles present), then go and feel The Longing for yourself.If you like, this game inspired me to found my  where I talk a lot about this kind of games that move. Feel free to join me .For german readers:Wer den ausführlichen Test lesen möchte:

_childDocuments_.review: I will 100% admit I looked up guides for this game, and still thoroughly enjoyed the experience. Granted, I'm not quite at the end, though I know there are numerous, as I'm waiting up some time to celebrate The Shade's birthday. Regardless, for the first three weeks or so after buying the game I was playing every single moment I could. Exploring, gathering, decorating, anything I could get my hands on without too much waiting; there is a surprisingly large amount of things you can do just in the first week. Granted, I was then left with large swaths of time without much purpose, but it was still deeply satisfying to leave the game open and watch The Shade read, to construct a sort of lore about what he may feel, and just idly listen to the sound of footsteps against the steeping background tracks. I was afraid of missing any little detail I was so obsessed, and the fact that the wiki is barren and the RNG is only vaguely understood only made me more invested in ensuring I saw everything possible.To put it simply, this is not a game that was made for someone like me, someone who isn't content with just waiting for the first wall to come down, and yet it was still so deeply satisfying to finish the lengthy tasks and hear The Shade's commentary that I just never stopped.The price was a bit of a pickle for me, at first, but ultimately I was far more enthralled than I could have predicted, and over 50 hours soon flew by, very much worth my fifteen bucks, in my opinion.I had maybe a few issues with loading, it's fittingly slow to start and slow to exit, but it does a good job of saving frequently, and only had the very minor stutter every once in a blue moon. The walking takes time to get used to, I'd recommend double-clicking for stairs in particular, but you won't often have to babysit once you'd marked useful locations anyway; a system which simplifies and heightens the idle experience.Suffice to say that, in the end, you'll go from questions to care, and will soon want the best for The Shade, as if he were your own, more than the living alarm clock he's been dubbed by the king. He'll voice his wants, in time, even establishing his lack of care and, later, excitement about breaking the rules and seeing more and more. You'll teach him to dream, to think, to feel, and to live, maybe even a name that only you know, and it's all so very special, as if you're the only two people in the universe, and I think there's something truly beautiful about that. I don't know what comes at the end of those 400 days, but I do know that time is flying by in the home we've built together, and that I'm no longer longing to see the next big thing, but, instead, to spend my remaining time waiting, content with what we've built, ready to help The Shade face whatever we choose to do next.

_childDocuments_.review: Given time and loneliness, what can you discover? Can the dark halls of a mountain hold more secrets than darkness itself? The longing is a unique point and click adventure game with an impressive art style that permeates all in the game, accompanied by a haunting soundtrack that fills the halls with solitude and mystery, and a story told very slowly, through exploration.  Released in 2020 with its development starting in 2014 by Studio Seufz, inspired by German legends of a King under a mountain that waits to be waken in the right time. Follow a shade in a 400-day journey, receiving a simple request from the King: to wake him up after that period, you are allowed to explore, but warned not to leave the caves, because once the King wakes up, all fear and longing will end. Although you can simply choose to start the game and wait 400 days for one ending, you can explore and make shade’s existence more comfortable. One thing to consider is that no matter how you choose to play, time doesn’t stop, so the timer once started will continue, but considering the allotted time there is no sense in hurrying anything.  The game can be controlled either by clicking the left mouse button to a specific point, clicking and holding either the left mouse button or the spacebar to guide shade, right clicking to interact with elements of the game and double clicking to get moving automatically.  Considering the main point of the game, shade walks very slowly, so patience is a good thing to have when considering playing this game, but if you allow yourself to be immersed by the ambience this game provides, you’ll slowly learn more about shade, and even discover the many secrets hidden in the game.  Exploration is also something intrinsic of this game, where paying attention to the background, shade’s questions, and even reading may be important, as waiting because, like all other things in this game, time is a key to most puzzles.  Although this game may not be up to everyone’s taste, the slow pace, the story, the soundtrack, all combined make for a refreshingly unique experience that I highly recommend.  If you enjoyed this review, I would like to invite you to visit  my curator page for more recommendations and reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: Plenty of things to discover, but as is the nature of this game you will find yourself having to come back to play this game in small increments at a time.It starts out with about 1 hours worth of things to do, but leaves enough intrigue to bring a curious player back to it every couple of days to find out what has changed.Thankfully when the game hints that something will happen in 1 week, it does not mean you have to physically wait that long. In the mean time you can find items and accomplish tasks that will increase the rate at which time passes while you are not playing. This means something that takes 1 week, will actually be only 1 day of real time while you are off doing whatever you do when not playing The Longing.The puzzles are minor, but the mystery keeps this game interesting. The hints found both at your home and around the place will clue you into what you can do next.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I would recommend the game.The game itself is very unique in its game play, and I found myself growing very attached to the little shade and enjoyed decorating the cave and exploring the realm; however, the endgame is quite frustrating, with particular actions ending the entire game abruptly with no opportunity to finish the remaining sections. If there are any remaining things you still wanted to do (e.g. for all the achievements) you will have to start the game from scratch (at 400 days). Therefore, if you want to play the game, I strongly recommend that you make a backup of your game-files before initiating an ending, which can be recognised by the following actions (very light spoilers, but in my mind safe to read):I am aware, that the game was not intended to be played with making backups of your save files, but I don't like the feeling of "trusting the game" and then being cheated of the full experience. Especially as a "completionist". Despite all of that: I do recommend the game, and I think it is worth playing. _childDocuments_.review: Absolute adoration. The minute you start the game the clock ticks down, whether you have it open or not. The slow burn is the entire point and my god does it deliver: our little black dust sprite moves on slow, meditative walks through narrow dark tunnels, to the sound of distant dripping water and soft synth music, with the sense of time and space spooling out forever in every direction. You can let the game count down the days second my second, or you can end it early in a dozen ways that get more and more Jungian the deeper you explore. This is the exact sort of thing I wish games did more often and it's the exact opposite of what most gamers want. And I adore it for that.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing was a game that I knew I would love from the moment I heard it pitched to me. This game forced me to think about my shade and how lonely he was and how I could make his existence just a little bit better when there was nothing significant for him to interact with. This parallel very well with current feelings surrounding social isolation with the pandemic and has encouraged me to focus more on my well being and self care. A game that can help change a bleak outlook on a real person must be doing something right.

_childDocuments_.review: I literally don't have words. The game seems really dumb but while playing it, i've never been so calm, the solitude, lack of excitement, lack of urgency to get things done. It's such a needed break. I find it actually gives me motivation to finish other games and do chores I procrastinate on, I also find myself thinking about where my shade might be if I left them to go somewhere or whether they finished a book yet. It's a surreal feeling, almost sharing loneliness with this little character, waiting for a king to wake up - alone, finding their own things to do in order to stay occupied during the time. There's so many little activities to work on, mining, music, reading, drawing, collecting. There's definitely more. I'd say this game is about emotions and teaching patience. There is no rush, just waiting, but waiting doesn't have to be boring or stressful. It can be peaceful too. You don't even have to finish the 400 days, there are multiple endings and ways to speed up (or slow down) the timer. The fully hand-drawn map, mysterious soundtrack and purposeful ambience all pull it together for something as scenic as listening to rain when falling asleep. This is background noise with a game built-in. I am loving it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you, developers, for creating this wonderful game.Playing this has been an experience. What do you have to do?You have to wait 400 days, and walk in realtime.I absolutely adore the game's aesthetics and style, the questions it philosophically brings upon encountering yourself (such as having to wait and impatience, or certain feelings attached to certain situations), and all the little things, like what the shade says, and other little things (I am writing broadly as not to spoil anything for anyone).The best, in my view, is the beginning of the game, but I enjoyed all of it. Similar to another game where I enjoyed the artistic style (the dream machine), the only thing I can say about this game that is critical is that I was not super enthousiast about the end I played: I could have avoided that end, and I wasn't ready. But in my view, on deeper levels, this was philosophical as well: all things end, in ways you like or do not like. And you've experienced a life and a longing in between. So that's what it is about. The title says it. So it's fine.Overal, I can recommend this to players who are curious, patient, like the arts, and enjoy realtime walking. And to all others, as a test in patience, and as a new experience:) It may not be for everyone. It's great in the beginning and middle, whereas the endings are probably debatable indeed if your longing is satisfaction (I recommend to not watch teasers, look for images online, or read walkthroughs, as that will surely spoil it).Also, to those still playing it, I recommend to enjoy the waiting while it lasts.

_childDocuments_.review: For the most part, I think this game is an extremely cool experience. The aesthetics are truly excellent; the more I look at the art the more it sucks me in and really impresses me with its attention to detail and great style. I also love the somewhat avante-garde premise of making a game where everything goes so slowly because all you've got is time and all you've got to do is wander and wait. I have mixed feelings about the execution of certain elements, though. The game wants to frame itself as a one-time experience you can't repeat, but that's not actually true; it isn't very difficult to start a second run after a first playthrough is completed. I also think that, while clearly this game is more about the journey than the destination, most of the endings are pretty underwhelming ways to wrap up the experience, which would be especially frustrating if the game followed through on its intent to be a one-time thing. Separately, for my money, the game's core focus on waiting is honestly cheapened significantly by the extent to which you can accelerate time by making your home more comfortable. I stayed pretty involved on my first run through, making sure to try to explore and map out everything I could, and (while it turns out you can take as much time as you want after the 400 days have passed and there's no deadline to miss) it eventually almost felt more like I was running out of time to uncover particular secrets than that I was stuck waiting.Overall I loved the game and was really engrossed by the ideas and art it puts forward. I mentioned those few things I would've liked to see done differently, but if you don't agree with my complaints, you might love the game even more than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love The Longing, and I think people will either be entranced or bored by it, one of the two. It's definitely a slow game: the Shade walks slowly, and you have to wait in real time to solve several puzzles or explore hard-to-reach spots. It's a delicious kind of melancholy, and I'm super-invested in making my Shade comfortable in his cave while pushing him to try new things.The soundtrack and art are gorgeous, too. I keep thinking of 80's fantasy and The Dark Crystal while I play it, which is honestly worth the purchase price all on its own for me. Plus: little lonely person stuck in their house for days on end, trying to find distractions to pass the time? Relatable.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was in Paris I visited a modern art museum.One of the attractions was a large room with a projection of a video.The video consisted of the "artist" crumpling up a piece of paper. Then uncrumpling the paper. Then crumpling it up again.It just repeated over and over.People were staring at the video with fascination.I stared at the people. I was mesmerized at how anyone could be interested in that video. To me it was boring. The Longing is a bit like that. If you are the kind of person who can stare at nothing for hours then this is the game for you.But, I'm not going to play a game where you have to wait 2 hours just to open a door.The pace of the game is incredibly mind-numbingly slow.If you are interested in an atmospheric game that offers emotional and fantastic storytelling then check out "What Remains of Edith Fitch". Don't be fooled by the positive reviews. This game is a dud.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Before you go into The Longing you have to know that this, by design does not respect your time.You will be told to sit and wait for minutes at a time doing nothing. You will go through tons of hoops to get to certain areas only to result in literally nothing. And yet If you accept the game's dreary fairy tale atmosphere, and somewhat tedious gameplay. I think there is something uniquely compelling here.It's the kind of game you play in small sessions a little bit a time over the course of many weeks and months. Pesonally it took me about 7 months. The Shade has a surprising amount of thoughts and is endlessly endearing. Probably the most, "not for everyone, but if it's for you it's REALLY for you", games I've played in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: It was great at first. Majestic and slightly spooky visuals and music. Interesting story revealed gradually. A unique world to explore. Sadly, the middle of the game is much weaker than the beginning. VAGUE SPOILERS FOLLOW....My favorite part was the new areas that I had to wait to unlock. This built anticipation and encouraged me to find ways to pass the time faster. But most of these unlocks, instead of unlocking a vast new area to explore and repeating the process, led more or less to a dead end. After about 50 in-game days, I realized I had unlocked almost every area in the game, with 350 days still to go. Without the promise of exploration, excitement turned to boredom.So while I appreciate the care the developers put into crafting this world, It's effectively a much shorter game than advertised and doesn't live up to the expectations I had for it at the beginning.

_childDocuments_.review: The first part of this review is spoiler-free, and only references things in a way that people that haven't seen what I am referencing will not understand what it means. This is an amazing game. From exploring to collecting coal and moss and the such to overcoming darkness and so much more, this game was very fun to follow along. The best part is, nothing is required of you. Not just in a skill sense, but in a game play sense too. Want to sit in the Shade's room for 400 days straight and do nothing? Go ahead. Nothing is stopping you. You can play just a few minutes of this game and beat it, or you can play hundreds of hours reading books and exploring the caves you inhabit. I recommend not looking anything up, as experiencing everything yourself is what I believe this game is about and it kind of ruins the whole experience if you look it up. However, if you want to, go ahead. Like I said, you are not bound to anything. There is no pride lost in looking up what this green mushroom does when you eat it or how to grow these patches of moss over here, because it is *your* game to experience how *you* want to experience it. I personally did look up a certain mushroom puzzle since I couldn't really figure it out, and there's no shame in that because this isn't a game that asks you to be good at anything. This is a game about choice and patience. To commit a sin? To defy the king? To wait here at the bottom of the world? To experience a wonder? It's all your choice, it's whatever you want. That's what tells me that this is an amazing game. ! ! Spoilers below ! ! I have only 1 criticism; the fire. Specifically lapis lazuli fire. I had left my game for a few days and came back too late to be there for the Shade's birthday, so late in fact that there were only 4 days left. I went to the crystal cave area with the water to see what gift waited for me there since the face in the wall told me that on my birthday I would get a present there, and I found that the water was now blocked by a singing crystal and there were lapis lazuli at the bottom of the now-dried pond. I picked them up and finally made a blue fire, happy to know that it rewinds time. Of course I tried playing the instrument, and it rewound time 10 minutes every time I played the fast forward melody. It took me a very long time of just lighting the fire, playing the music and lighting fire, repeating this annoying process to get back to day 35. I am very glad that the mechanic exists, but there has to be a way to make it less grindy. That isn't what this game is. This game isn't Runescape, that's not what I played it for.My suggestion to fix this annoyance is this; when the blue fire is lit time still passes the same as it does forward, just backwards. This means that if time goes at a rate of 20 in-game seconds every 1 real second, it rewinds 20 in-game seconds every real second. This would've made the annoying process go by so much faster, and I wouldn't have been so annoyed at it. Instead of 2-3 hours every minute the fire is lit, at least for my comfort level in the Shade's home it would go 2-3 hours (the music) + 20 minutes (passive time). This doesn't sound that much faster, but when you scale it up to rewinding 31 days it adds up. This goes from about 6 hours of clicking back and forth to 4 hours. Those 2+ hours make a huge difference.

_childDocuments_.review: What an interesting game this is.It is very emotional in the sense that topics like  loneliness, hope, and despair will be presented to you at regular intervals.It makes you think and ponder about such things but in a positive way...at least I did.It will not be a game for everyone, I believe it to be very niche game. Almost everything in the game requires time, and I mean real time hours/days for things to start developing. But if you allow yourself to get to that point you will find a great game to sink your time in to.Exploration, crafting, puzzles and a good story will be there for you
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The king of the underworld creates a shade, and orders it to wake him up after 400 days while he recovers his energy. Talk about an over-designed alarm clock! As it says on the box, the in-game time passes in real time, and the time keeps passing when you shut down the game. Your task is to wait the 400 days, and help the shade pass the time.Some people say this is an idle game, but I don't quite agree. This game is not about making numbers go up, or exponential systems. This is a narrative/empathy game: as you play, you will grow to like the shade and feel empathy for it as you share your time with it in the underground kingdom. The game will give you as much as you give yourself to it.I am usually very chill with spoilers, but for this game I highly recommend that you go as blind as possible. Avoid steam guides or YouTube videos. There are just a few head-scratching puzzles, but walking away from the game, and them walking back, and trying something else, or just looking at the shade happily flip the pages of a book is a large part of the experience.A few notes:- Graphics, Music and SOUND EFFECTS are very beautiful in this game.- I played this game on Linux, it has that common problem with some unity games where it will use all your GPU and make your GPU fan spin even when it is a low-powered game. I recommend configuring your system to disable GPU before playing this.- Content Warning: Suicide
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: :THE LONGING: is a wonderful game that elevates the industry as a whole. The core concept might seem boring but it really is what makes it so special. Right from the bat, you're already given the very tough choice of whether to obey the king and wait 400 days, or leave the cave and betray your creator. This might seem like a very black and white, good or bad type of choice, but you'll eventually understand it's much more of a grey area, and your understanding of this will come while you wait 400 days.Time, however, passes faster in your room through furnishing it or certain activities. So, in reality, the 400 days could go by a lot faster if you play the game a lot.The story is very "show don't tell" in the most charming manner, the game-play is simple and very creative. The few characters are iconic, especially the main character, whose constant presence and meek nature will likely make you love him as a friend, a pet or an extension of yourself.The scenario, ambience and music of this game are all of the highest quality, creating one of the richest and most beautiful experiences you can have in a game, even through its slow and purposefully tedious pace.It's an amazing world that anybody with enough patience and time should experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes a special place in my heart. This is definetly, as many other people said, not a tipical video game. It's an experience. _childDocuments_.review: So the devs are here trying to teach us about waiting and delayed gratification but they stick the credits in the beginning of the game because they know most will never reach the ending but still want their recognition. Talk about hypocrisy and disproving your own point.This is an obnoxious and overpriced game. I applaud the novelty and doing something different, but this could have been executed so much better in ways that don't actually push most players away. One idea is to make speeding up optional and count how much the player has done it/show repercussions. Introduce upgrades that speed time up, minigames that make time go faster and not just passive activities, etc. You can keep the concept while not torturing those who do not wish to be tortured but still experience the game.I CAN sit and stare at the wall, but I don't. if someone is insane enough to do this to themselves I find it sad, but go ahead and waste your precious life moments watching a cartoon character walk, I'm sure the reward would be worth missing out on thousands of actually exciting and interesting games.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% ReviewThe Longing is, in short, an idiosyncratic experience that tests your patience and commitment to a paramount degree. Everything, and I mean EVERYTHING in this game takes exponentially longer than it reasonably would in literally any other game. Opening some doors takes entire minutes, altering some terrain could take upwards of weeks, even a month in some cases, even walking from point A to B takes ages due to the speed of your character: The Shade. The Longing has a myriad of activities that it leaves you to discover and complete while waiting 400 real time days. You can discover hidden parts of the cave, find alternate endings, decorate your room, read, solve puzzles, etc. It's really difficult to even define The Longing as a game, for it's more of an menial undertaking, a "chore simulator" if you will. But its art style, theme, setting, atmosphere and allure just leave you intrigued to continue. Even if "continuing" is launching the game every few months. It just has such a palpable, morbid charm that seemingly no other game captures as well as this one. I highly recommend The Longing to anyone for the unique way it utilizes patience as the core gameplay mechanic, as well as its art style and setting. Remember, patience is a virtue.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Let me tell you a story of loneliness, and how through slow walking, high spirits and a little music, one little shade proved it wasn’t so bad.I’m only two days in and I love this game already, I’m invested in the little shade and just want to take care of him. Something sad and lonely in me resonates with him so fiercely and I just want him to be happy and loved. I want to explore and find all the secrets in hidden corners. I want to make his room warm and cozy, filled with books and pictures and a bed for when he just wants a nap. This game touches places in my heart I’ve tried to ignore, and it brings me comfort knowing that I’m not alone, that there was someone else out there that felt kinda like me. Just a little lonely. Someone who went out of their way to make this game so they could share a shade’s journey through 400 days of being lonely and patient and making the most of it or nothing at all. They made this game and left the choice in your hands, how much time you spend, how far you delve, what you collect or ignore. How will you help a lonely little shade go about his day to day, waiting for the king to awaken, or looking for a way out, or finding lost secrets, reading a book, drawing a picture or growing mushrooms? So many little things to make the wait bearable, to make the lonely a little less. What will you do? What are you waiting for?

_childDocuments_.review: "The Longing" is an extraordinary experience that defies conventional gaming norms, providing a uniquely contemplative and introspective adventure. It is a game that masterfully captures the essence of time, solitude, and the power of patience. As I embarked on this unconventional journey, I discovered a profoundly captivating world that left a lasting impression on my mind.First and foremost, the game's concept is both audacious and intriguing. You play as a Shade, an immortal creature tasked with waiting for 400 real-time days while your King slumbers in a deep underground cave. This unorthodox premise immediately caught my attention, as it presented a challenge unlike anything I had encountered before. The very notion of patiently enduring the passing of time became the crux of the gameplay, intertwining with the player's own existence outside the game.The art direction in "The Longing" is breathtakingly minimalistic, creating a melancholic atmosphere that perfectly complements the game's themes. The hand-drawn landscapes are beautifully rendered, with a subdued color palette that evokes a sense of quiet isolation. Exploring the depths of the underground world was a captivating experience, as every corner held secrets waiting to be discovered. The attention to detail and the subtle shifts in lighting further enhanced the overall ambiance, adding depth to the immersive experience.One of the game's greatest strengths is its ability to encourage introspection and self-reflection. The vast stretches of time provide an opportunity for players to contemplate their own existence, desires, and motivations. As I watched the seconds turn into minutes and the minutes into hours, I found myself pondering the meaning of life and the choices I had made. This meditative quality is a rarity in the gaming world, and "The Longing" excels in creating a space for such profound contemplation.The sound design is another commendable aspect of the game. The hauntingly beautiful soundtrack perfectly captures the mood of the underground caverns, immersing you deeper into the world of the Shade. The soft echoes, distant drips, and occasional musical interludes add a layer of ethereal enchantment to the already mesmerizing experience.While "The Longing" may not appeal to those seeking action-packed gameplay or instant gratification, it serves as a profound testament to the artistry and innovation that can be found within the gaming medium. It challenges the boundaries of what a game can be, offering a unique and deeply personal adventure that lingers long after the 400 days have passed.In conclusion, "The Longing" is an exceptional work of art that rewards patience, introspection, and a willingness to embrace a slower pace of play. It invites you to delve into the depths of your own thoughts and emotions while journeying alongside the enigmatic Shade. If you're seeking an experience that transcends the traditional boundaries of gaming and leaves an indelible mark on your soul, "The Longing" is an absolute must-play.Additionally, for completionists and achievement hunters, "The Longing" offers a tantalizing challenge. The game features a myriad of achievements to unlock, each requiring careful exploration, keen observation, and resourceful problem-solving. From discovering hidden rooms to unraveling cryptic puzzles, every achievement adds a layer of satisfaction to the overall experience.The sense of accomplishment that comes with obtaining these achievements is unparalleled. It encourages thorough exploration of the vast underground world, prompting players to uncover every secret and delve into every nook and cranny. While the journey towards completing all the achievements can be arduous, it is undeniably rewarding, offering a sense of mastery and fulfillment that few games can match."The Longing" understands the allure of achieving completion, and it provides a rich and varied set of challenges to satisfy the most dedicated players. Whether it's locating elusive artifacts or deciphering enigmatic inscriptions, the game constantly engages and surprises, ensuring that the journey towards unlocking all the achievements remains engaging and deeply satisfying.For those who revel in the pursuit of 100% completion and enjoy the thrill of conquering every challenge a game has to offer, "The Longing" delivers an exceptional and gratifying experience. The achievements not only add an extra layer of gameplay depth but also serve as a testament to the game's meticulous design and the developer's commitment to providing a comprehensive and fulfilling experience.Rating: ★★★★★

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird, beautiful, poignant game that ponders big questions. What is waiting? What do we want? What is a life without fear or longing? By an accident of timing, "The Longing" also captures this unique moment in history better than any other contemporary work of art. 2020 is the year when the world waits, not knowing how our collective waiting will end. But perhaps the wait - and what we do with it - will end up being more important than the end. And isn't that always how life works?

_childDocuments_.review: How to unlock the Never-Ending Ending: There is no ending. The Shade stays with you. Forever. Your Shade can have a good diet of homegrown mushrooms. Growing it's own food is very fulfilling to the Shade. But make sure they have a bath before you tuck them into bed. Never let your Shade go to bed dirty. Encourage your Shade to express it's feelings through art and make sure to proudly frame the art on a wall while making a big fuss about it! Shade should get regular exercise by taking walks through your favorite areas. Respect that sometimes Shade needs time to sit and stare. Try putting crystals nearby since they emit a pretty hum & chime sound. Or have Shade make a fire to relax near. Encourage your Shade to play music and always, always clap after a performance. Finally, reading together is one of the best activities you can do with your Shade so remember that you can read anything you want together through the neverending notebook!

_childDocuments_.review: The aptly named "The Longing" is a game about waiting that happens in "real time", even when the program is not running.There is a huge, timed, world to slowly explore and a bed room to furnish.  It accurately renders a feeling of loneliness.For a while, I kept hearing the eerie background musics.Given some of the themes depicted by the game, particularly on a psychological point of view, the game may not be appropriate for all ages nor for individuals with a tendency to depression.As far as I'm concerned, I've loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: No spoilers, but I do talk about the ending in broad terms.I often wish that steam had a more neutral choice than just thumbs up or down, because this is a hard one to thumbs down.  The music is nice, the shade is charming (my 6 year old daughter was there when I started the game and instantly fell in love with him), and the core mechanic is novel and weirdly engaging.  I like that this rejoices in it's slower pace--the guts it took for the dev team to embrace that is laudable by itself.  I don't think waiting is a problem...but how was I waiting, and what was I waiting for?  Events take forever, but happen in real time, so you'll find yourself closing the game and coming back later.  Some slower games (think like walking sims) have long events, but try to leave you in an emotional state for the duration.  60 seconds spent waiting while enjoying the atmosphere or drinking in some emotional music is more effective than a simple 'come back in an hour' text window.  People will just close the game and do something else.  That breaks the immersion the way a shorter wait that FEELS long (and requiring a player to wait patiently even a couple of minutes real time feels like an eternity) would not....and at the end, what?  The game seems to be based around the idea that patience is rewarded, but if anyone found the endings rewarding, I'd be curious to know why.  I did the standard 400 day wait ending and was so flabbergasted by its lack of payoff that I looked up the other endings online on the assumption I'd messed up somehow.  Typically I tend to think that disappointing endings aren't really a big deal if the gameplay is solid, but the entire game was centered on waiting for one event.  You cannot fumble that.  A couple of the other endings have some charm, but none feel like an appropriate counterweight to the patience they require.  I realize this was a small dev team to put together a flashy ending, but dialogue is cheap.  At least expand there a little.Again, total respect for new and interesting game concept that Studio Seufz came up with for this, but I'm just not sure the final product is worth the wait.

_childDocuments_.review: I have many thoughts and opinions about this game—almost all of which are positive—but I specifically wanted to write a review for it as a caution to potential players. The reviews I’ve seen so far don’t bring up the aspects of the game that could very easily be upsetting and even triggering in certain ways.I don’t want to spoil anything, so I’ll be vague, but I’m also going to hide most of what I have to say for those who want to go in completely blind. If, however, looking at the darker aspects of the human psyche has the potential to cause you emotion harm, I suggest that you read below before playing this game.Warnings aside, this game has kept me riveted despite its slow pace. It’s mysterious, and if you pay attention it’s full of foreshadowing and metaphors. I will be playing again to discover even more.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of The Longing fascinated me. Hooked on that I immediately downloaded the game and set to exploring. The silence of the game is just as oppressive as the cramped, dark caves. Discovering a new feature is always exciting after the time it takes to get anywhere. It's perhaps the most expansive and atmospheric idle game I've come across. But more than that, what's truly fascinating about the game is how it has released (by pure coincidence) into the middle of a global pandemic which requires people staying in their homes as much as possible. I can think of no other game which mimics this situation more than The Longing. And to think that it released just as the pandemic started! Regardless of this, the game is interesting enough to warrant your time!
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game I've ever played. The art direction and music lend the world such a beautiful and unique atmosphere, and the Shade is a deeply endearing character. The game has the potential to be dark or wholesome depending on how you play, but somehow maintains a relaxing and often whimsical tone either way. I played during the height of quarantine, and it almost feels like that's exactly what the game was made for. It got me through a really tough time and I have a lot of appreciation for it thanks to that.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is THE game to play in 2020. I'm only three weeks into the in-game calendar, but I'm already getting drawn into the mystery. Who is this Shade? Did they have a life before their current existence? Do they actually want to wake up this king after 400 days? Figure it out together while you wait out your real-life pandemic lockdown.The art looks like illustrations from a Scandinavian fairy tale. The soundtrack sets the melancholy mood effectively, although I would have appreciated slider bars for the SFX and music volumes.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Impressive hand-drawn graphics, interesting concept and very atmospheric music.What little "gameplay" there is, however, is extremely tedious because of the character's movement speed. (The promo videos did make that clear, so I've only myself to blame.) Nothing wrong with idle games, but this isn't idling! It's forcing the player to waste as much time as possible, making the little dingleberry limp about the brown underground labyrinth.Why have an explorable, maze-like area and then have the character move as slow as molasses? I get that they were going for "the game is about the journey, not the goal", but really. You can use a button that makes the character walk to a random place, alt-tab out of the game, do something and return later - but that way you'll have gained zero knowledge of the "map". It wouldn't be as much of an issue if the character could automatically pick up items, but he can't.It's also possible to bookmark locations, which eliminates some of waiting, but that still leaves the mapping issue.I guess I'm just salty because I expected the game to be about the character wasting time in surroundings the player helps them set up, NOT making the player waste their time as much as possible. I wish there was an "automatically explore and pick up items and solve puzzles" option for players to enable, allowing them to quit the game and return in X days to see what's been going on.The refund window came and went, so I guess I'll maybe return to this if I'm unemployed at some point, or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Think you're a patient person? Download this game, it will show you how patient you are. It is the ultimate test of patience. Maybe one day I'll revisit this, one day when I'm suddenly a much, much more patient person than I gave myself credit for being when I tried it. But for now I'm actually really sad and disappointed that I couldn't get into this game just because of how ridiculously sloooooow it is. You know the base speed of your character in Stardew Valley? With no coffee or buffs? I can't even stand to run that slow, I use a mod that allows me to speed up the pace a bit and I can't play without it now. Yet that is warp speed compared to the shade. I truly love the art and I love the concept and the music and the story but, as you can see, I lasted six whole minutes before I was ready to pull my hair out with how long it takes the adorable, sad little shade to walk halfway across the screen, let alone do anything else at all. I sat there for at least a full minute watching it scribble one simple picture to hang on the wall. That didn't feel like playing a game. It made me feel like I should get off my laptop and just go draw an actual picture myself for a change. Not sure that's what game devs want. I get what they're going for here, to an extent. But this really is a $15 monumental waste of time and I don't appreciate that. It's just TOO dang slow. It doesn't have to be that slow to be different and slower than other games and to put you in a different head space. As another reviewer pointed out, this should be more about you creating an environment for the shade to waste time in, it shouldn't force you to waste a ton of your time to get ANYTHING done. That pretty much sums up the whole game and its one fatal flaw, at least in my opinion. A lot of people seem to like it but I have to agree with everyone else who just can't get past how punishingly slow it is. I almost suspect that a lot of positive reviewers might not want to admit that it was too slow for them too and they recommend it anyway. It just doesn't make sense to me that many gamers in this day and age actually have the patience to get anywhere with The Longing. If they adjust things and speed the shade and it's activities up I'll try it again. I really hope they do. This seems like a really special and definitely different game but it truly, really, seriously does not need to be nearly as slow as it is. It's just not even fair.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very weird game. You start as a shade whose task it is to wake up the king after 400 days. Realtime days. Time progresses while the game is closed. So you can install it, play it and come back 400 days later and finish it. A game about waiting sounds terrible. So why does it work?One of the interesting mechanics of this game is the shade's house. You can decorate it, make it more comfortable and time passes faster while the shade is at home. This makes exploring the caves and collecting stuff a worthwile effort. The slow pace the game takes makes the moments you spend with the shade something memorable, as you quickly become attached to the little monster. Waiting for moss to grow becomes an achievement. And you may find other ways to end the longing.It may not be a game for everyone, but I think its worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is a difficult game to assign a single genre to, it’s a slow-paced, meditative exploration game mixed with idle-game elements (that’s quite a mouthful) . You play as The Shade, I like to think of him as a cross between a soot-sprite and the main character from Samorost. The Shade is a shadowy fellow who is brought into existence by an Ancient King with the purpose of waking the King up in 400 days. Sitting around doing nothing for 400 days isn’t exactly appealing, so you set off on exploring the cave you find yourself trapped in.Everything in The Longing is related to time. There are activities that make time go faster, such as reading a book or drawing a picture (so you can actually finish it in less than 400 days). Time also starts to pass faster as you decorate your room. Then there are things found throughout the cave that take a certain amount of time. For example, there’s a door fairly early on that takes two hours to open, so you have to wait two actual hours for it to open (time out of the game counts towards all this, don’t worry you don’t actually have to play it for 9600 hours). Your time in the game will be spent exploring the expansive, often confusing cave system. Some areas will having nothing but background in them, while in others you’ll find items to help you pass the time or other interesting things. In theory you don’t have to explore at all, you could just buy the game, play it once, and then wait 400 days, but I don’t see why you’d want to do that.The Longing won’t appeal to everyone, but if it does appeal to you then you’re in for a treat. It’s meditative, it’s unique, it’s mysterious. This is an easy recommendation if you’re into games that are more than a little different. _childDocuments_.review: Though it’s one part idle game and one part point-and-click adventure, :THE LONGING:’s commitment to its concept and its ability to gamify it make it more than the sum of its parts. While many puzzles are solved through simply letting time pass, it never felt like a chore to wait. I would leave the game on overnight and wake up excited to finally explore the next part of the cave, or find another piece of wood to build my bed. The Shade’s quips about loneliness are both funny and sad, which felt good from here in quarantine. If this is an experimental game genre, then this experiment was a success.

_childDocuments_.review: A very enjoyable and charming game that I found interesting every step of the way. Don't expect a fast-paced, action-packed experience, but if you just want to enjoy something deep and slow, then this is definitely the game for you. There are multiple endings and lots to uncover, with new dialogue and information being gained as you move along, adding to the mystery of the cave. If you are worried about the game taking 400 days and just don't have the patience to wait that long, then don't be, because there are tons of ways to speed up time in the game. As long as you play it and progress through normally, you can knock it out in a few weeks. Overall, this is an amazing game for people that like mysteries, multiple endings, and slow, yet meaningful gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely can't recommend this game. I admire it for what it's trying to do--game design and the field deserve a game so audacious that it asks the player to wait for hours for a door to open, or weeks for a stalactite to fall, or 400 days for a singular goal. It's an inspiring design idea, and I can't wait for other studios to expound on it. But the problem comes down to engagement. If you force a player to wait for something in real time, such as the door which takes 2 hours to open, then you are inviting them to tab out and do something else while they wait. This doesn't breed any interest in the game. It becomes a chore that you have to return to every now and again because there is no continual flow between interacting with something, seeing a result, and then interacting again. In the end, I was fine with waiting--but I didn't care what happened afterwards. I was completely apathetic towards the game by the time I finished it that I got nothing from the experience and immediately uninstalled. A lot of people clearly like this game, and I'm not going to step on any toes by saying that this game is bad. But as a player who values engagement and immersion, I got absolutely nothing from this game and can't give it my recommendation. If this game is your type of thing, you should totally go for it. The art is great and the sound design is extremely effective. But if you're like me, this ain't for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe not my absolute favorite game ever, but at least in contention for it. Assuredly the most unique game I have ever played. The overwhelming feeling of helplessness a shade feels is given directly to the player. All you can do is walk, interact with things, and wait. Yet in spite of this, I was paying attention more than 80% pf the time I played, despite it being an idle game. I felt compelled to do as much as I could for a shade, and to stop and think about a great many things.The music and sounds in this game lean exactly into what its trying to do, at least from the perspective of a player. A shades pitterpatter of feet slowly shuffling around as they move from place to place helps reflect how silent and empty the cave otherwise is. Slowly ambling through the caves really emphasizes how weak and alone a shade is. Thankfully, there is plenty to discover.If I have much negative to say about this game, its droplets in a vast ocean. Coal dropping in a place where I cant get to it on time? Puzzle too cryptic? You have time to figure it out for sure! The first time this happened to me, I felt a twinge of frustration. Then I stopped to think about it and burst into laughter. Admittedly, there are many things one could consider a "problem", but in the same way Undertale is a deconstruction of JRPGs, The Longing is a deconstruction of expectations in both games and real life. Therefore I don't see these "drawbacks" as such.While I want to write much more, but I feel like this game is best experienced, not read. Just remember your choices matter, and sometimes all you can do is wait.... alone... But with how extreme instant gratification in modern society has become, perhaps its for the best. I think we could all do with some introspection from time to time, and this game is an excellent catalyst for that.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, first: What is this game, right? It's a point-and-click puzzle game with a grim tone--figuratively and literally, as in . You are the servant of a slumbering earthen monarch tasked with waking him in 400 days, . The King tells us that when he awakens, he will have enough strength to "end all sadness and longing". No red flags there.So our job is literally to wait around or explore his empty, subterranean kingdom until we are ready to wake him up or escape on our own. There are lots of interesting things to collect and clues to find about our world. You could turn the game off and return in 400 days to see the ending, but if you are very clever (or a big cheater), you can end the game significantly sooner than that, about , most of that time hands-off. If you are very patient or very clever, time will never be an issue for you.The world and story is evocative, the characters are cute, the puzzles and secrets are phenomenal. I only wish there were more of all of it (the alleged 400-day game!). I strongly recommend you pick it up.Caveat: You will be pissed at first about how slowly the character moves, but I do think he gets marginally faster the longer you play and spruce up his little room...maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that is sweet and calm, curious for those who enjoy exploring and don't mind taking their time, it's like a background-game that works well being more in the forefront.If you dislike slow speed or things taking time, then it's not for you, but for those who don't mind taking their time or enjoy finding out the bigger picture in a slow and time-based way, you will love this as much as I have.I won't spoil anything, and I suggest you don't either.Keep yourself from spoilers.Keep yourself to memory and to remember places in the game.Some things are really easy to notice what you might have to do, everything just takes time.I highly suggest giving it a try, but if you're someone who loves fast action and instant skinner-box, this won't be fun, or enjoyable at all for you.I am still hooked and can't stop playing, and it's something about the slow reward, having gotten to an amazing point, I got elated and excited beyond what I've been in other games where I've won matches or figured out a puzzle, I actually jumped up and laughed and got so scared and excited, it was amazing.I've not regretted buying it.

_childDocuments_.review: The true game-breaker for most will be the main character's walking speed. It's utterly glacial. It's by design. And you'll either love it or hate it. The authorial intent is plain as day. But that doesn't mean many or even most will be willing to put up with it. Crossing a single screen-sized room takes about 30 seconds. The game is very vertical and going up 3 or 4 switchbacks can take 60. So what gives? What's the point?Pacing.You're one little guy. By himself. Underground. Alone for 400 days waiting for your god to wake back up. You're not forced into the situation. You're not unexpectedly lost and looking for a way out. Your job is to...wait.The Longing is a meditative game. In slowing down the in-game character, the game is also slowing down the player. What seems like a crazy design choice at first, slowly reveals itself as inspired mechanic (again that won't be for everyone).As you slowly plod from one room to the next exploring new areas, your guy talks to himself. Reflecting on the nature of being. The impact of loneliness. Sense of purpose. The slow pace of traversal puts you into your character's shoes. You feel the weight of 400 days in isolation. It's a melancholy experience. And the game triumphs in transporting you to that moment. But at the same time it asks a lot of the player to get there. It urges one to give themselves up to the glacial pacing. I can honesty, with zero judgement, see how many will view it as a bridge too far.I think the title of the game is apt. The whole experience reaches in and touches that lonely, longing part of us all. That existential, "We really are alone in the world." tenderness inside that we spend so much time unconsciously covering up with extracurricular activities and relationships.It's certainly a mood piece. A successful one at that. Not gonna be for everyone, but it doesn't need to be. It's gonna resonate for some, not all. The lucky ones that stick with it will discover a valuable experience that just doesn't come along very often.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is more than just a game, it is a piece of art. The art of "waiting".Although I am far from completeing the game, everything about the game has been above my expectations so far. Most of the time, you are just walking around, hoping to get somwhere, or waiting for something to happen, whether its for a door to open so you can enter, or for a spider to build webs so you can climb up, or for the water to fill the hole so you can continue exploring the unknown. But, there is something more to all that. The character is as unknown as everything else in the game, but you can feel it, you can feel the sadness, the lonliness and emptiness the character carries with itself, and as times progresses, these emotions become stronger.This game might not be anyone's cup of tea as it requires a considerable amount of patience. But for those who enjoy it, it is beyond perfect. The art used in the game is really beautiful and lovely. Everything feels like a melancholy.Other than walking and grabbing items, There isn't much of a gameplay, not that you need it with this game.I can't write enough to express the special beauties of The Longing. It is something you have to experience by yourself. This game is unlike anything else you've seen before.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a little girl, I loved to draw, and I used to draw 2D cross-sections of underground caves or snow tunnels. I would draw pathways that split in all kinds of directions, leading to rooms with treasures, friends to find, food to eat, or even dangers. I had pages upon pages of these, crudely drawn in ballpoint pen, and sometimes I would cut out characters to "explore" the tunnels I drew. This game sent me right back to my childhood and the tunnels I made: There's endless paths to follow and unmarked doors to enter as you explore the world of The Longing. This is a SLOW GAME. You cannot run. Your character slowly plods along. You can double-click to make them auto-walk up to the point you clicked to. You can bookmark favorite locations and make them auto-walk to said locations (including to walk back home, something that I had a passing anxiety about my first time exploring deep into the caves). Without these auto-walk features, I'd call the game unplayable, but I will say that the slow pace makes this game unique, strangely thrilling as the next scene slowly comes into view, and makes the stakes of taking risks (like entering forbidden rooms or waking the King early) that much heavier. Since, if you really screw up...how LONG is it going to take you to start over?Steam invites you to review games after 3 hours by default since for most games that's a good enough time to get to know them. Given the pace of this game, I'm sure I've barely scratched the surface. This game hits all the right notes for me, though: You are rewarded for exploring and taking the twisting, unknown paths as you discover little treasures along the way. Your "shade" character regularly shares their thoughts, helping break up the time and add some humor when you hit a dead end. And the timer isn't quite precise... much like "time flies when you're having fun" in real life, there are ways to speed up the timer in this game, too.There's still a ton I need to explore and find out. I need to find the pick-axe. I need to unlock the library. But as you learn early on, not all discoveries are instant. A door might need 2 hours to slowly crack open. A spider might need several days to build a web for you to climb. So your best bet is to explore regularly, set these things in motion, bookmark the location, and return later to see them manifest into your next course of action.I love that the game continues when you're not playing. That, combined with the auto-walk features, make this an excellent idle game. I haven't quit my childhood drawing habit, and I find this game is excellent to have in the background as I'm working on art to give myself mental breaks now and then. I went to bed very excited to get up in the morning knowing enough time had passed for the next stage to be unlocked.Again, this is a SLOW game, but if you're curious and like to explore by nature, and you want to have something casual to return to regularly, this game is for you. I'm a bit too busy these days to really invest my time and energy into the grind of an MMO, but this game soothes that addiction to gradually build up to something over time. I can start or stop it as I please, and every time I have something new to discover.

_childDocuments_.review: A review that tries to serve its initial purpose of helping you decide on a purchase; joke-free (may contain traces of sarcasm):1) The game is_not about waiting - it's about figuring out how to minimize waiting time, which includes finding other ways to complete the game. You do so by casually exploring the cave you're entrusted with, at your own pace. So If you're cautious about spending 10+ bobs for the experience of pure waiting - fear not.2) However, if you're too busy to invest your time into gaming, or simply prefer when someone else does the job for you - the game can perfectly serve your needs, too. Just launch it once, and then it will do all the dirty work towards its inevitable completion/win in less than 1.5 years. Profit!3) If the idea of doing the job yourself sounds more appealing, please be aware that it's not a casual game emanating care towards the precious consumer. It's full of unobvious puzzles & solutions, so if you aren't a hardcore beast _and_ if you call walkthroughs 'spoilers' - that's probably not for you. The reason I made it to the end (and relatively painlessly) is that I'm pretty comfortable with using walkthroughs.4) Unlike the devs' weird desire to make a one-time experience, the game has some replayability in it. Rather naive to make different endings and hope for the one-time experience, after all. So if you're cautious about spending 10+ bobs for the 'one-time experience' - fear not. Just be aware that it's not that easy and obvious even to replay the game (see p.3 'Devs hate their player'). If you consider replaying, read forums in advance to be prepared and know what to do when the time comes.5) Humour and drama of the game weirdly refuse to mix together, so you better pick a side in the beginning whether you wanna long or chill, to avoid the dissonance.6) The game is rather unique.Hope this helps, thank you for reading the most boring review.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't get it twisted, The Longing is an idle game. That means there's a ton of waiting! Magically the developers were able to convert idle game mechanics, from something like Cookie Clicker, into an exploration game. I'm impressed! They even included more active mechanics, which speeds up the game a little. This is the slowest game I'm excited about!Like in other idle games, you can close The Longing, and the shade will continue with whatever they were doing. So you do not need to be actively playing. This comes in super handy when you learn of the second quality of life feature the developer added. The shade will walk themselves to a location. You're able to save up to twelve rooms that the shade will automatically walk back to. There's a random choice as well if you want to take a chance. Early on, it's useful for finding new areas, but later it will take to places you've already been to. So good luck!So while four hundred days seems like a long time to have a game running, you probably won't have it open the entire time. You can choose to send the shade where you want them to go and close the game. Then open it later to play more active and keep performing that loop. Some parts of the cave are blocked behind a time wall. You will need to wait for days or weeks or months to get to new areas. So the game keeps changing as you play, and even nine hours in, it feels like there's even more for me to find.Overall, It's impressive the developers were able to translate idle mechanics so thoughtfully. It has a great style, and they nailed feeling alone without being too sad about it.I created a video,

_childDocuments_.review: True isolation. That's what this game is. You are a small shade, and your mission is to wake your king up... after 400 real time days. Until then, you are trapped in a complex layer of caves. You will both be curious to explore the place you are trapped in, and eventually beg for a release from your prison. I can't help but to shudder when . Soundtrack is sublime, sometimes filling me with wonder, sometimes with dread. All in all, very few games made me feel such strong emotions, and :The Longing: is certainly one of them. If you like fast paced games though, this might not just be your cup of tea. The main character walks very slowly (not with an unbearable pace, but if you rather like running in games, you might have a hard time). And you only live once . Make it count.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This unique adventure/idle game had plenty of places, things, and mysteries to discover. You play as The Shade, lonely, in a cave system with a King that asks you to wait for 400 days as he rests to regain his strength. It is then up to you to choose how he spends his time while he waits. You are rewarded for being patient, as the game moves slowly, but there are still plenty of things to discover over time. It was an experience I did not expect to enjoy as much as I did, but the story really hooked me in.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually I don't review games until I finish playing but well. The Longing is an incredibly charming game. I usually hate slow-paced games and consider myself pretty impatient but something about The Longing just feels rewarding enough to keep me going. The need to wait for more exploration as the cave shifts with time actually ends up preventing me from burning out. The artstyle is delightful and the atmosphere and dialog are just foreboding enough to make you think twice about your actions, even if you can't help yourself going on anyways, it just adds some good gravity to the experience. If you're down for a game that'll stay with you for a long time, like, over a year, here you go.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this morose little gollum of a Shade like he is my own precious child. When I downloaded this game at the beginning of quarantine, I thought it seemed cool and arty and maybe worth a lil cash and had NO IDEA how much it was going to get me through the whole world breaking down around me. Why do I love this character so much? I so tenderly want to bring him happiness and freedom (and rugs. Many rugs.) Made of coal and longing, he is exactly what I needed. I take a perverse delight in the fact that there is no fast forward or "run" in this game (well, except ... I'll let you figure that out for yourself.) The music is cool, the art is nostalgic of I don't even know when, and hey, you can read Moby ♥♥♥♥ if you want to!

_childDocuments_.review: You walk around a dark cave at a speed so slow that you will check your keyboard settings thinking there has been some sort of mistake, but it is no mistake, and for that reason, you might want to keep a book nearby or something fun to do to balance out this lethargic crawl. The core game mechanic of 'The Longing' is waiting. You must distract yourself for 400 days while the King takes a power nap and you are left to draw on cave walls with chalk. The gameplay is slow by design to accentuate the games hopeless narrative. The tedious pace allows the player to fully appreciate the hand drawn art style, which is the games most definitive strength. Arguably, the game could get by just as a visual piece with exploration. The story is cryptic and somber, and entertains some dark endings for our little shade friend. The player is not given much context/backstory and thus the story tells itself through subtle lore found throughout the caves, which makes discovering every little thing that much more interesting. As for gameplay, the interaction is limited, even for a point-and-click style game. Unfortunately, the slow movement and limited activity debilitates initial interest in the game over time. Overall, 'The Longing' is an impressive visual feat from a small indie team but lacks the engagement and polish to be a true masterpiece among video game artistic greats, and maybe that is why I am so hard on it. 'The Longing' could have been so much more, but ultimately falls short in giving the player an interactive and engaging experience. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Even if you have to wait for 400 days to finish the game properly, there are legit ways to do it faster, so it's sadly shorter – and I mean sadly, because the exploration is really soothing and the character and setting of the game are so as well! Generally, I relly recommend it, and I hope for more games following a similar pattern to this game :)As far As playing on Linux goes, it it native, it works great, it's based on Unity 5 and uses OpenGL by default, but the Vulkan version can be forced using "-force-vulkan" switch. Sadly there's no native Wayland support in Unity 5, but it's buggy in newer Unity games anyway, and Steam as well as various game-related utilities still rely on X11, so it doesn't matter. If you don't want to stress your GPU, you also need to limit the framerate with an external tool, as the game uses all it have available to render as many frames as possible. I sometimes gets some small hangs for a second or so, but it may be because I play on Vulkan, XWayland, have the framerate capped to 60 through MangoHud and/or I don't use a kernel optimized for gaming at this moment.

_childDocuments_.review: It's more of an art piece than it is a game. While it can be enjoyed in this aspect, it would be delusional to call it a good or enjoyable game for the average player, which is one of the reasons I can't recommend it.I found the game on reddit and it seemed very unique. I seem to remember that I purchased it for $12 while it was on sale. I enjoyed it to an extent, or at least I tried to convince myself that I was enjoying it. I tried to get 100% of the achievements (ended up with 20/25) but ending the game (escaping the cave) itself was such a tedious process that I never bothered doing it. Therein lies the issue with this game.The game, as advertised, takes place over time. It takes long periods of time to solve certain puzzles, which points to the theme of the piece: waiting. Everything takes time, so let things take their course. While this is fine, it does not make for riveting gameplay. The point that the game is trying to make is made in the first 4 hours of playing. Afterwards, it becomes too annoying to stand, and it makes you feel like you are wasting the time that the game tries to convince you that you have so much of. Having an extremely slow walk speed to get the message of "you have time/be patient" is too expensive to player experience to be justified.The message itself tries to be deep, and I imagine that it can talk to some people. But the in-your-face message of how lonely the shade is or how things take time seems to take away from the story itself. It makes the message feel 2D rather than complex.Soundtrack is nice. Story is alright. Locations are repetitive, drawn out, and frankly disappointing for a point and click exploration game. There aren't actually very many puzzles, maybe 25 to 30. It just feels like more because it takes so much gosh darn waiting to finish them.This is not worth $15. It's worth maybe $5 if you're interested in an art piece.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is a nice change of pace (literally) from my more recently played games like Call of Duty. It seems like the Devs intentionally made things painfully slow, but I appreciate it and understand that's what I'm signing up for with this unique experience. It's a great game to leave running in the background while I do other things, since The Shade (your character) walks what I would guess is approximately 1 mph and can take a while to get from one end of the map to the other.It feels a bit like Terraria in that it's fun and exciting to explore the caverns, though the map never changes between playthroughs like Terraria's procedurally generated maps. I've throughly enjoyed the mystery behind every corner, and the hidden or secret paths that you accidentally stumble upon.Now that I've spent several hours roaming the halls, I find that there isn't much else to do but wait around just like The Shade (there go those Devs again), as certain timers and events take their course to allow me to explore further. Some of those events will take way longer to complete than there is content currently available to me to explore and experience, so my only complaint is that it seems to force me to close the game and wait days or weeks to come back at that arbitrary time to continue playing. It does produce a lot of longing, so I guess I'm still getting what I paid for. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: General: Rating: Not listed but probably EPrice: $14.99	Genre: Idle/Adventure	Time played: 84.6 HoursAn ancient king creates the shade and tells you to wake him in 400 days. He also tells you not to leave the caves.  Then he falls asleep leaving the shade alone. So now what does the shade do? Gameplay - 10The game is different.  It is an idle game.  You’re not going to finish it in one session.  The game counts down the 400 days second by second.  The shade will not run, he slowly walks everywhere which is at first frustrating, then later.  It’s still damn frustrating. But the shade points out, he’s got plenty of time, why rush.  The adventure part is you exploring the caves, discovering various things.  Some of the mechanics are interesting, your shade is not a hero, he’s not strong.  Some parts of the cave you have to discover, then wait weeks/months (in game time) for them to finish their part so you will have to come back later.  They included a mechanic to allow you to save an area and you can set the shade to auto walk there.  Looking for more objects to make the shade’s home more comfortable.  He can read books to pass the time, eventually you can make a bed so he can sleep away the time. Story -  9The king has created you to wake him in 400 days, when he wakes he’ll put an end to all things.  Ominous no? The story is the shade trying to not be lonely and sad.  He reads, he walks around, he searches for things that will make his home more comfortable. The story is not meant to be played more than once. It’s a unique experience but I don’t see someone coming back to this game. Graphics - 9It looks hand drawn and quite beautiful. The various locations are interesting and add that personal touch to the game.  Controls - 10(mouse/keyboard) 6(controller)The controls are pretty simple, click the left mouse and he’ll turn and look that way, hold down the left mouse button and he’ll walk that direction. Double left click and he’ll auto walk there. The right mouse button is how you interact with things.    Controller isn't much different.  Left Trigger/L2 was your left mouse button and same for the Right Trigger/R2 replaced the right mouse button.   You used the right joystick as your mouse pointer.  The speed of the left joystick was a little fast and could probably be fixed easily but I just went back to the mouse/keyboard.Repeatability - N/AAs i stated before this game is really just for 1 playthrough.  It’s about discovering things and once you know where they are it’s hard to have the same experience. Music - 10Soothing, it changes depending on the room you enter.  The room with the king has somber almost militaristic music other places just soothing sounds.  The sounds are interesting, you can listen to the shade’s bare feet slapping as he trudges towards whatever destination he’s heading towards.   There’s a waterfall you can stand under and just listen to the peace and quiet.Multiplayer -  N/AInitial Thoughts: This could be interesting.  Let’s see how it plays out.   Okay. Okay.  Jesus this guy is walking so slow.  Oh a door let’s open… I have to wait in real time for the freaking door to open? ugh.Soma Says: I’m not much for adventure games that are point & click.  This one however struck a chord.  You’re told you have to wait 400 days.  Then watch as the clock starts winding down, 399 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes and 45 seconds.   That’s a long time to watch the clock.  So you start exploring things, the shade will make comments on things, usually about how sad/lonely he is at the moment. As time passes the Shade will drop hints on things you can do to help make time go faster. Exploring the caves is vital.  Of course you could wait the year + by turning on the game then coming back a year later but that defeats the purpose. I won’t spoil any of the game. I’ll just say at times I understood the shade’s pain,  he’s a lonely guy looking for someone to be around. *edit  Finally finished the game.  I was able to get the 5th ending which i felt was worth it.  And without too much spoiling, use the blue fire to go back in time, read the books backwards!If you enjoyed the review check out my curator page :
