_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this, I've played for 67 hours total, beaten it at least once, and restarted. For a game where the main gameplay loop is literally just waiting, I feel like that says something. One disclaimer before I continue: when the game says it's going to take 400 real life days to complete, that's not necessarily true. I got my first ending with about 30 days left on the in-game clock about 40 real-life days after install, and other endings can be gotten sooner than that. There are ways to end the game early and speed up time, but even then, it's still a game about waiting.The Longing is a pretty unmarketable experience. I think it would be hard to explain to a friend why I think they ought to play a game where there's no boss fights, no combat, and minimal puzzles, but lots and lots of waiting. But The Longing is one of those games where you play for the story and experience, and furthermore, it's a story and experience that only as effective as it is BECAUSE it's a game. It wouldn't work as a novel or movie, because The Longing gets its point across by making YOU wait for the same thing the Shade is waiting for.Because after the brief introduction of your purpose, there is nothing to do but wait. You can explore the king's extensive underground kingdom and find instrument pieces and art supplies that help you pass the time. You can find books that let you skip a minute whenever you turn a page for the first time. You can expand and decorate your starting home until it's a cozy little den where time can pass up to 24 times as quickly. But all this stuff just makes the waiting easier; it doesn't remove it. You can find all sorts of ways to pass time for yourself, but in the end you're still just waiting for an inevitability.And when I started up the game for the first time and started to explore the underground caves to look for supplies for the Shade's home cave, hoping to find something that would tell me more about the King and the Shade and the reason for the wait? My mind was absolutely buzzing with thoughts and feelings about the Shade and what he's got to go through. What happens when the 400 days are up? How am I going to fill that much time? What happens if I miss the deadline? I could decide to just leave the game and go live my life for a year and a bit, but would I even remember to revisit the game after leaving it that long? How can the Shade stand to be alone in these caves doing nothing but wait for up to 400 days? I'm pretty sure a human being would start to go insane after a week, and even the Shade himself seems crushed by the loneliness and emptiness of it all. On the other hand, the goal is far away, but it's also inevitable. Just wait long enough, and you *will* complete the game. The Longing is going to end. Your loneliness is going to end, if you just tough it out and see what's waiting for you on the other side. This is temporary, and you can find ways to make the wait easier. Make art. Read books. Practice music. Decorate your room. Oh, this door needs 2 hours to be fully open? I'll just take a break and fold some laundry. Oh, I need another week before this stalactite falls and lets me access whatever's beyond those stairs? Well, time now passes at 10x the rate in my room due to all these decorations, so I'll just check back tomorrow evening. Oh, the Shade needs 5 real minutes to mine out this crystal? I'll go watch this Youtube video and he'll be ready to pick it up when I'm done. The Longing is a constant battle against waiting, but waiting is a battle you will always inevitably win. Waiting is simultaneously the easiest and hardest thing to do in life.My heart started to hurt for the Shade the moment the reality of his situation sunk in, because I was sharing in his reality by having to wait with him. I was also feeling impatient and lonely with the whole thing, and I at least had the luxury of being able to turn off the game and go to sleep. I was able to finish in a little over a month with the various waiting cheats, but the Shade still has to tough it out for 400 days (or however long it takes for you to find another way to escape the longing.)The fact that The Longing puts all these thoughts in my head is what convinced me to stick with it. That is all.

I wanted him to read all the books, build his bed, lay down the , paint numerous pictures - I wanted him to be in constant comfort. When I finally received the  I wrote a small letter addressed to him. I had a nightmare that I ran out of time and  It got to the point that I spoiled myself the game so that  At one point I rang my sister when I was at work to move the Shade out of his home because  And when The Longing did eventually end, my hands were  I was so worried that I had done something wrong and my little Shade wouldn't be happy (For those curious about the ending,  ) It has been so many years since I've played a game that I've reacted so strongly to. _childDocuments_.review: Over the course of 19 hours I did next to nothing. The pace was excruciating at times, and the reward for almost everything was little more than a long walk home or a confusing lore tidbit. That said, the pacing of the game and the surprising depth to the game's core thematic all play to its strengths. There is genuine longing, and curiosity, and fear, and impatience, and delight as you traipse through the halls of the kingdom and find new things. As the days go by and the hours pass there are little joys like a new book or a new color of chalk that help to enhance what is otherwise doing nothing. To say the pace is slow is an understatement, but I think if you go into it with an almost meditative mindset you will come out the other end enriched and entertained. Learning of the endings, finding the secrets, and exploring the beautiful and surprisingly detailed world was a genuine treat. I highly recommend this game, although I will likely never play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game fully expecting it to be very slow, and for me to be waiting for a fairly low amount of content spread out over 400 days. This game doesn't provide that. You quickly learn as you play the game that exploring and finding things speeds up the game's clock, and if you actively play the game at all you can easily get through the 400 days in what seems to be under 3 months. Once I realised that I was a little disappointed, but still expected the game to deliver the same promise over those 3 months.After having the game for less than a week I can already access most of the endings and almost all of the rest of the game. I really don't feel like a game based around waiting 400 days should have what seems to be the "Good ending" easily reachable in 3-4 days. I checked a guide when I got to the ending to check if it's permanent (it is, but you can mess with save files), noticed the length of the guide was shorter than I expected, and decided to spoil the rest of the game. Reading the guide I found out there was barely anything left for me to discover or wait for.So the game is actually 20-30 hours of slowly walking around exploring a maze of caverns, solving about a half dozen puzzles (plus a few well-hidden secrets), plus some idle backtracking and mining. It's not a terrible game, but the ways it betrays its premise really disappointed me. The game may be about waiting 400 days if you do absolutely nothing, but if you actually explore what the game has to offer you're likely to get through it in less than 20.

_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is a wonderfully unique point and click game. I recommend installing it asap.You are the Shade and your job is to wait. Great for quarantine. While waiting for 400 days you can idle, explore, and collect your way to comfort. As you can see from the pictures on the store page, you start with quite a measly hovel. You slowly make this more of a home for yourself as your patience is rewarded. From your nook of the castle you venture out, slowly and introspectively. The thoughts of the Shade are super entertaining. There is a smart mechanisms in place to auto-walk to a saved location. Not only does that help when you're lost, but it may help if you feel bored or impatient. Sometimes the slow pace of the Shade is perfect for super casual gameplay, but sometimes you want to check out a specific area. Exploration and collecting are crucial!I love how rewarding this game feels. It's fun to check in on and chill out with. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Too little content to be worthwhile.The longing is a game that doesn't respect your time and makes no notions about that not being the case. Almost every puzzle in the game is solved by waiting an abhorrent amount of time. Trying to explore the world of the longing is also it's own degree of tedium since you can't run the large walking sections in the background until after you've seen an area once. The controls are also not very good and I've spent a good amount of time struggling to get the shade to walk the direction I want him to.The most troublesome aspect of the game however is just the lack of content. I wrapped up nearly everything in the game within the first two weeks of the 400 day counter with the only things stopping me being the 1 month and 1 year roadblock achievements. I'll fully admit I'm not into artsy games like this but I'd be a bit more forgiving of this concept if all of it's features didn't run dry incredibly quickly.I actually really like the art style however and while the music wasn't very memorable it certainly worked for the game. I've noticed a lot of reviewers love to talk about the shade's character. While it's true he's got a nice laid back personality, there really isn't much to write home about him to make it a selling point of the game. Some of his lines are funny but if you're going into this expecting to get really attached to this character I'd tell you to not get your hopes up.In short, it looks nice and has a unique idea but there isn't enough content to be worth a $15 price tag for the experience. If you're into games like this, get it on sale. Otherwise skip it.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I am torn on this game so much, I wanted to like it so badly. The concept is great and different, but it really just felt like a hurry up and wait game. I played it for a good chunk to explore the map, do the things, and make note of when things would change. Then I closed it and set a reminder in my calendar, came back and did the little bits that had changed, set another reminder, and then finished it. I know there are multiple endings, and youtube let me see those, because quite frankly I cannot praise the waiting process. The idea is unique but it just bugged me that I had paid for a game that I just had to leave sitting there until a clock ticked down.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend you play this game. Not because of the jokes "it's slow, boring, nothing happens." That's all part of the game itself, that's the deal you make when you buy the game.The fun of the game comes from very slowly figuring stuff out, making your little home better and making time move faster.The game is designed in a way where only one of its many endings is satisfying.My main issue is, there is a point in the game where you know you've won, you know you've got the satisfying ending, but you, as always, need to wait for it to happen, it's a long wait but you need to be present for it, so you can't tab out, this ending throws away all your hard work because no matter how nice your house is, no matter how much work you've done for your little gremlin, time moves at 1 second/second, it eventually gets to a point where you don't feel like you've won anymore, you're just waiting for it to be over.That is sort of what the final 1/5th of this game is, just waiting for it to be over, while the whole game is technically waiting, the final fifth just makes me feel... Apathetic? Towards the game, which is a real shame because the rest of it is amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is a pretty hard game to recommend, because the whole gameplay is pretty slow. You explore a cave system while you wait 400 REAL TIME days for the king to awake. While you explore the cave you come around several areas, where you have to wait a certain time to progress further; it even has a few little puzzles to solve.The whole game is centered around it, so do yourself a favor and don't let yourself spoil anything, because exploring it and finding secrets is the experience, which makes the game so great in my opinion.Also you can find things for your home cave that makes time progress faster than real time if you stay in your home cave.You can even find books like Moby-♥♥♥♥ in the game that you can read there.So all in all I would recommend this game to everyone that likes a unique "gaming" experience and like to explore a game on their own.Ps: The game has quite some depressing themes to it, so if you don't like that then you should stay away from it.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently about 1/4 through this pretentious art game and not happy with the purchase, even after getting it on sale. _childDocuments_.review: A few minutes into the game, you find your adorable critter (who I call Shady) sitting in an armchair in a mostly empty room. Behind you is a fireplace: empty, cold, and quiet. A few minutes later, and I have the pieces of flint and coal I need to start the fire, and begin the slow walk back to my room. Shady takes a long time to go anywhere or do anything. When you find a piece of coal, you can have Shady pick it up. The shuffling walk stops, and Shady slowly bends over to grab the black chunk. Yet, you can’t be upset about the sloth, because (as the game observes very early), you are waiting for 400 days. Why hurry?If you collect enough coal, you can start a fire in your room. It crackles in the background, pleasant and homey. You sit in your armchair with the warmth behind you, and the timer ticks slightly faster. Each tick of time passes four seconds instead of one. Then, after a few minutes, the fire goes out and time slows back down. 400 days.I have Shady wander the caverns, looking for any useful items that might be lying around, or areas that might be accessible later. Every now and then, a piece of coal falls from the ceiling, and my heart jumps a bit. Fuel for my fire!400 days.After finding a few pieces of paper to draw on, I return home. As Shady’s slow patter trudges on, I think again about what the game said in the beginning. Why hurry? I think of the fire back in my small room, and the fourteen days I have to wait for moss to grow before I can harvest it. I think of the five pieces of coal it will take to start the fire up again. Then, a resigned understanding sinks in: nothing I do will significantly speed up this game. I just have to wait... for 400 days.A piece of coal falls right in front of Shady.I don't stop to pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: while I liked the game (and beat it with the secret ending), gotta say it gave me x1 disappointments.So there's only a few things that are actually time gated based on cumulative time, the longest being 30 days. After that it's nothing. You can get the good ending within an irl week, 2 hours if you're willing to click your mouse a lot in your house. Like it's fine that there's endings that are semi quick to beat, that's expected, but for those that actually wait out the clock, there's like nothing to look forward to after your 1st week of playing. There's no, oh, here's a thing that will take 2 months to get past, or behind a 2 week time gate you find month long time gate you have to start. No wall that he's like "oh it'll take me a week straight of mining to get through". No stalactite or big pillar that will take a year to fall, there's nothing. The only things you have to look forward to are the halfway mark, but idk if anything in game even mentions it (and it's a real nothing thing too) and your birthday near the end, both are small and not even really worth it.So within 2 weeks of me playing for maybe an hour or 2 per day I basically exhausted the game of everything fun it had aside from reading the books I've never read before (man those old fairy tales are messed up), and there was nothing left to do for the rest of the 2 months I played the game except have the shade sit in his chair and check back every couple of days to make sure I didn't miss his birthday. It really needed something to do in the mean time like I mentioned previously: time gated access to new areas with something else there, whether it was just something to look at or something new to talk at or a new decoration, literally anything.So my advice to really enjoy the game is to just get the good ending when you can, then just look up the other endings online cause they aren't worth it. What you think happens happens at the end of the 400 days, secret ending would have been better to see on youtube, the bad ends are exactly what you think they are. Should take like a week or 2 of casual play unless you just can't figure out the puzzles (two of them are kinda weird).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough call; giving the game either a thumbs up or thumbs down. The main point of the game is to be slow. From travel to being forced to wait for events it's all slow. On paper I like this idea; a gaming experience where you are by all means forced to feel the slow passing of time from the point of a lonely shade. But ultimately, I lost interest in the game, put it down for nearly a year, then came back for an ending I don't feel I earned. The problem is this game both promotes exploration and the forced slow passage of time. This combined makes the game tedious which I think outweighs the game feel that is intended.Overall: The concept is a good idea but I think the execution doesn't do the game any favors.

Small favors.)Your first option in how to make all that time flow slightly faster? Reading Moby ♥♥♥♥. As in, the full 1282 pages novel, in real time. _childDocuments_.review: Now I just started this game, But I wanna make sure people know what its like at the beginning.The biggest disappointment I have is not being able to explore everything from the start.You're pretty limited at the start, the biggest things I've found I've been doing are reading my few books, or just walking around.Anyone who likes action/fps games to death is not going to like this. I'm a fan of fps but I actually like more slow-paced games.If you like story, this game is kind of for you, but not entirely.Where this game shines is that it is not actually a game, it's a piece of art.I mean that in a literal way, even only an hour in I could already relate to and feel attached to the shade, I already smile when he cracks a bad joke, or whenever I pick up coal.This is not an extremely fun game, but it's a damn good one, it's an amazing game for anyone who wants to relax and enjoy themselves for a while an hour or two a day.This game isn't for binging, it's something you play an hour or two of every once in a while, this is something you either spend an hour playing, or you don't play at all.The greatest part about this game isn't the interaction actually, it's the way it utilizes waiting and boredom.In essence, if this game didn't make you wait for hours, or however long, it wouldn't be good.In order to enjoy this game you need to be willing to be patient, otherwise you won't enjoy it at all.I still don't recommend this game because, it is not fun, this game will make you love this character, it will make you happy when he does something, or makes a remark about how lonely he is. But It Is Not Fun, it is a damn good game, but this is not for everyone, it's for a very few amount of people.Because you need to Long for your entertainment, because only then will it truly be fulfilling, and that's a hard thing to do.

_childDocuments_.review: The art style immediately sold me on this game. The premise of waking the king in 400 days is partially true. The real game play is finding things that speed up the clock (more books to read, items to add to the Shade's home, etc.). So the clock can move faster than normal under these conditions. The primary way of acquiring these things is through exploration. It has been years since I drew a map for a game and this game I have dedicated an entire notebook to (basically drawing the rooms and then labeling the doors). This is my go-to game for relaxing now.Absolutely would recommend this game to anyone who loves to make maps, needs something to relax to, and anyone who wants a unique experience.A recent update gives plenty of reasons to explore over time to find new books and I imagine other secrets as well.

_childDocuments_.review: :THE LONGING: is visually beautiful (with a fun little Monty Python element to the art style), the atmosphere set by the music is amazing, and even for someone like myself who usually hates these kinds of adventure / point & click style affairs, I've been won over by the gameplay. And absolutely none of that has the teensiest bearing on why I think this game is so special.I've never had a game give me such a bizarre sense of responsibility to a character before. I don't want the clock to speed up because I want to see everything but I can only quit the game once I've walked my Shade home and sat him in his big, red, comfy chair, otherwise I feel genuinely bad for stranding him in the middle of nowhere. No game has ever convinced me as well as this that the characters exist in a proper world, and that's all because of time. I don't care where I leave the protagonists in other games because I'm not "leaving" them there. When I boot it up next, one of two things happen: either I pick up at the exact moment I quit and thus, effectively, never left, or the game has moved the character and changed the skybox to try and simulate the passage of time meaning that, in this dumb scenario I'm crafting, the character has autonomy and can exist without me. When I leave my Shade, his world doesn't stop and he doesn't move. He sits exactly where I left him for as long as I leave him. He neither freezes in time nor carries on while I'm gone and no matter how often I remind myself that he's just a collection of ones and zeros, the idea of just abandoning him somewhere gets me in the heart every time.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely worth it.A joke: This game is like another particular title about a man in a pot with a mattock, but for people with taste :)Jokes aside, and with the hope that I haven't offended any fans of the previous title, this game is amazing.  The art and music are superb.  Full of metaphors that can be noticed by any students of deep psychology such as C.G. Jung, philosophy, myth, or certain spiritual lineages.  Also if you personally have any Teutonic, Nordic, or Slavic heritage, The Longing is very likely to evoke a strong unconscious response from deep within you that will be intuitively understood.In wandering these lonely halls and watching moss grow, or a slow drip of water into a pool, with nothing in particular for a mind to do, The Longing has reconnected me with the feeling and power of patience.  True patience.  And the understanding that situations in life are not absolutes- they are processes.  Even if all you have energy for today is to cut one tiny section of your hedges, or to repair your window blinds, well, it isn't nothing.  It makes a difference.I have gotten more long-unfinished real-life tasks accomplished in this past weekend playing The Longing than I think I have in the past month.  Leaving my little Shade on my desktop to remind me what it is to have no reason to rush or to hurry, or to pass judgment upon anything at all.Thank you The Longing for reminding me that slow and incremental change is still real change.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I have played to three endings in this game (yes, that's possible):One badOne happyOne ... uh... wrong.I feel like I've had a full experience with it.This game is unlike any other I've played before, and I like it for that. It is definitely one that demands patience, but not because of difficulty (except for the secret room puzzle, which is mostly irritating because of large scale timing, not reflex timing). It is a fairly passive experience, but still requires user input if you want to guide how it ends.The game is definitely slowly paced, and very melancholy.I'm pretty easy, with emotional connection, but I found it rather extraordinary how emotionally bonded I was to the character of the Shade. The bad ending I accidentally triggered was so upsetting that I HAD to undo it (a hack; see the discussion groups to find out how).There's something about spending so much time with a character who is as lonely, naive, innocent, and melancholic as this one that made me feel like I had done him wrong, with that bad ending. I almost cried. Is that how all the kids with dead Tamagotchis felt?When I got the happy ending, I was so relieved. I consider that the proper ending. It's cute and appropriate.I couldn't leave it alone there, though, because I wanted to see what happens when the time runs out. It was what I theorized, and I did not like it, so I hacked it back to an earlier state and now I just visit the Shade every few days, giving him another book to read, in his cozy little home. I did not get all the achievements, though, and the time running out makes that now impossible, unless I reset the game. Too much effort to get that last secret...I hesitate to recommend the game because it does require a lot of patience... but, if you are unafraid to emotionally connect with fictional characters, and if you enjoy melancholic things... You might like this.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game, it's a work of art. Art on many levels and a privilege to see it unfold on my own screen, to interact with it and enjoy its many facets. What is the longing of the title? Is it the Shade's desire to see his king restored? Yes. Is it the player's desire for everything to just get a damn move on and stop taking so long? Yes. Is it also the player's inevitable ambition to furnish the Shade's cave with pictures, books, multi-coloured fires, rugs and curtains? Yes. Is it the player's inexorable need to explore every inch of the labyrinthine cave system? Yes. Is it the player's wish to find all the stuff? Yes. Yes. Yes. The Longing is a commentary on modernity, our desperate need for immediate gratification, instant satisfaction and short term gains. It sets the table with patience, long games and the kind of reward you only enjoy if you put in the hours. That's deep given the fact that few people will even read an article these days if it stretches to more than three paragraphs.There are no evisceral machine gun battles, no turn based strategies, no big puzzles to solve or over-arching exposition. There is just you, the Shade and the sleeping King, his mighty kingdom waiting to be explored and the sense that there is no hurry, no demand on the player to think fast, act quickly or try to remember which key arms them with which weapon. In many ways, this is like meditation translated into digital and graphical form. Relax into the slow, steady pace of the Shade's plodding lifestyle enhanced by a dour soundtrack designed to make you feel detached. Accept the fact that everything takes an age to accomplish and think of the experience as an enforced and much needed slowing down of the hectic sense we all feel. Believe it or not, not everything needs to be done yesterday. The Longing is the slow steady drip of water to the sculpting of stone. Watching water drip is boring, but nobody can deny the extraordinary nature of caverns, stalactites, stalagmites and river channels carved by the steady drip of water.There's a deeper longing in the Longing than those already mentioned. There's a primal sadness, a melancholy enhanced by the character of the Shade with his big yellow eyes, skinny body and forlorn expression, the solemn synth music that accompanies him through the dungeon and the trudging pace of the game. We, as players, are asked to reflect on what it is to be alive (yes, really!). Something few games do and something even fewer games do well. Well... what is it to be alive? The answer is, frustrating as hell and very, very slow paced. We're all waiting for something, though we have no idea what. We're all longing for something. Again, we don't know what. Is it transcendence? The return of a saviour? Someone to rescue us from the mess we've made of the world? I think yes, both these things. But more. The exploration of those dark, barely explored channels within ourselves. Endless passageways and chambers of memory and emotion surrounding the safe haven of hubris, self affirmation and comfort where we regularly retreat to find solace and protection from the things that really screw with our heads.There's something profound in the psyche of human beings, a pathos and wistfulness rarely drawn to the surface without very focused therapeutic pressure - and even then it remains ambiguous. The Longing doesn't tell us what the nature of that pathos and wistfulness is, but it says, "hey, look. This exists and here is a way to touch it, feel it and wonder about it. Don't feel obliged to invest your entire being into thinking about it, but drop in and out and when you do, give it some thought. Not too much thought. Just a bit. We won't put any deadline on how quickly you think. The little guy will plod and you'll muse. That's how this works."Whatever that elusive Longing is, it has to do with primal desires, caves and tunnels, exploration and discovery, fungus and cozy homeliness, a lurking, sleeping patriarchy which will eventually arise and spoil the peace and quiet of solitude, of personal reflection, of art and choice. The colours, music and aesthete we use to express ourselves. The lack of ego within the context of service to a greater community and something more than ourselves - service to a sleeping idea that will one day rise and change the world (for better or for worse).Play The Longing, but also experience it, think about it and muse over the message it wants you to grasp. There's plenty of time to do this. 399 days, in fact, which is probably long enough.

_childDocuments_.review: The more I play this game the more I realize how unique and creative it is.   I don't even know if there is anything out there that I can directly compare it too, although it reminds me of that part in Undertale where you have to wait for Sans - there are many puzzles that require you to idle. Some of the secrets in this game are very unexpected as the game often compels you to do things that no logical game ever would. While I do find that game has a painful walking speed, when you discover those secrets, there is an undeniable sense of satisfaction when your curiosity is being rewarded. Despite the slow pace of the game, it is very playful when it comes to its writing, and I really enjoy the dev's sense of humour. Essentially the goal of the game is to wait up to 400 real days represented by the counter at the top, making it kinda like a negative idling game where you are trying to reduce the timer through exploration. Now you don't actually need 400 days if you play actively, I only played for 2 and I already speeded up the time by 1000% (I assume it will take about 30 days if not less). It seems like any additional upgrades to your hideout speed up the passage of time, including drawing, making fire, and adding furniture - the comfort of the home, making it less painful to wait. Honestly, the worst part of this experience is the first 3 hours because you have to map out the areas, but once you do that, you can automatically walk to your bookmarks which also works when you not in the game. + love the sense of humour, the devs make fun of you the whole way+ actually really good narrative so far, you feel for the main character+ rewarding exploration + enjoyable atmosphere, that strong feeling of isolation + obviously the game has plenty of content, maybe not the type of content one would expect, but hey... + very good use of achievements, they are kinda like little puzzles + some customization, like moving paintings and carpets  - this is the game where you complete 90% of it in the first 3 days, and then you wait 20 days to get one of the endings. It would be nice to have a little content patch with more events later in the game, I mean the game is selling well so you might as well add more secrets. - it's not uncommon to get stuck. Usually restarting the game will eventually fix it. But man, you obviously do not want to run into any game-breaking glitches as the game is somewhat of a commitment. Fingers crossed, it has not happened yet.  - the character navigates on his own if you have a location for him to walk to, however, if you do it manually walking up and down the stairs can be annoying. Also, I think all of the doors need an entrance icon next to them - right now only some of them do.  - many people would defend this one, but honestly it would not make a huge difference if you walked faster. First of all, the time would not be affected by walking speed or the resources that you find. There are roadblocks that require a certain amount of time to pass, so even if you flew around like a Flash, you could only progress so far. There is one area where you can collect resources infinitely, so that is the only place where walking speed would be a problem. I kinda got used to the speed, but still, it feels unnecessary to me because even if I walked fast, I would have to quit and come back often anyway - you just forcing me to do the same thing more than I can tolerate. And when I say the character needs to be faster, I really mean like 20%, I have seen these rooms 30 times, I don't need to see them so much if I have to wait for event anyway.I have mixed feelings about the pacing of the game, I think it would not be very different if you walked just a little faster, but I can't deny that just about everything else is very compelling. Even if I occasionally hate certain parts of this experience, the creativity and enjoyable writing ultimately shine through its flaws. I think the immersion is by far the game's biggest asset, there were a few moments where I really felt 'Alone in the Dark'.

_childDocuments_.review: (This review is not spoiler-free; however, I will mark the section in which there are spoilers with “spoilers begin here” and “spoilers end here” inline.:THE LONGING: is a video game; however, it is very, very different than other video games. It has no legitimate gameplay mechanics other than single-click interaction with objects. There is no object of the game; there is no “winning”, no “losing”, no “bad guys” to defeat. It is simply an experience, and while you do control it to some degree, it is something that happens to you as opposed to you happening to it. The thing about :THE LONGING: that sets it apart from other games is that the games ends after 400 days in real time. You can’t set your computer’s clock foward to skip days (if you do it punishes you.) However, the time can be sped up slightly, which I will explain later.:THE LONGING: is an experience, a form of art, but not so much a game. I would still consider it a masterpiece.Mild spoiler begins here, but it takes place in the first 30 seconds of the game so it’s not a real spoiler.The game opens with the introduction of you, a cute little guy known as “the shade”, and a giant stone wizard-looking man with a massive crown and beard, known as “the king”. The king tells you that his kingdom and his powers have faded, and that he is going to sleep for 400 days to gather his remaining power. When he awakes, you are told, he will end all fear and longing. You, the shade, are all that he has left, and your sole duty is to wake him after 400 days.Mild spoiler ends here.The gameplay consists solely of two things; walking and interacting. The Shade’s little den has an armchair and a very sparsely populated bookshelf, as well as a hole in the wall he calls his “fireplace”. The “walking” element is simply hold-clicking in one direction to make him walk either left or right, and diagonally to make him walk up or down stairs. The shade’s walking is very, very slow, and the only noise is the echo of his footsteps, which very much contributes to the vibe of sheer solitude in the caves. Occasionally, you will encounter items throughout the multitued of snaking hallways and huge open caverns; lumps of coal, bits of paper and books from the library cavern. The books are real literary text, and you can read them from the Shade’s bookshelf. I will admit that I did want to read all of them (there were some good classics in there), but sadly I didn’t have the time.One feature that I did not like whatsoever at all is that the more you pimp up the shade’s home by making art with the paper and coal, and using the fireplace, etc., the faster time passes in the game; which means you can complete the game in less than 400 days. It’ll still take many months, but not all of them.The game is designed to make you very, very emotionally attached to the shade. Every so often, text will pop up on the screen; it is the shade talking to himself. The shade has a lot of personality, and he is ugly in a cute way. (Especially when he smiles.)Spoilers begin here. There are four endings to this game, I am told. I only know of one ending (the one in which the shade is obedient to the king and wakes him after 400 days.) There is a portion of the king’s underground kingdom in which the shade says “this is the entrance to the kingdom. I don’t think the king should like me to go there.” I reckon this leads to another ending. I believe the shade can escape the caverns. I don’t know about the other endings and I don’t want to look them up; I might replay the game someday.I was very, very emotional when I chose to wake the king. I know it would mean the end of the game, and I was very emotionally attached to the shade. The giant stone king slowly, slowly rises from his throne, and the caverns all around crumble and crash down. The king says he has ended all fear and longing in the world by killing everyone in it; the king and his faithful servant, the shade, are all that’s left, and they can rule over the underground kingdom (and the entire world) in solitude, forever and ever. Some months I finished the game, I emailed the developer and asked a few questions about the shade. The game starts with the shade coming out of the king’s hand; does that mean the shade was created by the king? How does he know English well enough to speak and read if he was never “born” and never taught English as you or I would have been? In the shade’s artwork, he depicts things such as daggers or spiders; how does he know what these things look like if he has never seen them before? To what degree can he understand the books he reads. For example, he has never seen a “whale”; therefore, how can he comprehend Moby ♥♥♥♥? The answer that I got back is that the shade was created by the king, and that the shade’s knowledge is simply a subset of the king’s knowledge. Also, knowledge of the external world and of things he had never seen comes from the ideology of Plato’s Theory of Forms.Spoilers end hereAll in all, I highly, highly recommend this title. It was a very emotional experience. However, I don’t think everyone would enjoy it; if you don’t see yourself as a person who would get emotional from that type of thing, or you would only play games for the “fun” mechanics or story as opposed to simply a medium of emotional expression, it’s probably not your thing. I know people that would just see it as a waste of their time. Still, I recommend it. It will probably inspire me for quite some time.Also, after the game ends, it doesn’t let you keep playing. I reckon you have to install it on a new system or purge some file.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing I liked about this game was the aesthetic and how the game is conceptualice to challenge common sense in video-games, like waiting so events will unlock instead of time-trials, forcing you into a slow-paced but rewarding experience.This game isn't gamer material if you are used to mmorpgs and shooters, but those who are hardcore explorers and obsessive completers/achievers might enjoy a different thing (like what happened with Undertale, lol).I always try earning all the Steam achievements in 'short' games and wonder why the creators wanted to offer a game with a single gameplay, with 5 possible endings, but with the complete achievements requiring one of the endings to unlock. You also need to have your computer connected to the internet to be able to play, which I highly disagree with since it forces consumers into an awkward relationship with the game and even adds an eerie element to it, hard to fully enjoy if you don't have regular access to the internet.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: My big concern going in was if I had enough stick-to-it-ness to make it through 400 days.  It turns out that you can get to the end of the game in considerably less time. The graphics look hand-drawn rather than CG and that was part of the charm.  The drawings are very detailed and something I'd frame and put on a wall.Right away you have a bookshelf with a few books.    Some are game specific, but others are out of copyright classic literature.  I did not take the time to read most of the books, but the ones I read that I have read in the past were the exact same story.  I wish I had delayed finishing the game and just took some time to read the books.  But that's what second playthroughs are for.There are puzzles, a large range of complexity but none were seemingly impossible.  I found simply exploring the map was the greatest puzzle as it's not logically laid out in important places, I'm certain on purpose.Travel to places can be time consuming as the clock runs at a set pace and your character isn't that fast.  Make sure to allow real time if you want to go someplace pretty far from your current location.  There is no option to "teleport" with an appropriate amount of time removed from the clock.And a little tip, if you are taking your laptop to work and playing this game on your lunch break,  you care about your character's virtual comfort, don't like a smelly fire on your lunch break.  He'll have to sleep on the stone outside his room until the fire dies out and you can log into your computer again to move him.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Patience.That is the key to the game, for you will need a lot of it. There are positives and negatives to this game but overall its a good buy and id highly recommend it.Highly addicting, the Longing provides a vast cave world for you to explore in at a mild walking pace. You will not go any faster than walking, and walk you will, quite literally everywhere. while there are a lack of 'exciting' events going on, i find myself coming back to this game everyday to see how things progress, the game runs at real time (for the most part). The connection you make with the shade really sinks in and you find yourself caring for him, his wants, his thoughts, as if they were your own. ill keep playing till 400 days past me by, and ill most likely keep playing after that as well.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: If this would be another game, I would say, "I'm wasting my time with this, I will stopp here", after a few minutes and seeing how slowly your chacter walks and that everything needs a lot of time to progress.But that is the point of this game, and thereby you will have the chance to think about time, patience and what it's worth.It's hard to say if you will like this game, I liked it, but this could have been MUCH more, because even if patience is key here, there could have been way more things to do and investigate in this world.I will be honest, at the end I checked some walkthrough to see, if I missed some major points, but it would have needed just much more time, to get some additional achivements. _childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an enigma. It turns exploration, "crafting" and "basebuilding" into idle mechanics. It pushes you over boundaries by grabbing hold of your curiosity and rewarding your patience, and using time, REAL time, as the mechanic makes every decision feel weighty. The result of this is you feel what the character feels. You experience it, and consider it, just as he is.This game is truly an artistic journal on loneliness and longing.★★★✰✰/★★★★★ Outstanding art pieceI have a feeling this rating will go up once I've beaten it >.>

_childDocuments_.review: (This review contains spoilers. Do not read any spoiler tags, as the game is best played with no prior information. Trust me, the game is definitely worth playing if you are currently on the fence.)Here are the best things about this game:- Tim Burton meets Dr. Seuss art style.- This game is hilarious. The character has an amusing sense of humor about his situation with a dark streak to it. He can go from ambivalent to suddenly depressing in his tone, and that juxtaposition was very funny to me. You'll know what I mean after traveling through the first few areas. The humor keeps you entertained throughout the slower pace of the game. - Moody synth/ambient soundtrack. It perfectly captures the mystery and uncertainty of the game.- Unique usage of idle game mechanics to augment the more central puzzle/adventure game play.- A relatively simple/vague story that immediately builds intrigue and maintains it throughout. I absolutely recommend this game. I found myself easily warming up to the slow pace of the game, and it truly felt like a long and vast journey by the end of it. My only complaints are some minor performance issues and some obtuse puzzles, but overall these do not ruin the game. I tried to be super completionist and locate everything and do everything I could, but honestly you'll be less frustrated if you just go with the flow of the game and not worry about missing anything. The devs did a great job with making sure you know when you are doing something that will have permanent effects on your character's journey.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most engaging games? I've played. Well done, and thoroughly enjoyable, if a bit mysterious and difficult. I'm playing it a second time; yes, I know it was intended as a one-shot experience, but consider how it might be to live your life over again, with full memory. Life is full of pitfalls, missed opportunities and mistakes. How nice it might be to live it again in the same circumstances with the ability to avoid the pitfalls and take advantage of the previously missed opportunities. yeah, I know, life's not like that - but this isn't life, it's a simulation of a Shade's life, and I like the little guy. _childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to give this a thumbs up, truly.  The story and goal is original, especially among idle games where the vast majority is about climbing numbers.  The art style is unique and well done, the controls easy.  From a technical standpoint, it's really a good, simple game with an interesting concept.  It's the execution of said concept that I have issues with.  I'm okay with real time games, considering AC and it's many iterations.  But there is a quirk here, I'll call it 'precise randomness', that ultimately put me off.  Let me explain.Certain events, especially optional ones, occur at very specific times, .  No, the time won't be wrong, but it's a 50/50 if the event will actually occur despite the time being correct.  In order to guarantee getting the event, you would have to practically babysit the game, which is not quite how idle games tend to work.  (I gave up on one optional event because no matter how many times I went to the correct spot at the correct time, it never occurred.)Even getting the ending I wanted had this issue, because while the event did occur, if you're not paying attention or know what to expect, the different between a good end or a dead one is down to 50/50 on whether the circumstances are correct, or you have to wait an entire day and hope this time they will be.  You can speed up or reverse time (the second happens late game) but it felt less like an idle game and more like a waiting game, that you had to watch very carefully.Given the concept, the balance of precision and rng I feel was flawed, and kept a unique game from being truly outstanding.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: "I don't need to rush. I have all the time I could ever hope for."The Longing is a curious and unusual game. At the onset of the game you are given your one and only objective: to await for 400 days, until your King awakens from a deep slumber. Atop the screen there is a clock, counting down in real time. The game tells you that the clock will keep counting down even if you are not playing.And if you so choose, that is really all there is. Sure, you can roam around the Kings underground domain, collect things into your home to make it a little more comfortable. And maybe, just maybe, there is more to this game?I guess it's not too much of a spoiler to admit there is. The game even hints as much early on, and does so repeatedly and more strongly as time goes on. I don't know how many endings there are, but I found mine after some 23 hours.In fact, this is the only real issue I had with the game at all. I found an ending to the game almost by accident, without meaning to, and once you end your game there isn't really a way back.Aside from the potential to accidentally end your game earlier than intended, The Longing is impeccably well made. The lonesome dialogue of the protagonist, the somber ambient music that envelops the Kings realm, the particularly lovely hand drawn art style and rich animations whene appropriate, it all serves perfectly to create a haunting, lonely feeling in which finding a shiny rock is truly a delight and a marvel!This type of slow game is definitely not for everyone. There is no grand sense of progress, no action sequence to unlock. In fact there is very little to do, and it's quite telling of the games nature that you can read entire full books as part of the game. I did, though only some of the shorter ones.There was surely still much more for me to see...Playtime: 23+ hours (A single playthrough)Ratings (1-10)Visual: 10Audio: 10Story: 8Gameplay: 9Overall: 10
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Wait forever just to be depressed, yay.The Longing like it advertises itself it's a waiting game, but far from an idle one.You'll be stumped at places where it will take weeks, even months to open up but still leave you with stuff to do, like explore the caverns of this world, gather materials, read books, draw suff and more, this is also unfortunate one of my biggest complaints, there isn't enough stuff to do to "keep busy" and maybe that's the point of the game. If I could update this game in any way I wanted I'd make the world much bigger, have the clock always tick down in real time, have to manially drag resources back to the various homes you could build in the kingdom as well as many other ways to pass the time like making an ant colony, or talking your time to sketch maps of the places you visit.All and all was a novel idea that needs some working in to make the game great, but right now it's still something precious.

_childDocuments_.review: I had never played an idle game before (at least not this kind of game), and this was quite an intriguing and compelling game to play. But this might not be a game for everyone. If you enjoy exploration games and are patient enough, this might be a game for you.We play as a lonely shade living underground, who is given the task to wait 400 days before the awakening of its king.Given that the Longing is an idle game (the game progress on its own), it means that after starting the game and watching the intro, you could just shut it down, then launch it again 400 RL days later (or modify your computer clock, which should work too) to see the game ending. But you bought the game right? So I assume you might want to experience some gameplay. For the exploration lover, there is a huge labyrinth of caves to explore, secrets to discover and objects to find/collect/make to decorate the little shade home cave. You will also find ways to make the in-game time go faster. You can easily complete the game in one or two months depending on your choice of gameplay.As time passes, our little shade will share various thoughts/observations about its life, wishes or discoveries, which gives a philosophical aspect to the game. In-game events will also occur and affect the game progress.The pace is slow (the shade walks very slowly and events/actions takes time) which is actually really good if you just need to relax. The game gives you all the tools to take your time and manage it as you want. In all, this is a very unique game with nice art, a beautiful soundtrack that fits perfectly the game atmosphere, and a lovable but pitiful main character we just wish we could make happy.I really enjoyed it, but it really depends on what kind of gamer you are.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this so much that I'm debating buying the plushie for the shade, but depending on what you want from this game - you might not enjoy it at all. It was none of the things I expected going into it. If you aren't sure you'll enjoy this, ask yourself the following questions: Are you patient? Can you make your own fun and set your own goals? Are you tenacious about solving puzzles and vague hints? If you answered no to any of those questions, you might really hate :the longing:, purely because you'll be doing a lot of waiting, thinking, and trial and error. You'll probably play this a few times before you get to the ending differences.That being said, this isn't really an idle game in the same sense that a lot of people might be used to. A "run" is real-time 400 days and you basically have to entertain yourself in a massive cave until the old geezer wakes up. Thing is, the cave itself is pretty small and you can walk from one side to another in about an hour and the halls of eternity -which is the only place you CAN perpetually walk- stops your timer. So for the large majority, you are sitting around waiting for time-based puzzles to finish - ie "wait for the moss to grow, wait for the rock to fall, wait for the pool to fill" in actual weeks. You'll only log on to check, then go offline again. Or you can sit and read books with the Shade.(A quick side note to that is the game will get angry at you if you "cheat" and change your windows time to trick the game. But unfortunately it's only way of noticing the "cheat" is by going "this person hasn't played in a while, they must've skipped" and doesn't count on the fact someone might just be outside touching grass or playing different games. That's very aggravating.) Now this would've been fine and a neat experience in and of itself to hang out with this shade for 400 real days and just enjoying the frankly immaculate vibes this game gives you. I personally love games you have to dig your heels in with, and was ready to spend a long time with this game. - But your "house" which is arguably the nicest, cosiest place you can vibe with Shade will speed up time considerably the nicer you make the house. At once point, I was playing the 400 days thirty times faster than I was supposed to. Every 1 second was 30 seconds in the game, which artificially lowered the waiting time because of the brief "time flies when you're having a nice time" joke. Which was cute, admittedly. But I bought this early December, I've only played 60 hours and I'm 200 days in. It's definitely not the idle game it can appear to be, and you never have to actually wait 400 days - ever. Maybe that's not a problem to you. I enjoyed my time with Shade, and the vibes of the game, enough that I was endeared to it despite it's flaws, and the only thing this speed-up gave me personally was sadness that the runs end quicker. But it wasn't what I was expecting and had I answered "no" to any one of my earlier questions - I would've given up and been mad I couldn't refund this because there is admittedly very little to do - and coming to any of these conclusions for yourself would be well outside the refund period. Consider it a social experiment about yourself, I suppose. You'll lose £13 either way, but you might really enjoy yourself. Either way, it's a game I'm glad I can say I played and tried out.

_childDocuments_.review: All my life I thought I was fairly patient (well up to a point of no return that is). This game took me to new levels of patience. You learn to just take things as they come. Ok - I understand it is not your type of game.Those who do not like this game and played less than an hour? You have no idea whether you actually like this game or not. Play it again. Go back to a time when getting to the summit as fast as possible was not the goal. Go back to a time where how you made the climb was the actual reward.Play it or play it again. _childDocuments_.review: Picture you are the shade, as a human, trying to get out of a permanently depressed state with limited resources, and it feels like no one can help you, and any positive thing you do doesn't matter. What if becoming the darkness and acknowledging your longing, but also actively trying to escape it, was the key?You have to change yourself, and your environment, even if no one else will. Even if it feels like you're getting nowhere, or the impact is small, to beat the darkness.And maybe then, you'll come out of the longing with intercession from a loving family, a higher power, or self-fulfillment from the knowledge that you were really the king all along.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing it´s def one of the most surreal experiences I have had over many years of gaming. Not in the sense that the game it´s fill with odd things, but because it´s a game which you play by waiting mostly. It´s a completely unique way to approach a gaming experience that I have no idea how the devs came up with and also masterfully excecute it when there are no precedents of it.You start on the day the king creates you, a shadow, just a small and slow humanoid dark thing that looks weak and fragile. Your only reason to be it´s to wake up the king from his slumber of 400 days... that occur in REAL TIME. From that moment you are completely free, you can wake up the king from the go, you can explore, but most importantly, you can wait. The game is always running, this character lives under the same time rules as you do in real life. You could play one day and not return in two months and the shade would have just stay there, for 60 days, sleeping on the cold floor of the massive cave he and the king inhabit, dreaming. The character is, and exists, just as you do, bound in time. You cannot pause the game, you cannot return to an old save, you cannot change the date of your computer to a later day or it will notice and punish you. Completionist now are probably thinking better to avoid it then, but don´t worry, you have plenty of time in those 400 days to achieve anything in the game.As you explore the cave and found new things you start to interact with the main puzzle or challenge of the game, waiting. Drops of water that fall from stalactite will make a pond, mosh will grow, mushroom will repproduce, and all of it can be used to either progress your path or just create decorations for your own small piece of the cave. But you gotta wait for it. The game becomes quite frankly meditating, with a soundtrack that hits you on specific moments with what I can only describe as "cave dweller wave", the sense of imprisioment it´s there and yet our character doesn´t seem to be weighted by it in a way more fitting to horror games even when there´s certainly some horror themes presented but from the perspective of the shade, they are just things that are because they are meant to be. The shade can remember places and you can go from one to other, you could spend 15 minutes playing just watching this critter walk from one place of the cave to the other and just dwell on the atmosphere and ambient of the game.It´s the equivalent in gaming to video experiences like Wavelength (1967, from Michael Snow) or Sleep (1964, Andy Warhol), except that unlike those filmed experiences, this one does have a real narrative, it has a point, it´s actually saying something rather than just experience with a new format without really adding art into it (which it may have being the intention of those movies, but gaming it´s a far more active entertainment). I have being completely mesmerized by this game experience and I really think a lot of people would if they give it the chance, it may not be for everyone, but if it clicks for you, it really clicks, and you are provided with one of the more unique games I played in the last decade for sure. A rate it 34 out of 34 coal rocks and 3 crudly painted spiders.

If you can't, his struggles should bring smile and you'll find his commentaries funny.I had a lot of fun wandering around and getting lost in the underground caves (don't worry Shade would always find his way home on its own), and then I was having another fun part by drawing my own a map on a piece of paper (this place is a labyrinth). _childDocuments_.review: 10/10. A beautiful game about loneliness that is charming, melancholy, and atmospheric. After the weeks I spent playing this game I felt a genuine connection to The Shade, which lead me to open the game everyday and do whatever I could to help end their longing. Their infrequent  dialogue is quaint and sad, and gives them a believably real personality. The way time passes in the game is very unique, often requiring you to slow down and wait for several days in real time before being able to explore certain areas, and it made me all the more immersed in the story of the game. This is not a game you can speed through; you have to be patient, and let yourself enjoy exploring the game and getting to know the mysteries around you. When I finally finished the game (no spoilers), the story and The Shade stayed with me for a long time afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a review, but I think this is exactly the game I was looking for. I'm always on the computer. Even worse, I'm addicted to social media and games in general. _childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly as advertised. It's essentially a game you'll ignore a lot of the time, and have running in the background other times. It's definitely not a game I would classify as my "favorite", because it's not really a video game so much as it is... an idle game. The difference is instead of microtransactions and hitting that dopamine spike when you click some big number or roll that rare loot, it's story based. And it really builds up this old feeling of nostalgia for me. Remember when you were a kid and you'd spend an hour doing something really pointless in your favorite video game? Just to explore and see what's going on? And then the rush when you finally do it and you see that stupid easter egg or some other thing you had never seen before in the game? I mean, some people still have that as adults, but I feel like I lost it as I got older. In this game, that's really all this is. A huge time wait for the simplest reveal. But somehow it feels worth it. It has really reinspired my drive to explore in a video game instead of rushing to finish it or trying to get all the achievements or any other thing I've come to do in my adult years. I have spent hours in this game, actually paying attention to it, and I've spent hours of this game idling it. I'd say about half-and-half now. I think it's worth the $15 just because the story is captivating and it has gotten my attention for at least an hour or two a day. Which is better than Animal Crossing, these days, considering the lack of updates. lol.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I would definitely give it full points. The whole story takes patience to go through but the lonely feelings revoke the peace and complicate emotions inside of me. Trying to find more profound things out of this game after enjoying (cuz i just played for 3 hrs so far). Anyway, recommend it to those who enjoy being alone and get plenty of time to "waste". Hopefully there's going to be more games like this type, I love it so much!
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of fun with this game, but I can't say I'd recommend it to others. My favorite part of the game was discovering and reading different books, and the timer gave me more motivation to get through as many as I could. But since these books are open domain, I could just read them for free, so I decided to interact with the actual game:I played the game entirely blind, so I missed a ton of things, but when I completed the game and looked it all up, I had very little emotional attachment to any of the endings or secrets. Some of the puzzles I loved, most were stupid. And the rewards are decorations that speed time up, which gave me less time to read the books and to my knowledge there's no way to get rid of them - so that frustrated me. I only found the way to reverse time at the end of the game, which couldn't rewind faster than time moved forward so it was entirely useless.All in all, it's a very novel time waster. Interesting in concept, sometimes even fun, but it's basically a time soak like it says on the tin. The themes about depression and the finite nature of life fell somewhere between sincere and "overly artsy" so I wasn't sure if it was supposed to be comedic. I'm definitely getting that reading list though, and I'll read them next to a real fire this time.

_childDocuments_.review: From the moment you begin "The Longing," it becomes clear that this isn't your typical video game. Every ounce of the experience has been designed to challenge your preconceived notions about time, patience, and the role of the player in the narrative.Playing as the last servant of a sleeping king in a vast underground kingdom, you're tasked with waiting 400 real-time days for your monarch to awaken. The premise alone should be enough to intrigue anyone with an interest in unconventional storytelling methods.But "The Longing" is more than a mere experiment in video game narrative structure. It's a breathtakingly beautiful exploration of solitude, contemplation, and the passage of time, wrapped up in a package that's as enchanting as it is unique.The game's art style is a major standout. With its hand-drawn graphics, the kingdom's echoing caverns and towering halls exude an atmosphere that is haunting yet captivating. The game's use of color and light combined with a minimalistic yet effective soundscape takes the player on an emotional journey that feels profoundly personal."The Longing" also introduces an innovative layer of interactivity. The things you can do to pass the time - reading books, decorating your home, exploring the vast network of tunnels - aren't merely distractions. They're integral parts of the game that help to build a deeper connection to the character and the world. The pacing, though slow by conventional standards, is a masterstroke. The real-time countdown isn't just a gimmick; it fundamentally alters the way you engage with the game. The creeping sense of time passing, and the anticipation of the king's awakening, is a constant companion, lending an intensity to even the smallest actions."The Longing" isn't just a game; it's a reflection on solitude, a meditation on time, and an exploration of the human condition. Its unique gameplay mechanics, atmospheric visuals, and thought-provoking themes come together to create an experience that lingers long after the king's awakening.In the end, "The Longing" is more than worth the wait. It's a testament to the power of patience and a beacon for games as a medium for storytelling. It doesn't just invite you to play; it invites you to ponder, to reflect, and to feel.So, if you're ready for a gaming experience that will challenge your perception of time and leave an indelible mark on your psyche, then dive into "The Longing." It's a journey you won't soon forget.

_childDocuments_.review: One day I stumbled upon The Longing, but I didn’t fully grasp what I was signing up for. A game where time itself is stretched endlessly, where progress was defined not by battles or skill, but by patience. The Shade, who now sits by my side on the computer desk (just a plushie), a lonely figure, tucked away in a dark cavern, waiting for 400 days with no instruction, no purpose, just lots of time. I thought it was just a game, but as days turned into weeks, and weeks into months, I began to realize it wasn’t merely about a kingdom, its king or its servant. It was about me. This was not my first time meeting myself in a game, for I had traveled inwards into my own mind with Mountain.I was accompanying Shade. Lost in the quiet corners of my own mind, waiting for something to happen. But as time wore on, it became clear: life doesn’t hand you transformation. It’s something you must carve out of the stone walls of existence, one slow, deliberate pickaxe hit at a time. Just like Shade had to do to progress in the mines. At the beginning, the first dreary steps, Shade walked slowly, almost agonizingly slow. I was impatient. I found myself wishing it would move faster, explore quicker, cover more ground, see more places. Yet, as I watched the small figure tread carefully through the dark tunnels, I began to confront something I hadn’t expected: my own discomfort with stillness.The Shade’s pace opposed my own restless heart. In most games I was always rushing without truly noticing where I was going or why. In the game, there was no choice but to slow down, to accept the pace, to be in the moment. And with that, a shift began. I realized that in my life, I was avoiding stillness because it revealed all the things I wasn’t ready to confront: fears, uncertainties, boredom. Sometimes I felt like making progress and then came face to face with a place I couldn’t go through, or I had to wait 2 weeks. These roadblocks felt rage-inducing to me at the beginning.Just like The Shade, as days slowly went by, I started to accept that movement is not always progress. Stillness itself is a form of growth. To sit with yourself, in the quiet, is to face the parts of you that the noise drowns out. I would sit in my room looking at the screen, and Shade would sit in his small cave. The cave started as a cold empty space, and as days went by I found stuff to bring back to the cave and make it feel more like home.see my shared screenshotsThe Shade slowly walked through the sprawling underground world, and there were moments of discovery. A new cavern, a hidden room, a charcoal buried in the ground after falling from the ceiling. Some of these things held value immediately, while others seemed meaningless at first. But everything in this subterranean world had a purpose, though it was not always immediately clear. From time to time I got lost, thankfully Shade’s ability to return home came in very handy. Everytime I arrived back home all those things I found while exploring waited for me there, looking at the Shade’s yellow eyes for some short of emotion to surface, but none did.And so it was in my own life. Each new experience, each challenge, each hidden corner of myself I unearthed began to weave together into a greater understanding of who I was. I had long been seeking instant gratification, instant meaning, yet this game, with its slow revelations, reminded me that not everything important is immediately visible. Sometimes, meaning grows slowly, like moss or mushroom in the dark tunnels. You have to tend to it, nurture it with patience and care. At the time of playing this game I was going through some strifes in life, and everything I learned from Shade I could use myself.I watched Shade collect books to pass the time or make art in solitude, I reflected on the some pursuits I had once abandoned. I remembered important people in my life  again, not because it would improve my life immediately, but because the act of reaching out to others and acknowledging their importance itself was worthwhile. I began to explore new horizons, new places, not with the expectation of finding immediate purpose but because I was learning to trust that meaning would emerge in its own time.Shade was alone, but so was I, in many ways. Not physically, but emotionally. The game’s quiet, desolate atmosphere became a mirror to the isolation I had felt but hadn’t acknowledged. It forced me to sit with my solitude, to question why I feared it. In the stillness of the game’s world, I realized that loneliness wasn’t something to be escaped but something to be understood. Turns out loneliness is not to be avoided for the sake of it, it’s meant to be understood so when you fill that emptiness with something meaningful, you can cherish it. Solitude can be fertile ground for growth. It can be a place where the truest parts of yourself begin to emerge. In those long, quiet hours, I learned that I didn’t need to fill every silence with noise or every moment with distraction.This perfectly ties into the gameplay, Time Manipulation. Filling the emptiness of the cave we called home helped. That's what I meant with “filling emptiness with meaningful stuff”. Items like books, drawings, a lit fire in the home and shiny crystals help soothe Shade’s loneliness, subtly accelerating the 400-day wait.Every achievement I unlocked in the game came not from rushing, but from slow, consistent progress. And I began to see that my life, too, was like this. That the small, seemingly insignificant choices I made each day were slowly carving out a version of myself that I could be happier about each day.Suddlendly, the 400 days dwindled, I had to decide what to do. I won’t spoil anything about the endings, I will just say that I reserved the best one for my last playthrough. And since I left the game rolling with the good ending cinematic, I could appreciate how long Shade had come, and how long I should also expect myself to go. We are never truly passive in life; we always have the choice to shape our own path, to decide when to break free, when to remain still, and when to move forward.The Longing was a game, but it became a metaphor for my life. A reminder that transformation is not a sudden event, it is a slow, quiet process that unfolds in the background, in the stillness of everyday choices. And in that waiting, I became something more. I became myself.The atmosphere in this game is absolutely incredible. The art style is really on point for those of us that enjoy underground kingdoms. Caverns went on for miles in the background, making me feel a very small thing surrounded by dark vastness. Helping the atmosphere was also the music, the soundtrack really pulls everything together, specially The King. Everytime I heard that song play my mind would start drifting, imagining great halls and what the kingdom could have been before its unexplained downfall.

_childDocuments_.review: This is another one of those games that makes me wish there was a middle rating between Yes and No.I liked it, I really did. _childDocuments_.review: I honestly wasn't expecting much from this game, I only saw a youtube video about a game that was 400 days long and I was interested in checking it out. My main mindset when I first started playing was as if the game was some sort of challenge that was testing my patience and I needed to beat it (like any sweaty gamer) but honestly the game didn't even feel that difficult? If that makes sense. The game is more about making the gameplay more enjoyable by coping with your current situation and doing things while the timer ticks down. Oh and yes, just for clarification, the game doesn't actually take "400 days" to complete. I finished it in about 4 months because there are ways to increase the timer's speed and the timer still goes on when you aren't playing. That is why I only have 40 or so hours in the game that supposedly has 400 days worth of content. And honestly, this game has uber amounts of content. I hardly even finished a quarter of the game's full content and I had 4 months to do it all. I don't want to spoil too much about the game but you will always have *something* to do when you boot up the game. The problem though, is that the content is not very... high quality, according to what she said ;). For example most of the content in the game is reading. Yep. Reading. In this $15 game there are at least 20+ books to read with some of them probably costing more than the game itself and I didnt even unlock all of them. I personally like reading but I dont have the will to read THAT many books. And these are REAL books too, you can literally read Moby ♥♥♥♥ in this game. So even if I don't think the game itself has too good of content, if you like reading a lot of books, this game might as well be saving you money on all the books you would get. But regarding the rest of the gameplay every moment you are walking around you will be able to see amazing hand drawn art in every scene, as well as pretty good music to accompany it. Sometimes I would just walk around just to look at stuff because it was so well made. It honestly looks like someone painted it. The problem with this though is that there really isn't that much area to explore. At the beginning sure the whole cave seemed like a lot but I was able to explore around half of the whole map in 2 days as well as memorize all the passageways. And while the content the game does provide does relatively make up for this I did feel like that I was only able to see new stuff for maybe 10-15 hours of my entire gameplay? And dear god some of the things you have to get to take forever if you need to go back there for something. I kid you not there are some points in this game where you have to wait so long for something to be done you either just have to leave the game to do something else or just play another game. That though is probably the only downside I had with this game since I really don't feel that you should have to play another game in order to play this one. But other than that I don't think I have found another game more chill than this one. Sometimes when I got pretty heated playing a competitive game like TF2 I would come to this game to chill out and relax. So in conclusion, you should totally get this game if you love books as well as video games but if you absolutely have no patience for anything you should definitely not get this game since you will probably die of boredom. But personally I really enjoyed it and the ending seemed pretty nice for the whole struggle I went through playing it.
