_childDocuments_.review: This is a very slow paced and relaxing game. The Shade is very good company. It's a pleasant experience over-all, and when the game ended, I found myself missing it. It's like nothing I've ever played before.I struggle with insomnia, so I spent sleepless nights quietly exploring the cave systems with my little shade buddy, scavenging things to make the home base cozier and increase the books available to read there. It was such a calm and relaxing way to pass time, it was easy to sleep afterwards.Other times, I'd use the little buddy for body-doubling, an ADHD management tactic where having someone hang out with you can help you stay on task. I'd set Shade auto-walking somewhere and listen to the footsteps, or in the chair auto-reading a book and listen to the pages turning while I focused on my own task. It helped me finish a few projects I'd been neglecting. I couldn't believe it actually worked! I think it's because Shade makes slow but steady progress and takes a long time to do things. _childDocuments_.review: The Longing is a good game, but it's more than just a game. It a game that speaks to the player about our existential place in the world. It does this by leading by example as we are forced to relate to the Shade. Progress is gratingly slow, pushing the player to be patient and tenacious, just like the Shade. This extended waiting period compels the player to thoroughly examine both the game's world and our lovely Shade. The experience forces you to coexist with the Shade as intimately as the Shade coexists with the caves he inhabits, finding similarities in many ways.I interpreted the moral of this story somewhat differently from others. I believe it centers on finding semblances of happiness regardless of one's situation. It is about discovering sweetness in bitterness, glimpses of light in utter darkness, and the end of a tunnel that stretches to infinity, whatever end that may well be (). I recommend The Longing to everyone, as the Shade's journey speaks to every one of us.My interpretations & spoilers (only for those that completed the game):

_childDocuments_.review: While others have done excellent reviews on what you do in the game, I will attempt to explain the point of playing it. Right off the bat, I just want to make it clear you, the player, does not actually have to wait 400 days in real life to beat the game. The exploration of the environments reveals items that make the countdown go more quickly, even while you're not playing the game.Onto the actual review...I am not one to write reviews, but this game is wholeheartedly different from any other I have played. I am of the opinion that if you come to this game with a traditional sense of what a video game is then you will find it in some way boring, tedious, or shallow. If you, however, purchase this game and come at it with an open mind, then you will enjoy an experience like no other. This game is purposefully slow. Your character moves with little more purpose than to put one foot in front of the other to get to its destination. Throughout your mutual journey, the Shade will reflect on who it is, and the world around it. Some other reviews have expressed frustrations with mistakes they made that wasted their time. I was the kind of player who tried to discover every nook and cranny; many of the frustrations expressed by others were actually cleverly forewarned throughout the environment. Overall I would call ‘The Longing’ one of the few actual experiences that I have had in video games. Though I personally was not happy with the ending I chose (there are four that I know of), that does not mean I regret the journey I had with the Shade. This game means more to the player, the more they related to it throughout their journey. If you play this game with an open mind, then I can almost guarantee you will enjoy a very thought-provoking and unique journey.

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely game! Slow-paced for sure, but that allows you to take your time and check in a little every day - or not. _childDocuments_.review: Not exactly the greatest title to hold, but it's a noteworthy title nonetheless. Idler games are notoriously known for just being time wasters or often even worse, money wasters. The Longing is not that at all. With its interesting character study, handling of certain themes, and unique art style, I think it's a potential buy for some people. I definitely don't think this game is for everyone, but it has a crowd that it'll appeal to. The Longing is a game that I recommend doing a bit of research on before buying it to find out if you're in that crowd, but I can make that research all plugged in right here. Regardless, I originally thought this game was going to be one I never even played after picking it up in a bundle, but I'm glad I did.Let's get to the breaking point for the majority of people. The main mechanic of The Longing isn't some action-packed combat or intelligent puzzle design, it's waiting. It's objectively the most boring thing about any video game. But The Longing had the balls to make this drag of a feature in most games into its focal point. The primary goal of The Longing is to wake up a sleeping deity-like king 400 days into his slumber as his living alarm clock. You'll be spending hours waiting for doors to open, days for a stalactite to fall into place to make a bridge, and weeks for moss to grow. And all of this is in real time. Well, technically. As you progress through the game you'll find ways to make time speed up at a faster rate in your room. Having paintings you make and decorations you find to liven your room up causes time to accelerate at a faster rate by itself, but you can also read books and play some music to make it go by even faster. All of the books you find are real world ones, available through the game without a fee on the dev. You start out with all of Moby ♥♥♥♥ right away and it's easily one of the longest ones you're ever given. The time acceleration, the fact that it counts down when the game isn't open, and the fact that waiting the full 400 days is only needed for 1 of the multiple endings means that waiting game isn't nearly as bad as you might think. I think this idea for a game is outstandingly risky, but I think there should've been more to pass the time for the player. The only thing you, the player, do is read a book to pass the time and it's objectively faster to just let the Shade idle it over time. I think it would've been better if there was more to do in your room after you find stuff in the cave, like allowing you to create your own custom drawings or playing full-on songs with your instrument. More decorations to personalize the cave would have been nice as well. It's an innovating idea, but it needs work.I don't give out a gold star and a "good job" for just making a good waiting game though. It's the handling of this mechanic tied into the game's storytelling that makes the game for me. The story of the game is simple and small, but it's drawn out for the course of the 400 day journey to make the player connected to the Shade, the playable character. Even if you only spend a week with the little guy, you still spent more time managing his activities than most game protagonists. It's attempt at personally connecting the player to its main character without the use of meta storytelling or fourth wall breaks. And it works. The Longing covers themes of isolation and loneliness and the way it ties back into that mechanic is dark. What's a waiting game for you is a never ending nightmare of being alone with desperate attempts to sway away boredom for the main character. The Shade will briefly mention looking for a friend or wanting something as simple as the noise of running water to provide him entertainment. It's a spin on the horrors of isolation from someone not suffering from it, but rather seeing it through the eyes of someone who's only ever experienced it. You might be decorating your room to beat the game faster, but the Shade is doing it to actually keep himself sane. You do end up actually meeting other living things while playing the game but your interactions with them are minimal. Mostly because they're either a living face in a wall or a measly spider that's incapable of real communication. And the Shade feels overjoyed at these interactions when they aren't even real relationships with another person. I felt myself caring about the little guy a bit and you ,as the player, have the job of giving him a proper ending. Whether it's a happy ending, a sad ending, or an oddly bittersweet ending is up to you. But whatever you do, he won't be suffering from loneliness anymore.Oh and as for some important notes on actually playing the game: I mentioned earlier that the in-game timer keeps going when the application is closed. This applies to everything in the game. This includes whatever you tell the Shade to do. Walking somewhere, mining some coal, reading a book, etc. can all be done while you're doing other things. So read a book of your own, play a different game, do some chores or anything really to pass the time on your own accord. Sort of loops back to that relationship with the Shade since you're both just passing time waiting for the big moment. You can even turn off the soundtrack and sound effects while running the game so it's less intrusive. Speaking of which, the soundtrack is alright. It's something I'm never going to listen to outside of the game, but it does fit into the game's theming like everything else with its foreboding presence and the fact that it loops endlessly. Also I really like the art style! I believe Anselm Pyta and Laura Brosi were the game's artists, and they did a really good job. I love the big eyes and sort of texture everything and everyone has on them. It feels like an old fashioned fairy tale story. I'm tempted to check out other games they've been involved in just for that art style since I'm a fan of more unique-looking games over realistic-looking ones. I'm rambling at this rate but the art direction is good. Oh and there's even more ways the game mechanic ties into the story than I mentioned.So what do I think about The Longing in short? It's a neat little experimental idea of a game. I like it. It's nowhere near the perfect attempt at the goal it's trying to achieve, but I think it's cool nonetheless. Again, I'm applauding the handling of its major mechanic and its connection to the game's storytelling. With some minor praise towards the artwork and the fact that it gave me faith in a genre riddled with monetization and laziness. I feel happy with giving this game a 7/10. And hey, it got one update in the past, so here's hoping for more in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know exactly, what this game is doing right. Maybe it's the hand drawn backgrounds, maybe the slow pacing or the sad but cute main character. This game is hypnotic. And, it makes me smile for some reason. It makes you think about all the long times you're waiting for something, and what you're doing with the time given. The game has a soothing effect, definitely. I like it, and I wonder what will happen in 394 days.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Dont buy if youre looking for something fast paced, but if you like to relax and enjoy artistic scenery at times then this is the game for you.Upon further reflection from my initial review, I've come to the conclusion that this game is like raising a plant. It requires time, attention, and energy, but not a ton. It doesn't demand those things like most games do, rather, if you come back to it you find it becomes a facet of your life which grows alongside you and brightens your day (despite it's dark aesthetic).I love this game, but I certainly don't think it's for everyone. If you like raising plants, you'll probably love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game is profound. It pulls you in with its incredible artwork and keeps you coming back. Building an emotional connection to the shade and watching his journey through the 400 days is an experience I will treasure for life. This game makes you consider your connections to those in your life and appreciate the experience of being human. I am so glad to have experienced this game. My shade will be a part of me forever.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game filled to the brim with exciting content full of action, exciting gameplay mechanics and an enticing plot with twists and turns hitting you at breakneck speeds, The Longing is not the game for you. There are plenty of games out there sold at a similar pricepoint which will be able to deliver all that. If you're, however, looking for a long-term commitment that will actually require you to pay attention to your environment and be patient to progress - as opposed to just running through the entire game in a few hours, learning the meta and then doing the same thing again, but quicker - or a game experience that is most likely unlike anything you've ever played before, consider it.The very premise of The Longing, which is "Wait for 400 days and see what happens at the end," seems absurd, and if you do decide to give this game a go, you may decide to just quit and get it refunded after realising there isn't really much else to do but , and nobody would blame you for that. The fact the main gameplay mechanic is  is diametrically opposed to everything we've become accustomed to in modern gaming.If you can, however, come to terms with this, you're in for a delightful experience. I've been playing for a few days now, and I've caught myself multiple times thinking about how I can't wait to get back home and check out the caves to see if anything's changed, or feverishly waiting for enough time to pass for the next area of the caves to open when the moss in a pit has finally grown enough to break a jump, a wonky stalactite has finally fallen from the floor and filled in a destroyed flight of stairs or water has filled up a pit droplet by droplet so I can finally swim across in order to climb up a previously inaccessible ledge and go on.Thankfully, you don't need to constantly  for time to pass - when you decide to close it, time will keep running just as it would if you were in-game. Decorating, making a fire, taking a nap or reading in The Shade's home will make time pass faster while The Shade is at home, so you can improve the place a bit, leave the game for the day while you're out at work or running errands or whatever and come home to find a full day has passed in the few hours you were gone. You can also just do  and forget about the game, then come back in 400 real-life days and finish it instantly if that's what you want to do.The aforementioned Shade, the character the player controls during the game, is also strangely endearing. It has no personality whatsoever and seemingly exists only to serve the King, but the oftentimes humorous bits of dialogue (or, since it's always by itself, just , I guess?) will probably make you form a strange kind of connection to it.The art style and soundtrack are also marvelous. The soundtrack introduced me to the genre of dungeon synth (which, really, everyone should check out) and, together with the art style and the Shade's quotes, reminds me of Salad Fingers or Courage the Cowardly Dog, if anyone even still remembers those. The atmosphere is gritty, strange and always at least slightly unsettling.That said, I'd suggest playing The Longing in tandem with another game. Especially after you're able to get to all the areas of the caves and have explored all of them fully, which doesn't really take that long, the game quickly gets boring (even if you're into more environment-oriented games) and doesn't really offer much content. It's pretty much like one of those browser strategy games; you do a thing and then eventually a timer comes up for the next thing and you leave it be until that timer is up, since there's not really much else to do.In terms of replayability, there simply isn't any, unless you really want to get all the different endings. The core principle remains the same regardless of which ending you go for; All in all, I would recommend this to someone who doesn't necessarily need a lot of action in the games they play and is maybe looking for something to just check in on periodically while doing other things/playing other games.

_childDocuments_.review: I somewhat enjoyed this game, but it's not entirely what I was expecting. There are not in fact 400 days worth of gameplay in this game - I was not expecting 400 full days worth of material but maybe interesting new secrets to discover every day for 400 days. I would LOVE that game. This is not that game. I've seen almost all of the game material in a couple of weeks.The puzzles can be a little bit frustrating, and I eventually resorted to just reading the solutions in the forums. A lot of the puzzles involve standing in a particular spot and waiting, and it can be annoying to find that you've been wasting your time standing in the wrong place for no reason, or needing to have done a particular thing before waiting. One puzzle even involves . I'm extremely glad I did not waste time trying to figure out that particular puzzle on my own.Wait for it to be discounted, or part of a bundle.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly interesting concept masterfully portrayed. Very experimental, The Longing forces a sense of loneliness and desolation onto the player, as well as demanding patience, in a way very few games even attempt. In ignoring the typical rules games follow involving player engagement, The Longing is an unusually gripping game for the right player. It should be noted that The Longing will not take most players 400 days to finish, as there are ways of speeding up time. This does not change the fact however, that players will still have to wait significant real-world time to make progress.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry, but you don't need a lot of time to figure out where this game is going.  This game is literally a waiting simulator you do literally everything, unbelievably slowly.  Reading the other reviews, I didn't really understand how far the developers took this.  When I saw 400 days, I thought those were "game days"....  No, those are real life days, 400 of them, each lasting 24 real life hours.  The game runs, even when you exit and sleep.  Every action in the game is excrutiatingly slow BY DESIGN.  From drawing a picture to opening a door to walking around.  The player controlled character will literally take 30 seconds to cross from one side of the room to another.  2 minutes to draw a simple picture and I quit when I saw the door opening at an almost non-existant pace.  My character had to go back and kill time to wait for the door to finish opening....I wouldn't have negatively reviewed the game had the developer made it apparent that the game was THIS SLOW.  I was expecting some point and click adventure gaming.  not a literal 400 day waiting simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: :THE LONGING: is a very clever little game: a game about patience, a Metroidvania in which your main enemy is time and you are slowly learning how to kill it, little by little, it's basically a waiting game where you get to explore and find stuff you can use to make that wait shorter and if you’re the kind who gets bored easily you can very well just treat it like an idle game and let it play itself for the time needed, in other words, let the wait spend itself without allowing it to drag you along, but that would take the "longing" out of it and it would stop being wait, just... time passing, and that would rob you of most of the experience, because the way it deals with the psychology of idleness is pretty great, how they built the world and the protagonist around it, the whole thing about enduring time, finding ways to cope with nothing happening for long stretches of it, thinking of tricks to make it go faster, like growing mushrooms or reading a book – hey, I’m even writing this review because nothing is happening in my game at the moment and the game taught me that writing down your thoughts can help with it – who would have thought of making a game about reading books, but this game is quite about that, and about rearranging your carpets, and finding inside yourself what you cannot find in the world, and looking for a mattock, I don’t even know what a mattock is (seriously, what the heck is a mattock?) but if this game is any indication it must be a wonderful tool of soul searching and self-discovery!I played  for almost 600 hours -- with those looong voyages between its many islands -- and I thought I knew what patience was, but :THE LONGING: is just a better teacher.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game thats rather opportunistic, the 400 days is real, so imagine you're a person physically unwell waiting and waiting for that year to end so you can be better so you can live your life the way it was again, this game is sure to bring you catharsis, for if you are someone in life already desperately waiting, this game is waiting to share that moment with you, whether its good, or bad, by the time its over it will have you look back on if you are where you wanted to be, was it worth it? If you're feeling helpless and existential as if your own life is on a timer, this game could bring you comfort, it exists to remind you that there is purpose in a nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: “Longing, we say, because desire is full of endless distances.” - Robert HassAn experiment, a patience simulator, a face in the mirror, an insight into isolation and existential conditions in a world gripped in a pandemic or just an idle game you open once and come back in 400 days, if you remember it, The Longing defies easy classification. This fascinating experiment based on a student project that has its roots way back in 2014 uses the King asleep in the mountain folklore motif to tell the story of a lonely Shade that is tasked with waking the King in 400 days. 400 days in real time.If you decide to play it, The Longing wants you to learn to wait. Yes, you really can start the game once, close it and come back in 400 days to see the ending. But, in a world rushing on steroids inexorably onward to faster and faster gratification, in a “culture entirely hypnotized by the illusion of time, in which the so-called present moment is felt as nothing but an infinitesimal hairline between an all-powerfully causative past and an absorbingly important future”, The Longing wants you to stop. To slow down. To hear the Shade’s footsteps echoing across the vast caves and to feel the moss clinging to his feet.It’s easy to relate to and sympathize with Shade. Releasing into a pandemic, lockdowns and prolonged isolation issues, he was, and probably still is, a catalyst for a bit of self reflection for many. As you roam the abandoned kingdom, in a plodding, but still determined manner, looking for ways to pass the time, you’ll have ample chance to resonate with him. I know I have. Since the beginning of 2020, I’ve had an odd, outlandish feel for the passage of time. I’m certainly not alone with that feeling and Shade’s escapades are somehow a perfect metaphor.Your exploration is slow by design. Shade is in no hurry and you will find some parts of the caves blocked off or inaccessible until a hole fills with water or a stalactite falls to bridge a gap. And those events can take days, weeks or even a month to happen. A door opening can take a few hours. There are ways to speed up the passage of time. Just like in real life, finding and creating things to decorate your cave, spending time in a familiar place and doing comforting things can make time flow faster. If you find a pick, Shade can mine glowing crystals that will light up his abode. If you find different colored stones and some paper, he can draw increasingly complex, colorful and evocative drawings that you can place around his room. Finding scattered and discarded books, all real life ones, courtesy of Project Gutenberg, will fill up his bookshelf and bring out a toothy grin whenever you sit in his favorite armchair and read. But, if you wait anywhere else and close the game, Shade will fall asleep on the floor and time will flow just like yours. There’s not much gameplay in the normal sense of the word. You’re just keeping company with Shade, making his days go faster and more enjoyable.Shade’s quips and comments have made me consider some things and his grin brings a smile to my face. We hang out a few times a week, him reading The Count of Monte Cristo, Metamorphosis or something we found recently amid the rocks of another discovered cave in, and me doing some work or just relaxing to the game’s thoughtful, slow, atmospheric dungeon synth soundtrack. 400 days haven’t passed for me yet, but I’m already slightly dreading the end of it. And the end of my friendship with Shade. The Longing is made to be played once, as an experience. It does have multiple endings available, depending on your actions and exploration. I’m not sure if I’ve done enough to uncover and put together clues for different endings, I’ve managed to refrain from any spoilers, but Shade and I will do our best. The only guaranteed ending is the passage of 400 days as time waits for no one.The Longing will certainly not be everyone’s candle in the dark. It’s slow pace and lack of “real” gameplay will be off-putting to many. But if you wish to slow down, reflect and listen to yourself better, its experimental, unconventional gameplay, unintentional metaphor for today’s world that it brings and the firm hope that games could be art it delivers are more than worthy of you sharing your time with a lonely Shade in the dark.: Due to the experimental nature of the game, many achievements are missable. If you explore everything and pay attention, chances are you will gain all of them. There is a guide on Steam doing it's best to not spoil anything, but still help.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're the kind of person that sees patience as a virtue, you will not regret playing  The central idea is to wait for 400 in-game days, and awaken the King. But there is so much more in these caves and caverns to be explored, and surprising amount of things to be done. The average person may see it as a waste of time, I know my brother did when I started out, but the point of the game is the experience of solitude; the gift of patience and introspection. I feel very satisfied having 100% completed the game, exploring every cavern and discovering every secret. I'm sad that it's over, but very happy that I played.

_childDocuments_.review: 400 days is a lot of time, and sadly there is not enough content to fill out all this time.In the beginning I was very excited to dive into this. I liked the concept of everything going at a low phase, going from place to place was a big commitment, and you can not even run~! This droplet is creating a pond of water, come back in some days or weeks and see how much progress has been made. This Spider is making a web I can climb, hopefully he will be finished tomorrow! I understood how the game works and I enjoyed it. The themes of this game is some deep depressive thoughts. The Shade as you play as talks to himself about death and wonders if this is worth doing. "I can drown in that pond if it was bigger", and it feels very relateable if you have been through the same mindset your Shade is going through now. Most of the game you hear the footsteps of your Shade walking, flop, flop, flop, and loud or quiet eerie music playing. You can tell when you approach an important part of the cave as the music will get louder and overwhelming. The game does this best.You can make your little home in the cave comfy with decorations, do activities like reading, playing music or drawing to make time go faster. Time will go on ingame even when your game is not launched too. These are the reasons I reached day 0 in 41 real time days and not in 400 real time days, and I do not actually like that. I wish the game stuck hard to the 400 real time days as the game makes you believe in the beginning.When my ingame timer reached 300 days I started losing interest in actively playing. I explored the cave that was available to me at the time, I found the decorations available to be found, and I ran out of things to do. I would launch the game once in a while and see if anything new happened, but most progress is made at the beginning. In the last 300 ingame days I found the really cool "late game" things, but it was so far in between and so few. It did feel like a huge cave, but it was so empty. I waited in my little home for the timer to reach 0 days and did not bother to leave it until then.I get if this huge open empty cave is on purpose, and you need to be patient and wait for the timer to reach 0. I understand the concept and it is fine. But how come am I able to speed up time so much, instead of sticking to real time only? Because of this conflict with the game's identity it did not feel rewarding to reach day 0. ( ´･ｪ･｀)

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely recommend The Longing. It's atmospheric in sound, visuals, and story, making it interesting to come back to over and over between idle sessions. There are certainly enough mysteries as well as secrets to uncover during active play to make it interesting. And while I didn't make extensive use of this, the ability to read full compendiums of tales, stories, and even Moby ♥♥♥♥ within game play was a nice added touch.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a game for the patient person. The Longing lives up to its name, in that every action feels intentionally slow, and methodical whilst you traverse the magnificently hand drawn, underground labyrinthine world. The shade slowly lumbers from place to place, letting you take in each zone in full detail and absorb the ambience if this pain-staking quest of isolation. I loved it, personally. I can see why the slow pace would put many off, which is why I recommend a high level of patience, it truly pays off as there's so much to discover within.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: As of this review I've played for about 16 hours. My compy specs are: i5-4460 3.2ghz, 16gb RAM, GeForce GTX 980, Win 10. I've experienced no crashes and one small bug with a door not being aligned but, a quick restart of the game fixed it.What kind of game is this? A point and click with idle elements maybe? A walking simulator? Some kind of game art piece? I'm not really sure. I personally see it as an Idle game. Your little dude has to wait 400 days (real time, although you can speed it up to 10:1 seconds in your little cubby hole) for your king to gather his power at the end of which you must wake him up and he'll bring an end to all fear and longing in some kind of depression apocalypse. During your 400 day wait you are free to explore the realm and discover it's many mysteries or just read Moby ♥♥♥♥ thousands of times. The game will auto in the background happily and there is even an "Idle Read" function where your character will sit in his arm chair and read books (I actually have it on my 2nd monitor right now while my dude is walking back home). The map isn't huge but, your dude really takes his time getting around which makes it feel huge. You can remember locations which act as a sort of "slow travel" system (your dude will just path to the location). There's a bunch of stuff to do (not 400 days worth tho lol) while you wait (including reading full books like the aforementioned Moby ♥♥♥♥) and your dude will keep an updated list in a book. There are time locked events throughout the realm such as the stalagtite falling in one cave (from the trailer) and when you reach those locations it tells you how long you have to wait so you can save the location and come back later.Things I liked:+Pretty: nice to look at in most parts but, I think with the small scale of the map more detail and variety could've been added.+Neat Concept: The idea of waiting 400 days and being the caretaker to a dead kingdom.+Good Mechanics: For the little there is it works well. The location remembering is especially nice for QOL (I can't imagine walking back through the halls of eternity TWICE).Cons:-So Slow: When you're first starting the walking pace is KILLER. Once you've been everywhere and have all the important places remembered you don't notice it as much but, the initial exploring faze can get really anoying.Overall, neat game. I'm enjoying my time with it and hopefully i'll make it to 400 days ;).

_childDocuments_.review: I waited the full 400 IRL days to get to the end to post this review.I am all for artistic games and I do admire the work that went into this game. However art is also subjective, and from my subjective viewpoint I did not like it. The movement of your character is slow. I got lost in the hallways a lot. Everything I found that looked interesting needed something else or required me to wait longer. I know there's a message here, but I never felt myself combine with that message. There is also something to be said that I myself have very little patience. I felt like the game was forcing me to experience patience instead of training me to relate to patience. Game mechanics can be very helpful in training players to become better at said mechanics. This can be achieved by trial and error or by gradually easing players into a mechanic. What if your character could walk 2x as fast but that walk speed slowed to normal over the course of the first 30 minutes of each play session per day? Something like that would have encouraged me to continue to engage with the game and slowly learn to enjoy. That's just one humble suggestion. The game has a Very Positive rating; so there are a lot of players who enjoyed the experience. However, if you're someone who has a low tolerance for slow mechanics or you need some type of gratification  per play session in order to stay motivated, this is not your game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing is an extraordinary piece of art. It is a game like no other. When I first got The Longing, I thought "huh, could be fun." _childDocuments_.review: So, first off I do not hate or even dislike this game, a end game mechanic is the reason for the down vote, and further in the post I will explain the mechanic and not spoil it for those still undeterred from my recommendation.    I waited the time away. Starting from day 400 and explored what I could. After a week of poking in and out of the game, waiting for water to fill, or a plant to grow, or something involving the environment. I found the endless room, a lot of books, coal, colored rocks for paintings, the horn for music and upgraded my room. I did a good bit in the in the short time I played.   I found the game interesting at first but when I couldn't find anything more to do or uncover myself I used one of the steam guides to figure out my options. So this is the big kicker as to why I do not recommend this game is that the game has apparently multiple endings and outcomes, but you only get one. NO RESTARTING NO SECOND PLAY THROUGHS, ONE AND DONE. However, with a steam guide you can go through a few steps to reset your game or use a console command, but the Dev states this is a one time experience. Which I do no disagree with on the whole, but when presented with the variety of end game options, and all of it based on how you spend your time and what you look for, to me, defeats the whole purpose of a game.  Not being given a proper way to go back and try things differently, to go right when you went left, choose this instead of that, is part of making a game. I.E. Replay value. But if your going to down vote this because the whole point of the longing is for it to be a one time experience, then go ahead, and I agree with you on that point. This game is meant and built for a one time play, but the type of person I am wants to restart the clock, like in a dating sim, or an RPG, or any kind of visual novel. I want to go back, and go through it again, even if I only put in about 10 hours as of this review, and try for a quicker way to get through the 400 days. Maybe experience some more ways to kill time or even go to that one place and see how long I can bare it.    But ultimately the game has no reset option that I can find without going into the steam files or game files. I have had several tell me to just wait on the endgame screen which the game boots up too and stays on with the droning music, and they tell me eventually I will get a reset option. Well, I left it on for thirty minutes and got nothing. Which I think is a unreasonable wait time to just want to start the game back up again and wait some more if it would have popped up at 31 minutes. So I'm glade I got to experience it, but do not recommend it for anyone who looks for anything more than a simple experiment presented in a rather interesting and sometimes touchingly deep package.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Bought for the inclusion of Nietzsche (I'd love to hear from the developer why they chose to include Thus Spoke Zarathustra, aside from it involving a cave), stayed for the incredible emotional undercurrents, outstanding ambient tunes, and beautiful world design. I grew very attached to the Shade over the course of the few dozen hours I played, and I think that working (and waiting) hard to get the outcome I wanted for the Shade motivated me to apply a similar mentality in my own life. This is a thought experiment as much as it is a game, and to return to Nietzsche, it appears to me that the game encourages overcoming of the self, however hopelessly buried and worn by the onslaught time the self may be. Life and the world itself, for many of us, can be an absolute slog; it can be an unrelenting struggle to move forward in total darkness. I think that art, including digital media, can assist us in finding the means to overcome real-world resistance to our pursuit of happiness. This little Shade exudes spirit and willpower when you push him to overcome himself, and hopefully, if you're finding yourself lacking in spirit and will, the Shade's overcoming will help you find the drive to keep moving forward. All that said, that was only my interpretation of a particular way of playing and relating to the Shade's circumstances. The Longing offers more than an ostensibly Nietzschean experience, and those of you more accustomed to nihilistic or absurdist ways of thinking and engaging with art will surely find a current to drift in. It also offers access to an abundance of classic literature that may not exactly be cheap these days, at least compared to the game's price tag. In any case, if you're a patient type with an appreciation for mythology, philosophy, dungeon synth, or introspective art, you'll find a lot to love in The Longing. If you do love The Longing, perhaps you can take what it evokes within you and create something just as meaningful: I fully intend to do exactly that.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I'm just starting this game, but everything is so calming. even though I've explored a huge amount of the map, I keep finding new areas. everything is interesting and creates a sense of exploration. I love the books you can read and its been an amazing game to get away and just relax away from anything going on around me. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants to expand their patience. even just walking around collecting things isn't annoying or repetitive like a ton of other games I've tried to pickup. over all if your considering this game and your willing to wait a bit (its nice waiting though, not too much or anything annoying) then I'd definitely tell you to go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: First off I'd like to thank the developers of this game. After about 45 hours of playing this game. My save file became corrupted during a windows update. With their help I was able to revert back to an old save file. Without their help I would be stuck with a game that does not work. I lost a bit of progress in the game but was able to continue playing the game.FIRST off, if you are not a patient person, this game is not for you. It is purposefully slow. There are obstacles that take literal days, weeks and even a month to work past. The best part about this game is the exploration. Trying to uncover the map and figure out where to go next is what made me keep coming back. It was weird how connected I felt to your character. When my save was corrupt, I couldn't help but think about my Shade being alone in his dwelling. I definitely recommend not reading any guides to this game unless you are absolutely stuck. The puzzles are logical, and some of them are solved simply by waiting. The problem I ran into when I started searching for ways to fix my game was that there are a lot of spoilers out there. Part of the charm of this game is not knowing what will happen next or what you may uncover. If you crave a slow paced, point and click adventure game with an intriguing and mysterious story, then this game might be just for you.MINOR SPOILERThere are ways to speed up this game, but only in one place specifically. Once I discovered this, I was constantly trying to figure how to make time go by faster. Another interesting puzzle to solve.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to Unlock all the achievements and complete the game before writing a review and since I just did complete it all I feel that I have a proper perspective on it now. This game is Amazing, in many ways. As you have already probably read it is different from most games for it's extreme length which already gives it a reason to stand out. 400 Days, all alone, in a kingdom, deep, deep, underground. I found this game to be really atmospheric as the Dungeon Synth Music helps to make the isolated and dark yet wondrous underground kingdom that you are given free reign to explore as much as possible. You don't have to explore though, in fact you don't have to do anything, at all. I found myself at many points just walking through the caves or reading pages from the in-game library soaking up the world and it's atmosphere. I'm very aware the extreme length isn't for everyone but I would 100% recommend you give this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most impactful games I have ever played.  can recommend.This game is entirely reliant on what you choose to make of it. You can complete this game never interacting with the world of The Longing, or you could sink a hundred hours into getting to know your Shade and the world. The point of the game is being just as lost as your Shade, learning with them, exploring with them, . In this game you have all the time in the world, and you can spend that time however you like. It is entirely freeing to have all the option to do whatever, and however much of it, you like. This isn't a game that requires anything from you. This game comes with 5 unique endings you can find and choose through the gameplay. And while it is possible to play this game more than once, I agree with the creators that it  only be played once.   You truly cannot recapture the feeling of your first playthrough.This truly is one of the best gaming experiences I have ever had. I cannot recommend this game enough. Thank you for creating the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game on the caveat that you can tolerate it's abominably slow walking speed for many hours.It's got a good atmosphere, and the drip-feed of info and mystery and whatnot is pretty interesting, but after a while, I was experiencing diminishing returns, and just didn't care enough to keep playing. Admittedly this is partly due to checking a guide for help and getting some minor spoilers (deffo go in blind), but it's also because I just couldn't stand the slooooooow walking speed anymore.I don't begrudge the dev their decision, I know it's in-line with their vision and the themes of the game and whatnot, I just didn't care for it. Even if after a certain amount of time the Shade would drink some G-fuel or just decide to jog, it wouldn't be so bad, but once I discovered most of what there was to discover, it became even more of a pain to walk between areas. _childDocuments_.review: I love spending time on this game in creative ways. Everything takes a lot of time, just like a life without internet. Embrace your time, learn no get bored and regain the ability to spend an entire day staring at a wall, no matter how long a day can be. _childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game towards the end of my pandemic year staying at home with my children. It was kind of a fantasy to me, to be alone with my thoughts, to have all the time in the world to sit and read, and to enjoy atmospheric silence. I liked the existential question posed by the game where your god is sleeping. It was also a nice game to play while feeding my toddler, because it did not require any fast responses. I loved the music. I ended up drawing out a map of my own to keep track of where everything was. It would have been nice to have a mini-map in-game (besides the one tied to a certain location). I didn't get past the mushroom caves... but I did awaken the king of the mountain, to a depressing result.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most unique take on the idle genre so far.The game starts and you are given a real time 400 day countdown. If you choose, you can simply wait the 400 days in real time for the game to end.However, you are able to explore a decently sized realm of caves and secrets. Finding things will advance the time faster. Making some choices and solving some mysteries (all hinted within the game itself) will lead to a few different endings.A good engaging experience overall. However, I feel that the world could have been larger - 400 days is a long time, and the world can be explored in a relatively short amount of time. So if you find everything, you can be forced to wait depending on your choice of ending.Waiting may be the point, and it is probably a very deliberate design decision. However, it eventually overstays its welcome for the game play experience - more areas/mysteries could have blunted this.Still a positive review.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't play this game. I just installed it, puttered around for 35 minutes, thought about playing it more when I had more time then I put it down for more than a year. My intention was to see how much I could grow in those four hundred days. What I learned was that even though I had learned and grown so much in that span of time, I was still kind of the same person underneath it all. As I finally opened the game for the first time in who knows how long, I felt like the exact person who had bought it the first time.And the ending was poignant. Without spoiling it, it was enough. It satisfied me. I do still Long however. I think that's the point. We grow and change and the Longing is there. I feel like the Mountain King. I want to sit down and become stone and become still and rest.Five stars out of five. Great game. Thank you for the experience.

_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Adventure, walking simulator, puzzler, idler? All of these traits combined make The Longing, a totally unique game that could very well turn out to be a pioneer in idle games, since there's nothing even remotely like it on the current Steam market.You control a lonely Shade and your duty is to wake your King up after 400 days have passed since he falls asleep, while wandering in a vast cave system. How will that time pass and what you discover is entirely up to you, but you have to remember that this is a SLOW game.It's a pure idler (not a "clicker" like the vast majority of idle games available, though) and if you aren't patient or not prepared for this kind of game, it isn't for you. You WILL have to close the game and let the timer run quite a few times, since there will be intervals when you will just have to wait for some events to trigger and items/places to be available and accessible.On the other hand, if you're willing to take your time and explore every nook and cranny for a nice array of achievements and secrets, you will be rewarded. The devs really wanted to convey a true feeling of loneliness through this game and if you get into it, you will definitely feel it too. Although the latter part of the game will definitely test your patience, personally I finished the game with a feeling of satisfaction. It was well worth the wait.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: In The Longing, you play as a servant, a little shade, tasked to wake up your king after 400 days. During this wait, you can explore the caves you dwell in and try to spruce up your little home. The more comfortable you get your home, the faster time will go for the little guy.I have become incredibly attached to the shade. There is something about him that is incredibly relatable. Making the most out of such a depressing situation felt surprisingly fulfilling. The fact that this game got me excited about moss growing over a month or that I consider finding an ordinary spider somewhat of a spoiler says a lot about the atmosphere.Now this game is  for everyone, but if the premise of sitting around and waiting sounds like a good idea to you, I would highly recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is possibly one of the chillest games I have ever played. Take a stroll through a maze of caves, gather some moss, pick some mushrooms. Make friends with a spider. Speak to a face in the wall on how to overcome the darkness. Or maybe just read Moby ♥♥♥♥.There's no rush, you have 400 days to kill.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I got this game free from Keymailer shoutouts to them and the devs for allowing me to try the game.This is a rough recommendation because of the nature of the game about patience. If you're not into games that revolve around waiting for things to happen. I tell you right now, you should not get this game because you'll get bored of it.With that aside let's look at the Pro Cons of the game.Pro:- very chill, because of the nature of the game it is relaxing as you just roam around exploring the cave until time runs out.- artstyle is nice.- you can have memories/beacon to return to an area without having to physically retread places you've been to get back OR if you are directionally challenge and could use some help finding a place of interest you saw. good feature.- Your main character is endearing, you get to experience the passage of time with them as they wait for the days to go by.- You can actually read the books in the game to pass the time. it's interesting and it does speed up the time in the game a bit.- You don't actually have to wait the 300 days to pass normally, there are ways to speed up the clock by doing certain activities.- The game plays itself offline so you don't have to keep the game open to make progress.- The concept of waiting and doing things to kill time is interesting, most likely will not be for everyone.Meh:- Travelling is slow, but that's what you signed up for if playing this game.Con:- This game would be better played on a mobile device like a phone or the nintendo switch, maybe a laptop. I say this because if you think about it. Are you really going to boot up your PC tower to play a waiting game simulator. If I could revert my game key choice, I'd have ask for the gamekey on switch just to have it play on side.- I don't want to say there's not much to do, but there's not much to do while you wait for things to happen so you can get access to certain areas.I picked this game up knowing full well what I was getting into and I got what I expected.I am more on the recommendation side since it is a nice game and there's nothing bad about it. BUT the gameplay of waiting is not for everyone and I'd imagine most would get bored of the game.I'd recommend not playing the game on a stationary game system since it seems like it'd be better on mobile devices where you check in on the game once in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally thought that 400 days would take forever. However, the game rewards you by exploring. The more you play and collect items, the faster time goes. There are lots of puzzles, mining, and time stamps to go through. While the game does run idly, I have spent 40 hours on it so far, and counting. _childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really liked this game concept. I sympathized with the lonely little shade and deeply enjoyed the sometimes tedious but generally rewarding gameplay of simply waiting. the ambiance was there, the style was there, the puzzle aspect was enjoyable. He was like the lonely tomagotchi I could set to a task, walk away and do other stuff around my own personal cave IRL, and I deeply enjoyed when I got him to smile inside his own cave after making it cozy enough for him.My problem comes with the end game.  I get that the game is about waiting. I really enjoyed how different the concept was, but everything about the endings was just unfulfilling and downright frustrating compared to how attached I had become to my little shade. I will never finish this game myself, and feel pretty upset that it had such an unsatisfying "endgame" for such an engaging and original game.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I finished the Longing a few months ago, but I haven't stopped thinking about it.  I found this game to be incredibly emotionally impactful, maybe even the most memorable gaming experience I've ever had.If you are someone who gets attached to small, helpless, wide-eyed fictional creatures ("little guys"), you will likely enjoy being emotionally wrecked by this experience.  I don't mean to imply that this game is outright sad, but the hollow ennui is crushing in the most beautiful way possible.There is plenty to explore and find if you are patient.  I looked forward to coming home every day to log in and see if I could get just a little further along in this journey.The art and music evoke fuzzy, possibly-imagined nostalgia for late-night animated foreign films and uncomfortable picture books, and it never got old through my playthrough.I drew my own map as I went along, and I highly recommend that experience.I cried after I completed the game.  I even called my mom about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've really got mixed feelings about this game.  For one thing, everything you do in this game takes FOREVER.  You can't just start up the game and "speedrun" it, though I wouldn't want that either.  There's a very slow, methodical, calm pace to every one of the shade's movements and there's not anything you can do to speed things up.   Just walking from place to place can take up the bulk of your time.  The only saving grace here is that you don't have to actually sit there controlling the character.  You can tell him to take a walk to some place random and off he goes. Ten minutes later maybe he stops and you can take over from there, OR you can tell him to take another random walk, OR there are some other options that you have to find out yourself.Not only that, but the game also takes place over the course of 400 days, so you COULD just start the game up , shut it down and come back 400 days later and end it.  That would probably be the most boring way to play it but you could do it that way.  Later you find out that by decorating your little home, you can make time pass more quickly.  Sit and read a book and with each page you turn you jump a bit forward in time.  Make some drawings to hang on the walls and now you can watch time speed on by just by being in the same room.  There's a couple of goals to the game other than just "wait 400 days to wake up the king".  You can also try to find a way out of the caves, you can look for more stuff to decorate your house with (including building a bed to sleep in), and there's all sorts of secrets to find in game.  Unfortunately everything is time based, so there are some events that you can't just stumble upon unless you're at the right space at the right time.  Some events will happen whether you're there to see it or not.  This game demands a lot of time from you in order to get the most out of it, but if you happen to play it a bit, then put it down and forget about it, you'll come back to find that you missed out.Technically there's a way to reverse time so that you can be there just in time, but you have to find the stuff you need in order to do it.  If you're willing to spend a little time each day, and if you're willing to wait for certain events, there's lots of stuff you can see and do.  BUT if you don't have all the time in the world to dedicate to playing this game at the right time to see everything, you'll just miss it.You could say the lesson is "Good things come to those who wait" but after waiting 400 days (that got compressed down because I stayed in my home too much) I can say the ending I got was kinda disappointing.  It comes off as rather nihilistic in tone and depressing in the presentation.  I won't say any more than that.The game is meant to only be played once, so if I abide by the wishes of the developers I just end it right here and I don't ever go back...and that actually makes the game more disappointing for me.  If you get to the ending and just wait a while, it'll give you two options:  Start over (against the developer's wishes) or go back in time to before you triggered the ending (probably also makes the devs unhappy but less than starting it completely over).I don't really want to thumb this game down because it's an interesting concept forcing you to wait for stuff, but I've had more fun with some virtual pets or playing Animal crossing (which also makes you wait for stuff) than I did here.  Anyway, I'll just say that if you dedicate yourself to this game and play it every day for a bit you can probably get some decent amount of enjoyment out of it.  For me, it was interesting for a while and then I stopped playing it as the holidays came around and things got busy and I forgot about it and came back to find the clock had stopped at 0 days, 0 minutes and 0 seconds left and the only thing left to do at that point was to finish it. Not very fulfilling... Is it worth a purchase? I guess that depends on you.  If all of this sounds boring then probably not.  If it sounds intriguing then maybe?Because I fell asleep in my house (where time is sped up) I actually got cheated out of some time.  I wanted 400 days and only got 288 days... Or even just 365 would have been something.   So yeah, if you want to get the most out of this game, make sure to leave your house before you quit.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game literally helped me form new habits. One and a half years of university forced my brain into a constant state of multitasking. I couldn't ever focus on anything because I had so much work to do that focusing on one thing would cause me to fall behind. I developed the habit of quickly bouncing from assignment to assignment, never bothering to think deeply about anything. This also affected my leisure time as well. I gained the impression that if I wasn't force-feeding myself as much content as possible, I was wasting time. I was in a productivity trap. Everything I did had to be efficient.Then I played this game. Yeah, it was slow at first. It was honestly a little painful getting used to how slow this game felt at times. The artwork and the soundtrack, however, were more than enough to keep me interested, and I continued exploring the caves as best I could. Slowly, I found myself getting accustomed to the game's pace. It was genuinely fun to boot up the game for a few hours each day to explore some new corner of the cave that had become available to me. Pretty soon, I realised that I liked the speed of the game. It gave me time to really think about the situation I was placed in and really immerse myself in the game's small bits of lore it sprinkles throughout it.These habits found their way into my academic life. I found that I was finally able to focus on things properly. I was actually learning material, and I felt motivated to keep learning. I was able to hold longer conversations with people that didn't simply revolve around watching them play games. Best of all, I didn't feel bad about spending my free time more loosely. I no longer felt guilty that I had only read a little bit before going to bed instead of cramming as much YouTube into my brain as possible.I understand that these are very much first-world problems, but this game legitimately gave me my life back. I feel like I'm living again rather than slaving away on work and university matters. I don't know if this game will help anyone else in the same way it helped me, but I still highly, highly recommend it. As mentioned before, the artwork and the soundtrack in this game are great, and the intricacy of the caves makes exploring them super fun (even at a snail's pace!). The only bugs I ever experienced were minor visual bugs that didn't affect anything and disappeared upon restarting the game. In short, this game is a must play for anyone looking to immerse themselves in a slightly mysterious, slightly threatening, slightly comforting world. I could say a lot more about the game's themes and such but that's something that should be discovered by the player in the game, not from some random Steam review.

_childDocuments_.review: Every once in a while I think back to this little game I played back in September of 2020... well, it's more accurate to call it an experience.  Or perhaps a journey?  An incredibly slow one.This game refuses to move at your pace, and forces you to move at its own.  That isn't a bad thing... not a good thing, either, but not a bad thing.The main gameplay loop is... waiting.  Or finding new things to wait for.  Or finding ways to make the wait go a little bit faster... but it's all about the waiting.  The game timer goes down even when the game is closed, and when sped up as much as possible, still takes a few weeks to zero out - which is the ending I went for.  I stayed true to the promise to the King and woke him up, even though the wait was agonizing.What happened, and was it worth the wait?  On this, my lips are sealed.Whatever end you work for, just know that the game won't let you play it again.  Pretty sure it's account-bound, even.I would not call this a game to be enjoyed in the moment, like most.  It's a game that exists to make you ask yourself questions - and gives you all the time in the world to find your answers.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game and went in knowing it would be slow. I thought maybe it could be a game I could have running on my dual monitor where I just click and have my character explore while I work, but the pacing is just not right for me. It's too slow for me to watch but too fast for me to complete a task and check back to click. And it's not consistent where I can just set a timer for each stop either, distances vary before the character stops, and you will have to pay attention if you don't want to miss out on collecting the rocks. I don't really want to just babysit a super slow character. If it weren't too late I would get a refund, I'm sorry. It's cute but I wouldn't recommend, I don't think the game would have suffered if it were a bit faster.

_childDocuments_.review: its a slow but fun game, centered around waiting and exploring.when waiting for the time to awaken the king you come across many locations where you have to wait for up to a month to pass. but in some cases like when you meet the little spider and accidentally break the poor things web, it starts to make a new one in a different location over a few days, when done you can climb the web and get to another location on the map

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game!I started with something to see everyday and each time I kept loving my little shade even more. I wanted it to have a good house, with a lot of comfort and I also wanted it to be happy. I think I accomplished that in the ending!Ah! _childDocuments_.review: After a long time and after finishing this game 2 times, I can really say it was a hell of a ride. I mean, a slow ride, but still.The longing is a hell of a slow game, but not an uninteresting one, it has it's lore and little secrets and a lot to explore, altough at a slow pace. The game, however, rewards our patience with nice moments and discoveries, making us feel like time is really passing in the caves and making us apreciate the time we pass with Shade, our little friend that we control. It's narrative and the affection and worry for Shade that is created within it leads us to make personal choices that will carry us to different endings, it makes us think - "Should i wait and let Shade do it's duty or should i let him free?".Overall, a game i wouldn't say is for everyone since most don't have the patience, but I would still ask them to give it a try. Also 2 tips: Play it during a time were you have a lot of free time (like during vacation) and you can restart the game, altough it's not intended to (we all do that though).

_childDocuments_.review: The Longing: Disappointingly ShortThe longing is a game about a little black sprite, told to wait 400 days to wake his king. In this time you can explore caverns, draw pictures among other things to pass the time. The game is almost the inverse of a typical idle game, waiting for numbers to go down as opposed to making them go up. However, if you play this game regularly, you'll be able to get time to go 10-20 times faster. This means that with a little dedication 400 days can become less than 4 weeks, not to mention that several endings of the game don't even require that you reach that goal.The Shade is a lovable, depressing protagonist, typical of other point and click indie games. Throughout you're time with this game, you'll form a great connection with this little creature.While the gameplay is quite simple, I very much enjoyed my time with this game. I managed to  and it was well worth the investment. My biggest gripe with this game is that it doesn't follow through on the core premise, for better or for worse. Aside from that, I'd recommend this game to anyone already interested in it. If you're on the fence, go for it but if it doesn't seem like it's for you, I'd pass on it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unusual and unique game. I loved exploring the world and finding ways to decorate my home cave. There are mechanics in place which make the game more accessible than one might intially assume. The slow pace is appropriate for the mood and style the game goes for. Still a little patience is requred for an enjoyable experience, which is a good thing in my book. It's not for everyone, but those who are at least a bit intrigued by the game's description will not be disappointed (also notice how every negative review until now had less then 1h playtime).

_childDocuments_.review: It is my first experience with idle gaming and I am really surprised! I am a very busy mother of three and wife, working 40 hrs a week on top of it . In this point in my life I don't have a lot of time, which makes this game perfect . I don't need to worry about checking in at certain times and I can come and go and check when I have time, which our little shade has plenty of ;)when things calm down and have more time , I'll be able to go back to those games like RPGS that I loved .This game though is perfect for the puzzle and mystery seeker. If you're the "AHH HA!" Junky like myself and like to figure things out, then this game is for you . The graphics are nice and make you feel as of you're a part of the story. The only downfall to this is that sometimes it will glitch in the form of pause , not often enough to annoy you but enough to notice.The stem chats are very helpful if you are really stuck and don't know where to go next.what I like as well is that the developers update the game with new material time to time from what I've read. so there will always be something to discover. All I know is .. I have come to really like my little shade am excited to see what happens at the end of the 400 days :)
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is defenetly game for most of people, but if words "longing" and "lonely" speaks to you, it might be. Something in this speaks to my melancholic soul. Game is very s l o w and mysterious. It is simple game about waiting and exploring, and updating your home... or it can be just about waiting.  But don't wait for breath taking action. Just wait......and wait...
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game honestly feels like such a change of realities from real life busywork to sitting down and watching a little guy hit a wall for hours. The perceived slowness of the game really makes it work wonders on your feelings. Without it, the game would lose all it's spark. Then there is the slow connection you build with your little shade and the desire to make him the happiest he can be stuck in a hole for 400 days. Honestly, for such a grim game, it has provided a lot of happiness.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This saved my life, I was in a deep state of depression and playing with the shadesaved my life. If this didn't exist, I wouldn't be alive... Thanks to this amazing game my life and mental state has been restored to its fullest. With the coming of the Covid-19 virus I was left alone with just me and my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop. I have found a new love for the confines of isolation that I never knew never existed. Over the past days I have sat with the shade for many hours. My mother considered me to be lonely, and practically disowned me. This lead me into an even more depressed state... Then I realized there is nothing to be depressed about I HAVE THE SHADE. One of my truest friends who I can share my isolation with, So now I will share my love for the Shade and this game to you <3

_childDocuments_.review: Very relaxing and ... humbling in its premise. The Shade's intense loneliness, the slow movement and tapping of his feet, the inevitability of the king's slumber and the overall gloom sound like a horrible experience, yet I cannot express how soothing it really is. Like a warm blanket after a bad day, a withered flower tied to a happy memory, sentimental, bittersweet.

_childDocuments_.review: The 400 days of waiting sounded like a really unique premise and the artstyle was also very captivating. Technically it's a point & click exploration game. It reminded me of The Neverhood somehow. I loved that game too. I've spent a little more than 26 hours with the game to complete it and achieve all the Achievements. I was cheating a liitle by looking up the solution for the mushroom puzzle. It would have been solvable with a little more looking around and thinking. Time flies much faster in your room if you play actively and find more and more stuff. It's a fun and charming game, not boring at all. It involves some waiting, but it's really not tedious. I recommend it if you like these type of games!

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game, but not too heavily. It is a humbling experience, with many melancholic undertones that set a very depressing stage. At least at first. Then it becomes like a mobile idle game, to be checked in on once a day or so, until an ending can be achieved. The Shade is adorable in their sad, self-depricating little way, and the world feels just as desolate yet mysterious as the developer intended, but without patience to see it to the end, without the ability to remember it and stay with it, without the true drive to see the ending, I wouldn't really recommend it to anyone unless I'm certain they would take the time to see the game to the end, for little to no satisfying reward for doing so. Even to someone like myself that can appreciate the fact that the novelty and the journey in and of itself is the reward, it just felt meaningless toward the end. Not in a depressing or sad way, but in an empty and boring way. The "400 days in real time" and "you must wait for literally anything to happen" gimmick was foreboding and intimidating (and a little aggravating) at first, but it quickly faded into a nothingness once the player finds ways to speed up the time. Paintings, fireplaces, decor, and especially books made the game pass in a flash. Once everything was done, all there was left to do was let the shade read and then come back the next day to see the timer hit 0. 43 hours of playtime was even a little too long as it was, as I personally aimed to do everything I could before letting the game end. The timer hit 0 multiple times, and I used the hidden Lapiz Lazuli fire mechanic to rewind the clock more than once just because I refused to believe that a game with such a high and poetic opinion of itself was already over with by hour 20. In the end, I forgot about the game entirely, not having touched it for months until just now, when I reopened it just to finish it and write this review before uninstalling to reduce hard drive space, and I still had not done literally everything (I could have grinded for 100 coal to give to the wall-face just to earn every one of his musings, but I did not). In the end, I chose the "Wake the King" ending, not out of necessity, but simply because it was the most convenient. At this point in the game, I could have chosen any of the 5, but I was just ready to have it done with so that I didn't feel guilty about letting it sit on my desktop untouched for another 6 months. I see what the dev was going for, but again, once you find out how to speed things along (or if you know things in advance), it just doesn't hold your attention any longer. If you're going to play this game, do yourself a favor and do NOT look anything up about it beforehand, like I did. Not because it ruins the story, but because once you realize how little there is to do, it becomes depressingly shallow and empty.TL:DR - Its a neat enough concept at first, but the novelty of it quickly fades, even to those of us with the most extreme patience. Play if you want, but don't spoil yourself. Not because there's anything worth spoiling, but because there really isn't; if you do, you'll be asking yourself "wow. is... is that really it...?"

_childDocuments_.review: YOU CAN ONLY EXPERIENCE THIS "GAME" ONCE!This is more an art piece than a game.  There is one "puzzle," really, with a couple exceptions.  Your solution?  Wait...  Just...just wait.  Wait some more.  Then you wait a bit more...and every day, you log back in...wait, what?  Yes, not only is this game very slow, it requires a connection to a server, which means it's on life support.  I would say, you already know if you want to experience this art piece.  Otherwise, watch an edited version or a lets play.But, yeah, you can only play it once, so you better get everything done you wanted the first time through.

_childDocuments_.review: A seemingly long game that doesn't require much interaction if you choose to play that way. Watching as time slowly speed up as I gathered and discovered new items and places of interest felt rewarding. There were some challenges along the way and while I'd recommend playing it blind, I wouldn't hesitate to get some help either if you need it. Took me about 2 months with 48 active hours. Give this game a shot and if you don't enjoy it, just return in a year or so.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like the antithesis of most games. You have to wait real time days for almost anything to happen, walking is incredibly slow, there is negligible dialogue, a small map, any number of other non standard choices.And I played 30 hours of it, and fully intend to play it again.I feel more attached to this depressive shade, meandering through the underground passages of a decrepit kingdom than I have felt to nearly any other character in my life.I don't think I know many people that would actually take the time to get into this game, but I firmly believe that anyone who can will be in for a thoroughly memorable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun game. I'm not as much of a gamer as my friends but I find this game to still be enjoyable. If you have a lot of free time on your hands or if you just want something to do while watching Tv, this is a game you could play. You also do not have to wait 400 days, there are different endings, so you can choose how you want to complete the game. I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't say that this game is fun, but more of a relaxing meditative experience. While walking through these caves, you get to know the shade. It makes many remarks about what you find, that allows you to connect with it. While this game does have a story, the main appeal is finding out more about your patience and your relationship with problems that you may come across. The game will run without it open, so you can continue to make progress on tasks that may take a few hours to complete. The slow nature of the game was frustrating at first, but after about an hour, you get used to it, and going any faster would feel wrong. I highly recommend giving this game a try, but it is, in my mind, a guided meditation instead of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I loved it.It's almost like EVE Online, but cuter and set up in the random fantasy non science fiction world.The effects of the ending on you, when you are clueless about them, are overwhelming because you are imbued with sympathy to Shadow. Though I'm glad I had made several backups of the savegames before everything got bad.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game with the condition that you'll make a lot of progress with your home and the environment in the first 2 weeks, but will have to basically wait for another 2 weeks until the game is finished. It felt unfulfilling at the end, but the overall game was a joy to play. This game is more idle than adventure and should be treated as such.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: Nowadays there's no room for patience, there has to be something happening at all times. No room for silence or boredom. This game is designed against efficiency and fast paced life. Sometimes things just happen when you just wait. I didn't realize I got emotionally attached to this little shade during 50 days I played this game, until I found myself crying after one stupid, rushed decision. I'm sorry I failed you, little buddy.
