_childDocuments_.review: While I have to say I get some satisfaction playing THE LONGING (the capital letters not shouting the name, but uttering it in a deep voice like gravel landing on a coffin lid), I would not recommend it to all players. Everything moves so very slowly in this game about A Shade waiting for 400 days until the King can be awakened, no running and very little jumping allowed and you best believe that the game will punish your avatar if you try and cheat. Only the very patient completionist player inured to disappointment will see it through. Perfectionists will suffer torment too, no spamming saves to go back to. As far as I can tell, the only way I could restart the game after a mistake (I  broke A Shades' mattock on the unbreakable glass in the treasure room), is to delete save files which sounds like cheating?The good news is it still counts down the 400 days, with the timer running even when you've logged off and forgotten all about A Shade and his peaceful life deep underground. Will I be able to play it through after the King awakens & puts the happiness back in A Shades' life? I can't wait to find out.

_childDocuments_.review: MOBILE DEVELOPERS HATE HIM! Find out how The Longing Challenges Players with this one werid trick!This game is something special.  Humans hate waiting. We will do anything to not wait, to not be bored, so much so that sleezy game developers using the tactic of making players wait in an effort to get us  to shell out cash for microtransactions. This game makes some incredibly brave decisions.RAID SHADOW LEGENDS: "What's your game about?"THE LONGING: "It's about waiting."RAID: "Waiting? What!?  That's can't be ALL you do?"THE LONGING: "No, you can do other stuff, like explore, build your house, grow mushrooms. But you got to wait to do it all."RAID: "THAT'S BRILLIANT! HOW MUCH TO YOU CHARGE TO SPEED THE GAME UP?"THE LONGING: "...sigh..."So, no one can claim that The Longing "moment-to-moment" gameplay is exciting, griping stuff. To make a game around one of our most hated activities is nuts. That it works is amazing. On my first night with the game, I played for about an hour, slowly exploring all of the caverns that I could. I admired the beautiful 2D artwork. That night, as I started to drift off to sleep, I thought about the lonely little shade, in his little cave, just waiting, and I knew I had to help him.  The shade is an awesome character and he will get to you right away.A day or so in, I asked myself, why I am playing this game? This is a LOT of time to invest, I could be doing more productive stuff.  Very quickly, the game had me wrestling with my own tendencies. The awesome thing about the Shade is he is never worried about time, about how long something takes, and that makes him incredibly powerful. If you knew that in 400 days, you could be an good piano player, or artist, or you could write that book that has been in the back of your mind, that all you had to do was just do it a little each day, what would be your reason not to?  You hate waiting. You hate wasting time, you don't see "progress" fast enough.We need to be more like the shade. If you put one foot in front of the other, you'll eventually walk 3000 miles. This game isn't going to win any awards for funnest game of the year. No one's going to proclaim it the next big thing in gaming like a Fortnight. But, this game can help us learn to master our fear of being bored, of lack of progress, of waiting, and that's something I can't say about any other game.I'm far from finishing this game, as I write this, I have 383 days left until the King wakes up. Of course I want to know how it ends, but the shade and I are going to figure it out together, no spoilers. I fire up Unity and start working on my own game project that has been languishing. I keep the longing running in another window. I like keeping the lonely little shade company.

_childDocuments_.review: The longing is one of those games whose use of the passage of time, as both theme and design, is novel. Is it for you? maybe. It is slow, but make no mistake, there is a surprising depth to the game as a whole. It's an interesting world to be sure. Personally, if you have patience and an interest in discovery I'd say this is worth the try. I personally found the game compelling from start to finish, and, as crazy as this sounds, am looking forward to my next few play-throughs.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say... I'm really going to miss my little Shade buddy. However, I believe that this is the type of game you should only experience once. As soon as I realized all the ways the game could end, I made a decision on how I wanted the game to end for my little guy and I stuck with it and I was happy with it, because it was the narrative that was created during our LONG journey of exploration and discovery.It takes 400 days, maybe less, maybe more, it depends on if you figured out how to manipulate time in game.  The art style is unique and beautiful and I think the sound was done very well. The puzzles and exploration was very interesting and I managed to still discover new areas even very late in the game.I think the developers did a very good job and I really enjoyed the experience. The game however does cater for a very specific audience, as you need A LOT of patience, but the Shade teaches us that we sometimes need to take things slow and sometimes we need to look around and appreciate what we have but also have the courage to explore new things.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: What an experience! A game with puzzles that would fit seamlessly into any classic point-and-click adventure game but with an atmosphere and ponderous pace I have never seen before. The fact that most things happen "real time" really adds to the overall tone of the game as sometimes there is nothing but the wait for something to change, explore other parts of the kingdom or just go back to your cave and read a book or sleep - and even when that happens you get a glimpse of the shade's thoughts, doubts and emotions.In terms of playable content the game is short, but well worth the price. Equal parts point-and-click adventure and idle game this turned out to be a very interesting concept: surprisingly gripping and absolutely charming in terms of its art, music and narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: You have to be patient to play this game. I do absolutely recommend it, but do recognize that it is very much a purposefully slow-paced game, and much of the game is spent waiting.I love the dark and somewhat spooky atmosphere, and the game does a great job of making you feel absolutely and completely utterly alone. It's haunting in such a beautiful way. It gives you time to breathe and think and feel and exist, and I spent my time in the game ensuring that the shade's home was as wonderful and comfortable as possible (which is the main aspect of gameplay outside of exploration).
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: "The Longing" is like nothing you've ever played before - an atmospheric adventure game that features a slow pace and a unique time-based mechanic. You play a character called "The Shade"(*), a melancholic creature waiting underground for 400 days for its King to awaken. The game's meditative and introspective nature encourages players to reflect on the passage of time, making it a must-play for those looking for a contemplative gaming experience. Moreover, the gorgeous hand-drawn graphics and spine-tingling atmospheric soundtrack create an unique and captivating experience."The Longing" is a game that will stay with you long after you've finished playing. You'll come to love, understand - and miss! - "your" Shade. (*) Who looks like a miniature, black version of Mr. Burns from "The Simpsons"!
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a slow burn. Kind of obvious on the surface given it's slated to take over a year if you only sit and wait, but there is a good amount of stuff in the game to keep you occupied. Might even make the time feel like it's going faster ;). It has a lovely art style, a soundtrack that can go from daunting, to lonely, to oppressive, to beautiful. Just take your little dude around and explore the great underground, see the sights, and maybe even make some choices. It's a rather unique experience, at least compared to other games I've played, and that alone makes it worth the price of the game in my opinion. A fun little experiment of mixing genres that has turned out well.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I just wanted to point out that locking content behind a long timer is one of the strangest, yet smartest things ive ever come across in video games. It makes you value time, slowing it down with the big timer always ticking one second at a time. It reminds you of the game as you are doing other things (in real life or while playing other games for instance). Sometimes the timer comes back, running in your mind. ''In one month i can go check that place out. I should come back then.'' It keeps you intrigued in the game for longer, and it makes the world feel a lot bigger than it actually is. It literally makes you long for the moment the secret will inevitably reveal itself to you. I really wish there were more games that tried implementing this kind of feature (even though i understand it's quite a bold move).Ever since playing The Longing i've been looking for a game similar to it. I have, however, come to the conclusion that similar games do not exist. The Longing is one of its kind. An experience i will remember and cherish for the rest of my life.

_childDocuments_.review: A walking simulator, but also an idle simulator, but also an exploration adventure game. There is so much to discover in these caves that you will probably need 400 days to find it all without using a guide. Find odd bits and bobs around the caves to decorate your room. Collect and read old books. Sketch drawings with various colored stones. Wander the caves aimlessly, just to see where you end up. Or you could... not do any of that at all. You could spend the entire 400 days sitting in your chair, and that would be a perfectly valid play style. It really is up to you, but the one thing you will always need on your path is patience.You're not going anywhere. The caves aren't going anywhere. The sleeping king isn't going anywhere. So just make the best use of your time as you see fit.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This game disappointed me only by the deep and uncompromising work of art that it initially seemed to have set out to be. I love the concept of this game and how the solitude in an (at first) intimidatingly extensive and complex array of caves coupled with a series of tasks and events that endure far beyond the limits of your attention span create a world that seems far more momentous than you and the current moment. I believe that this 'largeness'  is the main aspect of this game's unique vibe, and is why I felt quite disappointed when I learned that firstly the game progresses while not being played, and secondly allows you to speed up the progression of time. Now the first of these I admit is a very unrealistic expectation and is more of a personal letdown than any sort of genuine complaint; the 9600 hours this would require one to play for would put off anyone who wanted to play the game remotely casually and would mean that only very few would complete it, but I would argue that this would create a world that felt far beyond the player in size and that the game would be all the more respectable for it. Now the second of my disappointments I was met with when I learnt that time could be sped up by methods that were in the hands of the player, as it was as if suddenly the daunting 400 days on the clock that made me as the player feels so small, was (to an extent) under my control. This felt very much like the game trying to be playable, which made it feel a lot less intimidating and thus 'smaller'. Anyways I love this game and the things it  do. I have not played anything like this and I am happy I came across it. The Longing is a mysterious and atmospheric experience that - in it's gameplay - encourages you to slow down and be weak (Although you can just have your character following commands in the background if you want to play more casually). I would highly recommend the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not for everyone, and that includes me.Given how this game is marketed "the game that takes 400 days to complete!" I will first say that it is not only possible, but encouraged, to end the game earlier than that and the game gives you many means to do so, so don't (necessarily) let that alone dissuade you from trying the game if you feel like you may like it.That being said, I think the message that this game portrays through its gameplay is very heavy handed and overstays its welcome. You the player are given a task, for which we famously know, you can just sit on for a 400 days and come back to check off. By playing the game and not just sitting around, you explore the area, find new ways to make time go faster or end the game early. The catch is that doing so is a chore. Your character walks at a lazy pace and just about everything takes days or weeks worth of time such that generally for any day you have a short checklist of things you can do until you come back at some point in the future after more options open up. It's true that if these things weren't the case, the game itself would be quite different, but the more I played, the less I thought that would be a bad thing.It places you in an interesting fantasy world that I naturally wanted to explore, but I pretty quickly got burnt out in doing. After about 12 hours of playing I was ready to forsake learning every nook and cranny of the place to just get the game over with already. Isn't this the "longing" that you're supposed to feel then? Maybe. And it's exactly for that reason that I don't recommend it. This is a lesson that nobody hasn't already learnt and all that we really get is a game that stresses out completionists.I'm glad that I was able to at least end the game and explore a good bit of the area, and I don't feel like coming back to do so again. Check it out for yourself if you find yourself with a good amount of free time over the course of a few weeks and no game that you actually enjoy available to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. I wish I could play it for the first time again.Overall the experience is exactly what you'd expect. I enjoyed exploring the caves, and the shade is an interesting character. While playing I found myself wondering a lot about what this world was like before my time. This game is artful exploration of loneliness, solitude, and desire (The Longing).You really feel the weight of The Shade's responsibility, his isolation and his curiosity. There is a sense that there might be more to life, and The Shade doesn't know if he desires or fears it. Ultimately, It's up to you to decide The Shade's destiny.The atmosphere is strong, greatly enhanced by the sound design and music, and there's no choice but to take it slow.This game is full of little surprises and hurdles to overcome, and the mysteries have delightful little solutions. The atmosphere really makes The Shade seem small. Think outside the box while playing, and take a good long look at everything.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: To describe The Longing as a game would be an inaccurate statement.There isn't really a goal, there is no clear conflict, there isn't challenge to be had or threats to overcome. It's all just a humble piece of art trying to convey the themes of loneliness and having plenty of time but nothing to do with it.And it does it very well. Calm and eerie music, the plodding walk of the character teaching the player patience, well drawn art and well written dialogue. This clearly had passion in it's creation.This is not a product for everyone, I wouldn't even say it has a target audience. It is intentionally slow, it forces you to wait minutes for simple things and a month for a path to unlock. But it does so on purpose, something which what few negative reviewers this game has seem to pointedly refuse to understand. You don't buy this for the instant gratification of an action game, you don't play it for the tragedy of a dark fantasy game. You buy it to wander the empty halls of a forgotten kingdom, listening to the shade's slapping footsteps echo into the dark.If you're the kind to spend some time in meditation and calm reflection, give The Longing a try.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this semi-passive slow-paced game. _childDocuments_.review: :THE LONGING: is a unique mix of game and art project. That is the best way I can describe it. No matter what you do, the game will take 400 real days to beat, from the moment you launch it for the first time. If you play for 1000 hours in that time, or if you play 1 hour, after 400 Days, the game ends.    You are a shade, the sole and trusty minion of the King, your only goal is to wake him up after 400days have passed. What you do in that time is entirely up to you. I don’t want to spoil anything, besides, that what you do has an influence on the ending, and that there is more than one.   :THE LONGING: is a very slow game, the shade isn’t in a hurry, and so shouldn’t you. The game requires a great deal of patience, but why would you be in a hurry anyways when you have that much time? While you explore the vast underground area of the Kings Kingdom you will find items that help the shade to decorate its room, but reaching certain areas can, and will, take a while to reach. For example, there is a cliff you can’t jump down, but after 2 (real) weeks, enough moss has grown at the bottom of it, that you can jump down. You will travel a lot. What helps that there is a system to safe positions to which the shade can talk again without your control, which is definitely a great addition, to find places again in the vast caverns, or just don’t spend 10 minutes by yourself to reach that one place again.   :THE LONGING: definitely won’t blow you away with its graphics, but it has its charm, and together with the ambient sounds, it generates a really nice atmosphere.   I can only recommend the game, its such a unique experience, unlike anything I ever played before in my life. The only thing I would say that is a requirement to enjoy            :THE LONGING: is patience, from start to finish, :THE LONGING: is never in any hurry. But if you can open yourself up to experience the game offers, I am sure you won’t regret playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: A combination point-and-click adventure/idle game that has some interesting ideas, but doesn't do the best job at executing them. The mechanics failed to maintain a balance between encouraging patience and inducing tedium, there isn't enough meaningful content to occupy the time it expects you to spend on it, and a gameplay loop that benefits from frequently ignoring the game made it hard to get emotionally invested. I knew going into it that it wasn't a game for everyone, and I suppose that it's just not for me either.  is part point-and-click adventure, part walking simulator, and part idle game with a very unique time-based gameplay hook. The story is that the king of a once-prosperous underground kingdom has run out of power and must enter a deep sleep in order to restore it. He instructs his final servant, known only as the Shade, to wait in his kingdom for 400 days until he awakens, after which he will "end all fear and longing" in the world. That's 400 real-world days, as the game keeps track of the flow of time even when you turn it off. The concept is fascinating, but the execution left something to be desired for me.First off, . The Shade has this little house that can be expanded and filled with different objects you find from exploring the caves; and as you provide the Shade with new amenities or keep it occupied with activities like reading books, time will advance at a faster pace whenever you're inside the house. The difference is negligible at first, but keep at it and you'll find that a single real-time second can advance the in-game clock by over 10, 20, even 30+ seconds at a time. , though your exact time will vary depending on the actions you take.Before I continue, I need to go on a quick side tangent: after spending some time mulling over my playthrough, I feel like the ability to speed up time is a double-edged sword. From a pure gameplay perspective, it makes perfect sense: a game that marches towards its end regardless of whether you play it or not needs something to get the player to actually engage; otherwise they can just run it once, turn it off, then come back 400 days later and have the same result with much less effort. That said, I think that it ended up taking away from the emotional impact that I feel the developers wanted me to have. Since speeding up time only occurs inside the Shade's house, it made time spent outside of it feel tedious; and I lost the desire to revisit old locations or just stroll to take in the scenery because it felt like any unnecessary time outside was detrimental to my overall progression. The fact that individual events can take anywhere from ten minutes to several hours, with nothing in-between to hold your attention, means that the best solution to moments often meant for quiet reflection is to just close out the game and come back later when the event is over. I played for a couple hours a day at first, and I managed to see everything that wasn't locked behind a timer in about 2-3 days. Those locked areas opened up after a few in-game weeks—only a few days in real-time for me—and nearly all of them gave me just an extra room or two to explore along with a few more goodies for the house. As I ran out of things to do, my average playtime decreasing with each passing day, a quick look at an online guide confirmed that . That may not sound like a big deal, but at this point I was only 100 days into my 400-day timer, and now all that was left for me to do was wait—nowhere else to explore, no more reason to regularly check in, and only one last time-gated event (the Shade's birthday on day 365) to look forward to.  other than read from a selection of public domain books you can find around the caves, and there are more comfortable/accessible ways to do that than through this particular software.You might be wondering why I keep complaining that a game I have over 30 hours of playtime on "doesn't have enough to do", and that's because . The Shade walks at a snail's pace, and getting to locations of interest can take up to half an hour of unimpeded movement in some cases. This isn't because the map is very big—despite references of a "vast" kingdom, it's actually quite small—it's just because you move so very slow. You're unable to auto-walk to places until you visit them at least once, so your first trip to any new spot on the map is a tedious manual process. Mouse users need to double-click in front of the Shade every few seconds to move them forward since the camera limits how far ahead you can see, and keyboard/controller users will need to hold down the walk key/control stick respectively for the entire trek to your objective. , something that's exacerbated once the late-game puzzles start to introduce a degree of trial and error in order to solve them without a walkthrough.Ultimately, the payoff for the patience and tedium didn't feel worth it to me.   I don't regret playing it, though, far from it. It had the guts to do something truly original, and I have the utmost respect for that even though I don't feel that it fully accomplished its goal. If you're into the more experimental side of games, there's a good chance that you'll get something more out of it than I did; and I'd still encourage you to give the game a try if you think you can look past the issues I had with it. If nothing else, it's something I imagine that I'll remember for a long time, and that's more than I can say for a lot of other games I've played in the past.

_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely one of the most unique games I have ever played. It is most definitely not for everyone. You can't really sit down and blast through it in a weekend. It's more of a marathon than a sprint. Setting goals and reminders for time gated objectives to beat hours, days, or in some cases weeks after you've encountered a road block. While that may not sound exciting I found myself thinking about this game a lot while not playing it. I definitely got a sense of accomplishment overcoming seemingly small hurdles that took time and patience to overcome. I really do wish you could move the character a little faster, but it's clear that the glacial pace of the game was very intentional. He's not in a rush, and if you are then you're going to be frustrated by this game.I am recommending this game, but again it's really not for everyone. I would recommend NOT looking at any spoilers since a lot of mysteries are much more fun to figure out for yourself. I know there are things I've missed, and I will play through it again in the future. The Longing might not be the best game I've played all year, but I won't forget it or how it made me feel for quite a long time. Then again maybe 2020 wasn't the best year to play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: THE LONGING

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game in the conventional sense.I'd compare it to "The Stanley Parable" or "The Beginner's guide". It is a meta-experince.The game is an excericise in time and patience.What does it mean to spend time in the game? How do we spend time in a game? Whats the goal of a game? Is sitting in a chair and reading a book a game, once its in a videogame?Those are some of the questions I had for myself, while playing the game.If you decide to play the game, I'd recommend NOT to watch the different endings beforehand. Looking up where different secrets are hidden is okay in my view, but the endings shouldn't be spoiled before you havn't had atleast one playthrough by yourself.I do recommend the game, even though not for the full price. The experience is worth paying for though.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m doing this writeup about a year after I started The Longing (life happened), so it’s to the game’s credit that I still remember so much of it so vividly.Let’s state the obvious first: The Longing has among the most distinctive art and sound design I’ve ever played. Art-wise, the entire game is hand-drawn, and the cave backgrounds are huge, such that every screen feels like a piece of a vast tapestry. In video games, caves are typically dull grey polygons; these caves drip with atmosphere. The character design of the player character, The Shade, feels so perfectly expressive that I’m confident there’s an alternate universe where he breaks out as a sort of emo Hello Kitty.The soundtrack goes all-in on evoking longing and loneliness, not through generic “sad” music, but through vast and sombre compositions that emphasize the size and age of the cave, and the weight of the Shade’s quest.But how does it actually play? Here, The Longing is more of a mixed bags. It does clever things with its formula, giving you active things to do (exploring the cave and figuring out how to delve further) while forcing a certain amount of waiting that is core to the game’s themes, and there are some wonderful puzzles and moments of discovery. But there are also a number of things that are too opaque, puzzles solutions that you are more likely to stumble upon through dumb luck than lateral thinking. This is doubly true for the paths to the game’s different endings, which were (to me) unintuitive—a significant issue because the game is explicitly designed to be played only once.Yet overall I really enjoyed my experience with The Longing and The Shade, and I suspect it will stick with me long after I’ve forgotten most of the other games I played in 2020.

name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree
detailed_description: The Gods have abandoned Midgard. Once a prosperous land teeming with mythical beasts and beings, it now rots from the inside, tainted by unknown forces. Odin’s chosen guardians of the realm are gone. In their absence, the sacred Elder Tree they swore to protect is exposed to abuse and manipulation. Now, the only remnants of hope reside in Estra, the daughter of mankind’s last great leader. With a heavy emphasis on narrative, Estra’s journey through Midgard is filled with Nordic lore, mysterious twists, and consequential decisions. Players will converse with a variety of characters and share in Estra’s discoveries as she learns more about her family’s past and the looming darkness spreading across the realm. Estra’s path is fraught with difficult decisions and untrustworthy characters that can lead her astray. Her story is intertwined with the player’s ability to discern fact from fiction and to decide right from wrong. Avoid battle, help companions, save your people, but remember that the consequences are Estra’s to bear. Along the way, players must solve incrementally challenging puzzles that reveal insightful secrets, fantastical abilities, and hidden passageways. While trial and error is useful, patience is necessary. Not every problem allows for multiple mistakes and failure is most certainly an option. The answers you seek may be lost if you make the wrong decision. Violence isn’t always necessary, but, when push comes to shove, ATONE’s combat is a delicate dance of sword and axe. Combat is grounded in the rhythm game genre and the mechanics of titles like Guitar Hero and Dance Dance Revolution. Music is a crucial component, with each fight receiving its very own song. ATONE’s music and sound design are composed by a variety of incredible artists, including: Julian Ratschiller, Australian artist Luminist (a.k.a. James Shuar), who blends a synth-heavy score with the digitally corrupted sounds of period-specific instruments, and Andrew Prahlow, whose name can be attributed to the critically acclaimed hit Outer Wilds and epics like Star Wars and Blade Runner .

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first play through, I'd say a general run of this game will typically take players about 4 hours- but what a fun journey it is! The music and art is fantastic here, it's a beautiful world and story to travel through. Honestly if you're someone who enjoys atmospheric games with a strong story-line, this is the one for you! Strong character design, tons of Norse mythology lore in animated cut scenes, and a little froggy best friend!But if you're looking for incredible mechanics and puzzles, I'd advice you look somewhere else. A lot of the puzzles weren't clearly established in the world- as in there were no hints as to how to solve them, aside from spending some 'puzzle points' you can gather throughout your adventure to gain a hint. I'm no puzzle extraordinaire, but if you give me instructions I can figure it out 9/10 times. This game just . . . doesn't tell you how to solve them. There's literally a puzzle in here called The Impossible Puzzle (or something like that), and all you do is pick 1/20 dots on the screen at random with a single chance to get it right.As far as the fighting goes, it's incredibly forgiving. I was on the hardest level and just kind of. . . tapped around? I did my best, but it was nothing fancy- never died, never had to heal. Enjoy the little musical cut scenes going on in the background, you really only need to pay attention to the actual battle so much. Whether that's a deal breaker is up to you! I think total there's only about 6 battles in the game either way, so come here for the flavor, not the fights!All in all, loved the experience and getting to support a smaller game. If you like the trailers, check it out! Great game to binge over an evening.

_childDocuments_.review: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree is an interactive story game that combines puzzle solving and rhythm-based combat. As a young warrior named Estra, you must journey through Midgard to learn about her family's past and stop the looming darkness spreading across the realm. With difficult decisions ahead and a deep narrative, this norse-mythology inspired game will keep you engaged with its delectable soundtrack and unique visual style. Will you be able to discover the truth and rise up against the corruption that is manifesting?Through my time playing ATONE, I was captivated by the music and the story. I am also a sucker for Guitar Hero-like gameplay, which is the combat system in this game (prompts coming down a rail to the beat of the music). I also loved the art style in general, but the art pieces that came up during combat were especially appealing. I also like the difficulty selection, which allows either 2 or 4 rails of button prompts. But one question remains: How does ATONE run on the Steam Deck? Well, I have the answer!ATONE has absolutely no issues when it comes to performance on Deck! The game itself performs flawlessly at 60 FPS with a 6W - 8W battery drain. No changes to any settings are needed in-game to enjoy this game optimally!The one issue that I see is the cutscenes not showing up when playing without any forced compatibility. But, if you use Proton GE, this will be completely fixed! I used Proton GE 7-47, but any later version, and possibly some earlier ones, should work just fine. You can follow our guide on how to get Proton GE for yourself, as well as the importance of why having it is a good idea!Otherwise, I found no issues with playing the game on Deck. Controls worked great, no hitches in framerate or stability, and battery drain being so low allowed a long battery life of 5.5 - 6 hours.ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree is an awesome game and one that I can see myself chilling out and getting lost in a captivating story with a mesmerizing soundtrack. The difficulty selection is a nice touch and I enjoyed the rhythm combat and visual style. And to top it all off, the game runs near-perfect on the Steam Deck without any changes in-game, just make sure to use Proton GE for the cutscenes! I am happy to say that ATONE is a Best on Deck game and definitely one worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: This game almost got a recommended status for me.I'll start with the good and later show why it didn't get a recommendation1) Norse mythology (yes I'm a sucker for it) and the game has an engaging story2) Cool and unique art syle3) Good music selection for the rhythm gamesPuzzles get a neutral rating for me. I enjoy the IQ-type of puzzles, quite on the easy side, but there are 1 chance-only puzzles that can be interpreted with more than one possible solution.Now, onto the downsides:After the unique art style fades its novelty, you'll find that the gameplay is boring, especially at the start and mid-game. Too much downtime and I can't help it's because of the slooooooooow walk/run speed. The game's concept and ideas are admirable, but the major ones are undercooked. 1) Branching story, but a snoozefest.  There are 4 endings and 6 possible paths, but they don't offer a duplicate saving mechanic so you can split your choice and easily go back the critical point. Instead, you have to start ALL OVER AGAIN to attempt a new path. There are skips, but the rhythm game battle battles are mandatory. I can't replay the game with it being boring gameplay 2) Rhythm game as a battle sequence: cool idea, Fantastic music, decent note mapping. However, the inability to modify note speed is a major downside for a rhythm game connoisseur. This has the added downside that it's harder to determine if you need to press a note pattern simultaneously OR in rapid succession. The lane distance is large enough, it could use an indicator to show when notes are paired or synced

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of the abstract art & aesthetics, love the color and contrast. Fun character stories and holy m, I would be lying if I say I wasn't confused at what was going on at the start, no spoilers but I was losing my sh*t as I discovered who Estra's mom was and what happened.... Everything makes so much sense.Really appreciated the effort of the team to reship such a great game -- or rather, a piece of art, to Steam so I get to finally play it as I didn't get to play it when it was on Apple arcade. Gameplay-wise, this is the best music/rhythm game I've ever played, the music is nice and soothing & full of depth. The key in the battle are so well matched to the music and felt great getting perfect combo.I'm that type of player who loves to try going into every single corner and to see if there's a secret path to anything, and if you're like me, Atone is not going to let you down. I absolutely loved all the Easter eggs (Lord of the rings, Pokemon, God of War .. even Berserk!) in the game and feel greatly rewarded after I discovered them. Whoever in the team that sneaked these Easter egges into the game poured so much passion into game making and I just loved to see that.You can't miss Atone if you're a fan of story-driven game, because I am one and I never regretted any single minutes that I spent to play ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree.

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review: I first picked up Atone in a game bundle. Ironically, I only really wanted to play the main game in the bundle, but it happened to be less expensive to buy the bundle rather than the other game by itself, so I decided, why not give this a try? I am a huge fan of the old Norse mythology stories and a sucker for puzzles, so I figured it wouldn’t be too bad to play through it. I have to be honest and say within the first ten minutes of the game, I wasn’t a huge fan (keep reading as that wasn't my ending opinion). The story starts off pretty rough and sad. On top of that, the rhythm game ended up giving me a headache due to the fact that the line moves and there’s a lot of stuff going on in the background during the game. Considering that we have serious ooh-shiny disorder, it was a tad overwhelming. It actually led me to turn on story mode, which makes it so that you can’t fail the rhythm games, just so I didn’t feel like I *had* to do a rhythm game if I didn’t want to. There is also a hard mode that makes it so that the games have 4 buttons instead of 2, but that was definitely not an option for me (lol).After having said that, I will say that while I disliked the rhythm portions at first, by the end of it I wasn’t too bothered by them. The boss battle music that plays in the background to them is enjoyable and I found myself bopping my head to the beats and enjoying them more than I thought. Despite turning on story mode, I did do all of the rhythm battles and I didn’t feel like they were a struggle so, something to bear in mind for your playthrough should you buy the game.Aside from the rhythm games you have a huge mix of different puzzles. Some you can’t fail, some you get only one try, and yes, I did fail a few of the one-try-only puzzles, leaving me frustrated and wishing I could reload my save to try again. All of the frustration led me to want to create an “all puzzles” video for you guys so that you don’t have to be in the same situation that I was, staring at the puzzles for 20 minutes wracking my brain for the tiny detail I was missing or the most obvious solution sitting right in front of my face (I was too stubborn to google it). It made me chuckle that I got to the end of the game and the last “impossible” puzzle, I solved in a matter of a minute or two and I actually found it to be incredibly easy with all the clues it gave when the puzzle right before that one left me stumped and staring at my screen annoyed. What can be extra discouraging is the fact that a lot of the one-try-only puzzles unlock hidden secrets or lead to the “good” outcomes in the story, and failing them led to… well, I’ll save you the spoilers but it wasn’t always great. Of course, all of the main story puzzles gave you infinite tries so that you could still “progress” but as a completionist, failing the side puzzles bothered me to no end. Aside from the puzzles and rhythm games, the game is quite beautiful to just wander around in. You walk through the world, encountering creatures, monsters, and people, all painted in an art style that I grew to quite enjoy. It’s simple and has a very “digital” feel to it, but it fit the theme and mood of the game. The thing I enjoyed most was how well the story was told through the cutscenes and the voice acting. It was all well done and it made learning about Norse mythology quite exciting. I’m positive getting to watch the story can be enjoyed all by itself. All in all, I would recommend Atone. I can happily say that if this is your style of game, you should definitely pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty boring. There is a lot of running around, looking for the correct text to read or puzzle to solve ( most are pretty simple). _childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Atone: Heart of the Elder tree is a wonderful game about a girl who’s been through a lot of loss in her life. I feel like the game portrays grief and loss very well. I am glad it mostly stuck to the actual Norse mythology. Finding the lore notes is fun and the animated lore book that sometimes appears when you interact with characters is very neat. One thing that they could have improved on is the voice acting. Some characters did it really well, others were mediocre at best. The art is stunning and there’s so much to do that you cannot see everything in one playthrough. It makes sense, since there are four different endings to the game. The puzzles are fun and challenging as well. I would like to go back and get all the endings with time.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: The story is great, I was hooked from the start. Just enough worldbuilding to get sucked in, without too many walls of text that could get you bored. I adore stories loosely based on mythologies.Superb artstyle - the geometry, sense of scale (and giants!) remind me of Hyper Light Drifter.The rhythmic elements make a good change of pace from the usual exploration and dialogue, although they aren't the main draw of the game for me.Minor annoyances - not being able to rebind controls or use a mouse. Other than that, great stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely  Atone. I actually wasn't expecting to like it this much!The story is really good. The cutscenes are voiced and while it's not super polished, I like them, they have their own charm. You get really into it as it goes on.Your choices will matter for the story. I've done two playthroughs so far to see the different story diversions, but have yet to get all of the achievements. The second time, I couldn't stop playing. It's addictive!Other positives:→ The puzzles are good brainteasers. There was only one where I couldn't understand a part even after the answer was shown, otherwise I'd say they are all pretty fair.→ The music for the battles, cutscenes and world is awesome. I particularly like the tranquil and pretty music that plays when you walk around.→ I love the art, too. Clean, simple and very nice.Just some thoughts:There is odal power, split into three types of odal energy.You get odal power from battling and coming across stones (a few stones have puzzles attached to them).Collecting enough chaos odal power will allow you to open two or three side doors. And if you want to retry a puzzle it will cost you an odal power (if you have a certain item). Other than these few instances, I'm not sure what else the odal energies do. Do they influence the story depending on how much power you have? Maybe?A character called Veldin will ask you questions based on things you read on your journey. If you get the question right, sometimes he gives you an item like a crest or cloth. But they don't show up in the menu, give you money or add to any of your power/health.Maybe they also influence the story? Some clearer information would be useful.Battling is done with a rhythm game. You can change the difficulty of the rhythm sections at certain locations on the map, rather than on the menu. You can choose to not play the rhythm parts at all, play with two buttons, or play with all four. As I've never really played a rhythm game before, I went for Normal Mode (two buttons) and was fine!You can replay battles in the Arena section, but you can't select a difficulty there. Some of the battles are really hard and it's just a slew of inputs that I can't wrap my head around. It's a shame I can't practice them more slowly first or on an easier difficulty and then build up from there. Some achievements are linked to high scores on these harder battles; I'm not sure if I'll ever get those!But all that aside, I still really love this game. I will be playing it again for sure. If you like puzzles and a good story, pick this up!EDIT: I was able to get the rhythm achievements I thought were impossible! Just by playing for fun and somehow improving!
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine.Visually it's obviously amazing and the story cutscenes are crazy cinematic. The problem though is that there's simply too much fluff in between the rhythm battles or there are simply too few rhythm battles spread throughout the game. Also, the rhythm fights are way too easy for my taste. I instantly turned it on hard mode and still barely felt challenged. However, the mix between Hyper Light Drifter and arcade rhythm game was really cool.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: A unique genre-crossing musical adventure. Some echoes of Superbrothers Sword and Sorcery and Hyper Light Drifter. Somehow the writers managed to make me care about even the most minor of characters even though the story was short and concise. But what really sets this game apart is the heart-pounding musical battles.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: The story really exceeded my expectations by a lot. I really wanted to keep playing to know what would happen. The Norse mythology was excellently woven into the storytelling. I especially loved all of the little secrets you can find (quite a lot of them!). The rhythm combat adds a nice layer to the game, with good music. In fact, it's a soundtrack I'd buy if that was available. You can change the difficulty of combat in the story, but not in the arena, which is just playing the combat scenes (I found normal fairly easy, but hard is definitely hard to get perfect at). The only downsides are that there is no key rebinding- I couldn't even get it in a round about way through Steam (not only is this a critical accessibility function, but also very useful for everyone else); and no separate saves, so if you want to see how a different choice impacts the story, you must replay the entire game. I think saving wherever whenever should be mandatory in this digital age of gaming. That being said, this game is actually worth replaying from the start.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game with a choice-driven narrative that really helps you feel like part of the world. Although a lot of the puzzles are easy, there are some tougher ones. And a variety of them. There's also riddles (which I'm horrific at) which is fun! A unique aspect of this game is the rhythm game combat. This is super fun, and has a normal mode and a hard mode. The normal mode is pretty forgiving, so even if you're terrible at rhythm games, you'll likely survive. But there's also a story mode that lets you bypass the rhythm game elements entirely. So that's a really nice feature. Would highly recommend! :)
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game, I have only positive things to say about it. First the art style, it is beautiful and simple yet detailed. It has an angular style to it but it all flows together so well, will make some very nice screenshots. Next the game play, the battles are done in an interesting way, it is what drew me to the game in the first place, and I can easily say that I love it. If you don’t want that much challenge in the battles they have 3 modes Story, Normal and Hard, so if you want you can focus solely on the story. I love that you have the arena to replay the battles, I found that it was good place to practice to get better, I have never played a game like this before(battle mechanics), so it was really fun to play something new. The music is so good it sounds so nice, I am not doing it justice the way I describe it. The story, I’m not that good at describing this but, it was amazing it made you want to see what happens next, which is what you want obviously, the characters are well written/you love some you hate some. It is a puzzle game its not that hard, any of the puzzles that you need to do to continue the story are not really challenging to the point you want to give up, but they do have hints which is always nice. Your choices matter so you can guide the story a bit more how you want. So to sum it up, If you like the look of it, get it, I think you should.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the logic puzzles are sometimes very simple, solving them is satisfying. While exploring the world, I also appreciated the collectibles, which were often hidden in an interesting way, so finding them was even more fun (it's nice that they often referred to other games or movies).I think it is a great game, especially if you appreciate games focused on building immersion and not afraid to mix, in their form, genres seemingly extremely different from each other.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Initial impressions are that this one is an odd duck, but boasts some strong visual direction and if nothing else, it has character aplenty. _childDocuments_.review: Had no idea what I was getting into with this one, but man I’m glad I gave it a go.Incredible visuals hit you first, with a colour palette so gorgeous it’s utter eye candy. The animation style is sick (I don’t have the words to describe the style but loved it lol).The whole game is like an ode to Norse mythology, with names you’ll recognise and tales that are beautifully told via excellent and fitting narration. The gameplay is mainly puzzle based, but very much symbols and riddle type puzzles which personally love.Then there’s the rhythm based aspect which is how combat is portrayed. Think guitar hero but you’re fighting, I guess. Sometimes wish I could have focused more on the actual fights themselves, as the animations are just that good, but of course loved the flow state feel you find yourself in when bopping along to the brilliant OST.Overall, loved it. Perfect length, well developed story with multiple endings, characters you care about, and gameplay that hits the sweet spot.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: This was... Hm. I don't know how to explain what sort of game this is. Rhythm combat, story-rich, puzzle based. Some of the puzzles were ridiculously easy and felt great to accomplish, and some were like getting hit with a sledge hammer. The art design was a little off-putting... it felt like a Nordic version of Teen Titans where some of the portraits were done in a zany! anime-esque style, but then there would be some incredibly smooth animations / cut scenes, only to have another blocky sort of... weird... picture? I don't know how to describe it. It wasn't BAD just... jarring.Really liked the mythology/lore tidbits, and I'm glad to have played it. Though since you have to replay the whole thing multiple times to get all the achievements and endings, I probably won't (I just don't have the time for it).Overall, I actually enjoyed it and hope you do, too.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Atone: Heart of the Elder Tree is really a great game! It's got a unique and fun gameplay style, nice art, and beautiful music throughout. The story is good, if a bit lacking, but I don't believe that's the main draw and appeal of the game. But the music throughout the entire game was truly phenomenal, the tracks always got me hyped or sad for what was to come. While the playtime was shorter than I wanted, the game has multiple endings for you to go back and check out. Additionally, there's an arena mode so that you can redo earlier battles, and also unlocks a couple new battles against characters you didn't fight against.My main gripe with the game is the lack of being able to create save slots, as there were many times in the story where the path diverges. And while I really do appreciate how you have to deal with the consequences of your actions, if I want to see how something might have played out differently it means I have to play through the entire game again from the beginning. Not cool Sonic.The puzzles in the game are fun. For me, they were all really easy, and I'd figure out most at just a glance. The "Impossible puzzle" had been solved within seconds just by looking at the screen and the information given. But they were still fun nonetheless, it made me feel really smart whenever I solved something.As a note for the developers, if you're listening, the only recommendation I have for this game is explanations for everything. With a vast majority of items in the game, such as menuing, battles, and even some quests, it's entirely unsaid what you're supposed to do, or what the function of the thing your using is. I never understood what food was supposed to do, even at the end of the game. I didn't know what any items did, I didn't understand what the artifacts and mead potion stuff was until the end of the game, and overall trying to understand and navigate the menu at the beginning of the game was a nightmare, and almost made me stop playing the game entirely because I was just so confused. But outside of that, I really do think that this game is great. Would highly recommend, and I hope that the issues that I had may be fixed in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Jack of all trades, master of none. This is a nice little dabble into different game mechanics that I like (rhythm, Undertale-esque RPG, pick-your-adventure, puzzles), but I was left wanting more out of everything. Like drinking a lukewarm orange juice—it’s satisfying, but doesn’t hit that nice refreshing satisfaction that iced/cold orange juice does.The game is meant to be replayable, but there isn’t much difference between playthroughs. The different endings are really only dependent on a few choices you make throughout the game, and the rest is pretty much linear otherwise. By my third one, I was already feeling burnt out because dialogue and choices really only have an impact on about 25% of the actual events in-game, give or take, with most of them being towards the end. This wouldn’t be too bad, but they took away the save system, so you HAVE to run through everything all over again. Definitely recommend using a walkthrough after your first or second run. I had to restart a handful of times when I realized I just made a choice late into the game that just cost me a new ending. I wish they had kept the save system, because I thoroughly enjoyed the story and gameplay during my first run, but because of having to restart from the start and speedrunning to get the new endings, my satisfaction with the game fell.The music is honestly pretty damn good and the rhythm sections are pretty nice, but the difficulty was just a little underwhelming; this is a good rhythm game for beginners and early intermediates, but for those that are more experienced, you may be wanting more out of the maps like me. I liked all the references and little humor interjected throughout. Overall, it was a nice game to spend some time on despite the things I said above. Definitely worth running through twice, and if you like it enough, completionist isn’t too far out of reach.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: I just submitted a refund request, but I thought I'd leave a positive review to boost the game a bit to those who would enjoy it more than I have. By my personal taste, the overworld portions had too little gameplay, too much dialogue, and too many cutscenes. I may have been able to grow into liking it if the story had a more steady progression in terms of story intrigue, but the prominence of the story in the gameplay felt like it would make puzzles confusing and be tedious if I were to skip all dialogue and cutscenes. However, the part I wish I could have played separately were the rhythm battles. What I played of them were really fun, and I wish I could have played more without all of the story. If the devs ever add a way of just playing through the battles individually without getting to them in the story mode first, I may consider re-buying the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Atone was a great experience! I liked the spin on the traditional Norse mythology and how the characters played into the story, I feel like the game did a great job at creating and playing out the themes of grief, self-confidence, and religious contexts like Atheism. The art-style and look of the game is flawlessly done and the environments are designed to feel so massive despite the game not being open world. You can really feel the world go beyond the screen you're on. The game play and music of course are where this rhythm game excel. The puzzles were plenty and well-crafted, I'd even say too well crafted. The puzzles started off great, but quickly got quite difficult because math and obtuse symbols. The hint system could have done a better job, sometimes it flat out gave me the answer, other times it did nothing to help me except give me more questions. Despite this, I didn't feel cheated by them, just stupid. The music and combat f*cking slapped, I stg. The battles were fairly easy, I played on normal, but towards the end they got quite challenging. I had to fight the final boss a handful of times to get it just right. The progression of the story was evenly paced, and there were a few side missions and puzzles I did, I'm pretty sure I did all of them so 5.5/6 hours is the time to beat. Besides my gripes with the puzzles, the game was a blast to play, and my chat had a fun time helping me with puzzles, and we were all gripped by the story. I would love to go back and try hard-mode!
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Very atmospheric game with an interesting mix of genres, I liked it a lot. The haunting music makes it a very special experience, the narrative is pretty obscure at the beginning but becomes more clear later. I loved the puzzles, their style and how there are inserted into the game reminds me a lot of the Layton games.The game rewards exploration with the unlock of new options or choices in the story, which can bring to several different endings. The downside of this is that, since there is no backtracking, it's easy to miss something that is required for the best ending just because you didn't noticed a path that may be hard to see.This may be a little frustrating, as I was always afraid I'd miss something, but in the end I actually got the best ending on my first try, so if you keep your eyes open and don't rush ahead you'll probably be fine without a guide.

_childDocuments_.review: At the beginning, it's worth noting Wildboy Studios have already made games that are focused on narrative and unveiling mysteries of the game world in creative way. Or should I say, Atone was the first one and their other productions follow the stream. As some may have already noticed, Atone isn't brand new game, originally it was launched in 2019 as part of apple arcade and was ported now to other devices. Don't take me wrong, I really appreciate they have made effort to let more audience enjoy this piece of art but unfortunately remnants of mobile game past remain. Lack of mouse support, non-existing settings tab (I'd love to be able to rebind some keys) and worse of all, however that might be just my case, low framerate animations and blurry art on resolution I'm using.Now that we are past some of the game's shortcomings it is time to move to it's strengths.Story so far was enjoyable, I've enjoyed cinematics most, however sometimes I felt that voice acted dialogues didn't covet emotions characters felt, but all in all, that's good part of the game.Another thing what bamboozled me a bit was camera perspective. It's different, kind of top-down 2D, but with some quirks. It somehow fits into the style of the game.The mechanics part I've enjoyed the most, as the player of other rhythm games, was combat. Relatively easy but enjoyable guitar hero simulator. Only flaw I've noticed was key binding that couldn't be changed and I'd love to be able to rebind those 1 2 9 0 keys.Last thing that is a big surprise are easter eggs hidden in the game. I won't go into details, just go and explore yourself and be rewarded. :)All in all, if you are looking for story-driven game in really unique graphics style accompanied by beautiful music and don't mind some quirks existing from mobile past (that don't really influence gameplay that much), the game is definitely for you!
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: Another indiegame gem from Untold Tales. Wonderful, unique mix of engaging narrative, adventure, exploration, great puzzles and pinch of (optional) rhythm battles. Gorgeous artstyle allows for atmospheric environments and impressive visuals, matched by fantastic soundtrack. If you're fan of Norse mythology, don't miss this one. Plenty of great lore here, with variety of characters and story shaped with your choices and consequences.
_childDocuments_.name: ATONE: Heart of the Elder Tree

_childDocuments_.review: This game mixes so many different element, that I am suprised it works so well as a whole. First there is the story, that's more mature (and sometimes brutal) than it seems at first glance. The decisions matter a lot and can lead to completely different outcomes. Voice acting is used sparingly, but when it is used it's more than solid. Then there are puzzles and exploration. The puzzles are mostly simple, yet satisfying, but sometimes they also provide a challenge. There is an in-game hint system so there is no way to get stuck and most of them are optional anyway. Same goes for exploration - there is A LOT of optional content, that sometimes affects main story and when it doesn't you are still getting rewarded by getting gold or items.Lastly there is combat in a form of simple rhythm game. This is probably the weakest part of Atone, but it's easy and visually enjoyable, so it didn't manage to bore me. There is also the excellent battle music and the fact that a lot of conflicts can be solved without fighting. In my opinion the game is definitely worth it, for the branching narrative alone and everything else is just icing on the cake.

_childDocuments_.review:
The Gods have abandoned Midgard. Once a prosperous land teeming with mythical beasts and beings, it now rots from the inside, tainted by unknown forces. Odin's chosen guardians of the realm are gone. In their absence, the sacred Elder Tree they swore to protect is exposed to abuse and manipulation. Now, the only remnants of hope reside in Estra, the daughter of mankind's last great leader.

With a heavy emphasis on narrative, Estra's journey through Midgard is filled with Nordic lore, mysterious twists, and consequential decisions. Players will converse with a variety of characters and share in Estra's discoveries as she learns more about her family's past and the looming darkness spreading across the realm.

name: Littlewood
detailed_description: You defeated the Dark Wizard. The world of Solemn is finally at peace, but at what cost? You can't quite remember... The Hero Who Saved the World Explore the vast world of Solemn. Enchanted Forests, Bustling Fishing Towns, & Dark Mining Caves are some of the few places to visit. Meet Townsfolk and convince them to stay in your town. Perhaps meeting people will unlock your memories of the past… Collect rare items and materials found across the world and bring them back to your town for selling and crafting! Customize Your Town Harvest materials by chopping wood, mining ores, catching bugs, and fishing in rivers and ponds! Unlock new structures to build by meeting new Townsfolk. Want a Tavern or a Lumber Mill? How about a Fishing Hut or a Magical Library? Your town's design is all up to you! Fulfill your Townsfolk's requests. Some may want to live on a higher elevation, others may want to be surrounded by trees and water. Fulfilling the requests of your Townsfolk will earn you their hearts and unlock new relationship paths. Master New Hobbies & Crafts Gathering : Whether you’re picking fruit or picking weeds, your gathering skill will level up! The Gatherer’s Glove is needed to unlock this ability. Mining : Looking for shiny ores to collect? Interested in rare materials for crafting? Then mining is for you! Woodcutting : Those pesky trees and debris that keep popping up all over town needs to be chopped! Wood is an essential material for building new structures and furniture. Bug Catching : Craft a Bug Net and catch all sorts of critters. Be sure to go bug hunting during each season and at different times of the day! Fishing : There's nothing quite like relaxing by a pond with a fishing rod in hand. You can sell fish for a decent price at the Shopping District, or use them as ingredients for new cooking dishes. Farming : Plant some seeds in tilled soil and wait a few days. Veggies are an essential ingredient to many cooking recipes! Also, they make your town look pretty. Cooking : Once you've built the Tavern and have become good friends with Bubsy, you'll be able to start cooking delicious meals for your Townsfolk! Maybe you can attract rare Townsfolk by serving unique dishes... Crafting : There are tons of structures, decorative monuments, and furniture to craft. Often times your Townsfolk will request specific objects that they would like to be placed in their home. Make sure you gather enough building materials! Merchanting : Selling items at the Shopping District will net you large sums of Dewdrops, which is the main currency in Solemn. As you become a better Merchant, rarer items will appear for you to buy! Tarott Master : Once the Dark Wizard was defeated, all of his monsters were sealed away into Tarott Cards. Many Townsfolk collect and battle with these cards, and there is even a big competition held each year in Dirboros. Get collecting! Make New Friends Willow : A cheery young girl who wants to rebuild Littlewood. She found you in the middle of the forest and took care of you for 3 days while you were unconscious. She likes working with tools and is quite proficient at building things. Dalton : A ditsy boy who loves going on adventures with you. Despite his forgetfulness and silly demeanor, he actually can tell some very clever jokes. He enjoys fishing, catching bugs, and shopping for cool furniture. Lilith : A Wizard who graduated at the top of her class at Alexandria's Magical Academy. When she's not reading a book she's mixing random things together to make potions that may or may not explode. Also, she is your biggest fan. And many more!

short_description: The world has already been saved. Now it's time to rebuild your town, learn new hobbies, and forge lifelong friendships in this peaceful and relaxing RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is a fun game honestly. Throughout the time I've played it, I've always had something to do in the game. One of my favourite parts is the unique personalities of each of the NPCs. Although the dialogue for them can be repetitive, I think each thing they say showcases who they are. As well as that, the music is quite nice and fitting for the game and its activities.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute and enjoyable game. Offers to live as a completely ordinary mayor of a city in a fantasy world. Gradually, we will be introduced to many characters, with them there will be a lot of interesting events and activities. Unfortunately the game gets too grindy at the end and the latest achievements are just boring to get (i.e. you need about 1000 fish, 3000 trees and stones to complete the game, but you need twice as much to get all achievements).It's nice that almost all the mechanics are explained in the form of dialogues with the characters, so you can walkthrough the game without a guide. But, unfortunately, that's what "almost". Three times during the game, I get a quest that was simply impossible to complete without Google. Nevertheless, you are guaranteed 30 hours of pleasant relaxing game, and another 30 hours of minor fun if you want to explore the game to 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest with you: My first impressions of Littlewood weren't great.  I remember glancing at this pre-release and I immediately thought it plagiarized Stardew Valley.  I quickly dismissed it and went on about my life.  But Littlewood popped up in my recommendations a few days ago, and I saw far more positive reviews than negative.  It was also on sale, so I bought Littlewood, and it immediately surprised me.I can imagine there's quite a few people comparing this to Stardew Valley like I did, but Littlewood does a lot to distinguish itself in that this is more of a town building/managing game.  Sure, you can farm crops, but it doesn't focus as much on farming as Stardew Valley did. Not only is the priorities different from Stardew Valley, but Littlewood's world building is also drastically different.  The game takes place on a land called Solumn, which is seemingly more fantasy inspired.  You control what I can best describe as a "blank slate" known as the Hero of Solumn.  The character is pretty much an extension of you, the player.  The Hero is an amnesiac who saved the entire world from a mysterious entity called the Dark Wizard, and much of the world is in the process of rebuilding.  The Hero wakes up some time later in an empty house, and your comrades Willow and Dalton wait outside, and you begin the process of building up your town.  Over time, you will gain more building types, crops, citizens, and home and town customization.  What you choose to do for the town is up to you.  You're pretty much given freedom to do what you want with your town, with a few caveats.  You're obviously given quests and objectives to do.  The town comes with a woodworking building and a stone masonry from the onset.  You cut down trees to make planks at the woodworking building, and you can mine rocks to get stones for bricks.  It's necessary to make use of these buildings in the beginning, and you need to acquire blueprints from Willow and Dalton to get started on building homes and customizing them.Beyond the gameplay, I really enjoy the music.  It's incredibly relaxing, and it fits the atmosphere of the game.  The best way I can describe it is that the instrumentation sounds more acoustic than synthetic, which adds to areas with a lot of nature.  My favorite tune comes during excursions in the Endless Forest.  If there's anything that might turn some people off is just how little detail some of the character and animal sprites have.  Littlewood actually reminds me more of an early SNES game, and if that's the intent, it was nailed perfectly.  I'm just saying that some might think this game was made cheaply, or they're not a fan of the style.  Fortunately, there's a lot of people like myself who do sort of yearn for the more "retro" look.  I also think there could be some more options for character customization as well, but for what it is, it works.  If you're the type of person who is into city or town building or management, with a hint of Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon, then I think Littlewood is great.  If you want a game that's more relaxing and mellow, Littlewood succeeds in spades.  There's no real in-game clock to be had, and time only passes when you do certain actions like gather items, cut down trees, etc.  I've only played the game for about 12 hours now, and I'm nowhere near the end, but I think I can say what's here is excellent.  Littlewood greatly exceeded my expectations, and then some.  I went into Littlewood with trepidation, but I was left pleasantly surprised by what I've seen so far.  I can see myself building my town and exploring the world for a while.  I hope Littlewood gets more updates or DLC in the future because I can see where more stuff can be added.  Not much else to say other than 'keep up the good work'.  Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: The energy of this game feels very low and steady - I enjoyed playing this game as a means to simply unwind, have little-to-no pressing objectives, and an objectively open degree of autonomy in how I progressed. It provides a slew of various mechanics to pursue ranging from fishing, farming, crafting, collectables, even town management, but with the complexity levels of each mechanic dialed down to 1, maybe 2. I've seen some comparisons to the likes of Stardew Valley, and I can see and appreciate the comparisons in regards to aesthetics, pace, and general tone but while it shares a lot of the mechanics, it does so at a very shallow level – not necessarily in a bad way, it certainly seems to be by design, but the idea is that while Stardew Valley has an almost encapsulated experience for each of the mechanics it introduces as a part of the whole, Littlewood’s mechanics act as shallow appendages to its pace, being slow and steady.Fishing, as an example, isn’t a minigame with a chance to lose the fish – you simply click and it’s caught. Relationships don’t involve elaborate gift guides, attention to NPC schedules, and lengthy interactions that denote advancement in the relationship – it’s visit every day, click the flirt button if it appears, and meet in the port city square for a kiss sound effect at the end of the dialog. Oh, there’s marriage sure, but it’s, again, a rather shallow mechanic. They move in and they give you blueprints.Pretty much all of the mechanics operate this way: as a sort of collection of garnish without a cake, but with that said, in this instance, I don’t regard it as a bad thing. I think part of the allure comes from the open-endedness of its objectives, and the constant rewarding feeling of the leveling and content unlocking as you progress. It has a grind, but at least in my experience, it doesn’t feel like a grind with long stagnation between rewards. As a result of that, you feel like you’re constantly unlocking things, you find yourself compelled to continue playing “just one more day”, and can freely stop and resume at a later date should you find yourself full enough to the brim with “chill”. I think the key to avoiding the feeling of “the grind” in this game is that you have to avoid having any *hard* objectives. Once you start narrowing yourself down to the specifics of tasks you want to achieve or items and upgrades you want to unlock, the shallowness of the mechanics become an obstacle to the intent of its premise.In short, I think if you’re looking for a game to sort of “shut your mind off” to, and play it that way explicitly, you’ll find this game to be a pleasant and relaxing distraction you can sink 20 or 30 hours into, maybe more if you endeavor to 100% it.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely adorable. The game play is relaxing, and gives you vibes of that sort of Stardew Valley thing but far less farming. Tasks are easily laid out and explained, you can easily understand how friendships work, and generally a relaxing game that's fun to play for hours. It's easy to lose track of time while you're playing and keep telling yourself "just one more day."The only complaint I really have is there are times the RNG seems against you to get the higher tier items to show up for harvest. Not impossible, sure, but sometimes you can go days before that one tree or ore shows up.

_childDocuments_.review: This... this is brilliant. I backed Littlewood on Kickstarter a long time ago, and when I last checked it out, I thought "eh, it turned out ugly" and abandoned it after 10 minutes.It was a mistake. It's charming, delightful, optimistic, beautiful, and also the sort of time sink when you think "one more day" and somehow it's morning already. I love it so much and I wish I didn't have job and stuff to distract me from playing.Also the whole conceit of "you're THE HERO and now go and enjoy your heroic retirement" is just  absolutely sweet.edit after playing more: this is cure, sweet and lovely HEROIN. The characters have a lot of personality, which is needed in a low-graphic game. The scenery is beautiful, which is hard for a low-graphic game. The world-building is super cool as well. I adore it so far. :)
