_childDocuments_.review: It has taken me 8/9 months to write this review because this game left me with so many mixed feelings.  I loved the concept of playing the hero AFTER the world has been saved. I love that you get to customize your whole village and that the desires of each new character force you to make creative choices you might not normally. I think most of the characters are really cute and have interesting/compelling dialogue. I even adore the art. What I don't like is that as you play the game (specifically through characters like Dark) it feels like the story is building to something epic and going to explore the meanings of good and evil, of forgiveness and friendship. Only to find out that it's actually....not. It actually wasn't building to anything at all. None of the characters that seemed to have really important things going on are actually going to get any resolution.I was SO excited and nervous to unlock the final area, only to get there and it's empty. It was such a huge disappointment. It felt so bizarre, I thought for sure the game had to be unfinished and that the conclusion would be in a later update, only to google around and find out that the game is considered complete and that the dev had actually moved on. The incredible letdown of this (lack of) ending soured my feelings on the rest of the game, mostly because it felt like I had just been wasting my time. If you like mindless grinding (and to completely level skills and/or unlock the final area you WILL need to grind), then I guess this game is for you. Otherwise, I can't recommend this game because, despite liking the town building and characters, when I think back on this game mostly what I think of is the disappointment I felt. - I have read that some people actually consider getting married to be the real ending or goal that you're supposed to work to. If so, that makes the game even more disappointing because depending on who you romance you can get married very quickly and easily. I got married halfway through my play through and it only took that long because I kept holding off on proposing until I had met all the characters. If you ended the game after marrying it would also mean all the post-marriage dialogue the characters have would be a waste.

_childDocuments_.review: The game I never knew I needed.A beautiful mix between Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing NH - you have complete control over your village and it's easy to progress fast but it's still a challenge.I'm not yet far into the game but I really enjoy it already! If you like relaxing games like these this is a must have <3
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: A very cute town builder game for relaxing. It's extremely good at not putting any kind of time pressure on the player; the world only moves when you take actions, not at a set pace that moves on regardless of you. The characters are all cute and charming, though admittedly a little shallow. Littlewood is a good game for a rainy day or destressing after a long day of work, but the simplistic mechanics can get a bit stale after a while.I'd describe it as the video game version of sweets, or perhaps cotton candy, in the best way. Sugary, charming, and cute, and terribly tempting to binge. But if you're looking for something deep or complex, you might be better off elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a promising little game. Delightful pixel graphics, and solid music. It feels a lot like Stardew Valley, but with more focus on building a town, which you micromanage in various ways. There's definitely nothing super original in the gameplay, except for the fact that it's very gamer friendly.  You don't need to Manually pull out tools, you can teleport to any spot in your town, the menu is really fluid and simple. The main problem though, is that the game is EXTREMELY grindy. If you want to upgrade your buildings/locations it takes a lot of time grinding in the very boring Forest/mining locations. In general, cosmetic items are far to expensive to craft most of the time. It's just not worth the grind to get to the late game, because there is no end game content yet. Obviously, it's still early access, but it's still extremely lacking content. I also think $15 is a bit steep.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: While the game stil has some glitches and a lot of content that is "to eb added later" (primarily events in town, as well as some portions such as new locations to visit), it's still a very addictive and animal crossing-like game with a lot of things to keep you going.I can't wait to see the monster card battle being implemented!
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I've played many other Harvest Moon / Stardew Valley -esque games before, so I love both the familiarity of this game and all of the unique aspects and mechanics. Being able to literally change the terrain is awesome and having each villager have "housing requirements" is a fresh take from the fetch quests I'm used to. (There are fetch quests too, but they're optional and unassuming.) Definitely one of those games I can play for hours and not realize it. Well balanced and very enjoyable!
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful, effervescent little game. I kinda love everything about it.For me, it hits a sweet spot between Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing -- you get some farming but not so much you'd just rather play Stardew Valley instead, and you get some village customizing, but not so much you'd just rather play Animal Crossing instead.It's lovely.

_childDocuments_.review: Animal Crossing/Stardew Valley vet checking in. I've been sick in bed for a week and this game has been exactly what I needed. I'm the kind of player who tends to overcomplicate things and research every topic. Littlewood is a simplified "CrossingValley" that's just fun to dive into. I've really enjoyed exploring and building my town and getting the classic aesthetic I was craving, without feeling like I'm going to miss anything or rushing against the clock. The simple controls make it easy to play without a mouse just on my laptop. I think this would be a good game for younger players or newcomers to the genre as well. Well done!

_childDocuments_.review: Preface:Going into this game I was a bit skeptical to say the least. As a little bit of background for the developer of this game Sean Young is the mind behind two other games that while fun in their own right are inherently flawed, and were never finished: Magicite, and Roguelands. Two games that I though could have been great, but never lived up to expectations.I'm happy to say that Littlewood is neither of these games, and that it has blown my expectations of the water, so lets get into it.TL:DRLittlewood is a rich vibrant game with charming interactions, dialogue, and a satisfying gameplay loop with a slight grind. The game mixes the best parts of Animal Crossing and Stardew Valley for a fun, casual experience. The visuals are simple yet gorgeous and allow the town that you build to really shine. Plus the game is an absolute steal at 15$ for fans of this genre of games.Story:A serviceable and basic premise that follows the events of after the hero (you) saves the world from a dark wizard. Following with you losing your memories and waking up in the middle of the forest with your old adventuring companion Willow. The destruction left behind by the battle requires that you rebuild. Meeting allies new and old to build the best town in all of Solemn, and rediscovering your past.The best part of the story (and maybe the whole game) however is the interactions between not just the NPCs and the player, but how they interact with each other. The humor in this game is quite on point, and the dialogue is absolutely fantastic. The best word that I could use to describe this game is charming.Graphics:The graphics in this game are very much Sean Young. This isn't a bad thing, as it allows for a very colorful fun looking game that is also easy on the eyes. The game is actually quite pretty, and makes the town that you build come to life.Gameplay:The easiest way to describe the gameplay is as a mix of Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing. You collect materials to build buildings and upgrade your town. Level up skills as you collect materials to collect materials better. Form relationships between the NPCs of your town, and build a beautiful town for your NPCs to inhabit. There is a Museum to collect things in, a Tavern to discover and cook new foods in, quests to complete for your NPCs and a world to explore. And a Collectable Card Game.It is quite satisfying to grind your skills up to max in this game and be able to effectively turn the game into a creative mode of sorts after earning it through the progression. But this is also a double edged sword and is probably the one criticism that I have with this game, many players may be turned off by some of the grind in this game (this is a fairly grindy game), primarily in the mid game and the pre-end game. Additionally some of the achievements for this game (while optional) can feel like a chore. I'm not exaggerating when I say that the last 10 hours of my play time were spent on getting 3 achievements, which feels a bit much for such short game.Content:Overall I'd say that you get a good bang for your buck in this game. Even without achievement hunting like I did, you can easily get 30+ hours of enjoyable content out of this game or more if you want multiple town with different layouts. Which for $15 is a steal.Final thoughts:I'm happy to see the developer finally find  and stick to a vision and fully realize it. This is proof that they can make amazing games if they stick their mind to it, and I hope that this sets a precedent for Sean's games going forward. I want him to succeed and I hope that he continues to defy my expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very conflicted whether to give this game a thumbs up, or down. On the one hand it did give me roughly 58 hours of things to do  However many of those hours were SUPER grindy. Don't get me wrong, I like grindy games. My job requires a lot of thinking, so a game that lets me turn my brain "off" at the end of the day is refreshing. The game is pretty straightforward. You start your day, go around town doing various things until your energy runs out, then go to sleep and start all over again. These things could be fishing, mining, farming, and things like that. Every once in a while there are "special events" but they are kind of rare. Straightforward, right? Well, there are aspects of the game that came off as very tedious. One example is progression in the game. Eventually you hit a wall where you can't do anything different. It wasn't until I realized that  before it will let you proceed/get farther in the game. Another example is the whole flower system. You can't even start growing flowers until you unlock a certain feature, and even then it doesn't tell you "X flower + Y flower = Z flower".....which a lot of end game items rely on certain flower combinations. Eventually you get to a point in the game where you do 1 action in a day (like watering flowers), then go to sleep. Wash, rinse, repeat until you meet your goal, which gets annoying after a while. To sum this up - I guess at the end of the day if you love to "collect" things, and want a game that you can turn your brain off and play  then Littlewood is for you. Some suggestions for the developers that I would suggest:- Make the watering can available without tying it to home decorating (maybe after X days someone gives it to you?)- Better describe how to grow flowers (You have a cooking recipe chart, why not a flower chart??)- List where items come from in the description (e.g. Cavern Wart comes from FISHING in the caverns)- I personally don't like having to require a town layout with certain homes being close/away from other objects. The game seems to contradict itself. You give the player all this neat and cool stuff to decorate your town with as you see fit, but townsfolk reward you based on where their houses are located (e.g. 20 spaces AWAY from the smelter). Which option do you want of players - optimal layout, or freedom of choice???- Some features seem deliberately implemented to make the game time drag out more. For example the "Dark Matter" visitor. It feels like the amount of dark matter needed for their rewards is way too high. Or pictures needing 50 of some rare item. Why????- The game seems to have a lot of RNG built into it. Maybe throw some of that to keep players on their toes? For example there is a 5% chance of this special event/visitor from appearing in your town.- Don't force players to sell rare items to make visitors show up. It really irritated me in the end game when a visitor needed a rare item sold at the merchant, yet a different item needed that same item for me to craft it. (For example sell 3 of X to have a visitor show up, but you need 5 of X to create a special item). You're just encouraging people to sell items, only to later realize ****! I needed that!!!- There's probably more, but if you are somewhat forcing a player to skp, skip, skip days on end then that gets very boring and tedious, and probably needs some mechanism for the player to look forward to. Not "I hope I get X rare item today. Nope, on to the next day." Otherwise people get bored and move on.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is... almost great. Parts of it are fantastic, enjoyable, delightful, memorable, you name it. Almost all my complaints are things that could be fixed in updates/patches, but for now I gotta give this a thumbs down.First, the good. The town-management aspect is actually really nice. The game gives you a fair bit of control over the layout of your town, allowing ponds and hills up to 2-layers above ground level, and a lot of cosmetic additions. Not a phenomenal amount of customization, but at least enough that you can sort of set up parts of your town that each feel special. There is a pretty wide variety of tasks you can do during the day. Music is adequately good, and the system of upgrading buildings to unlock new features is nice.So what's wrong? First and foremost, the NPC interactions with the player character are practically unbearable for me. Because the game story is that you are a hero who defeated the Big Baddie, who then lost your memory, basically everyone you meet swoons over you like you're some sort of, well, Hero. But you, the human playing the game, haven't done anything to earn that. So to me it felt exceedingly creepy. You have multiple NPCs practically falling head-over-heels in love with you basically on sight. And they ARE creepy with it, and their swooning just doesn't stop. Even the ones that don't love you per se are often super clingy. As if they have no life of their own other than fawning over your character and/or your town. It's... just a really weird vibe that keeps me from sinking into the game world.There are small cutscenes and dialog that give some of the characters more depth, which is nice, but it's all pretty limited and a pale imitation of how relatively fleshed-out the NPCs are in other similar games. And some of the 'depth' given to characters is also just more creepy weirdness. Secondly, although there is a lot of content, much of it is really pretty boring. There are three cave and three forest levels, but all three are always identical (in content) as far as I can tell. Unlocking them just means you can grab some more free dewdrops if you walk through them each day, and have more chances of seeing a rare tree or ore, which hardly even matter for core game content. In all three levels for the forests/mines, the same materials spawn, the same enemies spawn (with no real combat in the game, which is weird considering you are a hero warrior), the layout is basically a pretty boring randomized grid for each. It gets old. Fishing requires no skill, the card game you unlock is super basic and quickly loses its appeal. Bug catching is even easier. It all just gets incredibly easy and tedious.Those two things keep me from recommending this. The entire NPC system needs a massive rework in my opinion, and most of the rest of the content requires grinding to unlock things, but that grinding is just not that fun or interesting. Building a town up is pretty good, if you can bear with the personalities of people living there. And the visuals are cute. That's about it though.With polish this game could be fantastic. It's just not there.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is a game where you are an amnesiac hero who just saved the world. Your quest is over. Now it's just time for you to relax, make friends, and rebuild the town!I got a lot of serotonin from playing Littlewood as a Collectathon game while checking things off the list. It gets very grindy the further you play, but I was able to still have fun because I always knew my next goal and would continue playing towards it.The most charming aspect of Littlewood is the casual time system, which is much more relaxing than most farming sims (such as Harvest Moon, Rune Factory, and Stardew Valley). In those games, time passes in real time. In Littlewood, time only ticks forward with each action that you perform. This makes the game a truly casual and relaxing experience, and I personally loved getting cozy with the game before bed.My major criticisms are as follows:- I 100% the game after 40 hours, meaning I unlocked everything there possibly was to unlock and collected everything there possibly was to collect. I am still missing a handful of Steam achievements and will not be getting them. Some of these achievements are so incredibly grindy that I can't justify spending 10+ more hours on the game just to get them. I simply have no reason to grind anymore -- there is nothing left to unlock in the game apart from the achievement itself.- Littlewood characters are all super cute and have distinct personalities, and you can date/marry most all of them! BUT they run out of dialogue so quickly that you'll find talking to them to be a chore by 5 hours in.- The best part of Littlewood is how casual it is, but there are a few gameplay factors that are counter intuitive to this. Fishing is a reaction/timing based game like most fishing minigames. There are also creatures that you have to dodge when mining/foresting. I think the game should have fully committed to being casual and played at the player's pace.I give Littlewood a 7/10 overall. I don't think the grind is for everybody, but if you enjoy the mechanics of farming sims and you are a completionist that enjoys clear checklists, I think this is game is made for you.

_childDocuments_.review: All we have is time.In the first hour or so of playing, I wasn't sure if I was going to like it. There's no stress, nothing to really overcome at first. I was chatting a few of the characters up, kinda mindlessly exploring the game. I thought it was cute, but maybe not enough to really hold my attention.  Working on tasks uses up time in the day, or your "stamina", but socializing/traveling does not. The only limitation is really how much stamina your character has, which doubles as a representation of the time in a day. When I was growing up, my dad used to tell me, "All we have is time. Don't rush." I used to think he was just telling me that I didn't need to speed while driving or something, or to look where I was walking. Littlewood subtly made me realize what he actually meant. I noticed that I started to min-max my stamina usage for the day. Each new character brought into my Littlewood created additional things for me to prioritize for every day. Since socializing and moving around doesn't use up "stamina", I would always make sure to talk to everyone at least once per day.  When I got into Summer in-game, it hit me. I realized that I always had time for a chat. My motivation at the start was to "build" as much as I could simply for the sake of playing the game. As I played, it developed into a desire not to "produce" as much as I could, but to get to know each new person more. I went from thinking "I'm going to spend the whole day chopping wood," to, say, running into Bubsy, hearing the intensely-eyebrowed bird-person say something funny, and then wondering what he'd want in his house, then having him tag along while I built things for his house, just so I could hear what else he's got to say.You can only do so much in a day. We get tired, eventually we have to rest. But in-between all our hustle, there's always time to listen to what someone else has to say. The game helped me understand what my Pops was really trying to say. All *we* have is time. Its what we all share. It's not an original thought, right? "Take time to stop and smell the roses," and such. I've heard it said, but Littlewood just kinda nudged me into really getting it, and I honestly appreciated that. The game is neat. :) It's a chill time, the writing is fun, and I really started to care about my town. I recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is honestly such a delightful game, there's so much to do and it's all very easy to manage!In a way it's similar to Stardew Valley, however, only in this game do you have free reign on decorating the whole town how you want it to look, with terraforming, planting etc, you get to name it as well.You gather berries, cook, farm produce and later on animals, mine, chop wood, fish, craft and catch bugs, these all have meters that will increase with exp the more you use these skills, the higher your skill the less energy you use, allowing you to do more each day.Via the town hall, you can purchase "wishes" from the townspeople that increase certain aspects of your town, for example, you can purchase the wish to grow more berry trees/produce, the wish for an extra fish to appear in your rivers/ponds, the wish to gain energy back throughout the day etc.With each building you have a chance to upgrade which naturally requires money and materials, these you will gather in plenty if you keep on top of your jobs.Every townsfolk that wants to join your town will have specific requirements, like they want the interior decorated a certain way, they want specific objects and once you place a desk in their house, you can use that as a guide that shows you a checklist of what they want and don't want. Example being Dudley (the old man) wanted to be 16 paces within the coffee shop but wanted to be at least 20 paces away from the lumber mill.It can be fiddly with the more people that come to your town, but that's part of the fun I find, that you're always changing and decorating your town, improving it and watching it grow.Unlike Stardew, Littlewood doesn't operate on a time limit, so you can stand about in one place or walk around all day without losing hours of the day in-game, instead each day is measured by the amount of energy you use. The fuller the bar gets, the less time of the day you have left, which I prefer by a mile, no more limitations or worrying that I'll accidentally forget to pause the game to go to the loo and come back to find 3 days have passed.The music, like Stardew is very relaxed and I found myself being swept away into the game. So for anyone that has troubles with focusing or anxiety, having the music on low as you play will surely help calm you :)I found hours have passed before I have to remind myself that I do need to sleep, it's very addictive and so fun, but pulling yourself away from it will be the challenge!Another great feature is you can romance any character, you-yourself aren't given a specific gender, but you can make your sprite look a certain gender. I've yet to try this feature out as I'm still in the early stages, you do get a great diversity of characters in-game so I'm waiting until I have more people in my town before I decide one someone I want to romance.There's also mini-cutscenes quite frequently, every week or so in-game and as the treasured "hero" of the world, everyone wants to be your friend and willing to kiss your booty to do it! ;DIt's definitely worth the price and I've gotten so much joy out of it so far, I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a similar experience to Stardew Valley but without the constant need to upgrade tools and clockwatch.Speaking of characters, they're all unique and amusing in their own ways with their own little stories, literally, one is a birdman-thing who came from a nest of 16 brothers and sisters, he's also a tsundere and washes in the public fountain xD

_childDocuments_.review: Very chill and fun to play. Will update as I get further but in general, as you may pick up from the synopsis it's a Stardew Valley -like game with a simpler look.The best, key mechanic differentiating this game is that each day progresses based on what you *do*. You progress the game at your speed as things like chopping wood, gathering weeds, farming, fishing, etc. take up your energy and when you're out of energy you need to sleep. The game neatly switches to nighttime as you get around the 75-80% mark of your energy (or it may be 90%, not sure). Altogether, this makes the experience much more chill, and you can talk to everyone in your town without having to worry about running out of time.So think of Stardew Valley, but with no constant time component that keeps you running from point A to point B to point C, and it focuses on building up your town rather than a specific property you own (i.e. a farm). You decide how long each day runs, though you'll notice that days are relatively quick as your energy bar fills up quickly to start.Altogether, this is basically an almost-finished game for Early Access. Other than benefiting from more content and events, the game mechanics work great and fit together well, and don't seem to require more polish. This is worthwhile picking up if you like Harvest Moon / Stardew Valley / Animal Crossing / etc.

_childDocuments_.review: I have past experience with some of the Harvest Moon series and Animal Crossing, and if you enjoy those games like I have, you'll definitely enjoy this as well. I do like the grindy-ness of these kinds of games with mechanics like collecting the same materials and items over and over, although I find that I eventually get pretty burnt out (as I did with AC New Horizons, unfortunately). However, Littlewood's pacing and exp system makes it very easy to stay engaged. As you do activities like chopping wood and collecting crops, you gain experience for that activity which in turn fills up a total exp bar. When it is almost full it turns to night, when you sleep and start a new day with an empty exp bar. This makes planning your day an important part of the game, which greatly extended the enjoyment I got out of it. On the other hand is the town building and management aspect, which is also really well done and acts as a nice balance to the work routine. As of writing this I have yet to play Stardew Valley, the other  F A R M I N G  game, so I am unfamiliar with how it handles these kinds of repetitive tasks, but I really liked Littlewood's system. So much so I wanted to 100% the game, which was a nice way to move on after I did eventually run out of things to do.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this type of game. Littlewood is a solid contribution, pretty much what I expected, although lacking the depth of titles like Stardew or Pacha.There's a little grind, as with any game of this type, but it's a comfortable and relaxing grind. Littlewood doesn't feel like it's asking too much or being disrespectful of your time. Sometimes, however, it can feel repetitive when there is only one fish or one bug you can access per season. You'll spend your days woodcutting, mining, fishing, and checking what's for sale. There is essentially no time pressure; time of day depends on your remaining energy. You could play an infinitely long day by simply decorating the town. I enjoyed the lack of pressure, though I wouldn't mind more.Speaking of which, farming isn't a big focus. Very little strategy or time management involved. Everything grows quickly and at the same speed, all year round, and you'll mainly be farming to help with cooking.Endgame is the weak point for me, and I will elaborate in hopes that the dev plans to flesh out this part. Maxing a skill gives excellent boosts, but you'll barely get to enjoy them, because what else is there to do? Same for a building that gives you boosts--I spent a lot of effort collecting upgrade materials, but couldn't actually reap the rewards by the time I could afford the upgrade. It turned a big achievement into a let-down.Finally, it seemed like I was working towards a final piece of content by unlocking all destinations, but there was none. Just another reward I no longer had use for. I settled for my own endgame: grabbed a few more achievements, made the town pretty, got the furnishing rewards (which, yet again, would have been more useful earlier in the game--but obtaining all the blueprints requires lots of time and endgame wealth), and closed the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming world full of fun characters and creative takes on familiar mechanics, Littlewood hits the town-building, resource-hoarding, upgrade-all-the-stuff spot. Breed new flowers, grow crops, cook meals, mine ores, travel by hot air balloon and more as you make friends with those you meet and invite to settle in your expanding town. The passage of time being action-based swaps the comparative hustle of Stardew Valley for a relaxing stroll as you plan your day, explore new areas and chat with townspeople at your own pace. Choose to "hang out" with NPCs to have them join you in your travels, build your friendship...and maybe grow a little closer.The ability to actually build/shape your town (NPC home placement, some terraforming, landscaping, layout, stat-boosting) really made this for me in comparison with similar games; once I finish the story, my town is probably becoming a chain of river islands. :) There's also no penalty for crafting (dismantle the object and get all materials back), so the freedom to really try anything assuming you've collected enough material encourages imaginative layouts and themes.I thought the in-world card game (Tarott Monster) was a clever idea; easy to learn, lots of ways to build a winning deck, and a fast play with only 10 cards per player. The ability to turn up the speed of this part of the game was also a thoughtful plus!I'm heading toward the end of the story after taking my time through it, and have enjoyed it immensely.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood, Developed by Smash Games, a passion project of developer Sean Young, improves on the classic Stardew Valley farming, relationship-building and time-management formula in every way.Stardew Valley, released in 2016, is a classic farming simulator, tailored directly from the nostalgia of farming sims like Harvest Moon. It is, by all intents and purposes, a masterpiece. It is the tireless work of a sole developer named Erin Barone who spent over eight years creating it, and continued to develop it for years after its release. Stardew Valley surpassed its predecessors in every way and created a cottage industry of farming, crafting and relationship-building games like My Time at Portia, Moonlighter, and Sun Haven. One unsung Stardew-like that I rarely see talked about online is Littlewood, released in early 2021 by Smash Games. What is Littlewood?The premise of Littlewood is that you are a hero who, along with a couple of friends, has just defeated a Dark Wizard plaguing the world of Solemn. Now that the world is at peace, you decide to settle a new town which you can name or leave eponymously as Littlewood. You can customize and decorate your town, harvest crops, and complete quests to attract new townsfolk and forge relationships with each of them as well as upgrade your abilities.Similar to Stardew Valley, there are caves for mining, woods for cutting trees, fishing, gathering, and farming, but additionally there is cooking, bug catching, crafting, flower gardening, and even a battle card collection game within the game called Tarott Monster. While Stardew focuses primarily on its farm-building gameplay loop, Littlewood focuses more on laying out your town and relationship building. For instance, at a certain point in the game, it seemed perfectly OK to just let my crops exist as decoration. This is just one of the ways that gameplay evolved over time in a way that kept Littlewood from getting stale and pushed me to the endgame content that I never reached in Stardew.A Queer HavenYour settlement in Littlewood is a haven for Solemn’s misfits. I loved almost every one of the characters that I attracted to my town. They were often outcasts, flawed individuals with dark pasts, or eccentric artists. Some of my favorite recruitable denizens included: a witch that can’t control her powers, a snobbish bisexual bird boy and a half-orc who was cast out from her tribe for reasons you’ll come to understand. These are just a few of the fifteen citizens that I fell in love with. I always looked forward to cutscenes between the townsfolk that would unfold as you progress in your relationships with them. They were often touching, funny, or surprisingly dark.One thing that really stunned me happens before the game even starts. In character creation, most games follow a pattern: choose a name, choose a gender, choose some clothes and choose some hair. In Littlewood the developer made the canny decision to forgo the gender choice altogether. You are not defined by any gender, rather just by what you decide to wear or who you decide to associate with. The social interactions are all non-binary. I found this really refreshing and as a side-effect I felt more comfortable experimenting with different styles for my avatar. Ultimately, I went with pink, soft-serve-ice-cream-top hair and black overalls.While in other Stardew-like games, I always feel like there’s an obvious choice for my romance option (in Stardew it was Shane, I can’t help but try to fix him, he’s just so sad and cute, uwu), in Littlewood I honestly had a hard time picking because I identified with so many of the characters. The nice thing is, once you pick your one-true-boo and slide that glitter ring on, you can continue all of your relationships and see all of the cutscenes, besides the date scenes, with all the other townsfolk.One of the other things I’d like to mention is that while most Stardew-likes are mostly non-violent, Littlewood is completely non-violent. There are monsters but they’re not malicious and there’s no way to “kill” them. You can put them to sleep or tame them but they are just part of the natural order in Solemn. Following in the footsteps of other RPGs like Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor, the game simply leaves combat out of the picture even where it might make sense as a game mechanic. I really appreciate this approach to gaming and, while I have no problem with violence in video games overall, it’s refreshing to see RPGs breaking the norm of game progression.At the same time, the game is not entirely without competition. In the aforementioned battle card game Tarott Monster, you collect monster cards that can be bought, found by battling other players, or hidden in the forest and caves. You can battle certain NPCs and any of your fellow townsfolk, in what I found to be an engaging and sometimes challenging card battle minigame. Collecting all the cards had a really fun metagame as well which tied them directly into the lore you unlock over time.Never Regretting DecisionsIn Littlewood, I almost never regretted any decisions I made. This was due, in large part, to a number of quality of life choices the developer made that I’d love to see in more games. When you build your town in Littlewood, for the most part, all resources are refundable. That is to say that you never lose out on your resources if you make a mistake like putting a crop in the wrong spot or by crafting something by accident. You can always break it down and get exactly the resources you used to create it back. That goes for building up the terrain, placing houses or any other decorative object. This approach gave me a lot of freedom to experiment with my town, move stuff around or tear it apart completely and start from scratch without having to farm more resources. Some of the NPCs in your town have special location request questlines like being close to a store or placing their house at a certain elevation. So while it was sometimes a lot of work, I always looked forward to reorganizing my town to suit the needs of all its inhabitants. The only truly finite resource in Littlewood is time. However, unlike in other Stardew-likes where a holiday might come up and I’d have to weigh the decision to water crops or to participate in the town activities, in Littlewood, your crops never rot or fallow and day-to-day activities can always wait until the next day. I did still find myself trying to squeeze every possible moment out of the day in the early game, however, I never felt stressed out at the end of the day that I’d missed something crucial or regretted doing one thing instead of another. Everything you do in Littlewood feels like progression.Not Completely PerfectI completed just about everything I wanted to do in Littlewood in my 61-hour playthrough. Which, as a full-time working human with lots of video games, books, podcasts, and social events on my list, I appreciated it. I’m actually pretty sure that I could have done everything there is to do in Littlewood within 100 hours, if so inclined. This is great for completionists like me, who also usually get bored of games after the 100-hour mark, but the short game span could be seen as a plus or minus depending on how you look at it. On the one hand, completing a game feels really nice, and on the other hand, it didn’t really give me a reason to pick it up and play it again. All of the townspeople’s quests and requests are the same game-to-game so while you might build out your town a little differently, overall there wasn’t any incentive to build again.The only other complaint I have is the build screen, which can be cumbersome, especially when you need to make large changes to the town. You can only move the cursor for the organization as fast as you can run as a character, which especially with keyboard and mouse, just felt too slow.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is a great game I thought when I first started playing this game. The first couple of hours (1-4), where the most fun I've ever had when playing this game. The gameplay was interesting, building and collecting materials were fun. I wondered whats next? Unfortunately I was met with disappointment. I've unlocked every single citizen so far, and am in my second year of the game for those wondering. As I said at the start the first couple of hours are great, you get loads of buildings to place, collecting materials is fun, and most of all you get the ability to decorate your citizens houses! I had a load of fun with this feature. It was quite fun going into the general store each day to see if they the furniture you citizen wanted in their home, and meeting of requests, like 'I want my home at this height, or this close to something', allowed for creativity and problem solving. My second favourite part of the game was upgrading things, like the balloon thingy, and port city deluca, and the museum to unlock cool new additions was great.Then the cracks started to show. I unlocked all the items in the general store, I finished the museum and I unlocked all the locations on the balloon thing. Now that raises a question. What now? After you do these things, there's only so much you can do, buy things, fish, mine, chop wood, cook, sell. At first this seems like a lot to do, but it gets really repetitive. Seriously! It starts with a story opening, now rebuild the town, you do a bit of that. Then thats kinda it. At the start NPC's give you blueprints and quests to do, but after that they don't. And you ask yourself, what do I do? I mean, you can grind and level up skills, but that gets tedious quick. The next and last gripe is the environments and of the forests and the mines, and item variety. They're just the same thing over and over. After you unlock the next mine or forest, its just the same thing, may a bit of navigation variety but it ultimately looks that same. Which gives me my next gripe, item variety is LACKING! There are three types of forests and mines, but only three types of variety in wood, and ores.Littlewood, a great game at the start, with poor long term enjoyment. I loved this game but it makes me sad that a game with such a strong start turns out so boring. :([4/10]

_childDocuments_.review: "Grind, the Game." Littlewood is an off-shoot of Stardew Valley in the same way that SV was an off-shoot of Harvest Moon. But it is ultimately sterile. If you're looking for that kind of game, play SV, My Time at Portia,  or Yonder instead. There *are* some clever ideas here: the opening story of the game is really intriguing, the ideas about flower breeding are interesting, and there's a much better puzzle game hiding in this game about village building and villagers that want to live close to this part of the village but far away from that part of the village and close to this person but far away from that person. The developer should make *that* game.The rest of Littlewood is the unholy, unholy grind. Some other reviewers call the game "repetitive". Stardew Valley is repetitive. This one is mindless, numbing grind. IF you just want to rack up a perfect achievement game, then this is for you; none of the game-play is remotely challenging. But count on spending two or three hundred hours doing the same actions literally thousands of times to do it. And as usual for this kind of game, fishing is an RNG nightmare. You will spend whole seasons and dozens of hours fishing hundreds of times trying to catch four of several particular rare fish. It's awful. A second RNG nightmare involves furnishing the houses of the villagers.If you accept those limitations, the game is... fine. The graphics are serviceable: you can recognize the people. You can recognize when crops are ready to be harvested. You can differentiate between various types of rare items. It's a little disappointing that buildings don't visually improve as you grind to upgrade them. The controls are little awkward: the run key is badly placed. The music is repetitive but fine and the sounds are fine. The story is really intriguing but I only got to the mid-game before being driven off so I can't comment on whether it has a competent ending or not.Basically, only go into this one if you can get it inexpensively and you accept its limitations. Otherwise, you will soon be bored out of your skull.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is non-violent, relaxing and pleasant to play, and gameplay flows without need of a tutorial.As you build up your town, there's a little farming, a little mining, fishing and a fun card game...The characters are cute, likable but also unexpectedly heartfelt. (Don't neglect Dudley!)The world is small but interesting, revealed as books are collected for the library. The story, presented in bits of dialog as your friendships with the villagers grow, drew me in and I'd love for there to be additional content and/or a sequel. _childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun game, well worth the money. Think of it as a cross between Stardew Valley & Spiritfarer. You are a hero who lost his memory and is rebuilding a village. You get new villagers, build them houses & some other structures, go off to get crafting ingredients, etc. It's a really fun (but addictive) loop and the villagers are really well written, I like it. HOWEVER, the last 2 characters (ESPECIALLY the last one) are kept between unbelievable grinding walls by which I mean pure RNG. The RNG in this game is among the worst I've seen since the really rare stuff has abysmal show rates. I did end up completing what I had set as my personal end goals, not sure if I'm glad I did so or if I should have cut it before, but I did. That said if I ever replay (and what I would recommend to anyone playing it) play it for as long as you enjoy it. After about 8-15 hours the game comes to basically a crawl because now it's just brushing up against the RNG wall. The game isn't going to get better after this. That said, I do not regret my purchase at all, it is a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: Arelaxing, low-key, sincere game of rebuilding a town after the world is saved from evil.  The game takes many "light" versions of mechanics (crafting, town-building, farming) and combines them into a fun game of making stuff, arranging buildings, and meeting friends.  Plenty of things to do will keep you occupied, while the clever story mechanic - your character is recovering their memory as they help - adds to the overall positive feel.  A must-buy for fans of build-em-ups who want a relaxing experience.Littlewood is a game that is a challenge to describe because a lot of it is "This thing but not overdone."  It's in the vein of many town-builders-and-shipper games from Dark Cloud to Stardew Valley, but kept light and breezy so the game isn't stressful.  There's plenty to do, but it's a game that feels like a day out with friends, not a job.Story-wise, the game starts as if it's the end of another story.  You helped defeat an evil wizard and saved the world - and you also ended up unconcious, with amnesia, near the ruins of your old town.  Nursed back to health by your friends, you help rebuild the world while finding out more of who you were.  It's a simple idea, but it grounds the game and is a fun way to tell a story that already ended.The game consists of multiple interlocking mechanics.  Let's take a look at them.YOUR TOWN:* Townbuilding.  Put down structures or modify the land as you need.  These efforts can yield resources, new characters, new services, or just fun things to do.* Decorating.  Yes, it wouldn't be the same if you couldn't decorate houses and town.  However everyone has their own requests, and fulfilling some unlocks others.  Prepare to look for the right wallpaper . . .* Farming and botany.  Raise trees, crops, animals, and flowers.  Make your town practical and beautiful!YOUR FRIENDS:* Socializing.  Meet characters and get blueprints, unlock stories, and more.  You also have some basic social interactions like complimenting or hanging out, and relationships deepen over time.* Stories.  As you raise your relationships, stories and backstories unlock.  More is revealed over time . . .* Dating.  Build enough relationships and you can date characters - and find out more about them!* Marriage.  Finally, you can get married - and it even lets you pick your wedding date and theme!RESOURCES AND EQUIPMENT:* Gathering and refining.  Get ready to catch bugs, fish, mine, chop down trees, raise crops, and harvest trees.  You'll need all sorts of resources to make your new town.* Making money.  Over time you can make money (Dewdrops) at various things, from selling items to cooking food.* New equipment.  You can get new equipment over time, mostly by leveling up skills.EXPLORE:* Quests.  Everyone has their own needs, including your character, and random quests are also generated by certain structures and decorations.  There's always a fun new challenge - and it's fun to find ways to fulfill quests and goals in effective ways.* See the world.  Your town isn't the only place.  Over time you unlock other locations with resources, opportunities, characters, random events, and more.* The world's history awaits, from talking to characters to filling a mysterious library . . .IMPROVE:* Skill building.  As you perform actions, your skills go up and net you rewards from your friends, or unlock certain things.  Just running around chopping trees pays off.* Upgrading.  You can upgrade your town, buildings, and some locations to unlock more stuff.*Get fashionable: What, you want to keep the same hairstyle and clothes?THINGS TO DO:* Card Battles: Play Tarott a surprisingly deep card battler game you unlock.* Pets: Find and buy various pets for your town - some of which will find objects for you.* Cooking: Make money, find new recipes, follow clues, and experiment.  Your food also helps you make money and fulfill quests.* Sell: Sell crops and bugs and more - and clever town design helps things pay off even more!  Plus selling certain items might just result in other events!* Gamble: There's a chance to win that table blueprint you wanted . . .* Flowers: Raise flowers and find new breeds.* Learn: Travellers appear in certain places and under certain conditions, and in time they'll reveal more of the world.* Collect: Completist?  Try out the museum and more to try and find it all, find every blueprint, and more . . .* Events.  Various things happen day to day to provide new challenges and opportunities.The game's various mechanics are simple and never become overwhelming or confusing.  Plant an object in soil it makes crops.  Plunk down a fruit tree and you get fruit every now and then.  X boards and Y rocks builds a house.  Everything is straightforward . . .. . . but these simple elements interact.  Raised crops can be sold or turned into food to sell.  Selling items may unlock a new visitor.   You can delay a task so you can do it as part of a social event with another character.  Building one structure creates other opportunities.  All the simple mechanics fit together to make a rich whole.Oh, and no death, no destruction, no loosing.  Just hang out and do whatever.  It's sincere, relaxing, focused, and fun.The developer also takes feedback, ensuring an even better game!  The developer - and the community - care about this game.Who's the game for?* If you like town-builders with social/exploring elements, it's for you.  Buy it.* If you in general like crafty/building games but want a break from giant resource and crafting trees or just want to relax.* If you want a low-key, fun game that both focuses you yet isn't stressful or frustrating.* If you're curious about town-builders and social explorers, but haven't played many, this would be a great entry point - once it's done.Who is the game NOT for?* If you don't like harvesting/crafting/skill grind.  I know it's part of the genre, but it's not for everyone.* If you don't like skill/activity gating.  A fun part of the game is certain elements are gated by skills or certain activities, giving it a puzzle-like quality.  However not everyone may like that.* If you don't like the cute aesthetic.  That might not be for everyone.But for people like the above, it's quite a fun journey.This is one of those games that sets out to do exactly it's thing and achieves it not just perfectly, but goes beyond.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood: A Tranquil Gem Pros:Littlewood is a game that instantly sweeps you away into a world filled with wonder and tranquility. Here are some aspects that make it truly special:1) Emotionally Engaging Story: Littlewood weaves a tale that tugs at your heartstrings. As you rebuild a forgotten town, you'll uncover the mysteries of the land and forge meaningful connections with its charming inhabitants. The captivating narrative keeps you invested from beginning to end.2) Delightfully Simple and Addictive Activities: Foraging, farming, bug catching, mining – Littlewood offers a delightful array of activities that are elegantly simple to grasp. It's incredibly satisfying to explore the lush forests, nurture your crops, catch colorful critters, and unearth valuable resources deep underground. These activities blend seamlessly, providing a harmonious and addictive gameplay experience.3) A Haven of Relaxation: In a fast-paced world, Littlewood stands out as an oasis of tranquility. There are no timers or pressure to rush, allowing you to lose yourself in the game's serene atmosphere. It's a haven where you can unwind, forget your worries, and savor every moment at your own pace. Littlewood truly understands the power of relaxation.4) Welcoming and Accessible for Everyone: One of the most beautiful aspects of Littlewood is its inclusive design. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or new to the genre, the game warmly embraces players of all skill levels. Its accessibility is a testament to the thoughtfulness of the developers, who have created an experience that can be enjoyed by gamers of any age or background.Cons:While Littlewood shines in so many ways, there are a few areas where it could use a touch of improvement:1) A Dash of Challenge: Littlewood's tranquil nature may not satisfy those seeking intense challenges or complex gameplay mechanics. While the simplicity is part of its charm, some players might crave a bit more excitement or difficulty to keep them fully engaged.2) A Desire for More Content: Littlewood offers a wonderful gameplay loop that keeps you hooked, but after a while, you may start to yearn for additional variety. Expanding the range of activities, events, and surprises could inject more longevity and freshness into the game.3) A Tinge of Wanderlust: Although the world of Littlewood is enchanting, the scope for exploration feels somewhat limited. If you're someone who enjoys vast open worlds or the thrill of uncovering new territories, you might find yourself wishing for more expansive areas to discover within the game.4) A Yearning for Multiplayer Adventures: Littlewood is primarily a solitary experience, and while it excels as a single-player game, the absence of a multiplayer mode may leave some players longing for shared adventures with friends or loved ones.At last, Littlewood is an absolute gem that wraps you in its tender embrace. Its emotionally engaging story, simplistic yet addictive activities, and the soothing respite it offers make it a must-play for those seeking solace and serenity in their gaming journeys. While there's room for a touch more challenge, more content, and expanded exploration, Littlewood's gentle nature and inclusive design ensure that it remains a captivating and heartfelt experience for players of all walks of life.P.S. _childDocuments_.review: This one was very hard for me to thumbs-down, but I think it's appropriate (and I'm glad it's balanced by the overwhelming support).  I think it's at the edge of being a great game, but I think it will ultimately disappoint people after initially liking it.  It just mixes different playstyles, but doesn't manage to quite complete them.Is it casual?  Yes, but it gets grindy.  The start of in-depth systems does give an advantage to people who think them out.  Is it an in-depth RPG with useful choices?  Yes, at first... but that quickly becomes less meaningful and balance goes out the window.  Does it have a good story?  At the beginning it starts to build an interesting world, and has some lore behind it.  But that falls flat by the end.  The characters have some interesting quirks at the beginning, but they're very repetitive and all the romance scenes are very similar.I think the game could have done with more focus on either being casual or engrossing.  It could have gone either way, but ended up with a weird middle ground that didn't shine particularly in anything and feels a bit unfinished.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a little like Stardew Valley, except you're basically the founder of the town. It's also, in a way, more chill than Stardew. It's easy to sit there for a couple hours, going through each day fairly quickly.Time only "passes" when you complete actions that lower your stamina, and I actually kind of like it that way. Sometimes I'll get distracted by my phone, and when I'm playing games like SDV and MTaP, time passes by because I forgot to pause, and the next thing I know my character passes out and the day was wasted.Also, no inventory limit! And items in your inventory are separated into different categories so you don't have to sort them yourself.I'll say that it is a little annoying that there are limits on how many fruit trees/vegetables/town decor you can use at one time, but it's not that big of a deal.It's also annoying how I'll have the town all laid out how I want, only to later find out that a character wants to be a certain amount of spaces close to or away from a particular place, and I end up having to rearrange almost the whole place.The characters are pretty simple but still unique. In my opinion, some of them feel more two-dimensional than others, but the main thing of the game is more about helping the town grow. It is nice though that, like SDV and MTaP, none of the romanceables are gender-locked

_childDocuments_.review: great game if you like animal crossing in principle but are overwhelmed by the graphics/options it hasbought this game yesterday because i wanted to play something where i can gather, farm and build stuff. this game is literally everything i've been looking for: no pressure to do anything you dont wanna do, no time limits or very fast reaction time/good motor skills necessary (i have trouble with coordinating my hands), very cute graphics, relaxing music, lots of options to build/terraform, gather, craft etc. i didn't play very long yet but i already had to stop myself twice and force myself to go do other stuff instead because it's just really easy to get lost in it and overlook the time. it's not got too overwhelmingly many options (like animal crossing does in my opinion), there's no moving through threedimensional space, it's clean and simple and relaxing. the main things i'd really love to be different is that i don't like how the camera moves in a very fitful manner, it'd be cool if that was smoother at least when you run because it makes it hard to look at the screen in my opinion (its too shaky?)and the other thing is that it'd be great if there was an option to play the game with mouse instead of keyboard clicks. especially moving around and terraforming is a bit tiring after a while if you have trouble coordinating buttons. but those are both mostly accessibility issues and i still think it's a great game and will definitely continue to play.

_childDocuments_.review: There's really not a lot that can be said about this game that hasn't been said by just about every other reviewer on Steam.I bought this because it was pitched as "Stardew Valley minus the stress", and by gum, that is  what this game is. Instead of a timer marching ever onward, an energy system—I know, right? The same system that makes mobile games hot garbage?—gives you a limited number of actions you can take in a day.Done with the actions? Done with the day. On to the next one. No need to spam your friends or pay 99 cents, which is why this is no mobile game. It takes a system and actually figures out how to do it right.But here's the thing. Absolutely nothing in this game is time-sensitive. You can farm one day, catch fish the next, farm relationships with the obligatory cast of characters (introduced -style as you meet certain conditions to get them to come into town), date and marry, all while keeping up that utterly relaxed pace of play of "whatever you want to do in that game day, go right ahead, no pressure, no problem, just have fun."This game is so committed to being casual and player-friendly that it runs the risk of being a little too easy, but so what? Some games are meant to be hard. Dark Souls. PGA Tour 2K21 with the range-finding and putting assists turned off. Super Meat Boy. Battletoads. You get the idea.This is the game you'll want to play when you're feeling a little too beaten up by those "git gud" super challenges and just want to have some easy, relaxing fun. Because Littlewood is all three of those things. It's easy. It's relaxing. And most of all, it's fun.

_childDocuments_.review: While it has its flaws, Littlewood is generally a fun game with a pleasant, nostalgic vibe.+ Over 20 hours of gameplay+ Cute, retro pixel graphics and unique characters+ Lots of variety and novelty in the early to mid game+ No time limits, so you can go at your own pace+ Amusing side quests (exotic pet rescue, deck building)- RNG-reliant mid to late game with lackluster rewards- In-game currency, shops, and skills eventually become obsolete- Repetitive interactions- No story resolution or major late game events- A few very grindy achievements with no incentive for completionDespite the comparisons to Stardew Valley, this game is quite a different experience. Littlewood is not a farming sim so much as it is a city builder with similar activities (fishing, cooking, etc.). Importantly, there is no combat system and days are not timed. Instead, daily progression is determined by stamina depletion from performing specific actions. Customization requires no energy, so as long as you are willing to grind for the materials, you can take as much time as you want to build and decorate your town.I've seen previous reviews call Littlewood "unfinished," but that is simply not true. Is the final area unsatisfying given the expectation set by the narrative? Maybe. Was the game abandoned by the dev shortly after release? Yes. However, the lack of late game content does not make it incomplete, although it will be disappointing for many players. I definitely wish there were some new events or a greater sense of accomplishment after completing the town, but the developer has moved on. It is what it is.I would recommend Littlewood to most people who are already interested in playing. Just keep in mind that there is no real ending, so the game is only over once you get bored.

_childDocuments_.review: After convincing myself I would give this game a good review in the first dozen hours of playing, in the later stages I realised how incomplete it feels and I couldn't bring myself to give it a positive review. It's very grindy. EXTREMELY grindy. But not in a fun way, because you aren't grinding for lots of materials. You're grinding for the chance to get one material that doesn't even have a function aside from fulfilling an arbitrary goal, because you own more than enough, you just got them before this goal appeared. (potential spoiler incoming, not part of the story though)XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXBasically there are personal quests you need to fulfill, like catch 10 fish or find X item. You have to complete 5 before moving onto the next 5. After being stuck on one set of quests for an extremely long time, I completed it and moved onto the next 5. To my surprise I completed 4/5 of them instantly, because the goal was to get to lvl 50 in 4 skills but I was already level 99 in almost all of them. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXI suppose my issue is that the actual gameplay seems like an afterthought. The worldbuilding is mostly fun (unless you desire complete creative control - the townspeople have demands that you have to cater to) and it's a really pretty game, but the story is extremely childish, it relies on the cliché amnesia trope, there isn't much dialogue (it repeats) and it's clunky af a lot of the time due to the lack of MC pronouns, and very, VERY little of it is relevant. A lot of items unlock long after they have any function, for example an item that allows you to harvest more of something rare despite having collected more than enough of said rare item. I buy every item in the shop with 0 regard for what it is because I have more than enough currency. Some shops have been empty for "months" because I bought them out, yet I'm still not even halfway through other aspects of the game.The minigame Tarott Master is fun, but the only increase in difficulty is that your opponents have more HP while yours remains the same. They aren't particularly better at playing.I'm gonna finish up now because I've realised I could go on for a WHILE about what I don't like about this game. I'm going to continue to play to get all of the achievements,  but I can't give it a good review because I just think there are far too many problems with it. I just play mindlessly while I watch Community on Netflix for the 4th time. Yes, I can rewatch a TV series 4 times in a year but even this game is too repetitive for me.It is gorgeous though, aside from the character portraits which I think are kind of hideous. But yeah. Don't expect a game if you plan on buying this.EDIT: I've struggled to play much more since I posted this review and after discovering that this game has basically been abandoned, I'm requesting a refund (long shot) because I'm not happy with where my money has gone.

_childDocuments_.review: A sweet little game in a lot of ways, but lacks the emotional depth I expected in a feel-good game about finding your own happiness.  The characters are too simple to feel at all real, and none of them develop or progress through a story as the game advances.The game generally takes pains not to pressure you.  Though a few mechanics break the perfection of that zen calm, it mostly works.  For dozens of hours, most likely, you'll make steady progress, no matter what you do or what order you do it in.  Only in late game are you likely to feel irritation with the RNG's steady refusal to grant you one or two rare items you need for completion.Overall, I was disappointed.  I feel like a little more plot, a little more writing, could make this game a lot more rewarding to play.  As it is, I put in a lot of time and don't feel like I got that much in return.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I quite like this game, though it does have some glaring issues that I think should be considered before purchasing. things like, if you don't like decorating the town you're gonna have a hard time finding things to do after a certain point, the stores run out of things to sell you pretty quickly and then there's no use for all the dewdrops you will have at that point. The rewards you get for maxing out your skills are mostly pointless, I already completed everything that requires the resources they generate so why do I need help to get more? Tarot monsters is a fun mini game but instead of the stronger opponents having better strategies or rare and powerful cards they just have more health than you so it just feels kind of unfair  (as far as I can tell there's no way to raise your own health). The final destination you unlock is also a huge let down there's very little there and for all the effort I put into getting there it kinda pissed me off.

_childDocuments_.review: If this was an early access game my opinion would be very different. I love these kind of games and especially the graphics. But since this is a released 1.0 game my expectations were higher.Missing ItemsIt is incredible annoying when you have to play a whole year before you get access to something both your quests, villagers and animals request. I couldn't make any animals that wanted potatoes happy for a year, nor make the recepies I got "hints" for because I was missing potatoes for so long. When I finally got potatoes it was in the shop. I had the same issue with other ingredients too but nothing was as frustrating as potatoes because they are concidered "earlygame" material.IncitementsThe sense of reward is very lacking. You spend alot of time leveling up relationships and skills, but there's barely any reward for spending hours to do it (if any). The additional forests/caves you gain access to are pretty much copies of the earlier ones so it ends up depending more and more on stamina, which you can't really affect more than getting lucky with the +5% cards in your office. When it comes to the powerups to increase your skill leveling, you can stack them, but stacking doesn't work. You don't get anything extra and they are all used up simultainously. I opened most of the level 60 chests but don't remember any of their rewards. I think it was decorative things that pretty much translated to getting more dewdrops in the market.TimelineThe random events doesn't seem to effect the world at all, it seems to mostly be lore. The merchants that appear from time to time appear to be set to "endgame" even if it is the first time you see them. The mysterious merchant showed up two times during the last two seasons of my first year. I couldn't buy anything even if I spend all my stamina whenever he showed up. I ended up getting 250~ when his cheapest thing was at 400. The egg hunt was impossible to complete because it required me to build things I had recepies for but not materials. Seasons doesn't seem to affect anything other than which fish you can catch. Crops and trees work the same all year. Encounters in forest/caves stopped after like, one season? The only encounters I see now is  the bee and the blue flower guy.UpgradesUpgrade crystals are very weird. Sometimes you can access them next to the travel plattform, other times you have to run back and forth. It would have made more sense if you had to run for the first upgrades and then get closer to it, or well, even more sense to have an upgrade center... Anyway, when you get access to the forge and need to do "low level" upgrades, it's just weird to have to run there. Concidering the "rare item" rewards they hardly seem worth the material cost. It is also very frustrating when you gathered the correct amount of resources for an upgrade, and the game eats up your resources by creating a rare item instead of the materials I need.No pauseOne thing I found very confusing are the way monsters appear and act in caves. You can't pause the game, and the game doesn't pause. So when you enter a cave you somtimes get thrown out because a fast moving moster walks into you before you can act. This seems to have been "fixed" in forests but making the attacking trees that spawns next to you sleep for a while. But back to the caves, it seems very confusing that the game doesn't pause at all. I've been thrown out several times because I opened a chest without thinking of how the monster would move, so I ended up having to plan for the inability to move to avoid that.SandboxThe last thing I'm going to mention here is the limitation of trees/crops. In this kind of game it is very confusing to have such a limitation placed upon you. If the limitation is set to affect the dewdrop economy it makes no sense. You can level the grass and sell it for more dewdrops than you'll need for most of the first year. The building mode also lets you teleport around and customize the world just as in any sandbox game. But you can only have a few crops and a few trees.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life, you'll love Littlewood. It takes a few few in-game days to realize what the game is all about (i.e. play it for 2-3 hours before judging).Tips:-Lift/Elevate buildings & objects to move them rather than destroying and rebuilding.-Level the land / destroy dirt mounds and then create your own layout from scratch to make it easier to fulfill each citizen's desires (view their desires by building a desk in their house). -Place the hot air balloon structure ASAP.-Get a free drink daily at the coffee shop.-Fish by casting 1 tile next to the fish, NOT on top of the fish, then wait 1 second for the pop.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this is going to be hard. Because i like 2D Games very much and i wanted to like Littlewood. But the game makes it hard to like it. I just spend 11 Hours on it and now i cant recommend it anymore.First, the visuals. Like i said, i like 2D games and their style, each game has its unique style. So is the style of Littlewood, but after a while it seems off. Look at the water/ocean in deluca. Yeah thats it. Thats just poor. There is a impressive lack of detail even for this humble style of art.Secondly, the gameplay. I never saw a game getting that repetitive so fast. You just harvest ores and wood over and over again. Yeah, its nice to have control over the complete terrain, being able to lift or lower the ground, creating ponds and stuff like that. But once your finished, its over. no real Quests, no real meaning, just harvest materials and upgrade stuff to unlock new things and harvest again to upgrade and unlock more. Nothing more, it gets boring. Nothings happening, the festivals are boring. There is just no content, just grinding.Third, the sound and movement. Why cant i walk diagonally? Come on, that was already basic on the Super Nintendo... About the sound, why does it sound like a cheap game made from the RPG-Maker? Seriously, i thought i would be playing Vampires Dawn at some point.Well dear reader, its your choice. I told you my experience with this product honestly. Choose wisely.Well, or just watch you don't play over 2 hours so you can refund it, i am beyond that point.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is all of the fun from a game like Stardew or Harvest moon, wrapped up neatly and cutely into an easy to absorb, play at your own pace package. If you want to try your hand at farming, mining and forestry all in one sitting while befriending an ever growing town of loveable villagers then this is the game for you. My absolute favorite part of the game by far was seeing all of the Goblins that call Littlewood their home. Running into a monocoled purple coated green fellow who's only words to you are Poogy Woogy was just one of the many charms this game has to offer. Laid back, stress free, and adorable is the best way to describe this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a little torn on recommending this game. It's fun, but it hasn't taken many hours of gameplay to start running into placeholders. Many of the festivals are non-existent even though they appear on your calendar, and I've already advanced to locations that exist but aren't playable.It's a fun, playable game, but you're not going to make it far before you see areas that still need work. I'm going to uninstall for now, with 10hrs of gameplay, but I look forward to reinstalling later to see what updates have been made. I think the devs jumped the gun a little on release, but I think they've got good ideas and this could be a really terrific game in the future.Keep up the good work devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted a game where you can go at your own speed? Something relaxing after a long day? Then this is definitely for you. The way days progress isn't based off a timer, but instead an energy bar (similar to Harvest Moon). When the energy bar is gone, the day is finished.You can place items just about anywhere in your town, it feels honestly rewarding as you advance through your resident's requests, and to put it simply, it's just a good game. Most definitely worth the cost. Be patient with the developers (they upload progress images on Reddit!) and I'm excited for the Library update soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood was a game I kept my eye on. When it first came out, I was skeptical, and couldn't quite understand the game. After watching some Youtube footage, and paying attention to reviews, I decided to get it. After all, I'm a veteran to Farmer Sims and RPGS and such, and have played all the AC's and some HM's, so this seemed like a good choice.The music is nice, The graphics are cute, and thats about it. It has the feel of a mobile game, on a PC platform - in both mechanics and controls. Everything is very stiff and the response is odd, and boy oh boy the gameplay loop is extremely dull. You get to the loop about thirty mins to an hour in, and the rest of the game is just grinding that loop (by extension, all the subloops) until completion.As of writing this I have %100 percented the game, though I didn;t have fun much of the way through. Sometimes I found myself falling asleep. This game is not for everyone. I wouldn't even recommend this game to anyone who liked it's muses, because it can't apply to the entirety of that audience either. If you decide you wanna try it, DEFINITELY wait until sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is about life after the grand adventure, the world has been saved, you're done now hero. It's time to rest, and well why not build a life and a beautiful little town now that you're retired?Your days now run on your time adventurer, there no clock to worry about. You just need to be mindful of your energy, the day ends when you're tired and out of energy, so why not head to bed and get a good nights sleep before tomorrow?Also you've vanquished all the monsters hero! Well most of them at least. There's no combat, no more having to choose if you're going to wield a sword, bow, or spells, instead you are equipped with an axe for chopping wood, a pick for mining, a fishing pole, and your legs for running AWAY!Speaking of chopping wood and mining (of which you'll be doing A LOT if you're after those achievements hero), there's no more inventory management, no debating whether you need to save those herbs for healing or that shroom for mana as you climb that mountain to face off against the dark wizard. Your bag is now infinite and has room for everything you'll need.Last but not least, as you build your little community you'll welcome new friends and neighbors to your growing little town, build them a home and get to know them, the stories may be short, but they each have one to tell.

_childDocuments_.review: Beloved. This game is beloved.It's a farming/life sim loop, but the pressure of TIME is taken out. I can get distracted chasing butterflies, and it'll only negatively impact my day if I catch so many I run out of energy. Otherwise, I'm free to decorate, socialize, explore, and just BE without the unnecessary pressure my ADHD self experiences playing other games.The play loop is satisfying (provided you don't sell your rare stuff that you almost ALWAYS need later), the characters are cute, the music is soothing, and the art style scratches my brain just so. The UI is pretty intuitive/easy to use for the most part, though there are a few putzy areas that are holding me back from "finishing" my first town. I do also wish there was a bit more to socialization, but everyone/everything is so cute that I don't find it super lacking. I DO wish the bee and/or the wizard would move into town, though, particularly the bee monster since he's so lonely :( They're precious and I'd enjoy their company. That's about all I'd really want to change about this game though, honestly. It's about as close to perfect as I've seen a game get. All my love and appreciation to the dev~!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a 8/10! I love cozy, pixel-aesthetic games, so this was right up my alley. Really loved the pokemon-esque card game segments as well. Overall pretty laid-back, though if I had to be nitpicky, the plot's overall ending was a teeny bit of a let-down compared to the lore / set-up (MC being a world savior with amnesia, Dark's interesting past etc.), which had potential to be expanded into something that could set it apart from other games in this genre. There were also some parts that seemed rushed, specifically at the very end (eg: an invisible cloak that seemingly no contribution, except for making MC invisible)That being said, I had a really fun time playing this and would def recommend this people who wants to kick up their feet and relax at the end of a busy day
