_childDocuments_.review: Take away all the bad parts of Animal Crossing and add a sprinkle of Stardew Valley, and this is what you get. My only regret is playing it so early; I think there will be more to come, but I've fully exhausted what there is for now! It will be interesting to see if there's anything to bring me back further down the line :)
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a comfort game for me. I discovered it because a streamer I liked at the time was playing it, and now it's one of the games I turn to when I'm in a bad mood to cheer myself up. The little item pick-up noises and menu sounds are really pleasing, the style is really simple and easy to look at, I love the characters. I still haven't finished it out because it took me way too long to dig into menus to figure out how to get traders to show up, among other things, which I'm sort of glad for, because I like still feeling like I have something to do when I open it up. I've also never delved too deep into customizing my town because I'm just not good at that sort of thing, but the tools are easy to use, so if you are, go wild. Very recommended, super cute. I love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: This game really just isn't my taste. It's enjoyable enough at the beginning. Once the game finishes its tutorials, you're left to your own devices for the most part. You'll need to talk with npcs, fulfill their house quests, and upgrade every building to open more of the world. As the town gets larger, your daily maintenance also grows. At some point in the middle of month two for me, it become unmanageable and I had to start focusing my efforts day by day. Unfortunately, the more your town grows, so too does the grind. Levels have no meaning aside from being gatekeepers, and the quest rewards don't feel worthwhile after month two.I enjoyed what I played, but got tired of it after a while. At $15, it isn't much of a risk to give this a try if it sounds like your cup of tea.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played much yet and have not had any experience with combat, if there is any, but so far it's adorable. I really enjoy the little interactions with every character and the art-style is very cute. I also appreciate the energy system that doesn't rely on actual in-game time but simply on actions. It makes figuring out what to do each day easier.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a mellow game in the vein of Stardew Valley.The gameplay follows a simple gathering loop, where you collect resources to craft, donate, cook or sell. The day ends, unlike Staredew Valley, when you run out of energy and is not gated with a real time "clock" which gives you much more flexibility than would be allowed otherwise. There are small touches that show the care put into the town - for example, the terraforming system.  The only critique I have of this game is that they do not make it clear that flower breeding (one of the activities you can do in your town) is essential for unlocking the final area, and I didn't realize that on my first playthrough which made end-game a never ceasing loop of waking up, checking my flowers and then sleeping again.Overall this is a nice game that can be picked up and put down at will. I am not entirely sure how much replay value it has for me personally, but the bones here are well worth at least one playthrough or completion run.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is exactly what I needed right now. I grew up on games like Harvest Moon and Animal Crossing, and loved Stardew Valley, but they all became very repetitive and less fun as time went on. Littlewood takes all the stress of plants dying or missing events, and really taps into the fun of a farming/village sim. I've been recommending it to everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game on a whim. At first I was on the fence if it was worth it.Since using a controller and mouse and keyboard can cause camera stuttering which made me feel slightly nauseous.After restarting the game that issue was fixed.The gameplay loop is gather resources to craft materials for buildings. Rinse and repeat. While also having a limited amount of actions per day as your character has stamina. Each use of the stamina bar also advances the day so when you use an extra action your character gets knocked out. If you wake up knocked out you only lose 20-25% of your stamina bar which is faster than going to your characters bed... It's just a pointless mechanic which adds tedium to the game in general.After a while you'll reach a point where certain characters have desires such as certain furniture or placement next to other buildings. This mechanic is interesting as pushes you to build your cities in a certain way to get these needs... Unfortunately the only reward for appealing to these needs so far is money which is not worth it for the effort.... which should of been active bonuses that affect increased resource gains in certain fields. In the end the game has so much potential i just hope it isn't wasted later on. I can't recommend the game in it's current state. Maybe in a year or so when there is enough content then i might change my mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: characters are very cute. I had a tough time picking a wife out of my favourites. terraforming and designing town was the easiest I've found out of a handful of my other favourite farming games. i found the ending unsatisfying, but the upgrades available gave me something to strive for and continue doing after ending story. my tip would be work towards upgrades throughout game rather than having to quickly do them at the end when they're kinda useless.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I have about 4 hours in the game so far so good. Super chill game with a cross between Animal Crossing and Stardew Valley.  Just build up your town and have fun exploring. I think the only downside I would have to say is that the build mechanic feels weird since your character seems to just get dropped all over the place randomly after you finish building. Game is amazing and I hope one day it comes mobile. This is the perfect pocket sim game since you don't need to worry about time. Overall AMAZING game and keep up the good work.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. It's so very addictive and calming. I broke my ankle and have been place-bound for three weeks with three more to go before I can even start physical therapy, so this game has been a moodsaver and lifeline. Based on my personal experiences with other games, this game is like a mix of Harvest Moon, Stardew Valley, and Minecraft. I was 100% worth the tiny price tag, and I have played it for 36 hours so far. I'm so close to level 30 in Fishing! The only downside is that, like the games it reminds me of, it puts you in the "one more day" mentality and I have to force myself to stop playing so I can get my actual work done :)
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the chillest game I played. There is no risk or tension at all. Even inventory management is eliminated as a tedious mechanic! Just watch the cute story unfold as you carve your cute village and explore the impressively large variety of mechanics, new areas, and activities ^^ 20 hours in and there is still content! Exactly the game I needed to wind down <3
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: Littlewood is one of the most relaxing games I've ever played. I really enjoy the mechanics, specifically that, with the exception of a very few enemies which are confined to specific locations, there is no time limit on anything. The day progresses with your energy meter, meaning you can take things at your own pace. I am also intererested in the developments of the plot so far. The mysteries I've found are presented as low-priority, but they're intriguing.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: My marriage to snobby fashion bird is a sham and my hands  are calloused from chopping wood for a month straight to grind out that 100% cheivo completion back pat. Send help.Early and mid-game are fun and chill, relaxing; late game can be tiresome and progress is dependent on RNG coughing up specific items. Game is not great at rewarding progression, ie later areas are underwhelming and fail to offer anything new or exciting. Very chill thoughWas delighted to have 3-4 romance options that strongly appealed to me. Hot Orc girl, Unstable Witch, [Redacted], and a couple other mid-game additions. Was devastated to learn that accidentally marrying the wrong person is unforgivably easy and irreversible and am now forever stuck sharing my house with snobby fashion bird instead of Hot Orc Girl or [Redacted]I really enjoyed the early game, though. Love rearranging items on a map and building a little town. Love checking off lists and getting presents from townies. It has a lot of the same appeal to me that Staxel had. It is a good little game and at the $15 price point it's maybe a little underwhelming, but if you pick it up on sale it'd be a decent value.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, it's a little underdeveloped but it's still a nice little casual one to kill some time. Very wholesome. Gets a little boring at times because their farming does not really open up very much (still only allowed to plant six individual crop plants at level 30 farming). And the mining and woodland gets a little stale after a while.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: A cute game with plenty of content and things to do. It's mostly focused on building up your brand-new town, befriending new villagers, and creating/collecting materials to use or sell. The collecting can be a grind, but if you don't mind that in similar games (daily chores in Harvest Moon, for example), you should be fine. There are lots of potential villagers, each with their own backstory, personality, and desires, such as where they want their house built. You can hang out with them as you go about your day to get bonuses and build relationships, either romantically or as friends. There isn't much storyline, but there usually isn't with these kinds of games.In general, this is a nice game to relax with, especially for players who enjoy making friends or managing the needs of a growing town.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: So far, one of the best games I have played, ever.How I was missing a title like this, where you dont need to rush or you dont have to have all sort of things planned.The lack of objective is bad in one side, but, in another, give the game a so free and refreshing aspect. You dont have a sense of urgence. The "world " now is in peace, so do the player.The progession in the game is the interactions at your citty. Is see how your citty changes and spending time constructing it. And Im not talking anout a Mega citty or the Capital of Something.You only are rebuilding your hometown(?) with "friends" and catching uo the past and upcoming days.Is a really sweet and nice game. Dont expect a stardew, harvest moon, moonlighter, etc. The focus in the game is only enjoy a good time with a tea . hehe  :)
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't even put 20 hours into this game, but in spite of that I can say it's very addictive. Somehow it is different from Stardew Valley, or, say Animal Crossing, and I think that's because it's almost got an "arcade-y" kind of feel to it. Time doesn't exist, really and you just tackle your little chores and activities as you see fit and just cram a bunch into one day and move on. It's a satisfying loop and after having invested too much time into Stardew Valley across 3 systems (y tho?), I find Littlewood to be just what I need. The content updates and patches throughout early access have been great and I think this game has a very bright future. 10/10 would buy again on a second, third possibly fourth console or other gaming device!
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: If you're ever in the mood for a relaxed game with no ticking time, adversarial enemies or anything of that nature than Littlewood is up your alley.What comes forth is a game that takes inspiration and is a facismile of Harvest Moon, Stardew Valley and other farming sims. Yet the pace is ultimately decided by the player so they can do whatever they wish to their hearts content. Want to mine a rock then venture across the map to plant some trees? Then this game's for you.It's lovingly detailed from the time you help put your first down to adding the finishing touches on your village. Villagers will ask you for certain things that they'd like for their house, whether it be some new furniture or moving the entire thing to a different area.However? The game's a bit of a grind and only increases so. Though i've played a while and been enjoying myself I quickly lost interest once the methodical game of 'Go to 'X', collect 'Y'.' started becoming more and more omnipresent throughout the late-stage. Though there are things taken for you to work it. I tried for a bit of time before laying the game down and considered it completed.It's a really quaint and nice little game. The developers aren't asking too much for a price and I hope you can enjoy this little treasure trove as much as I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: Let me just say I really enjoyed this game! I loved the way we are able to move things and place things in the town. it was such much more simple to get things moved and build the town the way you want without all these extra steps. Which is a win in my book.  I enjoy the story and characters. its nice that as you progress with the characters you get those cut scenes in the morning. (Sometimes can be a pain to get cut scenes to trigger and in this game you dont need to worry about that). I also like there is not combat its truly a cozy game. Farming, gathering, mining, and building relationships. The art style is very simple and personally I love that. If you like games like Stardew and ACNH you'll enjoy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game in early access for about 2 hours. The graphics are very cute, the villager personalities are adorable, and I think this game has a lot of potential. Obviously I've hit a few bugs and weird things but this is early access and the game only launched last night. I hope the developers continue to support this game with frequent content updates because it is a very promising start. I recommend picking this up and helping to support this project.
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really relaxing to play. Things I like about it:- days are not time-based but based on energy spent,- being able to customize the town and people's homes, discovering new blueprints over time, build mode not counting toward energy spent- new things constantly introduced - characters, locations, objectives, items, etc.-  the mechanism of discovering dishes to cook- the aesthetics- the return to home button- the card duel mini game
_childDocuments_.name: Littlewood

_childDocuments_.review: The world has already been saved. Now it's time to rebuild your town, learn new hobbies, and forge lifelong friendships in this peaceful and relaxing RPG.

name: Spellcaster University
detailed_description: In Spellcaster University, you take on the role of the director of a magic university in a colourful world of heroic fantasy. Build your school, manage your budget, recruit teachers. Will you turn it into a black magic academy, with the best professors of necromancy and demonology? Or a place in harmony with nature to train druids and shamans? Or why not train adventurous mages, offering them options to learn how to fight and be stealthy? But this will require surviving the ruthless attacks of the orc tribes and the controls of the education authorities. Build your university using an original magic decks mechanism. Each game will be unique. Access different decks according to the magic taught in your schools. Make choices and take advantage of opportunities to create a unique university. Explore the Arcane Deck to access artifacts with strange powers and rooms that defy reality. Dive into the Deck of Light to take care of your students and teachers. Use the Nature Deck to gain access to a wide range of magical beasts. Choose the Alchemy Deck to boost the production of mana and potions. Yield to the Shadow Deck to teach real discipline to all those nasty students. Manage the well-being of your students by building refectories, dormitories, rest rooms... and ensure their discipline with a dungeon. Select your students: traits, personality, alignment, wealth... each aspect is important. Push your students towards a glorious future. At the end of their studies, discover their future (necromancer, archimage, peasant...) according to the success of their studies, and win new bonuses. Upgrade your rooms with powerful artifacts like the World Tree Wood Table Set or the Soul Eater Bed. Fill your school with legendary creatures: dragons, fauns, pegasus, janitors... Choose the rules of your school: exemplary punishments, recruitment conditions, organic meals, paying dormitories... Choose, through multiple-choice events, how to interact with the different factions of the world. Negotiate with the Adventurers Guild. Ask the king for help. Discuss shamanism with the orcs. Threaten the Dark Lord. Pretend to listen to the grievances of the staff representative. Lie to the witch hunters. Every choice can have short or long term consequences. Be careful before saying “No” to the student delegate! Flee from the armies of darkness by building your university in isolated environments: lake, mountain, desert, volcano, giant turtle back, etc. Collect powerful grimoires to strengthen your university and face increasingly hostile environments. Find new allies to help you in your fight. Take advantage of your trained students' bonuses accumulated throughout the campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty satisfied with this game, there is some issues, but the concept is relly refreshing. the future your students gets slowly but surely influences your future schools, and the campaign is long enough for you to see those tiny modifiers lerge into real bonuses. the location-specific challenges are neat and ensure you don't get bored even though you're building your fifth university.there is some issues though, and to be honest, while playing you will kind of see that this is a first iteration of the concept because there is some rough edges. like professor traits that may or may not be applicable, tipically a janitor having the trait "isnpiring", does that work ? who knows ¯\_(ツ)_/¯Also there is generally little to no purpose in rejecting a student, unless you're really strained in accomodation or the dark lord's army is litterally scratching at your door like a needy cat. You'd also think it could be fun to make a dedicated house like slitherin where everyone is an evil a**hole, but really, you can't, i mean you can, but that woudl be shooting yourself in the foot.Students can be poor, middle-class, rich, good, neutral, evil, they will stay for 3, 5 or 7 years, be well mannered or little punks, funny and entertaining to others or lonely and depressed, smart or dumb and so on. they have so many properties that it is impossible to really care for all of them, and by far the most important is what magic they like or hate. like a goth kid who hates light magic will suffer a 50% penalty when trying to learn light magic even if he's otherwise a real parangon of virtue and kindness. so just put him in another house and he'll do just fine.As the dean of the magical university, your goal it to decide for each student what he has the potential to become. Say you have a kid who is bright but will stay only three years, do you put him in a generalist house and hope he picks up enough skills to come out as something good ? or do you put him in your "house of dark magic ™" that studies only that one element to make sure that he maxes out in something? In the end that is really well thought of because that really puts you into the role you're playing.Otherwise there is a bunch of things that lack polish but are really fun, like the dungeon quests that send you dungeon-crawling with a team of students (who may or may not come back, and that will be all your fault), or the way you interact with the other factions to trade or get other bonuses.On the negative side, the UI is a bit clunky at times, and the RNG can really f*ck you up. sometimes the game slaps you in the face with bad events at a time were you have no way to dodge them which can be frustrating, but that's pretty rare in my opinion. Overall i don't regret buying and playing this game, and the bad points really make me think "I'm eager to see what Spellcaster University 2 will be with those issues fixed" rather than "Dear god, what were you thinking ?"

In all honesty, the game was not built as an open world, where the world is your oyster. The game is built around a little story and you complete it. The end. Thanks for playing. Buy our next game.

_childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University is  a surprisingly deep and engaging game which will absorb you for hours as you try find configurations of your school which will allow your students to earn the futures which will in turn benefit your school. There are some bugfixes and additional features I would appreciate if the developers are interested in continuing to patch or even making DLCBugfixes1. Currently, at least in the English version of the game, there are two different futures named "Shapeshifter". Less confusingly there is also a future called Werewolf, seemingly unrelated to the Werewolfs you can recruit as students.2. Some futures give an amount of resources for interacting with specific factions, if those factions then give a request to the player with the option of "let me think about that", the player can repeatedly interact with that factions and theoretically farm an infinite amount of that resource.3. Sometimes cards can be hard to place in a room, despite trying to drag them over an open slot, this can be fixed by centering the players view and then placing it. Similarly sometimes cards will not actually be placed and instead hover in miniature form, requiring the player to click on it again and drag it fully into the slot.Recommended changes/ additional features1. More dungeon delves per schools: On most levels of the campaign you will be able to delve into one or two, or at maximum three, dungeons with a team of students equipped with the magic you have taught them. The gameplay is effectively like an rpg autobattler with the students capabilities defined by what magic they've learned and what traits they have. This in my opinion is a really cool mini game, and I find it a shame that it usually will only happen twice per school. I would really love it if there were five or six such delves per level and a wider variety of possible adventures.2. More campaigns: While the one campaign in the game is very fun and extremely replayable, I would really enjoy more possible campaigns with different win conditions. I would love a much longer campaign which would allow you to build a much more OP school, but also give challenges worthy of such an OP school.3. More in depth futures: One part of the game which I find slightly disapointing is the future system. One student who earns the future of Archmage might have very different traits and education then another with the same future, but with the current system the only difference would be what chance they have to earn each future. This makes the actual students feel kind of indistinct from each other. I think one way to change this would be have each student earn multi semi independent futures which flesh out different aspects of the students life. However the developers choose to change it, I would very much appreciate a future system which makes me view the characters as people.Overall I give Spellcaster University a strong 7 to a light 8.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: I find the game pretty fun, it's got a simple concept with repeating the whole 'dark lord' to restart the schools but I find it enjoyable. I like exploring the different areas you can build the schools, the little side missions you get depending on where you've built the school really add to it's depth.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyable, chill base building/aquarium kind of thing. You build your wizard tower, with classrooms for students to learn in and the facilities they need to keep them (and the staff) happy, then they graduate into whatever class based on the magic they learn, which gives you bonuses for the rest of the campaign (individually minor bonuses, but they definitely stack up later in the campaign)I wish there was more ways to 'use' students, I assumed there would be some actual big battle at the end of the campaign where you would fight the lord of evil which would go differently based on what students you had graduated, but unfortunately that isnt the case.You get some of this with the dungeon crawling which is fun, but by the time your students are powerful enough to really push into the dungeons (and they become available to do) you probably dont really need the rewards anymore. Trophy rooms are OP.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting game, and while it probably isn't for everyone, I find it very enjoyable. The game is a management sim with a random component, where the rooms you can build are dictated by the cards you draw. The result is that no two schools turn out quite the same. This is also a game which has continued to grow overtime, with even more new additions on the way. As someone who backed the game on Kickstarter and played off-and-on during the pre-launch phase, I was very impressed with the rate and quality of new content as the game continued to evolve, and based on their latest news announcement there is still at least some more new content coming. If you enjoy games "building" type games and enjoy the pseudo-randomness that comes with card mechanics, this game is probably worth checking out. And how many other games let you build and run a magical school?
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: This review is very hard for me. Did I enjoy the 22hours I put into this game? Yes.Would I recommend it to somebody else? Probably not, if you want it grab it when it's on sale.It's lacks replay-ability and I played 2-3 full games, I got bored because it feels good to explore the world once, but after you have seen everything once the game fails to keep me engaged.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Great simulation game. I thought it was so unique how your students' future depends on what magic they learn, their race, and their personality traits. Over 150 different future outcomes and some have permanent buffs to help with your run, while others give you instantaneous rewards. The card system of getting your buildings or items also allows for a lot of variability and difficulty to adapt to whatever your luck pulls.I love this game. There are definitely bugs, but none that break the game or mechanics. Just UI bugs. My other gripes have to do with some balancing things, ending options, and other things that were more of a subjective bias. But all in all, it was a worthwhile experience and definitely the unique from other simulation / colony sim games. I am definitely inspired to try and make my own version of this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Very well made, I love all the customisation options and all the different qualities of students and teachers alike. Though the minstrel is annoying me to no end, I'm enjoying turning all my students to the dark side and forcing them to live with an abundance of weird and wonderful creatures >:) 10/10 would recommend

So now I have 0 complaints, and I'm still addicted!I love this game. It's incredibly addictive. There's a few quests I haven't been able to complete that frustrate me, but in a good way that makes me want to keep trying. _childDocuments_.review: The game is great, but it still needs some polishing!I hope quality of life improvements will come with future updates. For me the most important would be to toggle a view of your school in which all the rooms would be marked with colours (according to their types) and with names written on them. Right now we have to click on each room separately to check what kind of room it is. Dungeon delves should be triggered at least 2-3 times per level, and not just once as of now. This mechanic is great, but it can be frustrating when you train warrior mages to go for those dungeons, but the entire level passes and no such events are triggered anymore. It would be a good idea if we could revisit unlocked dungeons or earn access to new ones by interacting with certain factions on the map. It would also be useful to get a way of managing students and staff. If I want to look at the students in a given house to check how much they have learned, I need to click on each of them. The hitboxes are basically on their heads but not exactly (and very tiny), and sometimes you click on one person, but you open the dossier of another one. I imagine it should work like in other games, and namely: when you open information about a student in a given house, you would use arrows (left and right) to open the information about the next student, being able to quickly and easily review information about all the students in a given house, one by one.Sometimes it is not clear what are the requirements of each room to be built. Especially, we had problems with gazebos not attaching anywhere. Also, PLEASE add a demolition card to the deck, that would allow us to demolish one room of our choice.Moreover, I would like to have the option of making multiple save files (I'm kind of paranoid about my saves getting mixed up. overwritten or corrupted), and the escape button should close menus. In spite of the game being slightly rough around the edges, we had hilarious fun with it and still haven't finished the campaign in almost 30 hours. We love the sense of humour, and the variety of cards is already quite satisfying.

I do feel like that's a major problem of the game, having to do random draws of only three cards from six different decks. _childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: The way that this game works is you build up a university with the goal of getting students to graduate with different professions, based on how much they learned.  The better professions provide permanent bonuses that last throughout an entire campaign.  This is important because every 45 minutes or so your university gets destroyed and you have to rebuild on a different map.  Initially rebuilding is hard, but it gets easier as you get more higher tier graduates.  After going through 6 universities you end up on a final map that has some reasonably hard objectives to complete before your university gets destroyed again, and you need to have a lot of high tier graduates to be able to do those.All in all its a unique, fun game.  It doesn't require a huge amount of interaction or micromanagement - you basically just place classrooms and approve new students.  I can see how that's not going to be everyone's favorite game, but I like games that I can play while I do something else on my other monitor and this is perfect for that.

The game would also benefit from a more fleshed-out tutorial, e.g., took a while to learn how to use basic potion/equipment cards, and had to watch YouTube videos to understand some mechanics.With that said, the game makes up for it with good vibes, a decent soundtrack, and a surprisingly broad experience portfolio - e.g., dungeon, different maps, progressing each level with one boon and one curse.

_childDocuments_.review: is a building game where you construct rooms and amenities for your teachers and students at the school, as well as dictate your students by placing them in customisable school houses. You must manage resources from gold to 5 different magic types, maintain relationships with outside factions; that regularly have actions you must enact which influence others, and build up your efficiency of different school houses, teachers, and classrooms.The campaign mode is a succession of you building many types of universities in different locations that have variables for different playthroughs as well as quirky unique characters and quests on each location site. If you love games involving magic and fantasy as well as like games involving resource management and quirky gameplay, this is great fun.- Great Stylised Graphics- Fun Soundtrack- Customisable Houses- Cool Alchemy System- Lots of Factions that add benefits and disadvantages- A Great many cool items and classrooms to unlock- Lots of great scenery and decorations- Lots of fun locations with unique scenarios- Gameplay can get a bit repetitive in campaign mode since you rince and repeat building a new school after the army of darkness finally catches up to your university, there are many augmentations that hold this back but it is inevitable. _childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University is a casual management game about building and running your own Hogwarts-like school for witchcraft and wizardry. I can honestly say that the game gives a great first impression. The opening hour of Spellcaster University is among the best I've experienced in gaming this year. The graphics are charming, the ambient music is catchy and thematic, and there's a level of charm that permeates the entire game. The levels themselves look like cross-sections of a dollhouse, and I find it all really appealing to look at. That said, the management elements of the game are quite basic, and a lot of the decisions confronting the player throughout the campaign turn out to be quite superficial. If you're looking for a casual experience to play while listening to music or browsing, and if this kind of setting appeals to you, Spellcaster University is definitely one to check out. You might find that the price is a bit steep for what's offered here. At the time of writing, I was able to play through the entire campaign in four hours. However it should be noted that I played on an easier difficulty setting, and mileage might vary.If you're into humorous writing, and if you're at all interested in reading about my personal playthrough and impressions of the game, feel free to check out my in-depth review here: And as always, have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: The other reviews about replayability are the biggest reason this game gets a positive though mixed review from me. I really, really enjoy the concept and even the game play is fun, but I don't like how short each individual school session is. I get that the campaign mode is about restarting several times while progressing through a meta Arc with quest goals (and to be honest I am still enjoying playing those objectives), but ultimately I still find it bittersweet how it's still a game about short sessions instead of a University that you feel some pride or ownership over.  I don't know if there's room for a gamemode like this with this model but this game definitely makes me long for something a bit more expansive/longterm in terms of a Magic University Management type game. A game might last for an hour or so and it's definitely a great way to fill time when you haven't much to commit, but if you're looking for something to get lost in for a few hours and then pick up the next day and get lost in again, this ain't it.  However, if you're OK with not getting to attached too each University you start (or anything really), the gameplay is still dynamic, challenging, and interesting enough to be worth quite a few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DRVisuals:very goodMechanics: very interesting and simplestory(lore): understandable, simple and not boring====================================================================good to both casual and tactical playerWhat a wonderful game, that is also hard to beat!I played it for 5 hours straight and I love the atmosphere and balance of traits, versatility and customization.It has some mechanics similar to Darkest Dungeon, I wouldn't be amazed if this game was inspired by that title, but here you are offered a lot more customization and this game is generally more casual. It takes a strategist to get the highest score, alright, but the game doesn't punish you if you just decide to play 'sandbox' in the campaign. Objectives play a big role in this game. They can impact the way you play so that you get the best reward possible from completing the objective by the end of the round. For me one round lasted around 4 hours and I was gripped by the feeling of managing "Hogwarts".I recommend this game both to those, who seek a tactical challenge and to those, who just like to chill and enjoy the game. And you don't even have to change the difficulty for that! (poggers, right?)
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University is a neat little building sim where you build a magic school.Pros:-An actual campaign, you go through 7 levels, each with a different faction and goals to meet, all on your quest to either defeat or escape the forces of evil.-An extra dungeon mode that actually lets you use your students in an interactive manner.-nice little universe, there's extra factions that you won't actually meet them all in one playthrough, which encourages replay-ability and there are also different modifiers for you to mix things up. Cons:-Once you've completed 2 or 3 levels, you've basically experienced the core gameplay loop in its entirety. Once you reach level 5 or 6 it can sort of feel like you're just doing the same thing, with a slight adjustment based on faction.-Wish the dungeon feature was more core to the actual game as opposed to being side content, without it you don't really interact with students beyond assigning a dorm and seeing their end occupation.-There is a factor of rng that can screw you on higher difficulties in terms of getting the rooms/resources necessary to complete some of the goals-would be nice to have a way to move rooms around like you can with accessories, at least as option in lower difficulties or endless mode.Overall I was pretty bought into the game's concept and I enjoyed exploring and seeing the different levels and factions.I recommend playing about 1 level per session, if you grind out more the game can begin to feel tedious/repetitive. I think they put a nice amount of effort and really did create a novel experience, I would just like to involve more ways to interact with the students, such as the dungeon system.Rating: 6.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: It's OKIf you're interested, I strongly recommend to wait for a discount.There are some interesting ideas, such as drawing cards from a deck of cards from a specific school of magic and using those cards to build out your university.A campaign consists of starting a university at ~5 different locations of your choice + 1 final university. Each location has it's own challenges, including a unique group of locals to interact with. Aside from the final location, you need to to your best completing 3 objectives and move on to the location.Each location has a (kind of) time limit.Some rooms have access limitations (entrances and exits) which makes placing rooms awkward. I'd prefer using incentives like proximity bonuses. Instead, I must ensure students can access rooms without having to travel far.After completing campaign, I find little reason to continue.However, if the game interests you, I encourage you to buy it so that the developers could hopefully one day release an even better version of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: (tl;dr   You can get a perfect score by accident. Good games don't work like that.)Can't recommend and I'm not sure why anyone is. This game can take your time from you easily which is pretty odd considering how boring and repetitive it is. I really don't think your choices matter all that much and here's why. I build one school with a solid plan going in, only to have it turned upside down by missions which didn't line up with my build. I put in 100% effort, was very selective about who I enrolled, and managed a 3 star school by the end. Sweet!I then built a school around a theme of rich-kids-only with a focus on Dark Magic just for luls. I focused all their studies to dark stuff (you can decide what they study) and let them run wild. Got some missions which required that I incorporate Light magic and some Arcane studies. I panicked a bit and just started taking any student who applied. Long story short, I was making mana and money like crazy even though I couldn't possibly feed or house 100 students. Ended with a 3 star school.Do whatever you want and recruit everyone. Doesn't seem to matter as long as you manage studies. This is a very shallow game which, in it's current state, is easy to learn and easy to master. There are very few things you have control over so its dead simple. I put in 6.3 hours and I'm fairly certain I've gotten everything from it.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so, after finally completing a full campaign, I can honestly tell you this: It's fairly fun, and easy to start up a game.If you have a busy life, and really want to play a game and get a bit of gratification in going from zero to one hundred, then this is something that might interest you. It's got a kind of roguelike element to it, wherein the better you do, the better rewards you get at the end. Campaign mode lets you play across the game's continent as you run out of places to run away from the Dark Lord and his army.It takes no time at all in setting up, and once you know what you're doing, you can jump into each game pretty quick. I think my biggest critique is that I was left wanting more at the end. Maybe an endless campaign mode, or New Game +, where I could continue my school (the game DOES have a time loop mechanic in it for when you fail). But those are small gripes really. It's for sure worth the price, and it'll keep you pretty entertained while you play!

_childDocuments_.review: Charming if a bit clunky Hogwarts Sim Tower, card-draw based room choices. Can generate different mana as resources, which allow you to draw more cards of that mana type.The mechanics are enjoyable, and the game is a great calm, casual experience. The campaign could use a lot of adjustment, it can feel a bit arbitrary and the only real direction is either provided through trial and error or community written walk-throughs. There isn't particularly a feeling of progressing difficulty or even a real link between the areas as you progress. Challenge cards (You can optionally set a challenge at the start of the campaign, and completing it will unlock the card for future runs) are a cool way to provide goals, but they feel like a side piece rather than a main progressing thread. Some functionality/depth seems underwhelming on it's impact on the game. Cool ideas, but they don't actually end up doing a lot for you if you spend time manage them (ex. get 3-5 school "houses", set priority to different types of magic for the house, drop the people gifted in those types in those houses, stop thinking about houses. There's rarely a benefit to tweaking house settings beyond the initial setup). A lot of it is that the time limit on campaign levels by default means that you rarely get to see your vision for a tower through, and the kinds of adjustments you get from some features aren't needed for the specific in-area goals, more for min-maxing or seeing your personal vision for the tower through. Despite my issues with it, I find myself returning to the campaign again and again, and the core gameplay loop is straightforward enough that I don't have trouble settling back in if I want to put the game down for a week and come back to my partially-complete campaign after.Devs seem to be continuing to provide updates and make tweaks, which is great to see. Took a chance on this game with limited reviews at the time, and it's overall a wonderful twist to the sim tower style building/management that there's been a lack of for a long time. I could see some people not getting what they want from this in its current state, but I'm completely happy with the purchase, and really looking forward to/hoping to see larger scale updates as this progresses through EA, and hopefully eventually a sequel to refine and follow up on the ideas in this game from these developers.I rarely write reviews, but this is exactly the kind of creative takes and great ideas getting polished that I hope for from early access games. If you're wondering, it's worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: I hate this game. Let me just state and reiterate that first of all. I. HATE. THIS. GAME. Now don't get me wrong, I like the concept of building/running a magical academy á la Hogwarts or the Unseen University, and the graphics are charming enough. But the gameplay, OH, THE GAMEPLAY! MY DOG, IT MAKES ME BLOODY FURIOUS! I've never liked gambling in any way, form or shape, and this "game" is exactly that: GAMBLING. You have ZERO control over how you progress in the game, whether in regards to what you specifically teach your individual students, what rooms you want/need to build, or even what staff you hire.Get this. For everything, AND I MEAN EVERYTHING, you do in the game, it's a roll of the dice. EVERYTHING you do in the game is based on an utterly garbage RNG system. To build rooms, place artifacts, or even just something so insanely basic as creating a new house (think Gryffindor or Ravenclaw, not a bungalow or cottage) you need specific cards for all of that. And the chance of getting any of those cards during a draw is absurdly low. Worse yet, the cost of drawing cards increases exponentially AND permanently, AND WITH NO UPPER LIMIT, each time you draw a card. So if you draw 6 "general" cards bought with gold, well... you're soon paying a literal bloody fortune for crap like another dining hall or a dormitory. Stuff that's so basic you get them FOR FREE when starting out.But hey, at least you can always choose where you place your rooms, right? WRONG. See, there's this insanely insipid thing in the game: you can't even remove or replace an existing room. Honestly. What kind of developer could EVER think that being entirely unable to adjust the layout of a structure after construction is in any way "good game design"? Have these people never even heard of the concept of renovations or restructuring?!For those few of you who know me from my earlier reviews (Subnautica, Cities Skylines, etc.), I'll extend an apology right now that this review is more of a hateful rant than the usual in-depth analysis I make of games. For those who're just reading this while looking through the comments about this game, I'll say this: whatever your motivation may be for wanting to buy this game, DON'T WASTE YOUR MONEY. There are far more and far better games out there with similar-enough motifs that Spellcaster University isn't worth the investment. Hell, even if this game was entirely unique, I'd still recommend not buying it. At least until the developers realize that there is a HUMONGOUS difference between a "gamer" and a "gambler".

_childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University is a cute, relaxing game full of missed opportunities. I don't know whether to recommend it or not, because it is a fun little time waster. But the choice you have the most control over is the look of a "House" or class group in your school. Everything else is random.As a management game, it's frustrating. You have very little control, and very little consequence, as nearly all of your decisions are a selection of one of three drawn cards. There is little actual difference in the types of magic, except for the way the equipment that you randomly draw may behave or be focused on. For instance, you'd think your Beast Mages would do something with the animals you get, your Enchantment laboratories would allow you to create or enhance items, your Scriptoriums might let you make magic scrolls or books? No, no, none of that. It's mostly just flavor, and really the important thing are the color codes. I thought the Majesty series was shallow with its schools of magic and classes, but Magic University manages to fill in much of the wading pool to the depth of a puddle.To compensate for the lack of actual control, the game bends over backwards to make itself easy - though it has to, to deal with the utterly chaotic randomization. The game is still cute, and relaxing. It IS fun. It just ignores so many opportunities laying on the ground in obvious reach.

_childDocuments_.review: I got sucked in to this pretty well.You manage a school for spellcasters until time runs out, using a deck system, which you can add to as your students gain mana/your school earns gold. I'm not super familiar with deck systems, but a little trial & error made everything clear.For a beginner, pick Novice alongside the longest timeframe available. It'll give you time to get comfortable with the game. You can reset the tutorial in options if needed.Then you flee and start again in a new place. The tutorial bugged out for me (or at least wasn't compatible with my learning-style), so I turned it off and found my way around the hard way. Similar to idle games, your spellcasters will graduate, bringing you temporary and permanent (any with a %) bonuses. Once you flee, you pick a new location and start over again, maintaining only your % gains from students.You don't have to micromanage individual spellcasters, and while the animations are cute, you can zoom all the way out and still function fine. There's no blood/gore. Battles are hands-off. There is a lot of fun flavor-text on cards, but I didn't catch much of the backstory.I'd like to see the tutorial less buggy.Overall, really really fun to play, and I expect to return to it regularly when I need to lose track of time. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game straddles the line between game and simulator, and it might leave people looking for either one disappointed. I, however, love this game, so I want to talk about it a bit.The gameplay almost exclusively involves making choices from a mostly-random selection. You draw from a deck or speak to a faction, and then you choose the option that seems to serve your needs best. You have a limited time to make these choices because the Lord of Evil makes you move along almost as soon as you get rolling. The overall idea is to emerge from the storm of randomness with a healthy selection of graduates who buff your stats for the rest of the campaign. Ultimately, you run out of places to hide, so you have to find a way to survive the final level.The simulator aspects are broad in scope, complicated, and absolutely delightful. Students and teachers have positive or negative traits and Good-Evil/Lawful-Chaotic alignments. Every person has three bad stats that slowly fill on their own and must be addressed by rooms in your school or by going home (going home means less total time in the school learning/teaching). Every person also has two good stats that decline only in certain conditions, and they have to recover those similarly in your school or by going home. There is also an intelligence modifier on each student and a teaching skill modifier on each teacher that affects the rate of student learning. To pay for all this jazz, you manage Gold as well as five types of Mana. The idiosyncrasies of the different rooms (entrance directions, adjacency restrictions) leave you to manage randomness on randomness to ensure you can pay your teachers, please your neighbors, and still churn out good enough students to help you beat the campaign.One of the issues that might make people say this game has low interactivity or that your choices have low impact is the fact that easy information is all lagging measures. You find out if you're making enough money by seeing if you have any left after paying teachers. You find out if students are learning well when they graduate. The interface does a poor job of collecting and projecting information that should be expected as core UI info in a game like this. You CAN dig into these by tracking how many teachers you're paying manually and checking the progress of students manually. However, this can feel frustrating when other games will just... tell you if you're making a profit or if you can expect to complete your quest to graduate a certain number of specific professions. I am able to look past this issue, but some other aren't. Furthermore, this design decision means that unskilled players come away thinking their decisions don't matter. The decisions matter, but you need to seek out the high quality information that is the most useful feedback.Overall, I was expecting a cute game with limited gameplay, but instead I found a deceptively difficult and complicated game that is a far better simulator of academia than it has a right to be. The love and humor that went into crafting this game is evident all over the place. Definitely worth a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: This is so close to being a really great game :( Almost all the pieces are here. But they're poorly communicated, rarely pop, and lack a feeling of meaningful progression, or a satisfying pay off. If it were re-balanced to -    1. Make dungeons a regular mechanic, instead of a random event (because these are the best part of the game by far!).    2. Create a meaningful sense of progression by letting me keep some of what i earn in each chapter when i move on to the next (my house cards, my items, a bonus to faction relations i maxed out, some special "you got an arch-mage!" bonus starting card, and or the bonuses generated by my graduated students [this one might already be a thing, there's no indication if it is or isn't :/] Right now its just six consecutive games strung together.    3. Have an actual interaction with the forces of evil at the end of a chapter, not just a title card with my stats.............. At least a text based battle that somehow involves all the progression i made over the last 4HRS!!!    4. And i would love to have some kind of effect on the random events, like buildings that defend the school during attacks, or being able to click on negative room events to stop them when a teachers not there. Right now there just things that happen, i rarely even notice, and never care.     5. Also, let me adjust text size! Its super tiny, brown is a terrible color for pop up texts, and the click and drag button SHOULD NOT be the same as the deploy-able removal button!!!!!!! Also the screen movement is janky as hell. This game has a fun, though repetitive, core game-play loop. And everything else just feels tacked on, instead of complimentary. I like it, but as it is i wouldn't pay more than $5, maybe $10 for it. _childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly fun game that combines colony builder games with card games in a Harry Potteresque world. The artifacts, rooms, spell schools, factions blend together and interact with each other a lot, offering a very rich gameplay full of interesting choices.Positives:- The theme of the game is very strong and well thought out. - Solves a lot of colony builders' shortcomings with the time limit and the card system- A lot of content, fun interactions- Students give short-term or long-term bonuses to your school, so there is overarching bonus system.- Campaign that use the aforementioned bonus system and also have some other clever mechanics, takes about 10 hour (6 levels). It is highly replayable. - You not only build rooms, you also manage the furniture and sometimes the extra abilities of a room. Want a dinner hall that also teaches kids demonology? A bed that changes them to vampire? All possible here. Negatives: - Sometimes it can get a little too random, which can be solved in the game with cleverness, but can be annoying.- Some stuff aren't really explained, like why it is useful to have the same equipment multiple times, or if the effectiveness or pedagogy of the janitors matters at all- There are really a lot of decisions sometimes. At the end of the level, I just assigned students randomly among the houses.

_childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University is a fun idea poorly explored, resulting in quickly repetitive gameplay and very limited replayability. The gameplay mechanisms essentially centers around the idea of diminishing marginal returns, denying diversity in strategies: It is always better to have your university offer all classes of magic than to specialize in one. It is always better to improve relationship with all factions than to ally with only one. This is especially problematic since the main campaign is practically the same stage repeated over and over, with only minor and insignificant modifiers and carry-overs offered at each stage. Also, the lack of statistics and overlays makes it forbiddingly difficult to understand the inner workings of the game economy and devise deeper strategies. This, along side some redundant options (combat related traits and items are absolutely useless, for instance), makes it more likely for one to resort to a one-size-fit-all solution for the monotonic levels. At its current stage, the game offers no more than 2 hours of meaningful experience before degrading into a dull click simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since a humble game piqued my interest enough to not just install, not just play, but finish at least a run through it's campaign. So there's that. It's not amazing in any particular way. The reliance on RNG for the gameplay loop made it not as fun as I hope when installing as it makes it difficult to really plan your school. This RNG clashes with some of the mechanics. Early on you are going to select your three goals for the map, but sometimes you just can't get the cards you need to achieve that goal. The RNG was never so bad that it became unenjoyable, but it did hold it back just a touch.Otherwise, what you see from the gameplay videos is what you get. And odds are you've played some varent of games like this before. I would have liked a little more control to get around the rng limits, like more specific settings for the students. But again, nothing outright hindered the game or made me want to stop playing or ever get frustrated at a series of bad rng. So it's a solid game that at least for me personal could be great with a little less rng or a little more control.6

_childDocuments_.review: This is an odd game.  It's not very active, but there's always a lot of stuff to do.  It's kind of a weird combination of sim-city and hogwarts, with a slight plot, and some randomness to what you have available to build. _childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much fun. I'd write a more in depth review but I'd rather play more than write a review. But this game is awesome. There were a lot of reviews a few months ago that complained about crashes and bugs, and things have gotten much better. The developers have fixed the problems with the game crashing (I'm on a fourth campaign with no crashes so far.) _childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: These game developers need a tutorial on tutorials. This game looks like it could be fun, and could be interesting if they took any time to make sure you understood how the mechanics work and what you're supposed to be doing. Instead they just throw large chunks of text at you at the very beginning, cross your fingers you'll retain it and know what on earth they're talking about, and leave you with some lovely music playing as you scratch your head and wonder what on earth you're supposed to be doing with all these cards. Is there an order? Do my choices matter? What is happening? Who knows. All I know is that I feel badly for my partner who purchased this game as a gift as it seemed pretty and neat, and it turns out that any fun it might've provided is completely sucked out by me having to read a novel of a how to guide to get even basic information on game mechanics. Pass on this. Derpy adorable dragon isn't worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: There's nothing else out there really that's like this that gets you close to a Hogwarts Simulator, which is unfortunate because I think this is overall a mediocre attempt. You won't grow attached to any particular student, don't care about your teachers, and there are lots of other choices that don't seem to particularly matter. For instance, why would I turn down students when ALL of them have crappy traits and there's no real reason to min/max their acceptance? Or I finally get enough points to purchase a card, and then draw a bunch of junk I don't need, so which least crap option should I choose? There's also no direction for your school for the first 1/5 of the game...you're forced to start building and then can all of a sudden find that the direction you started your school in is completely opposite of what the randomized objectives end up being. And guess what? Too bad, because you're stuck with what you started building. It just all feels very cobbled together, and done so in ways that don't help generate any sort of narrative experience for your school. Why isn't there a system to replace teachers? Why can't I replace rooms? Why aren't there some systems for generating personal investments in particular/special students and/or teachers so I actually care about their progress? Again, just all too random combined with very inflexible systems in ways that detract from what this game could have been. There's little "management' past dealing with the game's RNG, and no narrative you'll care about to speak of.

_childDocuments_.review: wish there was a middle option for this game. _childDocuments_.review: Let me say i really want to like this game as it tries to scratch an itch and is a good idea in general.TL;DR: its a nice simulation that lacks all comfort functions of a simulation and is still quite unfinished, it looks like an alpha atm (in line with EA)But the lack off tooltips, polish, "quirks" and missing quality of life makes all enjoyment vanish.Of cause it also lacks balance as it is still EA.The current build also have all achievements not working.It starts by room cards that dont show indicators in choice select if it is a 1x1 or 2x1 room and more important if it can be vertically and/or horizontally entered. This is quite important info, better memorize for everything!!If you upgrade rooms they get "efficiency" - while it its obvious for the teaching stuff/food/sleep buildings ... what does it the other buildings is up to your guess. A clear message what it does? nope.Alchemy cards to craft potions are a mess & most stuff you get there is useless.(only good potions are the one "closing the portals and douse the fires" & the 2nd one is the cleaning potion).Cleaning is also a mechanic that is very iffy.  if you have 20 rooms and 3 janitors they can only keep half the rooms clean ... and unclean rooms reduce efficiency.So in the end a lvl 5 room (base efficeny 40%) can drop to -10% ...My biggest gripe with the game are the oversights.For example: animals, weapons, pictures, ect. have slots that are different for each room.What each room have is shown on the card while on your hand, but once placed that info is not accessible anymore.Thats super frustrating f.e. if you get the choice of "a room or a animal" ... the UI shows you if you have said room/animal allready ... but for the animal it doesnt show if you have a slot left. GL guessing - or making an extra list.Same problems with bed slotsSidenote:  Why can you place a student bed in your janitor room? Why is your janitor a teacher? , why does your janitors negative traits influence the room he is cleaning? Why can you not fire teachers?There are also no real statistics to see if what you do is efficient."Do i need more teaching rooms for X?"  "Why is no one in the lesson for Y?"Other things are there is a consultant that improves chances to get better jobs ... however it has no tooltip/icon if done for a student. So its anybodys guess if it even works.The "combat" (you get attacked 2-3 times) is just a bad joke.Monsters run past your students, jsut to randomly attack one and then they "fight".And the fight is all students nearby stay still, shoot at the enemy - mb run away or die - until the enemy is dead. Sidenote: the combat potion ("greatly damages attacking forces") doesnt seem to have any influence when used.Hit scanning for clicks is also questionable at best."wanna click the sleeping student?" sorry, impossible."wanna place that picture there?" sorry, the wal/student/something else is near it, so noThe game does also a poor job at best to display your modifiers.Play a card that specific students get wings? Go for it - it will never show that it was played. You can find it on a student that has the effect activated.Your graduates give you Boni (1% efficency for a room, 0.5% rep from king) ... a list where you can see all modifiers added up / card effects? This does not excistWanna find out WHY you have a specific efficeny in a room? noWanna know what modifiers are in a room (f.e. from teacher, animal, students, mobilar)? also noGraphics:It is functional.This game sadly has no Borderless window mode. There are outside programs to fix that but ... why isn't that a normal feature?Update 15/03/2024 ... sadly still the same.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw some people on youtube playing this game and really liked the idea. I've enjoyed similar games like this such as Project Hospital. This has a similar feel but more magical.Strategy matters to get the best out of the game and to achieve goals and i've found it easy to lose hours playing this game. Although a very simple idea, this was well worth the cost as I've relished trying to achieve all the outcomes for my students and have been considering sharing my gameplay online on twitch and youtube.One small point - currently they have a character trait called 'deaf' which makes a character learn all types of magic 15% slower. I am a disabled gamer and there is a definite issue in society with people assuming disability is a negative word. The irony being I noticed this in the game during Disability Pride Month. I don't learn slower than anyone else and i'm currently a disabled heard of hearing person who is doing a PhD. _childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University (SU) is a strategy card game about building your own magic university. It has deceptive depth, a functional art style and some fun components but ultimately it falls short of keeping my attention. A terribly designed save system combined with too much RNG makes for an annoying rather than enjoyable experience.The goal in SU is to build your university up from the ground before time runs out (which is essentially the Big Bad comes to attack, requiring you to leave and move elsewhere). You do so by spending different currencies (gold and various types of mana) to buy a random choice of 3 cards. You select one and either place another room, place an item that enhances the room or play the card to enhance the university ("get this bonus if your students meet these qualifications"). When you place a room you select from 1 of 2 random professors, each with a random trait or two. Your randomly get students and place them into various houses, each with a different emphasis of your choosing (again, usually among 3 random choices provided) or send the really dumb recruits packing. Notice the word random over and over in that sentence? Yeah, that's a recurring theme. Most everything in this game is random. While there's surprising depth to each selection since they involve multiple variables, this game ultimately is a very random experience. Get good cards, good students or good traits and you can sail along. Get screwed in the RNG, especially early in, and it's not much fun because like games of this ilk, things snowball.Music and graphics are adequate but nothing to write home about. This isn't a game that will awe you with its presentation but it's not bad enough to detract from the experience.The game play loop is kind of fun, I'll give it that. I like the premise of running a magical school. And I encountered no bugs, which is always nice. But I can't give this a positive recommendation.First of all, this game is very RNG heavy and if you get the wrong series of cards, it's not fun because you - as the player - didn't do anything wrong. This happened to me on my 2nd university of my 2nd campaign. Got a series of cards to start and placed the rooms and the stuff. Then I got the choices for my goals - NONE of which had anything to do with any of the rooms I had already placed. And 80% of the initial 15-20 recruits were either dumb or poor. While there's no way to "lose" as far as I can tell, that's just a start that I have no desire to even play. Which wouldn't be so much of a problem except....The save system is absurd because it keeps one save for your entire campaign. So if you get a crappy start (as I did), make just one mis-click (as I did on my previous campaign) or just want to try again, you're SOL. Not only can you not revert on the level, YOU CAN'T REVERT AT ALL! Your entire campaign is impacted because there's no way back. It's simply a mind-boggling idiotic decision by the developers to allow your campaign to get hosed because of bad RNG or a simple mis-click of the mouse. It's nonsensical and frankly idiotic. If I could go back and replay a level, I doubt this would be a negative review. But for a game that relies so heavily on RNG, not allowing a player to revert - even if they had to restart the level - is Riddikulus.  When you bring up the card selection, you can't actually interact with your university. You have the 3 choices and must decide right then and there. So if you can't remember whether you already had room "x" (and it's not easy to remember everything you placed), you may select it again. Can't remember whether you placed a student's or teacher's lounge? Too bad! Take a guess! And if you guess wrong, you just wasted your precious resources on a useless card. The tutorial is an exposition dump that did a really poor job of explaining the game. I had to seek out YouTube channels to figure out what I was looking at. In my 2nd campaign, I received no pop up for the dungeon. I don't know if this was a bug or if there's some sort of trigger that didn't fire but this was annoying since that's a good way to get resources mid-game. And since I had prepared my students for a dungeon adventure, it was quite the letdown to not be allowed to explore the dungeon. Not that the dungeon is a compelling part of the game. In my first outing I got two rooms in and ran into a dragon who proceeded to facewipe my entire party. I guess the enemy difficulty is also random, eh?If I could restart a level I'd probably give SU a positive score. But the extreme randomness of the game coupled with no ability to restart beyond having to start the entire campaign over again makes this game a waste of my time....and yours. Avoid.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I really enjoyed even though I'm usually not a fan of card based games. Those saying that there's a lot of randomness are plain wrong. There's a lot of strategy here even if there is some randomness.The game is not perfect though, the most annoying things for me were:1. I want to see the rooms I can place artifact before I choose one.2. Alchemy is really annoying mainly because I can't just click on potion I want, but have to drag ingredients separately. It doesn't even highlight recipes I could make with ingredients I have.3. It would be nice if the game grouped cards by their type, since it doesn't it becomes one more annoying thing to do.4. Dungeons are a bit of a mess, abilities are not very well balanced (e.g. healing & paralyze specifically seem to be really powerful) and it usually results in a lot of cards you don't really want. Not saying that they're not worth going to, since you definitely get a lot of value out of them, but I just didn't find it engaging basically stomping through the whole dungeon until you find enemies that one shot your heroes & kill them all.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first campaign, and I absolutely love this game! That being said, there are several small things that I'd like to see changed/fixed...The good:- The general concept - I loved building my universities!- The unique aspect to each level - from the bard to the monk to the giant turtle, every level had its own delightful twist!- the cards and the building system - overall unique and very fun!In general, I had a great time playing this game!The bad - - The tutorial was very quick, I had to watch several YouTube videos to really understand what was going on or what to do. I'm still not really sure how to manage a lot of things or how to get certain careers out of my students. I would've preferred a whole tutorial level, maybe one that could be played as a prequel? Something that teaches you things like ways to organize students in houses, how to stack rooms, how to achieve stars, etc!- I couldn't move rooms around once I placed them. I've seen a bunch of other people mention this, and let me tell you, I had some funky looking castles where I really regretted certain rooms. Unstacking would also be nice, but I think that might remove the challenge of it. Maybe on easier difficulties?- The ending of the campaign was a little underwhelming. I would've liked to see at the very least a few zombies and the lord of Evil come to the university and get destroyed, but instead the level just ended.Overall I highly recommend this game, especially for the price! The few complaints I have could probably be addressed if I just buckled down and did my own research, but I do prefer learning hands-on instead of through youtube videos!
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Not gonna mince words: This game is *rough* around the edges. The performance breaks down like an old man walking up to the 6th floor when your school gets too large, dragging cards onto room slots is like trying to piss through a needle's eye, characters get stuck on walls and each other like Skyrim NPCs on skooma, events repeat so much it makes me feel like I'm playing Outer Wilds... you get the idea.And yet - AND YET! The game's charm shines through all that stuff and more besides. For what it's worth, none of the problems really break the game, they're more of an inconvenience - an inconvenience that I was willing to forgive, in the end. Because the enjoyment and pride from having my students grow up to become Vampire Lords, Plane Walkers, Druids and Archmagi was just that nice.So yes. It's good, albeit flawed as heck. Want to hear more? Let's go then.The main thing you do is buy cards and play them. There are 6 currencies: Gold, as well as 5 kinds of mana from the 5 schools of magic. Each currency can only buy cards from it's own deck. Initially, every deck draw costs 100; but the more you play, the more it costs. Each draw lets you pick one of three cards - you'll get a random mixture of classrooms, utility rooms, artifacts, room upgrades and critters. Classrooms are the most important ones - they generate mana that allows you to purchase more of the discipline's cards. So it's a 'spend money to make money' kind of situation. Gold, however, is it's own category and requires different ways to procure it, and figuring out how to actually keep the dough rolling in is one of the first challenges you have to face.So it seems simple: spend mana to get more mana. Yes? No! Turns out every now and then you get random events, which often requires having some mana/gold on hand to respond to them favourably. Also, every mission has it's own special faction to interact with, and those often require not only mana but possession of certain rooms/artifacts. As such, resource management, smart investing and long term planning is the main skill utilised here.It's important to note here that the campaign is split into 'missions' - you start from scratch every time due to the Evil Lord destroying your old school, and he'll come again after some 10 years or so; this is what marks the end of a mission (it's possible to delay it slightly). Until then you have to complete as many objectives and train as many students as you can. Objectives can be selected and they determine the quality of the upgrade book you get after the mission, while your graduates give you currency and permanent microbonuses (0.5% increased efficiency of a given classroom, 5 gold every time you interact with the King, etc). And you'll need those, because every mission throws additional curse at you, making things more difficult - they stack, but so do your upgrades. So it becomes an arms race of sorts.I found this entire thing rather well balanced. The challenges keep mounting, but if you're aware of your perks and specialities, you can often make things work in your favour. It is possible to get screwed over by the RNG - naturally - but there are plenty of options to help you get started if you can't find sources of given mana. There's plenty of events, even if they tend to repeat (that can be used to your advantage actually). The students have a lot of traits which you can use to determine which house to assign them to, which will determine their classes (you can fully control this aspect). It quickly becomes a game of "make the best of what I got", and it always keeps you engaged. There's a truckload of artifacts and modifiers which are very situational, but if you play your cards right you can always make things work. Get rid of your students' bad traits by giving them a spikey bed. Get that overpaid teacher to sign a contract with the Dark Lord, nullifying his pay. Lots of accidents in the alchemy lab? Get an artifact that protects your students from aberrations. And so on. It's a little hard to pay attention to the entire school, but it's doable.You get the idea. The game's fun. It doesn't take itself too seriously, which is very nice - although I do wish some of the rougher parts were improved. If you can't handle FPS drops then stay away from this one. But if you enjoy a suprisignly complex city builder with magic and humour, then consider playing this - for what it's worth, I had fun, and I'm not easy to please. Enjoy!
