_childDocuments_.review: A terrific little game, atmospheric and charmingly brought to life.  Complex enough, with lots of room for strategy and meaningful decisions to be made, without feeling like you need to be fiddley or obsessive about micromanaging every detail (unless you want to).A single play through the campaign leaves me feeling like I've mastered the mechanics of the game, but like there are still a ton of tiny details left undiscovered.  I'll definitely be coming back - there is plenty of replay value here.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game on a whim, because who doesn't want to start their own magical university?? I got to create custom houses that taught different schools of magic, build my school from the ground up, and fight monsters! The mechanics were a little clunky in the beginning, but I eventually got the hang of it. Definitely has replay value because I know what I'm doing now! Next time I'm going to venture off to unlock different encounters and really tailor my student's developmental features.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: This is ostensibly a management sim game where you build up your own little Hogwarts to fight against the Dark Lord, but it doesn't really work.On introduction, it looks like you're going to need to pick and choose students based on their traits and sort them into houses to maximize their learning.  In practice, all you need to do is enroll every student that appears, and throw them into whatever house you've set up to grind out your quest objectives for the  map, and let it go.  Quantity trumps quality by such an overwhelming margin that paying any other way is just playing wrong.  This happens because there dont appear to be any real limits to quantity; classrooms don't have a max capacity, and the stressors like tiredness, health, and sanity never have a large enough impact on your students or staff to matter.This is for the best though.  If you did have to micromanage your students, the user interface would not be up to the task.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, Addicting, Easy to pick up, Hard to put down.  At first some of the mechanics and building techniques can take a minute to get used to, but once you get a good rhythm going man, this game gets flowing. Seeing your students advance and the different futures, the challenging but really rewarding dungeons, some of the really neat location based quests... (the zombies were a personal favorite of mine, so charming) Just beat my first campaign, but I know there's still so much more to explore as well
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: The game does not immediately let the player know what it is. From the description it may seem that this is a Fallout Shelter with mages, but this is not at all the case.Spellcaster University is an amazing combination of card roguelike, management game and Hogwarts. This combination makes her game experience unique (a bit like Ratropolis, but with mechanics that allow you to get strong buffs in subsequent playthroughs and more management bias).There are three main drawbacks of the game in my opinion:1) Inconvenient UI2) Management mechanics are poorly disclosed. It is not clear how AI works, it is difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of each artifact and room. As a result, at some point you stop thinking and start choosing randomly.3) Complexity is a snowball. The first map of the company is hard to play, but if you do it successfully (and get a lot of strong destinies), the further passage becomes extremely simple. And each next map only gets easier.But despite the cons, the game is good and unique. 10 tentacles for Gryffindor!
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Nice enjoyable little game but this would be more of a sideways thumb because of several issues.The main one is that it is repetitive, you basically do the same thing every game although there is a big part of random. Speaking of that, this is another problem. You get random cards to place, sometimes you will stuggle to get what you want especially in the beginning of a game. You manage to gather some mana hoping to get a classroom but the game might throw items or pets at you for a while. Random is also a factor in the outcome of studies and can be a pain. As for the management part, it's not prominent. You can influence things but in a passive way and with your decisions. You sort of give guidelines and then everybody just goes and does to his liking and according to their needs similar to a theme park, instead of being able to plan/schedule things. It is quite annoying to not really know the impact of many factors to help make the right calls. Also the game is missing visual help to know what you already have placed, used or what can be upgraded and what's the benefit of it, you can't move items or rooms plus you are stuck with picking a card once you draw. You get random events forcing you to choose an option while you might not have the ressources and can't postpone it. Some rooms don't seem to be very efficient like the guidance counselor or janitor. There are bugs also with items not placing in the slots (unless zooming in very close), some objectives not validating, and achievements not unlocking. I might have forgotten a few things.For now I'd say wait or get on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my second campaign, and this game is worth the sale price! That being said, there are a few issues. The good:- Building universities and seeing the careers that come from certain things. - The repeatability of play. There are so many unique levels and challenges. You can easily play through them and have a different game. - The building system is a fun twist with the cards and room variations, love the details as you upgrade them. I defiantly recommend the game. I bought it on sale 60% off and it is well worth that price. I will say with the amount of games I own, especially colony sims or base building games; I'm glad I didn't pay full price for this. The bad -- The tutorial was very quick, its difficult to understand what is really going on, how to do anything, fight back, overall objective, or how to get your students to level up to complete the level star missions. I should probably watch a few YouTube videos, but I do wish it would give us more than it did. - You can't move rooms. I started over 2 times because I hated how my layout was because I didn't understand the room design requirements (such as where doors are. - The ending is abrupt and underwhelming. Nothing happens except you get a pop up message saying the lord of Evil has come to the university, you graduate your remaining students and move onto the next world. - Similar to the tutorial there is no direction on what to do in the levels, I feel progression is hard. You cant fight the Troll because the Orcs gang up on you. Its difficult to get the requirements for the Lake Monster as well. You don't learn the requirements to get an arch mage, houses aren't really explained for the benefits of them, and its easy to lose track of the buffs you have. _childDocuments_.review: A cutesy looking 2.5d building game about training wizards which incorporates strategy and luck/rng - recommended for those who like board gaming (engine building deck drawing games) with a little challenge and luck.Overview:I picked up Spellcaster University after having watched a few youtube tutorials and walkthroughs, and if you have no idea what it's about I suggest you go do the same.  It's not Harry Potter, and it's not Sim city, but it's something entirely different.  The premise is that you are training wizards but there is a great evil lord who is building up their own army.  Your goal is to face the evil lord in the final round, but before you do, you spend each round creating a new university that trains students, before the lord of evil comes along and destroys it all.  You then get to do it again next round but in a different location. Each location has unique flaws/perks and a round specific challenge.  Also towards the start of each round you will be tasked with two other challenges, for instance to train a certain number of a type of wizard for example, or to have earned over a specific amount of money.  Whilst you don't have to complete any of the challenges, you will find as you progress through the game that getting three stars for each round is very beneficial as at the end of the round you will be cursed and also have the opportunity to draw a unique perk.  The more challenges you complete each round the better the perk you get.  In addition your graduating students also earn you perks.  There are also random events and potentially dungeons you can send your students in to fight and earn rewards.Game play:The game plays in real time as you build rooms and see your teachers train students.  As they train they get better at specific magic, and potentially spend money on food on other things.  This earns you money or 'mana' which can be used to draw three cards from their respective decks.  There are 6 decks, money, nature, light, dark, arcana and enchantment.  When you have sufficient amounts in a pool, say for example arcana, you can draw from that deck.  Each deck has specific types of cards, some of them are rooms, some of them might be trinkets to place in rooms, or some might be special abilities.  You take one card form the three and this goes into you 'hand'.  You can then play them if you are able or you can cash them back for a small refund.  At the top of the screen the lord of evil meter shows you their progress, and is it fills you time in your current location runs out, until it fills completely and you have to abandon the current location and it's students.Eventually the students finish their studies and they graduate.  At the end of their studies, depending on their background/race/abilities/perks/flaws and most importantly on the magic and levels of magic they have trained in they will get a random job.  Certain jobs can only be accessed by students proficient in certain magics or from racial backgrounds or even sometimes with certain perks/flaws.  These jobs can be something mundane like peasant or incredible like Archmage.  Every job a student gains will give you some perk, either ongoing (ie game long) immediate or rarely a mix of the two.So now you can see that the strategy in the game is train to lots of students that give you lots of ongoing effects that help you through the game.  You increase the likelihood of that by having better teachers, more satisfied students or having ways of changing things about them.  I won't go into much more as this review is already too long, but it's kind of delightful when you train a specific type of Wizard that requires a host of specific requirements.  I once completed a round with three stars and only earned two of those stars in the literal last seconds of the round.  I really like this game and have played through a number of times, and plan on playing through a number more, just to see different abilities/jobs and scenarios etc.  It is also frustrating and it's not always easy to plan out the layout of your university given the complexity of how the rooms fit together and the limited space you often have.  There are at least two endings possible, and even if you fail at the last hurdle, the game can start you again on the last round with a little leg up to help.Recommendation:Overall I would recommend this game to anyone that likes board games that involve building a engine.  Something similar to Terraforming Mars or Dominion.

_childDocuments_.review: I do enjoy this game, however I have mixed emotions with it being out of Early Access. What it currently has, has mass amounts of potential. I like the different schools of magic, each map has its own objectives. However, one thing I have a gripe about how each map, after 45 minutes - 1 hour, your school faces the inevitable. There are things you can do to delay this destruction, but all in all, all that you do in the end will either eventually end to the destruction of your school, or at the final map, if you're lucky enough to get all the cards, you can avoid it. There's no middle ground, there's no objective that I've seen that offers a chance to fight back or prevent the invasion outside of the end map. What I like about this game, to a point, there is some management with how you spend your "resources" and I like the variety of schools, you can custom design each school attire, the name, flag, and what lessons your students can learn based on the school of magic you put them in. I think the biggest improvement can go towards the objectives/end-game themselves. Every map you do, you're basically maximizing all that you can do and what your students can learn in the time you're allotted before you have to go to the next map, which kinda leaves you feeling, "well what's the point of trying to produce all-powerful students if they can't fight back?" Apparently in this game, there are "mini fights" (students vs orcs?) However from what I understand they have no bearing on the map's time limit. One additional small issue I've noticed - if you have janitors, and your students have produced "art" on the walls, there's a shocking percentage of how little your janitor actually notices the graffiti on the walls before going into the next room. I've had graffiti on the wall that's sat there for a good solid while as multiple janitors go in and out of the room before it's actually taken care of by someone/something.It's a cute little management game, however I feel like it should still be in Early Access. It needs a little improvement, possibly an endless skirmish if you don't want the time limit (but maybe still have those mini fights to keep your students on your toes), and more objectives that make you feel like you have some control over your school's fate.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, the game's a lot of fun and I certainly recommend it.The idea is really good and the game does well to approach its potential.There is an unfortunate general lack of polish and finish, standing in the way of it being truly great.For instance: - The loading bar completes in about 2 seconds, then it consistently takes another minute for the game to decide whether it's crashing or actually loading.- If you click a room for too long a fraction of a second when buying it, the game will take that as a drag and drop it behind your cursor - there's no way to undo it.- The filters are completely bugged and wouldn't be very useful anyway - there are no filters for the different object types, so good luck finding where to switch out a pet or a painting. _childDocuments_.review: Basically a "Hogwarts" simulator in which you build and run your own magic school until the Dark Lord arises again. Card drafting - in the form of new classrooms, artifacts or familiars that grant various upgrades - is a core mechanic that makes options less overwhelming and add replay value, since you need to build around what chance throws your way. The game has its share of glitches though, and it's crashed on me a number of times. Recently, I've lost a campaign save file as well, probably due to a Steam cloud issue, but I'm unsure if it's a Steam problem or a problem with the game. The game does not explain itself as well as it could too, so you might want to watch a YouTube video or read a beginner's guide, especially once you want to dig deeper into it.I'm having a great time with it though so far, and it strikes a nice balance of being pretty chill while being somewhat strategic too.

_childDocuments_.review: Review: Early Access 10/1/2019SUMMARY: A clever, low-key Not Hogwarts Really management simulator that mostly avoids the problem of other management sims - boredom and feeling like a spreadsheet with some game attached.  It's a game that manages to achieve exactly what it says - you manage a school of magic.  As various teachers, students, and more come to your school you build rooms, add features, negotiate with factions, and try to save the world.  As of this writing it's Early Access, with several flaws in stability and focus, but shows lots of promise and is authentically fun even from the start.Let's get it out of the way - Spellcaster University is the Hogwarts simulator we've wanted, because who hasn't wanted to have traumatized children taught how to handle dangerous forces to fight evil!The goal of the game is to raise powerful enough mages to defeat the evil Dark Lord (or perhaps ally with him).  You do this by designing schools, recruiting students, making houses, and choosing certain priorities and policies.  All of the different elements interact, so though it's easy to pick up, many other challenges away - namely making sure the world doesn't end for real.The game loops are pretty clear:* Build an initial school with some options by selecting cards you recieve.* Recruit students and teachers, choosing who will best fit at your school.* Make management decisions like prices, pay rates, and so on - don't worry, there's only a few options so it's not overwhelming.* Watch your choices generate money and mana so you can draw new cards.* Interact with different factions to take advantage of what they offer.* Have your school be inevitably destroyed - and run from place to place until you prepare for the ultimate battle!There's some RPG-like elements to this all as well.  Characters have personalities, equipment cards grant boosts, and you can even zoom in to see how people are doing.The core elements are straightforward and easy to pick up - generate resources, make choices, get cards, build the school, try to raise good wizard.The subtlety of the game is that all of these factors interact.  Do your teacher's personalities clash with students?  Is it worth bringing in wealthy dumb kids for the funds, or poor brilliant kids?  How do you deal with the Orcs?  Do you specialize in a given kind of magic?  How awesome is it to have a school on a back of a giant turtle?The game knows exactly what it is, and is busy being it to the hilt.  It's not just a solid game - it's a solid identity.  On top of that it maintains a good-natured humor that pokes gentle fun at itself and fantasy tropes, while being compelling as there's many options and paths.There are a few flaws:* At this stage, the game does lack an effective tutorial or guide, and some of the management tools where you do look at charts isn't clear.  Sure there's always mystery, but I'd like a little more guidance on optimal class sizes, routines, etc.* There are definite stability issues.  The autosave helps but it can be frustrating.  These have improved over time.* The usefulness of some elements is questionable.  It's not clear what they do or if they matter - like alliances seem to just be gold factories.* Certain adventure elements have frustratingly random requirements.* The games goals and victory conditions are NOT really clear.  This may be intentional, but it's a little annoying.These flaws aside, the game is FUN and easy to dive into.  There's some muddles to be cleared up, but it delivers a lot of its promise in Early Access.So who is this game for?* If you ever looked at Albus Dumbledore, Professor Ozpin, or All Might and said "I can run a school better than you" then here you go, step up to the challenge, and see if you can raise heros as opposed to creating a legion of child soldiers with  emotional scars.* If you like management sims but want something that's not like going into the office - while still having the tools to tweak things.* If you enjoyed some of those "fantasy management sims" that had RPGish elements and management elements combined.The devs are responsive and on top of this game as well.  So if you get Early Access, they will listen.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I hated this game. Its unintuitive, tooltips do not do enough to explain. But the strange part about this game is, its really damn fun and it's REALLY damn addicting. I liken it to the feeling i get playing Game Dev Tycoon, trying endlessly to get that perfect 10 game, in this case being that Archmage graduate. This game is way more roguelike that they make it seem and its a good thing. The campaign is where its at, you have to built a total of 7 schools, the first 6 being destroyed by the army of darkness after the time runs out and the 7th either you win by defeating the dark lord, escape, or die and try again. On medium and lower difficulties you get to try again on final map while on hard and master you cannot retry the final map. The roguelike elements come with your graduates. The classrooms, teachers, mana and item buffs you got on the previous school are all wiped out but your graduate buffs remain. Some are immediate and provide no benefit past the student graduating while others, the harder ones to get as they require a more learned student, provide permanent, small buffs to rooms, mana gain, reputation gain ect ect. Each school's graduates build on the next, the better you do the better buffs you get for that final map. On top of that on each map you are given three quests, you have a fair bit of choice when it comes to what they are. Each quest completed grants a star and each star grants a better end of map buff. You get 6 of these and some are amazing. (if you see the one for rune scriptiorium GRAB IT. 30% buff to the entire floor its on and you start each map with one is incredible, stack it on your first floor with starter magic rooms to buff their teaching speed) You also get a curse at the end of each map, making some thing worse/harder (you get a choice of 3, as per usual)All in all this game ends up being extremely complex. There are buffs for every spell/school of magic and half the battle is learning them all. As you play you'll start to realize which are rare objects and which are common, you'll start grabbing those rare things earlier and watch your school get better and better.This game will keep you coming back, despite it's lackluster ui. Be warned once you select into an action there is no override or go back. So if you open communications with the merchants and you don't have as much gold as you thought you did, you're ♥♥♥♥ outta luck. That communication is burnt and you'll have to wait for the next one to ready up. Also be ready to want to fire the head teacher when she comes demanding a coffee maching four times in the first four years and burns half your starting prestige. Stupid witch...
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the look of a management/simulation game but it has a bigger focus on management of randomness and resources. All decisions you make in this game are influenced by randomness. Events, rooms, students, teachers, interactions with the neighbors. Everything is random.What rooms do you want to build? Draw 3 cards and pick one, hopefully you can make a meaningful decision.What students do you enroll? Pull a handful from a completely randomized pool. Maybe they will be interesting. But most of the time you enroll all of them.What kind of houses do you want in your school? The choices available to you are random.What teacher do you want to hire for this classroom? You can pick one from two. Hopefully you will draw a card that can improve them.Which neighbor do you want to speak to? Pick any! But what you can talk about is limited by default with some random choices added. Hopefully you fill all the rquirements to make all of the choices. (You need to get lucky and have the right rooms and items.)This game is not interesting to play. The things you have any control over are some limited options for how you run your school and where you put your rooms (if you get them), but you have to be careful so you don't build yourself into a corner. Otherwise the game plays itself and you only try to navigate through all the randomness.The ultimate goal is to be lucky enough to build an efficient school so your students hopefully study well.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: I almost didn't get this game due to the negative reviews but I'm glad I picked this one up.  It's definitely worth the asking price.  To be honest, I'd gladly pay $30 for this title.  As of this moment, I've spent 22 hours playing this by logging in each night right after my kids go to bed.  Since I bought the game, I've been excited to fire up my PC and start where I left off the night before.  That is a good sign.  It's also a good sign that I have played this many hours and still haven't beaten the campaign.  I'm on the last level of the campaign and haven't gotten bored of it yet.  So, why so many negative reviews?  I wanted to take a sec to comment on some of the concerns that other players brought up:o Is it repetitive?  Maybe a little.  Yes, after playing the first map you will get the same cards over and over.  That said, you can use those cards to create another class so more students can attend the same class at once.  OR you can upgrade the class by dropping the same class card onto it.  Each time you play, you can have your houses focus on different combos of magic schools and unlock different occupations once they graduate depending on how high the members get and what combos of magic they learned.  Race (elf, human, orc, werewolf, deepkin) all affect the outcome of the occupation as well and there are a lot to unlock.  Like I said, I've played for 22 hours and I'm still excited to finish up the campaign.  I'm even thinking of maybe playing it again: this is because, at the end of every level/map, you pick a modifier that modifies the game for the rest of the campaign,  Looking back, I wish I would have chosen a different modifier.  I'll do that next campaign...o Is it random?  Yep.  it is.  However, it is no more random than many of the board games I play.  Any deckbuilder that you play that has a random market that changes as you purchase cards is just as random.  The difference is that, instead of building a deck, you use the cards to build a school.  There are also a ton of random events, random traits for each student/teacher, and the occupation your student gets at the end could be less than ideal, even if they have only a 5% chance to become a peasant... they can still become a peasant.  I have a LOT of board game buddies that hate randomness.  If that is you, then this game isn't for you.  That said, I enjoy randomness in my games.  I like to weigh my options, even if none of them seem appealing.  I'm cool with choosing the least "least appealing".  I like a lot of dice chuckers and luck of the draw games.  I also love "Euro" board games where there are very little chance encounters and the game is almost 100% strategy.  If that is what you are looking for, then look elsewhere.o Is it buggy?  I haven't experienced any bugs or performance problems.  That said, I've also played games where I seem to be one of the very few people experiencing bugs.  Pretty much any new release you buy is going to be a gamble on whether you experiencing some funky stuff.  This was is stable for me.This ended up being a much longer review than I wanted it to be and has cut into my play time.  The kids are finally asleep and I have a University to run so, ummm, bye.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game from a Humble Bundle set. This game was very fun and interesting at the start. As you progress, your choices from previous levels can affect your run. Every time you beat a level objective, you get a star. The stars give you different buffs that can help your next school. Along with beating each level, you also get a curse. The curses affect either your staff or students, very little or drastically. Each new level you start, you pick a new area. Which adds to the massive amount of RNG this game with special modifiers. I had to start over a good amount of times because of RNG bull crap. This game uses RNG far too much to really be considered a strategy game. There are also factions in the game, that also rely on RNG for reputation with those factions.!! SPOILERS !!After I finally made it to the end of the game, there are 3 ways for it to end:1.) You fight and beat the Villain and are super cool and stuff.2.) You live on the back of a giant flying turtle with a bubble until you find a planet.3.) You die.This game could've been better but this fell flat. People might like the randomness of literally everything, but I believe that it ruins it completely. The endings are pretty dumb, if you manage to remain successful for that long, and I was playing on the difficulty right below the standard.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are waiting for a AAA game coming out in 2022 and are still bored, this might be a game for you. The game is pretty basic and amazing at the same time. Your school will be defined by the different rooms you provide, and your students will be a mirror of your choices.  It took me around 24hrs to complete a marathon in hardest difficulty and it was a weirdly satisfying experience. Dungeons, however, give you the 'something still missing' type of feeling, and they are OK at best. It is def something the Devs should improve further in the games to come. Some side missions (simulated) would be a good addition. Lastly, if you are a fan of H.P., there are orcs here so please don't be toxic and expect this to be the perfect Harry Pot game. Just go back to wizardingworld. Gracias! PS: Def worth $20US. No more than $25US.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying Spellcaster University. _childDocuments_.review: Great idea; poor execution. It's a rogue-like base builder in premise. My issues with it are as follows:- The game encourages smart building placement and synergy between systems (schools of magic and specialisations within) along with needs-management of students and teachers. What it doesn't do is give you any information to see what exactly is going on. You can't see if needs are being met without clicking on characters individually, which, when there is usually upwards to 30+ characters, this can be incredibly cumbersome or just downright impossible. There's no graphs, no stats, nothing. - Efficiency. There are various stat modifiers for classrooms which can increase or decrease teaching speeds or even reaching the classrooms. This can severely impact your game, but you have little to no way of knowing how this is impacting your game without carefully watching every student -- which, as I said before, it's basically impossible.- Synergy. The game encourages synergy between magic systems. Different combinations can lead to different 'end' classes for a student when they graduate (which has no impact except for a very marginal bonus or some tiny rep gain.) These spells that students learn can also be used in dungeons... if they ever show up. As mentioned previously, there's no real way to see the skill level of a student without manually clicking on every single one individually, so it can be difficult to time when to go to a dungeon to make sure you have a handful of well equipped and learned students. Dungeons also rarely occur and offer little in terms of reward. If it was me, I would have a dungeon be available be available before each graduation and offer rewards which are unavailable to get through other means. Right now it feels, and seems like, a total afterthought. - Collectables/unlocks. There is a plethora of 'codexs' to unlock. Potion recipes, classes, etc. There's so many, in fact, that it's incredibly difficult to keep track and the game offers no way to help you with that. Making potions? You have to awkwardly drag cards to a screen that will pop up and dissapear. It also won't tell you if you have already made that recipe before, so you're left repeating the same recipes again and again because you're overwhelemed with the amount of ingredients you have and you're just trying to clear your hand. Same with classes. The game will throw a quest your way to 'specialise' into a class, which usually requires magic combinations - but it will give you that quest a good bit into the start of the game, long after you've already spent your early resources placing buildings -- which are permanent. So, if you screw up - tough. That's you stuck with that for the next couple of hours. - Game loop. After a period of time, monsters come, destroy your tower, and you go rebuild in a new place. At the end of the round, you get to choose a reward and a curse which carries through into your next game. The buffs are marginal and the curses are way unbalanced. It actually encourages you to do the bare minimum because the buffs are so lackluster compared to the curses -- or worse, downright detrimental if you do well in the round. Frankly, with all these half-baked systems and ideas, with no way to track, manage, or even see what is going on with your build, the game loop is very unsatisfying. This game isn't undercooked - it's badly cooked and needs reworked. This is all without me even mentioning the UI.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a fun magical school simulator game. The controls are fairly simple while the complexity of the game is deep enough. Would have been nice to have been able to create a physical description, a more detailed back story, maybe some personal elements/story thereof? That said, the game itself flows nicely, letting you create the style of school you want with a celebratory manage to all sorts of fantasy tropes. For those wishing to go to wizardry school one more-or a dozen more-times, this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Its hard to really compare this game to any others I regularly play.  While it does have a "card" mechanic, its more of a strange combination of multiple systems that feels unique.Basically you are building a school for aspiring wizards, but your control of hte teachers and students is very limited.  You can if you have the right card generate a "house" which allows you to prioritize some kinds of magic and ban others for students you place into that house (you are your own sorting hat).  But the classrooms end up randomly selected by the cards you discover.  As you gain mana of one type or another you'll have the ability to draw 3 cards and then use one to expand your school.  Of course, you can end up not getting anything useful, which can hamper your schools growth.and that's probably why I can't really praise this game too much.  Its very much influenced by RNG, and that is always frustrating since strategies can be ruined when you don't get the classrooms/items you need.Its still fun, but I just wish I felt I had more control.

_childDocuments_.review: This is very much an unpolished gem. -Gameplay loop is fun.-You run a magic school.-Your strategy will impact your game experience.-Things are often unclear. For instance, there are two cards called "library" which do different things and need different placement. When picking rewards you can't see which one of the two you get. _childDocuments_.review: Welp. that about does it.  I sunk my teeth into this game but it doesn't have enough meat on the bone to saisfy.On the surface, spellcaster university comes with an interesting premise and some semi-interesting mechanics.  You get to play arch-mage at a wizard school.  Most of the game you're going to decide what rooms to build in a magical university, whether to accept certain students or teachers, and how to respond to magical events and factions in your land.  Yep that's it.  I think there are some dungeons, but these are unpolished. Every "run" you have a finite timer, so no matter what, eventually your castle will be overrun by an impending evil army.  You can delay this somewhat but never indefinitely.  What's kind of cute is watching all your students and teachers interact admidst the castle, but you can't really do anything directly with the cast of this game.  You just watch passively.  At the end of their schooling you can see what career path the students obtained and potentially re-roll these, but nothing else. in theory there are rogue-lite elements where completing a chapter in one location allows you to unlock new locations with new challenges, but each run feels pretty similar to the last.  Also in theory I think you're supposed to graduate enough students with high-tier magical abilities so that you can permanently unlock more efficient ways to train them, but there's not a great way to see this feedback loop in action.  The central dilemma of the game is resource management, where you need to both accumulate resources for the chance to build new rooms or items, and have resources on hand to deal with issues or factions that create issues-- but this is surprisingly not that fun.   Overall it became a "meh" experience for me after a few hours when I realized that no matter what, all my careful optimization or planning for a particular wizard school would amount to naught.   Another big issue is understanding your capacity for training new students.  Space in classrooms, dorms, and rec-halls is limited, but you don't have a great idea of how many students are having their needs met or not over time or what % of a room's capacity is being used.  If you accept too many students at once, some of them will graduate with little to no magical training because they never actually attended classesAnother gripe is that if you do manage to get a student fully trained to level 5 in a specific magic, they appear to still attend the class to train in that specialty-- a total waste of their time and taking up space that other students could have used.  I think it could be more fun to have a competitive mode where my students had to become smart enough to compete vs. students at other schools, OR if the questing mechanic were more developed to send bands of students off into the world to solve problems at the risk of peril.   The simple inevitability of failure makes this one less attractive to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Smart, deep strategy.This game is tricky at first, because each decision you make has little short-term impact, yet colossal long-term implications. You play the long game - build a school, produce as many skilled graduates as you can, gain permanent (i.e. lasting the whole campaign!) bonuses from graduates and spellbooks, repeat until you slat the big baddie after a few levels.I must disagree with the opinion, that all of the levels are the same. Each level gives you three quest to fulfill before the "timer" runs out, e.g. produce 110 graduates, produce 3 archdruids, befriend the orc fraction. The more quests you manage to do, the better the spellbook you obtain (and better spellbooks mean better bonuses). You don't get the quests at the get go - you gain them progressively in the first 1/3 of the level. This brings a challenge and is, in my opinion, the main tension in the game - you have to start building a functioning school since second zero, but don't know what to aim for, so you need to be very flexible. A challenge indeed!I also disagree with the opinion that "you cannot specialize in this game". While it is true that it is most prudent to have all 5 magic types in your school, there is nothing stopping you from being a school specializing in a particular type of magic, as every type of magic gains cards that are useful for other types of magic.To sweeten the experience even further, there is a bit of customization involved, as you get spellbooks and curses each level. And if for some reason you really want to specialize a type of mage (like e.g. you're really into necromancers), it is a valid way to customize your school through specializations.I hope this review was helpful for those, who were undecided about trying the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun but I can't recommend it at full price. It has a lot of potential but I feel like the game still needs some work.Pros* Get to make your dream Hogwarts!* Seeing what your students become after their studies is really cool! It feels great to see students graduating as time travelers, Litches, master assassins, adventures, etc.* Each branch of magic is really interesting and offers different benefits and mechanics. Being able to combine different branches of magic together can also create really interesting builds for dungeons.* The "rouge-like" element of having a timer is actually really interesting. Its nice to be able to dive into different branches of magic and try new things out. Each area also has a fun twist to the game which keeps things a little more interestingCons:* I don't mind the card aspect of the game but it leaves you at the whims of RNG too much. The game would really benefit from adding ways to manipulate the pull of cards to make it easier to get what you want* One of the best and most interesting parts of the game is dungeon delving but you rarely get to do it! It takes certain events to happen that you usually have to store up resources like money to make sure you can unlock the dungeon. After that you only get one shot at the dungeon and I have found the rewards to be lack-luster* The core "story" of the game is that you are trying to train students before evil comes again but your actions don't have any effect on the coming evil. I would love to see alternative endings on how the world fairs against evil based on how successful you were at training your students. Big missed opportunity!* The main gameplay mechanic is similar to a colony sim (loosely) but I feel like the game lacks having enough tools to be able to tell how effective your university is. You don't get notifications if a lot of students have certain unfulfilled needs and your forced to just keep an eye on the averages of each need (which isn't always very helpful)* There is no way to move rooms once their placed. If you have poorly placed rooms you'll be stuck with it for the rest of your run

_childDocuments_.review: This is a relaxing university builder game with some serious rng. You can sit back and enjoy, or carefully calculate the odds and play to maximize probability of success as you choose.Each round becomes more challenging as you travel around the land trying to avoid evil and build up the best university possible. There are different approaches you can take as well as many unique areas offering their own challenges and rewards.It could use some improvement in terms of viability - like maybe having a better clue as to what resources you're going to have to build/upgrade with to meet student needs (less rng) or before locking in to quests. The location-unique quests are also sometimes completely out of reach depending on rng. So if you are looking for competitive or max efficiency gameplay, there's something left to be desired.But this isn't your typical AOE, Star Craft type game. It's supposed to be chill and fun. Where you can sit back and watch the animations and enjoy what you've built. So yeah, there's strategy, but in a chill way rather than an intense or always optimized manner.

_childDocuments_.review: So I thought this was a simple base building game and completely missed that this is a deck building game. _childDocuments_.review: A rather interesting magic school simulator with roguelike elements. Your job is to manage a school, which can be done in some depth as you need to keep both the staff and the students happy to stay in your school, which includes not just giving them places to study, but also to rest and recuperate. You are not alone in the world though - there are six factions around you, plus extras in some levels, and there's also the minor inconvenience of an evil army approaching to wipe your school off the map, which serves as your time limit to sort out your objectives and get as many students graduated as possible.Managing your students is vital, and the game gives you a fair amount of tools to do so. As one would expect from a magic school simulator, you can set up houses that will define their curriculum, allowing you to either forbid, allow or prioritise certain schools of magic. After a certain time, they will leave your school and pick their path in life depending on what they learned, with the options ranging from lowly peasant to lofty archimage. Each graduating student either gives you a boost (a certain amount of resources) for the current level or a permanent bonus for the remainder of the game (e.g. all new students are more likely to have some positive trait). Once discovered, the game lists all the requirements for a certain profession, so you can adjust your houses and your long term strategy should you for example prefer your students to become midwives instead of liches. There is a brief tutorial at the beginning of the game outlining how things work, and I recommend spending the few minutes on it.With this out of the way, is the game fun as it is right now, despite the Early Access? In my opinion, yes, but there is still a need for some polishing. There are still some rather glaring bugs, for example with the placement of rooms and objects, and at times your students get stuck pathfinding. The events need more work, too, although some balance overhauls might not go amiss in general. At the moment of writing, the game is receiving updates and I am again happy to say you can get a fair bit of entertainment out of it if management sims are your thing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has its flaws. The text needs a good proofing, there are no text labels on the stats pages for the different types of magic, making the bar graphs there basically useless, the filters that show student sanity/health/skills/etc. don't work when paused, and without better information on what carries over between builds of schools and how, each of the schools that come before the big boss battle one seem kind of pointless. Better data on what my students and staff are doing -- how many leave the school and for how long, how much time is spent in each class, etc. -- would also be helpful, instead of having to guess at what impact my choices are having based on the movement of several dozen sprites across the screen.But overall, I like this game. The mechanic of building the school is one I've always enjoyed in tabletop games, and is nicely executed here. The choice-based roleplaying aspects are well planned out; some can be completed quickly, others require some really long-term planning. There are so many different aspects to the game -- building rooms, placing artifacts, communicating with others and taking advantage of the additional options they offer, making potions, sorting students in to classes, etc. -- that you can really change your play style and have a pretty different experience based on which aspects you focus on.I really hope the developers keep putting work into this and make the changes the community is suggesting, because it has a LOT of potential. If you're okay playing a fun game with some bugs, it's definitely worth buying into the early access still.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really want to like this game, but it gives you a taste of something good and then flops. I love the art style, the music, that fact that I can zoom in on rooms, the cute help book, the hilarious and adorable animals, the idea of the game. All fantastic. Just...the lack of information for us to use, and the frustrating randomness grates away at me. A few tweaks and this game would be fantastic IMO.My main issues are as follows;1. Not enough information. It feels weird, some information is very easy to get to, and other's not so much.What does the synergy between teacher and student do? Is it powerful enough I should care or is it just happy accident when it happens?Why are some traits blue, and others not?(I learned what this means through reading forms, that shouldn't be there. It should be in the tutorial or help.)How much do werewolves prevent misbehavior? How much more is "more" in negative or positive traits? I can't tell how much I need to care.Are bonuses multiplicative or additive? All of that is information that has to already be in the code, its not like its asking for extra systems to be implemented to tell me these things.EDIT: Why can't I poke around the information I do have when making a decision? Why I am I frozen looking at the cards/options.2. Why can't I fire people?If I roll poorly on the teacher select, I can't do anything about it. I can't fire the teacher and hire a new one, I can't destroy the room and replace it, I just have to suck it up. I would expect this to be expensive, but it should be an option. Especially if student/teacher synergy matters. Its frustrating because I can't make a school of "Law" or "Good" or "Chaos".EDIT: I've learned after more play that you can *technically* make a certain type of school, you just have to get very very lucky and shoot yourself in the foot.3. Why care about the characters?I have no reason to personally become invested in a character, and this game feels like one where you are supposed to care about the characters not a mass management sim. No real story, no personal buffs I can give, no customization(I honestly don't care about that but some do), just...nothing to make me care. If anything, the pure numbers of students and teachers make me want to *not* care. The pure randomness of the Xcom games makes me care more.4. Most buffs and debuffs somehow feel both lackluster and frustrating.A lot of the buff/debuffs I can't tell the difference between characters. I don't have the information to know. Cool, that ones insults are more brutal...how much? Others, I can see the difference, but I don't have the management tools to do anything about it and it feels like its purely better to have more students than refuse that student, and from what I have read that is mostly true.5. QuestsWhy does it take so long to get the quests on a map? That's brutal. You can start building your castle one direction, for some time as well, and then get completely botched by your quests. Sure, you have some minor control, but multiple times I've had quest options that where only terrible for my school due to previous RNG not giving me rooms that could due that type of training.6. Quality of lifeSomething that shows the chance of them misbehaving, or a bar like their needs that once full they act out. Something so I can tell how much that stuff matters. Filters should be organized by Character and then room, and within those two groups alphabetically. A filter to show unused item spots, or someplace that has a count of them.I think this may be harder to due, but something on a characters sheet that shows what they have been busy doing. Walking, learning, sleeping, eating, entertainment, ect.Some visual sign of the change of the season or pop up. All i've noticed is the word change next to the time manipulation.Save house/university emblems so you don't have to redo them every time.It would be nice to have more dungeon dives. They are a lot of fun but so rare, and I really like that mechanic. Perhaps nerf their loot output and make them happen more often?Why does ESC not close menus. I know right click does, but years of gaming has trained ESC to close out of menues, not right click.Destroy buildings. Missclicks happen. Would also be nice that if we did it within like...1 minute we got the card back.EDIT: When talking with a faction their current relations status needs to be visible somewhere.When selecting a card option during adventures something needs to pop up showing what each card reward in an option does. Same for some interactions in the normal area.Curriculum quests are frustrating in how often all 3 options are *not* what you specialized your school in. Smarter "randomness" to favor your school specialty more, more options for that selection in specific, or ability to choose magic type of specialization(nature, aracana, ect) and then choose from 3 would be amazing.When selecting a building you get to see its efficacy from all bonuses. Right now you don't see room bonuses from previous students you've trained when you click a building.When you mouse over a rooms efficacy a pop up that shows list of current buffs and debuff sources.FPS limiterSomething that indicated max height of your university.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend this game!The gameplay itself is complex enough to be interesting, but easy enough to pick-up. You start choosing a location to first host your university. Once selected, you will have a standard set of room you begin with and can purchase additional rooms to specialize your castle. These can be general rooms or from one of five magic specialties. There are also dozens of items, animals, and bonuses mixed in to further boost your university. This means you can go all sorts of directions with your castle each playthrough. Specialize in one or two magics or try all five.Then, after your students graduate, you have the (somewhat random) choice of what careers they enter into, depending on their knowledge level in the various magics. So sometimes not specializing means your students get less prestigious job opportunities.Further, the campaign mode is a really fun option where you play through several maps, with each maps earning your bonuses and curses depending on how well your students performed and meeting certain objectives. Ultimately, you hope you have built up enough momentum going into the final map to overcome the darklord.I have very few negative things to say. First, mistakes are somewhat costly. Choose the wrong rooms or location early on, and your entire campaign might be shot. So be willing to experiment early on with the best starting combinations. Also, because this is a relatively new release, the events and quests portion is a little under developed.That all being said, I would highly, highly recommend this game!!! This game has a ton of potential for new quests, more events and maps, new artifacts, and some scenarios if they wanted. I am excited to see where this one goes!

_childDocuments_.review: Spellcaster University fulfills this site’s brief of being both quirky and cute - a wonderful time with strategy and randomness, set in (as the title would imply) a magical university.The aim of the game is to build up your university with a variety of different classes and facilities, to enable your students to achieve the most prestigious careers after they graduate. These careers range from the basic Peasant, Village Mage, or dead, to the mid-range Librarian, Warlock, or Perfume Maker, to the truly prestigious Archimage, Spirit Seeker, or Psionic. The various careers come with different bonuses for the school, meaning that as you progress through the game it becomes easier to train your students into the better careers.To build your school, you must draw from different card decks and place the rooms, artifacts and animals down on the screen. There are five different magical decks corresponding to the different magical disciplines and a ‘general’ deck which provides things like dormitories, staff rooms, and new students. Each deck costs mana or money to draw from, growing more expensive each time, but the cards you draw will (theoretically) enable you to earn more of that mana or money.Various events will occur over the course of the game,  with your options for responding shaped by the amounts of mana you have, the cards you hold, or the rooms you’ve built. The main method for triggering these events is through the use of ‘goony pigs’ - flying guinea pigs used as messenger pigeons. They may also fly with the aid of a catapult… You can use these goony pigs to improve (or damage if you wish) your relationship with various factions, which will help or hinder your progress.The limiting factor in each game is the fact that the Lord of Evil is gathering his strength, and will attack the school. There is a progress bar at the top of the screen to let you know how close he is to this goal. In the campaign mode, you move from location to location, building new schools as his influence spreads, until you reach a point where you decide to make your final stand and either succeed in a variety of challenges to defeat the Lord of Evil permanently, lose to him, or take the mystery option from the final special character. You also gain various permanent buffs and debuffs depending on how well you do in each section, so by the final stage you’re generally creating absolutely ridiculously high-powered students.In case you couldn’t already tell, I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game. It moved into my favourites list almost immediately after installing. There’s enough storyline to be interesting, without being overly complicated. This is, after all, basically a deck-builder. The graphics are utterly adorable, and the music (at first at least) is happy and bubbly. Everything looks great both completely zoomed out - the way I normally play games - or ridiculously zoomed in. And it runs well - so far I’ve only experienced one crash, and the game auto-saves often enough that it wasn’t a problem.My major gripe is that the mechanics aren’t really explained. The basics of how to build the school? Sure. But how the different characteristics interact, how dungeoneering really works, how different races give different buffs, how sanity actually affects things… so much is trial-and-error, or looking up a how-to. A more in-depth tutorial would make a lot of this easier to understand. That doesn’t stop the fact that I still enjoy the hell out of this game and love it to bits.Top 5 Pros	- Comical but suitable graphics	- No faffing about with mystery, big bad is literally the Lord of Evil	- Flying guinea pigs!	- The story builds on itself	- Challenges are generally difficult but achievableTop 5 Cons	- Game mechanics aren’t fully explained	- The looping music can start to get irritating	- Relying on random special events to be able to go dungeoneering is irritating	- Once you’ve drawn a room card, it’s hard to see where it can be placed without dragging it out to try and place it	- Saying it twice but it’s a big gripe: needs more explanation for game mechanicsWould I recommend?	♥♥♥♥ you, Lord of Evil! _childDocuments_.review: I love this game. Been playing almost nonstop since I purchased it. I was looking for a game with a good amount of RNG without being impossible, and that's what I found with Spellcaster University. My only hang up is that there isn't more content, but considering the Stadium was recently added, I'm hopeful more will come with time!I can imagine it might be sluggish with replay value for others, but I've played a few campaigns now (with varying success) and still find it enjoyable. Again, with more content and events, this game would be even better! For the completionists, there's still quite a few Futures I haven't managed to get after my 50+ hours at the time of writing, and there's a handy little statistics option on the main menu to show what you've got! There's also some challenges that will unlock new items if you complete them.It gets a bit dull at some points because a lot of it involves keeping things well organized, but plenty of people love that sort of thing. It can also be a bit frustrating for things to not go the way you want, but that's to be expected with a game that has a bunch of RNG elements. For each bad run, there's an amazing run to contrast it, and you aren't exactly doomed to fail if you get unlucky. It will be hard, but it's possible!Very excited to keep an eye on this game for any updates. I would also love seeing workshop stuff, but I totally get if that's too much to ask for. I think this game could benefit a lot from workshop support, in the case of a dev maybe checking reviews and being on the fence (wink wink). Recommended to anyone who enjoys a mix of RNG and skill within a simulation style of game.

_childDocuments_.review: A management game where you run a school for wizards. The twist is that instead of buying specific rooms from a list like you would in other management/builder games, you buy a draw from a deck and pick from three options. There's one deck from gold, which you get from enrolling students, and then one deck for each type of mana (Light, Shadow, Nature, Arcane, and Alchemy) that generates as you students study that kind of magic. In addition to rooms, you can also pull room decorations, pets, equipment your students can wield that gives them buffs if they meet certain requirements and so on. In the campaign, each map gives you objectives to accomplish before a timer runs out representing an evil Sauron-like bad guy attacking your school. After a certain amount of maps, you reach the final level where your goal is to beat the evil overlord and win the game. It's fun, the RNG presents a challenge but I've never had it totally screw me, and it's a nice twist on your usual management game.

_childDocuments_.review: I held off on this game for the longest time. When I did eventually buy it though, I sunk hours into this thing. At the same time, it's all RNG based, which might frustrate you. Personally I kind of liked the extra challenge and how you're forced to alter strategy. I'd call it an easy to learn hard to master type of game, because you can still have a good time without delving into optimisation. That being said, it can get a little boring after a few play throughs, when you see the same events popping up over and over again. I do really wish they'd add a creative mode though, where cards could be freely selected and placed without RNG. _childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

_childDocuments_.review: Almost really good, but missed the point somewhere along the way.Basically, it has a lot of depth and is very interesting, maybe the first three levels as you try to figure out the game.  But the game's mechanics hold it back, once you realize how they workEach level of the campaign has three goals; nothing else you do matters except to achieve those goals.  They are generally in the form of, gain a lot of mana in X school and train people in Y school.  And so, the general winning strategy is to not build anything except the (up to) two types of classrooms required to beat your objectives.  If you do accidentally build others, you can restrict your people to not visit the other types, but for example if you need Assassins, you can't stop them from visiting other subclasses of Shadow.  You can't demolish things, so the only option is to not build.  There are minor events in the game that ask for various other types of mana, but you can largely ignore them. Worse is that, once you've met your three objectives, the game doesn't stop.  I've met them before it was even halfway through the timer to end the map, and I just had to sit there and interact every minute for new recruits, waiting for the level to endAlso, the teachers and students - they're almost interesting because they have unique traits.  They miss the point when you are encouraged to accept every student that applies, and when there are only 2 teachers to choose from each time you build a new building.  The student traits become meaningless because you're not filtering based on them, and the teacher traits are almost the opposite; you have no choice because one is always obviously better than the other in the important traits, and most have no important traits at all.  Each classroom is permanently linked to one of two professors it gives you to choose from when you build it, so it's also possible that a given classroom just, has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ professor - both options were bad, and there's nothing you can do about it.All in all it's very nearly, very good.  The intermingling mechanics between the magic types, and the interesting new ways each map can go depending on how you focus on magic and politics, all are interesting until you recognize that you are given win conditions that force you into a specific branch, and any choices you might have had are stripped away
_childDocuments_.name: Spellcaster University

Just make a solid foundation before trying to keep it relevant. This tells me the core gameplay and the bugs are not priority. I can't recommend this game in this state. _childDocuments_.review: I got this game through Humble Bundle's monthly subscription, so keep that in mind as I did not have to pay full price for this game. If I could sum up this game in a few words, it would be 'lost potential'. The initial presentation of the game seems so rich and ready to offer hours of fun gameplay, because on first blush the game looks like a Tycoon sim game ala Tavern Tycoon, Rollercoaster Tycoon, and so on, where you get to build your own magic school reminiscent of a certain YA book series everyone and their mother has heard of. But...then it's also a roguelike card game. For some reason. This leads to massive conflicts of identity and design between the two genres, and it really feels like the roguelike card game aspect was crammed in not because it would make a better game, but because the developers set out to make a roguelike card game and refused to budge from that position.The tycoon side dangles this potential to flex your creativity and management skills, with each student and teacher having a grab-bag of positive and negative traits, five different 'schools' of magic that the game actively encourages you to narrow down to a specialization, and a variety of different 'rooms' to build, including classrooms, dormitories, common rooms, and more. When you load up this game, you get excited to create your very own Wizard School. And then the roguelike card game aspect of the game slaps you over the back of the head with a steel chair. Did you want to make a school specializing in Potions and Elementalism? Tough ♥♥♥♥, your specialization choices are all Nature and Shadow magic-school based with one random Enchantment option thrown in. And then the game won't give you any enchantment-related cards until the level is over halfway done, which means you can't complete the specialization objective, which means your campaign is crippled at the knees. The roguelike aspect also completely negates any and all reason to be picky about your teachers, students, or House specializations. Each student has a notation marking their intelligence level, their wealth, negative and positive personality traits, and absolutely none of it matters. Because the game has to account for RNG, the negative effects of teachers and students are completely negligible and I completely blasted through the games default difficulty without even looking at them beyond flavor reasons, just accepting every student the game threw at me. So with the roguelike RNG completely roadblocking your ability to actually create a cool wizard school in your own image, is the game at least fun when you play it -like- a roguelike? No. No it isn't. Because if you play it like a roguelike and not a Tycoon game, the game is extremely boring and extremely easy. Your school inevitably becomes a haphazard mess of rooms and classes filled with random ♥♥♥♥, there's no logic or cohesion to your school because not only are the rooms you have access to -entirely- random, there is ZERO way to move, demolish, or replace a room after it's been put down. So not only can I go 90% of the game without getting a SINGLE greenhouse building, even if my selected specialty at the start of the level involves Herbalism, when I finally do get it, I might have no place to put it because my franken-school is too cluttered and there's no place to put my Greenhouse where any of the characters will have access to it. In short, the roguelike-card-game aspect of the game design completely torpedos any potential this game had to actually be fun, interesting, or engaging. The RNG not only stifles your creativity and vision (which is the entire purpose of a Tycoon game), the way the game has to be balanced around the RNG means that at the "normal" game settings, the game is far too easy and extremely boring. I played through one campaign, and while I might try out the endless mode a little to see if that makes the RNG of the game more tolerable, I definitely won't be touching the campaign mode again.So at the end of the day, I can't in good conscience recommend the game at full price, and honestly even at 50% off I'd be extremely hesitant to recommend it. If the price is below $10 I'd say it's worth trying out if the idea of building your own magic school appeals greatly to you, but if you're looking for a good fantasy Tycoon style game, you won't find it here sadly. And if you're looking for a good fantasy roguelike with wizards involved, you won't find that here either and you probably already own Wizards of Legend anyways, which is a much better fantasy roguelike with wizards involved. It even has cards!

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing, adorable, and hilarious game that makes magic fun. My spouse nearly broke down crying at how adorable the dragons are. There are plenty of squees with just about every pet when it gets placed. The game will start slow and build up to a rapid pace by the end of each level pretty consistently so don't be shocked if in the beginning you feel like there isn't much to do.Play the campaign instead of just a quick run, it is far more entertaining. There isn't much of a story (that I have seen so far) but the campaign makes each university impactful and lasting on the future universities so it is much more interesting this way.I wish there were more dungeons in the game, both in type of dungeon and in frequency of dungeon, but wanting more of the game is honestly a good thing. _childDocuments_.review: A great game, I can't stop playing and it's not even finished yet.I feel this game has been well thought out in its design especially from a base building perspective and It has a great handle on simulation, saying this, it is still lacking on campaign a little and sandbox especially. I believe we need to the ability to attack and send mages on assignments in the world map as this would give more incentive to produce mages suited to certain tasks. I feel we also need to be more rewarded in sandbox and campaign for our design of school such as, magic focus, happiness and efficiency rather than just meeting goals that don't seem to mean anything before the school is destroyed. Currently the incentive to play is solely driven by the dark lord end game timer and achieving goals doesn't seem to matter. When goals and base quality are achieved in campaign we need access to good buffs and base additions, on sandbox we need unique room upgrades and events e.g monsters, unique event chains.When I comes to sandbox the flaw of "little to do once the base is built" show and I don't think the standard end game timer give the same sense of urgency that it did in campaign. The need for more map interactivity and political issues needs to happen here and the sandbox needs to feel interesting even without an end game timer. I think it's also essential we have a way to redesign the base in sandbox or at least change room upgrade positions.I believe this game could also benefit from a few more room upgrades and some more chaotic melt downs for good measure. Even though I believe this game has some ways to go, the fact I have enjoyed it so much already means Iv'e got my money from it. Its cheeky design makes it addictive and fun to play even without a fully fleshed out game.

_childDocuments_.review: It was fun for like an hour, with the expectation that eventually you will have a lot of control for your university. It feels the devs half-made the most basic aspects of the game, and then started expanding before finishing the simplest things.
