_childDocuments_.review: Funnish, quirky game. I haven't read any other reviews, but I imagine lots of people would compare it to Stardew Valley. It's quite a bit lower on content comparatively, though good for a bit of time out doing something different. I spent over thirty hours and a lot of that was mucking around, but I also got all the single-player achievements, so that's about the extent of it if you're interested. I imagine it could be good with friends, though more so if you're all playing it for the first time and figuring it out together.Some criticisms/suggestions: There's a number of tasks you can do for task masters in the game. But you can proceed and probably finish the game without ever having to talk to 4/5 of them, if I'm thinking about it right. They provide some perks (I went for all the movement speed ones, which seem to be the most helpful), though by the time you get them (and the endgame tools or weapons) you don't really need them. It would be good to see the task masters integrated with the main flow of the game so you're more dependent on their rewards. On integration, taming animals and catching insects doesn't really enhance the overall gameplay. If certain insects and tame-only animal products were required for exclusive items or builds, that could make it more interesting. The buildset is also quite limited (at least compared to other similar games), and there's definitely room for expansion here (even aesthetic, e.g. blueprints for the different-coloured fires in the labyrinths). On the other hand, I really like the number of trinkets available and the artwork in that area. I think I found exclusively two Japanese items on 4th island too, so again always room for expansion. Technical things: I found it annoying having no quick-stack-to-nearby-chests, and when your collection grew it's hard to find particular items. It would be good to be able to put placeholders in chests so that when you run out of an item a monkey puts new ones in the same place, etc., and to be able to name chests. The monkey interface is very fun (I loved the twist in the final cutscene), but it can be awkward sometimes, such as having to reteach a monkey something rather than simply being able to reassign it to a task it's already learnt, etc. Also various bugs, though I didn't make specific notes, e.g. the Beast Master and taming rabbits on another island, monkeys sometimes not following you through teleporters (not first use of teleporters, randomly on subsequent times), monkeys you had following you ending up on islands you hadn't been to yet.In conclusion, a fun exploration game if you're after something small. The base game shows promise though, and it'd be cool to see if it goes anywhere further in future. Not really replayable yet in my opinion, even in multiplayer, unless maybe the majority of people playing haven't played before.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not too bad but I wouldn't recommend it.Overall, this game is a bit short for a survival/crafting game. It is also quite simplistic and completely devoid of challenge. This is particularly problematic because I feel this lack of challenge is perhaps what drags down the crafting and questing part of this game the most. Every item or building seems to be lacking both in usefulness and in novelty. Since I never truly wished for any item, the steps required to get them seemed more like a chore than it should have. Or, perhaps, it might be more accurate to say that both the rewards and the process needed to get to those rewards are somewhat boring.Apart from that, here are some of the main clear flaws of this game:-the UI is poor overall. You'll spend eons looking through all your chests to get that one item that you wanted. The way to give orders to your monkeys is unnecessarily convoluted and takes more time than it should.-in multiplayer, for some unknown reasons, the developers decided to make it so that only a single player may profit from any kind of progress. If a player builds something, only he will unlock further recipes. If you get some unique item, only a single player will be able to use it, and it will bind itself to that player, forcing the other two to start again from the beginning with another host if they want to get it. Anything unlocked by questing will only be unlocked for the host.-another strange multiplayer decision by the developers: beds can only be used collectively. A single player can't benefit from his bed's buff alone, and the host can't save whenever he wants.Once again, not terrible, but not good enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Not Worth the FrustrationI had high hopes for "The Survivalists," but unfortunately, it falls short in several areas.Firstly, the multiplayer mode is almost unplayable due to severe lag. It's incredibly frustrating to try and enjoy the game with friends when everything is delayed and stuttering. The UI also needs significant improvement. It's clunky and not intuitive, which adds unnecessary difficulty to managing inventory and crafting. While the exploration aspect is cool, it feels empty and the game progression is very confusing. There's no clear direction, leaving you wandering aimlessly much of the time.The monkey automation feature, which should have been a highlight, is poorly executed. It's so bad that it becomes more of an annoyance than a helpful mechanic. The monkeys often fail to perform tasks correctly, making the automation system feel like a chore. Gathering materials isn’t too difficult, but crafting is another story. It requires an excessive amount of tedious work that takes the fun out of the game. What should be a rewarding experience feels like a grind. Lastly, the controls were decent at the start but became awkward and difficult to manage as I progressed. This inconsistency made gameplay increasingly frustrating.Overall, "The Survivalists" has potential, but these issues make it hard to recommend. Until these problems are addressed, I'd suggest looking elsewhere for a better survival game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. It helps immerse yourself if you don't google everything for what you need. If you like crafting, adventure, dungeoning, fighting, building, and farming, this is a game for that. I really like that there are different types of moster for each island. The monkey helper is really great and well designed for automatization. The materials can be reused as other more important materials using the one of the crafting benches which really saves time farming them in mid to end game. I like the online gameplay as well only using gestures to communicate. But I have a few feedback for the devs below.I just think it's not too big of an area to explore (half of the total area of the map is covered in water with nothing to interact, even the sharks/big turtle only shows near the shores). Maybe if you guys make the enemies in the ocean more like octopus, poseidon,etc. Also there are no fishes in the open ocean?? At least make that so we can fish more. (also more types of fish please) I don't get the water and green antidote functions as a repellant of heat/bugs if there's no drawback when you don't use it in the lava ash/deep forest areas. The additional status effect for the enemies is good but the enemies need to use this status effect more (burn, poison, explosive, life steal) because it doesn't show as much even though there are enemies that give burn damage but doesn’t show much. The enemy raid event could be better if they also attack the players base instead of only the player so that the player can utilize the building part of the game to defend. If only attacking the player, we can just take a boat and wait in the middle of the sea until the raid is over. I didn’t have a need to build walls, traps, nor attacking plants to defend my main base (which has all the main crafting station).The beach bottle quests are really uninteresting. Most of the rewards are the lowest level of the equipments except the multitool. Maybe add higher level tools/even equipments for the rewards like 20 gold plate or a special equipment only given from the bottle quest or something better so it’s not boring.I guess just extend the lore on how/why the monkeys wanted to help us and maybe a boss monkey to fight against?? Just a thought.An input for the player death by enemy fights, one of the monkeys that was with us gets kidnapped and put in the underground dungeon area. Or maybe the player shows up in the dungeon and must escape without weapons to survive.I guess that’s all my rant. I like these types of games because it’s at times peaceful. They don’t need high end pc to run either. All in all, a good game, but maybe need more polishes here and there.Cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently on the 4th and 5th island. For some reason they are joined together in my game so I had trouble distinguishing which is which.This game is really fun so far, but really the enjoyability sometimes comes down to RNG about the layout of the island.Likes:1. The fact that you don't have to sleep everyday. If you do, it heals you and allows you to save. But you can also save anywhere on the map.2. The fact that you don't have to eat all the time. The balance is just right. You definitely need to eat every 2 game days or so, but that is like half hour of playtime. Most of the time, I wind up eating because I need to heal not because I am hungry.3. There is enough food available. Unless you started off in a bad RNG and get enclosed with rocks all over the place.4. Crafting is easy enough to understand.Dislikes:1. Inventory management is a bit of a pain. I suspect it gets better after the 1st chest update.I want a rename or recolor chest option.2. The terrain is bad, either it is too empty or there is way too much stuff clustered in an area and you cannot move properly. 3. Monkeys. I don't like training or naming them or coloring them. The interface sucks. Please just implement a right click function so that we can just assign the monkeys to : fighting, cooking, crafting, chest carrying, emote, dismiss or follow. I keep accidentally giving them the wrong item and they wind up not able to do what they need to do. How about a lock function to prevent accidentally passing them items?  Why do the monkeys back away when you are trying to swap tools with them. HIGHLY ANNOYING!I would also have much preferred human than monkey companions, just saying.4. I want more hair and clothing options. There isn't enough. And the character customisation should have a colour wheel instead of randomly scrolling the bar to get the colour you want. Who tested this UI and passed it? It sucks.5. I want the character to stop complaining about crafting stuff. They are shipwrecked and need to suffer. _childDocuments_.review: I would really like to recommend this game, but in its current state i can't. So many parts of the game are a glitchy mess with no clear instructions on how to progress.The monkey taming, teaching, and working, was such a amazing idea for this game, however, it was horribly designed. Monkeys must be taught each time you need to change their job instead of teaching them once and allowing the player to easily switch between jobs with a spin wheel, or something of that sort. Monkeys also do not often work perfectly, and stand completely still doing nothing.The puzzles in temples were fairly simple, perhaps too simple. Most puzzles were very simple if you ever completed one before, but on your first one, it would be a struggle to even get past the first room. For example, the simplest of puzzles must be that you do a certain emote on a pressure plate. However, in many temples a lack of indication of which emote to do,  or even if you must emote, was present. This, made temples feel very clunky and unsatisfying, as if you finally figured out you had to emote it was just like a punch in the gut and a thought that said "That was stupid', and if you already knew how to do it beforehand, the items you obtain weren't very helpful anyway.Moving back to the monkeys from before, their confusing priority system and seeming lack of a brain made it difficult to automate things, something i was looking forward to. Mining and crafting everything you need for a okay looking base would take much too long, and since the monkeys were so dumb, mining everything on your own would be the only option. Honestly, these monkeys probably dropped out of school in kindergarden, I do not understand how their AI could be this stupid.The multiplayer in this game was the one, last thing that i thought could save this game. However, as many other things in this game, it was poorly executed and clunky. It took about 30 minutes to even set up a game, and upon starting the game, my friend was immediately softlocked for about 20 minutes. After that we got a monkey, and the game promptly crashed. Several times. I can't even review the multiplayer gameplay because multiplayer was simply too buggy. In conclusion, this game was a low effort, poorly executed, boring, drag on game that would have been a wonderful game with a great future if it had even a shred of love put into it. Right now, I can't recommend this game. Hopefully, sometime in the future the 4 IQ AI will be reworked, bugs will be patched and i can take down the hard work and significant brain usage i used to make this review. Anyway, that's my game rant for today. Cya'll

_childDocuments_.review: I was extremely disappointed by this game. Survival crafting/base building is my genre and I have/played 1000's of hours of games in that category. I picked this up on sale thinking the art looked very charming and the game had a good premise. The idea of being able to automate things so you don't have to do tedious tasks is a good one! However, the process of setting up those automations is finnicky, frustrating, and downright annoying. Sometimes I craft things by hand (which takes much longer) just to avoid trying to select a monkey, give them the appropriate tool, and demonstrate what I want done. You have to do this every time you want to make a change in your production lines. Did you select the right monkeys? Who knows! they all stand on top of each other and move whenever you take a step. Let me give you an example of a typical process of setting up a temporary base on a new island in early/mid game: Go to a new island with your handful of monkeys, bring ALL your tools because if you need a tool, the process to create a basic crafting bench takes 5 whole minutes, 3 ingredients, and 4 inventory slots to complete. You have very few inventory slots and will spend roughly 1/3 of this game tossing stuff out of your inventory and nearly 1/2 of the game managing chests. Then to make a basic tool takes 4 more ingredients (2 of which require 2 steps). If you want to avoid the long crafting time, you can reassign your monkeys to do it, but that will take another minute, at which point you'd rather just sit there and craft it yourself. In summary, making a crafting bench and a single tool takes roughly ten minutes, several different ingredients, throwing stuff out of my inventory to make room for all of them, and a bunch of micromanaging my monkeys which are supposed to make my life EASIER. I want to explore the world, which I think is one of the strengths of this game, but the exploration is an agonizing process of overpreparing, micromanaging inventory and monkeys, squeezing things into chests, and mostly being a pain in the ass. 23 hours in, I realized this game wasn't even fun, and the rewards I get for progressing in the game leads to more of the same annoying, frustrating, tedious gameplay. Things that would improve the game, in my opinion: A complete re-work of the monkeys. They are there to make your life easier, not more frustrating. For example, only having to "teach" a monkey once, and then being able to assign them freely to tasks without having to do the whole process again. Dedicated tools or a small inventory for monkeys so I don't have to carry multiple tools for every monkey anytime I leave my base.Better organization tools for chests, such as filters. MORE. INVENTORY. SPACE. (or fewer intermediary items needed to craft something simple) Why can't a crafting bench require only wood, for example? It would greatly improve QOL. Balancing can be addressed elsewhere. Cute game with a great premise but the gameplay is about as fun as yanking my fingernails out.

_childDocuments_.review: The Survivalists is a delightful game that captivates with its satisfying crafting mechanics. The process of gathering resources, building structures, and crafting items is immensely rewarding, making every moment spent in the game engaging and enjoyable.One of the highlights of The Survivalists is the automation system. While there are some rough edges regarding how much can be automated, the game’s length is balanced in such a way that these limitations never become burdensome. The challenge of optimizing your crafting and resource management adds a layer of strategic depth that keeps the gameplay fresh and exciting.However, it's important to note some technical issues. In my experience, I encountered corrupted saves and crashes, which seemed to be specific to my PC due to some compatibility issues. Fortunately, the majority of other players have not reported these problems, so it appears to be an isolated case.Despite these setbacks, the charm and creativity of The Survivalists shine through. The game’s vibrant world and quirky characters add to its appeal, creating an immersive and enjoyable experience. The cooperative multiplayer mode is another standout feature, allowing you to team up with friends to survive and thrive on the island together.In summary, The Survivalists is a fun and engaging game with satisfying crafting mechanics and an enjoyable multiplayer component. While some technical issues may arise, they don't overshadow the overall positive experience. If you’re looking for a game that combines crafting, exploration, and survival, The Survivalists is definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games! For a long time, I wasn’t interested in trying it because of the concept. Unlike other crafting games where you have to gather resources yourself, build things, and cook... here, that tedious part is removed. You can capture monkeys and train each one to specialize in a specific area—mining, building, gathering, even combat! Plus, there's a pretty interesting element with the labyrinths you need to explore.The game is still in the survival-crafting genre, and that remains the core concept. But with the new and interesting mechanics they introduce, the gameplay becomes significantly more enjoyable.(No need to mention the beautiful design; you can just watch the trailer and see for yourself.)

Hunt (or be hunted by!) animals for food and an array of mythical enemies, who aren’t necessarily pleased to see you. Get quests from a Mysterious Stranger or find them washed up on the shore. Prepare to trek into a procedurally generated wilderness, with a variety of biomes, for an adventure that’s unique to every player. Build Together, Survive Together. Finding the perils of island life too much or just looking to share your building expertise with friends? The Survivalists has you covered! Complete joint adventures, gain loot, trade and ultimately survive together and as you and up to three fellow castaways explore an island paradise.

 

Monkey See, Monkey Do! 

If you’re in need of a builder, a lumberjack or even a soldier, the monkeys on the island can be tamed and trained to help you with everyday tasks or back you up on raids to a fanatic camp! The Mimic System means a wide variety of functions can be performed by your banana loving friends, with monkey management becoming key to surviving the island’s challenges.

About the Game 30 years on, the battle for our world's future continues. Super Robot Wars is a tactical RPG that brings characters and robots from a variety of mecha anime together to battle their mutual foes. Players follow characters through adventure and battle. Take control of giant robots on a battle map, commanding them to defeat their enemies. The battle switches between ally and enemy phases. Once the player has moved and attacked with their robots, the enemy takes their turn. When all enemies have been defeated, the game proceeds to an Intermission. During Intermission, the player can use resources earned in battle to train pilots, upgrade robots, and earn bonuses for their army. They then can proceed to the next chapter of the adventure. In Super Robot Wars, players can enjoy a unique experience that combines all-star mecha series crossovers, action-packed attack animations, and the chance to upgrade your favorite machines and pilots. _childDocuments_.review: There's lots of "buy to support" reviews here, so I'll try to take a different route and speak to the completely unaware audience who probably lean towards the younger spectrum of gamers.For the uninitiated, SRW30 is the latest in a line of just under 50 (mostly) SRPG titles (including spin-offs) in a series that started in the early 90s.  It gained notoriety especially as videos of earlier entries were made available on YouTube, showcasing incredible pixel animations of fan-favorite mecha duking it out.  It is the ultimate mech/robot fan's dream, answering burning nerd questions like "How awesome would it be if Gundam and Getter teamed up?"  Thing is, up until recently, the series has been locked to Japan, so if you wanted to play it, you had to know the language and import the games because Bandai (or Banpresto, back in the day) weren't going to mess with the weird licensing issues West of the border.Over the last decade, however, interest in the series has grown as the Asia region started getting English-translated (hit or miss) releases for the PS4 and Switch, making it far easier for Westerners to get their grubby hands on the games and enjoy them.  This includes a few releases in the SD Gundam series, of which Cross Rays has been officially released on Steam, as well!  So SRW30 is quite notable for being an officially-released SRW game for Western audiences and thus, lots of fans aren't waiting for a discount to show Bandai that there is indeed a market for the games here, with all the licensing headaches that may be involved.  The only other title that made it here was part of the OG sub-series which features only original content and no licensed stuff (which doesn't mean they suck, btw, so worth tracking down if you care).So what the heck is it?  Essentially, it's a high-spectacle, low-challenge grid-based SRPG that typically blends elements of established anime robots and mobile suits with a few of Bandai's original creations.  Mostly this involves slotting new characters (weakly) into the plot of your favorite anime series or some you may have never even heard of.  Thing is, most of this stuff comes from the 70s to the 90s and perhaps if you're of a younger age, you might not have any interest in what you're seeing beyond the really slick battle animations.  Fear not, however, as there is extensive character and robot/suit info contained in an easily-accessed encyclopedia that will key you into where these things are coming from so you never really need to feel lost.What it all really boils down to is that you're getting a fairly-simple grid-based strategy game that doesn't really demand too much thought.  The battle animations are the big showpiece here as they are slick and full of cool effects and high energy, but they start to wear thin after the 5th time you've watched the same attack and they're mostly just masking that there isn't a whole lot going on except lining up your units to take shots.  Sure, there's some resource management stuff going on (manage your energy/ammo), some maps will require at least a decent approach to strategy, and there's a whole bunch of upgrades and special actions that round out the game, but it's pretty straight-forward and won't be much of a challenge unless you pump up the difficulty to the highest setting.It's not going to be everyone's cuppa, but take a look at the roster of licenses and if you have any interest in seeing them in action, go ahead and get SRW30, but don't pick it up just because you want to see more in the West.  Us crazy-ass fans have (hopefully) got that handled.  Take a look at the other stuff that's available in English (X, V, T, a couple of OGs) and see if those rosters tickle your fancy more.  You get the most out of these games if you are familiar with the licenses that show up and importing the one you'd like most might be worth it.  Find the right place to jump in and then come back to 30 if you so desire.

_childDocuments_.review: + Awesome attack animations.+ Interesting and funny crossover interactions.+ Customize and upgrade your favorite units to make them super powerful.+ Choice of main character and two different endings add replayability.+ A great time for fans of the featured series and people who want to find something new to watch.+ Autoplay function for ease of multitasking.+ Runs on a toaster.+ Excellent translation.- Gameplay can be too easy and simplistic for hardcore tactics players.- All the customization options can be a bit overwhelming to new players.- The game is long and completionists might burn out before finishing.- Very pricy especially with all the DLC.One of the reasons the Super Robot Wars series has managed to last for 30 years across more than 60 installments is how engaging the stories are. Without fail I can say that every single one of them has made me a fan of at least one series I knew nothing about beforehand. It's a really good gateway into mecha anime. The plots themselves aren't anything super special, but the writing is consistently charming and the interactions between the various anime series are very interesting. Your choice of main character, the order in which you do the various missions and the plot routes you choose to follow change the events of the game in various ways, making second and even third playthroughs stay fresh.The gameplay of Super Robot Wars looks complex at first. It throws a lot of stuff at the player right from the beginning: What are spirits? What does MxP do? What should I upgrade? I have good news and bad news here. The good news is that the game is pretty easy so you can get away with doing almost any strategy and your mistakes won't be punished too bad. Want to build your whole team for maximum offense and zero defense? Sure, sure why not. Maximum evasion to make everyone unhittable? Yeah, you'll be fine. Invest everything into the crappiest units around to do a challenge run? Sounds good to me, fam. The bad news and downside of this is that the game isn't challenging to tactics rpg veterans unless they're doing some kind of challenge run. But that's the beauty of Super Robot Wars, it allows a variety of playstyles.I don't even know what to say here. Just... Just look at the trailer. And those aren't even the best ones, which they always reserve as a surprise outside of previews. Super Robot Wars has some of the finest sprite animation in gaming. The bigger robots are weighty, the smaller robots are zippy, all of them are awesome. The visual novel scenes are mostly portraits with dialogue as is the norm for the genre but the variety in expressions and the occassional cutscenes keep things from getting stale.The music is full of both original epic jams and catchy game renditions of anime songs. The word "epic" is overused, but it's the best descriptor I can think of for when the hot-blooded music starts playing against a supervillain. The best part though is the voice acting, because you can tell the voice actors are having a LOT of fun in the studio. Try switching the pilots of various units around and see what funny things they have to say! Most of the important boss fights have really good battle lines against many of the characters that you probably won't see coming as well. Finally, try using the save & quit function during a stage sometime. The skits you get when you do that can be pretty funny.Super Robot Wars games are long, and 30 is the longest one yet. While 30 lets you choose which missions to go on and lets you skip big chunks of the game, it's still a 60+ hour affair to beat even once. Completionist runs are looking at 100+ hours of playtime and that's without doing NG+ to see all the stuff you've missed. Point is, these games are very meaty and have a lot of content to go through. HOWEVER, this one has an autoplay function to let the AI beat the enemies for you while you do something else, which helps you multitask if you don't want to dedicate entire afternoons to one videogame. Super Robot Wars 30 is a fun romp with giant robots that is especially good for fans of mecha anime.

_childDocuments_.review: SRW30 is extremely repetitive and strategically shallow.  If your main draw to this game isn't checking out all of the attack animations and seeing characters from a bunch of mecha animes interact with each other, than this game isn't for you.  Luckily, that's exactly why I bought it.7.5/10My biggest gripes are that the enemy designs and animations leave much to be desired, some of the ally attack animations seem half-baked (although there are enough cool ones to make up for this), and the writing is pretty terrible. It could just be translation issues, but i doubt it. I think the main issue with the writing is that there's just way too much of it. Almost every interaction seems to last way longer than it should.  It reminds me of how One Piece episodes can be 20 mins long but only have 5 mins of content; same vibe.All in all, its a good game for a very specific audience, but with a few shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: How do I even begin?...Okay, look. If you like a single component of this game, giant robots, tactical rpgs, or just one of the series that are involved... you're frankly doing yourself a disservice by not playing it. You may not know it, but there's been like fifty of these things but none of them made it here because every single one is the most ambitious crossover of mecha anime and that means a licensing nightmare here in the west. And the shame of it all is, almost universally, they're pretty much all exemplars of the genre, with excellent storytelling interweaving a massive number of different mecha anime series into a single coherent plot. Fire Emblem  it was as fine a game as Super Robot Wars. Avengers looks upon the sheer number of series crossing over from different series, different  even, all woven together like a beautiful tapestry, and despairs. I've seen depressing series uplifted by characters from upbeat series, I've seen characters who should have died be saved thanks to the whole team coming together to save them. I still don't know how they managed to bring this game west, but you owe it to yourself to buy it, and play it. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game singlehandedly convinced me to watch all kinds of mecha shows because of their existence within it. It's got everything from the weird combo of gritty pseudo-realism and utterly surreal existential BS that always manage to merge in later parts of Gundam, to the over the top explosiveness of Getter and Gridman, and yet somehow still manages to fit a pretty happy story where the power of friendship beats all in J-Decker. Also, there's a quartet of old Mexican guys in a super robot that they saved the world with as kids, and they are quite possibly one of my favorite parts of the entire mecha genre at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Super Robot Wars 30 is a mecha game in a long running series that is ACTUALLY the most ambitious crossover ever created. This game has given me the most amount of anime recommendation of series I have never heard of than any friend has ever given me. But also it has also made me enjoy the Mecha genre more than I already have as the only series from this genre that I cared about or seen were Gundam, SSSS., and a few others but they are not in this game. Some I never knew about were series like L-Gaim; Majestic Prince; and Brave Police J-Decker for examples.SRW 30 for short is a very long game for a singular playthrough. Within a single playthrough you will quite possibly have done about 80 to 100+ missions. I am 118 hours in and I have not finished my playthrough yet, others have finished their playthroughs close to the 100s, but I have not.  But that's a good thing, because you can take it at your own pace and you will be fine. So, here are some things to take note of. You will have 50+ units to choose from, but you will only be able to use a limited amount of them on each map, so the game recommends you to use the characters you like or have an attachment to and that it is okay to do so, because that is the point of this game and that's nice. So pick the ones you like and enjoy the game as this game has very beautiful animations, which really took me by surprise for this type of game. One major thing to take note and I mean major because this is great. You can add in your own BGMs to the game. So you can add in Gallant Char from Mobile Suit Gundam on Char as whenever he fights or an important moment happens, his theme plays. You can pop in COLORS by Flow; Stand Up To The Victory from Victory Gundam; Sorairo Days; HEATS; or even Yusyaou Tanjo as it is sung by Masaaki Endoh. (If you haven't heard him sing, listen to CLEAR MIND or the first OPM op.)Another little tidbit which I really enjoy is that if you go back to the title screen you will get an intermission and they are very enjoyable to watch as they give you tidbits about the game or even tidbits about their own series that they are from. Which brings me to this, as you play the game the story from their series will play in the game, but it will mainly be the MAJOR plot points and they will be edited in a way that doesn't spoil their series too much. It still spoils stuff but you don't have the context and build up to it along with certain characters being around for the MCs/side characters to be around and save or motivate them when they really needed it. Or seeing like Zanscare working with the Sleeves. I do recommend this game as it is a great game and I can see why this series has lasted 30 years. You can see the love and effort put into the franchise to the point that you might revive your love of the genre or even introduce to the genre. So, take your time with this game, have fun, and use who you want to use because there are no wrong answers, but there are hidden characters that are locked behind certain characters. If you are interested there are guides online from a very dedicated website.

_childDocuments_.review: Super Robot Wars 30 is one of the most infectiously fun games I’ve played - every new mech, weapon, and character makes me grin from ear to ear. The animations are so fun that I always join in with the characters - going  with Itsumi when Gridman does Gridman Beam, or  when Masaki does Akashic Buster.The game knows where its bread is buttered and knocks the most important thing out of the park - the attack animations you’ll see thousands and thousands of times. You pick the mechs you know best and are most fun to watch, and you overkill enemies with your superweapons, because there’s a reason this series became well known in the West through Youtube compilations of attack animations.Speaking of which, it’s a miracle that this game came to the West at all. Super Robot Wars is huge in Japan and beloved by SRPG and mech enthusiasts, but due to nightmarish licensing, the only official Western releases were the Original Generations games on GBA. Even the PS2 remakes weren’t released here. That Super Robot Wars gets a chance to shine on Steam feels impossible, and the hope of getting more in English is arguably worth picking it up for alone.Unfortunately, it’s also a  hard sell at the base price of $60, much less the laughable price of $130 for the game and every major DLC. No matter how fun the animations are and how fun it is to see series I recognize like SSSS.Gridman, the game is so poorly designed and mediocre that it just isn’t any fun to actually  it.The primary problem is the difficulty, or lack thereof. The difficulty is done in the laziest way possible, as all but one of the higher difficulties increase enemy stats without changing anything else. But, comically, the highest base game difficulty is so badly designed that it makes the game  - Super Expert increases enemy levels by 20 universally without adjusting your EXP, which mean you struggle at first, but soon your units level extremely fast and you snowball past your opponents. The only issue is early and new units, since your unupgraded units are severely outgunned, which is frustrating even on regular Expert.That wouldn’t be as much of a problem if everything given to the player wasn’t so busted, so that the level scaling mattered. Unfortunately, there’s a lot of strange choices. Every type of upgrade you have (AOS, unit upgrades, skill upgrades) uses different resources and is just a raw boost, so there’s never an opportunity cost. The most ridiculous is the AOS system, which just gives you cheap, exponential benefits. For instance, you can spend resources in AOS to increase how many AOS resources you gain each mission, so it pays for itself and then every other upgrade instantly. The stacking AOS benefits make you and your units so strong they feel like cheats.Even more strangely, there is a paid DLC including Super Expert Plus (yes, a DLC difficulty) that redesigns the game and seems like a response to these criticisms. Among other changes, experience gain is significantly lower and upgrades are significantly more expensive. It’s a bandaid, but it’s a great idea for people who want a challenge.  that it is intentionally designed to be feasible only if you’re on NG+, and it inherits all the problems of base Super Expert, so unit introduction missions where you fight massive hordes of level 21+ units with your unupgraded level 1 unit are completely unfair.There’s very little reason why the rule changes in Super Expert Plus couldn’t have been a separate mode, or even just the option for an Expert Plus difficulty that has the rule changes but is more reasonable. Instead, Super Expert Plus goes the complete opposite direction and is far too difficult unless you’re playing New Game Plus... meaning somewhere around 100 hours of play-in-your-sleep gameplay later. Why bother?People will argue the game is a power fantasy, but even the most overt power fantasies exist to feel like you’ve overcome something. Doom with God Mode turned on might still be a power fantasy, but it’s a boring one when you can’t ever lose.You will never die in Super Robot Wars 30, even on Expert. There are so many upgrades, all of your units start off ridiculous and only get better, and even light upgrades make already busted units invincible. The “evasion” stat is the worst, since it completely nullifies damage, so units with massive evasion stats ARE using God Mode. Combine this with equipment that makes it so that enemy units with a low chance to hit  miss, and it’s GG.The lazy design decisions extend to the rest of the game too. Terrain is entirely vestigial from previous Super Robot Wars titles. The maps are almost entirely flat, unmodelled squares with no relevant terrain variety. There are almost no enemies that have to be fought in the air. And yet, I have never noticed a unit with less than a B in any terrain stat, and weapons have nonsense stats that contradict the game’s own dialogue.For instance, Gridman has an entire mission about struggling against Air units, but the Sky Gridman it introduces - the weapon that literally has “Sky” in it - has an A in Air, not S. All of Gridman’s other attacks, including his Melee attacks, have an A in Air, meaning he’s just as effective fighting with a sword. And, in those animations, he just floats, since they couldn’t bother to make it so that Gridman can’t fight Air enemies without Sky Gridman, or to adjust the sprites so that he’s standing on the ground afterwards. It’s goofy and cheap.OK, fine, but you’re not here for gameplay. It’s Super Robot Wars, you’re here for crossovers and characters. Well, those elements of the game are... questionable. At the game’s best, the characters and dialogue are a lot of fun, and a hugely appreciated amount of effort has gone into taking the game’s non-linearity into account and integrating DLC characters into the dialogue and story. If you know the series, like I do with Gridman, you’ll be over the moon at seeing them represented so well, and if you don’t know the series at all, like me with Gundam: IBO, you might enjoy what you see so much you check it out.At the game’s worst, the dialogue is excruciating, while the presentation is so cheap it’s astonishing that it is in a $60 game. Sometimes, this is because of horrible characters, like those from Knight’s and Magic, a stereotypical, embarrassing isekai series. But most of the time, the localization is at fault. The localization for SRW30 is by a team including members of Carpe Fulgur, most famous for Recettear, and it  Characters are snarky and use slang-y, How Do You Do Fellow Kids tier dialogue regardless of their personalities or series. If you’re someone who hates “Whedon dialogue,” you’re going to find it very hard to sit through.And, oh boy, will you be sitting through it - the presentation is embarrassing by the standards of RPG Maker 2000. My breaking point was the first Code Geass mission. The opening cutscene goes on for an . During this sequence, characters are represented with nothing but a few static sprites. There are no animated sequences or scripted fights. There is no voice acting. Characters get into fights with each other or shoot each other, which is represented with just sound effects, so characters have to explain what just happened since there’s no visuals to indicate it. Calling it a VN is doing VNs a disservice - visual novels released for free on itch.io have better presentation than this.While I’ve had a great deal of fun, and I know there’s plenty left I’ll enjoy, the game often is a total slog. At $60, I can’t recommend it at all, and $130 is a complete joke. If you’re an enthusiast of SRW or mecha, or just really love Gridman, consider it in a deep sale. Otherwise, I’d really suggest sticking with fan translated entries and holding off until the next title.

_childDocuments_.review: I have zero history with this series and like 95% of the represented IPs, and this is still one of the hypest games I've played this year. If you like turn-based grid tactics and want some suggestions for mecha series to check out, by all means give this a shot.   POST-DLC AND COMPLETION UPDATE:I still love this game and will continue to put hours into it, but I felt it important to come back after all the DLC has come out and I've seen through to the end of the game and expand on things some more.Firstly, the Deluxe OST. It's definitely overpriced, but I understand this is due to licensing fees with JAM Project, and JAM pretty much exists to give artists more power and leverage when negotiating usage of their work, so...here's the end result. It's still worth it to me, but my biggest complaint is that it's incomplete. SRX and Cybuster have lyrical themes from the past, and they're GREAT. But they're still not included in the Deluxe OST for no reason I've been able to find word of. TL;DR it's entirely optional and only matters if you have some favorite tracks you really want to hear.    The "main" DLCs are pretty good, but the quality feels inconsistent at times. Gundam Barbatos' attacks mostly feel minimalist and rushed, like they wanted to use as few frames as possible aside from his two finishing attacks. Yet the other Iron Blooded Orphans units have much longer animations and more frequent shots of the models in their fully animated form, rather than "sprite" form, pretty much upstaging the poster boy himself. On a similar note, the Ultraman units can be made OP fairly easily, but their attacks are even more rushed and bare-bones than Barbados', which I can only chalk up to the difficulty of capturing a 100% CG anime in 2D sprite form. I feel like if it was that difficult, maybe don't do it, but they probably had the crossover agreement made in advance, so w/e. Now, those being the main complaints of the DLC, I should move on to the positives, which are just as if not more important. Aside from the better animated units in this and other DLCs, you also get new side missions to go with them, and the side quests pretty much always lead to unlocking new attacks for related units, as well as unique "break point" bonuses they can activate by performing well enough in a deployment to reach a certain threshold of morale. And despite previous complaints, the attacks unlocked via side mission are always on the higher end of the quality spectrum, being both stronger and more visually impressive.   Now, on a final note, I should really address the elephant in the room, because it's far and away my biggest complaint of all. The localisation quality. From an objective standpoint, there are STILL at the time of this writing numerous grammatical and formatting errors (including text just running off the edge of the screen instead of continuing to the next line down) throughout multiple characters' dialogue, including fight dialogue that *will* appear multiple times. This alone is frankly unacceptable for a full priced product, and I genuinely hope whoever was hired for this localisation is now looking for work elsewhere. Beyond that, injecting memes into translations is always destined to age poorly, and it's even worse when you pick decade-old memes that were stale and Facebook Mom-tier back when I was still in high school when Crates had just been introduced to Team Fortress 2. ("Boom goes the dynamite"? F*cking REALLY?!?) There are some genuinely funny character moments, quite a few to be honest, but I attribute the comedic value to the original writers and whatever limited restraint the localizer arbitrarily expressed. I'm aware there's controversy around how a bunch of character dialogue about gender identity was translated regarding Majestic Prince, but as I have never seen the series, I can't speak to the accuracy of any of it, and don't honestly care. From what I've seen of side-by-side comparisons, the character in question is ambiguously portrayed in both versions and the EN version just has other characters being weirdly hostile about people asking about a third party's identity. It's a pointless change, I admit, but it doesn't get one hundredth of one percent of the ire that seeing an early 80's legacy animated character like Daba Myroad saying "Cray-cray" does. When the localiser isn't projecting their frustrations or awful stagnated meme culture into the dialogue, it's C+ adaptation work and leads to some enjoyable moments. When their restraint slips, it becomes D- cringe and makes you appreciate the better moments more. An unfortunate half-in-the-bag case that I hope is rectified with a different hire for the next game.   All in all, having finished it, I'd give this an 8/10. Strong replay value with the branching/locking mission paths and a wealth of hidden recruitable units, along with a good old fashioned Secret Real Ending. I would pay double digits for DLC that is just a more professional translation version.

_childDocuments_.review: one of the most fun games ive ever played.  SRW 30 manages to weave together dozens of different anime shows together into a single universe with a coherent, albeit convoluted, story.  The characters all interact with each other in fun and charming ways.  Even the DLC characters will pitch in and get involved in conversations; they don't feel as tacked-on as DLC characters usually are.SRW30 knows what it is and what it isn't.  It's not a very deep game; its a game about watching all your favorite mechs across dozens of shows fight alongside each other against the combined forces of all their enemies.  It's like fanfic, but with better dialogue.  Despite being a "tactical" RPG, there's not a whole lot of strategy to this game; it's a total breeze even on the highest difficulty level, so if you're looking for something like Final Fantasy Tactics then this ain't it.  SRW 30 is the digital equivalent of smashing all your childhood action figures into each other and just having fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to like this game as someone who has been playing since the very first SRW, but I just can't.Every single game in the series starting from about half a decade back has been dumbing down the difficulty of the game such that the game becomes extremely boring very quickly. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who has not watched any of these mecha anime, this game is a an absolute blast to play and experience.Pros:- Excellent English translation.- Attack Animations are visually breathtaking.- Killer Soundtrack containing classic and original tracks.- Stellar sound design.- Satisfying gameplay and character progression.- Faithful and well-done vocal performances.- Great and varied cast of characters and mechs that each mostly feel unique and fleshed out.Cons:- WAY too easy for anyone remotely experienced in strategy games. Exploits in abilities/spirits/equipment are far too common. Recommend starting on Hard Mode and then switching to the highest difficulty after a while, but even then the fear of a mech falling in combat let alone failing a mission will be a rare occurrence.- While the writing and world-building are competently handled considering how many shows and characters it has to account for, LOTS of lore from previous games and mecha series are referenced and discussed, which will make casual players like myself feel a bit lost on occasion. There are reference guides for each character and major events, but it's still a lot to ask for newcomers. Some visual recaps of important scenes from previous games and the animes would have been appreciated more than walls of text.- Clashing artstyles of character CGs make it feel more like a low budget fanfic (albeit understandable and unavoidable; a nitpick really).- The budget was clearly focused on the attack animations because everything else in this game, while not bad by any means, feels very cheap in its presentation. This is mostly an issue of the visual novel sections being minimalistic in its visuals with zero voice acting whatsoever, as well as the combat map overworld being very simplistic, low resolution in its textures, and completely barren in animations for enemies and allies.Despite having a lot to say about the Cons, I do feel that they're pretty easy to overlook/ignore considering everything else Super Robot Wars 30 knocks out of the park. Easily one of the best games to release this year for me. 8/10 for newcomers. 9/10 for mecha anime and SRW series fans.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit of a fan of this game, as my hours will likely show.Pros- First Official SRW Title on Steam in the West, a huge plus for any strategy RPG/Mecha fan!- Thoroughly enjoy the flexibility of the new mission system, not only allowing extra grinding if needed/wanted but not being forced down one route if you want to use specific units really opens up playthroughs and adds some extra little dialogue depending on the order you choose.- Great title to start/continue the series thanks to the increased customisation, multiple difficulty options from the start and extra QOL features such as auto battles help save time especially if you are time poor.- The Soundtrack/effects are fantastic as always, especially liked the extra ability to add visual reminders for your various sounds (you can import your own soundtrack by the way, just put them in your SRW30Music folder). - Well rounded cast, definite hit of nostalgia as a long time fan but also was impressed at the newer series such as Gundam Narrative, SSS Gridman and Brave Police J-Decker.- The modified Skill/Upgrade system feels really nice, on top of the side missions sometimes providing skills it made everyone feel usable.- Supporter system was a nice extra touch since it allows individual/whole squad buffs, some of which were upgraded over time due to plot providing crazy synergy, such as a turn 1 map wide armour debuff.- New Game plus options, what a beauty! More customisable than it's ever been, allowing you to choose to use your past funds/PP and so on or start from scratch with some parts from the previous playthrough, really like this addition.Cons- Minor visual glitches when using specific settings, any Anti Aliasing seems to cause tearing of sorts so I simply turned it off- Rare crashes, normally fixed from restarting Steam/PC and thankfully only a handful during my first playthrough.- MXP System still needs some adjustment, specifically the parts available after clearing a path can be rebought for 20,000 provided you have the funds... - Auto battle system could use some extra tinkering, why is it that units always use the most powerful attack on player phase but are far more reserved in enemy phase? Would be great to have an option to have energy saving or simply choose the strongest attack. - PP Gain seemed somewhat low, even as someone who did 10-15 hours of grinding on top of regular levelling from missions. This may simply be the particular builds I was aiming for, with my main pilots maxing out their main offensive stat (CQB or RNG).- I'll just say straight up, the Original enemy units are some of the driest and most basic I have ever encountered in a game, could have sorely used some more variety even if it was a simple paintjob to differentiate between leader units/basic enemies. - Pre-order exclusive units/missions is a big no no, it punishes those who don't buy the game in advance and considering how powerful they are (Cybuster and SRX) can limit the enjoyment of the game to someone who isn't a longtime fan/doesn't want to invest in the title so early in release. Please consider a small fee of say $5 or so to access them post launch, they really added to my first playthrough due to their wide variety of attacks/options. Note: The Free update April 20th will allow everyone access to SRX/Cybuster+extra parts, glad to hear they listened to the players! While that is a couple of negative points, I felt it was important to address all of them since, again, this series is near and dear to me and I want it to sell well on PC and other systems.SRW OG Series on Steam next perhaps Banpresto?

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRThe Good- Lovingly animated 2d that mimics the style of the original source material.- Gameplay starts off easy, but offers a decent depth for min maxing.- Special side missions with puzzle-like mechanics that force you to exploit the game's mechanics to succeed.- In-game library to explain the component anime series and their terminology to those unfamiliar them.- Story does a generally good job of blending several stories from different franchises together into a seamless whole. The non-DLC characters aren't some interdimensional travelers. They are part of a living, breathing world.The Bad- 30fps locked. This can be forgiven a bit since it's hand-animated.- The same faithfulness to the source material can be jarring at times such as the (deliberately) choppy animation of the RX-78-2 Gundam.- Super Expert starts tough, but even then can get too easy too fast.- Some franchises are just there, and barely contribute to the overall plot.- Forced story repositioning in missions can frequently leave critical units exposed to precarious positions without support. In the worst case, they are dragged along to the other side of the map.Verdict: Overall, yes.As a whole, a not particularly difficult SRPG, similar to Fire Emblem, that places more emphasis on fanservice and flashy animations.The story isn't particularly hard to follow if you watched the component anime series before: Simply mash most of the stories together and blend them together, and throw in an overarching original story to tie the whole thing together. With that said, some of the series such as Zeta Gundam, and Char's Counterattack barely have a plot presence since their story is already over, and are simply tagging along for the wild ride.If you have NOT watched any of the component series, fear not, for the game supplies an in-game library that you can read at your leisure, giving an overview of the relevant plot of each series, biographies of every single named character, and even highlights story references which can be viewed in more detail on what exactly just happened.In terms of gameplay, the game gives tips and an in-game manual to explain various systems. The early missions also eases you in to the various unique mechanics in the game, such as their Extra Orders and Supporter system. While it won't cover every single mechanic, it gives out enough to play the game well enough.Difficulty-wise, as mentioned it's not particularly difficult for most part. Easy mode should be for those completely unfamiliar with SRPGs, and normal is a good balance at learning the mechanics and providing a challenge. Hard felt good for those familiar with SRPGs, while Expert provided a bit more of a challenge. Super Expert is aimed at hardcore fans and will actually be challenging enough to force players to use various quirks and unique systems the game has to offer. No, the real challenges come in the form of accomplishing feats such as destroying an enemy that would normally run away when it's at low health, and being rewarded with an otherwise rare item and a boatload of cash for the trouble. Or certain side missions pitting a choice of, say, 3 or 4 units, sometimes just one, against an overwhelmingly large force, and having to destroy them within a tight time limit.Aesthetically, the 3d graphics aren't particularly special, and is light enough to run on weaker machines. Instead, emphasis is on the lovingly made 2d animations that mimics the source material as closely as possible. It goes so far as having older series such as the original Gundam and Combattler V having retro anime-style sounds and choppy animation reminiscent of the 80s era, while newer series, such as Narrative Gundam and Code Geass, tend to have smoother animations and cleaner lines like modern animation.All-in all, highly recommended if you're a fan of Japanese mecha anime, or just want to play something comfy. SRPG fans looking for a challenge may at least want to start the game on Expert right out of the gate, or else look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I think after putting in 100+ hours of this and still not finishing all the story content, I think this is a bad SRW. However, I also think it is a good game.As someone with experience in basically every single era, from the winkysoft days up to OGMD and VXT, I think this is both one of the best and worst designed games in the series. It offers more content and a bigger series list than basically anything else out there, but the way it delivers it is honestly just a mess. The appeal of an SRW for basically the entire lifetime of the PSX era onwards, is multiple playthroughs. There is always a reason to replay a SRW, because even if you only have a single protagonist/mecha like in Z2/3, you always have alternate routes. There is always something more there. This game, by virtue of effectively being open world, kills this part of the franchise. There is less than zero reason to EVER replay the game, because you can experience 100% of the game in one playthrough, sans the character interactions between the OG character you pick at the beginning. I just think this overall kind of sucks. Route splits sometimes aren't fun, or take your favourites away, but this progression is what I, as a long time player, expect. I see the good things that come from this and what feels like a much more boring, standard, ironically more linear game. Modern SRW has also consistently had a problem with difficulty. From around Z2.1 onwards, every game has been getting easier and easier, topping off with the end of the VXT trilogy, where in T you could completely max out upgrades on all units by mission 40. Beyond a cakewalk. Theoretically, this game should be harder. You can choose your difficulty level and at least at the start, they feel impactful and while still not as challenging as the early 00s, they could get tough. But very quickly, because you have access to replay missions over and over, and the ability to do every single mission that would normally come through a route split, you're almost immediately overflowing with cash, and because you're never missing units due to story or route split, you always have your ringers. Hell, by third act, you have a single unit that can steamroll an entire map solo, and the further you get, you get more and more units like this. Gaogaigar, Mazinkaiser and the other supers become so overpowered that it feels pointless to even try to run most of the real robots. It leads to some of the worst balance in the series, in a game that is already too easy. The EXC system from VXT is also here, a system that at a glance would make you want to manage your new points better, but once again, actually trivialises the game loop horribly. Suddenly you can have a unit that can act 5+ times per turn. Constantly recovering EXC or burning EXC to gain more and more damage and actions. For a series that recognised the power of Extra Action and made it unpurchaseable as a skill, it baffles me that they included ways to cheese it back in but considerably stronger. Seishin, in the same way, follow the trend set by the last several games of infinite respawning points. This means you never, ever have to play safe or smart with your seishin, because it will always recover. No more carefully taking hits and playing intelligently to clear a map before hitting the boss all at once and burning everything you have to survive. Simply use all the points you want and they'll recover by the time you reach the boss. It makes everything feel like a slog instead of a nail biting strategy battle of math and forethought. The DLC, while genuinely great if played as it released with a completed game file, is a good experience. Regardless of what you feel about the individual series, their inclusions usually have alot of effort. The keyword being usually. While IBO clearly has a massive budget of beautifully traditionally handcrafted animations and effects, special conditions and activation types, the SRW OG units are meanwhile beyond budget. They're at the quality level of the mobile game, DD, where the "sprites" are just cut-up 3d models that look unbelievably bad compared even to Gridman or the Ultraman units, that are MEANT to be CG models cut up and worked into the SRW animation style. The quality gap between these instances is so stark within the game, let alone comparing it to decade old games that it just constantly teeters between being amazing and being horrible. The Hi-Nu from the Alpha series on PS2 should not look higher quality than the Hi-Nu in a game released in 2021. Same as the Combattler and Voltes stuff. It's all over the place.But the annoying thing is that while I really don't think this is a good SRW for veterans, for someone getting into the series? It's an easy recommend. The game would probably be reasonably challenging to someone who doesn't know the systems and is playing on a higher difficulty. The series list is wide enough but not swimming in Gundams and recycled units like so many of the games on the Z engine tend to be. The lack of route splits and the way you can simply experience the full thing at once makes a playthrough (probably) more appealing than say, Alpha 2 and 3 where there are 4 entire games because there are 4 unique protagonist routes that you NEED to play NG+ over and over to experience. All in all it is just maddening. I want to reccomend this to anyone who enjoys SRPGs, but I also want to say to go emulate OGs in english. I want to say try the DS games or the Alpha and Z series. Like I enjoyed my time with this game but I was constantly wishing that it didn't try to break the mould so much and instead stick to what worked, because it simply doesn't work as well as the original formula.It is a good game and it's worth the money and you SHOULD play it, but it diverges so far from the established series formula that I can't recommend it to vets, and ironically we've probably all already completed this years ago at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Clarification: My opinion might be biased because I like this kind long-text/visual-novel and tactical RPG game, my best advice would be look for a youtube video with the gameplay and make your own choise.It isn't for everyone because you need to have some patience, dialogs are long like those from gacha games but the bright side you don't have to pay to get the characters you like (outside from buying the DCL and in that case you aren't gambling like in a gacha).In general this game is very beginner friendly, if you like the japanese mechas seen in Animes, you are going to be at home playing this game. It is highly recommended to play it with a controler if you have one. Once you start playing you need to decide your protagonist gender but the important part is your birthdate, make sure to always use November 11th and Blood type 'B'. You get a good start with your protagonist skills that saves your other mechas units from missing enemies shots or to avoid damage early game.Next is WHERE you want to start your game, this only affects which mechas you get at the start of the game. At the end you are going to get all the non-secret mechas just in a different order.Earth Route is all about series where robots fight aganist gigant monters (Mazinger, Getter Robo, SSSS.GRIDMAN, etc)Space Route is Mecha vs Aliens or other Robots. I chose this one (Majestic Prince, Mobile Suit Gundam NT, Heavy Metal L-Gaim, etc)If you can, play it with all the DLCs. You can get some good items to equip your meachas and make your run far more enjoyable with their quality of life aditions like more movement, Experience boosters, buffs for all your units for a single turn or max out moral at the start for a single unit. Had a weird bug that couldn't allow me to take screenshots once I checked the DLC shop in game.If you want to buy the DLC do it from Steam before you start up the game.The game is a wild run to be honest, I only play it for the 'Rayearth' characters and because I like the mechas. I got more than I asked for, the game had the JP VA, their anime theme plays when they attack and they have their signature moves from their animes. The other anime series I was unfamiliar with them, I know is better to experience them in their source material animes but they realy made a good effort to bring them together and have them interact with each other. I grew found of some characters I neved knew they existed until I played this game (Team Rabbits, Jona Basta, Amuro Ray, Lelouch, Ryoma Nagare, Ray Lundgren, Ichiro Ogami, Akihiro Altland and some originals like 'Gilliam Jaeger', 'Masaki Andoh' and 'Caruleum Vaull').The game had some good maps but you will play on them once or twice. The best maps are from 'Heavy Metal L-Gaim' and 'SSSS.GRIDMAN'. The best mission for Rayearth is the final battle aganist ZagatoMost of the times the maps you can replay (to level up some new mecha or older one you couldn't deploy before) are somehow repetitive and boring after a while, might be my only complain. The good news is that you have an auto play option, the bad news is that it gets stuck when you kill a boss (called 'Ememies ACE Pilots' ) and needs manual input to close their dialogs; sometimes you can cancel unintentionally the auto battle when you close those dialogs.If you enjoy a mecha but its early attacks are hard to handle, try using the DLC supporter "Orga" from "Mobile Suit Gundam Iron-Blooded Orphans" he fixes almost evey unit. Just play with the mechas you like over gameplay reasons(protagonist of each of their series almost always have at least two broken skills: 'Intuition', 'Resolve' and 'Seal'). Ignore the skills in that case and make a Morale/Ex-Multi Action build, almost every mecha is compatible with that build, belive me you are going to enjoy the game more that way (Always deployed Rayearth trio after they joined).You can check this web site for a deeper game progresion guide:Only managed to "Clear" the game, didn't start 'the post game', but might do once I clear some back log games. Hope you enjoy the game as much as I did. This is a hidden gem in steam. PS: Cleared the game with a party composition like this one:1.- Maxed out the main protagonist Mecha and installed all the available skills (CCQ, RNG and SKL to 999) make sure to add 'Hit & Run', 'Fighter's Spirit', 'Morale+', 'Break Morale Limit', 'Ignore Size', 'Attacker','Dash' 'Full Counter', 'ExC Bonus', 'Second Attack','SP Recovery', 'Save B' and 'Save E' NOTE: The trick is to use the Ex Command "Multi Action" before you attack to have an extra turn and keep using the spirit skill "Resolve" to get other 5 Ex points to reactivate "Multi Action" and clear with a single unit all the bosses on the map. 2.- Other 17 mechas I liked and altenated them each mission to make sure they always get at least 1 kill per mission.3.- Maxed out the 'Dreisstrager' (main blue ship) with all its 'AOS Updates', belive me you need to get ALL the updates from ALL the available skill trees BEFORE you start unlocking the parts at the end of each skill tree.4.- 2 Extra ships outside of your main ship (these are limited only managed to get 4 because some are hidden with secret requirements)

_childDocuments_.review: All your favorite mecha from all your favorite anime, piloted by all your favorite characters, wrapped up in a strategy game package with awesome music and sick animated fight scenes that pay homage to the source material. What's not to like?Well, a lot, unfortunately. For starters, the "strategy" or "tactics" tags should come with heavy air quotes. The enemy AI is brain-dead, simply charging at your units with no thought given to positioning or even like, targeting the same mech with multiple units in order to bring it down? Expect the enemy to spread their fire very thin, making them easy to mop up. Maps are gigantic and generally feature little to no terrain, with space maps in particular being massive voids with absolutely no terrain to form a strategy around. Even if there were terrain, movement and attack ranges are generally so massive that positioning doesn't remotely matter anyway.Mission variety is another point of failure. Most maps are simple "route the enemy" affairs, and if you thought you'd face different classes of enemies that cover each others' weaknesses like in XCom or Fire Emblem, be prepared to be let down, as most maps will spam 10-15 of the exact same enemy at you, spread out in a loose formation that will run straight at you so you can pick it apart with boring, repetitive, focus-fire tactics. Sometimes there will be a boss enemy in the crowd of minions, who will usually politely wait for you to slaughter all of their men before charging you solo and getting obliterated by your entire team.But hey, maybe the mooks will exhaust your ammo reserves and you'll have to conserve - nope! Most missions seem to last 3-5 turns, and even your most powerful weapons usually have quite generous ammo or energy reserves, making attrition and ammo conservation more or less irrelevant. You will kill all your enemies long before you run out of ammo to kill them with. The closest you ever come to strategy is that some weapons cannot be fired after moving, which I guess makes careful positioning almost matter, sometimes. Granted, these weapons usually have longer ranges to compensate for limiting your mobility, so, this downside is fairly well mitigated, and half the time they aren't even the mech's best attack, so there's almost no reason to ever use them anyway.The absolute pinnacle of this boring slog was a mission early on where my objective according to the pre-mission cutscene was to defend a space station, but when I got to the map, the space station was just part of the background PNG and it couldn't be interacted with in any way, and my actual lose condition for the mission was the usual "your warship gets shot down."Speaking of cutscenes, there are too freaking many. The writing tries to cram in as many plot beats from its source material as possible, so expect extremely long intros for most missions, sometimes up to 20 minutes of "cutscenes". These are not animated or voice acted, and the game's system can only show 2 character PNGs on screen at once, so expect to spend a lot of time staring at pictures of two characters over a static background with text in front, with one PNG swapping out for another each time a new character speaks, with generic walking or punching sound effects played with obnoxious frequency to attempt to convey any action that might be going on.Expect to spend a lot of your time not really understanding what's going on in the story anyway, as the game takes a "yes" approach to all its source animes' canon, and tries to smoosh characters from different franchises awkwardly into a shared universe. This is sometimes neat, you'll have the characters from, say, Gun x Sword knowing (or humorously having no idea about) the events in Code Geass, for example, and characters from different franchises either knowing each other or having fought together in the past. The game just has SO. MANY. CHARACTERS. Nobody really has much time to shine and the free-form mission select actually hurts the narrative a lot, as you'll suddenly be flooded with new characters and plotlines every mission, most of which won't go anywhere for an extremely long time.Finally, I'll point out the atrocious UI and boring upgrade path. All your mechs and pilots can be upgraded, though for mechs you can really only upgrade their base stats, aside from one "custom bonus" for doing a certain number of upgrades. The game tells you that these are powerful and unique to each mech, but many of them are boring, generic, or weak, and some are literally shared between multiple units (I'm looking at you, Dreisstrager and Huckbein 30). You can purchase new skills for your pilots, but these are pulled from a shared pool that anyone can grab, same as your "extra parts" for your mechs, which can be swapped on to any unit and provide one of the few actual points of customization in the game. The upside to this is that if you have a favorite obscure mech or character, you can turn them into a monster with enough favoritism, the downside is that pilots and mechs are extremely homogeneous, differentiated only by base stats, base skills, and base weapons - none of which you can ever change.As for the UI... it's like this game doesn't want you to play it. Basic functions like swapping which weapon you're attacking with, canceling movement, or even bringing up a pilot's stats require you to grapple with the controls and perform multiple inputs. It's atrocious, and for a franchise this old, downright embarrassing. You know how in most tactics games, just putting your cursor over a unit will bring up their HP, level, XP, and maybe some other stats? That is hidden by default in Super Robot Wars, and requires you to RIGHT CLICK in order to bring up. If you'd like to keep that stat screen up, too freakin' bad, because any input will hide that screen again, necessitating another right click to bring it back up.Enemy health bars are only shown at certain times, and since most maps are just one unit spammed at you over and over again, it can be a chore to search for which enemies you've damaged and which you haven't. I could go on, just know that every basic action that other tactics games figured out how to comfortably display decades ago, this game will make you fight to perform. Every tooltip, every stat screen, every movement, every attempt to target an enemy, every "spell" your pilots can cast, expect to struggle to do any of it until you get used to the absolutely horrendous controls and UI.My biggest gripe is this: how do you take a premise this over the top awesome, get this many companies signed on to use their IP, and somehow push out a product that sucks this much?If you're a big fan of mecha anime and just want to read some truly wild crossover fanfic and watch Gundams cut Kaiju in half, this might be for you. If you enjoy gameplay, narrative pacing, or a functional UI, stay far away.

_childDocuments_.review: After putting a good 100 hours into it, I have finally beaten the story of SRW30. This game absolutely rules if you like mecha. Having watched about half of the series contained, I got to clap my hands countless times as my favorite characters used my favorite attacks to kill my favorite villains. The crossover stuff was also fun, with things like the Magical Knight Rayearth girls being inspired by the Getter Robo boys and Lelouch encouraging Daba in his war against Posaydal adding plenty of spice to keep me interested. The DLC bumped this up even more by giving me Voltes V and some other cool characters, and the nice thing is that the DLC characters get to chime in here and there during the main mission plot, even if they don't majorly influence anything. That being said, this game is too got dang long. By hour 50 I was begging for it to be over and the game laughed in my face. If you're a completionist like me who is incapable of skipping/missing anything, you're in for dozens upon dozens of hours of gameplay, as my 100+ hours don't even include the post-game stuff I've just gained access to. Unfortunately, a  that content gets quite repetitive, so your mileage may vary as to whether or not the story and crossover interactions are enough to keep you going forward. SRW30 is a game I recommend if you're a mecha/super robot fan because it is effectively 100 hours of having keys jingled in your face. Just be prepared for it to be the same keys being jingled over and over and over and over again.
