_childDocuments_.review: After all these years, a mainline entry in the Super Robot Wars Series has made it to the US! It may seem like an odd thing to get so excited about this kind of thing, but you gotta understand that this series had something of a mythical reputation among anime fans that came up in the 90s. We about it second or even thirdhand, and very few of us were able to get a chance to play it. Until the English Asian editions came out for V, X and T, the best we could get were the old Original Generation Games on the Gameboy Advance. A lot of us mainly got to experience it through watching attack animation clips on youtube. But, nonetheless, despite all the odds, we finally get to experience it for ourselves.The game, much like it's predecessors, is at its heart part visual novel, and simple strategy RPG. The strategy RPG aspect is simple and fun. You can choose to synergize the myriad offensive, defensive and support skills for some units, to strategically whittle down the enemy. Or, you can simply sending out your most powerful unit to mercilessly annihilate anyone dumb enough to stand against you. The choice is yours. The big attraction is getting to see the attack animations; lavishly animated showcases of the unit's abilities, and in some cases using obscure attacks and weapons that may have only been mentioned in side-materials, or concept art is a joy.The visual novel part is the hidden pleasure for the fans. Each chapter contains a set of scripted dialogs essentially playing out what would be an entire 24 minute anime episode. Getting to see character interactions between your favorite heroes and villains from different series, and also seeing how their own stories are changed by the interactions is simply amazing. These led to moments and events that people have heard about and discussed for years. Stories of how "Evangelion's Shinji Ikari becomes a badass because he gets cool friends like Koji Kabuto and Ryoma Nagare!" or "SRW somehow made Gundam Seed Destiny's story GOOD!" Finally getting to have a chance to experience these kinds of What IF style stories instead of just drip feeding off of second hand accounts is amazing. Unlike much hyped "Crossover Events" you might see in movies like The Avengers, or your latest Comic Book crossover, it's clear the writers put effort into giving fans the fun experience they want to see. The interactions are fun and sometimes oddly insightful, and they don't devolve into meaningless posturing or snarky comments.The series lineup for this entry is a solid mix of old school series, long time mainstays, and some new and even unconventional choices. A lot of the gameplay has been refined from the previous VTX trilogy, and the interface is a bit more simplified to make it easier to navigate. I will admit if you're not much for mecha anime, the game might not have a lot for you, but for my part, finally being able to play something that I've literally spent most of my life only hearing about as a distant rumor is an amazing experience. Thank you Terada-san!

_childDocuments_.review: Super Robot Wars is finally here in the west in an accessible way! And what a great game to form people's first impressions of this long running series! Super Robot Wars is a tactical turn based RPG series that involves the crossing over of various different mecha (and now Tokusatsu as well!) proprieties into its own original story where these characters stories are bound to be different despite any similarities to their source material due to the new settings and elements. This crossing over of series is a gateway to a variety of interactions that are bound to amuse and entertain, have you ever wanted to see Shinji from Evangelion find a positive male role model from a man known to crush dinosaurs heads with his own hands? Boy, do i have a series for you (this isn't in SRW30 but I'm sure I got your attention now)! SRW is full of this stuff and its witty and fun writing makes for a great time.For those who may not know tons or even anything at all about mecha, i think you will find no issue with jumping into this series, the in game glossaries will tell you what you need to know about past events and the many characters you'll encounter and you'll never truly feel lost. If anything, I think this series is a great gateway to mecha for newcomers to this genre as you'll get a taste of all these characters and their mechs and the feel of their respective series', so you can find what you vibe with most and perhaps go watch/read their source material afterwards and slowly dig deeper into this genre and the many, many franchises that know that deep down, people just love seeing robots beat stuff up.The way I would describe this series to my friends who don't know mecha really is is "It's like Fire Emblem but your waifus are gaint robots" which may not sound cool but get this. Robots are cool. Giant robots? Even cooler. If you have any interest in tactical RPG's and think what you've heard of this franchise from its fans and the reviews sounds up your alley, I can't stress enough how much i think this game is worth your purchase and time. This is the first time this series has gotten this sort of chance in the west and people like me who've played this series for a long time wish to see SRW continue to get such wonderful western support! So give this game a shot, I believe its a wonderful game for SRW beginners and by the end of the game, you'll be calling out all these attacks names alongside the pilots!

_childDocuments_.review: A full review may be coming later, after a full play-through.For now, I recommend it to anyone interested. This is also likely the most beginner friendly SRW yet, with a gentle easing curve and many hints for things that should be obvious but may not occur to someone who's never played a S/T RPG before.For returning SRW players, here are some key notes if you haven't taken a deep dive yet:- As a B.B. Studio SRW, it's a bit on the easier side so far like the last three (on normal).- Open Mission structure with minor exploration elements!   - Pick Super or Real starting route   - Plot involves building up battleship by getting into SRW style nonsense around the world   - Mission select lets you choose which units to go for first; there seems to be some variation in story elements in stages       based on what you do in what order.   - Map screen has extra patrol missions (free XP and other benefits for two random[?] pilots) instead of the old training       rooms   - Map screen also has relic missions for power parts, they are mostly difficult puzzle maps where you'll need your best       units or system mastery to win. Sending my weakest units, they ended up quickly over-leveled with careful play if they       were capable of completing it. They don't scale, speaking of which...   - Scaling in most(?) battles, not sure how it works exactly but so far balance feels just like most more recent SRW's (on       normal)     - Map screen has another bonus for exploration, a rare fairy that grants some benefit (hasn't appeared for me yet).    - TacP and other system upgrades replaced by MxP which is spent on the battleship. Some things provide good passive       bonuses or economy discounts like other BB Studio SRW, but others affect the ship directly like doing full damage on       some support attacks, giving it the repair system, and more.    - Optional chats from achievements, ace celebrations, and sim missions are back but accessed from a new tab in        the mission screen. The ship itself and main character take up the Sidekick/Pet role from past BB SRW games.    - Supporters are back but now include passive bonuses if set, altering rewards, ExC costs and more.    - Ship repair/EN restock is faster than most SRW, I don't recall rates from last three but I think base rate is 50% a turn        based on upgrade path information; closer to G Generations boarding.    - Ship can recover from adjacent tile in addition to units boarding.    - Base ExC costs reworked.    - The orchestral reworks of classic SRW scenario and map tracks are great.Cons:   - The UI in general favors aesthetic over readability (matching the ship design) and takes a little bit to adjust to. It is       arguably more functional than past iterations outside of the visuals themselves, once you become accustomed to       looking at it.   - Some of the early stages are a little too generic for their introduction, the tutorial is essentially a couple hours long. Early impressions in, I'd heartily recommend it for anyone looking to jump into SRW, who likes giant robots at all, or even just a healthy interest in SRPG's.UPDATE 1: Almost 200 hours in and still haven't beaten the game. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I've been enjoying my time with this latest version of the Super Robot Wars franchise.  The series list for this game isn't among my favorites but it's definitely pretty neat to see some new additions. _childDocuments_.name: Super Robot Wars 30

_childDocuments_.review: Super Robot Wars 30 is an example of what love and care can do to the franchise. While a lot of the earlier games in the franchise rely heavily on reusing of assets and animations, 30 manages to change things up enough to show why this sequel is truly worth your time.First off, the series list is pretty good. Shaking things up with some newer anime like SSSS.Gridman and debuting some welcome additions like J-Decker, really make the roster feel fresh. Don't worry, the staples are still here. Koji and the Getter team have not been forgotten. I don't wish to talk much about the roster, as it is entirely subjective. Some people will sorely miss the TTGL crew, while some others welcome a break from recurring series. Subjective. I just personally really dig the narratives they chose for 30. The animations still have some jankyness to them. The anime cut ins that you can find in V are still present in some actions. Some of the returning units do show their age and are screaming for a revamp. However, the newer Robots get some stellar animations, I am very partial to the fluid motion Gridman has. I was hoping that 30 was going to be the title where the team went all out in this department. We have a mixed bag of fantastic animations, to some you'll be skipping.Gameplay is where the most polish is shown. I personally felt like a majority of the maps felt interesting enough to keep my attention. There were a small batch of missions I saw as pointless but it was a small minority. SRPGs' lifeline depends on coherent and challenging map design, this is what makes them replayable. Previous entries have left me wanting in this department, usually depending on route splits or route specific units to create replayability. While this worked, I much rather play the same maps with varying difficulty and challenging designs, than 100+ different chapters with almost no thought put into them. 30 has some missions that I was excited for, and would gladly replay with a different team. While there are still route splits, you are no longer just forced to play the next story mission. 30 now offers the ability to choose what mission you want to tackle next. This is an excellent breath of fresh air, specially for those looking to recruit their favorite characters early on. However, I can't exactly praise 30 for this, as Fire Emblem was doing this years ago. I can only commend them for finally moving on with the standards. I can certainly say I will be happy to replay this. My main complain would be that I wish each protagonist would get a specific mech.You won't find an extreme level of complexity here, SRW for all intents and purposes is a simple RPG. 30 does add a few things to spice things up, but if you're looking for a super difficult and deep system, maybe this is not your bag.From the character designs, the animations and the music, the overall aesthetic of SRW 30 is nothing to scuff at. Sure, there are SRPGs out there that are pushing the boundaries of graphics and art style. But as a mash of a ton of beloved Mecha? SRW 30 accomplishes what it does, it looks like an anime. I highly recommend getting the anime tracks, it really does the game wonders.Overall, if you love Mecha and SRPGs, then I assume you already bought this. If you love SRPGs, but have no idea what SRW is, or why the Mazinger Z is awesome, I would still check this out. There's a ton of entertainment to be had by all.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been with SRW since MX back on the PS2 and importing them from Japan ever since. name: Endling - Extinction is Forever
detailed_description: Will a mother fox manage to keep its little cubs alive? Experience a world ravaged by mankind through the eyes of the last fox on Earth in this eco-conscious adventure. Discover the destructive force of the human race, like it, day after day corrupts, pollutes, and exploits the most precious and valuable resources of the natural environment. Explore various 3D side-scrolling areas and defend your tiny furballs, feed them, watch them grow up, notice their unique personalities and fears, and most importantly, help them to survive. Use the cover of night to stealthily guide your litter towards a safer place. Spend the day resting in an improvised shelter and plan your next movement carefully since it could be the last for you and your pups. Features: Explore devastated environments based on real current issues. Hunt other animals to feed your cubs and avoid becoming the prey. Put your survival instinct to the test and get involved in emotionally taxing decisions. Find new shelters to be safe from natural and unnatural threats Care for your kits, feed them, and teach them new skills to make them less vulnerable. Survive.

short_description: As the last mother fox on Earth, your cubs need all your care to survive in a merciless world that slowly destroys itself. You have to help them, teach them and save them. And you should never forget that extinction is forever – in the real world and in this 2023 BAFTA award winning experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Endling - Extinction is Forever is a short game, similar to the Shelter series. The main goal is to ensure your cubs survival, but with the added intensity of being the last mature female fox on the planet. It features current worldwide issues such as habitat defragmentation, pollution, illegal poaching, but most of all, the greed and selfish nature of the human race that underline all of these problems. The game is tender, heartbreaking, heart-warming and real. It unfortunately released on the same day as Stray, missing out on the attention it deserves. Playing as the last mother fox on Earth, it is up to the player to help the four cubs survive the harsh world. Teach your offspring about the many dangers, what food to eat, how to hunt and many more much needed skills to give them a chance at survival. The most brutal element of the game is the heart wrenching reality it portrays. Watching the natural environments become slowly polluted, burnt down and simply over-used due to the greed of one species is emotionally devastating. Although no words are spoken, there are clear visual signs to interpret about the world., for example, the air is no longer clean, with most humans wearing masks, there are no more fish in the water and prey species become near non-existent.At the beginning of the game, one cub is stolen by a human from the den. This begins a game-long mission to try and retrieve it through following scent trails. I believe this is actually optional, but comprises the main (and only) storyline of the game. I enjoyed the focus being solely on the survival of the cubs (and retrieving the lost cub) and although more plots or optional events may help keep players' interest for longer, I do think this approach results in a forced focus on the decrepit environments and thus highlights the developers' core environmental message, which I see as a positive.Shortly after beginning the game, the mother fox gives birth to four utterly adorable offspring. These cubs, full of fluff and adventure are inherently unaware of the dangers that exist outside the safety of the den and their survival solely depends on the player. Gameplay is similar to Shelter, but less linear. You must first find food during the night and bring it back to your babies. Once they get a bit older, they will shadow you and have opportunities to learn new skills, which will also help gather food for their siblings. The main premise is to get back to the den before sunrise, to protect them from harmful predators and ensure they do not starve. I completed the game with no cubs dying and did not find it necessarily difficult, unlike in Shelter where it was quite brutal and unforgiving. Although food is not an infinite resource and live prey species such as rats or pigeons do not continue to respawn (highlighting all creatures struggle for survival), some caution should be made to ensure longevity of the resources.  Be warned that Endling is made to evoke emotion and it delivers its poignant message silently, but brilliantly. There is a small map that guides players to fast travel locations or events. There are not many special events to witness, but it is a handy addition. There are around 30 nights, and after leaving the den, sometimes there will be a pink scent trail, this will lead to information about the missing cub. I suppose this is optional, but not doing this would result in there being no real aim of the game, besides repeatedly going out to gather food, which would become boring quite quickly.Endling has a unique stylised look and features countless hints in its backgrounds to portray the awful state of the environment. With "preserved species" signs crossed out with graffiti, rubbish piling up everywhere and a lack of living creatures. The world is empty and drained. This barren landscape is in complete contrast to the colourful fox family, highlighting the rarity of the species, or any wildlife presence in general. There are no words spoken for the entirety of the game, but there does not need to be. Despite such a bleak landscape, with what seems like every human trying to kill you, there is some good. Endling also showcases the rare but unmistakable kindness that some people possess, those willing to share what little they have with the fox, when no one else will. These moments are highlighted beautifully through the soundtrack, especially the ending. Approximately 4.5 hours. The game is noticeably short and I recommend purchasing at a sale if concerned about the cost-hour ratio. Yes No, only for achievement hunters.Endling is an example of a video game portraying such a relevant and important, yet devastating message. Simply put, I loved this game, and I will remember it for a long time. It is a simple premise, similar to Shelter, but focuses on the hardships of wildlife and their offspring’s survival in a world that humans have destroyed. It is a hefty price tag for a short 4–5-hour playthrough and I recommend it at a sale. That being said, this game deserves more  recognition than it has received. If you like animals, care about the environment which you live in and/or like the Shelter series, I highly recommend this underrated title.
_childDocuments_.name: Endling - Extinction is Forever

_childDocuments_.review: I delayed writing a review about this game as, like for many people I believe, was deeply touched by the story and the setting. I played the game three times in order to see every single event and the feeling that you are trapped more and more over time is omnipresent. I once got stuck in the poultry factory, there were people all around, the furrier running after me and the babies unable to follow me. The feeling of distress enhanced by the eery music as the sun begins to shine and you know that you have no other choice but tempting your luck and you'll probably end up dying.At that moment I felt not just stressed, but hopeless, in that world dying, every character, every animal was doomed to die at some point as the world is decaying faster and faster. This isn't a game I would recommend to people stressed out by timers, nor would I recommend it to people who can't deal with animal and people dying. This will happen. Would you get attached to the humans or to the animals around you, you will certainly end up finishing the game mourning the lost of many of them.For those who wonder what  is about and how it can lead you to such deep feeling, you're playing a fox who is trying to survive along with her three kits and in search for her fourth one which is kidnapped day 2 in the game. While you try to survive and walk around what is left of nature around you, you can see how people live around, how they evolve and even how they die. You're not the only one going through a tragic change of lifestyle and in the end you can't even be angry at the one who stole your kit.I really loved the game, it was hard to swallow some of the events, I would love the dev changing the icon when the "event" on the map isn't an event, but instead the position of an enemy.. How many times did I run into the furrier while trying to see what was that event on the map ? I ceased to count after 4 times in a row. Beside that small issue, if you can deal with the hopelessness, loss and grief the game goes towards from the beginning to the end, then you will probably enjoy that game, if that's too much for you, maybe look at a let's play of the firsts chapters before deciding to buy it.As for those wondering why you would subject yourself to something which ends up being so tragic ? It's simple, this is only an accelerated end we're running towards if we continue to treat nature as something we can benefit of and reward with more pollution and considering it as a landfill. As disheartening as it sounds, with those in power leaving the task to the next one, we're heading right there, in a world where our comfort's price is the life of others. It's already like that, we're just looking to the other side and ignore it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game left me heartbroken. But at the same time, I know that it's definitely the Game of the Year for me.Everyone was so invested and hyped about Stray, but Stray in comparison to Endling is... bland. This is how you make an immersive story-rich game with the animal as the main character (don't get me wrong, I liked Stray, but seriously this tops it in every possible way). The art and the music (which for some reason brought to my mind Mononoke Hime) are both exquisite. Perfect in every way. It was impossible for me not to fall in love with every aspect of this story from first sight.I don't remember the last time I cried so badly at the end of a game. Well, I also cried at the beginning, to be completely honest. I don't remember the last time I felt so scared, and I've played my share of horrors. But this fear... it was different. More real. The immersion of this game is so deep, that fear for puppies was even painful.Can I recommend this game? Yes! But should I? No, if you don't like to feel awfully heartbroken. And especially when you know that's what will happen if nothing changes.I want to replay this game. To find all the secrets and achievements. I need to. But right now I can not bare going through the ending one more time. One day for sure, it's too beautiful not to. But for now... I only hope that everyone will see and play Endling. It's a painful experience but there is wisdom in this pain. And it's important.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game- It has an amazing art style, mostly entertaining gameplay, and a pretty good story. Pros: The game is gorgeous. The game will make you cry. I believe the devs have hinted at multiple endings, but given the game's very story driven nature, I don't feel like playing the game several times over, potentially having to let one or more of my pups die, to see them. I thought after I beat the game there might be more in the "extras" section, but sadly not. As of writing this review, I have about 4 hours of gameplay and I have completed the game. If you knew what to do, you could probably beat this game in two or three hours if you tried. Personally, I'd recommend getting this one on sale. If you're sensitive to animal death, you might want to skip this one.The story can be a bit vague or confusing sometimes.I encountered a few bugs, one of which was nearly gamebreaking. Overall recommended, I'd give this a 6/10.Update: I have managed to 100% this game in less than 12 hours. Take that as you will.

_childDocuments_.review: Endling was NOT the game I thought it would be. Sadly this game missed the mark and could have been so much more. [No spoilers] PROS: I loved the graphics and enjoyed much of the story. I am also a big fan of the message about our impact on the environment. It was not a super easy game and had some challenges. CONS: [Time] Each "day" in the game is WAY TOO SHORT. I understand the short time for a day makes you a little more on edge, and pushes you to plan out your moves. However this game is clearly begging for you to explore the map. The map is pretty large, with a LOT going on. But there is NO TIME to see much of it. (If you played the game already, you know you have to search for items that show you where your lost pup is at. Just searching for those items takes most of a day, then you have to run home.) I really wanted to explore the landscape, see all the critters, and check out what the humans are doing. But there is no time. The game pushes you along and you beat it in about 4 hours max. [Design] The map is terrible.... You have to pull the map open ALL the time. It really sucks you out of the immersion when you have to pull open a MAP! You start to feel connected to the game, and then you get lost and need your fox-GPS.. The map should have been a little mini-map circle in the bottom right. The enemies in the game are really annoying. I understand the humans are a hazard and you need to protect your pups, but several times I got checkmated by being sandwiched between two humans and died. This happened WAY too often. You are stuck walking in a 2D plane, and often a human will be on your left and right... ensuring your death and wasting your time. There are ways to bait the humans off your path, but they seemed horribly ineffective... (The marking posts)TLDR: Fun graphics and good story. No time to explore the world... But it feels like the game is begging you to explore the world.. Many design flaws suck out any immersion. Great $10 game, not full price though.I really wanted this to be an awesome game. :(

_childDocuments_.review: Specifically, it’s an animal cruelty simulator. It does not overtly advertise itself as a horror game, presumably to make all the sucker punches hit harder.  There are starvation mechanics, sparce resources, jumpscares, roaming unkillable enemies, cruel and depressing themes, sad endings, and a  of disturbing, atrocious imagery to witness. Make no mistake: if this were a story of a human trying to survive as the world is invaded by invincible heartless aliens or monsters who kill indiscriminately and terraform the land to their own will, you would correctly identify this as a survival horror game. That’s exactly what this game is, except that mankind are the monsters, and the survivor is the last living red fox. is a game with a message. I won’t spell out what that message is – but I will say that this game is built specifically to make you feel  about what humanity is doing to the world, to the animals who are trying to live in it, and to themselves. It lures you in with cute foxes and then rubs your face in the message from beginning to end. If you’re not in the mood for that, simply don’t play this game; you’ll probably find it quite overbearing and exploitative. But if you’re the right kind of audience for this, it will probably bring you to tears. As the developers put it: “As long as we can feel empathy for the struggles of the world around us, there is always hope for a better tomorrow.” And yeah, to be fair, it does that. Fair play. Just… maybe the store page should have had a few more prominent trigger warnings, or an actual “horror” tag, that’s all I’m saying.With that out of the way, how’s the game? Well, the presentation is just about perfect. The environments, the music, the character animations… I have nothing but praise for them, and I want to recommend the game based on that alone. The mother fox is beaming with personality and has so many adorable little mannerisms which are sure to tug on the heart strings. As far as presentation, I would only have to take off a few points for the “scent cutscenes” which tell the story of the main antagonist; I found them overdesigned and visually incomprehensible enough that it took several playthroughs before I began to decipher the story they’re trying to tell. (Most of them look like a giant heap of dark purple polygons grabbing a smaller heap of purple polygons, and sometimes a bathtub is involved… yeah, I didn’t get it at first, either.) And maybe a few more points off for some tonal confusion. So you make this heartbreaking game meant to depict real-world horrors we’re supposed to take totally seriously, then you make the antagonists Pyro from TF2 holding a sniper rifle, and a lanky-legged man chasing after you with an axe while obnoxious punk rock music plays. Also, the prologue briefly showed a futuristic Star Wars floating sentry drone, while the rest of the game featured only realistic modern technology? It seems like something from an earlier game concept they forgot to remove.The world progression, the way the game conveys its overall narrative, is wonderful. The environment changes a bit each day, sometimes in big ways, and every change tells its own little story about what’s going on in that region if you’re paying attention. Really makes you feel small and powerless in a huge world.But now for my big criticism: I think they dropped the ball hard on gameplay. There was a promising start, but as the game progresses and the world opens up, it gets so boring and hollow! Most of the gameplay involves passing the time until the next areas unlock. Sometimes the game marks points on the map so you can go there to watch a brief set piece, but most nights don’t even have any cutscenes to watch. If you’re feeding your cubs well, there’s just nothing to do. It even had to punish you with a hunger penalty if you skip the day too soon.You’re supposed to hunt around for opportunities to teach new skills to your cubs, which involves stumbling upon triggers that aren’t marked on the map, but the game seems to discourage exploration by making navigation a nightmare. You can only run on linear paths that sometimes don’t correlate well to the actual terrain (). The game likes to spawn unexpected enemies and obstacles not marked on the map; it doesn’t mark one-way junctions or cub-inaccessible points; some connections aren’t even shown at all. Worse, the map doesn’t mark places you’ve seen from nearby but haven’t traveled. So if you’re hunting for those cub skills late in the game, you just have to scour the whole map without any sense of direction, without knowing where all the daily random obstacles have appeared, and getting hopelessly stuck in or out of the region you wanted to explore. It’s about as fun as it sounds, and you’ll probably give up trying and just check a guide.Also, as this is a horror game, I have to be careful about spoiling the mysteriousness of the game mechanics, but suffice to say it’s far too easy to break the illusion of risk and danger. If you don’t go into this game with the willingness to stay immersed and role play as the mother fox, you’ll quickly find that many basic assumptions and gameplay ideas don’t hold up to close scrutiny.  In all, though it may not be a  survival horror game, I can appreciate its visual and emotional beauty, and I can easily recommend it to those who understand what they’re getting into. It’s a decent fox game that tells a heartbreaking story.6.5 / 10.(4-6 hours to beat blindly, depending on how much you die/obsessively restart when you mess up. About 8-10 to 100% complete.)

_childDocuments_.review: Endling is a thoroughly enjoyable yet gripping survival adventure of the very last fox to wander,the story starts when you get new puppies and you will then have to make sure they have enough food and are also taught enough basic skills such as climbing and looking for food!Check out a snippet of the game's gameplay here: In the game world you will find several shelters where you can hide from poachers who wander, also very quickly at the start of the game one of your puppies will be captured by such a poacher, and you will have to find it again and you use it for that your sense of smell, which can also be used when looking for food.You should also make sure that you always return to your hiding place before the sun comes up, especially with the little ones there, because during the day you rest.If you are too late, it is not done immediately, but you will have to look for extra food more quickly.At night it is best to stay in the shelter, and every new day there are some interesting places worth visiting.On the one hand, this can be a tree trunk with which you can distract poachers, but also events that help the story further or unlock new paths, because not every path is immediately available to walk.The gameplay is simple in the basics, and I find that quite pleasant for a game with this concept, but surviving takes some getting used to in the beginning but certainly not a real challenge.The game also has good support for ultra wide resolutions, you can watch a vb at 3840*1080 here:

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following the game since the first announcement and was looking forward to the release, which was helped by a pretty nice demo.The story originates in a world where people preferred progressive technologies to the detriment of the environment. People polluted the environment so much that it became disgusting for them to live in it, and there are so few animals left that the question of their extinction becomes rhetorical. In this terrible world, we have to play for the last fox, which, somehow reaching its hole, gave birth to four charming puppies.The main gameplay is based on the search and extraction of food, as well as modest stealth, so as not to get caught by people and other predatory animals and birds. At first, for very young puppies, the mother fox will carry the food herself right in the logo, but when the crumbs grow up a bit, they will already travel with her and learn. Every day in this game is special and you need to use it to the maximum, trying to explore the surrounding area and carefully consider the rate of food consumption, since the living creatures in the area are not endless, which can lead to a situation where one day you will simply be left without food nearby. In parallel with this, people begin to roam around the area, eventually opening up previously closed paths, which you can also use. At the same time, it is important for you to engage not only in collecting food, but also in finding a trace of the fourth puppy that was kidnapped by a person.A modest visual component sets its own charming style, since the picture conveys all those present and the environment itself quite well, and all this charm is complemented by a very melodic accompaniment that plays very well on the general atmosphere.People who empathize with animals will clearly appreciate this game, since the horror of a dying ecology is clearly felt here due to the environment, and the fact that you need to play not as a proud lone predator, but as a mother who is trying to protect her offspring, further fuels emotions.This is not an action movie with explosions and shots, not an adventure with freaks and a sharp-eared clown, but a sad story about the survival of animals in a world destroyed by the irresponsibility of "progressive, intelligent and self-conscious people." Who did not understand - it was a spit in the direction of those degenerates who love to shout about the superiority of man over animals, it is because of this attitude towards our smaller brothers that a future similar to what we see in this game awaits us.

_childDocuments_.review: : Endling is a 3D side-scrolling game where you take control of a mother fox that gives birth to 4 adorable cubs, which one goes missing later on. The game's storyline focuses on the mother and her babies surviving in this post-apocalyptic world, while trying to find and rescue the missing cub. The game successfully shows how humans affect the environment and wildlife, and doesn't shy away from controversial topics, such as global warming, factory farming and illegal poaching. That being said, the story was fine, wasn't a "tearjerker" like most steam reviews have claimed, I wish it was longer and focused on more than one storyline.The gameplay basically revolves around you trying to feed your cubs every night, where each one can have unique events, different weather, wildlife and even humans (friend and/or foe). They will also learn new skills along the way that can help them access new paths and scavenge more food. Even though you can lose one or more of your cubs if you aren't careful, the story is very linear, as there is only one ending, and the gameplay can get repetitive at the end. Other than that the soundtrack is fantastic, the artwork is amazing and the post-apocalyptic world is beautifully depressing.The game is 3 hours long and has no replay value, so paying $30 for it is a little bit extreme. I recommend buying it on deep sale (not more than $15 in my opinion).

_childDocuments_.review: The game's message about climate change and human mistreatment of the environment should weigh heavy on everyone's shoulders. It is conveyed very nicely both through subtle and overt changes of the background scenery and short action set pieces that play out while you can move around freely. I felt that the gameplay loop of balancing foraging for your pups with the discovery of this dystopian world was satisfying. Towards the end of the game, when all areas are discovered, it lost a bit of it's original intrigue for me, but luckily the game does not overstretch it. The mix of 2D movement in a 3D world felt fresh and was really a joy to behold.Animation, artstyle and atmosphere were great, but I felt the main story did not have the emotional impact that it could have had, if it had focused more on the animal characters rather than shifting to humans.I can recommend it regardless, but do get it on sale!

_childDocuments_.review: An atmosphere-driven game about being a fox mother trying to feed her offspring in an increasingly hostile world.Endling has you take control of a vixen right as she’s giving birth to 4 cubs, tasking you with scouring the world around your den for food to give them every night. To do so, you use your sense of smell in order to discover new food sources, exploring various paths through the surrounding area. While the world is beautifully realized in three dimensions, you’re mostly limited to moving either left or right, using your climbing ability at set points to move between different paths.The overall area available to you expands throughout the game’s runtime, adding many rather different areas for you to explore and scavenge. Food can be found in many forms, be they natural, like fish-filles waters, berry bushes and unguarded bird nests, or human-made, like trash bags or chicken coops. After a while, your pups will also start joining you on your trips, unlocking different skills to aid in finding food as you progress.To add some challenge, your surroundings tend to be rather hostile towards you, with owl looking to catch your cubs and hunters ready to shoot you when you cross their line of sight. You’ll also have to watch out for traps and roaming humans, the latter of which become especially problematic as the night ends, urging you to return to your den beforehand. While I managed to get through all of this rather well, there were certainly some tense situations, with the game overall striking a good balance in regards to its challenge.During all of this, Endling also tells a basic, yet quite compelling story, in which one of your cubs is kidnapped by a human, leading to you trying to track them down. This narrative continued every couple of nights, when a scent trail leads you to different items left behind by the kidnapper, allowing you to reconstruct what they were doing and where they were going. Along the way, you also become familiar with the workings of Endling’s world and witness it changing in rather dramatic ways. For me, this resulted in a pretty emotional journey, with the game’s ending in particular feeling quite powerful.To mix things up, there are also different events happening at various locations at different times. While some of these can merely be witnessed to get more information about the world around you, some allow for interactions, resulting in you receiving help on your journey or furthering a couple of small but enjoyable side-stories.All of this is presented with frankly beautiful visuals that looked honestly stunning during certain scenes, with the opening alone blowing my mind with how gorgeous everything looked. The game’s soundtrack is similarly great and fits Endling’s atmosphere wonderfully. Further adding to this wonderful presentation are detailed animations and mostly superfluous but charming interactions, such as playing with your cubs. All of this combines to create an immersive atmosphere, which the developers clearly put a lot of effort in.I found Endling to be a fantastic experience that kept me hooked throughout its runtime with a mostly relaxed yet enthralling gameplay loop and a genuinely beautiful presentation. Make sure to give the game a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished the game with the closest good ending that they could give us... It's still deeply sad and you will not feel good about it. I recommend this for any player that loves having hunting and survival mechanics in a game with an animal protagonist while enjoying a story that is already carved out, yet offers them to make their own choices. It will be the perfect experience. Be warned; ready yourselves to also be emotionally struck at times if you lose a cub or the mother fox to a predator or a human. There's lots of tragic realism. Not to mention the art style and animation is truly beautiful and very fluid! It has captivated me the entire time I was playing. There's a diverse range of areas to explore on the map with your cubs, from man-made structures to patches of nature, it's adventurous. There's even seasonal change! So, yes, I think lots of people who love the post-apocalyptic theme with surviving animals can really enjoy this story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is as brilliant as it is difficult to sit through. Of course, that is by design. Endling tells a tale about the insatiable greed and cruelty of humanity through the lens of a fox mother, struggling to keep her cubs alive as the world is plunged into apocalypse.Pros:1) The entire story is told brilliantly through imagery and actions. No words are ever spoken in the game and yet the game has so much to tell.2) The concept of the game is simple an straightforward - forage for food so that your children can survive while you explore and navigate the environment around you. (I have seen people criticise the game for being too simple, but I think that is a bit silly. You are playing a somewhat realistic game as a fox, what more do you want from it mechanics-wise?)3) A powerful, moving ending that makes you think about our own insatiable hunger and desire for material things as well as how it is affecting the world. Cons:1) There is a timer on each day, indicating how much time you have until dawn. One has to be back in one's foxhole by dawn. Unfortunately, this timer is not constant on the screen and shows up only at certain instances as well as when time is about to run out. I wish it was visible throughout to allow us to manage our time better.Note:If you have made it this far into my review, I would humbly request that you consider getting the "Save Our Planet" edition of this game. For every one of this edition purchased, HandyGames will plant one tree via OneTreePlanted, a non-profit organization focused on global reforestation.If you don't want to do this right away, play the base game, and if you're satisfied, come back and then consider upgrading. It is a small thing to do, but maybe if we all do a little, we can make a difference together.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased Endling extinction is forever, while it was on sale, even if I paid full price. I don’t think it would’ve been enough, this is a beautiful game left an impact on me that I know will last a long time, I myself am Republican and every time I heard about climate change, I always brushed it off as crazy, left-wing shriekers, however, after playing this game, it certainly open my eyes in terms of the fact that I need to be aware of this kind of stuff and not just brush it all off as nonsense, I think it’s very hard for humans to think far outside of themselves and see the impact that we’re having through action and sometimes inaction to do things, this game, paints a picture of a grim future that could happen if we don’t step up. I think the best part about this game is that there are no words spoken, we don’t have a multi paragraph dialogue about how gas is evil and America is terrible. We have no idea what country we are in, nothing is ever said it’s only shown and I’m unable to deny that corporations are and would do this, anyway, as somebody who has never once given much thought to this issue, I can gratefully say, thank you all for crafting a story that didn’t lecture me or talk to me or blame me for problems that I didn’t create, but instead showed the future that I don’t want to happen as a cautionary tale, and allow me to decide my view on the state of the world and come to my own conclusions, from the bottom of my heart. This is some of the greatest media I have seen in a long, long time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers a well crafted experience where art and music create an atmosphere that’s both beautiful and evocative. The environmental storytelling is impressive. Without a single word, it tells countless small stories that reveal themselves the more you play. Paying close attention to the details brings the world to life, and as the days pass, you see nature slowly degrade. Safe spots vanish, and natural beauty fades, capturing the effects of human impact in a way that feels real and grounded.The game also does a great job of showing the good in people and their struggles. It’s not one-sided. You see humanity suffering as well, adding layers to the story that feel authentic. Emotional moments don’t feel forced. They fit naturally with the world around you. Even after three playthroughs, I was still making new discoveries and connecting more dots, giving Endling a lasting impact that rewards a closer look.A standout aspect is how your actions have realistic consequences, both positive and negative, that impact the game and it's characters in meaningful ways. Choices you make feel rewarding and carry weight, creating a sense of responsibility and connection to the story.While Endling delivers a lot of great moments, there are a few frustrations. The changing camera orientation often makes it hard to keep track of where you are in relation to the map. As more obstacles appear and the environment becomes more dangerous, navigating in and out of certain locations can become a real chore.I also encountered a recurring bug when carrying food into scripted events. When a scripted event would trigger, the mother fox would drop the food, causing the kits to try eating it during the sequence. They would then get stuck in the eating animation, making it impossible to feed them or use their skills for the rest of the day, which was a troublesome setback.Additionally, death can feel a bit punishing on days with purple scent trails. These trails are crucial for progressing certain story elements, but if you die, you’ll have to follow them all over again at a slow pace. This can be especially tedious when you’re eager to advance and find yourself retracing steps repeatedly.Despite some minor hiccups, Endling remains a powerful and memorable experience. Its storytelling, atmosphere, and depth make it an adventure that’s absolutely worth diving into. I will never forget my cubs—Tod, Copper, Speck, and Blue—and the journey we shared.

_childDocuments_.review: This game kind of got buried under the release of Stray, and while it's not as good as the former, it's still worth a look IMO.  In Endling, you play the role of a mother fox trying to protect her cubs over the course of thirty days while humanity is on the brink of collapse. This involves keeping them well fed, away from danger, and teaching them survival skills so that they can learn to be on their own one day. One of your cubs is kit-napped at the beginning of the game, and a good chunk of the gameplay revolves around trying to find out what happened to them and if you can get them back. What I really appreciate about this game is that it shows how environmental destruction isn't just a problem for animals; it's something that will affect us humans as well. It does a good job of emphasising the need for climate action and environmental protection without condemning humans as inherently evil or stupid or hammering in its message too hard. It's also a very beautiful game that tells its story without any words. Overall, I think this game is worth a look. It's short, and a bit pricey for what you get (I recommend getting it on sale), but it's still good, has an important message, and the foxes are adorable as heck. Just be prepared for some tissues because it doesn't sugarcoat the reality animals face when extinction comes knocking at the door.

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who is incredibly fond of all animals and wildlife, The Ending Extinction warmed my heart and also broke it through every step of the wonderfully tragic journey this game presents. You play as a mother fox trying to keep her 4 baby cubs alive in a very real and nasty  world much like our own, what stood out to me the most were the environments and scary dystopian atmospheres the game created. While I won't spoil my favourite moments as they are fairly significant story-wise, there are some cut scenes and moments through the journey where I was stunned by what the game had to show off.People can learn a lot from this game, as Game play shows how humans impact the environment and wildlife and doesn't shy away from controversial topics such as global warming, factory farming, and illegal poaching. However, I wish the story had been longer and focused on more than one storyline. The steam reviews are correct in saying this game will make you cry and really hit you in the feels.In essence, your goal is to feed your cubs every night, where each one can experience unique events, weather conditions and wildlife, as well as humans who can be friendly or enemies. Along the way, they will also learn new skills that will allow them to access new paths and scavenge more food. In spite of the fact that your cubs can be lost if you're not careful, the story is very linear, with only one ending, and the game play can become repetitive. Brutally savage world, soundtrack, and artwork are spectacular.Gameplay is limited to around 3 hours and the game is unfortunately unreplayable because of its same ending but despite this I do highly recommend this game if you want a story with intense game full of desperate moments. I was very kindly given a game key free by THQNordic but id happily of paid for this game at a value of around £15 to £20 mark for this game just because its and excellent game but short with only one path and one ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Endling: Extinction is Forever in an unusual indie sidescroller, in which you play the last mother fox in a self-destructing world, protecting and providing for the three pups she has left, while searching desperately for her missing fourth. I enjoyed the game for what it was, and while I'd recommend it to anyone with interest in the natural world and/or wildlife sciences, it offers a relatively limited experience considering its thirty dollar price tag. Below is a list of pros and cons. Pros: - Beautiful assets and design. The art in this game is gorgeous. - Compelling music- Touching narrative - Unique and engaging game play Cons: - Immersion issues - Some bugs - Low incentive for replayability A quick, nitpicky aside: In the beginning of the game, after mother fox gives birth, the pups are depicted curled up next to her but not actively nursing. In real life, this would be a huge indicator something was off - neonate pups should be nursing and huddled up against their mother, trying to keep warm and competing for the best mammary glands. This game is fantastic in a lot of ways but it was immersion breaking for me to witness these pups behave abnormally and wonder if something was wrong. I would really like for this to be changed but realize it's probably not going to happen. Oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: Endling is an incredibly beautiful game that tells a poignant and moving story but who's gameplay is so often at odds with it's own emotional beats. By fixing your interactions with the characters and the world to arbitrary mechanics that are so abstracted from the emotion of the story (watching health or day light meters, engaging with stealth mechanics, racing to activate events around the map, etc) and then removing agency from you as the character during the most powerful moments of the story, I think the game leaves me, the player, feeling a bit beaten down in the end. It seems to be saying "Here, do your best, but nothing you do will matter". It encourages me to min/max my interactions, but then punishes me with sadness and tragedy regardless. If played plenty of sad games before, but telling a tragic story with player interaction is a difficult line to walk and I feel that Endling doesn't quite do it.There's a version of Endling that is less "gamified" and more focused on exploration and emotional narrative choices that I would have loved to play. This is still a thumbs up, but I think that's mostly for the art and because I think that ultimately the game's heart is in the right place and I want to see more stories set in the aftermath of a climate change that is now going to be innevitable. But if someone asked me if they should buy and play this game, I think I'd recommend something like Before Your Eyes first, and then Endling second.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially had high expectations due to overwhelmingly positive reviews, but I found myself disappointed with the overall experience.The gameplay in the game is quite basic. Players can move left, right, or branch to a different path at predetermined points. The game features only three types of hazards: quick time events, static obstacles, and red light-green light sequences. (I also consider the chasing enemy as more of a static obstacle since they despawn after a few seconds of being out of sight.) Exploration is restricted by locks that only unlock after a certain number of in-game days have passed. This means that once you've explored an area, you're left with little to do other than passing time and ensuring your pups stay fed. However, this isn't all negative, as the game provides environmental changes every few days as a form of storytelling. There is also a series of scent memories in image form that tells its own little story that unlock every few days.The story is marketed as the game's main selling point, but it is also where my greatest disappointment lies. The game attempts to convey a narrative about survival and hardship in a world devastated by human industry and climate change, but the gameplay fails to support this theme effectively. In my playthrough, food scarcity was initially a challenge because I had to travel far to find food which was difficult because of the short nights. This changed after leaving the first area. Throughout most of the game, I struggled not to waste food because it became abundantly available. Even in the heavily polluted garbage areas, there were ample rats and garbage to eat. The human characters didn't seem to be enduring severe hardships either. While many wore gas masks, there were times when they didn't, and they appeared relatively healthy. There was signage proclaiming "Oxygen is a right!" but this seemed inconsistent when there were humans in the same area sitting around campfires without masks. Myself and the rest of the wildlife seemed completely unaffected by whatever toxins or lack of oxygen there was. I imagine food was probably somewhat of a problem for the refugees, but the only evidence of this was a refugee dying for stealing food. Others had enough food they were able to share it with a random fox like myself. There was only one human character who appeared to be severely suffering, but it seemed related to a lack of  rather than food or air. Given that this character was also a refugee, it gave the impression that the problem was more inequality than scarcity. A functioning industrial chicken farm, which both refugees and I stole from, emphasized the issue of inequality more than climate collapse. The ending was where the story took a turn for the worst though.Beware ending spoilers!

_childDocuments_.review: Endling is a beautifully crafted and emotionally charged game that puts players in the role of the last mother fox on Earth. As the protagonist, you are entrusted with the vital task of guiding and protecting your cubs in a world that is gradually collapsing upon itself. With stunning visuals, a captivating storyline, and a profound message about the fragility of life, Endling offers a unique and memorable gaming experience.The game's atmosphere is both haunting and mesmerizing. The desolate landscapes, coupled with a melancholic soundtrack, create a sense of urgency and despair. The visual details bring the dying world to life, emphasizing the devastating consequences of human actions on nature. As you navigate through various environments, you'll encounter breathtaking scenery, polluted areas, and remnants of human civilization, all of which serve as a constant reminder of the urgent need to safeguard our planet.One of the game's standout features is the bond between the mother fox and her cubs. Endling portrays the struggles and challenges of parenthood with authenticity and tenderness. You'll have to provide for your cubs, teach them essential survival skills, and make difficult decisions that can mean the difference between life and death. The game's mechanics emphasize the emotional connection between the player and the virtual fox family, creating a deep sense of responsibility and empathy.The gameplay itself strikes a balance between exploration, stealth, and puzzle-solving. Each area presents unique challenges and dangers, such as predators, toxic substances, and human interference. As you progress, you'll need to utilize the fox family's abilities, such as digging, scent tracking, and stealth, to overcome obstacles and protect your cubs from harm. The puzzles are well-designed, requiring both strategy and quick thinking, which keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.While Endling is a deeply moving experience, it does have a few minor shortcomings. The controls can be slightly clunky at times, leading to occasional frustration during precise movements or time-sensitive situations. Additionally, the game's pacing could have been better balanced, as certain sections feel a bit slow compared to others. However, these issues are outweighed by the overall strengths of the game.Endling's most significant achievement lies in its thought-provoking narrative and underlying message. It serves as a poignant reminder of the impact our actions have on the environment and the urgent need for conservation. The game successfully blends entertainment with education, offering players an opportunity to reflect on the consequences of human negligence and the importance of preserving our planet for future generations.In conclusion, Endling is a captivating and emotionally charged game that explores themes of survival, responsibility, and the fragile balance of nature. Its stunning visuals, compelling storyline, and immersive gameplay make it a worthwhile experience for anyone seeking a unique and thought-provoking gaming journey. With its powerful message, Endling stands as a poignant reminder that extinction is forever, and it's up to us to protect the world we inhabit.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a problem where the 2.5D map/movement design makes the movement so linear, yet all of the challenge of the game is built around it. The only stopping force in the game is a point on a linear path (a OHKO event), which means you take a different path, and thus beat the challenge. It's a point of frustration for the movement to be funneled so narrowly, yet all of the gameplay is built around it. It would have been a massive improvement to add actual 3D movement and rework the enemies around that.I have beef with how the last sections played out as well - the first tragic fakeout was cheap, but following it up with a second tragic ending is like... a weird, almost sarcastic way to end? It was so silly and manipulative, everything past night 29 felt so tacked on and out of place. The game deserved better than a clumsy misery porn wrap-up.

_childDocuments_.review: Smooth movement - check Beautiful stylized environment - check Immersion - check Horribly heartwrenching - absolutely.There's really a lot to like about Endling if you're into story driven exploration games. Gameplay elements are comparatively sparse, but I feel like they provide enough engagement to keep the player entertained throughout the story. The story itself, which will take about 4h~ to complete, is fairly linear and will play out the same everytime, excluding the amount of cubs you manage to keep alive. Despite this, I didn't find myself bored as I reran the game for achievements and the full extent of the environmental storytelling can perhaps only be appreciated on your second and third run. _childDocuments_.review: This game sure does HURT.I played this game on stream at request of a friend who purchased it for me. I'm real glad I did, so others could feel my pain with me as I slowly watched half of my children starve to death. Essentially, you are playing as a mother fox in an end-of-the-world type scenario. Animals are going extinct left and right and humans are hunting down the few that are left. Your job is to protect your four cubs - one of whom gets kidnapped pretty quick into the game. You spend the rest of the game hunting it down to rescue it, while trying to keep your other three cubs fed and avoiding predators (most of which are humans).The art is amazing. The tone of the world is really well done, with trash littering the areas, and the 'bad' humans definitely having a good villain vibe, post-apocalyptical gas masks and all. The further you delve into the world, the more destroyed it feels by humanity. It was… very interesting, and a very terrifying look at how our world may be. So much trash.The story is heartbreaking but so well done. I don't want to spoil a single thing for it, but just go into it knowing no matter how well you play, it's gonna hurt. But be so incredibly worth it.The gameplay was pretty simple, but engaging. You're constantly hunting down food for your starving children, avoiding traps and predators. You have to be careful not to lose your cubs by going places they can't reach, but they can also develop new skills to help hunt for the skulk. It's pretty interesting and keeps you engaged for the 30 days of gameplay. It was terrible, though, I could be doing real well for a bit and then suddenly we are all starving to death.One mechanic I really appreciate is that all your cubs will not starve at once. You only have one hunger bar, and once one cub dies, the bar does go back up about 1/4th. And no, it's not because you eat the cub. It's just nice and made it so I did not immediately lose the game, which I appreciate.The achievements vary in difficulty. One of them is to finish with all 4 cubs alive which… I do not foresee myself doing to be quite honest. There's a few for story progression, a few silly ones like barking in the rain 3 times, and a few sort of secret ones.I had a great time, but I don't think I'll go back to 100% it. It was kind of intense, but in a good way. I just feel like trying to grind out missing achievements would ruin it for me - it's not the kind of game I want to use a walkthrough on, I just want to. Vibe and do my best. And I did, and I had a great time with it!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give it a thumbs up since I played through it all and was invested from beginning to end. I think I mostly enjoyed it but it's pretty short and depressing AF - I don't know if there is a good ending or not(?), but I saved all pups and seemed to be doing fine, but it didn't matter. I think the devs are trying to make some large point about the world and such, but it's just a slap in the face for a gaming experience imo... The game also pushes you to return to your den before night, but I never really saw the negative impact of hanging out past night other than maybe not being able to move the story line and unlocks along. TBH, Im glad there was no punishment for not getting to the den I guess, since the night cycles come up crazy fast, and there's no real way to tell when night coming up until the warning starts flashing at you.  The survival aspect and getting your kits to learn skills is fun, but I dont think the game lasts long enough for you to really enjoy all the skills they learn. It would have been a little cool if there was a bit more conflict management in the game. Seemed like conflict was mostly just walking away from enemies (general avoidance), but if there were some more clear ways to distract or throw off enemies, and even have some way to deal with the hunter/trapper dude, that would have added some more interest in the game. Getting to where I was going was constantly disorienting for me personally. I kept having to check my map, then the camera loves to change around on you as your moving through the areas, which is cool visually, but I could not seem to process which direction to go in after that happened a couple times. I really wish there was a mini-map option, that would have solved about 99% of my map checking needs.TLDRPros: Gorgeous, motivating, uniqueCons: Short, Disorienting, not very rewarding end game experience

Right from the start you will be playing as a vixen(Female Fox) that is running away from a massive fire spread in the middle of the forest that is caused by the humans. You will eventually find a small hideout where you gave birth of 4 cubs. You will have to take care of them by finding and hunting for food and feed them. They will grow bigger and will be getting older. They will eventually leave the cave and join your adventure to assist you by unlocking new skills. They are able to learn, Hunting, digging, high jumping and a few other skills. The day and night cycles from time to time. It doesn't impact of the game other than having a bit more roaming enemies but sleeping in your cave will allow you to start a new nighttime. Their will be new events and resetting some of the food resources. What is important is to keep an eye on your cubs, They could starve or get under attack by some other hostile creatures and yes they are able to die. You are able to pet your cubs once they are frightened by an event and they will always try to follow you around if they are able to do this.The game isn't super long and you can easily finish this game within 1 or 2 days / 8-10 hours. The graphics are simple but effective and honestly i don't see much of a difference when playing it on a medium graphical settings or higher. The game is sorta like a side scroller as you can only move to left or right but you can change walking course by jumping up or down. The game scenery and details itself (like little detail) are amazing and show are the cut-scenes.None.-------------------I Give this game a 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure what to expect coming into it, even after the demo. But the demo does give you a pretty good understanding of what to expect - it gets bigger, the threats get meaner/scarier, but you get a solid 30 days worth of surviving, finding new homes, escaping threats, the world opening up as you go. The game is very scripted in terms of how it opens up to you, which felt stifling at first but makes sense given what they're going for. You are mostly just trying to survive as a passive, helpless creature in this ongoing story. Every day brings new changes, and they might help or hinder you in your goals.For the most part, gameplay is pretty simple. You're running and sneaking around linear tracks through the environment which loop and twist around each other, avoiding people and traps, trying to keep your pups fed and chase down a scent trail every few days to advance the story. It's tight, responsive, and makes for some good tense moments. But the main draw is the storytelling, and the ever-changing world/map.Aside from a few cutscenes, it's pretty much all environmental storytelling. Your only goal is survival, but with each passing day the world around you is changing, the humans greatly impacting your habitat. But they're not just an evil plague of fox-murdering, tree-chopping psychos. You get many opportunities to witness the devastating effects their industry has on their own health. The seed of humanity blossoms forth even in the most treacherous environment.Overall, it's pretty small. You won't get a whole lot of value in terms of hours played here, for your dollar. I don't get the sense that the decisions you make in the game impact things greatly, so for the most part I consider it one-and-done. Or if you're a bad mom, maybe a second try to get it right. But you're likely to get less than 10 hours out of it even if you do multiple playthroughs, so at least for now I'd recommend waiting on a sale if that sort of value is important to you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game shows the dark reality of the Anthropocene in a beautiful way. It breaks our hearts, but the message is very clear. Sad and moving.“To walk attentively through a forest, even a damaged one, is to be caught by the abundance of life: ancient and new; underfoot and reaching into the light. But how does one tell the life of the forest? We might begin by looking for drama and adventure beyond the activities of humans. Yet we are not used to reading stories without human heroes. (...) Over the past few decades many kinds of scholars have shown that allowing only human protagonists into our stories is not just ordinary human bias. It is a cultural agenda tied to dreams of progress through modernization. There are other ways of making worlds. Anthropologists have become interested, for example, in how substance hunters recognize other living beings as persons, that is protagonists of stories. Indeed, how could it be otherwise? Yet expectations of progress block this insight. Talking animals are for children and primitives. Their voices silent, we imagine wellbeing without them. We trample over them for our advancement. We forget that collaborative survival requires cross-species coordinations. To enlarge what is possible we need other kinds of stories, including adventures of landscapes.”Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, The Mushroom at the End of the World: On the Possibility of Life in Capitalist Ruins

_childDocuments_.review: While the premise of the game is incredibly compelling, the story ends up relying too heavily on it. Artistically, this is a beautiful game. There are moments that are incredibly touching and wonderful. The greater message of the game is a good one. The gameplay is fairly repetitive, days feel too short, and I longed for more player agency in affecting the storyline even in small ways. My overall take is that the visual and musical elements of the game are incredible, and the story and gameplay are both underbaked, relying too heavily on ineffective, cheap, heartstring-tugging shortcuts.Below contains non-specific, mild spoilers about game end:......I love sad games. I love gut-punches, bitter, and bittersweet endings. However, this game felt like it punished the player just for the sake of doing it without a satisfying narrative build to, or justification for, the final outcome. I'll also be clear that I got the "good" ending. One of the loading screens says something to the effect of, "there are still good people out there," but the last few days leading up to the end erased all of that complexity and left me feeling bitter instead of what I believe was likely intended to be bittersweet. To put it simply, it felt like a cheap, unearned emotional manipulation instead of an effective narrative close.

In some ways it is already a reflection of modern society and given recent changes, it might even become more significant in the future.On multiple occassion it is impossible to tell if tears arise from joy or from sadness, both being so close together and so interconnected. The game lives up to the expectations the demo set and goes much further, some outcomes certainly being unexpected. A personal hint: Allow yourself to be curious (while staying alert), expect the unexpected and sometimes give the benefit of the doubt.I wholeheartedly recommend this game to everyone who is ready for a highly emotional story about unconditional love, care and the struggle for survival. _childDocuments_.review: Endling was off to a great start when it banged me into a fierce chase sequence with the impressive graphics painting a drastic scene of a motherfox trying to escape from a wildfire. This sequence almost teared me up when I witnessed how ruthless our species is, the destruction we caused to nature and the innocent animals in the middle of all of it.Unfortunately, when Endling transitioned into the open-world section (99% of the game), it was littered with repetitive gameplay and a lack of conflict.It was fine at first. The tension remained as I learned to scavenge under a tight time limit. But the urgency quickly decayed when I am essentially repeating the same formula every night: 1. Avoid enemies2. Find food3. ReturnThe enemies are barely varied and don't pose a challenge. Once I encounter an enemy, I just open the map, and walk the other way around.Finding food became difficult when I needed to venture further and further away each night because I'd already depleted the area nearby- until the game started spawning birds all around for me to grab. Congrats! Poverty is solved! Just hold crouch and walk to the same bird spawn a block away from the shelter and eat it!At this point, it's hard to connect with the fox because of a lack of conflict in the gameplay when it's primarily what's pacing the game forward.In the meanwhile, I find the story pretty sweet on its own. But the forced repetitive gameplay kept it on the back-burner and hindered it to feeling severely underdeveloped to provoke any meaningful impact.The only possible redeeming quality left is Endling's world-building. It's also the most important element because it backdrops the player's exploration and holds the responsibility to depict human's merciless actions and their consequences to the environment.There are a few heart-moving moments, like witnessing the mother fox who almost suffocated in a trash bag or meeting a kind girl who gave us apples.However, these world-building moments are either too rare or too repetitive to keep up the run time of 4-6 hours. And I expected much more from an environmentalist-themed game.The chicken industry wasn't brutal enough. Show me the effects of fossil fuels. Where are the mass hunters? I want more ferocity from humans. Where are the meat eaters bruh- SHOW ME THE VEGAN PROPAGANDA.The wildfire is one of the most emotional moments in video game history, warning us about the consequences if we continue to neglect the current environmental issues.Too bad they showed it all off from the beginning and left with a lackluster filler.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is highly overrated. Played it through with all cubs alive. Neither narrative nor gameplay are compelling. At around midpoint the game SEEMS to open up, but it doesnt. Instead it starts randomly restricting access to certain areas, which COULD be interesting if some new gameplay resulted from this, but it doesnt. Not even a new challenge through scarce ressources arises. You are just stuck in a relatively small area for the night, thats it.  Lots of your actions are inconsequential. I got  "stuck" in like 50 plasticbags and 20 beartraps. (Almost) no consequences. And now that Ive finished the game I see why. Its tedious to replay only a single night. Gameplay is extremely basic, besides exploration the game has basically nothing to offer. The narratives only Pro is that its told from the perspective of an animal. No spoken words, only vague associations and the environmental telling. But thats it. The plot is almost non existant, the environment tells some tragic sidestory and general background, but at some point you simply have seen it all.The game has a clear message, and thats it. Thats seems to be its whole purpose. One might argue thats okay, especially if the game isnt "fun" since its such a serious and important topic. But thats not enough, the game should still offer me more than a sidescrolling Walking simulator with some ludicrously shallow and easy-peasy survival gameplay. At least I was spared the crafting...The conclusion of the game is a joke if you ask me. It feels like the devs simply didnt know how they wanted it to end. Both predictable and messy. Pretty unique combo at least.

Mother hunts for food = Ultra kill 3-Just FYI, all fox species are under the class of mammalia, which means lactation is necessary in their reproduction cycle. No milk for cubs = Ultra kill again It’s acceptable to alter some of the animal habits so they can better fit the game design. Not recommended.
