_childDocuments_.review: The game features a very interesting 'time shifting' mechanic whereby you can rewind time in battle by a certain amount... and it's honestly something that I've never seen before outside of Superhot... You also have a 'talent tree' of sorts, although one huge let-down in the game is that you don't have equipment or an inventory, so you can't change your character's equipment at all (because your characters doesn't even HAVE any equipment to change). Do you want to fight with a 2hander sword instead of a shield and hammer? NOPE! You can't change nuttin!!And while we are on the topic of 'Superhot'... my bloody graphics card's temperature gets hotter than the core of the sun while playing this game! My 1070GTX struggles to get above 50FPS on MEDIUM graphics with this game... so the graphics engine optimization leaves a lot to be desired.Look, the game is OK (I'm actually a big fan of TRPGs, so I'm a little biased), but I feel that €30 is too much for this game. It provides too little actual content, I mean sure you can complete the story in 20hrs-ish which is pretty respectable, but the ACTUAL CONTENT of the game is lacking ie. you can't level up, or equip items, or customize your appearance, or create different 'builds' for your party. The game only really allows you to select a single 'talent' or skill at the end of each mission, and that's it! That's really the only input that you as a player has with regards to how your character progresses... and I'm sorry but that's EXTREMELY lacking for a TRPG... just look at other TRPGs like 'Divinity Original Sin' or 'XCOM' or 'Pillars of Eternity'... all of those games allow you to radically change each one of your characters to fit your own playstyle and taste... yet this game doesn't allow you to change hardly anything. The game also heavily features puzzles, which I am not a fan of, because it makes this already slow game even slower (and I found the puzzles boring, not fun or meaningful).If this game was still in 'early access' or 'beta' then I would have given it a 'recommended' simply because there would have been the possibility that many of the game's core features (like maybe an equipment system!) would still be missing, however since this game is currently in full-release, I simply can't recommend it at the current price point, because there's simply other better TRPG games out there, that cost the same or less than this game does, with more features and more content. I want to emphasize that it's not a bad game by any stretch, but it's not in the same league as other TRPG games at this price point... I mean, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is only €22 right now, so WHY ON EARTH would I pay €30 for this game, when €22 can get me a TRPG that is literally 5 times better?For more reviews, visit my curator page: For my full recommended list of games:

_childDocuments_.review: My first ever review. Normally I wouldn't enjoy playing games that employ a similar mechanism to Dragon Age: Inquisition and Greedfall, in which you have to keep pausing and deciding what to do before executing your actions. This game takes that tactic to the next level. Tired of dying and not achieving something due to mishaps like wrong clicking and poor dodging? Get ready to manipulate time itself with the game's provided 'time bar'. Die as many times as you like and the game would automatically pause for you even if you die stupidly due to hidden traps or when you encounter monsters that are difficult to spot.  So far I find this game very noob-friendly to players who are acquainted with this style of turn-based RPG. HIghly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself looks pretty good - graphics, sound, interesting time-based mechanic, but...It is really confusing how the game becomes repetetive and extremely boring with each battle - new skills and character change are not really bringing much variety. Maybe, playing it a mission per day would not feel as doing absolutely the same thing on different maps, idk.The story is also not the strong part of the game, though, it exists - you are chosen now, must save the kingdom.About RPG part - you don't really control how the character grows - no character stats, you only get a chance to upgrade one of skills after almost each map, though, it seems like upgrades are predefined for specific characters after corresponding maps, which is also confusing. Upgrades themselfs are quite boring - you simply can't choose to improve specific skill stats - only if you want to upgrade it or not with defined stats increase.

_childDocuments_.review: Iron Danger is a Real Time Tactics Adventure.Most of the time you control two different characters during a mission.The only choices you make is what skills you want to upgrade after each mission.The rest of the game is pure linear without any choices or consequences.You proceed in the game by playing through levels with objectives.When you enter a fight you issue commands for your characters and can rewind if the outcome of your given commands do not turn out how you expected they will turn out. This mechanic makes the game almost non lose able. However, you will still die a lot but with a quick rewind the death will be prevented.The Story is a basic fantasy plot but the world and lore is unique.To bad that you can not realy explore the world and lore in the game. So even if it is unique, you won't experience much of it.The game concludes on its own but with a non shown to be continued sign.Overall I enjoyed playing the game.If you don't mind linear games and also like time manipulation mechanics, go for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: The most important thing to understand is that it's a tactical puzzler game rather than an RPG. Combats in Iron Danger are about accurate solutions in given circumstances rather than gearing up and upgrading skills to beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of monsters. Rather Incubation that XCOM if you know what I mean.I love art style, I totally love the story - it has this nightfallish northern myths (Finnish Kalevala to be precise) that most western fantasy really lacks.I can't tell if the price suits you as I received the game for free, but the first two hours I was so immersed I felt I should've paid for it. I guess you should try the game yourself before judging it. Just remember that it's not what you might think it is from the trailer.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Is time mastery your favorite superpower? you'll love this game.This game is rare, where you manipulate time in a tactics manner.Its fun when a lot of things are going on and you need to decide how to rewind time and take different actions to mitigate damage or even death!The combat is satisfyingly special and the sound effects too, enemies have decent designs and the powerups keep coming regularly. Its great to stop time and control your chars to pull off amazing elemental combos. Pretty cool AND hot.Achievements are easy too, just play the game and in some missions you need to do certain things, nothing is missable since you can replay any mission whenever you want once you clear it. Honestly, I want more challenging achievemnents for the game, that would rock.The voice acting and dialogue is top notch for the most part and the graphics and music are good! The story is nice, its original enough to keep you invested in it, it just wish it had more surprises but I liked it nevertheless, the spoken dialogue between the main characters kept it enjoyable and interesting and everything is skippable so you dont have to review it on multiple playthroughs. Didnt care much for the cliche villains though. That ending though.. hahaha.. came out of nowhere.But anyway, game is good! Sign me up for DLCs or a sequel.As for downsides, wish you had more control of the camera Im kinda used to moving it with ASWD, move the minimap where I want (SW corner), and you cant remap keys either, also text is a wee too small for my aging eyes, Im so glad the story is voice acted.I also want trading cards of this game and more looting please.I give Iron Danger a rating of 4 hightlightable locked doors without keys out of 5 time frozen flying burning Northlanders.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice game with it's flows. Just the way I love it. Realy love the way you can turn back time and select other actions - you don't see this much.Game is not an RPG - it's a story with tacktical combat. Nothing hard with official story-related "save-scumming". Characters (mostly one) get new skills and this is all - no more advancements in the RPG territory.At first I thought that inability to save a game on map is bad, but after completing I am ok with this - not needed. I have encountered bugs only 2 or 3 times forcing me to restart a level, but when you know map and don't try to kill every moving thing - most levels can be completed in 5-10 minutes.Another thing that some people struggle with is controls and ui - for me it's pretty much ok. Sometime some skills may work in unexpected ways (fireball killing character in open air), but as you can rewind game without any issue and loading time - it's become very minor issue.A little sad that game is short. And don't have much of a challange. For the first one I can wait for the next title. For the second I would love some New Game+ mode, but it's really hard to make this game harder. It's not like ton of enemies and their HP will solve anything mostly because of time gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: I think the fact that Steam Achievements show that only 50% of people have met the healer  - the 2nd achievement that comes about an hour into the game, and is a steep dropoff from the nearly 90% for the 1st achievement - kind of tells the tale. It just...doesn't quite click.I think the idea has a lot of promise, and sometimes when things work out it can feel pretty good - cast a fireball, swap characters, attack with sword, quick kick to get some distance...things like that. But most of the time, it is just a weird puzzle to solve. I'll say that should be up my alley, an RPG combat puzzle situation, but it just doesn't quite work well enough. It's just a little too fiddly, with how you have to do actions with one character, then rewind time, then do actions with the other character, play those action timelines together, find out if what you did worked, if it didn't, try to rewind far enough and try again. I think cooldowns also play into why it doesn't feel great all the time, with somewhat limited options early on making it feel like you use your 1 or 2 obvious cooldown skills & then, waiting for cooldowns to expire, find yourself with enemies in close range and are left with few options aside from just moving away and trying to basic attack or block before they hit you. And then doing that for 2 characters.There's not many chances for ultimate failure given the rewind mechanic, but it just means a lot of rewinding and tweaking. You do get some mild options for improving some skills between each level - no open world with expansive skill trees here - but that's about the extent of the RPG systems I can see (at least after playing a bit more than 2 hours). No real gear or anything to look for, no RPG dialog typed choices. I'm not quite sure - I feel like you could make something compelling out of what they have here, but I just couldn't get into it. It's not a terrible game. It isn't a badly made game. It just...doesn't quite work, at least for me. I'd definitely be willing to see what these devs do next, though.

Over 3 years into its release.  And now you can't continue playing without doing the tutorial over and over again until accidentally getting past the bug.Completely unacceptable.

_childDocuments_.review: CON: The time manipulation and stop-and-go combat system is a noble idea, but in practice it doesn't work. The timing is EXTREMELY unforgiving, and you get to watch your character die 10-20 times in every encounter. All opponents attack faster than you do, so you either spend most of every combat blocking or die even more. Further, the block is on a cool-down, and with the really fast-attacking opponents, your block against their first attack puts you on cooldown so you get to take their second attack right in the teeth. Further, if your fight starts near an NPC conversation, you get the listen to the comments 5-10 times as you replay the first few heartbeats of the battle trying to save your characters. PRO: the story is interesting, and if you can get past the frustrating combat system then you'll probably enjoy the writing. Also, the art is pretty.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, a game that gets me and my savescummy ways.With Iron Danger, save scumming isn’t something to be ashamed of – it’s a game mechanic……so despite the name don’t expect no real sense of danger.It like a weird blend of Fable and Baldur’s Gate with the rewind mechanics of Prince of Persia.You know when you were a kid playing knights or whatnot. That one kid who was always being obtuse. You know, the one who’d be like “Nuh-uh, that didn’t hit me, that didn’t hit me - I dodged it”, and you couldn’t argue with him cause his parents spoiled him? Well… now you can be that kid. Workout some of that childhood trauma you’re holding.Honestly it’s a pretty average game. Iron Danger’s gimmick is it’s interesting spin on turn based combat. It basically plays the same way as Baldur Gate’s II on hard mode, except you reload the entire save in BG whereas, you only reload a couple of seconds each time here. The time mechanic is actually interesting, but it’s poorly implemented. It’s both really cool and annoying at the same time. If you just make sure not to advance too far, there’s no risk of actually dying. Really it’s more of a puzzle game than a strategy game. At times the gameplay felt like I was doing video editing. Literally video editing, or animation, turned combat system. Interesting but very tedious. Thought it would feel like playing Dungeon Siege but it just reminded me of work.I loved the premise, but it was a letdown that there’s no reward for going off the trails. It makes the world seem bigger and gives the appearance of there being more to the world than there actually is. The temple areas are very distinct though , as are the levels leading up-to and from them which had beautiful scenery. The story like the game mostly feels pretty forgettable.So it’s an “idiot proof” tactical RPG… but it looks pretty, so if you’re more of a casual gamer you’ll probably enjoy it. Definitely only buy on sale.6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: And this goes to show how you make a game in todays AAA economy.A most unique combat system, a character with actual relatable decisionmaking and some companions which are actually very different each of his own. The story is easy, short and still packed. It is action based, yet you can try the stealth approach and did not contain any bugs for me. Each character develops on his/her own and is not based on "killed that many enemies for XP" but has a "planned" system.The beautiful soundtrack (which goes into my playlist now), a timeless and lovely art style and the great balancing rounds everything up. You are probably the most powerful being amongst humans but still you are afraid of your enemies, what kind of game does that? Finished on normal difficulty in 12 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:*The timeline based combat is unique and makes you feel great when you do a perfect no damage run. This is why you play the game, but it's also the *only* reason to play the game.The Bad:*Game is *short* for its price. I beat it in 9.4 hours. There is no replay value.*A dire lack of mechanically interesting boss fights outside of the floating zombie bastard.*The ending sucks ass. Completely unsatisfying. Not that the story was good in the first place. It was mostly "Meh", but there were a few really bad sections that bring it even further down.  (Main character having out of nowhere feelings(?) for her sister's husband, which is then never mentioned again.)*Stoneskin instantly removes any and all difficulty from the game by giving the target 100% damage resist.*There were a few game breaking bugs. Such as the camera getting stuck after a cutscene, or not being able to pick items up.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Controlling time and playing out fights as puzzles is a really cool idea. The problem is that the game is just too fiddly. Timing attacks is an exercise in madness.Each attack has a duration, the amount of time it takes to windup, execute, and recover. During this attack time your damage will be applied at some point, all attacks are different in this regard, so you'll need to figure out if an enemy attack will land and disrupt your attack before yours executes. This might require you to play back the same attack five or six times to figure out which one can fit in between the enemy blows.Most of your attacks also have really, really long cool downs, so you'll mostly be using an ability then running around like a chicken with its head cut off waiting out the timer to let you do anything again. The constant rewinding of fights is just exhausting. Even low level enemies can one shot you so you'll get to hear those death screams a lot.The camera too is annoying as hell. They wanted to cater to people who don't like moving the camera, which I guess I sympathize with, but the result is the camera controls are too limited and crummy. I'm sure they thought that this was "simple" and dare I say this without vomiting "elegant." You control the camera by holding down the right mouse button and wagging the mouse. Like everything else in this unpolished train wreck it's fiddly, clunky, slow, and unresponsive. Like punching water, the camera just doesn't move smoothly or point where you want it.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: There are two parts to this game:1) The good is that the story is interesting, at least up until the point I quit on it.  There is some character tension that I see coming that could lead to cool narative elements.  It also has really cool mechanics (the heartbeat and rewinding time).  It really makes combats feel like a puzzle that can you figure out (I tried to play every combat with the goal of taking no damage).2) The bad, unfortunately: the mechanics of playing the game can be very wonky.  Often times, if you only want to take a single step, the system will have a hard time processing that and sometimes your character won't step until you move the perspective around to select the same spot from a seperate direction.  And what drove me to stop playing is the aspect that the ai has issues dealing with the rewind of time, especially at the start of battle.  If you are trying to sneak past an enemy and accidently get spotted, often times the enemy will lock onto you even if you rewind time until before they spot you.  They will then walk toward you and start the battle all over again.  Or they might de-aggro, but then stand still instead of following their path.Overall, the bad frustrates me too much to keep playing (for now).  I hope some of this gets patched if possible (or maybe I need a bit of time off before picking it up again).  I look forward to more content this dev puts out!

_childDocuments_.review: Game has no key rebinds.Sorry but for me, left handed, it's a no go.  I almost hate to give it a thumbs down but a PC game in 2021 not having this simple feature is crazy, I haven't coded since BASIC but I cannot believe this is a great big task.  I'm sick of people assuming everyone is right handed and/or uses WASD.  It's ridiculous really.  If it wasn't a Humble Bundle I'd refund.If you are right handed the tiny amount I played seems fun but I can't really say.I mean, yeah I grew up playing games with just the mouse for everything back on my Atari ST but c'mon.  When you hover over an action and the tool-tip shows the corresponding key you COULD use then no.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: First off I absolutely love the concept of the timeline combat, but the execution in this game isn't for me.Every little encounter becomes tedious, because even with time powers you feel underpowered and managing the action of even two characters takes a good bit of time.Your attacks have windups that last a couple heartbeats (the time currency), but the enemies attacks rarely feel like they have the same windup.This means you rarely get to properly predict melee hits to avoid them, you take them and rewind to avoid taking them.Managing multiple timelines is tedious due to the timeline moving on when you initiate an action, meaning the action plays out and then you rewind to initiate an action for another character.Aggro seems dodgy to influence even with dedicated skills to do so.On the positive, the voice acting is very nice and the OST sounds beautiful and is worth the purchase if you buy the game
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for some unique and fresh gameplay mechanism, you'll certainly find it here. Further reasons to be interested in Iron Danger are good graphics, likable characters and some really good voice actors.While good enough for the game, the engine and controls aren't perfect. In that price range I expect something slightly better.Of greater concern is that while the game design is new and unique, it doesn't offer much variety or depth. Personally I wish it would be more about strategy than a puzzle. And evading / running away while luring the enemies around is way too effective.Ultimately I consider this game a mixed bag. You can tweak combat events till you are pretty invincible, but there is no real reward for being so ambitious. I registered that I got the second shard achievement, while I missed many others already had gained for dying, killing or healing. Meaning that I ended my missions far more efficiently. That sounds good, but at the end it made no difference. And tinkering too much isn't exactly fun, when it doesn't matter. Especially when it's repetitive.So yes, I do recommend the game. Consider it a nice and short experiment, but don't expect too much. For this price you can get a more eclectic menu by other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Perfectionism is exhausting.I think this best summarizes the Iron Danger experience. Now don’t get me wrong, the first few hours of the game were a joy to play. Kipuna starts off with a wide variety of spells and actions to play with, allowing you to duck and weave through combat like a rhythm game on steroids. It feels rewarding to be able to dodge a crossbow bolt, and then follow up with a fireball which blows up the oil barrel next to the enemy. Add on my habit of save-scumming my x-com encounters, it was great to strategize and think of the best way for a no hit run.Character interactions were also sparse but meaningful, providing a clear “why” as to their motivations. Kipuna’s growth throughout the course of the game was something that the player could identify with. Presentation-wise however, I did feel that more could be done when talking about them. Other than, just “Oh I’m joining you because of XXX reason, and this is my XXX backstory which is why I want to join you.” Come on, each of them have unique origins and unique relationships. Lemichen seems like he’s more interested in banging Kouko than Ayeling for ****. Also, secondary character kits could be more distinct from each other. I love how there was the ability to fire arrows and different kinds of arrows, which provided opportunities to start kiting and managing cooldowns.However, what irked me was more of the mid-late game. As you get introduced to more and more spells and mechanics to keep things fresh, but these kits end up being so weak that you don’t really end up using them? Furthermore, the game also starts throwing at you more of the same mob characters, so rather than think about more varied ways to take out your opponents, you instead have to use the most effective strategy again and again. A.k.a the grenade. root/freeze, grenade then fireball, taking out enemies at range rather than in the heat of the combat. Why? Low risk and your melee weapons are just too weak and don’t scale. So combat encounters in the level become this slow chore where you just nuke the enemy, and try to dodge as much what they throw at you. If you decide to switch it up, more often you would just be surrounded and die, which means more time reversing. There’s also no incentive in certain cases to even engage in combat. One level I just skipped all the mobs because it would just be too much of a chore to fight them all (which I guess could be an intentional design choice?) There were also quite a few puzzles in the game, but those were pretty easy and the game does do a good job of explaining the mechanics to you and letting you figure things out on your own.Lastly, the ending. Wooo oh boy I think the ending was the main reason why I gave this a thumbs down because I did enjoy the combat in spite of its flaws. Spoilers below for my disappointment.Spoilers for endingWhen I was reading up on this game, reviews, marketing, game videos and all, it was never once mentioned to me that this was like a trilogy or it was supposed to have a sequel or something. So imagine my surprise when I defeat Kouko, who I thought was going to be a mid-boss before fighting Lowhee in the north, to be greeted with the credits right after. With the fates of the characters unknown. Now come on, you just reached the climax of getting all the shards. Lemichen resolves his major character arc. You feel like the team is finally getting somewhere and you are on to a new chapter. And credits roll. It was a huge disappointment, and it is appended by the fact that either I would have to pay more money to see the ending, or god forbid the game development is not complete and I have no idea what happens to these guys. It’s just sad that there really did not feel like there was a payoff after grinding through all the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: The concept for the combat is cool, but the execution is bad. The AI wanders around confused or makes sudden leaps at you, forcing you to use the rewind time mechanic because there's no actual good way of engaging with enemies. I know that's the point of the game, but it makes combat such a boring slog. Wait for the enemy to hit me so I can figure out what to do so he doesn't hit me.On top of that, the UI is awful. The time mechanic looks like video editing software and Excel spreadsheets look more fun than the menus. Dialogue scenes awkwardly freeze time so characters will be facing wrong directions or in awkward positions, making it even harder to actually care about what is going on. There isn't much of an "rpg" element to the game either when you your skill upgrades just lower the cooldown slightly on 'swing sword' and exploring houses and environments only rewards you with things like fish to heal your HP with.It's a shame because the actual dialogue is well-written and the voice acting is good (though the story was hard to discern apart from any other vague "bad guys invade" trope.

_childDocuments_.review: The fairy-tale world of the game "Iron Danger" feels incredibly thin and right. Starting from the smallest details, such as a global map made in an amazing ancient form, detailed artistic descriptions of each enemy, and ending with serious details of the game design, the game constantly positions itself as something solid, fully developed. This helps the player to fully plunge into the adventures of the main character and her friend, entering into complete unity with a vibrant game world filled with events and adventures. On the question of the incredible elaboration of the world, this game even reminded me of “Druidstone: The Secret of the Menhir Forest”, and then she pulled out her ace of trumps from her sleeve - time manipulation, which will be discussed a little later in the text.There is a certain share of charm in how much of the excess is cut off from this game. There is no replaceable equipment giving you statistics, there is no experience gained, there is only a gradually growing understanding of the main game mechanics, and there is the possibility, after each mission, to slightly improve one of the game skills, forming your own line of behavior in battles. At first, the main feature of the game seemed a little cheating to me, but as the complexity of the fights increases, you begin to understand that it both makes you stronger in certain elements and shows your weaknesses. The whole point is that in turn-based combat you can rewind time, trying to fix the mistakes that led to the death of your character (and then creating new ones, naturally). And if at first you feel omnipotent, instead of dying just making a clumsy enemy dash behind his back and giving him a dagger on his back, then later you find that a poisonous grenade is flying into your face at the same time, a huge orc is ready to take you off the run , and the enemy you want to make dash behind your back will not be so awkward and will have time to turn around and give you kick between your eyes. Oh, and the earth beneath your feet burns, because you managed to get a fireball over a spilled pool of oil. And then you understand that every battle here is actually a puzzle, but not with the template rules set by the developers, but all the rules and solutions for it are created exclusively by you. And this is a great and very fresh feeling.Yes, there are certain drawbacks in the game. It is very linear, sometimes the camera behaves very awkward in non-combat situations, stopping by some strange camera plans, I would like more some additional quests that would help to further learn the history of this world. But I can honestly admit that this incredibly charming plot story and characters, combined in an interesting game mechanics, completely fascinated and conquered me. And I hope that the sequel, if it happens, will add even more meat to the skeleton of the game (in the form of more game content), giving me even more interesting sensations, I definitely want to return to this game world again

_childDocuments_.review: Core mechanic - time manipulation - is really unique for this kind of game but the more I've played it, the more convinced I was that turn-based system would work much better here... Sure, it's nice that devs tried to be original but I'd rather play non-original game that's actually pleasant to play. Believe me, Iron Danger sounds fun but combat isn't pleasant at all. Planning movements for both characters is inconvenient, especially when you're fighting with great number of enemies. What's left when combat isn't fun? Story. To be honest I can't say much about the story as a whole because I didn't finish the game. However let me tell you one thing. Last time I've played it few days ago and I don't even remember the names of main characters. What did I enjoy? Character development - it's simple but you can feel that your heroes grow stronger with time. Graphics and level design are good as well... some islands remind me Zelda games. On the other hand voice acting and sounds are annoying.I was going to finish this game but I've got tired after so many frustrating fights. Still.... if you're looking for something unique you should give it a try and see it for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but the lack of saving really hinders the gameplay session and the combat is very dull.If you are going to start a level, you better be prepared to run it to conclusion or you will need to start from the beginning and the levels tend to be looooong, so if you don't have an hour or more available per level, you are better playing something else.The time traveling mechanic is novel and fun at the beginning but get old fast due to a boring set of abilities that don't give much tactical choice, the enemies tend to rush you and you are trying to dodge the blows while connecting a hit or two before having to dodge again.There are very few things in the environment that you can use to your advantage but with enemies rushing you or throwing things at you and not moving, there is not much you can do. Dodge, hit/spell, run dodging projectiles, rinse and repeat. Some more control over the enemies and better environmental hazards could have improved the tactical choices and therefore, the combat.There is a limit to the rewind that can get in the way when you are trying to get that perfect fight that is logical but sometimes a blocker to improve the fight. The game could use a controllable replay of the action to see all those "perfect" moves in real time.The plot is very obvious and not compelling...

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ did this game surprise me. I had gotten it in a humble bundle and completely forgot I had it.  During one of my "what should I play this week" search in my steam library, I came across it again and installed it on a whim. It blew me away with its amazing voice acting (seriously some of the best I've heard in a video game), excellent visuals, engrossing storyline, and an incredibly addicting game mechanic. Game Mechanic: I adored the heartbeat mechanic, where I controlled going back and forth in time. Instead of seconds, heartbeats are used, where for each heartbeat of the character, there is a step forward or backward in time. In this trance-state, time cannot progress until an action is chosen. I can choose what each character does separately, so they can do actions simultaneously, and I can rewind time to avoid them getting too much damage in a fight or dying. I also can lead the denizens of the forest toward our enemies, where they end up accidentally fighting on my side (like leading a troll to the Northlanders, that will never get old, ha!).Visual: The details really stood out on each of the levels. The individual feathers on the Tyrannogrouse, the leaves on the ground, the roots from trees -- all exquistively drawn and rendered. For an indie game, far better visuals than expected. Characters: Kipuna and the characters she meets are fully voiced with dynamic personalities. Each have their own motivations and thoughts to add to the scenes. They also served very different purposes -- the blacksmith that pounds his way through enemies, the rogue who shoots and slices, and the healer with her spear and magic. Kipuna is a reluctant hero thrust on a typical hero's journey, but her character evolves and grows as the story progresses. She goes from being an uncertain fisherfolk to a confident magic-wielding hero, and that journey is worth the play. Plot:  It is the typical heroes journey, where Kipuna has the call to adventure in the most visceral way. Kipuna eventually meets her mentor, the Healer, and with the blacksmith, Topi, goes on to the second call - where Kipuna grows into some of the magic she is gifted with. Each act has an arc that kept me rooted to my seat eager to keep playing. She eventually meets Lemichen in the  'reject adventure' phase of the hero's journey, but despite that turn away from adventure, Kipuna will be faced with no choice but to continue. The way the dialogue and character interactions happen really help dig into the personalities of the characters and how Kipuna is convinced to continue on despite her fears. It shows the growth of each character, the way their motivations and loyalties start to change, and reveals a lot of wonderful lore about the world and the main combatants. Overall: I give this 5 out of 5. This game is top-notch writing and designing. It's definitely worth the play, and now stands as one of my top 5 favorite games EVER. Thank you developers for this wild and satisfying ride!

_childDocuments_.review: When it works, the main time control mechanic is genuinely so unique and satisfying.Unfortunately that mechanic is wrapped up in a game that's ropey in every single way. The UI needs improving. Encounter design can be infuriating. Character animations are really bad making the action often difficult to read. There is no meaningful character development outside of picking one skill to upgrade after each level. There is nothing to do outside of combat, no reasons to explore levels. No items to equip or upgrade.And there are some pretty game-breaking bugs. My game bugged out about 45 minutes into the final boss level, leaving me completely unable to control my main character. Unfortunately I couldn't stomach the idea of replaying the whole last level again so I uninstalled before seeing the ending.There is definitely fun to be had here, and it's interesting as a curiosity, but very hard to recommend with the caveats above. I'd rather recommend waiting to see the same idea executed better by a more skilled dev team.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely not for me.I think what many praises (the combat system) end up being more of a chore rather than a real plus of this game. It's just trial and error really, no real skill involved. You got hit? Don't worry, just roll back time and either evade or parry.I will give it to them it's a fresh approach but not one i can stand behind. I'd rather get punished and learn how to properly deal with a type of enemy, than what this game offers.Another thing i didn't like was the camera. Simply atrocious to control (at least with keyboard and mouse, didn't bother with a controller, but this is a pc game primarily, so...).I also hate the fact you cannot save whenever you want, nor the game does anything to tell you you reached a checkpoint. _childDocuments_.review: Iron danger is a small, but well done adventure/tactical game that superficially looks a bit like a fantasy RPG. I wouldn't actually call it an RPG, though, as the story is linear, the player doesn't have any choices outside of how to approach combat and which skills to upgrade, and there's no inventory that goes above a singleplayer FPS game, either. The combat is clearly the star of the show here, based on the timeline you can scroll back on up to 7 seconds. It is clearly stop and go, but not really turnbased - well, it has 0.5 second turns, if you will. for lack of a better descriptor I'd call it pause-able real time. The player over time gains access to a wide range of skills to engage enemies with, or shape the environment through judicious application of fire or ice. It is actually quite fun, and while it can be frustrating at times and has no in-level saving, the ability to just revert any bad decision alleviates a lot of potential issues with collision boxes(that the game does have; Like having to smash a box of grenades because it's somehow impossible to grab those grenades out of the box from all but one specific angle that happens to be facing a wall). It is just immensely satisfying when things 'just work' after having tried five different angles to line up that perfect shot.I somehow completely missed this game when it released until I got it in a magazine deal. Then I binged it the entire day and a few hours of the next; The playtime shown on this review is how long it took me to beat the game on hard(and write the review, so probably closer to 12 hours).The story looks relatively simple, but the world is interesting, and the musical score is just beautiful. I can obviously not tell you if it would be worth your money, but it was definitely worth my time.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: A difficult downvote. I feel complicated to its core time manipulation mechanic. In other games that you can S/L the combats, even you could save scum it you still have to sort of think and plan it. And when the plan works through it is fulfilling. But in this game you are S/L in every moment and hardly involve any planning. You just let the time pass a few heartbeats (the unit of turns in this game), and then load back and react to it. I just feel like a machine and dont find any enjoyment after some encounters. The enemies and encounter design also heavily depends on this feature. Attacks of enemies are fast and deadly you can no way to survive without using it. Sadly this constantly S/L without actual planning give no excitement to me.and a few more cons:1. your characters are shortsighted; their view range are really limited.2. limited camera angle control; camera is centered on character and the rotation and zoom are very limited.3. sluggish control; character movement, grab item etc.4. limited rpg elements; you got nothing in games (exp/loots) from killing enemies other than your enjoyment, but since the combat quickly feel dull after constantly S/L, i cant find the reason to fight the monsters. p.s. you have to collect 6 shards in game and the steam achievement shown only 16.7% people have done the second shards...

_childDocuments_.review: Note* I did not complete this game as I only played it to Chapter 5 - Part 4. I stopped due to a bug that infuriated me. Below is the detail.The game is fun, like immensely so. I enjoy the puzzle action nature of it. This is not an RPG as some would say it is, it's a prince of persia style puzzle where you control 2 characters at a time and attempt to find the best way to complete a level. The time mechanics are great in my opinion and work well with 2 characters as you try to time attacks and movement to create a ballet of death and destruction.The story seemed interesting but not so engaging, the Main Character herself can feel very hit and miss especially early on. But overall nothing too exciting nor too bad.The bad part is the save system. So each level is relatively short and as such does not have saves within them. Instead, if you wish to restart a certain segment of a level, you have to restart the entire level. Now this isn't bad on paper itself with how short a level is and the game's time mechanic. This does however become a problem when you get a certain bug.The bug essentially makes it so that one of the characters just doesn't move or respond to your clicks, it'll also fiddle with the time mechanic. The issue with this is that at the end of *most* areas, you complete the game by boarding your ship and the ship will only leave when both characters are on board... see where i'm going with this?You essentially can't beat a level when you get this bug due to the fact that both characters can't be present on the ship. Besides that, the game has been designed to rely on 2 character combat/coop so much that having one out of the frame makes everything else much hard by a large margin. This problem becomes a major headache in the later levels when the fights are tougher and larger with more enemies. So now combine this bug with the lack of manual or autosave and you have an issue that can completely ♥♥♥♥ your entire progression in that level simply because you had bad luck.I say ♥♥♥♥ THAT ♥♥♥♥. The game is genuinely fun, but i ain't taking a step further with the knowledge that my progress can be reset due to the games save design combined with bugs. So if you wish to buy this game, do so at a sale and do sale with the knowledge that this can happen to you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not an easy recommendation for me. The combat mechanic is fun, time warp lets you rewind time to plan out moves for the two characters in the party. It's really satisfying to be able to 'foresee' what is going to happen, move a character into position in advance and perform all kinds of coordinated attacks, combos, or just a sneak attack where one person threw an oil barrel, while the other blew it up with a fireball. There are tons of fun to experiment, especially after unlocking more abilities later into the game. That is the good part.The bad part. To me, the writing in this game is very bad. It is very crude and boring to read. Characters reacts strangely to one and other or speak entirely of gibberish. Maybe the writer see that as clever, but it aren't actually making the impact they are hoping for. It's just seems really amateurish to me.And that bring us voice acting. With all due respect to the voice actors, they really tried to make it entertaining with these badly written dialogues. But they are just trying too hard. The fake accents are very well...fake and emotions just doesn't match with context. It is very awkward, and makes me wanting to skip the dialogues even more. All in all, the story is just something I cannot get into at all.Finally. This is probably the thing I don't like the most. There are no manual save in the game. Every time you quit in the middle of a level, you'll have to play the thing from the beginning again. Some of those levels have pretty long encounters that lasts a while, and if you want to take a break after that? Nope, you'll have to start all over, or force yourself to go through the whole level first.Bottom line, I am recommending this game based solely on the combat mechanic and it's generally a fun experience to have. Other parts of the game such as presentation and music are just standard. While the story and the voice acting are simply awful. Get it only if you are not expecting anything from the narration perspective.

_childDocuments_.review: Generally enjoyable game, with some flaws. TLDR: I enjoyed the combat. What I found frustrating was the camera controls, and lack of manual saving.Most importantly, I believe the only point to playing the game is the combat, as the game is so linear, you don't make interesting choices to create a unique story about your character, and the story is mediocre enough that it's not going to carry the game if you don't enjoy the combat.To that point, I enjoyed the combat and rewind mechanic quite a bit, but I don't think it's for everyone. While overall I thought it was a little easy (there are options to increase the difficulty, which I did not use), it made me feel very clever, even though I know I am no tactical genius. The biggest thing for me was that I enjoy futzing around with optimizing, then testing it, then refining it, then testing, then refining, and so on, and that's exactly what you get here. If you don't like repeating similar choices repeatedly, you may not enjoy the combat. I do wish enemies better telegraphed an incoming attack, so you don't always have to get hit before you know when you will get attacked.There are several things that are different from typical RPGs. One of those differences is that the game is played very linearly in levels (like Mario). Start with chapter 1 part 1 map, then you go to chapter 1 part 2 map, and so on, and once you finish a level you can't choose to come back. After each map, where there is combat, you usually can choose 1 ability to upgrade among several options, or pick up a new skill from a very small selection.My biggest frustration by far was autosave at end of levels only, which can range from 10-40 minutes, with the average being in the middle there somewhere. That frustration was compounded when at the end of one of the levels, a bug prevented me from walking through the exit door to complete the level, causing me to have to restart and play the whole level again. My other main frustration is camera controls. I just want to zoom out and see more at once.Game is not long if you compare it to most RPGs, but it's repetative enough that I was glad that it did not overstay its welcome. The game ends with some apparent loose ends, so I expect a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: -Eye catching graphics and really pleasant music-Core mechanic (time manipulation) is always a fun tool to play around with and as you get better at it, at it's peak points aligning the moves of your characters almost makes you feel like a ballet coreaographer set on producing a play of the perfect kill-A couple hours in, while the story admittedly doesn't seem mind blowing, but seems solid enough to make you want to continue playing-Opportunity to play around with mixing elements borrows mild Divinity vibes-Due to the above points, combat feels more like solving puzzles than pure action which is a nice change of pace-Might just be my personal taste, but I definitely had the feeling the game starts super slow-Call it nitpicking if you want, but the way your characters meld together when just roaming freely triggers me slightly-While setting up heartbeats (turns) for one of your characters during combat, as soon as you issue an action, time moves to show the "results" of your choice which on one hand makes perfect sense, but therefore guaranteed forces you to turn back time to set up your other character - once again, I see why this makes sense, I jsut wish there was an option to tick that would allow time to only start moving again once I want it to, aka once I've arranged all actions I want at given timeThis is clearly a first impression review not a full playthrough one, but from what I've seen and experienced so far,

_childDocuments_.review: Putting a label on Iron Danger is a tough one, because it sidesteps a lot of neat, tidy classification. It's kind of an RPG? But not really. It's super strategic? Yet there's a lot of puzzle to it as well. But I don't think there's a point in trying to label Iron Danger, because I'd much rather talk about how cool Iron Danger is.Iron Danger reminds me a lot of , in the sense that both are fantasy-based kind-of RPGs, both are built around a super strong, super interactive gimmick, and both were unexpected pleasant surprises. Here in Iron Danger, the gimmick is a time-bending mechanic that adds a whole new layer to Real-Time with Pause.Each fight takes place on a slowed down timeline, where you control a pair of characters and queue up actions that cost a certain number of heartbeats—about half a second each. Abilities have a ton of different outcomes and effects that can really muck about with the environment; kick the enemy into the spike trap, knock over the tree just as they walk by, throw the molotov at just at the right time to set the oil patch ablaze. Think the kind of environment tricks you can pull in Divinity Original Sin and you'll get a solid idea of the potential combos in Iron Danger.Unlike Divinity, though, fights in Iron Danger are constantly in flux thanks to your scroll-wheel. All of your actions are logged on a handy timeline, and until the heartbeat in question goes offscreen you can mulligan and rewind beat by beat to change every action. It really feels like editing a fight scene, scrubbing back and forth to find new angles for better outcomes. Set up a perfect little attack-block-knockdown combo with your sturdy warrior, then scroll back and enchant his weapon with your rogue-wizard. Set off a raging wildfire, then rewind to make sure your other character dodges clear. Watch your warrior die, then scroll back and interrupt the kill with a quick backstab. You can't go back forever, but six-ish seconds is more than enough time to completely change the engagement.As you can imagine, there's a ton of butterfly effect possibilities with this system! It's a lot of fun in action, with a real puzzle vibe in turning things to your favour with the limited resources and cool-downs at your disposal.Like I alluded to, it's not quite a "true" RPG because there's no gear and little customization. You do get ability upgrades at the end of certain chapters, but aside from restocking consumables there's not much incentive to go off the beaten path. It's kind of nice in some ways, though, to know that pausing and rewinding to surprise a couple dudes and sneak past the rest is just as rewarding as an all-out brawl.There's a couple of quirks. Most are minor ones, like not being able to pick up the occasional consumable or a very rare frame-stutter. A couple are a bit more medium, like the way changing your actions impacts the AI—I almost think the game needs a threat meter or something, because changing a character's position can completely alter how enemies behave. Even shifting a step or two from across the room can completely bork up their partner's queued up flurry if the AI suddenly changes targets for no good reason—it's particularly noticeable with the hard-hitting ranged enemies.The big one for a lot of people though will be that the game doesn't have a manual save. I definitely understand why it was cut; there's a lot of moving parts in levels and saving that much variable data isn't exactly easy. And the game was clearly designed with this weakness in mind, since most levels are very short and the time-bending means it's exceedingly rare to lock into an unwinnable timeline. Personally I think sticking with between level saves really encourages you to dig deep and explore every possibility to scrape through a seemingly unwinnable situation, rather than just quickloading and stomping the second attempt. I think I only had to restart one super early level once, because often some rarely used spell or item ended up being the exact thing needed to save the day.But seriously, even with a few minor complaints I still really enjoyed Iron Danger. My first impression was of a pretty alright looking action RPG, but the time-editing gimmick is so cool and so interesting that it elevates the game well beyond what I was expecting. I would definitely recommend at least checking out the demo, because it's a super creative mechanic that's a lot of fun to mess with.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me be VERY clear. I DO recommend this game. The story itself is very good, simple and straightforward, but good. The gameplay is excellent. I've never played a game quite like this, it's kind of like Superhot meets Baldur's Gate. The gameplay does have problems. Even though you are travelling as a party of 4 all of whome fight at several points, you are only allowed to actually fight as a pair(one of which being the lead), which is dissappointing. The other problem it has is that the lead has a total of 2 offensive spells, and the rest are either buffs or de-buffs which means that, weirdly for a protagonist, she plays a support role to her friends who are the ones actually doing damage.So, why have I given this a thumbs down? What the HELL was with all of the man hatred?! Here are 2 direct quotes from the game:"He is a man, and men long in their hearts to crush all others underfoot." This, by the way, was spoken by the "great good" in the game, basically a God who guides the lead in her quest."I knew how grateful she was, and that, unlike an ordinary human, especially a man, she felt no shame for having relied on me to find and rescue her from danger."And it's not just those. The lead has 3 companions, a man who is portrayed as a simple, though loyal, person: a harmless idiot. Another man who is given 1 trait: a hatred for one particular individual...until he says out of absolutely NOWHERE "Hey, come over here and give me a kiss." to the lead. This is not taken as a joke and it is never mentioned again, like the writer suddenly said to themselves one day "Wait, I forgot to make him unlikeable. I know, I'll throw in some casual sexual harrassment, that will have no long-term repercussions. That will sort everything out!" And finally a woman, who is the ONLY PERSON the lead trusts and goes to for advice or help (the second quote is a reference to this woman from the lead).Mechanically this game is great. It has a good few bugs, I only experienced half of the final boss fight because the other half died off screen without me doing anything, but it is a very fun game with a really interesting gimmick. It's just a shame the writer seems to be sexist.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Despite Iron Danger being paraded as being an extremely innovative RPG with time manipulation mechanics, to me, it felt the same as if I was playing any other RPG (think Divinity: Original Sin) except this time the combat happened in (mostly) real-time and wasn't strictly turn-based: I am convinced that you could beat the entire game without ever using time manipulation by just being patient and paying attention to your surroundings, but I am not patient enough for that. As it stands, this "innovative" new mechanic is basically just an in-universe way of savescumming and thus correcting the mistakes you make in combat: It can revive you, can stop you from getting hit and can tell you when exactly enemies are going to attack. You're free to use this mechanic however much you want. There is no usage limit in fights so you're pretty much invincible.While I enjoyed the combat system well enough and I'd say it's pretty much the sole reason I finished the game, it quickly became worse and worse the more abilities the main character got. Since Iron Danger is your typical "Chosen One" story and there is no gameplay and story segragation in this game, your main character quickly reached a point where she could take down entire armies by herself. Now, this wouldn't be so terrible if her companion characters, which you are forced to take with you on missions, also got stronger at an appropiate rate but they didn't. Mid- to lategame missions all felt like escort quests because of this: You now had to prevent the nearly useless companion characters from dying. They were an active hindrance. As I have already alluded to, I can't recommend this game for its story either. In Iron Danger, character motivations are just completely all over the place: It also features banger lines like "Men are inherently untrustworthy. If they gain power, they seek to crush others underfoot" and has a shaman constantly flirting with the main character despite having known her for a grand total of 2 seconds and despite looking like she (the shaman) is about twice her age.But that's not all: The main cast doesn't even seem to get along with each other: They constantly start conflicts between each other for next to no reason at all... which is why I actively started rooting against them and hoped for them to fail by the time I reached the midgame.The dialogue in this game honestly just made me uncomfortable to read. I picked up this game because I expected to get an RPG with innovative gameplay and an epic story but I ended up getting neither. Even worse is the fact that the story didn't even get finished and ends in a cliffhanger. I cannot recommend playing this game to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Quite an interesting style of combat.Time is at your disposal and you can turn back time to a degree and deal with the enemy and puzzles the game throws at you.It is quite a unique way of handling the combat, and for the most part, it works rather well.There's not really death per say, the characters can die, and you can't progress if they do so, but you can revert time to avoid that, characters are extremely vulnerable and it's a challenge to see how to succeed in combat without recieving any or as less damage as possible.The game will have you control the main character Kipuna and 1 of 3 other characters that each have their own abilities.Who goes with Kipuna is determined on the level, so you don't have to worry about that.You're encouraged to use not only the characters abilities in combination with eachother, but also the various  items you pick up throughout the game, such as bombs, barrels with oil or fuel, bear traps  and "enviromental triggers" such as trees being able to fall over damaging enemies, or to destory a log pile and they tumble towards the enemy and it's fun to get a "combo" going where the 2 characters support eachother in dealing with the opposition.However some abilities seem vastly more useful than others and some seem downright useless except for rare instances.It takes a bit getting used to, but it's fun once you've realized the idea behind it.Sadly the game is quite buggy where you hardly have a mission/level without some sort of bug appearing, enemies stuck in the geometry, player characters getting teleported a short distance because of the enviroment glitching, certain items you can pickup won't register, enemies will walk into an object for eternity, some enemies will bug out and not attack you nor can you attack them, interactive elements not working and so on ad nausea.One thing that might put people off, is that there is no save state in the missions, challenge wise i don't mind it, but you can't exit the game either and have a "load the game up halfway through this mission".If you start a mission you need to complete it until you reach the next loading screen.The levels and missions themselves aren't terribly long, so it's not the biggest issue, but is still there.Pathfinding can be a bit wonky both for the enemies but also for your characters.Visually it looks nice, and has a great style for itself, it's a great mix of steampunk, fantasy and finnish folklore. But i wish it had a colorblind mode to change the color of the poison from green to blue or purple as that would stand out more in the green forests, but it might be deliberate that they have made it that color for the sake of being a "hidden trap" and it's a minor nitpick on my end.Voice acting is quite good, especially for the main cast.There is dialogue in the game where your characters discuss certain areas and enviroments, but is only conversed through text.There is also an issue with the dialogue popping or cutting off when going from 1 voice actor to another, it does not happen all the time but was noticeable.Music is great and sets the mood perfectly and was varied greatly.While having an interesting world and lore, the actual story is a bit on the "meh" side, it's a bit "generic" for a lack of better word, it's not terrible, but it does not feel unique.It's a lot about how each side is trying to "manipulate" kipuna into doing their bidding and be the "right thing to do", none of them are entirely incorrect from their viewpoint, but it is in the end the choice of Kipuna.Most of the time it's "go collect this shard and learn about a new set of spells". Plus some of the writing just feels out of place.It also ends on a cliffhanger, and wheter or not we're getting a sequel for it, or the ending is supposed to be left up to interpretation i do not know, but keep that in mind that the conflict of the story didn't really end.If you've been intrigued by the combat, i could definetly recommend the game, it was overall great fun, but the story was lacking a bit and there was a bunch of bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: "I ain't got time to bleed", I mutter to myself as I turn back the clock a few moments after taking some minor damage from an especially vicious mutant chicken. This would happen several times throughout the fight, where I would find that my chosen action would result in one of my characters getting nicked by a talon or bitten in the behind. I simply couldn't allow it, and because Iron Danger allows me to rectify my missteps by undoing them in real-time, I'd never have to.The ability to literally role back time in the midst of combat is, short of using an exploit, one of the single most powerful mechanics available to players. Some might consider it to be equivalent to an ill-regarded practice known as save scumming, which is the act of rolling back to a previous save as to avoid penalties when a playthrough goes awry. However, Iron Danger's gameplay schtick hinges on the player's ability to turn back time to, in essence, achieve their most ideal outcome. While some my turn their nose up at this, I think the game is much better for it.For a bit of backstory, Iron Danger is a fantasy CRPG heavily steeped in Finnish folklore (thanks Wikipedia). The story revolves around Kipuna, a village girl who, through a series of unfortunate and catastrophic events, becomes imbued with the power to manipulate time and defy death itself. Soon after, Kipuna finds herself at the center of an idealogical war that will ultimately prove to be the test of her strength and loyalties.The graphics are adequate, and the world itself is visually pleasant. The art style is reminiscent of the Torchlight series, which is fine by me. Additionally, much of the dialogue is voice acted, and I actually find myself caring about the characters. For the most part, the chemistry between Kipuna and her chosen companion is fun to watch play out, so no complaints there. However, Iron Danger's selling point isn't its graphics, story, or characters - though those things definitely help. Rather, it's the gameplay that makes Iron Danger stand out amongst its peers.Think contemporary RPGs such as Divinity: Original Sin, or Diablo 3 - except with a more inviting color pallet. Then consider how either of those games could possibly intersect with an audio editor such as Audacity or Garage Band. What you end up getting is Iron Danger, which blends the hotbar driven gameplay that you've come to expect with those aforementioned titles, and a slider interface that's used to manipulate the passage of time. It sounds a little weird, but it actually works really well.I've talked at length about how much I'm into Iron Danger's time-rewind mechanic, so I'll try not to repeat myself too much. However, it really is the lynch-pin of the whole game. The ability to harness time itself fundamentally changes the way you approach gameplay, which creates an interesting dynamic between the player and their journey.In most RPGs, I tend to feel like combat is more of a means to an end rather than a destination - whether it be to grind out levels, develop character stats, or to simply advance the storyline. That is to say, combat can end up feeling like a bit of a chore. While combat does indeed contribute to your ability to advance the storyline, Iron Danger doesn't really subscribe to those other constructs - such as leveling or stats. As a result, combat becomes the central focus of the game, which I imagine is why the developers made it as dynamic as it is.For instance, when there's only one or two enemies on screen, it's fairly easy to get away with taking a more cavalier approach to dispatching them. With two active characters under your command at any given time, it's not unheard of to simply shock and awe your opponents into the ground without any consequences. However, when you get up in numbers and find yourself facing down a small militia's worth of foes, you need to be a little more calculating if you've any hope of surviving.Your characters aren't particularly beefy and can easily be overwhelmed, which it's why it's so important to maintain awareness and a level head during combat. At first, I found it to be a little difficult to juggle two characters at once, and honestly, if not for that coveted allowance of 5 seconds to explore frontwards and backwards, it would actually be untenable. However, being that I'm able to focus on one character for seconds at time, then switch over to the other and replay those same frames from their perspective provides for some satisfying moments where proper coordination can pay off in a big way. Alternatively, if things don't quite pan out the way you had hoped then you can always roll back the clock and try something else. It's almost as if Iron Danger just wants players to be the best versions of themselves, and to play without having to compromise.If there's one thing that I learned from playing Iron Danger, it's that I don't have to accept anything the way it is if I have the ability to change it. A powerful sentiment in the abstract, but even more so in the context of a game that literally lets me time travel.What more can I say about how much I enjoy Iron Danger. It's an understated fantasy RPG that's both charming and straight to the point. The built-in rewind mechanic is a literal game-changer, and allows an otherwise tedious process of button smashing to become much more calculating and rewarding. For these reasons, Iron Danger has earned its place as one of my favorite games of 2020.

_childDocuments_.review: If Divinity: Original Sin, had a child with Vanilla Skyrim, it would be Iron Danger. Trust me when I tell you, however, that this game will still have you hooked to see Kipuna's journey through to the end.Iron Danger is a tactical, RPG-ish game where you take on the role of Kipuna, a civilian who, during a Northender raid of her village, falls through the floor to her death. Impaled by the Aurolith shard, she is suspended in time and space and a spirit tells her that the shard has reacted to her and granted her the power to turn back time. She does exactly that to avoid falling to her doom, and realize that the shard is forever impaled in her chest, and if she attempts to take it out, she will suffer the fate that the shard helped her avoid in the first place... Reminds me almost of the jewels worn by the red priests in the Song of Ice and Fire (Game of thrones) where if they take them out, they instantly turn to dust seeing is they are supposed to be long dead but the jewel keeps them going! Anyways, meeting with a Smith who saves her from the raid, Topi, Kipuna must now, under orders, travel the world in search of other shards that would also grant her more power... Power to burn and destroy, power to regrow, power to freeze. As with all storylines like this, the true evil is always closer than you think, and the Iron soldiers of Northend are the least of the dangers you'll face in your journey.Let's talk graphics, and this is basically Original Sin! Minus the interractions and in-depth gameplay. Iron Danger's core mechanics are really, really simple to get a hang on, until you're tasked to control TWO characters... Space allows you to go into Trance Mode, which is basically Baldur's Gate combat mode, every character has got a timeline associated to skills, if you fail you can go back in time and try other tactics. You should also get accustumed to how using your mouse to activate a skill on an enemy glitches your character out so sometimes they get bashed before they can get out their skill... However, this becomes easier to handle once you unlock Kipuna's Swamp magic (you can then suspend enemies in place, making it easier for Topi to eradicate them). I said "RPG-ish" because there is no level up system, except for maybe leveling up your skills after each chapter. The game also has got very limited exploration, with it being split into chapters, much like an FPS game... a cutscene plays at the end and then you're in the next chapter, and it just works! If you come into Iron Danger with the thought that it's an exploration RPG, then you might get really disappointed.At first, I thought the voice acting was cringeworthy but a few hours in, I gotta say that it grew on me! It's really that good... Kipuna's distress really shows through her voice and Kopi's protective fatherly behaviour towards her reminds me of famous father figures from videogames I played before... They make a great team. Iron Danger is, for me, an  tactical action game which is straight forward, simple to grasp but could do without the clunkiness of your characters during vital moments of combat where it is imperative that they don't fail to respond.

_childDocuments_.review: After an hour played for my coverage of the Humble Choice October 2020Ever feel like you wanted another chance in a video game to fix a mistake a few seconds ago?  That’s Iron Danger.  The main character here dies and then gets the magic power to go back about 7 seconds.  From there she can change any action that she or another character makes.  So suddenly instead of taking damage, she can dodge out of the way. It’s an interesting concept but it feels like it gives the player entirely too much power to balance.  I’m sure there’s a difficulty to the game, but it’s like being Superman. You have to come up with ludicrous ideas to even get a balance. Also this is a level based game, rather than an open world, though it certainly looks like a MMORPG or a typical Western RPG. Pick this up if the concept of manipulating time interests you at all.  It’s done very well, and I do applaud the developer.  But it’s very fiddly, so you’ll be jumping back and forth multiple times in the hopes of surviving each encounter. _childDocuments_.review: Sands of time as a turn-based ARPG.There's nothing inherently wrong with the premise, but the execution is bland to the point of utter boredom. The main character gets dragged through the opening stages of the Hero's journey the way I get dragged through my morning routine. There's no sense of wonder, even when literal time travel is involved, because I'm simply not invested in any of these people or places.The gameplay doesn't help here. Infinite amounts of retries via the time manipulation removes all sense of stakes, and the absurdly high lethality makes anything less than perfect play a losing proposition. These two facts combined result in tedious timeline-scrubbing while you look for a "perfect" solution, and when you finally get through combat unscathed, it's an anticlimax.

The whole system is working against you. The gameplay both in and outside of combat ranges from mildly annoying to unbearable to infuriating.The only good thing about this game is the soundtrack which you can probably find online, just avoid this garbage.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't want to write this, but after not one, but two game-breaking bugs, I uninstalled the game, because I am not replaying another level. Manual saves and/or frequent autosaves? You wish! The game only seems to autosave when you leave an area and it can take quite a while to open up the next area. The first bug didn't let me finish the tutorial, because there was no "Sail away" icon to click on. It appeared the second time I played it and the tutorial wasn't long, so it didn't bother me that much.The second bug I encountered was after a particularly hard fight roughly half-way through the game fighting an evil forest spirit called Kade (one of several tough fights on that Foxwood map), where I had to activate "light pillars" with some fire magic to gain access to a temple, but the pillars were gone, so no way to open the temple, no way to go the next area and thus have the game autosave. There were in-game arrows pointing downwards where the pillars were meant to be and it was far away from the fighting, so while my fireball has plenty of splash damage, it couldn't possibly have damaged them. If it still did and there is a way to actually destroy such important items, well, that's just stupid design. The game has its flaws, besides the game-breaking bugs, but the rewind time mechanism often allows you to undo mistakes, like characters running in the wrong direction or not doing anything at all. This game is micromanagement paradise or hell, depending on your preferences. The combat abilities are useful and you control two characters with different skill sets, meaning you have plenty of options. It has very good background music and voice acting and I kind of liked the story. I will probably look up the rest of the game on YouTube now, like I've done with other games that are great in several ways, but fail in the gameplay department. At one point in the story, our reluctant heroine says "No! I don't want to do this anymore!". Same, girl, same.

_childDocuments_.review: A story packed game with the ability to reverse time.  + Artstyle/Graphics+ Story+ Soundtrack+ Voice acting+ Unique gameplay  - Content- Occasional Freezing/Crashing  Decent game, not perfect.The game is very colourful.I liked the soundtrack, unfortunately, it kept on repeating quite often since there are not many songs.Voice acting was really nicely done, but some lines of text are not voiced.The ability to go back in time during the fights is great at first but gets a bit annoying after a while, especially when controlling 2 characters which is like 90% of the time. Towns are pretty empty, even if they are filled with NPC, there are almost no dialogues and some chapters are just a filler with no other content in mind whatsoever.No sidequests, no decisions just a streamlined story.It feels like a lower budget or a rushed game.The fights are fun once you get to a chapter 4-5 and learn some useful skills. I had some issues with the game not loading from the save after chapter 3 and freezing. I expected more from the ending.   15 - 20 hours   Easy (can be done in a single playthrough)  8/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you were to tell me you wanted to mix turn-based, rts, rpg and throw in some time manipulation.. I would expect it to fall flat. There have been a handful of games that have unconventional mixes of genres and maybe some do ok. Action Squad nailed it. Gaining XP, improving your skills through riskier gameplay instead of end-of-level upgrades. More than 2 party members! Finding the best way to destroy enemies without dying and having to rewind time and try a different way. More of a narrative than a full on RPG game but still very good. One issue - Turns my GPU into a jumbo jet and even then the temp went up by 20c. Hopefully this can be optimised soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Danger

_childDocuments_.review: Man I wish they had a 5 star system, instead of thumbs up or down. This is a very good idea badly executed. The game embraces save scumming, but doesn't allow normal saving, so you have to redo the whole level if you make a single mistake. The plot is boring and unoriginal, the voice acting passable.
