_childDocuments_.review: this is one of the most unique game I have ever played. the puzzles are not too hard but require significant creativity to solve them. this is true for the other aspect of the game. navigating through different part of the scenes and retrieving/finding the required information may be challenging sometimes but this is what makes the game rewarding. it forces you to think and be creative. the story is thrilling and interesting. I would not say I loved the end of it which was a kind of "meh" but at some degree it was an acceptable outcome and it did not ruined the whole experince :) in this genre it is a 10/10 piece to me and it worth the price (got on 75% sale).

_childDocuments_.review: Like many other reviewers have said, the story was amazing. My girlfriend and I were completely engrossed by it. Like you ever play a game where you just get completely sucked into it to where you forget you are playing a game and feel like you're actually there, actually have characters speaking to you? This game is the first in a while now that has done that to me.UNLIKE many reviewers, I have absolutely no problem with the controls. I really liked how you switched between the cameras and controlled the sphere. I think one of the people reviewing it here didn't know they could control the cameras...and I have no clue what the people talking about needing three hands to play the game are talking about. I finished the game last night and there are zero times you need three hands to do something...Maybe those reviews were before an update or something, because I also had no bugs.Anyway, the visuals are amazing, music and sound effects are amazing, the story had me piecing together theories of what's happening each step of the way, and I was engaged in a way that I felt emotionally connected to the characters and world. This is a great game that I highly recommend.Also, I'm a giant wimp, so if you are worried this game is too scary for you, I promise it's not!

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the game with mouse and keyboard and I've suffered unforseen consequences. Like seriously, it was a real pain the a$$. Honestly, it's not bad, just don't play the game if you're dumb when it comes to navigations/puzzles and if you're not playing the game with a controller. Sadly, I check all the boxes and my experience was a pure torture of a 5-hours session playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the discovery part of this game. Everything is a puzzle and figuring out what to do is sometimes a little frustrating, but satisfying. When you make progress you feel really good about it and look forward to the next challenge.It took me just over an hour to get through the intro and big reveal about what you're actually up to. I really loved that. I thought I was just past my first mission, but nope a big reveal is made and you realize this was just the appetizer. I'm really looking forward to the main course.There was one thing I didn't like and that is the key mapping. I'm hoping to be able to change as I hate WASD mappings and never use them because as someone who types a lot I find that position annoying since those positions aren't under fingers with more control. Anyway it's a personal thing but leads into a puzzle I found annoying as it required some extraordinary speed using WASD and I don't know if you're supposed to fail the puzzle, but with that mapping I have no chance. It's a timed challenge. Maybe it's just a tension builder. Who knows?Overall I feel drawn into this game and want to go play more to see what is going on.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best narrative games I have played. Instantly fell in love with the story and the setting. It's like a mix of 2001 and Alien. Most of the gameplay is puzzle and mystery solving. The camera movement speed when using the stationary cameras is a little too slow IMO. I didn't encounter any glitches. The graphics are beautiful. Had a good time playing this and would for sure play again in the future. Would make a great movie.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like so many others in its genre. There's space, there's an alien signal, and there's black goop. No, none of it gets explained, and there isn't a narrative, just characters reacting to things and then a vague ending. It's not tense, it's not intriguing, and the worst thing about it is that it's short. Don't play this game if you want real intrigue or a story of any kind.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Great cinematic game with practical puzzle solving and a cool story.  The perspective from the AI makes for some interesting gameplay.  Very clear inspiration from Space Odyssey 2001.  There's a lot of hidden little things in the story that you may not immediately notice, and they don't explain outright - which is nice.  Good for a playthrough, but not much more than that.  It could have expanded a bit on some of the missions/story lines, but I suppose it could have thrown off the pacing.  The idea of being an AI handling station warnings and fixing stuff could be a game in itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: On a serious sale I would definitely recommend this, but under any other logic just skip this one. Their previous game, Stories Untold, is a great example of a studio making the best of what they have, and this one is no exception to that. The reason I don't recommend is that the game is frustrating as hell. Online, the game claims to take 6-7 hours to beat, but i beat it in 5ish, and I feel i could beat it in 2 if the game didn't leave me struggling to find what I'm supposed to do so often. The game mostly sticks you in a navigation sphere or observation cameras with an fps that looks like 50, there is tons of visual noise to add immersion at the cost of visibility, and the map is a migraine to navigate. When given a task you're often left wondering what it is you're actually supposed to be doing. For example, you may get asked to do something such as turning power back on for the space station, but they will neglect to tell you how, where, or what you're supposed to do in order to achieve that goal. The answer could be on a small post-it note hidden on the station or laying within an unpowered laptop you have to happen upon. To make this worse, the game always gives you the option to have the characters repeat their orders for you so you never forget your mission, yet having them repeat the order never provides any additional help. You can ask for repetition 10 times and they will never change their phrasing or give any hints to make locating the task easier. I could get over the lack of guidance the game provides if the story remained as interesting as the introduction. The game really starts firing on all cylinders, but progressively seems to add more confusing sifi surealism instead of continuing off of a great opening twist. The game ends up making sense, but not in a way that really makes you care... Surely not worth the headache of getting through the game. I would blame myself for having trouble with this one, but various people i've personally talked to as well as reading more comments surrounding the game seem to agree with me. It's a really cool concept and definitely has some good moments in it, but the overall lack of clarity and shallow gameplay really bogs down the game as a hole. For the sake of the visuals, the studio, and a story that could have been much better, I'd say wait for a sale and play Stories Untold first.Pros:Great intro and story hookAmazing conceptVery prettyGreat sound designCons:You will not care about a single character If there was ever a game that needed a waypoint marker it's this oneOverly confusing mapHorrible visibility (granted you can remove some of the camera aesthetic gimmicks in the settings)Story gets worse the more you playAll gameplay is akin to Among Us tasks
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is an exceptionally well crafted narrative game which has you take the novel role of an AI helping a human character. I really enjoyed the role reversal at play here, and how the gamified elements were designed as if you were interfacing with computers / code around your environment. Really clever.Voice acting as very cool, animations were very good for a non-AAA title and the story and space station(s) looked great.Like other users, the game is unforgiving when it comes to telling you what to do next, and you will frequently need to google what the next step is to understand what you missed or where you need to go. So as long as you expect to have this 'barrier' element, which could have been matured more by the developers then you'll have an enjoyable experience.On a really small note, but one that annoyed me considering how much detail was put into crafting a realistic space experience;
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The story is the best thing about this game. But the parts that make this game a game really let it down and I wouldn't recommend buying it unless it's frustration you desire.Some minigames feel downright impossible with the keyboard/mouse controls (which were clearly an afterthought), and the connection spheres, which you're in for half the game, are frustrating to control regardless of whether you're using a controller. A lot of the minigames serve only as useless time sinks and quickly become a chore. Accompanied by an otherwise fine but confusing story, you'd be forgiven for ending up disillusioned with that too.The best way to enjoy this game - and you  probably enjoy it this way - is watching a playthrough, where the boring parts are edited out.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of the comments say the game is boring, I have to be honest, I'm an anxious person, so I get bored very easily. I didn't felt bored playing Observation at all. Also, the game is not too long, you can finish it in one day.What could be frustrating was that at some points you are not sure what to do, and I have to admit, that in 2 or 3 puzzles I had to google them because I had no clue what to do. But that is how puzzle games work right ?The space station graphics are so real I thought, in the beginning, it was real video footage lol only realised it was not when the main character showed up, and you can see in her face and movements that is a game.I can only say I liked it and recommend, specially for everyone that likes space/sci-fi games, is a very different concept.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.user: im sorry im not that good
_childDocuments_.review: Honestly an amazing game that gives me similar vibes to the movie cloverfield paradox at first. But it goes into a whole new feeling of something lovecraftian as soon as you start getting into the real exploration of things. I can't reccomend this enough to anyone who likes atmospheric and story rich horrors. The fact that it's in space only makes it the more enjoyable to me personally.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: While Observation isn't the most "fun" game out there, it's enjoyable the same way that watching a film or reading a book is, providing good intrigue, and keeping me entertained for the 5 or so hours it took to complete the main story. I personally think that £20 is a bit steep for the time it takes to finish, but getting it on sale is well worth the price
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This game won't be for everyone but I absolutely loved it. The most memorable game I've enjoyed in 2020.It's essentially an interactive SciFi thriller from the same vein as Moon or 2001 AD. Make sure not to read any spoilers because that's the best part for me.Also, I highly recommend you use a controller if you have one. I played most of the game with a mouse and keyboard but there are 2 puzzles in the game that are bloody impossible with keyboard controls - I suspect this game was designed with analogue sticks being their preferred play style.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The plot might be good and actually interesting, but I will never find out, since this is the dullest game I have played in a  long, long time... "Hey Sam, why dont you fly out of the space station and do some pointless, tedious tasks? Oh, a map would help you to find your way and help with this god-awfull navigation system? Nope, can't have it! Sorry!"If you enjoy a walking simulator where you are basically one-legged, blind and randomly turned around and random intervals, then this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Overall had this game for some time now and finally being able to make it work with zero help from the dev team was a let down.  There are methods to make it work but it might take a little effort to get the game started just be warned.   After that... smooth sailing, no crashes just an odd glitch that would reset my default resolution down to its lowest setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Dive into “Observation” for a thrilling adventure in space! As an AI, you’ll team up with a crew member for an intriguing mission aboard a space station. The game’s fresh perspective and engaging story will keep you hooked, while the creative gameplay brings a new twist to the sci-fi genre. It’s all about fun and discovery in this well-crafted universe, where every moment is designed to delight and surprise. Get ready for a space exploration that’s as entertaining as it is thought-provoking!
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: For any person who enjoys Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey or practically anything written by Heinlein will enjoy this game. You play from the perspective of a rogue AI. The game can be a little droning, but you are literally a program, so it makes sense. I'm an analog control gamer for the most part, and this was easy for me to play KBM. The story is pretty good. Lots of suspense. And the ending, really the last third of the game, had plenty of twist. It was one of the few games that each time I put down, I wanted to go get back on and see what was coming up next. Loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10, above average due interesting setting. Console game ported to PC without polish. No thumbing up or down, but Steam forces me to do it.Positives:+ voice actors are ok.+ sphere controls are completely ok (played Descent 3D a lot). Lot of players complain about this but just fine-tuning sensitivity fixes any issues.+ space ship interior and exterior is exciting to explore (first time, until you have to backtrack)+ graphics are sort of ok on Ultra High but I would like one notch more for gfx settings as we can't make sense from printed labels etc. which are around the ship. Turned horrible Motion Blur and Film Grain off. I don't know why every developer pushes that blur and grain crap as 99% of players turn them off anyways.Meh:= story is full of itself. Keep it simple and it works better. In 80-90's movies hero grabbed shotgun, said catchy one-liner, blasted the aliens, got the girl and I'm 100% fine with that kind of simple story. You really aren't new Kubrick so just do not try too much.= expected to be HAL-9000 with potentially nefarious motivations but story is in rails and choices do not matter. Wasted potential right there.Negatives:- mouse is laggy and sluggish at UI menus, developer cope-explained in discussions that "conveys space-y movement during gameplay". Well, IMPLEMENT CONTROLS WHERE IT IS USED, not at UI menus!- cameras do not use mouse for movement, instead you push slowly them around with WASD because game consoles use controller.- options to select things and puzzle responses are limited to four. Why four? Because game is completely made for D-pad brains. We have Fallout4-syndrome here again.- damned autosaves do not save even when the game shows saving symbol. Also there is NO saving at quit. Played from beginning and upon reaching UN I was hunting document for an hour and then wanted a break. Ta-daa, game starts from start of the UN-module without documents... Looking at game discussions/comments gameplay is on rails anyways so finding documents do not matter. This kind of issue is game-breaking problem.- animation freezes a lot so Emma looks like robot. I'd assume she would slap the sphere bumping on her face but no, frozen expression is all I get.- on comments some players complained about resolution setting resetting and keybindings do not work for puzzles. Therefore I didn't bother to rebind most keys to mouse where I usually set them.Game window-shopped & purchased from HumbleBundle store with several others, pricing was under 8€ which is in the ball-park if game would have more polish. It's somewhat telling I made the purchase two years back and didn't try the game until now.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Superb from start to finish.I really enjoyed this game. The story is mysterious, trippy, and classic sci-fi. The game's pacing also had me engaged throughout the whole play through. The voice acting is excellent across the board. Technically, the game looks great and sounds great. The graphics do a great job to convince you that you are the AI of the ship looking at the world through a camera lens. The game's art style in anchored in reality as the ship you're on looks and feels like the international space station. The gameplay can be a little finicky and frustrating at times, as you are asked to perform certain tasks with little guidance or explanation, and certain mundane tasks take a lot buttons to accomplish. However, you get used to it after a while, and it did not impede my enjoyment of the game. I do think that the controls are bit console centric, as I had a better experience playing with a controller than with mouse and keyboard.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this a lot. It's claustrophobic, disorientating, occasionally tedious and occasionally confusing, but those are all good things that add to the story and atmosphere. As in, I'm happy that there were times when I had no idea what to do (I'm a broken computer program on board a space station, I shouldn't have my hand held), and the tedium of waiting / fetching things / entering codes and connecting to systems enhanced the immersion and made it seem more authentic. Plus the visuals are incredible - the sets are really well done. I had to laugh occasionally at the temporal inconsistencies ('Come on SAM, we haven't got much time' - SAM then spends the next hour wandering around the empty corridors and bumping into things), but there's no way around those.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine 2001: A Space Odyssey.Now imagine if it was told strictly from HAL's point of view.Now imagine if it was a found footage horror movie.Now imagine if Stanley Kubrick actually WAS on drugs when he made it.Now imagine if it was a video game instead.That's Observation.And in all seriousness, playing as the AI is a great concept that's dragged down by the sections where SAM controls the sphere.  The writing and intrigue are great until it becomes clear that the story is going to explain even less than 2001 did.  The human characters are astounding, assuming you don't stare at their faces too long.  The whole "found footage" trope works really well in its advantage, until it starts mimicing the methods a little too well and sets up obvious jump scares.  In all, there's a lot of good that is slightly held back by a lot of not so good.8/10, definitely worth a play if you like surreal space horror, found footage, and/or weird trippy games that push the boundary on what someone would think of as a typical game,
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like jump scares you can see from a mile away?  Do you like repeating the same puzzle over-and-over throughout your play-through?  Have we got a game for you!  I got this because I enjoy puzzle games and this looked like it might have an interesting story.  First I'll say that the controls are infuriating.  You control either cameras or a sphere that can fly around.  Either way you're moving too fast for one or too slow in the other.  And inverting inverts for both, even though you use a keyboard for one and a mouse for the other.  I found a keymapping workaround for that, but still.  The controls are also very squishy.  Trying to make it "feel right" for flying around the sphere I suppose, but instead of helping you immerse yourself it just gets annoying.  As for the puzzle aspect, it's literally the same mechanic over-and-over.  It doesn't change for most of them at all.  Docking clamps?  Yup, those are the same simple W-S combo all three times you see it.  The fast paced procedure of using WSAD in quick response?  Yup, same every time!  It's hardly worth calling it a puzzle game.  In fact it's the furthest from.  It's meant to be scary in parts, but in reality it's just tiring honestly.  I played through it hoping to at least see what the story was about.  In the end you don't find out anything.  It's just this vaguely mysterious ending that doesn't really tell you much.  I'm sure it's incredibly "deep" if you feel it, but I didn't.  It is a beautiful game, and the art is rather fantastic.  In that regard it's really well done.  And the voice acting is very nice.  Beyond that?  I wish it had something more to it.  A tragic waste of an awesome opportunity I suppose.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game where figuring out what to do next is a puzzle in and of itself. The game will wait quietly forever until you do what is needed, there is no hand-holding here (but nothing had me so stumped I had to google it), control is constantly taken away from you (sometimes jarringly) to watch scripted sequences, characters will speak but their mouths don't move. Yet I couldn't stop playing until the end. I had to know what happens next every time I thought I would stop playing. And the ending leaves more questions than answers.Not for everyone but I enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Horrifyingly atmospheric, making for a beautiful background that will scare you in such a strange and unnerving way. Devolver Digital has done it again with another great horror game. The feeling of being a malfunctioning AI makes a game that is surprisingly easy to get immersed in.I would recommend for anyone looking for a different kind of horror game.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I have neutral feelings on the game. The way you play it is very different, using cameras and occasionally a 'Marksman-H training remote' x 'AUTO' thingy-sphere. There was an atmosphere going, I can still feel part of myself in the environment, my mind replaying that feeling-I-can't-name, and it was immersive enough that I didn't stop playing until I reached the end. However, it didn't find a place on the shelf of "oh I love this game, this story, go play it NOW" like the other games I've happily completed or am working on. There were moments where I got a little frustrated and plenty of confusion that conflicted with story progression. It was cool play as an AI, and not be the chosen one for once. I just feel like the story should have been darker, and had more going on, such as the AI becoming more corrupted, and interfering with crew activities. Unfortunately, I have to click not recommended, steam has no neutral option. I only recommend it to add to your own database of gaming experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Had high expectations for this game lmao. But the mouse is so sensitive its not adjustable at all. When you control the sphere, just a slight movement would just stagger the whole direction to eternity. Seems like a good game with interesting story, but nope, bad controls = bad game to me. The game has an option to lower mouse sensitivity, but it's not efficient at all. Lowering the ingame sensitivity makes the mouse slooower. After researching throughly, heard that there is negative mouse acceleration with the controls. I heard that turning hardware acceleration for the mouse would help, but i'm not sure why on earth I have to go through the effort of changing my system settings for a single game.  I was very readily trying to accept the wonky donkey mouse sensitivity but when it hit the sphere controls, i totally lost my patience. I requested for an immediate refund. Very funny since its like point and clicky type adventure game and the devs do nothing about the control coordination. Good god.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, you will not be dissapointed with this it honestly felt like a movie. You are playing the game through the eyes of S.A.M, System Administration and Maintenance. As you progress through the game, you find out that your purpose is to "Bring Her " the main charector Emma Fischer. To a certain place at a certain time in multiple dimension happening all at once. _childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The feeling of this game is phenomenal. Sensational sound design and very realistic sets makes this immersive in a way you don't often see. The story, while wonderfully creepy with some awesome ideas, falls apart when you think about it for too long and didn't leave me feeling either satisfied or curious. I think if the gameplay was a bit more open world-ey I would have been more incentivised to gather all the relevant information, but as the game handholds you throughout I found myself lost when asked to use my noggin to solve problems later into the story. If you like immersive horror and cool space stations definitely give this a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: If you've watched the video and think you'd like to play a walking-sim (note:  a puzzle game!) where you're the space station AI rather than the human, then I'm positive this game is for you.It isn't  - notwithstanding what seems like a game-console-compatible playmobil interface that studiously ignores my number pad, I found it difficult to do what the game was asking of me for the first few hours.  (I think I was still finding entire screens available to me a couple of hours in to the game)Figuring out *what* I was supposed to do was also sometimes difficult - later in the game I was able to list objectives, but either I overlooked that earlier somehow or it just took a while to get the feel of the game.Despite all that, I'd give it a B+A walking-sim's heart is the story and the characters, and while I might not have known exactly what I was supposed to be doing or how, at all times I knew the situation the characters were in, the information (or misinformation) they had available to them, the perils they were facing and their emotions as they faced them.The environment was also at all times believable, and rendered really nicely.Overall it's an innovative entry in the genre and deserves those awards listed on the store page.Last notes:I assert this isn't a puzzle game - you do sometimes have to look for notes, or assemble pieces of data together, but it's nowhere near Monkey Island.  If you think video games require gameplay you'll be unhappy with this.The game  have a waypoint system; you can activate it from the map.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This would have probably made a nice movie, but I wouldn't recommend it as a gameThe good:- Story- Atmosphere- Space station and space suits designThe bad:- Extremely short- Impossible to save whenever you want, there's only an autosave feature in some not very precise points in time, this made me have to go through the same parts several times, otherwise I would have probably finished the game in 4-5h instead of 7 (yes I've watched also all the final credits).- Lip sync is absolutely horrible.- Extremely annoying bug related to resolution changing, even applying the windows registry workaround won't fix it, it will always and continuously switch back to random low resolutions modes.- Without a map of the station you end up wasting A LOT of time wandering around trying to get your bearings.- Controls are extremely annoying and slow, if that wasn't the case puzzles would have been even faster to solve, when trying to solve some of them especially the unlock sequences it makes you feel like you have some sort of handicap.- Puzzles again: they're pretty much quite stupid, the only real problem relies in the clunky controls, feels like they did this just to make the game look not as short as it actually is.- I'm not quite sure what the ending was supposed to mean, not entirely at least.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: It's a short linear atmospheric story.The game has many pros: the visuals are amazing, the music/sound/voice acting really sell the ambiance, the concept of being an AI on a space station is pretty cool.However the surreal aspect of the game wasn't for me. I had fun on the first half of the game while I was trying to figure out what was going on. But the more the story advanced, the more surreal it became, and the less I ended up caring. Without curiosity, it became a "go to hinted coordonate, find the solution to the puzzle, watch a cutscene you don't care about, rince, repeat". I enjoyed my first few hours, but at the end, I was just glad it was over.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I was let down previously by Moons of Madness, a lovecraftian first person horror game set on Mars. I'll admit, I'm a huge fan of sci-fi, and further still, I'm a huge fan of works inspired by lovecraft, so what should have been a slam dunk for me ended up as just a very tedious experience due to awful optimization, bland gameplay, and a design that felt dated by 2012 standards. Why are you bringing up a completely different game, you may ask yourself. Well, it's because Observation was a complete 180 for me. I came into this knowing very little outside of a Zero Punctuation review I half remember and the splash art. My expectation was for a somewhat subdued sci-fi thriller set on a space station, because not being able to read means I can't actually look at the store page for help.Instead? I got a game that felt tailor made for me. A game that managed to almost nail all of it's core elements in ways that made me specifically absolutely enthralled with it. It's not a game for everyone. But it's a game I've really grown to love during my playtime, and I recommend that everyone give it a shot. It sticks around exactly as long as it needs to, so you won't be pumping 30 hours into a mediocre experience. Just pick it up, give it your time, and be amazed.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The only reason I don't recommend this game is the price. I got it on sale for 10$ and if I bought it for any higher I would be pretty upset with myself. The game itself is a mix of good and bad. The visuals and the story telling are great and together make an eerie sci fi story with a few twists and turns. I will say in terms of story if you, like me are not the one to go out of your way to find every little nugget of information the game has, then you will miss out on a lot of the information and characters in the game. Observation seems to rely pretty heavily on your ability to do everything on your own which can be frustrating. The gameplay itself was fairly boring at times, because for the most part you are either operating out of a drone or a camera and solving different puzzles and mini games. Some of the puzzles are fun and some of the mini games are but I found myself looking up a lot of them. I'm willing to admit that I am not the smartest person but the lack of clarity on a lot of the puzzles can be frustrating, and it gets even more frustrating when you use the feature to ask Emma what to do, and she just says the same thing over and over. All that being said I did not hate the game, but I would recommend anyone who is interested in this game to wait until the price goes down, or until the game is on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: A convergence for the last 60 years of transumanistic space operas.A storytelling immersed in an uncanny void of mistery.Puzzles are weak, but not frustrating, either too easy or just a "find the item thing" but can't get annoying because of the fantastic immersion of being an AI, moving with a sphere o the station systems and cameras.Definitely a must play, turn off the light and immerse yourself in this voyage
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Cool setting, cool theme, cool ideaBUTthe keyboard and mouse controls are atrocious and feel like an afterthought and the autosave checkpoints are weird, forcing you to replay a lot of what you've already done. Very often it's also very unclear what the game expects you to do, so it feels more like a hidden object game than anything smart.I haven't finished it and probably won't for those reasons, and won't recommend it unless you play it on controller and have some tolerance to repetition.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Great cinematography. But that's about all it has going for it.It's like it's someone's horror movie plot they couldn't get on film, so they made a 'game' instead that is basically a linear narrative with little to no actual game mechanics beyond 'push the glowy button'.If you're in to being trapped inside a horror plot as an AI, play it! Otherwise, I want my five hours back.Side-note: At one point you're "supposed" to do a thing a character doesn't want. I tried doing a thing to let them avoid the fate waiting for them. The character didn't even realize I had provided them a way out, and just sat there, twiddling their thumbs. Broke what little immersion I had left.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Jesus. I don't even know what to say. I was bored, so I bought this game on impulse. I'm an anxious person, so I usually don't play horror games, or even psychological horror games, but this was an experience everyone needs to have. It's one of those games where you just sit back in your seat as the credits roll, after 4 straight hours of gameplay, without even a break for the bathroom. One of those games you play in the dark, and experience life as someone else. Beautiful game.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. Story was good, but the interface was the best bit. Playing as the AI was a novel experience that really stood out from other games because of the way you interface with the game. Yes, most of it came in the form of puzzles and didn't require any actual knowledge of systems, but it's not branded as a sys admin game is it? I'd love to see this sort of genre take off. And the voice acting was excellent!All in all, I took my time and completed in about 7 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: this game is nothing like i've ever played before! it's so different, you play as an AI, SAM, guided by an NPC, dr emma fisher. it's more of a thriller than a horror, with lots of self-explanatory and challenging puzzles and controls. very well made this game! i loved every moment of it! one of my favourites!
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a really neat engine for being an AI, flipping between cameras and controlling station systems and stuff.The potential of which is entirely squandered. You spend more of the game than not operating as a drone inside a station, which essentially makes you like any regular person. There's potential for interconnected station systems making you do things like track movement on cameras and figure which doors to open and close to influence things or needing to juggle power to decide which systems were important to you or things of that nature - none of which is ever used.Everything you do will be to go to the place, click on a thing and do a simple self contained minigame. The challenge comes from ambiguous instructions, the interface being clunky, and the environment being confusing to navigate. You have the option to ask for clarification at any time but they could have an audio clip that just says "Do something" that played every time you asked Emma what she wanted and it would be exactly as helpful as her actual responses. The story follows the same pattern as the gameplay, setting up interesting and exciting possibilities and then failing to bring them to a satisfying conclusion. Halfway through the game I was invested in Emma's survival and on the edge of my seat. By the end I didn't care what happened to anyone and was hoping that just one thread would resolve in a more satisfying way than someone wiggling their fingers and saying "It's magic!"The whole thing comes wrapped in a "no manual save" system which tends to place its saves in front of unskippable dialogue preceeding long exploration sequences so if you get fed up with a puzzle half way through there's no way to save your current progress and quit, you'll have to start the section over again if you leave the game. There's also an aspect of exploring the station and obtaining recordings of dialogue snippets to give some more backstory and character to the crew, but finding one doesn't appear to save the game so you'll lose your progress if you don't have time to finish the next puzzle after finding a few pieces.This game has so much potential for greatness in both gameplay and storytelling, offering a compelling set up for both, but it doesn't stick the landing with either one and winds up being more disappointing than a game that was simply bad from the outset.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Being a gamer for many years, I have played numerous titles to completion.  After a first-time play-through, I have to say that Observation was truly thought provoking, cerebral, and left me with more questions than answers - which is a good thing!  The game takes from numerous science fiction greats, most notably 2001: A Space Odyssey, a dash of some Asimov, a sprinkle of Interstellar, and a drop of Rama to finish it off.  Kudos to the devs for making a fantastic journey that left me in awe!  I can't wait to play it through again to BRING THEM ALL!
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice re-imagining of {spoiler}. Not that {spoiler} needed re-imagining. Nicely done. I was surprisingly drawn in and to Emma and, eventually, the AI SAM. My only complaint is the inability to save. The auto-saves were too far apart. When you finally shut it off to get some sleep you come back to find you have to replay 30 minutes to get back to where you left off. I suspect that may be why I didn't get some of the achievements. I hurried to get back to where I left off and probably missed some things. Either auto-save more often or allow player saves. Basically a walking sim in space. Recommend using a controller. There are some time essential bits where using the keyboard will drive you mad. Well, if you're old and a little slow on the hand-eye coordination thing, lol. 9 of 10 for this. 1 off for the saves. Cheers.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is an amazing sci-fi experience. The story is well crafted and does not overstays its welcome. It has suspense and thrilling moments where you'll be on the edge of your seat. Gameplay is good, some moments may be slow especially when navigating and the puzzles are easy, though some might be confusing because of the UI.All in all this is a great game that makes you wonder what's going on!8.9/10 recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game so far. Requires a lot of thought and exploration. I wouldn't buy if you're looking for something fast-paced or full of quick action; this is slow-moving plot full of suspense. Reminds me quite a bit of Alien: Isolation which I love, and some of the same team worked on this game, which shows.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I really did. I don't know whether it was originally designed for a specific platform or something, but the controls for pc are horrendous, especially when it comes to the free-roaming sphere, and trying to rebind them fixes nothing. I lost track of how much time I spent fiddling with the mouse sensitivity, trying to find some middle ground between 'so low that it's completely unresponsive' to 'moving the mouse literal millimeters at a time results in wild pitching motions of the camera on-screen', and couldn't find it. Trying to center the camera on a single piece of paper taped to the wall felt like trying to play Operation with boxing gloves on. I ended up having to take motion sickness meds just to try and keep playing, and I don't normally have that issue with games. The mouse sensitivity being so unbelievably janky doesn't help the experimental reactor puzzle at all, given how fast you have to move between nodes, ending up making it one of the most obnoxious puzzles I've ever encountered in a puzzle game. The puzzle itself is relatively straightforward once you figure out what it wants, but the combination of the time limit paired with how slow the magnets move and how jank the mouse sensitivity is turned it into a nightmare that I spent 30 minutes repeatedly missing clearing it in time by 1 or 2 seconds each time.The difficulty in this game is ultimately caused by the controls being uncooperative, which doesn't make it feel like a challenge or make it interesting, it just makes it extremely aggravating to play.I've tried to play this 3 seperate times, trying to give it a fair shot each time because I was genuinely interested in the story premise and thought that the idea of the player character being a station OS was cool and novel. But ultimately, the horrible controls ended up making me stop in overwhelming frustration each time. I'm just going to look up a let's play instead so that I can at least get some closure on the story; if I hadn't had the game in my library for as long, I would be trying to refund it. TL:DR  =  promising game with interesting concept that was unfortunately utterly kneecapped by terrible pc controls, rendering it borderline unplayable given how crucial those controls and being able to maneuver are to doing literally any of your objectives.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend this game because I have so much respect for what the small team at No Code achieved. Certain parts of Observation were obviously made with love! The blurb and trailer tickled the same corner of my brain as certain slow-burn space horror films and since existential horror is my bag, I ignored warnings about the puzzles in other negative comments. I regret. The "puzzles"** are a constant obstacle to story progress. That's what puzzles are supposed to do, but the puzzles in Observation are so insultingly easy and repetitive that it's impossible for the (honestly good) story to keep up its thin veneer of reality.When all the atmosphere of the setting and story faded away, I was left alone with the stark realization that I was wasting precious hours of what life I have left on this blue marble pretending to putz around an imaginary space station at a snail's pace. Yes, this game gave me an existential crisis, but not the one it wanted to give me, I'm sure.The only advantage of putting puzzles this dumb and pointless into a game is that they add a significant cushion to the playtime. That's an insult to players, full-stop. If Observation was half the length, it would be 200% better. It's sad to think that such a promising indie dev team would choose to deprioritize player experience so severely. They got their BAFTAs, but I doubt I will ever buy another No Code game. Observer actually delivered on most of my expectations, but when it didn't, I felt patronized and confused about how seriously the game wanted me to engage its story. By the end, I was too hostile to appreciate the finale, and that is by no fault of the story. SUCH A SHAME.**scare quotes because these things barely fit the function of puzzles. At best, they're a round of Bop-It, at worst, they're just button press simulations.tl;dr: My experience has always been that good stories can salvage weak game design. The puzzles in Observation have changed my mind.The look: great. Eerie lighting, sexy planet, and neat-o level design.The world: awesome. Sometimes chilling. Cool payoff.The gameplay: ROTTEN POO POO YUCKY YUCK STINKY DING DONG :'(

_childDocuments_.review: (or at least watched a video tour of it), you are going to love Observation — and very likely for precisely the things that other people wouldn't. The game tries to convey the messy and mundane feeling of a very real space station, the slow, finicky procedures, glacial camera movements, bad framing and exposures; these minutes and hours of tense waiting in order to get things just right.Nothing happens fast in Observation, and if you waffle about peeking into corners (to get all these pieces of data - BTW, there's nothing obnoxious about collectibles here, and I've managed to 100% it on the first go), or go around reading instruction manuals and logs before doing an objective — it doesn't feel as if an action plot was set on pause; this is exactly how you'd do things in space. The game also features a cast of eminently competent, professional, determined, and smart people that actual astronauts and cosmonauts are in real life.Conversely, if you'll glance over these lovingly recreated stylizations of Salyuts and ISSs and Skylabs just like you would over any old, generic sci-fi interiors, you may blaze through the game very quickly and with little engagement, only seeing a blur of similar space corridors and haphazard junk. Thing is, again, all that elementary stuff is there only to help you play this "theater of the mind": to feel as if you really did some terrible things to a space station systems, or debugged your own electronic mind, or saved a person on the brink of asphyxia, while following byzantine checklists and sweating in binary. Like Battlestar Galactica's CIC or a war movie's strategic planning scene, they don't REALLY do the thing they depict, and would fall apart under any pedantic scrutiny, but they make you FEEL like a beleaguered astronaut.This is probably important to note: people who are allergic to any kind of arbitrary "lack of realism" will find a lot to criticize here. I'd say developers succesfully justified style with substance, and willing (and conscious) breaks from simulation-like realism work well here. It's not a hardcore-hard sci-fi, although it's often quite smart about its science or space minutiae. how you feel as an AI who watches and explores things through whirring cameras, or as a clumsy flying ball equipped with a glitchy GoPro, or as a helpless ride-along on a terrifying plunge into space. Also importantly, how you feel as a pedantic computer driving its user crazy by calmly listing every piece of information they didn't ask for before getting to the point (you can do that here if you want!). It also does the aforementioned fake interfaces and procedures very well — sometimes they veer into laughable, but they've got THE FEEL in spades. Cutscenes and gameplay are not that different here, but not because you don't have anything to do (IMO the game gives you just enough agency to feel engaged, and takes it away to make you feel helpless), but because of great art / sound direction. a generic-looking prop turns out to be actual real sleeping cubby or exercise machine just like on the ISS; the walls of cameras, ledgers and binders with post-its saying "DON'T MOVE", messy storage modules, weird spaces with alternating "UP" inside one room, but also with very helpful stickers saying which way is up as well (OVHD/DECK for up/down, and PORT/STBD for left/right wall). Consistent and well-delivered, it was not overdone and didn't take any unfortunate left turns, and was supported by good voice acting. Like  from the same developer, it doesn't try to impress you with blistering originality, but instead infuses humanity into its goings-on: its plot may be a shadow of all the other sci-fi cosmic mysteries about unknowable alien things, but it has a very warm story of Emma and SAM inside of it. Interestingly, their relationship is developed not only through dialogue, but through physical interaction as well: you constantly alternate between being a big omnipresent entity which tiny Emma is inside of, and being cradled, carried, comforted, and even thrown by giant Emma as a cute melon-sized flying ball. personally, the prologue gave me chills and even frightened me a bit with its intensity — Observation offers a rather cerebral and voluntary fear, not proper fright or jump scares, but that's frankly the kind I like best. It has a couple of likewise spooky twists up its sleeve later, as well. I also advise you to think about the alien symbol puzzles — I suspect they mean rather concrete statements, although I haven't looked it up yet; but I know for a fact that they have meaning (e. g. their symbols for "subordinate/member of" and "leading/head of" match with symbols for your crew if you look closely!). I will note that I did encounter a few bugs (had to turn off controller support once to make the keyboard work, caught a strange minor bug with menus, and credits video in the beginning freezes a lot), and restarted a couple of times, but in the end I played through with no issues.

_childDocuments_.review: I have attempted to complete as much as possible, but I see that none of my critiques are changing so here goes.Pros: -The plot is very interesting. Aside from the initial selling point of a story told from an AI's perspective, throughout the game the story remains engaging. I will definitely end up either finishing the game because of this or watching a walkthrough to see how it ends.-The games mechanics for you as an AI are very well interpreted and convincing. For example, the means of communication with the crew is through the AI's response mode in which you scan for information to relay to them. In addition the various information tabs and being able to link information fragments together in your memory to make a whole document or idea really sells the idea that you are controlling a computer. On a similar note, the visuals also do a great job at representing that you are a computer, and are probably the best at trying to accomplish this that I have seen so far.-The game looks pretty good. The people don't look amazing, but that is probably asking for too much when most other games don't do great in that regard either. Other than that the game looks great.Cons:-Ruined Tension. Unfortunately a large part of the story and tense moments are completely ruined by the player's involvement. In most instances I would have preferred a cutscene in order to preserve the mood and gravity of the situations. This leads into the next point-Movement is painfully slow and clumsy. I get it, you are supposed to feel like you are controlling cameras, not a player's eyes. This being said, when objectives are hard to find and you are expected to repeatedly search through rooms with multiple cameras, it gets old very fast. I understand the decision to not make the position change instantly, however even a slightly faster speed would give the off the same effect and not make using the cameras feel like a drag. -This game is very disorienting. Some disorientation is expected since the setting is space, but it is taken to an entirely new level when your movement and even just the ability to look in a direction already feel heavily restricted. It becomes a legitimate frustration trying to position yourself toward a door, reposition yourself at the next and then realize that you are going the wrong way and have to turn back. This on its own might not be so bad if you were just able to freely look around for where to go. I believe that a significant part of the playtime is dedicated solely to positioning your camera. And I am not talking about sections where positioning the camera is so that you can interact with devices in your crosshairs. I mean parts of the game dedicated to exploration inside the space station.-Instructions can be confusing or incomprehensible. The game treats you as if you were actually the AI on the station, so it is up to you to somehow know where everything is and what everything is called with no instruction. Sometimes you will be told to perform a task but not informed what accomplishes the task. This might not be a problem if you were introduced to the equipment beforehand, however the game often thrusts you into situations you are completely unprepared for. Many times you are flashed a puzzle and are just expected to know the rules. Your only options are to have the same vague instructions repeated or check your objectives list. In addition, by the time your objective list begins to be useful to you, you have already decided to ignore it because it shows similar vague instructions for a large portion of the game. This is really where tense and interesting moments are literally killed because of the player growing frustrated at trying to figure out where to go while having to search for where to go at 1 inch per minute. A specific problem I had with the game is the fact that the AI can speak, however can not inquire further about any task it can not figure out. It would be great if for instance you were able to use response mode to talk about almost anything and have the characters try to steer you in the right direction when off topic and give you hints when close to your objective. As it stands though, it seems to be a purely scripted 'mode' that only serves to advance the narrative rather than a tool to help the AI (and the player) communicate with the crew. I want to use this section to throw in a comment about a very specific part of the game. How on earth are you supposed to figure out you can go through vents? This really got to me but I will end it here.-On the Topic of Movement and Instructions. I feel like this game would have greatly benefited from some kind of objective based HUD and a marker system. You play as an AI so both of these things are definitely in the realm of possibility. For example, if you analyzed what someone said to do and connected that to equipment which then showed up on your minimap. Also an outline once viewing a camera for ease of finding it, since a lot tends to blend into the props in this game. Equally as useful would be a marker system where you would be able to ping a location or device from a camera or the minimap. This is especially necessary in the segments where you will be using the cameras to look and the sphere to move around. Disorientation here is a big problem and this simple addition would be a huge help. Almost forgot the first spacewalk segment. Probably the most infuriating segment and best example of useless instructions. You have to survey damage on station but you can only survey very specific areas. You have to look for the specific dents on the station when there are a lot scattered all over it. This part of the game gets 0/5 and probably forty minutes of my time.-Inconsistent. This point is a bit pettier, however some gameplay mechanics such as response mode or the computer memory are inconsistent. For example, it is demonstrated that to use information, that the AI must have access to it in its memory first. Some things, namely passwords, break this convention. I get it, the player would know full well to use this, however it would be nice to be able to link up the clues with the information found in the memory as some other sequences do.Summary:Overall, I went into this game wanting so much to like it, and have attempted playing it multiple times for this same reason. I didn't go into the game with even the idea that I would't like it. Each time I made a decision to try to think differently and use the game's clues to try to form a semblance of any pattern the game was trying to get me to pick up in order to succeed. Perhaps my IQ just isn't high enough but there isn't one there. This game is incredibly frustrating and it feels like it tried its best to portray a realistic experience at the player's expense no matter the cost. This is evident through the gameplay, mechanics, and limited functionality of the AI's communication. I wish I didn't buy this game because you can get the same enjoyment from the story from a walkthrough without any of the frustration. And therein lies the problem. This would have made a great movie. It essentially is a movie. Problems have only one solution and only one way to arrive at that solution. The narrative overtly comes first and foremost without regard for the player's enjoyment. It is inherently a game that has to take itself seriously however somehow takes itself too seriously. My disappointment is immeasurable, and my day not quite ruined. I can not recommend this game to anyone.1/5 for the cool storyEdit: Previously mentioned strange axis acceleration which I have found to be incorrect. Something is still off about the sphere camera positioning but I can't quite place it

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is one of those titles that muddies the definitions of movies and games as separate entities. The visual and sound design in this title is mostly excellent (though there remain a few glaring clipping bugs in the penultimate sequence), it achieves this partly by having a very constrained "set" and thus series of locations and on the sound side by using fitting performers such as Robin Finck. The narrative is also very compelling.The gameplay is so-so. Consisting largely of a mix of mini-games, from "spot the clickable item" in the quite busy space station interior to Simon-says style watch and repeat puzzles to timing based button presses with screen prompts to bypass certain safety controls.Why is this acceptable? Because you aren't playing the central character, Astronaut Emma Fisher but the station's AI - SAM (Systems administration & maintenance). It thus pulls off a kind of Bioshock homage, where your gameplay actions are helping an NPC (i.e. Anna / Elizabeth) at the same time as pointing out that as a player / AI you really have no choice in the matter. There is a distinctly Andrew Ryan "A slave obeys" moment, where an apparently "under the influence" Emma says, "I have the feeling you're going to help me anyway". This is rather clever because roleplaying an AI, you aren't entirely clear where the "good" actions are (presuming you have some form of ethics code alongside your clandestine mission directive) or whether in assisting Emma till the bitter end you're breaking your programming or simply obeying the ranking officer aboard. And as people don't we sometimes end up helping or enabling people we know we really shouldn't as well. If you've been corrupted by an external force and are on your way to become something else, are the actions really yours?If this makes it sound like you have some choice in the game, you really don't. However, missing information about how SAM is programmed, what happened to the crew, what the motivations of the various factions and actors that appear during the game are in reality, and whether lovecraftian black tentacles that send signals requesting young female individuals by their DNA signature are always a bad thing will remain after you've finished the game and... perhaps that's for the better.There is a scene towards the end of Bioshock Infinite that deals with some of the same themes Observation seems to touch on, to the extent that Observation in some way feels a homage that deals with a different side of the coin (or lighthouse), either in relation to B.I or to any of the myriad works of fiction that have dealt with similar themes (i.e. the end of Stephen Kings Dark Tower series). You could perhaps feel unsatisfied by the end of observation, but if you know what happens at the end of Bioshock Infinite's DLC, or what happens to Roland Deschain if you keep reading the last Dark Tower novel after the point you've been told not to if you want a happy ending, you might look at Observations final message of "BRING THEM" and decide...... that after all...... perhaps it's better just not to know.

_childDocuments_.review: A "walking simulator" in a new format that comes close to being interesting but ultimately fails in its execution.The idea of playing as the station's AI is intriguing, and at first it feels like it might turn out to be an engaging, immersive experience.  At the beginning, there is a promising moment where it appears that the game has let the player loose to gobble up all the knowledge and gather control of all the gadgets and systems on the station.  However, the effect is quickly lost once the player realizes a few things: - You are mostly restricted to whatever systems are required for the current objective, unable to interact with anything else.  This breaks the feeling of casting out all your tendrils of control as you "wake up", which I think is a crucial part of the fantasy one wants to experience when playing as an advanced AI. - Further to the above, the player doesn't really have any opportunity to "play around"; in this setting, one expects to have lots of things to interact with, and hopes to see characters and the environment reacting accordingly.  But, as one soon finds it impossible to take any action until the story demands it, one comes to understand that this is no sci-fi sandbox, but rather as linear as can be.The immersion is further compromised by the style of dialogue.  The writing itself is fine - it's just that there is such a clear pattern that the entire game feels like playing through one long tutorial.  A character gives an instruction, our current objective updates accordingly, and nothing else happens until the player does the one possible thing that follows.  Few games have given such a strong feeling of "going through the motions" to progress.  It's clear to the player that events are waiting on their little bit of input to progress - thus, even when dialogue seems to indicate urgency, the only real tension comes when a timer is slapped on the screen.The gameplay is unfortunately not exciting enough to save the experience.  This is a collection of not-quite-puzzles, where anything resembling challenge arises not from clever design, but from lack of clarity and awkward controls.  The closest we come to satisfying puzzle-solving is when we have to find an access code for a laptop by looking for sticky notes pasted nearby.  As for the look and feel, the interfaces of all the systems we interact with are satisfactory, and panning the cameras about is surprisingly not too tedious, but navigating with the sphere is awkward and not very rewarding - one would think it would be liberating to no longer be confined to the camera views, but I dreaded having to possess the sphere, bumbling around through the station and even worse, outside the station, where one will encounter some inexplicably low-res textures which mar an otherwise decent-looking game.All of this might have been a sacrifice made so that the story could have the room it needs to shine - the linear nature could be to preserve the pacing, the "puzzles" could be so insubstantial so as not to distract the player from the plot...  One might think the story must then be where all the value lies, here.  But for me, the story was the worst disappointment of all.  I feel that much of the satisfaction of a story like this, filled with and driven by uncertainty, comes from the understanding that arises when it all comes together.  This story introduces a number of intriguing threads, and is paced well enough to keep the player engaged throughout... but, halfway through, I began to fear the inevitable disappointment that would come if the threads failed to resolve to something clever and meaningful.  Sure enough... as the player is plied with more and more flashing symbols and cryptic dialogue, the threads fall away without being resolved, and in the end it all comes to nothing, in that the player is shown things that are supposed to be mesmerising, but are not enough to distract from the questions: "What about x?  What happened to y?  What was the point of z?"By the end of this, I found I was playing for the same reason one decides to finish a disappointing book once they're most of the way through, and I can't recommend this any more than I could recommend such a book.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game that makes me wish Steam had a "well.....it depends" button. Overall, its a unique and memorable experience, but brings alot of the same problems that weighed down Stories Untold, their last game. No Code at this point obviously specializes in immersive, highly interactive puzzle games that have you interfacing with complex, beautifully realized UIs and machinery with very little hand-holding, relying on player intuition to both complete said puzzles and advance the story through contextual interactions with characters and the environment. At Observation's best, those mechanics all come together to deliver some truly involved-feeling experiences and plot progression. However, at it's worst, just like in Stories Untold, those mechanics can be WAY too vague and can absolutely ruin the pacing of the story as you desperately bump around looking for an item to interact with until you give up, look up a walkthrough, and find out you had to use a specific function on a seemingly irrelevant object, or a menu you haven't used since the beginning of the game.If I didn't thoroughly enjoy the setting, sound design, and mechanics that worked, I would have left a negative review, but even with the numerous frustrations I ultimately enjoyed it. With their next title, No Code seriously needs to learn the difference between denying players info so they can figure things out on their own, and denying players important contextual clues, that without, make some of the most basic things such as advancing a cutscene a cryptic chore. Buy it on sale and keep track of that 2 hour refund period.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game; another in the very short (3 hour) narrative games.You are the AI on a space station where something has gone wrong. There's a survivor, and you are trying to figure out what happened. You'll control the different cameras on the station to open doors, activate systems, etc.  You might call the gameplay something of an "interface puzzler." You have to attache some clamps outside the station, you go to the clamp, and figure out it wants you to push and hold this button, then hold a second button, and release the first button. Later, you go to a the comms computer, and you need to align the dishes, so you have to figure out what the interface for that is. "Ok.... it wants me to enter the numbers 82 36 47.... how do I do that?" It's a unique take on the puzzling, and I enjoyed it.The game has a wonderful naming system for the different rooms, and you can essentailly fast travel most of the time. But sometimes I still found it frustrating to figure out where the game wanted me to be, or what to do. I liked the puzzles, I just hated when I did not know what room I needed to be in for the puzzle. But if you like short suspensful narratives, it is a good time and does some unique things.

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is a visually immersive space (station) "walking" sim with detailed graphics, good voice acting and sound design. The game's story, though chaotic, manages to remain intriguing. However, despite its promising elements, the game falls short in execution.The biggest drawback is the excruciating slowness of every aspect, from navigation, camera movement and zooming to some UI elements. Unlike other walking sims that embrace a slow pace, Observation's very task-oriented and thematically time sensitive nature clashes with its sluggish navigation. This results in unnecessary padding of the game with playtime that serves absolutely no purpose.Furthermore, the game's navigation through similarly designed space station modules, which lack clear orientation guides and offer 6 degrees of freedom movement, could have been an enjoyable challenge. However, the sluggish movement amplifies the frustration, transforming any mistake into a painfully punishing experience.In conclusion, I cannot recommend Observation.

_childDocuments_.review: simply if you don't like "security camera games", don't play it.great and unique story that everyone must know of. but the gameplay is too painful... gameplay constructed of minigames, minor sound bugs, i also got a game breaking bug. the real problem is that it's very confusing and not much of a clue on gameflow/gameplay side. -The minigames are very confusing and one most easy minigames could've been done with copy-pasting numbers. why would you add a pointless minigame between these amazing scene? -you will mostly get to play with security cameras and a 360 degree walking simulator that collide easily with small objects, hatch frames. drove me mad...-you play with 'W' all the time like a unity3d spectator mode (but have no Ascend and Descend controls) which just rubs salt to the wound.Somehow space themed fps games always suffer from these similar problems : UI bugs, stuck in a menu or a ui, bad saving checkpoints, sound glitch.
