_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed it, BUT KNOW WHAT YOU'RE IN FOR:This is not a game where you are given free reign over the station and then manage its various functions, this is a game where you very linearly find clues, flip switches and solve puzzles to progress the story.The devs put a lot of care into the presentation for both wirting and audio/visual (it's film quality), so it's a shame that there's not more freedom in regards to the gameplay. It's a horror game, but in a psychological thriller kind of way. And since you're seeing everything through cameras the entire game, it has a found footage feel to it.A big part of the game are the software interfaces which have that wonderful CRT military-grade aesthetic, you'll be reminded of Alien Isolation. In fact the game's director was the UI lead on Alien Isolation and Observation is in a lot of ways a spiritual succesor to Isolation. There's no hiding from an alien monster, but it's also about a woman trying to survive alone on a damaged space station orbiting a gas giant as things keep getting weirder and tenser.The game is purposefully confusing and clumsy - not just the puzzles, but the station itself, and the fact that it all takes place in zero g where there is no up or down, making it easy to get disorientated. My advice: sometime after the intro take the time and learn the layout of the station, and use shift to enter a 3D view mode, it will really help. You being confused though makes perfect sense because you play a damaged AI that's supposed to be operating poorly.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, not as good as Stories Untold, but a more than worthwhile followup. A masterclass in verisimilitude and diegetic gameplay. Like the weird lovechild of Tarkovsky's Solaris and Kubrick's 2001. Super ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. It does have the problem of (for a 'horror' game) not being scary (or even very tense). Putting the player inside a dispassionate robot shell made me play like a dispassionate robot. Probably objectively better than Stories Untold, at the very least Observation tells a much tighter and coherent narrative and is more technically proficient. But subjectively, I just *liked* Stories Untold better. Goes to some more surreal, artsy, interpretive places, and that's more what I'm looking for. Buy them both.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: is am 6.5/10is a very generic sci-fi story if you have seen a lot of alien/robots movies with vague story plots you have seen  all. I was really hoping this game to be like a rogue AI  that start killing the crew though. But the game is a bit too expansive considering that is very short. a game that last 4 hours cant cost more than $10 despite the over budget motion capture they did on a few scene and yes i have play another No Code game called untold stories and despite not liking the end of the story i still enjoy the puzzles i cant say the same with Observation.PS i recommend playing at a discount
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great scifi horror game. Kind of like 2001 X Event Horizon. That's probably all I should reveal if I don't want to spoil the story further. Gameplay wise you play as the space station's System Administration & Maintenance (SAM) Operating System whereby you are relegated to moving about from camera to camera operating various things after pairing up with them to accomplish many tasks essential to the crew's survival. Your companion for most of the game is the station scientist Emma Fisher. Together, you deduce what's going on with the station and what happened to the rest of the crew. Eventually, SAM gains access to remote bodies that allow it to navigate about the station to further its duties.This is a slow burner of a game and navigating SAM in 3D space in dark, confined, samey-looking areas can be confusing. Some of the puzzles you'll be solving can be cryptic, consult a guide if needed, I managed without one. Lastly, this is definitely and KBM game and not a controller one.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved the story. I don't have much love for puzzles but the atmosphere and almost Lovecraftian / 2001 space odyssey vibes kept me hooked all the way to the end. Would love to see a Movie adaptation or perhaps another game to this. For the price i paid the visuals were really solid. I'm glad to have been apart of the ride and hope to get more experiences  like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Overall it is a great game in terms of the story line and the visuals. The puzzles (the main point of the game) are not properly designed. Half of them do not make sense at all and you will be forced to look answers online. The puzzles that require memory, eye-hand coordination, etc. make sense, but any puzzle that requires to explore the station are extremely hard since the visuals aspects of a space game like this are unnecessarily hard. For example, the fact that the lighting overall is limited (it being a space station in distress) makes the exploration puzzles hard enough. Combine that with the difficulties of physical orientation, and its too frustrating and gets in the way of fun. Pick one of the two. Either improve the lighting conditions or make orientation easier. Overall, I found it more frustrating than fun, but if it wasn't for that, this game would be awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Top contender for the most boring game I have ever played.The novelty of the concept got me through the first 20 minutes of the game but once the novelty wore off the horrible controls and terrible game mechanics hit me like a truck. And the cut scenes .... in the words of great George Carlin, it was like watching flies F..k.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is a fantastic puzzle game with heavy 2001: A Space Odyssey influences. You control the A.I. of the space station, "Observation" that's in Earth's orbit, until you look out the window and are greeted by Saturn. The story while not nearly as convoluted as 2001, is much easier to follow but doesn't skimp out on the heavy subject matter that comes with this genre. Multiple times during the story did it take a turn I didn't expect, and kept me genuinely interested the entire playthrough. The game is well paced, not spending too much time on either aspects of the game being the storytelling and puzzle solving. While not necessarily a horror game, Observation keeps a consistent feeling of tension and unease the entire duration. Throughout the game you're given tiny snippets of what's going on under the hood of the story, you will piece things together by the time it ends. Observation is a science fiction mindf*** resembling some of my favorite aspects of 2001: A Space Odyssey, and in my book that's a buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving a positive review, but the game suffers from poor direction in lots of cases that made certain sections a chore to slog through. Overall, the story was a great experience and had a decent ending that left just enough open to interpretation, but explained enough that most things made sense.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This game was exactly what I expected and I really enjoyed it for that. It seems many of the negative reviews were simply expecting something the game isn't. So with that said: this is basically a walking simulator. There are *some* puzzle and action elements, but nothing particularly challenging. Mostly some following some very simple instructions on a computer screen and navigating yourself around a sometimes confusing space station in zero G (which I personally enjoyed).This game is about the atmosphere, tension, and watching a sci-fi thriller unfold whilst being an active part in its unfolding. It's gorgeous graphics and environments, great believable voice acting throughout, and a solid sci-fi story. Comparisons to 2001 are not without merit, so if you're a sci-fi fan already you're not necessarily going to be surprised by this one, but it puts enough of its own spin on things to justify its existence.I personally didn't find the controls clunky as some other reviews say, and I didn't notice a single bug or issue in my playthrough but obviously YMMV.The story does end a bit flatly as what feels like a set up for something new, but according to their website No Code has no plans for Observation 2 which is a bit of a shame because I would definitely pick it up.An easy recommend from me for fans of sci-fi and thriller themes who appreciate an immersive world and story, but DO NOT play this for action or puzzle elements because, whilst those elements are here to some degree, they are absolutely not the purpose of the game which is instead the story and the storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is a unique experience, this shows us what games can be as interactive story telling. It's not a game about mechanics(though the puzzles are interesting to complete), it's a game you can play with someone(like a movie) and the curiosity kept me going. I completed it the day I got it (5 hours) because I couldn't stop myself wanting to know the ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: 4/10Semi interesting rail game, no real way to fail, just infinite retry attempts on incorrectly solved puzzles.Puzzles are not hugely intricate, very basic 'receive commands and follow through with them' (in most cases with infinite time to complete).No ability to adjust audio in game.Some choices don't actually affect results.Second last puzzle was frustrating because of lack of accuracy in response from key inputs.Game obviously made for controllers, making some keyboard inputs fiddly.Graphics: 4/10Facial expressions look unnatural.In general also very boxy.Story Line: 4/10Maintains interest throughout story, but simply through waiting for story to make sense. BTW the ending doesn't fix this.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice Sci-Fi Thriller with a unique story spin and stunning visuals.You are playing as a space stations artificial intelligence, operating the control systems, cameras, and tools as the horror progresses. No jumpscares in this one, but still very creepy atmosphere.Only big minus is the rather complicated UI and the regular occurrence of a "what does the game want me to do?!"-feeling. Puzzles felt unique and overall non-repeating.My rating = 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is very divisive game, and for good reason. Now, my personal experience with it was extremely positive, but that's partially because I am very biased towards these sci-fi psychological, existential, you-dont-need-to-understand kinds of BS, and because I was lucky enough to get through the game without any of the apparent game breaking bugs, or having to deal with the awful checkpoint system. The gameplay and the UI leaves a LOT to be desired. You will fight with it every step of the way, and you WILL get lost and disoriented all the time. I spent at least half of my four hour playtime just trying to figure out where i was and where i needed to go, and good luck trying to read the map, cause chances are you will be upside down when you return back to your sphere and be totally turned around.On the other end of the spectrum, the story is very good at keeping you invested. The acting is good, not great but its believable, and the graphics are incredible. The atmosphere of a barely functioning and busted space station is a great one, and they do a good job of really making you feel it. There are visual shots in this game that are downright beautiful, but others kind of drag. Finally, the strongest point of the game, it's story. Honestly i want to give this one a 10/10 JUST for delivering a satisfying ending, something that almost no game, movie, book or show in this medium can manage to do for some reason. The story built up slowly overtime and the payoff is very very worth it. It's one of those games that really makes you ponder after it ends, the kind that makes you want to find someone else who has played it and discuss theories all night long. No spoilers, but the main concept surrounding this game is fairly unique if you really think about it and take the right context clues from the game itself.All in all, if you have some patience and just want a really compelling story and a few creative puzzles to go with it, i highly reccommend it! Otherwise, I'd suggest watching a playthrough on youtube just to get to the story without all the hassle. Solid 7/10 for gameplay, but 10/10 for story. Just don't forget to BRING HER.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with an interesting premise. Not only is the story and setting quite unique, but the gameplay is too. However, unique is not always a good thing, for although I like the main story beads, and I in theory like the gameplay ideas, this game was, at best, boring and repetitive to play, and at worst, incredibly tedious. Some of its core issues are: - The autosave feature does not really tell you when the last autosave moment was. There is a small, very missable icon showing, whenever the game saves, but it does not always save when you expect it to. I returned to the game to find out I had to solve two puzzles and watch two cutscenes again, as it had sent me far back. There is no real reason why this game should not have a manual save option.  - The puzzles/minigames are really repetitive and are generally not fun. It feels like much more of a waste of time than anything I enjoyed doing. It is made even worse by having so many time-waster associated with things, such as having you hold down a button instead of just pressing it. Having you enter three digits instead of just automatically linking you to something. It is a bit cute the first four or five times, but when you have to do it a hundred times, it starts feeling like the game does not care about the time you spend on it. And it also doesn’t make much sense, as this is futuristic technology we are dealing with (granted it is the near future), but everything is operating slower than a five years old IPhone. - Another issue is  that the game decided to have some characteristic graphics – something that makes you feel like you are an operating system. The issue is here that it is, again, looking like it is from the 90ies and the resolution is therefore so bad that it can be a huge struggle to read any icons, the legendary or simple notes you find (which can be affected a lot by your lights too). I tried adjusting the graphics in several ways, but nothing helped. In fact, another problem with the game is that it keeps altering the graphics settings I set for it. - The game can be very hard to navigate. Even when you can use the waypoint system (and that is not always an option), it can be misleading. In the end, I really wanted this game to be over after the first two hours, as I really didn’t enjoy my time playing it. I was however intrigued by where the story would lead and kept going. I can now say that it just isn’t worth it. I yelled at the game on multiple occasions and generally just had a bad time with it, relying heavily on YouTube videos for the last two hours of it as nothing interesting was happening gameplay wise and I just wanted to get to the ending. TLDRNice concept, terrible execution.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where I wish there was middle ground between Recommended and Not Recommended.Observation is a atmospheric scifi thriller with a great story that keeps you invested the whole way through. The problem is that the story is really the only thing it has going for it. Gameplay is passable but limited to either switching between cameras that you can pan and zoom to find and complete simple puzzles, or controlling a camera drone/sphere to fly around and complete simple puzzles. There are additional data logs and notes that you can find to learn more about the characters and station, but these are not required to complete the game and don't provide much in the way of meaningful lore.There are some minor bugs but nothing I encountered was game breaking. Some odd model collisions during cutscenes, and at one part I had the cutscene audio play without the visual forcing me to reload (fortunately the game autosaved just before the cutscene).You can complete Observation entirely in 5 to 6 hours - which includes collecting all documents and achievements (word of advice, there is a section of the game where you will end up somewhere you cannot get back to, if you do not collect all documents while there you are out of luck for that playthrough). Once completed there is no reason to go back and replay the game. There are no choices that change the story, no information that you've found in the first playthrough to impact the second, and perhaps the worst thing - you cannot skip cutscenes or sequence break making any second playthrough just as long as the first but much more tedious.Ultimately Observation is about the story, and you have to make the decision whether the going price is reasonable for you to pay to spend 5 to 6 hours in a  story that you won't go back to. I bought this on sale for 50% off at $18 AUD, and while I think it's on the pricey side I still enjoyed my time with it and recommend it. I would not recommend this at full price ($36 AUD at time of this review).
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, so much so that I played it through in one sitting. I have no major issues; I think my only complaint is that the game could probably have been longer without the story suffering, perhaps adding some optional parts? Technically I think the only issue I had were some z-fighting artifacts on the outside of the station. I'd also like to praise that switching between keyboard and controller was seamless, with the caveat that some of the puzzles were much easier on the controller, making it necessary to switch; the seamlessness rescued this, though someone without a controller will obviously be a little dinged.Of course, what better can be said of a game than I wanted more?
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: It's three hours of mildly competent sci-fi followed by an hour of metaphysical hand-shandy. (Go look the term up, giggle, then come back). If Bioshock infinite is how you want to spice up a low rent version of Event Horizon then sure, go for it but as far as I'm concerned this is basically Tacoma but with a few puzzles and an animated protagonist (which right away puts it above Tacoma).The story is a really low budget version of Event Horizon (instead of a rescue mission, instead it's "Send out a bunch of completely unprepared scientists to go poke a potentially doom-scale event with a stick because WHY THE HELL NOT") and the inevitable happens, everything goes horribly wrong, people die and you get to play budget HAL-9000 and try to stop the ship from falling apart whilst figuring out how the doom-event keeps trying to pick on the one STILL LIVING person who eventually goes "I'M GOING TO NOT ONLY POKE IT, I'M GOING TO HUG IT."Allow me to reference Laurence Fishburne when he realised what happened to the Event Horizon: That is the correct route when dealing with something that clearly intends to do horrible things not only to you but quite possibly your species. IF SOMETHING IS GOING "BRING HER" OVER AND OVER YOU DO NOT OBEY. YOU RUN LIKE BINGO.A good plot needs you to suspend disbelief. For the first half, yes, it worked, it actually worked pretty well, but once the reveal happened and the protagonist decided to hug the idiot ball, well, things started falling apart fast.Games like these -live or die- by their narrative. It's what sells these story centric games. It's not like most others where you're pitted against the puzzles set by the designers (the puzzles here are pretty pumpkin spiced latte) and the graphics, whilst pretty, are not blow your socks off. This was designed to tell a story, so it gets judged on that in the main.The ending made me a very annoyed Tiger. People do not hug the thing which clearly has bad intents, if they do, they're morons.GAH.Verdict:
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Wow that was it? What a short and tedioius game. From time to time you might catch a glimpse of the intended atmosphere when the clumsy controls and unimpressive graphics aren't getting in the way, but mostly you're just being frustrated when trying to find the next trigger to advance the game. I might be hard to impress by 2020, but in the very least I expected a much better and deeoer story. I could go on, but I have better things to do with my time and will just say I would pay max 5 € for a game of this quality and length without feeling robbed.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Observation tells a fantastic and compelling science fiction story, combining elements of 2001: A Space Odyssey, Soma, and Alien Isolation.  The player taking on the perspective of a space station A.I. makes for unique storytelling opportunities, the puzzles are challenging without being frustrating, and actress Kezia Burrows does a wonderful job bringing the character of Emma Fisher to life.  A short but remarkably well-written game that is a joy to experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of the films: 2001 A Space Odyssey and 2010 The Year We Make Contact, than you will probably love this game.These days I find it hard to play one title for an hour at most. I couldn't put this one down until I had finished it after 6 hours.I found the setting and gameplay extremely immersive with a narrative that just pulled me in and wouldn't let go. There were entire sections that had me on the edge of my couch with anticipation, with suspenseful moments that almost made me hold my breath.The game isn't super expansive or complicated nor at the top in terms of graphics quality, but than again it doesn't need to be. It's essentially an interactive story, but It does what it does extremely well and like the films this title takes inspiration from it leaves many questions unanswered and open to thought provoking interpretation. I will definitely dive into it again.I know this is essentially very high praise for what is just a video game, but for me it is the first in a very long time to pull me in and keep me playing.Many people won't have the same experience I had, some will say "it's garbage" or "just so so".But I feel this was worth the time and money spent.In addition: In the middle of the night after writing this I woke up and almost ♥♥♥♥ myself when I saw what looked like a floating black hexagon in my room.Turned out to be my desk chair.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking forward to playing this very much, but after an hour was ready to get a refund (which I did) and call it quits.My main problem with it was how the AI resolved the tasks given it. How does it make sense that by "looking" at something using a camera, only then the AI can magically access it... that makes no sense at all. If I am the AI, I would be able to access it anyway because I'm apart of the electronic's system and computer. How does "looking" at it give me that access??
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This is amazing.If you like atmospheric horror and mystery, if you like computer-themed puzzles, this game is for you.It took me about 4.5 hours to finish the whole thing, but it was amazing.Some people have complained about the sphere controls, I found them fine. Might be that my mouse sensitivity is very high and therefore they're less cumbersome.Biggest complaint is that occasionally it's not clear where you have to go or what you have to do to accomplish your objective.But overall, really good. Definitely worth a playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10. MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD.I would recommend this game if you want something really different from classic Dead Space experience. The tension is definetely present, the atmosphere, the unusual game mechanics, all the (surprise!) satisfying spacecraft realistic details are here. But bro, what is all this for? I have been solving these damn puzzles to know whats behind all this, and the answer I get is "a mysterious alien force". Like WHAT??? WTH??? Have you ever read Azimov, Lem, other great sci-fi classic writers? Take some notes from there, guys. Overall, a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, if you can pick this up for the price of a movie ticket ($10 or less), I would recommend it. I would not recommend it at full price.As a fan of story driven linear experiences I was really excited to play this. I had just played Tacoma and A Plague's Tale and was looking for similar games, and I love the sci-fi genre so this caught my eye.There was a game breaking bug that I ran into about 3/4ths of my way through that I spent nearly an hour trying to solve as a 'puzzle' before looking up a playthrough and finding out that this was a bug. Not to mention that my ultrawide 21:9 screen isn't properly supported (no option for it in the menu), and the numerous camera/view bugs (like character models disappearing and re-appearing at random, and props glitching in and out of existence).My biggest gripe was probably the complete lack of a good waypoint system. I understand that exploration is a major premise for the game, but it was frustrating to the point of ruining my experience when I couldn't figure out what unlabeled panel in a completely different side of the station I was supposed to randomly happen upon in order to progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic story and gameplay, different take on camera angle lends greatly to the experience. Facial animation is garbage though, so much potential there. Would recommend for the story and gameplay, that facial animation is just a big ♥♥♥♥ on the whole experience though. Still a strong 9/10 despite the flaw though
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: You control the space station’s AI system known as S.A.M, (System Administration & Maintenance) as you try and figure out exactly what happened after a strange event has your crew scattered and leaving your system massively corrupted. You will be assisted by Dr Emma Fisher, who helps you get to grips with how you can interact with the ship’s systems aboard the space station, Observation. Within the first half an hour or so, some of the mystery starts to unfold, whilst also creating more intrigue.To recover S.A.M’s memory you must collect data which is either taped on walls as documents or on files located within laptops. Finding every bit a data will give the player a deeper understanding of the Space Stations crew, even giving SAM schematics to unlock new areas previously inaccessible.The majority of the game and its story is told from the perspective of the space stations cameras, you as an AI don’t have legs or arms to get around the many cramped corridors. At certain points within the game, you’ll be able to possess spheres, which look very similar to the cores in Portal 2. The spheres themselves are easy enough to use, although certain areas of the space station will make traversal slightly more difficult.Puzzles are plentiful within , which could be memorising a series of patterns or numbers which you then input manually or hitting specific buttons in a short time limit. These aren’t too taxing but will build tension, as one mistake could cost the integrity to the space station. is a tremendous game, from start to finish you’ll be hooked into wanting to uncover what exactly is happening.- Captivating story- Smart puzzles- Unique experience- Fantastic visuals- Great atmosphere- You might experience motion sicknessDISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT |  | MASTERPIECE
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty awesome gameplay - camera movement were stiff and clunky at best, little to no responsiveness or precision.The characters, what little you saw of them was okay.After getting to the the half way point, guessing the story became utterly easy.Nothing really surprised me as the first half did.The path the story took (and at least it did not appear as if there is multiple endings) was actually a bland path.It kind of felt like the game could not really figure out weather it wants to be calm and suspenseful or pick things up.Little to nothing is ultimately explained.The ending felt like they were trying oh so super hard at figure out what to do with this game, and rushed the ending...In short, watch a youtuber play through this... you'll have a bit more fun this way, seriously.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: If it was a movie I would say that Ive seen a similar story too many times, but its not.  its a game, and a very original one. You play as SAM an AI of an adrift space station called "Observation". A great point of view to play a SCIFI game.You can move from camera to camera of the station, or move as a floating sphere from module to module, and interact with different elements, of course. I think the difficulty needs a little tweaking. Even if you know the next goal you need to achieve, its very difficult to know where to go in the station to resolve it. I had to google the solution too many times. The game needs to underestimate the player a little bit more.I think this game its a great achivement just by its gameplay, and a little by the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: This game hook me enough with the story to keep me going. Then gave me a disappointing ending after making literally look at everything in game. Just so that I could find the next piece of the stupid puzzle. I would have preferred to see this as a movie to be honest, but I got this frustrating game instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: pretty good game. At first I thought I would get bored of it as I was just clicking away at things but the story had a grip on me and the more I played the more I enjoyed it. The audio is awesome, the visuals aren't too bad either. gripping story and decent enough puzzles. Also i think the length of the game was just perfect. Any longer and i probably would have started to get bored but all in all its a pretty solid game imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: So i'll be reviewing this based on it's story. I didn't play anything outside of story.This game was a roller coaster ride, from start to finish. I started it thinking, it's gonna be a cool suspense horror with a nice space feel added to it. I hadn't heard of it before buying it so i thought: "why not?"Wasn't i surprised to find out that it's an incredibly well told story.The "Puzzles" (not really puzzles but sorta) are unique and cool. When i first started i had played on a worse pc so i lowered the graphics but after i had upgraded, the graphics were amazing. they weren't top notch AAA level but still incredible. I loved everything about the game.You start off as an AI who needs to help an Astronaut called Emma Fisher, get back to Earth intact. Slowly over the course of the game, you encounter some "being" which keeps telling you to bring her to where you currently are. The Space Station drifted near Saturn somehow. Afterwards you find out that you aren't the only one that got sent there. You're but one of dozens, hundreds, maybe thousands, of spaceships. All with the  same crew.The graphics were beautiful. It's one of the more new games i've been able to enjoy fully on it's highest Settings. I still thought despite everything that it's brilliant. I won't be specific and just say, it's beautiful.I saw none. I didn't see any Bugs, Glitches or "Features". It's incredibly well written (code, not story).
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Whats going on? I was expecting to be space walking or something but instead I'm just answering commands. She says she needs diagnostics to see if it's safe to open the doors and the only response I can give is asking her to repeat the command in different ways. What else am I supposed to do because nothing is working for me to progress past this point. Not fun at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know exactly what to think of this game. At full price i wouldnt recommend buying it. I bought it on offer, and for that price it was worth it.For those thinking you'll be freeroaming, you'll be wrong. Its a very linear game, where youll have some exploration but that's more to gather collections and unlock achievements, and get more out of the story.Outside of that its more of a do-this, do-that, fetch-this, fix-that kind of game with a lot of puzzles. Most puzzles were enjoyable, but there were a couple that for my brain were very wdsa-unfriendly and clearly designed for a controller.The story is good, maybe even very good, until the last 10 seconds. Without spoiling anything, but that ruined most of the game for me. Id suggest just ending the game when you do the very final puzzle and be satisfied with that mystery of an ending. It suits the game better also.But if you want to have five or six hours of gameplay (without hunting collections) that are enjoyable, and you're not looking for a horror game (the game did have that label on steam when i bought it, but thats really non present) and you can buy the game for around a tenner, Id defo advice getting it :)
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: A very, very quality HAL simulator/interactive movie kind of game.Intense, captivating story, Thiccccccc atmosphere, heavy and punchy sound, beautiful contemporary space station environments, and an absolute what the– ending and realization.Very light on any challenge, "puzzles" aren't really puzzles and more like... actual station routine which i REALLY appreciate, especially in the way we are doing it, the Station AI way.I wish there was more games about being either an AI or a similar entity, helping someone or impeding their progress through cameras and control of the environment.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The first 2 hrs of Observation for me were stressful, nauseating, and disappointing. The "puzzles" were simple Simon-says type tasks, presented with yelling and alarms to simulate difficulty. At one point you essentially become a floating camera with awful movement controls and effects that left me feeling ill enough to take breaks. Then it crashed...and then crashed again.Maybe it's one of those games that redeem themselves post the 2hr mark, but I had no desire to keep going.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: A really interesting story let down by terrible choices by the developer. This game has some really bad mouse acceleration applied that makes it really hard to control anything, even just clicking around menus are a chore. On top of that the game does not support ultra-wide aspect ratios, despite imposing it's own letter boxing. This just results in a view of the game that is both letter and pillar boxed. Refunded
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep it simple. If you're a fan of point and click adventures full of suspense and mystery you need this game. I played almost all of my first 6.5 hours in one day. Even if you aren't into the point and click genre this game will still keep you intrigued with just the story.My only complaint is the cameras move a bit too slowly and searching a room can take more time than it should if you are searching for something small and obscure.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The environment of this game is very compelling - your exploration is limited to what you can see from the perspective of the station computer through a few camera angles. The ambience leans towards horror, but you won't need to worry about anything jumping out at you. This game relies purely on the setting - a labyrinthine space station  - to keep you on the edge of your seat as you help what remains of the crew to make sense of their dire circumstances.Navigation can be disorienting and unresponsive at times, but I think this contributes to the experience of observing reality through the lense of a computer AI.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't read any of the other comments, so right now all I can think of that this game has got going for itself is the visuals. Everything else is on a scale of ok to borderline trash. The space station looks great: the cramped corridors, the stuff strapped along the walls, the GUI of the AI SAM (who you play as), and the various qualities of video feeds you have access to. But when an actual human shows up the game nose dives into the Uncanny Valley. Emma (the human astronaut you are lightly babysitting through the majority of the game) opens her mouth at weird times, stares blankly, and none of the facets of zero-gravity are appearant in her , besides the vague floatiness of it all.Ok, so the visuals hit a bit of a wall, the gameplay should make up the difference for this radically acclaimed game? Absolutely not.Besides the camera clunkiness (which actually has a reason for existing) most other gameplay elements are either completely arbitrary or down right lazy. You get to pilot a little ball drone in this game, in free-fall, in space. So what should that mean? It should mean that it's a little hard to control, that you fly off in a direction you eren't intending and have to actually get good at flying it, like the slowly rebuilding space station AI you are supposed to be playing as. But instead the damn thing stops on a dime, only runs out of fuel for plot reasons, and is completely invincible. Ok, fine, fine, maybe it's about being the AI, maybe it's about doing cool hacking ♥♥♥♥ and puzzles. Wrong again! The puzzles are straight up easy. And I don't mean literally pointing and clicking, but straight up infinite chances, no risks, low reward homework puzzles. Here's the "best" puzzle trio: Hacking is simple, collecting all of the data on all of the laptops is tedious and only yields a damn achievement, and there is no urgency whatsoever in any of the "action" scenes. So people can't be raving about the gameplay.It has to be the story. The sci-fi horror, the loneliness of space, the silence, the death just a few inches of steel away. It's not the story, folks. Spoilers for the story for the next paragraph or so, then the wrap up, if you stuck around long enough, thanks for reading, the password is Rootuledge.Horror is the utilization of a metaphor to remind us of a factor of the human condition. There is nothing, literally nothing, scary about this game. It isn't horror, it is not a good or developed story, it is not a good puzzle game. It literally only looks good.Do not buy this game. Get Outer Wilds if you want a sci-fi puzzle adventure game with existential horror elements. Read Contact or The Light of Other Days if you want sci-fi craziness. And watch Annihilation if you want the presence of  talked about in even a minor coherent manner.

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is an atmospheric puzzle game set in space and is heavily inspired by films like 2001: A Space Odyssey, and Interstellar. It nails the atmosphere. The setting is creepy, dark and tense. Whilst also being beautiful and serene at the same time. 10/10 in that area. The puzzles are very underwhelming. I call them puzzles put they're not really. The only times I ever got stuck was when I felt like the game didn't give me enough information to solve the puzzle. Sometimes this is cool, you feel like you're solving many puzzles by simply looking for details in the environment. Sometimes though it can be fairly annoying. Especially when the game asks you to navigate to certain part of the ship. Many parts of the ship look the same and it's very easy to get turned around by accident. Especially since it's a space station and doors and floors aren't always in the same relative orientation to each other. Sometimes a door is where you would expect it to be. Other times it's directly above you. Aside from these fairly minor annoyances though the game was enjoyable.If you enjoy atmospheric games, or plot heavy games revolving around space as a theme then you will enjoy this. Just don't buy it for the puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: In this game, you play as the AI of a space station whose mission has gone awry and had your memory erased after a catastrophic event. Your goal is to piece together what happened and support Dr. Emma Fisher during this process.Mechanically, this game combines many of the activities of a "walking simulators" (investigation, exploration, atmosphere, world-building). Of note, the way the player interacts with the camera feeds and station subsystems seems influenced by similar mechanics popularized by FNAF (of all things!). The game largely delivers on its premise; graphics are compelling and the environments really do shine. It is interesting to see how different a game of this nature feels when the perspective is from that of a "Robot."Playtime is likely 8-10 hours for the average individual, perhaps a bit more if you wanted to seek all the achievements. Recommended if any of the above is of interested or you like games of this nature.Overall, this is a solid game

_childDocuments_.review: My 15-year old daughter and I played this and we enjoyed it.  The visuals are beautiful and the story is intriguing.  The gameplay presents a few challenges.  Early on in the game you need to rapidly push specific keys, after only the briefest instructions.  It all happens so quickly that we screwed it up and the game doesn't allow for traditional saves (autosaves only), so there was no way to go back without going back to virtually the beginning.  There were a few other situations like that throughout the game.  We wound up having to "cheat" a couple of times by going to YouTube and watching how someone else figured it out.Another challenge is that it's very easy to get turned around and disoriented in the levels/rooms, as many of them are quite similar.  Also, often the only way to view certain areas is through mounted cameras, and scrolling through them to find the right angle and item you're trying to spot is occasionally frustrating.Despite those issues, the dialogue, visuals, and sound combine nicely to create a very eerie, tense atmosphere.  While the story borrows from some well-known sci fi films and books, it was compelling.  If you like puzzle solving and mysterious plots, you are likely to enjoy this game.  Given the price, it was good value for money, in our view.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first negative review I have ever posted on steam, but I'm really irritated with this game.This game is a disappointment. It's a sort of Sci-fi short movie with an excuse of gameplay. The puzzles are fustrating and the gameplay flow is heavily inconsistent, with the player having to guess a lot of things, and I imagine some of it is intentional. But the bad design makes the experience more frustrating than anything else. _childDocuments_.review: It's a rare horror game that leans so hard into creeping dread like Observation does. It's more Lovecraftian than most Lovecraft games.Rather than frighten the player with monsters at the door, Observation prefers to perplex its player through unsettling insinuation. Its puzzles are largely unraveled through careful exploration. The controls are ponderous, but the game itself makes no effort to hurry the player through its 6-8 hour campaign, so I didn't mind this much. I did encounter one bug later in the game the prevented me from closing a hatch that was necessary to advance the story, but quitting and reloading resolved the issue.You really should use a gamepad to play the game; keyboard/mouse controls are poorly optimized, but a controller works well with it.The narrative pits creeping uncertainty against the player's curiosity and takes a restrained advantage of the inherent vulnerability of being very, very far away from a breathable atmosphere. I wasn't as satisfied by the ending as I might have wanted to be, and the character twists might have been more impactful with more development, but those are all secondary to the growing blur of claustrophobia and agoraphobia the game inspires in its player.

_childDocuments_.review: Observer does not manage to be a satisfying story, mystery, or even a puzzle game. Even judged solely on its signature device -- playing as an AI, rather than the usual unwitting, human survivor -- the game does not propose any insight nor deliver an experience that merits the contrivance in the first place.As an investigative game, it is shallow. As befitting a haunted space station setting, there are audio logs to find and puzzles to solve. Most of the audio logs are banal, and provide little to no value in moving the story forward or gaining an understanding of what has occurred. The puzzles are superficial, mechanical exercises: typically about figuring out how to unlock doors and activate devices by messing with unfamiliar user interfaces. One would think, as an AI, that adjusting six magnets inside a fusion bottle would be effortless. Here, it's so clunky as to barely get it done within an imposed 60-second timer. Solving the puzzles moves the plot - usually via in-game cut scenes that follow, before interactive control is restored so that the player can proceed ... to the next puzzle - but they contribute nothing at all to a greater understanding of the central mystery.The problem may be that there's very little to actually understand. The trappings are technological, but the story is fantastical. The ending is unsatisfying and unhappy. As an environment, the game's music, lighting and audio work sets the mood well. But, as a story, it's the typical linear malevolence and pessimism that science fiction horror has been putting out for the last 40 years, and one doesn't even have to look back more than 5-6 years to find games in the same genre that plot, play, and look better, even at a cheaper price.Considering the player-as-AI concept that the game dragged out, one would think the game would actually reveal some profundity about the condition; insights on the limitation of being an entity with circumscribed mobility, or demonstrations of cognitive shifts. Observation is unfortunately unambitious, and all we get to do is unlock laptops, restart air circulators, unjam docking clamps, and vainly try to understand supernatural phenomenon that the game writers intend to be incomprehensible.

_childDocuments_.review: This was quite an impressive game to play. I was really amazed by the realism put into the game to represent life in space.This is not something I have ever seen presented with such RL accuracy in a video game before. Kudo to the devs for achieving this!You play as SAM, the spacestation AI. You have no body. Just imagine yourself playing as HAL from 2001. You are the spacestation eyes and brain, the station watcher and crew assistant. You are able to observe anywhere from any of the numerous cameras on the station, and gain access to/interact with any computers and systems on the station. Creepy much? Of course not, because you have to follow the 3 laws. Hum, do you?You will be able to possess a mobile sphere bot at different points later on in the game, but most of the gameplay consists of exploring the station by switching between cameras, and assist Emma, a station astronaut, helping her figure out what happend to the rest of the station crew.I would qualify Observation to be an sci-fi adventure puzzle game with a very strong emphasis on exploration. You have to like snooping to enjoy this game. Take your time to understand and figure things out. Try things, look everywhere, connect to anything, scan any documents, listen to any recordings... The more data you collect, the more info you will uncover about the story.There was one pretty hard QTE at the beginning of the game that took me at least 10 tries before I got it right. And one puzzle I didnt understand that I just solved using trial and error. But other than those, puzzles and QTE are relatively easy, as long as you pay attention.There is only one autosave, and the game automatically saves after some important event or after finding a document. You will see a round icon appear at the top right of the screen while the game saves. Pay attention to it if you want to quit the game. Otherwise you might have to replay some part of the game next time you load.I was absolutely delighted with this game and finished it in 2 days. I loved spending my time looking at every details in any corners of the station but I dont think this is a game that would appeal to everyone. If you are looking for a fast game with clear objectives on what to do, do not play this. This is a slow game that requires patience and time to discover what it is all about.

_childDocuments_.review: I do like puzzle games, so Observation started off as being quite intriguing. _childDocuments_.review: Observation is so close to being a great game, but unfortunately it's just an okay game. I'll tag major spoilers, but there will be minor spoilers.Overall: There's a real disconnect between the gameplay and the story here.At first they sync perfectly: the player as the AI (SAM) is slowly waking up, jumping between fuzzy camera feeds as our main character tries to figure out what happened. The slowness of the gameplay and camera perfectly compliment the dread and atmosphere just oozing from the early sections - and I appreciate the attention to detail given to the SAM's interface and actions. Every time I switched camera feeds I held my breath.But very quickly SAM is given control of a little robot to navigate the world, making the player just like any other human in this situation - having to fly around and interact with components up close. You spend the majority of the rest of the game using this little guy, and I can't understand why the developers decided to dump their unique method of story telling so quickly.As the game progresses further, it becomes clear that puzzles are never going to advance beyond "find and click this thing with your very slow moving camera" or "play this Among Us busy-work mini-game", which is a real shame. There also isn't any real sense of SAM becoming more powerful as the game goes on - it takes me just as long to unlock a door 50 minutes into the game as 5 hours into the game. As the player, I don't feel like a super-advanced AI - I feel more like a space intern. And a bad intern at that, as I repeatedly got lost both inside and outside of the station - which immediately killed any urgency the game was trying to portray as it waited patiently for me to find the right door/panel.By the time we reach the mid to late game, the story is growing more fast-paced, tense, and urgent, but this is undercut by the fact that the gameplay really doesn't change at all. This leads to an almost comical level of the story pausing while SAM very slowly goes through the motions, and just wrecks the pacing of the final act, which is a dang shame given that the story here is actually really good.Consider what could have been (SPOILERS): The story and atmosphere here are enough for me to still recommend this game, but unfortunately I still can't help thinking about how good it could have been instead of how good it actually was.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is  awesome, but ends up being a movie with bad pacing because of the game parts, and a game with less interaction than a choose-your-own-adventure book (save for a select few interesting puzzles) because of the movie parts. I think with a few small changes, this could have been an excellent hybrid of both.The fiction is great - I loved the story, it was thrilling to see it unfold when it was meant to be. The graphics and sounds are great and contribute immensely to a tense atmosphere full of thrilling mystery. I enjoyed the running "call and response" theme, which was used to set up some impressive scenes. The dialogue was interesting and the lore you can find on the laptops really added to the intrigue in ways that many other works with a similar/identical mechanic fail (e.g. Bioshock's audio recordings).The grand majority of actual interaction (gameplay) comes in isolated puzzles, most of which are fun to figure out. The player is rewarded for experimenting while solving some puzzles, but others become less of a puzzle and more of a waiting game. Overall, the gameplay has decent pacing and relatively engaging mechanics in isolation. However, some parts that may be considered "puzzles" end up artificially extending the playtime of the game by having incredibly contrived "solutions" that bring everything to a complete halt while you bugger around trying to figure out what to do. "Investigate the damage to the exterior": okay, well these whole modules have been torn asunder, let's check that out. Oh, no, not  exterior damage. No, not that damaged part either. No, not those structural beams sticking out into space, . Ah yes, you've found the singular, specific dent in the hull we were referring to, congrats on solving this pixel-hunt equivalent challenge.Additionally, the developers' approach to the fiction as an interactive film gets in the way of that fiction in many places; the medium they chose to tell this story in interfered with the storytelling itself. It often feels like I'm watching a movie, but there's someone else with the DVD remote who keeps randomly pausing for a few minutes. I got to about halfway through the game before I realized I had been waiting for things to "open up" and I would be given control and tasked with handling the situation - I was waiting for the game to start, in other words. This never happens. You are shown a big map of the station, told how to perform tasks such as opening hatches or accessing terminals...and then you are never really allowed to do anything they taught you except in the specific scenarios where someone tells you to. The only activity you are allowed beyond the puzzles is exploration, but this really falls flat because there's not really anything to find beyond the laptop files and pretty graphics. They wanted it to be like a movie, so the player has no control or choice. This is incredibly disappointing considering that with the in-text presence of  the developers had a  setup to let the player fail in any way at any time. Sam randomly decides to shut down life support and flush all the oxygen? This could literally happen and it would make sense for the story to continue, but No Code was too invested in making this cinematic to make it a great or even mechanically interesting game, despite how little would have to change to really elevate this work to the next level.And none of this is even to mention the bugs, but . Luckily, I never encountered anything game-breaking, but a bunch of random visual things really screwed up the experience at times. Hatches and panels would glow like I could interact with them, but there was nothing to do with them (and this one is really confounding to me because objects I could interact with never glowed anyway, so why can objects even glow like this in the first place?); hatches would disappear when looked at from certain angles, leading me down the wrong hallway (once I was actually looking directly at  through a bugging hatch, so I was led to believe things were going a WILDLY different direction than they did); at one point there was even a duplicate corpse sticking halfway out of a wall just around the corner from where the real one was. I spent a good minute trying to figure out if this was supposed to be some weird intentional effect, only to be disappointed yet again.It's really concerning to me that this would win so many "best game" awards when the "game" of this work is virtually non-existent. These awards aren't for the game, they're for the well-crafted fiction and the dazzling visual and sound design, like a Space Odyssey collector's edition of Candy Land.All in all, this a brilliantly shiny, beautiful series of setups and disappointments to an incredible soundtrack. Although, the graphics are very pretty, so I understand why IGN would give this a 9.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice little puzzle game with cassette futurism vibes. Reminded me of "Stranger Things" and "Alien Isolation" a lot. The VCR video filter makes certain scenes look photo-realistic (e.g. views outside the station). I'm amazed how far gaming has come. Took me about 7h to finish the game and would have 100% it if I had used a guide for the 3 items I missed to collect on my own.The puzzles are fairly easy and you don't need a guide for them. Making the player be the on-board AI also neatly explains why you have to do these chores.Perfectly playable on Stead Deck, just set the runtime to be Proton 8. And I'm glad I gave it another try.I will start with cons;Agonizingly bad game mechanics: I haven't seen anything like this. Throughout the game I felt I was a disabled malfunctioning entity. Maybe it fits the story well, but the game experience was definitely not fun.Minigames are not really puzzles. Its all about finding the solution before trying to solve some random problem.Controls in Quickime events were terrible. _childDocuments_.review: While the game is completely linear to my knowledge, the game is a fun variety of puzzles to progress the plot line. The visuals are startlingly impressive, the atmosphere is very gripping and the story unfolds in a direction that kept me rather hooked the entire time to see the ending. While not 'horror' in the jump up in your seat sort of way, it's much more horror in its presentation of the story, visuals and startling plot twists.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Observation is one of those rare thriller games. It's more akin to an interactive film but far more immersive than you would think. The premise is that you are on a space station called observation and some kind of accident has occurred and it's up to you to help the station crew survive and figure out what exactly happened, the twist here is that you play as the space station's A.I, called SAM, short for System Administration and Maintenance, and he is very much in the thematic vein as HAL from 2001: A Space Odyssey. As SAM, you have to assist the crew in keeping the station working and in doing so work through the game's well implemented and occasionally challenging puzzles. Observation is a great experience and I highly recommend this for players fond of narrative games. However, due to its short length, about 4-5 hours, I suggest you wait for a sale unless you are really dying for a good space game.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: It was like watching a very slow, very boring movie. You are on a railroad this entire game. Of the little choices you are given, they put your right back on the same track every time. You will get lost, ALOT. You will frequently not know what to do, because the response system always plays the same audio clip. When you have to pair with a system, just flail your fingers on the 1-4 buttons to unlock it and skip the puzzle. Weird graphical errors occur, including one where a hatch looks completely transparent, and you can see straight into the eye of the storm, but then the hatch magically reappears when you bump into it. Its so hard to know what the objective is, even with the prompts from responses and pressing "O." Ugh, I'm so disappointed. I really hoped Stories Untold would be the first stepping stone towards more immersive, branched storytelling. This was not a step forward. Its like they stayed exactly where they were, or maybe even stepped backwards. I didn't feel excited past the first hour once I realized, I was an AI in a space station, and there was nothing for me to do, other than follow the prompts to slowllllly progress the plot.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: The controls and user interface are obnoxiously unintuitive.  You play as an Artificial Intelligence program of a spacecraft where something has gone wrong and you have to help the lone remaining crew member figure out what.  Fantastic premise!  But it's never clear from the interface what you're supposed to click to communicate with her.  Sometimes you bring up a map and click on the location to tell her something.  Other times, you're supposed to use a computer terminal command to point to something on that same map.  I wound up watching a walkthrough not because the game was difficult to understand, but simply because it was difficult to figure out exactly how the interface works in new situations.  A lot of potential, but an overall disappointment for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been on my list for a while and I finally got time to play it. I am so happy I did. It is a wonderful sci-fi story. The way they make you play through the eye of the robot(SAM) the entire time was brilliant. It is a beautiful looking game, and the atmosphere was fantastic. Flying around in SAM looking in all the rooms, laptops, and walls really makes you get immersed into the game itself and the characters. Took me around 7 hours to beat it but I took my time and enjoyed every second of it. It made me feel like I was playing a movie rather then a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game.  I think it was worth the asking price.  Strong points:The story is good. _childDocuments_.review: Observation was so much more than I expected it to be. I've always believed that a great game has at least 20 hours of play in it, though looking at my 8.4 hours of play time, and I finished it, I'm going to have to change my beliefs. Observation has an excellent pace and by the end of the game, it just feels like it was the right amount of time for this story. Speaking of story, as a fan of this genre, this was one I truly loved. Kudos to the writer/s. The voice actors were both great and obviously had excellent direction. A masterful effort by all those involved in making this game. It is a game I will not forget. _childDocuments_.review: ZERO SPOILERS. I recommend going into this one knowing as little about it as possible, actually.Sharp, interesting science fiction with a neat premise. I finished it in six and a half hours and was sorry when it was over, but the experience carried me along from the start to the finish in one sitting -- I wanted to know what was going to happen next! The lack of filler content made for compelling play. It doesn't overstay its welcome.It can be slightly disorienting, both because it takes place in space, where direction is relative (no true 'up' or 'down,' etc) and because the environments can be a bit samey, which makes sense for the setting -- standardized modules, etc. Which is not to say that the environments are boring! They're well crafted, full of detail. That said, it can be a challenge to navigate the station reliably, or remember exactly where you saw certain things, making for some amount of backtracking -- which is for the most part painless, given the way you typically 'move' through the rooms.
_childDocuments_.name: Observation

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet, very well put together, not too difficult. Not too much of this, not too much of that... just a nice little game to play and then move on from.You play not as a human character, but as an AI helping a human character through a space station catastrophe. Something bad has happened and you're trying to help her - and also trying to further an unknown cause... (no spoilers here)As an AI, you have access to all the cameras on board, and also occasionally a small sphere that can move around freely. You interact with ship systems and perform basic tasks. You work to advance the story.Not everything is as it seems. Strange things will happen.Ok, so it was a neat story, but not something that moved me to my core. The atmosphere was grim and frightening, and they captured the feel well. Voice acting felt fairly on point, and sound effects fit the theme very well (including LOSING sound during vacuum scenarios, which was nice). Overall, I very much enjoyed the setting - graphics, sounds, themes, locations etc.The puzzles were not terribly difficult. There are a couple spots where you might be unsure what to do next, but bump around for a few minutes and you'll figure it out. If you're looking for real brain busters, this isn't it, but if you're in it for a good time, look no further - puzzles not too hard, but not one of those games with constant 'busy work' either. It feels just about right.This is one of those 'open ended' stories where they don't fully explain everything. Or, if they do, I didn't find it in my playthrough, and I don't want to play it again. Not because it was bad, but because I just don't. So you'll get to use your imagination to interpret the ending as you please.Overall it was fun to play and I enjoyed it. I liked the uniqueness of NOT being the main character, but being the assistant to the main character. Pretty cool.Final question I ask in every review: Worth full price? I don't think so. As nice and fun of a game as it was, I have a hard time recommending that people pay $25 for it. Great atmosphere, but you can beat it in a few hours and there's just not a huge amount of challenge. I feel like $10 would be fair; $15 at a stretch, if you wound up being the type of person that was just blown away by the game. No, as much as I do recommend it and as much as I did have a lot of fun playing it and found it really interesting, my advice would be to wishlist this game and wait for a sale. It'll happen sooner or later, and I imagine you'll feel better for not having paid a full $25.I do recommend, though, on sale. Great fun little time, and then on to the next.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Finished it since. Unfortunately, I have to give Observation a thumbs down.Pros: - Story is pretty cool         - HAL simulator         - Atmospheric, looks pog on a good machineCons: - Some of the worst zero-g controls I ever experienced          - Disgusting amount of distortion, every time you bump into anything (which you'll be doing a lot, see the point above) your entire screen ♥♥♥♥♥ itself. No, there is no way to turn it off          - Puzzles are mostly trivial and tedious, but a few times it jumps to a "what the hell" territory. (I am looking at you Astrophysics co-ord console)          - Facial and character animation is.. meh          - Honestly, feels like a lot of missed potential          - At least one game breaking bug that I encountered, has been around for 2 years and still has not been fixed          - Finished it in 5 hours, as someone who takes his time to soak in the atmosphere and explore aroundVerdict: Get it on an extremely deep special, or watch a playthrough. _childDocuments_.review: This game had a great story line & interesting puzzles. I was literally enthralled the whole time & thought I had really found one of my favorite games. But then I get to the final puzzle and my keyboard/mouse set up will not enable me to press the correct key/click sequence within the time frame necessary to advance & get to the ending.I've spent 15hrs playing this game & now I can't even play out the ending myself. If I want to know what happens, I have to go watch someone else do it on YouTube. I don't have a cheap keyboard or mouse, either. I have a mechanical keyboard & a gaming mouse that are a few years old but kept in rather good condition. And I've had literally 0 other problems in the 30+ games I've completed *solely* on computer in 2021. Also - there have been comments made in Steam threads about older people having less dexterity & being unable to do this particular type of puzzle. I'm in my 30s with no known dexterity issues at all. I suspect that the older folx who stated it was dexterity based are actually blameless - I think it's really the game functionality for this puzzle.The issue, if you want to keep reading:From the research I've done (without having too many spoilers here), you have to press WASD keys in a certain sequence & then click the mouse in order to confirm your keyed in selection. I had to do research in the first place because I was not able to use the controls as instructed (it literally tells you use WASD to move the cursor & then click your mouse to select) and I thought I was going crazy.My research confirmed the controls, and I even found a literal image diagram of what keys to press to get the puzzle to advance. When I tried the verified diagram, my white/red box 'cursor' wouldn't even move to select the correct 'puzzle piece.' So I'd time out of that piece & fail the puzzle. I tried countless times to no avail. I read that when using a game controller or playing this game on a console, this issue simply does not exist with this puzzle.I loved the game but am just really sad that I personally don't get to experience the end after FIFTEEN HOURS of play time. :( :( :(  If the functionality of that final puzzle was different, my rating would be positive. That really is such a big flaw in my mind that I can't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a bit of a mix of 2001: A Space Odyssey and Event Horizon, which is intriguing. _childDocuments_.review: I played half the game at 1066x600 and was barely able to make out the UI because the game constantly fought me and lowered my resolution randomly. I thought it was a stylistic choice for the sphere camera since I'd just played Signalis with the CRT effect turned on, but no, it's just a really buggy game. There's constant animation bugs, and I had to restart the first spacewalk section twice because of two unique bugs that stopped me from progressing on separate occasions. This game has a fairly interesting story (that I wish could be expanded in a better game), it's fairly well-acted, and the overall production value is good, but the puzzles are tedious to the point of tears, and they're stupid, and they're incessant. The whole game is a maze, especially outside of the station where nothing is marked in an obvious manner and directions aren't explained precisely enough, so you're likely to spend a lot of time wandering. I played with a guide just to get through it more quickly. The sphere camera is also extremely floaty and carries a lot of momentum, which controls horribly when you play with a mouse.I could keep going, this game has a lot of problems and unfortunately the writing isn't nearly good enough for me to recommend that you force yourself through the experience like I did. Maybe this dev team will do better next time.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is very slow and there's not a whole lot of action, mostly just puzzles. At first, you're tasked with helping Dr. Emma Fisher find the rest of her missing crew, which gives the plot a nice touch of mystery. However, halfway through the game it starts to get really out of left field up until the "finale". The original air of mystery is gone, and you're just left thinking "wtf??" That can be a good or a bad thing, depending on the person. Moreover, it's not a long game at all, so if you're looking for a game you can play for hours and hours, Observation may not be for you.Take everything said in this review objectively. If you enjoy slow-paced stories and lots of puzzles, you would enjoy Observation and in that case I recommend it. If not, then I wouldn't spend the money.

_childDocuments_.review: A really great, atmospheric game where you play as the AI for a space station as *events unfold*. Very descriptive, I know but it's a story-based game so I don't want to say anything specific. I'm really impressed by the game's commitment to its design/aesthetic. It feels extremely immersive, even though the somewhat floaty/slow panning can be annoying it still helps really sell that feeling that you are working these real systems. That paired with great environments and dark, blaring synth musical motifs all contribute to a sometimes oppressive atmosphere. The graphics aren't the best, especially for the human character and I had a few animation/positioning glitches which were unfortunate in how much they marred the meticulously crafted feel. Still, it overall worked really well and I loved where it went.Note: while there are some creepy moments this isn't really a horror game so don't worry about jump scares & the like. Also, there are some missable collectables so if you care about that sort of thing be careful. I didn't look anything up and ended up missing a single log which was a bit annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: 70/100Overall nice experience, certainly worth the few euros I got it for during one of the discounts. In detail I do have some mixed feelings. The approach is certainly unique enough to stand out and from the story/artistic standpoint the devs did a very good job. Some people were criticizing the controllis but you can certainly get used to it and I even think the cumbersome camera movements are intentional so that you have something to overcome in the otherwise easy to solve puzzles. It felt more real.What I won’t defend is the other technical issues, which certainly did hurt my overall experience.1) Resolution / aspect ratio - TLDR: complete unstable mess. I have a 3440x1440 monitor, which I know is not that common so I would not judge negatively a flawless 2560x1440 experience. But the game natively “wants to” be rendered in 21:9 aspect resulting in horizontal black bars, which with my vertical black bars due to a wide monitor made a fat black RECTANGLE around content. After finding this unacceptable, I came across an official side-patch (3 libs copied next to the game) which removed the horizontal bars and that was how I’ve played the majority of the game, tho some cutscenes ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it up and I was back in rectangle. I also tried to set my native resolution manually, which someone on Reddit suggested, which worked, but only until I opened a menu, so not really. Finally every time I open the game it sets itself to completely illogical 1920x1080.2) FPS locked at 60 without VSync ON… because that makes sense.3) Autosave - pretty scarce autosave without any indications when.
