_childDocuments_.review: Juno Markev & Lev Arris walk into a bar ...I don't review games often, but when I throughly enjoy a game that's getting mixed reviews, I fell an obligation to pay a little extra for my pleasure.Like many of the gerontological gamers here, I've played every Wing Commander and X-Wing game I could get my hands on, and plunked down thousands to upgrade my system every time a new one came out.  I've flown Battlecruisers - some that even worked.  Enjoyed both 'Lancers.  And more recently, I've dutifully tossed fifty bucks into a black hole like a good Citizen to fly a ship around for 10 minutes and run into a few asteroids.  So RGO definitely piqued my interest.  However, I waited to post this review until I pumped over 70 hours into RGO, completed the story and side missions, and got all the achievements.  Nitpicking aside, the game is really fun - more fun than a barrel of Kilrathi.The atmosphere is great.  They absolutely nailed it, even if they "borrowed" from all over to do so.  A little Firefly slide guitar here, some GTA radio there (go Dark Country!), grainy interlaced WC-esque vidscreens in the ships.  And who doesn't like to flip off a baddy while you're moving into range?  3-D character models, good voice acting, lots of cutscenes (which I can conveniently bypass when impatient).  Bar games that I can actually win without save-scumming ("Greetings, StarVenger" - what a surprise!)  A lotta indie love went into this thing.The gameplay is more fun than its ancient primogenitors.  Thank you for autopursuit & inertial dampening!  It keeps the action hot & heavy, without all that loop-de-looping over-and-over to bring around the bastids on my butt.  Sure this takes the "sim" out of it, but it makes it a heyuluva lot more fun.  I didn't come to RGO for a "sci-fi-realistic" spacesim experience - or the fleet battles of its predecessor.  I came to pilot my fighter through exciting battles with ships and missiles and lasers & explosions going off all around me while beeps and buzzes and warnings tell me my ship is seconds from breaking apart ... and I'm spilling my drinks & snacks all over my desk while I'm cussing out the bad guys and pounding the crap outta my keyboard and working up a true gamer sweat.  This game delivers, and I sure ain't gonna gripe about the Epic Games wait or paying full-indie-pop for this much fun!There is a learning curve, but that's there with any cockpit game.  Short basic tutorial - show me how to keep from flying into asteroids & turn me loose. I enjoy reading the guides and tips online during my lunch hour and learning new tricks that way instead of through in-game mega-sized hand-holding tutorials - the big three: (1) Map the "energy to shields" button real close by; (2) Balanced power drain in weapons beats the BFG's; and (3) Baddies start out flying flat like they are commanded by Khan Noonien Singh.On the tech side, there has been a pleasing lack of bugs or problems.  I play the game on both a 43-inch Predator 4K, and a junk POS work system with 1280x720 integrated graphics.  Both work great with no problems.  I've never hit a bug on any of the missions - once I learned to scan for stray baddies when mopping up a battle.Everybody says use a gamepad, and I don't know why.  I tried this with a gamepad, hotas, mouse, and for me the mouse absotively posilutely takes the prize.  I'm right-handed, but like any serious mouse-key-teerer, I mouse with my left, and gain the use of the entire keyboard with dominant right-hand accuracy ("When Grasshopper can use left hand to snatch mouse from Master Kan's hand, then he become true fragmaster...").  Left mousing works great here because there are keys o' plenty that have to be mashed like a mofo to fly the ship - just have to remap a few of them.I utilized all three types of piloting tracks: trade early on to learn the ropes, mining when I wanted some quick income, and mercenary for the fun of intense combat.  I appreciated that the game let me flit back & forth between ships without losing money (and having a good auto-transfer of my equipment between ships).  While the money's the easiest through mining, it's far from a cheat because that gets boring.  So I'd only use it for a quick cash infusion on the books for a needed upgrade.  By midgame, I was making plenty of money from mercenary work by stacking up all four missions nearby, and tossing in a pirate lord and some bounties to boot.  I don't get the griping about difficulty spikes.  There's plenty of options to work around a hard mission, which is sure better than those old WC days where you'd have to do the same mission over-and-over for days, until the Thrustmaster WCS was cracked & scratched from being repeatedly rage-flung across the room.  If I'm jumped in that tradeship that looks like the pig from Okja, half the time I can talk my way out of it, or with the afterburner upgrade I can usually scoot out of trouble, or throw the power to my shields for the final showdown with the one I can't shake.  If a mercenary mission kicks my butt I either add a wingman, abort with apparently no adverse effects, or mine to get more upgrades & return.  Case in point, the first time I started that misison to knock out 6 cops with ECM missiles, I couldn't tag a single one - I got there too early with a lame ship.  So I mined & upgraded awhile and returned, but I still could only fry about 3 of them.  Then I finished upgrading my base and bought the fighter with four missile racks, put ECMs in all of them, and fried all the cops on my first try.  That didn't frustrate me, it challenged me.  And now by the end of the game, I can finish any mission out there by the second or third try (with Ruth on my wing).  Last but not least on this topic of difficult missions, a big help to me in finishing a tough misison has been targeting mode.  I really don't like to use it because its a total buzzkill and funnus-interruptus to freeze the action, but when there's a tough mission, it really helps me get a feel for what's going on or find the bastid that just knocked out my aft shields while I'm pounding the poopchute outtofa cap ship.  So I'm glad its there for when I need it.One thing on my wishlist would be a money-pit to spend the excess cash on and keep me interested after squeezing out all the mission juice.  Following the game's example of borrowing from others, I would suggest "teachers" scattered in the bars where I could spend 100K a pop to "learn" a tiny, less than one percent buff to various game functions, with the bump decreasing in size and increasing in price each time I buy it.  Like the crusty pilot who can teach better gun accuracy, a mechanic who can teach how to get a little more speed, a trader who can teach how to make a little more profit from sales, or a miner who can teach how to mine better things from asteroids.  You'd really only be getting a buff of a couple percent out of these things after investing millions, but it would still keep the moneymaking interesting.  Another obvious place for spending bucks would be to make the painting program into more of a "pimp-my-ride" option somewhere on the map where you pay for the paint or skins (and maybe for a little more more bling than Burt or a bobblehead - I want my fuzzy dice!!!).I'm sad that the mixed reviews will probably make this be a one-and-done game, because this is the closest thing I've had to a true Privateer chub in twenty years.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game so much, but it seems every time I start to have fun, this game sucker punches me.I loved the original Rebel Galaxy. Loved the arcade ships-of-the-line combat, loved the lite single player space simulation, loved the 'cowboys, but in space' aesthetic. This game does a lot of the same, except trading in capitol ship combat on a 2D plane for flying a one-person freighter/fighter craft in full 3D. Controls are again arcade inspired, so less full 6 axis movement of Descent or Forsaken, and more like Rogue Squadron or Ace Combat. Still has fun aliens, a sim-lite experience that is pretty hands off, and that space cowboy feel.But every time I get rolling, the game sucker punches me; and I don't know why.So to save time, you can auto-pilot from place to place. Cool. Happy to see the game doesn't waste your time flying through the massive expanse of space just to get from point A to point B, cause that's where the cool stuff happens. Just point your nose in the direction of your mission waypoint or map marker, hold a button, and off you go. This is safe and time efficient way to get around 95% of the time. But, you can get stopped and ambushed. So far, I've only ever gotten ambushed when I've either tried to escape from a fight going really bad, or from a fight that I've narrowly survived. If I'm at full health and shields with everything in working order, I can fly free with no trouble. If my power reactor is toast and my hull has been breached, and I desperately need to just make it back to a station to get repaired? So far that has resulted in 100% chance of getting intercepted, and placed into a 4 v 1 fight that I lose (cause I quite literally cannot fight back, cause the reactor can't maintain power high enough to fire weapons for more than a fraction of a second). This has happened half a dozen times in less than my first 10 hours with the game. Again, every time I start to get on a roll, the game sucker punches me with absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that makes me want to quit the game in frustration. I don't know if I just have the worst luck, or if the game is programmed to kick you when you're down, but neither are fun.This is outside the times when a simple bounty mission (and not even a high threat one either) turns into a complete ♥♥♥♥-show cause a random pirate FRIGATE with escorts shows up, and now your already lopsided 3 v 1 fight is 6 v 1 with a freaking frigate. Its a fight you have to run away from, assuming you can manage to put enough distance from you and the horde to jump away.Or how about auto-piloting to a mission objective, only for it to drop you right smack dab in the middle of a minefield? No option to leave auto-pilot early and maybe NOT get yourself super ♥♥♥♥♥♥. No way to know ahead of time if you'll land in a minefield, since the missions and the areas around them are dynamically generated. I've gone back to redo scout missions after a minefield has destroyed me, only for there to not be a minefield there anymore on the next try. Great and all, but that doesn't erase the frustration of losing time and progress (sometimes a lot of progress if you get screwed at the last jump point in a 7 section scout mission, you done after 2 other bounty missions).But other than that, the game is at its core, quite fun. The combat is a blast, until it's not (you jump into a mission and have to dogfight in a minefield, or the enemy gets overwhelming backup mid fight, or you get intercepted when you quite literally cannot fight back). The game is entertaining and engaging, until it inevitably makes me want to chuck my controller through my monitor in frustration. I have died from more stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in my first 10 hours of Rebel Galaxy Outlaw, than I ever did with all my time with the original Rebel Galaxy.So if you enjoyed the original Rebel Galaxy, and you can jive with the different take on combat, you'll every likely enjoy your rime with Outlaw. However just be aware that this game, unlike its predecessor, will go sideways to ♥♥♥♥ you very hard and do so very quickly, quite frequently, and without apology. Be prepared to stop back at a station to auto-save after every mission, if only to prevent redoing batches of missions after one bad turn causes a cascade of failures that kills you.EDIT: Actually, the one time I did manage to beat the 4 pirate interception squad with a damaged reactor and no power reserves (hooray for missiles that take no power), only to get intercepted a 2nd time right after, preventing me from reaching a station and ultimately killing me. So the game kicked me when I was down, and even as a struggled to get back up, it kicked me again; cause ♥♥♥♥ me, right?Here's another not-fun no win mission. Get a low-risk station defense where pilots are urgently needed cause the local security forces are 'overwhelmed'. What happens when you fly there? Local security forces are NON EXISTENT, and instead of the usual fun dog-fight free for all of station and pirate forces, you get blasted out of the sky in a 8 v 1 fight and swarms of enemy missiles. Again, a low threat mission, that the game has bugged out or outright lied and put you into a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ scenario that in no way is represented by the mission's text or its reward/payout.Want even more not-fun ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Every freakin' time you have a mission that takes you to some seemingly abandoned point in space to check on a transmitter or some other space doohicky, you will be swarm ambushed and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ six ways to Sunday. Every. Single. Time. They force you to slow down and keep proximity with the black box/transmitter/whatever, then half a dozen pirates will drop right on top of you from every direction. Hope you enjoy having 2 dozen missiles coming at you from every angle all at once!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great love letter to Wing Commander Privateer. As space sims go, that means:1. The game systems are all pretty streamlined and straightforward to grasp. It's more "in space" than "space sim", although to its credit RGO does include some things that Privateer doesn't have.2. It has an excellent sense of atmosphere and world-building. This world is not the Wing Commander world, and it doesn't have the same sense of bombast, but it's a credible "alter-verse" that captures the basic themes and also brings an over-the-top Old West vibe to the table.3. The combat is focused on efficient dogfighting against multiple opponents that scale to your level. Systems management and evasion has some importance but ultimately, the most important strategy is to blow them up as fast as you can in a glorious combo of destruction.For Privateer players, the main thing that is new is some additional in-flight controls and systems. The old strats basically work, you just have to figure out how to express them.The main downside to this style of gameplay is that you won't get to geek out too much over loadouts, build armadas or similar. It's a "now trade to the next one up" type of deal with a few sidegrades along the way - and the best parts of the game occur in those early stages where you have a scrappy rustbucket and somehow make it work.Some further thoughts after completing the campaign: The story missions drag things out a bit more than necessary to make it a 30+ hour game. Every buddy pilot has their own optional mission set, and I did every one - it spaces out the main plot missions with mandatory downtime and then has the character phone you back, GTA style, so I ended up in a loop of optional-main-optional-main-optional-main because I would get a new entry in one while working on the other. This can probably be cut down if you play more selectively. The writing suffers from a common game writing problem - it's heavily character driven, but the characters are written to constantly propel the player back into the game loop, which leads towards a dry "mystery box" style of story where there are questions and answers, and occasional character moments, but not really thematic or environmental storytelling. Everything happens on a singular timeline, through dialogue spoken in-character to Juno, the characters are always soap operatically trying to steal credit, place blame upon, or take revenge on each other, and the game world is kept at arms' distance from the story beats - progress is nearly always a matter of reaching a destination or winning a set-piece battle; there are no puzzles, and few genuine discoveries after the first hours. There are some neat locations to visit and it does pick up a little towards the end, but it concluded on a "to be continued". Basically, it is the exact style of storytelling Privateer leaned a lot on, but the way it's presented is just a tad less impactful, and its content a bit more everyday hustle and less wistful lark.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I begin, lets be perfectly clear on what this game isn't and what this game is. It is NOT a game of mechanically deep economic trading with billions of star systems. It does NOT have a constantly shifting field of dozens of independently motivated factions. It will NOT require you to wander aimlessly across the stars to grind or farm for hundreds of hours to work your way up to fleet level carriers to execute trade runs with twelve-digit profit margins that only serve to get you to the next ship that will increase your profit margin by one more digit. This is NOT a cutting edge, industry-changing game.This IS absolutely a fun, nostalgic, story-focused love letter to the likes of Wing Commander: Privateer and Freelancer. Imagine those two games made with today's computing tech and you get an idea of what Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is all about. The visual and game play style lend to this clearly intentional homage. I mean, c'mon! Juno Markev (the main character) even has the exact same jacket as Grayson Burrows (Privateer) and Edison Trent (Freelancer)! If you're not on board with that concept, you might as well move along right now. The trade system is simple and designed to give you a cinematic if superficial taste of being a smuggler. The space combat is straight forward, action-packed, and (if the assist settings are on) a bit casual. The story line is slightly canned but lovingly executed. The main character is charmingly derivative of the archetypical space rogue. You have more ships and equipment options than were available in Privateer, but it is a bit of a linear progression from bad to good with only one real choice to make along the way (fighter or freighter). You will have fun blasting pirates, following leads, and avoiding the law when your cargo hold is filled with... questionable items.This game won't blow your mind. But it will give you many hours of fun.Here are a couple negatives: Flying with the the flight/targeting assist mode can (by some standards) remove a little bit of the white-knuckle piloting of the old-style space sims. You hold the right mouse button down and your ship automatically tracks your targeted opponent while you fire when they're in range. You can choose to not use this feature, but the manual controls can be a bit jumpy. I tried a lot of combinations of the mouse dead-zone and sensitivity, but nothing seems to calm the controls down to a point where it felt smooth. Having said that, I don't really live in a world where having a joystick on my computer desk is realistic anyway. So being able to casually control the ship with the mouse (and not look a scrub in the process) isn't hateful. And the experience isn't robbed by the assist. You still have to be on your toes and avoid enemy fire.Here are a couple noteworthy positives: The game drips with nostalgia. Not that it wouldn't be good for new players. But if you liked Privateer and don't want to deal with messy control conversions and dated graphics, this is a solid replacement.The game also features a pretty cool paint customization tool. You can paint the hull of your ship with a sick degree of detail, right down to the logos and scratches. The paint tool even has an option to "print physical copy." Not sure if that works, but its interesting.A pretty creative addition: The in-game music is a neat mixture that gives setting a wild-west, almost Firefly atmosphere. But, even more interesting is that you can enter a file path with music of your own. So add whatever you like to the music list (and still get the fun commercials on your ship's radio). In the end, if you're looking for a game that will top Elite: Dangerous with respect to the complicated trade system, number of ship options, and endless, mind-numbing, aimless grinding, this game is probably best skipped. But if you're looking for a casual, action-oriented, story-focused, cinematic, Privateer-like throwback, look no further.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that punches above its weight for a small outfit. It's an insanely fun space sim, with a great freelancer vibe and interesting characters. The combat mechanics are very different from the original Rebel Galaxy (also worth checking out) and resemble a classic space sim, like a combination between X-wing and Freelancer. It has one serious flaw, however. There's no level progression through the story. The best ships, weapons and gear are unlocked from the start and beyond a small cost difference, nothing prevents you from skipping all the intermediates and going for the best. In fact, one of the early main missions is so difficult, you need to max out your ship to complete it. This means that around 20% into the game story, you are maxed out, most combats are repetitive and completing missions to gain more money is meaningless. If better ships and equipment were unlocked with main story missions, you could explore more of what the game has to offer. For this reason, I could not bring myself to complete the story.

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game as a huge fan of Rebel Galaxy. I also enjoy space combat sims in general, but Rebel Galaxy is what brought me here.If you are looking for more Rebel Galaxy, I suggest you replay Rebel Galaxy.If you are looking for a space combat sim, there are better ones out there.Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is not a bad game. It is tediously ok. I doubt anyone is looking for a tediously ok experience, though.Growth is very shallow and over quickly. I spent most of the game flying the same ship.Initial mission difficulty is high especially combat missions. 10+ enemies is not unusual early, and later in the game swarms of over 20 enemies is not uncommon. This difficulty contributes to the shallowness of player growth since it pushes to player to max out their upgrades early.There are a ridiculous amount of pirates in the game. Dogfighting ceases to be interesting or worthwhile and I found myself accelerating past enemies not because they challenged me but because I simply did not want to waste time on them again.Most of the game is quite tedious requiring the player to fly back and forth across the sector. I spent a good chunk of my time traveling form jump gate to jump gate.Missions are pushed on the player at seemingly random times and the player's tracked mission is automatically changed. Several times I neglected to change it back to what I was doing and ended up flying in the wrong direction.Inability to dock or jump when hostiles are near added more tedious combat.Oh and there are minigames. Maybe they are ok,  I didn't bother with them, though. I didn't buy a space sim to play billiards and wish the developer had instead improved other aspects of the game rather than spending their time making minigames.

_childDocuments_.review: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is a single-player, space sandbox game developed by Double Damage Games. It was initially an Epic Store exclusive in 2019 and released on Steam and other platforms a year later.Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is infamous for being the first Epic store exclusive. This decision led to review-bombing and bad press. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is also not the best space sandbox game available. Elite Dangerous and its peers do just about every game loop better. However, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw packs a lot into a small package. The poor early reviews had little to do with the game itself. Double Damage Games is a small indie studio and lacks the resources of a AAA behemoth.You play as Juno Markev, an out-of-luck ex-space pirate. The opening cell-shaded cinematic shows her crashing on a planet after unsuccessfully confronting her husband's killer. Juno calls in a favour to get a modest replacement. She then must juggle repaying her debts, upgrading her ship and unravelling her past.Rebel Galaxy Outlaw's gameplay consists mainly of combat with some trading, piracy and asteroid mining. These earn credits to afford better ships and equipment. Experimenting and exploring are helpful but optional. They can reveal poorly explained mechanics, side quests, rare weapons, lucrative mining spots or beautiful nebulae. Unlike Elite Dangerous and similar games, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw has a light, grungy, blue collar, "space trucker" style. The default radio station plays heartland rock and advertises discount ammunition and cheap beer. All technology looks retro-futuristic, old and second-hand. Many star systems are named after working-class southern or central US states. The region of space is called Dodge, like the famous lawless US frontier town. You can play eight-ball pool or dice poker to unwind, the genre equivalent of fishing. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is the prequel to Rebel Galaxy, Double Damage Game's previous game. They share the setting and style. However, the games are different. Rebel Galaxy is about flying capital ships on a 2D plane fighting with broadside cannons. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is about 3D fighter combat.Instead, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is a homage to Wing Commander: Privateer and Freelancer. While there is a central campaign and side missions, you can ignore them to explore, fight or trade as you see fit. You can unlock buddies to fight with you temporarily. You can side with the law, against it or both. Even the graphics look like upscaled MCGA, used in Wing Commander: Privateer. The cockpit and HUDs are blocky and favour the old EGA colours. The stars are square. The game renders debris as sprites. Ships have distinct silhouettes and blocks of bright colours. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw plays best on a controller. While not as precise as a keyboard and mouse, the vibration makes you feel every shudder of acceleration and weapon recoil. The game's aim-assist helps, too.To be fair, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is not flawless. Encounter difficulty can vary considerably. Auto-saves are regular and reloads quick, but unexpected deaths can still be frustrating. One mission requires non-lethal takedown of enemies, but you must manually remove any turrets beforehand. It is easy to miss some side missions, like those in Eureka.However, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw surprised me. I had a fun 40 hours or so. You can complete the campaign faster if you do the minimum. However, getting distracted and blazing your own trail is part of the point. Fans of space sandboxes, Wing Commander: Privateer or something light and stylized will enjoy themselves. Do not let the poor early reviews fool you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is essentially a love letter to the original Wing Commander: Privateer game from 1993.  The interface, factions, detailed cockpits, weapon types, guilds, cut-scene transitions...even some of the one-liners said by NPCs and the camera angle for your ship sitting on a landing pad are directly from Privateer.  So if you grew up with that game on the top of your "best games of all time" list (like I did), then you're going to like Rebel Galaxy Outlaw.  It's not perfect - the pacing for upgrades vs mission difficulty isn't great.  I ended up just grinding out enough money in the starter ship to jump straight to the most expensive ship with fully upgraded components and only then moved on with the story and companion missions, which meant I had no reason to do any more generic missions or mining for the rest of the game.  The combat is chaotic and fun.  I wasn't sure if I would like the auto-pursuit mechanic, but it ended up being a really nice feature.  It almost made the combat feel more tactical by letting me think about other things (switching from energy to projectile weapons so my power can refill, dumping energy into my shields, uses the afterburner in combination with countermeasures to evade incoming missiles, etc) instead of just "staying on target".  You do still have to watch where you're going, your ship will happily auto-pursuit right into an asteroid or capital ship if you let it.  Also, I highly recommend using a controller instead of mouse / keyboard.The mission types and game mechanics are actually more varied and interesting than I expected.  There's general combat missions and cargo runs, but also defend, escort, patrol, resource gathering, etc.  Bartenders are even useful - if you're trying to hunt down pirate lords (for fun and profit, or maybe just an achievement), you can look at the map to find a station that has reported seeing one and then fly to that system and talk to a bartender (with a little bride) to get an exact location.  But even with different generic mission types, without anything to upgrade to they eventually become uninteresting - I would have definitely welcomed some more main and side story missions to fill in the time.  This is one of the few games where I bothered to get 100% achievements just because I wanted more reasons to keep playing.The bottom line is that if you remember and loved Privateer or Freelancer, you should definitely give this game a shot, but if you missed both of those games, your mileage may vary.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Juno Markev is tailing a bounty of a killer, and when arriving at his last known location, she gets ambushed by him from behind.But she is not giving up without putting up a fight, which ended with Juno shooting her last bullet at him and only kissing the side of his head. Calling it a retreat, depending on the current situation. Chased by the killer, luck strikes on Juno’s side and causes the killer to retreat, but not long after that, luck turns.Damaging her spaceship after the short-lived retreat and making her crash down near a trading outpost. She calls her old buddy for help, and in return, Juno needs to run a little errand for him while borrowing one of his junk ships. Out of money and out of luck, acquire bounties and gamble away your credits. You choose what your destiny will be. Go along with the story or go offside and earn some money.When the player is in the main menu, they can choose to continue their game, make a new game, test flight, and more, including the exit.The game starts out with the backstory cutscene that fills the player with what happened, which then leads to a small cutscene of Juno talking to an old buddy. She gets a mission and needs to travel to a mining facility, where she will find the man who is supposed to have the goods standing inside the bar.After getting the information that he does not have the goods with him in person was bothersome, and June had to go through with his little plan to steal the goods from his own company, which are owned by his brother. The flight mechanisms are very confusing, and I do think more than me thinks that too. It is understandable since you are in space where up is down and down is up, along with trying to learn the controls, the aiming, and all the buttons and settings.But overall, the game is a lot easier to play with a controller, and it is a lot easier to change the spaceship settings while flying or in a battle.It took a little while for me to see that there is an ammo counter that needs time to reload or load up again. In Rebel Galaxy Outlaw, a sequel to Rebel Galaxy. The player can proceed with the main story and will have to do some side missions to earn cash and upgrade their ship. But they can also choose to be good and help out space reinforcers or choose the path of piracy and crimes.The player can see a tab that shows where the player is currently standing, whether they are towards a pirate legend or a lawful assisting citizen.The circle menu is where the player can change spaceship settings or apply all power to a specific action. It’s an easier way to handle the spaceship with all its controls.Targeting mode allows the player to see a certain distance around the ship on a 3D map. This way, the player can select a specific enemy and lock onto them. Good way to kill pirates without looking all around for them during a fight.Allows the player to take a photo of their ship. The player can change the FOV, lens, and more.Allows the player to capture a clip or record the gameplay.The local map is shown on a 2D flat screen and shows stations, missions, points of interest, and jumpgates.Transfers all power to the shields, making the craft slower but able to take more heavy damage.Transfers all shields to power, making the craft faster but more vulnerable.The sector map shows which jump routes there are to get to a specific sector. All sectors are named after most states in the USA, and the player starts in Texas. Some sectors don’t have a state name, but most do.Automatically put a lock on the closest mission that you have in your mission logs.Scan area does like it says. It scans the area around the ship and detects pirates, loot, or reinforcers.Puts a waypoint at the closest station for the player to follow and take on new missions.The game's graphics are both very good but also not the best, depending on the situation.The floating trash bag looks amazing inside, as do the small, detailed animations for the character switching buttons and pulling levers as you are adjusting your spaceship for better defense, stronger firepower, or just faster acceleration.Literally, any adjustments the player makes will be shown inside the ship. Either a small light goes on or a bar or text changes. Every piece of information that the player needs is literally inside the ship on the board, as if it were a “real” spaceship, like in movies and such. Being able to see the ammunition level on the board is cool, but it was at first confusing to me since I did not know what it meant, but shortly after I realized it.It's just all this small but big detailing that makes the game so much better. I’ve said a lot before that to make good gameplay, the game also needs good detailing, even if the textures might not be top-notch.With all the flickering lights and detailed interior of a spaceship, that itself brings joy to me. But not only do the ships look well done. While the player is at the trading outpost, you can see the good-looking structure the main area has and each individual area. For example, there is the bar where the player can gamble or bet credits to hopefully achieve more with luck or maybe lose some.But other than gambling, the bar has information on bounties and missions, and though they might not be cheap to get, they are worth doing in the outcome.Other than the bar, there is the missions area, where the player can take on missions. There is the ship salesman to buy some new piece of art. A garage to upgrade and repair, or refill your ship. And some more areas with more missions.Everything looks very good, and you will not be disappointed in the look.For all country rock lovers, this is the game for you. As each continent out in space is named after the American states, and the player needs to jump between continents. Knowing Texas and some country ads on the radio, imagine them again, but more space-related.There is still a lot of rock, guns, and meat.The player can switch between radio stations, or they will be switched automatically at times.The voice acting in the game is truly dedicated and gives passion to the dialogs. The voice actors did a great job and gave life to the story, and not simply just a text dialog but voice-covered.The characters have different accents depending on which continent they are in, and every voice line/cover is just remarkable. The given depths and focus on the role that the voice actor was acting/voice covering.My honest opinion of the game is that it's enjoyable, but it takes some time to learn the controls, which can make the gameplay a bit less fun. But when all learnt then I’m sure it’s even better.The game is huge with multiple sectors, so the player has a lot to explore and can choose from either following the story or going free roaming and exploring.I tried the devs first game, Rebel Galaxy, but I didn’t like it that much, and it was quite confusing. But this game, which is a sequel to that game, feels completely different or just more fun in a way.Either way, I recommend this game, and I hope you have a controller and that you will have fun playing it.Rating: 8/10Floating Trash Bag

_childDocuments_.review: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw (RGO) loses a lot of the charm of the original and gets dumbed way down.RGO drops the "naval combat in space" aesthetic and goes for a space fighter sim, though not a terribly impressive one. There are many games who do fighter combat better. The game doesn't tell you about all of the stats on the ships so that a your beginner ship running the max powerplant cannot run 2 gauss cannons & keep your power charged, but the next upgraded ship can easily with all the same equipment. The game recommends a gamepad but the controls feel unintuitive. The systems are small. You lose all of the random events. Guilds do not have specialized equipment to earn. There's a paltry number of ships to fly. There's not much choices in equipment. Ships have 2 subsystem slots which is good, because there are exactly 2 subsystems in the game. A mining scanner and a repair bot.It's not a bad game. It's just a disappointing game. I was expecting an new and improved version of the original. Instead the graphics aren't really as sharp. The gameplay is nothing alike. It feels like a cheap console port. While some of the character animation is marginally better, the whole game feels like a giant leap backward. This feels like the first attempt by a small, not yet established studio, not the sequel to a solid game that I enjoyed, a lot.Long and short. I'd wait for a sale. Maybe half off.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit sad with the negative reviews, because I think people have their expectations set wrong. This is a true spiritual successor to Wing Commander Privateer. I would know...I just came from playing Privateer on my GOG accounts. The gameplay, the guilds, the trading, even some of the lines that the patrols say feel like an updated, 2020-version of the old Privateer.So this is NOT a 'true' space sim in that sense...this is a stripped-down, simpler and more accessible version of the genre. Think of it more as the 'Ace Combat' of space sims, as opposed to 'Microsoft Flight Simulator'. If you want something along similar lines but much more serious (and more intense), you're looking for something closer to Elite Dangerous and the like. Which are great games, but not what Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is about.The  gameplay here is simple and intuitive, and there is a lot of assistance in flying (auto-docking, for example). Even mining gives off enough hints to make the tedium a little more bearable and shorter.While people seem to complain about the combat difficulties, it feels very clear to me that the game is forcing your ship selection to dictate your gameplay - you're either trading/mining or doing combat. If you try to do both, you're going to have trouble.It does have a few rough edges, and can feel TOO simple at times, but if you want to just kick back, travel through space and whatnot without the hassle of spending hours poring over documents, wikis, reddits and Youtube clips (like what I had to go through with Elite Dangerous...I mean, just learning to undock and get out of the space station takes skillz over there), then this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: While taking the role of a pseudo space trucker/dogfighter, Outlaw does NOT know how to balance the world, enemies, controls, or equipment to facilitate a good experience for that theme.Obviously the music stands out as the highlight of the game, much like its predecessor. The heavy country rock music fits the space western vibe perfectly. Visually it matches the previous title with clean clear vibrant graphics, but the motion blur effect is horrendous due to the game taking a more first person perspective (with TONS of camera shake). And the controls, while heavily console-focused, are simple enough to pick up and play with, and can be customized.The game is designed pretty much just like the original  in that you essentially take the role of a space trucker, only difference is that you use a much smaller fighter/freighter craft instead of a selection of large freighters and massive warships. While that sounds enticing, it makes up the core of the game's problems. The game now expects you to face pretty much the same kinds of threats the previous game has (many fighters and some larger turret-covered vessels), but in a much weaker and vulnerable single-man craft instead of a heavily armed and defensible battleship/transport. And enemies in this game love to focus on you and you alone. If you jump into a massive mini war with dozens of ships, you may stand a chance, and even enjoy yourself, since there are so many threats around that enemies can't focus on you as well. But those are few and far between the many interrupted autopilot jumps with random fighters ganging up on you.Then there are the larger frigates that show up accompanied by multiple small fighters. These things have a place in the universe the game takes place in, but have no business being in a game like this. There are big and slow, but armed to the teeth and take ages to destroy. Defeating them becomes a choice between carefully hiding in their blind spot (to the rear at the engines) and unload all your guns into their butt, while slowly following behind and becoming a very easy target for fighters; or focusing on the fighters zipping around, missing most of your shots even with the best targeting system, and getting torn to shreds by the frigate's numerous turrets.The biggest problem is the core combat design is nearly identical to the original: You, alone, versus many other threats, and maybe some allies will help. The problem is that design philosophy does NOT lend itself well to a game built around dog fighting in space. It takes very little to get obliterated when the enemy decides to make you the galaxy's most wanted. And that's not even getting into how the game loves to mess with you on seemingly easy tasks.The game has some MAJOR underlying design flaws, some of which feels outright broken and unfair. Since missions are randomly generated, that allows the game to keep having things to do, but that RNG is the core issue with the game's biggest problems. It's pretty common to take an "average" threat mission, only to find yourself surrounded by 2+ heavy frigates and 10+ fighters halfway through a fight that started with a mere 1 frigate and 5 fighters. One common mission involves investigating a black box: Simply jump to the spot, hang close by the box to scan it, and you're done. Of course, it'll never be that easy, and upon getting to scanning range, the game will spawn a horde of fighters and frigates literally right next to you. And since they get to show up so close, you are now unable to escape, and a fight is pretty much unwinnable due to their numbers and arms. Most missions are like this, with the game throwing ludicrous odds at you, even for supposedly easy missions.Then comes the mechanics of fighting itself. With the exception of beams, all guns are projectile weapons. So even when you're in range, your shots WILL miss if the enmy moves fast enough (which they can do all the time, while the fastest fighter available to you can't). They also have  a tendency to ignore attacks it seems. So many times, it's just me and one enemy charging straight for each other, no evasive moves, unloading all weapons, with me melting their front shields and armor, and somehow they still survive long enough to zip by me. Now I'm chasing them, facing their rear shields and armor, trying to do it all over again, but now they're avoiding my projectiles, even if the guns are in range. It genuinely feels like the game allows enemy fighters to survive a little longer than they reasonably should, in an effort to make fights seem more intense and challenging. And while your shots are avoidable projectiles, I've never faced an enemy that ever missed a shot taken at me that wasn't a missile, even when I take the fasest evasion maneuvers possible by my chosen ship.Missiles are another major issue. They were both a mild annoyance, and a deadly threat in the original game, since while you couldn't avoid them you could pop a shield to block all damage, and the challenge came with carefully timing your shield to avoid draining it too much. Here, you have a "flair" type system that simply disrupts the targeting of missiles. Only problem is it's never guaranteed to work. Even the best upgrade only has up to a 75% chance to scramble missiles, and when enemies come in vast numbers, all equipped with heat-seekers or swarm launchers, it becomes a serious issue when they can just fire when your scramble is on cooldown.In the original, facing multiple frigates similar to yours or greater, along with dozens of fighters, felt like a fair challenge. Here, you face MANY craft that, regardless of how they match up to your ship, will usually always have a significant advantage due to how the games weapons and core mechanics work. You simply will never have enough to stand and fight all the odds the game throws at you. You WILL be outmatched, you WILL be swarmed, you WILL be overwhelmed, you WILL be ambushed trying to escape to the nearest station, and you WILL have to deal with this kind of experience every time you depart on your next mission.Given how your ships are pretty much the same spec-wise as other ships, it feels like every time you depart from a station is like jumping into a Battle Royale game, only instead of a free-for-all, all the other players only want to kil you, and they all know where you are.

_childDocuments_.review: Outlaw is basically the same as the first game, only you are now flying small freighters and fighters in a full-3D plane, meaning you have a lot more direct control over your ship.  Other then that, everything else is nearly identical.  The factions, mission types, and progression system is almost identical to the previous title.  But I did like the first game, so I figured I still couldn't go wrong.  I've loved space privateer games ever since I first played Wing Commander Privateer back in the 90s, so I was really excited to try this out.Unfortunately, the game is a complete mess, to the point of being almost unplayable.  The main problem is the difficulty.  It's just way too high.  All the playable early-game ships are crap.  They are essentially inferior to literally every enemy ship you encounter other than the lowest ones in your starting system.  Combine that with obscene amounts of enemies whose sole purpose in life is destroying you, and the results are many many times you end up in total no-win situations, where the game basically says "well we've rolled the dice, and based on this roll, we've decided you're gonna die".  It also doesn't help that the wingmen you find in the game can only be summoned on a temporary basis and then go away until a long cooldown expires.So basically until you get the high-end ships and the high end component upgrades, you are going to be stuck in the starting system grinding the same boring low-risk quests over and over, or just mining asteroids until you can afford a ship and components decent enough to give you reasonable chance to survive most enemy encounters.   Have fun doing that for the first dozen or so hours of gameplay.  Want go explore the outer reaches of the galaxy?  Forget it, the increased enemy difficulty isn't worth it.  Want to take a high risk mission for a change at a big payout?  Forget it.  It will probably be either unwinnable, or take so many tries to succeed that you could have easily made as much money from doing safer low-level quests in that same time-span.But even after you get the best ship and upgrades, it's pretty easy to get overwhelmed by the staggering number of enemies.  Unless you are fortunate enough to be in battle with a large amount of friendly ships, you're going to have to use hit-and-run tactics to stay alive.  You destroy one ship, spam the afterburner until you are safely out of range of all the other enemies, then turn around, destroy another ship, afterburner away, and repeat the entire process until only a few enemies remain so you can take them head on.  Sound boring?  It is, but that's literally the only strategy I've found to be viable for surviving large-scale encounters, so have fun for doing that for the entire duration of the game.Another problem is the game doesn't encourage a lot of different playstyles.  Every playable ship in the game is either a pure fighter or a pure cargo ship.  There isn't any moderate middle of the road ship that is decent at both roles.  I found playing as a cargo pilot was not viable anyway.  It takes way too much cash to increase your cargo space enough to make simply trading runs profitable, and if you take cargo delivery missions from the mission board, you are almost assured to run into enemy contact before you get to your destination, forcing you to fight your way out of the nightmare difficulty in a lumbering sitting duck freighter.  In any case, the story missions have mandatory combat anyway, so you might as well just take the fighter craft.Another thing is you can't be a smuggler without being "pure evil" and allying yourself with the bad guy factions.  Want to be a Han Solo type who trades in illegal goods but for the most part stays on the right side of the law?  Tough luck, you hardly find any base to sell your contraband.  Almost none of the standard planets or space stations have black markets or smuggling networks.  The ones that do are so rare and isolated that it simply isn't worth taking the time to go all the way to them just to sell your contraband.  It's particularly annoying since the standard enemies often drop valuable contraband, and if you aren't playing as an evil character, you just have to leave it floating in space.One final infuriating thing about this game is the constant radio chatter.  In every major battle, your screen will be constantly filling up with allies, enemies or neutral pilots telling you something, which is almost always useless.  This kind of communication is common in games like this, but here it's just way too much.  In a major battle, you'll have someone saying something to you almost constantly for the entire time.  It's the worst case of backseat driving (or flying) I've ever experienced in a video game, and what makes it even worse is that the video display for the communication screen is the same one used to display enemy targets.  Meaning you can't see your enemy target until each message is finished.This game had a lot of potential, but due to a wide array of problems, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw simply does not work.

_childDocuments_.review: So, basically this is a Wing Commander Privateer homage (the first one, not the second), if you played that game you know what to expect. In many ways the game is uncompromisingly retro (remember when you took two mercenary missions that happened to be in the same place thus getting double the enemy fire? Yep, same here) in others it improves on it and tries to be accessible to people that haven't played a spacesim in their life and probably only have a gamepad to play these games (there is basic HOTAS support for us nerds though, it just needs to be mapped manually). Of course by raising the difficulty these helping features get gradually disabled with Old School difficulty not even allowing for third person flying (which means that like in WCP you'll have to contend with the claustrophobic cockpit of the starter ship), difficulty other than that only influences the starting equipment (yes, on Old School you also start with a radar without color coding). The art style mimics the colorful pixel graphics of WCP in a full 3D engine, even the skybox has the bright stars and a bit of the blue-ish tint of the old game. There are countless quality of life improvements, the jump to a full 3D engine alone does sand off a lot of the rough edges of Privateer's sprite-based engine but there is also more variety in the money-making activity and side-missions, a better trading interface and they also took out some of the nonsense in the original. Combat is also much more X-wing-like than in WCP: there is energy transfer using a radial menu or keyboard/HOTAS shortcuts and a tactical map. Landings and long travels like in WCP are automated (this ain't no Elite: Dangerous). Another great addition is the GTA-style radio with different radio stations, quirky DJs and the occasional hint to a sidequest. In many ways this is the retro-spacesim revival we never quite got with the SC/E:D/NMS kickstarter wave, a smaller game perhaps but not all games need to be huge time sinks.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying the game is fine.  I really debated whether to give a thumbs up or down for this game, but ultimately what made my decision is that I feel like it was a bait and switch.  I absolutely loved Rebel Galaxy.  I'm not blind to its faults, but it was a game that just clicked for me.  As you might expect, I was really excited for a sequel, thinking it would actually be a sequel, building on the strengths of the first game and maybe improving the weaknesses.  This is something else.  Maybe a cockpit shooter spinoff set in the Rebel Galaxy universe.  If you're looking for a basic arcade style cockpit fighter and haven't played the original, this is a good game.  If you're looking to recapture anything from the original, this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first steam review, but this game felt like it was worth the words.  I have been searching, fruitlessly, for something to scratch the itch of a couple really old games in my head....  Sundog and Wing Commander: Privateer.  I tried Star Citizen, but its just not there....  Elite Dangerous, just too complicated and weird.  But this little gem dropped out of hyperspace and into my lap, and its perfect.  Its got the right balance of difficulty to keep you coming back, and a decent story to follow along while you are learning the ropes and figuring out your place in the galaxy.  The trading is simple and fun, the combat is tight, the controls are slick and smooth. (Enable your "track nearest hostile" function for best gameplay!).  The main character is funny and sarcastic, and the voice cast is decent.  A nice little film-noir-esque adventure through space.  I got 100+ hours of fun out of this little gem, just to grind enough to finish the story.  Don't forget to unlock "Bountiful Harvest" in Eureka System early on for more options to play with.   A great game, and worth a look on sale or at full price!  :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't *terrible*, but I can't recommend it.There is some good stuff: The combat is significantly more exciting and challenging than the first one; they got rid of the silly broadside attacks, and ships are no longer restricted to the system's primary ecliptic, so you can actually *maneuver* your ship. It's not nearly as strict as the first game was about making you slowly coast out of asteroid and debris fields before you can re-enter autopilot. It's also far more polished, with good voice acting, writing, art, and character animation. Unfortunately, I can't say anything else positive about it.The UX is just bad. The menus are the worst I can remember seeing: they're horizontal, so that you can only see 3 or 4 options at a time, and you have to slooooowly scroll through them just to see the full list of options.The ship status displays are dense and unlabeled, with a lot of (admittedly pretty) decorative cruft that makes them almost impossible to read quickly in a combat situation. And while it's awesome that you can maneuver fully now, that change needed to be accompanied by some sort of HUD component equivalent to an artificial horizon in order to maintain your orientation. One thing they did add to make it easier is a dedicated button that tracks a ship. Once you're behind the ship, it will match speeds. Mostly it works well, but it keeps you pointed at the ship, not the point where you have to lead it to score a hit. If you try to nudge your guns the extra little bit you need to score a hit, the controls will fight you. Eventually you get the hang of engaging follow mode when the ship dodges, then releasing it, then nudging your aim to fire a few times, then engaging follow again. It works. It would be nice if you could adjust your aim relative to the follow point and the difference would "stick" as long as you keep holding down follow.When you're putting weapons and modules on your ship, there's no display that shows you all your stats; if you don't want to just fly the thing into combat only to discover you can only fire your guns for a second and a half before your ship loses all weapons and booster power, you'll have to take a bunch of notes and work it all out by hand.The 10% of you with color vision deficiencies will just love how everything important in the game is color coded green/red/yellow and there is no option to use colors that everyone can distinguish. This is a trivial improvement to make to a game, and it's inexcusable to leave it out nowadays.The controls are *terrible*. In order to target a ship, you have to hold down LB on the controller while navigating through ships with the d-pad. Try doing that in combat when you need to be operate both sticks constantly to stay alive.The player is limited to fighters and small cargo vessels, while your enemies cruise around in small capital ships with 3-8 automated turrets, attended by fighters. Because you can't use an appropriate vessel for most encounters, you're essentially forced into using a single strategy over and over and over: stand off out of range of the capital ships, eliminate the fighters one at a time, then rush in and spam the crap out of a capital ship, ideally parking your ship right next to it so only one or two turrets can target you, pick off those turrets, then just spam it with your underpowered weapons for a minute or two while hiding in the hole you made in its defenses. (Just to make sure the combat wasn't going to get any better, I edited my save file to give myself a few million bucks, and even with the best ships and weapons in the game, you're just going to do this same fight over and over.)If you want more than one automated turret, you're stuck in a cargo vessel. Rather than concentrating on one main weapon and letting the turrets take care of everything else, you'll have to switch between weapons constantly based on enemy distance. There's an option to fire all of them at once, but none of the ships available to you have enough power capacity to actually run all weapons for more than a few seconds.While *missions* are coded by difficulty and based on your level, the random mobs you run into aren't. You will get ambushed every other time you enter autopilot and until you've managed to upgrade yourself into a mid-level ship, you just have to put all of your money into speed so you can run away from these impossible encounters. Every time, it will take you 2-3 minutes of running your boosters and waiting for them to recharge over and over and over to get far enough away to re-enter autopilot.If you get caught with contraband (which is easy enough to do accidentally), you no longer have an option of turning over the cargo and taking a reputation hit. Instead, all local police and civilian ships immediately become hostile, and if you've got a turret that fires back automatically, they'll call in reinforcements, too. So if you pick up a case of narco cola accidentally, you can either restore from your last save (which, due to the far-too-frequent random encounters, may have been 20 minutes ago before you tried to make a single in-system jump), become a pirate after slaughtering 50 police and civilian ships, or die.

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY wanted to like this one. I like the characters and I loved the first game, but this one feels like it has had NOTHING put into it. Rebel Galaxy had tons of ships, and ways to customize those ships, great combat and while a bit grindy was tons of fun to play. This one has a better story I guess but that's all. The combat is horribly unbalanced with enemies setting up in  circle around you and just pelting away while you chase one ship. The only way I found to play at all was to mine till I had the best attack ship. Hardly any ships in this btw, especially compared to the original. Lack of ships, lack of weapons, and no capital ships means no chance against those big swarms, you pretty much have attack and run away, come back, attack, run way, rinse and repeat. Oh and things will never get better than they are right now in the game because one the main devs threw a tantrum and quit after he took some flak for the deal they took from Epic. _childDocuments_.review: I desperately wanted to like this game, I was a huge fan of the original rebel galaxy and assumed that this would offer a similar experience by providing an interesting story and a variety of ships, modules to fit them with and a fun, quirky, retro themed art style.However I was starkly disappointed with what I received, the story had no underlaying narrative driving everything along that unwound as you play through missions into a coherent plot. Instead it feels like a string of unrelated fetch quests and search and destroy/ escort missions given to you by a bunch of bland unmemorable NPC's.The few ships that are in the game, 6, or 12 if you count the re-skins which can be obtained a little into the game, would be forgivable if there was a range of modules and weapons to equip them with to customize them to your taste, or more realisticly, your budget but the reality is that there is only between 2 and 4 modules to unlock and few weapons worth investing in after you buy the best  options available to maximise DPS without exceeding your power output. So before I came close to finishing the game I found myself with the best possible hardware to obtain in the game and a hoard of wealth that was no longer realivant. When I finished the story (and in turn the game) I was quite frankly shocked, that it just kind of ended the way it did, I did not even realise the plot was wrapping up until the title quickly popped up on the screen, I genuilly sat for a moment wondering what just happened. The art style, in all fairness, was everything I had expected, bright, colorful and retro sci-fi themes such as the display screens in the cockpit and the grainy vid feeds which pop up when people open a comm line with you. And the dog fights, chasing craft and manuvering to avoid critical damage are very exciting and fast paced, at times it even feels more like a looter shooter above all els. But the combat feels repetitive after a while of using the same ship with the same modules, and redundant when you have nothing to buy with the loot you will inevitably convert into credits, at (in my case) the middle of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy playing this after Everspace 2 well that's a big downgrade if you ask me... 🤦‍♂️Bad flight controls, weird physics, eveything in Rebel Galaxy Outlaw feels floaty, slow and imprecise.This game literally have the worst control scheme, worst UI and most confusing menus system i've seen in a while for a space game, easily can give you a headache the first 20 minutes you boot the game.The gameplay is boring and repetitive, it's mostly a constant grind the entire playthrough.The graphics are alright but nothing very impressive tbh, bonus there's no custom fov options, current fov is too narrow and it looks nauseating !Poor graphics settings, just like the trash controls it feels like a bad console game ported to pc...Just wait for Everspace 2 or get Starpoint Gemini 3 instead.Way better games and lot more enjoyable.Don't get me wrong Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is not completely terrible, it's just too boring IMO and the controls are way too frustrating for me to recommend it.Story and characters are interesting, exploring the game's universe is cool, radio stations are nice with many great songs.Sadly everything is ruined by the repetitive missions and the terrible controls.There's also some game balance issues and it can feel very unfair at times.Getting ambushed and outnumbered by outlaw pirates that will pop out of nowhere with flawless accuracy shredding my ship in just a few seconds and losing 30 minutes of progress well nope i'm sorry but that's just not fun.If you like space games and exploration i'd say give it a try, maybe you will enjoy it if you can tolerate boring dogfighting and trash tier controls.It kinda pains me to give this a negative but there are too many problems and it's also missing way too many qol features.Oh btw Double Damage Games aren't you ashamed making steam users wait a whole year and not even giving us a launch discount, like seriously ?Big middle finger to steam players again IMO.My advice wait for a deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is a very close clone of Wing Commander: Privateer 1 and then adds a few pieces from Rebel Galaxy onto it, such as the sector map and RG lore. Unfortunately, it follows that design so closely and ignores the progress made by other space flight sims or open world games since. The whole experience just underwhelms and was a chore to slog though to reach a letdown of an ending.This game should be held up as a case study in poor cockpit design that would have lead to actual fatalities if it was actually implemented on military aircraft. Why is my cross hair obscured by a "cute" picture overlay of my own ship hull just to show me the status of my guns, when enemies are really small and hard to see at firing range? Wouldn't I know what I am flying from the cutscenes already? Why is there literally only one actual MFD and you need to rely on that as it is only reliable source of target status information? Every time you are about to blow up some target or an event occurs, that MFD toggles away to either show Log of events or a video call of some bandit screaming as he gets shot down and you completely lose vital combat information in acquiring your next target. It's absolutely terrible and even toggling guns/missile launchers turns that MFD to guns display and you have to scramble to switch it back to targeting again. When targeting an enemy capital ship, good luck trying to cycle between turrets that are lined up and the actual hull of the ship itself so you can isolate which quadrant is unshielded without having to go into the Radial Menu.Heck, there isn't even a current flight speed or target status indicator on the HUD so you are constantly forced to look up and down all over your cockpit at monitors and energy bar, which is absolutely against the concept of a HUD that is supposed to keep your HEADS UP in a fighter craft. And oh, on the Foxbat, one of the end game fighters, on my UW monitor every time you pull up, the cockpit view pans up and you lose enough pixels at the bottom of the screen to obscure the range to target. *slow golf clap*When you receive shield damage, your shield indicator flashes red... and it keeps flashing red because weapon cycles very quickly and you can't tell if it is tiny amounts of damage or large amounts and it takes a while for the constant flashing to go away so you can actually estimate how much shield you have left. The impact of weapons on your shields is so soft and the feedback so minimal that often time your real warning is when your ship's computer tells you shields are down.. and sometimes because there are so many other messages queued up, it tells you like 2 seconds after a shields are down just to tell you all the "Missile Evaded", "Missile Detected" first. In Privateer 1, the combat speed was slow enough and the shield "THUD" was loud to let you know you taken damage. COME ON! Thank goodness the hull hits are way more audible and visible and you also get your MFD toggled off enemy info to tell you what systems are mildly damaged urgh. I guess they really want you to play in 3rd person eh?In summary, I really wish the devs had spent some more time on proper design instead of focusing on nostalgia and remaking the outdated systems of old in a modern pretty graphic game engine. I had more gripes but those are the main ones that Steam Review would let me fit.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: This is disappointing compared to the original game.Constant interruptions from warping, hyperspace gating, taking off and landing break immersion excessively (many stations involve 3 cut scenes to land on a station and another 3 cut scenes when you take off. How did this get through any level of playtesting?). Use of Command menus during combat (encouraged by the devs) is the only way to see the battlefield in 3D but is also immersion breaking. Animated character graphics are clean and cartoony, a real step down from the less often used but far more detailed and realistic look of the original. Cockpit graphics are low res and quite blurry. The art program looks like it could be phenomenal (although the detail and resolution are far greater than what will ever be seen in game. Unfortunately they are also way too complex for someone who does not professionally use an art program (like the game devs) so I could not even manage a simple colour swap and gave up. Something more along the lines of SPORE would have been far more approachable for the average player. The music is still good. There is a lot more of it but many of the songs have very few lyrics repeated excessively. The advertisements on the radio stations were a highlight and all the more for being unexpected.  They are consistently funny and add to the world building. The game play is ok. Everspace has far better controls for a keyboard and mouse game and allows for skilfull play in 3D. The normal play approach to this game involves pausing the game to select a target in a menu and using a follow target button to do most of the flying for you. I avoided using the menu for targeting for most of the game but the radar did not have a display that could be used to read distance and the targeting command buttons were frustratingly poor. I imagine trying to play with keyboard and mouse without the follow button would be tantamount to suicide. I had to remap controls almost entirely to make keyboard and mouse work and I am sure there were still some aspects of the game that I was not using because of the controls (eg side strafing with inertial damping turned off).Difficulty is a bit of a mess. In the original game, the threat level announced by the onboard computer fairly reliably tells you how likely you are to get blown to dust. It also starts combat situations with your ship almost always at a distance that allows you to avoid combat if you want to. Outlaw has a very bad habit in the early game of putting you into a combat situation that is far too difficult at close range and without the ship speed to get away. The story missions also seem to have some very noticeable difficulty spikes on the first time through - even with a fully upgraded ship (which takes hardly any time with some efficient mining - leaving nothing to spend money on). But it turns out that there isn't much difficulty really - just that there are not many variations of ship and equipment that are viable for the hardest parts of the game and only one  effective approach to play. The only sensible way to handle most of the big combat scenarios in the game is to keep yourself on the edge of the field of combat, picking off the smallest and fastest ships and then circling around quickly to approach capital ships from behind or platforms one at a time out of range of the others. In my second play through I died just once and that was only because I did not follow the prescriptive combat approach above.The story arc is not epic like the original game but a series of seriously petty squabbles between members of the same gang or, even more often, the same family. Despite all of this I did enjoy the game enough for the price, but I only paid about $1.50 for it AND a copy of the original which I gave to a friend. Unlike its far better predecessor, which I bought at full price and would do again, I just don't see myself going back to play it many times. My first playthrough was 60 hours but that involved multiple hours of 8 Ball and 100% achievements including some frustrating hours on Star Venger (Asteroids but without a hyperspace) before getting the top score. The second playthrough was 10 hours and there probably won't be a third.If you want a skilful dog-fighting space game Everspace gives you far more control and sense of achievement. If you want an RPG space flight game Rebel Galaxy (and not Outlaw) is something I would wholeheartedly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is pretty much Wing Commander: Privateer - 2020 edition.The game is firmly, and intentionally, stuck in the 90's, and I love it for it. (Note: I've only played the game on the "Old School" difficulty setting)So there's a couple things to note about this game:1. The beginning is . The starting ship they give you is truly garbage (as Juno, the main character, says it is). It's severely under equipped, with  a main gun that will struggle to take down even the weakest of shields, no afterburner, no secondary generator, no extra armor, no missiles, no tractor beam, no jump drive, no pretty much anything. You'll have to spend a good amount of time at the start of the game running in-system delivery missions and mining to be able to afford upgrades to make the thing usable.2. The game pretty much assumes you're a space combat vet (or maybe it's just the difficulty I'm playing on). The enemy ships will actively maneuver to juke and dodge like pretty much no other game in the genre. They'll regularly rapidly change directions, do barrel rolls, circle with afterburners, etc. to try to shake you. This may or may not be easy enough to manage on normal difficulty settings (with aim-assist guns that adjust to aim at things in the center area of your screen), but you'll probably have a hell of a time trying to tag enemies on the Old School difficulty, where your guns only fire straight. Even assuming you  have aim assist, since projectiles have travel time, the fact that the ships don't move in straight lines for long means they'll probably dodge quite a bit of fire (particularly with the stronger/slower projectiles).I should note the game has an auto chase function, but I have no idea how strong it is, because it's disabled on the higher difficulties, so I've never had access to it.Anyway, if you're looking for a classic Privateer experience, this is it. I was looking for this, and I love it. While most games try to do their own thing in some way or another, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw does pretty much everything in its power to feel like Privateer, other than keeping the whole space western style of Rebel Galaxy, that is.

_childDocuments_.review: In a lot of ways it's clearly more polished than the first game. It's got the same good music, intuitive controls and menus, and the gameplay loop on paper is the same, but a bit more streamlined so there is less down time between combat.On paper it should be a good sequel to a hidden gem of a game. Unfortunately it isn't the same game. Instead of the 2d plane combat, with increasing scales of ships building up to massive broadside naval slug fests, the game has taken it's larger budget and thrown it into creating yet another space dogfighter.Unfortunately it is just worse than all the others. The world is barren of anything interesting, combat is frustrating and unrewarding, finding and targeting things around you is implemented horribly.They should have just stuck with and improved over what they had. This just doesn't work. Get Everspace 2 instead.
