_childDocuments_.review: Good but flawed modern approach to Privateer/Freelancer in a Redneck-Space-Setting. Less deep than freelancer, but better combat action.pros:+ outstanding music, radio channels like in GTA with even a customizable channel for your own music+ great overall atmosphere+ challenging and spectacular dogfights+ good voice acting, though a bit repetitive since few voice actors+ nice visuals+ very powerful ship painting tool (you can import PNGs and stamp them onto your ship, work with multiple layers, etc)+ extremely useful auto-aim function (not fool-proof though, it can often make you crash head-on into other ships if you never let go of it, so use it wisely)+ very well made gamepad controls (in my opinion)cons:- NOTHING IS EXPLAINED. Theres a small piloting tutorial in the menu but that's about it. No explanations of how most things work in the game. I heavily advise to watch tutorials/read some wikis when you start with the game, otherwise you'll die often and get frustrated soon- poor character animations- the balance varies throughout the game. At the start you'll barely have a chance, at the end you're almost unstoppable, but in the main part of the game its mostly luck if you enter a fight you can win or not. This could be seen as "realistic" but it seems as if most players dislike this approach of balancing- some bad game design choices. Tractor beam for example is on the same button as fast travel, which means that you'll sometimes accidentally fast travel away instead of getting that sweet sweet loot. Also, don't leave areas too early until the screen clearly says "mission accomplished". If the npcs thank you for your service and you leave the area too fast before it says "mission accomplished" you will fail the mission. Especially annoying in combination with the tractor beam/fast travel button issue.- not a lot of ships to select from. 12 ships in total, but 5 of them are just modified versions of other ships, so it feels more like 7 ships- World is big, but everything is already explored, no "huge, mysterious space" feelingOk, so why the mixed reviews?1. This is the sequel of a game called "Rebel Galaxy". Fans of the first game are disappointed because the gameplay is very different: RG had twodimensional "big ship" battles with huge ships, RGO has 3d dogfight combat with small ships2. The first hours can be harsh. There's pretty much no explanation at the beginning and enemies will often shred you to pieces with rockets (and they LOVE to shoot rockets at you). Also, you have a terrible ship at first, so you'll have to grind a little bit with small transport missions, cleaning minefields, mining asteroids or even playing billiard to earn a better ship and some decent equipment. Getting used to the controls and the energy management on your ship will take a while.3. Not every fight can be won. Whenever you enter a fight, scan the area first and check if you can handle the fight or not. If in doubt, flee. People seem to think that every fight can be won, that is not the case, especially in the beginning.This game gives you the best "Freelancer" experience if you were ever looking for a similar game (or Wing Commander/Privateer). Police patrols scan your cargo, the galaxy feels alive (police, traders, pirates/bandits), it fulfills a lot of points that I was missing in other space games. It is not as deep though; it has great combat mechanics, but the galaxy doesn't feel "huge and unexplored" and there's less functionalities to play around with. This game focuses more on flashy action than a space sim.You can travel in two ways: sublight flight and autopilot. In sublight, your ship enters a "travel mode" until you reach a point, autopilot shows you a skippable cutscene and instantly teleports you to the next point of interest. The thing I missed the most was that flying in sublight is barely interesting.In Freelancer, I always loved to enter those sublight "highways". While in this travel mode, I liked to look at trading prices/routes, read through upcoming missions/lore, check the map/cargo while I was flying towards my goal. In RGO, time slows down when you enter a menu. So instead, you'll just use the autopilot function a lot. This means: Aim for a point, fast travel, skip cutscene, arrive and aim for the next point, fast travel, skip cutscene. I mean it's better than no fast travel, but it would be nice to give me the option to check/read up on stuff while using sublight.Golden advices for a better experience: - early in the game, get into mining, it's really lucractive. You'll need a mining laser and a scanner for that- stick with ballistic weapons, they have to reload but dont require energy, you'll need the energy for your thrusters- get the best ECM (countermeasurements for missiles) as soon as you can. Enemies love to shoot rockets at you. Also try to dodge rockets- put a bit more energy into thrusters at the beginning of a fight, you'll be faster and afterburners will cost less energy- scan at the beginning of a fight to estimate if you can handle it or not- if you hold B, you can keep floating into one direction, but aim into any direction you want. This is very useful if you fight bigger ships or turret platforms- if you don't understand something: read up! The game sadly won't really explain it to youNot a GOTY, not a game for everyone, but a pretty neat space shooter game with action packed combat, great music and a southern states setting. Yeehaw!

_childDocuments_.review: Now I really enjoyed the first game and was really excited to see Travis dropping little nuggets of information about a follow up. I had no issue with it being fighter based rather than capital ship based as most of my star-fighter experience from XW/TF days were itching for something like that.When DD & Travis announced it was to be an Epic Exclusive upon release I was very disappointed as a Steam Purist I will not support Epic at all. However I understood why an indie team of 5 people would take that option in the current climate. So I waited patiently for the Steam release and left it there. However there was enough backlash from the sludgy part of our community which directly attacked and harassed Travis and his team to the point where Double Damage games threw in the towel and are no more.This is truly sad as 5 people had crafted this universe of characters with great gameplay and graphics and its now over.I hope the people who were involved in this feel ashamed that they had a hand in killing a fantastic indie company that could have flourished into a beast.Outlaw is a different style of game compared to the first as its based on small fighter ship to ship combat as opposed to capital class broadside style. However the main loop is similar. Follow the main mission, do side quests, trade, mine, pirate, bounty hunt.The graphics are great and have some of the best explosions you have ever seen. Some incredible lighting and flares of of stars and explosions.The sound track is again amazing for the atmosphere and style of the game. Very similar to the first lots of Dark Country and Hard Rock and even a station dedicated to Hardbop/Jazz for when you need to feel those Cowboy Bebop vibes.Controls where very good for me, I used an XBO controller and everything worked really well. One very cool feature is the Inertial Damper Cut which when activated allows your ship to stay on course while being able to rotate fully in any direction.Selection of mini-games, like Dice, Slots, 8-Ball, Arcade Cabinets.My only gripes with the game were - Auto pilot inhibited just like in the first game and the sheer amount of jumps in story missions was sometimes annoying.Overall I enjoyed my time again in Rebel Galaxy and am genuinely sad this is the end. There was going to be more, DLC, modding tools, 3D printed custom ship models but all of this died with the closure of DDG. To get a pair of games of this quality made by only a 5 person dev team meant things could only get bigger and better, this series had the real chance of blowing up to be something massive and now we will never get to see that.For shame people.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game for the soundtrack alone!   I played in Veteran difficulty with a gamepad and the auto-tracking system enabled... this way is kinda easy mode but it was the best dogfighting I have ever seen.  If you like Firefly or Cowboy Bebop you'll probably feel something familiar here.  This game also includes an impressive tool to customize your ship painting.This is no space simulator and you won't command huge battleships neither, but you can buy your own asteroid and build a comfy base with several perks.Some things I did not like:- Even if I tried to play for the "good guys" I was forced to play pirate in several missions, killing a lot of space cops in the process and making my initial choice irrelevant.  The alternative is not to help your old friends and  pass on the "Unlock all buddies" achievement.  I'd rater have an stealth / hacking / trading option in those cases.- Fast travel is annoying AF- You need to make several jumps just to pick up a lot of missions that should be given by radio contact.  This only makes fast travel more repetitive and boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a huge fan of Wing commander Privateer back in the day, and Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is a fantastic spiritual successor. While the ending left a lot to be desired for (I think they left it open ended thinking they'd make a sequel or DLC), everything in between is fun. You hall cargo, run missions, fight the power, and make money however way you can. The ships control well too. Don't listen to the reviews that compare it to the first game. There is no comparison since this game is completely different. If it was named anything else, it would have received a lot more positive reviews.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: The first game had a real vibe, but had some shortcomings.  The developers tried to address those in this prequel, but a few things were lost along the way.  But overall, I really enjoyed it.PROS:- Music is chef's kiss.- Visuals are pretty good.- Story is stronger than previous game.- Combat is 3D this time around, and and very fun.- You can paint your ship!CONS:- Seems to be less ship choices.- Less customization options.- A little heavy-handed with assist options (but can be disabled).- While the story is better, you are locked into playing a character, so really no immersion or self-insert ability here.FINAL THOUGHTS:  Would really like a game like this with more pilot customization as well as ship customization.  Being able to do those two things is what makes these games exciting.  I love the universe that the developers have crafted, and hope they make another entry.

_childDocuments_.review: So far the game looks nice. It doesn't take too long to take you into action, the tutorial is short and intuitive.The characters animations are awful, like from 15 years ago but they're secondary so I don't give a damn.The ships feel smooth, like a crossbreed between Everspace and the X's series.The overall feeling is of the old Freelancer, moving between planet bases and star ports but with much more freedom.The soundtrack is the top gem of the game, a combination of rock and dark country goes together with a western aesthetic that make you feel part of an episode of Cowboy Bebop while bounty hunting or kind of a Han Solo doing some shady smuggling.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a bit different from the first game, but as an arcade space simulator this is pretty decent. Its as hard or as easy as you want to play it, the ship options are limited, but enough that you can pick what you want for how you want to play. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game.  I really liked this game's prequel, for that matter.  It has all the ingredients for a game I'd really enjoy, but it failed to come together.  This soufflé has deflated.So it's basically a wild-west sort of space fighter combat game, in the vein of Freelancer and many others of that ilk, and lashings of plot so it's not the comparatively empty-feeling directionless experience of Elite: Dangerous.  I don't care about the western stuff much, but it gives you a lot of theme and lore to draw from, and "wild west" is short hand for "lawless frontier" so there's a lot of theme-setting done without having to do much of anything, and I'm okay with that.Where I'm not okay with it is actually flying the ships.  If you play the game the way it's intended, you basically right-click to auto-track and follow enemy fighters, and left-click when your guns are in range.  And if your kit is good enough, you'll win the fights.  So no meaningful pilotry is called for.If you try to use a flight stick (and I have a full-on HOTAS arrangement), well, it just doesn't work right.  You can't trim the control scheme properly, so it's all wiggly and hyper-sensitive and equally frustrating.It's too bad.  Like I said, I wanted to like this game, but I want to feel like I'm flying my ship around, and this game won't let me.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this, since I liked both the original Rebel Galaxy and Freelancer.But the overall presentation of the game is just too painful to actually be fun. I would have loved the cockpits... in 1997. It's as visually claustrophobic as playing Wing Commander in 640x480, except back then we didn't have anything better. The background starfield is literally just composed of pixels with a distracting glow effect that blows out what little visual real estate remains. The menus obsessively simulate 90s CRT monitors, complete with extremely annoying wobble effects and excruciatingly low-resolution text that succeed only in causing the very eyestrain a modern high-res, high-refresh LCD/LED monitor is designed to prevent.Even the audio succumbs to this bizarre obsession with lo-fi nostalgia simulation. It's compressed, scratchy, hard on the ears, and compensates for this with as much volume as possible. Great for a heavy metal album, not so much for a modern video game; and unfortunately the developers' musical tastes go in a different direction anyway. To be fair, this is no surprise after the original Rebel Galaxy's Texas blues-rock aesthetic, but the expanded catalogue in Outlaw doesn't offer the sort of variety you'd expect from a Grand Theft Auto-esque radio selection; it's pretty much just everything wrong with modern FM radio simulated in video game form.That's par for the course for Outlaw: rather than take Freelancer and give the formula a 2020 (or 2019, thanks Epic) update with modern visuals and sounds and new ideas, Outlaw just simulates all the worst parts of the 1990s and justifies it as nostalgia. Which is a shame, because a retro-90s aesthetic would be cool... but I'd like it without the suffering of an actual 90s CRT, please. I was there, I don't need a reminder.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not want to leave a negative review for this game, because it has a lot of the functionality and expected features of a space sim the likes of which hasn't been created since Privateer 2 - unfortunately, the implementation is just plain not good, and the devs seems utterly disinterested in fixing even the most glaring issues. The game has been released for almost two years, and they haven't released so much as a patch since a month or so after the game's release. They could have released a mediocre game, then listened to player feedback and spent the last 22 months polishing and improving.They have not.Anyway, to the meat of the issues:-The controls are inexcusably clunky. Seriously, unbelievably crappy for a space sim in this day and age.-Enemies scale in difficulty immediately and dramatically as soon as you begin to upgrade equipment. Want to kick around the home system for a bit fighting lowbie pirates and improving your equipment before fighting tougher enemies? Too bad, those lowbie pirates are no longer lowbies the moment you install a nicer weapons system or a bigger cargo hold.-The UI is clunky, literally less intuitive than Privateer 2, released more than 20 years before this game and after which it was clearly and obviously modeled. How the hell are you going to copy a game from the 90s and make it worse?-Many things simply are not explained by the time you first encounter them. For example, contraband - you can obtain contraband items in the home system, where no station will allow them to be sold, long before you have a jump drive and can go to other system, where I assume there are pirate stations or something at which to sell such items. But who knows? I sure don't, because there is no explanation in-game. Obviously the player should be able to sell contraband anywhere, since that is the nature of how contraband works... Where an item is illegal, it has the highest value.There is a fair amount of content implemented, and a lot of thought went into things like ship types, ship systems, costs and relative values of upgrades, etc. There is significantly more depth to the ship equipment than in most comparable space sims.It seems that a lot of effort went into writing a compelling story. For those characters I met in the first few hours of gameplay, the voice acting was excellent. I don't want to defecate upon the creative team - those things that are wrong with this game are almost entirely design decisions, rather than creative decisions. The creative team deserves massive kudos for doing a great job producing story, audio, and visual content, and they aren't responsible for this game being a bit of a turd.In this game, there are a wide variety of commodities, and a fair amount of thought clearly went into the economy - different locations have different items they produce, and demand/prices vary seemingly based on an idea of what such a colony or station might lack. However, the quantity of commodities available is not only unrealistic, but makes for crappy gameplay. Why does a colony of 8,000 that produces ores have 1-4 tons of iron ore available at any given time? How often do colonies produce more ore? Again, no explanation I can find anywhere in-game. A side kvetch - we're in space. Tonnage can be important too, but the primary measure of cargo space should be volume. For extra immersion, it's always nice when a space sim accounts for both - if you pack all your volume with extremely dense materials, acceleration and deceleration become sluggish.I played for less than five hours before becoming too frustrated with the limitations and poor design decisions to continue. I truly hope the devs choose to improve this game down the road - but after almost two years without any kind of support or updates, it seems extremely unlikely. This has the basic bones of a truly excellent space sim, and with significant modding it could probably be the best such game released in years.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying that I'm a huge fan of the first Rebel Galaxy game. I thought it was tight, polished, and had a great vision of 'high seas piracy, in space'.RGO is a disappointment. Every aspect of the game just feels undercooked.Firstly, the 3D spaceflight model. It's a huge downgrade. The map is utterly impossible to read, with all the same problems as elite dangerous. However, with no 'contacts' UI element, I have no way of telling which hostile ships are near me, which are the biggest threats, or which are approaching me. To dogfight, I have to select a target, then aim for the lead indicator. That would be fine, but since this game focuses on fighter combat, the pirate ships are very fast and dogfights become a repetitive cycle of zooming 10km towards a target, shooting them a bit, they blow up, and something attacks you from behind, so you turn, shoot them, they run away, and you chase them.You can bump into Pirate Lords in the first system, with their huge retinues. Good luck working out what they are or how to escape them. The game is balanced for a well-built ship, with all the modules and a full rack of guns, not the starter-ship you have to begin with. Oh, and the enemies scale against your ship when you start upgrading it, so you never feel like you've progressed at all. When I realised this, it was time for me to stop playing.The art direction in the story cutscenes is interesting, but jarring against the realistic style of the main game and stations. The sound design has highly-processed, monotone vocals. 'CRAFT HEAVILY DAMAGED' being chanted as loud beeps warn me about incoming missiles, for example. It's annoying, it tells me nothing I don't already know. Graphics are muddy, looking pretty ugly at 1080p and coming with an atrocious film grain effect as standard, which hurt my eyes. I do not like the artistic choices Double Damage have made in this game - they've tried to make things more complicated than Rebel Galaxy, and it just didn't work.The economy is dull. Early missions don't pay enough, you'll buy your second ship by mining ore in the first system, not by doing the story or side missions. In Rebel Galaxy, I smashed out dozens and dozens of missions without realising there was a story at all, and worked my way through all the ships having an absolute blast. RGO makes everything feel like a chore, like it's gated behind upgrades which don't help me at all. It's taken all the worst aspects of Elite Dangerous, but on a lower budget.When I got my ship of choice, for a short time I did feel like I was having fun. It was manouverable, had plentiful hardpoints, and gave me a couple of higher-grade systems to feel a but of a power curve. But unless I underpowered my guns, the aforementioned enemy scaling makes the combat tedious, and I just don't see the point of throwing good hours after bad.I can't recommend that you play this game. Play Rebel Galaxy, instead.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'm giving this a thumbs up, but it's a pretty specific recommendation. There are basically two groups who I think will enjoy Rebel Galaxy Outlaw:1 - Old-timers with fond memories of the 90s Wing Commander franchise, because in all ways this is basically a modernized remake of WC Privateer. It's almost uncanny how much it feels like an old Origin flight sim.2 - People who like the idea of space life sims *in theory* but simply don't have the extensive free time that games like X and Elite demand from their players. Because RGO plays like X on fast-forward. Missions typically only take a few minutes. Visits to a space station can be handled within a minute or so. Autopiloting (complete with swooshy flyby) cuts in-system travel times down to seconds. This is a rare space sim where you can have meaningful sessions in less than an hour, and the main plot can be finished in 20 hours or so. Maybe double that if you're doing all the side content, but it's still very zippy compared to every other major space life sim out there. RGO is not trying to become your second life.The space combat itself is streamlined and enjoyable in an arcadey way. We're in Star Wars style non-Newtonian space here, so ships handle more like WWII fighters. One of the game's big additions to the WC formula is a paused tactical mode, which lets you see every ship in a battle - and this is invaluable in later missions which could have a few dozen ships from several factions all flying around. I do wish there'd be a little more variety in the guns and missiles, though. With only rare exceptions (like an EMP missile you get midway through the story) it's simply a matter of paying more money to make bigger explosions. Although you do have to balance your energy use for your guns and shields vs the size of the power plant in your ship.I also really enjoyed the game's production design, which is going straight for a retro "blue collar space" vibe from movies like Alien, Outland, Space Truckers, etc. The addition of a series of radio stations are a nice touch. You probably won't recognize any of the tracks (aside from the classical station) but they do enhance the vibe. I especially appreciated the jazz/psychedelia station that was clearly aiming for a Cowboy Bebop feel.But the game does have a couple problems.First, it can have a very rough difficulty curve for the first 10 hours or so. Enemy difficulty is scaled based on the total value of your ship, and it's easy for a newcomer to build a ship whose value exceeds its combat potential. Be conservative about upgrades at first. Only buy what you *need*, especially until you can afford a better ship. Also, the mission variety is fairly limited, and even with the game's short overall runtime, it will probably start to get repetitive before you hit the end of the story. Especially at the point you've fully upgraded your ship and/or home base (if you want) and don't have anything to spend your money on.And, speaking of the story - it's incomplete. The whole game feels content incomplete, like they only implemented around 2/3 of the missions and story they'd intended to include. And since the developers are basically defunct at this point, there'll never be more. Then again, the plot and characters aren't that interesting anyway.But still, if what you're looking for is a "pick up and play" space sim that lets you get in an hour of enjoyable privateering pew-pew now and then, without it trying to take over your life, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw still offers a fun experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Wing Commander Privateer only worse. I grew up absolutely in love with Privateer, and thought Rebel Galaxy Outlaw would scratch that itch. It comes SO close, but I cannot recommend it.  First of all, it all but needs to be played with a controller. It was clearly designed with this in mind, where you “pause” the game and use a radial dial to scan, set engine power, pull up the map, etc. You can’t look around the cockpit while flying and are relegated to a single straight view. I attempted to play at first with a HOTAS, and it felt borderline unplayable. With an xbox controller, it controls alright, but still feels “floaty”. They also made the bizarre choice to include an “auto follow” button which if used takes all the flying out of this game. Maybe this was my downfall, but I refused to use this because I wanted to actually, you know, FLY my ship. However, possibly to make up for the auto follow mechanic, the difficulty is cranked to 11, and you can be swarmed by 10s of ships and literally annihilated in seconds of entering a mission area with the best equipment in the game. Also, enemies can “teleport” right next to you in mission, and do, and then destroy you in seconds. The only way I could deal with missions at all was to employ kiting tactics and separate the massive globs of ships by tagging a few, running away, killing them, and then repeating. I finally got pushed over the edge doing this in a plot mission where about 15 super soldiers showed up, and were again killing me in nanoseconds, and I just couldn’t be bothered anymore. With tighter controls and a balanced difficulty, this could have been a great remake of Privateer. As it stands, I still put many hours into it and enjoyed my time, just not enough to see it through to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: So Rebel Galaxy Outlaw aims to shift the series from two-dimensional to three-dimensional navigation and combat, and yes many claim the game is a radical departure from the original, but in my experience not so much. The game makes commandeering a craft much more of a dog-fighting experience than the battle-cruiser experience of the first game, which is the biggest change.The controls are funny on mouse and keyboard, it feels like your ship is constantly swaying as you aim to centre its course. One does get the hang of it eventually. I'm sure it was designed for play with a game controller primarily but I didn't try because my controller broke recently. There is an auto-lock and roll feature which makes guidance and navigation much easier... almost too easy. However, the game grades encounter difficulty on capability of guidance and there is a steep curve to unlocking and building a better ship, and even so encounters can remain difficult even after building a pretty good ship and many encounters requires decent tactical nuance in its approach. So... while it becomes relatively easy on smaller encounters, you can often unexpectedly be ambushed by hordes and obliterated in seconds.There are many areas where the game expanded its horizons and a few areas where it has shrunk. The world is much bigger, the great soundtrack from the original is much bigger, but the amount of ships and upgrades has shrunk rather dramatically. But there's still enough to suffice.The economy of the game is similar than before. But the earnings now aim to rein in the grind of the original and rather locks the economy behind difficulty rather than stretched out task repetition. I often have to guess which missions to tackle for earnings that are within the capabilities of the vehicle and more than occasionally find my craft outmatched either deep into missions with plenty of resources on board or right from the start, returning you to port and losing all resources gained and having to start the same mission or something else over which can be frustrating.There is a disparity between the two games as the original can be picked up for like a dollar and its excellent value, but accordingly I wouldn't recommend this at the $20 RRP expecting to get more of the same game. But if you get a good deal on Rebel Galaxy Outlaw, you can get more of the same Rebel Galaxy goodness, with a little bit of a twist.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game a year ago on Epic Game Store, and so thoroughly enjoyed it I have bought it again to give further support to the developer.Simply put, this game is a love letter to Wing Commander Privateer (Sept 1993).  If you played any of the 90s Wing Commander series games, this game is for you.The cockpit-POV intense action, atmospheric music and in universe radio station are all amusing and fresh. The way that you have a choose-you-own adventure style of how to play the game to progress your character and abilities of your ship.  The storyline is there, but you can play it as rapidly or slowly as you want.  Plenty to explore, and lots of factions to interact with as well.This is a modernized take on a frontier life-style space pilot, with a blue collar touch.The attention to detail is noticeable in all the small things like the landing pad officer with their light batons, or how a ship shudders upon touching down.  Things like this are just wonderful to see.A quality made game by a small developer.   It doesn't try to do everything, but what it concentrates on, it does exceedingly well for what it is.  The price is more than reasonable for a near-AAA production game.Many thanks again Double Damage games.

_childDocuments_.review: oof, I'm glad I got this on a deep sale. I never found a flight/space combat game that got the feel and AI so wrong. Enemy fighters have 3 moves, fligh straight, hard bank, or corkscrew; all of which they cycle between so they are always doing any one of those at any one time. Capital ships just go in slow circles from the point you engage them or sit stationary. It's all way to simple and boring to engage with.I enjoyed the combat of Rebel Galaxy enough to replay through a criminal playthrough and had a blast right up until I finished the game a second time. I just cannot bring my self to do it with this prequel. You will have to grind up out of the starter ship and at least reach mk II components to continue on the main quest in the first few hours of play. Once that mini-grind is over, everything else will be the same and you can just do the most boring side quests (because you already saw all their variations in the generic auto-generated quests you grinded in the first system already) to get the endgame ship and full upgrades. So the last 80% of the story campaign and side quests just feels like a slog.The ending mission (no spoilers) is like sitting through your neighbors firework show for 4th of july, and when they hit the grand finale, they launch 2 fireworks (the same you've seen a dozen times already) simultaneously instead of one at a time. No resolution to anything in the story either, it's just pointless. yet the script and voice acting both last the character that contributed so much to the fun in the first game.It seems the devs have abandoned the DLCs or any other future updates for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Game is decent but everything above normal difficulty is BS cheating AI. Pick it up on sale under $10 USD or not at all. Also the dev just dipped out a year ago. 6/10 when under $10 4/10 when $30I like this game overall as I liked the universe of the previous one and I love Freelancer the game it is kinda copying. That said I wish I could give this a hard recommend instead of a very light one with strings. Combat:Dog-fighting in this game is kind of hit and miss literally and figuratively. I use a X52 HOTAS and the scaling for acceleration is NOT reading the inputs for the stick at all properly. This game reads the inputs as 0%, 5% 20% and 100%. If I push the stick forward 3/4 of the way that is read as 100%. If I push it halfway that is read as 100%, push the stick 30% forward? That is read as 100% to this game. There is no option to turn off this acceleration so from a flight stick user this is TERRIBLE input reading. What does all this mean for combat? Well get used to overshooting your targets and having to adjust back multiple times per encounter. I have Elite combat ranking in Elite Dangerous and I am a damn good pilot in every game I have ever tried EXCEPT this one. I feel like I am only a passable pilot in this game and I know most of that comes from the abomination that is acceleration in this games configuration. Scaling/Difficulty:I played my first save in this game on the highest difficulty Old School for 45 hours. I got a bunch of the combat chevos for blowing up enemy ships and collection their cargo. I was dealing with the control problems and just making due with the weird acceleration. The Snipe Hunt mission was a solid brick wall and a complete slap in the face. This SECOND LOWEST difficulty mission was spawning enemies who do not miss no matter what evasive maneuvers you take, and also can tear through a fully reinforced level 2 shield AND max level armor on a medium ship in under 4 seconds. The AI aiming is very similar to old Need for Speed AI. It is not able to keep up with you in terms of pure skill so it cheats the physics and rules the player has to abide by. Much how NFS AI would warp through corners to catch up to you, the AI in this game just turns 180 degrees in a second at full speed while firing and hits you with shots even if the fixed front mounted weapons are not facing you. I was able to pause the game while one of them was turn firing and with the photo mode it was clearly shooting directly at my ship while also facing 90+ degrees away from the guns aim point. One ship doing this is bad enough but the game spawns in a whole wing of ships doing the same thing.  Sound/MusicThis game has some amazing sound effects and is a outright treat to hear the audio of everything in it. From the sound of a ship taking off to the impacts of rounds on a hull this games audio engineer needs a raise.I do the same thing in every game, I play for about 10 minutes with the music on then I turn it off or mute it completely because the music is garbage. I left the music on in this game because it is absolutely great. Nuff said. Conclusion:At $30 just go pick up Elite Dangerous and you will get a much better experience than this game. At sub $10 this game is an "OK" game at normal difficulty. Do not expect anything from the game devs either they have not done anything for this game in a year now.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Rebel Galaxy (the 1st one from 2015) over and over, it was a lot of fun.I grew up playing Wing Commander, Starlancer, Freelancer, Independence War and having a modern space game that is reminiscent of these old classics with amazing graphics, excellent voice acting and all the Greel Whiskey you can get?It was an instant purchase, twice in fact(!) as I bought it on EGS and Steam.The humor is on point, the cliches are there and delivered in such a way that it entertains you, the soundtrack is pure ear pleasure, just like the 1st one.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game deserves way more love. Yes, it's quite different from the first one. The devs have stated RGO is what they had in mind all along but they didn't want to release it too close to titles like No Mans Sky (even though it plays very differently). At first I was sceptical because of the mixed reviews but after watching a few videos I realised that with all the customisation options, exploration and dog fighting combat this would be right up my ally. As far as repetitiveness I can't say I agree with some of the reviews here. Sure you get to do the same things over and over but thats true for most games. I think it just boils down to wether you like doing these things or not. And the grind here is more than bearable I think, especially considering there's an intriguing main questline you can experience.Now the game isn't perfect though and here are the aspects I didn't enjoy:- Even with good gear you can be overwhelmed by enemies quite easily. A few generic side missions are just not possible to do, especially on your own.- Speaking of fighting on your own, theres gonna be quite a bit of that. The buddy system from the first installment has been revamped. You now unlock buddies through story missions and call them if needed. They will help you for 10 minutes and have a cooldown lasting another 10 minutes. I think this mechanic doesn't fit the overall pace of the game at all and I really preferred the original system where buddies stayed with you until dismissed. The way it's handeled now I sometimes go afk and wait for the timer to reset before a difficult fight. Doesn't feel like it serves a purpose.- Theres a good selection of weapon systems, although they don't come in different grades like in RG, which means less grind but also less flexibility because without tiers some weapons are just better than others, period. You will find yourself using the same loadout for the rest of the game once you've been able to afford it. Also most weapons consume power and some of them consume so much compared to their DPS that you probably won't ever use them. Tl;Dr weapons could have used more balancing.These are things to consider but they didn't make me want to play the game any less. It's just some unused potential imo.So in conclusion I really like the game. I got it on sale for 5 bucks though, so maybe that put me into a more forgiving mood.

_childDocuments_.review: Some pointers.* Texas is a dangerous hellhole, do not underestimate it simply because you start there.* Do not idle outside of the Amigo tablet menu, otherwise the game will pause for you by blowing up the ship.* Flying manual through sublight is this game's hard mode, I would  recommend doing many easy jobs quickly using the auto pilot. You do this to escape the garbage box and get a better ship faster.* You will fly into rocks, CCCP "decommissioned" satellites, Musk's dumb rockets, Space Force corpses, and various another objects as you try to break into sublight. >>>Check the Amigo tablet<<< make sure you don't need repair and just start again. There's no reason to get frustrated about it.*  of your sublight approach to planets, the orbital gate and space stations are placed there as bait by the hungry planet. If you need to correct; always-always set the waypoint at far angles from the planet, become a Saturn Ring until you have a completely safe fight path that's dead on.* Later on, you can use your woman power to enslave a man. Do so. Make them come help you everytime they are available.* This is not some fancy pants game like EVERSPACE 2, if you are not into Cosmic Western or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in Space this game might not be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Wing Commander: Privateer is one of childhood favorites. This game is a great spiritual successor to it. The gameplay is smooth and satisfying, especially using HOTAS. I highly recommend old school mode which only allows gameplay from the cockpit and is more challenging. Dozens of planets and stations to explore. Purchase various ships and upgrade them. Play dice poker and pool in at the local bar. Pickup missions from the Merchants and Mercenaries guilds. Although the game can be somewhat repetitive at times and could use more content (which the devs have planned with dlc) I enjoyed it quite a bit and blowing up baddies never get old.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a beautiful hommage to the space sims of the mid and late 90s. You can tell that a lot of love went into it, giving it just the right feel that many older gamers miss in today´s polished AAA-play-safes. There are also some nice easter eggs that people of my age (early 40s) can appreciate. The controls might need a short adjustment period, but that is to be expected when something new is attempted. I still remember all the hate that the first RG got for its broadside system. A lot of noise was also made by people who seem to be personally offended by the 1-year-exclusivity deal with Epic. Their downvoting does not have anything to do with the quality of the game, so don´t let that keep you from giving it a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun space game with dogfighting, mining, trading, and exploration.Has good accessibility, including an auto pursuit mode when your target gets a bit too swirly whirly, and respects your time with good old Wing Commander style autopilot to quickly transition across the system, but if you like long waits it includes the warp from the original RG1. Don't go into this expecting to be the same as RG, this is all about flying fighters instead of cruisers and you can now fly on all axis.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe it's more cartoonish, more streamlined and a little less epic storywise, yet the game shares a lot of the Freelancer DNA that you can't find nowadays anymore.The gameplay resolves around easy-to-learn-hard-to-master  and/or a  simulation. While cringe-worthy at times it provides a  atmosphere. There are only a few ship models in-game and the designs are hit and miss based on who you ask, but they provide different ways to play the game and are done well. Mission design could use more variety. On the other hand, it is very polished and nearly bugfree. The game does not the best job at explaining itself well, so you can run into difficulty spikes if you don't learn the game mechanics properly yourself (Hint: power management). Once you get it, it is a fair and polished experience. For its price and taking into account that it is done by a team of five, .

_childDocuments_.review: For those who liked the first Rebel Galaxy, this prequel is a familiar, but different, new, but classic feel.  Instead of commanding a frigate, cruiser, or dreadnaught, you now get to play Aunt Juno from the first game in her younger days.  It's in cockpit mostly, with the focus on flying fighters, gunships, and light transports.  The feel is that of the 90's cockpit space games, like X-Wing and Wing Commander.  And when I say it's "like" them, I mean it's really like them:  there are limitations such as the inability to look around your cockpit, or adjust your camera range in 3rd person.   The space combat takes some getting used to, especially since, unlike those other OLDER games, there's no way to quickly target either close enemies, or enemies attacking you, or allies.  You always have to open up a new mini map, which pauses the game, and lock on to a target there.  Another annoying thing is that the enemies do scale with the value of your ship.  So if you think you're getting an advantage by upgrading your systems and ships as soon as you can, think again.  Upgrade too fast, and suddenly "Easy" missions become deadly and nigh impossible to complete as you're swarmed by enemy fighters who, as long as they're off screen, (aka: behind you) can vaporize your shields in a matter of seconds and end your game early.  I'm pretty sure if Star Wars: Squadrons had a more in depth story mode, it would've been better.  But again, it's clear that this is a throwback to the space fighter games of old, and in that capacity, despite all the shortcomings, it's still a fun way to pass the time.  The GTA-like music stations you can listen to while you're flying helps.  Bottom line, despite the clunky and sometimes annoying combat elements, it's still a fun game to play and definitely worth the few dollars I paid during the summer sale!
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: An arcade warp gate simulator with some bad design decisions.I wanted to like this in spite of the mixed reviews but having thoroughly played it I can see why it has the score it does.The single biggest gripe I have with the game is that there is one UI element that shows your target and its damage, your nav point, any comms and any status message. So any time a log message comes up or someone talks to you you lose the status of your target or you have to wait for it to disappear to verify if you have the right nav marker because they don't know anywhere else.Other stupid decisions include making the tractor button the same as the travel button so if someone drops cargo right near a warp gate you either tractor it (and risk getting busted with illegal goods sometimes) or get really close to the nav point.Another annoyance is that new missions will pop up at any time, usually in the middle of a current mission, so you have the comms chatter issue, which also prevents you from warping so you just have to hang in space and listen for a while. Whenever you get a new mission it immediately sets it as your current mission, so you lose your current mission marker, mid-mission!The game recommends use of a game pad but even with aim assist and a follow button, combat can still be ridiculously difficult and unrewarding when you do destroy stuff, knowing that your cursor was never really on the hit marker.The game lets you fast travel as much as possible but that just means that you spend forever travelling between regions via warp gates. There are a large number of sectors but most of them are extremely boring and not worth taking the time to explore. Maybe that is why they went with a mid-west theme :PTrading seems to be pretty meaningless because even the largest ship can't carry much cargo, and a lot of places run out of goods to ship very quickly so you have to move on to other sectors.Most of the missions are more trouble than they are worth. Early game I just took the low-reward missions that I could just fast travel through so I could make small amounts of money every 10-20 seconds or so.The best money/time come from mining but it is incredibly boring and tedious because you only have a very small cargo hold.The plot was actually okay but it tries far to hard to be edgy. There was a certain amount of pleasure from choosing to walk away from everyone else in the end.Hopefully the devs can take this on board for any future games.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: A bit baffled by the number of negative reviews for this game, so I decided to write my own.Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is pretty much a modern version of Privateer, where you are a space fighter pilot free to do as she wants (mining, trading, mission running etc). It has interesting combat mechanics, immersive characters, excellent music and atmosphere, rewarding exploration, lots of content.Of course, it is not perfect : the controls and interface are designed for consoles, and take time to get used. The difficulty is noticeably high, I really would have liked difficulty settings.Still, this is a very good  game that I would happily recommend to space fighters fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed and completed all content in the first game, but the extremely slow grind to get a ship/components capable of comfortably fighting outside of the first system along with problematic controls/ui make this successor not to my taste.Visuals, music, atmosphere and combat sounds are great.Combat style is fun, if also different from the 'naval' style of the first game.Plot and ship design is passable.Controls and UI are poor, and the low FoV first person view is awkward without a horizon indicator.Progression curve feels horrible, with components and new ships requiring dozens to hundreds of thousands of credits each, while transport or early jobs only offer 1-4k per run, and attempting to move up a few systems gets you horrifically outmatched.

_childDocuments_.review: 3/10 - It gets one point for not costing $60, and one point for some decent music...NOT a replacement for FREELANCER, as many have suggested.  The general idea behind the two games are similar; open world space trading/combat across multiple systems, upgradable ships/weapons/equipment, multiple faction/alignment diplomacy, etc...  The execution falls short.  Aside from slick animated cutscenes, the graphics are somehow equal/worse to Freelancer from 20 years ago.  The information display (HUD or cockpit) is jumbled and uninformative.  More than half of the screen is obstructed by non-essential fluff in cockpit view, or your wildly flailing ship in 3rd person view.  The selection of ships and equipment pales in comparison to Freelancer, and it doesn't appear (as of Nov 2020) that the modding community has found a way to expand upon it.And worst by far, is the control scheme (at least for keyboard and mouse).  I've played games with unresponsive controls, I've played games with twitchy/imprecise controls, and I've played games with inconvenient/contradictory key bindings.  I think this is the first game I've ever played to combine all three of those.  I've only got 2.3hrs on record at the time of this review (unfortunately 0.3hrs past the refund request cutoff), and roughly 1.5hrs of that was spent trying (unsuccessfully) to reconfigure/rebind the controls to something manageable.  Trying to use keyboard flight will get you a clunky 90's Privateer-like scrolling/rotating movement with no inertial feel and instant damping, and you will likely need to choose between having yaw control OR roll control if you still want throttle and targeting near the left hand.  Trying to use mouse flight will get you a wildly oscillating roller coaster that somehow feels both uncontrolled AND over-damped.  At engagement distances, enemies are typically rendered as a few pixels with a targeting box around them, and some hieroglyphics on your dashboard that offer little insight into the enemy's stats or threat (assuming you don't mouse over something else while wildly spinning about trying to make sense of the BattleZone type radar display wedged into the other side of your dash).To top it off, there is no manual save/load option, and you can only work off one slot at a time.  The game autosaves when you dock at a station, and when you exit or rage-quit.  So remember that then you are randomly jumped by a ridiculously overpowered quad of pirates for the 114th time in a row while trying to warp to a station or mission point.  If you rage-quit with half your sh*t blown up, the game will overwrite your only current save slot with your ship half dead in space...Lastly, the menu system is abysmal.  The quick menu of a few common actions was obviously designed for a console controller; it is a slick flashy rotary dial with pictographs instead of text, probably intended to be a "hold, point, release" style menu, that loses both the hold and point function when transcribed to keyboard and mouse.  The rest of the game's functions are crammed into a blue and white scanline style terminal display intended to look like a late 80's word processor display for some reason.  Mousing over a command will highlight it, but not activate it for modification (pressing a key at that point will modify the LAST thing you had clicked, that is no longer highlighted), and the keyboard controls for navigating the poorly labeled and organized sections are apparently another homage to late 80's word processors.Since I'm past the refund period and loath to completely waste the purchase price, I'll keep at it and update the review if conditions improve (or I decide I was being a cranky old man when writing it).  As of now, I'd give it 3/10.  It gets one point for not costing $60, and one point for some decent music...

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really close to recommending this but I just can't quite get there.The good stuff:- The world is just cool. This "deep south in space" vibe is great, very Firefly.- The flight model is pretty cool, I fly with a stick and I feel connected to the ship and I've had some pretty good dogfights).The bad stuff:- It tries so hard to be just like Freelancer and in a lot of ways it does well! The story for me though falls a bit flat, I know I'm not that far but it just doesn't really grab me, none of the characters are that interesting and the set up is just too much too soon.- The main thing for me though, there's just no sense of exploration here. Every sector is pretty much identical and you can instantly fast travel through an entire sector to the jumpgate and then instantly travel to the next. Cargo runs just become: Autopilot, Jump, Autopilot, Jump, Autopilot, Jump. You lose any sense of where you are, especially given there's no discernible difference between any of the sectors. In Freelancer every part of every sector felt hand crafted and ready to be explored by the player, there's just absolutely no sense of that here, it feels even more generic than Elite Dangerous.If you're just about the grind to better ships and components then go for it but if you want any sense of immersion and exploration then pass on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: this game openly states that it is not a space sim. Do not go into this expecting something with the depth of x4 or elite dangerous. This is a rooty tooty fun shooty arcade space game with a great theme. Too many negative reviews from people expecting something that isn't promised to them in the first place. A drastic departure from the gameplay of the the first game, rebel galaxy, this shifts from black flag style capital ship combat, to fighter dogfighting. If you're looking explicitly for a continuation of the same gameplay of the first game, you won't get that here. What you do get is quite good, though. I'm roughly 30 hours in, mostly on side missions and just moving around cargo. There isn't a stunning amount of variance, but the gameplay loop is entertaining enough. and enough of the fat has been trimmed to make it much less tedious than in the first game. cross-system trips in the first game could be a nightmare because of the sheer time it took, but the autopilot (basically fast travel) makes it much more bearable, meaning that you find yourself far and wide across the map instead of trying to isolate yourself like in the first game. The controls on m/kb are awkward to say the least. They were already awkward in the first game, but if you're coming from an actual space sim, it's going to be very hard to adjust. They very heavily recommend a controller, but I've managed to adjust to m/kb with some time. To put it into a single word, the controls compared to a space sim are "simple". Autopursuit isn't necessary but it's nice. The weapons are gimballed by default so you just have to be near. There is a difficulty option that removes both autopursuit and weapon gimballing, but I wouldn't really recommend it. A lot of cool things to see. Some interesting, if few, ship designs. Very good choices in art style and music.And DLC is planned, so watch this space.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a love letter to Privateer, it can be seen in the ship and station models and the overall atmosphere.  It is a very different game from the first Rebel Galaxy, but still has the same goofy aliens, great voice acting, sense of fun.  The economic model driven by special events that you can control and influence is really great.You can stop a science ship from reaching an archaeological dig site which will in turn prevent a tech boom which would change market prices, and all the various economic fluctuations work like this so you have direct influence over price changes in a meaningful way -- which in many ways is far more satisfying than the dynamic economy of the X-series, for example.I was surprised to find myself enjoying playing pool and dice in the bar, it really makes the universe feel alive.  It is just a super charming game with a lot of character.I'm not as good with cockpit sims as I was when I was younger, so I really appreciate all the flight-assist and auto-aim features.  It gives me just the right level of action and challenge, making combat more about picking the right approach to a battle and not getting surrounded, rather than how well I can execute an Immelmann. If you are a better pilot, you can turn all that stuff off and play in hard mode.The game is definitely setup to be played with a controller, which is a little bit of a challenge for me with my mouse and keyboard but once I got used to the idea that Q and E were back and forward, then all of the menu navigation that was frustrating me fell into place.  You can obviously re-map all that, but the menus are definitely designed to be navigated with the back/forward concept that is natural for controller users.There are certainly some rough spots, but it is an absolutely charming and enjoyable game, and totally fun to just fly and run missions.

_childDocuments_.review: I dont know what to say, its not an all in one spacegame. Very few games are all in one spacegames. You dont get spacelegs, you cant leave the spaceship while flying, you cant build bases, upgrades and ships are sparse. But its all saved by the missions. The missions and custom soundtracks. So much of this game is unfinished, even "casinos" are just another space station, it hardly seems like 40 people exist in the whole galaxy based on atmosphere, but the missions save this game. If you threw these missions on no mans sky or elite dangerous it'd be the be-all-end-all space game of a lifetime, but its common-sense approach to gameplay and missions is just enough to be worthwhile for the 6 dollar pricetag. Its cheesy its meh, but the missions and shortcuts to otherwise grindy gameplay found in other "ultimate all in one spacegames" really save it. There may never be a universally entertaining space game, we may forever have to jump from space game to space game to get pieces of what we wish were in just one game, that said, this one is a valuable piece to the puzzle between Space Engineers, NMS, Elite Cash-graberous. The community is dead, the modding scene is dead, the dev has left, but for 6 bucks, eh, close enough. Its starcraft 2:starfighter, dont expect more. 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a retro-mod Privateer, and a good one. If you ever played and enjoyed Privateer, you'll enjoy this game. 5 minutes into the game and I was loving the updated graphics and feel that still managed to capture the grittiness of the game it was modeled after. Some reviewers complain that this is too much of a departure from Rebel Galaxy for them. This is not supposed to be a sequel or followup to the first game, it is listed as a prequel, but is very obviously a spinoff, just as Privateer was a spinoff of the Wing Commander series.Other reviewers complain that the game doesn't give you the pertinent info and stats you need to properly fit your ship. My first visit to the ship and equipment dealers gave me all the info I needed, from engine output power to weapons stats that showed how much each component on your ship draws and even how many seconds of sustained fire you can maintain before depleting your engine power. The things we had to calculate on paper in order to keep track of in Privateer has been addressed.The base layouts, the cockpit, the hud, space flight, and combat, this is all straight up Privateer, just modernized a bit. Although the game may recommend using a controller, if you've played Freelancer, the other Privateer inspired game, then you'll feel right at home with your mouse and keyboard. This game is not designed for you to start a new game, jump in your starter ship, and take on the galaxy. It is going to take work, lots of mining or cargo runs, lots of patrol missions, and lots of time to get proficient in the path you take. Those that use mining to quickly get a good ship and weapons without putting in the combat hours running patrol and bounty missions will inherently hate the game as there is a lot to be learned when going into combat outnumbered and outgunned. The soundtrack is good, the voice acting is good, the graphics are spot on, the ambience (Privateer with some Firefly mixed in) is great, and although there may be a few bugs here and there or some minor polish work that needs to be completed in  a patch, overall this game is a winner and I foresee many, many hours of exploring in my future. Well done Double Damage Games, and thanks for bringing such a classic back to life.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite dogfight space sim.The controls, the handling, the optics, the soundtrack. Everything is so good. The fast travel system is one of the best in my opinion. The dynamic animations during fast travel give the illusion that you are still flying through space by yourself.Sure, it's not easy to get into, but here's how I did it the first time on the Switch:   - Start by doing low-risk cargo runs.- Then join the merchant guild and do merchant runs to make a lot of money.- Buy a bigger afterburner and then install a power plant. If you run into enemies with this setup, switch all power to the engines and push the afterburner to the max (999 speed) until you can activate your fast travel again. You can outrun any pirate this way.Do this for a few game sessions and sooner or later you will be able to buy a bigger ship with powerful weapons.Give this game a chance. It deserves one.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much Wing Commander vibes on this one.Positives -*Good story (for what little I've seen of it so far)*Very open as far as going out and doing whatever you want to do*Good variety of things to doNegatives -*A bit confusing on how to get into any specific menu, but nothing outlandish*Do we really need 2 or 3 seperate landing/launching cuts every single time?  They are skippable but it seems excessive.I haven't put a great deal of time into yet but so far, I'm enjoying just the Texas system.Tips -*Get a couple mass drivers, and a tractor beam asap, it helps a lot (need the tractor anyway)*You could play merchant right out of the gates but with the limited hold space, I'd say just sell when you get to any port for the first bit*Check the bartender for news of places to visit later*Check to job board and try and pick up several jobs at once*You can pick up pilots sometimes for bounties/rewards (if you have a tractor beam)*Scan often*On mine clean up, approach, cut your engines, scan as needed and just destroy what you can without moving. Even the side missions suffer from the same issue - difficulty level often jumps from easy to impossible within the same mission, even after upgrading ships and components. They're far too sim-ish for this kinda mood.The controls are decent, the graphics are colorful, and much like the first game REBEL GALAXY, the music is top notch.It's a grungy, dirty, honky-tonk galaxy, and it really doesn't like you.Great at $30, a STEAL if you get it on sale.(Note: I had some issues with the game not recognizing my X52 HOTAS flightstick, but Anna over at Double Damage did wonders on helping me figure out the issue. _childDocuments_.review: It's Privateer 3. It's literally just Privateer 3. This isn't a bad thing at all, mind you, I just find it funny how blatant it is. And honestly, it's kinda all it needs to be? Give Privateer a control scheme not designed for an autistic octopus and a banger soundtrack and you've got yourself a quality arcade space sim of the sort you just don't see nowadays. As for the story... look, I can't even remember it. I can barely remember the main character's name, all I know is she looks like every lesbian's dream girlfriend and kills people for money and that's good enough for me. Like in most space sims the story is entirely perfunctory anyway, it's just a device to give you a guided tour of Wacky Space Texas and a few setpiece battles while you're still learning the controls, and I had the most fun just ignoring it in favour of doing my own thing in the sandbox. It's superior in this regard to Rebel Galaxy 1 IMO, with no levelled gear or level gating stopping you from just doing whatever you want in the sandbox.And the messing around in the sandbox is good, you've got a pleasantly uncomplicated arcade flight model, weapons that feel fun to use, a half dozen-ish (plus a few variants) ships to upgrade to to fit your preferred play style, all with their own bespoke cockpit interiors (complete with the customary Privateer style deeply questionable visibility), two fast travel modes that make flying between points of interest a breeze and a soundtrack full of licenced C-list-radio country, blues rock, metal and other, less appropriate genres. It's got nowhere near the depth of Elite Dangerous for instance, but this is IMO a strength, it's good, brainless fun. It helps that it's got very strong presentation as well, with every corner of the universe oozing with run-down space hicksville vibes that fit the game perfectly.The one criticism of the game I have is that, while it is generally a good looking game (more for its strongly Foss and Elson-inspired art direction than any particular graphical achievements, although I do value the former more highly anyway), it does overuse bloom and window dirt to the point where it's legitimately hard to see what is going on sometimes. It also has a truly bizarre implementation of motion blur that makes the background stars double in brightness whenever you turn even slightly. It's horrible and I hate it and because the studio went under a while ago it'll be there forever.But these really are minor complaints. If you see this on a sale, definitely grab it for a couple hours of classic-flavoured space sim joy.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: If your reading this then you are probably like I was.....you like this type of game but the "mixed" reviews worry you.  Well...I can tell you that there is a good game here...especially if you get it on sale (I got it 80% off).  Don't let all the bad reviews fool you.  They are from people who either didn't give the game a long enough chance or they were fans of the first Rebel Galaxy and were turned off by how much different this one was.  I firmly believe if this game had either come out first or had no predecessor it would have been received more favorably.  Yes....the controls are a bit clunky and the mission can be a bit repetitive but the graphics are crisp (if not a bit too colorful) and in the 3 hours I have played so far I have not encountered one bug.  The dog-fighting is also a lot of fun.  So if your willing to over look a few things and invest the time to learn the somewhat weird controls you will be rewarded with a fun space sim.....not the best one ever made....but also not the worst.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes me back to Wing Commander days of dogfighting with some delightful twists.  There are some minor complaints or improvements I wish I could see, but overall it is a fun game with interesting characters.The radio is amazing!  Regardless of your musical tastes I haven't heard the same three songs played over and over (and over and ...) again, but it feels like actual radio.The combat is fun and challenging and that option to follow a locked target is such a game changer, but not overpowered. _childDocuments_.review: For a casual gamer like me, someone who normally plays turn-based games or third-person RPGs/shooters, this is a welcome foray into the space sim arena. I played the original Rebel Galaxy and really enjoyed it, though sometimes traveling place to place was tedious. My favorite things about both games are the music (I've never heard anything quite like it before and I love it), the sense of humor and the overall style & aesthetic of the ships and universe.As a fan of Cowboy Bebop, it strikes the right chord for what they describe as the "blue collar" life of merchants, pilots and pirates. It's a lot like being a solo Mal Reynolds (Firefly), trying to keep your ship in one piece taking any jobs you can handle. As you scrape together enough credits, you can upgrade your weapons, defenses (armor, shields, ECM), ship components (like bigger power plants, a tractor beam, etc.) and even add a little "flair" to your cockpit. Eventually you can even afford better and bigger ships.It took me awhile to get used to the new flight controls, and I'm still certainly no ace, but the auto-aim assist makes it possible for me to actually keep up with moving targets and have a fighting chance. The original game doesn't necessarily need it, since you're not flying a small fighter/cargo craft, but this is essentially a prequel game since you're Juno's nephew (as I recall) in Rebel Galaxy. Juno Markev sounds a bit like Jennifer Hale from Mass Effect, but I'm pretty sure it's another talented voice actress, though I'm not certain who. She deserves a lot of credit for making Juno entertaining.For anyone who wants to dip their toes into the space flight sim genre, this, or the original Rebel Galaxy, are a great start!

_childDocuments_.review: Okay the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly.GOODThe game is chalked full of great music! This helps add to some of the flavor of the world. I love the feel of the world and some of the NPC's you meet along the way.  It scratches the Wing Commander and Freelancer itch of by gone years. The bar is a great way to get some gear. Play against the patrons which offer you upgrades.BADI'm playing on the easiest level and man it had me sweating bullets. You start in garbage scow. Basically a flying brick with a huge target on its back.  I had to grind out cargo runs to get some basic equipment.  Going on combat runs in the starter ship is close to suicide if don't have the right upgraded gear. I spent more time with my finger on the afterburners instead of fighting. UGLYOkay the game is grindy until you can get some better gear. Mainly a ship that does not suck!  To do that you take on missions like cargo runs which are usually pretty safe.  Combat runs can cost you time and money because your ship gets shot up and your spending hard won loot to re-arm / repair. I found the best way to make loot is mining!  With mining you can make 20k - 40k in the Texas home system as a good starting point. This is far better then your standard crummy combat runs and luke warm cargo missions. Also the time is minimal around 10 or so minutes a pop to fill your cargo hold. (Note: This might take longer in a bigger ship)Here is a link to a mining guide  SUMMARYThe game is fun with the right gear and ship. Get out of the Garbage Scow and have plenty of the upgrades before tackling harder fights. Use mining as a fast way to make cash and to buy the upgrades you will need.  Fighting will be a little better once you have enough money / gear / ship.Good luck Citizen and watch your six.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked everything about the original Rebel Galaxy, like I did, skip this crappy installment and just let it exist as it was for you.Rebel Galaxy: Outlaw is... a floaty controlled, 3D, poorly animated, loading/transition screen filled, interruption filled, less customizable, less engaging, less interesting far cry from the prior installment.Gameplay: 1/10~On the second difficulty level, it boiled down to holding down auto targetting/chase on whatever little thing I wanted to kill, and then just timing my guns to not run out of energy. In the big fights, it took all the tactics of just running away and isolating units to not take too much damage and then proceeding with mild caution. These 2 strategies carried me through the whole game, using the Gauss guns.~You can get all the weapons and meaningful ships pretty early too, so before I had my shielded jump drive(for convenience's sake), I had the full loadout that I would end up using the rest of the game. I tried several combinations and mixes, but they all really end up feeling pretty similar beside range of engagement.~Shielded jump drive seems to exist just to make you spend some amount of your quickly pointless funds. It stops risky gates from potentially obliterating random parts of your ship and lets you refuel less. (My second risky jump deleted my shields so that part needed to be bought again, no big, but annoying).~There was nothing interesting to see or explore in this game, environments were less destructible than the original(pretty much entirely indestructible) so I didn't even get to spend time merrily clearing out entire asteroid belts just for fun (not that the mining lasers are good anyway).~Half of the end game missions make you go through a minimum of 10 loading/transition screens each just to progress as it sends you several times half way or further across the map multiple times.~Enemies will just be in your path constantly as fodder and interrupt your quick travel. This manages to add hours to the game with 0 additional fun!~Exploration is not encouraged as you don't control your warp drive movement unless you place a checkpoint on your map and then use it as a target. You can't just explore freely, so you're effectively more locked down in a game that has a full extra dimension of movement~Don't worry about getting too attached to a tier 1 ship. Unlike the original where you have multiple classes of ships with wonderful designs completely different classes, tiers, and ways to use them, your ships are basically all tiny fighters in this game with a base form and a minor evolution of each one.~Guilds and mining serve no real purpose after you get your basic setup. I stopped doing guild quests after I got out of the fourth system, did mining once, and never ended up running out of money. The only reason to do these quests is to...to...I guess try to get the 3 million dollar achievement? Maybe do them as a flyby as you're on your way to something that progresses the game.Story: 3/10It started kind of interesting, a classic little revenge plot, with some quirky characters to pick up and work with along the way...which quickly derails into a whole bunch of introductions of characters with no real background that you supposedly know for some reason and once you're done using them (and they're done using you for their stupid sidequests) you just never interact again really. No quirky dialogue or random encounters, nothing, they just exist somewhere doing whatever, not that you need them to help, but it would have been nice if your travelling buddies had character, or meaning after bothering to give them names and supposed importance.I feel like there were supposed to be some big reveal moments, but they fell flat and I really don't remember them. This game only gets a few points for story because some of the characters started off interesting.Music/sound: 7/10The music is still fine, there are a few that really don't fit the space cowboy theme imo, and that wouldn't really bother me either honestly, the variety is nice. This topic loses points for commercials, during the music, which is kind of interesting at first, but VERY quickly gets bland and feels kinda bad in the middle of fights. The same goes for interruptions from enemy pilots that you're killing. I have no desire to hear their last obnoxious words every time I take their shields down or take one of them down. This also has crossover with the gameplay interuptions because, their screams are always accompanied by an image over your hud screen. Which may and likely will get in the way of something you're trying to look at at many points in time.Animation: 4/10They decided space needed to be blurry for some reason? I really don't get it. It feels like they went backwards with animations in general and the opening cinematic is somehow lesser quality than the infamous animated Legend of Zelda scenes from yesteryear (see: Excuse me princess). Overall: 2/10Rebel Galaxy: Outlaw hints at all the things a good game could deliver, then just decides to do none of them instead.
