_childDocuments_.review: I had to be in the right mindset for this game. Quick background, I come from the Wing Commander era of space sims. You had quite a bit of control and a bit of management but otherwise it was gameplay that might seem too simple in today's grand space simulations. My long time favorite is Wing Commander Privateer so when I hear of a game that is exactly a modern version of that, I'm all for it. The first time I booted it up, I went through the flight tutorial and decided the game wasn't for me. I wasn't feeling the cowboy twang soundtrack, the fake corporate sponsor messages, and the fact it had an auto-chase function for space fights. Recently I got in the mood to play another Privateer or Freelancer kind of game. I first tried a game that was heavily following the design of Freelancer. But that particular space sim's third entry just... lacked. It just did not have any real personality and nothing was particularly noteworthy despite nailing the design and open space feel of Freelancer. Disappointed, I decided to try Rebel Galaxy Outlaw again and I'm glad I did.This is not your modern space sim. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is your old school "simpler" space sim. The trade off is that this game has a lot of personality to it! I may have been turned off initially by the soundtrack and fake commercialism but I greatly appreciate it after the experience with the other game. I am also likely a bit biased toward this game because it is following Wing Commander Privateer's design document almost to the letter. You start with a low end trading ship complete with a single laser as its only gun just like Privateer's start. Depending on the difficulty you select, this will either be an okay laser with a color coded radar or full "Old School" with a worse laser and a gray color only radar that doesn't show you if someone is friend or foe. Your difficulty also determines what gameplay assistance you can expect. The standard difficulty lets you access the auto-chase and assisted aiming where going down to the "Old School" difficulty removes it all. You can also choose somewhere in the middle by turning off aim assist and not using auto-chase. While the difficulty pacing remains the same, I like the options are there to either appeal to old hands that have done this before or newcomers that may not have the flight experience.Just like with Wing Commander Privateer, don't expect a lot of flash and glory. You are a working pilot. You need to spend time earning credits and making small upgrades to your ship. Rush into danger and you'll be blown out of the sky without a second thought from pirates or radicals. It's a slow satisfaction and Rebel Galaxy Outlaw always lets you know the expected difficulty of each mission before you accept it. Even main story line missions have the same warning if you look within the universe equivalent PDA. If you get blown up, try again to see if your luck is better or abandon the mission to try something else. Clearing out minefields, shuttling cargo in-system, or just answering random distress calls as you travel around can offer rewards without getting too heavy. Thankfully there is the quick travel Autopilot or you can travel at Sublight speed if you prefer to stay immersed listening to the radio as you travel around.tl;dr This is not a heavy space sim and it's not full of flashy set pieces. This is a game you either kick back and ride the waves between calm and space battles for a few hours or you come back in small increments to do a few missions at a time. Play it slow. Don't rush to an endpoint. And if you keep an open mind, the game's world just might pull you in.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this as I take a break from RGO after it's hurt me, again, by crashing and losing my save file. Yet I'm still recommending the game because I think it's just a great, fun, space shooting experience. The in-moment gameplay is fun. The combat has a visceral feel. It gets chaotic, and is at its core a good time shooting things in space. Just flying around is a joy. I like the very strong style. There seems to be a Firefly influence - a western in space - that comes through in the cheesy rock radio, the myriad grungy details added to the setting, and the drawling accents of the various NPCs. I like that the game gives you a lot of freedom. Right from the start you can go where you want and do what you want. That whole story thing sound boring? Grab a mining laser and go and make some money shooting at rocks for a while. This game feels to me something akin to GTA in space: there's a heavily stylised and detailed setting, mini-games in the bar, constant voiced reactions from the player character, factions and reputation, and the radio station complete with in-universe adverts and jingles. But they clearly didn't have a GTA-sized budget, so while there are such things, there's nowhere near as much of them as you'd find in GTA. All things considered, there's a lot to like in Rebel Galaxy Outlaw.But. (Of course there was a 'but' coming.) There's also a lot to dislike. There are some really obvious major features missing, such as: the ability to own multiple ships; have weapon loadouts; any more than token economy options. There are other things that do the job but only just: the station menus are kind of sparse and in places un-intuitive. The controls have some weird quirks, like one of the main control keys also providing context-sensitive options. But probably the biggest problem - probably the main issue with the game - is the difficulty scaling. Right back at the start, when I realised you could just take yourself off mining to grind money, I did so for a while. I bought a couple of new weapons and was pleased to see that the pirates I met were dispatched more easily. So I spent a chunk of time amassing more money and splurged it all on a new ship and a host of upgrades. Cockily I went back to an area I'd been before and found pirates, expecting to show them who's boss. I got my landing-gear soundly thrashed. It seems the game just decides to spawn enemies based on the value of your ship and its equipment, so if you take a break from combat to upgrade, you'll go back to combat only to find the enemies much harder. It rather takes the fun and the point out of upgrading. Rather than becoming more powerful over time, it's almost the opposite: you find yourself less well equipped against strong enemies. It's annoying because the game also includes a location-based 'danger rating' system, which you would expect meant deadlier enemies were in different places. But no, everywhere is dangerous once you upgrade.Rebel Galaxy Outlaw feels like a game that had big ideas, but ended up rushing to release before they were all fully implemented. There's a lot in there, but some of it isn't as well developed as you'd want. So there are big problems that may spoil your enjoyment. Even so, I recommend the game because it's fundamentally just fun to play. But probably wait until it's on sale to pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: I had such high hopes for RGO when I heard about it. I played a ton of the original Rebel Galaxy and enjoyed every moment of it. I'm not the biggest fan of first-person flight-sim games though, but I thought "Can't be that bad, let's give it a try." When I saw it on the winter sale, I figured, "Awesome, no time like the present to pick it up."It's worse than I thought.A floaty dead-space and sensitivity slider that can only be increased by increments of five means you'll never find that sweet spot where your normal mouse motions register correctly. It's nearly impossible to align your ship to any point in space, with your cursor dancing in an orbit around the exact point you want to go. It'll also feel like you're too sluggish or like your ship will be jittering around like a squirrel on crack, no in between. At this point, I figured, "Okay, maybe they only did extensive testing on gamepad, that's understandable. Let's plug in the ole PS4 controller and try that out." Nope, no native PS4 controller support, you have to download a third-party application, configure it, and THEN the game -might- detect you have a gamepad and give you the correct button prompts. If it doesn't, good luck figuring out what "button 6" and "button 9" are.TL;DR: If you were looking for a sequel to Rebel Galaxy that improved upon the first game's combat, this isn't it. If you were looking for a space-flight-sim with smooth controls and a dash of that space western feel, I'm sure you could find better elsewhere. Double Damage disappoints in this installment sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Game is hard, but that's to be expected if you have any memory of Wing Commander Privateer.  Game is great if you remember Privateer, and introduces a lot of features that we could have only dreamed of back in the 90's.  Control scheme can be remapped to your liking, so I don't think that should count against the game.  I see a lot of people using the "privateer vet" tag, and I can say that I'm one too.  If you've never played Wing Commander Privateer (the original...not privateer 2), and I'm assuming most of you haven't, this game is going to feel unreasonably hard.  Well people reading this review, I can honestly say that Wing Commander Privateer was considerably harder than this game.  You think the swarm missiles in this game are bad?  Try the missiles from Privateer!  You couldn't shoot down those missiles, and your ECM only worked when the missile was fired.  If the missile maintained it's lock, then it'd be on your ass for a good long time.  Do you like taking ammo-based weaponry and diverting your spare energy to shields?  Me too!  Guess what you couldn't do in Privateer.  That's right!  I hear people complaining about the controls for this game, but isn't that what the button remapping feature is for?  Also, if you're having problems with the mouse flight characteristics, then just remap the mouse buttons to the keyboard, and you can bypass mouse flight controls all together.  Now that I think about it, I don't think you could remap any of the buttons for Privateer back then.  The only real control feature that is missing that is sorely needed is a key that targets the next enemy ship.  It's pretty annoying when you're cycling through targets, and you need to move through a capital ship's entire stock of turrets before you can actually target an enemy fighter.  There are a lot of other things I didn't like about this game, but nothing that would completely turn me away from this game.What I love about this game:  The variety of weapons in the game.  The music.  The art style.  Exploring.  Fighting Pirate Lords!  Being able to call in allies.  The mini games.What I don't like about this game:  No Target next enemy button.  Cycling through turrets on a capital ship.  Ships that I took the time to save scooping up all the good cargo drops.  Dropping out of autopilot/warp directly in front of an asteroid.  Multiple enemies spawning around me at less than 1km away after scanning a black box.  The LACK of variety of subsystems (why only 2?).  The lack of variety in overall gear (no shields or armor with different properties, only one different type of afterburner aside from normal upgrades, etc.).  No deflectors (unlike Rebel Galaxy 1).  The LACK of variety of Pirate Lord exclusive drops (only weapons drop).I know the downsides section seems pretty large, but none of them were deal breakers (at least to me). Anyway, if you're having difficulty with the game, I would recommend hot-keying the transfer energy to shields function to a convenient button and loading up on ammo-based weapons.  That way, you can divert all of your energy from weapons, and  keep your shields up a lot easier than before, giving you a much longer period of time that you can fight for before you need to put distance between you and the enemy ships to regen.  Be sure to target the weaker ships first to reduce the numeric superiority of the enemy as quickly as possible.  If you're willing to trade shots with a ship, cycle through targets until you find a enemy about 6 km away.  At that distance, they'll usually be trying to make an attack run on you.  If you have faith in your frontal shields and armor, then you can usually kill them in a very short amount of time, or at the very least ding up their hull pretty badly.  Also, missiles are cheap, so until you have the number of enemy ships down to a controllable amount, keep firing them out!  You can always head back to base to restock without interrupting a mission.Anyway, hope this was helpful.  Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: The ship painter is a genius idea, getting to be one of the little ships is quite fun, I don't mind the repetition, the grind isn't totally egregious, the cockpit views aren't nearly as annoying as the videos make them out to be, but this is a big nope from me for three main reasons: The weird way difficulty is handled, the way the jumps/long distance travel works and the continuing bug that takes you out of a jump/auto-pilot and smashes you directly in to a ship/asteroid/station/debris.Jumps/long distance travel: This is nothing like the first game when it comes to your in-system jumps or the warp gates. In this game, any long distance travel is accomplished via a cut scene that ends and dumps you at your destination. That might sound like it saves you a lot of time watching your ship travel - which it does, personally that never bothered me though - but you don't get to see what you're flying in to. This means no spotting enemy contacts on your way in so you can change your approach, and for some kinds of missions which end up on the higher end of the difficulty scale (which is totally random), means you're dumped in the middle of any enemy that might already be spawned at the destination.Difficulty: The risk rating on missions can be totally ignored since it simply doesn't give you any indication of how difficult/dangerous the mission will actually be since the number of enemies and their ability to gank you is random each time you play a mission. There was some degree of this in the first game, especially when doing missions involving Murath pirates or Greel Syndicate in harder/later game areas, but those were predictable and the first game's jumps weren't cut scenes that dumped you directly in the middle of the mission area, so you had some warning flying in most of the time and could react accordingly.For example, one average risk distress beacon mission had me facing a half dozen easy mode pirates that had already spawned in the mission area when I arrived, and while I was spawned in amongst them, I was able to destroy them and complete the mission because I wasn't instantly annihilated. The next average risk distress beacon mission had the beacon in an empty area which shortly after spawned three difficult pirates directly behind me, which was still doable. However, finishing them and scanning the beacon triggered a small fleet of around a dozen pirate ships including two capital ships which spawned above and behind, destroying me before I could even manoeuvre, let alone attempt to get out of gun range or run away - every single time.The usual answers to these difficulty spikes are "get better gear" which won't stop the above since the capital ships drills through the highest tier armour and shields almost immediately. "Transfer power to shields/to engines and run away" which absolutely is a valid strategy...but not when you had no idea you'd be so vastly outmatched that you're killed in seconds with no time to even transfer power, let alone run away. Or "be a better pilot" which I don't understand since no amount of skill can stop two massively overpowered ships that spawned directly behind you with masses of weapons from immediately destroying you before you can put any form of strategy in to play.Jump bug: The above can be handled by just walking away from missions where the difficulty skews that way after you've died a few times and realised the game has borrowed Xcom 2's RNG. What can't be avoided is when the game decides its going to drop you out of a jump face first in to a ship/asteroid/station/debris. At best this results in being faceplanted and having to quickly try to manoeuvre away while you're taking a lot of costly damage. At worst you'll hit something that you can't fly away from and you'll be destroyed. Some jumps between certain locations will always result in this kind of thing so - yes - you can just avoid those places or jump to a different location and then on to your chosen destination from there. That is an odd thing to allow in the game on its own, but this happens between random locations every few dozen jumps as well which you can't do anything about until after you've been smashed in to paste and reload at the previous checkpoint.This is a regression from the first game and I find the design choices around long distance travel and difficulty bizarre. I would recommend you pick up the first game for the exploring/trading/larger scale combat and pick up 'Enemy Starfighter' if you're after a more narrow focus on just smaller-scale fighter/gunship combat.

_childDocuments_.review: A big disappointment, I enjoyed the first game but this one is simply mediocre. The developers should have stuck to what they know, a broadside capital ship game, instead they went for dogfight space game and failed miserably. Only get this if you like "space mining" and even then on a 75% off discount.Pros:+ Good music.+ Mining is good and provides decent reward for time spent.+ A couple of decent ships.+ Some decent looking areas in space.Cons:- Very limited ship variety.- Combat is poor with floaty controls and swarming enemies.- In higher risk areas your flight is constantly interrupted by enemies taking you out of "warp" drive (not its actual name).- Enemies never drop anything of real value.- Mission reward is extremely poor for time spent, the only way to make money at a meaningful pace is to mine.- Story is very bad, same goes for characters.- All sectors feel very samey.- Basically, combat is to be avoided since the mechanics are bad, the rewards are miniscule and there is real risk of spending more in repairs/consumables than you get from mission rewards and salvage.- "Illegal" cargo is completely pointless, it's worth very little, there are hardly any stations that will buy it off you and if you are scanned with it, the police start chasing you.- Trading is pointless, between low price delta and very low stocks on stations it's even less efficient than combat missions which are already less efficient than mining by a factor of 5 to 10 depending on sector.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an awesome remake of Wing Commander Privateer with lots of improvements over the original. It also plays inthe Rebel Galaxy universe which is leaning heavily on space western themes. It's worth buying for the soundtrack alone. It's an open world "do your own thing" space simulator with a strong focus on dog fighting. Trading is possible of course but you don't expect a space trucker sim. There are also a lot of quest lines to follow and wingman to unlock.There is a bit of consolitis, yes, but it's not too bad. Every button can be re-mapped although a few are always double mapped.The devs clearly intended this to be played with a joypad/controller but you can also use your flightstick or HOTAS. The only downside here is that the joystick deadzones cannot be adjusted. Otherwise it would be the perfect space combat sim for flightsticks.

_childDocuments_.review: Holy god how did Double Damage go from making the joy that was Rebel Galaxy to this trash (Rebel Galaxy Outlaw).  TLDR : Space combat game with some of the worst UI/camera(s) for SPACE COMBAT ever encountered in 30 years of flight sims.  All the good music, writing and atmosphere in the world doesn't help when your core gameplay is this un-intuitive, clunky and indecipherable.The UI is awful, whether we're talking about settings, the planetside UI or UI menus...  but the CARDINAL sin here is that the UI inside the cockpit for gameplay is EVEN WORSE.  And speaking of Cardinal sins....  the flight controls and camera(s) for gameplay are also amongst the most awful I've ever encountered - I thought hey maybe its me using the mouse/keyboard and switched to a joystick...  which eventually ended with me throwing the joystick across the room.  In 30 years of playing flight sim games this MIGHT be the first one that I actually regret paying for.  This UI was excusable back when I was playing LHX Attack chopper back in 1990 but in this day and age?  Seriously - and honestly the controls were more natural and properly responsive back then which is....  beyond depressing.If your into masochism then enjoy!  Otherwise stay the h--- away, go play the original Rebel Galaxy or any of the Starpoint Gemini games or go oldschool and play Tie Fighter or something - it'll be cheaper AND more enjoyable!  Should have listened to the other reviews, this isn't even worth it on sale, its unplayable unless your in it for the politically correct female main character and a continuation of the play for the Rebel Galaxy universe - or maybe the music which I have to admit is pretty awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an alright game but the controls seem very clunky. Digging into this it makes more sense because the developers designed it to be played with a gamepad/controller. Combat isn't very interesting and feels very arcade-like. Even though you can damage specific components of ships (not through targeting) combat just comes down to simply blasting at something until it dies. If you get a missile launched at you, you simply launch an ECM to counter it. If you are outnumbered, your character will say something like "oh boy I should leave" and that's your cue to punch out.The game uses the main quest to give you goals in an attempt to motivate you to improve your ship and travel to different systems. Each "stage" is essentially just you grinding for money. You'll probably end up grinding delivery missions until you can get some decent combat gear or mining equipment, then grind combat or grind mining. Both of these are very simple and get boring fast. It's very tedious and it doesn't feel rewarding when you upgrade a component or buy a new ship. Rather than getting excited I often felt myself saying "well at least it will be a little less tedious."On the positive-side you can play pool in this game which is more fun than the game itself. The downside is that you are stuck betting whatever the game feels like you should bet, and there's only 1 person to play at each bar, which never changes.It looks like the developers were inspired by things like Cowboy Beebop and Privateer, but the game formed around the joining of these two great sources of inspiration is very lackluster, dry, and tedious.The biggest downfall to this game is that in its entirety it feels like a console game. I've heard people compare it to freelancer and even privateer, and it doesn't come close. As a game designed specifically with consoles in mind, it sacrifices a lot for PC users. Anyone who plays it for the first 30 minutes will understand what I mean. This might be a fun game to buy for XBox or the Switch but I can't recommend it for the PC.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay...do the smallest jobs, rack up the cash, build yourself up drip, drop, afterburners here, twin mass drivers there, make sure you save up a decent powerplant and Rebel Galaxy Outlaw will deliver, an enjoyable, solid, space truckin', bounty huntin' asteroid minin' 8 ball pool hustlin' [yes you read it right], retro arcade gamin' [yes that too] and barkeeps with their finger on the sectors' pulse so you know where the credits can be made... glad I picked it up. Use your sub engines [Seta-ish drive] when you come out of a jump gate the very moment an enemy starts talking smack, or if you hear "ship has entered the area" there's 90% chance you'll be gone before they start shooting3. This game is not a patch on Elite Dangerous, NMS etc, do a few missions to get the cash together/till you can afford better gear and just carry on with the main/story missions.5. if you can get some space between you and ship[s] chasing you [whilst in retreat] dump power in engines 1st/Max, Shields 2nd and get the hell out of there then Auto/Sub jump when ready....After 34 hours:6. Dumbfire missiles, tricky to line up, seem like a no, no...yes, yes! small fighters = 1 hit, you'll know when to fire and even the heaviest of fighters can only take two in the engines before its punch out time.7. long range Solid projectiles vs long range energy weapons: Solid shot/Auto Cannon every time, why? solid shot doesn't use alot energy so that's more power to the shields and engines!8. Use the Platypus for a very, very, very long time! fully kitted, she's a fast, nibble little ship capable of going toe to toe with ships armed with several times the fire power and power systems, can carry enough cargo from A to Z to make healthy bank, has an excellently small profile and almost flies like a Starfury from Babylon 5 when you truly get used to her; I kid you not I am still using the Platypus, 34hours in.Note!! _childDocuments_.review: This game is good but not great.  I was looking for a replacement for Star Wars Squadrons and this was adequate.What I liked:- Story mode- Side missions- Customizing ships: choice, weaponry, paint job, name, cockpit flair.- Infinite playability, post-campaign completion (Sure, I'll eventually get bored but I get to choose how much I play)- The "Buddy System"Things I wanted:- VR-support!  (I loved playing Star Wars Squadrons in VR and I wanted it here too)- The ability to customize my avatar (I can customize a ship but not my toon?)- Better cockpit flair: more of it, animated flair (e.g., bobbleheads that move... like Star Wars Squadrons)- A way of speeding up jumps even more (jumping 8 times and back again gets monotonous)- Commerce at Bountiful Vista (makes sense for in-game and gameplay reasons)- Default stickers/flash in the ship painter (like the game Space Crew)- More background on the "Buddies" e.g., strengths, weaknesses (not all Buddies seem to be created equally)NOTE TO EA AND MOTIVE STUDIOS: Please make a sequel to Star Wars Squadrons that is closer to this game.  PvP/E-Sports is fine but what I *really* wanted from Star Wars Squadrons was the sort of gameplay available here: story mode, side missions, infinitely spawning sector-based missions.  If Star Wars Squadrons had this game's campaign mode depth, ally missions, and infinitely playable side-missions, in VR, I'd never bother to play another game again.

_childDocuments_.review: I know that i haven't played it long, but i doubt that any of the points i have a problem with will change drastically over the course of the game.The controls with Mouse and Keyboard feel awful. Or better, the deadzone in the middle where you can freely move your mouse, while not steering your ship is an absolutele godawful idea in my opinion, cause the sudden acceleration once i move outside of that deadzone, is so sudden that precise flying/aiming seems to be impossible, at least it makes things way harder than they should.Also, being disintegrated by an enemy within seconds, while being at the very start of the game and in a mission that didn't had a high threat level, feels a bit like overkill.It also feels like the cockpit is suffocating me and blocking 70% of my view out into space, which seems like an odd choice, cause the game definitely doesn't look bad. Though it feels a bit too colourful and distracting for my taste.The soundtrack is definitely great though.Anyway, there's a lot of frustration talking out of me, cause the game looked fine in the trailer and i hoped for a game that might give me similar things that Freelancer gave me back in the days.Unfortunately, that didn't work out and the odd design decisions and in my opinion bad controls just don't let me enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: "YES" I would definitely Recommend this game... but with a Massive Warning!!!The game is fun... Action Packed... Should have been made VR... But provides Great Combat, Good Choices of Ships and Weapons and Missiles (not Massive Choices like going to Jack in the Box, and staring at the menu for half an Hour; but more Like In-and-Out Burger... with a Few Really Good Choices.) :) If you like Space Sims... JoyStick Game Play... and Space DogFights... You will love this game.However... and this is the Warning:This game is Massively UnBalanced, and will leave You Rage Quitting on more than one occasion.  Example (without making it a Spoiler); there is a Quest You must take to Move the Story forward; it's You and your Wingman against a Target and 5 of their Wingman.  EVERYONE shots at YOU... and Just You!  If you run too far away, and go outside the INVISIBLE "You Left the Mission Area" area, you Fail the Mission; Of course... if you don't run, they will Tear You Apart with guns that hit from up to 10km away; Note: Your guns hit around 2 or 3km.  It took me 5 tries to complete this mission; by that time, of course, I wasn't even having fun anymore... I just wanted to get passed this mission, so I could continue the game.  This was the second such mission I ran into; and based on what I've read, it is not the last :(.Another annoyance are the ship's Monitors.  There are 2 primary Monitors on your HUD; one shows Your Ship (very convenient, you'll find yourself looking at it often to know your status), the second one changes depending on your actions.  When You target another ship (such as the Enemy) it will display the target ship on this monitor.  Which is Excellent as you can see their status such as Shields and Hull Damage.  However... if you do anything to your ship like; change weapons, your ship now displays on the second monitor for about 10 seconds or so; meaning you are no longer able to see the status of the Enemy ship.  Or if you change your Power Management (Energy to Shields, Engines and/or Weapons) again the Display shows information about those changes instead of the enemy ship.  This is very inconvenient... and Annoying... since this information has a lot to do with the decision you make during battle.  Is their shield is low enough to changing to an Armour damaging weapon; should I fire a Missile, or wait... are they close enough to blowing up, that I should do... WhatEVER!!!  Bottomline is:  there is plenty of HUD Space to place several more monitors; and these other monitors could have been used for this information; or better still, use the first monitor with Your ship information which would have made more sense.So there are your warnings.  If you can deal with that; the rest of the game is Awesome.  I even love the music.  In Every game I play, the very first thing I do is Turn the Music Off... I really don't care for Music in General.  However... with this game you have a number of Radio Stations; I find 4 of them play music which I consider perfect (fitting) for this game; but what I truly enjoy are the Commercials; it makes the whole experience seem more realistic.  I usually change the station after 4 or 5 Gaming Sessions; allowing me to hear different music, different DJs, and different Sets of Commercials (it's not really different commercials, but in a different order).  I'm not sure how many hours of Radio they have per station; but it takes a few gaming sessions, before it feels redundant; but after going through my Fav 4, it all sounds new again when I start from the top.Oh... and another warning; setting up the Joystick/Throttle is a bit of a Nightmare; some of the items are not common names, so you have to figure out what controls what; but once completed... and getting use to the controls; it's very comfortable flying this ship, and making changes to anything/everything purely with the JoyStick.  Note: I have the X-52 JoyStick and Throttle, so I have lots of button choices to map; but again... once done; I can control everything without Keyboard or Mouse.So... all in all; I'd give this game 4 Stars out of 5... but a Strong 4... and a Must Have Game at Full Price!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Ooof..  This is a VERY qualified "thumbs up".  I'd give it a thumbs down but there's a lot of work gone into this game and it's not BAD, it's just.. meh.  Where to start?tl;dr :    This game had SO much potential.  A large sector of space, but 99% of it isn't used.  Trading that's rubbish and samey missions that lead to a disappointing ending.Story : Lacklustre.   Takes FOREVER to get somewhere... and just at the point where you've assembled your posse, you've got to the bit where you might unlock some actually GOOD ships, boom. Story over.Missions:  Every mission is the same; Go here, blow up those, go back.   *shrugs*  Trading:  Pointless after the early game.   Pirate hunting and mining eclipse the money per unit time you make from trading.   They needed to multiply the potential profit by, like, 5, and properly stock the space stations!Dogfighting:  Passable.   They've made the enemies bullet sponges with miniguns that can auto-track you.  To balance it they gave you a one-button "Point at enemy" console-ism.  So, the dogfighting turns into "hold both mouse buttons until bad guy goes boom, then press 'next-target'".  Music / audio:  Great, like Rebel Galaxy. But a choice of good music doesn't really rescue this game from being lacklustre.Voice Acting:  Pretty good, on the whole.  I liked the protagonist's voice.. Just the right level of sarcasm, weariness and hostility.  Everyone else was a little cartoony, but pretty good on the whole.Side Missions:  The sharky missions can get in the bin.  The other companion missions are fair, I guess.  The 8-ball is a nice distraction, but the Slots is pointless.  I had 3.5  mil in cash and left a macro mashing the 'spin' button and went for dinner. Came back an hour later with... *drumroll please*  3.5 mil.   Just pointless.  The poker dice was a fun little thing to tinker with.   Painting your ship was nice, with the stencil option and everything. I wish you could have had glowing paint though, opportunity missed there :)  Graphics:  The insides of the statations and the planet surfaces are really nicely rendered.  Whoever did those really earned their pay.   The ship designs are nicely clunky (feels like a cross between Privateer and Borderlands), but you can just get the Durston quite early on, and that does you as an iron ass for most of the game, and then you need to move into something nippier like the Coyote or the Dingo to finish things off.  The game feels like it was trying to be Privateer, but just about missed the target.  It also feels like they reached a halfway point in the story and ran out of cash/steam. All in all, I miss the capital ship combat of the first game. That was truly something different.   If the devs ever want to return to the franchise, they need to make a DLC for this that lets you move onto cap ships and start taking over the sector.   I think we're all weary of 'space fighter' combat now.  All in all, I give it a solid 'meh'.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this on sale for $4 USD and still felt I needed to return it for a refund.  I haven't seen anyone mention the flying and aiming mechanics.  I seem to be the only one lodging this complaint.  Aiming is incredibly counterintuitive and uncomfortable.  I've played the original Rebel Galaxy, No Man's Sky, Battlefront I & II, EVE Online, and an assortment of other games that directly or casually involve flying a craft and aiming its weapons at other craft in space.  All of them, including the limited 2-dimensional maneuvering of Rebel Galaxy,  outshine the flying and aiming mechanics in Rebel Galaxy Outlaw.  For the life of me, I couldn't get even remotely comfortable piloting and fighting in this game.  There are some really successful and intuitive formulas for flying and dogfighting in space in other games; I don't understand why the developers felt the need to abandon that tradition and invent a square wheel.I REALLY wanted to like this game, since I thought the premise sounded like a lot of fun.  No dice, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved the first Rebel Galaxy and I'm really enjoying this one so far. The way I play these games is rather grindy. I like to run missions back and forth between systems and just spend times cruising through space. In a lot of ways this game is more like a sim for me than an action combat game. I've seen it described as Elite Dangerous lite and I think I agree with that. Combat has changed drastically from the first Rebel Galaxy. It's no longer a 2D broadside based game. It's a fully realized 3D combat environment. I like it just fine, although frankly I think I enjoyed the big ship broadside combat aspect of the first game a bit more. _childDocuments_.review: The original Rebel Galaxy is one of my all-time favourite space games, and this is most definitely up there with it, this time replacing capital ships and naval-esque combat with dogfights in smaller ships.I wouldn't say it's a step back with this decision, as the original Rebel Galaxy definitely had its own good thing going, but more of a step sideways. The atmosphere, design and soundtrack are as brilliant as the first, and the Ship Painter is second-to-none, giving you the ability to properly make any ship your own.The only properly negative thing about RGO I feel was the Epic exclusivity, which totally killed the buzz in the lead up to the original release date, as well as having features disabled by the time it's hit Steam (like the ability to send your ship away to get 3D printed). I understand the Devs decision - it just sucked to see as a fan.Speaking of the Devs, they're absolutely top-tier. I noticed the Mattock was missing its Paint Mask in the files of the game and messaged them about it on the Double Damage Discord, and not only did they send it to me, they patched both it and some other missing ones into the game once I raised the issue. Absolutely nuts support there.

_childDocuments_.review: Came to this game after playing Rebel Galaxy on Epic Games. Was initially dissuaded from playing it by the negative reviews, and they do have a point. This is not Rebel Galaxy 2, but in many ways they improved upon the gameplay of their first game. I do have one very important piece of advice for anyone who picks this up: There is an unmapped command to "Dump power to shields." Map it. It will save you much, much grief. You are very, VERY squishy, and using this command will instantly recharge shields from your capacitor. This is naturally more useful if your weapons are less energy intensive(I personally favor the Gauss Guns/Auto Cannons as my combo).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one.  It's not that I'd not recommend it, I just cant honestly recommend it, it's 50/50, not a no, but not a yes.  The problem with the game, is it just feels like a bare-bones version of the game it should be.  There are mainly two varieties of ship, haulage, or fighter, so ultimately, there are 2 ships, the best freighter, and the best fighter, the few other ships are just filler.  The fighter cant carry much, and the freighter cant fight well, so you have to decide.  In the original game, items did not devalue, so you could try a ship, fly it for a bit, and swap it for another, at no financial loss, but in this game, you lose money if you buy a weapon, an upgrade, a ship, etc, so you cant really 'give it a try'. There are many improvements on the original Rebel Galaxy, but the downsides also detract from this game, it generally feels like a grind, rather than a pleasure.  I find I fly a few missions, then just lose the motivation to do more.As I said, it's not a bad game, I've got 17 hours out of it so far, and I'll probably get a few more, it's just, it could be a lot better.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it so far. I wish there were more equipment and utility components, or ship types. I wish the costs of each respective ship was further apart so you can't just go straight to a sandhawk, than to a coyote. The early game is very poorly paced. It feels like it's missing some bells and whistles that is much better handled in similar games like Elite Dangerous, or Everspace. I feel like naming most of the sectors after US states is kinda sus. And it doesn't pace it self well at any point in the game really. The first game felt like there was a lot more to it. It takes a lot longer to get up to the final ships. There is a wider variety of weapons equipment and utility components. I wasn't sure what to expect when I started this game. I was expecting an RG clone. It is in some respects, but being able to move in 3D and actually play a fighter I actually like that part. Even if the ship always feels paper thin, even if the late game doesn't make you feel completely invincible like it does in the first game. I like the wider variety of music that came with it, and I only really used the custom music path for the dock/in-station music. Stuff like Wild Side and some other goodies that break up the tracks that I keep running, which are usually from Grinder or Backbeat. I like seeing Juno's back story fleshed out. I like seeing the universe more fleshed. I like playing a character that actually has a visible audible personality and a considerable one at that. I like seeing what lead to the events of the first game. I like the Wing Commander nostalgia. I find the combat here more accessible than Elite Dangerous or Evocron Legacy. I got good with using the targeting ui to figure out what's attacking me. I make use of the intertia locking to autopilot away from enemies faster, take passing shots on cap ships and turret platforms, or turn faster before waiting for momentum to catch up. The auto-pursuit kinda makes things a lot easier than it should be imo, but the combat is still difficult to master. But careful targeting and quick dispatching of targets with efficient use of afterburner, secondary weapons, and the targeting ui makes some of the impossible fights actually winnable. I feel like the cap ships move way faster than they should, they always seem to be right behind me no matter where I move to, but I can deal with them easily with all the strike craft out of the way. And it doesn't feel like I'm playing a brain dead plug-in character like in the first game. Juno has personality and I like seeing her backstory actually fleshed out. It's just lacking content and could've been designed a bit better pacing wise. The first game does feel like a much longer game, with a lot more to actually do in it. The mining system though still terrible, was still better. Trade is still as much of a side thing as before. Getting constantly stopped by contraband scans is pretty annoying. It's missing some quality of life that even the first Everspace seems to do a bit better in terms of equipment management and the ui for viewing your equipment status. I noticed there's only two subsystem components also. I can think of a number of ideas for subsystems including combat specific ones that would've been nice to see. This game feels like it had a lot more planned for it but they had to cut it short. You can't trade with npc ships or anything. So that's my biggest gripe with it. It does feel more alive character wise than the first game though, and I appreciate that part. I appreciate the music. And while late game doesn't make you feel invincible, I actually don't mind that so much.

_childDocuments_.review: This game tried to bill itself as the new privateer. Which I think threw alot of people off. It has the same balance issues Privateer had. When people talk about old school in the worst way, its rarely because of UI, and more to do with design decisions. I played about 30 hours of this game back on Epic. The problem is that it bills itself as a open-ended combat thing, but the game actively punishes you for doing any sort of combat before you are in an end-game ship. It happily spawns 20-30 enemies on a 'patrol' and you find yourself facing swarm after swarm of missiles. You can use the newtonian physics, you can use the auto-follow, nothing matters when you have that much ordinace flying at your face.This is because you are meant to trade/mine and get out of that first crappy ship. The game doesn't tell you that leaving the first system is a death sentence. It doesn't tell you that your ship's WORTH dictates what your enemies are flying. It just throws you in the deep end. There is a reason we abandoned old school to the neckbeards. Mechanically this game is amazing, and alot of fun, you have such FEEDBACK for shooting things. The sad part is, that you will probably spend your first ten-fifteen hours doing cargo runs just to afford a ship that isn't crap. Its extremely frustrating, and proves why Freelancer was always the better game. Progression. Doing things that where actually enjoyable. Decent game for 5 on sale, but be prepared for alot of frustration and throwing things.Also the developers... no longer develop video games. Says alot really.

Plus it's got a great range of music to listen to as you do your thing.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played Privateer but I used to play Freelancer, and I've been looking for a game that felt the same (but looked better) ever since: an accessible, fun space trading/combat game, with cockpit view. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is all that and a bag of dry-aged YikYak. I didn't play the first Rebel Galaxy (no cockpit view) so I can only judge RGO on its own, so: I get to customize my ship, ignore the main story, pick up trade missions or do my own trading, mine asteroids, fight pirates, run from pirates, beg them for mercy or flip them off, build my own space station, make space buddies, all with a gamepad in hand, feet up, trucker hat on, and no need for a manual. Not only is this as fun as Freelancer, I put the subspace radio on Backbeat and it's better than the live-action Cowboy Bebop.

_childDocuments_.review: Feels a bit like Privateer/Freelancer. Although the previous Rebel Galaxy had capital ships and that was the reason I fell in love with that game. Worth a buy at the current price point ~A$25.I have a HOTAS for Elite Dangerous but i found the Mouse/Keyboard controls just fine for this game. Only needed to change a few keys.

_childDocuments_.review: In the same spirit of the old Privateer or Freelancer games this space adventure is tons of fun. _childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: I love the original Rebel Galaxy. This was a huge disappointment. Tremendously shallow in every aspect. Ship upgrades and components, factions, mission variety, and combat mechanics are all far inferior to its predecessor. Travel is joyless at best and just plain obnoxious at worst. You can either teleport straight to your destination instantly with a chance of being interrupted by random enemies or travel over the course of minutes via sublight, but only in a straight line from point A to point B, which is far worse because it often results in ramming an asteroid or something face-first en route. The broadside weapons from the first game are gone, which is an absolute shame because it's really the one thing that set the game apart mechanically from other space sims.

_childDocuments_.review: It is like if you turned the show "Firefly" into a video game, mixed in with a little cyberpunk and a little Battlestar Galactica.  Great solo play, with many different ways to make progress.  Don't like combat - no problem - you can play as a trader.  Don't like to play as a good guy?  You can play as a pirate, or as a law-abiding space farer, or any combination of the three.  The controls take a little getting used to, but the 'aim-assit' and different combinations of ship upgrades make this only an initial inconvenience.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: its really fun to just rock out to. TBH there is nowhere NEAR as much to do in this game as other EV/Freelancer clones. That Open-Source once comes to mind. As a result the difficulty curve is insanely high unless you are willing to do a crazy amount of grind. The voice acting and the music make it worth the buy though - for sure!
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: It offers a perfect mix of sci-fi western, an awesome soundtrack and the arcade action of games like freelancer but with a nice facelift, when it comes to action impact. The game also breathes the spirit of Freelancer, which is isn't all that good, when it comes to the mission design and the core gameplay that gets quite repetetive at some point. Anyway, its a nice blast from the past with some really unique ideas and when it comes to the pew pew part, it delivers a good feeling of impact like in the typical popcorn action movie. Its easily worth the price, and when in doubt, at least the sale price.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Played the first one and was excited to get into Outlaw. I'm quite satisfied and went 100% on the achievements. Definitely worth playing especially for fans of Privateer and Freelancer. Outlaw shifts back to dogfights compared  to Rebel Galaxy's capital ship approach. It can get rather difficult when the odds are stacked against you, but it's part  of the challenge to figure out how to come out on top.  I'm left wanting more, but unfortunately Double Damage is done with the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Anybody who likes space games should be able to appreciate this one.  Especially if they play for a while.   It has elements of  immersion that are good.  The missions are non linear and you can take new missions from all over the galaxies stations.  In bars and guilds there are harder missions.   Tons of dogfighting pirates and other enemies.    Plenty of action , and also scanning down targets sometimes you find secrets.You will die alot in random fights when you first start.  Actually throughout the game lolz   beware of distress signals, because they bring boons as often as they bring a trap.    It is really fun if you actually survive a trap and get to loot the enemy ships.It is its own game , and has some fun minigames inside of it. You can find most of them in bars. Different bars have different minigames to play that are actually whole games integrated.  I like how they did that.  I am not much of a gambler, but Pool and Blasteroids are fun.There is lots of content , and I can tell I am still just getting started.It is a space Roguelike with ship progression, and stories that take you on adventures.   I also have to say the soundtrack is really well made.  The station talk is hilarious if you listen to it sometimes.  The music is also really good.  This game is a hidden Gem.I was waiting for some other spacegames and was lucky to find Rebel Galaxy Outlaw.  I feel guilty buying it on sale.  I feel like it is worth much more than they ask.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: The presentation and gameplay are reminiscent of a mod rather than a fully released title. During combat the AI often flies into you. The audio balance is off, I experienced audio clipping with some explosions. They try to hide the low resolution textures with terrible gimmicky post-processing and the controls are horrible. Take away the nostalgia and there is no reason to play/buy this game when there are so many superior space games available on PC.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the most a game has ever disappointed me, though because it is particularly bad. It is a game that shows so much great potential, especially in its criminally underpopulated niche. Because of the immense scope necessitated by the immense setting, space sims are a very rare breed. Rebel Galaxy, its sequel, and older titles like Wing Commander Privateer and Freelancer are a sort of "light space sim" that have the scope in setting, but not the scope in gameplay, and looking at what "true space sims" have been able to accomplish when they have reached the theoretical limit of scope creep imaginable, these lighter variants may be our only chance at an actually stable and finished experience. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw, then, in theory, is the perfect harmony of all these ideas, building upon years of evolution to bring us the perfect compromise between scope and realistic expectations.Unfortunately, the core gameplay loop is nearly unplayable. I could put up with the limitations of ship and station variety, no planetary surfaces to explore, and the limited range of career paths. But even if you only focus on what is contained in within the vision of the developers, it can't even do that. The combat is so frustrating I can't even begin to describe it, though I believe it stems from the broken level scaling system. It comes as such a disappointment when the previous game did it nearly perfectly. I played this game for 27 hours but it felt like 100. I was ready to quit after 15 but kept pushing through because I could see the sheer potential.It would have helped if there was a half-decent story to keep me going, but again unlike its predecessor, it just wasn't clicking. No undercurrent of mild intrigue to serve as a simple hook, just a string of busywork.When I finished the last of the side missions, I remorsefully uninstalled the game with tears in my eyes. If in a bright future year we receive a true sequel to Rebel Galaxy that gets everything right and gives us the best of all worlds, a light space sim that humanity can forever hold up as an ambassador of its achievements, I will die a happy man. Until then, I wait for that day with infinite patience. As infinite as space itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Months ago, I was feeling nostalgic for Privateer and wanted to try it again. Unfortunately, I couldn't find where the disc, or my disc drive, went, so I didn't manage to get it going. Luckily, there's Rebel Galaxy Outlaw now, and from what I remember, this is almost the same thing (but with more saturated colors and sounds).So Privateer is one of the oldest jiminy cockthroat games, and not all of it holds up to scrutiny. Oddly enough, a development that I think would have been particularly useful here is the way modern cockthroats use multiple different currencies: since as an Outlaw I'm only trying to maximize Credits income, there's little incentive for me to branch out and try the other activities once I've committed to an approach that I'm pretty sure is effective.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: ok, right off the bat, just trying to do the flight training. WHAT DECADE WAS THIS DESIGNED??? Seriously. I've seen better keybind mapping in games from the late 1990's. The inability to use ctrl or shift key options is one of the worst possible decisions a game like this can make, and cuts my keybind options by a huge factor.  The graphics on the setup screen would seem to indicate that the designers last saw a game in the early 1990's, which kind of explains their decisions on the matter.Example. It's been "standard" for quite a while in many flight games that "roll" is mapped to Q and E. But since the developers gave Q and E *dual* purpose, I *CANNOT USE THESE*. As they also removed the ability use use Shift-Q or Shift-E, well, I'm less than pleased.  This is but one example of many of the issues I'm having mapping the bloody keyboard to suit my play style. Yes, I know they use "space" to modify the mouse movement to add roll, but this isn't the damn 1990's, game inputs adapt to users now, and have for years, not the other way around. Muscle memory is a wonderful thing, if they let me use it.*Freelancer* had a better control scheme! wow. Just... wow.So, just for making it damn-near impossible to map the keys to something that suits me, I have to say that this game already sucks farts from dead goats. Glad I got it for CDN$9.  Of course, I should have suspected something when it got that low so soon after release...Also, this is one of the least intuitive interfaces I've EVER come across, and I include games from the 1990's in that list. Sure, I can learn it. The issue is... do I want to? Time well tell. Enough for initial impressions. Side note: 8-ball minigame. I've seen better implementations of this in first bloody year bloody computer science classes by people who are only taking it as an elective! No ability to choose which ball, no ability to walk around and check angles, no retargeting, nothing. Just a guess and a golly and fsck you by Double Damage. I'm going to keep playing this game for a bit, because it's been a LONG time since I have come across a game this badly designed, this badly executed, and this badly put together. A very, very long time. I'm SO glad I didn't jump on the bandwagon and buy this game at launch!
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Average and simple gameplay, minor quirks, decent graphics, amazing sound & Music (and the music is there to be exported to YOUR music library!), and amazing ship editor.The gameplay is nothing spectacular.  You shoot, things blow up.  I found there were only a few ships that were endgame viable; meaning, there is a best in class ship and gun to use and little room for variation.The quirks are minor.  I encountered, I think, 2 crashes.  The Jumpgates are excessively loud but you can skip them.The graphics are nothing to write home about.  They're pretty, but Juno could stand to do a better job washing her cockpit windows.The music is amazing.  And, like the first game, the music files are unprotected in .ogg format. [Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/RebelGalaxyOutlaw/Music]  There are at least 300+ songs by my estimation that you get by purchasing this game.  The game is worth buying for the boost to your music library.The ship editor is an amazing feature of the game.  You can go from painting your whole ship black to creating a detailed police cruiser (like I did) with a little bit of research and YouTube instructional videos.Overall: Get the game and start sorting through the music for what you like.  The rest of the game is, unfortunately, forgettable, which is a shame; the developers clearly put love in making this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A good, but flawed, love letter to Wing Commander Privateer and Freelancer.Finished all of the main and side quests, and I had a blast with this game. I was a huge fan of Privateer when it came out, and it’s one of the few games I go back to for a replay every few years. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw follows in Privateer’s footsteps to a tee, sometimes to its own detriment.There is a grind to this game.  Just playing through the scripted quests won’t give you nearly enough money to upgrade your ship to where it needs to be.  You’ll have to rely on mining, commodity trading, or random combat missions to fill the gap, and it’s here the game falls short.Mining is by far the most time efficient way to earn money in this game compared to the random combat missions, which feels wrong. Combat missions, being a high risk choice, should in theory return the biggest gains, but it just isn’t the case. In the 20 minutes it takes you to fill your hold on a merchant vessel with ore, you could easily bag 20-80k. Compared to the 15-30k on average a combat mission awards for 20-40 minutes of work, and you’ll quickly find yourself reverting back to the low risk high gain miner’s life.As others have mentioned, you sometimes find yourself outgunned by 20+ ships which swarm you and take you out way too quickly. I’ve only experienced this on random side missions. None of the scripted missions had this issue. I only died once during the regular missions in a fully maxed out ship and that was because I was flying lazy.Some people have criticized the graphics, but I find them to be just fine considering this game was made by a 5 man studio. The cockpits of the ships definitely take up too much real estate and the text can be hard to read. Fortunately, this isn’t an issue in third person, but it kind of destroys the Privateer vibe.All in all, if you’re looking for a sandbox space sim, this game will scratch your itch.  It’s a good game that has an opportunity for greatness with a little more polish and maybe some DLC to add some more swag to spend your money on.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Want to spend all your time autopiloting between jumpgates and occasionally finding huge pirate fleets camping next to them, meaning you can't escape? Then this is the game for you!Want to get a crappy cargo ship, run hours of pointless cargo missions and then still not have enough money to win a single fight against anything larger than a fighter? This is your chance!Want to be wowed by beautiful vistas and then get slammed by three pirate capital ships? Your game is here!Boring, repetitive, many unwinnable states.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw
