_childDocuments_.review: Like other reviewers, I have mixed feelings about this game. Mainly because there really is some good gameplay here hidden under a flawed set of story missions in the early game. I'm leaving a positive review since I do think the game's current price ($30) does represent decent value given that the music alone would cost you that much. The value will only improve with a sale and if the developer is willing to make a few simple changes. Read on below if you want more details.The Good----------As a fan of the original Rebel Galaxy, I like that Outlaw adds to the world by filling out the backstories of the characters from the original game. The radio stations are a great addition with spoof commercials and great music too that also help to make this universe feel like a real place in a similar way as some of the Grand Theft Auto games. The switch from capital ships to fighters also gets you closer to some of the neat details on the ships (i.e. being able to see and targeting individual weapon mounts) and space stations (you can see individual window lights, docking ports, biomes with visible vegetation inside).The ship-to-ship combat is fun when you're facing off against similarly specced ships AND you've started to learn the ropes enough to deal with the garbage pile that is your first ship. My trick was to direct all power to the engines and use the option to temporarily boost shields if they got depleted. That gave me a fighting chance and got me through some great fights. Also, I do agree that auto-follow is essential to making pursuits enjoyable for myself. You may want to look elsewhere if you want more direct ship control. And make no mistake - this IS NOT the same 2D capital ship warfare you enjoyed in the first Rebel Galaxy game. It is a 3D fighter sim and feels notably harder than the old game.Pretty much all of the features that I enjoyed in the first game are back (a simple economy for trading, basic missions based around shipping cargo, pirating, or helping law enforcement, hidden treasures out in deep space) with some other neat additions like winning ship parts through games of 8-ball. Sure, there's nothing ground breaking to these activities and they can get repetitive but I mostly play this game to relax at the end of the day so that's fine for me. And I know the graphics aren't mind blowing (they're pretty much the same as the old Rebel Galaxy) but I do like the art style of the game and it has some really cool touches like the way the stars get brighter when you turn and the visible smudges when light hits the cockpit windows.The Bad---------I would say the biggest fault of this game is the fact that it sorta throws you into the deep end when you start the story missions. Yes, there is a minimal flight trainer outside of the story but that wasn't nearly enough to keep me from dying at nearly every encounter. It took me a while to figure out how to manage my engines and shields, and even then I would often find myself stuck in situations where I would get into trouble just by jumping into the wrong system with no way to outrun the higher class enemy ships pursuing me (what's the point of getting a jump drive if you can't go anywhere with it?!). A big part of the issue is there are so few story missions within the low-threat systems to show you how to use your ship and also to give you the cash to equip it properly before heading off to the higher threat places. The only way I could enjoy the game was by ignoring the story altogether in favor of side quests within the two low-threat systems (I think they're called Texas and Kansas). Those easy missions helped me learn how to handle my ship better and build up the cash to upgrade. I think the developer should consider making some of these easier missions part of the story in the beginning. Doing something like winning a 4000 credit ship part from a game of 8-ball is much more satisfying than dying 10 times as soon as you  arrive on the other side of a jump gate.The story cutscenes that have you talk to characters at space stations aren't really enjoyable with bland voice acting and animations that falls a bit into the uncanny valley. I just skip right through them and I remember that being true of the original Rebel Galaxy too. Oddly, I found the best voice acting came from the in-ship dialogs and radio commercials. I would have much preferred the story be told through quick, in-flight snippets rather than making me dock all the time.Minor gripe: every time I open the star system map, the cursor defaults to the central system rather than the one where I currently am. I felt like the old Rebel Galaxy had a much more intuitive map design, but maybe I'm mis-remembering. Though I do like the addition of a side bar with space stations and their economic data listed.Should You Buy?-----------------At the moment, it's hard for me to give an unequivocal yes since the early gameplay isn't good enough on its own to win you over if you're a doubter. The two reasons why I said yes were:#1 - I really enjoyed the original Rebel Galaxy and didn't mind that the gameplay of Rebel Galaxy Outlaw would be different (arcade-like 3D space fighter pilot instead of arcade-like 2D capital ships in space). The fact that I like the universe was enough to keep me on through the more challenging controls and the bad parts of the story mission structure.#2 - I like the developers because they're very passionate about building a cool space outlaw experience with some awesome tunes to match and they've definitely made a game that has $30 of value.That said, I can easily see a number of reasons why you might say no if you're either:#1 - Looking for a direct sequel with the same gameplay as the original Rebel Galaxy or#2 - You're a more hardcore space sim fan (I haven't tried the harder difficulties so I'll defer to some of the other reviewers who thought the controls weren't tight enough to work as a more hardcore sim)But I do think the developer could easily make this a better game to recommend by adding more early story content to help set players up for more success in the later missions. We'll see if that happens in the future. Final Dig at Epic-----------------Overall, I think it's a shame this game didn't go through something like Steam early access. I feel like a lot of the issues would have naturally been fixed before launch with feedback from the Steam community. Maybe Epic isn't setup to funnel that kind of user feedback to developers yet? I do favor their competition (lower prices for players and more money to devs is great) but they should offer the same tools if they want to compete. I couldn't even find user reviews on their site (though they do now have Open Critic scores aggregated from typical game review sites).

_childDocuments_.review: Came for the dogfight, stayed for the sountrack (and the dogfight).I gave it a second try and I´m liking it. I`m having trouble taking the leap forward in terms of ship, but I have already been able to upgrade some stuff on my initial vessel. The visuals are pleasant, the soundtrack, awesome. I tried to be a merchant this time, but I´m leaning towards being a mercenary - again. After mining a lot and making lots of cargo runs, I started to get better gear and better ships. Mining was what did the trick for me. Ignoring Iron (too cheap), and getting gold, obtanium, pure water, alien fossils... Of course, it´s grinding, but the soundtrack is so awesome that time passes in a pleasure manner.And you gotta understand the architecture of the game.Rebel Galaxy: Outlaw, more often than not you´ll find yourself outnumbered/outmatched, especially in the beginning. So you gotta run or try to talk your way out of the battle.Also, don´t go into the distress beacons in the beginning. Go straight to your objectives.When you have spare money, join one or both the Guilds (merchants and mercenaries). They will offer missions with better pay.In time, you start getting extra money from loot dropped by defeated ships, bounties (when you defeat a guy with a price on his head), rewards (when you save a convoy and they pay you in gratitude). Then you will start to get confident and explore more, upgrading your ship.There are few ships available (like ten or so), but that´s not bad. Same for weapons and components. The interesting thing is to find a ship that fits your play style. If you wanna be a space trucker, buy a Durston or Beluga, with heavy armor, turrets to protect you, lots of cargo space, but less maneuverability and speed. Or, if you want to be a star fighter, get a Blood Eagle or a Foxbat, more agile, with lots of teeth, but less cargo space, weaker hull, etc. There are even ships with more missile slots and others with more shooting slots. Every ship, even the better one in my opinion (Dingo), has some feature that another ship is better at it.As for the combat, you gotta get used to it. Maybe tweak a little with the key bindings. There´s an auto-aim feature that is awesome, specially if you play with keyboard/mouse (my case). And the game has three kinds of maps: Sector map, system map and surroundings map. In the surroundings map, the game pauses, so you can assess the situation, plan your next move, mark the target you want, etc. When I started using this map more, the battles became easier (the AI will shoot at you from all sides if you let them!).And the visuals are beautiful, bright, colorful... The explosions are spectacular, I don´t remember seeing better explosions than these lately.And there´s the soundtrack. It´s GTA-level. I will do what I can to rip several songs to a CD or mp3 before eventually uninstalling the game (I´ve finished the main campaign, but there is a lot of side quests to do).My only complain is that they make you travel through too many jumpgates in the end game. Each mission is six, seven jumps away from the previous one. It was unnecessary. Other than that, all good.And Juno Markev is a fox. Slender, smart, hot. I already miss her (no, she doesn´t die).

_childDocuments_.review: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is the sequel to Rebel Galaxy, an open world space trading and fighting game and spiritual ripoff of games like Elite and Privateer. There's problems, however.  The gameplay is a bit shallow and the UI and combat seem to be more than just spiritual copies of games from the 1990's, they also look and feel like them... but the industry has moved on.   That certainly pushes the game below the kind of standard I'd mark as recommendable.Speaking of moving on, here's where the review gets dark.  The developers have shown an abhorrent degree of amorality, greed, and sheer anticonsumer sentiment.  They advertised this game on Steam and used the Steam community to drum up support for the game, then immediately pulled the plug and accepted a large up front bribe from the largely Chinese/Tencent owned Epic Games to withhold the game from Steam.   This kind of anti-consumer, anti-gamer crap cannot, must not be tolerated.  I cannot in good conscience recommend a game from such highly unethical devs.   These guys make Russian asset flip scammers look like legitimate and kind businessmen. Game reviews are about games and not developers, yes.  But gamers must be advised of flaws in products before they buy them, and unethical developers like Double Damage Games put gamers at risk.  Their unethical behaviour in the past shows they have zero concern for the rights of gamers.  This means if you buy this, you could be shorted, dumped, or they might just pull the game right back off Steam again leaving you, the consumer, in a place of risk.   You should not expect any guarantee the game will be patched, maintained, or your key (and right to play the game) retained on Steam, should the developer choose to go back to EGS and screw everyone on Steam once more.  Keep your money safe, look into a better alternative game than this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This review doesn't downplay the game price of 3€. It sat still on my library for a year or so until i finished all my other games (never have i left a paid game unfinished), it took a while to get used to controls, by default it requires a gamepad but you can turn it off in options, that makes using a keyboard and mouse tolerable.For these of you who played the first rebel galaxy:-You will be disappointed with the new controls, no more 3rd person broadside fire, just a more normal space fighter simulator now.-Character animations and variety much improved, still not very good.-Maintains great tunes, now with more variety and styles.For everyone:-40 hours to complete with all side missions.-Good space sim that is rare these days.-Overall easy missions save for a few final ones.-Good story with leaps and twists yet with no replay value, linear development except for last mission. Save and reload to see all endings.-Music is great and full of different styles and choices.-A few too much fetch quests with encounters 7 or 8 lanes away that take too much travel for minor chores, you end up doing them just to finish side missions and story progress because money gets useless too early.-You can maximize your ship early in the game, and having full specs means money gets useless. Besides, you can almost finish the game with your starting ship if you are a good enough pilot.-Useless money means no more value in mining, random quests or trade.-Reminds my of tachyon the fringe or freelancer but really not as good.-Oh, you can ask the attacking pirates to "please do not attack me" and often they will comply.Conclusion: At this price the music alone makes it worth buying. Good old space simulation, not much of a choice nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I'm lukewarm on this one. Rebel Galaxy: Outlaw is a sequel that improves upon everything I loved about the original Rebel Galaxy, but unfortunately it doesn't fix any of its primary faults. If you want an open-ended space cowboy simulator, this is one a good one. However, while fun at first, it quickly devolves into a grind-fest with a very unpredictable difficulty curve. This is a tentative recommendation, but overall I think there is more positive than negative.Good:Music - This was a huge strength of the original and did a lot of heavy lifting for the tone of the game. The sequel turns it up to 11 in every way. There is so much more music on this game it's almost overwhelming. The non-diegetic music is very similar to the original, but much more varied and syncs better with the action. The radio stations are awesome with tons of music from different genres. It makes flying around so much more fun. Art Design - RG:O nails the space-cowboy feeling again. The ships and stations that looks like they were soldered together from spare parts. The cockpits are amazing mesh between 80's computers and science fiction, and they are all unique. Buying a new ship is fun just to see the new control panels and light up.Immersion - All of the above, plus the sound design and very open / freelancer feel of the game really helps you sink into the fantasy. This aspect is the biggest improvement over the original and I think the switch to first person contributed to that. Sometimes I forget it's not really an RPG until the main character talks.Speaking of the switch to first person...Mixed:Combat - The switch to a dog-fighting style from a broad-side capital ship style was a controversial one. Personally, I like both styles combat. I miss the broadside stuff from the first one, but this combat is still fun, just different. The devs even included some optional assists that solve some of the most frustrating aspects of dog-fighting games. Perhaps starting out in a fighter and working your way up to a capital ship would have been ideal, though obviously that's a huge scope increase.Attention to detail: This game goes way above and beyond in some weird places. 1) The bar games, especially the pool, are incredibly detailed for a space sim. Like we're talking Read Dead Redemption II you could forget about the main game kind of detailed. Seriously, this game is unexpectedly the best pool game I've ever played. 2) The ship customization. When outfitting your ship, if you select the customization option, it opens a full-blown professional-grade design tool. I think this might actually be the tool the devs used to make the ships for the game. So... why mixed, then? Well, because this game has some features that are amazingly detailed, but are so far away from the core of the gameplay, that I can't help but feel the dev time would have been better spent on fixing the game's pitfalls.Speaking of pitfalls...Bad:Balance - This was the original's biggest weakness, and unfortunately it's not better in the sequel. Once the novelty has worn off, the game gets really grindy really quickly where you have to play a lot of repetitive missions to earn enough money to upgrade your ship enough to progress the story. Luckily, the mission design is more varied than the first, and the good immersion makes it feel slightly less like a chore. Also, the estimated risk of a mission that is not a good indication of how difficult a mission will be. The difficulty is very unpredictable. Sometimes high risk missions will be a breeze. Sometimes low risk missions will kill you in mere seconds. It kinda kills the fun. Meta-game - Speaking of the grind, while upgrading your ship and getting stronger is fun, you hit a "level cap" or sorts when you buy the best ship and all the best equipment in the game. Unfortunately, there are still missions that will annihilate you even when fully maxed out. Also, when you die, it sends you back to the main menu instead of respawning, which is super jarring. It's almost like the game is showing you the door.Story - It's kinda boring tbh. Admittedly I never finished it because of the issues described above, but I barely remember any of it. I like the main character, but I found the rest forgettable. Luckily it's not the primary focus of the game.Character Models/Animation - While the space stuff looks good, the characters do not. The look of the people / aliens is slightly improved from the original, but it still leaves a lot to be desired. I know the studio doesn't have the budget for hyper-realism, but maybe a more cartoonish/stylized approach would have been better.

_childDocuments_.review: This is really a great "spiritual" successor to Privateer.  Immersive game play, great graphics, good story.  My only wish is that this concept is carried on into MMO and online play. I would give them ALL my money for a more "sandbox" like experience set in Rebel Galaxy Outlaw universe full of players.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: After playing a string of games that just don't work its good to play one that does.  Not falling through floors and seeing every NPC in a T pose is nice for a change.  Not a sim way more arcade style but love this title for what it is .. well worth the price just for the music and games in the bar alone.  Love the explosions as well !! If your looking for a space game that is just pure fun without brain and game breaking bugs .. this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: First, the good things: The music is great and fits the gameplay. The graphics and art style are actually fine for this kind of game and match my expectations. Furthermore, the game's complexity is just right with a lot of things to configure on your ship (including customizing the paint) and a lot of stuff to do. (There are some minigames, guilds, a big sector map and many sidemissions.) You could do so many different things... ... if the game just explained them to you. But it doesn't. When starting a new game you just get thrown into the world with all possibilities already unlocked and none explained. Sometimes one of the rare 2-sentence-explanations of some of the mechanics pops up, but that's about all you get. There is a separate flying tutorial but it doesn't explain a lot. Also, the menu navigation is terrible.However, I could deal with these smaller problems. The biggest issue I had was the core gameplay (flying and shooting). It is just not fun for me. I have never played this kind of game before and I find the controls to be really unintuitive. Also there seems to be no hit feedback but maybe it's just really subtle. That is why I found the fights to be really boring. But this is of course really subjective, so you should judge for yourself.I can imagine this game being actually pretty solid and fun if it was just a bit more polished.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line up front, if you loved Starlancer or Freelancer and have been searching for its spiritual successor, buy Rebel Galaxy Outlaw when you can get it on sale. If you haven't, Outlaw may not be for you.I completely concur with the comments about the clunky interface (I burned at least an hour getting the control where I wanted them on my HOTAS) and the grindiness between main story missions. But Outlaw is SO similar in play style to Freelancer except with live action dialog and better graphics I got my $6 worth on the first day of game play.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and entertaining game about shooting space ships listening to rock music. Gives Freelancer vibes. As fun as the first part of Rebel Galaxy - this time with a charismatic character, free 3D controls, neat controller support and mini games. Though it took me 16 hours to learn that you can actually switch radio from rock to other genres. =D
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of fun, satisfying gameplay loop that doesnt feel grindy, characters are kinda funny, radio chatter is comical. The game clearly doesnt take itself seriously and I love that. Radio music is really good also, bonus points for being able to play the radio while painting your ship. The ship painting editor is amazing too. Connect a drawing tablet with pressure sensitivity and literally draw artwork on the hull, I love it. I'm definitely going to put some time into that alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fun space shooter with a old school feel. Graphics and art are cool, and the music is great and fits the theme of the game perfectly. Combat can be tricky to get down at first but once you have it down its alright.  That being said, combat situations are unforgiving so doing a bit of trading and upgrading your ship is crucial before taking on any missions that require you to leave the starting area of the game, including the main story missions. I like the first person option and ability to fly fighters and trade ships. An update I'd like to see is more camera control options, like follow distance in 3rd person view, and ability to look around in 1st person view.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a freelancing space pilot trying to find her husband's killer. You can buy different ships and equip it with various pieces of equipment. You can fly slow and bulky trader ships or fast fighter crafts. You can take conrtacts or just fly through the galaxy and play procedural missions. It's a great sandbox spaceship themed arcade shooter and the music is A+. It's not perfect and could use more meat on its bones but it does a lot of things right and, in the end, I bought it and finished it twice.Gamepad required.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Firefly in space...overall the game is very enjoyable and a jolly world to spend over 20 hours in. Plenty to like:+tracking system makes it easier to follow enemy ships;+lots of controls but not too complicated, staying on the arcade side;+nice graphics: cockpits, stations and ships look good, particularly when destroyed of course :-); +good sense of humor in the game, you encounter hicks and religious fanatics in outer space, goofy aliens. A lot is inspired by present day southern USA and westerns, with a wink;+the 8 ball side game is actually superior to many other pools games!+you have a lot of choice in music and can even arrange your own soundtrack which was cool. Four things things I disliked:-investments you made can be wrecked in battle;-travelling costs a lot of time. I would like to jump between 2 very distant systems instead of having to make 5 jumps;-not enough black markets;-also the animated intro is inconsistent with the computery art style.Overall a mighty fine game and a worthy alternative for those like me who can't get Freelancer to work on their system. Check out Spacebourne too, a bit more serious but it also rocks. Galak-Z is also a blast.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the original RG, and always wanted to play in a fighter instead of a capital craft, then you'll enjoy Outlaw as well.If you didn't like the first one, I'd spend some more time on reviews before committing to a purchase. If you did like it, why not buy? It's a fun time killer and you get to look into Juno's past before the events of the first game.What you'll get here is a lot of the same from the original. For me, that was trading and mission running. I worked my way up to whatever had the largest hold size and just started banking missions one after another, occasionally taking a break for a story mission.The only serious upgrade I feel like this game has over the original is the inner-system jumping mechanic. If you've played the original, then to get to your destination you'd find yourself entering sub-light and waiting until you either got pulled out by other craft or objects, or arrived at your destination. In Outlaw, you can either preside over this process or skip over it entirely.Graphically, it's nothing impressive but it's also no slouch on my 5700xt.Eventually game-play can get monotonous but I do feel like the game largely accomplishes what it sets out to do. I jive well with the western feel and enjoy it's general atmosphere and the game soundtrack meshes well.I got it for $10 while it was on a sale and feel like I've gotten and will still get my moneys worth once I complete the main story.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Rebel Galaxy, you'll recognize the characters, sounds, and some of the controls.  I play this on my pc so gameplay is not as great as perhaps with a gamecontoller.  The story feels a bit like RG original so I'm good with that and overall, I will keep playing as RG orginal is one of my fav games and i want to keep Double Damage in business.  What I don't like is that there is no attempt to translate the controls for mouse & keyboard so it is wonky.  I watched the author do a run through on youtube and he pretty much said as much.  I'm also not a fan of the interior of the ship graphics...way too cartoony and no real help aside from the radar.  Switching to exterior control feels more like orig. RG but the controls aren't as smooth.  another disappointment is that I'm kind of lost when playing side missions.  Not alot of information on what you are doing or at least it is not very clear.  Also, the controls don't exactly translate.  I've picked up some illegal cargo and the designer said that you can eject selected cargo.  I can't find any keybinding for this so I've been losing my reputation with the local law enforcement.  Maybe I'm supposed to be an outlaw but I'd like to dump some of my cargo.  All that said, I like the game and will continue learning and playing.  Overall, not a satisfying compliment, at least so far, to the original RG.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: A highly underrated gem with stunning art direction, a very enjoyable core loop and solid combat that keeps you on your toes.One of the most beautiful looking games I've played in years, I can't praise it's stylised aesthetic enough, and I can understand that not everyone enjoys the risks the developers took with the custom UI for every ship, but I personally loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: 1st: some of the reviewing detractors obviously aren't paying attention.  For instance at least one complained there is no tutorial but "Training" (i.e. tutorial) is literally a title menu option. I read some other unfair complaints in the reviews.  To begin with, this game is worth WAY more than the price asked.  Not quite as in love with this game as with its predecessor, but it's definitely worth playing.  In fact I think it's pretty good.  Play the first one before you do though, that's the only way this prequel will be meaningful.  The fighter builds seem more limited than the large ships in the prior installment, but once you get the hang of the controls/interface it gets pretty fun dominating enemies with speed and freedom of movement.  Use your lock-on map.  A lot.  And use a controller; I can't imagine playing this on mouse & keyboard.  I'd say I got access to the best fighters around halfway to 2/3 through the playthrough, which made me a little sad, but also put me in a good position for completing missions and the main story.  There are lots of characters you can meet and work with, and the buddy system can be super useful.  The minigames are fun/clever but I really only put time into them as needed.  There are some meaningful choices that affect the story, which is cool.  The soundtracks (there are 7 radio stations!) are a pretty great feature too.  Got 2 or 3 crashes in 58 hrs, which isn't bad (although one was during the climactic battle so I was kinda mad to have to do it over again; but it IS a pretty good battle).  I was super addicted to Rebel Galaxy and have played through it 3 times, about 40 hrs per.  This game carries over many similarities, and while it loses some things I loved in the first, it adds more new stuff than it takes away old stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game for what it is, it has short comings but its still fun. I bought it on Steam and Switch because of how much i enjoyed it. 19 hours in on Steam and 45 Hours on switch. It shows its shortcomings if only because it aspires to be like elite dangerous. Except this game had a Dev team of 5 and a tight budget. So while i was unhappy that it was on epic for a year, (Time that was spent porting to Switch, Xbox and PS4 rather than fixing shortcomings) I can't blame them for taking the money from epic. An indie dev should not be burned at the stake of game reviews just because they took the guarantee of a profit. Just look at the jump in quality between their first game and this, i would bet their next game will be even better. I for one am now a HUGE fan of the devs and can't wait to see whats next. This coming from someone with 600 hours in Elite(and hoping for something similar) i was not disappointed.

_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Privateer, but I'm running into issues that I feel like if this is a mostly finished game, I shouldn't be running into these issues.  I really love how I can drop in my own music.  I've played a lot of Privateer and Privateer: Righteous Fire.  I was able to find the Privateer music and I dropped it all in.  But there's a few things missing as far as sounds go.  I wanted to change the jump point sound in this game to the sound from Privateer, but I can't find the .ogg file to change.  For me, just having the Privateer music and sounds makes it worthwhile to play.  Like literally the most easiest thing to make me perfectly content, music and sounds.  Can't be too hard I wouldn't think.So moving on to when I first started playing.  So, I could go from one station to the next in the Texas system, and there'd be no problem.  Then, out of the blue, when I went from Austin station to Lubbock, every time I go to Lubbock, it puts me smack dab in front and heading for a huge asteroid.  Then I have to turn so hard just to avoid it.  Well, now it's doing something new.I'm at Austin station in Texas and I left clicked on Equipment Bay.  After I clicked on Equipment Bay, there were no other options to click on.  When I clicked back it took me back to the main listing, but now it's like the game is locked up because pressing ESC does nothing, clicking on different menu items like Commodities, or Ship Dealer aren't doing anything either.  I have to force quit the game.What gives?  Is this game still early access or is it finished?  I'm really trying to figure out now, because I'm getting frustrated.  Do the devs still work on the game?  Is there this feeling of "well, ugh, I'm having a bad day and can't be bothered." going on?  If so, well then that's on you, shouldn't have made the game if you're not willing to put in the full commitment your players DESERVE from you.I get it, we all have bad days.  But if you're not even willing to listen and take action on something, then in my mind, you've given up.  If you have a plan, and life gets in the way of that plan, I can accept that.  But what I can't accept anymore, is this extreme positivity of "HEY Let's make a game!!" and then either abandon it completely, or just about ignore your CUSTOMERS, who PAID MONEY for YOUR product YOU created.Why do you think Notch, the guy who initially made Minecraft left?  Because, he couldn't handle all the nagging about adding this and this and that and this and that and this and that and this and that and so on.  I'd like to feel like I'm not nagging about anything.  Just be there for your customers when they present a problem, and do your best to be able to help them, because ignoring them just because you're having a bad day, can really put a lot of people off.It's a good game, just fix the minor bugs and please give more flexibility on music and sound changes.  I'm a simple man who just wants simple things.  I hope that's not too much to ask for.  I'll recommend it for now, and see where the direction of the game goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: A prequel to the 2015 "Rebel Galaxy", here you play that game's main character's aunt. As a result the game keeps the "Old West in Space" theme from the previous. However, where in the original game you flew 'battleship' sized ships, in this one you are back in standard space fighter sim 'fighter class' ships. Otherwise the gameplay loop is mostly the same only in better resolution and prettier graphics. The soundtrack has no right being as awesome as it is, which also continues the tradition from the original. However this time the company has made concessions to the streaming crowd and both includes as 'streamer friendly' toggle and a boilerplate letter you can send to your platform if you receive a DMCA claim while streaming in that mode.Altogether I'm loving the game so far and will enjoy seeing how the events of this game led up to the events of the previous.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Game is awesome. If you've played the legendary Freelancer, this game is its successor in spirit. Though story line and characters are little bland and earning cash can be a chore, soundtrack slaps, combat is satisfying and ship designs are beautiful however limited. Though I believe such things can be amended by mods.

Even if the mods work it's cancer. _childDocuments_.review: Its Privateer (the original) reborn. Same ships, same missions, same cargo, even with Mercenaries Guild, just update for 2021! I loved the original, and I love this game. If you were a fan of the Privateer/Wing Commander series, you'll love it. If you are after a great fun space sim, you'll love it. In short, you'll love it!
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: You should know upfront that this is NOT a sequel to Rebel Galaxy.   (That reasonable assumption might be the cause of many negative reviews for this title.)BE WARNED - This is a completely different game from Rebel Galaxy."Outlaw" is a homage. - no, wait, - it's a LOVE LETTER to a classic space game that I have adored for nearly 30 years - Chris Robert's "Wing Commander: Privateer" which was released waaaay back in 1993.If you loved Privateer, there's some very strong nostalgia value in this title.The dog-fighting is challenging but fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Great sound track!Gorgeous explosions! Seriously, I've never seen explosions rendered more beautifully than this game. The debris generation is spot on, and awesome. Something about blowing up pirate ships to tiny little pieces is quite satisfying. Lots of fun (but optional, not forced) mini games !Graphics are pretty good.Missions are your usual space sim bundle: protect a convoy, gather commodities, go here and kill this, investigate that, explore here, etc.There are also "random" events and encounters in the form of "distress calls" which you may choose to intercept or ignore. There is a basic (single) wingman system in place but nothing fancy. You can tell your buddy to either watch your back, break and attack, or attack your target, and form up. However, form up and watch my back are pretty much the same, as well as break and attack (default setting) and attack my target. You can not, for example, tell your buddy to defend a target or escort a certain ship.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game for the first time almost a year ago in the Epic Store version, but loved the game so much I had to get it again for Steam :)Rebel Galaxy Outlaw is a space dog-fighting simulator clearly inspired by the Wing Commander and Privateer series of old, but with a new coat of paint.If you enjoyed these old classics, you own it to yourself to try this game.Highly recommend playing with a Joystick or H.O.T.A.S. as it will greatly contribute to the immersion and avoid the auto-targeting system like the plague, as it really takes the fun away from the game. Learn how to pilot properly and play it without aids, you'll thank me later.Overall the game is great, but the story is really lacklustre and falls flat at the end, detracting from the game's other many positive points.Would love to see this universe expanded, the number of ships, guns and add-ons significantly increased and a story worthy of a space opera.Anyway, don't let the low points keep you away from this great game. If you like the genre, you'll love Rebel Galaxy Outlaw.

_childDocuments_.review: A prequel story to Rebel Galaxy, and while I miss the limited 2D plane and firing broadsides of cap ships of RG, this game still hits a lot of the good notes about the previous game. While there isn't a lot of depth (not a lot of different ships to choose from, not a lot of weapons to choose from, there are only basically move and/or find "item" missions where sometimes you have to blow it up), it is still fun to play. A solid 6.5-7/10 game to enjoy on a rainy weekend or long holiday weekend. Wait for a sale of $20 or so and you'll get your moneys worth.

_childDocuments_.review: Ship goes boom. thumb go up.Edit:After finishing the game there is sadly not much to do except making money, but as the ships and equipment also doesn't cost that much that is done quickly enough.There needs to be a bit of endgame content like randomized missions from your buddies, or building your own empire. Also the Story sadly was really short and the final missions were hasted by a lot.Still a really really great game and I really hope the developers will add some Updates or DLC later on that will fix the issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though it is arcady and sometimes generic on the missions/enemy front, I like the overall feel and atmosphere of the whole game. It's just fun to haul some cargo from one end of the sector to the other, while listening to a large selection of radio channels as well as nice background music both in space and on stations.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the game has some quirks, this is essentially Wing Commander Privateer for a new generation.  If you ever played and enjoyed that back in the day, recommend Rebel Galaxy Outlaw 100%.After beating the game, a few minor suggestions if you are about to start:- Do side missions, but don't ignore the main story too long.  The game is more fun if you don't max out your ship before leaving the first sector.- Use a gamepad.  I almost quit trying to use mouse and keyboard controls.  Gamepad made it 1000x better.  HOTAS would work too of course.
_childDocuments_.name: Rebel Galaxy Outlaw

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a bliss and a torture for fans of the old freelancer game and is nice for some arcady adventures in spaces in contrast to the epic scales of No Man's Sky, Elite-Dangerous or Star Citizen. It's clearly inspired by freelancer but differs in many aspects, which makes (me at least) long for the original.The artistic style is great, the colourfull space is a nice touch on the usual greyness of space games, the interior design and clothing style which is pretty much 20./21. century stuff with Jeans and Suits etc is also great (it's a little weird to imagine this as a future, but it's also kind of how fashion works...they just came back to that old fashion style). I think style is more important than graphics alone, graphics are just meh, but what to expect?The music is really awesome. The sound design is pretty heavy and has punch in the right moments.Gameplaywise:Controls are fine after some trainingMission design is pretty simplistic, but good enoughShip, weapon and equipment diversity is a little on the shallow side, I would have preferred more varietysome of the artistic choices with the colourful space compromise the visual clearness of combat situations

name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION
detailed_description: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION is an isometric adventure set in a distant future. Explore a post-apocalyptic landscape, solve puzzles , meet new friends and make powerful enemies, mediate conflicts, and fight for your life as you unravel the secrets of the world around you. Mark, a man out of time, searches for his lost brother Don in a far-flung futuristic era ruled by highly advanced technologies, which are both revered and reviled. Your surroundings hold echoes of a desolate past and glimpses of a dark future that has yet to be written by your actions. Be prepared to face many tough choices that will shape this land long after you complete your journey. The inhabitants of this world will help and hinder you as you make new discoveries and navigate the spectacular African-inspired landscape. Negotiate your passage with local leaders, healers, and warriors, or find yourself embroiled in a battle against nanite swarms, enormous scorpions, and rocket-equipped robots. From thriving villages to crumbling cities, petrified forests, and bone-dry ocean beds, this strange new world holds a multitude of terrains to uncover. BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION features music by MICK GORDON , known for his work on Wolfenstein®, DOOM®, Prey®, Killer Instinct® and Need for Speed®. A story-driven adventure set in a dystopian post-apocalyptic future. A unique aesthetic and 2D isometric rendered and painted environments. Simple Point & Click interaction with profound puzzles. Classic adventure gameplay. Bizarre creatures, animals, and vibrant characters await. Thousands of lines of dialogue with multiple conversation paths. Tomes of lore and a world, unlike anything you have seen. Over 40 Unique Characters to meet. 4k and Ultra wide native support. 90% PCGAMER 9.5/10 PCINDIEMRACE 9.5 /10 GAMEPLANET 4.5/5 PENNYWORTHREVIEWS 8/10 THEGAMESLASHERS - '...the world of beautiful desolation is like a binder overflowing with artistic creativity...' 10/10 SHOWGAMER 5/5 SAVINGCONTENT - 'Incredible' BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION is brought to you by THE BROTHERHOOD , the studio behind STASIS (Adventure game of the year 2015) and CAYNE .

_childDocuments_.review: The artwork is beautiful, the story interesting and well told, with a lot of local flavour thrown in to spice it up and make it very uniquely South African.The story pulls you in and you feel involved in everything that happens.This is a subtle point-and-click adventure with a lot of information, so pay attention! Everything is important. Don't expect this game to hold your hand.There is no quest log, though you do have a journal (called a codex) that all the important information is saved in — lots of clues and tips. A quest log would have been great just in case you forget something from one play session to the next and you need a nudge to pick up where you left off.I found that playing with good old pen and paper handy worked for me. It is a lot easier to write down clues than opening and closing the codex constantly. And you will need the codex.One other thing that bugged me is that there is still an element of pixel hunting to the game. While exploring an area you can run past something on the floor a few times before you see it. There are gold items that you can turn in for credits to buy items in the game and they are very well hidden.Overall, Beautiful Desolation is brilliant.The voice acting is great and characters are well developed. POOCH, one of your companions, just crawls into your heart. Combined with the music and visuals, the game's atmosphere is fantastic.As a local, there is something special about seeing our local slang, places like Brakpan,  words like shongolo and shebeen, and the TIK game immortalized in a game. It will be interesting to see how this nod to South African culture translates to players outside of the country

_childDocuments_.review: (BD) is a post-apocalyptic isometric adventure game with strong emphasis on player choice, puzzles and narration. Players impersonate Mark Leslie, an average South African man that like many others, gets involved in the world-changing appearance of the Penrose, an enormous floating construct of unknown origin. A series of events catapults Mark and Don in the far future, where they find themselves in a completely alien time, populated with unbelievable denizens, rife with devastation. Their only goal from that moment, is to get back home by any means necessary.🟩 🟥 Starting out with the (many) good points, one of the elements carrying BD to its Masterpiece status is, undoubtedly, the art direction and sheer quality of visuals, ranging from 3D models in dialogue boxes, to the extremely well made CGI cutscenes. Everything in this title is realized with painstaking attention to detail, from vegetation, buildings, quest items to characters and NPCs. Moreover, the setting created with such mastery is entirely unique, reminiscent of the Torment setting at times perhaps, just a little bit. A game title has rarely been more apt, as the world depicted here is beautiful and terrifyingly desolate at the same time. BD makes an excellent work in focusing on its strong points, delivering consistent character that act accordingly to their personalities or agendas, encompassed by solid writing and quality acting. Other than that, it also builds a deep, interesting lore to accompany each location and item found. The gameplay is largely typical of story-based point'n clicks, though it does diverge on many occasions, introducing even turn based combat and gambling in some parts. Player choices are ever meaningful, down to the very attitude used with your companions, that goes a long way. The only bad thing I could think of, is that certain puzzles or interactions to continue certain quests are a bit too obscure to decipher. This is an exception, not the rule. 🎮 Gameplay is divided into Exploration, Puzzles, Dialogues and Minigames. Is performed on foot while in one of the various locations, while the world is instead navigated using your trusty Buffalo, a salvaged military transport acquired very early on in the game. While traversing a place on foot, most interactions such as talking to an NPC will be visible at all times, while hidden items will have a minimum visibility radius to become detected. This makes thorough exploration of each environment almost mandatory, as many of such items are critical to progress. The sheer beauty of each location makes exploring them all the more pleasant.The open world map is divided into several fixed points of interest, each explorable on foot. To switch province you'll need to use the Wardens, huge portals providing near-instant transportation between them. Several areas however will need special authorizations, protection systems or specific items to be accessed, and be unavailable at first.Are a consistent part of the experience. The most common type are "fetch puzzles" where you need to collect and combine a series of items, along with talking to the right NPCs sometimes, in order to get a final product that will actually help you. This can be just a few phases sometimes, or become a much more convoluted affair where multiple NPCs and items are involved. Generally the game will give you hints in the form of dialogue information as to where to go next, and what to do. Consulting your dialogue recorder to review them can be very helpful. Other forms of puzzles include logic-based ones such as finding the correct sequence of symbols in a display, or programming a computer the right way by copying protocols. Are with either NPCs or your fellow companions. The former will often be available to talk with when you first encounter them, then stay inactive for one reason or another until the need for them arises again, or some time has passed in the story's timeline. Depending on how you approach an NPC and what choices you make, the story can take significantly different turns. Your companions will often voice their opinion about your possible choices, other than just stop by for chatting - again, the way you answer them and the choices you make will modify their attitude towards you, with lasting consequences. As this is not an RPG there is no such thing as "skill checks" or anything like that, just plain talking.Are apart from each other and consist in a gambling table with some creative twists, and an arena with turn-based combat, unlockable factions and character abilities - just like in a real RPG. Both are integral to the main quest though only one of them is mandatory. None. Good, resource consumption is within expected parameters.  The game runs without problems in 1440p, 85hz. Very few minor bugs noticed, otherwise good polish. None.Beautiful Desolation is a really unique, extremely well made isometric adventure that I can fully suggest to anyone that has a knack for exploration based sci-fi games. There isn't anything else like it around.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: The good:-- Visuals are great. Has a nostalgic 90's game vibe to it, with modern comforts and improvements.- Sci-fi world and lore is pretty interesting- The South African setting and history/culture added quite of lot of interesting aspects to the story and art style. The bad:-- Lists that it's an RPG, but it's not really an RPG - Has a lot of the worst aspects of point and click adventure games, with the added punishment of making you travel long distances, through many loading screens, to prolong the pain.- The main character and his voice acting didn't really seem that interesting. (The background story is interesting but sort of peters after that. Might be a bit subjective here.) - The game play is basically just all non-stop fetch quests it seems.  (It can be argued a lot of good games boil down to fetch quests I suppose, part of the art is making it enjoyable, or at least obfuscating it, in my opinion.)- There's a lot of non-intuitive elements to this game. Specifically for using items, triggering events, and some aspects of game play and/or UI.The neutral:-- The voice acting is good and bad depending on the character. Not really consistent quality overall, IMO.My experience of this game is that I was enjoying aspects of it to a point, a point where I got stuck and couldn't figure out quite what I needed to do. Got really bored flying around various maps and loading screens to try to trigger some random event or pick up some random item I'd overlooked. I logged off for the night and ended up playing another more enjoyable game. Coming back two weeks later to this game, I finally broke down and looked at the official walk-through. Once I figured out what I missed, I just felt I was done with this game at that point, though I tried to keep pushing through and continue on. Basically missed the femur item at a location I'd already searched, because it's not very visually obvious there's something there. I tried to get rolling with it again regardless, and started progressing the quest the item was needed to complete. Where I then got stuck up by a lot of non-intuitive UI, or gameplay I guess maybe. In regards to getting a certain NPC to go into a certain state. Basically there's a tablet you access in the game, and it's not quickly obvious what it is doing or that it's connected to the NPC when you click something on it. Only figured it out when I walked away from the monitor and saw the character had changed to the state needed to continue. (Trying to be very vague here not to ruin the story if people care, but just want to state this to show the problem in regards to it not being intuitive in a lot of aspects.) Then I continued on to a new location, where I found I needed a whole bunch of other items to further progress after talking to "the 5", and I just don't really care anymore. The visuals and world/lore is great, but the game play is really tedious and slows the story down so much, I'm just done with it personally. I'm fine with what I paid for it, while it was on deal, but probably would have preferred to not have bought and spent my time on it really.If you like old obtuse point and click adventure games, you might like this, otherwise best to pass on it. Additionally, there is mention of RPG elements to this game, but I believe that's really stretching the genre to cover this. There's a glut of good point and click adventure games on the market, so I feel it's fair to be a bit picky here. Like one that kept coming to mind which is similar but actually does have RPG elements, and an interesting main character, is Disco Elysium. There's many games of this type though to be clear, and why I'm leaning more towards not recommending it personally. If you really want to get, best to get it while it's on deal, and be aware of the return period.

_childDocuments_.review: **A DARK AND DELICIOUS APOCALYPTIC SCI-FI STORY GAME SET IN A UNIQUE SOUTH AFRICAN TECHNO-HORROR LANDSCAPE**My review is going to be a little more nuanced because, not only am I South African but I am also a historian specialising in South African military history during the Cold War - so for me, this game pushed all the right buttons and this review will reflect my take on things.But first and foremost let me just say this is a wonderful game and if you're looking for something with an engaging sci-fi story, intriguing (and almost horrifying) characters, and gorgeous isometric scenery - then this is for you. I also recommend this especially if you're NOT South African and are looking for a more exotic universe to sink your teeth into.This is also NOT an isometric RPG (though I really wish it was) even though it has a very strong Fallout feel. Rather, it is a point-and-click adventure/puzzle game.[PROS]-Great music and sfx-Great visual style and artwork-World feels alive and worth exploring-Characters are unique and interesting-Lore is an utterly fascinating blend of Lovecraft, Fallout, and Mad Max worlds with a thick coating of District 9 and Elysium science fiction-Detailed references to 70-80's era SA history, war, and politics and explores war veteran PTSD through heartfelt dialogue between the characters (for me as a historian who works with Border War veterans, this was especially interesting)-The MC reminds me of Thomas Jane from the 2003 Bronwen Hughes film "Stander"-Does a great job in making you care for some characters, even a troop transport AI!-A great mixing of African lore, language and culture with a post-apartheid sci-fi world[CONS]-Voice acting is not consistent. Some voices are amazing, whilst others are bland and emotionless (especially the MC and brother)-The lack of a Journal is a pain - the Codex  does not cut it and leaves a player with a disorganised mess which sometimes leads to lack of in-game progression.-At times, you will miss a prompt somewhere and will spend ages moving back and forth between places trying to find that one item or dialogue bubble you need to progress. A quest tracker or journal with notes and progress would have been helpful to prevent this.-The autosave feature is sometimes bugged and at one point I lost 3 hours of progress when my game crashed and it hadn't autosaved in that time. (I know, I should have been saving but this is still an issue.)-Non-English words should have translations available (maybe through a hover-over-text feature?)-Would prefer more inter-companion dialogue or banter as we walked through the world to foster more of a team experience.-Though the MC and his group are interesting, I feel the game missed out on having a black South African on board to explore the world from a different perspective - especially considering the heavy African cultural themes.-I feel the story makes Africans feel a little too exotic and alien in their own country. Though it is a sci-fi, post-apocalyptic story set in the future, and it does have some fantastic African influences, I think it fails to make any "normal" African characters and factions for the player to interact with, and rather makes them mostly techno-tribal barbarians who seemingly aren't capable of Western-style "civilisation" like many of the other factions.[CONCLUSION]A fantastic game that I am obsessed with. I would LOVE for this world to eventually make it into an isometric RPG-style of game one day, but for now I am happy with the story and lore this game allows me to explore. Beautifully dark, South African game with scope for many a science-fiction/horror fan to enjoy.VERDICT: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is quite an odd game in a sense. It has so much going for it and yet it makes some really poor decisions and has some key weaknesses that stop it from becoming a classic. Such a shame. Here's an overview:THE GOOD- it has gorgeously designed locations with ridiculous amounts of detail- the story is very original and well thought out- the interface is clean and works well- it's very polished and feels very solid- the voice acting is pretty great with South African accents all overTHE BAD- there's a lot of walking - a LOT of walking- the puzzles are all simplistic - this is less a puzzle game and more a "find all objects" game.THE UGLY- the biggest flaw of the game, is how you can only spot items when they're up close. This is NOT a classic adventure game where your character is quite big and everything is within arms reach. You're tiny on the screen and you walk around huge difficult-to-navigate overgrown wastelands with items that are only visible within maybe two meters distance from you in areas spanning hundreds of meters ...This problem is compounded by there not being any real direction to the game with you only being given basic tips. This is not unusual but the problem is that you basically have to crawl through large maps, walking over every inch to make sure you catch every clue or object. It's very easy to become stuck because you didn't find a clue or object this way ... meaning you'll have to go through every area you can visit and do it all over again.They could have made the game a hell of a lot more fun if they had added more hints as to where certain items or hints could be found. The maps are difficult to navigate as-is but when you're going over them to find an item you may have missed ... well let's say you'll quickly turn to a walk-through guide because this is anything but fun.Other than this, it's an incredibly beautiful game so if you're willing to cheat from time to time, you can enjoy a beautiful game.

_childDocuments_.review: Well first of all, please note this game is not an RPG, some people say it should be obvious from the store description, but the game has some combat in a form of a mini-game late into the story (like 6+ hours in), so you can see why it can be a little confusing if you saw those. Besides, the game looks like a modern version of Fallout, and after playing the combat mini-game I wish it had more of that. Honestly, I would just compare this game to Cayne which is a free game by the same developer, the same format, just on a bigger scale. So as with any traditional point&click adventure, the focus is on the story, puzzles and choices (just with an isometric view). About 1 hour into the game you will realize the game has a limited open-world design, you have a little map with a few points of interest, but you will unlock more locations as you keep solving quests.I completed the game around 15 hours with no hints, a lot of it was backtracking due to confusing puzzles. It has some replay value, you can choose a side between different factions 3 times during one run. I am not exactly sure about the dialogue choices, based on what I saw I think the game has some form of karma system. There are many things that I like, mainly the visuals and certain characters. The beautiful locations of this game should not be underplayed, it is ****** gorgeous, the environments are very creative and have an insane amount of detail. There are a ton of animated character faces with unique personalities, and in general, the game just has a really good art direction.The UI in the game still needs some work, there are some missing hotkeys and it could use some questline updates instead of just reading old dialogue. So why negative review? There are a lot of issues but I can put them into two categories, the 'convoluted puzzle progression' and 'voice acting consistency'. Now you might be saying - "Beetle the voice acting in this game is great wtf are you talking about". The voice acting starts decently enough but it gradually declines to a point where it killed my immersion. I will say that the main characters did a decent job for the most part (the brothers). However, some of the side characters are hard to tolerate, borderline comical voice acting that does not fit the characters or the universe, you feel like someone is just casually talking into a mic. The actual writing in the game has some issues as well, for some reason you always have a choice of in-universe dialogue and '♥♥♥ OFF' - I am not offended by the cursing in the game, it just feels out of character with polarizing responses. Ultimately the puzzles are what killed this experience for me. Now, this is the game where you have to look for hints in a dialogue, which in itself is not a problem, but even when I managed to follow the hints, sometimes the game was not behaving as it should. I was doing a quest with 2 skeletons which for some reason stopped abruptly in the middle and randomly resumed 30 minutes later after I gave up. It often feels like you get new quest lines in random places with no obvious triggers, essentially forcing you to check every location just in case. You have the option to read the previous dialogue in case you miss the hint, but I think the game needs a summary of current objectives so you not looking for key-words through an ocean of old conversations. + best looking P&C game I ever played, gorgeous locations and animation+ many unique characters with creative personalities+ it has some interesting story choices and mini-games+ replay value is okey, 2 runs will cover most of the content+ achievements  - please add shortcuts to dialogue logs and radio, I was using those menus a lot.  - sometimes the quest items and interactive areas are hard to pick from the background. On some occasions you need the item to interact with something you thought was a background. I just realized something, I played the whole game with a robotic dog scanner, would have been kinda cool if she would run up to things if you idled in the area. Oh crap thank you robot scanner for noticing this stupid item that pulsates small waves that bland into the background.  - they killed immersion of the game for me. It sounds like a dude trying to talk like a robot, it's hilarious, I wanted to take this universe seriously to some extent. The quality of voice acting goes from 1 to 10 every 5 minutes, what happened? - it can be difficult to know if you are still doing a certain mission or if there are new events. Maybe you could have a summary of the current objectives. Perhaps if old characters have something to say they could have a sign over the icons in logs, "as in they contacted you on the radio". Honestly I would just put something over the map saying- "hey, you did not finish exploring this location stupid"To me, this game constantly feels like looking for a needle in a haystack. There are some great moments but they are spread too far apart to have an enjoyable experience. It's not just about good looks, I want that voice acting to be consistent, I want to take this universe seriously, but I can't because you were trolling with some of those side characters and it killed the atmosphere. At the very least, the objectives should be a bit more transparent. It could be a decent game, but I think the devs took more than they could handle, hence you have all these consistency issues with quests progression, voice acting, and UI.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Desolation is an isometric point&click adventure with a fascinating story, great world-building, mediocre puzzles, and a lot of aimless running around.You play as a journalist in an alternate world where, in 1976, a strange object appeared in the sky and changed human civilization. During an attempt to investigate this object, you, your brother, and an intelligent robotic dog get flung into the far future, where the object still exists, but humanity has been reduced to small pockets in a barren wasteland. Your small group explores this land, trying to find a way back into your own time.The setting is amazingly well designed, with about a dozen very different cultures, not all of which are human. While most of them play on various sci-fi tropes that fans of the genre will have seen before, the sheer diversity creates a setting that still feels refreshingly original. Unfortunately the presentation always remains a bit superficial (usually there are only 2-4 interactable characters per faction, and the conversations focus on the one or two quests that they have for you), but the ways how the factions interact, and how your decisions determine their future, nevertheless gives the impression of a complex, intricate design. Exploring this world piqued this old gamer's curiosity to a degree that few games do (Planescape: Torment and Star Control II come to mind, though they are both very different games).The story starts a bit confusing, with two time jumps and very different settings before you finally arrive in the world that the game actually takes place in. Once you're there, you conveniently meet a character who immediately tells you how you can get back home, and which three items you need to repair the respective machine. The rest of the game revolves around getting these items - they are usually important for the civilization that holds them, so you have to complete a major feat before they are willing to let them go. In many cases, you have to take a side in a conflict between 2-4 factions, and whole civilizations will rise (or get destroyed) in the process. There are many alternate paths through the game, and your decisions are rarely just "good" or "evil" - all factions have understandable motivations, and all of them do things that can be seen as atrocious. I appreciate this "shades of grey" approach a lot, since it makes a story much more believable and meaningful for me. But be aware that you'll rarely feel like a shining hero, there's always some darkness involved.While there is some linearity to the exploration (you have to complete quests in one given area to unlock others), you are otherwise mostly free to choose which tasks to pursue and when. Unfortunately the game is really bad at keeping track of the various quests that you'll be taking on. You do not even have a quest list. Instead, there's an auto-updating "ToDo"-list that's not only incomplete (lots of tasks simple don't appear there), it also just lists singular tasks with no context whatsoever. So you'll often see a task like "find item x", but you won't get a reminder of what you need that item for or which quest line it is relevant for. This is really bad for a game with so many contingencies. If you don't want to juggle with lots of information in your head all the time, or if you don't have the time to play without longer breaks, then I suggest taking notes. You _can_ blunder through without understanding the context, but then you're arguably skipping over the best things it has to offer.Gameplay consists mostly of three elements: conversations, puzzle-solving, and exploration. The conversations are well-written, but the dialog choices are a bit bland. Very often they are just three different ways (friendly, rude, neutral) of saying the same thing, and while your tone does affect some things in the game, many conversations will lead to the same result regardless of your choices, and some of the will feel a bit forced. But apart from that, the dialog felt believable and I enjoyed it.The puzzle design, which was already problematic in the developers' previous title (Stasis), is unfortunately even worse in this one. Usually you just need to find an item (which may just lie around somewhere on a wide-open map), and apply it at the location of the "puzzle". Sometimes you need a code (numerical or in symbols) to unlock something, and in one case there was a small logic puzzle. Generally, the puzzle design is fairly primitive, but this makes them also pretty easy, so they don't distract from the story.Exploration is engaging at first, since the maps are varied and often have large features that are interesting to look at. However, you'll also walk circles across each map to find items, which are only shown when you're close to them. So the game will waste a _lot_ of your time while you're walking across every area, looking for potentially important items to pop up. You'll also often just move around aimlessly since the game does not give you directions, lacks proper quest tracking, and it's often unclear where or how a quest will continue. The game tries to "ping" areas for you that you should visit, but that does not work reliably - sometimes there wasn't anything to do in an area that got pinged, and sometimes a quest progressed in an area that didn't get pinged. So I ended up regularly trawling through all locations just in case I missed something, which cost a lot of time that I would have preferred to spend actually _interacting_ with something rather than just bumbling around.A fourth gameplay aspect are two turn-based tactical minigames that you can play. One is a simple 1v1 fight with dice rolling, and one is a fairly involved 3v3 fight in which you build your team from various available units, which all have different values for hit chance, damage, armor, and health. Which units you can choose from, depends on the choices that you're making throughout the game, which is a neat idea. I like turn-based tactical gameplay, but the combat mechanics in this minigame were too simple to really make it enjoyable. There's no way to move, no stances like "defend" or "overwatch", no status effects, no synergies between units - you just take turns attacking each other until one squad is dead. It's not a _bad_ minigame, but it definitely dragged on for longer than I enjoyed it, especially since each attack involves a slow, unskippable animation, and every fight requires a repetitive, click-intensive "unit selection" phase. Thankfully it's optional - there are other ways to get the reward that it provides.Graphics in this game are hand-drawn, varied, and often well-done, but also often look a bit blurry, as if the source image was drawn in a relatively low resolution. They also don't use shadows very well, which sometimes makes it difficult to understand the layout of the map and the "depth" of various sections at a glance. The pathing across a map (which sections are traversable and which are obstacles) is also often unclear, which creates some annoyances due to the size of the maps and the slow running speed of the character. Movement animations look a little dated (the torso remains unnaturally stiff during running), face animations during dialog seem hand-drawn with very few frames and no visible lips, but neither is really a problem. The music is very well done, it is very subdued and contributes to the atmosphere without ever pushing into the foreground.... and here the dreaded character limit for reviews strikes again. ;) If you're interested in the rest of the review (with information about voice acting, usability features (including accessibility and UI), and the final verdict, please continue here:  . Sorry for the inconvenience.

_childDocuments_.review: So first things, this game is beautiful, stable has a nice interface and intriguing story.The problem is the puzzle/progression design is kind of broken. The company that made this game is a veteran developer and this isn't their first title but it's nearly unplayable without a walkthrough.Sometimes, progression requires talking to a character, leaving the area, and speaking with the same character again. WHY?There is a starting quest where a maiden tells you she will plant a flower only if you find her sisters. You don't have to find her sisters - give her the seeds, leave the map, come back and she gives you a free flower. You only find the sisters much later in the game.There is also the bass reactor - a puzzle where you need to stabilize a reactor by copying data from one terminal to another - the problem is, the way the copying is done makes no logical sense. _childDocuments_.review: 6/10 Decent.The dev team (Brotherhood) are very talented at two things; Writing superb storylines and creating atmospheric designs that tie into world building and characterisation.Beautiful Desolation is a decent game, the concept of a 1980's alien object appearing and catapulting your character into a dystopian future where man and machine merge in various awful ways, is quite interesting. The dialogue and characters are top notch, really showcasing the body/mind-horror on display.And then we have the environments themselves; again, superbly drawn, well designed, a marriage made in heaven for an adventure game basically.So, what let's it down?Two things; Firstly, UI design is quite poor. I always felt like I was battling the navigation of the game - it was slow to response, and the cursor constantly gave the wrong impression that I couldn't move to areas that I could move to. It was finicky to click on items/dialogue boxes, which made things labourious.Secondly, the game takes a semi-open world design, you have various areas you can travel to via aircraft, and each area has several points of interest to visit. The problem with opening up the game like this, is you cut through the tightness of the narrative, thereby diluting one of the key strengths of the Dev team (IMO). The back and forth of hunting down items and things to progress the story, just results in a tired game that wastes too much time and it slows the story elements down to a crawl.What essentially happened for me when playing this was; I started, was totally immersed and engrossed, started getting bored and then by the end was totally uninterested *and* disappointed with the ending. It just didn't seize the momentum from that initial opening of awe and newness, it just steadily declined until the damp end left me feeling rather let-down.That's my personal view. If you're a dedicated Adventure game fan and you don't mind semi-open world set ups, this is easily going to be one of the best in genre to recommend, but if like me, you want a stronger narrative design and less faffing about, then this is difficult to recommend, and I say that with some disappointment anyway, because as I mentioned, the devs are very talented and have put out some superb games so far, but this one, ultimately, misses the mark for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, but it has a good dystopian sci-fi story and I love that.Explore a post-apocalyptic, dark future of our Earth in this isometric point’n’click adventure.The brothers Mark and Don (and a stupid robodog), voiced with an accurate South Africa accent, are thrown from the 80s far into the future. Our civilization doesn't exist anymore, so they are trying to get back to the 80s. To be able to travel through time, they have to traverse across a marvelous landscape full of remnants of our civilization and inhabited by bizarre creatures, engage in conversation with them, and solve some puzzles. They need to upgrade a transport ship and find one required part after the other. A free prequel chapter called Cayne is available on Steam. Beautiful Desolation obviously uses an enhanced engine, but I wonder if I am the only one annoyed by the mouse cursor that always covers part of the hotspot description when I click on one. Hasn't anyone told the devs this? Click on a hotspot, move your cursor somewhere else to be able to read the description. Yea.One of the better p'n'c adventure games I’ve played this year.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though I backed this and paid full nickel, I was lucky enough to crack the nod and get early access for pre-release testing. Where to start, well, the game is stunning. The game is a visual feast depicting a post-apocalyptic Southern Africa dripping with atmosphere and steeped in a unique and often bizarre mythos. The game teleports you to a world like none other, a used and alien future that nature is slowly clawing back from the hands that misused it. Truly, the title captures this perfectly.Adding to this is an amazing soundtrack that's both haunting and exotic. Mick Gordon really knows what he is doing! And the Voice Acting is fantastic. Get ready to fall in love with P00CH.  But all of this is window dressing for a compelling and heartfelt story revolving around two brothers; one looking for answers and the other, forgiveness. Rounded out by an unlikely companion seeking a place of belonging and purpose. All the while, our heroes meet characters ranging from funny and peculiar to the outright sinister and macabre.There is however a caveat to all this. The game is somewhat old-school providing little in the way of hand-holding. Don’t expect to be told what to do. Decisions matter but they are yours to figure out. You’ll need to look for the solutions to the next rung of the story's ladder. Likewise, not everything is revealed in single exposition dumps. Pay attention and you will slowly start to piece together a bigger picture that carry’s a twist that’ll snap your back.
