_childDocuments_.review: I won't do a proper review since I have not finished the game and I don't think I will. Why? Let me be fair here, I love classic point and click games, I always look for them and I always support indie devs who start their careers making them.Beautiful Desolation is without a doubt a work of art. The dude or people that worked for this game and Stasis have a huge talent in art design, but that is it. I have 7 hours and I'm probably half-way in but I absolutely cannot push through this boring gameplay. It is not made with love, I can tell you that. The difference between visuals and gameplay is day and night. Point and click adventure games, the classic ones, most of the good ones, have great pacing, they know how to take your time and use it wisely. You don't just click stuff and that is it. No, the items you find, the items you combine, they all make sense in the backgrounds and in the world, and while most of these games can have some ridiculous combinations, they are still more engaging than Beautiful Desolation.Holy s&8t is the gameplay tedious. Every item you find or at least 90% of them are just placed with no care whatsoever in the huge empty maps of the game. You have to aimlessly move all around to find that small dig spot and pick it up. Whats worse the whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gameplay is a fetch quest. Every single thing you do is pick a hidden item and deliver it and you do that back and forth nonstop. No, I'm sorry, but no. BROTHERHOOD I love your incredible artstyle and hiring Mick Gordon to do the soundtrack was a genius move since the soundtrack is ace but the gameplay ruined EVERYTHING for me. For those who have more lenience towards this type of gameplay the story is unique to say the least, not something you'll love, but it is something you do not see very often and you might enjoy this but I could not. _childDocuments_.review: What a waste of beautiful art, sound, and characters. Too bad the sum of the parts doesn't make for a fun GAME. Beautiful Desolation had me hooked in for the first five hours, until I finally broke down and had to consult a guide for a hint. After that, the story was basically ruined for me, and it made apparent how player unfriendly this game really is. I've never had to do this much backtracking in a game before. You literally have to fly to one part of a universe, talk with someone, fly to another universe, exchange one or two lines of dialogue, then go back to where you were originally to get the next clue or item to further the story. The journal is practically useless. It'll give you vague hint topics, but can barely point you in the direction of where you should go. Things that would have  made this game a home run would be: 1. A fast travel system, and 2: a system to keep track of NPC locations once you've met them. There are a LOT of locations and characters in this game, and they are so unique that there's no context in remembering where they are. So you could be flying from space to space, walking through several screens, just to be in the completely wrong place. You then have to call your ship, fly to some other destination, rinse, repeat, until you finally hit the right spot. As I've mentioned in other reviews, having my time wasted is the biggest negative for me when playing any game. The developers were SO CLOSE to making one of the best point and click adventures of all time here. It really is a beautiful world, I enjoyed the dry humor, the unique and interesting characters, and the main quest. I've also played Stasis, another game from The Brotherhood, and it didn't do much for me either...but based on the good parts here I will certainly check out their other titles. I think they just need to refine the gameplay aspects to make the games not waste your time so much, and they could certainly produce an all-time classic. Unfortunately, Beautiful Desolation is not that game.

_childDocuments_.review: A rather mixed bag here.Pros:- pretty cool setting.- faction conflicts are interesting and require you to make some morally grey choices (though, in hindsight, one is generally the most sensible).- companions have good voice acting and interesting conversations.- maps and artwork are generally very good.- main menu looks great and unique.- cutscenes look pretty good.Cons:- some of the voice acting is very obviously autogenerated and sounds horrible.- the plot is very confusing to follow, with a time jump very early on in the story leading you to a completely different setting. In a quite stunning coincidence, when you start playing after the time jump, you are right next to an NPC who tells you what happened and exactly what you need to get home. How convenient! Then, when you eventually finish the game, further developments occur that add to the confusion even further and clarify absolutely nothing. As a result, it can feel like quite a disappointing ending.- questlines are quite challenging to follow. Turning quest markers on helps here, but without it would be quite a challenge. Sometimes where you need to go or what to do next is not at all obvious, and the in-game quest log is less than helpful.- the game is mostly one large fetch quest, from the very first NPC I mentioned above. This is made worse by the fact movement on the map is quite slow, and you may have to run back and forth on maps several times. I recommend a speedhack while travelling to cut down on the tedium.- items you may need are lying on the maps in random locations, and are only revealed when you are very close to them. I suppose this could be a way to get you to explore the maps in detail, but it feels cheap.- the arena minigame sucks. It's slow, clunky to control, has little strategy, and repetitive.- worst of all, as if the game didn't respect your time enough with all the fetch quests back and forth, you need to complete the game 4 or 5 times to unlock all the endings and achievements. No thanks.In summary, if you like old-school point and clicks, you might like this, but it's quite slow and obtuse with its plot. If you can't put up with that, and I got pretty sick of it towards the end, then skip.

_childDocuments_.review: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION desolation is a point and click adventure set in futuristic post apocalyptic South African Landscape. the gameplay loop is mainly talking to people, solving item based inventory puzzles and exploring the wastelands with your brother and cute robot dog companion. What stand out about BD is its lovingly crafted world, beautifully rendered in isometric perspective and every maps. literally every single map contains familiar, yet otherworldly vistas that makes you wonder. tribal huts protected with energy force field, settlements guarded by cyborgs, massive scars on the land reshaped by technology and weaponries beyond imagination, carcasses of massive mysterious creatures or dead machineries of war. the world are absolutely filled with sceneries that would blow your mind. the depth of the world don't end there. as you explore the world futher, its characters and cultures slowly become clear to you. you slowly piece the history and people of this world, and finally you are able to shape and decide their fates in your journey. this massive world is separated into several "worlds" that represent different regions of the wasteland. you navigate the overworld map with your trusty airship, similar to the map in Fallout 1/2. in each overworld, there are locations, whether it is ruins of past civilization, wilderness, or settlement. you "land" on these places and you travel the locations on foot just like game's source inspiration.Desolation is a game about exploration. the story isn't presented to you linearly. in most of the cases there are multiple ways to solve the puzzles, and tied to your decisions, whether in dialogue or action can shape your character's personality, their fate and everyone around you. the game dialogue is done trough a "talking head" window where the portrait of the characters are rendered quite in detail, and you have multiple responses to choose. there is no looking back. the dialogue never really repeat, so whether you choose to antagonize someone and be a jerk, or be kind and friendly you can never take it back. you will make friends, enemies, and you will eventually make a choice. the dialogue are also wonderfully voiced. whether you're talking to a robot, a mind controlling parasite or just a regular person. each of the characters background and personality are delivered wonderfully by the talented voice actors also the wonderful sound effect done. the Bzz in robotic sound, their gears whirring can be heard trough their voices and so are all the other characters. one part of the dialogue that is a bit jarring is the talking head itself. the character models are well crafted. they all look so diverse and detailed but it is more of a "wagging" head instead of a a talking head. when speaking there are simply like 2 different frames synced with the syllable so some of the characters looks like they have a little seizures. it would be great if each characters have several poses instead of just 1 and the wagging animation. considering the game's budget though, it is still fantastic. i can't stress enough how surprisingly good the voice acting are and every dialogue is voiced.the music is great, techno-ambient with some touch of tribal sound composed by one and only Mick Gordon. the game is most of the time silent,  but when music plays, it is powerful. the sound effect is brilliant. from the footsteps of the 3 main characters that played independently and react to different surfaces from dirt, to wet sloppy sound to the creaking of wooden floor or clanging of metal against soles. the sound effect that played in cutscenes or dialogue, weapons being fired, explosions, the heavy grind of machineries, wildlife and other ambient sound. playing with good headphones, the game is a feast for the ears. lastly the story. without spoiling anything, there is a great story being told here. it just doesn't hold your hand at all but you can really interpret what really going on by paying attention. at the beginning of the game, you will feel lost. there are terms that get mentioned, names, factions that will confuse you. but as you visit more of the world, all the terms, names, etc will be familiar to you, and you will revisit dialogue trough neatly sorted record of your dialogue that can be sorted by characters or chronologically. this serve both as a clue to solving puzzle or reminding you of your objective, or simply learn the things you missed in the dialogue because of your lack of knowledge. this is not a con at all for me. imo, it evokes the feeling of "stranger in a strangeland" you come into this weird world, knowing nothing, but you as the player and the character you control both learn naturally about the state of the world and its inhabitant. it is rewarding when you know a history of a faction that got mentioned early and you are able to piece the story. there are alot of open to interpretation part in the story, but i have pieced myself a long theory that got pinned in the discussion forum (look it up only after finishing the game and want some answer.) . i think it is a wonderful story told masterfully and don't hold your hand. i had alot of fun playing the game and tons of another fun playing detective and piecing the story and world together.this isn't an RPG and the combat is more of a minigame so if you expecting an RPG, even something like disco elysium, this game won't be. it is at its core a point and click adventure, where you talk to people, collect items, combine them to solve puzzles and advance the plot. i think it is worth a try even if you aren't a fan of the genre just to experience the wonderful setting the devs created. there will also a hint / clue system the developer will try to implement in the future that will make the game alot more accessible because this world is BEAUTIFUL. pun aside, it is one of the coolest setting ever created in fiction, not just videogame, with also an interesting story with strong science fiction foundation with a bit of philosophy and fantasy added.

_childDocuments_.review: Frustrated and annoyed.Full disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter. Beautiful 2D story-rich isometric Fallout-esque game? Yes, sign me up, definitely! Project started in the beginning of 2017, and I was prepared to wait, and wait, and wait.ONCE AGAIN, I should have read the description more carefully…For ♥♥♥♥’s sake! You cannot make a good game with good graphics alone. You cannot make a good game with a metric butt-ton of padded pointless dialogue (looking at you, Tides of Numenera!). You cannot make a post-apocalypse game without explaining how the game world EARNED that apocalypse first. And you cannot make a world without providing proper context and exposition.There may be spoilers ahead. Or not. I don’t care. Like I said, I played the game top to bottom and now I am annoyed, and frustrated.Forget about Fallout. There is no character progression, no combat, no Actions Have BIG Consequences, nothing.Forget about exposition. Most of the stuff you see in game is never explained, not even a tiny bit. Story time. So you… who the bloody, bloody, bloody hell are you is never properly explained… drive down this very dilapidated road towards something with someone who is somehow important, and then this Big Huge Thing appears and there’s an explosion or shockwave and the world fades to black! DRAMATIC! OOOF!And then it’s future! And it is the aftermath and it is not the apocalypse yet somehow is… because South Africa, and South Africa does not play Fallout because South Africa IS Fallout, only worse, and everything is made of rusty scrap metal and repairs are for wussies… and you get somewhere like an airfield which looks like is survived a nuclear apocalypse but it’s actually not because it’s actually the bright future (does not look bright or futuristic) and you wander around looking for something because you have someone’s eye (WHAT) that requires something for some reason, and you have to go to this Big Huge Thing to do something because GOVERNMENT CONSPIRACY… and then it all no longer matters and you literally never come back.If you read all that and have not lost my train of thought, congratulations, hop aboard, because you will need at least this level of resilience to trudge through gameplay.Full disclosure, again. Big Huge Thing will never be explained. It’s not even needed for the story, really. And it will never be explained why you have an eye and why it is called the way it is called.Come on, people, logs and books and codex entries and whatnot exist for a reason.Ok, so maybe the game presents itself through dialogue? Well, yes, kinda, but again, without providing any context. Most of the time all this incessant monologuing spat at you will be structured like this:“Something something of something does something something because something reasons something”Human mind that is properly learned can infer at least the structure of what is said even when you speak gibberish (provided that gibberish really does have any structure). So that will be you fallback option – try to grasp the basic relations between all those words that are not words and infer what is required to progress.Any immersion is immediately broken. Roleplaying goes out of the window, because if people speak gibberish but carry handheld guns that can one-shot future choppers, and you don’t carry anything like that and want to survive, you tend to be polite unless you have a death wish.Hint: there is NO direct combat system in the game. At least, not one that you directly participate in. So, don’t go my way – feel free to vent your frustrations whenever you like it.This brings me nicely to my next point.CHOICES. Developers drank deeply of the cool-aid provided by ELEX, unfortunately, and it shows. Most of the outcome of the game will be solely dependent on the WAY you spoke to people. Not what you did, not what genocide you caused, not who got what. A careful balance of naughty and nice will unlock you Four Colored Endings! Because we don’t want to go the Mass Effect way and have just three!Again, this is an adventure game, not an RPG, so consider this a long fetch quest that nests subordinate fetch quests. Also, be prepared for puzzle-quest logic, when items interact in mysterious what-the-heck ways.Like this one time when you have to play a game (only actually you don’t have to) and there’s an arcade machine and you have a guy who’s really proficient at arcades and there’s a token slot and there’s a little bit of gold economy going on… sooooo, insert some gold? Exchange gold for tokens? Maybe there’s a kiosk for that? Sounds reasonable? WRONG, go do multiple fetch quests, you imbecile.The auteurs went the Ace Combat 7 route – it is quite possible (I did not check) that you have to play the game multiple times to get what the heck is going on and what is what and what are all those words that are not words. What Desolation lacks is engagement to make you play all those additional times.I did finish the game hoping for some resolution or explanation or SOMETHING in the end. There will be none, don’t repeat my mistakes.BTW, see what I did there? Desolation? What about beautiful?Ahhh, this is my last point. The backgrounds are beautifully crafted. There are beautifully crafted backgrounds. The authors definitely poured a lot of work into backgrounds. Finding paths through them is a hot mess. Most of the time I could not even fathom what was a path and what wasn’t.As for beauty… I don’t know. Looking at all that made me desperately wish for more order and structure and even more explanations on what were all those things littering my screen like so much hot garbage. Mostly it’s just that – Desolation.There is no hope, no gains, no world deserving to be saved, no choices that will matter in the end for you personally, no resolution… only desolation.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: My very anticipated adventure project from the creators of the game Stasis finally saw the light of day. And since I really love their past game, I will try to get as far as possible from comparisons of the new project with it, making only one very necessary comparison a little lower. BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION is a post-apocalyptic adventure that shows us all the facets of a possible future - the merger of man and machine, bio-experiments, outlandish African landscapes (by the way, this setting was chosen very well), moral dilemmas and the need to know yourself. The player seems to fall into the anthill from the warring races of the future, each of which has its own truth, its own problems and goals that we can help realize. The linking of all these scattered storylines, small and large conflicts, important for the history of details, was made by the creators so subtly and interestingly that it is surprising. Before us is a truly full-fledged science fiction, in which we can influence the events that take place, several times the player will even decide the fate of entire races, which naturally increases the degree of tension.Technically, the game is flawless. A bewitching visual picture of the majestic landscapes opening in front of you, accompanied by the music of Mick Gordon, often makes you dumbfounded with delight. The appearance of various representatives of the future is also very diverse, the artists embodied a lot of interesting ideas in them, often again weaving them with the African setting, which inspired the game. The puzzles have quite a strong logical foundation, only one of them has caused me big questions. The work with the characters is excellent, their development in the course of the plot is pleasant to observe, you really begin to be friends with both of your companions, the emotional connection between them is established. The same applies to working with the plot, which is already becoming the brand name of these guys, great attention to detail, a lot of small hints that you can understand only at a certain moment, and love for the story being told.With all this, one cannot fail to notice that the game has obvious drawbacks. I really did not like the first hour of the game, when you literally run through large empty locations, not really understanding your goal (we'll talk about goals). The feeling of painful loneliness that Stasis so suited does not fit this project at all, so the game began to unfold for me only with the advent of many other inhabitants of this universe. But the appearance of many characters and locations revealed a completely different problem - there is no diary in the game. Well, the very diary where you can briefly write your goals, where there may be some kind of clue system, if you are completely lost, etc. Formally, he is, but he is not. And this is a serious problem, because when you have at your disposal more than 20 huge locations available, you don’t understand your goal, and all the action rests on the fact that you need to find some small object lost somewhere in the grass, then in these moments, the connection with the game is destroyed. But I don’t even doubt that this problem will be solved, especially considering the obvious attention with which the developers relate to the feedback of the players.The new creation of the talented brothers fully met all my expectations, once again emphasizing their talent. Very original, perfectly sensing its purpose, this creation is really unique and exciting, we are waiting for new projects!
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: A few years ago now, I was  highly impressed with the indie point and click game, Stasis. I thought it had a huge amount of personality, looked great, had excellent atmosphere and did a lot of things that game designers usually fail miserably at. When The Brotherhood announced that they were looking for funding for a new game, I didn't hesitate to put my hard earned dosh in. After all, it looked so promising. After all these years, it's nice to say that it was money very well spent.Beautiful Desolation is very much a point and click adventure game at heart. In ways it reminds me a lot on the previous game Stasis but has more than enough of it's own thing to be considered unique. The character design is quite fantastic. A lot of the characters look very unique and are all very well voice acted. I thought the different levels to explore were also very well done. Each area has its own distinct look, making the unlocking of new areas very exciting. There seems to be a lot of confusion from people who seem to think that this game is like Fallout. Whilst the adventure aspect is very similar, the combat mechanic is not. There is only one instance of combat and that's the VERY limited arena battles. The entire game is combat free, something I was grateful for. I'm a bit bored of mowing down the same enemies time and again. Those people like the exploration part of Fallout will certainly get a kick out of this. The areas to explore are all quite large and as I mentioned above, they're all unique and beautiful. Talking of the presentation, the UI is well made. It's simple, aesthetically pleasing and very easy to use. The bar at the bottom is pretty typical adventure game stuff. You'll be able to access the map, past dialogues with characters and of course your inventory. It's all pretty simple and easy to use. The music and cinematic cutscenes are all very well done. The score I found very atmospheric and did a great job of sucking me into the environments I was exploring. When I fulfilled my missions and was greated by a cutscene, it felt worth the effort. They were pretty epic. I don't have many complaints with Beautiful Desolation. I liked the way it played, the way it sounded and the design of the whole thing. If I were to complain about a couple of things, it would be the arena combat and the dice gambling game. I find the AI gets a bit too much of an advantage over you when playing these and it can make these parts of the game very tedious. I also would have appreciated a log to list your unfinished missions, just remind you what you have to do. I had the odd moment where I felt lost and this would have helped greatly. As a whole though, I loved my experience with this game and it turns out I didn't explore near as much as I thought I did. I'll have to re-visit it soon and I highly recommend picking this up to anyone into point and click adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: First off,  is an RPG.Not just an adventure game.An RPG.WITH adventure game mechanics.Because here be: multiple difficult world-influencing choices, deep characterisation and multi-layered interconnected questlines.So if glorified LMB-shatterer is still considered to be an RPG, excuse me if I believe this here thing should too.Now then...Mechanically - yes, it is an adventure game. You will have to scour locations for items, combine them and apply them. And just so you know, I usually hate this type of gameplay, but here it works perfectly! There are no illogical puzzles, and if you're stuck, there are always hints in the dialogues that you had over the course of the game - which are stored in your PDA, so you can access them at any time. And the location-combing doesn't feel bothersome in the slightest because the game is just so beautiful. is called that for a reason. It really is the prettiest of isometric games with 2D backgrounds. This grass, this heat, this absolute abundance of life: little flies, small animals and drones going about their business. It really does show that the authors observed the landscape they are portraying, and now are just replicating its feeling while simultaeously imbuing it with technological post-apocalyptic grandeur. Generally speaking, it looks like a game formed in a big way by a vision of a very skilled visual artist - the design of locations, character models, sketches and especially character-dialogue animated portraits are absolutely top-notch.And it runs very well too. On my level-minus-80-total-junk-laptop™ it ran at agreeable framerate and looked great at the same time!More than once I've seen this game compared to . No. Just no.  is a dusty rusty social-critique half-dystopian affair.  rather belongs into the league of the old 70-80 sci fi. If we talk in terms of games, it belongs to the  constellation. I.e.: it depicts a complicated amalgamation of a mystical-technological world that looks absolutely dizzying and surrealistic to the uninitiated, but begins to make sense the moment you start delving into it. Beautiful desolation nails it perfectly, world-building is just out there.1.Sometimes you are liable to do something that you haven't talked with anyone about - both in the dialogue and in the way of action. It is not a frequent occasion, but it happens.2.There is a contextualized combat minigame on the Arena loction - and it is atrocious. Maybe I just didn't get the hang of it, but it mostly consist of spamming the strongest attack over and over. A great pity that so much animation work went into it and it is feels so pointless. Fortunately, you can skip it entirely if you intend only one playthrough .If you believe an RPG with no combat isn't an RPG, consider going home and rethinking your life while playing . It is a wonderful game made all the more wonderful by the fact that it was made by just a handful of people while its production values are so high.PSThankfully, the success of  shows that this archaic line of thought is being slowly pushed back.PPSFor the love of everything, don't just click through dialogue! So much effort went into voice-over here, and it is so good that skipping it would mean doing yourself a great disservice.PPPSThree years later I've learnt a few things about the nature of RPG genre and don't stand for what I said here quite so vehemently anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightfully different. The setting, art, voice acting, soundscape, it's all brilliant. I love the "modern" take on classic gameplay of isometric RPG and P&C adventure game. The story was very enjoyable as well, with moments of triumph balanced by moments of poignancy, interspersed with some great humor. A total recommend from me!Small caveats: I have to admit that I basically played with a walkthrough open, but it was only occasionally necessary and even then likely only because I am an impatient gamer that only barely tolerates "puzzles." I do think that with enough patience, and especially if you DO like puzzles, a walkthrough would be unnecessary. Most of the places I got "stuck" were less actual sticking points and more just me wanting to get on to the next thing because, again, impatient gamer. :)

_childDocuments_.review: A game that left me with mixed feelings. I adore the art style, post apocalyptic sci-fi setting, story, various factions, captivating NPC's, voice acting and  dialogues. However the gameplay is severely lacking and I had to drag myself to the end of the game. I'll describe to you an example of the gameplay loop. You'll be in a town, talk to an NPC for a brief moment, get a quest, call transport, go to overworld, move to teleporter, teleport to next zone, travel to location, pick up item, call transport, go to overworld, move to teleporter, teleport to previous zone, travel to town, talk to NPC for a moment, complete quest, rinse and repeat. That brief moment of talking to an NPC is where the game shines, with outstanding characters, voice acting and dialogues, but the time spent on that doesn't compare to the time wasted on traveling back and forth. With a walkthrough you can go straight to the point, but without that it would be even worse. In addition to that the world is mostly empty so you'll be running around exploring vast areas only to pick up one story or collectable item or talk to a lone NPC here or there. Obviously it is a point & click game, and I appreciate the gameplay around that, but overall it leaves a lot to be desired. It has (optional) turn-based combat in one specific area, and a karma system, so I kept thinking why they didn't have more going on to engage with (think Undertale). Either condense the world (no needless traveling) or fill up the world with things to do.All in all I'm giving this game a positive review, but it comes with caveats.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: From the creators of STASIS comes another point and click adventure game, this time starting us off in an alternate history South Africa in the 80's, placing us in the role of Mark Leslie, a man investigating a colossal object that appeared in the sky and shortly thereafter dropping us into an acid trip in the form of a desolate, post-apocalyptic African landscape.The game consists of exploring an alien world via an overhead map in a ship, solving puzzles, interacting and carrying out tasks for the abstract characters/tribes you meet on your journey in hopes of finding your way back home and it too features a choice system which adds for replayability.The art style/graphics are beautifully done, these are the best pre-rendered landscapes I've seen yet in any game and the setting is reminiscent of titles like Planescape and Fallout except with an African twist. Visually, Beautiful Desolation delivers in troves. The sound design too is fantastic which manages to nicely compliment the insanely high bar set by other areas in the presentation.Overall a fantastic experience which no effort was spared in its creation..
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I can just hear some of the reviewers say, “I told you so”.I have always been reluctant to buy BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION. I have watched a lot of gameplay footage and read the reviews. But still I was drawn to this game because of the graphics. Maybe it’s nothing earth shattering but still, in my opinion, the graphics looks good, and one can get a “feel” for the postapocalyptic world.But …I find the story strange. Sure, I get it … it’s clear that the player gets dumped at some strange postapocalyptic place in the future. But then the story kind of falls apart for me. I just don’t find it gripping at all. And that brings me directly to my next point.I don’t mean to be rude, but the voice acting is really not on standard with many of the similar games that I’ve played. I’ll try and explain as quick as possible. The scenes where you character have verbal interaction with the characters in the environment is just bone chilling bad. It is clear that many of the dialogue is done by the same person. Your character’s voice is just in the same emotionless tone throughout. There is just no feeling and just don’t attribute to the atmosphere of the game. The response during the dialogue is equally bad. It’s clear that the responses are done by the same voice that is “camouflaged”, by mixing in a bit of Jamaican (for example).It also seem that the developers tried to mix in a bit of humour, but it fails miserably. At one stage during dialogue the jargon that was used is just a poor attempt at humour. I will give one example. Words like “kak” (♥♥♥♥) and “♥♥♥-of” (♥♥♥♥ off) where mixed into the dialogue but it just did not do anything to make the quality of the dialogue better. It’s just a terrible attempt at adding some emotion to the dialogue.If you love games where you run around like a headless chicken from point A to point B, then to point C just to go back to point A … well then BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION is the game for you. If not, then I suggest you stay away. When exploring the world, it get very tedious to play. You will just stumble onto some random object without even getting a visual hint that the object was there in the first place. I can only describe this a “pixel hunting”. During the puzzles you constantly have to guess what the developers where thinking. What is logical to one person is not necessarily logical to the next person. Not all people have the same logic. If that was the case our world would have been just as strange as the BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION world.And lastly, the amount of irrelevant onscreen information just don’t make sense. For instance, you will mouse over an object like a rusted car. Then the information will pop-up that informs you that this is “a rusted car that is overgrown by some plant”. Really? How does that contribute to the quality of the game? I mean, it’s clear that this object is an old rusted and overgrown car, why tell the player.BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION get a unequivocal NO.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice visuals and isometric 3rd person hint at open world party-based RPG, but that this is not.  This is a mostly linear point & click puzzle game.  While the story seems interesting, it simply hasn't been compelling enough to keep me wading through what I see as tenuous threads of logic in the puzzles.Perhaps I'm not a fan of the genre, but I do remember enjoying the old Sierra point & click adventures of the 90s.  The game play and story telling here don't really stand up by comparison (though clearly the visuals are great).

_childDocuments_.review: Wakanda place is this?Move aside Afrofuturism, District 9, Black Panther, Elysium, Chappie and all you other African takes on sci-fi, because one thing’s for sure… I can easily tell you that I’ve never seen anything quite like the world of Beautiful Desolation.If you are South African like me, then you must already know that you’re gonna experience it in a slightly different way to the rest of the world and may get a kick out of various elements that feel familiar to home. Beautiful Desolation is without a doubt, a whole new bag of Simba chips. It launches you into a future so far ahead that the South Africa you might know (and the people who lived there) are completely unrecognisable. The more this story of crazy futures and prophecies unfolds, the more interesting it becomes.Here’s what the official site had to say:“Your surroundings hold echoes of a desolate past, and glimpses of a dark future that has yet to be written by your actions. Be prepared to face many tough choices that will shape this land long after you complete your journey”.Dig InThe base gameplay itself feels somewhat inspired by the original Fallout games, sci-fi point and click adventures like The Dig and some of the more notable RPGs like Baldur’s Gate. One big difference (but more like point and click adventures) being that it doesn’t contain a consistent combat mechanic inside the main world, and instead relies on exploration that might have you sometimes partake in combat at certain times.Make no mistake though, none of Beautiful Desolation feels like you’re playing something borrowed from another game, or just some sort of spiritual remake. The gameplay actually feels slightly similar to Stasis and offers a slower, more patient adventuring experience and won’t be well suited for those looking for some sort of high-paced, sci-fi action extravaganza.The way this game wants to be played can best be summed up by my very own approach to playing it on my PC: Laid back, with one hand on the mouse and the other helping me sip a hot cup of tea. It wants you to take a breath, immerse yourself in the familiar but alien world, and figure things out. Figuring those things can get a bit tough at times though, and I definitely struggled at some points to piece together what I had done and where I needed to go to find what I was looking for. You definitely need to pay attention to get an idea of where you’re going next, but for that you also thankfully have the ability to review all previous conversations and notifications.It’s not for everyone, and definitely speaks more to those that have or took later interest in this specific kind of PC gaming from the 90s. So if you’re looking for a new Diablo, Quake or otherwise – you’re barking up the wrong Akacia tree.Ripleys In TimeIt’s immediate and clear that while Beautiful Desolation’s setting and concepts are incredibly unique, it’s one hell of a love letter to sci-fi and old-school PC gaming – complete with FMV cutscenes.You might hear a reference here or there, but it’s within the style, the music provided by composer Mick Gordon (DOOM, Killer Instinct, Need for Speed and more) and the atmosphere that I constantly found myself tasting the flavours of sci-fi properties of the past and feeling strangely at home in this nostalgic mixing pot. It’s a very strange experience to feel like you’re both revisiting certain feelings while also experiencing something completely new. This feeling is very subjective however, and may really differ from player to player depending on your past experiences with sci-fi.The music and sound really is a large part of the experience though, and when combined with the very South African accents heard throughout and the heavy layers of post-processing you get pulled into the world that much more. I particularly love the low-booming African-styled languages being spoken and traditional singing heard while moving through certain habitats.Love, Death and Road tripsSouth Africa in the far future is very different, and despite the sci-fi and robots (not the traffic light kind), the world is littered with strange healers, tribal leaders and religious zealots. The areas are filled with interesting characters, strange languages, unique architecture and echoes of a past world. You need to explore large areas, and so travelling mostly gets done with the use of an old SADF “Buffalo” transport airship. You mostly get around by using a map to select locations that the Buffalo can fly to, and make use of “Wardens” which are a sort of blend between Stargates and Mass Effect Relays.When at a location, you spend a lot of your time walking around small towns, bases and various other sites of interest, speaking with locals, finding items you need and figuring out what to do next. The locations themselves are something to behold though, and vary from tin shacks and various huts to grand structures and gorgeous, lush nature.ContactCharacters you meet aren’t what you expect either, and range from sentient machines to people stripped of their parts and modified into something rather ghoulish.Harkening back to old school PC gaming, you break away into a dedicated conversation screen whenever you speak with others. You have the option to choose from multiple lines of dialogue as you decided what to ask and whether or not you want to behave like a real poe bad guy.It’s made all the better for South African gamers when you’re able to tell someone in-game to “stop your kak”.VERDICT:The more I discover this unrecognisable, post-apocalyptic South Africa, the more I’m astonished by the original ideas injected into the story, visuals and setting.It’s a rabbit hole that has gripped me more and more the further down I’ve dared to venture. I’ve gone from just being intrigued by the concept, to staying up later than I should because I can’t wait to see what happens next.Considering its low price point ($20 at launch for the standard edition), Beautiful Desolation delivers a big adventure with lots of depth to the wild story and fascinating world.If you’re into the joys of 90s PC gaming or far-out sci-fi concepts then you’re in for quite a treat.

_childDocuments_.review: Welp, let me start by saying this game hits D I F F E R E N T. From the unique voice acting to the sheer atmosphere presented by the game's setting, this sh*t was one of the most enjoyable stories I've ever played in a game. _childDocuments_.review: If Fallout 2 and Monkey Island had a weird love child only a mother could love, this game would be it.It's an isometric, click-and-point adventure game with some RPG elements that looks like similar to games like Fallout 2, set in South Africa. The story takes you through some sort of weird apocalypse, and it's up to you to try to find your way back. There are multiple endings, though I only explored one of them. There is no combat, except for one small part, but that doesn't stop the game from being really interesting. I will say, though, this game can be difficult and it won't hold your hand.

_childDocuments_.review: Adventure game that deftly mixes the style and feel of the old Fallouts with Planescape: Torment and adds its own tribal african twist to it. Nostalgia over the remains of the old world and being disturbed by the weirdness of the new makes for a unique blend. Would prefer a more traditional oldschool RPG rather than a point and click adventure, but this was definitely a thoroughly enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's a huge fan of point-and-click games, I was really interested to play this title. The devs usually only make horror games, so a quirky sci-fi post-apocalyptic game set in South Africa sounded neat. Unfortunately this game is a complete slog. 90% of the game is just fly here, do something, leave, fly to different place, do something else. Every location is mostly empty and there is absolutely no challenge to anything whatsoever. While it's interesting to see cultures and different species in new worlds based on South African tribes, none of them are that fleshed out and the dialogue with them is extremely limited. There's a lot of lore that is kind of explained but not really (the devs are known for this) and it ends up being extremely shallow. When you have to make choices regarding which groups to protect and which to doom to death, you don;t really have any connection to them so it doesn't matter. There's also a karma system that is affected by the choices and dialogue options you make that is measured via your Simulacra card (this is never explained to you btw.) This affects the ending you get, but you can only build up so much karma in one playthrough. I've read it takes at least 5 playthroughs to get the "true" ending and I can't even imagine playing this game twice.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Desolation reminded me a lot of a mash-up of Mos Eisley Spaceport and Planescape: Torment. You travel a lot to deal with semi-skull-robot-alien-people you can't really relate to. Again and again you meet two equally unpleasant tribes and help one eradicate the other to get some strange device.  Most of the time, I had no idea what I had to do, and when I was doing something, I didn't understand it. Too many strange items. Too many strange names, goddesses, concepts, etc. I still have no idea what the whole story is about, seriously. What about that Independece-Day-Penrose-thing? What about that brother-and-brother-family-drama? Who exactly is this Daris thing?I can see how a lot of work and creativity went into this game, but I personally could just not get comfortable with it, so it was very limited fun.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I love post-apocalyptic anything. Just the curiosity of wondering what would happen when a man is on the brink of extinction is morbid yet fascinating. Beautiful Desolation takes the isometric point and click of yore and brings it to life with over 40 fully voiced and wonderfully designed characters and a time warping story. The game starts out with you, Mark Leslie, arguing with his wife about someone whose emotional mess you have to clean up. Suddenly a giant object slams into the ground from the sky and brings about the apocalypse with machines. You are now trying to find a way to figure out what the Penrose, the giant object, is and how to stop it from changing the world. The only issue is that doesn’t go as planned and you are warped an unknown amount of years into the future and must stop factions from fighting and chose between groups of characters.Choices mostly matter before the ending of the game. There are several groups of characters, some warring with each other, and some just single characters that don’t offer any rewards, and you must decide what happens to them all. You fly around an overhead map in your Buffalo transport and objectives are obtained by talking to characters. Each area is small and linear and there’s usually only one person to talk to in each area. The characters are really well done and the style of the game feels like a mid-90’s Fallout with pre-rendered animations in a box and the text appears below it. The characters look amazing from robots to weird fleshy things to plants and various lifeforms. There’s tons of imagination in this game and even the environments look amazing. However, there’s not much else when it comes to exploring.When you land in an area you will most likely find things that need to be used or find things that need something to be used with. Sometimes a character might need an item, or they might need you to solve a large issue that decides the fate of their race or faction. The issue here is that objectives are so obtuse and cryptic and you can easily miss an option to solve a large problem. For example, you need to ultimately find three items to restart the array to let you back on the Penrose to go home. One item needed is Red Mercury. There are two ways to obtain this and depending on your choices once will always be cut off. There is also one route that lets you fight a few bosses via a weird arcade game. You need tokens to put combatants in this machine. You need at least three tokens to even bother and that’s never explained. To get these tokens you must choose one of three outcomes for a few factions, or the fourth outcome gives you Red Mercury for the array. I wound up missing two of these and only got two tokens in the game so the item I needed from the final boss for the arcade game to get Red Mercury was cut off. This long string of outcomes that are hidden is a little unfair. I also accidentally decided a fate without even knowing that option would do that and I wasn’t given a second chance. I decided the fate of two factions early on and wound up doing the opposite because I didn’t realize clicking a certain option would launch that decision and it was too late. There are also some items that need to be bought to progress and you need credits that are exchanged for gold. To acquire gold you need to find them hidden in certain areas by just wandering around. This was also something never explained and for a while, I couldn’t figure out how to get credits. There are also some bogus items that you can waste credits on, so I’m not sure if you can end up not finishing the game because you have found all the gold and don’t have enough credits. There’s only so much gold in the game and there’s not much.One of my biggest gripes is needing to talk to certain characters before something would advance. Icons on the map flash if there is a new dialog for a character, but that’s if you have already done something to trigger that. It won’t flash for items not discovered or anything like that. I had to use a walkthrough through most of the game because there were times I felt l made progress and the next character would give me zero hints on where to go next. Some objectives I could figure out alone, but 90% needed a walkthrough. Just because the game looks mid-90’s doesn’t mean it needs to play like it. It still didn’t stop me from looking forward to the next area and character to talk to as they are so unique and interesting.Overall, Beautiful Desolation is a well-written and very stylized post-apocalyptic adventure game with lots of nostalgic feelings of the mid-’90s. However, the insane amount of cryptic and obtuse objectives makes the game very frustrating without a guide. I also didn’t like how often you would start feeling like you’re making progress and then get stopped dead at every turn with the only option is to wander around every area until you notice something you missed, and as the game progresses that can take forever. You end up unlocking over 50 areas towards the end and going back to them all is insane. I love the voice acting, the art style, and the story itself, but it’s so unfair and stops you dead in your tracks at every turn. Progress is incredibly grindy here and not to mention the major decisions in the game can easily be missed or skipped over.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I don't regret buying this game, but in the hypothetical situation of a mad scientist offering to give me my money back but take the game and wipe my memory of it, I would consider it. Frankly the concept and a lot of the world is amazing, but the execution is a little off. The main issue of the game is the amount of time spent traveling between places and trying to figure out where you're supposed to go next, because the game isn't always very intuitive. I say I recommend the game, but it's more that I don't hate it enough to "not recommend" it; what I do recommend though, is buying it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I am a massive fan of THE BROTHERHOOD games but this one is a bit of a disappointment. The world is fascinating, the main plot it's okay, POOCH is my absolute favourite, but this game it's just one big massive go-and-fetch quest, which makes it very boring and tiresome at some point. There is one really cool riddle and the rest is just: go to this character, ask what they want and go to another character to bring this to them. Add to this the fact that you need to spend some time travelling from one location to another and this game just loses its charm. I still think that it's beautiful, that the created world with everything in it's absolutely great, but the experience of playing it it's just not good after a short while. I really wish to recommend this game, but I cannot. Play it if you look for something beautiful and unique. Don't do it if you expect an RPG or interesting point-and-click.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: In this isometric adventure (which to me feels like a walking simulator) you'll traverse post-apocalyptic Africa, encountering bizarre creatures, solving intricate puzzles, and making decisions that shape the fate of the world. It's like a scenic hike with a side of existential crisis - perfect for those who prefer their exploration with a hefty dose of narrative depth.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this game.Yet another highly imaginative game from The Brotherhood, we have a far future, post-apocalyptic South Africa. There is a deep integration of local South African cultural ideas and aesthetics, which give this game a unique flavor that I haven't seen captured anywhere else. Additionally, the characters, societies, technology and more that accompany the setting are all brilliantly creative themselves. The party members you get are all likeable and have their own problems and issues that you can respond to in different ways. I think this game has some good replay value, especially with some of the different decisions you can make, and the attitudes you can have when talking to others.Visually this game looks great - fitting in well with modern takes on the isometric RPG. There is no combat, of course, meaning it does play like a point & click adventure game - so if you expect lots of combat like in Fallout, Baldur's Gate, etc - you won't find that here. Additionally, the game has a good soundtrack to go along with its nice visuals.The only cons I can think of that are that the interface, while simple and easy to understand, could be a bit quicker to use in places like the main menus, but this is never a major problem. There were also a few puzzles that took me a while to figure out, but that's just how it is with RPGs and adventure games sometimes. Overall an excellent game that I highly recommend - a fascinating setting with a good story and characters. If you enjoy story-oriented games, you'll like this for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent adventure "game".The art is beautiful, the dialogue is good, the voice acting and music are great, the puzzles are ok.The first two hours of the games were super fun, the scifi is top-notch and it really makes you think about how the world would be like in the far, far distant future but then, it started to happen.The multiple fetch quests are not ok.If the quests would take you to new places or old places that have now chanegd, it wouldnt be that bad but the game makes you go back and forth to places youve already been that show no change at all and it gets super, super tedious.Not to mention you need to finish the game 4 times to get all the achievements. ugh.As for the ending.. jeez.. It felt so.. convenient but also convuluted and disastifying. Kind of reminds me of those endings where you find out everything was a dream (thats not the ending but its similar) and I was so, so disappointed.Anyway, the game is very nice to look at and as a story is good but as a game, it sucks.Beautiful Desolation gets 26 fetch quests that made me waste 10 minutes to travel from one side to another out of 56 times I lost the position of my mouse pointer because its so tiny and everything is brown, the same color as the stupid mouse arrow. Get it if you like post-apoc sci-fi interactive movies but this is hardly a game.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I was fortunate enough to be involved in pre-release testing and I was a bit apprehensive.  I’m more of an FPS player and tend to get distracted with point and click games, and I was concerned this would be the case. I could not have been more wrong.This game asks for a lot.  It isn’t going to hold your hand, it isn’t going to give you solutions on a platter.  It expects you to use your wits and common sense.  It expects you to explore it and take your time and second guess yourself.  That being said, if you do all that is expected, the rewards are extremely satisfying.  The game left me satisfied, exhausted, wanting more.  I had more than a week to test, but I got caught up in the story and just binged it. When I wasn’t playing the game physically, it was running so I could listen to the soundtrack.The graphics and sound effects are quite pleasing and unique to the world, and blends well.  As a South African, I enjoyed exploring areas known to me in the real world, and recognizing birds local to my area.  The colourful blooms of one map made a stark and interesting contrast to the aridness of others.  I struggled in some spots to notice things I needed to collect, but not to the extent where I felt like I didn’t know what to do next. The initial lack of a journal made me a little anxious.  It adds to the feel of being lost in the world and I was concerned I would lose track, but that is far from the case.  As you get to explore, you meet amazing characters, hear amazing stories and you start connecting dots.  The story is complimented by outstanding voicework, with a special mention re the Mina, probably one of the creepiest characters I have had the (dis)pleasure to meet in gaming.Many have mentioned elements of Fallout but what really sealed the deal for me was how some of the mechanics reminded me of old school Kings Quest/ Space Quest, where you would collect items for interesting uses, sometimes not in the way you would expect.The game sets an easy pace, it doesn’t expect you to retain every single bit of information you get, but allows you to discover and rediscover just by playing and exploring.  No interaction is insignificant, no choice is without consequence and the end will make you feel like you were truly the writer of your own story.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Made with love, that´s to be experienced. Great story, nice sightseeing of postapocalyptic scenery, entertaining point&click-like elements (inventory, items combining, using them in the game-world), relaxing gameplay, you won´t fight, you have no time limit whatsoever. About 15 hours of entertainment in one playthrough. Different decisions deliver different endings, some decission pretty tough, morally. Will challenge your conscience. Main characters are likeable. NPCs in the world are pretty unique in the gaming universe.  Pretty fresh way of navigating the map by using a flying transporter. I have not seen that in all the years of gaming.  Game-world got a great atmospher. Had a nice stay there.  Got some not to hard puzzles to solve, too.  And it got a little taste of strategy, when you (optional) battle in the arena.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend Open world with choices matter on a point and click adventure. Theres a combat minigame at a point in the game but that's it. Most of it is just you walking around talking to people/mutants/cyborgs/robots and solving puzzles and it was a blast that kept me, a guy who doesn't usually play adventure games, very interested. I felt really connected to the player character's brother, Don, and the robot dog companion named Pooch. The characters you meet all around post apocalyptic South Africa are full of life and have their own problems that you have to solve or make worse. The art and design of the areas are very cool and add a lot to the setting and sometimes tell their own story. There are multiple endings, and speaking of ending I did not predict what would happen at all. I had the setting on that pulsates items because I don't like pixel hunting for objects, if you are the same be sure to check that out.Check this game out if it seems interesting, I don't think you will be disappointed if you want to have a good point and click open world adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to play this game to completion but I found myself at a point where I was running around in circles trying to determine how to progress the game. Online walkthroughs did little to help me ascertain my next point of interest, thus I lost interest in the game and found myself deciding to stop playing it. I think in some ways this is a very interesting game. It has the feel of a role playing game but without the game. I wonder what it would have been like with a full fledged battle system. Maybe at some point in development there was meant to be one. The world definitely feels like it could have added combat in there somehow. I think if done right this game could have been a lot more interesting that way.That said, the writing isn't bad and the story, while sparse, does hold some intrigue. Still, even the sum of its parts doesn't push this game into positive review territory.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely wonderful adventure game. In the vein of classic RPGs but without the combat, it is a journey to discover the truth and you get to meet a lot of interesting characters along the way. If you enjoy this game check out the other games by THE BROTHERHOOD, they are a bit more into the horror side but done in a similar no-combat item-puzzle solving style.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Desolation is a idiosyncratic, multi-themed adventure, bringing some interesting gameplay ideas to the table. Its story and distinct setting are its strongest assets and it will definitely take you places. Be aware though, there is no hand holding at all. You'll need to pay attention to the conversations with the cast of delightfully bizarre characters you meet, if you don't want to backtrack and fumble for clues constantly.Read more on:
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves more attention.It's quite an experience. Even though it's mostly bringing items to various characters and locations, said characters and locations, their aesthetics, together with the soundtrack and the world building, make the experience worth it. I didn't feel these "fetch quests" as something tedious, I could only look forward to the next line of dialogue and the next scenery to contemplate. The duration of the game is just right, without overstaying its welcome.It's a great (or should I say "lekker") game, and a wonderful work of art.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely incredible.  It is visually stunning and it is amazing the care and detail that went into each of the worlds to make them so different and all beautiful in their own ways.  The story is intricate and completely sucked me into it.  This game is huge, but with maps, quest markers and text logs of dialogues to help keep it all together.I just can't say enough wonderful things about this game.  I love how each world has it's own sounds.  Their tiny footprints in the sand.  How the robot dog liked to roll around on the ground every so often and the silly complaints and comments from brother Don as he accidentally eats bugs and gripes as he tries to keep up.  I loved and hated how hard some of the choices were to be made, because your choices in this game are literally world changing.  The many characters you meet are all flawed.  They have wronged and been wronged.  All are fighting for survival in a harsh world with their own belief systems.  This complex world your character has been dropped into and is desperate to escape from is compelling and I just couldn't get enough of this game.Highly recommend for story lovers that want to sink into another world that is rich and complex.Nominated this game for innovative game play award for 2020.  This is such a great game, it is beautiful but also has a very unique style to the controls and features that I thought it definitely deserved to be nominated.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, modern adventure game. Plenty of choices that will impact the ending, without resorting to banal good/evil score. Very original setting, interesting factions and characters, stunning visuals, and excellent music. If you enjoyed Stasis or Cayene from the same devs, or classics like Sanitarium, you will absolutely love this!
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Such a great game. Classic Point and Click adventure in a large world with numerous locations. Fascinating , quirky and bizarre characters, dripping with the sci-fi/apocalyptic theme throughout. Pays to really pay attention to detail for task requirements and this is really cool where you'll need to traverse numerous locations and talk to people to find out what you actually need. People desensitised to hint systems and inbuilt walkthroughs may struggle at first but this is what these adventure games used to be like in their hey day. Interesting story, great learning curve and let's support this company so they can make more :)
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: What a... Beautiful game. Art and story are wonderful, it was really easy to pick up and put down and I enjoyed the lack of hand holding. It really brought me back to the days of exploring and figuring things out. Plays perfect on the Deck, only wish it updated my offline playtime. About 20 hours to complete.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I have no words for how amazing this game is.  It's almost the ultimate in choices matter for point and click adventures, and everything feels immersive and real.  The art, the storytelling, the characters are all very real feeling and amazing.  On top of that it has fairly significant replay value.  I don't know why there are any complaints about the back and forth, as most of that is fairly standard for point and click adventures like this.  And most of the time there are obvious clues as to what options you have available to you when you are playing.  I can't wait to play more games by this developer!
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: For those of you who might be considering buying this as a Fallout-like game set in a post-apoc South Africa..don't. While it may appear otherwise at first its entirely a point and click adventure game that while fun has little in common with Fallout. _childDocuments_.review: It's not a good game, and it's not an RPG. It's an okay "interactive book." There are dialog choices, but they don't change the outcome at all. There are no puzzles, the game is all fetch-questing. The only actual interactivity you have is in the aggregate, in the dialogue choices: whether you decide to be "evil" or "good" or sometimes mix it up a little. All this does is determine which of 4 endings you get, which are all very brief, entirely unsatisfying, and have no connection to anything you did in-game. It's a long game that expects you to play from the beginning at least twice to unlock all the endings. I like the graphics, thought the music was fine, and really liked the exotic setting. But the lack of actual "play" here--instead it's all virtual page-flipping--makes it a bad "game." They're trying to re-create Planescape: Torment with these things, and it's not working. There was a lot of good and neat stuff in here, but the lack of player input, and the horrible way the endings were dealt with, leads me to say "hard pass."
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story, great isometric graphics, interesting areas, good sound design (though a couple music tracks had some pretty high pitched parts). Set in a world you want to see and learn more of. Pretty fantastic as far as adventure games go. Almost every conversation has at least 3 dialogue options at each point your character speaks, and that feeds into a kind of alignment system. I'll have to either get further into the game to see how things can branch out, and replay as a complete jerk to see how things change up.As long as you don't go in expecting a CRPG with combat and stat sheets you could get a lot out of this.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Another great adventure from the Brotherhood and a big step up in quality from Stasis.The game is undeniably beautiful with great presentation all around. I especially loved how it all came together at the end wanting me to run through it again at some point to try to get a different conclusion.The only thing I feel is missing is some type of notebook or reminder of tasks you took on. When I finished the game I still had a couple items in my inventory I picked up for side quests and totally forgot what and who they were for. A reminder or a simple list of current tasks would have been fantastic.An easy recommendation for sci-fi adventure lovers

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Desolation: Fallout SA Intro:I am a South African, and like any good local, I always want our entertainment industry to expand and grow.  Sadly there are few local development studios and fewer who use our unique setting and talent.  That is however changing with The Brotherhood games and Beautiful Desolation, a delightful isometric adventure game in the vein of early Fallout and Planescape Torment.Some of the plot pointsI do wish we could have stayed longer in 1970s South Africa.  The Penrose arriving during such a time in SA could have lead to some riveting alternative history.  How would have the National Party responded to the presence of aliens? How would have the world reacted to the extraterrestrial presence?  But once Don and Mark get sent forward, the past is so far away that it barely matters.  The character’s past doesn’t include the Penrose in any prominent way. The Penrose Alliance (set up as a nice juicy alliance between South Africa and the alien intelligence on the Penrose) had loads of potential, but it is never really explored.  I think Beautiful Desolation could have been longer, exploring both the rise and the downfall of civilization in SA.  It should have been longer as the ideas and themes could have created a true masterpiece. Gameplay:From a gameplay perspective, there is very little in terms of verity. This is not a bad thing,  I would prefer that if the game mechanics are limited, they should be tightly designed.  The two main pillars appear to be exploration and puzzles (normally combining two or more items).  All of these are perfectly fine…except for the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic!  One of, if not THE most unique and entertaining games I've played in a few years.  Gorgeous end to end, excellent audio design, wonderful companions, and a new spin on traditional adventure mechanics.  The closest game I could say it's related to is Planescape: Torment, and that is also intended as an extreme compliment.I'm not sure what the complaints are about the game loop, it's very traditional for adventure games to have you searching for items and trying combinations of things.  I feel like the negative reviews aren't fair, due to the game explicitly stating it's genre.  Have you guys never played an adventure game before?  At no point have I ever felt stuck, or that I was going out of my way to search for things.  There are clues in the story, and there are visual clues on the maps.  Look for pulsing circles.I don't know if any of the screenshots or game-play videos can prepare you for just how engaging and fun this world is.  I'm looking forward to everything The Brotherhood produces in the future now.  Such a gem!The only thing I wished for was an alternative control scheme.  I'd like to hold the mouse down and have my character follow the pointer, like Diablo.  This is probably just me, as I have some joint pain from all the clicking.Edit:  Just completed the game!  I will gladly run another play-through of this in time.  Absolute engrossing entertainment from start to finish.  9.5/10.  Planescape: Torment meets District 9 in an adventure game package.  Just phenomenal.  Bravo.
_childDocuments_.name: BEAUTIFUL DESOLATION

_childDocuments_.review: I grant this is much better than its predecessor, Stasis, which had too many illogical things required (see my review for that). But it suffers from the frustrating tedium of requiring way too many steps to accomplish anything with very little to go on to know what to do. You must do every step in order. So, a walkthrough is required. I don't play games for tedious frustration. And using a walkthrough for every next step becomes just following instructions.The South African touch of language and culture is different. But that's not enough. The main characters are nice enough, but the world is entirely populated by cartoonish monstrosities. The story is interesting enough. There is a gauge that measures between how nice you are to how bad, based on conversation choices. That is never explained how it works. But it's important in determining the ending. 40/100
