_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant mixture of japanese grotesque horror and Lovecraftian lore, in the form of a seemingly simple but in fact pretty interesting roguelike rpg game.Graphics and sound : 8The 1/2bit palettes (2/4 colors) and the crude drawings alongside the sharp chiptune music can make this thing feel "too niche" to some types of gamers, but there's in fact a lot to love here. Aesthetically the game is very homogeneous, feels like a labor of love, and I can't see how HQ drawings or a big ost would improve it in any meaningful way. It's a rare bird, that's true, but once you get used to it, it feels cohesive and well thought. Art is retro but not bad, music is a bit repetitive and stressing but it just fits the nature of the game.Writing and lore: 8.5It's not up to the standarts of, say, sunless skies, but there's definitely a lot of interesting stories to experience. The game is not overly verbose, and sometimes one can't help but wish they had gone a bit deeper in this department, but all of the main investigations, as well as the random events, are cool to experience and certainly creepy in their own way. Sadly, the game doesn't feature a lot of main investigations as of yet. In about 3/4 playthroughs you will probably come across most, if not all of them. Since the stories have many endings, there's always some new approach to take and some new screens to read, but more content is certainly required for this game to really reach it's full potential.Horror: 9.5It's hard to say what a good horror media is. Defining horror is hard because what's creepy for some people can be boring or even hilarious for others. The nature of the horror here is a mixture between the arcane, existential horror of the Cthulhu Myths (which is based on the feeble nature of mankind and its almost inexistant power to oppose the ancient horrors that lurk in the stars) and the more prosaic, yet still profoundly disturbing nature of japanese horror manga master, Junji Ito . Ito's horror is based on environments where obssesions are out of control, usually due to unnatural events, and not only for a few isolated people, but for the vast majority of a community. The strangest, most maccabre things happen and only a few remain sane enough to notice them. It's, in a way, all about the feebleness of human mind. I think that's the reason both styles can be mixed so well. World of Horror drinks from those waters without trying to hide it, but it manages to come up as something with its own value. I don't expect anyone who likes that kind of horror to be dissapointed.Gameplay: 8.5The gameplay loop is similar to games like Nuclear Throne, where you choose a character and perhaps a few perks , tweak some gameplay aspects (difficulty, seed, game mode) and dive into a randomly generated world. To overcome the random trials (5 investigations plus ending "dungeon") you will need to make the best use of the items and perks you randomly receive. The events you face are also random, so the same strategy won't always work. This formula isn't exactly new, but it has been sucessfullly applied to a genre with very few precedents, and that's something. WOH features 7 different characters (each with their own unique perks, starting equipment, expertises and stat distribution from the 8 stats the game features), many backstories to choose from (which add an extra layer of customization), three dificulty settings, and a decent variety of items, equipment, spells, shops, enemies and random events to face. The in-game archievement system provides a cool incentive to keep playing by unlocking new equipment, game modes and characters with each archievement. Some of them require a whole, very specific run to be done, so even if the gameplay loop can seem repetitive after the first pair of games, you'll realize you'll have plenty to do if you want to really taste everything this game has to offer.Lastly, since the game will apparently feature mod and custom stories support, the amount of content could potentially rise exponentially. If a decent community of horror writers flourishes around this game and the proper tools are given to them, we could  be facing something big. I certainly hope so.Overall: 9 I would recommend this game without hesitation to anyone who wishes to experience something fresh and yet familiar, and to those who love horror and roguelites. It has its flaws, sure, and it's still unpolished in some aspects, but the overall experience is solid, and It's cheap enough that even if you don't love it as much as I do, you won't feel robbed.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot honestly express how much I love this. It's unsettling and creepy, and it's all the best of horror all milked together without being jump scare. It's such a wonderful psychological and body-horror centric game, and it has so many wonderful little things. I've been playing since it all came out, and watching early access play-throughs and devouring everything that I could. It's such a great game, and there's so many little things that you'll never realize unless you're dedicated. I definitely recommend it, and I generally hate horror because of all the nothing-but-gore-and-jump-scares. Support the developers! This is such a wonderful game.

_childDocuments_.review: World of Horror is a story driven rogue-lite. You will be faced with a multitude of choices around every corner. Random events could bless you with rewards to assist in your investigation, or they could plague you with curses and other unfortunate events making your run hell. The difficulty is reasonable, once I found out how the combat worked the rest came naturally for me. There is a lot going on with this game, each investigation has multiple endings, and many events have good/bad/random outcomes. The game will be just different enough every run to keep you enjoying the game, while simultaneously giving just enough knowledge to perform better your next run. The more challenges you complete, the more items get added into the loot pool, changing your games even more. The atmosphere, art, and story telling is top notch, I just wish they had even more stories to choose from! I cannot recommend this game highly enough, and is certainly my style as a person who enjoys rogue lites, and the horror genre. If you too enjoy the spooky story telling through RNG based events, sprinkled with combat and investigation then I cannot recommend this title enough.

_childDocuments_.review: The thing that first pulls you into this game is the visuals. They are really the best thing about the game. It is obvious that the artist is taking heavy inspiration from horror manga, especially Junji Ito, and they pull it off really well. The game itself is strange. It is based off of 80s detective video games, and as a result is purposely primitive and bare bones. I've never played those games, so I didn't know what to expect going in, and was initially put off by the gameplay. It involves traveling to different locations and conducting "investigations" to find clues. Most of this is completely luck based, and most of your enjoyment comes from the visuals and the story, which are both very good, but a lot of the time it feels more like a very interactive visual novel than a game. That is not to say there is no strategy to it, you have to watch your stamina, reason, and doom levels to make sure you don't die, and you can buy items and increase stats to give yourself a better chance in events, but the majority of the game is RNG based.Personally, I enjoyed this game, but I don't think it is for everyone due to how weird and bare bones the gameplay is.I nominate this game for Outstanding Visual Style6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Gripping survival horror rpg that is a race against the clock to stop an elder god. The game's mechanics demand careful planning to receive spells, items, and companions. The art alone sells this game and got me invested with the mysteries.There are a few problems with this game. The save system is pretty janky. The player is slightly to punished to encourage playing the game without saving. I found that equipment would go back to storage, but the stats they give would stay. Injuries were similar in that the stat penalties would stay, but the injury would be removed. This gave me permanent stat decreases. Both these issues seem unintended because they were not described among the penalties for saving. This can be overlooked since the game is short enough to played without saving. However, sometimes I would get fatal crashes which would end the run and leave a bitter taste in my mouth. Overall the game is worth the buy in it's current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I see all of the Junji Ito fans here crawling out of the woodwork...And I'm one of them. And this game takes after him exquisitely.Typically I absolutely hate rogue-likes because of the RNG aspect, but this game seems very well balanced. Undeniably, as with most rogue-likes, you will get shafted by the randomness of it all sometimes- my shortest run on Normal was 5 minutes. Particularly once all of the kinks, bugs, and typos are worked out, I can see if being nothing short of a masterful homage to the master himself.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game hindered only by an out of date tutorial.The game is essentially a reskinning of a board game, Arkham Horror, but as a single-player rogue-lite RPG. It has a lot of unlockables, a lot of replay value, and modability to add the only thing that keeps it from living onwards further, new experiences. If you enjoy the existential horror aspects, the unique experience of retro PC gaming styles, or just a good run-based pool of decision making, World of Horror is a solid outing for the price, and fairly unique from a pure style standpoint.The one downside is that the tutorial leaves much to be desired. It doesn't do much to actually guide people into the decision-making process, it mostly just lays out a series of a couple of combat actions to do, and then sends you on your way, without explaining why you might want to do any of them. Nor does it point out any of what the information on the combat screen means. I've seen so many new players bump into the tutorial, only to do it 3 or 4 times trying to actually beat it.  Mostly because the tutorial gives them actions that defeat the purpose of items given to them by the tutorial, weakening them.Worse yet, when you go to the next complexity down, "Extracurricular Activities", it actually gives you the tutorial info for your stats, inventory, etc. Something that needs explaining in the initial tutorial as well. Plus, things like the main overview screen, where the sidequest isn't explained as a side quest, nor are locations like shops and the hospital. The UI does have a lot of information overload, and without a decent tutorial, I've seen dozens run up against mechanics they don't understand and get frustrated, lose, or simply miss the answers to the questions they have, because they stumble into the overload unprepared.Once you've gotten used to the UI, you look past a lot of these things. Especially if you're familiar with the board game, you get that everything is just a stack of cards and you're randomly drawing things and rolling a dice against a stat.  It isn't hard if you're used to a lot of info being crammed into small spaces. But just the amount of times I've seen streamers pick up the game for the first time and run into issues, makes me realize that the tutorial is clearly just too bare bones for the amount of info that the game wants you to process.

_childDocuments_.review: This game manages to blend elements of Lovecraft and Junji Ito's style of horror, and create something wonderfully unique. The old, arcade-like visual style combines perfectly with the eerie soundtrack, and creates a surreal experience that's rather haunting. It's tough as nails sometimes, but with so many different events, enemies, and endings to discover, I keep coming back for more. The customization for your runs is also very in-depth, and with the unlockable content and (I'm guessing) future DLC/expansions, the possibilities are endless. I've only just begun to scratch the surface of World of Horror, but I definitely want to dig deeper, and solve the eldritch mysteries lurking within. 10/10

While the game still has some more fleshing out to do, it's still in early access and I cannot wait to see what the dev does in the future. It is already a spectacular game and I highly recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, this game is awesome, I played it over and over until I got most of the achievements, I love the concept on the whole (Lovecraft's Eldritch/Cosmic Horror meets Japanese horror stories), and it's probably one of the better rogue-likes on a mechanical level with interesting and relatively balanced combat and event systems that leave you wanting to do 'just one more run'. ON THE OTHER HAND, I'm now going to vent & nitpick for a few minutes because I am irrationally frustrated at a few minor details that should be addressed*:1) Some of the events are a little wonky and need some fixing. A spontaneously gained Spell here, a double-registered loss of Stamina there. Just some small stuff that I only noticed on my up-teenth run, so it never ruined the flow of game-play (except on one very specific occasion, but ruining a run ain't no skin off my bones). (To be a bit more specific, the 'Falling Asleep' event spontaneously gives you a free spell for passing the strength check, which doesn't really apply as a reward, and the 'Cast One Free Spell' event with the stone statues does not apply to any spells that cost stamina, only experience and reason costs.)*UPDATED* - The specified events 'Falling Asleep' and 'Cast One Free Spell' seem to work as intended now. However, a few other events seem to be wonky instead, including the new Character-Exclusive events that were recently added as well as some of the old ones. I currently think it is mostly a bug with receiving certain types of healing rewards but I can't be certain. The Mimi event 'Life or Limb', for example, seems to give 2 Reason & +10 Experience for FAILING the dexterity check on the Surgery option. Although, this might be intentional when considering some checks tend to punish the player for finding out TOO much about a monster or horror, like with the 'Chat with Old Friend' event in downtown that takes away reason for succeeding in finding out more. Also, the Idol Girl event 'Price of Fame' has the 'try to forget' option which, on the screen's description after the blurb about her past, SAYS it gave you +10 Exp & 1 Reason, it actually TAKES AWAY 1 Reason instead.2) Some of the characters may need a bit of balancing. Some are damn-near unplayable without RN-Jesus smiling holy luck onto your run, such as the Priest guy you can unlock, while others make the game child's play in a few tries, namely Aiko the Fit Girl who can be absolutely broken with a steak knife, her many Dexterity and attack-based perks, and maybe a stat point or two in Dex. Either way, might need some fine-tuning.*UPDATED* - Aiko the Fit Girl has now been nerfed quite severely in the most recent update by making the steak knife (and other Dex-focused weapons) very inaccurate to compensate for their ridiculous attack speed. Thus, Aiko now has a CHANCE to do absolutely ridiculous damage unless you are compensating by lowering the enemy's power or simply being very lucky. The Priest is still fairly difficult, but considering he has such a unique mechanic and is a late-game unlock, I can buy him being a niche way to up the difficulty, so he doesn't necessarily need to change much.3) Remember how I said you can absolutely break combat with a Steak Knife on an Aiko-Dex run? Yeah, if you manage to get enough 'actions' in on a turn, such as with small attacks with the Steak Knife like so, you break the action meter that tracks how much time each action costs. After maybe eight or nine, the meter stops displaying additional actions but the INPUT for it still works, meaning if you click the button three more times after the display breaks, you have to cancel three times to bring it back. That's definitely not working as intended and should certainly be fixed. (Note: still not fixed as of most recent update.)4) Some achievements are a tad, hmm, unfair. For example, I (the foolishly obsessive lout I am) wanted to do all the achievements, including the one for 'Completing the Game on Hard Mode'. Naturally, I checked a few guides, the achievement itself, and the available difficulty settings, concluding that the 'True Despair' achievement did not mean the 'True Believer' difficulty, which was the SECOND-hardest, oh no, no. I thought 'It MUST be the HIGHEST difficulty' since obviously, that's what I'd consider with the information given. Yadda yadda, beat the mode, took a screenshot for proof, basked in the afterglow and... no achievement.Yeah, turns out the 'Hard Mode' that was referred to was not the HARDEST mode, but one step below that. That... that was pain. And now I propose to you, potential reader, a quandary: "Why the hell don't you get the 'True Despair' achievement after completing the even HARDER difficulty?" Well I don't flip-flapping know. In short, this (as well as some of the character completion achievement rewards, but that may just be a bug) did not work, and that makes no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense. Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk. (Note: I don't want to reset my progress & do this again to see if it was fixed, so it may or may not be fixed but I don't care enough to check.)Anyways, besides that I'm loving it.8/10 - Would throw a tantrum again.EDIT: Found another bug, so I'll note it here for documentation's sake. On the 'Upper Kingdom' other-world event, where you can use either an Empty Bottle or the Goblet to contain some of the blood from the waterfall, having both in your inventory (even with the Goblet above it in the list sequentially) forces the event to register the Empty Bottle as the only available option for containing the blood.This is a problem because it's a LOT of work, luck, and RNG to even ACQUIRE the Goblet in the first place and the chance of encountering that PARTICULAR other-world event with it in your inventory are pretty low.  Now, couple this with the fact that you normally have an Empty Bottle in your inventory anyway, whether you start with one or you buy one, and suddenly you get screwed out of the associated achievement, the bonus +6 to both Reason & Stamina, and are stuck with a bottle that, at worst, gives you +3 DOOM and needs to be thrown away. Also, of course, drinking the formerly-Empty Bottle kills you, which might be nice if you want to find all the endings, but as someone who already did that, this is an immense kick to the undercarriage.I swear I love this game, I really do, but some of these bugs make me IRRATIONALLY frustrated. Yadda yadda, thanks for reading. Still 8/10, but these bugs are making me tentatively give a 'buyer's beware' that this is STILL in early access for a reason, but is otherwise a great find.EDIT 2: Spelling, grammar, re-phrasing, & added instructions for Goblet quest.*EDIT 3: Some of these have been addressed in the most recent update to the game (Yay, the developer is alive and kicking again!) and yet more have popped up in their place. I'm going to put a big *UPDATED* for those that have been addressed or changed but remain problematic. Hopefully it's not too confusing, and I will update this as I experience the updated game for myself.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings a lo-fi cosmic horror experience I've been thinking about since the days of firing up the borrowed MicroBee at my Aunt's house and playing around with the weird adventure games on unlabelled floppies while the ambient sound of japanese horror films from the neighbours house drifted through window. It's filled with tight resource management, oozes atmosphere, and each update brings brand new art, items, stories, and horrible things to bother your character with.  The active and healthy mod community makes this a concrete FUTURE CLASSIC.
_childDocuments_.name: WORLD OF HORROR

_childDocuments_.review: junji itos works in their most enjoyable form yetBefore I start this review, I want to say that I have some bias due to my love for Junji. It works, and this game, being almost directly inspired by it, had me excited beyond belief even before purchasing it.I purchased this game long before its official 1.0 release, and I was worried it would fall into the early access curse that many games do, either becoming modern abandonware with or without a community supporting the game. However, I'm very glad to say it survived the long periods of silence from the developers, or more properly, the single developer who has clearly poured their heart and soul into this project.World of Horror is one of the first roguelikes I've tried, and it made me fall in love with the genre not only with its intriguing story and stories, the self-contained mystery service, and the game's overall plotline of reaching the lighthouse and saving the town from its demise. The heavy RNG-based gameplay encourages multiple playthroughs, and with the Steam Workshop support and various mods out there, the game is essentially endless.I recommend this game to anyone who is very into Junji and its works and anyone searching for a fun horror roguelike with an active community (at the time of writing, this could be subject to change, of course). It's worth the $20$, and it's even more worth it when it's on sale!
_childDocuments_.name: WORLD OF HORROR

_childDocuments_.review: World of Horror is simply an amazing game. Its fantastic 1-bit artstyle, combined with a great soundtrack succeeds in mixing together the H.P. Lovecraft-inspired world with japanese urban legends. And it all looks like it was drawn by Junji Ito! While the gameplay itself comes down to a fair amount of luck in each playthrough, the encounters, cases and atmosphere surrounding them more than makes up for it.In other words, if you are a fan of any of the genres/worlds mentioned above, give this game a try. It really deserves more attention and I hope the dev continues adding content.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially my review was a little negative, leaning towards a recommendation because of the fantastic art direction but some misgivings concerning the harsh roguelike mechanics that will keep new players locked into the early game for many, many cycles and new characters until a stroke of luck pushes you forward to the deeper side of the game.However, after the game has been fine-tuned and updated over the years, I think it has become as refined as the sharpest katana (find this weapon and conquer the game, seriously). A monumental effort that ranks with some of the best indie-horror I've played in recent years.Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: World of Horror is a solid turn-based RPG where most of the story takes place as a read narrative. The spooky text combined with the atmospheric music and the appearance of monsters is super effective at giving chills, like you're really immersed in this literal world filled with horrors. If you're into real life RPG and character stats, you'll love this. Even if you're not but are remotely into horror (like me), and you'll still love it because you can play by yourself, take your time with making choices and just enjoy the horror aspect without worrying about being alert and dying. It takes some getting used to but once you know where everything is, it's fun to try and get your character to survive and solve as many mysteries as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to articulate exactly how stellar this game is - the atmosphere is absolutely perfect, design choices range from gorgeous to unsettling to nightmarish, and the narrative themes drawn upon are diverse. _childDocuments_.review: A general rule among classic horror games seems to be that the true masterpieces are often more riddled with problems than the merely good games. World of Horror keeps to that. A love letter to Junji Ito and HP Lovecraft, World of Horror is a game dripping with aesthetic brilliance. From its engrossing 1-bit art design, to the simple-yet-not-overbearing music, to the rich world that will attempt to murder you at every turn, to the fun (and sometimes funny) touches in the game, the experience is thoroughly charming. The combat is simple but fairly deep; you have a limited time to perform a number of actions, and each action will take a different amount of time. If you've played Barkley: Shut up and Jam Gaiden, you'll be familiar with the style. The game is punishing, and often arbitrarily so. Sometimes a random event will just carve away a bit of your reason or stamina, with no means to prevent the damage. Encounters are often vicious, and the ever-looming threat of eldritch doom means that you won't want to escape said encounters too often. While it's certainly possible to beat, it's not easy to beat by any means. However, this is a horror-themed roguelike, so complaining about the seemingly-unfair difficulty feels a bit like going to a metal concert and complaining about how loud it is. You know what you're getting, may as well strap in and enjoy the punishment. The main issue I find with the game is that it could do with a number of quality-of-life adjustments. For instance, after certain missions, you can't get rid of items. If you want to change your moves in combat, you need to clear your entire queue and redesign your attack. The "find an improvised weapon" action feels really unnecessary; some tweaking to your unarmed strike and the enemy's strength seems preferable to just having to spend one turn per character grabbing a broken bottle and dodging. Finally, while I recognize that the unknown is a vital part of horror, I'm really not thrilled about not knowing my odds of succeeding or failing at individual stat checks. A bunch of little things add up to one major strike against the game. That being said, World of Horror is still a gem of a game, albeit a rough one, and given that it's still in early access, I can't take its flaws too personally. I heartily recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I will say WORLD OF HORROR has kind of a weird curve to adapt to because the UI is overwhelming, almost maximalist and at first I found the gameplay almost too arbitrary to be especially engaging but I found over time I started to warm to it as I viewed it more from the perspective of a game about "collecting different events" rather than simply always trying to win efficiently.I still think there are problems, playing WoH "well" is mostly a matter of committing to memory what every single event is going to stat check and making decisions based on that, so before you've done a fair few runs to have really zeroed on these, things are just going to kind of Happen at you arbitrarily without a lot of rhyme or reason and your grip on proceedings is going to feel pretty loose. I have a vague sense the game may be improved by just making it visible on the UI what stat an event is going to check, maybe after being seen once to at least preserve some of the amusing unpredictable occurrences of the first time seeing an event.But once you get into the swing of it, it becomes surprisingly breezy to play and fun to try and collect different outcomes and this is all buoyed by a really well-executed aesthetic sensibility, there's a lot of nice little touches that make your first couple of hours feel pretty tense and atmospheric, so it makes a good first impression, but after that wears off what'll make or break your time with WOH is going to be whether or not you can get into the mindset of trying to see lots of scenarios rather than trying to "solve" the game. For me, it was a bit touch and go but I ultimately came around on it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games because of RNG and "unlockable items" similar to The Binding of Issac, you'll dig this game on a purely mechanical basis. However, if you like some genuinely beautiful and horrifying art, the works of Junji Ito, as well as a really good mystery-hunting (not solving) game, you'll love this game. I've only got just under 13 hours at the time of writing this review, but honestly I am in LOVE with this game and I'm pretty sure it'll become my new favorite.There's so much versatility to get a really nice unique run, while also some ways to get standard ones if you just want a casual mode. The general vibe is top tier, there's so many little details here and there that will freak you out, and even when you think you've seen it all you'll notice something new and slight. However, this game is still a work in progress as well. I haven't ran into any major bugs in the game so far, however, there are still items without purpose and I've experienced a single moderate graphical glitch so far. If you do not like playing games while they're still in development, I'd definitely wait as I was somewhat miffed when I discovered that there wasn't a usage for the videotapes yet. More things to note, the learning curve is a wall, but once you get over it the game is smooth running. There's a slight tutorial in the game, however, I didn't know certain mysteries send you to "alternate maps" where you no longer had access to certain shops and facilities. I'd recommend watching at least one short lets play to have an idea of how the game work (as that was how I had interest in the game), and then going ham. Also, some monsters I fight so frequently they seem to lose their value while I have yet to see others even once yet. This can easily be changed by using a different "backstory" when creating your own run, however, I would enjoy having randomizer options even in the "choose your story" mode as I usually would at least like the god to be random.Ultimately, I recommend this game because: It's a nice RNG style with unlockable items/events/characters similar to my current favorite game. There's tons of mechanics overlapping with one and another, creating a highly intuitive gaming experience. The fighting system is very understandable while also complex, as well as the injury, curse, and other similar features affect it in really fun ways. Character level-trees are really fun to play with, and almost reminds me of Vampire the Masquerade Bloodlines in how you might have different conversations, event experiences, and other similar things based upon traits (some of which you may not have known could affect some things). It's got really gorgeous art with horrifying details, and retains a solid atmosphere through and through. All in all, this game is definitely a diamond in the rough and I can't wait to see the full version--but until then, I am quite happy and satisfied playing the pre-release as it was very much affordable for the amount of entertainment I'm getting from it.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:+ Fantastic events and exploration the first few times through+ Branching paths lead to different endings for many investigations+ Secret endings, achievement unlocks and multiple ancient evil options give a lot of replay-ability and customization+ Amazing fusion of Japanese horror and Lovecraft-ian horror, many events leave a visual and psychological impact the first couple times you see them+- I really loved the soundtrack. Retro-horror game music with track changeover from exploration to a combat version of said music works incredibly well for this style of game.The Meh:-Challenges are almost entirely RNG-based. Good preparation will almost always win you a playthrough on Normal difficulty, but you're really just at the mercy of RNG for harder difficulties and challenge modes-Many of the items in the game are worthless. You'll aim to get a couple specific items on each play depending on your character and ignore the rest. The fact that you have to buy 95% of them from a shop (i.e., you'll never see them as random drops from enemies/events) gives zero incentive to ever use the inferior items-Usually you want characters to have a mix of strengths and weaknesses so you can try different strategies. Unfortunately, the only difference between most characters is "which base stat is highest so I can go buy a weapon that matches it." There are a couple exceptions that start with an item or spell capability that changes how you approach their run, but the overlying strategy across all of them is about the same.--  Special shout out to challenge modes that turn certain characters into "Oops! All Weaknesses!"- The interface for exploration and especially combat takes some... getting used to. You won't even realize all of the options you have at your disposal because many of them are sub-menus that you have to click into. Even starting a custom run for the first time or two isn't intuitive because there's a lot of option clutter. Not to mention certain options only exist on the menu during specific encounters...Overall:A very good pick-up for the price. It's fun, replay-able, and has a great atmosphere. Moderate learning curve on how the interface works because the creators wanted to maximize options and customize-ability, you may want to find a guide or video of someone playing it to build some familiarity with where everything is.

_childDocuments_.review: A big "don't recommend" simply for how unenjoyable and bulls**t the "challenges" are. I would normally just ignore those things altogether, but of course the dev had to go and make them mandatory to unlock the secret playable character. It's not just that they're hard - with the Old Gods being random and difficulty always set on "hard mode", things that could change to make them more bearable -, but because they're a painful slog to get through, as well. The entire idea behind each of the challenges is "What if you had to play on hard mode with a character that's deliberately deprived of what makes playing them tolerable?" Not to say they're all equally hard, or equally boring to play through, but enough are, and there's a lot of them. I don't wanna spend hours upon hours trying and failing to get through those things just to unlock the character, therefore I do not recommend this game.

The gameplay is... well, very similar to eldritch horror boardgame, but in singleplayer.On the bad side, I understand that is a horror game and I should be scarce on resources, but I would like the game to offer me more choices, sometimes you just get "a bad hand" and you are dead. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this, but right now the only good thing about it is the aesthetic. After just a couple hours of playing, I've seen most encounters (only 1-2 seem to be relevant to your current "Mystery" and the rest are pulled from a generic pool via RNG) and most of the Mysteries as well.  There are *extremely* few opportunities to up your stats or even get a weapon, so most runs are spent hammering the default "Kick" button while watching your HP and sanity drop, and your chances to win coin flips don't get any better either (and it seems to default to about a 75% loss rate), and every time your "Doom" passes a certain threshold, you're saddled with a permanent debuff (like not being able to recover between Mysteries) that makes things even more annoying.The battling and encounters suck, but it's also clear that this game is still *very* incomplete. I've picked up items that can't be dropped or stored or used (I guess they're intended for future content, but until the appropriate content patch comes out, you're permanently down an inventory space if you find it), music that's supposed to progress along with the worsening state of the town will reset itself to the chipper starting version when you leave the screen, and there are so many pointless little threads or things that look like they should do something and don't. It only takes ~20 minutes to do a run once you start seeing the same irrelevant things over and over and over, and the game just feels massively unfair, so this one's a nope from me, dawg. The 80's PC game/Junji Ito aesthetic IS neat, but the novelty wears off quickly.  I wouldn't bother with it until version 2.0 or something, maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: This is basically like a card-heavy board game, for better or worse. The stats are pretty rudimentary and used mostly to pass skill checks, wherein the game tosses a d12 for you and if your stat is equal to or greater than the number you get, you pass. Other than that you have Health and Sanity, excuse me; "Stamina" and "Reason", which you can lose by way of enemies and events, and if you run out you die.The items and status effects and allies are all basically just asset cards giving you stat buffs or debuffs, and even the allies can be discarded for a boost in combat.It's main gameplay comes from investigating locations and tackling "events" drawn randomly from a pool, or you might say deck, of events. This makes it so said events might be jarring for the location and/or story of the current mystery, but imo that just enhances the board game feel so I don't even view it as a negative. The events are usually just a short relatively self-contained piece of narration followed by a skill check, or it often gives you a choice of actions before deciding which stat to check against, or to do a skill check at all, and then it might for instance give you an item or experience if you succeed, or maybe damage you or increase "Doom" if you fail. Or the event might throw you right into combat.The combat is the most video gamey part of it tbh, though that too is often just deciding to attack and/or defend, which is itself just a skill check, and the enemy usually just does a set amount of damage after your turn. But there are some more intricacies to it, like throwing and using items, or that weird ritual stuff against ghost enemies.Speaking of Doom; that's the timer you have, and it increases every action, or turn, you take, bringing with it the reckoning of the Outer God which you are trying to keep away. There are some few events that thankfully decrease this Doom though.Now, any fans out there of FFG's Arkham Horror series might be thinking that this is sounding oddly familiar. And they'd be right.This game keeps getting touted as a "Junji Ito meets Lovecraft" game, but to be precise I think it'd be better to call it a digital Arkham/Eldritch Horror with a Junji Ito aesthetic. I find myself sincerely doubting that the creator of this game hasn't played one of those board games.That's not a negative though. I probably rather like this game  of those similarities, and if you're an Arkham Horror fan you probably will too.

_childDocuments_.review: Three years ago I bought this game on a whim, being on wave of hype about roguelikes and roguelites of different sorts. I remember finishing ten or so cases, having played through tutorial and preset run once or twice. Afterwards, it seems, my knowledge of game comes from LPs and videos from influencers. Why? Well...For start, let's say, graphics in this game are great, if stylish. You could FEEL Ito influence from screenshots alone and Lovecraftiang motives are noticeable too. Its weird to see also chibi versions of characters time from time, I guess author thought making some cute horror will create contrast.Sound design is also okay, maybe even great. I tried to play WoH at night with headphones and it wasn't that scary, but atmospheric.So, point is, artistically this project is great and if it was all animation, like in release trailer, I will pitch this game to every my friend at every opportunity. However, problem is, this is GAME, you see.And how bad this GAME is! Its text adventure with random chances for this and that, which makes you feel you are just pilot of self-driving car, which already programmed to reach specific destination. Picking order of places to visit is MOST thing you could do. Maybe it gives sense of inability to act against elder gods, but gameplay wise this stuff sucks.Battles are also quite similar and repetetive. I never saw fights against more than one enemy and for most part I was picking same most damaging/healing options for play. There are many statuses, many relics and weapons, many enemy types... But compared to other roguelikes of sorts they feel artistically diverse, but same gameplay wise. It's not good.Compare this game to Yahtzee's Consuming Shadow, which came out ten years ago or so. It looked like sheet, but was more interesting to play overall, granting player more options to influence flow of game. Here, you can switch between few items you have, remove spells "tactically", but it nothing matters if you meet random event with powerful monster.GUI also needs a lot of time to get used to and it's just... a mess of numbers and text, which is bad even for text game WoH is. Each status and some actions have graphics, but this isn't enough to keep process of jumping through menus engaging.Obviously, last straw for me writing this review was release of 1.0. Game was in development for three years. Three damn years. Some games, even from solo devs, get huge updates, even change their nature due to new stuff. What we got here?3 new stories and 2 new characters. Okay, I've read about it in AUGUST news message. Release message says NOTHING about what 1.0 brings, not speaking about changelog. In fact, me and few of my friends totally forgot about release and weren't presented with message about release in PC Steam - and even mobile version message was easily missable. I learned about release from DreadXP channel stream of Horror Game Show which also was watched me by random. What is this promotion?So, what I was also shocked about? Dev is Polish, as it says even on wiki. There is no Polish language in 1.0 version. There were many people from Eastern Europe, especially Russia and Ukraine, who were supporting game with money and positive reviews. There is no Russian or Ukrainian in 1.0. Publisher did German and French translations for "their great supporters from Europe"... Even if statistically, most popular language, even more than English, is Spanish. So, in short, I can't even give a f about HOW priority of translation past English/Chinese/Japanese went.And, finally. Many games, even small ones, have such usual or nice features like achievements, cards, workshop support and could saves. This game got NOTHING of this on 1.0. Devs and Pubs basically hope you will enjoy game as it is, without any other inspiration for finishing it aside of atmophere and popularity it gained.Thing is, even popular games are trash. In fact, they even more likely to be trash, even from indie studios with solo dev. World of Horror is great art object, but bad game with too abstract narrative and not working repetetive gameplay full of random.Go play Consuming Shadow, some horror text RPG like Omen Exitio or just horror game, normal one, with multiplayer or puzzles which give you fun diverse gameplay situations. World of Horror will very likely stay all the same through all of runs. And new content we'll get in six or more months probably, if dev even plans to support game still. WoH feels like horror themed tunnel ride which you could enjoy once or twice, but then you need to be REALLY crazy about artistic presentation to play again.P.S. Chinese downvoting is bad, but apparently its once again because of mistranslations on publisher part. People, giving game good reviews to "counter-balance" that without describing anything about game, or even playing it are likely to be blamed for misinformation too.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam really needs to add in a "Meh"/~ review! Not a "bad" game by any means, but somehow, despite it's somewhat unique gameplay, still feels unoriginal and ESPECIALLY incomplete. Not a bad game, but somehow feels incomplete.  I would grab it to support the devs, but NOT at full price. I would go for the 25% discount at most.  Half price feels fair for what you get out of it.    The game is a good idea, but needs a bit more baking in the oven before we can call it done.As a general rule of thumb, I expect to get 1 hour of gameplay out of every $1/100円 I spend on a game, and this one falls a bit short.  It relies too heavily on the idea that multiple people will eventually mod the game and add more content for them.The art style is good. The music and sounds fit the retro style they are going for.  I genuinely love the looks of some of the monsters and how they bring a lot of japanese yokai/horror stories into the game. And although the tutorial is a bit lacking and the game doesn`t hold your hand, I don`t mind it at all. So why the "meh"?  Probably because the RNG on it is a bit TOO much RNG.  I don`t just mean in terms of combat either (which can be really finicky too), but rather how it handles the story generator.     There have been several times where it had me "Exploring the  of a school" and then suddenly saying "You found the swimming pool"!  Or "You ran into the boss of your current job! Should you get a tattoo for him?"     They just don`t fit and feel REALLY out of place.  A lot of variables default to "000's place" or "000 Company".  And Ⅰ mean that literally.  Half of the locations in the game are literally named "000"There is a good selection of missions, but they always play out the same. The appeal is purposely messing up or sticking strictly to what the game tells you to do, to get the other endings. Some quests allow a "half-complete" ending, but feel sort of shoe-horned in.  Combat is kind of odd too. There are no real "bad" choices to make during combat, but some feel kind of unneeded. Why would I spend 150 points to do a HARD attack with 60% accuracy and 30 damage, when I could spend 45 points doing 3+ small attacks with 85% accuracy and 10 damage for each?  No matter how you slice it, my 3x 85% accuracy for 10 damage, will ALWAYS trump my 1x 60% accuracy for 30 damage, so why bother having it in the first place?  Hell, I can sacrifice 10 damage to increase my dodge, while still having a good chance to do 20 damage...     The combat just devolves into a "can I kill them in 1-2 rounds, or do I need to default to the "attack,attack,dodge/block" formula? The prayer combat option for ghosts is nice though! It really breaks from the mold of the above mentioned combat style.  Don`t have magical weapons or spells that can hurt ghosts? Time to pray victory!...literally! The bestiary is kind of pointless too.  You can see the name of the monster you fought, but no details.  If you want details, you need to study it WHILE in combat, and only there.  The bestiary will just hold the name of it. Not even a photo.    I love games with some extra flavor-text but this game doesn`t handle it very well.  Same for items, quests and other "extras" we can "look at".   Stats feel REALLY pointless, due to the RNG nature of the game.    Try to lift a heavy box?  Game shows it as  (8/3), with your character having a STR of 5. Well, you failed... Why? Game doesnt say, but lets assume it is because apparently the 8 is larger than the 3.  So you think that "OK, We need the second number to be larger than the first!"  Later you make another STR roll with it being (2/7). You still failed....   Which side represents what you rolled? Which side represents the difficulty to beat? No Idea!  Feels like a coin flip every time, regardless if your STR is 1 or 10.Your stats don`t matter anyway, because nearly every level up has you putting it to gain +3 reason(sanity) or +stamina (health), since you lose if either reach 0.  It is literally more cost-effective to put the points in your health/sanity than in a character stat, where you risk losing 1-2 points in HP/Sanity.I have to say though, that despite its really bad flaws:  I REALLY like this game.  It isn`t perfect by any means, but sometimes, if the light is right, you can spot that bit of diamond beneath the rough of this game.  It isn`t good, but you can`t help but feel some respect for what the developers were trying to do.   I just can`t give it a positive review, since it still feels incomplete and relies WAY to heavily on it`s fans creating content to make it better.  Grab it if it is on sale, for the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Certainly a good game overall. If you're the kind of person who thinks something like this might appeal to you, it likely will. It's unique, and has a fair amount of replayability (probably somewhere between 5-20 hours worth, depending on how into the genre you are.) It's beautiful, though I suspect making a game composed entirely of handmade black-and-white pixel-art down to each and every background is akin to making an MMO in the sense that a friend would never let you attempt it. Again, it's gorgeous, but given the art style, it's pretty easy to see why - in spite of stellar sales for an indie game at this genre intersection - the game was apparently not finished, and will likely remain in something similar to its current state for quite a long time, if not forever.World of Horror, even in its 1.0 release, is still missing some critical features. The game has a robust achievements and unlocks system presented in a style most reminiscent of Risk of Rain and Vampire Survivors, but the game is not integrated with Steamworks in any way. This means no Steam Cloud (you will have to earn those achievements all over again in the event of a corrupt installation, failed hard drive, forgetting to transfer before installing a new OS, etc.), no Steam Achievements, and no remote play support. Further, the scaling of the game is capped at 3:1, which can make playing in 4K a hassle, particularly if you are streaming in lower resolutions on a personal platform like Discord. Finally, mods exist but there is no official toolset or support as of yet (beyond having place for them in the menu,) so their implementations vary from simple asset replacement to the sort of janky experience you'd expect from early 00's era CRPG mods like those found in WeiDU. There are also a number of places where placeholder content is plain to see: There is a "Talk" UI element, yet none of the recruitable allies will have anything to say beyond two universal, generic lines. A number of names of places and people are simply "OOO." (There may be some inside joke about this one, maybe it's to circumvent copyright or defamation claims, maybe it's a Lovecraftian "Scary Name So Scary and Inconceivable" joke, but I'll be honest in saying that it just comes off as lazy and immediately breaks immersion.) I'm certain that the difficulty settings could have also used another pass, alongside the spells. I've run the game three times and succeeded each time, up to the highest difficulty setting, despite having almost no experience with adventure games of this kind. The game is remarkably breakable. In one instance, I received a spell that allowed me to flee encounters for the remainder of the current Mystery (read: mission/chapter/level) at the cost of Sanity (a form of health.) Except that in this instance, the Old God I had selected made spells cost Doom instead of Sanity. Doom is a player stat that, while it can be trivially reduced, serves as a sort of time limit for a playthrough - reaching 100% Doom means you lose the game. And with this combination, for the normal cost of fleeing one encounter (~5% Doom), I could flee the half dozen or so that come up in each Mystery. Unfortunately, this spell and Old God combination were all that was required to break the game. As there are five Mysteries per playthrough, I could complete the entire playthrough fighting only one or two enemies who couldn't be run from, accumulating only 25% Doom. This made the playthrough entirely riskless, which would be a problem for a game in any genre, but doubly so for a horror game. This was far from the only broken combination I acquired in only a small number of playthroughs, which again, were all completed successfully up to the hardest difficulty setting. It's a shame when a potential game for all time comes out of Early Access this way. Again, it's more than passable, but it needs a lot more love to be great. All that said, I do recommend the game, with a casual warning about a largely untested independent developer - if they move on to a sequel while leaving this game in its current state, it's probably a good idea to pass on purchasing both as a matter of principle. It's one thing to release an unpolished indie game and let it be, and another entirely to use consumer money to reach a deeply flawed release.

_childDocuments_.review: Been waiting for this one and, even in early access, I'm satisfied with the purchase. I love the art, I like the game play and it just oozes with personality.I see alot of references to rogue-like and RPG and I think it does the game a disservice. It has much more in common with board and card games, think Arkham Horror.  If you come in expecting a contiguous storyline or deep systems you're likely to come out disappointed. The two primary "Campaigns" are just tutorials. The first scenario places you in an extremely linear scenario to learn the basic interactions and the second is the full game with a pre-selected setup. The core of the game will be the quick play and custom modes where you mix and match characters, card packs, dark gods. There is repetition because you're mixing and matching packs instead of running unique stories.Your overall goal is to solve 5 mysteries before the doom track reaches %100. After solving each mystery you'll encounter one global rule change that can impact the rest of the game. To help push back against the growing darkness you keep your items, stats and allies from previous mysteries. The mysteries themselves involve "Investigating Locations" which is basically just drawing a card based on the location and resolving the effects. These can range from mini-branching-stories to "You have bad dreams. Doom +3%". This is where RPG/RL players will be disappointed. Each location has a set pool of cards and repetition will happen often and quickly.While you can investigate any location at any time, mysteries will have you following a specific trail with 1 optional sidequest (Investigate another location X times). These 5-10 mystery specific events lead to branching endings.  While relatively meaningless, usually only offering a minor bonus/penalty per ending, it's fun to try and find all of the endings.This loop continues until either you or the dark forces are defeated. My play time both on my successful and failed runs have been under an hour total. The balancing needs some work because your RNG determines whether you steamroll the bad guys or they do you. The decisions themselves are fairly light and revolve around how to balance your resources. The last thing worth mentioning is that mod support and custom events are planned. This means that the repetition issues are likely to lessen over time as development continues and players get the ability to add content. Overall, I'm happy to have picked this up day one.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun 1-bit (or 2-bit if you are packing the latest in personal computing technologies!) horror point&click adventure with Time Unit based fightan system. Music is catchy and fun even though it's basically somebody violating a MIDI system. Combat is not hard to figure out it's basically just time management where you have 200 time units worth of actions and you try to shove in the best combination of moves to not die, go insane and kill the enemy. Art style is very good for what it's trying to convey and the little animation that the game has is used effectively (EELS!). The gameplay time is very short for a single run allowing the player to play the game in multiple quick spurts and not be forced to cancel weddings or funerals to find the time to play. You constantly unlock new events, characters and locations from just playing the game, though some of the achievements needed for unlocking requires some RNG. If you are looking for fun and playtime optimized gaming experience (and you don't mind needles near your eyes...) I warmly recommend World of Horror.

_childDocuments_.review: So, after the first 3 hours I would not have recommended this game. It's far more frustrating than enjoyable. For new players like myself, the best advice I can give...stick to investigating only circled areas in town and you'll have way more fun. If you get the bad water event early (first or second mystery), its probably better to restart.In my 4th hour of slogging through ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I finally won a play through. I stuck to the bare bones investigations and not being adventurous with any event choices. That and I found the Katana. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is this weapon insane. Not only that, I found the Demon Mask. I ORKO'd a boss fight with this set up on Aiko. After the stars finally aligning for me, the ending felt like a huge disappointment. _childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful old-school adventure game in the vein of Lucasarts/Sierra's previous work, but with a much more macabre theme.  Obviously inspired by the likes of Junji Ito and his brand of beautifully surreal horror manga, it pits you against a town haunted by the impending DOOM of an evil God. But it's a beautiful little rogue-like, turn based rpg game, with a simple, yet effective turn based combat system, complete with items, stats, and spells.  Encounters in the game can either be choice based ("You see a strange light, pulling you. [Resist][Walk towards light])" or combat based, or a combo of both.  Choice based encounters then do a roll check against your stats, leading to success or failure and accompanying consequenceEach play-through (Either Quick Play or Custom) consists of this: starting at your apartment, and picking your first mission out of five on your conspiracy theory wall.  Before choosing your mission, you have a few other options you can explore, like your closet, taking a bath, watching tv, and more, which add flavor or actual benefits to the experience.  As you spend time investigating your mission, you will most likely gain DOOM as you progress. As doom increases, the town you investigate can gain certain statuses that increase the chance of certain encounters happening each time you [Investigate].  Said statuses only have a chance of appearing upon completion of a mission.  Each mission has multiple branches/endings which are altered by your actions, choices, and items in your possession. The game does not have an easy mode, but it does have a "Tutorial Mission" of sorts, which is the story of the School Scissors Ghost .  A self contained mission, it allows the player a glimpse of the general experience provided by the other two Game Modes, Quick Play or Custom play-through. A cool story about a ghost haunting a school, featuring multiple endings, and a randomized set of events and encounters.  It will teach you about the turn based nature of investigating, combat, and encounters, while rewarding you with quite surreal, macabre pixel art.  This story can appear as one of the missions in the Quick Play or Custom game modes.A fail state in any game type will usually consist of a Reason or Stamina loss, but I think I have died by too much DOOM as well.  You can gain Acheivements, as well as keep track of the events, endings and enemies you've fought throughout your different runs, as the only real sense of progress.  There are things to unlock upon completion of run as the main reward upon completion, which i shall look forward to.The difference between Quick play and Custom is small, but game changing.  Quick play sets you with the same character, stats, and God chosen every time, Events are randomized like always.  Gods chosen alter things that seem small but have have a huge effect in the long term.  In quick play, your God forces you to rest less, as resting increases your DOOM every time.  In Custom, you can choose your character, which each have different sets of skills, spells and items that change the play style slightly, as well as getting to choose your own God.  You can customize it further too, with various effects that can be changed by the addition of mods and other features you can unlock.  There are 4 gods to start with, but there seem to be more that i think i need to either unlock or wait to be released by the developer.The best thing about this game?  The Mystery.  There's a little pantheon menu in the extras screen that allows you to click on four different little icons, like some sort of code.  I have no idea what it does, but i hope to find out through playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a product of passion and it shows. The graphics and music are really well done, full of charm and nostalgia-inducing. The gameplay is a mix of a point-n-click adventure and some RPG and roguelite elements, such as a levelling up system, random encounters and turn-based battles. Replayability is very high - you can basically randomise every element of the game if you want, and there is a ton (100+) of encounters, with more on the way. Moddding support is to be released, which will undoubtedly increase it even further. A playthrough is around 45 minutes, which consists of solving 5 random cases and a final dungeon. As it is still in EA, expect some bugs (I haven't encountered anything gamebreaking yet though). The price is fair in my opinion. Overall highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this game is really good. The visuals are great, and it has a lot of really cool ideas. The main problem that it suffers from is a general lack of cohesion. _childDocuments_.review: I've been enjoying this game so far and think it's fairly fun, it definitely has a few flaws being an early access game, but nothing that can be ironed out, the pixel art is well made and music is definitely enjoyable.I've always been a huge fan of the Junji Ito style, so to see this game be so inspired by it in their creation is quite nice.The only cons I have against this game is that the combat really feels on the weak side of RPG's, considering you can play the whole game just Blocking and Attacking to nullify most weaker enemies, and there also being no way to actively avoid being debuffed by certain enemies/bosses.I think a good way to fix this is to seperate the enemy attacks and debuffs, and make Debuffs only dodge-able and not blockable. Make it so we're not forced to just block all the time, but also have the option to dodge, maybe give bosses huge attacks that put them on cooldown so you're forced to have to avoid/block the attack or risk dying instantly, but then they're stunned so you can go all out.Lots of options for the devs to make it more intuitive, but as of right now I believe the combat really does need improvements, because I've only found that the block and attack prompts are the only real useful ones in the game.As for my other complaints, I think that there does need to at least be a few more "positive" encounters, because most encounters in this game, if not all, have some sort of negative to them, and it would be nice to have a couple positive ones snuck in there so it's not just all bad, even knowing this is the "world of horror."Oh and, I do believe spells could be a touch more useful, maybe outright make it so everyone has a beginner spell, since they all seem to have some form of downside you may as well allow us to just use it on any character.I rate the game 7/10, willing to go up to a 9/10 if improvements are made.

_childDocuments_.review: World of Horror is a cool game. The artwork is obviously based on Japanese horror like Junji Ito, and gameplay seems to be heavily inspired by old DOS choose-your-own-adventure style games from the late 80s/early 90s It is clear the developer put a lot of work into this game and I am thankful for that. Despite this, I can't personally enjoy the game, simply because it feels like it relies too heavily on luck. During the game you pass time and come closer to uncovering the mystery of the eldritch god by investigating various locations and resolving one-time events. For example, you may come across a doorway that is ominously pitch-black on the other side. You can choose to explore through the doorway or resist the urge and leave. There is a positive and negative outcome for both choices depending on a roll of the dice against your skill values, or sometimes by having a certain item. To me it is not an interesting game mechanic to have every decision be a risk, even the decision to not do anything. Like if you decide to leave the doorway alone, you still have a chance of losing vitality. Resource management is very difficult, and it can be really irritating to spend all your funds on healing up your vitals or wasting valuable time by resting to regain your vitals, only to lose 30% of your stamina in three turns due to bad rolls.Even on the easiest mode, the game is very unrelenting and it will often feel like it is simply up to fate to decide whether you progress or fail. I can see how this type of gameplay is interesting to some. I am reminded of popular games like Darkest Dungeon.I would definitely recommend this game even though I'm not personally a fan. I enjoy it as a piece of art, and I can see that for what it is, it's a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly replayable, World of Horror asks the player to singlehandedly thwart the coming apocalypse by investigating the surreal and strange happenings of Shiokawa, Japan (the default mode does, anyway). You choose a character, a backstory for them (an optional modifier to spice up a run), and an Elder God to throw hands with. This game has excellent art direction, an appropriately groovy soundtrack, and is well written for how fast things can go.My only gripe (and I imagine this will get addressed/ rendered obselete in the future), is that this game doesn't have Steam Workshop support. For a game so obviously inviting modders and creators to strut their stuff, I can't wait to see all the dumb-ass ♥♥♥♥ people put in their games. _childDocuments_.review: A fun and refreshing take on the well-worn rougelite genre, World Of Horror is immediately striking with its exceptional art and atmosphere, nearly unmatched by its ilk (especially considering it was made in MS Paint). While initially rather difficult and confusing WoH quickly picks up steam and becomes a great resource management RPG, with short (15-30) minute runs that don't overstay their welcome.The soundtrack and general mood is also exceptional, with many great tunes and designs that will get stuck in your head. In fact, the game has an absolutely amazing atmosphere overall, capturing that "found this game in an abandoned warehouse" energy perfectly. This makes it absolutely terrifying and exiting, especially during the early-game.World of Horror is short (It takes about 25-35 hours to complete 100% as of the latest update), and while this means that the game generally won't become boring in a standard play through, it also really shows that the game is nowhere near complete. Updates are extremely scarce (as this is being developed by one person), and while it is understandable this game is very limited in scope. I still highly recommend it, and while I strongly believe that it will one day become a cornerstone of survival horror, at the moment it is still a unique and truly nightmarish experience that you shouldn't miss.Overall: 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: World of Horror is an absolute awe-inspiring blend of Junji Ito and H.P. Lovecraft's works all packed into the poor, poor pixel village of Shiokawa. Armed with a combat system that takes time but is rewarding to master, multiple endings to many bite sized stories and stunning visuals, the player will find themselves playing over and over to fend off the old gods threatening to plague this unfortunate pixel world.I had this game on my wishlist for the longest time and waited for it to go on sale, only to actually be sad that I didn't pay  This game is absolutely amazing; the visuals are crisp and horrifying, the game plays smoothly and the content is very enjoyable for an 'early access' game. I genuinely recommend playing blind at first, though you'll likely still be playing blind even after the 'tutorial' the game offers; this is explained in the gameplay/combat part of my review. If you love all sorts of horror and tabletop rpgs, this game is absolutely something you should purchase.The game plays to me, like a table top rpg where you draw an 'event' from a deck of cards. From there, it is either a scripted event (Health loss, Item gain, etc.) or you get to choose an option which will make you roll a skill check. Depending on the outcome of the roll, you may get a variety of resolutions. If anything, the charm of the game is to find all of this out for yourself, but I provided a basic explanation. The Combat system initially seems a little clunky and confusing, even post tutorial but once you get the hang of things it becomes such a treat to completely eviscerate enemies. To be completely honest, after an hour or so of gameplay I had to search up a few guides to know what I was exactly doing, which is where I feel the game falls short. It isn't the best at explaining how to 'play' the game or what to do in certain situations such as exactly how stats affect combat. However, this made the game more enjoyable for me as I found learning my own 'playstyles' and playing how I wanted to play makes my run throughs significantly better. Now, you may be thinking: . Well, without spoiling things you can either 'jump' into a game with a randomised character and background or customise such. From there, you play through 5 bite sized stories that all tie in together before tackling the 'resolution'. The game is very replayable in the fact that there are many endings to these stories, events to discover, achievements and items to use. The charm of the gameplay would lie in either the randomised playthroughs you'll keep going through, or if you're more of the min-max type, trying to find a nice build for a character you enjoy playing as. Even with the latter, your playthroughs will likely be fresh each time as the stories you tackle will refresh and so will the events. All in all, I heavily enjoy the replay-ability of the core game and going through it blind to learn will reward players greatly. (There's also no harm in reading up on a few of the community guides out there! They're good at not spoiling the content.)The combat is turn based, you 'prepare' a set of actions to take against the enemy before they strike back. (A bit like the ATB gauge in FFXIII if you've played that before!) However, I think the combat is something a new player will struggle to comprehend at first, and even I don't fully grasp it. The game only quickly goes through it with you on the initial 'tutorial modes' and doesn't explain every action you can take as well as only briefly explains how your combat stats affect combat. One coming from an rpg background would likely think by increasing their dexterity, the damage done by dexterity weapons would increase; however, this is not the case. Instead, a weapon has a 'base' chance to hit and is tied to a stat such as DEX, STR, KNW, the more you increase the stat, the more likely the attack will land. There is also more about the 'speed' of your actions however I myself have not even figured this out. Despite the lack of information however, it is very rewarding to learn the basics and find out a combat style suitable to the strengths of the character you are playing as. Eventually, you'll be slashing through enemies with a Katana, bopping them in a single strike, or absolutely bludgeoning something with a baseball bat. What really got me on top of 'mastering the combat' was that some 'stories' allow you to act outside of just one's basic combat needs such as interacting with the room and various other actions if one is to 'explore' their options. The only complaint I have about the game at all however is encountering ghost enemies. For example, the game fails to teach you how 'ghost' enemies work and one can easily run into problems with these enemies, even if one knows how to do so. One cannot deal with ghosts through physical means, and instead must 'defeat' it through other means such as a ritual. The ritual is basic in nature, yet I find it more of an annoyance as dealing with a ghost usually results in a lot of damage to the player character if you are unlucky. I think the system could do with a bit of re-working or at the very least allow you to dodge or brace. In conclusion, I find the combat could be explained better but it is also very rewarding to learn.I am always absolutely floored by how beautifully done this game is in the visual department. World of Horror adopts a pixel art style and wonderfully so, as the enemies and events one will encounter are so horrific they will genuinely make your skin crawl, or you'll recoil in disgust. The combination of all the aspects of the game make it amazing, but the visuals are top notch. The designs of the various horrors you'll face during the game hit exactly what I want out of the 'horror' genre. You'll encounter familiar looking monsters alongside unique designs that are so unnerving they'll send chills up your spine. Furthermore, the visuals have a customisation aspect to an extent which allows for even more uniqueness through your playthroughs. One can choose from many colour palettes offered to them and you'd be surprised at how much they change the look of things! The soundtrack is another spectacular part of the game. There are very few involved, yet they are masterfully added in the various stories and replicate the feeling one would feel if placed into that kind of situation. The music adds to the tension and unnerving visuals, while also 'telling' you when you're in a safe area. In conclusion the visuals are stunning and the soundtrack only adds to this. Play it blind and do your best to not spoil yourself of anything in the guides. As of this review, these guides are mainly spoiler free and were what I went through. > > > But even still, I recommend playing as much as you can first!

_childDocuments_.review: The ideal kind of genre tribute, a game which is so clearly inspired by horror manga (and particularly the manga of Junji Ito) but which also manages to make the tropes, stories, and themes all its own without straying too far from their source of inspiration. On top of that, it's actually quite a deep and engaging game, with complex systems and a straightforward but robust randomization cycle keeping things fresh over multiple playthroughs. And there will be multiple playthroughs, as the RNG-driven RPG base of this game could make your horror story an Uzumaki-like triptych saga with a full and thorough resolution, or a bloody one-shot where you're devoured whole by some terrible beast two days after coming to town.I'm not a huge turn-based combat fan, but the depth of this game's combat system (without being an overwhelming mess in function or interface) allows for a lot of possibility in enemy encounters that can work both for and against your favor. Occasionally, you'll get jumped by a crazed rioter or some shadowy ghoul and get absolutely bodied, but this is balanced out by thrilling highs like an eldritch terror rising from the deep that you blow away with a single splattering headshot.Just like a character in a horror story, though, as doomed as you may feel, the best you can do to delay the inevitable is prepare, pay attention to your surroundings, and BE ON YOUR GUARD.

It does have some great shock moments though, like the ending of the Eel mystery.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has been pining for a fresh experience, eventually a little birdy told me of a game called World of Horror. Imagine a rogue-like, with eldritch inspirations and telltale signs of Panstasz's fascination with the world of Junji Ito, this is pretty much the game.You play as essentially a high-school student or, on occasion, an adult, travelling throughout Shiokawa in the hopes of staying the hands of a sort of "cult" attempting to bring about the resurrection or summoning of their Old God. Throughout your experience, you have to undertake and complete 5 mysteries that, while they're not actually related to the Old God in question, do add a touch of world-building, add their own horrific journey and, depending on how well you complete the mysteries, you will get an ending for it. The endings go from A to D/E, A generally being the best possible ending, and the lowest either being the absolute worst, or in some cases, a Timeline B ending. All you need to know about Timeline B is that it changes how certain mysteries will end, for the most part they will end up being more dangerous than their normal variant.To say that there is enough to do in this world is an understatement. Prior to a particular play-through, you can switch around what shops and services will be open to you for that particular run, and some will be more beneficial for certain characters or they could just be a boon to all. You can also have your chosen character wear new outfits, although it is a cosmetic choice and offer nothing besides. There is enough practical and cosmetic variety to freshen up just about every playthrough you could possibly want or get out of World of Horror.However, if I were to simply ignore how beautiful the music is in this game, this would be an incomplete and rather insulting review, especially one praising the efforts and creativity of Panstasz. The music is absolutely sublime, with every mystery having a sort of song based on a particular theme. If a mystery is to take you to the seaside instead of within the city, you would know because the accompanying musical ambience will let you know. Even with the music being different for each mystery, which all have a variation that you only hear when you get into battle, and the battle variation adds a touch of urgency and threat to whatever has found you and thus intends on ending your life.Speaking of battles, they are very much akin to Final Fantasy except that both you and your opponent take turns, with you having only enough time to perform a couple of actions before it is your opponent's turn to damage you. You can slip in more actions or increase your damage based on your stats, which are the following: Strength (STR), Dexterity (DEX), Perception (PER), Knowledge (KNW), and Charisma (CHA). You also have Luck (LCK) but it is hidden and not necessarily useful outside of a choice number of random encounters, and oddly enough, the other attribute that is governed but only helps with shops and services are your Funds (FND). Each of the characters you can play as generally have a skill they excel in, and one they're awful at. Your chances of completing a play-through is dependant on you either playing to the strengths or attempting to lessen/completely negate their shortcomings.As a final note, this game still has a lot it can offer. Panstasz will still look for ways to shove in more things for us to do, and we can also do our bit with help from the game's dedicated modding community. All the resources you could want regarding this game can be found on Panstasz's Twitter: With this glowing review out of the way, this duck needs to learn how to make mods to include himself in-game. See you all in Shiokawa!
