_childDocuments_.review: I honestly thought this was a really cute game that tried as it might to be more game-y. This is not a simulator game in the "Farming Simulator" sense. It's boring in a different way: lack of progression. I loved the flying, and I think that was the most important mechanic for a game like this to get exactly right. I felt like I had good control of my bee. Going into more technicalities; the voice acting was fine, I thought an effort was put in, and while not perfect, they did their best, and there was a cute charm to it. I can understand why others wouldn't like it though. The overall story was very short, I finished it in little over an hour, and spent the rest of my time trying to do side quests and get skins for my bee. This brought me to another issue: the map is huge, but it feels so empty; there isn't much to do besides collecting pollen, and I didn't want to max out, because my bee would not shut up about how much pollen she had. So I rarely collected unless I had to. Not collecting pollen somewhat prevents your bee from gaining her speed boost, something which is fundamental to traversing the map. I hate feeling slow, and the boost really helped with that, but I really didn't like how quickly it was depleted. When it's gone, you are slow, and you need to either rest for a long a$$ time, or find some sweets, which require some searching, which wastes time.The more I played after the story, the more bored I got, the cracks really began to show, and my 4 hours is about as much playtime you should expect as well. I finished all but one side quest, I think there are 10 of them, which isn't much added playtime. Bees aren't my favorite bugs, I like moths the most, but they are cute and important. I appreciate this game because it had a heart, and presented a lot of bee facts, as well as bringing up some awareness, but in terms of actually playing, I wasn't a huge fan. The more I played the more I wished this game could have done better, because I think it's such a good concept, but sadly it fell short. I'm happy I played it for the time being, but I would not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, it seems the vast majority of negative reviews this game has received are written by children masquerading as grown adults who are ironically unable to recognize that the game is *clearly* targeted at young kids. The dialogue and voice acting is simple, childish and poorly written, the controls are awful, the story practically nonexistent, etc. All of which an adult will notice, but a child won't.Is it a simulator? No, not in the least. Is it a GOOD game? Well, no, not really. It doesn't have any real gameplay elements besides flying around and completing mini-games. Is it worth the *exorbitant* $30 asking price? Absolutely not. But again, this is not a title for adults. It has about 2 hours of actual gameplay to finish up the "story", and after that it's just repetitive nonsense.OH! But it *does* have an absolutely fantastic soundtrack. I don't know why, but it seems like the developers wanted a fully-orchestrated score, which is wonderfully composed. This is a title that parents should buy for their kids if they want to educate them a little about bees, and maybe expose them to some nice classical music, and that's about the extent of its value. In that capacity it does a great job. It teaches kids that bees communicate by dancing, that they migrate to build new hives, that they have to collect pollen from 4 million flowers to make 1kg of honey, that they aren't friends with wasps and hornets, that humans are responsible for destroying their hives, etc. It doesn't really teach much about the life cycle of bees or their importance as pollinators, but it DOES teach. So. If you've got children and you want to educate them a bit about bees and maybe indoctrinate them into thinking bees are cool and important, you should buy this game and force them to play it, but only at a *steep* discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I was interested in this game when I first saw it. I don't know what I was expecting, maybe some kind of bee colony manager elements or I don't know what, but this wasn't it. This game would be amazing if you have a very small child that likes bees and wants to just fly around and be a bee. However, if you're looking for some kind of game that has any lasting value or any kind of depth then you need to look elsewhere. The gameplay cycle is literally flying through hoops for the most part, sometimes you're collecting stuff in those hoops, sometimes you're racing people through those hoops but mostly it's flying through hoops. The flight controls are somewhat weird, like on old FPS games where you feel like you're sliding on ice but through the air and a bit unresponsive at times. There's combat sequences that depending on the difficulty are either a rythmn game or if you switch difficulty it's no longer a rythmn game and now it's some kind of combat game with no apparent telegrams and what appears to be little sense in when to attack and when to dodge.The storyline of the game itself is attempting to be educational but does so in a manner which feels aimed at children under the age of 10, with the characters talking in a fairytale childrens book manner and lacks any kind of depth.I'd recommend the game if you have a very small child that likes bee's like I've said as there are literally no other options that I'm aware of, I'd still only get it on sale as I'd absolutely feel scammed paying full value.

_childDocuments_.review: It's cute, but not really a simulator. The game is clearly geared for younger players, and some of the information is not accurate. Honey Bees, for instance, can only sting once, and die after doing so. The workings of the hive is simplified. Most of the game is exploration and mini-games, though both of those things are very fun. The world is large and fairly detailed. It also looks really nice. You'll race other bees, fight wasps, collect pollen and find that everything seems to have a European accent. I am very happy that there is a game where you can learn about bees firsthand, but I wish it was more detailed. Bees are a very important species, and their problems are human problems.Again, I would like for their to be more detail. Why is one flower considered "epic" while another is common? How about some real world names to encourage people to plant these things and offer organic solutions to dealing with pests? You are able to unlock some of this information, but it still would have been insanely fun to manage a beehive as a queen or something.

Ultimately thumbs down due to equivocation on and exploitation of activist sentiment.

_childDocuments_.review: After controller support and achievement progress got patched I decided to give the game another fair chance and beat it.Overall its a pretty short but fun open world game. Main story wont take you longer dan 3-4 hours to complete but theres still a fair amount of (albeit much of the same) activities. I went in expecting something resembling an actual simulator but its more of an adventure game for all ages.Beating it is a cakewalk, but trying to get all the challenges can be a pain. The only way to find them is by checking your in-game compass which will pick up any challenges in your vicinity which is fine at first, but the more challenges you complete the more spread out the other challenges become, so after a while you spend more time looking for challenges than actually beating them. name: Coffee Talk
detailed_description: In Memoriam Mohammad Fahmi Hasni, co-creator and writer of Coffee Talk passed away on March 28th, 2022 from an asthma attack. He was only 32 years old. Fahmi had a big heart and was a wonderful person. He was known as someone who is really passionate about telling meaningful stories through games. He was a role model that inspired many of us, especially Indonesian indie game developers. Rest in peace, Fahmi. About the Game Coffee Talk is a game about listening to people’s problems and helping them by serving up a warm drink out of the ingredients you have in stock. It is a game that depicts lives as humanly as possible, while having a cast that is more than just humans. Immerse yourself in the stories of alternative-Seattle inhabitants, ranging from a dramatic love story between an elf and a succubus, an alien trying to understand humans’ lives, and many others modern readers will find strongly echo the world around them. The game features: Tales of people from an alternative-Seattle, a city where elves, orcs, mermaids, and many other fantasy races live together with humans in a modern world we will all find familiar Branching storylines, where the branches are determined not by the dialogue options you choose, but from how you serve your café customers 90’s anime-inspired pixel art visuals and chill vibes-inducing color palette help to immerse you in the game’s world Selection of jazzy and lo-fi music to accompany the late night warm drinks and conversations An experience to make you think, feel, and rest both your body and your soul

_childDocuments_.review: Coming into this, I knew I was going to have to make obvious comparisons to a certain other game. Certainly, there is a lot of overlap between the respective slices of life of  mysterious barista and that other game's cyberpunk bartender. The two games share a similar flow, similar mechanics, and much the same overall premise. Is there enough contrast between the two to make  worth a go? is set in the present day - in an alternate world where elves, dwarves, orcs, succubi, werewolves, vampires, and more all coexist with humans. To be honest, I approached that aspect of it with some skepticism and prepared for the same old overplayed high fantasy archetypes.  plays with it, sure, but I don't often feel like I'm playing a fantasy game. These are all just people who are living their lives, and dealing with the challenges being an adult throws at people. Where  is often, and rightly, described as cozy,  is practically a warm blanket and fluffy pillow. Both games have drama for sure, and both games have more serious thematic stories outside the periphery of the main scenario, but it's all softer for  world. doesn't do much different than  as a game. That is, it hits the same notes, and scratches the same itch, but it does not feel like it really innovates much past that formula. It doesn't need to. I loved  and I love . Just don't go expecting something radically different.Overall, whether or not you are a Glitch City veteran bartender,  is a fantastic experience. It will charm with its atmosphere, and leave you satisfied and relaxed.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun relaxing game that is easy and can be 100%ed in a day. There are some glaring contrasts between reality in the sense that Fantasy Seattle doesn't have heavy racism and a plague, but those are good things. The music is good, and the different story lines come together into something neat. The most difficult parts are collecting 50 collect drinks in challenge mode, and knowing what drinks to give in general, but that can easily be done through save scumming or pausing the game and using a guide... (the first part is even explained in story as something MC can do in lore.)
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't say that it is overly entertaining for my own personal tastes. If you are the kind of individual to really enjoy story-driven games, then Coffee Talk is going to be incredibly geared towards you! The overwhelming majority of this game involves listening to peoples stories while making them the occasional cup of coffee. It is certainly relaxing with pleasant music in the background, and utilizes a simple but pretty to look at graphics style. The game mechanics are very simplistic and easy to pick up, but sometimes it does take a while to really understand some of the more 'vague' instructions that you get. I found that the story lines were enjoyable and felt realistic (as realistic as you can get with a coffee shop in a fantasy world, that is) and kept me engaged for the most part. It does feel a bit repetitive here and there, so if you don't have the best attention span, you may have a bit of a difficult time getting through it. For my fellow achievement hunters out there: the achievements are very easy to get and complete, and very minimal grinding is necessary. Overall, I would rate the game pretty highly! 7/10! _childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk is pretty much what it is marketed as: a chill visual novel with well written characters, setting, and conflicts. How would I describe this game?I don't know what it is, but everything about this game is just so wholesome. From the lofi music, to the sound design and effects, to the beautiful artstyle, to discovering various new drinks, to attempting some digital latte art, to listening to different people's conversations and having your character chime in sometimes, it's all so... heartwarming.It was pretty much the perfect game for me when I was experiencing gaming burnout. It's very engaging without requiring much attention or effort as there's not much in terms of gameplay: you click through text and sometimes get the chance to brew someone a hot drink, which is just perfect for a game like this. There is a challenge mode, though, for anyone who enjoys making difficult, specific coffee orders. I just wish the main game was a bit longer because I really got attached to some of the characters. I guess I still have the sequel!Small note, I also played with VO modded in from the workshop and I absolutely LOVED IT! It was really well done and made all the characters come to life. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on a whim. I hadn't read anything about it, but the premise seemed interesting enough. Let's get this straight, this is a visual novel. The coffee brewing part is more of a mini game inside the story you are reading. The game offers some replayability as I realized I made a few mistakes that unlock other stories. Now, I have to agree this is not a game for everyone, as many reviewers have mentioned. First, as a visual novel, this makes it a more niche game. I have to be honest, if I had known this was a visual novel, I think I wouldn't have bought it, since this is a type of game I don't like. The other aspects is what made is special for me. Games are not made on a vacuum. Games tend to reflect trends and topics of each era; be it through the type of game they are, through the graphics or music that are used, or for the topics it touches upon. Coffee Talk is a game that clearly responds to modern trends in more than one way. While the writing, the character construction and the graphics/music selection truly represent a vision, it is the topics that this game touches that are truly the core of the game. This game brought me back to 10 years or more ago, when after work I would meet with my friends, once every 2 weeks in a coffee shop to talk about life. We would discuss our life, our career decisions, our significant others (or lack of), our families, politics, and of course the future. This is exactly what this game does. It throws you in daily conversations with a grain of fantasy about every day topics of conversations. The characters are interesting, each one very unique in their personality, even though I am sure some will be cherished more than others, but in general, it is their conversations that you are truly invested on. And it was a refreshing experience. It was a very relaxing experience that took me most of my evening. The game even made me take a break to go and brew me a cup of coffee to continue playing in the same mood as the characters. If you are looking for a "slice of life" kinda game, and you are not worried about reenacting some conversations you may have had about... the usual stuff, then, this game will most likely is for you. I have read other reviewers saying that revisiting the topics that are tiresome to see in news media and social networks is not for them, I have to agree. If you don't want to read about that

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to talk about Coffee Talk without mentioning VA-11-Hall-A. It's clear that Coffee Talk takes a lot of inspiration from it, both being games about serving drinks and talking to customers in a very chill environment. I don't think this is necessarily a bad thing, however, as Coffee Talk's characters and subplots help the game stand on its own as another game in the "drink serving visual novel" genre, rather than a mere imitation.The game is a lot more subtle than VA-11-Hall-A, perhaps due to its more sophisticated setting of a small coffee shop rather than a bar full of drunk people. I definitely don't find the setting as interesting as VA-11-Hall-A, partially because the focus is much more on the character than the setting, but also just because I personally really like cyberpunk settings, they're pretty rad.The only real criticism I have is that the main character, the Barista, is not that interesting as a character and a lot less involved in the story. Jill Stingray's character was fleshed out throughout VA-11-Hall-A, and the game wrapped up with finishing up her conflict that's alluded to throughout the game. Meanwhile, the Barista feels like an invisible deity that sometimes spouts wisdom at the characters.Overall, Coffee Talk is a great time that I can recommend to VA-11-Hall-A fans or just people looking for a cozy little story they can get lost in.

Anyways, I sincerely was expecting to love this game, but am a bit disappointed and therefore unfortunately wouldn't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk is a fun little narrative game with a few stumbling blocks that don't ruin the over-all experience.The first thing anyone will do is to compare this game to Va11-Hall-A because...well, it should be obvious. It's a visual novel about making drinks for people and chatting with them. There are differences here and there but I won't compare it too much, though sometimes the comparisons are unavoidable.So, for a game that is 90% writing, how is it? The answer is...pretty good. Sometimes the game can be a little on the nose with it's writing but that's not anything that really bugged me at all. It also tackled some decent topics, such as disapproving families, generational divides and fantasy racism (which is handled decently, tho analogues for real minorities in fantasy works are always a little awkward). The characters are fun and pretty good as well, tho you'll see only a couple faces the whole game. Which works out in favor of developing their stories more as you get to interact more than with larger casts. While there is no overarching narrative, each character story can wrap up in it's own way: good because you made the right drinks or bad because you didn't....which brings me to the negative I had about the game. The drink-making was fine for the most part, but I found myself messing up people's drinks because of either unclean instructions, getting the order of ingredients wrong (which it never explains to you matters) or because if I did get an order wrong it wasn't added to the drinks menu so I didn't know if I had made it and messed up before. As a result, while I understand they wanted to make the game a bit puzzling and so you don't succeed the first time you play the game (more on that in a sec) and see different story paths, it became frustrating because when you got an order wrong it felt like you didn't really have enough to figure it out. Sometimes it legit just felt like guess-work.Now, this bothered me less when I replayed the game and tried to get all the drinks right. I would HEAVILY recommend a second playthrough to do this as it is quick to skip past stuff you've seen and it really does unlock some interesting changes when you get everything right. The game is definitely meant to be played with mistakes first and perfectly after. I just wish that getting drinks wrong didn't feel so frustrating.With all that said, I did enjoy my time with the game and think it was a great 3 hours. It even has some other modes like drink challenges and a free making mode so there's some other content in there as well. I'd say this is well worth a purchase and even if you only play it once, get the best ending and never touch it again I think it's time well spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk is a great visual novel and just recently bought it at a recent Summer sale. Great pixel visuals, colorful characters, and an atmosphere that captures the real-life struggles of coffee enthusiasts who come in late at night for a sip of coffee, to have a temporary escape on the struggles of reality. Features an alternate ending that you can unlock by replaying the game.There's hardly any negative things to say about this game, only that they could have optimized the dialogues efficiently. For instance, why do I need to press the X button just to read 3 - 4 words on the next chat bubble if they could have been included on the previous one instead? This game has lots of text to read through but they solved it with the use of a Fast Forward button. However, relaxing games are meant to be calm and, well, make you relax - in a way that you want to finish the game faster. That's how I would have envisioned a relaxing game like Coffee Talk. There's a mode that challenges your understanding of the game that does not properly explain the mechanics though, so you may have to resort to reading a guide on how the bar works for each ingredient.Overall, it's worth the buy. _childDocuments_.review: Picture it's downtown Seattle, now picture the world of Shadowrun with different fantasy races with mundane jobs going through day to day life.  That is more or less, the setting for the game itself.  You'll play as a nameless barista working the coffee shop.  You'll be working day to day through the course of 14 days helping customers and learning about the problems of others, and by being a empathic listener will help to (hopefully) work through and solve their issues.One character you'll meet almost every day is Freya who is a reporter by day, and story writer by night.  She'll be someone you encounter nearly every day of the game, and plays the role of helping to explain the rest of the world lore, while you help her continue to chase her passions.  The in game app (your characters phone) you can open up the daily news site.  Specifically "The Evening Whispers" to read about fictional short stories based on the past day of the coffee shop.Alongside Freya, you'll frequently speak with Jorji, the comical police officer who helps provide fatherly advice during his time at the shop.  Myrtle, and Aqua, an Orc and mermaid who both seem introverted, but a common interest blooms into what could could be a great friendship.  Gala, and Hyde, a werewolf and Vampire who are great friends but somewhat opposite of one another.  Rachel, and Hendry, an idol singer and her father who worries about her getting involved in the unsafe aspects of the industry.  Lua and Bailey, a succubus and elf who are attempting to get through the trails, and tribulations of a relationship where their families disapprove of their relationship based on their race and culture.  And finally, Neil.  An alien being who seems to think he can save the world by---reproducing with an earthling.  That one is a little odd, I promise it makes more sense going through the game![/code]The graphics are great.  Definitely a 90s anime/manga pixel art aesthetic.  It's a lot of static game play and text, it's a visual novel game so you should know what to expect from the genre, not so much in the way of game play and almost more of an interactive movie of sorts.What stands out for me in this game is the music.  The entire Coffee Talk soundtrack was done (as far as I'm aware) by Andrew Jeremy and they really knocked it out of the park.  All very jazz inspired lo-fi music that I honestly can't get enough of.  The music in this game is what really sold me on playing it, and continuing to do so.[/code]This is where the game kinda falls off.  While mod support has been implemented, it doesn't seem like much has been created for the game thus far (That obviously is subject to change!)Aside from this, I do feel that in terms of replay-ability for the game, like many games of the visual novel genre---it is lacking.  This isn't a bad thing.  Often times the price for these games are cheaper so I don't mind only having reason to go through one or two play-throughs.Having said that, I do think I'll continue to play the game for the music, and also to help amp myself up for the next game of the series coming out in 2023.If you're a fan of the genre, you enjoy the music, aesthetic of the graphics and the calm relaxing pace and story line, yeah.  I'd absolutely recommend getting it.  Truth be told for my personal preferences, it is hard to nitpick for the game.  I did receive it via a humble bundle a while back so I got it for pretty cheap.  I honestly wouldn't have a problem paying even full price for this game as I really enjoyed it, the music, game play, story, and overall message all touch on the right spots.

_childDocuments_.review: Certainly similar to VA11-HALL-A in tone and mechanics. The setting is pretty different though.So, basically, you read dialogue and make drinks. If you make drinks well, you get good dialogue. If not, you don't necessarily. That is, good minigame performance is required to advance the story.The stories are fine, perhaps less interesting than in VA11-HALL-A, but that's probably due to the setting being less interesting for me. Oh, and the setting, as you can read in the game description probably, is alternate-reality Seattle, with all your fantasy races mixed into basically modern human society. So, think like Bright, but fewer stereotypes. On the topic of writing, I enjoyed the after-credits plot twist very much, so there's that.Some parts get pretty meta at times. This might be immersion-breaking for some, I thought it was fine.Anyway, the minigame is fun, the art is nice-looking, the length is average for the format (took me about 6 hours to finish). Overall, a nice enough read, so I can recommend this without any caveats.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: Wholeheartedly recommended! Make coffee, change lives :) This definitely reminds me of a  pixel-style bartender game, but with a lighter and more citizen-life story. The English writing is to the point yet playful. I like it. The lo-fi music is also fantastic and I plan on buying the soundtrack later.You play as the owner of a small coffee shop in Seattle in the year 2020, serving a diverse group of regulars like humans, elves, orcs,  cat girls, and mermaids. The story unfolds through their casual conversations, set in a world that closely resembles our own.The meta elements are a nice touch, but the story stands on its own fine without them.RIP Mohammad Fahmi Hasni. Thank you for making this awesome game. 🙏

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for this game and absolutely adored it. I love stories that experiment with creative methods of allowing the plot to unfold. For me, the secret ingredient that was holding the whole experience together was that the playable character's dialogue lines were left ambiguous. The game trusted me as the player to get in the role of the barista and come up with my character's lines on my own, which turned out to be really immersive.AND THEN I bought the full version, only to find out that in the real game, the barista's lines are all explicitly stated, which immediately sapped all of the goodwill I had felt for the game while playing the demo.tl;dr the game has one really significant difference from the demo. _childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible game to just relax with and wind down as you listen to the characters talk about their lives, occasionally brewing them a drink. I've seen over Twitter that it's got a whole bunch of people to experiment with coffee making in real-life, and I'd quite like to try it myself. Though, on the subject of if this game could help you be a barista, the answer is probably no. Personally I thought the setting would've been stronger if they'd ditched the urban-fantasy and just made it regular-ass Seattle, but I appreciate how they took it and world-built with it in an interesting way. With indie games become more popular in recent years, I'm expecting a lot more of these kinds of relaxing 'iyashikei' games in the future, which is great, because I love games like this and they're pretty cheap too. I want to see more games explore themes about human life. Coffee Talk is all about shining a light on those everyday stories that might otherwise get lost in the crowd. Because if it doesn't gain you fame, who'd wanna know, right? Everybody's interesting and everybody's story is worth telling, so why not do it over a cup of coffee?

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you enjoy the vibe of a rainy Seattle coffee shop and a good story, grab a cup of coffee/tea and sit down with this pixelated visual novel game. The list price is reasonable for the experience it gives you, but beyond achievements, there isn't much replay value if that type of thing matters to you though.This game is set in an alternative world where humans live among vampires, werewolves, aliens, and more in the year 2020. You play as a mysterious barista who owns a late night coffee shop which acts as a refuge for its customers. You not only make drinks based on what customers want, but you also hear out their stories and troubles about their lives. Although the concept is simple, this slice of life visual novel will have you invested in the customers that stop by, cheering them on and hoping for their happy ending. From an aspiring writer to quarreling lovers, there are all types of stories and conflict going on. And, if you dare, through a secret ending I won't spoil, you can even learn about the barista you're playing as too (and trust me, you want to, it was a satisfying twist).The achievements don't require too much extra effort but are fun to unlock, the graphics are beautifully pixelated, the characters are fleshed out and interesting, and the music captures the vibe of a rainy cafe. I'm not sure I have any complaints or reasons not to buy, assuming you enjoy this type of game and don't mind a lack of replay ability. So get out there and enjoy the vibes!
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

But that's okay because I heard that Episode 2 is coming and I hope I can enjoy it again in between my breaks. Light and fun stories like this are what I want from Coffee Talk."     - Overall : 8/10 [Hopefully Episode 2 will be better and more enjoyable.]

_childDocuments_.review: This is an edited review. My first impression was to buy the game on sale, but I have changed my mind on that.I woke up at 2am unable to sleep and decided to buy this game. My first review was saying to get the game on sale, but after getting some more sleep I decided to change my review. The idea of making coffee for fantasy and sci-fi creatures is really cool. I love the concept of the game. The art is also great, and the music is really soothing. However, I'm playing on my Xbox controller and besides making coffee, all I do is press A, over and over and over and over. That's literally all there is. There is no RPG element where I choose where the conversation goes. There is no money to manage. It's literally make coffee, press A a thousand times until it's time to make coffee again. _childDocuments_.review: I recently saw this game on sale and thought it was a decent game to pass the time on. However, after the first hour, I was immediately invested in it. The game has lovable characters and captivating story arks that make you want to know what happens next. However, some story arks deal with serious issues that I won't mention here to avoid spoilers. The game has a friendly vibe with suitable background music and a nice good 16-bit visual.Gameplay-wise, the game is just you reading dialog between your customers while you make their drinks. Of course, there's a recipe book for you to look at if you don't know how to make a specific drink. But in some cases, you're going to have to guess a particular recipe because a customer's order is not on your menu or for another reason.While I was playing the game, I noticed a News Post about the game stating, "Thank you for helping Fahmi's family in this difficult time and celebrating through his works." Of course, I was sad to hear that the game's creator has passed, but I am glad that Toge Productions used the money they received during the sale to support Fahmi's family. I know my money went to a good cause, and I look forward to Coffee Talk 2 when it releases to support an outstanding indie developer.Overall, I recommend this game if you want to pass the time and enjoy a good story. However, I can understand that this game is not for everyone. It might not be a puzzle or an action pack adventure like other games, but this game does give you a little life lesson(s) if you pay attention to the stories with its calming atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: Instead of mixing drinks & saving lives, you're brewing them. Not to say it's as good as VA-11, that would be quite a feat, but it does scratch that itch it left many of us. Instead of a dark neon bar in a dystopian future talking about societal issues, you're in a warm colored cafe with a constant rainy background, talking about modern day societal issues reflected in an alternate universe, where many species (werewolves, vampires, humans of course, & so on) coexist together. And while I appreciate the takes on race & immigration; the idea behind what they were trying to demonstrate -- it's simply not the best writing I've ever seen, but on the flip side, it's not the worst. I got a few chuckles here & there; it's just a slow burn sort of story. However, the original lo-fi soundtrack, the art work, the entire atmosphere, makes this game worth playing to me. I recommend sitting down with a cup of your favorite hot beverage on a rainy day to play.

_childDocuments_.review: It's impossible to talk about this game without pointing out it's a shameless rip off of a better game, Va-11 hall-A.  They're both visual novels with a (very) light gameplay element of mixing drinks.  Va-11 Hall-A takes place in the far future in a mysterious glitch city. Coffee Talk takes place in Seattle, oh but there's fantasy races! It's here that coffee talk makes it's first failing. It's does nothing to immerse the player to the setting, and it having fantasy races seems to just be a window dressing to make the game more interesting, rather than actually adding anything of value.Coffee Talk is low energy. I found it hard to care about any of the characters, the conversations boring, the humor falls flat.  I needed my own cup of black tea to actually power through game.  Lue and Bailey are the only characters where the fantasy setting actually seems relevant, in addition, those are the only two characters you'll actually want to read about. Unfortunately, your coffee shop regular is also the most annoying, an immature writer who...  has trouble writing.  What a great trope.  It also doesn't help that the player character, (you), is a bland self insert with no dialogue choices, but enough dialogue to be annoyed at, unlike valhalla which had a defined character.The music is chill, and pretty good, if a bit limited. The pixel art is also fairly nice, except for pretty much all the female portraits and their nonsensical noses. I'm used to minimal anime noses, but they're at least placed and sized normally. Instead in this there's a very tiny detailed nose right above the lip with a huge blank space between the eyes. It looks absolutely bizarre, and you can tell two different artists worked on the game because one of them can actually draw noses that don't seem out of place.Play va-11 hall-a instead, and if you already did, just play policenaughts or something. Not this.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes it's hard to know what to write here, but I think Coffee Talk stands out as a game that is obvious in its intentionality (pure hygge) and its inspiration (VA-11 Hall-A, visual novelry, peppered examples of modern-society-fantasy as in Shadowrun, that weird Netflix film with the orc-cops, and the 'lo-fi beats to study to' aesthete), and in being clearly stated as achieving them. It's a bit short, and the narrative arc doesn't have as much heft to it as other titles in a similar mould, but that's totally fine. In some respects, this brings the game closer to the warm, fuzzy vibes - less pressure, overall. The music is very nice, but I wish it played in the background by default - I don't usually find visual novels so engrossing that I don't tab out from time-to-time, and this is a bit jarring. At any rate, I suspect I'll want to listen to the tracks for a while after I'm done with the game. :)There's something weird about using fantasy tropes as foils for real-world issues, but I appreciate it enough in Shadowrun once I've suspended my disbelief, and I think the same applies here. It just takes a little while. You'll end up with some charming characters (and some banal ones, but taste is what it is) regardless, and the game's made me giggle a few times, too. I think the more fantastical elements (pretty much exclusively Neil) were honestly when it shined most, and that some of the everyday experiences of the others was a bit simple. The game spent more time referencing Indonesian variants of coffee and like-drinks, and I was happy to learn about them, but I would've rather learned more about the state of this hypothetical alternative 2020. The newspaper segments, borrowing from VA-11 Hall-A, hint at a world that's super interesting. I want to see that world a little more, and while I guess we did with ,  I wanted more!Whatever; the point is this: the game is charming, sweet, and super light. Like, snack-lite. It's not filling, but part of the hygge vibe is being contented with the world. And I'm content with this.

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk is a story focused barista game that was released on the 29th of January 2020. What I mean by “story focused barista” is that you are a barista in a coffee shop, and you listen to the stories of the customers. The stories of these customers are what the game focuses on. I played Coffee Talk for 11 hours, played through the story twice and got all 24 achievements.The story is really good. It’s set in Seattle, 2020. The setting is somewhat unique since it’s a fantasy setting in modern times. All the races are there, orcs, humans, elves, Atlanteans etc. I don’t want to go into too much detail but there are a lot of relevant issues in the game. Racism, immigrants and even Autism (that is how I interpreted it at least.)Coffee Talk plays half like a visual novel and half like and an arcadey coffee making game. The visual novel part is straight forward. You just listen to the customers talk. This is the main way the story moves forward. The customers will also order drinks. This is where the arcadey coffee making part come in. Drinks are made from 3 ingredients. There are 5 base ingredients and 6 additional ingredients. To keep track of everything happening, you have a phone you can use. The phone has an app to keep track of all the drinks that you can make. Another app keeps track of customers and information about them. There is also an endless mode.The graphics are nicely done. The characters have a lot of detail and expression. The coffee shop is well done for what it is. The drinks themselves looks good and some of the drinks actually looked delicious. The music of the game is good but blended into the background after a while.Coffee Talk is not a game for everyone. The story may be too slow for some. The gameplay may be too boring or slow for others, but if you are patient enough and like a really good story, Coffee Talk is 100% worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my all time favorite games is Va-11 Hall-A and ever since, I’ve been on the lookout for similar games ever since to scratch that itch it left behind. The closest I’ve gotten was playing The Red Strings Club which does have you literally pouring drinks to bring out certain emotions in your customers, but it turned out to be disappointing (for me at least). When I heard about Coffee Talk though, I knew I was going to pick this one up and play it as soon as I could. My decision was hammered home even more after I played the demo. Well, now that Coffee Talk is released how does it fare?Taking place in Seattle in an alternate 2020, you find yourself in a world that hosts not only humans but fantasy creatures like mermaids and elves. Though, that doesn’t mean this world doesn’t have it’s own set of problems. That is where you come in as the owner, and only employee, of a small coffee shop named Coffee Talk. What sets yours out from all the others is that yours is the only one that is open only at night. Ready for anyone to come in looking for a hot drink and an ear to air out all their frustrations.Coffee Talk’s cast of characters are wonderful as each bring in their own unique personality to the table and stories on what’s currently happening in their lives. Each one manages to interesting to where most players will want to hear more about them and hope that they’ll come in before you close up. You’ll start out with Freya, a regular that always comes in to write and is aspiring to have a book published. It’s not long before you meet up with an elf and succubus couple that’s struggling with their families not approving their relationship and what the future holds if they never do; a cop that’s totally not taking too many breaks to have a cup of your coffee; a vampire model that gives insight on and to whoever happens to be there; a werewolf that’s trying to find a drink that will calm him down during his Fury; and more. You also have some other world building elements through daily newspapers (headlines only sadly), Tomodachill profiles that opens up more information as you get closer to the characters, and you’re even able to read some of Freya’s short stories to give you a taste on how she writes.Brewing up drinks for your customers is pretty simple. At first you’ll only have a couple ingredients, but you’ll slowly get more as inventory comes in. You’ll pick a base, a primary ingredient, and finally a secondary ingredient. While you’ll brew the usual drinks like espressos, lattes, and flavored milk, there are also special named drinks you can discover and customers will occasionally request. However, you won’t have the full list, only having the basics already in your Brewpad, as you’re meant to discover them yourself. As some customers will request named drinks, with some giving hints and others not, it also means you most likely won’t be able to give everyone correct drinks. Luckily, Coffee Talk doesn’t change anything other than them saying it’s not what they ordered apart from two instances. These two instances are telegraphed so it’s not hidden away if you’re worried about that.For lattes, Coffee Talk also lets you create your own latte art if you wanted to. I personally found it hard to make anything, well, pleasing. Basically the long you hold own, the more milk will be poured and it’ll be pushed down. If you don’t like it when you try it out, you can completely ignore it.Coffee Talk also features an Endless mode with two different choices. First, you have Free Brew which lets you make anything. This is mainly used to let you figure out all named drink combinations as you won’t be able to make all of them in your first playthrough or be able to figure it out if you’re not given any hints. Then there’s Challenge Mode. Challenge Mode, well, challenges you to make as many correct drinks as you can for your customer before the time runs out. Each correct drink adds on more time so you can survive longer. It starts out pretty easy with them just saying what ingredients they want outright. It slowly brings up the difficulty as it brings your base to the end of their request and occasionally requesting a named drink (that you hopefully discovered before now). Lastly, it gets more vague on what ingredients they want, but more specific on how they want sweet, warm, cool, or bitter they want their drink to be. This is where it gets challenging as it first starts with only requesting one aspect to be a certain way to all of them. Though, this part is a bit confusing at first before you figure out what the customer actually means. Asking for a drink that’s not bitter and extra sweet is obvious, but what about less and just regular sweet. Especially when they just plainly say “I want my drink to be bitter” and they hate it when you just load it up. Well, you might not have noticed, but the coffee maker actually tells you what constitutes as a drink having a low or high amount in each. 1-3 bars is less, 4-5 is just right, and 6+ is extra. When the game asks for a normal amount of one of them, it will only accept 4-5 as anything more counts as it being too much.When you think of a game centering around being a barista, I would be surprised if the first thing on your mind wasn’t a cozy coffee shop where you can go and study or write. Coffee Talk certainly doesn’t disappoint if you’re expecting a cozy atmosphere. The coffee shop just shouts cozy vibes with how it’s decorated, the characters are wonderfully designed and brings in a pop of vividity, the soundtrack is relaxing and I could easily see them being in a “relaxing cafe music for studying” playlist, and the rain certainly brings in another addition for those that find rain relaxing.This game definitely reminds me of a 10 hour rainy mood loop of Beneath the Mask that I listen to sometimes while I write so I’m not writing in complete silence. Combining a relaxing soundtrack with the sound of rain pouring down outside and the image of you just sitting in a coffee shop watching people walk and drive by the window.One thing I do wish was that Coffee Shop was a bit longer. Not because the price doesn’t fit, which I do think it does, but it felt like there could have been more interactions between the characters. While these things didn’t bother me much, others might be disappointed that giving wrong drink orders doesn’t really affect anything outside two separate instances and it doesn’t show the complexity of brewing coffee. The latter is a shame as I would have been interested in learning about it, especially since I even looked up how baristas make latte art in an effort to understand how the latte art minigame worked.While Coffee Talk might not completely scratch that itch that Va-11 Hall-A left in many of it’s players, it will satisfy those that have been looking for similar games. While it can disappoint in some areas, it gives players a wonderful cast of characters, a cozy atmosphere to relax to, two endings, and a challenge mode for those who are looking for a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been eyeing this game for a few months before giving in and purchasing it. I had many expectations coming in, but I was sorely disappointed in the execution of this game. First and foremost, the brewing system is frustrating. I thought it was a cute niche idea initially, but it quickly became repetitive and borderline frustrating. It doesn't help that as the game progresses, their idea of increasing difficulty is just making the drink orders vague or giving you names of drinks that you've never made prior. I just resorted to using a guide to find the drinks' proper ingredients because I couldn't be bothered to go through the tedious trial and error especially considering you only have five retries before you're forced to serve.But the straw the broke the camel's back for me was the writing. The dialogue was shallow at best and cringe-worthy at worse. It reads like a first draft written by a pre-teen in a middle school creative writing course. It's predictable and superficial and tries way too hard to be relatable. There are many instances where some conversations just went on for too long. For example, there's a scene where two characters explain how dating works to an alien in an almost expository manner. I understand this character doesn't know how dating works, but I assure you that the people playing the game do, and they don't need it to be explained to them. It's boring and monotonous. This may also be a nit-pick, but the stories that Freya writes in the fiction column of the newspaper are just awful. They are the equivalent of a watt pad one-off story. They're pretentious and try extremely hard to be meaningful and humorous but fail miserably. There's a particularly disgusting story  about a girl revealing to her date that she enjoys french kissing her cats. I know this isn't supposed to be taken seriously, but I don't find a story of a girl taking advantage of her animals to be humorous. It disgusted me so much I quit the game after reading it. I know some people may think I'm taking this too far, but this kind of content makes me so uncomfortable that if I knew it was in the game before I bought it, I would've never made the sale. This game is beautiful aesthetically and has an interesting enough concept and ambiance. But the characters, the writing, the gameplay, and the stories all ruin it for me. All in all, I wouldn't recommend Coffee Talk unless you have a particular interest in eye-roll inducing writing or shallow characters.

_childDocuments_.review: To put it simply, Coffee Talk is the best virtual novel/coffee shop sim I've ever played. I bought it during a sale and the graphics and trailers interested me, but oh BOY I wasn't ready. It pulls you in such an immersive experience... So many incredible moments, some that make you think or change perspective from subjects in life, some that warm your heart and some that worry you, too! AH! And not to mention the characters... Freya, Bailey, Lua, Hyde, Gala, Officer Jorji, Myrtle, Aqua, Rachel and Hendry and of course, my favourite, NEEEEEIL! To be quite honest, sometimes during the many conversations, I even forget they're just "characters"... They're so well written, with such interesting backstories and moments that I forgot they were JUST characters, because they were so real!So much more could be said about Coffee Talk, and Episode 2, but I'll leave it up to you to find out and enjoy yourself.}Much love to Toge Productions, I hope Episode 3 comes out.RIP Fahmi.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: In an increasingly high stress community filled with anxiety, Coffee Talk feels like a moment to breathe at the end of the day. Serving one warm drink after another to an array of frazzled yet relatable mythical beings, I could feel myself winding down alongside the patrons. Accompanied by a wonderfully chill lo-fi music playlist with the sound of rain in the background, the stories of the customers unfold one drink at a time. Even though the main story itself wasn't that long, I feel like I'll be playing this over and over just to get that sense of calm I need after a long day...
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: oh gosh where to even start.i really like that this game exists. it seems to have been well received by many. i play  many visual novels and Coffee Talk has a level of polish and quality above a large sub-section of the options out there. there is clearly a large amount of passion and skill poured into making this game possible.that being said, i can not honestly recommend this as an enjoyable experience. the first few days of the story are tiresome as the plot grabs you by the lapels and pulls you through the administrative mud of meeting all the characters and getting a snapshot of their issues. this process feels anything but organic as random individuals plop themselves in front of you and immediately lay bare their box-standard issue & personality. the manner this is carried out feels incredibly stilted. they do not sound like individuals in a coffee shop chatting, but more like a list of attributes disguised as a character attempting to justify their own existence. speaking from my own playthrough, the opening week of the game bounced me off twice and i only managed to get through it after mostly skipping through the boring setup period.admittedly, the story does improve from this point, as the characters and relationships are all setup, you're left to wonder and explore how the characters change and how their issues get resolved. it doesn't do a lot to play with your expectations, but it mostly works. the part of the game that does not improve, sadly, is one of the main characters, Freya. i truly can not understand the appeal of this character. Freya is a writer, who is writing a novel about characters in a coffee shop. not just any coffee shop or characters mind you. she is specifically writing a novel using Coffee Talk's story. so you'll get weird meta conversations where some fantasy character will enter the scene and go "hi! I'm a cat person who dreams of being a pop idol!" and then Freya will lean over to tell you "wow! what a unique struggle! this is so interesting, i should use it for my book!". like, why is this here?? what narrative purpose does Freya serve? adding onto this point, the game attempts to make use of the old troupe of fantasy racism with little success. spread throughout the game are news clippings of how tensions are high between the different fantasy races and how orcs really aren't stupid i swear, elves are all hoity-toity, smarmy snobs, and are werewolves actually mindless beasts?? and yet racism between humans doesn't exist in this world. but like, it doesn't do anything with this. it doesn't use the twist to make commentary or explore thorny topics. it's there for mere world building? like, it's just there for the sake of being there. this is made abundantly clear when Freya mentions that her novel will only have humans in it, however it will still have racism in it because that's just how people are. flipping the script, you can clearly see that the creators of Coffee Talk had the same approach of "oh, well this story has fantasy creatures in it, but there's still racism because that just how people are". the most annoying part of this is that the conversation ends there. nothing is explored further, there is no commentary made. there is so much more you could do here, it's frustrating to see it wasted.as for the coffee brewing, barista mechanics, they are fine. like they're just fine. idk why it's there, it's super simple and changes mostly nothing, but it sure is there. it can be frustrating to get recipes right since the order of the ingredients completely changes the recipe, but it's largely harmless. additionally, the music is fine. i had it muted for most of my playthrough, but that was just because i wanted to listen to my own music. but again, it's fine. it works and sets the correct mood.all in all, idk it's not good. it tries. you can tell it tries to be something unique. but there are too many ideas that seem like they're the first idea that came to mind with no further attention given. if you're really curious, go for it. otherwise, maybe pass on this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: I originally got this game because I am a big fan of Va-11 Hall-a, as I loved its story, atmosphere and music. It was something different and a step above your average visual novel game. And I love coffee as its the elixir of life to me so this game seemed right up my alley. Unfortunately it wasn't. I will say the jazz inspired music in this game is wonderful and is definitely the best part. Valhalla had a chilled soundtrack with its synth club music and this game went for a more jazzy vibe which I like. My main issue was I just found the story a chore to play through. Characters didn't pop out at me as much as I would have liked and the dialogue was less interesting. My other issue (and I don't mean to overly compare) was in Vallhalla you played as Jill and you were following her day to day life. She was a compelling protagonist to follow and I enjoyed her journey of self discovery. In this game your just you, yourself and thats it. Your "character" has dialogue that you can't influence, and a simple backstory but that's it. It made the game less engaging to play because I couldn't connect with myself if that makes sense XD But I feel like if they were going to go with the approach of your character being you, then they should have changed the dialogue to be more RPG like in that you pick dialogue options and characters respond accordingly so that in that way, you can craft the story to how you would be in that situation. The other issue was the coffee brewing mechanics are very dumbed down from Vallhalla. In the latter game, you didn't just select ingredients and click a craft button, you had to mix the drinks correctly with the mouse otherwise the drink would fail as an example. In Coffee Talk you just pick ingredients and click craft and your done. There is a little more interaction where you make a latte as an example and you can make a drawing with the foam milk, which I thought was cool, but thats the only time where it requires skill on your part. Because of that I just found myself very bored most of the time. In the end Coffee Talk is not a bad game by any means, and I can tell the devs put a lot of work into it. I'm just not the biggest fan of it and despite numerous times of me trying to get into it, I just can't.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute little game where you are a Barista with their own little cozy coffee shop, and the stories of the people who come to visit. Take a seat, grab a nice warm drink and some snacks and enjoy a nice little story about different people and their different lives. The art style is cute and amazing, the comforting smooth music playing in the background. It was an overall fun little story. Its a game that pretty much plays itself, you just give the correct (or incorrect) drink orders. It really gives you that nice little coffee shop on the corner vibe, makes you wish you could visit a place like this and just relax and enjoy the company of many friendly people. <3If you're looking for a nice little relaxing game to come home after a hard day of work and just unwind to and just chill, this is the one! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing Coffee Talk.  The art is stunning and coupled with the lo-fi beats makes it a really setting a soothing feel to the game's environment. The characters and their story arcs are fun to delve into, and I did really enjoy the information that is revealed after you finish the main story arc for the first time.My one critique is that I wish the game length was longer. It would have been fun to delve deeper into the different relationships that develop between the regular clients. Or maybe have more options to expand further on the ending plot reveal.Overall, this game is definitely worth the purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk is a chill game with nice lofi music and a good story. The game is perfect for those who want to relax and enjoy a cup of coffee while playing. The game has a unique concept where you play as a barista who serves coffee to various customers. The customers come from different backgrounds and have different stories to tell. The game has beautiful pixel art graphics that are pleasing to the eye.The community’s voice over mod is amazing and adds an extra layer of immersion to the game. It would be great if the developers could add native voice over in the future.Overall, Coffee Talk is a great game that is perfect for those who want to relax and enjoy a good story. I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely intriguing game that can keep you interested in it for multiple playthroughs. I quite like it and haven't even finished my second playthrough. I definitely recommend trying it out to see if you like it, I think it's worth anyone's time If you enjoy this kind of game play, just with a bit of a twist.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Va11halla, I had to give this game a shot. Instead of being a bartender, you now assume the role of a barista working a coffee shop that stays open late at night. In the fantasy world of Seattle, you will be serving humans, elves, orcs, and more at your shop. Each character you meet has an interesting story about them and they become regulars. Serving them the correct drink will change the story slightly but overall you are mostly listening to their tales and what they go through in their daily life.I enjoyed the game overall. The art is gorgeous and the music was the perfect lo-fi mix you put on when you want to just chill. Add the fact that it rains every night for some odd reason in this universe and you have the perfect atmosphere for this game!I know some people gripe about that the game was too short, I personally thought it was a nice length for the price. You can even do an endless and free brew mode for fun. I especially love the artwork galleries, specifically the comics that give you a quick insight on why all the patrons you meet come to your shop.My single complaint about this game is that they don't give you all the coffee recipes. In Va11-halla, they give you all the drink instructions and from there you just have to use context clues and listen to what the customer wants and go from there. In this game they start you out with like 4-5 recipes and it's fine for the beginning, but later in the game, they will ask you for a specific drink that's you don't know and you just have to guess (or look up a guide like I did).Final verdict? If you like visual novels where you serve people coffee and have a nice chillaxin 3-5 hours to spare, I say check this game out. It was beautiful and I truly hope they make more of them with new or returning patrons, (plus I'm curious about that ending!) Thanks for reading!
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game in the summer of 2020. I was going through my first breakup when I first found this game. If you want a storybook through the medium of a video game, this could be for you. I love the story this game tells and makes you feel interested and entices you to build a connection to the characters while you hear their stories. When I went through my breakup, this game made me feel not so alone and made me feel like I was enjoying a cup of coffee with some friends. It is a crime not to drink coffee when playing this game. You also have to play this game at night in the darkness.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk

_childDocuments_.review: Before 2020 I used to go to cafés to either talk with the baristas when their shifts were calm or study or read and listen to the ambience. So when I bought this game I thought I could compensate with it during the lockdown, I was not dissapointed.Even though it is exhausting to read the conversations and follow the story from time to time, but not because the story isn't good or something, but because I don't like to read too much, contradicting what I was saying two sentences before. However this is my personal problem. And I love the game non the less, I just try not to binch on it.It was one of the games I own to compensate for the lack of human interaction during the pandemic and that's what is important to me. Does it have gameplay? Near to none!Is it relaxing? YesDo I brew a cup of coffee before playing this game ? Always!Is Freya cute? also yesBuy this game if you want to get away from it all but keep a realistic day to day feel to it!

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be the first to admit I'm not your average Steam user, and not a typical gamer or even merely game player. I don't spend a lot of time playing much of anything, and my gaming skills are definitely lacking. I'm very sure an 8 year old could beat my ass in Smash Bros. I may have unusual taste & playing habits, but I do know quality when I see it.Coffee Talk is a work of art, in many different ways. It's given me joy and a strange sense of comfort and belonging when I didn't know I needed it or was searching for it. Much like a good IRL cafe, Coffee Talk gave me a place to be. I found myself completely absorbed in every detail.It may not be the most complex or multidimensional game, but I fell in love. And you can tell every inch of the game is an experience that was created with so much love as well.Give it a go - maybe you're not a gamer, like me, maybe you're looking for fun story and interesting characters and comfy vibes - maybe, like me, it'll be something you end up deeply loving every moment of.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR:Gameplay-7/10Story-10/10Characters-10/10Graphics-10/10Music & Sound-10/10Replayability-5/10Coffe Talk may not seem like a whole lot on the surface, especially compared to VA-11 Hall-A(Valhalla), but if you take the time to get to know this relaxing yet event-filled tale, you'll find yourself immersed in a beautiful tale of unlikely souls coming together, their lives enriched by more than just the beverages they drink.Fun fact: I've never actually been in a coffee shop before, at least not something official, like a Starbucks. The closest thing I'd say I came to one was a little social hall at NWMSU, but it never carried that kind of vibe. It's never really bothered me that I've yet to go to one; I'm not the kind of person to seek out a barista joint just to mingle. Hell, I've officially quit caffeine(bad for my health, I've abused it over the years). That being said, when I first heard about this game on Steam, I was immediately drawn to it; I'd played VA-11 Hall-A before, a bartending simulator, and despite the fact that I despise bars IRL, I absolutely LOVED that game, so I knew I'd be in for a treat with this one.Now, I didn't expect Coffee Talk to be perfect. It isn't, but for a bartending simulator(may as well call it one, since it carries such vibes even though you never sell alcohol in it), It's pretty darn close.Picture this: It's 2020, in Seattle(no, I'm not joking, that's the setting), except the world is a bit different in that there aren't just humans, but also fantasy races-elves, dwarves, orcs, succubi...even werewolves and vampires! The game blends these races together in a world similar to our own, where, instead of waging war on each other, these races(species?) are finding their own ways in life. Of course, life is never easy, and there are a few stressful things going on in the world, as the occasional news headlines will tell you, but there is a place one can relax-Coffee Talk, the local coffee shop open at...nighttime. It's safe to say this isn't your ordinary world, and it certainly isn't your average Starbucks, but all of this only makes the game world much more intriguing. After watching the well-made opening cinematic, I knew I was going to have fun with this one.Story-wise, this game is a collection of smaller plotlines that interweave with each other in a clever fashion, and at certain points some characters will pop in to update their tales, then jump back out for a bit. The one  plot that is always there is that of a young, green-haired woman named Freya who is slowly but surely working on her first big novel. Even though she already provides numerous short stories to the game's newspaper, The Evening Whispers, she's ultimately hoping to get a book made of stories inspired by the many events and tales she hears in the coffee shop itself. While she doesn't get particularly invested in the other stories, I still love Freya nonetheless; she's very entertaining, she makes me laugh a lot, and the fact that she's going for a story based on the in-game coffee shop, a story about only humans no less, gives this game a bit of clever self-awareness you don't see in many others.Another thing I love is that you, the player, get sort of a character as well! When you enter a name you choose for the save file, that name is used for the barista(formless and genderless), who interacts with the characters on his/her own perogative. Not only that, but if you play the game enough, you'll find an interesting secret about said barista, too.Other stories in the game include Baileys the elf and Lua the succubus, a young couple in love, despite their relationship looked down upon by their families; Rachel, a nekomimi pop star looking to get her solo music career going, despite being at odds with her father Hendry, who is opposed to the idea; Jorji, a human cop that mainly gives advice to Rachel, as he is a father of three, though he has light banter with other characters; the odd yet shippable couple of Hyde and Gala, the former a vampire that seems to have an eye for the kinkier side of life, and the latter a werewolf who is not only looking for a way to control his transformation, but is also a war veteran with PTSD issues; Aqua the shy mermaid and Myrtle the stoic half-orc, a pair of ladies that come together to work on an indie project for a gaming convention; and Neil, the astronaut, or at least he looks like an astronaut, but is actually on a mission to breed with people on Earth for a special reason I'll not spoil here. As you can see, most of the characters are paired and, as such, don't always stand out as much on their own, but all the stories in this game were enjoyable in some way. Everyone gets a decent amount of screen time, and their unique personalities and looks help them add something special to the game as a whole. It does kind of stink that some characters get more time than others, but they are all memorable and loveable nonetheless.As far as actual gameplay goes, all you really do is serve coffee when a character asks you to. They'll usually give you the ingredients necessary(although a few brew recipes are given at the start, with more added as you discover them; can you collect them all!?), but sometimes you'll have to experiment, which adds a fun bit of mystery to the game. It can be a bit frustrating when you don't get all the ingredients, and thus you may screw up an order here or there, as I did, but you aren't really penalized at all for a mistake(at least from what I can tell), so you can rest easy that you'll still have fun, mistakes and all.Aesthetics are where the game really shines. There's no voice acting, which is fine by me, but the whole game looks positively stunning. The shop itself gives off a relaxing, calm vibe, even as you watch silhouettes walk/run back and forth in the outdoor background, a rainy nighttime city street. Each character is colorful and vibrant, eye catching, and they all have varying expressions and, as such, visibly react to certain dialogue.On top of that, the music...just, THE MUSIC! It is 98% easygoing and relaxing(there's one or two instances where it actually picks up a bit, mainly for story purposes, but it still works), and it really fits the mood of a coffee shop very well. I've played a lot of games, and many of those titles have very good music, but I've never had the enjoyment of basking in a title where the music fits so perfectly. It's even fun to listen to OUTSIDE of the game, so feel free to look it up on youtube the next time you need to study or relax.The only area this game really lacks in is replayability, which largely depends on whether or not you're fine with the endless mode, where you, erm, "endlessly" serve customers coffee. The main story does have a bit of replay as well; in addition to simply trying to get every single coffee order correct, beating the game once will clue you in on four different days where you're guaranteed new dialogue, which will ultimately, yet subtly, reveal the barista's true nature. Endless mode is a cool way to rack up some achievements, but I don't typically worry about achievements too much, and even then the repetitiveness of it all may not fit well with some people.Ultimately, I'm so glad I picked up this little gem. It isn't every day I see slice-of-life storytelling in a game outside of a visual novel, but Coffee Talk definitely gets the job done. It's not quite as engaging or memorable as VA-11 Hall-A, but it still managed to keep me sucked in with its characters, stories, visuals, music, and atmosphere. This title is a must for anyone who enjoys more story-based games, or simply likes the idea of a title themed around serving coffee(and that's considering the headache it must be to be a REAL LIFE barista in our current situation). So if you're looking for a more relaxing title, give Coffee Talk a taste. It's not quite a masterpiece, but it's definitely theraputic.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a Hybrid of Visual Novel and Cafe Manager.The drinks you make effect the results of the Storyline of the Main Game.There is also a Challenge Mode, where the player has to make drinks for customers, correct drinks grant bonus time to stay in business, and running out of time ends the Challenge Mode, leading the player to close up shop.Endless Mode is giving the option to the player to creatively create and design drinks and latte art, as well as listen to music on their phone. It is the creative mode of this game.Each mode has the ability to unlock a wide range of achievements, and I recommend playing through each.The story of this game is great, and I love the characters and the lore of this game.Many references to modern pop culture and other things is made in the game's story, making it filled with easter egg type stuff for folks to find.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a lot of mixed feelings about this game, but I ended up recommending it mainly because I had quite a lot of fun with it in the long run. With that said, there are some negatives to consider, so don't take my first sentence as a fact immediately.Coffee Talk takes places in an alternate universe where creatures that we normally associate with fantasy exist, like for example werewolves, elves, vampires, succubi, and so and so forth. In this world is a humble little cafe in Seattle owned by you, the self-insert protagonist. Throughout the game you serve customers drinks and listen to their stories. It's very similar in concept to VA-11 Hall-A, though instead of a bar it's a coffee shop.The game is fairly short, I finished it in about 7½ hours or so. For what content there is, it's a pretty entertaining read, though maybe a bit on the shorter side. All the characters are well written and they're all pretty memorable. Because there are so many characters, some of them have their own story arcs as well. The only problem I had with most of those story arcs is that they felt way too short. Before you know it, you run out of days and the story is over. That was a little upsetting for me honestly, but compared to what was given to me in the first place, I don't see much reason to complain. I'm decently satisfied.Gameplay wise... Well, I have some gripes to say the least, but let me first explain how the game works. A customer will order a drink, they will either give the name of the drink or the ingredients to make it. You then look up the drink and put it together with the required ingredients and serve it. There are some instances that someone will ask for a drink, but you might have to give them something else instead, which you have to determine from what you think the customer might really need. If you've played VA-11 Hall-A before, you should be familiar with how it works.But this is where we get to my gripes with the game. You start off the game with instructions on how to make only a few drinks, the rest you have to discover for yourself. On top of that, the game can be  picky about the order of the ingredients. You have three slots for those: the base, as well as primary and secondary ingredients. Sometimes customers will tell you to make a drink with certain ingredients, let's say for this example the character asks for a drink with "tea, ginger and milk." So you go start brewing it by adding them in the order the character said it in, but when you serve it, the game tells you that the drink isn't quite right, because you put ginger in before milk, as according to the order the customer themselves said them in. I think that's a bit cheap of the game to start pulling stuff like that out of nowhere.But that's not the end of it. Sometimes, customers will ask for a specific drink, and if you haven't discovered it earlier, you're kinda screwed if they don't give you a few hints at least. Because what ends up happening is that you'll be given two ingredients and you're just left to your own devices to figure out what that last ingredient is, not to mention you have to figure out the order of input as well. It doesn't help that you can only trash a drink 5 times before you  to serve the drink you made most recently. I could see that working if you have a failure condition, but there kinda is none. Not in the story at least, especially since you can just save before brewing the drink and then loading the game if you screw up (which, at least it has that, so good). But that doesn't change the fact that you'll be spending most of your time figuring out what the correct drink is through trial and error. It's by far the most annoying part of the game and the only way to bypass it directly is to look up a walkthrough.To give you an example of how bad it can get, there is a moment where a customer asks for a certain drink, and you think that they would need something else entirely. This other drink is a very specific drink that would guarantee a certain significant event to happen. The problem?  Never. The only reason I knew about the drink was because I had looked at a brewing guide before and I happened to see it on the list. This sort of trial and error design is one of those reasons that made me have severe mixed feelings about this game.The story, though short, is pretty enjoyable. The brewing, while it seems easy, is plagued with some mind numbing design decisions. But despite that, I'm willing to give the game a recommendation, if only to show some support for the devs. It's not a perfect game, but for what it's worth, it was enjoyable.
